_childDocuments_.review: Remothered: Broken Porcelain is a flawed, but still very solid and good horror, adventure game and a good sequel/prequel to Remothered: Tormented Fathers. Okay the story.Celeste Felton the adoptive daughter of the Felton's, years ago she had disappeared presumed kidnapped and she never returned home, that is what the general public believe. But in secret Celeste Felton had returned home to her family, where did she go? What happened to her well? Well we soon find out what happened to the young teenager and what she went through as we go through the past as well as the future seeing what happened after the events of the first game with Rosemary Reed, all this being told by the mysterious old woman madam Svenska.Now let’s talk about the likes, the story is really good it can be a bit confusing at first as it jumps around, but as it keeps going it starts to click, I think the story jumping around from different perspectives and not being in order is to represent fragmented memories the first game and this game has heavy themes of memory manipulation and forgetting. But like I said if you continue seeing the story play out it soon starts to click and in the story there were plenty of touching moments in it especially at the end this story almost made me cry it's that good.The graphics/levels are both very good; the graphics are pretty detailed with plenty of nice colors and pretty detailed backgrounds. The game itself takes place in the Ashman inn and it's a pretty interesting level/world as we explore it seeing the different parts of the hotel. I think the basement level was probably the best, it was not just a creepy basement, but also had a good mad scientist laboratory feel to it.The gameplay is basically the same as it was in tormented fathers IE running, hiding and avoiding the stalkers, but you also get a chance to fight back especially in later stages when you get a weapon to use against two of the stalkers which I really liked that. The atmosphere in the game is good and can be pretty spooky for first time players especially when you get into the basement level.Like the first game the music in this game is very good with plenty of nice tracks to listen too, the voice acting in the game is okay there are some voices that work but some are questionable especially for Celeste. The characters in the game are good I especially loved Lindsay she was probably my favorite character she was adorable, pretty funny and sweet.The stalkers in the game we're pretty good each one with their own unique look and weapon, my favorite has to be Porcelain he just has this great intimidating look to him and it gives off this great Jason Voorhees vibe.This game has boss fights where you have to fight the stalker, it was a mixed bag others were good others not so much. This game also has an upgrade system and I found it pretty interesting as you can upgrade your skills making the game a lot easier. Finally the absolute best in the game were all the notes and collectibles you can get, like I said in all my other reviews that have notes and collectibles those things can do wonders in helping in improve the game’s world and expand it. And these notes and collectibles are no different. Now let’s talk about the dislikes, the game does have some bugs in it, from what I read the game when it first launched had a lot of bugs and it was practically unplayable that's why I waited for so long to play the game until it was patched. But sadly the game still has some bugs in it.There are two that can be game breaking like in the west wing of the Inn where I was blocking a stalker from entering a door and after the stalker left for some reason I couldn't open that door no matter what I did.All so when I was running from a stalker I had to climb up to a window, I didn't climb up to the window and in fact just lost the stalker and when I went back to climb up the window it wouldn't like me do that, but those were fixed after restarting. There was all so little bug where I couldn't open the face in the first level but that was fixed when I use my keyboard, and some of those bugs can be quite frustrating when you're trying to get all the achievements for the game. And speaking of achievements some of them are a real pain in the ass to get, the absolute worst achievements are the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the bloodbath achievements; they were just so hard, annoying and unfun to get.As I mentioned in the likes the voice acting was okay but there were definitely some weird moments in it like Celeste she has a British accent which I found it extremely weird and kind of off-putting I mean she's born in Italy, now I'm not saying that she should have an Italian accent I'm just saying it's strange that she has a British accent with no explanation to it. Then there is old Stefano Ashmann at first his voice sounded good, old and kind of frail sounding. But as later in the game it sounds a lot different more pathetic and kind of like he has something in his mouth, I don't know maybe it was intentional it just sounded off putting to me.Later in one cutscene for some reason Lindsay who had an American accent in one scene develops a British accent but then she goes back to sounding American again like what happened did the voice actress get sick and they couldn't get her so they had to improvise? Finally sometimes when the character speaks it sounds like it's being recorded in a booth, I don't know it's those weird touches that just kind of pulled me out of the experience a little bit.As I have said this game has boss fights in it and it was a mixed bag, the two most annoying boss fights was the one with Stefano Ashmann and the second time you battle Porcelain they were both pretty annoying. And lastly as I said the story is really good, but I have to admit there were some parts that just felt kind of dumb like the whole telepathy/mind over matter thing, it just felt a little too out there.All right now that that's all said and done with Remothered: Broken Porcelain is a flawed, but still very solid and good horror, adventure game and a good sequel/prequel to Remothered: Tormented Fathers. With a really good story, very good graphics/levels and pretty good stalkers. So despite the game's flaws and shortcomings I do recommend this game if you like the first one then you're probably going to like this one, I do recommend playing the first game and reading the comic Remothered Lambs to the slaughter before playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is more frustrating than fun, not because it's particularly difficult but because it feels extremely unpolished. I think the graphics are the best part, as if the developers put most of their time into making a game that looks pretty with no substance.The AI is annoying, beelining for your position when they had no reason to; sometimes the prompt to stealth attack them just wouldn't show up despite hovering behind them for a good while. On the otherhand, the AI can be extremely exploitable; both of these extremes make for an experience that is simply underwhelming and not gratifying. The items aren't well explained and the "inventory" system is extremely clunky, which is made worse when being chased.I haven't played any other game in the series, but the writing in this one is kind of all over the place. It's a lot like the game: mostly boring with some things intended for shock value just sprinkled in willy-nilly. The audio quality too is totally wacky; characters in the same room will sound distant then super close depending on the camera angle.I really wanted to like this game; I received it from a Humble Choice and after getting Song of Horror from a different month, I was hoping Remothered would be an old school Resident Evil style horror game. But it's just too dang frustrating most of the time and flat boring the rest.

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★★★★★★★ + ★★★★★★★★ 18/10+) Intensely dramatic story.+) Great environment designs.+) Distinguishable graphics.+) Well planned mapping.+) Keenly thought-out checkpoints.+) Artistic music and ambience is excellent.+) Highly optimized control. (Especially door opening)+) Crouch-sprinting has been implemented. One might think this will make things easy but the way game is played is quite different from previous series, so this element was actually helpful. Very, in fact.+) Collectible items are added and they are also currency for upgrades. The upgrades aren't necessary but helpful.+) That said, yes, upgrade system has been implemented. You might say it's little off place for the genre, but it serves as a subtle contribution.🌀 Story of previous series felt very much forced. But when you play this prequel it makes all sense. Yes, there are still "as-is elements" but I find that part also interesting in this case, so no complaints from me. Most importantly, the story is very touching and immensely dramatic. I dropped tears HARD at the end. I believe this game has the most emotional story of all horror games, nay, of all games. Which is why I selected this game as one of my seven main horror games. Considering how fun the core gameplay is, it is only natural.

Even with the route with Andrea and just looping her with the TV and her office, it's such a tedious process. Visually, the game is amazing. Everything in this game screams "The Shining" so hard. And the last and the biggest positive of the game is the main character. _childDocuments_.review: Remothered: Broken Porcelain : By Triple F"Remothered: Broken Porcelain" is a survival horror game developed by Stormind Games and published by Modus Games, serving as both a sequel and prequel to "Remothered: Tormented Fathers." Set in the eerie Ashmann Inn, the game follows Jennifer, a troubled young girl with a mysterious past, as she uncovers the secrets lurking within the inn’s haunted walls. While "Broken Porcelain" ambitiously aims to blend horror storytelling with stealth-based gameplay, the final product falls short of expectations, hindered by technical issues, narrative inconsistencies, and clunky mechanics. Nonetheless, it remains an intriguing experience for those who appreciate psychological horror and character-driven stories.The story of "Broken Porcelain" is intricate, weaving together timelines and characters to create a multi-layered narrative that delves into themes of trauma, obsession, and revenge. The game attempts to build on the mysteries introduced in "Tormented Fathers," offering new insights into the sinister figures involved in the events of the Ashmann Inn. While Jennifer’s journey reveals some compelling moments of horror and suspense, the story struggles with pacing and coherence. Flashbacks and surreal sequences, though atmospherically intriguing, often feel disjointed, leaving players piecing together events in a way that can feel more confusing than mysterious. The game’s ambition is evident, but it occasionally feels weighed down by overly complex storytelling.Gameplay in "Broken Porcelain" combines exploration, stealth, and puzzle-solving, with an emphasis on evading hostile enemies rather than direct combat. Players must navigate the Ashmann Inn carefully, as Jennifer lacks any substantial means of defense; instead, she relies on tools like throwable items and distractions to evade enemies. The stealth mechanics are tense, especially in dimly lit areas where enemies lurk around every corner, creating a constant sense of vulnerability. However, the controls are somewhat unresponsive, and inconsistent AI behavior can make encounters feel unfair or frustrating. While the core stealth mechanics hold potential, they’re often undercut by clunky interactions that detract from the tension the game seeks to build.The puzzles scattered throughout "Broken Porcelain" add a layer of engagement and challenge, requiring players to search for clues, manipulate objects, and combine items to progress. These puzzles range from simple object retrievals to more complex environmental challenges that often contribute to the game’s atmosphere of unease. However, the puzzles sometimes suffer from a lack of clarity, leaving players struggling to understand their objectives. While the sense of discovery can be rewarding, the game could benefit from more intuitive design to reduce frustration and maintain immersion. Still, the puzzles play a significant role in adding depth to the gameplay experience.Visually speaking, "Remothered: Broken Porcelain" captures the horror aesthetic effectively, with dimly lit corridors, shadowy figures, and unsettling decor that create a foreboding atmosphere within the Ashmann Inn. The art direction emphasizes an eerie, abandoned feel, with detailed textures and subtle visual cues that help build the game’s unsettling ambiance. Character models are crafted with attention to detail, though some animations appear stiff or outdated, which occasionally breaks immersion. Sound design, however, is a major strength, with haunting ambient effects and tense musical cues that heighten suspense and keep players on edge. The voice acting is strong, especially for Jennifer and the main antagonists, adding to the game’s narrative weight.One of the game’s most significant issues is its technical performance. Upon launch, "Broken Porcelain" faced numerous bugs and glitches, ranging from frame rate drops and stuttering to clipping and AI malfunctions that impacted gameplay. Although patches have since addressed some of these issues, the game’s technical stability still feels inconsistent. These problems not only hinder player immersion but also amplify frustration during crucial stealth moments. For a game heavily reliant on atmosphere and tension, such disruptions significantly impact the overall experience, making it difficult for players to stay fully engaged with the horror elements.Despite its flaws, "Remothered: Broken Porcelain" offers an interesting narrative and an atmospheric setting that may appeal to fans of psychological horror. Its themes of trauma and revenge give the story a dark emotional edge, and the protagonist’s vulnerability enhances the game’s horror factor. However, the ambitious narrative and complex themes might feel overwhelming or disjointed for players seeking a straightforward horror experience. While it doesn’t fully meet its potential, the game remains a unique entry in the horror genre, particularly for those who enjoy character-driven stories with a psychological twist.On a final note, "Remothered: Broken Porcelain" is an ambitious yet flawed horror experience that shines in its story and atmosphere but struggles with gameplay execution and technical stability. The game’s eerie setting, unsettling story, and strong sound design create an experience that can be compelling for horror enthusiasts, even though it’s marred by control issues and performance hiccups. For players who can look past these limitations, "Broken Porcelain" delivers a haunting, albeit imperfect, journey into the psychological horrors of the Ashmann Inn. While it may not fully satisfy fans of polished horror titles, it offers a distinctive and memorable experience for those willing to brave its challenges.

_childDocuments_.review: Tentative recommend, and strictly for the story and atmosphere, not the gameplay.tl;dr: One of the most intriguing and heartbreaking plots I've ever encountered in a video game. I find the core gameplay rough, but I don't like stealth horror, so take that with a grain of salt. I highly recommend the story if you like psychological and/or survival horror plots. If nothing else, maybe just find a movie-fied let's play of the cutscenes and such, because the atmosphere is brilliant when the gameplay works.The long version: I haven't (and can't currently) played the first Remothered, but this is one of my favorite stories ever told in a videogame. It's pretty damn convoluted in the middle, but gets cleared up ENOUGH by the end. But every element-the atmospheric choices, the VO, the music-helps to serve the tense and tragic atmosphere of the scenario. If you like RE plots but want something sliiiightly more believable (once all is explained) and focused more on interpersonal dynamics than just running through corridors and shootan monsters, I'd imagine you'll dig this. That being said, I don't like stealth horror games. Like at all. I find them unfun and the monsters stop being scary after about five minutes. Remothered: Broken Porcelain is maybe my favorite stealth horror yet, but I still wouldn't say I liked the gameplay. Using distraction items is kinda awkward, enemies take a long time to wander off, and there are various corners of the maps where the camera doesn't wanna cooperate. I still found these enemies scarier than most Clock Tower-esque stalkers, but that's not a high bar. Regardless, I almost called it off at about the two hour mark, but I REALLY wanted to see where the story was going, so I pushed through. The most fun I had with this game was in the latter half, where it diverges from the stealth gameplay more often. Even then, R:BP strikes me as, shall we say, Kojima-inspired in that there are tons of cutscenes and not that much gameplay, all told. It's more like an interactive movie with stealth horror elements.I'm not sure if I loved the story so much BECAUSE of the gameplay experiences i went through, but I suspect the cutscenes and just a bit of the gameplay would easily make for a good movie. Hell, even the run time wouldn't be too crazy, since I cleared the whole game in five and a half hours. So yeah, if you don't wanna deal with the gameplay, I still recommend watching the movieBut also, fair warnings all around: I'm 90% sure this franchise is dead in the water. The devs are on to other IPs and the lead writer has abandoned the planned third game in the trilogy. That being said, this game stands alone incredibly well. The ending was so flawless that I assumed the series was meant to end with this one-or at least go in a completely different direction.

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't even consider trying this game until you've played the first one. It's entirely a story-focused experience that has LOTs of elaborate, intricate, and oftentimes frankly convoluted plots points. Before purchasing the game I think that's THE most important thing to keep in mind.That said, I think the game does a good job with closure to the story and continuity with the previous title. This doesn't feel like one of those situations where they retroactively made up a bunch of plot points to force a sequel/prequel to work with the previous title. The story is clearly deliberate and carefully planned out from the very beginning.Gameplay-wise it honestly isn't much of anything special. It's pretty engaging and most of the animations are very nicely done, but it feels immersive and story driven, nothing more and nothing less. Sometimes it's a little fumbly, and the AI isn't very good. Extremely basic behavior, no memory of player's actions/locations at all after breaking line of sight. Just very straight forward behavior. Disappointingly, this simplicity is paired with lopsided difficulty at times. You'd think a simple AI would be easier to wrangle into a consistent margin of difficulty but evidently that wasn't the case.Bugs were relatively minimal but a lot of transitions when interacting with hostiles (or vice versa) felt extremely strange with weird jump cuts and sometimes the AI even forgetting where I was immediately after, when I'm left right behind them at the end of a jumpy animation. Little things like that maybe 3-5 times throughout the course of the entire game.Art-wise this game looks top notch. Environments are consistently remarkable, graphics are good, characters are detailed, most animations feel solid. Music was repetitive at times (looking at you, high pitched whistle in the main menu) but it was good.Overall, I think this game has a lot holding it back but I recommend the game specifically for those interested in playing BOTH games. Do not deprive yourself the necessary context to understand the story. It's the primary content to the game. The story felt like I was watching a cult classic mystery horror TV show or something. Constant twists and turns, a couple really solid characters, and a pretty cohesive plot in the grand scheme of things.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start this review by being upfront with the fact that I haven't played Remothered: Tormented Fathers, I received this game in a humble bundle and decided to give it a try and thankfully this game provides a recap of the previous game. Sadly that recap is the only concise bit of storytelling you will get from this game. I understand that Chris Darril has a vision for this series especially since from what I read he planned on making a trilogy from this IP but after playing Broken Porcelain I honestly don't know how a trilogy would be possible since the story now feel closed and shut. But lets talk about the "story" if you can understand it and again in all honesty after I finished the game I read the wiki synopsis to better understand which is already troubling. The fact that I had to rely on an external source to better understand a congested story that feels like its riding an express flight to the conclusion just screams bad story telling but the fact that the RECAP for the previous game does a better job at explaining things just further boggles my mind. Story aside the gameplay? Jesus Christ HOW DO YOU RUIN BASIC GAMEPLAY!? Objectives sometimes never make sense, features are introduced only to be used once or twice, the gameplay loop of being chased is clunky and more frustrating than scary especially since hiding NEVER works, and the idea of upgrading your character is a throwaway idea that I rarely used. Pair these issues with an incredibly short play time and you literally have a game that YouTubers would play for some quick views and honestly its insulting. I'm not sure if there was studio interference or a lack of time but this game just feels bad. There's some moments where I actually enjoyed the chemistry between two of the characters but beside that everything isn't "half-baked" its just raw.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to recommend this but ultimately I do if you enjoyed the first one. I can see what they were going for it just wasn't as exciting or effective as the first game. You are able to fight back a bit more in this game and it weakened a lot of the tension the first game had and it felt more frustrating then fun. I waited a bit for patches as I heard the game was nearly unplayable at launch I ran into no technical problems that hurt anything (two times it looked like some animations didn't work right but other then that it was solid and I wouldn't have mentioned anything in my review but I heard horror stories with this game at launch that scared me away) I do think the story is better as it ends and wraps things up nicely. Don't try to play this before the first one despite it technically being a prequel not only dose it spoil stuff this game will be impossible to follow.  It follows 3 timelines and is somewhat convoluted as a story about mind controlled moths can be however if you pay attention it is an interesting horror story about 2 horrific families and is worth digging into.One final note this game is significantly less graphic imo then the previous entry. Just letting people know if the previous game turned you off because of it or were worried it escalated if you can handle the previous game you will be fine for this one.

name: Total War: WARHAMMER III
detailed_description: Immortal Empires is Now Available to all Total War: WARHAMMER III Players Immortal Empires is the culmination of the entire Total War: WARHAMMER series. Combining the campaign maps, races, and factions from all three games* into a single, epic sandbox campaign. It’s the most complete and definitive Warhammer strategy experience ever conceived! Immortal Empires is Out Now *All owners of Total War: WARHAMMER III can now access the Immortal Empires Campaign. However, there are several races available in Immortal Empires that are unlocked if you own Total War: WARHAMMER, Total War: WARHAMMER II or DLC across the entire trilogy. Join Our Discord Server
about_the_game: The last roar of a dying god ruptures the boundary between worlds, opening a portal to the Realm of Chaos. From this maelstrom, the four Ruinous Powers – Khorne, Nurgle, Tzeentch and Slaanesh – emerge, spreading darkness and despair. The stern warriors of Kislev and the vast empire of Grand Cathay stand at the threshold, as a vengeful Daemon Prince vows to destroy those who corrupted him. The coming conflict will engulf all. Will you conquer your daemons? Or command them? With seven unique races and hundreds of units under your command, raise an army and dominate in epic real-time battles across a world of breathtaking scale and spectacle. In the most ambitious and groundbreaking Total War title to date, dive into a captivating narrative that will take you to the mind-bending Realm of Chaos and back again. Forge your empire in a strategy sandbox that ensures no two campaigns are ever the same. Play as 10 Legendary Lords! Will you side with the Chaos Gods and take one of their Daemonic Champions, play as an ancient transforming Dragon from Grand Cathay, defend the frozen nation of Kislev with the Ice Queen or play the ultimate villain as the Daemon Prince? Customise the Daemon Prince to your own unique design with a huge suite of body parts and powers, creating billions of potential combinations to suit your own playstyle. Multiplayer is now bigger than ever. With the vast 8-player Realm of Chaos multiplayer campaign, the intense 1 v 1 Domination mode, the story-driven multiplayer campaigns built around Kislev and Grand Cathay and ranked & custom battles, there’s no shortage of ways to cause chaos with friends.
short_description: The cataclysmic conclusion to the Total War: WARHAMMER trilogy is here. Rally your forces and step into the Realm of Chaos, a dimension of mind-bending horror where the very fate of the world will be decided. Will you conquer your Daemons… or command them?

_childDocuments_.review: Total War: Warhammer 3 is a great game, but I can't recommend it in good conscience due to the recent DLC price controversy. The new Shadows of Change DLC is priced at $24.99, which is a 150% increase over the price of previous lord packs. This is especially egregious considering that the DLC only adds two new legendary lords and a handful of new units.Creative Assembly has defended the price increase by saying that it reflects the increased cost of development. However, I find this argument to be unconvincing. The previous lord packs were already well-priced, and I don't see why the cost of development should have increased so dramatically in the past year.The DLC price controversy is just the latest in a series of problems that have plagued Warhammer 3 since its launch. The game has been plagued by bugs and performance issues, and Creative Assembly has been slow to address these issues. The developer has also been criticized for its lack of communication with the community.I hope that Creative Assembly will reconsider the price of next DLC. Until then, I can't recommend Warhammer 3 to anyone. The DLC price increase is a slap in the face to the fans who have already supported Warhammer 3 and overall, the DLC price controversy is a major black mark on Warhammer 3. It is a shame that such a great game has been marred by such a greedy business decision.

_childDocuments_.review: Total War: Warhammer 3 isn't just the product of years of work on the Total War: Warhammer series, but in many ways, a culmination of all the work done on the Total War franchise to date. The Realm of Chaos campaign is impressively intricate for a 4X game, with a more robust story and more direction than its franchise predecessors--like Total War: Three Kingdoms. In turn, the Immortal Empires map is massive and integrates all the major factions from Warhammer I and Warhammer II. When everything is said and done, it is easily the largest Total War title to date, while also offering the most variety.This game won't be melting any computers with its graphical quality, but it will with its scale. With the camera zoomed out a good deal, there are truly beautiful battlefields, and the sight of massive armies crashing into each other is impressive to behold. On close inspection, the models and the terrain do a good job representing what they are supposed to represent, but are, understandably, fairly simplistic compared to what one finds in Triple A games like The Last of Us.The music and sound is, similarly, very serviceable for a 4X game, with the voice acting in the Realm of Chaos campaign being a highlight. None of it ever rises to the point of being truly inspiring or immersive, however, without any truly standout pieces, and there is definitely a difference in voice acting quality from character to character.As mentioned above, the scale of the game can also impact performance, especially on weaker PCs. This isn't just the case in battle either--as the game continues, weaker PCs will struggle to keep up with all the troop movements and changes on the campaign map as well, which can result in some lengthy waits and load times for everyone in multiplayer games.There's no getting around the amount of variety this game offers. I do not want to think about how many thousands of hours it'd take to play through a single campaign as every faction available even once, much less then going back and replaying through a favorite.There are no real cookie cutter factions either. While there is at least one faction, and sometimes two, from each race that has a fairly simple campaign with few additional mechanics outside of the race mechanics, things such as starting location and starting situation make even these feel quite different from each other. Every race, as well, is massively different from the others, focusing on different gameplay themes, with sometimes vastly different mechanics, different troop strengths and weaknesses, and of course, wildly differing graphical motifs.Even some of the basic mechanics that are shared across races can be quite different for some of them, with beastmen caring little for empire building or diplomacy, and chaos dwarves having a substantially more complicated economy.An impressive amount of new content continues to be added as well, especially for a game that isn't taking on a free-to-play or games-as-a-service model. While much of the content is locked piecemeal behind DLC, and which content is included in which DLC can be confusing, there are no microtransactions to speak of, and all the DC feels solid, especially when compared to other 4X games and strategy games.People hate spending money on things that aren't on sale, and they hate the idea that maybe to support a game over the long term, prices for some things have to go up. This game has, unfortunately, received a lot of undue criticism from "fans" as a result of this.Every additional DLC becomes harder to add than the last. It's easier to balance 2 factions with each other than 4 factions with each other... Each new addition takes far more work to add than the last.There is also no subscription cost for this game, so when the base game has reached its audience, such that sales begin to slow, of course the company making the game will have to raise prices on additional DLC content to continue to pay their employees. That is simply common sense. The choice, ultimately, becomes either charge more for DLC, or stop supporting the game and move on to a new one. The Total War: Warhammer series has done the latter twice already, and franchise-wise we've seen the difficulties with continued expansion cut DLC plans for other games, such as Total War: Three Kingdoms, short.I worry that the fan backlash will make that the case with this game too, but only time will tell.The game is not without its issues, but many of these are tied to doing so, so much. The scale of the game is simply huge, with variety and personality befitting the depth and history of the Warhammer setting.I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nah, 25€ for a 3-lord pack when Champions of Chaos gave us 4 for 16€ last year is actually insane. Don't listen to garbage "inflation" excuses, these corporations sure as hell aren't starving - just don't financially support them until they change their ways.Between 150 and 200 hours of my playtime were from the Realm of Chaos campaign alone, I bought WH3 solely for Kislev. I'd have recommended WH3 even before Immortal Empires, now I'd say it's a must-buy if fantasy Total War is your cup of tea. Never really cared much for fantasy Warhammer and this game was my gateway into the franchise and I've been in love with it since a few months ago.Don't have much to complain about except that minor settlement battles are a nuisance (got a mod that entirely removes them from the game), the player-focused AI is ridiculously annoying (I got the impression Immortal Empires exacerbated this issue compared to Realms of Chaos), and the price of the whole package can be a bit too much - for this I suggest using 3rd party key retailers, I myself have used Instant Gaming for about 4 years now."Oh, what a noob, he doesn't want to play the game the way the developer intended and had to mod out a deliberate mechanic" - after over 150+ hours of minor settlement battles in RoC, I can genuinely say I've had more than enough of them. When IE launched, I wanted to give new factions - such as Tomb Kings, Bretonnia, and Warriors of Chaos - a try, but my interest in the game would plummet immediately right after attacking that first minor settlement in the campaign. There's only one rule to singleplayer video games and that is to have fun - to me, minor settlement battles simply aren't. They were tolerable in Medieval 2, Rome 2, and Three Kingdoms, but the frequency and the gameplay concept behind them in Warhammer 3 is just a chore.All in all, I'm beyond satisfied with Warhammer 3 and will definitely put hundreds of hours into it.(Regardless, I'm excited to see where historical Total War goes next.)

_childDocuments_.review: BACKGROUND.This is gonna be a long one, plus i am only airing my thoughts because of the new DLC but this is for the game Total warhammer. However this should have been done ages ago. So some pre-text I was a huge fan of Warhammer fantasy back when it was around, then came into this series at the end of the Grom and Paunch DLC. So i had missed the travesties of Norsca and Warriors of Chaos. I had played TW Rome 1 back when i was very young. To which i own all of them and the DLC, at discount cause of my late entry to the game and i am part of the reason this happened.    MY REASONS. THE NEW VS THE OLD.Now to my Opinion of this game and i mean of all TW warhammer as the second and third are expansion packs with engine upgrades not a full game.  In terms of this being a Total war game, it is awful simply put it pales in comparison to older games, games that are 12 years old Shogun 2. 17 years Medieval 2 These games are complex and have soul to the era of a war game. formations, progression, complex trade routes and a full settlement overview to which tiers of armory buildings affect the armour the units recruited from that settlement look like, also on public order population density, showing trading routes and networks of what you import and export. Making trading products valuable enough to restrict buildings and unit production. The most striking of these is the simplistic nature of playing a campaign locations only matter for climate in other games had specialist resources to that settlement. Making them more of a prize than any other settlement. When recruiting units it actually takes population so you have to consider where you draw armies from lest you cripple your population growth. In warhammer recruit to your income. Yes easier but many less choices are made here diluting the game down. The army upkeep tax for each new army restricts the amount of armies you can make so people doomstack, which makes the armies the same optimal builds. Limiting the experience once can have. The Details in the older games are massive, seeing your trade routes presented on the map which you can raid for those special resources, The fact you have to build boats to travel by water, yes the automatic sea faring in Warhammer makes it easy, but you can't defend your border by sea they might as well not exist as i can sail to Lustria, empire, the elven kingdoms. How many times have you been invaded by a ai stacks just sailing across the world for you? In the older games, block their ports, block their ability to ever get you by sea, which the ai can do this to you, making another choice to focus on both naval power and land power. There armies useless sitting there on land. Where on warhammer if they are more powerful they get you no matter what. The fact of sieges is a point many know Ass ladders. referring to the fact every infantry unit carries ladders making those big walls useless as since they don't have to build rams and siege towers they can siege faster nothing the player can do to stop it, if they are more powerful and attack it's game. Gates equal as even if you don't bring monsters your horsemen, dogs/wolfs and lords can break them down, dumbing down siege warfare since so many things overcome your defences, where as in medieval 2 they needed to build such things, which if you destroy their siege equipment they lose the fight, making you spend time on gathering more thinking of what to bring. But since sieges are slower you have to consider if the enemy can bring over other armies in that time. Making the player choose when and where to siege. Bringing another decision to the players hands.  The ability to army split and , able to use an army to attack many issues. In warhammer one army can deal with only one issue, but if the ai sends a small force to siege a settlement you have to send your army all the way back for that. where in the two games mentioned, take out a force of your army to deal with it, making another choice of what you send as infantry, Calvary forces move at different rates but are slowed down if you put even a single artillery unit in the force which makes full army choices matter as you have artillery means armies can catch you. Full horsemen armies can outpace and outmanoeuvre. So you have to be careful, what you pick and put in armies as it all matters, so instead of sending a full army send 3 units of horsemen that can get there faster and deal with the issue then come back. In warhammer bring whatever you want. full hellstorm army, doesn't matter that your army is all horsemen move at the same rate, making again little thought in your choice. You have freedom sure but it came at a cost of tactical awareness of your armies. Lastly units mean nothing stats are everything, This is my biggest one for battles, if you have high enough leadership no matter what you do you can not break a unit. magic, outnumbered, charged in side or back means nothing. It does not matter what unit you bring to fight another if you have better stats and tier even match ups like archers vs cavalry which should be a nobrainer becomes a mess as a sister of Avalon unit can hold off cavalry charge. Why? Cause there stats are simply better. This can be done with any unit with better stats. making the role of a unit mean nothing. In warhammer it is all about stat stacking not unit type, I am not looking at What weapons they are holding and the enemy, i am looking at what the MA (Melee attack) MD (Melee defense) are to see if my stats are better and tier is good enough to overcome my target. In the older games matter of the triangle of type horse beats archer, sword beat horse, archer beat sword. (Yes killing them with arrows.) This made every unit type matter and targeting matter on the battlefield. Other terrain affects like weather, elevation, lay of the land mean nothing in battles in the warhammer games. In older games you could bring the lowest tier spear men vs the highest stat/tier horsemen and if they charge the spear men they lose no matter what. Did not matter the stat it was the type that won the day, Like it says in the tool tip for units, frightened by stronger unit or foe near by.  Nothing for being outnumbered, yes there is for being charged in the back by Calvary but again if stats high enough might as well not bothered. In Shogun 2 when charging in the back with Calvary it breaks units regardless of their unit size health bar. Which then can cause a mass route as the ai freaks out seeing how other units react seeing their fellow running, Yes there is a negative in warhammer but it's a stat difference. they won't run. In shogun you can chain this rout to cascade making a more powerful army run for the hills through tactical play, in warhammer if leadership stat high enough, even if half the army is gone, shrug the balance of power is not based on the amount of units left the balance of power is based on which of your powerful units is still on the field. two or three units can be half their balance of power. NOTHING NEW HAS BEEN ADDED. This section is to highlight the reuse of assets that came from Troy and Three kingdom or from other races and other games that are being passed around constantly. Going from Taurox the Brass bull rampage being Lu-Bu, The new Matters of state being from Cao-Cao, Even the Changling is just skaven undercity, pirate cove, normal chaos cults. The whole siege rework just three kingdoms. Agamemnon using the office system just like the vampire coast and wood elves do, Menelaus call to arms which turned in allied recruitment for warhammer 3, the diplomacy system from Troy.  Unit caps from the tomb Kings to Beastmen, Chaos Dwarfs. These are a few examples.     CONCLUSION. I would have never started playing this game if it wasn't for the IP and in fact that love for warhammer has blinded me to the decay the game series Total war has become. Indeed a shadow of change has begun and CA sit on a throne of Decay.

_childDocuments_.review: A very solid game in its current state, and the upcoming DLC looks promising.Even though you need to buy the previous games and DLCs for the full(er) experience, even with just buying Total War: Warhammer III you can enjoy the game for the value you paid. Although you cannot play as the previous games' and DLCs' factions without purchasing those, you can still interact and fight against them with the starting races (Kislev, Cathay, Nurgle, Slaanesh, Khorne and Tzeentch + Be'lakor (Warriors of Chaos) in Immortal Empires).It is very important to highlight, the Immortal Empires campaign combining the content of all three games is playable for owners of only Warhammer III as well.The game is receiving FLC content and reworks with time, alongside the DLCs, so you are still receiving some new content if you are paying for the new DLCs or not.Although the Warscape battle engine is always somewhat struggling in some way or form, it is rather polished, functional and enjoyable for the scope included in the Total War: Warhammer series.The campaigns are quite enjoyable, with some exceptions, notably the late game feels rather dull and limiting in comparison to the earlier stages of campaigns because of the climate system and lack of a meaningful challenge. Scripted hostile armies spawning in completely secured territory through end game scenarios is not an enjoyable late game challenge.With all this said, especially if you also buy the other games or DLCs you are interested in, you will have a blast in the first 100 or so turns of most of your campaigns.From the campaigns I've played, I especially recommend playing as Katrin (Kislev) and Wulfrik the Wanderer (Norsca - paid DLC from the first game) in the Immortal Empires campaign, and I'm looking forward to a Karl Franz (Empire) campaign in the upcoming 5.0 version of the game. The Realms of Chaos campaign is not bad by any means, but the Immortal Empires campaign offers a more clean and varied fun experience.As a conclusion, I recommend this game and I hope it will continue to receive support and new content in the years to come.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, this game is a mess. Continuous crashes to desktop, pointless war declarations, randomness of enemy actions, DLC (and game) price tags, and the ridiculous settlement battles make it really hard to keep playing this game. CA should have worked on giving the player the possibility to build more diversified defenses through the settlement building panel and it would have been a great addiction to be able to invest in the garrisons and tailor them to your needs. Give us customization, such as sliders to determine AI bias towards the player, choice of map size and number of factions involved, diplomacy and AI war declaration options (e.g. the AI can declare a war only if they share a border with you, or if you attack/get attacked by their allies), and such. _childDocuments_.review: I want to love the game but I'm finding I'm getting bored fairly quickly into campaigns. I think there needs to be much more clearly defined winning objectives for your campaign. The short, long and total conquest victory just isn't fun for me. I think they need to be more thematic for each faction. The main issue for me is the size of the map, it's so big that I think it makes the game more of a slog and a chore than anything else. I get burnt out and fatigue sets in after a while and then I get bored. CA might be moving into this direction, I just think they should redo all factions campaign victory objectives. You could still have total map conquest for those who enjoy doing that, but I think another option for winning your campaign might be also be good.Many others have mentioned before that the Dwarfs should have one sole campaign objective - retake/reclaim the Karaz Ankor. That's it, nothing else. I think that would be perfect for them. For the High Elves I think confederating/taking complete ownership of Ulthuan and then having to defeat all Dark Elf factions should be their campaign, you could maybe add reclaim former colonies as well. Then they're done. For Wood Elves I'm not sure what to do for them but the current campaign I don't personally find enjoyable. I think they need more settlements that provide income so they can have more armies. One campaign objective for the Wood Elves could possibly be to completely forest the map, so they have their main magical forests but they can also transform province capitals into mini-magical forests which they can construct buildings in and thus extend Athel Loren to the entire map. It could be done with a mechanic when after they capture a province capital they have the option to plant an acorn from the Oak of Ages there and in 5 turns they've created a new mini magical forest. Total map conquest just isn't fitting for Elves, Dwarfs or Humans lore wise and I think they need campaigns to reflect this. It's fine for Greenskins, Skaven, Chaos to go for that total conquest but it shouldn't be a campaign objective for all.Lastly I think a campaign victory cinematic at the end would be nice for each faction. I'm hitting recommend for the game more for what I hope it still can be, rather than for what it is currently.

_childDocuments_.review: CA have Knocked it out of the park with this one. Only 7 odd hours played at the moment but felt compelled to write something after seeing so many negative reviews. As far as I can see the negative reviews fall into 3 categories; 1. Poor optimization. I do not have a beefy comp (980ti) and I've been running high graphics (with trees/grass on medium) ultra units with no issues. I have encountered an alt tab bug which crashed my game, but that is the first thing mentioned on their troubleshooting page. It's not great, but hardly worth a thumbs down if you consider the game as a whole.2. A portion of the Chinese TW community are review bombing the game as they are unhappy with how CA handled which content creators got early access to the game. I do not know the full situation and i am not commenting on how right or wrong that is, merely stating the facts.3. 'I prefer the old historical TW games'Of course there are some negative reviews from people who just don't enjoy what they've played so far which is completely valid but those are few and far between compared to the reasons stated above.Is the game perfect? No. But in my opinion this is the best Total War game on release CA has made to date. If you have enjoyed any TW game in the past or are a fan of Warhammer Fantasy, I would highly recommend giving it a go.As i have only played 7ish hours I cannot give a full review, but after seeing the wash of negative reviews I just wanted to throw my hat in the ring. Thank you CA for a wonderful cap stone to the series. I look forward to putting in a few hundred more hours over the coming years,

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing total war titles for about 16 years now. This game is in the best launch state of any total war game I can recall. It's also in one of the best release states for any AAA game in recent history. If you were a fan of previous Warhammer entries, this will certainly be worth the price of admission.The game has a fantastic prologue that dovetails wonderfully into the available story campaigns. The factions are hugely unique, more so than previous entries, and really do their source materials proud. The campaign mechanics combined with all the qol improvements make this a worthy start to the bookend of the Warhammer trilogy and a must have for fan boys in it for the long haul. The ui experience and campaign coop changes are much needed and bring new life to the whole total war experience. If you're new to the series and want to try Warhammer, find a key for the second game to give this one more time to grow into itself. There are visual bugs, minor pathing and some obvious faction specific bugs ranging from comical to annoying. The only crash I had was when alt tabbing out during a load screen. I haven't experienced anything like Rome 2s horrible unplayable mess of a launch that broke me of the total war series for years. The game has been nothing short of fantastic for me and my friends group. I'm seeing negative reviews from people who are expecting a lot from older hardware and a fresh released game. If your looking at this game and it's reviews, manage your expectations to make your decision:-this is a new release, it doesn't have the same amount of content the 2nd game had after 2 years of development and 4 years of support, not yet anyway.-the campaign map has obvious graphical downgrades in preparation for combining the 3 maps into a massive, and functional, mortal empires map.-you need a good cpu to maintain high fps with all the complex calculations (dice rolls) the larger unit counts do.-you need a good graphics card to take advantage of all the diverse visual effects and lighting.-you need a fast ssd to load the huge campaign and battle maps.-if you don't have those things, adjust your setting down (unit count, graphics especially ssao and vsynch) or expect an experience on par with your equipment.

_childDocuments_.review: Embarrassing release.- Positives:1. Minor quality of life changes.2. Great prologue/tutorial.3. Alliances finally give incentives to have them.- Neutral:1. Minor Settlement battles. You will either like them, or get tired of them very quick and start missing open space battles.- Negatives:1. UI changes. Red color everywhere. Removal of unique art for races when interacting with settlement after victory. Glowing selected units (toggleable, but toggled on by default). Missions and quests moved from logical top left menu to side menu with tiny texts and no art. Tiny hourglass for magic pool (from readable huge container in WHII).2. Campaign and lack of alternative for it. After going through chaos realms as one faction and finishing one campaign, I have zero interest doing it with a different faction. Realms are annoying + there is time pressure for the campaign. This is worse than Vortex campaign, where you could take your time and ignore vortex until you are ready to engage it. In Vortex campaign you had to fight waves of chaos if you triggered rituals. Here you do not trigger anything, armies just spawn from portals, which you need to patrol and close with heroes to keep corruption and demon armies in check.Realms themselves are a major annoyance after going through them once. Except for Slaanesh they are boring aswell. And can give your LL horrible traits.(even if you are aligned with the Realm's God, Plaguefather with negative Nurgle disease traits, what?) To get rid of them, you need to waste turns in Capital, very engaging gameplay.And if AI LL got to the soul first, you are kicked out of realm and your progress is lost. This is especially "fun" in Tzeentch realm, which is random af and promotes save scumming if you do not want to suffer.3. Technical side of things.Bugs: Some embarrassing bugs, which went past QA. Some were reported by early access streamers, but were not patched.Slaanesh has a technology which breaks Slaanesh's gift and makes this faction mechanic useless.Disbanding armies does not decrease units upkeep, this is not only an old bug, but is one, that for sure has no place in a total war game on release. Some maps have glitchy docking spots, some maps have broken pathing, or outright destroy artillery pieces when moving through some terrain.Antilarge counter charge, a bug that was eventually fixed in WHII is once again present.AI: Your own units sometimes forget and ignore commands. AI often has breakdowns on siege maps. Docks for no reason during melee combat just to expose itself to flank attack. Etc, but this was to be expected pretty much, but it feels like AI is derping alot more than in WHIITechnical: It took me a while to setup a proper windowed mode, as fullscreen game changes resolution after alt-tabbing. Alt-tabbing also can crash your game supposedly. At first windowed mode is not aligning properly. Then it was constantly switching ui scaling to 200% despite me reducing scaling.Denuvo was implemented last minute before release, which halved FPS for paying customers, while those who will eventually pirate it will have a superior experience.Also, streamers got to play the game without Denuvo and their reports on performance became misleading.What solution CA provides for technical issues? Adjust amount of cores used, or, wait for it, install Windows 11.4. Evidence of rushed content for release without much thought or effort put into it:Many heroes/lords have very basic redundant skill trees copy-pasted from wh1, despite many other heroes now have disproportional better skill trees.Greater demons of Tzeentch not having arcane conduit, since it has a template of other greater demons, making greater demon a worse spellcaster lord than basic one or even a hero.Be'lakor as a "reward" for every single faction with dumb skill tree, making him a useless reward, as you will have much superior lords by that time.Great bastion siege attrition, which not only makes zero sense, but if you are playing as Cathay, Demon armies will just sit there trying to attrition the units. Your best option is to sully out, leading to open space map battle. As Cathay you simply wont be having those defensive walled battles of the bastion, or have them with half dead armies.Vassalisation is a broken mess, like it always was, making one of Slaaneshs major mechanics a dud.And so on...TL,DR: Campaign with bad replay value, which becomes more annoying on each playthrough, many nonsensical decisions, poor performance, major almost game ruining bugs and last minute Denuvo.WHII, even just a base game, at the moment offers much more, is much more stable and has modding community that fixes things CA does not bother to.Give this game half to a full year, it might get much better, but right now I have absolutely no heart to recommend it to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Botched launch, Botched DLC pricing, utterly botched ability to take constructive criticism... As is, this game is decently fun, but nothing like its predecessors or other, older titles in the series. Much of what used to be standard content, like naval battles (i.e. half the game), varied maps instead of the same three empty fields or boring straight town walls (enter GCCM), and proper game balance (enter SFO) either got axed completely or worse, dumbed down into oblivion. For a while now, the modders have been left picking up the slack - which they tend to do very well provided CA doesn't ban them from its steam forums...Meanwhile, most of the game's content is locked behind DLC, be it in this game or the previous two Total Warhammers. TWWHIII's juicy pricetag? That only gets you access to perhaps a quarter of the game's content - for the rest of it you'll have to shelf out a few hundred more on DLC of this game or its predecessors. And TWWHIII's DLC are very pricey and very lacking in content, and getting more so.If you are a dedicated Total War fan, don't bother with this one, it will only ruin your (remaining) trust in CA.If you are new to Total War, or you just want to play something Warhammer, try CA's older games, like Total Warhammer II, or Shogun II.If you are a CA executive, enjoy watching the consequences of repeated shortsighted decisions, of alienating your community, and of clawing mindlessly for short-term profits in a manner that destroys your company's long-term viability.

_childDocuments_.review: I was so exited about the release of this game as I would love to continue loving the series for hundreds of hours, unfortunately this game has tested that love. Warhammer 3 was a perfect example of CA and the major issues they always seem to have with their large releases and this game is no exception. In the base game their is a few very questionable choices for the armies and factions, Kislev being the one that I have the most issues with as they seem to have fully went into the whole "bear meme" idea with complete confidence. Why does the Tzarina use a bear mount instead of perhaps a ice tiger mount? same with the ice witches, instead pretty much every lord and hero gets bear mount and a useless horse mount that provides no real competition when compared to the *literal bear* I really enjoyed the Kislev reborn mod which added a unique army to the Kislivite faction in warhammer 2 and while I had my issues with that mod I have to say that the mod made for free felt better than the actual released army with seemingly an entire half of the army being nowhere to be seen in game. The second major issue is that as of now I and many other players are unable to play the game as it crashes seemingly randomly when certain factions turns come up during the cycle with no real explanation of way to get around it without rolling back your game which for me at least blocks my ability to play with any mods. A myriad of questionable choices have gotten us this far, and unless CA can manage to fix some massive glaring issues with the game then I can not recommend what was supposed to be my favorite game from what has been one of my favorite franchises since 2014.

Unfortunately, that means that negative reviews have to be left.There’s no good time to leave a negative review, and I have not taken this step lightly. However, the business reality is that developers and publishers must price their content fairly if they expect me to be willing to purchase the years of extra content that they currently have planned. I know this may mean your fanbase stops buying your DLCs at full price, only buys them on future discounts, or even boycotts them altogether. It's important for you to hear from me and I hope that, if nothing else, this helps clarify why a pre-order has not been made. I want you to continue to deliver competitively priced content I'm excited to see, and I want to support your doing that as long as I can.Finally, I need to ask you again to release bug fixes independent of paid content. Frustrated as you may get, the human beings responsible for patching these bugs should not have their work arbitrarily postponed and attached to DLC releases. _childDocuments_.review: This game could be so much better, but CA isn't interesting in doing so, because it wouldn't make them any money. Here's a list of problems this game has.1. This is the buggiest Total War game since Rome 2 launched, it's no surprise that the community bug fix mod is one of the most popular right now. I have never seen units fall off the map in any Total War game, except this one.2. Maps, oh boy this game has some of the worst maps in the series, both in siege and field battles. In sieges, every culture has like 2 or 3 different generic siege maps, which isn't that bad on it's own, but when you look at the scenery and the layouts of those maps, you'll realize that it's not just the city template that's being reused, it's the whole map. The best example for this is the Empire, just compare Altdorf, Nuln, Averheim, Pfieldorf and Talabheim, they're all the same exact map, with the same mountain range in the background. Field battles have the same problem, you're either fighting on the same map with the pit in the middle, or one of the various fields with one small round forest in the middle. 3. Horse cavalry is the worst in any Total War game, horses just get stuck on every unit they fight and when they get a charge in, it just throws the enemies in the air without doing much damage.4. HP pools for units were a bad idea from Rome 2 and they should get rid of them.5. HP regen seems kinda broken at the moment, you can kill an entire army but the lord will still be fighting with 100% of their hp because they can regen it.6. Campaign victory conditions are atrociously boring, not one single thought has been put into them, so for most factions your victory conditions are really generic.7. Same old boring settlement building system from Rome 2, bring back the Shogun 2/Empire/Napoleon system.8. Very repetitive and forgettable soundtrack.9. Some sound effects feel very cheap, especially guns and cannons.10. No naval battles, they could've made the most insane naval battles in any Total War game ever, but they didn't even try, so we're back to having no naval battles/naval units.11. Overpriced DLCs, Shadows of Change costs 25$ for 3 new Lords with rehashed mechanics and reskinned units. Meanwhile Fall of the Samurai for Shogun 2 cost 30$ on release, that DLC transforms S2 into a whole new game, with new rosters, new factions, new mechanics and a new campaign, it's arguably the best DLC Creative Assembly has ever made.12. Battles don't feel meaningful anymore, in older TW games, you had to conserve your numbers because you couldn't just replenish your troops immediately, this made elite units feel special, because you had to use them strategically and cautiously if you wanted to conserve them. In this game, replenishment is so strong that conserving numbers is no longer necessary, just spec into your Lord's replenishment skills and you can replenish a full stack in 1 or 2 turns.13. Doomstacking, no longer is army composition important, now you can just spam one type of unit and succeed. You can make entire armies of your best unit, as opposed to having a limited amount of them to recruit. Even the AI does it, it's getting ridiculous.

_childDocuments_.review: Half decent sequel to a much better Warhammer game. A game that had a terrible launch, a starting campaign that just doesn't work and that CA execs never bothered to fix, a ludicrous paywall to get access to all factions, bugs that go unfixed for months and months despite modders and creators endlessly highlighting them, battle AI that is dumber than Total War managed in 2007, campaigns that are boring as f*** by turn 50, without fail, regardless of faction or difficulty, and to cap it off, an endless increasing price for DLC that offers nothing extra as compensation for the price hike and merely adds flavour to the game rather than actually fixing what doesn't work with it. Don't get me wrong. I've been a Total War fan since Rome 1 and Medieval 2 were some of my favourite games as a kid, and Warhammer 2 was just as awesome as i hoped it would be. I've stuck by them despite the Messes that Empire and Thrones of Britannia were, despite the shortsighted, garbage way DLC was handled for 3 Kingdoms, despite the AWFUL launch for Rome 2 and the sheer greed around Rome 1's lame remaster and Troy's pointless Epic Exclusivity for its first year. I wanted to love this game. But the executives of CA are killing it with their greed and shortsightedness, just like they've slowly killed the Historical Total War side of the franchise. The DLC pricing is the final nail in the coffin. If Baldur's Gate 3 has proved anything, it showed what game developers are capable of and what value they can deliver for customers with the right resources and lack of executive meddling. Warhammer 3 is a lesson in how not to finish a trilogy and how to exhaust fanbase goodwill, and how underinvestment in their own team and pandering to shareholders only does one thing: screws their customers.The game itself isn't terrible. Some of the developers clearly tried their best despite their paymasters stupidity. The factions, units and lords are pretty well done, and the game performance and art design is pretty strong. But bluntly, after what Warhammer 2 achieved, this game being at best a 7 or 8/10 that will likely never achieve its true potential? Its not just disappointing, its a disgrace.I wish i could recommend this the way i could recommend Warhammer 2. But because of what CA are becoming, because of how they are slowly burning their own fanbase and IP to the ground? Screw them. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly I wish I could give this a "mixed" or an "average" instead of either a "yes" or "no". On it's own,however,  this is not worth the price tag.To be succinct, the game has enough negatives that outshine the positives. Let's cover both sides (these were the most significant in my experience with the game):1. Questionable  design decisions: Here I'm looking at you, Realms of Chaos. To be brief, it's just not fun and the game design works against the player and against the core design of total war games. You are actively discouraged to expand and conquer  due to the Rifts of Chaos mechanic. Coupled with how the economy works, you will not be able to field more than 1-2 armies before the first rifts open. From then, you will have to basically micromanage 2 "maps" (as your Legendary lord ventures into chaos to try and get the demon prince soul). It basically becomes a hassle and you get to barely scrape by before Chaos armies come through the rifts and invade your provinces if you don't rush to close them. Now remember, you can only field 1-2 armies realistically, and rifts open all around your realm, which means... you WILL lose provinces, and if that weren't enough, the corruption from chaos kicks in, and it's no joke either to clear that corruption. Added with the ticking clock element of having to rush chaos ASAP, it becomes a race that is significantly stacked against the player way too early. Back in Shogun 2, Realm Divide made sense, it provided an adequate challenge at the point in the campaign where the player would be ready for it. Here, it feels contrived at best.  Allow me to exemplify: In one of my campaigns, I was doing decent to get the Khorne Realm soul... won 5 battles in a row, didn't lose a single army unit, encamped to replenish, was a turn away from fighting the guardian... only to have Goldtooth rush into the chaos realm, win one fight, and in the next turn he rushes into the guardian fight, wins, the realms close, I get kicked out of chaos with empty hands, making 2-3 hours of work... pointless. It's extremely demotivating for the player. The randomness of it all, while thematic, makes for a poor gameplay experience. It says volumes that one of the most popular mods for this game is one that completely deactivates the campaign conditions and mechanics (Ursun does not roar, so the game becomes a sandbox).2. Battlefield mechanics:2.1 AI behaves erratically, at points ignoring units completely, at others not knowing who/what to attack but I didn't have too much issue with that. Let's face it, AI in Total war games was never the best when it comes to this (though TWW2 had significantly better AI, especially for the generals, at least in my experience). 2.2 Sieges: They've always never been the best, but now they are even more frustrating. Being allowed to build towers and fortifications WHILE the battle is ongoing is just nonsensical. That should be allowed only  during the deployment phase of the battle. 3. System:3.1 Loading times are still an issue. Having to wait 2-4 minutes with specs above the recommended still proves this game has significant issues with it's aging engine and optimization. Although, it seems that the most glaring issues from launch have been fixes, as I didn't experience some of the worst ones noted then.  3.2 Campaign map has frame rate drops, especially when snow falls. Now for the positives:1. Graphics: amazing. Chaos realms look fantastic and have ton of character to them. Each realm looks distinct and interesting in their own chaotic ways. Kudos to the graphics designers and artists here. The rest of the main campaign map also looks pretty good. 2. The Prologue campaign: excellent narrative for a prologue campaign that teaches the basics of TW mechanics and provides a cool background for this game's setting. Only hurt more that the realm of chaos campaign after it was such a contrasting experience.3. Diplomacy: Well look at that, finally I get told WHY my deal is rejected or accepted and I can base my proposal in game parameters, instead of a simple "low/moderate/high" likelihood of success. Not nearly developed like a paradox game diplomacy, but still, a step in the right direction. 4. Immortal Empires*: the one big reason to play this, especially if like me, you own the previous 2 games and has a bunch if not all the DLC. Finally we have the largest Warhammer map ever, and god it's fun. It's everything you wanted for the grand campaign we've been wanting ever since the fist game came out. * Immortal empires did not ship with the game at launch and is ONLY worth it if you have the previous games and DLC. Having almost 70% of the content and leaders locked behind those paywalls is otherwise a turn-off. Here in Japan the base came goes for 7,000 yen (and they lowered it after all the debacles) and the Shadows of Change and chaos dwarfs still go for 3000 each, lol.  All in all, this is a very mixed bag. I focused a lot on the negatives, as they are the main reasons why I am in the end giving this a negative but it does have good points. However, as a standalone game, it does not justify it's price tag. I got it on sale and still I might continue to play it, but only for immortal empires.  Edit 11/2024:Played more and finally dragged myself to finish a Realm of Chaos campaign. God that was BAD, both in terms of mechanics and narrative. Here are some highlights.1. Glitches, bugs: got so many weird bugs and glitches both in battle and campaign. Units not attacking, units glitching, a hero outright vanish from the army it was attached to, sieges being an utter and complete mess, etc. etc. My personal favorite: In the last campaign of Realm of Chaos the chaos army glitched so much it was insanely easy to win. Be'lakor just flew around the battlefield not attacking a single unit until his health was 10%. Half his army had issues with path-finding and could not reach my units. Clearly little to no QA was done here or was outright ignored. Unbelievable that at least some of this stuff has not been fixed in over 2 years.2. Narrative: Honestly, sort of lame ending for a game that had a good prologue campaign. No spoilers, but it was quite generic and I think more could have been done to give it some flavor, especially for Kislev. There are also some plot holes that are never addressed in this narrative. 3. A lesson for the future? CA, please think twice about these arcade-like modes in a game design that does not work well with it, or make it it's own thing entirely. Again, for realms of chaos, the best strategy is to not to play this as a TW game. 4. Engine: as people much better articulated than I have said, CA, it's time for a new engine. This engine is collapsing over its own weight. I keep having significant issues despite well above recommended settings, and loading screen time are atrocious.

_childDocuments_.review: It saddens me that I can't recommend this game. #3 has potential with some great new ideas but flops too hard on one of the fundamentals. Aside from the usual gripe that you need to buy extra DLC to make some factions tolerable to play, the game usually functions well and is enjoyable, so why the negative review? The simple answer is that in it's current state, it's previous title in the series is more fun experience.My understanding (I might be off the mark here) is that previously, settlement battles were an issue, with the new settlement defensive tower mechanic being too powerful and the bulk of fights being walled settlement battles. It appears that the devs response to this was to strip it all back. The buildable towers are now uniform between factions (that I have played), but worst offending is that they are so heavily RNG based. Keep in mind that with the best defensive upgrades to a minor settlement, most garrisons are pathetically weak. This is supposed to be in conjunction with the settlement itself being a multiplier but it's just not the case. In major settlement battles, the answer becomes obvious. The walls there are significant to slow down enemies and more importantly the towers built into them by default are both highly damaging and ACCURATE. Meanwhile any ones you build yourself would struggle to hit the broad side of a mountain at point blank range.In conclusion, with weak garrisons, no walls and defences that are often useless, it's mostly not worth trying defending minor settlements unless you have an army stacked there. I'm aware that people complained about playing "tower whackamole" to fight these and with very limited map selection it made the issue far worse (some of them are literally reskins of others with more/less trees). But the devs fix has changed it from tower whackamole to settlement whackamole on the campaign map instead. What turned from a good and interesting way to stop players slowly cheesing walled settlement fights (because the AI is and probably always will be poor at dealing with walls) has been stripped back to frustration in comparison to #2.TLDR: Don't buy this, #2 is a more fun and well rounded experience than this.

_childDocuments_.review: With games, I often have "phases" of playing them which last for a week up to a month at a time. Sometimes, a game's longevity will only consist of one or two phases, while others last a few more. Total War: Warhammer is one of the latter. Perhaps even beyond that, as I have been playing this game consistently for well over 2 months now. For me, that says something.I figured I'd have to leave a review when Creative Assembly made Immortal Empires available to everyone who owns the third game. Since I already had Immortal Empires, this decision had no bearing on me in terms of actual gameplay. However, this does tell me that the developers really do care about the community. Immortal Empires is an excellent experience and I believe, the definitive way to experience these games. Seeing all of the races & factions from every game come together on one map makes the experience feel complete. Each race is completely different in terms of style, roster and gameplay, allowing for countless hours to be spent on each one. They're all incredibly fun and there's a faction out there for everyone. Do you want to pummel the enemy with artillery and make them come to you? Try the Dwarfs. Do you want to swarm the enemy with mass numbers? Try Skaven. Or maybe, you'd like a more balanced roster allowing for a flexible playstyle- Empire.Something that I don't often see mentioned, and one of my favourite aspects of the game, is the amount of detail around the Warhammer lore put into this game. Descriptions of units, items and buildings are all interesting and varied. Having not read any of the books or played the tabletop game, I find this all very engaging, helping me to keep immersed in the experience. The unit card art, soundtrack, and dozens upon dozens of maps all help to further accentuate this feeling.All in all, Total War: Warhammer 3 is an excellent game. The main downside to me is the amount of money that needs to go into these games if you wish to unlock more races. Aside from that, blink and the hours trickle away...
