_childDocuments_.review: As of May 2024 it looks like the game is back on the right track.__________________________________________________________I can't recommend this game in its current state. I began playing this series somewhere the middle of WHII's patch cycle. It was incredible. I had been a huge fan of Total War growing up, and to see one that was so well fleshed out with a fantasy theme blew my mind. Sure, it had some issues here and there, but there was clearly a lot of love and effort being put into the game. The DLCs were worth the money and the FLC content was great. I felt good about buying up every bit of content, and even purchasing some for my friends to play CO-OP.Needless to say, I could barely contain my excitement in the weeks leading up to the launch of the third game. I pre-ordered, religiously watched Youtube content, and was practically counting down the minutes until launch.And then it launched.What a disappointment. It felt like it wasn't even the same people making the game. There was clearly no UNDERSTANDING of what made the title such a success. The campaign wasn't very fun. A significant portion of the new races had uninspiring mechanics, that were a straight downgrade from some of the recent game two reworks. The units didn't seem to be able to follow commands the same way. The UI was downgraded. Even minor things like traits for heroes and lords were so poorly crafted it was just... puzzling.I guess the word is regression. The launch of the newest title was a regression. It was actually worse in nearly all ways from the previous title.OK... Let's rationalize: it's hard to launch a game. I'm sure they were using a code base from a previous iteration of WHII that didn't include all of the more recent fixes and QoL changes. The DLC team will take over and make it a great game again. Most of these fixes really aren't even very complicated, right? By the time Immortal Empires launches in a few months they will have most of this stuff ironed out, I'm sure.Well, it has been a year and a half, and to be completely honest, the game is in pretty rough shape. It is clearly not receiving the attention it needs to get it into a condition where it is acceptable to push out DLCs that cost nearly half of what we paid for the base title. Paid content is routinely broken and left to rot for the entirety of their four month patch cycle until they attempt to fix it with the next patch. I say attempt because oftentimes what is relayed in the patch notes isn't what is actually put into the game. Each patch inevitably introduces a ton of new bugs and issues because they aren't dedicating resources to proper QA. The game three races, released only a year and a half ago, are almost all in need of some form of a rework. This was promised with each future DLC and what has been released in this most recent one is laughable. God forbid you are a fan of the Ogre Kingdoms, because they are going to be miserable to play for YEARS to come. They were born into this world between the thighs of the game three team, and it was an inauspicious start to say the least. I guess this is running a little long, but hopefully I addressed the crux of the problem-- the game was released in bad shape, and instead of dedicating the time and resources to improve it and sculpt it into something worthy of its predecessor, it is being milked for cash until it is time to take it out back and put a bullet in its brain. I can't understate how little goodwill I have left for the developers of this title, and just how many issues there are with the game itself. On top of that there is no communication. There is no effort. There is no love left.There is, however, a road to redemption. Pick up that broom and get to work.

_childDocuments_.review: It truly hurts me to give a negative review of a game I do love and can see enormous potential in. The pricing structure has gone out of control and the fans are being squeezed, we're being treated as if we're cash cows. That'd be one thing if the content was plentiful, high quality and worked but the fact of the matter is dlc such as this is not higher in quantity or quality than previous dlc yet demands a price increase of 150% on a digital product.They want almost half the cost of the full retail game on one low content dlc. All while the sheer scale of bugs in the game only gets bigger, the known issues list grows larger and basic optimization and clean up is not being done by CA. The game is swimming in legacy issues and new ones. They promised more dlc, more patches, more information and yet have failed to hold to their word. The shadows of change dlc was supposed to be a summer dlc and they're dropping it August 31st literally the last day that could be considered in the summer schedule. If thats not a massive middle finger to the players who're eagerly awaiting content and took them at their word for the schedule than I don't know what is. I'll change my review when CA change their attitude towards the fans and paying customers.An update as of now they're also using veiled threats telling customers that if they don't buy the dlc they'll shut down support. Someone from CA better come out and apologize for basically everything and tell us the're putting all available hands on bug fixes, optimization, and fairly priced DLC or we as a customer base will pull support from the company.Further update patch 4.0 broke more things and God knows when or if CA will even fix them.

_childDocuments_.review: The warhammer series is my favorite of the total war gene. Having said that this game is over price which is why I can't recommend it to newer players. The base game is whatever, only immortal empires (which is all the games combined) is fun. To truly enjoy the game you need to spend 180$ to get all three games, on top of that theres 280$ worth of dlcs. The strongest and most creative factions and lords are dlcs. But if money is no object to you then I would highly recommend this game and just buy the extra stuff as you want it. It has more to do than any other Total War with very unique and interesting ideas that you wont experience anywhere else, and you could easily spend thousands hours playing it. All in all it really is an amazing game that would had been one of the most played games up there with Minecraft and Skyrim if the game was 60$ (all three combined) with 60$ worth of dlcs. You would think a company that makes strategy games would understand that a higher player base would increase profits significantly with not just this game but all their past and future games, but their greatest project is anti new players. Instead they milk their dedicated players and release less and less content with each new release. Which the result is and going to be a less and less player base as people are over it which lead to a inevitable downfall of a great company, or at least a major set back.I love Total War and I love CA for making my favorite game. Rome 1 was my first pc game and I have thousands of hours throughout all the games. The amount of content has dwindle and dwindle while advertisement increase, the upside of the newer games is better graphics and animations, but this game is so fast pace you can't even enjoy those aspects even in slow mode. The game really is amazing and the things CA does are amazing. We don't need a new total war every year, one every 2-3 years would be great. I don't have a problem with a company wanting to make money thats the whole point of a company, but their hurting their costumers and their reputation. I love CA but until CA makes a total war or any game that they take their time on, and prioritizes gameplay over graphics (take a page from minecraft) I wont be buying another one of their games.

_childDocuments_.review: Even as someone who has over 1250 hours in the Total War Warhammer games, I can admit that Warhammer 3 had a rocky first year. A buggy launch, a much delayed beta release for Immortal Empires, and a strange lack of communication from Creative Assembly had many people thinking the End Times had come for the series. However, I can comfortably say that with the release of patch 3.0 and the Chaos Dwarfs, Warhammer 3 is exactly what I've wanted it to be since release. The variety of factions and lords is breathtaking, and it is an amazing accomplishment and fulfillment of the vision laid out in 2016 that we now have a fully realized Warhammer world complete with all of the factions from the tabletop game in a Total War campaign. With the breadth of content available, you'll find enough replayability to last a lifetime. Immortal Empires will go down as one of the best RTS experiences in gaming, and there are still years of support ahead to look forward to. If you are a fan of strategy gaming, then I cannot recommend Total War Warhammer 3 enough.

_childDocuments_.review: 165 hours in, I finally admitted I was having a miserable time playing WH3. Poor gameplay decisions aside, the sheer amount of content that is rushed, badly implemented or just plain broken is staggering. Especially when you consider that that this is the third iteration of this engine/game.For me, the most problematic faults lie in the battle system which, rather than improving in the migration to a new version, is rife with broken and rushed systems resulting in most battles ending in a laborious, dull mosh pit grind. If the core battle gameplay had been satisfying (which is mostly the case for the second game at present) I would have been able to grit my teeth and wait out the inevitable long round of patches. Sadly, this is not the case. I had been excited in the run up to launch to think that the third game would address problems still inherent in the second. Sieges for instance, were pretty janky in WH2 in a number of ways, and I had hoped that they when they were revamping the system they would come up with something fresh. Instead, we got a poorly implemented rehash of the Attila siege system. Additionally, the minor settlement battles can barely accomodate the models in the cramped streets, and they invariably end up being shorn completely of any tactical possibility beyond that of rushing some fast units to unguarded victory points. I stopped pre-ordering games a long time ago but, despite my grave misgivings over the 3K debacle, I trusted CA enough to deliver the third game in a state that would be both an iteration and improvement of the second game. Regretfully, they did not. Considering the problems I can see in the current state of the game's development I've uninstalled it and won't be coming back for a good while.As a counter-point, the art is astounding and the DLC team have now taken over production which suggests that it will eventually be a total war worthy of the name.tl;dr: Avoid for now, too broken.

_childDocuments_.review: The third and final Warhammer game in the totalwar series is the pinnacle of bombastic over the top strategy gaming. Its the best looking totalwar has ever been, its most fun warhammer old world has ever been and with the introduction of a new epic campaign to play until we wait for the game changing combined map; "Immortal Empires" or whatever CA decide to call it.The campaign map is bigger, containing more diverse battle maps with hauntingly beautiful scenery.The starting factions (knowing many more will come) are all diverse and a heck of a lot of fun to play. From skull collecting Khorne who is always on the attack to the every hungry ogre kingdoms, there is something for everyone.Performance and graphics are inconsistent. Oddly rendered models while looking around the campaign or zooming in and out of the battles. Occasionally the game stutters around, particularly during the end turn and the immediate moment afterwards as it loads all of the events which happened in the previous turn. The occasional bug may also hinder progress, such as events not ocuring when they should, pops up not appearing, and thus not being able to "remove them" to continue on with your next attack or movement.Overall I rate the game a solid 8/10 with points being removed for the bugs and inconsistant performance.

_childDocuments_.review: I need to preface this with the simple fact that I'm not a super duper, hardcore Total War player. With that in mind, I can safely say that I would recommend this game. Like others have said, there are some issues with the game:- The survival battles are interesting, but (in my opinion) they feel like there's still some work that needs to be done on them. They just don't feel like they're at a place that a player would always rather fight than auto resolve in subsequent campaigns.- The mechanics for a few of the factions are honestly just really annoying to keep track of while also dealing with chaos portal corruption and the race to get every flavor of demonic soul.- Extra supply line cost for new armies on top of unit/lord/hero upkeep. I will die on this hill and take everyone down with me.- Technology research trees for some of the races feel incredibly underwhelming and trade is...eh.- Possibly having a "DLC" that only adds in more blood effects and having the audacity to charge money for it. They haven't done it, yet, but we all know it's going to happen.All that being said, I still enjoy the game. They recently added in support for modding, and there's some fun stuff on the workshop to play around with. As someone who only started dipping their toes into both the Warhammer Fantasy and 40k lore a few years ago (because of Total War: Warhammer 1, actually), the stories for the Legendary Lords are interesting, and the prologue was really fun to play through from a narrative perspective. I honestly wish CA would do more narrative driven micro-campaigns like the prologue/what they had in the first TW:WH game with the Beastmen, but I can see where some people might not like it.Tl;Dr - Does it have issues that CA is still hammering out? Yeah. Would I still recommend the game even knowing such issues exist? Yup. Even with the issues it's fun to control armies of fantasy races and smash them into one another.

_childDocuments_.review: Review of NOV '22, early access and beta Immortal Empires. I played many hours of this and have a good grasp of what this game is composed of and what to expect in the future. I also have experience playing WHII and WHI across various patch metas, so it's not a blind perspective.Overall I am glad this was released in a playable state, despite the turmoil across the world and various game companies failing their own expectations in recent times. I am glad there is no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, despite being SEGA. I cannot stress this enough, no microtransactions, no skins ♥♥♥♥, it's just a classic pc style game with actual gameplay like way back in the day. Sadly, a rarer and rarer commodity with all the chinese neon colored garbage flooding every landfill. Positive:*Everything is there that you remember, plus new content and units. If you pay for everything, there is a con of content. Improbable that you can get to it all with a mere moderate focused effort and time commitment. You can play this for years to come.*The content fans have been waiting for, that this title focuses on (Kislev and Chaos) delivers in every possible way that you could expect from this company. I still cant even believe it's finally out and playable. Years ago it seemed like something that would never be released.*I am glad CA wants to stay true to creating the complete TOTAL WAR WH digital strategy experience with no compromise, in all of it's ecclectic, completionist glory, with massive bloody battles, as large and messy as your PC can support.*Playable, not many crashes after many hours and all bugs were gameplay and balance related, also kind of an oddity nowadays, a pc title which works in early access better than many AAA release on release day. Negative:*I think the worst thing is someone on dev played a Paradox title as inspiration. Focusing too much on campaign, when it's always (and in many ways still is) just an excuse to go from battle to battle, really hurts momentum. Especially when the main dish, the battle sim, suffers for it.*Some classic flaws in the game go unaddressed, from buggy movement, poor responsiveness and visual communication with the player, excessive AI cheating really begin to grow from quirks to full gameplay hinderences in this one due to scale and scope.*I think this game focus a bit too much on fighting undefended settlements that dont have a chance, hundreds of undefended settlements. Its too cowardly and strategic to be epic fantasy war, which is what you hope for. If I had one request, I would ask to remove the battle predictor entirely for the player AND the AI, because it serves no function and is comically broken and in this recent version seems to sway combat artificially which is completely unnecessary unless you start charging real money per battle. This way the game would just be about battles, win or lose and less gamey garbage and underhandedness ( dont know if its part of tabletop tradition ala card select in MTG for example.)*I failed to have much meaningful multiplayer experiences, but this is common for Steam titles. *In the BETA of Immortal Empires, I found most non-RoC races near broken. I guess it's expected but it still seems really odd. How do you break hitboxes between games? Neutral:*Surprisingly, this game's strongest suit is it's detailed graphics and iconic designs, charming characters and units. I found it surprising that more wasnt done to get the engine up to modern TECH standards to really put the graphics in front. If they were half assed that would be one thing, but in many cases the art is extremely detailed and legally required to meet certain criteria of quality. I hope the final version will really allow support of all the modern 2020~ era roboust diplay options of modern super graphics. I am no expert, but even I noticed it seems like the display engine or something just isnt even up to par with the graphics in game.  Overall, I am glad that this exists. I am glad it was released and is playable. Though it managed to piss me off more than previous titles with all of the problems related to early access and everything else that is well documented in more detail across Reddit and over complaint boxes, I am still glad I put the time in to explore the inner workings of this conclusive installment. Thank you for many hours of fun to this series and I hope to play it in its final state one day.There is a lot of negative views related to love for the series, love for WH, and disappointment at the incomplete release or feeling of the game regressing in quality in some respects. I am glad a feedback loop online exists now between player and company. Dont let them get complacent but be reasonable too, devs are people and you dont know what their situation is. I think its important to have faith and give the benefit of the doubt here, especially through these dark economic times be glad you can afford such an expensive game, remain strong and best of luc to you all. We can all make it through the dark times.

_childDocuments_.review: This has to be the most frustrating game in existence. No, not because of difficulty... There are so many great improvements, and yet every single one of them is ruined by some other issue. I have over 9000 hours in TWWH2. I loved that game so much. The only complaint I think I ever had, and it was only a minor thing, was sieges were a little dull.Now, sieges are simply awful. The pop up tower defense game that they have turned into is just plain terrible. I hate everything about it. It doesn't graphically look right, nor add anything interesting to the battle. They are just an annoyance that feels really out of place and makes the game look silly. This is especially annoying since the maps themselves are amazing. Why add this dumb mechanic? Who ever thought it up should be fired immediately. Then there is the level cap increase. I have no issue with this overall, but the fact that heroes often don't have enough skills to spend the points on? What the heck? You NEED a mod to make use of those points, or a skill dump... That's just pathetic. Another point of contention for me is the check boxes for notifications. I don't understand why these setting cannot be saved. Every single campaign I have uncheck a number of these that are useless and annoying. I know that sounds like a very minor thing, but its annoying. Likewise with unsaved camera setting. Modders found a way, but CA can't?Then there is balance... Or more accurately there isn't. Every unit seems wildly unbalanced in ways that continue to shock me. There are far to many units to go through to explain this in detail. But it needs a lot of work in this regard. Another issue is the new magic system. It makes no sense at all. The old system was great, why change it? Finally there is performance. Its horrible. This game runs absolutely terrible on any settings. What's even more annoying, is that battles run great, but the campaign map runs horrible, so the place where you are 99% of the time is the worst part. So, you turn the setting down to look terrible so you can get a stable FPS, and then the battles which would be fine look like trash. Very annoying. However, all this said there are many good points to list. Unit variety, impressive maps, great sound track, amazing audio, race variety with unique mechanics. The list could go on for hours as there are so many great sides to it all. That's why its so frustrating. I really really really want to love this game. There is so much work put into it that should make it great, but it all falls short over and over because of really dumb decisions. If I can say any one thing really ruins it, its those siege mechanics. If they dropped the dumb pop up towers and buildable siege tools in battle it would be SO much better. Also if they made siege equipment make sense instead of battering rams that are useless and the like. None the less, all complaints aside, I still recommend this game. There is enough here to keep it interesting, and one can hope they resolve these issues over time. We will see. (Also, this is including Immortal Empires, with out that, the game is 2/10 hard pass)

_childDocuments_.review: I am a big fan of Warhammer I and Warhammer II an have spent 1000s of hours in both together. I will describe my problems with Mortal Empires and Chaos-realm-campaign in this reviewMortal-Empires-ExperienceMortal Empires is no fun to play since the diplomacy is broken and driven by an anti-player-bias. The Ai-Factions (Factions played by computer) are totally obsessed with destroying the player. So every round a dice is thrown and with a probability of estimated 10-20 % another faction declares war on you. Even factions that are friendly or neutral declare random wars on you. So you get sorrounded by many many factions that have no other goal than bully you down and sent army over half the world to achieve this. Total-War-Series have always been tough, but the anti-play-driven diplomacy is just nonsense. Even if you manage to build up a kingdom, make the right technology-descisions, recruit good units to counter your enemy you will very often overwhelmed by many many hostile factions sending 5 too 20 Army to you and their combined powers is not to overcome. The typically Mortal Empire campaign starts easy. You build up a kingdom of 5 too 10 settlements. Than totally unprovoked war-declarations come in each round and your sorrounded by a lot of enemy that bring you down. For me it looks the game-developetrs where so obsessed with fancy units, new monsters and spells they failed totally that their diplomatic system is bad. Chaos-Realms-ExperienceWarhammer III is a very chaotic, unbalanced and boring game in my opinion, surely not worth 60 €. The problem is due to the winning conditions youre forced to walk into chaos realms. On the other hand often occuring rifts let spawn numbers of chaos armys destabilizing your kingdom. Forced missions and numbers of rifts spawning hostile armys in your land makes an expansion of your kingdom very hard. The charm of the Total war series for me was to build up kingdoms and conquer the map. The more scripted events and forced winning conditions, the less joy for me. Warhammer III is a extreme event-driven game, that enforces the player to a strict path. That takes away all the fun of the game. The Factions as such are interesting, but overall few fun in a scripted campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: I have 10k hours on Warhammer 2. Yes i may have been passed out in my chair for a good portion, but I still very much enjoyed the game. Which is why it truly pains me to write a negative review for Warhammer 3. There has been massive backlash about DLC prices, but hear me out here and I will explain why money has nothing to do with it.Now, for all its glory Warhammer 2 had its flaws. The most prominent among them being settlement battles. Minor settlements simply did not have unique terrain, or worse when walls were constructed in minor settlements they became generic major settlement battles. While major settlement battles consisted of a big long wall which prevented defending armies from effectively using their ranged units. Especially when those defending armies were controlled by the AI. This resulted in blob tactics and quite literally being able to solo conquer major settlements with a couple well placed wind or vortex spells. The first time you conquer Altdorf with the army that is Vlad it is pretty satisfying, however, it quickly loses its flavor as you thirst for dynamic, challenging, or dare i say it, "strategic" game-play. So how did they fix this? Well.....they may have made it worse.Warhammer 3 came to us with a promise. This was not a promise that every DLC would be $9.99; but a promise of minor settlement battles, a rework of major settlement battles, and a new AI that would make ChatGPT look like a ferby. So what changed? How did they go from blob fight tactics, and walls that you couldn't place rattling guns on. To sniper nests and artillery positions from which to rain death upon any man thing things that dare interrupt your experiments? Well they kind of did. I can genuinely say i enjoy defending MY settlements more. Just one small problem. 90% if not 100% of the battles you engage in are offensive. So how does that new AI do defending their settlements? Bad, just bad. Units walking in circles trying to find a home, and artillery nestled behind a building waiting patiently to point blank 1 unlucky swordsman before being completely overrun. Despite these derptastic moves by the AI it is nothing compared to how positively infuriating it is to get your own units to move around these new battles offensively. You tell units to walk through the open gate and they begin climbing the walls. The AI build a barrier and your melee units suddenly stop in place. AND FOR GODS SAKE LEAVE THE ONE FELLBAT BEHIND AND GO STOP THE QUARRELERS FROM FLANKING ME IN THE REAR! So all in all the settlement battles are better in the sense that they make me want to burn down one orphanage instead of two. Now it might seem like I am hyper-fixated on this one issue, but unless you are playing multiplayer these battles make up more then 50% of your playtime, and that's more roasted orphan faces then even Carl could digest. Yet have they done anything since Warhammer 3's release to improve this key, nay only real difference in gameplay? Sadly no. So i don't care if the next DLC is five bucks or fifty bucks. Until they improve how the units behave I don't care how many of them their are.

_childDocuments_.review: Update review:DONT BUY THE GAME AND AVOID CREATIVE ASSEMBLY!!!!!!I will avoid Creative Assembly going forward when I make new game purchases; because they're the stereotype of a greedy/evil company.We are in luck that the game developers pour their heart and soul into the game; and I love it, and I got hooked a long time ago. Now I'll still get scammed out of my money until the game is finished, because i'm addicted.Praise the developers, let the company rot.Edit: seems like they're turning the ship with Thrones of Decay and new additions to Shadows of Change. I will turn this review positive again if they keep on this track.Initial review:At first I played the prologue, followed by a Kislev campaign. I loved the story, lore and the immersive world of Warhammer fantasy. After Kislev, I played Grand Cathay, which I must say was even more fun than playing as Kislev. (Both gameplay wise and personal preference for the style and feel of the faction.) Defending the Great Bastion as Miao Ying, The Storm Dragon, was a blast. Let the hordes of Kurgan smash against my wall!  The hope of finding the lost dragon child, Shen-Zoo, was something that caught my curiosity. Really hope we will get more story and lore about Cathay, so I can re-unite the siblings! Speaking of which, it's a shame there are no quest battles for Grand Cathay. Not only from a story wise perspective, but from a rational one as well. Because it makes no sense that these ancient dragons do not possess any kind of unique artifact that they've kept throughout the ages. I understand that legendary items come from caravans for Cathay, which is a great add on for the Ivory road system, but the lords need their own special equipment for sure.In short: The game is great and I'm looking forward to everything that is still in the pipeline to really make the trilogy one of the greatest games of a lifetime!

_childDocuments_.review: While Immortal Empires certainly was a breath of fresh air for the game, there are still so many bugs and simply downgrades from game 2 that I would not recommend this game if you don't know what you are getting into. I still play it and enjoy it, but that's only because I can overlook the major issues that plague the game (and especially how incredibly slow CA has been at addressing any of them).  Just go play Total War Warhammer 2 instead, which is in a great state right now.A few specific (major and minor) negatives for Immortal Empires (The twwh3 campaign alone is awful so let's just pass over that)------------------------------------------------------------>the ui is just straight up worse than game 2. I don't even know what happened here except that they wanted to change it for the sake of changing it. The faction selection is terrible, mission panel is worse to use, etc.sound design is good for the most part, but once again projectile units sound like *** with very few exceptions. Almost like someone else did them specifically (both blackpowder and bows/crossbows)>many factions have been nerfed and a lot of their interesting mechanics removed. While I do understand the need to reduce power in some cases, the big problem here is the lack of anything interesting in its stead. Just ends up making them less exciting to play.>Bugs, bugs, oh so many bugs. Yes that's to be expected, but they could at least have done some hotfixes by now. Some of them make certain factions nigh-unplayable or remove key parts of their identity (lack of items, heroes, quests, etc.).>Hero traits ... what the hell happened here. The vast majority of them are just straight up awful, while some are very good. I don't expect all of them to be great, but at least something decent. Rn the difference in power is astonishing Ogres are especially notorious here, with some default traits providing bigger benefits than their unique faction traits in the same attribute. Cathay similarly has some very weird traits ... all the good ones are of one type (Yin), while the Yang traits are just plain useless. That's not even to speak of factions that pretty much only have useless traits.>Personal issue, but the game is generally too easy right now. The AI is way too passive even at legendary leading to extremely fast campaign burnout (by turn 50 the campaign is basically over, cause nothing can challenge you anymore).>Lack of field battles. This is especially notorious on higher difficulties due to the ai sitting in their settlements as soon as they even get a whiff of your army. Additionally, since the autoresolve is as forgiving as it is right now, you barely ever fight any field battles past turn 20. It's always siege or minor settlement battles, which are both incredibly easy to defeat (easier than field battles in most cases). This has a lot of knock-on effects, such as gunpower units being generally awful in actual battle (due to the ai behaving smarter by avoiding LoS and targeting them with archers) or ranged units in general being subpar (again due to ai perfectly microing to avoid being shot as much as possible). This leads to sieges being either a melee slog or being cheesed in the vast majority of cases.>continuing with the gunpowder issue, the obstacle detection right now is so jank, that often those type of units don't even shoot if there is virtually nothing in front of them. It was already bad in game 2, but so much worse now. You often can't even shoot larger targets stuck in your infantry, because they seemingly don't realize that 60% of those trolls are sticking out above the heads of their comrades. Add to that the fact that most ai actively targets gunpowder units (such as handgunners, ironhails, thunderers, etc.) and you'll likely get a better performance out of any bow/crossbow unit. Those can shoot above your own units, have less targetting issues and most importantly don't require 10 seconds of micro each to get into a position where they can actually shoot properly.There are many other points that irk me, but I think these are some that might give you an idea of whether or not you may enjoy the game in its current state. I do believe it will get better with time, but as it is now I can't see this being anytime soon.

Total War: Warhammer I - Released 2016, normally priced $59.99 USDTotal War: Warhammer II - Released 2017, normally priced $59.99 USDTotal War: Warhammer III - Released 2022, normally priced $59.99 USDAfter purchasing those 3 "BASE" games, it is $180 USDBut wait, you still don't have all the factions. I can understand having SOME factions available by DLC, it's the state of gaming today. DLC is unavoidable and is everywhere it is what it is. But to buy a new game, then have to buy the two older versions of the game just to get the locked factions in the new game is nuts. So be prepared to have to buy just about all of the Total War: Warhammer content to unlock all the factions. If you are huge fan of this series and already have Warhammer I and II and most of the DLCs, then it's not a bad purchase. Few DLCs and you're good. I mean, there is clear indication that there is no playerbase, so it might go down the path of Saints Row, Redfall, Starfield. As many companies learn today, there isn't much demand for another cooperative cartoon-style shooter with inclusive characters and monetization cosmetic shop (or even worse, pay to win). There's Overwatch (another recent flop), there's Fortnite and there's Apex Legends - the question each and every player of these is going to ask - "Why would I want to switch to something different, when I have already achieved so much progress in that particular game?"B) With the focus on new games, the good old TW: WH3 is getting very little love. I mean, I would be first in line to shower devs and publisher with gold from my bank account, if they could roll out a decent content DLC after DLC, no questions asked - but they don't. The updates come, squish some of the bugs, but yet more remain - so these are up to modders to fix, most of the time. And I mean, stuff like Mod Configuration menu should not be a mod at all, but an integral part of the game itself - the functionality should be included in the base game.So there you have it. You like turn-based strategy games with real-time tactic battles, which give you a feeling of being a powerful warlord, the war-hungry conqueror righting ancient wrongs and building a massive empire? You love Warhammer fantasy setting? Then this is a game for you. But bear in mind what I said above.

However I feel I need to change my recommendation to negative based on recent developments.I love this game but it has bugs and balance issues. Like a lot of bugs and balance issues. Nakai isn't able to recruit Kroxigors (as a Kroxigor lord), healing is conpletely overpowered to the extent that in multiplayer the meta factions almost universally have access to healing and it makes MP battles painful,  skill trees are broken for a lot of characters, feral mammoths are 1400 gold for a unit which does almost nothing, some units infinite rampage, lots of legacy units never had their stats rebalanced for game 3 (varghulfs, hellpits etc.) Making them functionally useless, I could go on. I think the problem is that these bugs/balancing issues (and a lot more) have been flagged to CA for a long time but nothing is ever done. I probably would have just put up and shut up but the pricing for the new DLC is just insane (50%  extra content for 150% price hike), this is a pretty expensive game to start with (you're looking at over $200 to get access to all of the races and the best units in the sandbox) and that is fine if the content is well supported and regularly patched. This isn't. To then release a DLC which is half the cost of Baldurs Gate 3 (nearly) is bizarre. I'm not going to be buying Shadows of Change on release but probably will eventually but that is only because I am so committed to this game now. For someone who's looking to get into it I would probably avoid for the time being, the cost/product balance is just not good enough at the moment. I can only hope CA does the right thing and gets the community back on side because this game has the potential to keep making money for years to come, but if you completely alienate the fanbase some people will go and not come back (I already know of at least 5 players with >500 hours each who are defecting to BG3 and starfield when it arrives) and trying to get new players in with such a phenomenally high financial barrier to entry is going to be a tough sell.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of strategy games and fantasy worlds, you're in for a treat with Total War: Warhammer 3. This game is the third and final installment of the epic trilogy that combines the turn-based empire building of Total War with the real-time battles and lore of Warhammer. I've been playing it for a few years now and I can't get enough of it. Here are some of the reasons why I think this game is a must-have for any gamer.First of all, the game offers a huge variety of factions, races, units, heroes, and spells to choose from. You can play as one of the six core factions: Kislev, Cathay, Khorne, Nurgle, Slaanesh, or Tzeentch. Each faction has its own unique gameplay mechanics, strengths, weaknesses, and objectives. You can also unlock four additional factions: Chaos Dwarfs, Ogre Kingdoms, Daemons of Chaos Undivided, and Kislev Bear Cavalry. Yes, you read that right: you can ride bears into battle!Secondly, the game features a massive and immersive campaign map that spans four continents: the Old World, the New World, the Realm of Chaos, and the Eastern Lands. The map is full of details, secrets, and surprises. You can explore ancient ruins, trade with exotic cultures, fight against roaming monsters, and witness cataclysmic events. The map also changes dynamically depending on your actions and the state of the world. For example, if you play as a Chaos faction, you can corrupt the land and spread your influence across the map.Thirdly, the game delivers epic and cinematic battles that will test your tactical skills and thrill your senses. You can command thousands of troops on the battlefield, from infantry and cavalry to artillery and monsters. You can also unleash powerful magic spells and abilities that can turn the tide of war. The battles are visually stunning and realistic, with dynamic weather effects, destructible environments, and blood and gore. The game also supports multiplayer modes, so you can team up or compete with other players online.In conclusion, Total War: Warhammer 3 is a masterpiece of strategy gaming that offers endless hours of fun and replayability. It's a game that will appeal to both fans of Total War and Warhammer, as well as newcomers to the genre. It's a game that will challenge your mind and immerse you in a rich and diverse fantasy world. It's a game that will make you feel like a true warlord. If you haven't played it yet, what are you waiting for? Get it now and join the war!

_childDocuments_.review: Warhammer 3 is like a deliciously chaotic buffet where you get to choose from an array of badass factions and unleash them upon your enemies with reckless abandon. Whether you're a fan of dwarves, elves, or something more exotic like the Ogres, this game has got you covered. But let's not forget the newest additions to the roster: the Cathay and Kislev. Who knew that wielding fireworks or riding bears into battle could be so much fun? The graphics are stunning, and the attention to detail is impressive. Watching your armies clash on the battlefield is like watching a high-budget action movie, with explosions, magical spells, and monstrous creatures wreaking havoc. It's a true visual feast for the eyes. The campaign mode is challenging, but it's also hilarious at times. There's nothing quite like watching a giant rat named Queek Headtaker lay siege to a city while his minions chant "Skaven! Skaven!" in the background. And let's not forget the legendary lords, who have their own unique personalities and dialogue. Mazdamundi, the giant frog wizard, is a personal favourite of mine.But what really sets Warhammer 3 apart is the sheer amount of strategic options available to the player. Do you want to play as a defensive tactician and hold your ground against waves of enemies? Or do you want to be an aggressive conqueror and crush your foes underfoot? The choice is yours, and the possibilities are endless. In conclusion, if you're a fan of strategy games, the Warhammer universe, or just want to ride a bear into battle, then Warhammer 3 is the game for you. It's a wild, wacky, and wonderful ride that's sure to provide hours of entertainment.So what are you waiting for? Get out there and unleash your inner chaos!

_childDocuments_.review: [Edit] It would appear that my initial review was too optimistic; though it is now outdated, I shall leave it here for posterity. Following 1) The horrific pricing of the Shadows of Change DLC, and CA's disappointing response, 2) A chronic lack of patches for egregious and longstanding bugs and 3) A mix of misguided reworks and gross inattention to core gameplay mechanics, e.g. sieges and AI, I can no longer recommend this game for purchase. Perhaps in the future I may revert my review to a positive one, but I cannot recommend the game in its current state. CA will have to work very hard to regain my trust and goodwill-trust that was gradually built up over the past half a decade, and has subsequently been eroded at an astonishing pace.[Original Review]Now that Immortal Empires has released, I think this game now deserves a positive review. Although there are bound to be many bugs and crashes in this beta, I am having infinitely more fun now than I was with the abysmal Realms of Chaos campaign (whose existence should be ignored).With the improved alliance mechanics (having Hellstorm Rocket Batteries with Tyrion is a blast), the introduction of item fusing, and a significantly expanded and reworked map, Immortal Empires is a great upgrade over Mortal Empires already. Sea lanes are a greatly appreciated mechanic too, since it did feel strange not being able to circumnavigate a supposedly spherical world.This is without mentioning all the new factions (and indeed the factions which have received reworks) which I am very excited to try. Having said this, with these new factions comes imbalance, and I wouldn't be surprised if we see many tweaks to the game's armies and economies over the coming months.After the massive disappointment I felt at the game's release, I now have renewed confidence that Warhammer III will be as grand an ending to a superb trilogy as it ought to be.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I play Total War because I want to paint the map. This game constantly prevents me from doing that in a very annoying and repetitive way. Whether you're talking about poor game design or actual bugs - there is always something preventing me from actually enjoying the game. I've tried letting go on my desire to dominate the world and to just play the story, but even then I find myself to be constantly annoyed by the way things are set up. No matter what faction you play, you always have to deal with high levels of tediousness. Maybe we got spoiled after TW:WH2, but IMO it's baffling how this game is nothing more than a reskin of the previous versions - and they still messed it up. Playing against or as chaos as a whole, both in the chaos realms and just as AI opponents is buggy, tiresome and just disappointing overall. The best thing about this game compared to Total War: Warhammer 2, are the actual units in the actual battles. All the chaos army rosters look really cool and their abilities are very well done. The other factions also have a very unique taste to them and I'm looking forward to playing them in the immortal empires campaign.  All in all, I can see the potential, sure, but it's quite hard to understand why they went with this campaign design. If you haven't bought TW:WH3 yet, I'd wait untill they release immortal empires. If you don't own TW:WH1 and TW:WH2 yet, my advice is to buy those two and play their mortal empires campaign, rather than buying this one. There's plenty of very good experiences in mortal empires, and as soon as you're tired of it you can always expand to TW:WH3 in a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a Total War player, I'm Strategy player in general. I enjoy all types of strategy games, from fast paced Starcraft 2 to slow Civilization, that's why I treat WH3 not as "next Total War" but as "another strategy game", which is probably why my opinions differ greatly from average Total War player. GraphicsThe game looks just as good if not slightly better than WH2. The common complaint is that game looks like Fortnite, which isn't true. Did the game had a graphic style shift? Yes but it was a minor one and I'll try to guess why it was the case. I think it's because of the advanced corruption mechanic. The Empire provinces in WH1 looked almost as grim as some uncorrupted Chaos Wastes regions in WH3, now they look relatively normal, without the grim. I feel like this change was neccesary to make certain regions look extreme in comparison, especially when they are corrupted/uncorrupted so that map won't get boring.UIYes, the UI does look boring and lazy with all the red, I didn't like the UI color in WH2 too if that matters. I only liked WH1 colors. Now for the spicy take: the UI in previous WH Total Wars was always bad, unnecesarily minimalistic, very unintuitive to navigate especially when you are new to the franchise. Many people that complain about UI saying that it was better in WH2 are simply dishonest, becuase it was ALWAYS BAD, the color is just irrelevant. On the plus side WH3 actually improved Character and diplomacy screens.FactionsThe starting playable factions compared to the previous WH titles are vastly improved when it comes to unique gameplay. Every player should find something for themselves to enjoy. The straight forward factions like Kislev, Khorne, Daemon Prince, the middle of the road Ogres, Cathy and gimmicky Slaaneesh, Tzeentch and Nurgle. I was able to beat the game on Very Hard/Very Hard difficulty with every faction and neither of them felt repetetive. CampaignI got the feeling that CA tried to experiment with the formula because they are eager to draw in other strategy players since there's not that many AAA strategy games, but that didn't end up well for them, their own community turned on them because every strategy game is created for a certain niche of players, from what I've read and heard from my friend that owns and played EVERY Total War title, this game was always a sandbox type, slow paced strategy game that you can't really loose in unless you play on the difficulty you aren't prepared for. Yes even the Vortex race map from WH2 was impossible to loose as long as you played at your prefered difficulty bracket. It all kinda changed with WH3. The game has clear distinct pace, it's own set of challenges you need to overcome as fast as possible, because they will pile up, very high, to the point where you will loose the campaign in an instant if you treat it as "previous Total War" titles. The campaign was definetly designed to pull players out of their comfort zone, me being relatively new to the franchise, and a fan of many different strategy games didn't affect me that much.The RiftsThe "impossible", "bullsh*t", "punishing" feature of the campaign according to probably half players. It's unreasonable exaggeration, the rifts always open every +/- 30 turns, you can always be prepared to close them all in 1 turn with agents because they have set spawn place. It's the most minor setback the game can throw at you. Some people complain that other races shouldn't participate in the race, but it's a very bad suggestion, why? Because your enemies will have 1 more army on the map gaining ground faster than the player. It's better for them to participate. The Chaos Realms are relatively easy and short. The quest battles are repetetive, but you can autoresolve them in most cases. Tzeentch Chaos Realm is definetly the trickiest one unless you remember to never enter the same teleport that looped you twice. Even the negative traits you get from the Chaos Realms are a minor issue, people like to exaggerate that it's the most punishing aspect of the rift mechanic, but you can get rid of it in 3 turns max depending on trait tier in one of the province capitals with trait removing building. The building stacks with capital bonus giving you 100% success rate. After autoresolving the quest battle you need to rest 1-2 turns inside a city anyway so it looks like it was literally designed in such a way to not stop progress of the player that much and simply add some Lore flavour to the game, yet many people treat it as something that is impossible to overcome or "too punishing" that will spin your campaign 180 degree into the ground. All I can do is simply shrug. Many people like to claim that the game will only be good once combined map is released, but quite often the exact same people will write on forums for upvotes that they can never finish the sandbox map for multitple reasons and that they prefer to start a new one instead. It's unhealthy and unfair perspective towards the game.DiplomacyIt was definetly improved, maybe not as much as I'd personally liked but I don't really have anything to complain about. It's easier to get the deals going and the alliances are much more beneficial.Battle/AutoresolveThe autoresolve on higher difficulties likes to give unfair outcomes, that's something that simply must be improved. The battles themselves are a bit more sluggish compared to WH2. At first I thought it was design decision to make some spells easier to cast after the nerf to entire magic system because AI is actually really good at dodging some spells. I'm on the fence here, if majority of community prefers units to be super responsive which will result in some spells being harder to use I don't mind. When it comes to mass and formation disruption - I actually like it. I don't see it as a bug, I see it as an indirect buff to heavy cavalry/chariots, which were absolutely useless in WH2 unless you played Bretonnia and even then cavalry could still underperform compared to other unit types. The duality of Total War community really shows here: when cav is bad community calls for buffs, when it's finally decent, community want it to be nerfed to the ground. Let's hope CA will find good middle ground here.BugsApart from some minor graphical glitches that happen in every game ever, I've only found 3 bugs, one of them being upkeep bug, I didn't noticed it till my 3rd playthrough though, Slaaneesh devotee bug, wich is a minor one because at the end of the campaign you'll have more devotees than you can spend and the movement bug, it's not game breaking it's actually beneficial glitch? Your movement stances should cost % of movement, but in reality they cost points, I kinda wish it stayed that way. I've also read some overzelous comments that some mechanics don't work properly but more often than not those people are not aware that UI of those mechanics only updates at the start of the next turn. That is definetly lazy coding, UI should update in the same turn, not one turn after something happened.OutroIs the game enjoyable? Yes it is, as long as you are willing to be pulled out of your sandbox comfort zone and try out faster paced campaign with higher stakes. But what if you are entirely new to the franchise? Should you buy it then? The Total War community loves to say that you shouldn't bother with WH3 right now and play WH2 instead, but they always forget that Total War games have steep learning curve, WH2 doesn't have any proper tutorial that will explain the game properly, on the other hand WH3 does have it and it's very good introduction to the mechanics, so the answer is: probably yes, maybe wait for the patch on 5th April, just in case, better yet you can try it relatively cheap on Microsoft gamepass to be 100% sure. The game isn't as atrocious as people like to say, for me it's solid 8/10. Paradoxically, people new to the franchise might have more fun than Total War veterans.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the many, many bugs and flaws that followed Total War: Warhammer III at its release, the result after a full year of release is amazing, and already packed with many, many mods that are ripe with content. The world map; the STRATEGY part of the game is massive.But, personally, the game lacks 'tactical depth' and, in battles, quality of life improvements. For example, in terms of QoL, ranged units will not "reload"; this doesn't just include the average musketeer or archer, but also siege weaponry, and the like. It has been remedied by mods; but this is a detail in basically every other total war title.Additionally, tactics in this game rely entirely upon the tiers of your units, as well as what faction you are; not what your units actually are. If I wanted to provide an example; Empire reiksguard are useful up until turn 40. Then you may aswell forget about them. They are a defensive cavalry; a.. defensive shock cavalry? Their primary use is to flank the enemy and cycle charge, however once the enemy is able to afford proper armies there is no reason to spend the money on them, and instead buy, for example, a wizard.Many units in this game suffer in their roles as they rely on the enemy not being strong in order to even try to kill them. Ranged units are a joke; not in a bad way, they can obliterate your army before your melee units even have a chance of getting to them, and they only run out of ammunition after a long, long time of consistent fire.So why do I recommend it? Because it's still a fantastic game with hours of content worth, and my 200 hours only consists of playing 3 factions (Tomb Kings, Chaos and Empire). In the end, I will still continue to play it as it is legitimately fun regardless. But, definitely if you want to play Immortal Empires, pick the game up. You can start right away playing major Chaos entities, or one of the 2 most uhh.. "unfulfilling" Order factions in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Following patch 2.1.1This review is concentrating on Immortal Empires.  Much has already been said about the Chaos Rift campaign, so I won't be going into any detail on why I think that's poor, beyond saying these are the main reasons:- removing player agency from timings (unlike Vortex from TW:W2),- adding completely random elements (Tzeench realm), and- adding tedious mechanics (the rifts themselves).Overall, I remain disappointed in TW:W3.  If this game were created in a vacuum, then I'm sure most people would have been blown away with how much is packed in.  However, it is not.  Strange design choices were made producing TW:W3.  I'm not convinced anyone was screaming out for things to be redesigned from the ground up.  The battle-space was redone and still has issues.  The economy has been redone for W3 factions, weakening economy focused factions (HE, DE).  Winds of magic was completely redesigned, severely weakening magic focused factions from W2 (mainly VC).  The list goes on.Fair play to the DLC team that had to smash TW:W2 into TW:W3.  They've done a fantastic job, but there's only so much they could do here to make W2 factions viable.  Even here, some decisions make no sense.  Why rework the DE slave mechanic completely?  Was it possible to "cheese" the DE economy?  Yes.  However, it required significant micromanagement, so maximum effort was needed for maximum reward.  In a predominantly single-player game, I don't see why things like this couldn't be tweaked without blowing them up completely and leaving an uninteresting husk of a mechanic behind.Then there's confederations.  Why are confederations almost impossible for all the factions that relied on diplo-annexation?  Part of the fun of TW:W2 was in gathering the collection of legendary lords.  The effect this has on the IE campaign is more insidious though.  With AI factions also unable to confederate there's no "final boss" in a campaign.  By trying to artificially balance everything, once you get into mid-game, it's completely over.  As an example, at turn 70 playing as Reikland.  In ME, I still have major threats in the Dark Elves, Greenskins and Dwarfs - all ahead of me in power rankings.  In IE, I can't see any faction rising up as a threat.  The challenge has been removed from the game.Confederations hamstring the AI, along with other changes that were made when CA inexplicably rebuilt the whole game.  The AI has been made far too passive.  They don't build large standing armies, meaning they won't try and drive you away.  They will hole-up and hide in settlements, because they don't have the on-field manpower to drive you off.  The only threat is the tedium of chunking through yet more small settlement battles _shudder_.All-in-all, it feels like CA have removed much of the fun from the game.  Rather than trying to balance things, they have gone with nerfing them into the ground so they are no longer viable.  Player agency/choice has been removed from the game in exactly the same way it was removed from the base campaigns (Vortex and Chaos Rifts).The only saving grace is the vast improvements in campaign multiplayer.  Having up to 8 concurrent players (though I wouldn't go above 4 if I were you) definitely improves matters, but I have the sneaking suspicion I will return to TW:W2 for single-player and leave TW:W3 for multiplayer games.Can a lot of this be fixed?  Sure, over time.  However, CA have signalled heavily with recent design choices that the fun factor of the game isn't important to them.  Even if that mindset were to change, it would likely take years for them to get IE to the stage that it felt as fun as ME (to me at least :)).tl;dr: Is TW:W3 bad?  No, not at all.  There is still fun to be had with the game.  IMHO it's just not as good as TW:W2 at this point, so I cannot recommend the game.  If you haven't got TW:W2 and played it to death already, get and play that :)

_childDocuments_.review: Usually, I prefer to review games on Steam when I have played them long enough to consider being somewhat knowledgeable about them (There isn't any exact number of hours I should play through, so for the sake of this review, I'd say something like 150-200 hours), but this case is different. This is something I've been outraged about for quite some time, because Warhammer III actually is a decent game, but I have to leave a negative review due to:- The disastrous 2022 launch, consisting of a large amount of bugs. The Realms of Chaos campaign, which was the default campaign at the time, is arguably the worst campaign CA has ever created for a Total War game. Not even the Vortex campaign from Warhammer II comes close to being as bad as the Realms of Chaos. Painfully uninteresting, requiring the player to spend too much time to finish the campaign's goal, which is to defeat Be'lakor, and even then I wasn't able to achieve this goal due to boredom. In fact, when Immortal Empires were released, I instantly forgot about the Realms of Chaos and never came back to play them ever again.- CA's DLC pricing policy. We get it - inflation is going rampant and people are trying to use whatever they can to achieve financial stability. This doesn't excuse the fact how Shadows of Change, a Legendary Lord pack, costs a whopping 25 dollars/euros (ignore the fact that it's at a -10% discount on Steam Store, I'd say it isn't worth pre-ordering) for the amount of content it brings. Sure, Forge of Chaos Dwarfs was expensive as well, but for its price, we got something big - a new, highly anticipated race for the game. The contents of Shadows of Change don't justify its high price and unless CA delivers a high-quality product, I won't even consider getting this DLC at a discount.- CA's handling of the situation mentioned above. This is a terrible statement in regards to the whole situation. There is no point which justifies CA's decision to charge such amount of money for the DLC; all that we get is something along the lines of "the prices had to go higher, lol, get over it". What I want to note is the fact how, at the end of the statement, it is mentioned that individual team members are being harrassed by the community. Is this supposed to have the community instantly turn into more empathetic towards CA? We get it - harrassment is bad, we shouldn't do it. But do we really have to resort to such low blows? Is this supposed to nullify any criticism? If the statement about harrassment is false, however, it paints CA in an even worse light than before, with them using despicable, manipulative tactics just to gain back the community's favor.It pains me to see the course CA has taken recently as I've played Total War games for over 15 years, starting with Rome: Total War and I'm quite passionate about this franchise. To see that a series I've been growing up with and I've considered as one of my beloved series suddenly gets butchered like this is most unfortunate. I hope CA changes its course of action, but honestly, I'm skeptical that it will eventually happen.

_childDocuments_.review: The ultimate Total Warhammer experience as the conclusion of a trilogy. This game gives a fantastic approach to major conflicts with large troop counts in a fantasy setting. Monstrous creatures, artillery pieces, firing lines, riders of all types, a multitude of factions and factions within factions, etc... The game can be broken down into 2 aspects:- The official Realms Of Chaos story experience is dedicated to the 3rd game itself. This part of the game gave me a mixed feeling as the baked in factions to actual Total Warhammer 3 are not very fun in my opinion to try the story campaign. However the DLC races as of this writing (April 2023) of the Ogres, Warriors of Chaos, and Chaos Dwarves can be a bit more fun for the RoC campaign (Chaos Dwarves in particular). The base factions have to race to collect souls and it turns into a bit of a whack-a-mole game. Ogres have the same thing, Warriors of Chaos are working with Black Fortresses and a different goal, Chaos Dwarves are running a drill to pierce into the realm of their god and it is much more fun than collecting soul pieces.-Immortal Empires is where the game truly shines as it combines the content of the past 2 games into a massive sandbox experience. Immortal Empires now is natively supported in just Total Warhammer 3 wherein you used to have to own TW1 and TW2. To make it brief you can play any races you own in the Immortal Empires map. If you own TW1 you can play TW1 races as well or any DLC you own you can play those races from the relevant game. If you are a completionist you can buy everything to have access to all races/factions in the game to choose from. This is a truly staggeringly large amount of content with loads of replayability.Total Warhammer 3 itself offers loads of quality of life improvements over the previous games and if you play TW3 it is very hard to go  back to TW1 or TW2 given how different the UIs are.This is a great game to play with friends as well as you can play Immortal Empires with up to 8 other players if you desire with a simultaneous or traditional turn based approach depending on which you prefer. (If you have more than 3 players I would recommend traditional turn based to cut down on lag and possible desyncs when too many people are acting at the same time).Overall a fantastic game that is showing to have very long legs as the developers are very active on bug reporting forums and planning of future content.A perfect end to the trilogy which I am sure people will be playing for years to come as the replayability is sky high with all the factions involved in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: As a dedicated fan of both the Civilization series and the Warhammer universe, diving into Total War: Warhammer 3 has been nothing short of a spectacular experience. This game seamlessly combines the intricate strategy mechanics I cherish from Civilization with the rich, immersive world of Warhammer.        The depth of strategy in Total War: Warhammer 3 is exceptional. The turn-based campaign map and real-time battles provide a perfect blend of tactical planning and dynamic combat. The game’s expanded roster of factions and legendary lords adds layers of complexity and replayability. Each faction feels distinct, not just in terms of their units and abilities but also in how they interact with the campaign’s overarching narrative.          The attention to detail in the Warhammer setting is astounding. The developers have managed to capture the essence of the lore and translate it into engaging gameplay. Whether you’re delving into the intricacies of the Chaos Realms or managing the geopolitical landscape of the Old World, the game does an impressive job of making each decision feel consequential.        Graphically, Total War: Warhammer 3 is a visual treat. The diverse environments—from the frozen wastes of the north to the lush jungles of the south—are rendered with stunning detail. The battles are exhilarating, with a level of scale and spectacle that truly does justice to the Warhammer fantasy. For fans of Civilization, the strategic depth and management aspects of Total War: Warhammer 3 will feel familiar yet refreshingly different. The game’s blend of strategic empire-building with real-time tactical combat offers a unique and compelling experience. The incorporation of Warhammer’s rich lore and factions adds a new layer of excitement to the strategic planning that I’ve always enjoyed.Overall, Total War: Warhammer 3 is a triumph for fans of both the Total War series and the Warhammer franchise. It offers a deeply engaging strategy experience wrapped in a visually stunning and lore-rich package. If you appreciate complex strategy games and the epic fantasy world of Warhammer, this game is a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played over 500 hours of this game, hundreds more in WH2, and I have played Total War games since the original Shogun came out. The reason I say all this is because I want to make it clear that I am not a recent arrival to Creative Assembly games, that I am familiar with their pre and post launch dramas and triumphs, and that I am definitely not some troll who smelled the gasoline and hopped over to add to the fire.All that said, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to prospective buyers in its current state.Why, you ask?Picture this: Total War Warhammer 2, despite having trip-ups here and there, was the pinnacle of CA's post launch support and DLC content. They had a system, a solid pipeline, and (mostly) accurate roadmaps that told us what we would get and the general timeframe of when it would happen. The DLCs followed the same kind of formula and they worked alongside free patches to update factions and mechanics that needed extra attention. Along with this, they made sure the game was running without any gamebreaking bugs for long.As the game winded down and we got closer to Warhammer 3's release, it was made clear there was a division of labor between the DLC Team that maintains the previous game(s) and the "A" team that actually builds the new games, expands the engine and all that jazz. Skipping ahead, Warhammer 3 had a very rocky launch with a lot of bugs (almost expected at this point since every release since Rome 2 has been especially rough), an unsatisfying single player campaign with Realms of Chaos mechanics being particularly criticized, and worst of all some very inconsistent communication from the developers concerning roadmaps to fixes and new content.But most everyone had faith that once the "A" team was finally pulled off the project to go do something else, that "B" team, the real stars that proved their salt with Warhammer 2, could get things back on track.Not to denigrate the DLC team's work too much during their time with TWW3, but that simply has not happened. Which leads me to believe that something happened in-between; the DLC team was downsized further, less attention in general was paid to Warhammer 3's post launch content schedule, the A team just screwed up so hard the DLC team still hasn't caught up, or something else entirely. I don't know, and I don't want to speculate too hard on stuff beyond the scope of a steam review.What matters is, in the timeline since release, we haven't gotten anywhere near the level of attention of bug fixes, game mechanic updates and tweaks, roadmaps and developer communiques, and other "content" as TWW2 did. Is the game playable? Sure. Is it fun sometimes? Yes. Is it worth the price? No.And the last thing to mention, and perhaps why I was inspired to write a review when I never write reviews, is the drastically increased DLC prices and what, in my eyes, appears to be a much lower quality product that does not justify the price tag. Not only has it been to the effect of pulling teeth just to get any kind of news on fresh content, but when roadmaps are given, they were never stuck to which has only led to more discontent. And when they finally released something substantial as the Chaos Dwarfs DLC, people balked at this $25 price tag. But people swallowed that pill, bitterly need I add, because it was an entirely new faction with new mechanics AND because inflation is a thing and people figured prices would rise eventually, though to this degree is still rough to see and accept.But now with the Shadows of Change DLC, they kept the $25 price tag but instead of adding a new faction, they are just adding some new lords and units, and not many might I add. This content isn't any different in scope to TWW2 DLCs of the same formula, and it just isn't justifiable with that insane price jump, "inflation" or no. Not to mention again how long and infrequent the DLC release patterns are in comparison to previous titles; it just shows a lack of organization and care to the post-launch of this game. The price tag, and the Chief Production Officer's out-of-touch response to backlash, is just the final nail in the coffin. Zero transparency.If you are going to say the price to run your studio and support these games has gone up, then you have to prove the value of what you are currently working on is worth further support from consumers. Ignoring the value of the DLC by itself, the actual handling of TWW3 since launch has been, in a word, inadequate. This DLC debacle just pushes this "Not Recommended" review further. I feel for the developers having to work in a clearly mismanaged studio, but I can't support that kind of treatment of the otherwise loyal consumer.

_childDocuments_.review: So I cannot fully recommend this game at the moment as it is currently a little under cooked. Which is why despite this review being positive, it comes with a caveat. There are still a large amount of bugs in the game and the patches released have come with their own specific issues. If you are new to this specific series I would recommend that you start with the second one. Since it is currently much more stable, easier to run on lower quality computers, and all the content in that game and the one before it carry over to this game. This means that any character you have access in the previous games will be available when the immortal empires update is released. Third the overall campaign of this game is a bit tedious to say the least. So if you want to get the gist of this game and don't want to deal with the issues it has at the moment, then the second one is a safe bet. However, there are a few things that this game does currently have going for it that a lot of the negative reviews (while completely correct in terms of issue accuracy) don't seem to be factoring in. For one this game is one of the most ambitious projects that I have seen in a while. This coming autumn there is going to be not only a full rework and accompanying DLC for the warriors of chaos (which don't suffer from the campaign's tedium), but an update/beta called the immortal empires. Which is going to feature the entire Warhammer Fantasy world as the campaign map. Making it easily one of the largest and most complex 4X/RTS games on steam.Which is why despite how bad some of the bugs are it kind of gets a pass from me. As I personally would never expect a project of this games scale and size to come out completely squeaky clean. This game is going to have bugs for a while until the development team at CA  can kind of stabilize everything. Which I genuinely believe they will do since all the prior games/DLC had tons of issues and bugs and gradually got fixed as time went on. For example the beast men were virtually half built in the first game and fully overhauled in the second one. This shows that the developers at CA clearly have their eyes on their community and are actually listening.  In addition as a Warhammer game this is one of the only games that fully features representation from all four chaos gods. With each chaos god functioning as you would expect with distinct and individual mechanics. For example I literally cannot think of any other game that fully features slannesh units in all their glorious depravity. Finally this game, assuming CA follows suit and continues supporting it, will likely be seeing new content and features throughout the next 4-5 years.  Overall I love this game so far and I think this has the potential to be an amazing masterpiece of a game. However Rome wasn't built in a day and this game still needs some building. Which is why this is a great game to either buy on sale or preferably later once everything is fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: There are two major components of Total War: Warhammer III The Campaign and Battles. The soul of the game is its battles. It is the entire point of the game: to fight. Without it, what is the point? This is the heart of the issue. The campaign offers cute little mechanics to make the experience of coloring the map "interesting." We can reduce it down to being a boring turn-based game with the rare RTS battle. TLDR: Campaign is drudgery and the multiplayer experience is lackluster and doesn't attract players' attention. There's no chat function. In the campaign enemy ai will only engage if it believes it will win. The player when engaging the ai can gauge this themselves, however they too will know if they will win or not. The problem is that majority of fights are auto-resolved in the campaign. Some fights have to be fought, but when the ai is piloting the enemy, it can be abused and beaten. If you have friend(s) with you in a campaign, they can take control of the enemy and make a fight fun but also make your life harder. It can result in the player not having an army if they are defeated thus putting their cities at risk. Essentially knocking them out of the game. A player losing their whole army is sometimes enough to make them want to quit out because of the number of turns it takes to get a new army out. Turns when you have friends in a campaign that makes it take longer, and the campaign becomes a waiting game. The campaign is a terrible way to experience battles in the game. It's rare that fights are balanced and fun. Playing with friends makes getting any progress difficult. Even the chance to fight battles comes into conflict with knocking friends out of the game if they lose their army. Not to mention how irritating it is when players perform actions that freeze everybody else when it usually results in a auto-resolve. The campaign does a lot to make the game not fun. There's no option to choose which of the maps you want to play. Whether that's the entire playable world, the old world, the eye of the vortex, or the realms of chaos. Money is difficult to produce to fund multiple armies to protect and attack. The other part of the game, the multiplayer battles lacks player population. It's a ghost town. I do not understand the allergy players have to the multiplayer aspect of the game. Why trudge through a campaign, thirty or whatever turns (this can take upwards of 3 hours) to get access to all your factions units when you can expedite it and just make your army in a menu and fight with your friends?  The multiplayer netcode can be hellish. Units walking in molasses kind of slow. It is abominable.
