_childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is a first-person exploration game with platforming elements. It’s a strange and trippy experience, but surprisingly fun.There’s not much of a story. You play as Ghost, an aspiring graffiti tagger, who wakes up in a small shipping container (which acts as your base/home). After a short tutorial, you’re free to explore a small open world—a polluted island filled with shipping containers and various industrial buildings, surrounded by sludge. The vibe is bizarre, with characters dressed in “gangsta-style” attire, plus some odd hybrid or animal-like characters. Nearly everyone you meet is rude or weird.Tagging is one of the core mechanics of the game, with 100 preset locations to vandalize. Figuring out how to reach these hard-to-access spots is part of the fun, as many are in tricky, high-up places. The game has three different endings, though only one involves tagging all 100 spots.While exploring, you can interact with various items—eating shrooms and slugs, drinking soda (or maybe alcohol?), and smoking cigarettes. As you progress, you’ll find helpful tools like a glider and a teleportation device, which make getting around the island easier. The controls are generally okay but can feel imprecise at times.The UI is designed like a computer desktop where you can install apps, complete with annoying pop-ups. There’s even a surprisingly fun mini-game included. I noticed after two hours that I hadn’t unlocked any achievements, but once I checked the to-do list on the computer, they began unlocking. The list acts as a helpful guide, providing direction with goals and challenges since the game lacks a structured story or quests.While the game’s strange music and art style didn’t fully appeal to me, they fit well with the overall atmosphere. There’s also a default VHS-style graphic setting, which adds a grainy, distorted look/filter. I preferred turning it off for a cleaner appearance.It’s a short game, but since it was given away for free in March 2023, I can't really complain.
_childDocuments_.name: SLUDGE LIFE

_childDocuments_.review: I think my attempt at writing a review of Sludge Life will be a failed one. If nothing else, this is a game unlike any other I've played, and it defies description at every turn. Not quite a walking sim, not quite a sandbox, with minimal gameplay or story to speak of, Sludge Life follows the player character Ghost, a tagger on a mission to graffiti all of an island for reasons unknown. The game lasts all of two hours, which are spent tagging walls, urinating in random places, and eating as many banana slugs as you can find while you explore a small open world filled with many characters, all of whom offer very few, but very unique lines of dialogue. The game features minor parkour, but the controls feel almost as irreverent as the game itself, with slippery movement that gives the impression that Ghost doesn't quite understand how their own body works. The game has a bright and colorful palette, with clashing tones and a low-key soundtrack that make Sludge Life feel like it was put together by someone on copious amounts of drugs after they strolled through a garbage plant. For all of its short runtime, Sludge Life offers an overwhelming, indescribable, and all-around absurd experience that I believe is worth trying at least once. I don't think this game is good or bad - it completely and utterly denies being classified in such an objective manner. However, I appreciated it enough to give Sludge Life a 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: SLUDGE LIFE

_childDocuments_.review: The presentation of the game is top-notch. One of my personal favorite presentations of any game probably, incorporating a mix of a colorful palette with well-done 3D assets. It just looks fantastic. The music is also great even if it doesn't feature too much throughout your playthrough.The game can be beaten in 4 hours, which is perfect because I feel that the simplistic gameplay would get tiring if it goes any longer. It's essentially a collect-a-thon where you try to tag up designated tagging spots within a tiny but reasonably filled map. Movement is just WASD and jump, so traversing the map can get kinda dull until you get some gadgets. The main draw of the game for me and what kept me playing is just seeing all the wacky stuff and quirky people you'd encounter as you try to collect everything.I enjoyed my time with the game. There's a Sludge Life 2 that I haven't played yet and I would love to see how that game fleshes out the mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is a great open world collectathon, getting tags and gliding around the highly expansive world is an overjoy to play in. For starters, the aesthetic is gorgeous. The mix with pixel walls and 3d buildings fit the mold for the game’s experience and attitude. There are also so many places to go, like Gen Pop or any of the stackers. There are also a lot of funny details in the backgrounds, like the massive baby near Gen Pop, or the chef that cut his hand open at the Glug Tower. Overall, the aesthetic of this game is one of the best I've seen in a video game. Gameplay however, isn’t as great as the inventive backgrounds. The whole point of the game is to spray paint your logo on every surface, along with many other things. At first, this is very fun and finding new sprays can be rewarding. But when you have got to the last few sprays, not using the vandal's eyes, it could be very tiresome and boring. Don’t get me wrong, there is a lot more than sprays in Sludge Life. You can find all of the items, smoke some ciggys you find around, and play other games in the control panel found around the world. Sadly, the game is very short, around two hours to get one ending and four to 100% the game. But in conclusion, Sludge Life is an atmospheric collectathon, with a beautiful world, and lots of things to do, however it does it in a short time frame.

_childDocuments_.review: The game strays away from other genre's but has strong vibes to things you've seen before, whether Jazzpunk, AngerFoot etc. 100% it yesterday and I have to say it's absolutely worth it while it's free.The game has a sensation as if you walked out of the era of MTV & Adult Swim from the 2000's. You tag along with a few pals and when you earn enough respect from the community you make collab tags with them, mix both your brand and their brand on a billboard. Go ahead and grab it while it's free! Take over The Sludge while it's still crumbling apart.To anyone whose having issues with the achievements, here's the errors I've encountered along the journey.- The achievements are programmed in with Steam, if you try making a shortcut (aka right clicking the icon to save it on your Windows bar) it won't give achievements. You have to open it only in steam.(Semi-Spoiler)- If you happen to find a helpful pair of an old legend's eyes on your journey, sometimes it'll get stuck looking at where a character used to be, like if you met a buddy on a rooftop and walk away it'll notify you that a tagger wants to collab with you if your rep is high enough. But the eyes might stay pinpointed and won't leave unless you reset the game.Personal thank you to the developers of the game for making this, and being the first game I ever achieved 100% on.Side question for Terri, what inspired you to make this style of art? Was there anything in particular like Getter's Music videos? MTV? What genre of art was your references?

_childDocuments_.review: First heard about this back when it was free for a while on EGS and got it there but couldn't make myself to just sit down and play it. However when the same case happens on here as a little promotion for the upcoming second game, said "Why not?" so make that as you wish. Despite almost all of the gameplay mechanincs being a bit janky and inconsistent, it still manages to be fun. Unique art style, low poly-cell shaded graphical style and the overall absurd world and the story which is just as weird end up making the game a charming one. I also can't make myself remember the last time when a game became actually more fun/entertaining while trying to go for %100 completion (AKA open world/collectathon done right), great job on that. _childDocuments_.review: definitely get this game if the atmosphere captured in the screenshots even mildly piques your interest because the game does an even better job of immersing you into that world through its engrossing LSD fever dream art style dizzied by the VHS-quality HHBF distorted positional in-world music crackling out of boomboxes cleverly placed all over a no-loading-screen open world as you parkour your way to leave your Ghost logo on a crazy overhang that makes other taggers think "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Ghost, you animal!". I really want to thank the devs for doing great job filling up the world and making it interesting. There's a whole culture of taggers in the midst of a workplace strike in a city flooded with sludge. You meet other taggers who when you get to their location you'll find them with their own theme song and tags which you'll also see around the city.In terms of vibe, it atmospherically feels like Happy's Humble Burger Farm with that hazy VHS style filter and location dynamic music. There are no boundaries, so you can go wherever you want to get those walls tagged and those toilets urinated. Yes, urinated. This game captures the early-to-mid 2000s South Park and Postal feel and humor. There's good worldbuilding in it too, lots of stories, events, and culture that you don't really find out much about but which you keep getting glimpses into by talking to other people you meet.In terms of gameplay, it's a parkour platformer that feels slippery when going up a ledge. The game won me over moreso because of the atmosphere and the visuals than the game mechanics, and that's not something that's easy for a dev to do without turning it into a walking simulator. But again, the focus is definitely on the art, the culture of Sludge City, and the source of fresh green eye-cucumbers for the CEO.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge, a word that resonates with a sense of stagnation, filth, and decay. Its very utterance conjures images of a viscous, dark substance oozing through the crevices of our society, polluting our minds and suffocating our progress. Whether it be in the physical or metaphorical sense, sludge represents the obstacles that hinder our growth and hinder the development of a better world.In the realm of environmental concerns, sludge takes on a tangible form. It is the muck and mire that accumulates in our rivers and streams, the remnants of our industrial endeavors. It is the result of heedless consumption, where waste is irresponsibly discarded and left to fester. The sludge not only threatens the delicate balance of aquatic ecosystems but also seeps into the groundwater, poisoning the very source of life. It serves as a reminder of our shortsightedness and the consequences of our actions.Metaphorically, sludge permeates through various aspects of our lives. It represents the mental and emotional baggage that weighs us down, inhibiting our ability to progress and thrive. Sludge can be found in the form of societal norms and prejudices that hinder progress and limit the potential of individuals. It can be seen in the bureaucratic red tape that stifles innovation and hampers the implementation of necessary reforms. Sludge is the complacency and inertia that prevent us from addressing pressing issues, leaving us stuck in a perpetual cycle of inaction.Sludge can also be found in our personal lives. It is the clutter that accumulates in our homes, filling our spaces with unnecessary objects and stifling our sense of tranquility. It is the toxic relationships that drain our energy and leave us feeling trapped. Sludge is the self-doubt and negative thoughts that hold us back from pursuing our dreams and reaching our full potential. It is the fear and uncertainty that paralyze us, preventing us from taking risks and embracing change.The effects of sludge are far-reaching and pervasive. They can be seen in the deterioration of our physical and mental well-being, the degradation of our environment, and the stagnation of our collective progress. However, it is essential to recognize that sludge is not an insurmountable obstacle. Just as sludge accumulates gradually over time, it can also be slowly eradicated through conscious effort and collective action.To combat environmental sludge, we must adopt sustainable practices and advocate for responsible waste management. We must invest in renewable energy sources and reduce our reliance on fossil fuels. Additionally, we must hold corporations accountable for their actions and push for stricter regulations to prevent further environmental degradation.Addressing societal and personal sludge requires introspection and a willingness to challenge the status quo. It necessitates dismantling oppressive systems and embracing diversity and inclusivity. It demands fostering a culture of innovation and empowering individuals to overcome self-doubt and pursue their aspirations. It requires creating support systems that encourage personal growth and wellbeing.In conclusion, sludge represents the obstacles that impede progress and hinder our ability to create a better world. Whether it manifests in the physical form of environmental pollution or the metaphorical form of societal and personal barriers, sludge reminds us of the consequences of our actions and the urgent need for change. By recognizing the existence of sludge and taking proactive steps to eliminate it, we can pave the way for a brighter and more promising future.

_childDocuments_.review: To the guy who sent the clown award: Thanks! But your wife's boyfriend still owes me $20- If you tend to gravitate towards visually impressive games that sell themselves on eye candy and impressive visuals, you'll wind up bouncing right off of Sludge Life. It's purposefully grimy and smoggy, likely to reflect the anti-capitalist counterculture bent of the narrative- When I say "smog", I mean "LA in the 90s" levels of smog. The concept of draw distance will become a distant memory after you load into the hazy open world of Sludge Life. It's like a flashback to Silent Hill fog- In addition to the omnipresent cloud of industrial fumes, there's an aggressive VHS-style overlay that adds yet another bit of visual distortion to the experience. In principle, I understand that the intent in most games like this is to make them feel more "retro", but I don't know how much scan lines actually make me feel nostalgic. I'll chalk it up to "artistic choice", but honestly, the game could have done without them- The music is perfectly inline with the visuals. doseone's alternative hip-hop stylings capably underpin the parkour action with synthesizers and Reagan-era samples. The artistic unity of the audio and visuals is impressive and probably the game's greatest strength- If you didn't expect a game like this to have much of a story, congratulations, because you're absolutely correct. You play as Ghost, a tagger (graffiti artist) in Ciggy City, a town that's more or less entirely run by the Glug Corporation. In addition to manufacturing all of the products available for purchase in town, Glug and its many subsidiaries also appear to control the police, schools, and all other services. The company's quest for profit has left Ciggy City a wasteland, with the ocean already flooding the entirety of the town while many of its citizens and workers are left to populate stacked shipping containers, tents, building crevices and other ad hoc living situations- As Ghost, you have no real stated objective. The main thing you're left to do is explore the town and plop graffiti on designated tag spots- The vibes are as chill as can be. There are no stakes. Dying has no consequences. The music is relaxing. There's plenty of humor- On that last point, Sludge Life employs an unfortunate amount of "lel randem" comedy, but without the level of try-hard spark that leads to a lot of inward cringing and eye rolling. Instead, it's a bit more carefree and lackadaisical its approach. If you can envision a game where all the dialogue is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Sludge Life would be that. When it lands, it can be pretty humorous, at least- To sum it all up, there's some interesting world building going on here, but without much to do within the world, it feels like a waste of potential- Due to the heavy emphasis on vertical exploration, parkour is the predominant gameplay mechanic you'll be experiencing. It feels like a lot of notes were taken from first-person "schmoovement" games like Lovely Planet, Cyber Hook, or SEUM, then subequently crumpled up and thrown in the trash. Without any pressing need to move quickly, the speed and free flowing aspects of those games are binned. What you're left with is sort of a mess- You can't see your feet, so you'll fall off narrow platforms and girders constantly if you try to go to fast. Jumping feels awkward owing to the first-person perspective, and how close you need to be to a ledge to mantle up it is something that I failed to get a feel for even by the end of my playthrough. Some walls are climbable through repeatedly jumping at them, but it's not clear which ones qualify. Altogether, the platforming feels janky and frustrating. The engine feels like is constantly at odds with the mechanics that were programmed into it- Unlike most platformers that have the sprint controls bound to a left stick click, that action merely makes you fart in Sludge Life. While funny, it doesn't actually boost your movement speed at all- The items you find do offer some respite from the horrible platforming. The Glider can help you soar from rooftop to (slightly lower) rooftop, and the Warper allows you to set a custom teleport point. About to attempt a tricky jump or need to cross a narrow platform? The warper can quickly return you to the start so you can try again after you almost inevitably fall to your death. You'll also come across warp stations that can help you quickly navigate between the small open world's major areas- Finding these items and warp points is helpful, but your main goal is to tag billboards, buildings, statues, and other surfaces you'll stumble across. The Camera item can help you spot these tag spots in the early game, but you'll later find another item, the Vandal Eyes (ha), which can provide additional guidance. You may also notice "Blue Caps", hallucinogenic mushrooms that allow you to leave your body and fly around for a short period of time before you rubberband back to your body and vomit all over what's directly in front of you. These are pretty helpful for scoping out hard-to-reach tag locations- Some graffiti you'll be making are collabs with other taggers scattered around the city. You'll have to up your cred by tagging a set number of locations before working with them, though- There are also apps that you can find for your laptop (menu screen), but these primarily seem to help with tracking achievements- From what I understand, there are three different endings: A "good" one, a "bad" one, and a "weird" one. The weird ending requires tagging all the locations, which I did not do, so I can't speak to it; however, it's safe to say that in a game like this, the good and bad endings are fairly weird too- I don't know that I'll replay it. I'm not sure I even want to go back and finish up the achievements. The gameplay just isn't fun enough to motivate any sort of revisit- Well, it's yet another game with really good audiovisual presentation and worldbuilding but with dogwater gameplay. Your enjoyment is wholly dependent on how much you value you assign to its strengths. As an exploration-focused platformer, I wouldn't recommend it, but as a piece of interactive art, it's at least interesting- I played through the whole thing on the Steam Deck, but I think I'd suggest playing with a mouse/keyboard setup. It ran very well and without bugs, but the frustrating platforming would have been less so with WASD controls instead of the analogue stick. If you like the music and artstyle, maybe throw it on your wishlist and wait for a steep discount. If you're looking for meaningful exploration or fun parkour, though, you're bound to wind up a little disappointed. I found the world interesting enough that I'll be checking out the rest of the series down the road, but more out of curiosity than enthusiasm

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game for free. Initially, I liked the vibe of the game, the odd characters you meet and the weird world Sludge Life is set in, but the vibe fades very quickly. The game apparently has endings, but try as I might, I did not find a way to end the game. Some objects you find and can use in the game don't seem to have a deeper meaning and it seems the main goal is to tag every spot - which is fun at first, but that too gets annoying really quickly. The biggest problem is the games lack of movement options. No double jump, no running and while you can heave yourself up ledges, it only seems to work half the time. You get a glider eventually, but it is very awkward to use and not very useful.As a game to just explore and spend a weird hour or two in, I think Sludge Life is fine (and it has a cool soundtrack), but the goal isn't very clear-cut, movement is a pain, there are a few hidden or locked areas I have no idea how to get into (with no hints) and the aesthetic of the game, it being a weird sewery dump, is only interesting for a short time. It also emphasizes how "random" it is all the time, as nothing seems to really have a point to it. That's charming in games like Crypt Worlds, but not here. Nothing you do really has a point to it, and I know that is the vibe the game is going for, but it is also kind of a waste of the thematic and aesthetic. There COULD be something cool going on here, but playing the game is like, well, like trudging through sludge. Fitting.Getting all achievements would also be a pain as some of them seem really annoying (like eating all sludges in one session). Maybe these things will be improved in a sequel, because I feel like this game could have been interesting, if it was fleshed out a bit more. And for what it is, 14.99 is way too high of a price if you decide to buy it - that is almost Highway Robbery for how little there is to do.

_childDocuments_.review: So this is a super weird game. I can see how some people might like this game and some might not, but I thought it was a blast. About 3-ish hours in I found the way 'out,' but I know I'm going to be going back to try to hit all the tag points and stuff like that. It's just plain FUN to play, even if it feels like you're mostly just goofing off.So what's the point? I have no idea. I guess you're some kind of graffiti artist living in this world of sludge owned by some greedy evil corporation. The ground is sludge, everything is haphazardly thrown together, everyone is grumbly and grumpy, and the entire place is cluttered beyond belief. You walk around. You talk to people. You find secret entrances, climb things, meet strange people, find bizarre things you weren't expecting, and paint your graffiti everywhere. Eventually you find an escape pod and take off, and credits roll.Now, you may be thinking to yourself, "That doesn't sound like a normal game where there's a point or a goal. It sounds like you're just wandering around doing random stuff." And.. you know.. that's pretty much the case. Had I consulted a walkthrough guide, I probably could've beat this game in no time. But the world was just FUN to interact with, so I had no desire at all to consult a guide. I had a lot more fun just wandering around, exploring, finding. Yes, this is one of those worlds where you actually WANT to probe every little corner to find what may be hiding - whether giant turds, cats with two buttholes, enormous sleeping babies, bored employees or anything else. You'll be heading into a room expecting more garbage and disarray, and all of a sudden, think, "WHAT!? What is THAT!?"I seriously enjoyed the careless, mindless gameplay. When you finish using an item, you casually toss it onto the ground. It's always THERE for you to use, somehow.. but for example, you finish using the camera, so you just toss it aside. That's the tone of the entire game - very little in the way of consequences (besides dying if you plummet from an enormous height), very little that's serious, and very little "need" to make any progress if you don't want. (And you know what I mean, where some games you feel compelled to continue ever onward.. In this game you're literally just kinda bumming around doing stuff.)You can pee, fart, spit, jump, crouch, climb, fall, glide, teleport, all kinds of random stuff.I really don't know what else to say about this game. If you're expecting an intense experience, or a very clear and engaging story, or well-defined goals, or anything like that, this isn't that. Mainly just explore, have fun, do stuff, find secrets, and find your way out. That's about it.That being said I had a great time. The characters are unforgettable. The atmosphere is gritty and gross. It's the VIBE you play this game for.Graphics fit the theme and are pretty decent. I've read about some people getting motion sickness from this game, but that didn't happen for me - I was fine in this case. Sound effects fit the theme.. I loved the music, though. It's just bizarre-sounding hip hop and weird stuff. The controls were easy to use and didn't feel unfair, and I never got 'stuck' anywhere. Overall great.Worth full price? Hmmm, that's a bit of a question. For $15, I think it's going to depend on how much you like games like this that are more about open-ended exploration, goofing around, and more about the vibe than the actual game. I can tell you that I bought it for THREE bucks, so it might be worth it to wishlist and wait for a sale. At three bucks it's a dead steal for pretty much anyone. So if you want right into this world right away, it might be worth full price, but if you're not sure, just take note that I got it for 80% off and maybe sit on it.End of the day, I'm glad I pulled the trigger on this weird little title. It made me actually laugh, which is not usually the case for 'funny' games. And, works PERFECTLY on Steam Deck, so heck yeah.I say go for it if you can get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Not worth full price, not long, not challenging, not even something I'd normally buy or play. However, it was free one day for the release of the sequel so I gave it a shot. Turned out to be a decent, casual timekiller if you're into open world collectathons, light puzzling and everything being a bit...grody.+A number of areas or mechanics that show attention to detail+A couple of very clever puzzles and a minigame to figure out+Unlockable fast travel and a way to re-do failed jumps+Items to help you find anything you missed+Multiple endings (all possible in one save)+Little penalty for dying+Autosaves+Lots of options+The default video filters (gave me a headache) can be disabled+Laughed more than once at some subtle humor+Only one short splash screen+No crashes and only ran into one very tiny bug~Movement control rebinding is a bit confusing~Mantling is over-sensitive~Only one save file~Frequent drug and alcohol references and usage~Unusual amount of detail put into sphincters and defecation~Minor swearing, blood and I guess technical nudity~Often no music or nearly any sound~A few typos, though this may be intentional~Kind of hard to tell what will kill you~There's probably an attempt at some social commentary in here-Not remotely worth full price for 2-4 hours of gameplay that isn't exactly innovative-Achievements only pop after checking the To Do ListPlayed on:Win11, i7-14700, RTX4060 Ti 8GB, 32GB DDR5-6000 @ 1920x1080using KB&M

_childDocuments_.review: Bizzare and stylish, yet somberly grounded parkour/collectathon game.Sludge Life oozes a certain type of vibe. The "kids fresh out of high-school goofing around behind a gas station, smoking cigarettes and talking about nothing in particular, trying to not let the overwhelming hopelessness sink in, because they know that staying in their hometown just means having no perspectives for the future" kinda vibe. It's heavy and soul-crushing. So how do you combat these feelings? Sludge Life's answer is: creative expression through street art, friendly competition and human connections.Okay, that was kinda depressing, but it's a video game, right? So what's the gameplay? Well, it's mostly a platformer with some parkour elements, gadgets to unlock and secrets to look for. Leave your street tag all around the town and create unique street art by comboing with your fellow street artists. It's not that complicated and it doesn't need to be. The movement feels fine and I didn't encounter any massive bugs or glitches.Sludge Life high point is definitely it's aesthetic. The graffiti are genuinely amazing pieces of art and I believe real-life artist were involved. The soundtrack is fitting and works well with everything else. The town you're  exploring is full of surprises and what the cool kids call enviromental storytelling. You're gonna find some unique characters and whacky stuff happening just around the corner. While the subject matter is essentially about being stuck in a dead-end town with no perspectives, while giant corporations kill the world for more profit, it's not a terribly depressing game in tone. I feel like the sparks of hope found throughout Sludge Life are there for a reason.Overall, I think you're gonna enjoy this game whether you like the movement based gameplay or just simply vibe with the style you see in the trailer. Oh yeah, there's this weird screen filter that's on by default and it was giving me a headache if I tried to play with it on. Thankfully, it can be turned off. Just a headsup.

_childDocuments_.review: It's so relaxing, not just in a gameplay way, but in a weird cultural way.  This is utopia, not the clean 1950s space program utopia, but it's a DIY slacker utopia where everyone just hangs out, ignores their job responsibilities, and listens to beats.  Goals are simple - climb stuff and tag stuff.  You'll think you get the whole dynamic within a few minutes and then come back a week later and realize there's another place to climb or another way to sneak through a window and get some puzzle-solving endorphins without even realizing you were solving one.  Because there's always another place to check out anyway.  Graphically & sonically, it's super stylized, but doesn't feel lazy - everything works smoothly and looks great.  The soundtrack by Doseone is cool too and adds to the low-pressure feeling.If you've ever been frustrated because you just wanted to wander and climb everything in some other game, but it locked you into a particular story or gameplay mechanic, this is the game for you.  Overall a great end of the day wandering experience.Editing after playing more to say that it's really well-designed (and relaxing) that you can play this game and make progress without realizing that there even is progress to be made.  As you achieve more things, it starts to feel more like an adventure game, there are even a couple legit puzzles to solve.  But that's not a complaint, I think all Myst-like games need this much jumping.  I got the Good Ending but felt sad about it so I'm sticking around till I get the Weird Ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Very reminiscent of "A short hike".Both games are about exploring a small area densely packed with content and upgrades. However, whereas A short hike encouraged exploration by giving you collectibles that upgraded your mobility throughout the game, Sludge Life lets you explore the world at your leisure and there are only a couple of unlockable items that drastically improve your ability to move around.The game has no real "objective". You might initially believe that finding tagging spots is the goal, but i don't think you need to tag a single spot in order to get two of the game's three endings. Rather, exploring is its own reward and the setting and characters are endearing and funny enough to motivate you to keep looking around.At full prifce, the game's short length makes it tough to recommend, but if you can get it on the cheap, it's a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: Wish I found this sooner as I discovered Sludge Life through the next fest demo of Sludge Life 2. After playing the demo of SL2 I dove right into this one and had a blast! Tore through the whole thing in one sitting which isn't to hard, but I did a whole 100% complete run. The main reason I did it one sitting, it was very captivating in the sense of old school 90s video game stylings with a modern feel. It heavily reminded me of playing Normality. You have a sense of what you can do, but what you should be doing just naturally happens as you explore and talk to people. The game world has its own things going on and it's not until later after you progress do people start acknowledging you, not everyone does which I find to be a good thing, not everyone needs to know who the "main character" is.Playing the game is satisfying all the way around, jumping and scrabbling on things is endless fun. I even noticed a small detail with the edge grabbing that is perfect; (might be hard to explain) If you jump towards a ledge and are still going up the edge grab will happen, if you try to jump from a distance and you're going to fast downward by the time you get close to the edge the grab won't happen. It sounds in text form not fun, but it's so well implemented that in game it works great.Every time you tag is a delight, that tag sound is pure excitement.The music is really good and the game underplays the music a LOT. It keeps the music to boomboxes around the game world so it's not always playing. I grabbed the album from Bandcamp and there are a lot of bangers on there that I don't think even show up in the game itself, do yourself a favor and check out the soundtrack.My final thoughts: I love the pure gameplay that's in here, the world is what it is and spends zero time trying to explain it to you, I love that. The dark comedy and weird stuff going on just delights me to no end.It feels refreshingly different with it's own sense of self, if anything it brings back stuff from 90s video games that I feel we've lost overall and I'm so happy it's here.It's just fun, pure distilled fun.Extra: You can turn off the VHS filter, it might not be for everyone, I went back and forth on it but finally just left it on.There are settings that make little sense when you first start playing, mess with them after you've played a bit and they should click.The camera is a lot of fun and I used it to recall locations of banana slugs when going for that 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: A great yet quirky game. I never expected to actually, to put it plainly,  this game. The whole grunge/trashy oil rig aesthetic really got to me. The story, while not explicitly the main focus is still a welcome presence in the background.The characters are actually quite humorous, with their dialogues being the actual way the player can get the background of the character we play as and the whole vibe of the area in general.Spray paint tagging is not a concept that I am well aware of, but the designs of the tags used in game are quite fancy and cool. The music is especially important that actually sets the tone for the entire game. the rapper known as 'Big Mud' has quite a few good songs in the game.Gameplay wise, the way this game sets particular 'objectives' is quite unconventional. You can go the whole game without even understanding what you are meant to do. There will be hints in the dialogues and the world around you, but there isn't a defined quest menu where you can see what you have to do (except there actually is, but you have to go to an end game area to find this list and install it as an 'app' on your in-game laptop). This was really nice, as there really isn't any hand holding done by the game and the player is actually quite free to do as they wish. The gadgets that are received to complete said objectives are also quite unique and nice - there is a glider, a camera, a teleporter and a tag spotter... which is actually just someone's eyes in a small jar.Unfortunately, as is with many games published by Devolver Digital, they are too short. _childDocuments_.review: SludgeLife is a game that defies traditional conventions and captivates players with its unique and unapologetic approach. As an avid gamer, I have fallen head over heels for this gritty masterpiece, and I can't help but express my sheer admiration for the experience it offers.One of the aspects that makes SludgeLife so remarkable is its immersive and atmospheric world. The game transports you to an industrial wasteland, where dilapidated structures and polluted environments create a sense of desolation. Yet, within this bleak setting, a peculiar charm emerges. The graffiti-covered walls, neon signs flickering amidst the gloom, and the hauntingly beautiful soundtrack combine to create an unmistakable ambiance. SludgeLife effortlessly infuses grime and chaos with an artful touch, making every corner of its world feel like a canvas waiting to be explored.The freedom to roam and explore is another aspect that truly sets SludgeLife apart. The game offers a refreshing departure from linear narratives, encouraging players to chart their own course through its intricate web of secrets and surprises. Whether I was scaling towering structures, tagging graffiti in hidden spots, or discovering hidden collectibles, the feeling of discovery and adventure never waned. SludgeLife rewards curiosity, allowing me to stumble upon unexpected encounters and mind-bending visuals that left me in awe.What truly sealed the deal for me was SludgeLife's offbeat sense of humor. The game doesn't take itself too seriously, delivering a healthy dose of satire and wit that had me grinning from ear to ear. From quirky characters spouting absurd lines to tongue-in-cheek references scattered throughout, SludgeLife kept me engaged with its infectious charm. It's a testament to the game's ability to blend dark themes with lightheartedness, creating an experience that feels refreshingly different from anything I've played before.Moreover, SludgeLife's art style deserves special mention. The deliberately low-fi visuals, filled with vibrant colors and pixelated textures, accentuate the grungy aesthetic of the game. It's a deliberate departure from hyper-realistic graphics, and it works wonders in creating a world that feels simultaneously retro and contemporary. The visuals are both rough and beautiful, capturing the essence of the environment perfectly and enhancing the overall experience.Finally, it's worth mentioning the game's excellent soundtrack, which adds yet another layer of immersion. The combination of electronic beats, ambient tunes, and lo-fi melodies creates an atmospheric backdrop that further engulfs you in SludgeLife's world. Each track felt meticulously crafted, amplifying the emotions and enhancing the gameplay experience.In conclusion, SludgeLife is an exceptional game that embraces its own unique brand of grime and elevates it to a work of art. With its immersive world, open-ended exploration, offbeat humor, distinct art style, and captivating soundtrack, it's no wonder why I've fallen head over heels for it. SludgeLife defies expectations and provides an unforgettable journey through an industrial wasteland where beauty can be found even in the most unexpected places. If you're looking for an unconventional and unforgettable gaming experience, SludgeLife is an absolute must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is an absurdist 3D platformer based around spray painting (tagging) various walls across a fictional shipyard. Reading other reviews, the game’s humour and stylistic content seems to have polarised reviewers who struggle to explain in words the game’s aesthetic beyond “grungy”. However, I feel Sludge Life’s awkward, surrealist humour stems directly from shows like The Eric Andre Show, Adult Swim and, taking it even further back, BBC’s The Mighty Boosh.Reviewers have struggled to categorise Sludge Life into a specific genre, with labels such as “walking simulator”, “open-world adventure” and “3D platformer” being handed around slightly hesitantly. For the most part, you’ll be trying to reach high ledges, jumping across shipping containers, gliding, jumping and crawling through vents and other tight spaces. And honestly, it’s pretty fun if a little clunky and lacking in depth. There’s a real satisfaction of ticking off your in-game to-do list that I feel will really resonate with late 20s home owners.Set in an abstract patch of the sea, players explore a shipyard complete with disgruntled striking employees, an anxiously leaking oil rig, dilapidated apartment block, laboratory, radio tower and sports centre. The game’s pull is in its deliberate lacks of cohesion and its illogical situations. For example, knocking door-to-door on the apartment block led to me discovering:🟢 A news agency run entirely by pigeons🟢 A sleeping baby the size of a lorry🟢 A group of students high on shrooms hypnotised by a TV show presented by an oscillating slugLater, I met a depressed self-depreciating bird sitting atop a stack of near unclimbable shipping containers who told me “Sometimes I just sit here and doubt myself”. It’s the type of humour designed to be made into viral content, YouTube shorts and reaction GIFs, but isn’t quite bottom of the barrel humour either. While it’s not laugh out loud humour, Sludge Life did elicit lots of big smile across its succinct 2.5 hour runtime.I had a really fun time with Sludge Life, and it became the perfect remedy for a long day of work. It doesn’t require too much thought, but is smart enough to hold your attention. It’s a short game, and it’s full £12.99 is certainly too steep, but it felt satisfyingly manageable and a welcome distraction from the real world.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is a unique and immersive first-person exploration game that takes you on a journey through a surreal, grungy world filled with unexpected surprises and strange encounters. As you explore the decaying urban environment, you'll encounter bizarre characters, hidden secrets, and a whole lot of sludge.One of the most striking things about Sludge Life is its art style. The game features a minimalist, almost abstract aesthetic that manages to convey a great deal of mood and atmosphere with very little detail. The world is dark, gritty, and full of decay, but there's also a strange kind of beauty to it all. The visuals are accompanied by a fantastic soundtrack that perfectly captures the game's strange, surreal vibe.Gameplay-wise, Sludge Life is a mix of exploration, platforming, and puzzle-solving. As you make your way through the world, you'll need to use your wits and reflexes to overcome obstacles and uncover hidden areas. The game also features a number of optional tasks and missions, which can help you unlock new abilities and items.One of the things that sets Sludge Life apart from other games in its genre is its sense of humor. The game is full of strange, absurdist humor that will have you laughing out loud at times. From the characters you meet to the strange objects you collect, everything in Sludge Life feels like it was designed with a twisted sense of humor in mind.Overall, Sludge Life is an excellent game that's well worth your time if you're a fan of exploration games, platformers, or just weird and surreal experiences. The game's unique visuals, fantastic soundtrack, and bizarre sense of humor all come together to create something truly memorable.(I recommend for people who are bored)

However I do like that part of it, it is uniquely charming and presents an interesting world for you to explore. The visuals are well done, and the music is surprisingly good, the only problem I have is the lackluster feeling controls. Movement is sluggish with unsatisfying jumps and a clamber that refuses to work half the time. Outside of all that this is a pretty well made indie with a good amount of stuff to do, just enough to not overstay its welcome. The concept of making tags is fun and gives a nice incentive to explore and find weird and wacky stuff along the way. As for the price I received this when it was given away for free so from my perspective its not really worth the full $15, partially cause of its brevity, but mainly because of its very love it or hate it style. _childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life does so much strange things with complete confidence. It's an exploration platformer with a unique art direction. Basically, you play as a character named Ghost and roam a polluted island and spray graffiti on given locations, and talk to the weird inhabitants.With a cell-shaded look and sharp pixelated borders stills from the game looks like art someone has made with MS paint in the 90s. It also makes the think of Pushwagner a bit.The sound design is very "in your face" and well made with a few exceptions, such as the jumping sound which becomes annoying after a while.Overall the game is very fun and does not overstay its welcome. I do have a few gripes with the movement though. Everything is presented in a way that encourages speed and sloppiness, therefore the controls must be extremely snappy and precise. right now you feel that Ghost doesn't do what I tell him. He stops too late and he fumbles when he climbs on a beam. This really takes away from the experience and feels like an artificial difficulty. It's not fun to climb the same stuff many times because the character doesn't do what I want.I hear they are working on a sequel and I hope they iron out the movement and maybe add some more parkour-like movement to enhance the fluidity of the game. _childDocuments_.review: WOW. This is good. Let me tell you that I got this game when it was free on steam (I think it was free on epic games too at one point?) just so I would have it in my library, on the off chance that I wanted to play it later and wouldn't have to buy it. I had no actual plans on playing it. Curiosity got the better of me, and I decided to play it, see what it was all about. The screenshots looked cool.I had no idea it was exactly what I was craving from a game.You play as Ghost, one of the graffiti artist from around this place. You have no idea what you look like, but you can only imagine you are some kind of goop or semi-solid creature (Your crouching is very, VERY low. Chin-touching-the-ground-level low).You go around, traversing this world, looking for tagging spots, and tagging them. Getting to the often-inconveniently-placed tagging spots is the fun part. Parkour mechanics are simple, but you need none more, they're exactly what you need.Along your adventure, you will meet other taggers (and ex-taggers). Once you tag enough locations yourself, you will unlock collab-murals with one of the taggers you will meet.You will also obtain items, which will help you find tagging locations and also reach them. The camera works just like binoculars, it helps you see tagging locations from longer ranges (tagging icon only appears when you are close to the location). The vandal eyes work like a compass, guiding you to the exact location of the nearest tagging spot.The glider helps you... glide.The warper teleports you to the anchored location.Let's dumb it down to some pros and cons:Pros:- great atmosphere- great concept- great execution- some lore- traversing the city is fun, so is platforming- 3 endings- multiple achievements- collect-'em-all style mechanics for tags, slugs, apps and items- decently big world- unique graphics and art style- some secrets- cool music- smart puzzles- you can get high from shrooms, smoke and drink sodaCons:- pretty boring NPC dialogue, semi-con- VHS filter on by default. I thought it was forced at first, but it was annoying. Turns out you can disable it, so also only a semi-con- limited replayability- some puzzles may be annoying. You might get stuck. I had to do some googlingTHING YOU SHOULD KNOW BEFORE PLAYING (I have not seen anyone mention this):Endings do not reset your progress. Only if you wipe it. (Make sure to agree to trying to recover it in the bad ending. It will go back to normal)Overall: 9/10. Initial playthrough is amazing. Replaying might be boring.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge life is a short little sandbox game that can be best described as a "Delinquent Simulator". You're incentivized to go out and spread your brand onto the city by tagging various spots with your name and character (the "Ghost").Despite your character being (allegedly) underaged, and fully capable of committing underaged-substance-use crimes, This game is not for kids- even though the swearing in this world is very-unlike real life's swear words.The worldbuilding is spot on. This clearly gives me a "Splatoon's-crunked-up-ghettopunk-neighbor" vibe in terms of atmosphere. Your home is a shipping container, the place is owned by a megacorp dealing with a strike and an incompetant CEO who's holed up in the corporate penthouse. Most of the populace has stopped giving a damn, the security guards are violent douchebags,  drunks are everywhere, half the people are mutated, and Taggers like you are the only ones gutsy-enough to stick it to the man.The flaws of this game? Well, first off, due to the premise of this game being an exploration game and delinquent sim, there isn't a terrible amount of combat, that's not a big deal. The one problem I have with exploring things, is that despite most of the game being relatively simple to figure out, there are a few puzzles in the game which require unusually-interactice solutions in order to progress.Also, the air physics in this game are janky in a rather unpleasant way, not as bad as some games but here it's a bit "bitter tasting" so to speak.Also, the collect-a-thon sh*t has never really set well with me, and this game has quite a bit of it. This game normally retails for $15. I generally can deal with short length if the game offsets it with replayability, or being lower-priced. Sadly, this game lacks in the replayability department, but since I got it for free, it counts. I don't think I would've bought this game for full price though.

_childDocuments_.review: A very cute little open-world exploration game with light platforming and puzzle solving. You take on the role of Ghost, a green goblin-esque fellow, who has made it his mission to tag all the good spots with their distinct graffiti in his city, which is a depressing mix of gray concrete, an oil platform and an industrial-chemical wasteland in the middle of a polluted ocean full of sludge. Over the course of the game you will figure out a path and climb to hard to reach spots to cover in your art and talk to some weird NPCs in this tiny but completely open world.  There are no enemies to speak of, the only way to "fail" is by falling from a high place and breaking every bone in your body.The main appeals of this game are mostly it's aethetic, which stands unabashedly on its own two urban graffiti-style legs and the fun exploration through a combination of platforming and puzzle solving, which rewards you with collectibles, items that make platforming easier or open new paths and of course a way to get too the credits. It's not just about collectibles though, you will also have some amusing moments by talking to eccentric NPCs, whos' dialog ranges from just funny too stories about drug abuse and the misery of living in this dystopic world, where greedy corporations have polluted the earth. It's sort of like a cyberpunkish story, but replace the cybernetics with graffity and cartoonish characters. The world of sludge is not just random dialog with no connection, it does have a small but funny background plot about a beloved mascot and a protest as you explore and fits the punk vibes, but I will leave it to you to discover. And of course you will encounter just some out of place weird, sometimes even dark but funny things in this world, it treats your eyes with a lot of diverse stuff within its small contrainsts and never feels lame or predictable.But when I talk about this game's open world being tiny, I really mean tiny. Completing the game while tagging all of the 100 spots will probably take you 2 to 3 hours at most and you will rapidly run out of interesting areas to explore as you finish them one by one until only the hunt for achievements is left. The game's platforming can also be frustrating at times. I often found myself accidentially vaulting over an object I just wanted to climb on, plunging to my death as my character just fall down on the other side. What surfaces are climbable can also be a bit unclear at times.All in all, I had a very pleasant afternoon exploring the small but colorful world of Sludge Life and if you enjoy games with a unique design, weird things to discover and some light puzzle-platformer gameplay, then the couple of bucks this game costs will be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend it enough - atmospheric, free roaming, and loaded with life. The music of this game, unlike High Hell, basically carries you through the world of the game on a cloud.I think one of the best aspects of Vellman's games is that they're so incredibly loaded with a sense of the character themselves - in High Hell, it was seeing yourself in the mirrors, burning money, vandalizing things as part of your objectives, and rescuing animals.Here, the little touches are what make the entire game have a soul. I've never gone out and tagged IRL but this makes me wish I did, and you feel like you're the character. You're walking around smoking, drinking energy drinks, getting high and hanging out on top of high buildings, breaking into stuff, causing shenanigans, talking to friends, getting accosted by weirdoes, and just living life.The collect-a-thon mechanics are only one aspect of the game, because it's really just a vehicle to make you experience the world that Vellmann and Doseone have made. It feels unmistakably cool. There's a whole lotta games that wish they were this game, and not very many that actually are. The things that make this game are the extremely precise sense of humor and worldview in a fantastical environment that feels incredibly relatable, and all of the visual gags that don't try to force themselves on you. There's a very strong sense of play, and the open-ended nature of the gameplay makes it extremely rewarding to find these things yourselves.Also, god, wear headphones for this. You absolutely need to experience this with bass blasting. It has such a huge impact on it.It's a blessing that it's so easy to play through in a sitting, and that's been part of why I revisit it.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever played a game that could be succinctly described as “Beautifully Ugly”? Sludge Life stands up to that description very much so. Its artstyle stands out from most games that come out these days, it’s the reason I bought it while browsing Steam using the Discovery Queue. The cartoon cel shaded art style caught my eye and rose to the top of all the white noise that is new releases on Steam. I am pretty picky when it comes to games, for example I used to only buy games when they were on sale. What I buy however, has been consistently influenced by visuals. There are other factors, of course, but a game with great art direction can really compel me to want to play it. The subtle VHS-like vignette adds a lot to the aesthetic, and the loud cartoon colors contrast greatly with the sludgy wasteland the game takes place in. The whole of Sludge Island where the game is set feels convincingly lived in, with people looking bored working at their jobs, sleeping midday because of the few prospects they have in life, Or just winning a bet super hard by spinning on their head for eternity. The main gameplay loop involves spraying graffiti in predetermined spots throughout Sludge Island as all the authority figures called “Clops” are either striking or busy. A veritable dream for an up and coming tag artist. You play as Ghost, one such tag artist and your goal is to earn the respect of the Islands five other prolific taggers by hitting as many spots with your sludgy green ghost blob logo as you can. There are also tons of other shenanigans to get yourself into like smoking, drinking, talking, farting, and finding lost snakes. I spent maybe half my time playing Sludge Life, finding graffiti spots and the other half goofing off, finding people to talk to, and laughing my ass off. Make no mistake, Sludge Life is a Funny game, not “funny” like it's trying too hard or is really cringeworthy. Sludge Life has great comedic writing and some of the dialogue is ridiculously hilarious. My only gripe is that it's too difficult to find the other graffiti artists. Once you impress them, by hitting milestones of spots tagged, some of them give you tools that make it much more fun to explore and keep you on track. While I had enough tags to have impressed two of them, I found three graffiti artists, all of which were not the ones I had impressed. And while I did find them eventually, I wish there was an easier way to track them down. I loved my time with Sludge Life, unfortunately that wasn’t a lot of time. The final time I recorded was just under two and a half hours until I found one of the game's three endings. I’ve definitely taken issue with games being too short before and Sludge Life is asking for fifteen dollars for, what most will play, a three hour game. Not a great ratio, sure, but despite that I think the game more than deserves a buy.

_childDocuments_.review: TOTAL COMPLETION: 100%TIME TAKEN: 3.5 HOURSSLUDGE LIFE is a delight. It has great humor, nice parkour, good music, and an overall fantastic art style. If you enjoy exploration games with plenty of charm to go around, then I would definitely consider picking this game up...... on sale.Now, do understand- I thoroughly enjoyed my time in SLUDGE LIFE. As stated above (in a new move I'll be trying in my reviews) I was able to 100% complete this game in just three and a half hours according to Steam. I could see ten dollars being reasonable, but hey, I'm not a game developer, so I don't really understand how to price a game in a manner in which they could still turn a profit.I personally don't regret spending the money. I feel this is something I can come back every now and then and play all over again. To me, this is a game I think I'd have fun memorizing. However, I know not everyone will think the way I do. a lot of people might not want to replay the game, memorize it, speedrun it, etcetera, and that same demographic would probably be better off spending money elsewhere on something longer and more expansive, say a rogue-like, or even Mirror's Edge.Rest assured, though, if you decide to purchase, you get a great little walking/parkour simulator with fun characters and art style, and the pleasure of listening to Big Mud's raps. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this game feels like a mash-up of  and  by way of . In my first two hours of play, I smoked a cigarette (a "ciggy"), took a photo of a dizzy pigeon, got bit by a snake, smacked by a  "clop", found a  baby, chatted with a half-insect kid whose mom is a Certified Public Accountant, talked to a guy about a literal s**t he took (and left in the toilet), then I climbed a tower, found a bird person chilling on a couch up top, and then I  backflipped off of the damn thing- falling to my death.And I respawned in a hospital bed, and now I'm in debt! You'll know quickly if this is your kind of jam or not. I bought into the vibe and aesthetic IMMEDIATELY. I loved this. One of the first games I actually intentionally lowered the resolution on. Visually, everything is line-traced, like a cartoon, and it comes through a lot better in 1280 x 720 than it does in 4K. I'm giddy to play more, and had to force myself to stop so I could savor the experience of finding more and more weird stuff in this delightfully gross world. Unless you're speeding through this, looking for objective based gameplay, there's no way you're gonna see everything Sludge Life has to offer in under two hours. But it's not the kind of game that gives you rigid, structured, goals and compels you to do them either. At the same time, I feel like it's reductive to call it a walking simulator. It's more like a "do whatever you want and explore to your heart's content" kind of game. Which is rad. If you ever found yourself playing a game with a cool world that you low key wish you could explore, but the gameplay is linear enough to prevent that- this game is for you. Provided you vibe with the toilet humor and low-fi aesthetic. Be a punk, screw the clops, go throw up some tags and backflip off a building. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Listen guys. This isnt a "game" per say.  Its an experience. Do not buy this game expecting some action and goals.  You are presented with a dystopian world.  I dont know if you have played HEAVY BULLETS or High Hell, but this game takes all of that and puts it into this walking simulator where you experience life as a tagger. The goal of the game is to tag and reach areas to tag.  Now that that disclaimer is out of the way.  This "game" is wholly unique and Ive enjoyed it immensly.  No, you wont get tons of hours out of this game. Let me be straight up.  Its a short excursion into a dystopian landscape that only the developers could dream of.  Remember this word. Walking simulator. I dont think it does it justice because there is a goal, but mainly this game is for the experience.  I quite enjoy it.  If you like psychedelic dystopian narratives and like smoking virtual cigarettes, youre gonna love this game.  I just dont want anyone to think this game isnt what it is.  Its an experience of runaway capitalism. 5/5.

name: Out There: Oceans of Time
detailed_description: JOIN THE DISCORD JOIN THE NEWSLETTER About the Game The cosmos is calling. Take the helm of an interstellar expedition of discovery spanning the vast and vibrant infinity of space. The definitive Out There: Oceans of Time experience is available now, with the new Redshift Update. New Oxygen management system on Rocky Planets Expeditions New class skills New Consumable Items New maps for all expedition types New way to explore maps (Tunnels, Ancient Portals, and Unstable Structures) Overall difficulty balancing The successor to the award-winning Out There, Oceans of Time blends resource management and interactive fiction for a space survival epic where death is one wrong decision away. As Commander Nyx, explore a vast galaxy that is different every time you play, as you search for the Archon; a cosmic villain set on dominating the civilisations of the galaxy. Encounter other strange lifeforms and learn to communicate, trade, and conduct diplomacy as you build a coalition of allies in your mission to find the Archon. Recruit new members from the alien races you cross paths with, and build a team capable of traversing the cosmos. Manage your crew, your ship and its systems; the mission’s success is down to your decisions as Commander. Experience a deep, branching narrative written by FibreTigre, dialogue by Christos Gage ( Daredevil (Netflix, 2015), Spider-Man (Insomniac, Sony, 2018)) and beautiful interactive cutscenes illustrated by renowned artist Benjamin Carré ( Transformers: Age of Extinction, Alone in the Dark ). Out There: Oceans of Time is developed by Mi-Clos Studio, the creators of Out There and Sigma Theory. FEATURES Navigate an expansive cosmos that is different every time you play. Explore unexplored terrain and collect resources for your ship, and the next leg of your journey. Recruit from a diverse range of Alien lifeforms, and build a team capable of surviving the furthest reaches of the cosmos. An epic space-saga penned by FibreTigre, with dialogue from Christos Gage.

_childDocuments_.review: so i played the beta or demo or whatever it was and they had a mechanic where by exploration was risky and challenging because you would run out of "energy" while exploring, this was over tuned in the beta and made the game very punishing/un-fun. they have decided to remove the "energy for exploration" mechanic entirely. which aside from removing an aspect of what made the process tense and risk/reward it has also left the game feeling hollow as a significant part of the character abilities and items are based around making the process of exploration more efficient which felt rewarding when it mattered but just pointless now that they don't? the strange thing is that lets say they changed the mechanic to something as simple as running out of energy results in your ship collecting you automatically (i.e you can no longer explore, this could mean you fail the main objective of said exploration) then it would by all accounts make the game design around this process of rewarding players with better exploration character buffs/items still valid. if i had to guess i would say they backed out of their original vision for the game in wake of many complaints about a system that needed work rather than removing.  which is a shame. Trouble is the game-play loop of exploring and levelling up crew really dose feel gutted without that distinct need for a challenge to overcome. right now exploration is really more of a click and point adventure rather than the tense decision making process it used to be.  then again if i had publishers/players protesting about a core mechanic then i too would feel very tempted to just remove it for the initial sales. hopefully they will add this component back in as an "option" sort of the difference between story mode and normal for those of us that like are rouge-likes punishing.

Fly, click, collect resourse. Repeat. Build ship modules that let you fly, click, collect further, faster, harder. Thats literally the entire game, the entire 99% of gameplay is exactly that. _childDocuments_.review: short version: original OT's resource grinding is a bad centerpiece for a longer roguelike space exploration/adventure game. long version: it pains me to not be able to recommend this. I love the original game (65 hrs on it & more to come) & waited patiently for this, but I don't think what they did here works. what makes me play the original is that's it's short, unforgiving, mysterious, and to the point (get home) and I love the art style & music. this game is easier, has expanded gameplay mechanics which are.. ok, neither good or bad, but make things take longer. since the game takes longer, it's more frustrating when bad luck wipes you out (although there are save points now in white dwarf systems). things I like: the music's great, being able to finally take hydrogen out of the scoop & put it directly into the engine is great, and the greenhouse mechanics are kind of cool. things I don't like: dropping the original's comic book style, the morale system is an unnecessary chore because the characters are void of personality, the character writing is really bad (apparently this game's dialog was written by a professional screenwriter, but you wouldn't know it), the character models are fugly, the planet models don't look near as cool or varied as they did in OT, planetary exploration is repetitive, the labyrinthine star path you have to follow feels arbitrary, the story is generic space opera stuff...  but the core of this is still a resource grinding game so there's little narrative depth (not w/these characters, anyway) or a conflict (since combat isn't a feature). the original game is about getting home & grinding resources because you HAVE to, this game is about saving humanity (or something) & exploring, but with no straightforward objective & expecting you to enjoy grinding resources & taking care of your unlikable crew for the fun of it. I don't know who this is going to appeal to. I think the hardcore fans of Out There are going to be disappointed at the generic new look & all the shoehorned-in time wasting mechanics. And I think anyone new to it looking for a space roguelike are going to find it strangely lacking in depth for an asking price of >20$. Pick it up on sale, I guess. that's all I've got.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, it's been noisy on our spaceship as of late. You hear that? That’s the sound of wasted potential, bouncing nervously wall to wall, echoing across the barren room, a sign that reads “gameplay” above its door. In the room across it – the one where the sign says “narrative” – you’ll find its occupant, the know-how necessary to translate all those great ideas the developers have had into a solidified narrative, completely checked out; its absence seemingly overlooked during development. They both came down to the same conclusion: that bigger isn’t always better, especially when the biggest chunks are missing.  is the sequel to , a 2015 space-exploration, resource-management roguelike which I haven’t had the pleasure of playing. Taking a quick gander at its store page, however, reveals a game that seems to be beloved by many. So why does this new game, one that’s supposedly taking everything from the old one and turning it up to eleven, have a much more mixed reception? Now, I don’t have the necessary experience to compare the two, but with how barebones and bloated of a game  is, it seems that too much time has been spent inflating and less so innovating as much as necessary to support this different, seemingly more narrative-driven approach.And that breaks my heart a little; I’m a narrative-loving kind of guy, but I think I’ll pass on going down this particular wormhole. It all creates this sinking feeling in my gut that slowly expands as the playtime counter on Steam goes up. Eventually, the intrigue wears off, and the understanding for what the developers were going for, but failed to do, evaporates. I become uncanny, and all that’s left are feelings of disappointment. Alas, for where I was promised considerable depth, I only found a puddle’s worth. The story begins with our two main characters, Captain Nyx and Officer Sergei, escorting a dangerous wolf-like creature known as The Archon to a space prison of sorts. It doesn’t take long for things to go awry, The Archon to escape, and our two characters to end up in a century-long cryostasis slumber as their escape pods limp away to the nearest habitable planet. While the setup seems as cliché as can be, there are glimpses that what’s underneath could be more inventive. Unfortunately, it doesn’t get much better. It’s all ideas and barely any refinement. Throwing things at the wall, seeing what sticks, then just leaving it there, hanging. What the universe that these characters inhabit is like, what The Archon’s grand plans are, and how have the past one hundred years affected it all are things merely mentioned in passing, or not at all. There’s no cohesive world to explore, no compelling mystery to uncover, no expansive lore to get lost in. It’s exposition dump after exposition dump, with some meagre attempts at characterisation thrown in. Some branching moments in the story try their best at tempting a replay out, in the hopes of there being a sudden realization that makes everything worthwhile, but the ordeal as a whole is so unrefined that I’m hard pressed for motivation to go looking for what I’ve missed.The gameplay is divided into two sections: interstellar travel and expeditions. You’ll be spending most of your time aboard your ship, flying from star system to star system, the goal being reaching the next objective. Along the way, you’ll be tending to its parts and crew by managing four bars: fuel, oxygen, hull, and morale. Should any one of these fall to zero, it’ll mean a game over in the vast majority of cases, at which point you’ll be sent back to your last manual save. Manual saves can only be performed at specific space stations, but these aren’t as rare as you might think, and should you quit out, you’ll be able to resume from the very spot you did so at, provided you haven’t died. Still, permanently losing progress in a narrative-inclined roguelite is a pet peeve of mine, so keeping these bars filled is non-negotiable. To stave off death, you’ll be visiting planets. As each planet is of a specific type, so are the resources you need spread out among them. For example, Hydrogen and Helium – both used for refuelling – can only be found by sending a probe to a gas giant, while you’ll have to land on a rocky planet and drill out Iron to repair your hull. Everything your ship does corresponds to a module or technology aboard, and they’ll wear off the more you use them, eventually needing to be repaired. Add in the fact that each ship – as you have the option of swapping between ‘em should you find one abandoned, adrift in space – has different stats that govern how efficient it’ll be when it comes to depleting these bars and you’ve got a decent foundation to add more gameplay elements onto. But, there aren’t any. What you do an hour in is the same thing you do after ten, albeit more efficiently. I don’t know where this “steep learning curve” other reviews are talking about comes from, as I’ve only died twice – both times to running out of fuel – near the beginning of the game. After that, for the next eight hours or so, I’ve never come close to it. It’s an easy system to learn from and figure out. Once you do, the game has no curveballs to throw your way to shake things up. Sure, a text-based event will sometimes pop up, urging you to decide on how to resolve it. However, most decisions will inform you in advance of their outcomes, so you can just steer clear of what isn’t in your favour. A decent number of events also have the option to be ignored, so it’s almost a non-feature at that point.  Planetary expeditions are similar in that regard. You can find them after scanning certain planets for anomalies, then landing and deploying your team to complete a specific objective and maybe pick up some resources along the way. They’re explored by moving across a hexagonal grid while avoiding tiles with hazards on them. These hazards can inflict a negative effect on one of your crew members, which can eventually lead to death. However, there’s almost always an alternate route to find as long as you’re the least bit patient, and even then, the chance of getting inflicted is only 25%, with possibilities to lower it further, making the tiles rarely a considerable threat. Nyx, Sergei, and any other crew members you recruit later in the game (though none other than the first two are actual characters) differ by abilities and classes, though these are negligible mostly. They’ll sometimes provide a nice benefit, but never will they pull an expedition from certain doom. They’ll be most important during text-based encounters, similar to those in space, that occur on certain tiles.  Each class has a limited number of action points, consumed when picking an option exclusive to that class during the encounters. Theoretically, you could find yourself in a bad spot, with no points to pick the winning option, but as each event informs you which class you’ll need to get the best outcome before you even find it, let alone step on its tile, you’re free to ignore any that might pose a risk to your party; a realization that turns expeditions into an assembly line of clicking around for as many resources as you can find. I’ve explored the stars and found… very little of note.  might be the next great space RPG, but only with substantial additions and reiterations to its gameplay and narrative. As it is? A bit intriguing, but hardly recommendable.

I can't imagine that it would have been too much of an effort to ask the devs to be able to create multiple save points, but not so with Out there: Oceans of time.Firstly, whoever came up with the idea of creating in-game save points at certain locations like white dwarf stars for example needs to seriously give their heads and wobble because the save game function in Out there: Oceans of time is flawed beyond credibility. _childDocuments_.review: I don't want to give that game a negative review but... I got to say, the biggest new feature, the away missions and the related new moral resource kills it for me. That despite I really liked the predecessor and had this one on my wish list for a long time,  me. These forced away missions turn a relaxing casual game into a pointless grind fest.  The game got quite an update regarding the visuals and story animations. Also there are multiple languages included right from start, although the game contains a lot of text! I also found no bugs yet except for quite huge frame drop  when you do away missions and don't use a good graphics card. The problem are the away missions themselves. You now have new resource called "morale", that goes down whenever you jump between star systems. You can only increase it by completing away missions and visit villages while doing so. That means, you are more or less forced to do these missions. On the other hand you can't do them whenever you like because there is a cooldown of two jumps per crew member. So you not only have to do them but also in a certain interval! Before you can start such a missions, you have to compelete a mini game that gets quickly annoying. The missions then turned out to be very time consuming for usually little rewards. In the first "Out There" game, you landed on a planed, talked to some aliens and maybe drilled for resources. Quick and simple. Now you walk arround like 20-30 minutes on a single planet, mostly because you can only move like 4-5 tiles per turn, no auto-walk possible to already explored areas. You also have to do some micro management and evade dangerous tiles by walking longer ways arround. That has probably to do with the system they had in place during development, where you could only stay on a planet for a certain time so you had to choose whether to take the risk or not. Either way, I can't get into these missions, they just take too long for too little reward and also get boring quickly. There should be a an option to auto-resolve these, like it is with any other event in the game. Probably to somewhat offset the annoyance that away missions are, you can now save manually in some star systems. I actually had no problem to lose in the old game without being able to load some save. But there are run took also only like 2-4 hours, if it went really good, so if you bascially complete the game, in average it was more like 30 minutes to an hour if you screw up. Here most of my playtime are away missions with very little overall progress.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm completely fine with the monotonous gameplay because it evokes the same feeling I would expect when travelling through space. It's fine to not have too much action at once, and I think this game is an upgrade over the original where objectives are much more clear and the paths to them are more defined. What does not pass the bar for me is the amount of gamebreaking bugs there are in a game like this. Objectives in this game are broken to the point where you will lose a significant portion of your save data, and literally be unable to progress in the game. There are no backup saves, or ways to revert saves to help fix these issues when they arise, and the devs are terrible at responding to bugs and feedback.
