_childDocuments_.review: The smoothest, most dynamic action game I have ever played. I'm not usually a fan of the genre, and honestly didn't love the previous Supergiant Games, but this title swept me off of my feet. There are six weapons, each with four aspects, some of which alter the weapons so much they are basically completely different, then you have dozens of "boons," which dramatically alter how your abilities work, or "hammer upgrades" that alter the weapon in more specialized ways. Each run you'll get random selections of these boons and weapon upgrades, you'll have to cobble together boons to create builds and alter your playstyle to work with what you get. It all works together so well I'm still surprised by each run.It's rare that I pick up a title and know that I will still be thinking about it 10 years down the line. Instant classic.It's not all completely rosy, sadly. The game definitely lacks in polish. Some terrain corners can catch you while others can't, the hitbox of magma on some maps is very, very hard to read, the forced perspective makes it hard to use pillars to block line of sight (very important for two boss fights), and one of the bosses has a charge attack that you are supposed to lead him into a pillar but he sometimes just slides around it like a cartoon character.My biggest gripe is the dialog system, to progress the story you often have to wait for specific dialog events, but they are drawn randomly from a pool of available comments, so you might have to wait very, very long for story events to trigger. The main story takes precedence over the side quests, so if you are beating the game and moving quickly you will have to wait a long, long time to trigger needed dialog. This is most noticeable with Hypnos, after filling his heart gauge you have to wait for a series of events involving his brother to play out, but Thanatos only rarely shows up at the house, and if you have other dialog options with either of them in backlog this can delay those events. Some dialog events are also dependent on you dying to certain bosses several times, easy bosses I should say, so it's quite possible that if you want to complete the story you'll need to find a guide and suicide a few runs.(While that might seems like a lot of complaining I love this game and I'm just grouching and nitpicking over something that I love.)The story of the game is based on Greek mythology. Zagreus, the son of Hades, desires his freedom from the Underworld he was born into, renown for there being no escape. Along the way he makes amends with the family and friends he may have been rude to over the years and realizes that he can't do this alone. It's a tale of reconciliation, love, friendship, and banging your step-brother.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty repetitive and grindy. Even after you beat dungeons after dungeons, the game becomes boring and lame, forcing you to work for the fun part (which is the next boss fight) . Altough that is the whole point of an rng it does affect the overall experience. This was my first RNG game, however i have played other games like nioh and sekiro, that also have rng elements to it. However those games encourage you to develop skill and experience in order to overcome extremely challenging bossfights, which then permanently lead you to the next stage. In Hades, youll be forced to restart the entire game after every death, making each playthrough more and more repetitive and boring as well as grindy. What makes this game somewhat tolerable is the lore, the gameplay and the soundtrack, but   like i said the main issue is that it becomes repetitive after every death. I would not reccomend this to anyone who isnt a fan of the rng genre.

_childDocuments_.review: ~~~Introduction~~~Hades follows the life of Zagreus the son of Hades, in his attempts to escape the underworld in search of his biological mother. Along the way you will meet your fellow relatives who will aide your quest to leave thinking you are going to Olympus to be with them. Along the way you fight various monsters, avoid traps, and kill bosses, all while collecting items to further upgrade your character, relationships, weapons, and home.~~~Gameplay~~~Hades is an isymmetric action roguelike. During your escape attempts you can wield 1 of 6 weapons. Each of those has vastly different gameplay and difficulties. Each run feels new and refreshing with all of the available upgrades and unlocks you can get. The combat and movement is the most fluid of all of the roguelikes I have played. It feels extremely polished to the point where other games just do not compete. Even after death you want to go right back in and play again. 10/10~~~Story~~~The story is top tier. Revolving around multiple stories woven tightly together between characters. After a run new dialogue options become available for you. The story is so well written sometimes I just want to die so I can go back and read more. The addition to increasing your relationships with fellow characters to unlock more dialogue is an interesting take on the story. The intricacies of how they pieced together multiple running story lines and how they revealed themselves is mind boggling.10/10~~~Sound~~~The SFX noises are great, each one of them feels like the real deal and fits perfect. But noone cares about the SFX when the music in this game is what it is. For a smaller studio I don't think anyone else has come close to the music quality that they have composed. Considering one of the main aspects of the story follows a muse you would expect as such. Once you complete the main story a cutscene plays that has hands down my new favorite video game song of all time.10/10~~~Difficulty~~~The game caters to both hardcore roguelike players and casuals. It has the ability to turn on a god mode, where after each death your defense goes up by 2% adding up to 80% in the end. This allows those who want to experience the story without being stressed about the gameplay able to. Alternatively the game has heat levels and conditions that make the game increasingly more difficult. 3/10 if using godmode for the story.10/10 at max heat levels.~~~Overall~~~Hades is one of if not the best action roguelikes to come out in recent years. It has everything great going for it. Unique story, amazing gameplay and music, and the ability to let casual players and hardcore players experience it without frustration.10/10 GOTY

_childDocuments_.review: It’s a cool breezy night here at the Temple of Styx and we’re back for another electrifying round of your favorite game show and mine, FIGHT… YOUR… DAD!As the first entry in a spicy new genre I’m prepared to call the father-fighter, Hades lets us join Zagreus, the immortal son of the eponymous lord of hell, as he works out some daddy issues the only way the Greek gods know how: trading mortal blows and expensive gifts until someone consents to stay dead. It seems that Hades’ erstwhile squeeze Persephone has wearied of the old man’s sparkling wit and sunny disposition, and lit out for the surface, leaving her godling son to absorb an endless torrent of divorced-old-man whining and backhands, and the underworld in a state of lockdown. Living or dead, mortal or divine, nobody gets out.Fortunately, Zag’s not the only one who thinks Dad’s being a little unreasonable about this. The cousins and uncles on Olympus have sent letter after letter, and Hades won’t even look at them. We get that he’s mad about being assigned the underworld, but that’s millennia ago now. At some point, you have to move on, fix up the house, find a hobby. Zagreus did — learned to fight at the knee of Achilles himself, and was that ever a mistake on his father’s part. Kick a boy around for thousands of years and then have the greatest warrior who ever lived train him to kick back? Maybe this is why they say all fathers subconsciously raise their sons to destroy them.No telling where he got the weapons, though — that must have been the Fates. Some of them haven’t been seen since Hades and his brothers sealed away the Titans. Some were already lost before that battle began. Most immortals won’t lay a hand on the powers Zagreus is stirring up, and most wouldn’t defy the Lord Hades to his face, but having found some kind of direction for his endless life, the boy moves through the underworld like a wave, like lightning, like an arrow in flight, wearing the blessings of his Olympian relatives and bringing change to this unchanging realm wherever he goes. Perhaps it’s because everyone else has a place here, of a kind — Mother Nyx has the old man’s trust; Thanatos a sacred duty that never ends; even Cerberus sits at the throne’s right hand. Zagreus has never once, not for a day in a thousand years, been allowed to forget that he is unwelcome here.There’s a term for games that are ridiculously demanding and yet satisfying to play — it’s becoming a little dated now, but we used to call that “Nintendo hard.” These days, Nintendo focuses on expanding gaming’s fanbase beyond its existing demographics, and there’s nothing wrong with that; anybody criticizing a game for being accessible or “casual” is a little boy trying to keep the other kids out of his clubhouse, and destroying his own hobby so he can feel superior. There was a time, though, when Nintendo was known more for making games that wanted you DEAD. There’s an appeal to that, if the game is well-designed, as the wild success of games like Dark Souls can attest. But the game must be well-designed — it can’t be hard because it’s obtuse, badly balanced, responds sluggishly or unpredictably, communicates poorly or lies to the player. That’s the kind of hard that makes a gamer quit, not the kind that makes her grit her teeth and reload from the last checkpoint.Hades is Nintendo hard, in the most beautiful way. So much of this is gamefeel — the experience of maneuvering around the world, the responsiveness of the character, the speed and elegance of the animation. Rewarding progress with power is one thing, but starting a player off limping feels punitive in a roguelike game where you’re always restarting — and Zagreus never feels weak. He fights like a god from the first step he takes, and grows more powerful from there, and the challenge scales accordingly. This scaling isn’t just bigger numbers, either. Too often, “New Game Plus” just means another zero tacked on the end of all your stats, and the only difference between “Normal” and “Hard” is that enemies have twice as much health in hard mode. And you can do that, in Hades, if you want — make the numbers bigger if it embiggens your… enjoyment.But you can also cause the Hydra that spat fire at you from the sidelines to hop right out of the lava and chase you on its dangling neck-stump, if that sounds more fun. Face Theseus and the Bull in Elysium’s arena enough times, and you’ll realize that raising the difficulty here actually makes Theseus easier to hit — he jumps into a chariot to charge you, but doesn’t carry a shield and block all damage from the front anymore. This is active, thoughtful game design, and it requires active, thoughtful play in response. You often find yourself wrecking shop through Tartarus and Asphodel, only to discover that your build is atrocious when facing a single, huge enemy, or you have no good strategy for dealing with armor. You have to adapt to what you find and when you fail. You fail more often than not.And yet failing never feels like a waste of your time. Only got as far as Asphodel before you stood in the fire while picking your nose and contemplating your build? (I’m in this picture and I don’t like it.) It’s fine, you got a fistful of gems that you can use to change the draperies in the hallway for the fourth time this week. I change ’em every time the option comes up; hearing Dad whine about it is worth ten gems a day to me. Even if you only made it to Meg before she spanked you (which you love, and you know it), so long as you ran into Sisyphus, you’re doing meaningful work out there in hell.The most wonderful thing is, often that work is just bringing a little joy to someone who sure as hell doesn’t deserve it. That’s the Supergiant special sauce — their complicated, flawed, heartfelt characters — and there’s not a single one in Hades I don’t want to cuddle all night long. Except maybe Dad. F*** you, Dad. But everybody else… I can’t tell who’s been in Zagreus’s bed and who hasn’t (my current ship list includes Meg and possibly all her sisters, Thanatos, Achilles, and Skelly, don’t judge me), but everyone I meet feels real, and like their life is bigger than just our interaction in this moment. They make bad choices; they’re emotional and shortsighted; they don’t always do what I want them to do. Sometimes I work very hard to help someone… and nothing changes, it doesn’t help. That’s sad, and frustrating, and most game devs haven’t got the courage to do it, because the Skinner box of “Do Hard Thing -> Get Reward” is so fundamental to gaming.Not every game needs to be a slot machine, though. Gaming can offer many kinds of experiences, nuanced with emotional and mechanical challenge, and Hades is one of them. It appeals to me as a profoundly absurdist experience: there is no win state, no possibility of escape. The only control you have in this universe is the ability to choose, to try when you know all too well you can’t succeed. It’s an irony wrapped in an irony — an unfinished game more beautiful and involved than many finished games; a journey that you can start a thousand times and never, ever finish; a fundamentally pointless and futile fight that, by its very existence and our choice to participate in it, rejects that futility. We know where this story ends… but we’re gonna tell it again. Smash that button and start over, because somewhere deep down inside, you and Zagreus believe the same thing: despite all the evidence of your eyes and the blood you’ve shed, despite every soul in the universe who insists it’s impossible… we’re going to win one day. Never know when it’s going to be. Just have to keep trying.

_childDocuments_.review: John F. Kennedy, the 35th president of the United States, was assassinated on Friday, November 22, 1963, at 12:30 p.m. CST in Dallas, Texas, while riding in a presidential motorcade through Dealey Plaza. Kennedy was in the vehicle with his wife, Jacqueline, Texas Governor John Connally, and Connally's wife, Nellie, when he was fatally shot from the nearby Texas School Book Depository by Lee Harvey Oswald, a former US Marine. Governor Connally was seriously wounded in the attack. The motorcade rushed to Parkland Memorial Hospital, where Kennedy was pronounced dead about 30 minutes after the shooting; Connally recovered.About 70 minutes after Kennedy and Connally were shot, Oswald was arrested by the Dallas Police Department and charged under Texas state law with the murders of Kennedy and of J. D. Tippit, a Dallas police officer. At 11:21 a.m. on November 24, 1963, as live television cameras covered Oswald being moved through the basement of Dallas Police Headquarters, he was fatally shot by Dallas nightclub operator Jack Ruby. Like Kennedy, Oswald was also taken to Parkland Memorial Hospital, where he soon died. Ruby was convicted of Oswald's murder, though it was later overturned on appeal, and Ruby died in prison in 1967 while awaiting a new trial.After a 10-month investigation, the Warren Commission concluded that Oswald assassinated Kennedy, that Oswald had acted entirely alone, and that Ruby had acted alone in killing Oswald. Kennedy was the eighth and most recent US president to die in office, and the fourth (following Lincoln, Garfield, and McKinley) to be assassinated. Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson automatically became president upon Kennedy's death.In its 1979 report, the United States House Select Committee on Assassinations (HSCA) agreed with the Warren Commission that Oswald's three rifle shots caused the injuries that Kennedy and Connally sustained. After analysis of a dictabelt audio recording the HSCA concluded that Kennedy was likely "assassinated as a result of a conspiracy". The committee could not identify a second gunman or group involved in the possible conspiracy, although the HSCA concluded that analysis pointed to the existence of an additional gunshot and "a high probability that two gunmen fired at [the] President".The U.S. Justice Department concluded active investigations and stated "that no persuasive evidence can be identified to support the theory of a conspiracy" in the assassination. However, Kennedy's assassination is still the subject of widespread debate and has spawned numerous conspiracy theories and alternative scenarios. Polls conducted from 1966 to 2004 found that up to 80 percent of Americans suspected that there was a plot or cover-up. The assassination was the first of four major assassinations of the 1960s in the United States, coming two years before the assassination of Malcolm X in 1965, and five years before the assassinations of Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert F. Kennedy in 1968.

_childDocuments_.review: I admit, I saw the word "Rogue-lite" on the page and my first reaction was to run away. That was a mistake. This game is excellent: easy to pick up, and easy to break away from. The music is great, the writing and voice acting are both witty and heartfelt, and the randomly-generated map somehow keeps the game from feeling like a grind (even though it is).For those unaware, the standard roguelike is incredibly difficult, requiring the player to memorize the map and get creative with whatever items the game decides to give you to avoid permadeath. Hades does a few things to make things easier. First, all items are useful. Second, the map is random; you don't have to learn which areas are more difficult by trial and error. Third, you get XP to use on skills, which are permanent. Each time you die, you go right back to the start, but those skills gradually make the game easier to beat.

_childDocuments_.review: This game does not respect your time, play it for a few hours and if you don't love the gameplay *stop* and watch the rest of the story/character interactions online.I love SGG's writing but in Hades it is drip fed to the player so slowly it's excruciating. To beat the game and unlock half of the character interactions you have to complete a 'run', in terms of a rogue-like, 10 times; I hit 30 hours and 40 attempts before I bit the bullet and installed a 100x damage mod and even then it took another 3 hours to reach the credits. _childDocuments_.review: It is safe to say that Hades is the rogue-like game I enjoyed the most by a long shot out of any other I've played so far. Here is why:As engaging as the gameplay might be, Hades is far more than a simple video game experience. It shows extraordinary development in terms of story, characters, hub world customisation, "post-game" content, and difficulty. Packed into one term this game could be defined as: Progression. Peak progression, to be fair. Honestly, it is that good, you feel immersed as if you were Zagreus himself, you feel like the incantation of "escape from hell". If this is as far as video games, especially rogue-likes can go, we've truly reached the top. No other singleplayer game has made me come back to it over and over nearly as many times as in this case, even though the mechanics stay the same and you'll have eventually found your weapon or weapons of choice. You'll keep on doing it again, fighting and escaping one more time, and then again, and then you say to yourself: "Alright, this will be my last run", well, it is not. Because Hades' world wraps its setting, music, characters and progression around you and it makes you eager to know it all, to dive deep into Greek mythology. You'll want to help loved ones who were separated by death, you'll want to find love for yourself, you'll want to become friends with a boulder (you'll find out eventually if you have not yet), and once you are fully invested in its world, the game opens up even more and reveals all its lore and gameplay options for the post-game. Over 100 hours into it and still I have not seen everthing there is to see and unlocked every single bit of dialogue there is to unlock. I will keep going, I will keep escaping hell. Because the game makes me want to do it. Supergiant Games deserve every last bit of praise they can get, as they created not only a rogue-like game that keeps on giving, but a story that keeps on going. Hades 2 is my most anticipated game of the year by far, and honestly, I wouldn't mind seeing Hades 3 one day, or even expand on the Norse mythology in future titles. I'll be there. Thanks for reading. Now go ahead, talk to Skelly, pick your weapon, and beat your father's butt. And don't you dare to forget to pet best boy Cerberus!

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5)I first played Hades on the Nintendo Switch, and I enjoyed it so much that I purchased it again on the Steam Deck. It's the perfect game for Valve's hefty li'l handheld and, before I knew it, I had pumped in ~147hrs into it. Nearly every minute of those roughly six days was a joy to play. I say "nearly" because there is a significant element of RNG and, while this adds to making each run different and fun, it proved to be a bit of a pain when I hit a string of bad RNG luck tracking down a certain chamber for my last achievement. I don't hold it against Hades, however, as any other players could feasible get lucky and frequently run into those chambers without even trying. In any case, the characters are all charming and I'd venture to go as far as stating that they are what make the game so great. Zagreus, Megaera, Nix, Dusa, Achilles, and even all of the Olympians themselves are such well-written characters and it's SO fun getting to know all of them. Each character's personality is so distinct and draws you into a unique take on the grand world of ancient Greek religion. But that's not all the game has to offer; the action is superb and the sheer amount of content and unlockables are mind-boggling. This is, simply put, the best rogue-like game I've played so far and I am really excited to see what SGG has to offer for Hades II.If you haven't already played this gem and are on the fence about purchasing it, I say go for it. Even at full price Hades is 100% worth it. Go carve a swathe of destruction throughout the underworld to reach the surface. Or you can try...there is no escape, after all!

_childDocuments_.review: Coming off of a nearly 70-hour marathon of this game over my week of owning it, I can safely say as a preface that Hades is a very enjoyable game with a lot to offer for an extremely affordable price. An excellent roguelike action game with tremendously well-written characters, beautiful evocative music, and fulfilling action and challenge make for a game suited perfectly to someone who wants something to get lost in for a long time.+The gameplay is stellar, controls are tight and everything feels very intentional. It's a fine line between speed and impossible-to-follow chaos, and Hades walks that line perfectly by maintaining a level of both fluidity and maneuverability that you'll find yourself feeling like an anime badass very early on.+The characters and story are so beautifully written that you may even forgive a few deaths just because you got to have another conversation with Dusa, Achilles, or Nyx. Great inter-personal stories dot the main questline and make the game feel very full and complete, and each character feel dynamic and alive.+Beautiful artwork and knowledge of Greek mythology fill the entire game with a feel of authenticity and charm, along with making mythology buffs feel very smart and clever (like me).-It's hard. It's really hard. Even with the provided "God Mode" option, players not accustomed to action games will not be able to clear the story that's frankly too good to be locked behind the immense challenge of beating the game nearly a dozen times.-Post-game is lacking. After you complete the story, there's little to do except aim for 100% completion of character stories, sidequests, and weapon upgrades. With the main story out of the way, a certain adversarial feeling the game emanates fades away, leaving one to feel like the only things left to do are busywork - a point all but acknowledged and conceded by the story's framing of the post-game. To accentuate this flaw...-Variation is somewhat lacking for a roguelike. Six weapons, nine (ten-ish) gods, 25 keepsakes, and a slew of randomized Boons and Weapon Upgrades sounds like a lot of content, but not when you'll be needing to do a hundred or more runs to achieve post-game content. You'll be finding yourself falling into patterns a lot with very few X-factors shaking up established routines, especially since the game has no variance in bosses, and only a handful of room designs per level.As a story-centric experience and an action game, Hades is an absolute must-have and must-play, especially for its remarkably low price tag.In this regard alone, Hades earns a 9.5/10 in my book. It's well worth the time and effort to play through it.However as a replayable roguelike, I give the game a passing grade of 7/10.  Replayability is low with few incentives and not much variation to make each run feel unique or unpredictable.Overall, I'd give it a solid 8.5/10. A fantastic, long-lasting game that only starts to wear and fatigue when you strive for 100% completion.

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore my hours played, I have 200+ hrs on my switch copy.I love this game. It's not my favorite game ever (I'm one of those weirdos that played Xenogears at that perfect impressionable time in life, so it will always be my favorite), but I 100% believe Hades is the greatest game ever made. I can come back to Hades anytime, and have a blast. This is the only game that as an adult, I can still catch myself up playing at 2am and saying to myself, "dude, you need to go to bed... ok one more run I swear".  I am not good enough with words to explain just how much I love this game.But I'll try to explain it like this:I have never been a real hardcore gamer. I've never really been the type to keep playing a game in an attempt to improve at it. I usually find my ceiling in a game pretty quickly, and I'm content with that. As long as I'm having fun I don't care, and since I hardly play multiplayer games who cares if I'm not "good". Hades is the only game I've noticed myself gradually getting better and better at over time. I'm no freak. I still have many many heats left to go, and a lot of weapon aspects I still suck with. The thing is though, I'm not getting better at it because I'm actively trying to learn the game, and get better. It's because I enjoy playing the game so much that I just naturally do get better. I don't know. Like I said, me no word good, but I do own 3 copies of this game if that means anything. The only other game I've done that with is Catherine, and one of those is the remake.Anyway, 100 out of 10. This game knocks it out of the park in every aspect. Can't wait for 2.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of roguelikes, but was going to pass on Hades because hack-and-slash gameplay is not really my thing. But a friend recommended it to me because of Dusa's storyline, and I have to say I love it. All of it. The voice acting is phenomenal, the art is beautiful, and the game's mechanics are integrated seamlessly into the story. I love that you're encouraged to try all of the different weapons and boons, and that there's no one correct way to build Zagreus's abilities from one run to the next. I love the inclusion of God Mode; I would not have made any sort of progress without it because of my aforementioned lack of talent with the hack-and-slash genre. But I also love that you still have to work at it: with the damage reduction capped at 80%, you can still die with God Mode enabled. I love that there's a LOT of content in the game even after the completion of the main quest; I finished the main quest at ~60 hours in, and I haven't unlocked the epilogue yet.But what got me to write this, my first-ever review, was technical help from Ellis in Supergiant's support department. I had to email Supergiant when my cat walked over my keyboard and it seemed my save data had been corrupted. He was able to diagnose that no, my save was not corrupted, it was safe, but that the game was looking for a nonexistent second profile. He sent me instructions for how to fix the problem, and I'm back to the game with no loss of progress.Hades is a great game, both from the story perspective to the people behind it. I nominated it for Game of the Year.

_childDocuments_.review: A fairly common problem I find amongst Rogue-lite games is the feeling of stagnation. Games in this genre are meant to feel different from run-to-run and must have tangible power progression that is frequently felt.Hades is an example of a Rogue-lite that delivers on the genre perfectly. No two runs are the same, and after almost every run you are barraged with a fleet of new upgrades, dialogues, vanity items and story elements. The aforementioned story elements are what really set Hades apart from other similar games for me. The story is compelling and lengthy, where every single character has their role and unique and charming (or not so charming) personality. What's more. even once you complete what is described as the 'main story', there is still much story to be explored in the form of quests for various characters and an epilogue of sorts.The gameplay does exactly what it needs to, asking you questions constantly and testing the full depth of your ever-changing arsenal. You can even augment the gameplay in many ways later in the game, providing that extra challenge and even more unique feel to the various encounters on the 4 floors you must climb through to escape.Hades also has the benefit of a great soundtrack, whether it be heavier tracks in combat or more solemn songs for story moments. And along with soundtrack is a distinct art style, with clear but impressive animations.For anyone that likes Rogue-lite games, Hades is a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited for finishing the main story to review it, then I waited for the epilogue, then I waited for 100% achievements on steam and I think it's now time to just do it.Hades is a good game, it makes you want to play more from start to finish and after 81 hours it still feels fresh. It doesn't have the biggest revolutionary and artistic story, but at the same time that's fine. The game is focused on being fun to play and on top of that the story brings much more than your average game focused on gameplay. The game tells this story in it's gameplay and this pacing feels very natural, the world and story feel like it's happening naturally based on things you do in the gameplay and nothing feels forced.That's it, it's a good game, and while I wouldn't call it one of the best games of all time like some others would. There haven't been many games that made me want to come back and play it more like Hades did.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally 100% the steam achievements, and I can honestly say this might be my game of the decade.What makes me love this game the most is the voice acting, and it gets even more incredible once you see the cast. At least half of them have more than one voice (one doing upwards of 6, Logan Cunningham is a voice acting god), and I would have never noticed if it wasn't for the credits. Also, with 55 hours on the switch, and 83 on steam, I have hardly heard any repeating voice lines, and that alone is a feat, but with how top notch it all is makes it that much more unique. Then there is the gameplay. Somehow it takes a highly repetitive game, and actually keeps you engaged. Typically, these kind of roguelikes start to lose me if the game is too repetitive with not much change, but this one manages to do it. The build crafting has a lot of depth to it, and the actual gameplay is very satisfying to perfect. The difficulty scaling is also brilliant. Early on, it is a punishing game that you start to learn, making it farther and farther each time, while unlocking more permanent powers to help you try and escape, giving you more and more of a fighting chance. As you get better and the base difficulty is not that much of a challenge, you can scale the difficulty with your skill, making it slowly harder and harder for yourself while you get better and better at the game, making you want to push for new heights and see how good you can get. The difficulty slider is also way better than most games difficulties, most games just increase the health and damage of enemies. While those are options, there are also a plethora of other options, potentially making each run a little more unique of a challenge. I could go on all day about how much I love this game, and will recommend it to everyone, not just people looking for a roguelike. The story sometimes makes it not even feel like a roguelike. Even failures push the story forward, and after almost 100 runs, I am still finding more and more dialogue with the NPCs in the House of Hades. Thank you, Supergiant Games for this masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: You're sick of it, aren't you? You're sick of games yoinking your hard-earned money and handing you a roadmap with your receipt. Open worlds full of nothing, missing systems, always having to compromise your expectations to enjoy them. Hades is the panacea for the ails of the modern game industry. An action roguelite that gives you so much enjoyment for the pricetag that it almost makes you uneasy. The developers clearly love the genre, as the systems of Weapons mixing with Blessings create an incredible number of possibilities. It has honestly felt like these types of games haven't really evolved much since The Binding of Isaac, but here is Hades to open a new decade, bringing all that excitement each run with a coat of paint and charm that means your eyes have to make no compromises. Artistically, the game is polished to a shine. It carves out it's own style that is never silly or lazy, the tone and art fit each other like peas in a pod. The characters are all fully voice acted, and at many points in the game you'll stop and think to yourself "Wow, they recorded a line for that?" The story is cleverly spliced to fit in with your progression through the game, and you'll be as excited to play the next run to see what happens next, and develop your relationships with the cast, as you will be to find a new build. My nitpicks are all minor, perhaps a few tooltips that could be helpful, a few story beats I would have liked more agency in, but if you love the roguelike genre and have been feeling like nothing is scratching that itch, this is it. If you also love Greek Mythology and the story resonates with you (it has some honestly emotional moments, in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ roguelike), this might be the best game you've ever played. The gameplay can be hard, but keep at it, it just takes patience, and there is a "God Mode" if you want to experience the story but can't reliably beat the game. Supergiant deserves your 20 dollars, and your thanks.

_childDocuments_.review: I never understood why this game had Overwhelmingly Positive reviews until I played it myself. This game sets the bar for rogue-likes. You will die. A LOT. However, I think that's the point. Each time you die, something happens. You might learn more about certain characters or the story, you may get some (often mocking) advice on what you did wrong and how to improve or even some sort of event can occur every now and then. Each run feels different, and never feels too grindy, as you unlock different weapons with completely different play styles, as well as tons of upgrades which make you just a little bit stronger after each run. There is a ton of variety in the upgrades you receive during the run, too, with each Olympian God you meet having a different set and theme for their upgrades. There is loads and loads of content. I still haven't seen it all. One more thing, the amount of dialogue in the game is absolutely ASTOUNDING! With all of my play time I still have never heard the same line spoken more than once (no joke)! This game is easily my favorite rogue-like of all time! It's a must buy!

_childDocuments_.review: By far the best Roguelike game I've ever played, it never manages to feel repetitive because of the vast amount of characters and dialogue which slowly builds the story and your character as you complete each run.I can tell I'm nearing 100% completion at my current playtime of 80 hours but I still have almost never heard a single line be repeated, I'm still discovering new things and my enjoyment definitely hasn't stagnated. If anything I just wish there was DLC to buy!There's not a whole lot of levels and a run can take anywhere from 30-50 minutes depending on your speed but yet every single run can feel so very different because of the insane amount of options you can chose from. The art-style being so pretty is a plus too.Anyone interested by Greek mythology will also enjoy the story, it includes some very famous characters and plots but also some lesser known ones such as you being Hades' son Zagreus whom most people probably never heard of before. I know I certainly never did before this game.I found myself hitting up Google after some conversations because I couldn't believe it was from actual Greek mythology and not made up by the developers but so far it's very faithful to it, which is very impressive. Don't know what much else to say other than the soundtrack being great and same with the voice-acting. 10/10 game in my book. I would love to see this same setup with Norse mythology!

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of fun, likeable characters, compelling story. Excellent game.There is a way that roguelikes tend to be for people like me, who often aren't compelled to play again and again by the gameplay alone, and Hades takes care of this very well using their story. Every character you meet has a story and dialogue that can be unlocked as you play again and again. Making it to the surface is about more than just beating the game again, it's about getting to learn more about why you're going to the surface in the first place. You want to play not just to win, you also want to see what comes next.

Set in the depths of the underworld, players embark on a thrilling journey as the prince of the underworld, Zagreus, battling through hordes of mythical creatures to escape his father's realm. _childDocuments_.review: I bought it just before its full release and even then was enjoying it.  The music is absolutely breathtaking, the art style is beautiful. _childDocuments_.review: A great game. The core combat mechanics are quite fun, although if that isn't your jam then it probably won't stick for you. There's a wide variety of weapons with different characteristics, and a whole lot of abilities (boons) that change how you have to fight and tactics you need to employ. And each of the different weapons are all fun to use in their own right, and on top of that can be modified later in the game for even more options. I really liked the story-telling aspects, it'll even teach you a little bit of Greek mythology. I think that's what really pulls this game above just being a fun gameplay loop, characters are entertaining and you want to learn more about them as you play. I like the variety available, for me it doesn't quite reach the heights of Binding of Isaac, but certainly makes up for it in character, and the core combat loop is exquisite.Played on Deck, handles perfectly, although it might be a bit too zoomed out for some people.

_childDocuments_.review: Hades rules.The game is a roguelike par excellence. The number of weapon variants you have and the unique perks offered by each god's boons allows for each run to feel, while tracing through the same areas, completely different in approach.The gameplay itself is also fast-paced and exciting, and the availability of God Mode (which I didn't use) and the Heat system makes tinkering the difficulty to your own liking effortless....but the real draw of Hades, in my opinion, is the characters. Zagreus is an eminently likeable dork, and the cast of gods and heroes are a delight to interact with and watch their stories. I'd definitely recommend this one to basically anyone who's a fan of action games and roguelikes. Blood and darkness, baby!

_childDocuments_.review: Why are you reading this review? Buy it already!As a certified Percy Jackson kid back in the day, hearing about a game that was based in greek mythology was very exciting. I got to the party kind of late but when I finally started a few days ago, I was hooked in the first few hours.The story is pretty good. The plot won't blow your mind but it is exciting enough to provide a motivation to keep playing besides the gameplay. The huge variety of well designed characters and their well done voice acting support the dry sense of humor and I found myself chuckling over a piece of dialogue more than once. The genius part of Hades design, in my opinion, lies in the fact how to the story is tied to the gameplay. When you're successful, you're rewarded with a part of the story and it really gives you a feeling of progress. When you fail, you at least got a little bit stronger get some fun interactions with side characters and can just try again. Even after "beating" the game for the first time, the story itself is good enough to want you to keep going.The rogue like gameplay is really great and fun. Hades reminded me of a mobile game in the best way. Just like the old school games like Temple Run or Doodle Jump are centered around simple mechanics that are fun when you execute them correctly, Hades doesn't overwhelm you with complex combos or anything like that. the gameplay is centred around doing the same thing over and over but in a diffrent way. It feels like going to school, sometimes you take the bus, sometimes you walk, sometimes your parents take you in their car. And then, from time to time, their is a new bully in the school bus, then you buy new shoes and can run faster, and then sometimes lits your parents car on fire. What I am trying to say with this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ metaphor is that the game provides enough variety to make every run feel a little unique, so even after multiple hours, you will find yourself using a playstyle that you never did before.All in all, I can just encourage everyone to buy this game. It is worth the price and I'm sure that everyone, from "cut-scene skippers" to J-RPG players can have fun with this!

_childDocuments_.review: I would like, in some time, for the designers of this game to write a book on how they worked out the mechanics and progress triggers of this game. The way the NPCs make note of what's happening game-to-game shows that a LOT of intelligent design work went into how they want you to feel as you progress towards your ultimate goal.  This is a beautiful example of a nearly perfect Roguelike:- The combat is intense but consistently fair- Progression and the development of characters is perhaps the best I've ever seen in this genre- Even after a hundred hours, there is still the feeling of "what will I find next?"- The writing and voice work deserves awards. These are characters that behave as immortals would; with all of the time in the world to become more like themselves, the writing conveys their senses of purpose as well as their trappings and exposes lore at a consistent pace that seems utterly bottomless. I think many can see a bit of themselves in each lesser and greater god they encounter.The game itself, is beautiful. The art and music are profoundly fitting for the setting. There's a muse around that I simply hung around with so that my wife could learn her song on the guitar. This game is already worth more than twice the money I've paid for it, and it doesn't even have an ending yet.This is a rare entry in the top tier of Roguelikes along with Isaac and Enter the Gungeon. I -strongly- recommend playing the absolute hell out of it.

_childDocuments_.review: When a game is so universally praised that it becomes revered as one of the greatest of all time, I tend to be hesitant. I like for my opinions to come from a place other than hype and will tend to visit these games once the hype is gone. So once I did this for Hades, I wound up kicking myself because it was exactly as good as everyone had said it was.A simple run through the game's four floors is but a microscopic glimpse into the sheer depth of its content. Beating Hades himself is not where this game ends, 'cause you'll be up to your knees in side quests, unraveling the game's lore, remodeling the House of Hades, romancing the Underworld's denizens, experimenting with different load outs, tackling the pact of punishment, and discovering the absolute magnitude of unique dialogue there is to hear from some of the most charming and lovable characters to be portrayed in Greek mythology. There is so much to see and do that it feel like an immaculate flex of creativity!And of course, the gameplay is a boatload of fun. The game expects you to fail. In fact, it expects you to fail A LOT, but the way it masterfully handles your progression makes it truly feel like you're defying the odds with Olympus on your side. Then there's mixing boon combinations with your weapons of choice all while relentless hordes of hell's servants try to stop you, which makes the combat feel addicting as sin. There's just so many things it does right that make your time playing it feel like a power fantasy!You'll barely find roguelikes as good, if not better, than this. If you've ever wanted to stick it to the god of the Underworld with phenomenal gameplay and an outstanding cast, don't hesitate. Play Hades.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not just a great game, but the greatest roguelike game of all time. I'm normally not a huge fan of this genre, and I was on the fence of buying this game but after seeing all the amazing reviews I just had to try this. And boy, am I glad I did! This is also my personal game of the year for 2020. Supergiant Games have truly outdone themselves and set an industry standard for what roguelike games should be. Let's break down the review below:-StoryYou play as Zagreus-son of Hades who has been kept in the Underworld since his birth my Hades himself. He never knew or met his mother, and therefore he wants to go in the world above in search for her. But this is no easy task as Tartarus is filled with monstrous creatures and godlike beings who guard the passage to the ground above. Zagreus will have to conquer the multiple regions of the Underworld such as Tartarus, Asphodel, Temple of Styx etc. Each region contains the undead wretched beings of the Underworld as well as Godlike beings that await Zagreus at the end of each regions such as the Sisters Of Furies. Zagreus receives boons from the Gods above in Olympus to aid in his journey. Each attempt Zagreus makes to escape the Underworld unlocks more story elements about the inhabitants of the universe. Overall it's a well crafted story with meticulously researched references to Greek mythology and witty dialogues.-Visuals and character/environment designThe art style is gorgeous. The character design is absurdly good. They are colorful, unique and oozes out personality. The likes of Zagreus, Nyx, Megaera etc have incredible character and costume design which gives a different dimension to their personality. The environment is beautifully crafted and each region have a unique set of color pallet which sets the regions apart and portray the state of the regions. This game is the perfect example that graphics do not necessarily need to be "realistic looking" or have the AAA graphics to appear gorgeous and beautiful. It's the creativity of the artist that truly makes a game shine.-GameplayAh, the gameplay. Where Hades truly shines. I don't even know where to begin with this. The combat is incredibly fast paced and requires quite a bit of skill to master. Zagreus has access to an arsenal of godlike weapons. Each weapons have their unique combat animations and special attacks. On top of it, you can gain boons from the Gods of Olympus which interacts uniquely with each weapon. This gives countless forms of playstyles which will bring you back to the game again and again. Due to the nature of the fast paced combat along with many different boons you get from the Gods which applies uniquely to each of Zagreus's weapons, the game ensures that each playthrough and escape attempt will feel unique and exciting. There's a wide varities of enemies with their own attack moves and animations which makes each levels fun and challenging. You will always have to be on the move and on your toes to dodge/deflect enemy abilities while unleashing your Godlike powers and Godlike weapons, making it an exhilarating experience. -AI and level designThis game has procedurally generated levels that shift and change with each attempt. The levels are fun and has a lot of environmental effects such as lava field, traps etc which you can use to your advantage (may also cause your death). For a roguelike game, the AI is surprisingly clever. Archers will position themselves behind traps and walls, and will dash away from you to create distance. Tank enemies will charge you down, while casters will always keep their distance behind them. -Voice acting and Sound designThe voice acting in this game is absolutely stellar. Every character has their personality oozing through the voice acting. I particularly love Zagreus's and Megaera's voice acting. Sound design is brilliant too, each weapon has unique sound effects and combat sounds are very good too.Overall, I tried looking for faults in this game have but there's next to none. This game is incredibly polished and meticulously designed. I wish this game comes out on Xbox/PS as well, more people need to experience this. I would be heavily disappointed if this doesn't win Steam/PC GOTY.

_childDocuments_.review: My review of Hades after 100 hours and completing 100%:✓ PROS and ✖ CONS:✓ Excellent, responsive and fluent gameplay✓ A TON of gameplay altering effects and weapons which make every run unique✓ Increasing the "Pacts" allows you to tailor the difficulty exactly to your liking✓ Insane replay value✓ The art design is absolutely beautiful and inspiring✓ Great audio and VA✓ Great sense of humor ☺✓ The synergies between different boons and gods are amazing✓ Fun game to speedrun (Disclaimer: some builds are way more OP than others)✖ The story was fairly basic✖ After a while the dialogue becomes really banal and the characters have nothing interesting to say✖ The romance subplots are really tame and unfold into nothing interesting✖ The quest system is incredibly rigid and time-consuming(It can take dozens of hours to get a certain quest completed, because sometimes you can't find the right NPC or they won't talk to you about the right thing. Completing the quest with Achilles and Patroclus took me almost entire 100 hours.)Verdict:Hades is an absolutely fantastic game, but if you're looking to 100% the game like I did, you'll probably run into frustration with the quest system and how long it takes to unlock certain story-related things. Otherwise, you'll have a great time with this.4 out of 5 Pomegranates ◍◍◍◍

_childDocuments_.review: To be perfectly honest, Hades had reached a point where so many people had talked about it that I wasn't really interested in playing it. Similar to what probably happened for Undertale and Helltaker to some people, tons of people saying this was an amazing game without ever elaborating on why and spreading memes about it everywhere left me kind of disillusioned on wanting to ever play it. It doesn't help that I personally didn't really care for Bastion, feeling as it was overhyped as well back when it first came out. It is to my pleasure to say that I was wrong for thinking this on all accounts and after buying Hades on sale during christmas I think this is probably my game of the year 2020.Beyond the art being fantastic, music being extremely well done, and the  being beautifully voice acted, Hades finally manages to bridge the "pick up and play" nature of roguelikes with the deep experiences of heavier story based games. It's the first rogue-lite i've ever played that felt like a full game experience; what I mean by that is that roguelikes generally feel like some entertainment you get for a few hours at a time and not something cohesive (for better or for worse). While there's no commitment to roguelikes (for example I have to be in the right mood to play a story based game), it also never really feels like i'm playing something immersive or rich with experiences. That's fine and i'm ok with it, but Hades is the first game to do both and get it right. I could get home after work and just start up Hades and not give a crap because it has that quick pick up and play feel, yet every time I'd play there would be more story bits to uncover... and even after completing the game I feel like I'm only half finished with all of it! The amount of dialogue between characters is stunning, and while the plot is relatively light and not super interesting, the family of gods and those around them is what steals the show. On my 30th escape attempt or so, and the fifteenth or so fight with the second boss, Zagreus gives him a nickname and it changes the boss's health bar. A funny gag I thought, but it permanently changes for the rest of the game. Stuff like this made every playthrough enjoyable and always made me want to progress further to see what kind of unexpected development could happen.That's not to say the gameplay isn't stellar either. It's a standard hack and slash game, but each weapon you can choose from has great synergy and flows well with the various upgrade trees you can find throughout the underworld. New stuff unlocks extremely frequently and unexpectedly, and even if you don't finish a run you still will gather resources to take back home and level up various skills to make the next run that much stronger. While the game does have some of that notorious rogue-lite "permanent upgrade grind" later on with things costing a ridiculous amount, it doesn't really matter since the world and characters change and evolve so much outside of that and things keep randomly changing that you'll find yourself going to play "just one more run" over and over again. If I have any issue with the game I feel like the difficulty curve was weird, but it's relatively minor. Once you "beat" a run once it is easy to do it almost every single escape attempt afterwards. But before that it is very hard and you will struggle quite a bit. In retrospect I don't really mind this since I still enjoyed struggling to escape from the underworld for my very first time, but it did feel a bit weird to me how much easier everything got after I had done it once. Other than that I'd say Hades is pretty much a perfect game. Don't miss out on this one if you like rogue-lites and want something character rich and extremely detailed.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a Supergiant game, so you know it's tight, pretty to look at and beautifully scored. It's a roguelike whose narrative ties very nicely into the structure of the genre. The game is full of character, voiced wonderfully, backed by a fantastic soundtrack and pretty visuals, but there's just not enough there for me to warrant playing it 10 times to get an ending. Some people can I know, but I find myself looking at things like this and Binding of Isaac and wondering where people find the motivation to do the same thing for hours on the promise of a cutscene or a new combination of perks and weapons that make big numbers go up. Mind you, I've never been big into MMOs or very stat-grindy games, yet I found myself really enjoying the first wave of roguey games (FTL, Darkest Dungeon) because they do a good job of keeping things fresh and allowing you to forget that you're stuck in a loop. Hades is built around being very aware of the repetitive nature, and the grind is part of the narrative, but you can't help but die so many times that it just feels like playing Pachinko: there's so few buttons it could be a NES game, and eventually it's going to give you enough power-ups that those few buttons score you a win. When I had taken however many deaths to get to the final boss and found out I'm expected to repeat it 10 times with minor mutators, though, I just lost interest.It's an undeniably beautiful game that's responsive and fun to play, and I wholeheartedly recommend it. I feel like I played it through as much as it deserves, and got my money's worth. I guess the grind is there if the game really captivates you, but I fell out of the loop after one go round: there's just too much out there to play nowadays for a game to demand so much of your time that it almost feels arrogant to expect it of you.

_childDocuments_.review: In general, I like it. But I don't think that the game will provide much interest after finishing the epilogue. So, the main strength of it is in its plot, characters, art design, simple combat system.Hades provides you with a very solid mix of action, lore exploring, dialogues and characters progression. The main source of satisfaction for me in this game was the next simple thought: whatever the outcome going to be, there always will be some lore uncovered for me back in the main hub. So even when I died, I haven't felt particularly bad, cause this lore and character progression was perceived by me as consolation prize of some sort. And this is where the game rocks: enjoyable plot progression, character progression in action-packed simple roguelike combat, accessibility for pretty much every player of any skill.By calling combat and difficulty progression simple I mean that it doesn't provide you with new challenges or skills to improve as a player (except for dodging and some timing with attacks), but rather some stats disadvantage. And if it would be the only foundation for the game, it would be pretty mediocre to play. But given that this is a game by Supergiant Games which are famous for their art, deep work on plot and character progression, we get what we actually have in this game.By finishing the main plot and epilogue I call this game accomplished for myself and I would recommend it for casual players who want to get acquanted with roguelike genre with a substantional focus on a plot. If you're hardcore player who enjoy the games like Dead Cells, Curse of the Dead Gods or something similar, the combat system alone won't get you interested at all.

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes the best from Bastion and Transistor and adds a fresh take with how the story/gameplay progresses. This was the reason for my horrible experience, for three reasons:1. It warps the learning curve.2. I'm at 30 hours and not even close to the end (might actually be faster to restart on normal).3. You cannot turn off Hell Mode (even by changing values in the save file).Aside from that, two more major gripes:- The combat comes down to three things ... level, luck, and not messing up. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing game, one of the best I've ever played. The base game is simple and easy to get the hang of, but the game gets harder as you progress. Following the play style of most dungeon crawlers, you will die, respawn, die again, and repeat. If you don't like games where you have to grind in that manner this game might not be for you, though i would still recommend trying it to find out. The story is interesting and progresses naturally as you play the game, without feeling too grindy ( except maybe the very end ). It doesn't take long to complete the "base" storyline, but even after completing the first section there's even more to the story you can progress if you choose. You can unlock weapons, aspects of weapons, abilities, and certain cosmetics as you play. Most are fairly simple to get, while other achievements and unlockables take a LOT of grinding. Each character in the game has their own story arc which makes interacting with the characters even more fun, and developing bonds with the different gods and friends you will meet is one of the best parts of the game imo. You will read some review by people who didn't like the game because of the repetitive loop; well, if you buy a roguelike expecting anything else that's your own fault. It CAN get repetitive at times, but the game never bored me even after I beat it 50 times in a row. Great game for fans of roguelikes and achievement hunters. Great characters ( not you Theseus ), the gameplay is slick and fun, the music is god-tier (pun intended), and the graphics style is one of my favorites. Highly recommend, 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: You like addictive, "30-minute at a time" gameplay? You like listening to some music that slaps? You like an art style that's vibrant and gorgeous to look at, all while giving enough visual clarity to not ♥♥♥♥ with your eyes during gameplay? You like a surprisingly cute and interesting narrative about Greek gods, and this cartoony yet earnest take on Greek myths?Well, look no further, fam. Supergiant's got you covered.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: Reached the true ending of Hades after 33 hours and I have to say this is SuperGiant's best game to date. I thought they outdid themselves when I played Pyre, but Hades combines the fantastic writing of Pyre with exquisite roguelike gameplay. In general, I heavily dislike roguelikes (exceptions being Darkest Dungeon and Dead Cells), so I thought I wouldn't like this game, but SuperGiant proved me wrong.What's so good about the game is you never feel like you have to start over once you die, you always get rewards be it with story exposition, more dialogue, NPCs reacting to the way you just died. You always make progress, you collect stuff in your runs that will make you stronger once you die, the progression system is very good!Music, as always, on SuperGiant games is superb along with narration. This is something you expect will be great before you play a game from this devs, their track record is clean!I hope someday we see a Hades 2 or explore other Olympian Gods, but if we check the devs history they never made sequels, still I will hope!
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: Huh, that's probably one of the few times when I write review of the game before I complete it. But, well, I'm not planning to do so anyway. Hades is a well-crafted rogue-like which is about escaping the underworld. Combat works very well, there are different weapons and different "variations" (called aspects in game) of them. If you are new to rogue-likes or just want some casual 15-20 hrs experience, than this is a good pick for you.My main problem with this game is that it rewards successful escape attempts mostly with storyline progression, not the difficulty changes, like TBoI: Rebirth does, for instance: there are no "extra floors" (idk, route going sideways, alternative versions of floors or whatever), completely new bosses or anything like that (well, at least to the point after finishing the main story there was none). Variety also isn't entirely here: we have roughly 10 enemy types tops per floor making it up to 30 - not very great for a game you want to replay for hundreds of hours. Bosses variation is even worse with ~3 variations in the first floor (not counting "aided versions" as extra ones since movesets are almost exactly the same - it's not a new bossfight). Boons are numerically have high variety (roughtly 200, I believe) but you get them in such abundance that you are likely to see ~80-90% of them in your options after 15-20 hours of you gameplay. So, well, not that great. So, most of these issues seem to be fixable with a bunch of dlc's with extra content, however, at current state, I do not see any actual reason, expect "completitionism" to play this game after you finish the main story and maybe grind for epilogue. Due to the issues I mentioned, my experience was somewhat like this (each number indicate # of escape attempt):1) Die at the end of tartarus2) Finish tartarus, die to hydra3) Kill hydra, die in the middle of elysium4-6) Die some more at elysium7) Reach hades, die to him in the first phase8-10) Some more unsuccessful runs11) Reach hades phase 2, die because of having no idea what was happening12) Kill hades12-24) Successful runs with 1 random death to hades 2nd phase25) End.So basically, once I reached the hades, game stopped from becoming actually harder in any noticeable way. I was basically replaying almost exactly the same game for over 10 times with only difference being that my character becomes stronger with further investments and I become more accustomed to enemies' patterns. So, I don't really see how this game is a goty material, but, well, it is an alright game after all.

_childDocuments_.review: Exhibiting 90's era Blizzard levels of polish, Hades is a game that surpasses its elevator pitch in every conceivable way. I could wax poetic for paragraphs about how Hades is an amalgamation of many obvious influences: Rogue and Diablo chief among them. But to hone in on the shoulders this giant of a game stands on to reach its meteoric heights is to miss what makes it such a colossus in its own right. As such, I'll put it simply:- One of the best isometric ARPG combat systems ever coded- Superb aesthetic so well suited to Greek mythology as to make one wonder how else these characters could be depicted.- A soundtrack that absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ melts faces- The greatest 'downtime' game loop of any game of its kind full stop, with a method of story delivery so surprising and so effective, it threatens to eclipse all of Hades' other monumental achievementsThis game took me completely by surprise. I knew it was going to be good. I didn't think it would be golden age of video games levels of good.

The way they tie the greek myths into everything (including how they spin their deviations from the myths as well) are very well written. _childDocuments_.review: So, after 73 hours of playtime I managed to 100% Hades - best roguelike I have ever played! My favourite aspect of this game is repeatability, no matter how many runs you have completed, you always want to go for another one with different weapons/aspects/keepsakes/companions/mirror setups etc. I would highly recommend Hades for anyone who like to progress and get stronger with time. At the beginning you have to learn the mechanics and movement, die some times (a lot) but after a while you will get hand of this and for sure you are going to like the combat the game offers :) Also, for those of you who like the plots in games, you will not be disappointed ;) 10/10 from me, now can happily move to Hades 2 and spend some unhealthy time there too :D

_childDocuments_.review: I expected nothing less from Supergiant. The visuals are impresive, the art unique, the characters charming and intriguing and of course, the gameplay engaiging and fun. I find the action pretty fluid and the controls tight. There are many weapon options to choose from (with more to come), each with its own play-style.I may be a bit biased concerning that I have a soft spot for Greek mythology, but I find the plot and world building interesting and well connected with the fact that you die all the time. Not that it matters much, being a rogue-like game and all, but for me it's a huge plus.To no one's surprise, the replayability is very high, with many abilities and perks to combine. You can make fun and interesting combos that make the experience unique for every run.The only issue I have is the fps drops that occur sometimes, but being in early access, such things are expected and will be fixed in full release.I really love this game and I'm very excited to see how it develops.

_childDocuments_.review: Art Style: 9/10Gameplay: 6.5/10Music: 5/10Story: 4/10Im fully willing to admit that my dislike of this game could be because it's my first Rogue-Like, but what seemed as a Gold Standard for Rogue-Likes, I was very underwhelmed. The story is really nothing good either, and yes Im comparing it to all the other masterpiece stories I've played because there does not need to be a bad story because of it's art-style or being a rogue-like. _childDocuments_.review: I really have nothing bad to say about Hades and I'm not even a big fan of roguelike/roguelite games. Supergiant knocked it out of the park with this one for sure. Takes something special to make being killed in a roguelike just as enjoyable as succeeding.Voice work is fantastic.Story is great.Gameplay is solid.Variety kept it fresh for a long time.Customizable difficulty is great.Unlocks feel valuable.Only thing I want is more content but I think any game you spend 100+ hours in you're going to want more content for.A+ game, totally worth the buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: Normally I lose interest in these types of games(roguelites) due to the limited story and repetition that often goes beyond typical grinding.  This game has that repetition for sure but what has made it more palatable is the near constant progression of story and flavor dialogue that's injected into every single run I've attempted.  I also don't think I've heard a single piece of repeated dialogue yet despite being 12 or so hours in, even for simple things like picking up boons from the various gods and entities.  Each character seems to have specific lines for each decision you make while in the runs and even those have yet to repeat as far as I'm aware.[This game has the combat Supergiant games is known for.  Solid isometric, action combat that allows you a fair amount of unique styles and ranges to pick from.  The melee and ranged combat are both satisfying and animated beautifully as usual.The backgrounds are absolutely gorgeous, character panels and pretty much everything regarding the visuals is as advertised and is always a high point for me with this company.][Audio is great.  Sound effects, voice over and etc are all to a high standard.  I find some of the distortion over voice lines to be a bit odd but I'm not sure I'd say it detracts from the performance.][Progression is done well.  Each run moves the various parts of story along and you can improve relations with characters via dialogue with them and giving them gifts.  You can skip anything you want to at any time, which is appreciated.][Item Progression mostly is great.  The keepsakes you get from various characters rank up as you use them and provide nice buffs that are maybe a little bit boring(more HP, more backstab damage, etc..) but some do offer some unique effects that honestly just get passed up in favor for the base stat upgrades since there's usually no conditional factors affecting their use.  We need more like "+X% damage reduction to frontal attacks, receive X% more damage from rear attacks".]My only real contention with the game is the unlocking of weapon aspects.  It's linked to a certain aspect of the game and isn't adequately explained as to what you need to do in order to get more.  I also wish there were more varied ways of gaining the upgrade levels without having to play weapons I don't want to use or hoping a certain vendor has it on off while I have enough of the required currency.  That's really it.If you like Supergiants games, I think this is an instant buy, there's a lot of content already and apparently more on the way.Roguelikes/lites I am not a huge fan but I think this a well made, competent RL that has a lot of flavor and interesting mechanics for you to explore.Recommend to anyone halfway interested.  Dusa is bae.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: All of Supergiant's previous games were in the "ALMOST REACHES GREATNESS" category.That is about to change.Hades is a top down rogue like Action RPG in ancient Greece setting, with the art direction showing some anime influence.Supergiant(SG) already had amazing art and writing team. The artistic direction is extremely well designed and the voice talent is suitably appropriate which brings each character to life. The Greek gods have been done to death in other media, so it was important that SG did something different to stand out.But Graphics and Sound design can only carry a game so far. What about the combat? They Nailed that too.The combat engine is possibly one of the best I have ever seen. Its smooth and reactive like Diablo 3 which makes the twitch based gameplay a joy to experience. It must have been a pain to design since they had to balance the player having enough information on screen to react to it without clutter but at the same time make the game visually stunning with explosions and enemies' swipes and projectiles going all over the place, yet they did it.The story is fantastic, and unlike MANY MANY games, actually incorporates the gameplay elements well and never feels like its there to give your character purpose. I will not talk too much about it to avoid spoilers.Normally, Indie games usually have a problem where their work is a labor of love but some elements of design, like Graphics/Sound/Combat, hold them back when compared to their AAA peers. Hades might just be the game that bridges the gap, its a awesome Indie game made by a team that loves their work and that stands up in technical departments with their AAA Rivals.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: Absurdly fun. Playability is super smooth, the story is unusually engaging, the grinding has so far never felt exhausting or tedious, and I've never played any other game that allowed you to fine-tune difficulty levels at late to end game like this one.Hadn't played any game in months, and all of sudden I've sunk eighty hours of this thing in a couple of weeks. The 'just another run' feeling is real.EDIT: Just to add that the Portuguese (BR) localization is pretty weak. Many typos, several really literal translations, little to no creativity, very weak effort to preserve the tone of voice of the source material and a few glaring screw-ups that really destroy the moment. A particular instance of 'goodbye' being translated as 'tchau' ("bye" or "see you") at a very pivotal moment was particularly egregious. This game really required care and dedication to the localization (more like transcreation, really), and the fact it came out so-so to bad like this kinda bummed me out. Missed opportunity, really.

_childDocuments_.review: Hades is my 2020 Game of the year. It's an incredibly innovative mix of story deeply rooted in greek myth (a fave since childhood) and legacy rogue-lite gameplay. Supergiant has been a hitmaker since Bastion. All of their games are worth playing, but this game shows they've taken best lessons learned from each predecessor and combined them into an instant classic. I don't exaggerate when I say I expect this is their Magnus Opus - cheers Supergiant, well done!

_childDocuments_.review: Hades is a fantastic game and an easy pick for my 2020 GOTY.  Supergiant's always had a knack for blending solid action/RPG gameplay with superlative presentation values, and they've outdone themselves this time.  The gameplay is rock solid in the moment to moment action, coupled with a huge variety of ways to build your character and push through on each run.  The game fits into a nice loop of "I'll do one more run" where you spend a few minutes talking with the members of the House of Hades, then a 15-40 minute escape attempt, then back to the House.Outside of the gameplay, the presentation values are impeccable, with an absurd amount of voice acted dialogue (that's incredibly reactive to the situation you're in, including specific lines triggered by things as small as carrying a particular artifact into a boss fight), lovely artwork, and great music.Even if you're not a huge roguelike gamer, Hades is worth a look and will give you a ton of value as you push forward to help Zagreus get to Mt. Olympus.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played any other dungeon runner type games and I probably wouldn't have tried this if a friend hadn't gotten it for me as a gift. I'm really glad they did! The 'god mode' setting means it scales to a difficulty that suits my play style and the amount of time I have to play it, which means I got to get through the whole plot, which was really enjoyable and the primary reason I kept playing. _childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: There is a bit of a learning curve, but instead of punishing you for it, Hades keeps gently prodding you and encouraging you to keep going. I'm not usually a fan of rogue-likes - when they get too tough or too stressful I shutdown and stop playing. However, I love dungeon crawlers (Diablo was my ♥♥♥♥ as a child), and I am happy to report that this game is very forgiving towards people, like me, who hate to die. With every death comes a new little bit of the story or a new tweak or change to something that ramps up the intrigue and keeps you engaged. Sometimes I even look forward to dying just so I can experience new conversations with the wide variety of characters.In addition, this game is absolutely stunning. Quite possibly one of the most visually stimulating games of all time. It's a work of art.Buy this game. It's worth every penny.

_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: Hades is a must play.For anyone who hasn't already seen or heard anything about this game, I can do nothing but recommend playing it. A beautiful blend of action, setting, narrative, music, and character create a wonderfully fulfilling experience of the Underworld from Greek mythos.If you've played any of Supergiant's other titles (particularly Bastion) and have been holding out of Hades, I can only ask why?If you aren't a fan of roguelikes/roguelites and are hesitant because you don't want to feel like you lose your progress after a particularly deep run -- then worry not. The progression system in Hades ensures that you never feel like a run has really gone to waste; with the protagonist growing incrementally more powerful depending on how far you get and how many resources you pick up along the way.If you're looking for something you can play in bite-sized chunks, then look no further. A deep run can take anywhere from 30-60 minutes (towards the latter end if you want to take your time to milk out every boon or bonus possible). I'm fairly certain that time can be cut down considerably if you figure out a nice build and intend to speed your way through.In any case, I feel that Hades has been an amazing game to go in blind to. The learning curve isn't super steep, but there is depth to be found should you want to look for it. If not the sharply responsive gameplay or amazing soundtrack, then the wealth of characters, lovely range of voice-acting, and visual pop of the art style should be enough to make the experience worthwhile.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: The greatest example of how to evolve a genre.
