_childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY:It's pretty damn good. The more you progress, the more crazy the animation effects get, so if you're overwhelmed by a metric ton of things happening at once it might prove challenging to adapt to.Otherwise, it's gorgeous, fluid, and supremely responsive. I played on controller, as this type of game seems to prefer it.The variety of weapons are fun and interesting, and they really encourage you to go for the win with every single one of them.There's tons of stuff to upgrade, improve, unlock, and indulge in as you go and it's easy to get motivated to go after specific items, bounties from the Fates, and other things to improve your runs. You'll start off feeling relatively pathetic but when the power starts to build and you start to gather boons in a run that work incredibly well together with your weapon of choice and the talents you've equipped up, you can definitely start feeling like a very confused god very quickly.The more you play, the less confusion. Occasionally leaving you with a satisfying feeling of "This build is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ broken" as you rampage through an entirely new region/level all the way to the boss only to realize your one or two mistakes earlier on spell your doom against your newest rival.This is 100% worth the buy and it's fun whether you want to grind it to completion or just explore the addictive mechanics.COMBAT:Who put bullet-hell in my God of War and then decided I don't get to choose all my mind blowing combos myself unless blessed by my chosen gods? Combat is fast, furious, full of technically challenging maneuvers and at the same time... Relatively simple. Rely on your boons from your gods, choose them wisely, learn your dash mechanics like your own nether region and you'll dominate. Make one mistake? It's going to hurt.EXPLORATION:Rewarding. Each new region offers increasing levels of challenge even as you grow your power and skill to mete out your thirst for freedom on the unfortunate lost souls of Hades. You'll find bosses that are surprising in their mechanics and challenging to beat until you learn what to expect (almost Darksoulsian in that respect). You'll also find chambers of welcome reprieve along your journey, as you would expect from most rogue-lite/like etc.STORY:No comment here as I haven't played through enough to gather up the juicy details. I'm interested in what's happening with all the characters and gods, however, and as I've progressed there are certainly implications that our fated escape could prove devastating to the natural order, or perhaps simply irrelevant. Looking forward to finding out!STUFF TO DO:I appreciate the cosmetics options that are available. From upgrading your undesired residence, adding new mechanics through conscripting gem-hungry contractors to simply selecting your favored colors for everything from rugs to chairs... It's actually fairly compelling to want Hades to look a little nicer and besides, there's an entire resource set aside just for that. You'll want to invest in improving options on your runs early on but as time goes, no resource ever feels useless. It's motivating to make a decision on what you want to upgrade next: One of my weapons? My own capabilities in combat? Make the place look a little nicer? How about becoming close friends with one of my compatriots or even one of my enemies by swaying them with an expensive bottle of Elixir? It's always fun and there's always something new to see.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I am really conflicted on this one. I really want to like this game. From a technical and aesthetical viewpoint this game is absolutely great. Runs smooth with no bugs other than a few minuscule visual ones. The story is really good with interesting characters and a ton of voice acting. However, the more I played the more I got annoyed by the combat and progression system. The first areas play very well, and thats where I have the most fun. But then it turns more and more into a bullet hell with spongy enemies. The screen gets clouded in explosions and particles which makes it really hard to impossible to tell what is going on. That compared with the environment that is sometimes blocking the view, especially around the walls at the bottom makes fighting really not fun. What I also don't like is how you receive damage. It is possible to get constant chip damage with no reliable way of dodging it. I think if would be better if the enemies hit harder, but less frequently. The thing that I don't like about the progression system is that it is build around playing the game to gather resources to make yourself permanently stronger. So you get farther every run, but not necessarily because you get better at the game, but because you made the game easier. You later get the option to make your runs more challenging to get extra rewards, but it's not a natural progression of the game. All in all it's a game with a great foundation but lacking game design, I personally didn't like the later gameplay, probably won't complete it.

_childDocuments_.review: Super Giant Games is the renowned studio behind the amazing game, Bastion. However, what started as a platformer studio, went ahead to make a TBS and now a rogue lite game. And frankly, this is the first time since Bastion since I could hear Zia in a game again.As far as rogue lites go, there are a few things Hades is excellent at. Story progression is done every time you die or the further you travel. The characters are developed well and the game has a great deal of lore (even past your first completion). The mechanisms themselves are complex, from boons that act as attack modifiers, a passive tree which you unlock over time , relics, which grant situational benefits and a variety of weapons, each for a different play style . There is a good amount of synergy to go between the four and the RNGness in the game is reduced.However, at the end of the day, the game is still a rogue lite. Which means it still has (albeit reduced) RNG, is overly punishing and revels in repetitive game play as an excuse for content. The story while fleshed out is mostly through voiced dialogue and is doled out in scraps. If this appeals to you, do pick up the game. But my recommendation for the game is, its more of a job than fun.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this review I've only played 10 hours, but hot damn is this game good in so many ways. The gameplay loop is great, lore and characters keep you entertained and interested, visuals are fantastic, soundtrack is really good, voice overs are nicely done and I genuinely can't come up with a single con, only pros. There are some things that I want to give special attention to, and the first being how the game gradually introduces new characters and mechanics. You think you've seen all the mechanics by now? Nope, here, have a new way to permanently upgrade yourself. Secondly, this game surprisingly handles roguelite upgrades a little bit different, where instead of unlocking new items that you get on your runs you unlock new possible rooms and objects that can spawn in there, which can indirectly boost your stats during a run (for example giving you money which you can spend in a shop). The fact that you can also ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fish and furnish Hades' domains is a definite plus. Honestly, I don't think that I can give this game anything lower than 9/10, and considering how I objectively can't find a single flaw I say this is a 10/10, at least for me. If you are a fan of roguelikes/roguelites - get this, you won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Very rarely do I find my way to the steam page in only 5 hours of play-time to write a review but I felt compelled to do so. Well - you're right where I was 5 hours ago!This is gauntlet legends meets risk of rain in a bullethell universe with an incredibly diverse skill/progression system that leaves EVERY game - EVERY ATTEMPT - Feeling unique, rewarding and epic!! _childDocuments_.review: It's not just a fantastic game, it's a true masterpiece that clearly has been crafted with a lot of love, passion, and care. I mostly play it on Switch, and cross saves work perfectly.Something that I gotta say as a disabled person with motor issues is, the game is surprisingly accessible while still being challenging even in god mode. The controls are perfectly balanced and pretty easy to get used to, which is important to me, and, what's also important, the game doesn't feel frustrating even when you die for the 20th time in a row because the story keeps advancing and moving forward. _childDocuments_.review: This would be one of my favourite games of recent years. It has a brilliant storyline that requires repeated playthroughs to move the plot forward. _childDocuments_.review: Hades is a straightup near perfect rogue-lite game. Sadly its flaws are irritating enough that you can not close your eyes to it. Unlike most of the rogue-lite games Hades leans on the story as well as the gameplay and this is good, really good if done correctly. Greek mythology is common knowledge and even if you don't specifically love the mythos it still has enough power to make you interested enough. But like I said if done correctly, mythology and its characters are a perfect base for a story and sadly Hades does not done that, at least for some parts.The thing is, towards the epilogue the game does not have anything to add gameplaywise but it adds another layer of story to follow and this is refreshing for rogue-lite enjoyers. As I said this is also less complicated and very much more welcoming to the new players of this genre, but it loses its spark at some point cuz unlike most rogue-lite games Hades does not have any real endgame boss, challenge, or anything. If it was a perfect story this could still be good but the game's story is hidden in dialogues and the dialogues are a bit problematic/immersion-breaking (sometimes the dialogue you sposed to have is blocked cuz of an in-game event, sometimes the character you are supposed to talk is absent, the character that supposed to give me the epilogue quest is talking with someone else so if I want that quest I have to do another run just to speak with her, the worst one was that one time my character was talking to himself and revealed a story spoiler cuz I reached the last area of the run (at that point neither I nor my character had the story hint to say that)).Even with its immersion-breaking events Hades is a well earned 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like short run-based action RPGs, the previous releases by Supergiant, and Greek mythology, I'm qualified to say that you'll love Hades.Despite being in Early Access, I'm still nowhere near the end of the content available. However, if you're the kind of person who want to just get to the ending of a game and move on, maybe wait until the proper release.Updating my review: I've now gotten every achievement in Hades on 3 different platforms. This is easily the second best action roguelike (while it has stronger fundamentals, nothing compares to the run variety and sheer amount of content in Binding of Isaac). Runs great on the Steam Deck, and if you don't have one of those, the PC version has cross-save with the Switch. I've at least beaten every Supergiant game and think they're all worth playing, but Hades is my favorite by far. Cannot wait for the Hades II Early Access to start.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the tightest rogue-like experiences brought to you by the minds behind other masterpieces such as Bastion and Transistor. Great writing, a fairly compelling that succeeds in making the repeat deaths compelling and canonical. Combat is hectic and fast-paced with plenty of variety thanks to the upgrades, or "boons" provided by a myriad of Olympian gods. As unforgiving as Hades can be at times, the "God Mode" feature does a great job to open this genre up to more casual players or players that simply do not enjoy rogue-likes. God Mode grants a stacking damage resistance buff every time you die, allowing subsequent runs to be a tad easier and give you a more evergreen feeling of growing strength.I would easily recommend this game to any rogue-like fan, or fans of Supergiant Games in general. 100% the safest purchase of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s one of those games that simply has everything in its favor. The soundtrack, the visual art, the character development, the storyline; you name it, this game has it, an excels in it.The game’s impressive replayability, however, is probably Hades’ strongest point. It has countless of modifiers, which make every run completely different from the previous one despite facing the same enemies over and over again.It’s remarkable how they manage to make you don’t care at all if you die, since this also moves the story along (unlike other rouge-like games); and it leads you to another core aspect of the game: the interactions between its characters. These are downright excellent, thanks to the alluring voices of its cast (I’m talking ASMR levels of voice acting here).To sum up, Supergiant Games has, once again, succeeded in creating a perfect blend between a compelling story and a superb gameplay, turning the loop that most rouge-like games tend to be, into something truly grand.

_childDocuments_.review: Right, where do I begin... This game is many things. Most good, and some not.It is a visual novel roguelite with an incredible soundtrack (and the first roguelite to encorporate storytelling into the games' core structure).It is a rhythm game (each aspect and boss has its own rhythm), which makes it an interesting speedrunning game. Let's not forget about the sound-design either, nearly every sound effect is a treat to hear.As a top-level runner for the game: It's roguelite-with-storytelling nature also inherently makes it therapeutic. It teaches how to emotionally deal with strings of unfortunate events, be it in games or IRL.One can play the game for thousands of hours without running out of run-ideas, due to the games' high skill ceiling. It's also a fun casual game, though the content generally doesn't last for more than 300-ish hours in that case. Technically more than 300 if your casual-player-objective is to get the optional Unseen One rank from the Resource Director, but I would not recommend trying this. It takes far too long.Everything (other than the Unseen One rank) the game asks of the player is achieveable to nearly anyone within a reasonable amount of time (the previously -stated 300-ish hours).Now, for the things I dislike about Hades. There is this weird phenomenon where the more you play this game, the more you see the ways in which it is terrible. Examples include the following:- the entirety of the last biome's mechanic- some enemies' AI, some attacks are bugged to happen multiple times or happen without cue to let the player know an attack is coming- the difficulty-scaling for most aspects above heat 45-ish, after which it becomes RNG-heavy even given perfect play- entity pathfinding, which may result in janky out-of-bounds behavior- bugged boons/hammers, some in the player's favor and some less so- bugged weapon-aspects, usually bugged in the player's favor- overextended attack hitboxes, meaning despite the visuals not lining up some hits (enemy -> player or vice-versa), some attacks will still deal damage.- collision-detection, some places look like they can be accessed from a certain angle and position using a dash, but actually can not- while many builds could be thought of (given how many different aspects there are to learn the rhythms of), most aspects involve looking for one of the same 3 or 4 builds. On some aspects, it even is best to ignore the aspect's gimmick entirely because either the mechanic was nerfed to the ground during development and thereby make it irrelevant to use over something else, or the aspect idea was inherently unbalanced.You may have heard that some players use a speedrunning modpack to remove some of the needlessly time-consuming parts of the game, and Quality-of-Life features the vanilla game lacks. I quite wish the developers used some of the ideas present in the modpack, but understand the people at Supergiant have more people to please than the top 1% of players. They produced a game that usually feels incredible to play and that's most of what matters.Oh, and finally the community for this game is likely the very best I've been a part of on the internet. Appreciate all of you. <3

_childDocuments_.review: This game is proof that a roguelike can tell a good story, and do it well. It may have have taken a very convenient setting and story to do so, but man, it did it good. _childDocuments_.review: Hades is one of, if not the greatest rogue-like of all time, it perfectly encapsulates everything that is great about the genre whilst pushing it to new heights of narrative-lead storytelling, character development and satisfying, meaty combat. The way in which Hades rewards death is flawless and every single run is a chance to test new builds, build new relationships with it's characters and explore the lore. The music, art style and animations are AAA tier but it's the combat which you'll keep returning to over and over again, which is pure ambrosia. Rogue-likes can often be unfair and punishing, with no sense of progression or learning, Hades is none of those things. With each run you'll get stronger, until such a time that you'll feel like an absolute God, smashing bosses with sub-optimal builds and adding more and more heat to your runs to change up the difficulty. There is RNG but it never feels unfair and there's plenty of room for experimentation and salvaging poor runs becomes second nature after a while. Hades is a strong contender for GOTY, and is as close to perfect as any game within the genre has ever come. This is Supergiant's masterpiece, and a culmination of everything they've learned and taken on board from the community. Don't delay, get it now.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, I am giving the widely-acclaimed , the 2020 title from darling , a thumbs down.The crux of it is that the core gameplay is really designed for players who can avoid taking damage. In a fast-paced game like this, I am a graceless klutz who will bluster ahead in pursuit of the enemy, discounting any nicks and scratches I get along the way as flesh wounds that are as inconsequential as they are inevitable.Problem is, healing is . There is no “rest to heal” button, no portable healing potions, no reliable campfire where we can recuperate or respawn from. Picking up a few of those nicks and scratches along the way means I didn't have much health left for the next boss, so I lose that fight.That's okay if you think losing is fun, right?Maybe. But it takes me twenty minutes to get back there, which is too-long of a feedback loop for learning how to perform in a boss fight, and the character's abilities are  randomized between runs, so my effective attacks and strengths and weaknesses are  different from the last encounter, which makes it really hard to benefit from practice.but hey, people really like this game, it clearly has some things going for it (I'll acknowledge those in the next section), so I stick with it for a while to see what it has to offer.I turn on . It helps— in the short term. It's certainly not the Wizard Mode known to those who have delved in pursuit of the Amulet of Yendor.On my 58th attempt—the 28th since I turned on —I see my first Victory screen.The story doesn't end there.You've heard this game has a story, right? It's surprisingly detailed for something from the procedural death labyrinth genre. I don't want to spoil anything for you, but I had really hoped that battling through to the end of the  meant that I got to the end of the . The game is clearly dangling all sorts of tidbits for completionists to follow up on, but I figured any of that New Game Plus-type stuff would be extras for people who wanted to stick around after the end.My second victory follows not long after my first. I'd say that's a sign I've improved, but honestly I feel that's more due to the slow power creep provided by  and a lot of luck in which boons I'd happened to run in to.It's clear this isn't the end either, but it's still scripted—I haven't reached some sort of infinite loop. So I look it up: People say it takes  victories to get to the “true ending.”Honestly, I'm around thirty hours in at this point, and I'm not really interested in spending another dozen hours hacking my way through the same dungeon levels to be allowed to finish out the last few pages of this game's visual novel.The game's main progression mechanic—plus the extra forgiveness factor added by —made the game playable for me. But not, I now realize, .That is why I say this was not a good game for me. If you're equally a klutz who is not good at staying away from the pointy end of a sword or the path of a magic missile, it might not be a good game for you either.As we've come to expect from Supergiant Games, the art style is gorgeous and wonderfully carried out. Our hero is agile and the hits feel impactful; it controls well, at least as far as my clumsy fingers are able to determine. The audio from this game may not stay with me in the same way that  and  did, but it's no slouch there either, effects lending punch to the combat and color to the surprisingly wide cast of voiced characters.Oh, and most importantly: . Just as importantly: at no point are you encouraged to  a dog.The conversational system seems simple at first, as the player is not provided any  during dialog. But as you progress, you choose which characters to favor and which goals to pursue, and the brief passages of dialog are remarkably good about reflecting that context.

_childDocuments_.review: Hades is a rougelike game that actually incorporates the concept of "doing runs over and over" in a way that makes sense into it's story. You're not just doing this because its a videogame, rather because in the context of the game its an actual mechanic and a "normal behavior".In this game you will likely die in early chambers when you begin, but this is pretty much on par to how the game is designed, as you play more you will not only get better at handling Zagreus and learn enemy patterns, but also collect resources to make future runs easier, as you'll be able to permanently upgrade yourself, making future attempts more likely to succeed.The main powers you acquire are derived from Olympian gods, each offering their own set of effects that you can equip to your main moves, or just gain passive buffs that might alter how you approach a given run, there's also 6 different weapons that can later even gain new alterations, even though the game encourages you to try all weapons by buffing the rewards you earn if you use a specific one during your next run, you might just find your favorite one and use it to achieve more victories.The game also has a wide cast of charming characters that you'll be able to interact with during and before/after a run, deepening your relationship with each as you progress and eventually even unlocking sub stories related to them, allowing them to grow more as characters and friends of yours.Overall this game is a great experience, and from popular word, even if you're unfamiliar with the rougelike genre, this game has proven to find their way to be liked by these people. There is a lot of extra unlockables you can pursue if you decide to, and the game even allows you to pump up the difficulty with set modifiers, to test the skill of those seeking for a greater challenge.The true GOTY of 2020.

_childDocuments_.review: Where the HELL to start. Okay, boyo, I'm writing this past midnight, high out of my mind, after I just logged my 84th hour and finished the final achievements for my 100% completion. No ones ever going to read this. Yet I persist.That is how good this game is.Lets take away the things that are just indisputable aces; Compellingly imagined Greek Mythology, beautiful OST, and a seamless art direction. Let us say it had none of those things. It would still be a tremendous game.The gameplay is a roguelike heaven. Your growth both in your individual attempts, and those gains you keep permanently are perfectly paced. There is a myriad of customization options and choices that truly means no two runs are the same and that you can conquer even the highest difficulties with the preferred character build of your concoction. On my last run I had an epiphany and crafted a beautiful build on a clean run that allowed me to finish this game in a manner I never experienced on a previous run. It's enough to make a grown man cry.I finally found a game I don't want to uninstall after I've 100%'d it. There is still a plethora of interactions I haven't seen, builds I haven't discovered, secrets I haven't found. I cannot stop gushing about this game. Beyond the gameplay, this game has one more flagship. Reactive dialogue.This story is as fresh at the end as it is in the beginning. You root for characters, you rip on them. You watch the NPCs in this world hone in and comment on everything you do,. EVERYTHING. Just when you think, "Oh, this fella couldn't POSSIBLY have anything to say about what I just did to that other dude on my last run." And then they DO, and it somehow remains true to their character. What I'm saying is the storytelling is without comparison. That's coming from a guy who nerds out over Hollow Knight's minimalist style. Mind-boggling.Let's wrap this up. Buy this game if you like video games in any form. And if you're a damned savage who doesn't like video games, or if you just can't handle that roguelike difficulty, put it on god-mode and EXPERIENCE. THIS. STORY.

_childDocuments_.review: I patiently waited for Hades to get out of Early Access in order to play the final product. I had high expectations given the reviews and the studio previous games (specially Pyre, one of my recent time favourites) and I am happy to say that my expectations were meet, the game is beautiful. In line with the studio signature I found great art, fluid gameplay, clever dialogs, superb voiceover and exceptional game design. During my gametime I noticed that there was a lot of content to unlock and I was looking forward to reach the end-game and explore those mechanics. It took me around 20 runs and almost 20 hours to finally kill the final boss on my third attempt. All that time I was hooked and amused.Afterwards I put an additional 7 or 8 hours and to my surprise I found the end-game severely unrewarding. I wanted to keep progressing and feeling OP but realized that to unlock the stuff needed to reach that state it will take me a long time (probably 100 hours or more). I usually have no issue on putting that time on other genres (i.e: CCG, ARPG) but to do that on a roguelike I need a higher ratio within time-invested and reward, and on that regard the game did not deliver.I would rate the game with 9/10 if I was just rating it to the point I got to the final boss kill, but considering the whole experience I rate the game 7/10.I do realize that for people more invested into the roguelike genre Hades is, without doubt, a must have, alongside the best games in the genre. If you like the genre, then you cannot go wrong with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: What a perfect game for 2020. The year that keeps hitting us with a seemingly endless wave of disappointment and loss. Hades is a game that takes place in the Greek realm of the dead and has a story that revolves around you dying as many times as it takes for you to complete your story. The journey itself is fueled by rage and loss. The art is stunning and the music is enchanting. This is my GOTY for 2020. Over 120 hours in and haven't completed it yet. I can't wait to loose again. Because this game reminds you "that sucking at something is just the first step at getting kinda good at something" - Jake the Dog (kinda).

So much so, it is easily my favourite game of 2020, but it might as well be my all-time favourite game. I absolutely and unabashedly enjoy every single aspect of . I believe there isn't a single thing I wouldn't enjoy in one way or another. This game makes me crave for more. One more run. One more interaction with the colourful denizens of Underworld and Olympus alike. One more punch, one for thrust, one more shot through the wretched souls of the underworld.  brings out the very best in terms of telling stories, combining it with gameplay, enhancing it with beautiful audio-visual queues to provide an experience worth every penny, every cent you spend on this game. In terms of gameplay, I would only request one thing and one thing only - give me -like farm in a need of care at the end, instead of the wonderful narrator with his wonderful lines of monologue - you know, to unwind and relax after gruelling battles. This request doesn't make any sense to you? That's ok, but I desperately want it! As I mentioned above, visually, this game is an absolute gem. Everywhere you look, everything you see is just so damn gorgeous and so pleasing for eyes. The attention to details in every frame, the details big and so small are so damn impressive. Now, combine this with sounds, music and impeccable voice-acting you are in for a true audio-visual treat, a masterpiece if I can be so bold with such claims. But, if there's one thing I can't get enough of, it's stories. Storytelling and stories of any kind are something that brings me true joy in life. name: Beyond a Steel Sky
detailed_description: From Charles Cecil, creator of the Broken Sword series, with art direction by Dave Gibbons, legendary comic book artist behind ‘Watchmen’, comes ‘Beyond A Steel Sky’, the long awaited sequel to the cult classic ‘Beneath a Steel Sky’. You are Robert Foster. A child has been abducted in a brutal attack. You have vowed to bring him home. The trail has led you to Union City, one of the last remaining mega-cities in a world ravaged by shattering wars, and political meltdown. Union City is a utopia, its people loving life under the control of an altruistic AI: ever-attentive androids, designer living, piazzas and bars. What’s not to love? But this City has a dark underbelly... ‘Beyond a Steel Sky’ is a dramatic, humorous, cyberpunk thriller in which engaging puzzles drive a fast-paced narrative set in a dynamic gameworld that responds to – and is subverted by – the player’s actions. Features: The World An adventure set within a dynamic world, populated by wilful characters driven by motivations that the player can subvert. In combination with a unique hacking tool, multiple solutions to puzzles emerge from player choices. The Story Unravel dark conspiracies, defeat a terrifying antagonist in this dramatic, humorous, cyberpunk thriller, which explores contemporary themes: social control, AI, and total surveillance. The puzzles Intelligent puzzles are interwoven with an intriguing dramatic narrative to deliver a compelling gameplay experience. The Look A beautifully detailed, comic-book styled world, from the mind of legendary comic artist Dave Gibbons.

short_description: From multi-award winning Revolution comes ‘Beyond a Steel Sky’, a groundbreaking 3D adventure thriller, set in an AI-driven future. Subvert the world, hack the systems and solve dark conspiracies to uncover the devastating truth.

_childDocuments_.review: 1994’s  is a dystopian cyberpunk point-and-click that’s a much bigger deal than you probably realise. Set in the awful future all dystopian cyberpunk scenarios have plotted for us, Robert Foster is an adopted citizen of the Gap, the new name for the new hell that has become the Australian outback. He’s kidnapped and strong-armed along to Union City where he has to try and undo the oppressive regime of tyrannical AI overlord, LINC.One of the things this game does well is bring the player up to speed on current events as it very quickly and efficiently reminds us of the main things that happened in Beneath. It is done so naturally and will help ensure that it’s not necessary to play the original if the player doesn’t have the time or the inclination to do so. Indeed while this game is a sequel it doesn’t rely on nostalgia or on the success of the original game and it stands well enough as a standalone game in its own right.The writing is of a particularly high standard. Much like their previous games, this game combines a serious overall story with plenty of humour sprinkled throughout. While the changes in tone in the original game from serious to comical were a little jarring at times it is handled better in Beyond and the humour is considerably more restrained this time.The puzzles can usually make or break an adventure game. More recent games have done away completely with traditional puzzles and only include choices as replacement for these traditional puzzles. Other games, in their attempt at creating challenging puzzles sometimes make them illogical and  frustrating instead. Thankfully they are logical and interesting and fit well into the story in . There's a solid adventure game in . The puzzles make sense and ease newcomers to the genre, the story is mostly on point, and the writing is robust. Whether you're a longtime fan of the original or just coming to its world now, there's plenty to enjoy in .- Foster remains an amiable protagonist- Conversation trees feel nice and deep- Great voice acting- New hacking puzzles are intuitive- Thoroughly modern feeling dystopia- Lack of puzzle diversity, particularly in the later scenesDISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY | GOOD | GREAT |  | MASTERPIECE

_childDocuments_.review: Beneath a Steel Sky was one of my favourite games on the Amiga 26 years ago, and I'm thrilled that Union City has made a return. The sequel is packed with some lovely references to the Amiga original, and it was magical to revisit these characters all these years later. The switch from a traditional point and click interface works well, too - and if anything makes the city far more immersive - plus the game has some brilliant new characters with some wonderful voice acting.That said, the second half of the game doesn't quite live up to the first, with puzzles and characters becoming much more sparse - it feels like the latter half was rushed compared to the first. And the main issue is the buggy nature of the game, with things like characters wandering through each other, audio fading down suddenly and all manner of other things.Hopefully most of these issues will be fixed with time, and otherwise I thoroughly enjoyed visiting Union City again - if you were a huge fan of Beneath a Steel Sky, this is definitely worth a look. _childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the original game (more on that later), I was extremely worried about this sequel. I wasn't sure if they could live up to expectation (at least not to mine) since the original game was so amazing and atmospheric but I think they (mostly) managed to do an amazing job.The first game has a very special place in my heart. Back in December 1993, the first issue of the magazine PC Gamer (UK) arrived on the shelves and with it came a Beneath A Steel Sky demo, specifically created for PC Gamer. It was my second PC games magazine and adventure games were unknown to me, having grown up on consoles and my Game Boy. Man, this demo changed my world - a gripping story, amazing setting, brilliant pixel art and an atmosphere unlike anything else I'd ever seen in a game! On top of that, the dialogue was witty, funny and just great. I became the biggest fan of BASS when it was a relatively obscure adventure game. As a freeware game, it became a lot more popular the past ten years but I never forgot this brilliant gem, even though people used to barely mention it among other games such as Secret of Monkey Island, Day of the Tentacle and Full Throttle. To me, it was better than all of those.So now we are 26 and a half years later and the sequel finally arrived. I was worried they'd lose the appeal of the first game: the mystery, the atmosphere, the huge scale of the city, the wit, etc. Luckily, it's all here. The city is amazingly well done - much better than I expected - and it took some pointers from Bioshock which I can only applaud. The scale of things is grand as well - you really do feel that Union City is absolutely massive. And the characters you speak to? They're very much in the same vein of the original game. The dialogue is sharp, offers many dialogue choices and even lets you dig deeper and deeper on a single subject multiple times which makes conversations quite fun and informative at the same time.Like with all adventure games, the puzzles have moved on from "use X on Y" to a more natural sense of progression - a mix of dialogue, logical thinking and using tools. While I enjoy the old puzzles, the new ones can get a bit easy - so far, I've yet to encounter a single hard puzzle. It's mostly about discovering something new to interact with that reveals a solution to a problem you were working on rather than having a bunch of objects at your disposal and not being sure how to use them. It's still fun but it's unlikely to get you stuck for long.However, BASS was never really about the puzzles for me - it's all about the story and setting and Beyond does a pretty good job at setting up a new plot for you to follow. I love the many references to the old game as well. You see remnants from the original game like an old LINC terminal or the art piece that used to be outside the insurance and travel agent in the original game (they even kept the original comment you made too).While I admit I haven't come anywhere close to finishing the game, I felt a review was already warranted since so far, it's clear this game deserves to get a lot of sales, more than it will likely get and since it's just been released, any positive review can only help. I will update this review later if I feel it's needed but fans of the original: yes, it's definitely worth a look!

_childDocuments_.review: There are excellent reviews written about this game already that cover the things I usually have to say so I will not reiterate them here.How about this? I loved this game.New mechanics are introduced; it still feels like a “good old point and click”.There are some clever and unique puzzles that you solve with your new tool: an excellent hacker device! I had a lot of fun with this and extended my game-play by doing many unnecessary, but fun things with it.You access your inventory and game options by the escape key or “I”. You almost always know your objective and how to proceed. If not, there is a hint function if you get stuck that provides one nudge at a time rather than the solution.You have many set-up options so tweak away to your hearts content.The game autosaves after a chapter/memory. You also have a manual save option (thank you!). Traditional WASD movement. A right click flips you around; that was a nice addition. Story, story, story, that is where it’s at for me and this was well written and engaging.I suffered no crashes, and it ran great for me. This was the best game I have played in a long time. I cannot wait to find out what those pesky humans and androids get up to next!My play time was about 14 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: As one of the doubtless thousands of people who have waited patiently for 26 years (and even created my own in AGS) for a sequel to possibly my favourite video game of all time, I can safely say I am not disappointed. It uses a brilliant hacking mechanic to make puzzles logical and fun to solve and really nails the aesthetic I think we all hoped for.Frankly, I think this is a wonderful return to the world of BASS and I genuinely cannot wait to see what Revolution do with this take on the adventure game genre with George & Nico (hint hint guys...).

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game, I enjoyed almost every minute of it (the minutes I didn't enjoy involved a smug poet and loud music). I'm truly sad to be finished this game, and looking forward to going back to get my last two achievements. If you enjoy point and click style adventure games at all, or good stories in a classic dystopian setting at all, then don't hesitate to get this game.  The logic gimmick that drives most of the game's puzzles is a lot of fun, even after you're used to it.  9.5/10Note:  The game ran pretty hot for me on a new mid-high-range gaming laptop; however, I had no problems.Pros:- excellent story- omg the fan service... for sci-fi geeks, that is XD- if you know Asimov, Star Trek, or any of the other oldies but goodies, you can see where the story is headed early to part-way through, but you *still* really want to see how it all works out, and the ending is *still* really cool- the main character is awesome- the graphics are perfect for the story- the music is good- the voice acting (English, in my case) is outstanding (I really loved it)- the secondary characters were very well done (both the good and the bad)Cons:- one puzzle that drove me nuts (okay, maybe not a fair con)- Orana should have had an action scene (mostly kidding, but I wanted to see more of her)- the GangGang birds are scary- only 10 or 12 save slots, but you only need them if you tend to save too muchHonestly, I don't have any other cons. I seem to have outwaited all the glitches, because the game ran smoothly for me.  Share and enjoy! (Brave New World, Aldous Huxley)~ Imp

_childDocuments_.review: Taking the courage to make a sequel to a classic after 26 years is no small feat. The fact that this sequel is as good as the original while being completely different in gameplay and presentation is mind-blowing. The story is captivating from start to finish, but make no mistake, you absolutely need to know Beneath a Steel Sky. I found the cell-shaded graphics to be appealing, though perhaps it is the weakest element of the package. On the other hand, it has Hollywood-grade epic orchestral music that is simply stunning. I enjoyed both games immensely (replayed the first one after decades) and recommend both.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for this game for a very long time - even was waiting with baited breath as it was a Broken Sword 5 stretch goal for the kickstarter.However, like BS5 (and the reason why I am still yet to finish it) Revolution seems to release games with gamebreaking bugs that can't be reset and therefore necessitate an entire gameplay restart. Does Revolution have any QA? Clearly they're not getting beta players like myself, where I will break a game to show the devs what's wrong so they can fix it BEFORE release rather than AFTER.It's a shame because the game is rather good, with some great visuals and sounds and especially characters and story. But why have all this when the game doesn't actually WORK? I've invested 9 hours playing and now I'm stuck either repeating all that to get back to where I was or shelving the entire thing for a few years until the bugs are sorted out, which is what I have done with BS5 and I've yet to go back to see if that bug has been fixed.So, my recommendation is not "no" specifically but "not yet."

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite point&click adventure game is Broken Sword 2 and since this one comes from the same developers I had to play it and I wasn't dissapointed. Although I still can't comprehend why this studio is so set on making their games 3D when they obviously don't have the budget. Nothing wrong with 2D graphics get this into your heads developers. Cheap, poorly made 3D graphics made with no budget don't age well. Just look at first two broken sword games and then 3&4. Which ones look more appealing today? Stop it, enough, 2D cartoonish look is amazing and ages well.So what's the game? It's basically a third person point&click adventure game. You arrive at the city and all the shenanigans start.You run around talking to characters and investigating everything around you just as you're used to in such games.The story starts slowly and honestly it's kinda hard to not be bored in the first hour but fortunately the more you play the better the story becomes. Overall the story is quite good and engaging.You meet lots of characters and get to know them, you even get a friend following you. You explore the dystopian city while solving puzzles and of course if you care hunting for achievements.Gameplay is good and is not too easy or too hard although i'd say some puzzles will make you curse. There's quite a few puzzles to solve and they're usually different so the game stays fresh until the end.There's also lots of secrets and easter eggs. On top of that the game is filled with great humour and will make you smile at least few times.Graphically the game looks alright? Again like I said why the 3D looks? At least it's cell-shaded which make sit a bit better. Animations are kinda bad and so are facial emotions.Fortunately due to good sound design, voice acting and general atmosphere compensates for the lack of graphical fidelity. Characters sound believable and and voice acting brings more life into the game.Performance for me was good although I had to use the ultrawide fix. Played on 7800x3d, rtx4080, 32gb, @3440x1440. So I can't say much regarding performance. It may need decent hardware to run but shouldn't be anything too crazy, especially considering the fact it's not a fast paced game.Overall a good adventure game with some pacing issues and outdated graphics. Worth a buy for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't expect the game to be this good.Mostly because of the 3rd person view, and the promotion material having me believe that it would be a barely interactive cinematic title.But they pulled off the transition to 3D, which is highly unusual for Point n' Clicks, and yes, it's still very much a Pn'C in terms of structure and gameplay.The first minutes seemed to confirm my initial worries, starting with a long cutscene, followed by a moment of pure walking between invisible walls.However, we quickly reach an area near the city with plenty to look at, things to do, and several cool characters to talk to.That's where I got hooked.Areas might be thinner later in the game, cutscenes more frequent in the final stretch, but by then I accept them because they are good, I'm invested, and I'm enjoying the sum of the parts anyway.No game has been flawless, at least technically, since 1993, and this is no exception:NPCs push you instead of walking around you; a hacking puzzle's glitch might require you to reset the entire area (it takes only 1 click to do so;) it's hard to use your inventory on a NPC that never stands still; some dialogue exchanges cannot be skipped; and once I ended up behind a barrier, unable to get back into the legal play field, so you'd better cycle on your manual saves.Nothing too bad, just could have done with a final layer of polish.The story is simple and interesting, but it's the storytelling that really engages, as well as the great world-building.It's all delivered with charm and personality, with some most excellent characters, from quirky adults to adorable kids to the classic, cartoonishly pompous villain.The game looks good and is very well voiced.The puzzles aren't really hard: when stuck, look carefully around for a hot spot you didn't notice.The hacking moments aren't hard either, but often enough (or is it ever enough?) they give you latitude to play around, annoy someone or create a mess just for the sake of it.Great sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine you are a big, big fan of Pulp Fiction, and they announce a sequel.After  using a Pulp Fiction avatar , they announce a sequel.It comes out, you get your ticket for the premiere, and the first thing you see is a 'for children' age label, awful camera angles and a plot worthy of a bedtime story.Now you know how I'm feeling.TL:DR; They tried to pull a BASS sequel in Pegi 7...I must admit some shy optimism; hoping that maybe they could still pull it off.Didn't take long for the blunt realization to come, there was no way.This game is decent, and maybe most people have enjoyed it. But this is not a sequel to BASS.The overall quality in this title makes it feel like a fan-game made by people who didn't quite understand BASS in the first place.And I apply that not only to the predictable story, but to the glitchy mechanics and the elevator audio design.Disappointment, and a black burnt aftertaste, that's what remains of the game after I finished it.I will definitely remember my  when I watched .The first five minutes of BeneathASS got my heart rate to increase, and that never happens.Visuals, sound design, initial tension in the story. It was intense.What I found in this sequel was the opposite.An easy-go, slow adventure, more akin to the start of a kid's JRPG game.There is no impact.Some big nostalgia spikes on the rare instances where music and voices actually reminded me of the original bass.But that's about as far as the resemblance goes.Even that was hard to enjoy though, with random volume drops making voices almost inaudible. Awkward camera angles, made worse by forcing it to the front when "".Robots getting stuck on each other when you're trying to get through trivial scan puzzles.Doors not working when they should. Robots duplicating themselves.A lot of reloading saves involved in my playthrough to fix these glitches. On the positive side, it has autosave (that's the only improvement, would be unplayable otherwise though). I had to literally save and then load the save I had just created to fix doors/interactables. This definitely made a bad experience worse.I have no one but myself to blame for my own disappointment. It wasn't a bad game. It wasn't a good game either.In the end, BeyondASS can't cast a shadow on the original.I am not changing my avatar, of course. I will not let this attempt at a sequel taint my view of the original game.But I do wish I'd never played this, I wish I never even knew it existed.PS: A note to the developers, in case they read this absurd negative write-up veering to a personal complaint. Forgive me for being so harsh and failing to see any good in this title. Beneath a Steel Sky was, is, and probably will always be one of my favorite games. It was the one game that made me realize how important the  aspect of a game is to me. It basically made me look for games with good stories above all else. So, in the end, it is kind of personal to me.

_childDocuments_.review: First, a disclaimer on the "Yes" vote.This is a wonderful story driven game, very much like Telltale Games used to create.  That's both a plus and a minus.  It's definitely not a classic adventure game in the veins of the original it's based upon, nor did it really need to be.  (But it would have been welcome)Beyond a Steel Sky takes place roughly a decade after the ending of Beneath a Sky Steel.  It does a pretty great job of picking up the plot where that game left off and building upon it... until, well, the ending.  But we'll get to that down the line.A bulk of the gameplay is walking around, talking to people, and inspecting the environment for the magical dohicky that will allow you to make forward progress.  It's usually pretty straight forward, barring a few cases where it isn't so obvious.  Thankfully, the game has a nice built-in hint system that helps resolve ambiguity in this situations and keeps the story moving.Since a bulk of the gameplay is literally just talking to people to exhaust their dialogue options and figure out where the next magic interaction point is that will advance the story, it's worth discussing the dialogue.  It's pretty well written and voice acted.  The performances are top-notch across the board, barring a few spotty audio quality issues with some bit roles that you can *totally* tell were done in a rush near the end of production.  Those little bumps don't really detract from the professional storytelling quality of the rest of game.Eric Meyers steps up as Foster's voice and his work is magnificent.  It's similar, but different Adam Henderson's work as Foster in the 1994 classic.  Honestly, if this man's vocal work wasn't as good as it is, the whole game would suffer tremendously.  His ability to portray Foster's idealism and revulsion with the society of Union City elevates the game's ability to pull the player into the story and keep them invested throughout.There's plenty more praise I could lavish on this game, but I think my point has been made pretty clear.  If you're a fan of Telltale style adventures, you're getting a solid storytelling experience from start-to-almost-finish.So... let's get into that nasty part I've been avoiding.  The ending.  Oh boy.Dave Gibbon's original work in Beneath a Steel Sky was an excellent warning at the time about the dangers of an unbalanced society, where mechanical efficiency smothers anything resembling humanist values.  The dangers of a literal corporate state run amok.  The message at the time was appropriate and well made.Beyond a Steel Sky seems to attempt to make the  argument in the closing minutes of the game... but it's a different story now.  And the arguments leveled against this society are generic, empty platitudes that don't actually build anything new.  There's no substance to the message. A couple of brief, spoiler-free examples.  It's revealed part way through the story that in order to keep up with society's conspicuous consumption, they've had to do some bad stuff.  But rather than condemn the means by which they obtain these goods for consumption, Gibbons takes this as a soap box to rail against the very concept of consumption.  That's... okay, I suppose, but it's a little awkward to condemn people for wanting to eat food and drink clean water and wear clothes.  His point tries to be specifically about "wasteful consumption", but it happens in the context of .  So it kinda falls flat.The real kicker where the entire ending falls apart is the dissemination of progress.  When humanity has successfully automated away nearly all tedious, mindless manual labor... that's a huge step forward, right?  We all have the time now to pursue our passions and work towards creating a better world.  Study whatever you want.  Become a scientist working on space travel or more efficient fuel sources or automated manufacturing techniques.  Lots to do, right?Well, no, not according to Gibbons.  He asserts a society's lack of ambition to make progress follows from complacency of their basic needs being met.  Essentially, if you aren't starving and working yourself to death to live... Well, I guess everyone becomes a lazy worthless jerk who has no interest in science, math, or philosophy.  They just sit around and choose to do literally nothing at all.These arguments are all leveled within the last 10 minutes of gameplay, and they're not very well explored despite being the basis for the entire setting and story of the preceding 8 hours of gameplay.  And they're particularly bad when the condemnation of these concepts is .If external forces are required for humans to make effective progress... then... at any point, the people of Union City could have been told what terrible things are happening to keep them happy, and something else could be done.  Thus, an external force for progress and development is discovered.  But that's brushed aside, literally never addressed, so the very concept of technological or social progress is outright condemned.And that's the crying shame.  The world built up to that point has some extremely good points to make, a modernization of a classic concept.  Collecting "likes" as a form of social status?  Spot on.  Wasteful, unnecessary consumption?  Definitely still a thing.  Baseless fear and paranoia of the outside, of others, of the unknown?  Triple check!It seems like the final act of the game needed another few drafts to sharpen its point and make a clear statement about what it means to live in a world of growing technology.  Instead, it veers off into shallow, fantasy storytelling idealism about how great it is to live in a barren, lifeless desert without technology and how bad it is to live in a city with technology... when it had excellent philosophical points to make about the shallowness of modern society and our wasteful consumption, it certainly isn't well made when the writer is saying "You should go live in a dirt hut without electricity and technology is only good if you build it from the garbage of bad people's technology"....if this sounds like a mess, that's because it is.  The final act is just god awfully clumsy.  I can see what message he was trying to deliver, but it fails miserably at making that point and in hindsight, it really ruins the rest of the narrative as... it doesn't make a lick of sense in hindsight.If all this sounds incredibly negative, mind you, the fact the game has me taking the time think about these concepts and explore them means it's .  And that's worth a whole lot of points.It's a fun ride until that last 30 minutes where the writing gets rushed and sloppy, in my opinion.  Absolutely worth a spin, especially if you've never played the original.  But in that case, I'd recommend playing THIS first before playing the free release of Beneath a Steel Sky over on GOG.  You might not get a lot of references, but that's okay.  They weren't important anyway, it's just for old fans and their nostalgia trip.  You'll likely get the same value seeing that relationship in reverse, except you'll get to end with a story that has a satisfying conclusion.

_childDocuments_.review: The original "Beneath a Steel Sky" was either one of my first, if not the first PC game I ever played back in the early 90s. And since then, I've replayed it countless times even. As such, it holds a very special place in my heart. So when I saw that it was finally getting a sequel, the anticipation was real.But after now having completed it, I really can't say that I'm not disappointed.I'd accepted that a lot of the feel of the original was not going to transfer well into this new game but held out in hope that it would be faithful in character. Especially with Dave Gibbons on the team. But it's safe to say that whilst the original had great art direction, this one looks like it was rushed together based on a few new to the IP design-evolutionary themes cobbled with a generic futurist utopia template. There are lots of callbacks to the original but very few evoke the feel of what they're trying to purposely recall (Exceptions being the transport robot and the cleaning droid shell). It's only served to remind me how good the original game's art direction was.The writing has also taken a big hit. The original presented a game world where you could sense that something was very rotten beneath... Union City's sky. Characters in this sequel feel much less layered and requires the game to actually inform the player that there was more to the public's general mood all along by the time of the game's ending. You never get a sense of Union City's denizens being genuinely dissatisfied until Foster has to spell it out for us. The game's attempt at humour is passable and there were moments were I actually laughed, but nowhere near the dry, tongue-in-cheek of the original. It has its moments but rather than being woven into the game's writing, feels reliant on set-pieces to deliver laughs.As another review and other players have noted, the game's challenge level compared to the original is lacking. Over relying on the new hack mechanic and the crowbar feels lazy, and giving us mostly set puzzle challenges rather than organic situations with which to solve challenges feels a little too disconnected. The original was adept at connecting our actions in solving problems to further the game's narrative. There was nothing in 'Beyond' that attempted the puzzle solving flow of say, the lab chapter from near the end of the first game. It feels far too simplistic and it just doesn't feel rewarding because of this. Tied to all this is the overall feeling that the developers seem to have made this game a lot more family-friendly. You no longer feel any gravity from mistakes you make, as opposed to the original where Foster is at risk of being shot, fried, crushed, strangled or eaten by a cave monster.Whilst I enjoyed the plethora of references and callbacks to the original, Beyond a Steel Sky feels less like a genuine sequel to its forebear and more like a museum showcase of what made the original so compelling. As such, it can feel both very short of its potential for diehard fans of the original, and likely a little bit alienating to players new to the series. It instead, serves to help me highly recommend playing the original either before, or instead of this sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: While the western world is eying China and its social credit system, glorifying posthumanism and technocratic ideals in its media, and dangerously increasing its formation of politically correct but emotionally plastic cultural value systems, it is Charles Cecil and his team from Revolution Software, who are producing the antithesis in the shape of Beyond a Steel Sky.You are playing as Robert Foster, a middle-aged man living a simple and rural lifestyle somewhere in the desert on the outskirts of Union City, a futuristic walled megapolis built on the dream to provide all of its citizens with the opportunity to a perfect life dictated by spotless happiness.Foster had saved Union City out of the hands of a tyrannical all-pervasive AI-system a decade before, but content with his recent lot, Foster could not care less about the goings-on in the city these days. That is, until one of the boys from his village is being abducted one night, with the traces leading him right into the gates of the beaming utopia.To gain entrance, Foster will engage in identity theft of a certain Graham Grundy, whose dead body we find outside of the city walls. Through his eyes, we will gain insight into the inner workings of the city and its unspoken tragedies. Over the course of the game, we will come to know many colourful characters and their ways of dealing with Union City's rigid social structure. Increasingly, Foster will have to deal with the question whether the city he had liberated might have slipped into a far more subtle tyranny.Spiced up with the usual eccentric humour that Revolution Software has become known for over the years, an interesting comic-book art style and a lush soundtrack, this game will provide for around 8-12 hours of intelligent and intriguing entertainment with some very good, old school puzzle design - depending on how many of the numerous conversations with the NPCs you want to engage in.Foreknowledge of the prequel, Beneath a Steel Sky, is not at all required. The basic plot is conveyed cleverly over the course of the story.As a writer, Charles Cecil is once again proving his ability to go down the rabbit hole with this one, without ever losing the connection to a more general audience. It's a shame that the technical framework of the game cannot support this artistic vision. As of its release, Beyond a Steel Sky is riddled with bugs and logic issues in its puzzles, some of them game-breaking. The performance is sub-par, there are many unfortunate animation and pathfinding errors that will break the illusion, and more...In an almost funny way though, these quirks manage to underline the message of the game: The perfection of the computer is incapable of adjusting to the imperfections of its users and programmers. Humanity cannot be systemized.A system in stasis will inevitably create unseen terrors to sustain it. And so, if we want to free the children, we must take the difficult decision of not playing the part, of dropping through the net, of killing the machine - generation after generation. Both figuratively and literally. Amen.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Sweet, short reboot of the original Beneath a Steel Sky, technologically updated but stylistically consistent. The new Union City is simultaneously brighter and darker than the original. The story and game-play still focus on human interaction and clever manipulation of your environment. Any fan of Dave Gibbons should check it out.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Well, the original Beneath A Steel Sky from 1994 is considered to be one of the best classic point and click adventures ever made by many of its fans. A dystopian story of an outsider abducted into a city state who in the end overthrows the evil mastermind running the city. I loved the beginning of the game, but was a bit disappointed by the ridicoulously incompetent security forces of the city, who were unable to stop me from moving around the city and finally destrying the ruling AI, although the ending somehow hinted at why they may have been so misguided in a city ruled by technology. Anyway, this is the sequel to that game, made 25 years later. The technology used by the game has changed completely, from the classic 2D view to a (third person) 3D game. Well, most adventures that switched from 2D to 3D were (more or less) failures, like Simon 3D, Gabriel Knight 3, King's Quest 8, Broken Sword 4, or Syberia 3... will this game be a worthy sequel?Despite my initial fears, I actually enjoyed what I saw. The cell-shaded graphic (think "Borderlands" or maybe "XIII" if you are older) looks good, and the interaction with hotspots works flawlessly. Click on a hotspot and options to interact (examine, use, talk, inventory...) pop up. The gamerplay consists of the usual talking to everyone, examining everything, using your inventory, although only options that make sense are available. This saves you from trying everything with everything. While the city is technologically advanced, bypassing its security is still a piece of cake. Actually it is so easy that it is - again - a bit childish. Using a manipulated scanner to re-program crucial infrastructure equipment? Driving into the well-protected city just... ah, I won't spoil it, but it was so easy. Even the US-Mexican border is protected better. The technology of Union City is easier to manipulate than illegally tuning the software of my car.The sci-fi story continues a few years after the events told in Beneath A Steel Sky. While your toy-robot Joey stayed in Union City to rule it, you, Foster (named after an empty beer can...) left the city again to live a humble life in the barren Gap outside Union City. One day, fishing in a mudhole in the wasteland with a friend and his son, a 4-legged machine comes out of the water and kidnaps the boy, while knocking you (and his father) down. Since the father is injured seriously, only you follow the tracks of the machine to bring back the boy. After a few days in the desert and losing your orientation following a sandstorm, you arrive back in Union City, the gigantic megapolis in the wasteland where you overthrew the last government and left your little toy back to rule it. Of course... a lot of things have changed, and Joey, while being revered by the Council, has left the city (or so it is said). The city itself is a perfect utopia, but who is the Council that runs the city now? And what utopia is really the paradise it seems to be?With a beautiful 3D graphic (and a few clipping errors), gorgeous cinematics, fully voiced (and subtitled), playable either by m+kb or controller, and with 3440x1440 support the game comes with high production values. The (third-person) 3D doesn't distract from the classic puzzle gameplay, although I'd wish to be able to move the camera a bit farther away from my character.One of the best point and click adventures in 3D. Discover the secret of the missing kids... and find Joey.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond a Steel Sky is a 3D continuation of the 90's point&click cult classic "Beneath a Steel Sky (1994)."You don't have to play the first game, but it is highly recommended as a lot will fly over your head.Made by the same British studio Revolution Software who are best known for their "Broken Sword" series.Beyond a Steel Sky is not a indie game and won't receive the same indulgence.It was refreshing to play a point & click in 3D, not my cup of tea, but most of the time is spent on traveling around.Games like "Stasis: Bone Totem" and "Samorost 3" have proven that 2D and isometric perspective are not only viable but also focusing on quality over quantity.As a point & click, I'd say it is one of the easier games. No ridiculous moon logic puzzles, instead we have very intuitive detective puzzles that can be solved if you have some common sense.While the world is beautiful and the voice acting is great, the writing outside of the main plot is annoying. Talking to characters is like talking in circles, a lot of repetition.Maybe it was made to hammer in important info to remember but a simple notebook with quests would have made it so much easier to keep track of tasks.Walking and running is very slow, yet if they were optimized we would soon realize that the maps are very small as is the game.It can be completed in 10+ hours where most of it is wasted on slow running or listening to repetitive time-wasting padding.(I fell asleep, left the game running over 2 nights, ignore my 40hrs)The story was great, instead of the previous cyberpunk dystopia, we have a more insidious retro-futuristic Utopian hell.The whole city is basically run like a cushioned prison that offers safe spaces and participation trophies. Real human interaction and genuine kindness are worthless as everyone chases a status."Beyond a Steel Sky" is everything "We Happy Few" wished to be.If you ignore all the typical genre flaws, lack of 3D experience of the devs and recognize that it is not a triple-A title,you will find a pretty decent game with nice characters and story.Not as cozy as typical point & click games but still nice enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: The first time I played the original game (Beneath a Steel Sky) was right after high school I believe (2008 off GoG) which was almost 2 decades after the game was released; I had always been a fan of point-and-click adventure games and grew up playing some of the classics like Day of the Tentacle, Sam and Max, Full Throttle etc. The thing I love about these games is that they hold up forever. I recently went through Beneath a Steel Sky again last year and I forgot the solution to many puzzles so it felt fresh again.Beyond a Steel Sky is a good game but might lack the replayability of the adventure games of ye olde tymes; I'm not completely sure this is the case, but time will tell. I could ramble about these games all day so I'll try to be succinct by just listing my pros and cons for the game below.Pros: + Decent story-telling/dialog+ Humor is here still, especially with the sidekick+ Puzzles can get chaotic and funny as a result+ Visuals are nice+ Very faithful to the first game+ Game has a few different routes depending on player choice+ Voice acting is pretty solidCons:- Some animations can get clunky (bugs)- 'not enough' locations. I wish we got to explore the high class wealthy citizens' layer- Puzzles are on the easy sideAll in all, I enjoyed the experience. This game just might be a testament to the impact and longevity of adventure games and I hope the genre never dies. Be vigilant.7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Decent fan service, and a pleasure to be back in Union City for people who played the original back in the 90s, but it feels quite a bit more sanitised despite the dark potential of the story. Even Joey doesn't seem as acerbic as he used to be, which is a shame. I'm giving it 'recommended' but mainly out of nostalgia. It has some nice moments - like the 'interview' early on - but it never quite lives up to its potential, and the puzzles largely come down to the same hacking mechanism which gets old quite fast. If you never played the original, it's probably not worth trying.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Even though I do not play many adventure games, some of them occasionally catch my eye, and I have to give them a chance.  is one of them, as I love cyberpunk setting, so it immediately looked interesting enough for me. I finished the game in about nine hours, and I think that it is a fair amount of time for the content the game offers for its price. The positive thing is that I still managed to enjoy it despite not playing its predecessor, , from . starts with a beautiful comic-book style cutscene, and it is a shame that it does not occur later on anymore. The plot is about finding the kidnapped child from your village. The trails lead to , which looks at first glance as a wonderful place to live. Citizens are supposed to be happy all the time, so they get every food and entertainment they desire. However, this comes at the cost of their free will, and the dark secrets lie behind this curtain of happiness. While the game presents it with a slightly serious tone, it manages to lighten up the mood with several humourous dialogues and situations. Robots are especially humorous, as they sometimes refer to . Most of the main characters are quite good, as well. Some characters are a bit generic but still enjoyable. And while developers did a good job in this regard, I feel that there should be one iconic character for which I would remember this game, yet there was not one for me.Dialogue wheel is present with a lot of topics you can ask about. Some give you just more information about the lore of the city and its characters. Unfortunately, sometimes the dialogue options feel a bit scattered, as the game sometimes requires asking about the same topic again, even though NPC already told you the mentioned piece of information. That topic looks like it has new, additional information, but that is not the case. I would expect this to be more fleshed out, as the game is mostly about dialogues.I must say that I enjoyed the game’s story from the beginning, as it was interesting to explore the city’s mysteries. Unfortunately, I would say that the last two hours are worse than the rest of the game, and the ending feels a bit rushed and disappointing. Main characters are also not challenged enough, and everything goes way too easy for them. However, the ending did not ruin my experience. It just could be a bit better. Few choices impact some cutscenes, but those changes are rather small, and I would not replay the game to see a different outcome.There are also several nods to the previous game. However, you can still enjoy  even if you did not play the previous game. The game explains the predecessor’s story and relationships quite well, and I never felt like I miss something or that I do not understand what is going on. So, in that regard, developers did a pretty good job.The gameplay itself is quite simple, so there is not much to say. You control the movement of your character freely (with  or ), so it is not just a point & click game. A white circle shows you interactable things or people. You always have a choice to examine it, use some items from your inventory, and in the case of the object being person, talk to them. You are always in a relatively small location, and to continue to another one, you need to solve an environmental puzzle. Those puzzles are well-made, as they are not very simple but also not extremely hard. There is also a hint system in the main menu for players who get stuck. A new hint occurs every 30 seconds, and if you activate them all, you have a tutorial that tells you what to do next. There are also several details you can notice while exploring the world in the form of pictures, banners, books, and e-mails. I loved exploring these small areas, as there was always at least a bit of new info about the game’s world.The hacking system is an important part of gameplay, as you usually need to hack something to continue on the level. Its controls are simple, as you need to switch various tiles. In your playthrough, you hack a lot of robots, doors, elevators, and many other environmental things, such as virtual banners. However, these options are quite limited, as you can only switch tiles between objects and not create new ones or delete some. I enjoyed the gameplay for what it is, as it offered what I would expect from this kind of game.As the game released firstly on  mobile devices, some of its graphics and animations, especially the facial ones, feel a bit outdated. However, I would say for the game’s price it still looks good, and the game’s colourful art-style helps a bit with it. All the locations look differently and present a different tone. You will visit futuristic plaza with gardens and shops, as well as oldish industrial skyscrapers or virtuál reality in . I also must admit that the game offers several nice views, whether it is over the city or in the desert.The game’s environmental sound effects are of good quality, as well as voice acting. As for the soundtrack, it does its job finely, but there are no compositions I would remember or even wanted to hear again.The game was tested with an , running at high settings at , at . The game ran mostly without any significant problems and crashes, except for  areas, where I got framerate drops down to . While it was unpleasant, these areas cover only a small portion of the game, so it was not a huge problem for me. Other people reported even some game-breaking issues, but developers seem to update the game regularly and are active on their , so kudos for that.One of the main “cosmetic” issues is that NPCs usually have problems with pathfinding, so they bumped into each other or the player and get stuck there. While it is not a big issue, it certainly breaks my immersion into the world, as it happened almost in every location. As the game is not that complex with its mechanics, I would expect that pathfinding issues would be minimal. However, those issues are still relatively small, and definitely not game-breaking.While  has a few aforementioned shortcomings, it is still an enjoyable and pleasant experience for adventure fans, even for people, like me, who have not played the original game.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: You need to play the first game - Beneath a Steel Sky - before you play this one.The writing maintains the same tone as the previous game, which I appreciated. The puzzles are good and not too hard. The hint system is very helpful and very good at making you not feel like an idiot when you *almost* have it figured out.The only minor gripe I have is with the animation and faces especially. Foster looks like he's smiling too much when he's delivering or being given bad news. And they turned the hunk level of Foster's face to 11/10 - I'm not sure why he has a crowbar when he could just use his chin.That all being said, I enjoyed it, and if you liked the first game, it's a nice revisit to the world and I found myself invested. You'll probably like it too.
