_childDocuments_.review: I love Revolution, so there's that bias upfront.  I also played the original game, but it has been a long time.  If you're wondering how well you need to remember Beneath a Steel Sky, this game tells you more than enough as you go so it's okay if you've forgotten nearly everything, or never even played the original.My bias to like the game results in me declaring it to be more than the sum of it's parts.  For example...-The game runs well enough, but I did manage to break at least one puzzle without trying.  And if you like to get all achievements, at least one appears to require you to fail and retry a sequence, which I didn't do.-The city is supposed to be huge and looks great, but in truth, you never really have freedom to go back and forth between more than a few areas, most of which are just a series of open spaces where you can run over to the handful of nodes that allow meaningful interaction.  I didn't feel like I was really exploring.-The story is really surprisingly good, but the design shuttles you forward in the plot without a lot of feeling that you're affecting the story.  Don't get me wrong -- I've finished a lot of adventure games in the last four decades and I love what they do, but some people might expect more choices and consequences.  Another disclaimer here: I also love Telltale, but I did NOT want that style of interaction, so I'm glad this was more open than those heavily scripted games.-The puzzles are seldom maddening, but they also aren't very original. There's a little bit of environmental manipulation and little bit of dialogue paths and a little bit of inventory puzzles, but the game leans HEAVILY on a hacking mechanic that is repeated over and over. The worst I can say is that sometimes you know exactly what you're trying to do but you can't seem to find the spot to do it in.-The hacking mechanic is cool at first, but then you see that there are very few combinations of commands you can string together, and the game simply can't execute some of those. You're just finding spots that allow you to shuffle around commands in your hacking device, and other than a couple of entertaining ways to mess around, you're just looking for the combination that triggers the scripted advancement of the plot.So if you don't mind the one clever puzzle approach that ends up being how you solve half the game, and you're okay with some typical adventure shenanigans like running dumb errands in the same environments while so much more grave or colorful goings-on are hinted at but never seen, then get the game.  I recommend only getting it if you plan to finish it, which is about an 11-14 hour commitment if you don't use hints at all.  Judging from the achievement stats, only about 20% of the players who start the game play to the end, and since the story has peaks and valleys, I imagine a lot of people stopped while it was lagging and didn't see it get good again.Despite my criticisms, I still love Revolution.  Overall, this was a decent attempt to get the feel of the first two Broken Sword games (big praise) moved over to the dystopian future setting (love it) and the full 3D environments, and while the game didn't experiment with gameplay the way the 3D Broken Sword sequels did, it sticks more effectively to traditional adventure style.  The story came with adequate surprises to supplement my general satisfaction with the fairly predictable gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Revolution Software might be best known for the Broken Sword series, with the first entry still being considered among the best adventure games of all time. However, their previous title, Beneath a Steel Sky, is liked as much if not more among some. It was their second Virtual Theatre engine game that had lots of innovative concepts not seen in other adventure games at the time, “grounding” every character in the game and giving all of them their own schedules. It was also a relatively short game, yet packed full of memorable scenes, characters and moments and it’s no surprise people wanted to see more of this game world. 16 years since the release of the original and 7 years since said original has been available for free download, Revolution released Beyond a Steel Sky – a full on sequel, exploring the aftermath of the events of the first game. And while it’s not as revolutionary (pardon the pun) as the original game may have been, it’s a really fun modern take on the genre.Having played the original game definitely helps, but thankfully, you can enjoy this game without prior knowledge and it will explain (or remind) you of the world Steel Sky takes place in. It’s a dystopian future set in Australia, where some people live in several technologically advanced cities and some live a simpler life in the Gap (current Outback). Robert Foster, the main character of both games, has lived in the Gap for 10 years since the events of the previous game, however a sudden incident leads him back to the setting of the first game – Union City.While the original game was a screen-by-screen point and click adventure, Beyond works as you would expect from a modern 3D adventure title with direct character controls. It feels really good, both with keyboard and mouse and a controller (apart from several menus where the controller has issues), and reminded me about just how far we went since the awkward earlier attempts at this type of controls back in Dreamfall in 2006. This being an adventure game, lots of gameplay is about solving problems, which, luckily just like with the first game, are mostly problems and not abstract puzzles. Though you do still get moments where you can formulate a plan only after randomly trying out an interactable object because it’s interactable, not because you knew what to do with it.A big part of problem solving is also delegated to the hacking tool that you get early in the game. It’s a fun simple concept, which basically allows you to swap instructions between devices you’re connected to with the hacking tool. It’s usually very limited in what can be swapped, so you don’t get overwhelmed, but developers left enough fun optional interactions that won’t solve problems, but will get a reaction from the game. They mostly put those during parts where you will be experimenting when trying to find a solution so you don’t get bored when, for example, swapping the voice tone of an announcement robot and learning that yes, they did in fact voice over all of the variations.Just like with Beneath, the game isn’t trying to wow you with constantly new locations and characters and rather tries to put the things you’re already familiar with in a new context with each new story twist. So you will be revisiting locations and learning more about different characters. Which will differ from playthrough to playthrough depending on how you play, mostly in minor ways, but there are a few moments that will change the fate of some characters. And there’s even at least one moment where you can “die”, though it’s not as much of a risk as it was even in Beneath and relying completely on auto-saves is fine for the most part (you can manually save at almost any point too, however).Despite so often being comparable to Beneath, Beyond is smart enough to be its own thing and not rely on the original for the most part, as far as a direct sequel can. That said, there are moments that feel like pure indulgence in nostalgia, or character returns that feel unnecessary and a bit gimmicky. Plus, the game has what has thankfully became a rarity in modern games – clear references, sometimes outright scene quotations, of movies or books. It’s been a very popular thing to do in the 90s adventure titles, so I guess it’s also nostalgia. But as someone who has never appreciated those, especially in games that have so much of their own identity, this felt jarring. As did the somewhat abrupt and lacking ending segment of the game. It wasn’t bad, unless you really hate story twists that you can call from hours before they are revealed, but it did feel a bit too simplistic and also handled rather poorly in terms of gameplay.All that said, however, Beyond a Steel Sky is a wonderful adventure game for a modern age. It’s one of the most enjoyable takes on the genre as of late, where you still get both the adventure feel and the problem solving aspect of the classics, without weighing too far into one or the other. And it’s a really good example of how the classic point and click adventure gameplay can be transferred into 3D with direct controls of the character. If you’ve never played the original game, I would suggest checking that out first, but if you don’t feel like it, playing Beyond a Steel Sky would still be a very enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up with point and click adventures and the original Beneath a Steel Sky was one of my favourites. I am also a fan of many of the games that have come through the modern revitalisation of the genre even though they are trying to achieve different things (e.g. Wadjet Eye, Daedalic, and even Telltale style games and walking simulators).Beyond a Steel Sky takes a different approach which works really well. I was nervous about the third person controls but it still feels like a point and click adventure despite technically not being one. The game looks amazing and the writing and voice acting are excellent. The puzzles are perhaps on the easy size and they could have done more with the hacking mechanic which was a nice replacement to the Joey shell-swapping mechanic from the first game. I was never opposed to inventory object puzzles but this game does not require objects to be combined in your inventory.There are some strange animation glitches especially with background characters when you are in a dialogue and the final frenetic conclusion could have been paced a bit better. I did appreciate the actual ending. The price point was very generous in my region (I would have been willing to pay 50% more than the baseline price). Thematically I appreciate how they addressed a more Huxelian rather than Orwellian dystopia in the sequel with with a firm nod to real world trends in that direction such as social credit scores.I recommend this game if you liked the original or if the look / themes of the game appeal in any way. I don't think you need to really have played the original but it is freely available from Steam and other platforms if you feel you would rather play it first.

_childDocuments_.review: Took me a while to finish this one off but I have to say its very enjoyable. No its not a traditional point and click, however if this is where modern adventure games go then I'm more than happy if they're like this. I must confess I never actually finished Beneath A Steel Sky. I didn't find out about the original game until a few years ago. Unfortunately it was one of the older adventure games that passed me by. Saying that you don't really need to play the original as I mostly understood what was going on (obviously there are some little nods and nostalgic moments for people who did the original back in the day). You are not required to play it to get what is going on in this. The story of the game....well Its funny really, you can see a lot of parallels in it's story that are actually quite reflective of what is going on today as of 2021. What a lot of governments are subjecting the people to I mean. Rightly so however, I feel the game gives the message that this is unacceptable and cannot be allowed for a multitude of reasons. But I left the game with a feeling of hope which is a great message to leave a player with. All that aside (its a game after all and it just happens to be a mere coincidence) The game is quite cinematic. With some amazing looking skybox art which harkens me back to the old days where you'd just be there staring at it for ages. The game frequents you with this and its excellent eye candy.The cinematics are well framed and flow nicely. The game also has some has interesting if not slightly confusing puzzles to solve at times (which there always should be in an adventure game) and they're mostly logical ones too (if you get stuck there is a hint system to guide you at all times). The game also has very nice production values. Especially for a game of its calibre and budget. The music is fantastic too. Alistair Kerley should be doing more film/game soundtracks. At times the score really reminds me of something from the likes of David Arnold/James Horner/Alan Silvestri/Elliot Goldenthal/John Debney. It adds a great sense of mystery and adventure at times just like their music does. Its great.Revolution has done a good job. Here's to more adventure games from them in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm slightly torn but it is often a trope of adventure games, that with all the mystique and intrigue by the end it will almost never leave a satisfying taste if everything is to be wrapped up neatly.The true testament of the game is that I struggled to put it down until I finished it, I'd of sorely loved an extra couple of hours or for there to be some more nuance in the final scenes, the final point is one that should be investigated and pondered to it's full but not just countered with less than a paragraph of dialogue.Regardless of my thoughts of the ending I had a great time with this game, exploring the world, messing with the computer systems, I think part of that enjoyment is tied to loving old adventure games but with the added benefit that this time I seldom found myself stuck or pixel hunting, and when I did, the hint system in-game was enough to hold me back from walkthroughs online (Bar one incident)Anyone who enjoys old point and click adventures should definitely have this game, the art style is a solid okay for me, but the lighting was phenomenal in a lot of scenes, the voice acting was really good and a nice variety of accents rarely seen in games.8/10 I'd say in the end

_childDocuments_.review: I gave "Beyond a Steel Sky" a thumbs down because it's arguably not good value for money (even 20% off @ $27.99 USD) and the bias towards "Very Positive" at the time of writing this review needs to be accounted for. "Mixed" would be a more representative rating and I would give it a halfway thumb if possible.Dzelgris' critique is excellent and encapsulates all my own criticisms with more detail than I can muster, In addition, I feel "Beyond a Steel Sky" clearly reads as a half-baked game.As it stands, by the time I got to the end of the game, all my good faith was exhausted and my disappointment was palpable. The story trips over its own feet as it rushes through the final act. It only took me 12 hours of real play time to complete the game while purposefully going as slow as possible. This was a let down.While I found the voice acting mostly great, I feel the direction wasn't very good. Again, I attribute this to a rushed process. The tonal dissonance between action and dialogue was jarring at points.I only recall one meaningful character arc (Songbird's) and her arc was only notable for the fact that it pretty much stands alone. I found it difficult to care about any of the characters. I went from being excited and invested in the potential of this new world to kicking myself for selecting a dialogue option that forced me to skip through exposition I've already heard nearly verbatim in another dialogue option. The writing as a whole is on par with an episode of Black Mirror no one really remembers, except without the polish.The game often beats you over the head with direction and narrative. This is most obvious in Foster's literal narration. While this is a perfectly valid artistic choice, in this case it reads a crutch for the developers lacking the time to flesh out a world and story that "shows" rather than "tells". Think Blade Runner Theatrical cut's annoying Decker narration, except in the case of this game, it also doesn't "show".All games are on rails to one degree or another but "Beyond a Steel Sky" somehow manages to eschew all lessons learned and extant examples of successful design in the last 30+ years of point and click adventures. Playing this game feels akin to following a flow-chart.Why does the camera auto-rotate when you sprint forward and strafe?I can't help but feel that given another 6 months to a year, this game could've had enough added depth and polish to make it a potential future classic.I would recommend giving it a shot for less than $20 USD if you are an avid fan of point and click adventures, though I warn you, don't expect much depth. There is far more sizzle than steak here. Despite my criticism, I appreciate all the effort put into this game and do sincerely hope to see more from Revolution in the future provided they find a way to allow themselves to fully finish their games before commercial release.If you really want a point and click adventure in a sci-fi settings, I highly recommend Technobabylon as an alternative.

_childDocuments_.review: That there’s something sinister about Union City is made clear very early on. Foster’s accent into the city proper is ruthlessly anchored in delicious bureaucracy. As a filthy outworlder, he doesn’t have the clearance to enter the city without first being chipped, which lets the city track his every movement. Even assuming he can bypass that, he’s barred from entering the city at the entrance he’s arrived at, because it’s an entry point for vehicles only. No pedestrians; rules are rules. There’s a gruesome solution in the ID of a dead man left rotting in the desert sun, but even hidden under the umbrella of citizenship, Union City’s waxen smile continues to feel false. The more you’re required to burrow into the suspiciously pristine world, the more it seems ever so slightly wrong.Case in point: let’s talk about Spankles the clown.On the face of things, he’s an innocent mascot for a soft drink, which is routinely offered to the citizens for free. You’re never too far away from a Spankles vending machine and, so long as you let it read your chip, unlimited cans are yours for the taking. In the confines of Union City, Spankles seems to be a Very Big Deal. Banners are draped across walkways, asking you if you’ve enjoyed a Spankles recently. Holo-adverts flicker and change as you walk past them, asking you why you’ve not tried any of the new Spankles flavours yet. Your private messages included sponsored polls about what new tastes you want to drop into circulation. It’s never pushed as part of the game’s narrative, but once you start noticing how hard the city wants you to drink nothing but Spankles, regularly and heavily, it’s impossible to stop noticing. You walk into a hip coffee bar, slices of cheesecake out on display and various syrups and lacquers lining the shelves behind an immaculate serving droid. But scan the service point to order a drink and it’s not a double espresso skinny latte with vanilla you might end up; it’s a Spankles. You’ll notice countless rubbish containers filled with countless discarded Spankles cans. A machine designed to regulate your health will recommend Spankles as an unlikely remedy. Maybe its slogan is starting to feel just a little more ominous: “Spankles - Explodes your mind!"I started hacking every vending machine I saw, making them oft inoperable. I didn’t need to, but it made me feel like I was fighting against something bigger than myself in the defence of the common man. Usually, rather than waging war against soft drink distributors, hacking forms the bulk of Foster’s offense against Union City’s new world order. It lets you mess with various software’s goto commands, borrowing a prompt from here, or a direction from there and mashing it together into manipulative program code to suit your needs. It might be as simple as changing switching positive and negative commands around –for example, a door is programmed not to upon while an alarm is triggered. Usually, this would mean finding a way to shut off the pesky alarm, but now you can take the command that lets the doors open with no alarm, and swap it with the active alarm function. The blaring alarm is now you ally, and your path is now clear.Hacking becoming your (ahem) goto tool makes sense because of how heavily automated Union City is. But it does mean a shift away from the original’s purely inventory based puzzling, making Beyond a third person adventure game in departure to Beneath’s point-&-click roots. But rather than distance itself from its founding title, Beyond a Steel Sky does everything it can to celebrate it, with little Easter eggs, sly nods and returning characters. Some of these are obvious, and some much more sly; for example, though the game is set in Australia, the original game’s voice cast were all hired from North England, where the Revolution studios were located. Casually browse information consoles, and you’ll learn the founding fathers of Union City were imported from Hull, alongside building materials and steel.

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond a Steel Sky is a mixed game of 3D adventure (third-person view), exploration, and finding solutions to problems through in-game actions, otherwise you cannot progress through the story. The challenge of the puzzles is medium-high difficulty. Sometimes the game does not give us an adequate explanation while playing; so, it is a game where your ability to find solutions is particularly important.The game can make your life easier through hints, but if you are an adventure gamer you must (and can) finish it without help. There are a couple of occasions where you really will not understand what to do, I recommend that you follow well everything you read during the game by NPC.The story is good, nothing groundbreaking, but it makes sense and is coherent.The average duration of the game is between 10 and 14 hours, it is more than adequate for an adventure. The graphics are cartoonish style, they are decent, but they are more than fine for this type of games.The gameplay is mixed. The character moves and runs slowly. You can play with a pad.There are choices throughout the game, but they are often without consequences. Normally it is just options for what to say in the dialogues, but no matter in which order you choose them, you can always say everything, until you run out of dialogue possibilities.Can you die in the game? Yes, but it does not mean anything, it's just always QTEs where if you take the wrong action the game simply makes you redo only that action to make you choose to perform others until you do the only right one. It is not frustrating, it's usually obvious what you need to do.The settings are almost entirely in the city. Only the first part (tutorial) is expressly external to it. All in all, you won't get bored because there are many types of ambient and a good number of locations.The possibility of changing the programming of electronic devices is nice, often the puzzles are related to this function. In practice, there are actions that you can exchange between two devices, but only if they both have a particular shape (ellipse, square, trapezoid, …) inside the programming phase.e.g. You can set a door to open if you are not authorized to open it by swapping the function with another device or inside the same device. Other times, you can turn off alarms, or have androids perform certain actions. This part is actually something you don't often see in other games, and it is a nice plus to have inside this one.Do I recommend it? Absolutely, if you are an adventure lover. If you just like shooting, finding loot, leveling, then this is not the game for you.Rating: 7.8/10. Good game penalized by a high difficulty caused by poorly explained situations and a technical realization that could have been better.

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond A Steel Sky..Let's start of with the fact that I HAVE NOT played the previous older game that this was based off of. I am basing this review solely off of this game alone (minor spoilers in basic plot are in this review)This game is a Dystopian AI future based story with a tie to child abduction. Child abduction/abuse I see as important as its not talked about enough in current times (These are both taken with more light heart then what they actually are like in real life. Easier to digest). "Kudos" to them for actually addressing serious concerns in real world within the game world. The main character in this story is extremely tame and relatable for someone who is trying to find the truth in a crazy AI controlled world. Some twists and turns with the story but it is mainly binary in path, and somewhat predictable ending given the start. There are puzzles you have to complete throughout that are very similar to basic programming (in my eyes). Some can be very confusing at first. There are "hints" on the ESC screen if you run into a brick wall on them.My full run of this game was around 11 hours (play time may show higher if I do another run). I also did this run at a very slow pace. If you were trying to do this quickly you could probably get it done in less than 9 easily. Which ties directly into one of the two biggest problems with this game entirely. The price.Price of a game that lasts this amount of time I would market to $20-25. Nothing more then that. I think the $35 price tag is far too high given the level of game breaking bugs from within the game still after release and time taken to play the game. I truly love the story of the game, along with the theme of the game in general. But the price tag is too high to recommend to everyone by default.The bugs in this game can be quite painful at times... Forcing you to completely go to a completely older save file just to be able to function the game correctly. To not spoil.. Everything from your "device" not working entirely to characters and interactions no longer functioning when they should be still. Most of the times when I was forced to reset back several saves I would take a couple days break as the frustration would be painful to just restart hours. I finally did end up finishing the game after around 2-3 rollbacks to stop bugs. Graphics in this game are kinda sub par, but I did not going into this game expecting S tier graphics in the first place (saw the trailer, images, was not click baited).The reason I am still leaving this as a "positive" review despite price and bugs:The game itself is a great story. The Dev team has a discord where players have been actively reporting bugs and they are getting squashed to this day. I love seeing active game devs that still try to fix their product past release. There was a bug with the "apartment" quest not progressing and they fixed that during my run, which relieved some of my initial headache. As long as they continue working on the game to fix the "headache" issues that break the story I will leave this review as a thumbs up.Pick this game up on sale, I got it on release for around $30 before it got put back up to 35. At current price I wouldn't tell my friends to get it, but for 20-25 it would definitely be worth it for the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Game aimed at the fast-consuming younger crowd and "family-friendly" experience without smart puzzles and lots of  bugsTL;DR expandedOverall game tone, mood, and puzzles got more cartoonish/kid, a lot of dull uncanny valley characters, cliches, and bugs. All elements feel disconnected from each other. Lack of QA and lots of annoying bugs. I liked graphics, models, level design, and lightning, but it's not enough for a good game. Verdict - Didn’t like it, get it when it’s on 70% sale. If you are looking for a good, smart and stylish cyber-punk adventure, check out oldies or indies like The Red Strings ClubWHY?Just to get the idea of how relevant is my review could be to your experience.I’ve played the original “Beneath a Steel Sky” back in the 90s as a kid. It was not even a cd-version, it was a floppy version without voiceover and if I remember correctly, the PC my family had just a pc speaker instead of a fancy “sound blaster” card, so it was mainly just beeping and clicks as a sound.I’ve replayed the original later though my life and played Broken Sword 1-4 from the same game development company “Revolution” as well as dozens of other quests, point-n-click, adventures, and whatever you call them games, including all the classics from Lucas Arts and Sierra of course. When I found out about the sequel called “Beyond A Steel Sky”, I was very excited, as good cyber-punk never grows old on me. I knew that it was already available through Apple arcade, but decided to wait, as I didn’t want to be affiliated with Apple’s “new gaming service” in any way. Well, fast-forward to me buying the game when the sale started on Steam.If you are not familiar with the original - then just a couple of words about the setting. The game is set in a dystopian future, the player assumes the role of Robert Foster, who was stranded in a wasteland known as "the Gap" as a child and adopted by a group of locals, gradually adjusting to his life in the wilderness. After many years, armed security officers arrive, killing the locals and taking Robert back to Union City. He escapes and soon uncovers the corruption which lies at the heart of society. The sequel takes place ten years later after Rob’s peaceful life is interrupted by violent events, that force him to return to Union City.Visually game set me right on the mood for a good old adventure game with a nice “comic book” feel, reminding some sort of Telltale Games mixture with Borderlands. I was surprised by the camera and control style (which is not point-n-click apparently, but a 3rd person action gamepad style), which gave me the impression of more action inclined adventure style.Through the first hour, I realized that it’s just a gimmick for a feel of “a familiar to contemporary AAA action” user experience, yeah you will have to walk around to find the needed characters and items, but no action per se of any sort. And by the way, physics for moving around is buggy - you going to be stuck in spots with plenty room, stuck into other characters, experience buggy pathfinding with your character doing a “moonwalk” while stuck in a coffee-table and similar stuff.The more I was playing, the more I was getting disappointed. And there are reasons for that. Minor bugs in character behavior, camera, and sound were annoying and distracting from the story, and puzzles were way too linear and not thrilling. As I got the middle of my 12-hour game (which would take less for a walkthrough - I would say I’ve spent 2 hours at least dealing with bugs, reloading savegames, and listening to needless dialogues) I realized that I’m not going to have a deep and fun experience, but decided to finish the game anyway.At this point, I didn’t have any connection with the characters left, nor with the narrative. Most of the characters and the plot were very cliche for my taste, and occasional fun dialogues of Joey and Rob are lost in the massive spineless waves of non-essential and dull dialogues of non-essential and dull characters. At some point it felt like it was the developer’s goal to waste your time on these and long walks around, just to make sure that average gameplay time would hit a certain mark.The game world is very beautiful but empty at the same time. It’s interesting to see the scenery once and basically, that’s it. Why choose the form factor of the open world and at the same time not introduce anything that will breathe in life into it is beyond my understanding. Technically you have dozens of NPC wandering around to imitate life, but with the fact that you can’t even talk with them (Hey, Little Big Adventure 2, an open-world 3d adventure from 1997 had more life in it) it just adds more to the uncanny valley.Speaking about uncanny valley - unfortunately, the animation in the game is terrible, very crude and characters don’t even blink EVER. Feels like the animation style doesn’t work with the actual models/graphics at all, which brings me to a thought, that the teams who were working on these essential tasks were in a sort of disconnectionAnd in general that what I felt from the game - a total disconnection of elements, like each department was doing their thing, and the result was assembled right before the release day. And you can spot it by seeing that the Ministry of Plenty is called the Ministry of Consumption in some other menus. Like "dudes, so which one is it after all? Why couldn't you just let all the departments know what you decided".Which is sad, because visually game is really nice. Sound and music are on the level as well. Voice acting is good in general, just sometimes you can feel like the voice actor didn’t know what’s going on and were disconnected from the characters.I could go on with clunky and unnecessary UI solutions, UI bugs, sudden memory leaks, and freezes on certain locations and other technical issues, but it doesn’t matter.After all, for me, an adventure game is about the plot and puzzles, but these are the game Achilles' heel. The overall tone of the game is not cyber-punk anymore, it’s kind of cyber-pop with very family-friendly content, which is not bad by itself, it’s just not entertaining if you are not under the age of 8.And regarding the “political commentary” in this game - don’t be naive, it’s a “political commentary” of Disney-kid level.Wait for a sale, if you really want this game.

_childDocuments_.review: First off: I'm a big fan of point and click adventure games so my opinion may be colored a bit by my general enjoyment of the genre. Having said that if you too enjoy the genre you will love this game.Taking place about 10 years after the original BASS (Which is free, if you haven't played it yet I recommend you do so!) it picks Foster's story back up. Things are a little different but the game made me laugh several times and chuckle constantly. The puzzles aren't particularly challenging but they are fun and do require a bit of thought. The story is fun and interesting; and JOEY!Overall I'd recommend this game to point and click adventure fans. The game's puzzles and story are pretty accessible so I'd also recommend it as an entry point for newcomers to the genre.EDIT after finishing the game: The puzzles get a little harder which is good. The story progresses nicely and overall this game is now in my top 20 of favorite point and click adventure games, and in my top 3 of modern point and click adventure games. At the time of writing there are still some slightly immersion breaking bugs here and there but even with those I can wholeheartedly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the first game, I had high hopes, and this game met my expectations.  IF you've never played Under a Steel Sky, download that (free) and play that first; it will make the story so much better.  I replayed it just before playing Beyond, so it was still fresh in my mind. Beyond is a visit back to that same city some time after the ending of the first game; but where Beneath is a 2D pixel side scroller, Beyond is 3D world, with 2D animation style.Beyond a Steel Sky nails the ending, too, great ending.  I recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond a Steel Sky (BASS) is an interesting game with a VERY simple gameplay. The story start strong with a comic book estetic with a Sci-fi theme and a mystery all put together. It keeps the played both engaged and intrigued, but it starts showing its true colors after an hour or so of playing. Awkward animations in cutscenes, barelly any (if good) facial animations that consist well with the situation, no skip cutscene options and probably more that i didnt pay attention to as i later on didnt pay attention much to what i needed to do but just enjoyed the thematic landscape the designers had really put a lot of effort in, which shows. Overall, its a game that losses its charm but is still an enjoyable play till the end. But would not recommend if you don't like pretty linear progression and a lot of talking and logic based puzzles (i would say there is maybe 3-4 different puzzle types in the game). I put it as a recommend for those that wanna have a relatively simple interactive story with no big impact on how you do stuff (beside how you interact with one single character). It is also very easy to 100% for those that enjoy that. Took me a bit over 11 hours (including doing some stuff in real life, like eating, while running the game). Pros: + Short + Intresting story and artistic theme (Sci-fi with a comic book look) + Good Voice acting (for the majority) + Interesting first 1/2 of the story Cons: - Losses it's charm after an hour or so - Awkward cutscene/talking animations - Laughable face animations (or the lack of) - Unskippable cutscenes - Lackluster second part of the game - Dissapointing ending sequence. Overall, would give this game a 8/10 in the first half of the game, then 5/10 in the later part. Hope this helps.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game.As far as Point and Click adventurers go, this isn't too difficult, I think all puzzles are logical and can be done without too much help, and there is a nice hint system if you do get stuck. There's no crazy use X with B to create P in this game. Although I did pick up some item that I had no use for.The dialogue is great and the d-RYDs are particularly funny, especially Tarquin and Chipworth.The story is good and has a satisfying ending, I wouldn't mind seeing more games in this series, as I feel like I want to see a lot more of the city. There's even some sly dialogue that makes jokes about the fact you do random things and use random objects with things, you will see what I mean when you play it.For now I'll have to go back and re-play Beneath a Steel Sky to get some of the back story.Recommended for all point and click adventure fans.

_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good sequel especially taken into account that the predecessor is 20 years old. The creators did not turn it into just another point and click adventure. They did not just revive the old dystopian setting. And they did not settle on the old plot and meaning. They did not go totally crazy doing something completely different milking a past century brand. They employed the old and made it new. They could have done too much in either direction, but they managed to avoid that.So here goes my heart felt respect to the creators and my recommendation to the fellow gamers.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game 8/10I'm easy to disappoint when it comes to sequels. And in fact this game fails to live up to its predecessor in my humble opinion. If this had the story and the dark atmosphere of the first game with modern graphics, I would give this a 10/10.That being said, I think it's still a fun experience with some interesting new mechanics. The story is not bad either, I just didn't like the conclusion that much. The end of the first game just blew me away. But I guess it's hard to achieve the same effect with a sequel. The game has its moments, though and I think is well worth your time, if you are looking for a classic point and click style adventure. This is certainly among the better ones of the past few years.If Revolution Software makes another sequel, I will buy it, and I wouldn't regret doing so, if it's as good as this one. But maybe next time, they should focus on a different part of the world they have created instead of Union City. The wasteland or some of the other mega cities for example. There's still great potential to be tapped into.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING: SPOILERS!! Mostly cryptic, but clear spoilers in the long text!!THE GOOD:> A feel-good story with a likeable protagonist> Beautifully rendered scenes that capture the artist's style> Something for players of Beneath, but also a good standalone game> Peppered with humour, but not flippant or nonsensical- the tale has heartTHE BAD:> Some lines spoken with emphasis that isn't contextually relevant - "would have gotten ME too" rather than "WOULD have gotten me too"> Dialogue often feels stilted/awkward, with odd pauses between lines/reactions> If you've played the first game, expect to repeat yourself- there's nothing new here - expect the same puzzles... in 3D! - expect the same jokes... in 3D!> Some scenes/interactions feel like redundant filler, eg: - *action* > *cut scene* > *walk* > *longer cut scene* > *mundane action* > *cut scene* - forced slow-walk along corridors for exposition; only slightly better than being on railsTHE UGLY:> Glitches and bugs galore- save often, or wish you had> Cel-shading sometimes feels inconsistent, or pops-in noticeably while panning - notable example during dialogue when first sat in the chair, panning to Robert's face (*pop*)> Textures often pop too- blurry after camera changes, for instance (loading from NVMe, too)> Philosophical confusion; kill the monster rather than correct the child? - using the word 'evil' seems a little strong in the closing exchanges - the message of the story is as confused as this review__THE DETAIL:Despite several bugs that irked me, I played this game through three times- once at a crawl, once for the alternate Songbird arc, and a speed-through to clean up achievements (grab the fish, try all the trinkets, view all posters, etc.)... and I enjoyed all of it. I learned to save more often, too.We have the same likeable protagonist returning to the scene of his earlier adventure to be the unassuming hero of the day, revisiting some interesting locations, gags and puzzles, and generally living up to what we experienced in the first game, but in three dimensions. Here, as a lover of the first game, I feel as though the sequel failed to add anything all that new or original. It could almost have been a reboot of the first game.As a consequence, the game felt quite short. Upon one of my restarts I walked away during the long, obligatory story sequence, and forgot I left the game running for several hours; this accounts for about a third of my recorded playtime. About three hours were spent on my final play-through. I explored almost everything the first time, so skipped much of the dialogue thereafter (there isn't much worth re-reading if you're not looking for clues).The story is good, and ostensibly makes some insightful comments on society- at least, the one presented. Ultimately though, after destroying recycling operations, collapsing civil order, and arguing against progress, we're left with a sense that our protagonist is more an advocate for anarchy than for liberty, who blithely befriends an active serial killer. If not for seeing to the the very literal duty of saving the children, all he really achieved was the destruction of something with massive positive potential because, well... scraping for survival among the scraps of a failed society is a better way to live? City-slickers can't do useful work? Humanity cannot advance without chores? Robots taking menial jobs is bad, m'kay?In the end he walks away from the city again, despite now knowing his error in doing so before.Despite the sermonised philosophical confusion at the tail end, it gets a lot of things right, and feels relevant. We've got obsession with social status, the evils of over-consumption, tyranny of a nanny state, fake news, some nonsense or other about automation, etc... it plays all the right notes as far as social commentary goes, and finds a few opportunities for humour both subtle and slapstick. It feels like these could have been played with a little more. More NPC conversations and interactions that offered opportunity for socially-relevant humour would not have gone amiss.There was a clear nod to Monty Python. It was unmistakable. This also missed an opportunity for a deeper and more humorous conversation tree with a certain defeated but stubborn character.Besides some funky new scenery, a classic towers puzzle, and a section that relies upon really bad mathematics, the bulk of the cyberspace sections were just a re-shoot of the first game. I feel there was a missed opportunity to really pull the stops out here, rather than closely re-tread the concept of the first game. This goes for the game overall, as it fulfilled my sense of nostalgia at the apparent cost of originality.If I had played this fresh, without ever having played the first game, perhaps it would have felt more substantial and new. I sailed through the vast majority of it just doing what I did the first time around in Beneath a Steel Sky. Even then, I missed some of the humour and interactions of Beneath; Beyond is not as explicitly humorous and feels like it lacks the diversity of characters and scenes in Beneath. It's a chimera made up of parts of the first game stunningly re-imagined, with a couple of new scenes tacked on. It feels short, if not for many cut scenes pinned together with mundane actions (like walking forwards).The moderate amount of exploration that is possible adds an element of world-building and space that only a three-dimensional rendition can provide, and the game delivers well here. As you climb higher, you are afforded ever-more impressive views of the city and the landscape beyond it. It looks amazing, especially from a precarious ledge atop the Citadel. Every moment of this game feels like a panel from a graphic novel, and the scenery is stunning.Puzzles are lacklustre to the point of being downright mundane. Most consist of walking between two nearby points grabbing one clearly-labelled thing and using it on another clearly-labelled thing, and never more than  'rotate these things until they align'. It's not brain surgery by any stretch.The hacking mechanic is fun, though it also feels a little contrived; once you've had some limited fun setting off alarms, changing soda flavours, mangling speaker bot announcements, and swapping holo-ads around, the actual puzzles that rely on it are not dynamic or challenging- you can't really do things the wrong way, and you can't mistake what needs doing because relevance is inferred by arbitrary overlaps of relevant nodes and the locking of irrelevant components.I feel like I want to say I was dissatisfied. I want to say I wanted more - that this was like 'chapter one' of a bigger story... but the truth is, despite the very personal opinions I've expressed above, I really love this game. It needs a little polish here and there, but it's a great story and a competent adventure game set in a beautifully-rendered world.There are some nice touches here and there. Stand around for a while and read what the NPCs are talking about- hang out near Greta by the cafe and the report of a missing ring pull, for instance. Mess with the laundry cycle. Note the colour of the paint you chose. See how many Gang-gangs you can get to follow you around (should be an achievement). Rifle through a random shelf of innuendo. Feed a goat (what, no achievement!?). Feed a hungry kid. Do things a less talkative way, then miss being called 'young lady' as a result. Smirk about soldering.Maybe I'm greedy. Maybe I just set my expectations of astonishment too high. Maybe I remember the original game being funnier and longer than it was. If I discard my prejudice, I can't help but love Beyond a Steel Sky. It should be played and appreciated. It should spawn more games in this genre.Besides, I want more of this universe. And Foster needs to fix that board, damn it!_____Next Up: Beyond the Walls - the open-world adventure RPG? If only... *sigh*

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time Broken sword series and Beneath a Steel Sky fan (games that bring me great childhood memories) - buying this game on release date was a no brainer for me. Any game Revolution puts on market, I'll buy it :) Just finished it a moment ago so I'll review it in the state it is now on launch. _childDocuments_.review: This game should not have been made, at least not as a sequel to Beneath a Steel Sky.They've made it too "family-friendly" and in the process everything good about the first game has been lost. There is an over-reliance on an inane "hacking"-game for solving problems, and the crowbar is used too often. The humor from the first game is no longer there.Additionally, it's too "cute" -- your mission is to rescue a child, and you'll meet a number of "cute" children throughout the game. Not everyone find children funny for their own sake. At 10 hours of playtime, I can't bring myself to finish the game.I picked up Beneath a Steel Sky again, and was unable to put it down until I'd finished it. It only confirmed how good that game still is, and how lackluster this sequel is in comparison.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: The original was one of my favourite PNC adventure games - so I was very excited to play this. The graphics were superb and I played it on my 4K 65" TV using a Steam Controller. However, there were a number of bugs with the interface, graphical glitches and on multiple occasions I had to force quit and reload. Trying to use your inventory items against something this is moving became a frustrating experience as the menu disappeared and you had to start over. Although none of these stopped me from completing the game, it did detract from an otherwise polished experience.The plot was perhaps a little too obvious for my liking and lacked the "dark" aspects of Beneath a Steel Sky. In the opening scene of Beneath, you see a man cut in half by a gun, and I'll never forget the doctors surgery reminiscent of the popular film, Minority Report. This felt tame in comparison, clearly targeted at a younger audience - strange considering the age of people who played the original. Don't let the TellTale-esque style fool you - this is not an interactive movie, it's still very much a PNC. There are some interesting puzzles to solve and overall it kept me rapt enough to try and finish in a single sitting. Is it perfect? No. Is it wonderful to see a follow-up to a childhood favourite? Absolutely. Could it have ever lived up to my expectations? Unlikely. So all in all, I would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed this game. The puzzles throughout all made sense, though it does have a built in hint system in the pause menu in case you get stuck or like me had a few days since you played last and don't remember what you were doing in that area. I played through it all with my kids and they had a good time playing it. They looked forward to playing it again. My 13 year old son said that he wanted it to be a couple hours longer. It took us about 9 hours to finish, so I took that as a compliment that he enjoyed it and wanted to play more of it. The people were unique and the areas were interesting. The overall story, while it is a continuation from the first game, didn't require that you played the first game. It had plenty of nods to the first game so that if you had played it over 20 years ago you'd go, oh yeah. Revolution Software has done a good job with this one. Just like the original Steel Sky and the Broken Sword games, which my kids enjoyed also, this one is a well paced adventure game that has tough enough puzzles you feel good beating them, and a story that makes you want to figure out the puzzle so that you can get to the next part. Great mix of talking, figuring out, environment searching, puzzle solving.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Sequel to a point-and-click adventure released in 1994 (made by the studio famous for the "Broken Sword" series; they even put their famous characters in display), that you can play for free  on Steam. It's advisable to play the earlier entry, or you'll miss a lot of context. I liked this sequel more than the original. Not only because of improved graphics and audio or for taking more than double the time to finish, but because the gameplay is more interesting and less frustrating (the original has a lot of pixel hunting, for example). The hacking puzzles, although not challenging, were interesting, giving the game more than the usual inventory-based puzzles.  The story is pretty linear, with no meaningful choices and consequences. If you're a stickler for plot holes, you'll find some, but thematically I thought that the game made some good points _ maybe inspired by the classic novel "Brave New World". Not a masterpiece by any measure, but I enjoyed playing these 2 games.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: this game didnt cut it for me. lackluster presentation, abysmal graphical fidelity, a story that still didnt hook me an hour and a half in, and very little to no gameplay.i usually love narrative games, even if they show very little in terms of gameplay and/or presentation, but the story and characters have to be amazing and carry the game forward and here, it just doesnt.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: So, yeah that was fun. It has been a while since I played a point and click style graphic adventure and I really enjoyed it. Thats not to say it didn't have its problems but certainly the game is of a high quality and was entertaining and absorbing. I finished the game in 14 hours according to Steam, I wasn't rushing anything but it honestly felt like a lot less and by the end I really felt it could have easily been twice as long, maybe this is a testament to how absorbing the whole game is that 14 hours felt like only 4 or 5, I really felt pulled into the story and the graphics and story are great.So, what could be improved? Well, some of the voice acting was a bit hit or miss, one really memorable character was the hacker "Leet" voiced by Shane Attwooll with a distinctive broad welsh accent, you can tell where this game was developed by all the regional UK accents in play. On the flip side the main character has a generic American accent and was almost instantly forgettable and rather boring to listen too.You can tell the interface was obviously designed for controller, and although navigating with a mouse is much more pleasant and realistic, using the in-game menu system could sometimes be frustrating.Most of the puzzles were fairly easy, some very clever and one or two just didn't make sense and I had to get all the hints to understand them. (The firework projector one comes to mind). The final puzzle where you twist some box puzzles could have been much better especially as it is the finale. Overall, I give 4/5 stars and I really hope they make another as this genre is one of my favorite.
