_childDocuments_.review: is... well quite frankly, a news room story driven game where instead of merely watching the news, you get to edit it! You play as the one that gets to make all the edits: all the camera jumps and adverts shown and other things... and your choices, they have consequences. A very story heavy and engaging game this one is, i'll try to stay spoiler free (or... as much as I can be)!This game heavily relies on ones sens to effectively multitask at times. You see and hear both the live and the two second delayed broadcast, as well as the 4 edit screens, a interference monitor, and even more! There is going to be a lot of panicky overlap where you quickly have to make a edit realizing it's on the wrong one, or you totally forgot your interference. The game can be very chaotic dancing around the various incidents and story steps and such along the way, it's honestly jolly great fun though! It's a feeling that you only get in games like this!The story in this game is SUBLIME. On the surface, it starts out as this cheesy poke at TV channels and politics as a whole, but it gets very deep, while still keeping a sense of humor and charm all the way through the entire game, but can quickly hit you in the gut with a sudden whiplash of shock, sadness, or fury. It keeps you on your toes, wanting more, even more so since the game is split into three "episodes" (as of writing, the game is 2/3rds done).  The story is deep, really full of amazing turns and unexpected twists, and you control them all! Every ad you show, every image you pick, every choice, it all adds up, and all changes the story. There must be a dozen endings to this thing, there are so many possible choices, even I haven't seen all the possible choices! I love how sometimes the game goes a bit meta breaking too, just to throw you off.For a early access game, this is quite the polished and well working game! I only had minor issues in the past versions, but they are all but gone in this newer version, so no more problems that i am experiencing anymore. The video and sound files are rather large however, this game is quite a big one so make sure you got plenty of space for it to fit. However, there's some really cool features like being able to see how everything looked without all the stress, you can see the individual adverts, and you can see what people said while you were cut away to other things. It really helps to sell the news room feel and helps you keep track of the story if you get a little lost.This is a flawlessly executed concept and a flawlessly executed story that is deep and rich and leaves you wanting more. It has comedy, it has stress, it has low times and it has high. But that's just the news for you, it's a chaotic mess, but a absolutely beautiful one at that. And it's not even finished yet! I urge you, dear reader, if you like the concept, by this now! You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece. Plain and simple. It takes the FMV genre and twists it so much that creates something new and spectacular. Through its quirky jokes and satirical speech, it tries to touch serious matters about propaganda, politics and war.You are playing as a live TV broadcaster, and mainly try to choose the "correct" or "best" information to convey to the public. Most of the times, you face the consequences of your choices, and most of the times they are pretty brutal...The amount of content in the game is beyond belief, with up to four different (FMV) videos playing at the same time with no cuts, which can last for more than a dozen minutes.The script is amazing, the gameplay is hectic and meaningful, with implications both on the story and your performance as a broadcaster. There are also choose-your-own-adventure type of chapters where you just read the story and make your choices. And boy do your choices bite back...With 14 different endings and a lot of interesting choices and twists along the way, the game has much to offer. Maybe even too much for an FMV game.A single playthrough is about 10 hours long, but the asking price for the amount of work that was put into the game is a steal. A completionist could easily get 40 hours out of the game, but that would prove to be too much of a chore.Definitely grab it, even at full price, and when you start, give some room to the quirky humour... Serious society issues will rise through this TV satirical masterpiece.The best FMV game I have played, and most probably by far. The whole team made an excellent job: UI, OST, SFX, Acting, Story, Script, Choices, everything...10/10A must play.

You take control of a janitor meant to help out a friend who keeps going out to parties and such (a kind of lame plot device, but it gives you a way to feel indebted to nobody). In what amounts to a combination of minigames you'll have to balance and micromanage to get a good score, you are tasked with taking over the broadcasting desk every few days (in game time). _childDocuments_.review: This is a qualified recommendation, as it depends very much on what you want from this game.A bunch of entertaining video clips? Absolutely. The performances and presentation are solid, there is a great sense of absurdist humour and there are more entertaining song numbers than you can shake a flard at (such that the absence of a soundtrack release on Spotify feels like a missed opportunity).Gameplay? Probably not. It is mostly there as a means to an end. The main appeal for some may be the choices, and there are certainly a variety of significantly endings. However, I found this aspect rather unsatisfying. Playing a middle-of-the-road option, which I thought befitted the role, resulted in muddled responses - one side would go from berating to lauding me in the space of a few minutes. Sharp political themes and a deep narrative? Definitely not. Both sides are presented as such ridiculous caricatures that I could not take them seriously. This would work fine if it was consistent with the silliness which is portrayed through much of the game, but these same caricatures are involved in terrorism and warfare which leads to such tonal whiplash that I was thrown out of the narrative. In isolation the segments are fine. The ending to chapter 2 for instance was quite powerful, and very well executed, but in the context of the game as a whole it was jarring. When chapter 3 ended with a similarly heavy scene, I just couldn't get invested again.It reminds me of Always Sometimes Monsters - the individual components of the story are good, but when looked at as a whole they are far less than the sum of their parts.Nonetheless, I had a lot of fun watching the segments, and that made it worthwhile for me. Your mileage may vary.

_childDocuments_.review: Not For Broadcast is a very original game concept which was executed very well. The game is still in early access so you are not getting the full experience just yet, however with more content on the horizon and the available sections hilarious and engaging I would definitely recommend this game to other players. I read some other reviews and completely agree that this game does NOT need gimmicks such as buttons breaking down or killer toys in order to be fun, the base game already introduces new mechanics at a frequent enough pace to keep the levels fresh. I think these features should be left for the challenge mode section which already exists. The game does have choice system, where you choose what makes it into the edit, what ads you play, what family choices you make - which offers some sort of replayability on top of improving your previous scores. As the game is still not complete it is hard to say whether or not these choices feel impactful later in the story. The choices are also not subtle, which is not necessarily a bad thing but the game always makes it clear to you "do you want option A or option B" or "picture A or B". Not something that annoyed me but some others seemed slightly bothered by it since its makes the choices feel shallow so I thought I would bring it up.The game is very polished, from the menu to the gameplay, everything runs well and plays well. The soundtrack is great and the game looks very nice. It touches upon political topics however approaches everything in a comedic tone. So if you want a laugh, a unique gameplay experience and a game that runs smoothly then this might be the game for you, I personally loved every second of it.

_childDocuments_.review: NFB is so terrified of interacting with its own premise that the plot goes out of its way to be completely nonsensical while still trying to convince the player that the decisions they make do matter, resulting in the story see-sawing between humor and drama and effectively achieving neither. Add to that the poor and inconsistent execution of its main mechanics, extraordinary tedium on replay and lack of QoL features, and clear over-ambition, and Not For Broadcast falls short in basically every aspect of what it could've been.First off, credit where it is due: The FMVs work better than I thought they would. A couple of single-appearance characters are less than convincing, but that hardly detracts from the 99% of the acting that create memorable and colorful characters. There's quite a lot of actors too, and it was impressive how careful they were even about reusing extras so as to not break the illusion. That's where the game's positives end. Now, as for the negatives:- Despite the title and hints given by the game, airing footage "Not For Broadcast" almost never makes an impact and is difficult to do in the first place. Now, all games like this (the obvious comparison is "Papers, Please", which NFB even includes a nod to) tend to include a drawback to the player breaking the in-universe rules, to present risks and rewards, but NFB doesn't give you any feedback about when playing not-for-broadcast material (that is, things you weren't supposed to cut to, were supposed to cut away from, or are happening during a commercial break) will have an impact. They had to include a **loading screen hint** for the time in the first level when it *does*, because they have no other way of signalling that information to the player! And whenever you do air such content, you are punished swiftly and harshly at even the normal difficulty. *A* punishment makes sense, but making it so players can't afford to experiment on an average run is really not conducive to the mechanic IN THE NAME OF THE GAME- Because they so royally screwed up the mechanic that, once again, is the entire name of the game, they change the rules halfway through the game. The only actual "not for broadcast" material that matters will be on clearly marked tapes or cameras. The player still has the choice to play it or not, but the entire process has been dumbed down, and the penalties for playing this supposedly "not for broadcast" material are a lot more nebulous and avoidable. So all the actual feeling of risk and rebellion is taken out of the equation, again rendering the entire point of the mechanic moot. Also this happens like, twice in the entire game.- Out of I assume a terror of accidentally offending someone or saying anything meaningful, the plot has been constructed to be utterly divorced from reality, with the side effect of giving you nothing to care about. The two political factions that, broadly speaking, can be considered to be vying for your allegiance as editor of the news station, are: 1) A fascist moron who commits mass murder, orders assassinations, and has people brainwashed, but seems legitimately surprised when her supporters turn out to be fascists and is also portrayed as sincerely caring and benevolent by the game, and 2) freedom fighter black Alex Jones, who was right about everything. Because you see, the left and the right are *both* evil. Only centrism is the enlightened path, the game tells you outright.- In case those stunning choices of groups to support weren't enough player motivation, they have also given the player a family. Who do nothing. And have no impact on the story. They were extremely obviously stapled on to the actual plot in a weak attempt at pathos. In Papers, Please, keeping your family alive was the entire *point* of the game. What happened to them mattered, and effected your options later in the story. In NFB, they're just fluff.- Despite the title image for this game, the player isn't subject to anyone's controls and doesn't suffer any consequences for anything less than purposefully running a show into the ground. Not to compare to Papers, Please too much, but in that game, you could be imprisoned for hanging a picture on your wall. If you played your cards wrong, the revolution would shoot you in your booth. There were real consequences to your actions, for you. Because you were just a cog in the machine. In NFB, no one can touch you. You don't work from the shadows to help your chosen cause, or just toe the line and try to get home to your family every day. People address you, by name, on national television. You are the most important person in the country, by the end. You, and you alone, get to decide the fate of the dictator of half a continent. But it doesn't feel earned. You're just magically untouchable for the sake of the game. It's really, really shoddy writing.- There's a lot of endings, but they all come down to a few inflection points. Does the game telegraph these? No. Is it even logical what leads to what path or ending? Arguably, not always. Sometimes it's not even clear what you can do differently, and what effect it'll have. And funniest of all is that most of these inflection points have little to do with something being "not for broadcast". You don't get punished for them, but then again, we've been over how little the game has to actually punish you with.- Because of the endings being wrapped up in a couple of events, all the other levels are just filler! You CAN'T do anything differently for most of them, basically the entire second half of the game. Almost all your choices are meaningless! You just have to sit through the exact same conversations and songs and dances every time you want to do a different route. Some smaller things can get changed, especially things they can just do voiceovers on still images for, but those don't really make up for 20 minutes of nothing! Clearly a game way too ambitious for its own good.- The pacing also feels really effed up. It's weird going a week or two between levels at first, and then YEARS at the end. I get that they were trying to make a point with it, but I don't think it worked. I think that the choose-your-own-nonventure sections were dull, and again, didn't interact with the main plot, so they really could've been entirely removed from the game with nothing lost.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really unique game and well worth playing despite some room for improvement. The primary loop of choosing cameras and formatting the show is great and feels like you're a real producer, most of the time (criticism below). You choose what goes out live and there are various mini games (for lack of a better word) to keep you busy and add to the challenge of concentrating on multiple things at once. Some of the aspects can be turned off in the settings to stop them throwing random distractions your way when there's less to do on screen, but I kept them on because I initially like to play games the way the creator intended. I'll probably get rid of a few of them for a future playthrough.The Story is poignant and entertaining, you have choices and they are reflected in realistic and somewhat unpredictable ways. You might not be able to to change the immediate events happening in the studio, but everything you do will have consequences down the line. They might have localised effects on your own life, family and finances, or you can affect the lives and careers of the people in front of the camera, ultimately having an impact on worldwide events. There is a lot of whimsy and comedy thrown in to remind you to not take it too seriously and overall it's enjoyable to watch things unfold.Constructive criticism:While the acting is great at times, and with certain people, overall it feels like an amateur theatre production. This might be a very specific criticism from me, but having spent a lot of time around performing arts students, it feels like they could have done with a wider and more experienced cast. I think some of this may be due to the extremely long takes making the acting style seem like that of a theatre production (by necessity), but the casting certainly skews towards the early/mid 20s too and doesn't feel like a "real" show because of it. To a lesser extent, some of the sets, and particularly the police costumes look really under-budget. The security people have guns, but no other tactical equipment or protection and wear shirts and hats that look like kids dressup. It's hard to take the serious bits seriously when you can't tell the difference between a mall security guard and a gestapo enforcer.Secondly, they made the obvious choice to leave the gender of your character and your partner open for you to interpret how you see fit, which I commend. However the awkward use of they/them pronouns in the written portions of text can be jarring when simply reading along. Maybe another specific criticism for me as I have dyslexia, but a couple of times I found myself reading over portions of text several times to figure out if it was referring to one person, or all of the people involved. eg, Alex walked into a room full of people, which made them feel uncomfortable. Who felt uncomfortable, Alex or the people? Again, I appreciate the effort to keep the characters gender identity and sexual orientation undefined, with gender neutral names like Alex and Sam but I feel the more elegant solution would have been a simple selection at the beginning of the game to choose your gender/pronouns and that of your partner.Lastly, I think background communication should be improved for future games. There is a phone that rings for tutorial and story stuff, but I feel like the player is left wanting for more information about the clearly planned out production going on in the studio. For example a little heads up that camera 1 is going to be on the presenter, but get ready to cut away because it is going to do a wild pan off to the left to track the guest coming in. IRL there would be a plan for these things and prior knowledge of which camera is going to be doing what during a production and/or a producer constantly chattering between camera operators and the control room. They have moments in the show where the producers look to camera and say "opening on camera 1" which is super helpful and immersive, shouldn't that be happening all the time in one way or another? Some quiet behind the scenes team chatter would really help for those that want to play it more like a simulator game and make the perfect broadcast. For those into the story, it would heighten the tension and drama when unexpected things start to happen and it all breaks down, and bring you a little closer to some of the production crew you see featured on the screen. It would also help to make you feel less disconnected and isolated in your little room, and more like the world around you is alive.I think those three criticisms are minor in the face of the unique nature of the game and the clearly huge amount of effort that went into creating the live action shows in the first place. Although not perfect, the game left me wanting more, another story with a different theme, more DLCs. More than anything I would kill for a more serious broadcast simulator game with less mini-games and more focus on actually running a show and creating a good broadcast. I loved going back and watching the tapes back to see what went out and if the camera feeds and timing was right. I think the upcoming VR experience will be a gamechanger too so looking forward to that.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a pretty good game, but the bugs and the way the game is designed make it frustrating to play most of the time. I can't even finish the game because the same level keeps crashing and freezing over and over again at the last minute, forcing me to reset, do the entire level all over again, only for it to freeze again. I tried to enjoy this with all my heart, and while I can recognize its upsides, like an intriguing story with unique characters and challenging gameplay, the freezing locks all that behind a wall of bugs and errors. The way the game is designed also bugs me. It keeps giving you unique and interesting challenges that keep you on your toes, but they never stick to what you've faced before at higher difficulties, instead opting to throw a new challenge at you, force you to learn it, and then discard it to the Challenge room for the rest of the game. This makes it unsatisfying as I spent so much time learning how to do these new challenges and how to juggle them with the main game only for that new skill to be completely worthless by the end of the level. Overall, an intriguing game with lots of potential, but ultimately the bugs, freezing, and CONSTANTLY differing challenges make me feel like the game itself wants me to stop playing altogether, and I can't recommend this game because of that.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic, refreshing and unlike anything I've played before. Cleverly written to be just close enough to real life personalities and world events that they're recognisable and relatable, but far enough detached to be able to laugh at. No matter where you are on the political spectrum, this allows you to play out what you believe in and even offers chances to sabotage your opposition. The innovative TV studio control room allows for a surprising amount of simultaneous challenges to keep you on your toes, from the obvious "show the camera of the person speaking" right down to the ridiculous intruders (no spoilers). If you like Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror, you'll love Not For Broadcast, it has a similar tone of extending our current reality to the worst case scenarios while keeping them believable enough that it makes you uneasy about where we may be headed as a society. The Devs' commitment to this game is incredible, having had to cancel all production on their planned Episode 2 due to COVID Lockdown, NotGames got creative and used it as an opportunity to create a Lockdown inspired, Lockdown themed update to the existing content, providing more gameplay for no extra cost - and all of this was done at a safe distance while under lockdown themselves!I can't wait to see what Episode 2 brings and will be replaying obsessively until then to get all the alternate stories available!

_childDocuments_.review: As of the Lockdown Update, the game is fantastic. It's hilarious, both subtly and overtly. I actually missed some of the ridiculous happenings during the first play, so it's great that they have the footage available after completing the broadcast. The undertones of serious political ramifications of the election day broadcast do shine through the humor, making for a very gripping story that I want to see unfold as the developers get the opportunity.Anyone that was a fan of the old Digital Pictures games like Night Trap or Double Switch should easily feel at home playing this game. Similarly, fans of Five Nights at Freddy's play-style should find enjoyment of the Lockdown level. Anyone unfamiliar with those titles, or just otherwise unsure should try to free Prologue.The game at this point is certainly far from complete, but for the offered price, it is more than worth its cost in my opinion. I'm grateful the developers were able to find a way to make content during the Lockdown, but I also realize that there might be a considerable delay in content due to the live-action footage required to make the game. However, I'm already down the rabbit hole, and need to see how far it will go.

_childDocuments_.review: It works for me because I enjoy the humour, but that's possibly an English thing.  As an insight into live TV, it is both interesting, stressful and funny, even without the specific stories being covered.It starts brilliantly, with you as a cleaner, thrust clueless in front charge of all the controls because the real producer has run away.  His 'phoned instructions for what to do work really well as an amusing tutorial but the game keeps adding 'features' to deliberately keep you feeling slightly behind the curve.As the mechanics of working the production control room become more complex, things can get fraught, which means you'll probably let a stream of profanity out on air, but that's fine - because of the interference you didn't control, no-one can hear it anyway.  Everything works well to seamlessly simulate the barely-controlled panic of a live and unscripted broadcast.[ex-wife, C4 News and documentary producer gives this game her seal of approval].

_childDocuments_.review: This was a game I really wanted to like.  The idea that you're playing as someone working in the News Room as a Communist party slowly takes over the government is very appealing.  It's even more appealing that you can choose how to react to the situation leading to several different endings.  And to be clear this game isn't a lazy cash grab, a lot of talent has been put into it, particularly the acting and it's not like there's only one talented actor, the entire cast gives an amazing performance.But I can't in good conscience recommend this game.  This is sadly an example of a game that was too ambitious and tried to do too much.  This game really needed someone higher up to pull back the developing team and force them to pick their favorite ideas and focus on them.  The game has major issues with both it's story and the game mechanics itself.Game Mechanics:The mechanics of the game have several major issues.1. The game is constantly throwing new mechanics at the player.  Even the final level of the game has a brand-new mechanic in it which is crazy.  What's even worse is that a lot of mechanics are only used once and then dropped.  Like don't get me wrong, many games have levels with a gimmick (ice level) but the issue is that the game doesn't establish a good enough flow to be breaking it up this regularly. The fact mechanics are changing constantly is made even worst by the second point.2. The game gives little to no player feedback.  The size of your audience doesn't necessarily reflect your actual score.  So you can have a green level of audience but be getting a D (A is the best) for your score.  The game doesn't ever tell you why this is but based on context clues I'm assuming your score is based on the amount of mistakes you made that level and your difficulty setting.  This is where the buzzing doesn't help, yes sometimes it will be obvious what mistakes you made but for the biggest core mechanic, editing videos, there's little to no indication on if you're doing a good job, except for the graph at the end which isn't helpful in my opinion.However the worst to suffer from this is the CYOA parts of the game.  While some major story choices will literally be spelled out to the player, others will be completely hidden.  In fact I'm convinced that unless you're using a walkthrough the game is designed to make players get a terrible ending their first time through.  Major mechanics such as public opinion on Advance (the communist party), Disrupt (the resistance) are hidden from you and you just get up arrows or down arrows.  Public opinion determines which ending you get so not having a solid number that tells you who the public likes more is very annoying and leaves you guessing based on how you've acted so far in the game.  Also I think public opinion affects the advertisers ending but I'm honestly not sure because the game doesn't make that clear.Likewise the game doesn't make it clear how you earn money.  Obviously, you can earn money through good performance at work but that's not true.  Only getting an A / B score will increase your wealth and there is no story events that will increase your wealth despite the game telling you having stock in said advertisers will increase your wealth.  This directly impacts some story choices for the player character.However the worst hidden feature is the Headliners.  The headliners that pop up at the beginning of every level DO change and have multiple outcomes but the game doesn't make this clear until the end.  And worst is that when you pick between headliners they give you the choice between two pictures and it's very unclear what the pictures are supposed to mean or what the newscasters will actually say.  So it's possible you might accidentally pick something you didn't mean but unless you replay the segment you won't know that.  This actually brings me into the third major issue with the game.3. Failing is extremely punishing!  It's very easy on normal to have your score drop from an A to an D due to a mistake, and look I like a good challenging rogue-lite like everyone but the issue here is that if you fail a segment you have to reload and watch the videos you had just seen all over again and hope you don't ♥♥♥♥ up on the same part again.  And some of these segments are 30 minutes long.  Like at times I was fiddling on my phone as I waited for the headliner section to be done so I could attempt the rest of the level again.  Halfway through the game I was ready to set it to story mode difficulty but again the game is very unclear if that's an option.  I was able to change it in the options menu but every time I quit the game it would reset back to normal and the game didn't feel that much easier so I don't know if the difficulty every actually changed.So if you want to play the game just for the story I beg you to set the difficulty to story mode, you will save yourself hours of frustration but the thing is the story itself isn't worth it in my opinion.Story Mode:To the game's credit, this isn't like your cheap telltale game.  Past choices are reference throughout the game and the game is FILLED with choices and outcomes (provided you know where to look for them).  The premise is exciting, watching the decent of a government from the eyes of a news team, there's so many things you can do with that.....and boy does the game do ALL of them.  Similar to the first bullet point of game mechanics the story suffers from over ambition and no one telling the writers to focus on something.The game's story takes place over the course of 5 years and you'll feel like the game has 5 years worth of stuff to talk about.  There's the story of the rise in power of the communist party and how they drastically change society, then there's the parody of business, the music industry, the film industry, politicians, rich people, scientist; and there's a war in there as well; plus we have the story of the PC (there name is Alex by the way) and their family, not to mention the story's of the news anchors (that's 7 people minimum, more if you count some strong supporting characters like the person who gets Alex the job).That's a lot to talk about and I haven't even gotten to the very complex themes the game wants to talk about.  The obvious issue with having all of this in the game is that there's no room to have a slow buildup or setup.  Like we don't see a slow descent as the communist party (Advanced) gains more and more power until they can only be stopped by an armed resistance; instead the party seems to get full control of the government in like 3 levels (but don't worry the time skip waves this away).Setups are constantly just not properly done.  Twice in the story they do a damasking moment, as in who is that character under the mask but neither is earned.  First off the mystery isn't properly setup since the masked figured isn't masked long enough for the audience to care, and there's nothing done to build up suspense and make the audience even ask the question "Who is under the mask?".  And second the answer is characters who we only saw once or twice prior and you can tell the writers want the audience to be like "OMG I can't believe it was them!" but more likely the audience will be like "Who are you again?".  This is made worse during the ending as each of the 12 stories the game is juggling will have their own multiple choice ending or mini character arc; which will just leave you confused as you try to remember who some of these people were.And then there are the themes which someone else can talk about because they suffer from the same setup problem.  The bottom line is because the game is so unfocused it makes for a sadly bland experience.  It would have definitely benefited from some cuts and a tighter focus but as it stands now while the game has many different endings you can find I have zero desire to sit through and rewatch that story again to experience them.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I write this review, I would like to warn whoever is reading this that this is an incredibly long review that will go over several topics, but I will do my best to be brief. If you have an hour, thank you for listening.Believe it or not, I was actually attracted to this game because of Jacksepticeye of Youtube. I suppose the marketing has been cut out for the Not Team. Regardless, I would still wonder what kind of commercial would fit it best. Since I played the game itself in its early release, I will go over some first impressions, move into the gameplay and experience, and end with some last thoughts, suggestions, and about its potential message. [SPOILERS INCOMING]I watched the youtuber who played the game for his channel, and I really liked how it was setup. Some light humor mixed with realistic interpretations of actual news coverage and production. When I first saw Jacksepticeye play it, it prompted me with the thought "I can do that better!" which is always the curse of the cocky/viewer. The $15 dollars did scare me a little, but considering the costs of AAA games that can range from abysmal $20 to over $50 (along with the promise of more updates without extra cost) it was worth what I saw. So I already had some foresight into the two levels. A dangerous prospect, now that I realize, because a youtuber could have easily spoiled the whole game. Upon entering, I already ran into the problem of lag. Don't get me wrong though, my computer can't really handle games more than several gigabytes, so this isn't particularly unusual. Playing the game without changing the graphics slipped my mind. Suffice to say, it was miserable. However, that part was my fault for not realizing the problem right away. I changed a lot of the graphics (although being confused about vertical sync, a description in-game is requested), and it predictably ran better. Unfortunately, better isn't the same as perfect. Playing the first three levels took a lot of getting used to. And I could have gone for better scores, but it doesn't really seem like that would have done anything aside from an achievement. The archives option is phenomenally well-called as I loved to see the works that went into the scenes. What I observed was either the best movie directing I've ever seen, or extremely well-timed and natural responses that flowed as a news studio. I was interested by the premise from someone else's perspective, and I was rewarded upon playing this myself.The first thing I will note is how the game and its mechanics are designed. There is a lot of complicated levers that move up and down, but its not so impossible that its incomprehensible. A few tries, and I usually blow it out of the water after the first time. Though the reason why I can do it so well seems more attributable to knowing what's ahead once I've played the level once. I suppose that's why I really appreciate it when the mechanics get harder in a neat learning curve without any real artificial difficulty and fair challenges. Although if it really is 10 levels, I think I will become remiss when I land on the final levels (kinda accelerates the difficulty a bit). I think the best part of the design is associating most of the actions to key presses because anyone who has even witnessed a FNAF game will understand that such situations respond quicker with the keyboard. Yet, having a mouse also gives a sense of REALLY needing two hands spread apart to finish the job. I think it gives the illusion of needing to take something seriously or harder simply because it keeps you occupied. But now for some problems I generally have, which unfortunately, is still consistent with the lag. I can't really ask what could make the game better for a crap laptop like mine, but the problem is more so from the gameplay translated into video. To be fair, I've seen a lot of gameplay and a little coding, so I'm semi-aware of what generally happens in a lot of games, but the recording and capture of single images in-game is more or less still a mystery to me (particularly because of the amount of RAM that would be required to keep it going, but I guess that explains the lag, next update is going to kill me). Whenever I would use the censor button, it always seem off in the video, but correct in the game. To some extent, this can be kinda confusing considering that the bleep should more or less align itself within the timeline when it was pushed (so if it's correct, the video should reflect that). I suppose it really does record the bleep at the time when the audio/video is playing. Speaking of, the audio, no matter what mode I'm in, seems to be ahead of the video. I suppose what's happening is that my computer is still technically lagging. Because of this, the video is slowing down because it's a part of the game, but the sound continues regardless because a sound doesn't technically slow down. Like, ever. Any game I've seen will usually prioritize the sound because a sound that is slowed down (if it gets to that point) would start skipping and cutting at certain points. At that point, that's either the game or the system that plays it. Still, it can be kinda weird, and I'm not sure if there would be a way of fully buffering the video/audio before it plays, but that is as far as my analysis goes. It gets annoying watching the play back when I get something right, but the video doesn't reflect it. In addition, the only decision I don't fully understand is the necessary role of the second, lagged monitor. They say that this is suppose to help you figure out the timing for the censor button, but it always seem more bothersome than useful. I could mute the second monitor and get away with the rest of the setup just fine. I honestly don't see the point. In between the main gameplay, there is the mini choose-your-own-adventure segments. These really do wrestle with some formable options that aren't really obvious. Its tough navigating through the surveys, but it does surprisingly well to convey the struggle in their story. Its sort of like the kind of "hero's story bit" that will eventually be overcome by the story arc of the entire plot where the main protagonist will eventually need to or forced to be involved. This kind of gives a character that can be interpreted in many ways. Kinda like Stanley in the "Stanley Parable", except this is an actual character who is capable of being either character, but not a completely different character altogether (if that makes sense). It can be a nice reprieve. When I looked at the videos without having to edit, censor, or maneuver around the screens, it made me appreciate the amount of directing and effort that went into it. As well as the fact that its f---ing hilarious. In truth, I've actually really liked this kind of humor for a while. In a way, it is reminiscent to a long forgotten show known as "The Monty Python Show". Though I find the reactions mixed with some of its absurdity really nails down the humor. The game is worth it on its own for its comedy and wit. However, the more amazing observation I realized is the individual characters themselves. There wasn't really people who weren't straying from their character (unless its camera on/camera off), and I could tell what they were like by the WHOLE tape. The news anchors were particularly interesting because of the sort of friendly, if not knee cap breaking, nature of their friendships and relationships. They deliver as much as they fire at each other in the sort of way I see actual people who spend time with each other act. It shows that they have been on air for a good while to develop such friendships. Aside from character dynamics, I think there will certainly be something interesting with the cynical news anchor when s--- hits the fan (I can't remember names very well).This game, despite some of the nit-picks I had, was a game worth experiencing yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Because I used to work in the journalism field, I knew I wanted to play Not For Broadcast. I also knew that there was no way I would have time to immediately, so it lived on my wish list for over 2 years while I got through other things. Almost 10 hours in so far, I realize I made a huge error in depriving myself of this for more than 30 seconds. Buckle up kids, we're about to go on a trip.I was expecting the game play from the demo and the trailers. Picking the news segments, choosing where to camera, play ads, censoring politicians who get drunk and swear, all the best parts of working in a newsroom without having to have your face on it. What I was not expecting was the absolute bonkers amount of content this game has and the massive variety of branches and options, all of which is seamlessly spliced together, and all live recorded and acted. TL;DR this game is exceptionally well made, well performed, and is an absolute pleasure to play. 8.5/10The game splits between two game play modes. The first is playing the operator in the studio, pressing the buttons that determine what the media shows the public, This will swap public opinion's views on the political and cultural landscape and affect the story you experience.  This portion has several minigames of varying difficulty, representing the production of different types of segments in a daytime news show. Each game is unique in its mechanics and each comes with its own challenges. The combined effect each of these interactions gives a stunningly accurate representation of how a show of that nature is created and produced. That's not to say all of them are *fun*, as there are definitely ones that I found more tiresome than enriching (I'm looking at you Shock Tower). But they all worked together to actually feel and look like a news broadcast. It truly felt like a really talented team sat down and had meaningful discussions about how a broadcast is made. It also shows that great care was given to combine the different toys in the their toolbox into unique and interesting game play.The second play mode is a text based dialogue with response choices. While the interaction itself is just a simple choice, this is where the narrative effects of the choices you made in broadcast shape and impact the world. There are parallel story lines with members of your family, celebrities in the world, technology, and so much more. The writers had to have had an incredible time taking real headlines and stories and situations from the news and adjusting them *just* enough to be distinct, as well as the hilariously absurd and obvious names for the characters in these stories. It's also a more relaxing comedown after the more stressful active play in the broadcast segment. The ability for the team to tie the characters here into the headlines in the broadcast makes a nice overarching narrative that makes the world feel so immersive.From a design standpoint, having a high number of branches and variations is an astronomical task to coordinate and layout. But what boggles my mind is how seamless things are cut together. The filming and acting are so well done that the pieces of content tied to the choices you make is put together with no noticeable jumps or cuts or broken transitions. That's basically impossible to do when hand animating stuff; to do it with recorded media is absurd. I cannot commend NotGames enough for that.All around, this is a wonderful game in every way. If I had any critique, the musical numbers feels really long and the rhythm game with it is not super forgiving. But it also doesn't seem to impact progression very much that I've noticed, so I phone it in and pay closer attention elsewhere.Highly recommend, buy this, support this team.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is unplayable for me in its current state. Runs like a slideshow. I'll be happy to give it some more playtime once they optimize it.edit: Since posting my review, the devs worked quickly to address the issues I was experiencing. Now the game runs fine for me.The game is a bit slow, in terms of pacing, in the beginning. I'd prefer to be left to my own devices sooner rather than later but instead you're forced to follow instructions in the first few missions. Gameplay is alright, though it may not be for everyone. They spent so much time and effort on the videos but you're constantly having your attention divided by small minigames that you must complete in order to keep the broadcast going. As you progress through the game you can buy modules which do these small tasks automatically for you, which is nice. There is an archive where you can watch all of the videos again after completing the mission, but why would I want to waste my time and watch them again when I could've watched them the first time?There is also a sort of "choose your own adventure" mechanic in between the missions. It is a nice touch though I wish there were more options sometimes. The choices are often binary and lack nuance.The overall story is interesting enough, but there are some places where it just goes overboard for me. I get it is supposed to be a satirical story, but it just gets absurd at some points. You're hit with some serious family drama and the plight of the average citizen then next you see some guy engaging in BDSM on national television.

_childDocuments_.review: PLEASE GO INTO THIS GAME RAW. This game seriously had me reexamining my personal beliefs. Reading the wiki or looking at scripts puts into perspective how much your choices matter. One choice you make about your family changes the entire game. You start to really feel the consequences for your actions, and you really feel bad if you make the wrong choice. There are literally hundreds of alternate timelines in this game and choices at the start pave the way for your end. Even replaying this game allows you to make tiny changes to how play and you can watch the vast change in how the future pans out if you had acted differently in your first run. You get faced with crushing choices that make you think about your consequences and if what you're doing is worth it. I'm not gonna say my personal beliefs in which organizations are better, or how you should play situations, but this game had me on the pause menu for at least an hour total just thinking of the choice that I wanted to make in situations. You start to really connect with the actors and the anchors' friendships with one another. Gameplay wise, the game is simple but changes itself as you progress to make itself more difficult, but more engaging. Every day brings a new challenge, and you suffer or biinefit in other situations in the game based on how you play (Family is worse off because of wealth etc.)

_childDocuments_.review: I have a soft spot for games where are you are a little man with a bit of power over others, like Papers, please or Beholder. NFB scratches this itch perfectly. You play as an editor in a major TV channel. You need to maintain broadcast quality and choose how the public will perceive the narrative. While in Beholder you mostly decide the fate of a single person or a family, here choices you make affect large corporations, as well as public opinion. The story here is about conflict of interests between government and radical opposition, with both sides trying to sell their vision of the future. What happens as a result here is up to the player.Gameplay wise, it requires 100% of your attention. These days I tend to listen to something while playing, but here you have to look at screens, as well as listen for slurs and interference SFX. Multitasking gets even harder when the game throws episodic complications, such as electricity that sometimes makes buttons painful to touch, overheating pipes that you have to manually cooldown or toys that press buttons unless you hit them first. There’s also a challenge mode where you can combine these modifiers in different ways.All in all, the game has been a pretty satisfying experience. You should definitely try it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Not For Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: lol this is absolutely brilliant!The gist of the game is that you are an operator of a TV News station. You have to control what people in their home are gonna watch and hear, switching the broadcast from 4 different cameras, beeping profanity, adjusting the signal, deciding what image to show etc..The flow alternates between broadcasting segments and home/family events, presented in the form of multi-choice textual narratives. The story unfold in a multi-layered fashion, where your decisions in the "home" segments affect your life. The kicker is that the decisions you take "in the control room" affect the political landscape of the nation, with ramifications in your everyday life.The broadcast segments will definitely test your multitasking skills and the home segments provide a nice change of pace. All the actors are very committed and it's clear that they had a lot of fun recording this. The content itself is generally politically loaded or hilarious and surreal, I know that there are a lot of interesting ideas in the indie/semi-indie scene, but I wasn't prepared on how unique, fun and original this game is. I've just barely started and can't wait to see what else there is.

_childDocuments_.review: Whilst not perfect I would still highly recommend purchasing this, even in early access. The price tag is a little much for what you get, but thinking of it as an investment in the ongoing development of the game makes it more than worth it. This is certainly a project that deserves an opportunity to continue and should be supported. Positives:1) A rather endearing sense of cynical humour that hits the spot. (I'm British so maybe that helped) 2) A well observed commentary on today's growing politics and news environment. (Again, it felt particularly applicable to Britain but I get the feeling this stuff is everywhere these days.) 3) The sub plot over a strained family life is engaging and has a slowly building sense of foreboding to it, which is impressive considering it's just a few paragraphs of text and a few options. I sense it will not end well, but I don't think any of the story elements to this game will have a happy ending. (but it will be a good story)4) On the above, the general narrative and plot is intriguing. In the game as it now stands we only have hints and seeds of future events, but I already want to know more. Not just about the main plot but also the side elements such as the established host having to face a thirsty challenger after his job, Dave's flight abroad (presumably to avoid new taxes) and so many others. 5) I have the feeling that the game is setting us up for a "papers please" style choice between diligently doing you job and supporting a questionable resistance at great personal risk.  Indeed, the rapid and time pressured checking of numerous factors combined with that sort of tone makes this whole game seem like a more advanced spiritual successor to "papers please" and that is no bad thing! Particularly as this game seems to give the player more choice.6) The acting! From self aware goof to surprisingly straight the acting in this game is on point and enjoyable throughout. Serious points go to the two main hosts, the Alex Jones stand in who might just be right, our leaders from Advance and Striker and Harris who manage to play the entirely fictitious and utterly ludicrous rubber ball game with just the right blend of straight and comedy. Negatives: (I should stress the positives outweigh the negatives in my opinion) 1) Difficulty curve. I made the papers please comparison earlier and it stands. However, whilst papers please gradually introduced new elements and challenges slowly allowing the player to get to grips with it leading to the end of the game being pressured but dooable with focus, attention and calm. This game asks a little too much a little too quickly. Especially since you have to pay attention to lots of things simultaneously. Maybe I just have the uncoordinated flailing of an octopus but in places the combination of factors all at once was overwhelming and it felt like the way to do well was to repeat sections over again until you learnt what would come next, rather than react. If the difficulty curve continues in this way the game would become far too hard and frantic, to the point it might even detract from the narrative. 2)  The replay archive section needs a fast forward or time bar feature like in a youtube video. In this game you have the opportunity to re-watch the broadcast as you sent it out, and re-watch parts that did not go to air. These are interesting features and I particularly enjoyed the ability to re-watch what was edited out, as it can be illuminating. The problem is you have to sit through the whole section (that you often just watched) to get to the bit you want. This can be dull. So the ability to fast forward or jump to a timestamp of your choosing would make much better use of this feature.  Summary: If you enjoy a good narrative and don't mind some mechanical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to enjoy said narrative, this is certainly the game for you. Funny, cynical, well acted, well observed, well written and an odd sense of foreboding all make this very enjoyable. The minor downsides only come in the mechanics / difficulty imposed by those mechanics. These are fixable and do not lessen the enjoyment mentioned above. As stated at the start of the review this is a project that deserves to go on and I would strongly encourage the reader to support this game's ongoing development.

_childDocuments_.review: While there are plenty of flaws, Not For Broadcast is absolutely a journey worth taking if you have even a passing interest in this game's premise. _childDocuments_.review: The game is really nicely put together, and manages to be funny and serious at just the right times. The Dev team are clearly passionate, (dropping multiple bonus episodes is definitely appreciated), the mechanics are great and constantly being updated with quality of life improvements, and I'm really enjoying watching the story unfold. I haven't encountered any bugs and I've played through many times, which is fab for an early access game!The only real criticism I have is plot based, and it's that between episodes 1 and 2 the antagonists seem to go from having actually fairly admirable goals and policies, albeit with controversial and highly flawed methods, to being cartoonishly evil. It's not that I can't buy that their goals were populism to disguise a hidden evil agenda, but the rapid descent between episode 1 and 2 leaves me feeling like a bit of the story is missing. This might be a result of trying to avoid alienating potential players by interrogating any specific politics too deeply, which is understandable, if a bit underwhelming for a game with politics front and centre. I won't elaborate further for fear of spoilers though!Overall I definitely recommend giving this one a go because it's an excellent game, but don't expect any great depth to the plot (as it currently stands).

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like NFB, I really did. Because the game borrows so strongly from bastions of satirical comedy Brass Eye and The Day Today (and due to the really innovative and exciting interface), I assumed I was in safe ideological hands and jumped in with both feet...Pretty early on you're confronted with a press conference in which a Nigel Farage-type character and a party co-leader are talking about health and education reforms, heavily taxing the rich, and cracking down on offshore accounts. All sounds pretty sensible until you realise that these characters are being played as naive, bumbling fools, and worse - that they've been amplified into picaresque caricatures that don't remotely align with left-leaning British politics. Taking away passports and closing borders...these are not the remit of the left. So the satire in this regard doesn't really work.Shortly after, you're confronted with a situation in which it's made clear your only options are to either tow the party line and be militant about completely unreasonable policies, or help some wealthy loser escape from having his own 'hard-earned money' harshly taxed.It's clear I haven't played very much of what is a truly novel and imaginative game, but, I got the sense I was going to be forced into more and more of these ideological corners, which would significantly hamper any enjoyment I could get from the game. To reiterate, the people calling for health reforms - in this fictitious version of Britain - are the bad guys. It's not offensive, it's just ♥♥♥♥.If you like neoliberalism, centrism, conservativism, libertarianism, or can just otherwise sever your political proclivities sufficiently from whatever game you're playing to be able to enjoy it, then this game is probably for you! If you are a sensitive snowflake like me and prefer to spend your escapist time with entertainment media that broadly reflects your values, then stay away.

_childDocuments_.review: While it can be tonally uneven at times, swinging one moment from goofball comedic to surprisingly dark, the game is nonetheless highly entertaining with a great amount of variety, memorable characters and a even a few memorable twists. The odd sense of humour baked into the plot worked for me more often than not and provided quite a few laugh out loud moments. The true selling point of this game is of course all the wonderfully produced FMV, always a treat in games, of which there was more than I was expecting. All delivered with suitable levels of ham for the subject matter.A single play through will provide you with perhaps a little over 8 hours of content. A more completist play through will take longer as there are plenty of alternate story branches to explore if you wish, with the fates of many characters varying according to your choices throughout the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Its an amazing game. At first I didn't expect much and I must admit I was turned off by the in-game live action videos because I couldn't stop associating them to those old obscure games from some obscure console but the videos in this game slowly grew on me and now I absolutely love them. The acting is top-notch, I love the acting and simplistic controls for the game. Playing this game was like going through a fever dream and somehow enjoying it. The story was really good and being able to go back to watch the conversations you couldn't hear because you had to focus on the broadcast really gives the characters more depth and contributes to the world building.EDIT: I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ HATED the rhythm mechanic. _childDocuments_.review: Definitely give this game a try! Not for Broadcast has unique gameplay, incredible acting and storytelling, and choices that actually matter. (No spoilers review below)Gameplay: The gameplay is super unique and fun! Between choosing cuts between cameras, censoring swears, cutting to commercials, and many other things to keep track of and mini-games the gameplay never got boring. The difficulty can be changed but most importantly the game does a good job of slowly introducing you to new mechanics so you're not overloaded.Story: The story is incredibly entertaining and a huge part of what makes the game fun. Live editing boring footage would put anyone to sleep but this game brings a really interesting plot and a ton of humor. I was so interested in the story that I found myself sometimes messing up on mechanics trying to pay attention to the videos (don't worry, you can always go back and watch the footage after). Two highlights of the game make the story really stand out are the acting and choices. The actors are all incredible and you can tell a lot of time was put into writing the script and acting it out. Choices you make actually make a difference, with branching story lines leading to many different endings.The only con I can think of is the story cuts in between broadcasts. I know it's not the focus of the game, but it does remind me of a lot of the cheap visual novel games you see on steam with simple 3d assets as backgrounds.I bought this game in early access and the devs were always working and releasing updates even through the pandemic. You can tell they really cared about this game and it shows in the full release. This is a great example of turning an interesting idea into a great game!

_childDocuments_.review: Not For Broadcast – A Broadcast of Chaos 📺🗣️Not For Broadcast is the political thriller we never knew we needed... until now. Picture this: you’re a janitor (yes, a janitor) suddenly thrust into the high-stakes world of news broadcasting during a political crisis. Your job? Edit and air the chaos, all while trying to stay sane. Spoiler alert: you won’t. 🧹🎥You’ll find yourself in the control room of a major news station, juggling live broadcasts, making questionable decisions (like what gets aired), and possibly altering the course of history, all from behind a desk covered in clutter. It’s like House of Cards, but with more malfunctioning equipment and less scheming politicians. 🤯📡The best part? You get to choose whether you want to help the new government stay in power or stir up some rebellion with your editorial choices. Who knew being a janitor could have such power? 💼💣The humor in this game is sharp, witty, and delightfully dark—perfect for anyone who’s ever wanted to sit in the editor’s chair and play puppet master, or in this case, propaganda guru. The ridiculousness of the situation will have you laughing and cringing at the same time. The pressure builds as you have to decide what gets aired while dealing with technical glitches, angry anchors, and the looming question: Will you save the government or expose their lies? 📰💥In short, Not For Broadcast is a satirical, wild ride that gives you power over the media (and your sanity). It’s chaotic, it’s clever, and it’ll make you wonder if maybe being a janitor wasn’t such a bad gig after all... as long as you’re behind the broadcast booth. 😜📺Created with <3

Good casting, enjoyable acting, dubious political messages - "unfortunate" wealthy people, displaced by some kind of "evil" socialist agenda - all add up to a hilarious and silly game reminiscent of other atypical games such as Guitar Hero, Papers Please, and Five Nights At Freddys. Sadly, at time of writing, there is only one three-part episode. Thankfully its narrative suggests future instalments are in the pipeline. _childDocuments_.review: INTRODUCTION:Not for Broadcast is a quite splendid game about main character, Alex Winston, working as a live broadcaster for the popular news channel, "Channel One". More so for the sub-channel, National Nightly News. As you play, you will be challenged with new obstacles to keep your viewers not only entertained, but also appropriately kept from not-so-safe sights.MAIN GAME>In the main game, you will play as the broadcaster, as I mentioned before, and take part in switching cameras, keeping the language clean, and guiding the wavelengths of interference away from the news channel. You will also control what "Adverts" your viewers see, which can take a turn for the world's story. So choose wisely.STORY>The story won't be revealed here. However, if you are interested in playing a game with loads of story and "lore" if I shall lean, then this game also has that.MECHANICS>The mechanics of the game are quite splendid. Especially the update to the "Interference" mechanic, which has more uses for further updates and also is more interesting and investing gameplay-wise. If you like unique mechanics to the likes have never been seen before, then this game might perk your ears up, both literally and metaphorically.VALUE>As for the value of this game, I'd say it is truly something to behold. Although I got my version for around 17 bucks, the full 25 (as of Early Release) is still quite worth the price, especially for the upcoming updates to come (with a predicted 10 Chapters for full-release). As for the emotional value, I'd say it still hits close to home, even though it is not another Earthbound clone or narrative-driven game (at least from first-sight). CUT TO THE CHASE (OVERALL RECOMMENDATION)>Good game! I'd give it a good 9/10 for overall promising quality. For the people working on the game who might be asking "why only a 9?", do not worry. I'd give a 10 if I had all the chock-full of content promised for the future. However, we are still waiting. For consumers, I'd say buy the game if you like the demo. If you haven't played said demo, try it! And if you don't like it then, I'd still recommend wish-listing the game in case you want to change your mind!FOR THE DEVS>The devs might be wanting a bit more "spice" to take from all this. For that, I want to say there are still some more challenges I'd like to see. And maybe even wackier performances from the actors! I'm sure you plan for all of that, however, in the coming updates. Tell the development team that I love the game and that they are doing fantastic!END REVIEW>9/10Note: Hope to see more in the next update! ;)~DaPlagueDoctor (PinkiePurplez)

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most ambitious, original and clever games I've ever played. Very funny at moments, too. Yeah, the elevator pitch is "what if Papers Please was an FMV game?" but it's a bit more than that. Every choice that you make early on matters later and the threads the game weaves with your choices is impressive, giving it strong replay value.The latest update gave the ability to adjust the difficulty of the mechanics, including the extremely frustrating interference mechanic, and there's even an option to turn any or all of them off entirely if you just want to see the story play out via your choices.It's not fully finished yet and it's crashed on me a couple of times but that's what you get with Early Access so I'm fine with it at the moment. I cannot wait to see what the finished product looks like after how high the bar has been set so far. It's worth it at the current $25 price and steal any time it's on sale.Bravo to both the devs and the actors involved, everyone's amazing in it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is mostly silly.  I was expecting something a little more dystopian or something taking itself a little too seriously.  It doesn't.  It's an interactive comedy.  I love the political party.  They go full communist so quickly and it's great.  I love how they show the formerly rich becoming bitter and angry after losing their wealth and how they transform into counter revolutionary terrorists, a side of the story often left out.  We often don't get to see the blood thirsty nature of the rich. Look at what chichita did in Latin America and the like over bananas.  Not that it get's very serious but it acknowledges it which is more than anyone else.  The game isn't built with Linux in mind but I'm running it with Proton.  There are pretty major frame drops which hinder the experience.  At the beginning it was as low as 7 Hz before stabilizing in the high twenties.  Usually this would be completely unacceptable.  I'd either have to boot into windows or refund the game if it wasn't worth it to me.  But you don't really do much in the game.  The video you're watching is likely 24 Hz while everything you're responsible for is on a still frame so it didn't really mater.  It's something to keep in mind for those using proton though.  There was one crash at the two and half hour mark that lead to a system freeze.  The game keeps good track of progress.  It didn't look like there was any major set backs as a result of the crash.

_childDocuments_.review: Not For Broadcast is a dark FMV-style comedy where you decide what gets screened, edited, and broadcast from a TV station to the masses. Gameplay focusses primarily on constantly switching between camera feeds, censoring foul language, selecting adds, and managing the quality of transmission (amongst a few other tasks). Your actions determine how the public sees major world events which impacts the story and endings. Each of the shows and segments has something funny, striking, or poignant that tries to grab your attention as you manage these various tasks. All the while you are exposed to behind-the-scenes shenanigans and the agendas of various parties who try guide you to determine what to broadcast in their favour. The game honestly had me alternating between smiling and laughing out loud, then riveted to my chair waiting to see what happens next. Absolutely, worth playing and while it is still early in 2022 this is a top contender to be my GOTY due to its humour and originality.

_childDocuments_.review: Not for Broadcast is a FMV simulator where you, as the janitor of the Channel One TV network suddenly find yourself as the editor of National Nightly News. You are tasked with switching between cameras during broadcast, managing ads, censoring things that should not be broadcasted live. As the game progresses, you will get many other challenges and find yourself in situations where you have to make choices, which will then determine the ending of the game.Firstly, the acting... It is phenomenal (especially the actor who plays Jeremy Donaldson) and easily one of the best acting you can find in a video game. Same goes for all the other actors with major/minor roles, they all did a tremendous job.As for the footages, the first thing to mention is Not for Broadcast actually scored a Guinness World Record, holding the most FMV footage in a video game. That’s +42 hours of live action footage, most of which you won’t even get the watch in your first playthrough.Your story based on your choices will be delivered to you after every broadcast. This is one of the less interesting parts of the game, as the presentation of the story is really poorly made. The gameplay also has some issues, once you realize the core game mechanic is succeeding on a variety of mini-games on a timely manner in each broadcast. If you get distracted and fail, you will have to restart that particular broadcast, which in some cases means watching the same 20+ minutes long footages.Despite its issues, Not for Broadcast shines with what it achieves. It’s one of the best examples of political satire in a video game format and everyone is in its aim from right wing to left wing, from governments and politicians to news media.Not for Broadcast may not be one of the best games released in 2022, but it certainly is a unique experience that you cannot find elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed a lot of this game, and it's well worth playing despite my issues with it. If you can grab it on sale, do. Go in blind & don't read the rest of the review if you haven't played it yet, if you can help it.1. The acting-- The actor who plays Jeremy is phenomenal. He's a joy to watch and has great dynamics with the other actors. His relationships feel real and emotionally convincing right from the get-go, he's super charismatic, and the game's humor, which sometimes fell very flat for me, was always funnier coming out of his mouth. I kind of stopped having fun with the game shortly after he left. The other actors were fine for the most part (Jenny's actress and the PM actors were pretty great especially, and even some of the bit parts were really fun to watch), but Jeremy was really carrying the broadcasts for me. I also wanted to note that the tutorial's VA was excellent, and this game has probably the best tutorial of any game I've ever played, in large part thanks to him. 2. The gameplay-- Except for the late-middle portion of the game where there's barely any gameplay, it's great. It scratched a very specific itch for me. Even though the live-action parts of the story are fairly linear minus the epilogue and probably a few other pivot points (I've only finished one playthrough so far, so I don't know for sure), the gameplay makes you feel like you're integral to the story and making a significant difference in it. Curating the broadcasts is fun and fast-paced, the additional core mechanics like the censor add just the right amount of stress, and it's really satisfying when you get into a rhythm. The grading is sometimes a bit obscure to me--there were broadcasts where I only made a couple of small mistakes and retained a high viewer count and got a C or E, and broadcasts where I was screwing up constantly and got an A or B (not counting the ones where you'll get super high ratings basically no matter what you do). The only mechanic I really disliked was the interference mechanic. When it kicked in during segments that were interesting, it took my attention away from what I actually wanted to do, which was watch the segment. When it kicked in during boring segments, it felt like a failed attempt to make the game less boring. It demands quite a bit of concentration without being fun or rewarding or at all stimulating. I'll probably turn it off if I play the game again. (And I do appreciate that you can customize the mechanics/difficulty extensively, even though I haven't fiddled with any of that yet.)3. The music--There are songs in this game that are intentionally bad, but the songs that are meant to be good are some of the best songs with vocals I've ever heard made specifically for a video game. The loading screen song is great and never got old for me. The end credits song was characteristically unsubtle lyrics-wise, but it was such a banger.  was an unexpected gut-punch and I loved it. I also liked the rhythm mechanic a lot.4. The story--This is where my issues with the game really start. The first episode and part of the second () gripped me right away. I was completely transfixed and could not put the game down. The pacing was perfect, the tone was great, the writing was good, and I was totally invested in the characters. There were parts that had me more immersed than I've been in a long time. The political commentary and humor were pretty heavy-handed, but in a way that felt charming because it wasn't expecting you to take it too seriously. I was meh on the lockdown broadcast, but I appreciated how absurd and surreal it was. It just felt like it went on for too long, and once I figured out that , which was pretty much immediately, I knew there were no stakes and stopped caring. Then there was a point where the game became excruciating and stayed excruciating for a while. The awards show segment in particular was so boring, so unfunny, and had so little gameplay that it was insulting. Actually, all of the parts focusing mostly on pop culture commentary were bad, except for the J-Zuss bits, which I found pretty funny and endearing. I agree that celebrity culture is dumb and vapid and fake, I'm pretty sure everyone playing this game does, and that point gets hammered into you so hard over and over and over again. Didn't help that some of the actors playing celebrities were either horrible actors or being directed horribly while working with horrible writing. I don't know why they put some of these broadcasts into the game. This should not have made the final cut. I get that the point is that , but it doesn't make it any easier to get through, and it just goes on for way. too. long. It gets good again close to the finale.I want to preface this point by saying I don't want to seem like I'm taking an irreverent political comedy too seriously, and I don't at all mind media that makes fun of the left and right equally. I just think this game didn't do it well. It somehow felt incredibly preachy while also sitting the fence, which I guess is an achievement. In the beginning it was gearing up to be an absurdist, showy, but still interesting piece of commentary, and then it seemingly gave up on that front altogether. There were a lot of ideas that could have been funny if executed well, but the way they were done fell completely flat for me. It didn't feel like it was being intentional about not wanting to be taken seriously--it felt like it wanted to be taken seriously but was too embarrassed with itself to try. And a character can be an over-the-top strawman while still being funny, but characters like the Alex Jones pastiche and the Scandinavian president or whatever were lazy and dumb and almost as brainrottingly on-the-nose as the celebrity characters. The core story, ignoring all the filler, is simple but not bad at all, and the gameplay and characters elevate it to being great. I really, really wish they had tidied up and tightened the middle. It almost feels like they had a story planned out, then they lost the script at some point and just came up with a bunch of disparate unrelated material to stay on their production schedule. I know that's not what happened obviously, but that's really what it feels like. It's baffling. 5. The humor--I don't think this game is a dark comedy. It is dark sometimes and a comedy other times. The comedy parts are "dark comedy" in the same way that, like, Shane Dawson skits in the early 2010s were attempting to be "dark comedy." A lot of poop and fart jokes (like a LOT of poop and fart jokes) and dull edginess with tired, overdone stereotypes that would only shock a 12-year-old. And that's sad, because the dramatic parts are really, really good, and they make it clear that a lot of heart and talent and hard work went into this production. And there's obviously not a total lack of comedy chops here--there were quite a few clever one-liners that I liked a lot, and a few skits and recurring bits that genuinely gave me a chuckle. But most of it didn't mesh with me.---I know a lot of that review was me complaining, but despite that, I'm still really glad I played this game and I will probably play it again. The good parts were so good that, in hindsight, it was worth getting through the bad parts. Mostly, this was me lamenting that this was a 7/10 game when it could have been a 9.5/10 game. I also want to highlight what a monumental achievement this was in terms of the production--it must have taken a crazy amount of planning and coordination. It's unlike any other game out there as a result. Give it a shot.
