_childDocuments_.review: re-reviewing after playing when i got boredthe game can be described as "forgiving british papers please"worth the price? i would say wait for a sale.all broadcasts (the actual game) are always gonna be nearly the same, until the build up for the final (and sorta the red carpet section on second to final), which kinda killed my motivation to get all endings, but it was still fun for a while.spoilers ahead sorry lolthe game's story in episode one (first few broadcasts) is lackluster and sometimes becomes a pain when replayed over and over again, but is still fine for a few times to replay. after Jeremy's meltdown, the game kicks into high gear, with many choices, stressful and real moments, and hard choices after that, with the story and writing also getting alot better and more entertaining.the entire game is a buildup for the final episode, which is quite boring and linear (there are disrupt hacks if alan james is still alive i believe), until the third segment. the third segment is the result of solely your choices, with there being 14 different endings or so.the writing for all endings and third segments is absolutely great, with the segment of alan james and jeremy surviving being beautiful, with you being able to choose between the oppressive advance, the disruptive (sorry) disrupt, and the truth.is the ending worth 10 hours of gameplay? absolutely.i would like to mention as a side note that jeremy donaldson is one of the best characters i've ever seen, with him visibly wanting the public to know the truth, and being honest about it. it sounds alright in text form, but is vastly better when you actually see it for yourself.one thing that is either hit or miss is the very obvious british humor. i'm not british, and i did have some parts of the game (looking at you, lockdown and episode one) be quite stale or just weird. i had a better time when i understood that i'm really not gonna be understanding most of it. however, there are some parts that can be universally hilarious.as for the mechanics, they are pretty alright when used correctly. some parts aren't used correctly and it's usually in the way of being boring. the red carpet segment has only interference with a miniscule amount of editing required, which made me want to sleep during the whole segment.nonlinear, kindof replayable, great writing after episode one, and a very worth it ending.

_childDocuments_.review: This is legitimately one of my favorite games of all time. You are the man behind the scenes, switching cameras and bleeping swears making the news the most enjoyable for the audience watching it. Just as you get the hang of it, new challenges come your way, making it more difficult to keep your audience happy. Not only are there physical distractions and challenges, but the humor of the reporters, the drama in the country, and the, interesting, celebrity guests keep your brain occupied enough to add even more of a challenge. You get the power, and what you choose to show or censor has consequences. The live action footage for this game makes it one of a kind. The cast bring so much to the table. The execution of story gets you really involved. The slow ramping of difficulty, and now included bonus challenges make the main components of the game interesting throughout the play through and for me they never became too repetitive. Watching this game grow as new chapters were added, and all the way up to its full release has been such a thrill. The Not For Broadcast team has put so much love and time into this game and the payoff is amazing. If the concept at all interests you, give it a shot. I bet you'll enjoy it.My only complain would be it has issues running on lower end systems unfortunately, due to the large amount of video footage and things, but otherwise I have loved every second I have played of this game.

Personally, this one has to be my favourite. The moments of foreshadowing, sudden appearance of dystopian elements which are placed very far apart in time, all of it made my heart drop when it occurred. I played in the way I felt my character probably would, and only restarted a segment when I made a mistake with tape order. Otherwise, all was done with just dealing with the consequences.I'm glad I did that. It made the regime's growing control feel more like something I could have prevented, made me feel horrible yet entranced. _childDocuments_.review: It's always interesting to see how game developers create gameplay using FMV, and this game definitely succeeds at that! The writing is fantastic, the jokes are hilarious, the acting is on point, and the OST is even better! It will definitely be interesting to see what happens to the jokes, because I hope that the story will try to take itself seriously in the later chapters when things get worse for the characters in this fictional universe. In a world where it seems game developers are only here for the money, it truly feels like the developers of this game are here to make a fantastic game. With all of the discounts, free updates, and giveaways, I have no idea how they're paying for all of this, but I won't complain about that!If I were to provide any nitpicks for the game, I would say that there are occasionally some odd lines of dialogue hinting toward the fact that the player is playing a video game, ruining the immersion. Also, the text-based sequences aren't exactly exciting.I would also like to add a few suggestions to this review. The challange modes are great, but the option to play through the entire game in Free Play Mode or Realism Mode would be nice. Different difficulty levels for the different challenges would be interesting, and it would also be cool to somehow combine some of the challenges. If I were to suggest some challenges, the two distractions from the Lockdown episode would be interesting in other episodes. Actually, the addition of the two new episodes to the challenges would be good. In the Archives, I would like to be able to view the bloopers, the trailers, the old developer messages thanking the player, and the Telethon without the filters.Even with all of that, I find it to be very frustrating just how many huge YouTubers seem to have forgotten about this game's existence, because this game deserves more attention! I can't wait to see what comes next!What did Dave do to the water cooler?

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine Papers Please and a choices matter game had a baby. This is the product. Not for Broadcast is an amazing video game where you control what goes on broadcast and it requires a lot of concentration. I’ve played a lot of this offline as well (5 hours total) so I absolutely have to recommend it. The gameplay kept me entertained for quite a while as I’m a fan of concentration and actions have consequences. The whole game mainly takes place in the broadcast room. The access to the room is a 180 view. Meaning you can look to your left, front, underneath the desk and to the right. The gameplay itself is really solid however I won’t reveal anymore because the tutorial is like 15 minutes long and you don’t wanna know much now and then have it repeated to you. The visuals are so beautiful and optimised that there isn’t even a settings option. As 90% of the game relies on live-action visuals from amateur actors from the developers, the game doesn’t rely on heavy processed graphics which is great. I tested this game on a laptop with 4gb ram, intel igpu and a weak cpu however I maintained a solid 60fps. This game is amazingly optimised and I love it.Sorry this review was so small. There’s so much that you should just explore for yourself. This game is a masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing this game. The mechanics and story are so interesting and hilarious at times that I couldn't even focus on what was being said, or what camera i should be focusing on. My personal opinions and suggestions would be as follows:1) The colored lights beneath each monitor should be wider and/or brighter. I didn't even notice them until halfway through the second broadcast. But once i did, they were an incredibly helpful tool.2) The musical section was almost perfect. The multiplier went down a couple of times when i thought I switched cameras on beat, but that could have just been me with a slight delay or lack of rhythm.3) I feel that the sportsboard game section of the third broadcast should have a bit more of a warning because there were a few moments that felt like i didn't have a camera to turn to. Also I loved how little it made sense and I was just too busy laughing to keep up on the cameras the whole time.4) I just want to let the developers know that the story they are telling is amazing. It isn't yet fully realized, but there are all of the little details in plain view that show what they plan for the "part 2" of this game. The descriptions of everything in the shops and the fact you can only get 250 dollars per A+ broadcast show that they plan for more playable broadcasting sessions. The obvious mention of a rebellious graffiti and hacking group whose goals are clearly to expose what Advance is really doing behind the scenes just makes me wish it were completed already. I really look forward to when this game gets an official full release and would even pay full price for it if this early access is any indication of what it will be like. Also, I love the sense of humor in this game. I had to play the sportsboad section 3 times all the way through just to figure out what the rules were supposed to be. And any game that makes you want to replay it, even just a section of it, is amazing in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: "Not For Broadcast" is a truly exceptional game that immerses players in the thrilling world of television broadcasting and challenges them to make tough decisions that shape the narrative. As a fan of unique and engaging gameplay experiences, I was captivated from the moment I started playing.One of the standout features of "Not For Broadcast" is its innovative gameplay mechanics. The game brilliantly captures the essence of controlling a live television broadcast, putting you in the hot seat as the operator responsible for censoring and managing the content. The real-time decision-making adds an exciting level of tension, making every choice feel significant. It's incredibly satisfying to see the impact of your decisions unfold on the screen.The game's narrative is equally impressive. The storyline is intricately woven, filled with unexpected twists and turns that kept me engaged throughout. The satirical take on media manipulation and censorship is thought-provoking, shedding light on the power dynamics and ethical dilemmas present in the media industry. "Not For Broadcast" masterfully combines humor and social commentary, delivering a compelling and relevant narrative.Visually, the game is a treat. The attention to detail in recreating a broadcast studio is commendable. From the meticulously designed sets to the authentic-looking news segments, every aspect feels realistic and polished. The graphics are crisp, and the use of multiple camera angles enhances the immersion.Furthermore, the voice acting and audio design are top-notch. The cast delivers stellar performances, bringing the characters to life with their distinct personalities and emotions. The background music and sound effects create an immersive atmosphere, perfectly complementing the intense moments and adding depth to the overall experience.The replay value of "Not For Broadcast" is exceptional. With multiple story paths and outcomes based on your decisions, the game encourages replayability, allowing you to uncover different storylines and consequences. It's a testament to the game's depth and complexity that each playthrough feels fresh and exciting.In conclusion, "Not For Broadcast" is an outstanding game that seamlessly blends immersive gameplay, a captivating narrative, and thought-provoking themes. It's a unique experience that challenges players to think critically about the media landscape while offering an engaging and entertaining adventure. I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone seeking a truly remarkable gaming experience.Rating: ★★★★★

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I wasn't expecting much going into this game, I got it from a Humble Bundle and knew nothing about it before playing short it being a bit like Papers Please, I almost gave it a miss.Let me tell you - I'm extremely glad I didn't pass this game up.It's genuinely in my top 10 gaming experiences, it ticks so many boxes and it's one of the few games I've bothered to actually play more than once, and I plan to keep going until I get all the endings and achievements.Does it have stupid but hilarious British humour? It does, in spadesA compelling story? Yup, quite a few of themActually good live action acting? YupEngaging gameplay? YupBug free? For me, yesImagine a "semi political" game like Papers Please, mechanics akin to "Please Don't Touch Anything", FMV scenes akin to old school Command and Conquer games and you're part of the way there.The humour is great if you are into British humour (as a Brit, it's semi compulsory) there were times I legitimately couldn't stop laughing, especially in "The Finale" episode. The DLC offers even more of the same humour and with a bit more flexibility to control how the humour works, which again works great.The story, I've seen some people say the central politics driven story line is quite hard to follow, not amazingly true to life and it feels difficult to pick anyone as the "winner" without feeling a bit dirty. I think that's perfect, because the world we live in isn't perfect, especially politics. It is very politics driven so if that isn't your thing then it might not be for you, but I found it compelling, and the side stories that you actively have an impact on depending on what you choose to show, or the celebrities you focus on is a great touch that keeps you involved and not just pressing buttons for the sake of it.Now the acting, it's FMV so 99% of the game is played through live action clips, if you're imagining pretty poor acting, you'll be wrong. Is it Oscar worthy? No of course not, and that's perfectly fine as that isn't what they were going for. Even some of the names have some TV roots, anyone with kids should recognise "Megan" from the game as the mother from Waffle the Wonder Dog...are you going to see AAA level names, again, no of course not. But the acting is great, and to say the majority of this game was developed and produced within Covid is another testament that shouldn't be ignored (watch their documentary)The gameplay, this might be the thing that might not be to everyone's tastes, and that's ok. It plays similar to Five Nights at Freddies in all honesty, you a fixed in place and you can turn left and right, you press buttons, listen to people on the phone and you can do various other parts from your chair. It can get a bit hectic at times remembering what to do, but if you get stressed, just switch to "Story" mode in the difficulty and enjoy the awesome story.I've seen a few comments about game breaking bugs, honestly I didn't see any issues while playing. Everything worked perfectly so I can't comment on this.I very rarely review games, good or bad, but this one deserves a hell of a lot more recognition than it currently has and I'd recommend anyone give it a try, you'll be pleasantly surprised.

_childDocuments_.review: This was A LOT of fun.  Started slow at first, but my goodness this made me laugh and cry.  Great characters and acting.  Jeremy Donaldson <3The game play consist of watching 4 simultaneous camera feeds of the news broadcast and switching between what is appropriate for the situation.  You can additionally edit the feed that audiences will see during a few second delay before it goes live by censoring curse words or certain political views, adding in sound effects such as a laugh track, or dealing with power outages and equipment glitches that would prevent your broadcast displaying smoothly.  There is a lot of (often hilarious) chaos going on with guests you interview that demand  quick attention to get the desired results in your broadcast. Its not all humor either.  The game does move into very serious and disturbing moments that are affected by your decisions.  I promise it is a lot more enjoyable if they remain unspoiled, but be mentally ready for the darker scenes in the game.  There are multiple good and bad endings that can occur based on your choices.  Choose wisely!

name: Skul: The Hero Slayer
detailed_description: The Demon King's Castle in Ruins The human race attacking the Demon King's castle is nothing new and has happened countless times before. What makes this time different though, is that the Adventurers decided to join forces with the Imperial Army and the 'Hero of Caerleon' to lead a full onslaught in hopes of wiping out the Demons once and for all. They attacked the Demon stronghold with overwhelming numbers and succeeded in its total destruction. All of the demons in the castle were taken prisoner except for one lone skeleton named 'Skul'. Side-Scrolling Platformer Action 'Skul: The Hero Slayer' is an action-platformer that boasts rogue-like features such as everchanging and challenging maps. It will keep you on your toes, as you will never know what to expect. Tons of skulls, tons of playable characters Skul is no ordinary skeleton. In addition to his formidable fighting skills, he can gain new and exciting abilities depending on which skull he's wearing. Use up to 2 skulls at a time, each of which has its own unique attack range, speed and power. Choose combos that match your playing style and switch them in the heat of battle to bring your enemies to their knees. The power is in your hands! The Adventurers Skul has crossed paths with a party of Adventurers! They are powerful foes that hunt Demons for sport. While Skul may be small, he still packs quite a punch. So just wait and see who really is the hunter and who is the hunted....   Bosses Corrupted by Dark Quartz At the end of every chapter, go head-to-head with massive bosses corrupted with Dark Quartz and powerful beyond belief. Derived from the pain and hate of life itself, Dark Quartz taints and takes control of everything it touches.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay in  is very straightforward with attacks, skills, jumps and dodges. Survival depends almost exclusively on the players' skill as all animations are very detailed and methodical, attacks are well telegraphed and dodges can't be infinitely spammed to get out of any and all situations.On many occasions you can either find or buy  to replace your own with and gain its abilities, and you can simultaneously own up to two different heads, making the approach to each situation pleasingly varied. Additionally, each of the different heads has a pool of abilities and which one you get isn't always the same. For example, the , an ice-based transformation, can either come with the  skill, an attack where you throw three ice shards at the enemies, or it can come with the  skill which will make you impervious to damage but also immobile for a few seconds.There are more than 20 different skulls available at Early Access launch and the variety is pretty amazing, with some skulls being more common than others. After a while you'll have figured out some favorites. For me they include among others the Werewolf, the Ninja and the Harlequin, although the  Easter Eggs are also pretty neat. Note that you have little to no influence on what skulls you find and that you can only carry two at a time anyway, so it doesn't tend to get too repetitive. Each skull also has an action that activates when you switch to it and much like the skulls' skills, these aren't always the same for each skull-type.In addition to the skulls, you can carry up to six different items that give you passive effects (like 10% more damage, higher damage output while airborne but reduced damage while on the ground etc.), as well as , an item that gives you an additional skill with a cooldown that is independent of your equipped skull.Occasionally you also find caged monsters. Upon freeing them, they return to the castle, offering new upgrade possibilities.This game is tough... but also very fair. In this regard it shares a bit of the  mentality where pretty much every death you suffer was clearly your fault and you can see where you can improve and what you could have done better, as I hinted at in the Gameplay section. Nevertheless some situations can be quite overwhelming and when the screen is full of enemy attacks there aren't many spots left to evade them.Personally, I couldn't do it, I'll admit. I couldn't clear the entire game, yet. But that's where it gets interesting: I don't feel like giving up yet, either!In short,  is one of those games that isn't  difficult but instead  so. It's probably not a game you'll boot up a lot when you've had a hard day at work - although that also works due to the soundtrack and art-style - but one you'll enjoy to challenge yourself with.The story is neither groundbreaking nor complex but it's a compelling premise nonetheless: The adventurers of the Kingdom have joined forces with the Imperial Army and the dreaded  to lay the  castle to waste and kill or kidnap its inhabitants. , an unimposing skeleton, affectionately referred to by the other monsters as "Littlebone" for being the smallest, is the only one left in the castle after the attack. He discovers that the  have been defeated, the  has been captured (he promptly frees her) and the  has been captured. After further discovering that even monsters have been attacking them due to some mysterious, black stones corrupting them,  sets out to free the King and Council and defeat the Imperial Army and the Heroes.The sprites all look either cute or epic or something in between and dialogue is portrayed in JRPG-style text boxes. The enemies all have a  aesthetic that complements the setting perfectly.Having played on a preview build before the launch of Early Access, I was able to witness how much the developers have improved over time and both the way the plot is conveyed and the English localization have improved immensely.This game is absolutely gorgeous to look at. The pixel-art is beautiful, the animations fluid and the effects are used... well, ively. The game boasts vibrant colors, flashy magic, convincing destruction and very unique and sometimes surprisingly recognizable transformations for the protagonist.Since you'll die a lot in this game, you'll be hearing the track of the first area a lot. It isn't bad music but especially the start of the track does get a bit repetetive after a while. Other tracks, like the title screen music or the tutorial track, are beautiful and fit the atmosphere really well.This game is probably for you if you enjoy  like ,  or  and/or prefer short games you can jump into for single sessions like ,  or .If you're into Rogue-likes and/or Rogue-lites, or if you enjoy 2D platforming, or if you like a fair but punishing challenge, it isn't hard to find something to like in this game. Most importantly, though, if you like good pixel-art, you absolutely have to give this one a shot. There is a lot of love and passion infused in this project and it really shows.Even as someone who tends to get frustrated after a while if much of my progress is erased/reset over and over, I really can't stop enjoying this game - over and over.So yes, I definitively recommend  - at least to !

_childDocuments_.review: Skul is a challenging Rogue Lite where you play against the good guys, you can switch skulls to switch your abilities, It great pixel graphics some funny dialogue and some very likable characters.In Skul you play the antihero side. The "Heroes" attacked, destroyed the castle, Locked up the witch and defeated the skeleton guard, You play as littlebone, You are the weakest of all skeletons but somehow you survived, You are handed a legbone from one of the dying skeletons to use as a weapon, You free the Witch and find the Skeleton guard chief, He gives you his skull and you use this to defeat your first miniboss. Later you will meet up at the Demon Castle and this is where the game begins, It is up to Littlebone to save the world from these pesky heroes.I really like the characters, The Heroes all have an ego that doesn't fit on the screen and the bad guys are just very down to earth people, and from my perspective they are not that evil. I especially like Littlebone, He is just too nice, Everyone picks on him and he doesn't even seem to bother, There is not a lot of backstory in the characters, but they all make one hell of an impression. I like the dark and serious but still colorful and funny style that is added to the game. It is rather unique.The game has just 1 gamemode and it is single player only, You start in the Demon Castle every time, Here is the witch who will sell you permanent upgrades for the Dark Quartz you collect during the runs, You will unlock more NPCs, like one that gives you a free random skull to start with. You start a run by jumping off the castle, You have to clear the area from enemies and the door will open to the next area, So it is very linear, you can not go back, But it is not like that you have anything left to do there anyway.The main gimmick of the game are the skulls, You take over the abilities of the skull you wear There are a lot of them, I counted at least 20. Some enable you to fly or hit very hard, or shoot, Some are just rip offs of popular media, Like the Ghost Rider skull, The Zelda Skull and the God of War Skulls, But I like that. Next to the forementioned Quartz you enemies also drop coins and health pickups. You can spend these in the shopping areas that you encounter at times during your run. There are also chests which mostly contain coins and a upgrade, There are also treasure piles which may be impossible to reach with your current skulls.There are a lot of areas before you reach a boss, There are areas with a ton of enemies, areas where you can buy stuff, areas with just a free skull and some training dummies and areas with minibosses. The enemy rooms are different each time, Also the mini bosses differ with each run, The endboss stays the same, After you beat it you will move on to the next level with new areas and a new end boss, There are 3 levels so far. If you die you will lose everything except for the Quartz and the upgrades you bought from the Witch. You can spend the collected Quartz and start over from level 1.The graphics look very nice, It already has a great variation in enemies, Most of the animations are done very well, but it is obvious it could use a little polish in some places. The soundtrack is also nice it is joyful most of the time but during the bosses it gets a bit more tense. Overal a nice soundtrack. I love the many ways Littlebone can look, All the different skulls really add to the game, ofcourse to the gameplay, but also visually, They all look great. One thing that does not really fit is the ingame font, It is not pixelated, It feels out of place.I had absolutely no performance issues, No crashes, bugs or anything like that, The game is locked to your refresh rate, Steam Cloud save has recently been implemented and this is also working fineSince it is a rogue lite it will score high here, The skull system really helps, But I do feel more could be done to extend the lifespan of the game, There is just the one gamemode, no difficulity tweaks, no custom runs, I think more mini bosses would also be vital here.Surely we need more mini bosses and levels with bosses, unique, enemies etc, It would also be nice if we could customize what skulls will drop, Somehow I never get the ones I want, Customize the run a bit more by tweaking some settings in the castle, A Stats NPC, which gives you a nice menu with all skulls you have found and their info, total amount of runs, fastest run, enemies killed, etc, Maybe an NPC who sells you temporary upgrades back in the castleI would love to see Custom seeds so you can compete with others or improve on yourself. It also offers a static experience if people want that. Also a few more gamemodes, Daily runs, Boss Rush, Maybe a local versus or coop mode? Maybe custom challenges for each run, or each area which can help or work against you depending on if you fail or complete the challenge. Skul just released and it will probably stay in EA for a while, They do have a public roadmap with every small detail in there, It does not look very impressive so far, but I think new ideas still need to get implemented in the Roadmap. I will keep this review updated, I will edit it when I feel a lot has changed or the game leaves EA.Skul is a nice roguelite with a lot of potentional, I love the skull switching idea, And I absolutely love some of the skulls, It has nice graphics and the hard challenge should keep you busy for a while, It is obvious we are in early stages but I can see this game becoming a masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: Before purchasing this game, I read a decent amount of negative reviews just to know what to look out for. I went into my first play-through extremely nervous that I was going to experience some cheap combat where enemies constantly get in random hits on me and I won't be able to enjoy my experience. HOLY ♥♥♥♥ WAS I WRONGMy first hours on the game were met with nothing but pure ecstasy as I slashed my way through each stage and discovered new skulls, items, and enemies with each run. The story is short, but enough to get you decently engaged in what exactly is going on in the world you are in. The combat is an absolute blast and was neither too difficult nor too easy. One of the two main complaints for this game were 1. It's too RNG heavy2. It's very repetitive.My opinion on these complaints: Honestly, the RNG in this game is just down to personal preference, but I personally love the RNG aspect of it. It makes every run I do different and forces me to learn new play styles that I didn't even know existed. What solidified this opinion was when I was at the second stage of the game and desperately in need of finding a decent skull to upgrade. The skull I received was "Grave Digger", a new skull that was added quite recently. However, this skull was a "common", so obviously I was extremely disappointed that RNG didn't bless me with a rare or legendary. After debating whether I should restart, I figured what the hell, and gave the grave digger a go. . . .That run ended up being the VERY FIRST time I cleared the game fully. I couldn't believe it, how could I clear the game for the first time with a maxed out COMMON skull. To make sure Grave Digger wasn't just some unique case, I tested other common skulls in upgrading and was mindblown to find that most of them could compete with the upper tier skulls in terms of strength. This switched my mindset on the RNG to "man I hope I don't get a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ skull" to "no matter what I get I'll just MAKE IT GOD-TIER". This revelation made me more excited to test different skulls and item builds in my future runs. Especially since the dev team showed that they planned to continue adding more skulls to the current 100+.Overall: A fantastic game to play at anytime. I personally have never been big on laptop gaming, but since this game has no need for a mouse OR internet, it was just the perfect way to enjoy an S tier game wherever I was. This game got me through an 8 hour plane flight, a 3 hour uber drive, and a 5 hour wait at the DMV, all in the same week. IF YOU LIKE RNGIF YOU LIKE ROGUELITESIF YOU LIKE CHARACTER VARIETYBUY THIS GAME

_childDocuments_.review: Skul is… Castelvania, MegaMan, & MapleStory. ALL-IN-ONE.It’s the perfect blend of the old genesis game, Kid Chameleon combined with Dead Cells difficulty in a Maple Story world.Indie games like Skull are a blessing in the gaming world. I used to think they were just crappy made games no one has heard of but some of them like this one have become my all time favourite games. Truth is, the older I get the more I crave these types of games. The art is cute and crisp, with a really nice, consistent feel. The controls are tight and responsive. The swapping heads gimmick is great fun, and the “monsters are the good guys” story really resonates with me. The witch is a bit excessively sexualized, but I don't really care. I’ve fapped to worse. Overall, lots of great stuff here, lots to love. Unfortunately the combat is where many get stumbled with this game. One of the reasons Hades is so approachable is because behind all the ways to die the game still very much “wants you to win” eventually. Skul is in the exact opposite category. It appeals mainly to the kind of player that sees “get gud” as a challenge instead of an insult. That may not be how you game and that’s okay. I’ve put over many hours into it without beating the final boss yet, even having maxed out the upgrade tree long ago, and I love that. It keeps me coming back for more and thinking of new builds to get a little farther. This is one of the few rogue I've ever committed to and I've played a ton of them. Getting a good run, or even getting a mediocre run and making it work, is such an awesome feeling. I also love that the heroes you fight all spout cliché phrases while they attack like a hyperactive anime character: LEROYYYYY JENKINS!!Honestly it is such a fun game, you can get extremely strong combinations that almost feel like cheating, but that is the fun of it, how absurdly strong you can become and the satisfaction of seeing health bars get melted. The game expands magnificently and is impeccably calibrated and balanced compared to most roguelikes. I've come to like it more than dead cells for the combat options and specifically for how it mitigates luck with several very smart design choices.There are some issues like the relatively small enemy and room variety, but the feeling of playing with and upgrading all the different skulls is more than enough to make it very fun in my opinion.I feel like many of the complaints are literally descriptions of what roguelite players like about roguelites. If you want a game where success is achievable without a great deal of skill, effort, and luck, where power-ups are game-changing, where you don't have to carefully weigh your decisions... saying this as a fan of both genres, what you want sounds more like a clicker game than a roguelite.Personally, Ive played almost 30 hours and I loved every second of it, I keep coming back for a few runs every couple days. It was honestly completely worth the price, if rogue likes are up your alley this game is a must.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don´t write long reviews for games; but I´ve seen some that have been downright lies about this little gem, so I feel the need to talk about my experience with it.Skul is a great rogue-lite with some flaws; the main one being the limited and uninteresting skill tree(although the devs have said they intend to redo it in the following updates) that limits which classes are truly usefull in the early game(I don´t recomend the power classes until you get some levels in life and physical damage) and hides some very important quality of life upgrades behind some grind. So beware of that as you start playing.Outsite this major flaw, the game is a masterclass in engaging combat and build progress.CombatIt's true that RNG defines what build you'll use, but you can try to reroll some items if you really don't want to play a certain way; or you can wait until you find something more interesting along the way. The combat is VERY skill focused, so if you know how to play well enough, you don´t really need that many items or classes until you get to the third map. And even if you get the best classes and items early on(it´s possible, but very unlikely, to get two legendary classes even on the first map) if you play badly you'll die soon. Position and pattern recogniton are key in this game; if you master both, you can make many weaker builds work.ProgressionEvery passive item in the game belongs to a set, which means no item is truly useless, since even the most common ones may give you passive bonus that stack to give you powerfull stats(like a massive increase to life, or constant crits); but some itens are more usefull to certain classes than others, so keep that in mind. This means that if you get some legendary magic class lategame, but your itens buff your physical damage, it won´t be as usefull until you manage to switch your build.Since rerolling items in the shop is expensive, you'll need to get used to deal with what the game gives you most of the time(a similar flaw that Dead Cells share); but since the introduction of class upgrades, this is not a major problem anymore, because now any class can get very strong if you invest in it. You no longer need to pray to find an unique or legendary class to carry you lategame, and there are far more unique builds possible now that all classes(outside the legendary ones) have at least one upgrade that makes it far more powerfull than before.DeathThis is the reason I decided to write this review: The enemies DO NOT GET STRONGER when you die. The devs have stated months ago that the death message "the enemies have gained XP" was just a joke in reference to traditional RPG games. So the game does not get harder as you fail(if this was the case I would always die in the second boss, but I managed to kill it without taking damage after failing countless times before).That being said: the game is hard, and death is common, so get ready for it(this is a rogue-lite afterall). So I recommend spending your upgrade points in the extra damage until you max it, and maxing extra life whenever possible; the game becomes WAY easier afterwards(though still a challenge).MapsThe game follows Hades formula: The maps are always the same, but their order changes in each playthrough. That means you'll start to see the same maps after a while(especially because this game is not as big as Hades) but each time your build and playstile will vary how you deal with them.Still, if repetiviness bothers you, I do not recomend Skul(or Hades for that matter); although I personally never find any of these games repetitive.ConclusionAlthough not as complex as Dead Cells or Hades, Skul manages to be it's own game by focusing on a brilliant combat system that seems simple, but has a LOT of complexity to it. And the sheer amount of builds possible  due to the item sets, class variety and class upgrades makes the game shine when things synergize and you no longer feel as a bone soldier facing an impossible task, but as the final boss mowing down hordes of enemies that dare stand in your way.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a lot of good reviews on here so I'll try to put in my thoughts on itRoguelite action platformer with a good amount of variety in weapons and items, but the stages and enemies tend to blur together after a while. The core of the game is that you pick up skulls across the game, which determine the playstyle for that run. You can have up to two at a time and swap between them, and each skull has up to two skills, all of which are unique to that skull. Each skull can be evolved, too, which adds quite a bit of progression over a run, as each evolution is pretty strong and getting to the final rung feels pretty impressive. Plus, you can get up to nine items, each with their own effects, and mix and match them for set effects, which gives a genuinely large amount of build customization for each run.The levels themselves are pretty meh for the most part - sidescrolling platforms where you fight off groups of enemies as you progress through each stage. Each level has a set boss, a couple of shops, and a miniboss. The only real highlights are that the minibosses are randomly mixed and matched together, which makes for fun (or frustrating) combinations, and you can usually pick whether you want to go to a stage that gives you a skull, an item, or gold, but for the most part it doesn't stand out and it's mostly the buildcraft that keeps you coming back.The game gets rather difficult, or at least it does for me, and it will cut you down pretty hard starting around the second or third zone if you don't already have a good build and good skulls, but ultimately I keep finding myself coming back to it even after I throw down my controller and call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's hard to keep track of things where there's a ton of enemies on the screen, which is annoying.Graphics are okay, music is good. The story is a fun twist on the general fantasy, where the demon king and the monsters are the good guys, and the heroic kingdom of golden knights and adventurers are the bad guys. In this day and age that kind of subversion is common enough that it doesn't blow my mind, but it doesn't come off as pretentious as other attempts have.The real make-or-break is going to entirely depend on if you find the mix and match gameplay of the skulls and items fun - I definitely do, which is why I'm positive on this game overall despite being trash at it. It's not quite as tight as the really big names like Hades or Binding of Isaac, but it dives into its particular niche and excels there, so definitely pick it up if you're prone to "just one more run" halfway into the night.

_childDocuments_.review: I really hate to have to review this one negatively but there are just some issues that make the game too frustrating to recommend. I have a few main concerns, and my first is that too often damage feels frustrating and unavoidable. Not always of course, here and there would be no big deal, but it's fairly frequent. Most of the greatest (IMO, obviously) roguelikes like The Binding of Isaac, Enter the Gungeon, Hades, Dead Cells, etc, make it feel like MOST, if not ALL damage is avoidable. This creates an incredible feeling of triumph when, as your knowledge and skill with the game progresses, you can avoid all the damage of the earlier mobs, bosses, traps, whatever with ease. Saving that often valuable HP for the stuff you have yet to make it to in a run so you can learn the nuances of those mobs, bosses, traps. Unfortunately with Skul, there are times where 10+ mobs spawn, all of your attacks are shattering background objects, debris flying everywhere, the enemies projectiles are going off, and you come out of the fight feeling good, look down and you've lost 20, 30 health and go "When the hell did that happen? I didn't even think I got hit".  It's just SO unsatisfying. The combat feels great, and if this were a typical RPG or something where after a fight you could eat, potion up, what have you, it wouldn't feel as discouraging; However in a roguelike, health is a resource, and when you feel like your resources are getting stolen from you with little input on your part, it sucks. This can make it feel like instead of jumping into a fight, you should hang back and just wait for your cooldowns, pop them on the mobs, and then run away and wait for CDs again. My second main complaint is one I've seen several reviews mentioning before purchasing, and can definitely agree with them now. The same bosses and floor layouts over and over and over gets really tiring. Most of the boss fights are pretty fun, if a little damage spongey and less mechanical, but they're mostly fun. But seeing the exact same ones, in the exact same spots, every run brings it down. And basically the same thing with the floor layouts/enemy spawns. A few hours in and you'll have seen the majority of floor layouts of each stage and that also just feels too repetitive, too soon.And lastly, the RNG/Skull and item imbalance. So, skulls have different rarities, and obviously the higher the rarity, the better the skull (common, rare, unique, legendary). The problem is that the difference between the capabilities of say a rare skull and a legendary skull is truly insane. A legendary skull and no other items can carry you far further than a rare skull and some top tier passives. BUT, they have an upgrade system for lower tier skulls! That sounds awesome! Except it takes a pretty atrocious amount of time garnering enough fragments to upgrade a skull, even if taking every skull drop door option available. So you're basically always just hoping you find a legendary skull, or at least a few unique skulls that you can upgrade a different unique skull into a legendary with. This is not common. In 8 hours of gameplay I've upgraded just two skulls to legendary, and acquired 2 Legendary skulls as drops. Now, something that really saddened me was that there is a passive item cap. You can hold only 9 passive items, along with one activated item, and two skulls. One of my absolute favourite things in roguelikes is when you've collected an arsenal of passives, stacking together in awesome ways that make you feel overpowered! That can make having a crappy weapon, or in this case, pair of skulls, feel much less frustrating, because your other items are helping carry the weight. That just doesn't really happen with Skul. With the 9 item cap, you'll mostly be stacking % damage increases of either magical or physical damage, obviously preferably whichever your skulls deal. But as I said earlier, even if you have awesome passives, and crappy skulls, you just often wont have the tools to get through some of the fights. Anyway, I doubt anyone has really read this far, but I hope you believe me when I say I truly would rather recommend this game, as I feel it is quite close to being known as one of the greats. These issues though I feel are quite glaring, and can heavily hinder your enjoyment of the game. I'm still going to be playing it, but just a run or two here or there before the frustration sets in. Hopefully in the future there may be some changes to address some of my issues and you can guarantee I'll be changing my review once I feel it's warranted. If you pick up the game, I hope you love it!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not going to get into the details of Skul, I don't think I'm qualified for that, but just based off my experience with the game and past roguelikes...I feel Skul is an example of a roguelike that refuses to let you get one over on it, if that makes sense.  It promises broken builds or cheesy strats or just really strong damage, but will always outscale you to the point where your damage doesn't feel fun or your skills feel borderline useless: From boss immunities shutting down status or blizzard builds entirely, to being seemingly incapable of ever maxxing out some of the large-scale set bonuses (I have yet to ever hit 5 Faeries. Despite forcing it as hard as I can any time I get 2+ of the items. Lord help you if you want a max tactics or empire setup...), to just scaling out Boss HPs so much (or damage scaling them; Truth be told, I can't tell) that even with some of the strongest items the game has to offer you often feel heavily lacking...I just don't find myself feeling strong in the game, not for long.Furthermore, the game...has some early design weirdness, with some skulls just being flat garbage even when upgraded to legendary (Demon King's Guard felt like a bad unique, not a legendary skull...), making it feel like you need to get lucky and roll Archlich + Magic Boosters to feel strong. They do plan on addressing this with some of the more notable offenders (Archer, Water Elemental, Raksha or whatever the stompy boy is called) based off the dev diaries just...idk.Overall, I hope a Dev sees this: If you add in ways to make it so I can break this game or just, get set bonuses, make it so legendary items actually feel strong and not just kinda boosted stat-uniques/rares, . The promise of future support has me hopeful for balance reworks, but right now, whenever I leave the game I just have a sour taste in my mouth. It's good enough for me to recommend it to others, but that's as much as I can do.

_childDocuments_.review: Every part of me wanted to enjoy this game, and I forced myself to play well past the point of misery to make sure I'd given it a fair shake. After 20 hours, I'm done. I love roguelikes, roguelites, platformers, 2D souls, metroidvanias, etc. I've played thousands and thousands of hours of these genres of games that can feel very unforgiving and deeply unfair, but Skul blasts past them all in that regard, quickly crushing my initial excitement into stony silence and leaving me seriously baffled at some of its design choices.To start off, the concept is great. Little skeleton hopping around, slashing his way through "heroes" and switching his head out in Skul's version of a class system. The sprites and animations are great, and the character design is coherent and satisfying. Then we get to mechanics. Immediately, this is where things started to sour. Many of the skulls are so awkward as to be unusable without serious practice (and good luck getting it, because you'll often go several runs without seeing certain skulls). Some are just flat out awful, and even a good skull might stall out if you get the wrong skill when you pick it up. Furthermore, some skulls might be awful or godlike depending on the items you find (or don't). There isn't much player control over what items or skulls you get. I'm used to RNG dictating a lot about a run in nearly every roguelike, but in Skul, it feels extreme, like the game just decides whether or not to give you interesting classes or pure trash.Now enter level and enemy design. I truly can't overstate how much these two made this game a "no" for me. At first, things are fairly balanced. Foot soldiers, big guys, archers, a variety of fairly tame trees. Then you get into the second zone, and apparently welcome to hell. Now there will be large, massive spongy enemies that do something hideously annoying, and unless you're rockin' around with huge modifiers, enjoy spamming your paltry attacks against the maids that summon three other maids, the alchemists that you just aren't going to stop from summoning golems, etc. Then you've got the "adventurers" who vary between utterly harmless and unstoppable teleporting juggernaut, and seem to be another way for the game to inform you your run was doomed from the start.Apart from the absolutely wild difference in enemy strength, with some rooms being so sparse and others being packed to the gills with aforementioned hellmaids, the way the game handles level design and healing is dedicated to your suffering. I have on numerous occasions had a nearly flawless run, deftly dodging around and taking my shots carefully, trying to lean into the "Skill over stats" ethos. Then you walk into the next room and there are sixty mages, archers, alchemists, exploding ghosts, spinning traps, and suddenly you're 200 HP down and wondering what else you could be doing with your time, because you definitely won't be healing 200 HP back. Here's your 10 HP blip from killing the archer, ninja and paladin adventurers, sucker. Don't even get me started on the "event" rooms. After testing out a couple, and giving serious consideration to the risk vs reward proposition, I skip every single one of them. I have what we'll call fairly serious disagreements with the reasoning behind whoever put these rooms together.So what's the big deal, right? Sounds like "git gud" time, yes? Well, sure, but now we have the question, "Why should I?" Most roguelikes have upgrades that carry over between runs, and Skul does too. However, the system in place isn't just bland, it's one of the biggest reasons I can't keep going. For starters, the upgrades feel more like you're just missing parts of your character, and you're handicapped until you grind up thousands of quartz so you can start actually playing with a chance. When I die ingloriously in Rogue Legacy, I get to say "Alright, well, let's spend some gold." When I die in BoI, I can say "Alright well, at least I got that clear before dying." Skul I just look sadly at the witch, and consider whether I ought to just stop. The answer was eventually yes. The magic of small incremental upgrades (gotta get them numbers, right dopamine?) fades rapidly in this game, and in no time I was disconnected from the character and had lost any sense of progression.So in short, I wanted to love Skul, but I guess the developers had other ideas.

_childDocuments_.review: With behemoths such as Hades or Dead Cells dominating the current action roguelite scene, an underdog like Skul has had way too little exposure for its value. This is by all means a truly excellent metroidvania and it pains me to see it so very close to the Overwhelmingly Positive threshold, so I decided to share my thoughts. Skul is a 2D roguelite platformer where you play as a cute little skeleton on a mission to free his best friend the demon king from the clutches of the mean humans. Your path is divided into rooms, which you must clear in order to proceed, and which give you a reward for clearing them. You eventually fight bosses, which give you better rewards, and so on, until you get to the final boss and hopefully kick his butt. In many ways, Skul feels like Dead Cells' little brother : the gameplay loop from start to finish lasts about an hour, you get to unlock new stuff between/during runs, etc, all the mechanics you'd expect from a roguelite are there and they are very well executed. If you are familiar with the genre, Skul will make you feel right at home in the best of ways. Where the game especially shines is in the unique mechanic it brings and focuses on : skulls. Your character, being an undead skeleton, can remove its own head and replace it with others to gain their powers. There are many skulls available, and they each come with their own unique abilities, synergies and evolutions. Skulls are the cornerstone of the gameplay and they open up a wide array of playstyles : perhaps you like the first skull you found in your run, and you want to evolve it into a late game war machine ; or you might want to make do with what you find until you can get your hands on a legendary skull ; or maybe you will find yourself using two strong skulls and rotate between them as often as possible, or use each of them for specific situations. This system gives a massive amount of leeway & replayability to the game, because which combination of items and skulls you decide to use can drastically alter the way you approach any given run.The game is also filled to the brim with references and cute little winks here and there : World of Warcraft, League of Legends, Adventure Time, God of War, Ghost Rider, Naruto, Predator, Dead Cells, Slime Rancher, various mythologies, and then some. Surprisingly, I've found that it gives the game its own kind of sheen. Skul does not overwhelm you with lore or storytelling. There is a cute little story, but that's about it. It is however very homogenic in terms of design and atmosphere, which gives it its own identity and makes for a discreet, lighthearted and comfortable ambience that feels bang on for a game you're meant to replay.As is usual for action roguelites, this one is meant to be played with a controller, but it is by no means a requirement. I play it with a keyboard and never had an issue. In terms of difficulty, the game is relatively hard. It took me about 30 hours to beat it for the first time, which is the average time according to google. It does not currently have a NG+ system, which felt like a missed opportunity, but from what I read it is the next order of business and should land with the next update. The devs seem to be still very much active & working on the game, with a recent major overhaul of items barely a month old, and quite in touch with the community - always a good thing. One complaint I have with the current state of the game is that there are not enough rooms and bosses given that those are static across playthroughs. It's not a huge issue, because you usually clear either of those in under a minute and move on to the next thing, but it does raise the player's feeling of déjà vu ever so slightly each time. I'm hoping more rooms and alternate bosses get added in the future, or that the order of the biomes gets randomised each run.  I'd rate Skul: The Hero Slayer a commendable 8.5/10, which I will upgrade to a 9/10 once NG+ is implemented. Cute, easy to learn, hard to master, crisp gameplay, dynamic loop, polished design. Very much worth your time and money even at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this game a NEUTRAL rating.The base gameplay is actually pretty fun, that's why I've sunk so many hours into this game. But after so many hours, I can't say all of that time was spent having "fun". I can have fun with a difficult game, and I can have fun with RNG in a game, but the problem with this game is that Other balance issues:There is little to no "choice" in the game despite all the skulls and item combinations. After you play for a few hours every run will start to feel more or less the same because there's only a few usable skull/build combinations.The inscription system is also really pointless, and seems like flavorless icing to me. You're almost never maxing out any of the inscriptions. You simply cannot play the game with the goal of working towards certain inscriptions without playing like a god, that is if you even get lucky enough to max them out. The worst offender is the spirit inscription, I only faintly recall a single run where I even saw 5 spirit inscription items. That means if I played all my runs with the goal of doing some spirit king inscription, I would have only accomplished it once.The item limit is too low to be creative. Inscriptions are either impossible to max out and would severely cripple your run if you try to obtain them, or negligible when maxed out.  This results in almost every build turning out into more or less the same physical/magical build. There is not much active itemization choice beyond "build lots of magic damage" or "build lots of physical damage". Again, the inability to work towards certain inscriptions means there is little to no point in the system, and the stats might as well be built into the items themselves because 90% of your runs will end up being similar item-wise.The better approach would be to increase item limit to something like 15, but nerf all items across the board. This means early game you might be slightly weaker, but mid-late game you get more creative builds without having to sacrifice usefulness. Now you can finally go full shield/protection while still maintaining enough damage, or go 5 spirit inscription king. Or actually build hybrid magic/physical damage (also I think there's only about 3 or so hybrid items).

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of the issues I had with this game have been fixed in subsequent updates. The devs actually responded to my review (in a deleted comment), said what changes they were planning on making, and delivered on them. I'm leaving the original review under a heading for comparison. Ironically, making a hard mode made the game easier. The devs stopped nerfing every good combo that players were using, and they made it easier to see what each item actually does as well. All the upgrades you get in hard mode make becoming powerful enough to no-hit bosses completely feasible, and they know where to draw the line because they didn't add no-hit achievements for the new bosses. They kind of fixed Power Skulls, but not really. Their solution to 1/3 of the skulls being really slow with less dodges in a game that requires dodging was to just make some of them really overpowered. So you technically CAN win on the hardest difficulty with Power Skulls, but only specific ones. I'm perfectly fine with this because the high-level enemies throw so much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at you that it's only fair that you can ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ them back. The new story stuff is cool, if not a little confusing as to whether something happens in the real world or the dark one. I still think that it's not easy enough to know what things are good together, it's better than before but it's almost required to watch Youtubers to know what's viable. Someone playing this game blind is still going to be really frustrated for a long time even with all the improvements made. I would not recommend this if you're not very familiar with roguelikes, it's really hard and requires your full attention for the entire run, which for a beginner might take up to 2 hours. It's most similar to Dead Cells so if you've played that, completed it, and were disappointed that it wasn't as hard as people said it was then pick this game up right away._______________________________________________________________________Outdated Review:Was scissors the last item you unlocked in Binding of Isaac? Do you play Enter the Gungeon blindfolded for fun? Do you think exhaustive wikis and actually being able to see your stats are for chumps? Then Skul is the game for you!The RNG involved in this game is extreme. You cannot win every run you play, not by a long shot. Every enemy in the fourth chapter is ridiculously tanky, designed to slow down even the most OP builds. A few of the hitboxes are wonky, damaging you before the sprite actually gets to you (especially noticable in the goo in the third boss fight). Even if you understand all the patterns an enemy is capable of, certain room layouts throw scores of hard enemies on top of you at once, making it almost impossible to completely avoid taking damage consistently. You do not want to take damage in this game. Healing consists of spending gold you could've spent on items on food in the shop, which most of the time will only heal you about 1/3 of the way, and some of the food's secondary effects are actually detrimental, like the pineapple preventing you from staggering enemies. The next best healing method is random purple orbs from enemies. These heal you 10 hp, which, past a certain point in the game, doesn't even make up for being hit a single time by a grunt. There's items that make you heal more or heal very slowly on kills, but the 9 inventory slots would be better used for offensive items to make you less likely to take damage in the first place. That's one of my biggest gripes with this game, is that not only is it absurdly difficult, but you can't keep everything you find. You can replace items, but scrapping extra ones for gold is locked behind the most expensive upgrade in the game, tied with an extra life. If a handful of gold is as valuable as an extra life, then I should be able to buy them. But maybe having infinite item slots would be too easy, especially if the damage bonuses are multiplicative instead of additive. Unfortunately, there is no way to know. The official wiki only repeats the info that's already available in the game, aside from what's outdated, which is a lot. And you can't see what your buffs do, either, you have to look at your items and inscriptions and guess what they are. The devs clearly don't care about making the game fair as they've instead added "rookie mode" which makes you take 50% less damage with no restrictions on unlocks or achievements. I hope future updates fix this game because I really don't hate it, there's a lot to like too.Firstly, the main mechanic of the game, skull swapping, is great. You can get a skull that does magic damage if you've picked up magic boosting items, pick a different one if you don't like its skills, and grind up some to upgrade the two you've picked out that you like. Sadly, almost one-third of the skulls are sub-optimal for the majority of the game, as they move very slowly and can only dash once on top of this. The graphics are also very good, with the enemies that do similar things in each chapter obviously being upgraded versions of the previous ones without looking like just palette swaps. The story, while not amazing, is a bit more thought out than just "standard RPG but humans bad and demons good." You can rescue some NPCs permanently, so you can get an item from them at the start of your run, or you can rescue npcs multiple times in different runs, that can give you an item, duplicate one you have, or just give a stat boost. I really with you were guaranteed to meet every NPC at some point in every run, because the werewolf that boosts your stats is amazing. Also, the music is pretty decent, each chapter having its own theme alongside different boss/miniboss themes and the menu/credits theme. The game is charming, but not without its flaws. The fact that they have the audacity to put in achievements for beating each boss without taking any damage is laughable. I wish the head-switching and skill customizing ideas were used in a better game.If you're a veteran of roguelites you should at least buy it on sale, everyone else stay away.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start with this, I like this game. But it's way too flawed, missing simple QoL stuff like showing what your buffs does, game feeling clunky at times with inputs, HORRIBLE enemy AI even for a roguelite game, biomes not being interesting. Skulls, and how they change the gameplay is something that is very well done, I enjoy playing with different types of Skulls and what they bring to the table, but for a roguelite game this game really has low replayability with it's builds, and how biomes works, while adventurer fights are essentially gank bosses from DS2. Lore sounds interesting at first, but it's also not explored properly when the main idea about the lore is quite good, I see that as a missed opportunity. Also, unlike some some games that made a name for theirselves in the genre, at times it feels like you really need a very good amount of luck with items and Skulls to have a chance progressing, since there are a lot of dead ends with both. _childDocuments_.review: This game looks beautiful and I really would like to recommend this, but I can feel that after 9 hours I'm starting to get enough because of how repetitive the game is and how the game mechanics and games systems ultimately seem to boil down to memorization and building muscle memory and nothing else.Initially, the game seems super fun. The upgrade system for switching the character class and building synergies with the different items seems very deep and makes your imagination run. But I get the feeling that it is never really utilized well. The game alternates between levels where you kill a huge amount of cannon fodder and then arrive at bosses. The bosses have clear patterns and usually, the fights consist of stages where these patterns remain similar but get faster and more damaging as the fight goes on. The issue is that the character builds and game mechanics that work in a fun way in the cannon fodder levels, such as mixing different status ailments, do not work  at the bosses. It's like the game discards everything about the mechanics in the boss fights excepts raw damage output and memorizing the patterns. And since you cannot practice the bosses, the game becomes a grind where you either get lucky and get a skull that has insane damage output and that is how you win against the boss or you re-run 30-40 minute runs 20-30 times to slowly build muscle memory against all the pattern and keep dying until you could win the bosses using any character, no matter how weak, because you can avoid most of the damage.In the end, I concluded that nothing else matters in this game other than trying to get lucky and maximizing just raw damage output. Or memorizing the levels and bosses and grinding the game endlessly so you upgrade the permanent upgrades which I assume makes everything easier. But that kinda takes away all of the fun from the game for me and makes all of the complexity and experimentation I thought would be here at the beginning vanish.

Great job on the characters, they're lovely, and I quite love the skull protagonist. I'm quite enjoying it 4h in, but I do have some points I think should be improved.First, the stages and enemies. Too few stages with set spawn points makes it get a bit repetitive. Adding more variety for this kind of thing would be really, really cool. More enemies would also be a bit nice. Second, most of the basic skulls are kinda boring and it feels like a chore to play them until I get a cool, fun skull. Thist isn't really an improvement, more like a suggestion: maybe getting alternate pathings, like in dead cells where you have 2 biomes to chose from in each transition would be really cool to have. But all in all, great game and on the right path to be one of my favorite roguelites*edit*More great content keeps being added, that's great

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? It can become one, but beware, it has just released into Early Access and it's content is a bit limited today. Seems there are only 3 worlds/large bosses so far. I didn't expect too much of this game... another platformer? Or a beat'em up? So - what did I get? An extremely cool roguelike!You play a tiny skeleton named Skul, who is the only one not taken prisoner by those so-called heroes that attacked and capured the Demon Lord's castle. Skul was the smallest member of the Demon Lord's guard. Supported by a pretty witch who can transform into a cat Skul has to fight those heroes and free the Demon Lord (and his friends). Skul does not even have a sword, so he takes the legbone of one of his dying comrades as his weapon to pummel the heroes. Skul is a bit headless sometimes, he can throw his (original) head and then teleport there. On his travels he finds additional heads (currently around 20 available) and gain abilities and a new look that way. Some are really funny, like the Ghost Rider head that allows Skul to race around the level on a motorbike and use a burning chain whip. Skul can carry two heads around at the same time and switch between them as needed.As usual in the genre, level exits open when you have vanquished all foes from a location. Randomized levels, a skill tree to improve Skul during the runs, well made pixel art graphics, and a jamming soundtrack make this a game to watch! I hope they continue to add content and make this a real masterpiece in the future.Cute roguelike in Early Access. Die and retry!

_childDocuments_.review: I think out of all the roguelikes, this game has the best boss fights in terms of animations and technical skill needed to dodge and beat the bosses. The Leliana Sisters feel much more epic to fight and defeat than Theseus and Asterius in Hades. This game also provides a dizzingly high array of item choices and skull combinations (skulls are what you equip on your character to completely change their playstyle through obtaining new skills and attacks with different effects). These two factors have encouraged me to keep replaying the game as I want to try out so many different item builds and legendary skull combinations. The variety is on a comparable level to other roguelikes.The big problem I have with this game though is that there is no way to vary the difficulty of the game or change the attack patterns and buffs the enemies have like you can in Hades (increase the heat gauge) or Dead Cells (go from 0bc to 1bc). The bosses and mobs remain the same throughout each playthrough, so once you exhaust trying many of the item and skull combinations and understand how to dodge and beat boss/mob attacks, the game becomes relatively easier and loses much of its replayability. Overall, for $20, you can easily squeeze out 20+ fun filled hours playing this game. It is close to becoming one of the best roguelikes like Hades or Dead Cells, but it needs more content updates through increasing difficulty in subsequent playthroughs as well as changing boss attack patterns and difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT:  this review was from a long time ago, when the game was in its early stage. It looks like some of the cons are still there, but hats off to the developers who are constantly trying to improve their work! I changed my review from "Do not recommend" to "Recommend."  Thank you for working hard!I respect the amount of work the devs put into this game.  The game now feels complete.  I do want to thank the devs for working really hard and listening to the comments people made.  I have played almost 300 hours, and it was mostly a good experience.  I still play a couple of games every day, and that's what's going to happen in the future, too.  It is a great game.With that said, here's my top two reasons I (still) cannot leave a positive review.1.  "Hard" isn't necessarily "challenging," and I wish the devs made changes toward the challenging side, instead of hard.  When many people commented that the game was too easy during the Early Access, I don't believe it wasn't about the enemies not hitting hard enough or too few invincibility frames.Having to beat scores of enemies who hit like a truck is okay.  Having a really narrow invincibility window is okay.  Having to fight enemies whose attacks can never be cancelled is okay.  Having to get through visual effects that masks pretty much everything that comes at you is... doable.  Beating a mini-boss or boss that attacks non-stop so you just have to memorize their offensive patterns is possible.  But all those put together?  Tiresome rather than challenging.15 melee enemies spawn, and others fire arrows at you from a screen away.  Some enemies just charge at you and explode, taking away a large portion of your health bar.  But you can't see any of those because of your own skill effects.  Worse, hitting them won't give you a window to escape.I am not saying it is impossible.  I am actually mildly exaggerating, as things like that don't happen often.But they do.And that's when you just feel tired and overwhelmed, rather than challenged and motivated to deal with it.  And that's why people go for overpowered builds:  not because of the difficulty, but because of the stress.This is only a personal preference, but I would not have bought Skul if I expected a Soul-like.  Difficulty isn't what got me into the game, and I would have been perfectly fine with playing a game or two each day just to relax.  After the 1.0 release, Skul became something I have to actually put my energy into.  Again, this is my personal feeling, but I do have a feeling that not everyone welcomes higher difficulty with outstretched arms.2.  RNG seems to determine much of, if not the entire, game experience.  Yes, it's a rogue-lite.  But if you get just the right RNG, you can burn through all of the stages without feeling any of the stress that I mentioned above.  That's the reason I call it hard and not necessarily challenging.  A few OP builds simply cannot be countered, while most other builds struggle.For example, if you have a Grim Reaper with the right skills and four of those little fairy things along with the item that gives you bonus Magic Attack depending on the number of fairies, you are one size fits all.  From a meager swordman to the final boss in his golden armor, there's nothing that can even come close to stopping you.  What are the odds of that happening?  Not much.But it does happen.RNG is good.  It makes games much more unpredictable, thus more re-playable.  But if the game is reduced to just looking for better luck, as luck is the primary determining factor in gaming experience, how is it different from a slot machine?Okay.  No matter what I say here, I know I will return tomorrow to play, because I love this game that much.  Maybe all the things that I said don't even matter.  But at some points, Skul feels so tiring that I just want to stop.  I hope I will be able to enjoy it more tomorrow.-Previous Review:I started playing Skul since its demo version came out. I fell in love with it right away and bought the EA version as soon as it became available. At the moment, however, I am not sure if I would recommend this game to others.The updates in the last few months were more or less a letdown. New skulls were mediocre at best; and some of them rather uncreative. For example, the Carleon soldier skull has a very uninteresting set of possible skills, which are too weak to be of any value anyway. Same goes for the items: the devs try and "balance them," but end up just nerfing the majority of them. I personally find myself going for the same skulls and the same items over and over. Trying new skulls and items was mostly a clunky experience where I go through each field desperately hoping for health orbs, and the game became stale very quickly.I thoroughly enjoyed Skul in its early days and still think that it has great potential. However, to be honest, the game has not been improving much up to this point.
