_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of roguelites, this is a tough not recommended from me. Skul feels like it has enormous potential but falls short due to a lack of polish in more or less all areas. The combat fundamentally has a pretty good feel to it. Hits feel impactful and so on, but the game has a problem with enemies overlapping. This isn't such a big deal in the first levels, where taking some damage isn't crippling, but later on in the game, it becomes a huge problem. The screens in the final area become extremely chaotic, with full of enemies that can shoot lightning-fast projectiles and melee enemies that can't be interrupted. This is made worse by the fact that the game doesn't give the player any post-hit invincibility frames (like every other similar game ever). The result is that you can lose devastating amounts of hitpoints in less than a second if an enemy hits you and it produces a chain reaction. Now, I don't have any problem with games being difficult, but when I can't see what's going on due to the chaos on the screen and enemies standing inside each other, it ends up feeling frustrating instead of fair difficulty. You can even be shot from outside the screen. Most of the time I was afraid to use my melee abilities because most of them tend to lock you into an animation so that you're a sitting duck. For example, using a charge move can often be a bad idea because you can, and often do, take projectile damage during the charge, and there might be an enemy that can't be interrupted in the chunk of enemies you're charging into.Taking some damage here and there wouldn't be so bad, but this game is exceptionally stingy with healing. Most other roguelikes, such as Dead Cells and Slay the Spire, allow you to fully heal between shops or major areas. Skul, however, does not. Sometimes it only lets you heal for 20% HP in shops. The average seems to be around 30% HP of healing. This means that taking damage is tremendously punishing, and careful play is a must. The limited healing combined with the difficulty of avoiding damage due to the chaos led to many frustrating moments for me. It also encourages boring, slow gameplay. In a game that makes damage avoidance so crucial, having clear telegraphs for enemy attacks and as little overall visual noise as possible is paramount. This game does the exact opposite: it has the most clutter I've probably ever seen in any roguelite, and yet avoiding damage is also more important than in most other similar games. Skul features a pretty neat system where character abilites are tied to upgradable skulls that you find along the way. You can also have two of them at a time and swap between them. There are a lot of different skulls, and there's an impressive amount of variety in the way they play. Each skull even has multiple different possible ability sets, so adding them all together adds up to a pretty impressive number. The problem, however is that some skulls are simply ludicrously overpowered compared to others. My impression after 50 hours is that magic damage is by far more powerful than melee damage. For example, a fully upgraded Samurai skull can't hold a candle to the Archmage or Archlich. Those skulls are capable of wiping entire screens with a single press of a button, while the Samurai struggles to kill even normal enemies despite having an inventory full of physical damage-boosting items, all the while having to endanger himself in melee combat while the magic damage-based skulls mostly don't. This is just one example of the imbalance between the skulls, and there are many, many more. Generally, magic is too powerful, even without the consideration that the magic-based skulls can damage their enemies without putting themselves in danger. There's also a good selection of items to build your character with, but my experience was that unless you go for damage almost exclusively, especially if you're a physical damage-based character, the late game will feel almost impossible because your damage will be inadequate. The problem with this is that ultimately you're only looking for damage, and all the interesting utility and defense items will start to look unattractive because you know you will need the damage for the final area and final boss, or they will be incredibly difficult due to how long you need to survive in those fights. I did have quite a bit of fun with the game, but the more I played, the more pressing these problems got. I just think there are many, many better and more polished roguelites than this. If you're a massive fan of roguelites and have already finished most of the popular ones, then give this a try, but probably not before then.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has played every roguelike/rogue-lite in existence (from most popular to the most indie, to games which have been abandoned during their development), Skul was an obvious purchase. There's a lot of things I want to go over so I'll discuss them as we go, with minimal spoilers as possible, as to why I wouldn't recommend the game with its price tag to players into this genre. Story: The game does in fact have a story, however it's very cliche, and shouldn't be a major factor in your decision to purchase it. The events of the game all happen due to a (spoiler)   .How it plays: Skul's combat is based on different skulls he equips throughout a run (all random), taking on the abilities and moveset of his fallen comrades - this sounds like a wonderful idea to add variety to the game play loops, however, its the main problem with the game in two categories: balancing and controls. Not all skulls are equal, and playing subpar skulls means terrible dps output, or terrible controls. This leads to frustration during a run. as to not getting 'fun' skulls. This shouldn't be an issue I thought because DPS shouldn't be a problem as a veteran player in these types of games, I just need to never get hit and plainly "get good." However, to add difficulty to runs the rooms just increase the amount of enemies in the room (with little to no variety), meaning taking damage is inevitable unless you manage to get lucky with items and skulls to 1 shot every enemy in one swoop. You don't feel you get better at mastering the game you simply get lucky. Now going over the controls, some skulls are perfect while others give force movement in attacks - this is such a terrible idea because many enemies are on ledges, so you are forced to fall, go back up, or hit hazards. You are forced to wait till you land so you don't accidentally do a diagonal ground pound instead of just swiping in the air. Once you land, then you can start attacking or your dps will suffer and you'll waste so much time fighting hundreds of enemies with belated HP's falling off edges or taking hits. So many skulls have abilities that lock you into animation, and for some reason do worse damage than just spamming attack. Another inevitability to get hit. Overall is was a frustrating experience, and I only finished the game on a few different skulls just to write this review, as the game gets so incredibly easy with a normal skull with a normal moveset with abilities that are better than spamming the attack button. My best way to describe this game is that it's a hack n' slash with poor balancing.Enemy and level design: In short, most of the enemies are just reskins of themselves throughout the entire game, and an extra 2 or 3 enemies in every area. It gets so bland fighting the constantly respawning foot soldiers, and the like. The actual levels are fairly bland with some exceptions, with almost NO variety. It gets especially worse near the end of the game (the first area had a large room pool to choose from) where it looks like they gave up designing new rooms as I fight the same rooms over and over again. Bosses:If you've played these types of games before, the bosses are extremely easy, and can be done hitless with some exceptions. As soon as you've seen their entire attack pool then you are able to dodge most of them. The major issue though, is DPS is required, so a good build is needed or you will be fighting a boss for a solid 5-10 minutes taking chip damage and eventually losing. I'd just like to comment as well that one of the bosses is sadly a reskinned worse version of a boss in Hollow Knight, almost an exact replica.Replayability:Due to lack of variability which is viable, there is not enough of the game to justify replaying it. Once you've beaten the game there isn't much else to discover after the next few runs. The combat isn't good enough to justify playing it again either (which is my personal reason I play these games). Items don't change much of the gameplay loops, just increase passive stats. If you manage to get lucky with consumable items it can carry you through to the entire game without needing a good run.Tl;dr The games difficulty is artificial, with large amount of enemies and large HP, annoying controls at the mercy of RNG (skulls). If you're into these challenging games then Skul isn't one of them, you don't get better at the game, you just get more upgrades for the game to become easier, as taking damage is guaranteed. It's a poorly balanced hack n slash in essence. I'm not saying these games are bad but I was expecting the normal Roguelike difficulty of doing runs and getting better at the actual game. It's forced artificial difficulty to bump up playtime until you can unlock more stats at the start of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I will continue to play this game, I can't in good faith recommend it. Having played many different roguelikes such as Hades, Risk of Rain, Enter the Gungeon, Dead Cells and so on, I can say that while it is indeed a roguelike, it relies on RNG far more than the other games do. All the games mentioned can be played to completion with very little in the way of good RNG and relying mostly on skills, in fact in most of them good RNG can only take you so far and it gets to the point that you require good skills. Skul is somewhat of the opposite, in which skills get you very little if you get bad RNG. This is EXTREMELY evident in the encounter generation. There are 4 types of gates to each encounter, one gives money, one gives an item, one gives a skull and the final one takes you to the shop. 1 or 2 Randomly generate every stage, and it is completely random. You can have a shop appear on the third encounter, and if you haven't taken a money gate yet, you are completely unable to purchase anything, taking you one step closer to the boss with no progression. There is no guaranteed shop or heal before a boss fight, in fact the encounter before a boss fight is empty, as if there is supposed to be some way to heal but they never implemented it. And after the boss fight there is only an NPC with the ability to upgrade a skull, if you actually managed to get enough bones to upgrade, no shop and only a small heal from the boss drop.Having only completed the first boss and reached the second without completion, I cant comment on any further bosses at this time, but the first boss is rather standard, telegraphed attacks that give you ample time to dodge, with a slightly harder second phase. The second boss however, becomes MUCH harder in its second stage, if you manage to make it. Attacks come much faster than you are able to dodge, so you have to be able to tank through several hits if you hope to win. So far, due to having to start all boss fights with less than optimal health, I have not beaten them yet. The mini bosses that occur half way between each stage are a nice touch, a chance to choose between a skull, quintessence and item upon completion.Skulls are horribly unbalanced, many strength skulls seem downright harmful to the player with how slow they attack, and since health is shared between your skulls and only items increase health, strength skulls have no real benefits when dodging is your best chance at surviving. For the first stage it doesn't really matter, but the second stage is becomes a hindrance to have slow attacks with the sheer volume of enemies in some stages. Speed types honestly seem like the best, but they sit pretty closely with balanced types. Some skulls, like the shield and lancer, seem downright worthless even compared to the base "skul" skull. The abilities on skulls are also a random one of 3 (Maybe 4) with some being obviously better than others. There is a good chance you can have a solid skull and a good set of items, but having the wrong ability ends the run. You can upgrade your skulls at a certain NPC that appears after each mini boss and boss fight, but only if you were lucky enough to get enough bones, something that once again is RNG. Unique (Legendary) skulls are obviously the best, but there is a huge difference between them. Map variation is pretty good, I don't recall getting duplicate encounters but I also don't pay that much attention, but some maps are quite inconvenient without prior knowledge, one map in particular has a roof that is covered in spikes with 3 levels. To jump to the third level you need to double jump to make the height, except double jumping takes you into the spikes whereas a single jump wont reach the platform. Small things like that where you need need to make an effort to either jump late or cancel the jump with a dash immediately makes getting around just that little bit inconvenient. I'm all for traps that require you to watch your positioning and your movement during battle, but it genuinely seems unintentional and it just punishes you for trying to move around the level normally.Overall if you are looking for a fun roguelike along the caliber of Hades or Enter the Gungeon, you should look elsewhere as this game probably isn't for you. If you wan't a hard roguelike that punishes you for bad RNG despite your skill level, go ahead.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Solid rougelike game; it's got a few flaws that prevent it from being one of the best but it's still very fun and worth a try if you like other games in the genre or 2D platform action games in general. Although you don't play rougelikes for the story Skul actually has a decently short, charming one that's actually quite good with some decent introspection and commentary on the 'hero' genre especially towards the end. Gameplay has a good arcadey fun feeling, and it captures the highs and lows of the rougelike genre well, albeit with two possibly major complaints. The clarity takes a big hit as you progress; debris and particles fly around and it's hard to tell what's going on or where your character is. This contributes (although is not the sole cause) to the bigger issue of damage feeling unavoidable at times. The iframes are a bit short on your dash/abilities and the game is a bit too fast and hectic to really 'avoid' damage consistently, and this lowers skill expression a bit and causes some frustration.The environments do get a little repetitive after a few runs, and the upgrade material for your permanent upgrades are a bit expensive, meaning the game does get a tad grindy at a certain point when compounded with the above mentioned gameplay flaws. The Skulls early game tend to be of lower quality and can feel clunky/weak before they're upgraded, compounding the issue.  Toggling on the rookie mode for -50% damage taken was a big helper here. Overall the game's good. Engaging, solid rougelike fun with a nice charming short story, I'd definitely recommend grabbing it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but at the end of the day I just can't. To its credit, the world it's set in is very charming and very creatively designed, and on paper Skul has a ton of really good ideas. But the one area that quickly lost my interest is the one that matters the most: Gameplay. The entire thing is a slow-moving, tedious, grindy slog from beginning to end (and this is coming from someone who had patience enough to beat Dead Cells on its hardest difficulty). The "randomized" stretches of the levels and the things in them, from enemies to other obstacles to items at the end, get extremely repetitive VERY quickly and basically come down to either "huh, that was a little TOO easy" or "OH GOD, please kill me NOW"; there is NO middle ground. You're either a Shredder-esque menace who encounters no challenge at all until a boss, or a Slim Jim who might as well be poking all of your foes with a dull graphite pencil (and probably breaking it in the process).However, all of that and even the overly grindy process of attaining upgrades that are frankly too small to make ANY significant difference still wasn't quite enough to turn me off to this game. That dishonor belongs to the boss fights. I'll be fair and say that the first two MAJOR bosses aren't that bad (in fact the guard sisters' fight was the one that brought me the closest to having any genuine fun here), but I'm mostly referring to the various random hero mini-bosses. Long story short, none of them are fun. Depending on which one (or ones, as you proceed further) shows up, you're in for a fight that is either boring and not engaging at all, or teeth-grindingly annoying. Special mentions go to the ninja (who is just flat-out the most overpowered enemy in the whole game) and the cleric (if she shows up in the later hero fight where you have to face a three-man squad, you might as well restart the run then and there because even if you somehow win the price you pay will not be worth it at all). No matter which of them it is, though, they ALL have absolutely ungodly-huge health pools, and you can not afford to try getting aggressive with them so you will be forced to dance around with these clowns for a long time. Not to mention in the middle of the fourth stage, the game will pick a random one to chuck at you again and make them even worse. Eventually when the game decided to throw the already unbearable ninja at me there, that's when I decided enough was enough. I dread to think of what even comes after, because that was the one that broke what patience I still had.Too sluggish, too tediously grindy, not enough interesting elements in said grind (or among your rewards), and it has no trouble at all making some extremely tall orders of you as a player. I really, really wanted to like this game, but too many things in it push all the wrong buttons. I just can't.

_childDocuments_.review: Skul: The Hero Slayer is one of the best rogue-like games I've ever played, and that's saying something. In my opinion, this game is up there with Hades, Binding of Issac, and Dead Cells. I've spent the last 3 days grinding and getting better at the game, and oh boy, it has been a journey. At first, I thought this game would be a cakewalk, but I was WRONG. This is one of those games where it's easy to learn, but VERY hard to master. I didn't even beat the 3rd boss until day 3 of getting this game, and I love it. Let's start out with the negatives:- The unique aspect of the game is that you can change your class by switching to skulls you find in game, and I find that really appealing. However, I find that some skulls are utterly useless, while other skulls are probably must haves. The balance with the skulls should be touched up, and it should be where I should actually have to think whether or not to pick up a skull or to turn it into upgrade currency. - The main boss fights are amazing. They are FAIR. You spend enough time fighting the bosses, you can get the mechanics down and take them down. On the contrary, the adventurers are not fair (the mini bosses in the games). At first, you fight one which is easy. Next stage, you have to fight two, which is harder than the first, but it's still do-able. The third time you fight the adventurers, you have to fight 3 at once, and that's where it's too much. Depending on the heroes that spawn, you're going to get taken down to half health, and if the Cleric is one of the heroes you have to fight, it is MANDATORY to target her first, or else you can't take down the other 2 without her healing them back to full health. So while you're targeting her, you have to watch the other two adventurers' attacks, and depending on the other two heroes, you're going to have a bad time. The 4th time you fight the adventurers, you just have to fight one super-charged adventurer, and I find that to be easier than fighting 3 at once. I don't know, maybe I just got to get good. -The rooms are not balanced, in my opinion. There are some rooms that are baby easy, and then you get the rooms where you find yourself thinking "wtf is this s***". -The NPCs are ehhh. After you first talk to them, they will just say the same thing over and over again, and you find yourself just skipping their one line of dialogue to you in order for you to get your stuff faster. The NPCs have no personality, especially the shop NPCs. After you first step foot in the shop, they have nothing new to say. No one has nothing to say on your progress. No story dialogue. Nothing. There's literally no reason to talk to them. You just buy your stuff and go. - The 4th level. IYKYK Now on to the positives: - Gameplay is similar to Dead Cells. It's a 2-D dungeon crawler where you have to go from one side to the other, defeating all the enemies on the stage before you move on. At first, I found myself just mashing buttons, hoping to defeat them before I take too much damage. However. sometimes that just dosen't work, and you have to precise with your attacks and your dodges. -Soundtrack is 10/10. Especially the boss music. Gets me so hyped while fighting against them. -Animation is pretty detailed as well. For example, if you pay attention to the 2nd level bosses, you can see a little jiggle whenever they slam down, and it's pretty distracting (in a good way) and it often gets me hit. You can tell whenever an enemy is about to attack because the animation is clear enough for you to tell. -Graphics are amazing for the artstyle its going for. It's visually appealing and it dosen't hurt your eyes. Overall, this game is pretty amazing. It has some balancing issues, but if the devs can fix that, it can be a damn near perfect game. If you are a fan of the rogue-like genre, and if you like difficult games, then this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: What most reviews neglect to tell you about the difficulty is that you cannot animation cancel most of your moves. This is where the word "clunky" originates from. On the other hand, I think there is some depth to the combat when you cannot animation cancel, just like in Monster Hunter. Rather than just mindlessly spamming your skills off cooldown, you have to take your positioning and the enemy into account. Most of the skulls are viable and fun. Furthermore, there is no harm in playing on rookie mode in singleplayer, which lets you take 50% less damage while the enemy keeps all of its move-set. I cleared the boss on rookie mode tooThere are certain platforming rooms with environmental traps that require you to jump/dash to avoid traps etc. Those rooms can be annoying and ruin an otherwise good run. Because you will probably not get the exact same room, this makes practising the platforming difficult.There is however little incentive to replay all the bosses on a new skull once you have everything unlocked. The game could use an expansion or DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: Skul: The Hero Slayer:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ The humans, with the help of the Imperial Army and the Hero of Caerleon, have finally defeated the Demon King and his army! The last onslaught was humungous and saw the Demon King and his Senators being captured! Actually, there was one small skeleton, named Skul, who managed to keep his bones together and avoid being taken away himself. From the ruins of the Demon King castle, he is making his plan to rescue the Demon King and his collaborators! Are you ready for the challenge? Become Skul: The Hero Slayer!Skul: The Hero Slayer is an action roguelike platformer developed by SouthPAW Games and published by NEOWIZ on the 21 of January 2021 on the Steam platform. The game consists of 5 chapters that each host several stages and mini-bosses, as well as a main boss at the end of each chapter. As you launch the game for the first time, you’ll go through a short tutorial that will bring you up to speed on what happened to the Demon King’s army and castle. After rescuing the first Demon King Senator, the witch in the tutorial, you’ll arrive at his castle. This is where you’ll restart each of your playthroughs. At first, the only person you can talk at the castle will be the witch. As you progress, rescuing other characters and defeating the main bosses in each chapter, you’ll be able to talk to other characters and receive skins (skeletons), skills and other goodies. In my case, after 16 hours of gameplay, I have 3 different characters to talk to, and from whom I can acquire goodies, before I start my next playthrough. You can add traits when you talk to the witch, but you’ll need to collect purple gems called Dark Quartz. These gems will appear every so often when you kill an enemy. There are three traits that you can upgrade, and each of them has four tiers. It will take you a while to upgrade to the maximum level of 10 in each tier.  In my case, I only have one of the first tiers on the maximum level to give you an idea. I do have a few levels 8 but I haven’t managed to unlock one upgrade on the last tier as yet. It’s a whopping 3,000 Quartz to unlock the first of each in the last tier!The second character in the castle is the Fox Hunter, where you can acquire another skull (skins). The first one is free, and you can use it or destroy it. You can ask for a second one, but it will cost you a few Dark Quartz, but that’s it. If you destroy it, you’ll receive bones which you need to upgrade your devilish skeleton halfway through each chapter. The third character is the Ogre Peddler, where you’ll receive one free gift/item and pay for another one if you have enough Quartz. The third one available to me is the Evil Druid, where I can be blessed with one specific ability in my next playthrough. I am not sure if there is another one or two extra characters that will become available to me before my next gameplay. Now I can manage to reach and defeat the second main boss, but still kiss my little pelvis goodbye at the third boss!  I really loved the gameplay from my first playthrough! After jumping out of the castle window or big hole in the wall, you land in front of one or two entrances (it will depend on each of your playthroughs). There are only three types of entrances; one is green with bones in front of it, the other two are made of stone but one will have treasure chests in front! If you decide to go through a green entrance, you’ll be rewarded with a skeleton skin at the end of the level. The bigger the pile of bones, the more chances to receive a special. If you don’t want it, you can destroy it and receive bones which you need to upgrade the skeleton you are currently using. However, it is not possible to upgrade Skul’s original skin/skeleton.  You’ll receive items at the end of the level if you choose to go through the door with the treasure chests in front, and you’ll receive gold if you go through the plain stone door. Bear in mind that you can only accumulate 9 gifts/items per playthrough.Each of the chapters is laid out with 3 to 4 small levels first. Then you’ll visit a store where you can buy more health and goodies. One mini-boss fight, and when you defeat him/her or them you’ll be able to upgrade your skin by talking to Arachne the spider, but you’ll need bones for that! Then you’ll have another 3 small levels and the main boss fight! As you upgrade your traits, the first two chapters will become easier; well, depending on which skeleton you have or change during the course of the chapter. But I must say, it still can be difficult to defeat each of the main bosses because of the randomisation of the skeleton skin at the start of each playthrough, as well as the gifts and skins you’ll get through that gameplay. It is entertaining and addictive; let me tell you! You’ll also feel your fair amount of frustration! In my case, I can’t beat the third boss at the moment, and therefore I have to start all over again, and pick up as many Dark Quartz to upgrade traits for my next run.Great variety of enemies as you progress through the levels, that are harder to dispose of, which is always fun!Beautiful pixel artwork, the mechanisms are fluid, and the game runs really well. Plenty of skins, gifts/items and the ability tree is simple and easy follow. I do feel that some of the rare skins you might collect during your playthrough are not as good as the one you might start off with and upgrade during the gameplay. In terms of the controls, you can play the game with your keyboard, but I strongly recommend using a gamepad for this game. There are not too many variations within the levels, which can become repetitive.  Positives:~~~~~~~~ +	Great pixel artworks+	Easy to play, addictive but hard to master+	Stacks of skins/skeletons and items to use+	Each playthrough is different+	Good variety of enemies+	Control support+	Epic mini-bosses and main boss fights+	Achievements and trading cardsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	A bit repetitive in terms of the levelsSkul: The Hero Slayer:  super fun and well made. An action roguelike platformer with a devilish punch all way through!  8/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a major problem that is not addressed by most other reviews. The gameplay is very fun and the graphics are nice. The music is nothing special.The various skulls provide great variety between the runs, and the abilities feel very satisfying to use.Unfortunately, 80% of your runs success is determined by RNG. Before you call me a noob, i have reached the final boss multiple times, but i refuse to waste any more time hoping for a decent run where you actually get what you need. Keep in mind that in order to know whether a run is good or not (and thus whether you should just restart instantly or not) you have to play for an hour or so.This creates an evil, repititive and boring cycle of starting runs for hours on end hoping for the 0.000001% chance that you might get something that can actually reach and kill the final boss. The reason you need to rely so much on rng is because most rooms and bosses have attacks that are nearly undodgeable, thus requiring you to have a certain amount of dps to finish them. If you don't care much for winning in roguelites, and just want to have some fun, interesting and varied runs, then this game will be great for you. But being unable to finish the game without playing pointless runs that go nowhere for hours is extremely frustrating to me, which is why i'm giving this otherwise great game a negative review.

_childDocuments_.review: "hey, what’s wrong?! what’s your problem?!  why the negative review, after all these hours?!"ok, this game is very addictive and while playing, you even get close to having some real fun.but in its current state, it’s much more frustrating than satisfying.why?i will compare it to "the binding of isaac". In "the binding of isaac" the whole game-mechanicworks with this crazy synergy effects, you know what you get and what to expect: always a surprise.but! even if everything seems totally hopeless there is this small glimmer of chance, there will be one item that combined with your already consumed ones, will make you very mighty.yes and even in a standard run, you can play carefully and reach one of the endings, if you have enough practise. (and the binding of isaac for me and many other players is about unlocking all the items and archievements, not merely to "win the game".)"skul", on the other hand is overhelmingly unbalanced; ok; until you reach the castle, there are not too many problems, nearly every combination of skulls and items and good strategy could bring you there – so the fun indeed is concentrated in the first part, as of course this becomes repetitive pretty fast -; from the castle on, most of the combinatons will make it incredibly difficult to nearly impossible to progress..And then you have the overpowered ones.For example, i had the grim reaper and a very good alchemist - yes, their attributes can differ -; in this combination i seemed nearly undefeatable, the grim reaper does so much damage, has so many advantages, you just rush through the stages, even the two sisters were some sort of child’s play, i died a little bit later, because i became superstitious.ok; then for another example, i put all my energy in a combination of fighter and rockstar, reached the two sisters, but no matter what i did, the fight lasted over seven minutes, they continued to build up their health again.you can use the quartz zu improve your character, but in such a limited way that you wouldn’t have to do it at all, if you got the grim reaper for example in the beginning and some good items. _childDocuments_.review: After many hours in the game I'm revising my review to reflect my experience. Skul starts off challenging but quickly becomes easier as you learn to fight the various enemies and gain new permanent upgrades. Because of this the learning curve isn't steep and many casual players can jump straight in and have fun. *Skulls*The unique mechanic for the game is swapping skulls (your head) with others to gain new forms and abilities. You can have two of these at a time and switch on the fly during combat. Think of it like tagging a character out for a second one during a fight. The skulls themselves have their very own abilities that are randomly given to them each time you find them. So just because you found a Warrior skull again doesn't mean it'll be the same as the last. Mixing your duo of skulls around to suit your favourite play style is a lot of fun.*Items*The items within the game are collected either from completing treasure rooms or from shops found during your journey. Their effects range from passive ones (+30% to Physical Attack) to more unique ones (Attacks fire Shurikens from your body!). Building a strong arsenal of items along with your favourite skulls can lead to absolute chaos on the screen as you shred through enemies. *Early Access*As of writing this (Late Oct 2020) the game is still in early access but is aiming to release in December this year. The full release promises new areas explore, more enemies, bosses and an entirely new system for upgrading your skulls during runs to provide another layer of customization and power to your play. If you aren't a fan of games that are in Early Access, I understand. However I still strongly recommend you take a look at the game after its final release to make sure you aren't missing out on something you could really enjoy. The game is still young with a lot of room for growth.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw this game randomly on "Popular Upcoming" by chance. I watched the previews, some gameplay and decided to dive SKUL first into this. I am a huge Rogue-lite fan. I have played countless of them: Deadcells, Rogue Legacy, Wizard of Legend, Enter the Gungeon, Spelunky...you get the point. I absolutely adore the challenges and different types of gameplay that you get with each run. It took me about 10 hours to finish the story currently, while I got to the last boss 3 times total. If you love rougelites, please pick this game up. It has a lot of potential it's already hitting. Comboing skulls together and absolutely destroying a map full of enemies is really exciting. This game rewards thinking quickly very well. It's a game to pick up if you love an original story, great music and really interactive gameplay. - Lovely Pixel Art- Very Rewarding Passive Traits- Most classes (Skulls) seem viable- Music is to die for- Challenging but not pull your hair out- Player Agency- Comboing- Easy to tell what's going on- Proper character progression- There are definitely skulls that are just not that great- Rewards speed over all else- Animation locking can get pretty annoying- Wish there was a small buffer when you received damage (Passive Trait?)- Item slots are super important, I wish health items were given to you but I understand why they aren'tHere are a couple thoughts the game design itself because I love the story. Power Skulls: Minotaur, Warrior, Fighter, Yaksha and Grim Reaper. These skulls can be very strong but I feel like the animation locks really inhibit some of the game flow. It just feels SO slow when you are trying to use their abilities when you have things like the the Spearman with the dash auto-attack cancel and the Djinn that rewards 1 button mash. I-frames would be a solution to letting them hit hard but not be punished for having to stand still a little bit. Give them proper reward for being slow. Skulls I frequently avoid:Clown: Slow attack speed even though they are ranged. I like the idea of a *3* hit passive but it just feels like the animations take forever.Werewolf: Speed like this could be important in a speed run when you have 1 skill carrying everything but I figured this guy was too crazy. He moves a LOT and I would prefer some sort of Howl move to perhaps fear enemies around it.Ranger: Long wind up, doesn't feel good to use most of the time. Most power skullsSamurai: Animations a bit slow and it feels like you get locked into them. Skulls I tend to almost always pick up:Djinn: Teleport + the Fairy Tackle gives you very large vertical hit box and also lasts a deceptively long time when it comes to the Swap + Skill use.Rider: Very good mobility and feels good to use. I wish this skull would be immune to the fire mages. Motorcycle is a good concept and really love how wild it is. Ninja: Get the right items and the right skills and you can burst a lot of stuff down very quickly. I love the ninja and he is super fun.Predator: Having skills to spam really makes you feel good as long as you can control it. Immense DPS and really gives you the feeling of a dual-wielding maniac. Has a weird synergy with the Purple Ribcage where you can infinitely use the skills. This might be intentional but each press of the button is considered an independent cast, so it's almost infinite resets.Mummy: Click attack fast = destroy people. After the most recent nerf it's not as good but it gives you immunity to traps so this man is a legend. Dark Paladin: Rewards swapping and smart skill usage. Does a buttload of damage if you can get the right angle on people. Super fun to use and makes you feel really bad ass when you can pull the combos off.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Skul system is uniqueHardmode is pretty interestingSome bosses have unique mechanics that are fun.Cons:Build variety is pretty limited, if you play sword you are only looking for bleed items, hybrid classes really have no identity. Item pool seems heavily tilted toward physical items, so it puts magic dealing chars in a strange spot of hoping for re rolls being in your favor at shops. You will become very bored of the same layouts and enemies over and over. I have played up to hard mode 4, and i have already come to "hate" specific rooms. Which with proper random generation would increase replay-ability. There are people trapped in cages but there seems to be only 5 of them so even events are lacking in variety. THERE ARE NO SECRET ROOMS, you will maybe see a unique room with treasure every 10 or so runs but typically there are no secret rooms, as I've mentioned there is limited variety in layouts so this is probably why there are no secret rooms or alternative paths. Certain bosses make melee characters cry, the mage in act 4 stays airborne for 75% of the fight is very annoying, certain skuls have abilities that are impossible to use on bosses such as the gravedigger and Otello on the Boss in Act 4, all the boulders just roll off the platforms and damaging the boss becomes a game of hoping she lands on platforms long enough for the boulders to do damage. I recommend this game if you are looking for a metroidvania style game with limited rogue aspects, with minor replay-ability.
_childDocuments_.name: Skul: The Hero Slayer

_childDocuments_.review: Skul has only gotten better over time, thanks to the continuous updates that this game receives. The variance in builds is high, and the replayability is there through the gameplay loop and difficulty modifiers. Each skull (equivalent of character class) feels unique and enjoyable to play. And while it's one of the harder games I've played, it never felt unfair.Skul's approach to difficulty increase is significantly better than most. While the game becomes more challenging once you activate this mechanic, it isn't due to enemies simply statchecking your ass, but due to adding new movesets to bosses, or new enemy and stage variants. However, the game also provides you with new toys to play with, such as a new powerup system or mechanics that increase the quality of a run. While not every run will be god tier, you'll be hard pressed to find a run that can't be won with pure skill alone.And now with the seemingly final story update, it adds a new incentive to see the game through as well as some incredible boss fights near the end. The music is underrated as well.Personally, if I liked the feel of the combat a bit better, this would have become one of my new favourites in the roguelite genre, but despite that, the gameplay loop and content still makes it worth playing for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Skul: The Hero Slayer

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game with items that really impact your play-style that can lead to so many different feeling runs.The difficulty of the game is a steep learning curve but it is done well as difficulty comes through increasing variety of enemies and traps.There are two things that make me not recommend this game:1. One of the three character types "Speed" is not possible to play well unless you are able to mash one button without tiring or hurting yourself. The game would benefit greatly by an option to hold button for continuous attacks.2.Visual clarity is not this games strong suit. There is some amazing work done with the pixel art and particle effects. Too many effects. Once you stack up bonuses through items, enemies and especially bosses are incredibly hard to see. All or most of these effects should layered behind/around the enemies to allow the player to see incoming attacks and enemy projectiles. Another option would be a toggle to highlight enemy models.If these two things do not bother you, this is an easy recommend for anyone that loves rouge-like elements, varied player builds, and button mashing action with some platforming elements.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is mostly against what people are saying about the game and it's "flaws". The biggest complaint I see about this game is the boss' health bars and how they are too big. The only boss I genuinely agree that this is a problem is the Chimera. Every other fight has some aspect that is either interesting, or able to be manipulated. I kind of cringe when I see people say the bosses take to long in this game because even on the final boss, it takes 3 to 5 minutes tops. That is also the FINAL boss. I enjoy fights where I have to pay attention most of the time or I could be severely punished. The chimera just kind of feels like a dps wall and the fight isn't interesting. The next problem people have with the game are the skulls you get and how broken some are compared to others. First off, this is the same mechanic as getting a bad or good gun in enter the gungeon. Similarly, some of the basic skulls can be amazing. Werewolf and Thief are godlike for commons, frozen skull and rider are the same for rares and so on. Slightly connected to this subject is bone fragments. I've put 38 hours into the game and almost have all of the legendary skulls. They are NOT hard to get. You get plenty of opportunities to get bones throughout any given run probably. While one run you may get a bunch of commons so you don't get enough bones, the next you might get 3 legendary skulls to sacrifice. This was the case in one of my runs where I upgraded two skulls to legendary and still had 113 bones remaining. It's a roguelike, there is going to be RNG. Next is the inventory and items. I would not compare the game to gungeon or isaac in terms of inventory. It is not that sort of game and there are twice as many levels in gungeon and you can potentially have a full restart while keeping your items in gungeon. The items are well balanced for a 9 item limit and they all give additional passives that can be useful in themselves. Having "the run" every run because you are good enough to get so many items every run gets boring. Having to pick and choose makes every run semi-unique due to RNG. Two last problems people say the game has are one, that the layouts get boring. I really don't get this one because this same thing happens in every roguelike I have ever played like of course you are going to remember layouts and spawns. It's a natural progression. I just do not understand this complaint. The second is that damage feels "unavoidable". The game gives you two jumps and a dash. Every normal floor enemy definitely feels avoidable. I'm so glad I can't just braindead auto through every map. If someone is really having health problems, get the vampire necklace. I could maybe see this complaint on some hitboxes in the sisters fight, but other than that, and I hate saying this, but get good.Lastly, I just wanted to say that I love this game. The variety of skulls are so cool and the mechanics of the game are so much fun to play around with. The boss fights are challenging for the most part (looking at you chimera) and are so satisfying when beaten. When you actually put together an op build with the perfect skull for the build, the gameplay just hypes me up. I'm looking forwards to any dlc this game has if any. P.S. My least favorite item is the green bone, and mummy sucks so much.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if I can evaluate the game properly, for I don't have too much technical knowledge. However, I can definitely say that, at least for me, the combat system; different characters, items, perks and the feeling of hitting the enemy, is "devilishly" addictive. I played it for 24 hours in 3 days! So in my opinion, it is really worth the money you give (regardless of the amount maybe). Besides all these, I think the plot and the story is also cute and is more than enoough for a game like this. However, please do not forget, these are my opinions!Lastly, I have a suggestion for the developers: It would be great if there was a mode in which we are able to use anything in order to try out different combos, different combos with characters etc. This mode can be available to the player after she/he defeats the final boss and finishes the game in normal mode. This mode probably would have caused me to play the game for another 40-50 hours...Thank you for reading!

_childDocuments_.review:
The human race attacking the Demon King's castle is nothing new and has happened countless times before. What makes this time different though, is that the Adventurers decided to join forces with the Imperial Army and the 'Hero of Caerleon' to finally succeed in the total destruction of the Demon stronghold. All of the demons in the castle were taken prisoner except for one lone skeleton named 'Skul'.

Skul is no ordinary skeleton. In addition to his formidable fighting skills, he can gain new and exciting abilities depending on which skull he's wearing.Use up to 2 skulls at a time, each of which has its own unique attack range, speed and power. So choose ones that match your playing style and switch them in the heat of battle to bring your enemies to their knees. The power is in your hands!

Skul has crossed paths with a party of Adventurers! They are powerful foes that hunt Demons for sport. But while Skul may be small, he still packs quite a punch. So just see who really is the hunter and who is the hunted...

name: UFO 50
detailed_description: UFO 50 is a collection of 50 single and multiplayer games from the creators of Spelunky, Downwell, and Catacomb Kids. Explore a variety of genres, from platformers and shoot 'em ups to puzzle games, roguelites, and RPGs. Our goal is to combine a familiar 8-bit aesthetic with new ideas and modern game design. 50 BRAND NEW GAMES - These are NOT minigames or microgames! Although the size of each game varies, every one is a complete experience, from its opening title screen to its ending credits. Some are small arcade-style games but there are also larger open-world adventures and a JRPG that could take many hours to beat. AN ALTERNATE UNIVERSE - According to the story of UFO 50, the games were all created by a fictional 80s video game company that was obscure but ahead of its time. Some games are sequels to other games in the collection and various characters appear in multiple titles as part of a shared continuity. AN INSTANT LIBRARY - All 50 games are available to play at the start! The concept was inspired by multicarts, retro collections, and the experience of going to a friend's house and perusing their game library. Jump in and out of games at a whim - exploring the collection is part of the fun! AUTHENTIC BUT ALSO MODERN - We carefully chose what elements to modernize. Every game shares a unique 32-color palette and we took great efforts to make them look and sound like actual 8-bit titles from the 80s. On the other hand, it was important to us that UFO 50 was fun and surprising for modern players, so we chose not to limit ourselves to the genres and design conventions of the past. VERSUS AND CO-OP PLAY - Half of the collection features local multiplayer, including co-op and versus. You can compete head-to-head in a new fighting or strategy game... or team up to beat a classic arcade game from an alternate timeline. It's great for groups! Here are some of games you'll get to play in UFO 50: CAMPANELLA 2 - The sequel to Campanella (another game in UFO 50), Campanella 2 features procedurally-generated levels where you can explore in your UFO but also hop out to enter shops and dangerous caves. You play as the intrepid treasure-hunter Isabell, but she hasn't always been a hero - by playing the entire collection you can learn more about her past. QUIBBLE RACE - In this unique sci-fi 'horse-racing' game, the goal is to win more money than your opponents, but why stop at betting? Thanks to the seedy alien underworld, you can hire thugs to tamper with the race or even sponsor your own quibble to earn extra credits. But your opponents can do the same, so the question is... how well can you anticipate their actions? Up to 3 players can compete in this turn-based game of betting and bluffing. PINGOLF - A fan favorite at gaming get-togethers like PAX, Pingolf is another fun multiplayer game that mixes golf with pinball. As you navigate 18 holes filled with bumpers, trampolines, and other crazy obstacles, a dot matrix display will light up at the bottom of the screen to cheer you on! SEASIDE DRIVE - Sometimes you'll want a break from long, open-world games and challenging strategy titles, so why not jump into a straight-forward arcade-style action game like Seaside Drive? But even in a popular genre, UFO 50 brings something new to the table - in this case, Ojiro Fumoto (the creator of Downwell) designed a stylish car-based shoot 'em up where 'drifting' across the screen is how you power-up your gun. GRIMSTONE - Yes, there is a full blown JRPG in the collection! Grimstone follows many conventions from 8-bit console RPGs, but is streamlined for a modern audience. Also, to make combat more engaging, we added a skill-based component to battles and encounters on the overworld can be strategically avoided. The story takes place in the American Wild West, where somehow the land has been swallowed up by Hell! Creating your party from the ashes of a burned-down saloon, you'll be looking for answers as to why it happened. And that's just five games! Out of 50! So come join us and enjoy this collection of 8-bit classics from another dimension! There's something for everyone!

_childDocuments_.review: Still playing and will write more later, but I want to leave this a positive review. Here's some praise from my Twitter.UFO50 is effing brilliant-- it's hard to not throw every adjective at it since there's so much going on. My expectations are always flipped on their head-- games look and sound beautiful. Super fresh, elegant, clever spins on old formulas and a lot of new stuff.By "fresh" I mean it's hardly ever "oh it's [x] game with this spin or coat of paint"-- there's so much thought to it-- roots in classics but super original.The games feel really alien to me, by which I mean there's such a unique approach to most of the designs I don't see often or have never seen before in my life.Main gripe is in some of the longer games, there's no checkpoints-- which makes sense sticking with the tough retro style-- but having to play through the easier levels again and going through those menus/transitions just to get slammed and sent back to the easy levels again later on can be a little slow and frustrating. I'm not sure what the solution to that is beyond checkpoints.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: UFO 50 is amazing! So worth the wait. While not all of the 50 games will be for everybody, there is an impressive amount of quality and variety across all of them. About half of the games have local multiplayer as well, and thanks to their simplicity and good design they are a great way to spend a few hours with friends. Me and my brother stayed up until about 3 AM one night playing just one game (Avianos, an adorable strategy game about birds and dinosaurs). You're getting way more than your money's worth with this one.Absolutely check this out if you're curious! It really is that good, and is one of the most inventive and unique indies I've played... well, ever.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: To list the caveats upfront: most of the games in this collection are difficult, without easy or assist modes to work with. Some throw you into what feels like the deep end and kill you before you know what's going on. They're probably better suited for players who have either already experienced the cruelty of 8-bit games or want to aspire to the challenge of them.The underlying design of the games, however, is very solid and fun. Tenets of game design that have been learned by the industry over the last 35 years very much shine through the games' sometimes unwelcoming and callous exteriors. If something is finicky or a "gotcha", it feels deliberate, something to overcome or wise up to next time. Restarting after a failed run is usually pretty quick, and the games do generally "want" you to get better at them if you stick to them.Potential accessibility concerns aside, this game is a wildly good value, but more than that, it simply contains some of the cleanest gameplay I have seen in any era of gaming. Some of the games work better by being part of this collection than they would as standalone titles. Some will scratch one person's itch and fall absolutely flat with someone else. Some are just plain great in any context, games I wouldn't give notice among others on a storefront but if I had paid $5 or more for them individually I would have been absolutely happy with that purchase. Personally, I will shout out to Party House and Warp Tank as standouts, but after almost 50 hours of play there is still a lot of ground I haven't covered. Every game plays a part and they all have more to them than it seems at first.Tldr: tough, fun, lots to discover, absolute banger in my book.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played about 15 of the games so far, and there is something to love about every single one of them. Most of these games are more individually more creative and interesting than most games I've played in recent memory. The music and graphics are wonderful. This is the most generous game I've ever played.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not just a smattering of minigames thrown into a value pack. Most of these games could do well selling for 5 bucks or more on their own. I was really impressed after playing the first 5, then after the first 10 realized this was something really special. I'm now 19 games in and I think this is probably one of the most ambitious and unique game projects ever done. Serious props to the developers pulling this off.The question of 'is this worth picking up' is such a resounding yes. Stop whatever you're doing with your life, and play UFO 50. Whatever you want out of a video game, you'll find it somewhere here, and then some.PLAY FOREVER.

_childDocuments_.review: The best video game anthology I've ever played. The variety, depth, and quality is incredible. The story/meta-narrative of the fictional video game company UFO Soft (formerly LX Systems) is fascinating as well. There's this progression of game mechanics, ideas, and characters across games that is so cool. It's a special game and a great value at its current price of 25 dollars.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: UFO 50 is incredible. Yes, this is a collection of FIFTY retro-style (think NES era) games. Each is a full experience. There are multiple games in this collection I would consider to be some of my all-time favorite games. These games hit essentially every genre. So if you are reading this, and have any interest in video games generally, it is a must buy at a price of $25. There are some games in the collection that are absolutely worth the $25 price tag on their own.So what games are the best, you ask? Well... this is what makes UFO 50 so special.  My favorite games will be different than yours. There is virtually no consensus on what games in the collection are "the best" and which are "just okay". In other words, this is not a collection of 5 amazing games and 45 games that were thrown together at the last second. Every game is someone's favorite.The game design is extremely fun and creative. There is a Zelda-like golf action-adventure game where your health remaining is connected to the number of strokes you have played. There is a platformer (and a sequel!) where you need to use your extra lives to progress through the stage. And the list goes on. The ideas were flowing when they made this game, and it's so fun to dive into each game without knowing what is next.One last thought - the games in the collection as a default are organized "chronologically" which means the first game most people select, Barbuta, has the most outdated audiovisuals and game design. I can see a lot of people playing this and immediately being turned off by UFO 50. Barbuta is really the only game in the collection that is meant to feel dated in this way. FWIW, I liked this game, but it's not going to be everyone's cup of tea.TLDR: Derek Yu and Co. hand-crafted 50 excellent games and you are bound to like many of them, and possibly all of them. This game is no longer a hidden entity, but I'm shocked it has not exploded in popularity more than it has because there is something in this collection for everyone. It's the only game I can confidently recommend to absolutely anyone who games.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: The variety and depth on offer is really impressive. The '80s design sensibilities won't be for everyone, but UFO 50 serves as a good reminder as to what has been lost in the pursuit for games with ever-increasing mass market appeal. Most of the collection does a good job of blending retro and contemporary game design, helping each game feel fresh despite having old school elements.There are a lot of multiplayer modes on offer which can be great fun with a friend. The soundtrack is also fantastic!
