_childDocuments_.review: UFO 50, unfortunately, feels as shallow as you can imagine a retro-inspired 50-in-1 game pack made in 2024 would. I think the idea is novel, and I greatly admire the amount of love and effort put into it by both the developers and the artists. I just get a sense of "we used pixel art solely because we wanted it to feel retro and nostalgic" vibe from this.The games themselves fall fairly flat—there's not much substance here. Everything it tries to emulate, it does so pretty poorly, and the original ideas weren't interesting enough for me to want to keep playing. Games tended to either not be that fun or deep, or suffered from an insanely steep difficulty spike—which, I assume, was in an effort to emulate the brutal difficulty of NES games, but it fails at even that. As a lover of retro games, it feels to me like UFO 50 wants so badly to recapture that "tough-as-nails" feeling those old games evoked, but tried to do that in most cases by making level 1 super easy, level 2 a tiny bit tougher, and level 3 impossibly difficult. In these cases, the games were sadly not engrossing enough for me to want to try and overcome that jump in difficulty, as attainable a goal as I think it may have been; I'd simply cut my losses and moved on to something else in the pack, knowing that there were 49 other options (one of which  to be better), until I saw it as a futile effort and gave up.It feels like the problem of having a thousand TV channels and nothing to watch. Sure, there may be a diamond or two in here, but even if I had found a game I enjoyed, the package by and large still wouldn't be worth the price tag to me. I don't think there's anything here to latch onto, as much as I would have liked there to be.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: well UFO 50 does exactly that and oh boy has each game so far been exceptionally good in its own category. there will be genres here that probably wont work for you, but even I could still appreciate the work put into those games (specifically even though Block Koala isn't really for me, I still enjoyed the gameplay)in terms of length per game some have exaggerated this fact, in reality it varies between an arcade style game that's beatable within 15 minutes, to a full fledged 3-6 hour experience, to time wasters that drag on even longer!so far I went through roughly 40 games and beaten 14 of them, I'd recommend that you take your time with each game to give 'em a fair shake instead of speed running through all 50 and then playing 'the best one'Highlights: Devilition, Kick Club, Mooncat, The Big Bell Race, Waldorf's Journey, Caramel Caramel, Diverson top of the massive game collection there's a "meta secret" sprawling through the games, kinda like how Animal Well has multiple layers, UFO 50 has a 'treasure hunt layer' of sorts.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: Too many games in the pack rely far too heavily on three things:1) The myth of "we just had to figure it out back then." Several of the games are not intuitive at all and the extremely limited "how to play" instructions will leave a lot of people cold. Games you purchased came with manuals explaining how the game worked. Rentals usually did. Arcade machines had bezels with instructions printed on.2) "Nintendo Hard" being a feature instead of developers of the time still trying to squeeze quarters out of your pocket (despite being home games) and/or stop folks from being able to beat games during a rental period, thus encouraging game sales. Several games in the pack require a "1CC" victory or have extremely limited continues. Some have AI that just never messes up or rubberbands SUPER hard. The Big Bell Race, for example, has the enemy pilots almost never attack each other, but hoo buddy will they mess you up at every chance.3) The two button gimmick. A good chunk of the games in the pack wouldn't be nearly as bad to play with even just one more button for one of the commands.These three things alone made a large amount of the games rather unfun for me to play, and I'm literally from the generation that these kind of games are supposedly emulating. There's a reason tutorials exist, difficulty is more of a curve than a cliff, and controllers got more buttons.All that said, there absolutely are some killer, easy to pick up and fun to play games in the pack. Warptank, Camouflage, Block Koala, Vainger (loved the way it feels like a hybrid of Super Metroid and Metal Storm), and Mortol come to mind, but the lopsided ratio of clunkers to bangers leaves me at "can't recommend."
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: An utterly incredible collection of games that has something for everyone, theres lots of secrets and hidden meanings in here, and the experience is truly akin to getting a pirate cartridge for a console you never had, choke full with games you have no idea how to play and barely any guidance if the game doesnt have a tutorial of sorts (and they often dont!)they can be extremely frustrating and the design can be quite evil at times, but all the same its quite modern and the frustration feels milimetrically measured to not be AS evil as actual retro games, they just emulate the punishing feeling they have while being quite merciful under the hood, some extremely hard games only last about 10 minutes once you get their rhythm down, and the variety is so large that you really should not feel obligated to connect or enjoy literally every single title, despite their quality, OCD be damned.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most game you can get on steam right now, 50 games for 25$ that's 50 cents a game, if you don't like one there's over 40 more, If you have any love for retro games, or a desire for something that emulates them almost perfectly, then you have to pick this game up! Literally something for everyone!
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: I can't imagine anyone would play all these games and not find at least 5 they absolutely adore. It's an incredibly diverse collection in terms of the genres being explored but in spite of that the familiar charm carries through in each game as you progress through this imaginary developer's chronological output. Even the games that didn't hold my interest had some great unique ideas and all of the games I passed on seem to be someone else's favourite. Also a lot of these games have a shocking amount of content considering it's basically a bargain bin 50 pack. The game somehow always manages to feel like it values the players time, everytime I open a new game I think "surely this one will be the inevitable dud or repeat" and yet it never is. UFO50 is truly a superb experience, and if you have someone to play the couch co-op multiplayer games with this is easily game of the year imo.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: The execution of this compilation exceeds even its clever concept: a fictional 1980's game studio's entire 8-bit catalog. Unlike Retro Game Challenge with its fan service (instructions, magazine articles), UFO 50 is intentionally obtuse for better or worse. What is doubtlessly better: There are way more games. While not all will suit your taste, I found many I loved - spending several hours on several of them. Pilot Quest, Mini & Max, Party House, and Vainger are favorites. Big recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: As a person who normally does not play Singleplayer games, I'm in love with UFO 50. It has so much passion and care put into it and so many of the games within are an absolute blast. I won't say every single game out of the 50 is a banger but certainly more of them are than I ever would have expected. More than worth the money, especially if you like to be a completionist or compete against yourself/others for times.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: This is a massive collection of games from the early days of PC gaming. I downloaded a list of the "10 best" and started to play them in that order. The first two were "run'n'gun" titles that seemed too hard for me to enjoy. Then I got into "Grimrock" which is a Western-themed RPG title. It is reasonably challenging and there is a story of interest. There is also a need for a lot of "grinding" in order to level up. Of course the graphics are not what we've grown used to in the 21st century. This is as much as I can say after only ten hours.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: This great is really great.  You can tell love has gone in to the development of it.  Some of the titles are better than others but that is to be expected with 50 available to play!  It reminds me of playing games for the first time on NES back in the day...renting the odd ball ones from blockbuster based off their covers to find that whatever it was was a gem.  Def up on the top of my list for this year!
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: I was hoping I'd finally have the right words for this at the 100 hour mark, but I'm still struggling. It's really good, might not be for everyone, but is ridiculously technically impressive.The developers have delivered a package that delivers 50 individual games that are all fun in their own right, but also tells a story about a company slowly developing mastery over game development over a decade.The first few games in the collection have rudimentary character controls, barely have sounds, don't have title screens, didn't have credits yet, but all innovate in their own surprising ways. Further in the collection, the games get far closer in feeling to what Rare or Capcom made for the NES, but with small callbacks to previous games in UFO 50 for anyone who's taken the time to explore them.If you're the kind of person that can appreciate the fact that this team included 2 JRPGs in two distinct styles, one where a game over requires the player to load their last save, and another where the player only drops money and is sent back to town, just to tell a story about developers getting better at their craft and ongoing experiments with save systems, you owe it to yourself to pick up this collection. Nobody at Mossmouth had to make any of these simpler games to learn. Instead, the limitations they've chosen aesthetically and mechanically help push this weird pseudo-narrative artistic interpretation of the collection as a whole. It's ridiculously cool and I don't think there's ever been anything else quite like this.Simply put, the amount of game development talent on display here is actually incredible.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute joy. UFO 50 is a festival of gaming, paying homage to gaming in the 1980s. The devs have crafted new games with imposed technical limitations to get the vibes right. There are fifty GOOD games in here! If you enjoy the classics from the NES & Amiga generation, you should absolutely buy this.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible collection of retro games, all made as though they show the history of game development for an imaginary 1980s console. There are tactics games, platformers, sports games, puzzle games, RPGs, sidescrolling shooters, beat-em-ups, and even a relatively believable for-the-period roguelike deckbuilder. Man of the games feature surprising depth once you've sunken into them. I could easily spend double the time I already have. It's an amazing piece of work. No wonder it took so long for them to finish it!
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: (There is a TL:DR at the bottom)I've put 6.2 hours into this game at the time of this review. I've played about 18 of the games and have "beaten" two of them. This is a collection of games with secrets to find, easter eggs to discover, and so much to explore if you want to go in deep, but it is also just 50 fleshed out NES/FAMICOM style games here to play if that is what you want as well. While I do recommend the game for people to explore, I will say it has absolutely frustrated me so very much to the point that I almost wish that I could refund the game because it makes me very angry, but at the same time the games and game as a package is so passionately created that I want to see more of this caliber of game. (And I completely understand that it is a  thing, but that is why I am writing this review)My (very personal and probably  shared among other players) anger stems from this being an alternate reality 50 games from an NES/FAMICOM computer era, where we are just playing around with them. That's fine, but if I would have read that in the description of the game, I wouldn't have bought it. I don't  to figure out the nuances of the games by trial and error. I didn't want a "figure it out as you go" META-GAME I wanted what was in the description: "the experience of going to a friend's house and perusing their game library" but there are absolutely zero instructions or instruction books for these games.  You basically click on a disk to play a game...maybe the game has a cut scene that tells you a little about it, maybe the game has an options menu where you can see what the controls do. I understand that "figuring out" how to play a game can be part of the charm...but I know that it is not for me. "Exploring the collection is part of the fun!" Yes, I agree that it is part of the fun, if I have the instruction books to go along with the games.Although you can view the controls for a game before you open it, they will tell you what the controls do e.g. "+=move ; a=jump ; b=attack". But it doesn't explain all of the controls and this is where my frustration lies. As a kid, I would always read the instruction booklets before playing the game. I want to know the lore, I want to know how to play. This right here is what raises my blood pressure. I'm looking at you MOONCAT where every button is move, and also Block Koala where I've never enjoyed a block puzzle game and would like to know what's going on. Avianos looks like a Romance of the Three Kingdoms, but I boot the game and am immediately frustrated and not knowing how to play. This is how most games just throw you in. You get more explanation about the 5 out of the 50 games listed on the store page than anything that you can see in the game (at least initially...maybe that changes with options?) For some games...that is ok, but for others it is so very frustrating. Imagine trying to play PUNCHOUT on the NES without knowing that the "start" button allows for star punches or what the concept of star punches are.UFO 50 is an impressive package of individual games wrapped in a larger game-lore. I am truly impressed by Mossmouth and I want to encourage others to try the game, but to realize that instead of getting 50 new 8-bit games that you get to experience for the first time like when you were a kid...you get 50 games from an alternate universe where you will have to figure out without instructions that the game  originally would have come with.Maybe I'm too old to put the time and effort to put on my archaeology glasses and figure out these games, to then figure out the lore of the UFO 50 and the secrets of the terminal, etc. Maybe I'm just not in the right head-space and am getting frustrated too easily, but wanted to share for others that are curious about the game.TLDR: 50 Games, easter eggs galore, only basic instructions per game that doesn't tell you  you need to know and you're going to have to figure out a lot on your own with each game. Be ready to join a discord group or watch a video to figure some things out.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: A very cool collection with some excellent games in the package. There are a few that aren't good at all, but overall there is enough variety and quality to entertain.My only real disappointment, though, is the wrapper for the games.I was hoping for something along the lines of Retro Game Challenge on the DS, with lovingly made manuals and a bit more presentation. Feels a bit bare-bones on that side, and lacks charm (when really that should have been an open goal).Overall, very entertaining and very good value.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: There's something really Special about this game. it's like the 90-in-1 nes cartridges you'd find at flea markets or yard sale except not completely awful or hacked roms. It's not even 50 mini games, its just straight up 50 games that are fully fleshed out. Bushido ball, being my favorite at the moment, I haven't even played all 50 yet, not even half of that. Worth the VERY long wait. Here's hopping to a 16 Bit sequel in 2030.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: If you are like me and grew up with the NES/ (and to a lesser extent the) SNES - you absolutely need to buy this . The games are all amazing and some are very clever throwbacks, one is like a metroidvania take on the chip and dale game, I sh*it you not - the game designs are all wonderful, clever and engaging, though some i find more frustrating than others - thats half the reason I love this thing. Reminds me of playing and losing TMNT as a kid - they did a heck of a job with this thing. I have it set up on my CRT for maximum nostalgia lol
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: If you like NES/retro games, experimental indie games, and you're fine with some of these games being hard as nails this is an amazing time. Plenty of really fun couch co-op games in this collection too and games that don't try to emulate the NES difficulty as much. The games are easy to understand on the surface and have a limited amount of controls but each one managed to surprise me at least a little bit with its depth. I love the way the games in this collection play with mechanics and mashup genres. I find myself referencing at least 2-3 games when trying to put my finger on what each one is inspired by or feels like.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: What to say about this game?! It's an absolute tour de force combining retro aesthetics and retro-style games with more modern design principles. Some of the games are - in themselves - modern classics and as a package the combination of value + quality is unsurpassed. I genuinely recommend playing them one by one in order to get the full experience and only move on after you have "golded" each game
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most impressive games I've played in... well, ever.The creativity, scope, and overall quality of this collection are astounding. Many of the games are obviously inspired by other titles, but remixed in a way that makes them feel unlike anything I've played. With just over 30 hours at the time of writing this review, I have barely touched the majority of the games in UFO 50, and I like almost everything I've tried. Even the ones I've completed are tempting me to come back for more. I can see myself spending over 100 hours on this, and I'm not a completionist.There's so much here. If you have any love for retro games, I can't recommend UFO 50 highly enough.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: 28/50tl;dr Just get this game and see what games you like.Not only is this a really fun collection of 50 games of many genres, there is also a good bit of extra stuff around the collection. There are collectable gifts for giving games a good try along with gold and cherry carts for finish and 100% respectively. By the nature of the variety, don't expect to like all the games and secrets that are here. (There are tough shoot em ups here) However, all the games seem to be of quality so I promise you won't be let down by the games you do like. Well, except for one. Check below for that review, you can't miss it.Barbuta is sour in play, but if I give it more time I’m hoping to be rewarded. Though it might be more fun to share notes with peers on what you find instead of trial and error. If not, you might get tired if you don't take detailed maps. Got cherry after looking stuff up due to getting tired of combing the game for secrets.Grimstone is really fun so far. Kind of harsh, requiring some grind to get stronger, but it makes that clear and makes the strategy of grinding more in depth than you will expect. Might gold.Planet Zoldath was a game I didn't like, and yet I chose to play it and get my first gold from it. I believe that means the game is good, but not because I was having fun playing it. Bug Hunter can get real challenging, but once you figure out the key features of the game, the game get's really good. Not a favorite quite yet, but I defiantly will return to play more runs. Maybe I can get the gold then.Ninpeck was a fantastic game to gold. It was also the first game I top scored on too. It was really fun to chip away at it.Paint Chase is alright. I might come back if I feel like it, but probably not getting gold on it.Mortol is such a clever idea done fantastically. Defiantly will chip away at it more and probably get gold.Velgress is a fun rogue-like. It's a bit tough so gold is only a maybe, but I might come back to it.Devilition is satisfying. Getting a good combo put together is great. Failing to detonate some units make me sigh though. No guarantee to gold.Kick Club can be quite challenging platformer, but it was great. Will play more and maybe gold.Bushido Ballin with the gold. Might even cherry.Camouflage Is a fun puzzle game. Will gold and maybe even cherry if collectible give the cherry.Campanella is the in-lore LX system bundle game for good reason. It's tough, but super fun. It even has secrets of it own for increasing score or beating the game faster. Might gold.Goldfaria is the gold RPG we didn't know we needed. This one will take a bit, but it will be a good one to gold for sure.The Big Bell Race is super fun practice zone for Campanella flight physics. Got the gold, but will only cherry if I decide to play it again.Warptank is a great puzzle platformer that is also tough to navigate outside of the puzzles. Also has hidden secrets where you have to touch everything hoping the secrets reveal themselves. Will gold and probably cherry at the same time at my current pace.Caramel Caramel is a fine shoot-em-up with a fun mechanic. Not my kind of thing to just keep playing, but defiantly great.tl;dr👎for the secret filler,👍for the secret contents.At first, I was thinking that the Lore and Meta Secrets in the game were level 1 overall (designed be found by yourself) due to what the community has said about them. Unfortunately, with the alertness requirements worsening my game sampling (there are more games sampled than I actually played for real) and the amount of theory crafting and interpretation of said secrets, I say that they are more Level 3 overall (designed as a community game). This probably could have been better if I had started some stuff way later instead of discovering a piece way too early. Regardless, my experience became worsened by some of the filler as I am calling it. Instead of letting the secrets getting in the way of your experience, I recommend you bite the bullet and experience the key findings rather than following the threads closely to find them yourself. The fan discord has document links in the pins of #code-hunters to see the contents yourself. Trust me, it is much more fun than solving the filler stuff. Unless you find it fun to remember the past 50 games you have played instead of 5.Mini & Max was a really fun exploration game. Who knew there could be so much just in a closet to explore? Got the Gold and will likely Cherry.more reviews to come later.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: This game hits the mark perfectly.It makes you a child again, roaming through a library of good games, not knowing exactly what they are or how to play them. You just go at it and discover.Not all the games in it may be of your taste but they are all well made, with a charming retro aesthetic and often with a surprising mechanical depth.Plus they are great for both quick and long game sessions.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: I've played many game collections. This is the best one I've played. Each game in this collection is a full fledged NES style game, whether that's an arcade with 4 stages and a high score list, or an RPG with towns and turn based combat. This collection is a testament to the idea that games do not have to be complex to be fun. Every game is a modern twist on a classic genre or formula in a way that freshens the experience while still being plausibly playable on the fake game console they present.Derek Yu and friends, thank you. Thank you for pouring your souls and effort into this masterpiece of a collection.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute triumph. Both of good gaming and the concept it pitches. UFO 50 is fully in conversation in the exact way you would want it to be; it's finding those jagged edges and then really exploring them. It's not just doing 'good ones of those' but also delivering new classics; taking old and new ideas and then executing them uncannily within the bounds of the hardware and the era. Just play it!
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: Great premise, great value with 50 games included. I am a sucker for 8-bit games having grown up in this era. The games all seem interesting so far. A few are not for me at all, others seem like a cute idea that gets less interesting as you play. But even those are fun to sample. I like quite a few very much, some have some downright addictive gameplay. My only "complaint" is that of the games I've beaten, you seem to be pretty much done with them after that victory, except maybe getting some crazy perfect run high score. Some of these (like Magic Garden) I would totally come back to play for hours with an endless mode, if there was one.Other than that it seems very well put together. I'd recommend this game to anyone who liked 8-bit/16-bit gaming, or even just likes fun gameplay over graphics. Very highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: A retro pick n mix in a delightful mixture of styles and genres that also makes me very mad because it also includes basically every flavour of retro BS under the sun. I absolutely respect the audacity of its concept and it actually follows through on its vision really well on the whole, you will find plenty to like in UFO 50 no matter what kind of games you like. But also you will probably find plenty that makes you cross, both due to the sheer variety and again, because UFO 50 leans somewhat hard overall?pingolf da greatest, but also it's the worst, but actually it's the best one nope the ball bounced all the way back to the start, it's the worst one but actually it's a hole in one which means its the best one. oh i love the fifty ufo games but actually i hate the ufo fifty games but actually i love them
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible. I love the faithfulness to the experience of playing old games and the thoughtfulness of when to include more modern elements (like the deckbuilder game), the in game lore as you play through the chronological releases from ufosoft, the gift system for the garden, the graphics, everything about this is a masterpiece. An incredibly fun multiplayer game too. 10/10 and a real GOTY contender alongside Balatro, which is the highest of praise from me.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: What a massive accomplishment, and an even greater value, this game is. When we first heard 50 games, I'm sure no one expected the depth and quality that we have here. It's truly remarkable. I've only played 19 of the games so far, and I can't recall the last time I was so happy with a purchase.It's not just 50 games ranging from decent to fantastic. So many of these games are so brimming with charm and personality, that they're already carving out a place in my mind alongside full release games. I look forward to seeing speed runs of these games, and people doing guitar covers of their theme songs in their bedrooms for years to come.I keep coming back to the thought that I really look forward to whenever this game releases on the Switch, since an even greater amount of people will be able to experience its greatness, and start the conversation about it all over again.And selfishly, I hope that one day some more gems from these UFOsoft devs are uncovered. Surely these folks didn't just stop making games in the 90s after the company folded? I'm imagining a rhythm game with an off color Waldorf lookalike, or perhaps a golf themed FPS....
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played 3 of the 50 games so far and I'm already nearing 8 hours. Each game so far has been high quality. They take the limitations and design of those classics they are emulating but use clever modern design philosophies to remove the frustration that often came with them. Every thing is quick to navigate and don't feel like they're wasting your time even when the game itself is slow. You can easily hop in and out of games, they're low commitment to enjoy but easy to get sucked into and lose an hour or two discovering secrets or chasing high scores.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: Some of these games I've enjoyed so much I gladly would have bought them just by themselves for the same price. The sheer amount of gameplay you get for your money here is insane.  I've put over 20 hours into it already, and I've barely even scratched the surface of what there is on offer here. UFO 50 is easily my GOTY, and I definitely recommend it
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a love letter to 80s gaming, not just to the classics, but to the stranger, more experimental side of the decade. Every sub-game is weird, unique, not always good per se, but always interesting. It is a fascinating collection of games that doesn't let up on the surprises the whole way through. I've heard this took 8 years to make, and it's not hard to see why. Derek Yu and his team managed to create 50 games that, though sometimes similar to the classics, are all unique in their own way, none of which have been a complete dud and some of which have been surprisingly deep and fun.It's temping to try to review every individual game and criticize this collection for none of the games being as good as the best games of the 80s, but that would be missing the point. This collection evokes nostalgia for the era when you could buy a box of mystery games or bootleg floppies from a garage sale and have no idea what you were getting. There's a certain joy in delving into the unknown, never knowing what the next game will have in store for you. That joy is missing from the modern era of gaming where you can easily look up any game and know everything about it, but UFO 50 brings that sensation back in grand fashion, and I kind of love it for that.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: It has it all!Short and Sweet Arcade Games, Mind-bending Puzzle Games, great (local) Multiplayer, some really unique RPGs and even a point and click horror adventure game... loving every minute I spend playing it.Completionists will have a hell of a time with this one, however, as each game requires you to be pretty proficient at them to "clear" it. Some can be beaten in under an hour, but others will likely require much practice and strategy.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feeling about Ufo 50. Yes you get 50 games, depending on your tastes you will find a handful of stand out games that you'll come back to again and again. Many (perhaps the majority) of games are derived from obvious classic 80's and 90's sources which reduces their appeal somewhat if you're old enough to remember the originals. Yes there are twists on the classics, but the core game-play for many of these games feels a little too familiar. Coupled with this and the deliberately awful control schemes in some of the games and I'm not sure UFO 50 is worth the sticker price. There's certainly original stand outs in here, so much so you'll wish they were separate games entirely, but of the 50 games, I can only see myself playing maybe 10 of them for more than an hour or two.The presentation of the games themselves is lovely. Jaunty music, delightful retro graphics, classic title screens, great idle cycles. Ufo 50's presentation is super polished here without question.I'm aware there's a meta-game and a lot of people are enjoying that aspect, but this seems of limited life once it's fully discovered by these bold early adopters (again, a nice riff on original cartridge style games). I understand Ufo 50 is designed so the more you put into the games, you more you'll get out. It's a bold experiment in that sense, but feels to me like it could have been Ufo 20 perhaps in terms of the games included.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: Shockingly jam-packed with ideas and mechanics, with surprising takes on a bunch of Nintendo-era designs and aesthetics at every turn. I don't want to say too much, as I think a big part of what's fun is discovering each game and figuring out what its deal is. I guess I just want to echo every other review and say that this is way, way more rich and varied and fun than I had any idea it would be. Oh yeah, and the multiplayer games (that I've played so far at least) have been really fun as co-op adventures, party games, and ones that you can play competitively.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: unbelievable value for an unbelievable collection of extremely high effort, in depth games. this isn't some action 52 collection of churned out slop. each and every game is thought out, fully developed and carefully crafted with unique gameplay mechanics and assets, all of which are wrapped up and beautifully presented as a historical archive of a fictional console with bits of additional lore.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: I have only beaten 6 out of the 50 games in the collection and I feel confident the rest of the games will be of an equal or greater level of quality. It's truly a work of art; an homage to retro games of the past with modern design ideas, but the same crispy graphics, simple sounds, and unbelievable levels of replayability and endless amounts of discovery
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: Solid game for retro enthusiasts but don't get too hung up on cherries or even beating some games.Its made with gamemaker and magical garden drops inputs for example. Be prepared to double tap every important input. Some games are better than others, don't recall having this issue with mooncat.If you like retro games, you'll love it, otherwise skip.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: Growing up, I didn't have many video games. Our household only had an NES that my dad bought on clearance sometime after the release of the SNES. Even as some of my friends started to own N64s and Playstations, we still had just that NES and about 3 games. Then, one day, one of our neighbors cleaned out their attic and found a box full of their old NES games. They had gotten rid of their NES years ago, and knew we still had one, so they gave us the whole box full of games. Suddenly, I had dozens of new games to play. None of them had their manuals or boxes, but I didn't care. I happily loaded up one game after another, learning little bits about each game, figuring out how to get a little further each time. It was one of my happiest memories related to gaming.UFO 50 immediately took me back to that memory. Playing this game, I feel like that little 7-year-old boy with that box full of NES games again. Playing through this collection is an absolute joy and I would have happily bought more that half of these games on their own. But having them together along with the meta narrative of the fictional UFOsoft just puts this game on a whole other level, and dare I say, makes it a masterpiece. UFO 50 might not click with everyone, but for those it does click with, it's something very special.

_childDocuments_.review: UFO 50 is a collection of 50 retro-style indie games, charmingly presented as the "all-in-one" digital collection of a fictional software company's game catalogue.Buying this game and booting it up for the first time is like getting your hands on a huge toybox as a kid. I have never felt such gluttonous, childish joy with a video game before playing UFO 50. Every game is unique, a wonderful balance between 80s and modern game design, feeling fresh while maintaining that retro feel. Don't like a game? Just leave and boot up a different one; you can switch games at any time in literally 2 seconds and as few as 6 button presses (start>up>A>A>up>A). There are turn based strategy games, arcade platformers, shmups, puzzlers, adventure platformers, you name it. Many games are short, a few are long, but nearly all have enough depth to demand at the very minimum an hour of play to master. I personally guarantee there is something (very likely many things) in this pack that you will enjoy. It made me feel like a kid again.Nintendo kid? Sega kid? Nah, I was a UFO Soft kid.

_childDocuments_.review: In college I tried playing through nearly every single NES game ever released as a fun endeavor between classes. While I didn't make my way through the entire catalog (stopping around the "N"s), the late nights of difficult platforming, old-school story-telling, and crisp chiptunes are ones I'll always cherish. UFO 50 is all those glorious memories sweeping back to me in a rush, with no dumb-ass bad games to get in the way. I think the keyword of the collection is "restraint". Sure, modern game development lets you do a LOT, but that's not what UFO is about. There is a certain considered quaintness, an intentional minimalism to the modern sensibilities of today. Mooncat has some of my favorite examples; a super minimal soundtrack and clever sprite techniques all make you feel like the developer was trying desperately to save memory. UFO 50 is special. It's the collaboration of some of the greatest artists in the game development world of today. I don't think I'm being even slightly pretentious to compare this to a hypothetical collaboration of Mozart and Tchaikovsky, a painting rendered by both Van Gogh and Delacroix. Don't miss this.

A game that is itself 50 other fully featured games, spanning all kinds of genres, and all of them made with so much care and respect for the era that they are pulled from, and for the entire medium of games on the whole.I've played 12 hours so far and only touched the first 10 games, not finished any of them yet but getting close with Mortol (Banger game btw). _childDocuments_.review: UFO 50 is nothing short of revolutionary within the category of retro-style new games. I'd like to use this space to consider the feat of this accomplishment by Mossmouth by way of comparison, to another collection of retro-style new(er) games: the much heralded Shovel Knight series by Yacht Club Games. Shovel Knight deservedly received much critical acclaim on first release a decade ago for bringing back the essence of retro games at their best while doing one better by bringing everything learned about good game design into a very satisfying package. They went on to expand the Shovel Knight universe with several other offshoot platformers which also received acclaim, and eventually released 4 or 5 offshoots in entirely new genres: puzzle, fighting etc. But compare Yacht Club Games offering -- 10 or so games, half of which are platformers -- released over a period of a decade -- to UFO 50: one single amazing collection of 50 fully-fledged *fun* games spanning a ton of genres while adding completely new innovations and ideas. Then realize that UFO 50 also created a whole lore and "alternate reality" 1980s in which a game development company grew and matured along with their games over a ~10 year period. It makes Yacht Club Games look like child's play. It puts YCG, and similar developers on notice: UFO 50 is the new reality of the competition. UFO 50 is the new standard bearer. UFO 50 is revolutionary because it becomes clear playing it that *this* is the new gold standard if you want to make the best retro-style new games. YCF can release Mina the Hollower and it may be a great, expansive action-adventure game. But it is still just one action-adventure game. You're still just controlling one character, in one way. I don't know how many styles of game play the game may ultimately have, and many "mini-games" may be included, but again, but it clearly isn't presenting itself anyway close in terms of gameplay variety and depth to UFO 50. Don't get me wrong - I love Shovel Knight and the series. But there is a new king of retro-style games. It is here folks. UFO 50. Nothing will ever be the same.

Some of the games will show a brief demo if you leave them hanging on the start menu.-- A few of the more approachable games, in my experience, are Party House (elegantly designed push-your-luck deckbuilder), Campanella 2 (roguelike where you swap between flying a spacecraft and on-foot sections), Pingolf (side-view arcade golf game) and Valbrace (first-person dungeon crawler with twitchy real-time combat)

_childDocuments_.review: Having hotly anticipated its release since it was first announced seven years ago, I think I would've been predisposed to recommend  just based on its premise and ambition alone. After all, a collection of fifty () faux-retro games centred around the fictitious narrative of their heretofore unknown developer is exactly the kind of high concept to kick my nerdy, retro-loving brain into overdrive.But as far as writing a Steam review goes, how do you talk about one game that's actually fifty games? You might be tempted to go over each and every morsel in brief, but to do so could end up devaluing the whole by robbing someone of the satisfaction of simply discovering what's inside. This collection lives precisely because its many parts, fun as they are, would have less impact presented individually -- the essence of what  aims to capture in its gonzo display of game design bravura and old-school visual style is in how what's on offer can be  and not merely . is a maximalist celebration of those small sparks of inspired ludological craft. It is unmistakably nostalgic for a time when mainstream games weren't so afraid to embrace absurd concepts, when consoles were mediums defined more by their unique limitations rather than raw processing power, and when a lack of ubiquitous Internet access made experiencing games more inscrutable and gave them a greater mystique for it. Many of its games are over fairly quickly, but they beg to be savoured slowly and often their sheer difficulty will ensure it. And although the collection's ethos is firmly rooted in the retrograde, its design philosophy fortunately isn't, feeling free to apply modern hindsight and slyly employ genre anachronism for the sake of a smoother or more unconventional user experience. Even when a game is maddeningly frustrating (looking at , Barbuta), it was clearly done with an eye for period authenticity and strengthens the notion that the human chops powering these games improved and evolved new ideas over time.The joy of  isn't just getting to see six indie professionals flex their creative muscles across fifty weird and wonderful games -- it's just as much about the incredibly geeky pleasure that comes from digesting gaming history as you forge your own path through its matter.And that's without even getting into .If all this sounds exciting to you, then dive on in. You really can't go wrong for the price. Enjoy the selection at your own pace. Find what you like and what you don't like. If something doesn't strike you right away, put it down and see how you feel about it later. There's no guarantee that every game here will appeal to everyone, but (as another reviewer put it so nicely) fifty games is still fifty chances to fall in love.

_childDocuments_.review: (Updated after achieving 100% completion: All 50 Gold and Cherry Disks)UFO 50 really is a package with something for everyone, especially anybody with an interest in game design or a love for old school titles (I'm both of these markets). Nearly every game offers a unique idea or a spin on a pre-existing genre and genuinely puts the modern game development scene to shame in so many instances with its well-executed ideas.Games like Warptank being a spin on Blaster Master's tank controls with gravity flips or games like Mooncat having one of the most interesting control schemes I've ever seen, there's a new idea in every experience for better or worse and I loved every minute of it.Eirik's music is also yet again nothing but bangers, but this should be expected if you're familiar with his work. The limitation of a 32-color palette across also games also lends itself insanely well to really creative color and stage design choices, its always vibrant but never eye-piercing. The only major negative I could give this game is entirely related to the type of person that may tackle it, like Spelunky/Spelunky 2 this is a game with three base levels of what someone could consider "completing a game" which are...Completing a minor objective in a game gives players an item for their virtual garden, often unlocked around midway through a game or trying out a specific mode. Completing the base game gives you a Gold Disk and if a player is really to they can go for a Cherry Disk, which is usually a difficult challenge or bonus objective to complete. Many people may get frustrated if they go for all completions in order as many of these games are old-school levels of hard, but that's the beauty of a 50-in-1 collection... you gotta figure out what methods or pace work best for you.But overall? This is an insanely polished project 8 or so years in the making, you can really tell how much heart went into every single one of these titles, especially alongside the meta-narrative story about game design and the people involved in the process of game-making as a whole.

_childDocuments_.review: UFO 50 is not a simple lament of a past gone by. It's a celebration of creativity. Framed in its own fiction as an official all-in-one cartridge from a lost and forgotten contender of the 8-bit era, UFO 50 lovingly recreates the era that is in many ways radically different from our current one. On the surface, the games are simple, as you only control a D-Pad and A and B buttons. However, learning how to play this game is harder than most contemporary games, as the gameplay mechanics are not taught to you. You’ll have to experiment to get the hang of each game. Barbuta is a great and brutal example of this: you can move and jump, but you do so slowly, and when you move to the right in the first screen, you immediately die.UFO 50 isn’t contended however to slavishly celebrate the old ways. There are of course the necessary “tweaks” to let these games play like you remember 8-bit games then rather than how those games actually were. For example, the games do not suffer from slowdown and sprite flickering: a game like Rock On! Island might’ve never happened on the NES with the amount of enemies it throws on you. But there are also other “inaccuracies”. The “sound chip” isn’t strict chiptunes but also includes synthesisers, something you didn’t hear on NES except on expensive Japanese exclusives. Your viewport is widescreen, which in many cases gives you a larger field of view than the 4:3 of yore; Sunset Drive plays with this heavily, as it’s about drifting across the width of the screen in order to gain firing power. Even in game design, UFO 50 is not afraid to be anachronistic. Party House is a deck builder even though the genre didn’t exist in the 1980s. Pilot Quest uses an in-game clock for its idle mechanics when The Legend of Zelda was already radical back then for giving you save files. It’s this combination of both familiar, nostalgic ground as well as fresh twists that makes UFO 50 unique.This experimentation is greatly helped by the other stand out, namesake feature of UFO 50: 50 games in one package. It’s a miracle that all these games are as good as there are (and even the ones which aren’t are deliberately constructed that way to explain the meta-fiction), and fully featured as they are. Granted, most of them are a lot smaller than what many gamers now expect. It would be silly of course to expect a 100 hours open world RPG amongst these games, but sometimes on a small game like Magic Garden or Big Bell Race, I wish there was more meat on its bones. However, the sum is definitely more than its parts. You are encouraged to mix and match games, play the ones you like and quickly skip the ones you don’t, and the short play time makes mastery of even a few games a realistic prospect: I played this game for about 50 hours (pun intended), and in that time I’ve beaten 10 games and completed 5. I can’t say the same for Tears of the Kingdom. The variety of games on offer means there’s something here for everyone: your top 5 games (and bottom 5) will radically differ from mine.UFO 50 would’ve been a way lesser game if all these games were just straight copycats of past glories. In fact, the hidden meta-game pokes fun at the impulse to prioritise the old over the new, with the foolish head of the company creating the UFO 50 in the first place as a time capsule in order to establish their legacy, to the point of even shelving some of the games in production like a more extreme case of Star Fox 2. UFO 50 reminds us that nostalgia is not, and should not be, inherently conservative. We don’t have to regret that the past is gone, nor do we have to preserve it untouched to the point of calcification.

_childDocuments_.review: Still cannot believe that we have been blessed with this tremendous achievement of a video game. If you are a sucker for cool game design ideas - get this immediately! all 50 games are unique and made with a philosophy where you don't have to go over lengthy tutorials, but learn while playing and discovering the mechanics in the process while playing.Those who have a huge backlog of games that stresses them out - get UFO 50! It is essentially a gamified backlog simulator that would give you a very tight and achievable experience of discovering a collection. In UFO 50 you'll have the games that you love and games that you hate, some that would appear too hard that you overcome, and some that you will beat easily, some that you'll try once and never touch again and some that you'll come back to make them your favorites.It might take a few games to get into the collection (first game, Barbuta is intentionally janky, feel free to skip it!), but once it clicks it clicks, and you will sunk hours into digging deeper and deeper and deeper into the collection. As for the actual games: I love Red Dead Redemption, but it kinda lacks compared to how Rail Heist simulates the slapstick bar fight from an old comedy western movie with cowboy sprites that have only like 10 pixels. Moon Cat is a 2D platformer with controls made like it is the first 2D platformer of its kind, completely ignoring all the genre established practices, like 40 years of Mario games didn't happen There's a lot of games that try to be bite-sized 4X strategy, but very few come close to Avianos, achieving the strategic depth with all info fit to one 384x216 pixel screen and NES two button gamepad controls.I can go on and on there, and can also name a bunch of games that I think are meh (pretty convinced that Golfaria's only reason to exist is for Derek to sound catchy in the interviews, wow, we made a Zelda where you are a golf ball, such creativity), but as I already said it is a part of the experience to discover the games and make your own opinions, and then question them and change themSo don't hesitate trying out UFO 50, which is the best game of this year, and the approach it is made with is also so hard to replicate that its central idea won't likely ever be repeated in our lifetime. An instant cult classic (better jump on our hype train now while the cult is still young)

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like the equivalent of a very successful gamejam with tons of entries and high profile developers. Except the twist is the top 50 entries were funded and fleshed out into full games. I've played about 10 hours and finished roughly 5 games (in chronological order, so from my understanding the remaining games get better and more intricate in line with developers becoming better at using the fake console's tech). This game is the antithesis of the AAA bloat problem that has been plaguing the industry for years. It's ironic that it has 50 full games - so a ludicrous amount of content too - but the package never compromises on identity by throwing the kitchen sink at the player and drowning them in time sink garbage. Each game serves up one core idea, and iterates on it until the developers feel like it's done. Some games are simple, some are as complex as major releases from the NES era (and even beyond). Keeping the game's overall constraints as being retro in vision but allowing for modern game ideas to flourish has also created an almost alternative timeline where pixelation is celebrated over graphic fidelity. This game feels like a booster shot to the industry, to be frank. A reminder of what games were, and why we liked them back then. As well as what games can be, and how stripping away the unnecessary auxiliary elements can reveal the passionate beating heart of games that are fun because the developers want you to have fun.TLDR: 50 cents per game and they are just, like, good *** retro style games. If you are a millennial that grew up with Atari and an NES, complaining online about "the good old days of gaming" - and you DON'T buy this - turn in your card.

_childDocuments_.review: UFO 50 is a compilation of 50 games created by the devs behind Spelunkey, Downwell, and Skorpulac among others. It's set in the fictional gaming system LX-III, a console which takes inspiration from 1980s consoles and personal computers, such as the MSX and NES. These are games that vary in scope and size, but act as solitary experiences. Some are very long, taking as long as 20 hours to beat. Each game is retro-inspired but have their own unique twist that makes each one standalone. Genres are all over the place, from platformers to puzzles to full-blown strategy and even a JRPG ala Deltarune. It's a huge labor of love that took over 7 years to finish, with tons of secrets and unlockable achievement-style rewards to keep players coming back.NO. Right from the start, you have EVERY game, as well as a quick and easy way to categorize by genre, multiplayer, and amount of time played. You don't even have to play them in order: just play whichever one you want. However, I recommend starting with Pilot Quest as soon as possible. You can read why in my short recommended games list below.Having played them all, I would say that a vast majority of them are extremely solid. Some are difficult or have odd design quirks, but for the most part it is an extremely solid list of games. There's just hit after hit, and I'm personally so excited for it that I would consider the compilation itself a solid contender for Game of the Year.The games that might not be a hit for you could be the following, which other players complained about. Doesn't mean they're bad perse, just that there's mixed opinions on them:- BARBUTA: This is an adventure game inspired by games like Citadel for the BBC Micro. Personally, it reminds me more of Spider-Man for DOS. A very simple but very slow game where you are a knight hatched from an egg attempting to explore the castle and defeat the boss. It's purposefully designed with cheap one-hit deaths, but a ton of room to find plenty of secrets the more you're willing to be patient explore. It is the most retro of retro out of every game on the list, and is the first on the list chronologically. Maybe it sets a bad taste in your mouth, maybe it doesn't, but whatever you're feeling is very much intentional.- MOONCAT: As praised as it is hated, this is an obtuse platformer where you play as a literal bean with legs and traverse to the end while avoiding obstacles. Seems straightforward, except the game uses only two buttons for every action, including movement. That means the D-pad acts as one button while the buttons on your right thumb (A, B, etc) act as the second button. The way your character controls is odd, but very clever, and I won't spoil it for you. It's an unexpected treat to play this game, and I'd say give it a proper chance before you judge it too harshly.- COMBATANTS: Definitely the most hated on the list. This is a simple RTS game similar to Pikmin where you are a blue ant building an army to destroy the red ants before they destroy you. As simple as it sounds, it's very slow, and the AI is pretty obtuse. It's also very hard, as the red ants deal more damage and take more hits to kill. It takes a lot of patience to play this game, and it's probably not for you if you're like me and get frustrated easily.It was hard to narrow it down to just a few, but here's some games you might really enjoy:- PILOT QUEST: An idle/adventure game where you're a space pilot who crash-landed on an alien planet, now on a mission to find the parts to your spaceship. A mix of Legend of Zelda 1 and Cookie Clicker, you're able to collect resources automatically, even when you switch to another game. Once in a while, you're able to spend limited resources to go out into the wild and explore, but make sure you return before the time runs out or you won't collect what you've earned. Dungeon and item locations are also randomized, so it makes for a slightly different experience each time you play. A super addicting game, and highly recommend starting this one ASAP so you don't miss out on resources.- PARTY HOUSE: The fan-favorite. This is very similar to a random card draw game where you're the host of a happenin' 80s party, and you invite guests over by clicking on the front door, which brings in a random guest from your Rolodex guest list. End the party with tons of guests and cash in Popularity resources to expand your guest list. Make your house bigger with Cash to invite more guests at one party. However, some guests can be trouble: have 3 or more people who cause trouble, and someone calls the police, ending the round early. The game ends when you invite four Star Guests, such as aliens, dinosaurs, and mermaids, all with different abilities. It's super original, easy to get into, and a blast to play with friends. This is definitely a must-play if you purchase this game.- MIN & MAX: One of the longest games on the list. This is a huge Metroidvania game in the style of Super Mario Bros. 2 meets Alice in Wonderland. Play as a little girl named Min as you shrink down in size and explore the vast world of the Closet, making friends with all sorts of little things like bugs, toys, and dust bunnies. Later on, a whole other world begins to open up, making what seems to be an 8-hour game into a 20-hour exploration game. Tons of people to meet to help with their problems, as well as new abilities to float, store items, and command enemies. Not to mention it's extremely adorable and great for kids. If you've got the time, this is a very fun and satisfying experience.- AVIANOS: A very simplistic turn-based strategy game in which you manage bird soldiers to capture and hold castles. Pray to different deities for different actions, and build up your army to rush the enemy castle. Attacks are done on-screen in a semi-automatic way with a few minor control options at the bottom to give outnumbered soldiers a fighting chance. Even if you can learn all the rules fairly quickly, the depth of this game is surprisingly pretty vast as there are tons of ways you can take the game. The story mode is unfortunately very short (3 levels), but there are many trials afterward if you want to put your skills to the test. There's also 2 player versus with a lot of home rules to mess with in the options setting.Keep in mind that there are tons of other games that fit into many more genres. I've only mentioned 7, and there's 43 other games on this list. Try them all out!This is an amazing lineup of games for all players. Even if this game is retro-inspired at heart, there are still a ton of clever modern mechanics that they use to keep a lot of games from being too frustrating. Half of the games are two-player, and is highly recommended for Steam Deck. If any of this sounds interesting, this is a must-buy, even at full price. You'll get more than your money's worth out of the amount of hours you'll be spending.

_childDocuments_.review: This is almost certainly my game of the year. Stats:* 170 hours or so* 48 games tried* 26 games completed (13 gold 13 cherry)It should be clear from my hours that it takes a lot of time to get a full taste of all the games in this collection. If you're browsing reviews, maybe steer clear of any review that doesn't have 10, 15 hours. This is just one of those games where the refund window is not enough time to know if it's for you. There's so much variety and creativity among the games that it's hard to write a single recommendation, but...here goes.Here's some people I think will really like this collection:* Speedrunners, challenge runners, and arcade score-chasers who want a bunch of fresh challenges to pick from* Anyone with 1-2 specific genre interests who is also interested to try new things* Those with nostalgia for 80s and 90s games* Game design enthusiasts looking for inspiration or just something new to nerd out over* Meta lore enjoyers who are looking for an experience full of secrets* Anyone with a friend who also loves retro gamesAlso, keep in mind that UFO 50 is very low commitment if you think you're interested! I am confident that anyone who's interested will find 5-10 games that really appeal to them, and those games alone will be worth the price. And while games themselves are full games, they're more bite-sized, so people with less time on their hands don't have to worry like they would committing to, like, a full JRPG or even the average Ubisoft game these days.Here's some reasons I think someone might not like this collection:* They aren't satisfied by games that take 2-5 hours to complete* They want complex stories in their games* They dislike difficult and/or punishing gamesThe biggest reason people will bounce off of this collection is probably the way these games reflect their inspirations. Like the classics, a lot of these games are hard, punishing, confusing, or awkward, and there's little to no handholding. There's a lot that borrow from the arcade style, where after taking a few hits you go all the way back to the start of the game. The "Controls" tab in the menu helps with some of the confusing games, but unless you're willing to sometimes treat the learning process as part of the fun, many games may leave you frustrated. A decent amount of games in the collection are forgiving, straightforward, or very tight to play, but overall the collection has more intentional rough edges than the typical modern game.I, however, love this design philosophy. In almost every case, my struggles with difficult games paid off with satisfying wins, and my confusions with games turned into rewarding moments of realization. Where classic video games were often challenging because they were poorly balanced, or mysterious because they didn't teach vital mechanics, these games have felt challenging because of their carefully crafted difficulty curves, and mysterious because they had me learn by experimenting in situations designed to teach me. Plus, the games are not too big -- games that feel too difficult don't last too long, and games where you get lost have a small number of points of interest so you find your way easier. UFO 50 takes from classic games an increased amount of friction and a decreased scope. This way, it packs more dynamic, intense experiences into smaller games. It's unusual compared to modern games, and I really appreciate the difference.Some of my favorite games are:* Barbuta, an unwieldy, secretive nonlinear platformer seemingly inspired by Maze of Galious* Bushido Ball, a 1v1 tennis-like game where each character has a unique secondary and super-move* Vainger, a Metroid clone with gravity-flipping mechanics* Mooncat, a secretive platformer using only two buttons* Rail Heist, which consists of sixteen levels of trains to rob that are guarded very creatively* Porgy, a nonlinear underwater exploration game* Valbrace, a classic dungeon crawler with combat reminiscent of Punch Out* Campanella 2, Mossmouth's new take on a 2D platformer roguelike, in a UFOThis list -- probably even just half of it -- makes the collection worth it on its own. But there's 40 other games I got to try and enjoy! There's a few I bounced off of and haven't played much at all (e.g. Divers & Rakshasa), a few that grew on me (e.g. Magic Garden & Pingolf), a few that I loved at first but mellowed on over time (e.g. Bug Hunter & Camouflage), and a few I just don't really enjoy (e.g. Devilition & Combatants). But I have things to say about all of them! And that's without mentioning all the secrets hidden among the games.

_childDocuments_.review: As a child of the early 2000s, I cut my teeth on games from the sixth and early seventh console generations.  One game in particular that I spent many hours on was Midway Arcade Treasures, a compilation disc of arcade hits from the 80s and very early 90s.  I didn't care at all that the games looked rather rudimentary compared to the other, more modern games I had.  I was quite happy with the variety of simple games I could cycle between and play to my heart's content.  I've always been quite fond of similar compilations; the best ones offer a ton of value for modern gamers and grant old classics and hidden gems alike a new life on contemporary hardware.UFO 50 has all the trappings of games like that.  Here are 50 games from the 80s, packaged together and running flawlessly on modern computers.  The big catch, of course, is that the games here are completely original, made by a sextet of talented indie developers over the past several years.  These games have one foot in the past; a limited color palette and highly simple controls, and one foot in the modern era, presented in glorious 16:9, no slowdown or glitching, and (your mileage may vary) ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-free game design.  Sure, very few who play UFO 50 will adore every single game.  A lot of titles here, especially the "earlier" ones, can be pretty obtuse and hard to figure out at first.  However, there's enough brilliance and fun at the heart of this collection that just about everyone can find something here to enjoy and return to.  For anyone who's had enough of the always-online, microtransaction-infested, games-as-a-service cruft that pervades today's biggest titles, UFO 50 is a fantastic alternative that respects your time, your curiosity, and your wallet.

_childDocuments_.review: BUY THIS NOW. This is a collection of games, an alternate history, a school in retro game design, a school in modern game design, a loving homage, and an unbelievably amazing collection of truly interesting retrogames. As a collection, it's astounding. As a WORK, it's a monumental accomplishment.  It succeeds in telling the story of LX System/UFOSoft through the medium of games.  When it's an early game, it SHOULD be clunky and slow-ish, and it IS. If it is a later game, it shows polish, learning, gamedev maturity.The art is appropriate and fantastic, the mythos is wonderful, and the games are exactly what you'd expect from a retrospective of a prolific 80s game company. Variety, because people were just trying out stuff. Nuttiness, because the rules weren't written yet, and you had to stand out... AND they were made by individuals/small teams back then.One thing about revisiting old computer games: often the memories are better than the game was.UFO 50 is like a collection of those games, but the way you lovingly remember them. They WERE that good! See?!?So get this game collection -- and marvel all the love and care this project is made with. Enjoy exploring at your leisure, like we used to. Try stuff.  It's like getting to really be back in the 80s and going down to the computer shop. Everything was an adventure. Everything was kinda amazing. Even if it wasn't, it was -- because it was NEW. Different. Magic happening on your screen.Get it, play the games, because no one is likely to go to the effort of capturing that feeling again. This is pure retro-gaming nostalgic joy. The undiluted elixir of playing early games in the 80s.

_childDocuments_.review: When I looked at this game I was concerned that the high amount of games would mean it would be a  quantity over quality situation. I bought it anyway-reviews were good and it was from the creator of spelunky. Unfortunately the developers didn't seem to make this game because they had 50 great game ideas. They came up with the gimmick first to exploit nostalgia then came up with the games after, filling it with shovelware.Take Ninpek for example. It's a simple scrolling platformer. You can jump and fire a projectile, and of course you die in one hit. That's it-no mechanics or gimmicks. That's the whole game. The collection is filled with crap like this. The excuse from defenders of this game is it's supposed to be like this because it's inspired by their boomer consoles. That doesn't make these games any more fun.While there is a ton a games here covering many genres, they are so shallow there is no reason to play them over dedicated alternatives.There is a JRPG here-but why play it over dedicated games like Sea of Stars/Chained echoes etc?Why play the crappy beat 'em up over Streets of Rage 4?Why play the Metroid clone over the many, better games in this genre on Steam?Why play the crappy platformers over the hundreds of better games on Steam?There are a few good ideas here, but you have to dig through the garbage to find them. Even then, the good games feel undercooked-but I guess that's what happens when you have to meet an arbitrary target of 50 games.If you're an aging millennial 'retro gamer' who is obsessed with collecting boomer consoles and nostalgic about shovelware you will probably love this game. If you are not a part of this group, and just want to play good games, stay away.

_childDocuments_.review: It is incredibly generous that this is only $25. There is a humbling wealth of game design mastery at work here.UPDATE (31 hours): By now, after many more hours, the "sampler platter" phase has dropped off and I've begun to dig into games knowing what I prefer and what I don't. I miss the feeling of taking a chance on a random game and consistently being pleasantly surprised (although truth be told, there are still games I've logged just a few minutes in), and as such I highly recommend going into UFO 50 blind, with perhaps the understanding that Barbuta is an intentional outlier among the 50 games, and some players may find it helpful to start Pilot Quest early. Most games won't give you an explicit tutorial, but figuring out how each game works is extremely rewarding - each game *demands* your engagement and rewards you proportionally. 31 hours in, and I'm nowhere near finished gilding/cherrying everything I want to, and I've barely touched the Terminal. _childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a retro experience similar to that of most NES games, UFO 50 may disappoint you. Its main inspiration mainly comes from the games conceived in the 80s for microcomputers like the MSX, C64 and ZX81; where genres, conventions and standards for controls were still not set, and every company in the business was experimenting, exploring the systems and shaping the rules of gaming itself.People who grew up in a different age and context need a very open mindset to appreciate what UFO 50 has to offer, even with all its concessions to modern sensibilities. For someone like me, who grew up with a C64 and played copied games with no manual or instructions, UFO 50 is a delightful callback - I found myself drawing game maps on paper, and fiddling with odd controls with a smile on my face.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: Ludicrous value. There are several games in this pack that are arguably worth $25 individually. It's a glorious smorgasbord of unique experiences, every one presenting a fresh take on mechanisms both new and old. Some games feel like they really are lost relics of the golden age of arcade games, while others might take inspiration from a more modern design trend or mechanism, but still present an interesting deconstruction of it in a consistent retro aesthetic.There's enough quality content here to keep you busy for months, spanning just about any genre you can imagine. Even though some of the games might not be for you, there's something here for everyone. It's great on PC, but this might be the best Steam Deck title of all time, effectively giving you a full arcade at your fingertips.

_childDocuments_.review: In many ways, the work of a critic is easy. We risk very little, yet enjoy a position over those who offer up their work and their selves to our judgment. We thrive on negative criticism, which is fun to write and to read. But the bitter truth we critics must face, is that in the grand scheme of things, the average piece of junk is probably more meaningful than our criticism designating it so. But there are times when a critic truly risks something, and that is in the discovery and defense of the *new*. The world is often unkind to new talent, new creations. The new needs friends. Last night, I experienced something new: an extraordinary game from a singularly unexpected source. To say that both the game and its maker have challenged my preconceptions about fine gaming is a gross understatement. They have rocked me to my core. In the past, I have made no secret of my disdain for Mossmouth's famous motto, "50 games in 1." But I realize, only now do I truly understand what he meant. Not everyone can become a great game studio; but a great game studio *can* come from *anywhere*. It is difficult to imagine more humble origins than those of the geniuses now coding at Mossmouth, who are, in this critic's opinion, nothing less than the finest game designers in America. I will be returning to Mossmouth's soon, hungry for more.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited to write this review until after trying all 50 games contained in the title. wants you to have that experience of finding and playing one of those unlicensed multicarts for a bygone console, and it succeeds in doing so. The thing about those carts is that they're garbagey and released into the market to make a quick buck. From rip-offs of other, more fun games to total WTF finds, the only life those carts might have years later is in the novelty that such a thing exists.  totally has this going on yet I don't think this was the developers' intentions.There's possibly the gamble that, with 50 games on tap spanning multiple genres, everyone is going to find at least one that they will enjoy. I didn't have fun with any of them. Even with the ones that should have hooked me, I found boredom settling in quickly and no real interest in swinging back around to revisit them later.The game knock presentation out of the park, but it's as if too much focus was placed on the audiovisual experience and the "lore" instead of polishing the games to be approachable and a good time. There's a thread of continuity across the games that I thought was clever but, again, it's all filler.Too challenging for casual gamers. Too slow for challenge hounds. To be fair, and unlike unlicensed multicarts, none of the games here are unfinished or felt like they had been slapped together in haste.If I had to choose one of its games to highlight, it'd probably be  but you have to be really, really into tabletop dexterity games and pray regularly to RNGesus. Some people call out  (which is charming but tedious) or  (too difficult for what it intends to be) as hidden gems and I can understand how they've come to those choices. If only they were fun to play!Is it just me or does anyone else hear sampling from  in ?
