_childDocuments_.review: I've seen the 50 hour review trend so I will hop on the wagon. In short, I  this game. After a little over 50 hours of UFO 50 I can say this may be the game of the year. The sheer amount of depth, difficulty, and craftsmanship that is in this game will astound anyone that touches it.In a time in gaming history where the mainstream is laden with remakes, reboots, and re-whatevers, creativity feels like it has been abandoned by game companies in the pursuit of the $70 AAA game that went over well in focus groups. And it is arduous to shift through all these copycats that observe the success of small developers and pump out their copy in a matter of months. UFO 50 is a nostalgic homage to retro gaming that makes you wonder what companies that spend millions of dollars making games  do with their time. This is as good as "Nostalgia Bait" gets. Unlike some larger game companies that constantly sell us reiterations of the same game with nostalgia baiting as their main marketing strategy, UFO 50 does this in a rather unique way: Creating 50 completely original retro games that don't rely on an existing IP to carry it! Additionally, they have created their own lore for the mythical UFOSOFT company and LX system, so you can unravel the mysteries and history as another objective if you'd like. As a popular streamer put it, "The best compliment I can pay this game is that I wish I had it as a child." I concur.It is incredibly hard to pick out my favorites among all 50 of these games, some of them I haven't played enough to really offer an opinion on, but I will tell you my current top 5, in not particular order, after 50 hours.Quibble Race is insane, my partner and I were yelling at the screen, mashing buttons that do nothing, and betting unreasonably as bankruptcy loomed after a lost race. I haven't paid enough attention to tell whether the stats are random every time or not, but this should be case. Mossmouth pls make quibble stats random every time thx :)As a strategy guy this is one that I naturally gravitated towards and "Cherry'd" as soon as I could. The whole loop is rewarding yet crushing if you do not plan properly. In the end, I really enjoyed slowly crushing my enemy and leaving them alive as I took each tile one by one but leaving a single flag short as to not win the game. Then having my hoard of owls, drones, and birds take their final square with a single solider defending it. Quite poetic. Incredibly fun, I strongly recommend this one. Another strategy game that will have you wondering what exactly is happening for the first couple minutes you're playing it. Once it clicks for you though it becomes a matter of buying hippies, dogs, and Unicorns. Getting the Cherry Disk on this one is probably one of the more difficult ones to do in the entire game because of how luck based it is. Or you're just bad at the game. All the deckbuilder Andys out there will love this.  Another one I strongly recommend!Can you tell what kind of gamer I am yet?  strategy game. Unlike this others though, this is real time and will have you mashing either your stick or dpad to move around your units to capture their base. This one was pretty easy but I imagine has great replay value with friends. Pretty easy to Cherry Disk I'd say.MOONCAT is one of the most interesting games in the bunch. I can't remember a game I've played with a control scheme like this. The fact that there are people creating controller layouts to "fix" MOONCAT is ironic and I need to put a mirror in their face. This could be the most political game in UFO 50 and I'm here for it. Rise up MOONCAT enjoyers, do not let Pilot Quest Time Wasters steal your pride!No matter what type of game you're into, as long as you have love for retro in your heart there's something here for you. I see many future hours being put into UFO 50 and, hopefully, more Cherry Disks. If you're disillusioned by the mainstream and need a retreat to a game that feels far away but has modern sensibilities, UFO 50 is for you. I played Spelunky when I was younger so it's cool MOSSMOUTH is doing something different now. Check it out!

_childDocuments_.review: [pre-emptive review]I'd seen some videos and a few tweets about the game before its release, though I'd never heard about it until then, nor did I know about who actually went and made it. I did actually try to go for a refund because of just how wary I was about the price of it and what I'd be getting out of it going in, but now that I've sat down and played it for a while longer, I can say that it's a worthwhile addition to anyone's collection if even a few of the games included are appealing.Yes, there IS a "side game" or "meta game" as you may quickly find out, but it is NOT the main focus of the collection, and it isn't required at all for completion. This isn't some ARG horror tripe with some tired old twist, it's an honest, straight up collection of 50 retro styled games, nothing more, nothing less. Do NOT buy this if you're expecting something like that. Think of it as a nice bonus and a hidden 51st game.Go in without a guide. Figure everything out for yourself. The only one I've played so far that's really and truly obtuse (and it's on purpose) is Barbuta, and it's a shame that it's the very first game you encounter in the collection, because it sets a bad precedent for the others unless it scratches that VERY particular itch for you. If you can push past that, then you'll probably have a good time with it.

_childDocuments_.review: The knee jerk reaction upon seeing this is to compare it to the infamous Action 52 on the Nintendo back in the day, but the games in this compilation are all amazing. It's a love letter to old school gaming while also showing just what new indie games could be bringing to the market. With little hidden easter eggs and secrets all through out.several of the games alone are almost worth the price of admission by themselves, most likely party house, mortol 1 and 2, and mini and max. Though there are a couple of games that I feel could have been replaced, puzzle stacking games akin to columns or tetris are strangely absent, and a 2.5d racer like outrun or pole position would have fit in comfortably, as well. Long Story short, this is an amazing game compilation, and it's garanteed to have at least one of your games of the year within it's contents.

_childDocuments_.review: A collection of brilliant and fun games. Brings back the excitement of exploring each games in a cartridge your parent(s) bought you.Most likely you won't enjoy every 50 of these games. Especially the first game, Barbuta, might leave a bad first impression with its clunky gameplay. But the more you explore UFO 50, the more likely you'll find a game that has the power to keep you hooked for hours. Genres are so diverse in this collection.I tried every game, and completed 3 of them so far. Mooncat is captivating with its surrealistic visual style and hauntingly beautiful melodies. Control scheme is quite unconventional, I believe this is for reflecting the difficulty the protagonist having while moving in this alien world. It is a reason you might dislike Mooncat, or enjoy Mooncat *despite this*, or enjoy Mooncat *especially for this*. Nonetheless, that unconventional control is inseparable from Mooncat's identity.Attactics is a fast paced strategy game with an easy learning curve. New unit types are introduced as you progress in the campaign. Your computer opponent doesn't really have an AI that makes any decision, but its troops are more than yours and sometimes even more powerful, which makes the game sufficiently difficult.Warptank's game mechanic is brilliantly creative. Pure fun. Levels get really hard when it's close to the end, but never to the point of becoming frustrating.UFO 50 is a monument of indie creativity.

_childDocuments_.review: The price is wrong. This game should cost $200. maybe more? A few years ago I spent a few months building a home arcade cabinet with a raspberry Pi inside of it loaded with all my childhood nostalgic games. It was a fun build but I hardly ever play it. Most those old games don't hold up well and its mostly the memories and  nostalgia that is delivering the dopamine not the gameplay.  What a wonderful gift UFO 50 is... Instead of struggling through borderline unplayable titles from my childhood and scraping the bottom of the barrel of my mind for those last bits of nostalgia, UFO 50 just sets down a brand new fresh pot of fun games that an alternate reality me is probably nostalgic for. They are good in the way you remember those old games being, and not how they actually were.  The day I got it I played for 14 hours straight and I have only opened about 20 of the titles. _childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for many years for UFO 50 to come out. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible game, my game of the year for sure. I never really feel the need to leave a review for games, but this one I had to. It feels like even with all the positive praise this game is getting it still deserves tenfold more. The fact that this is 50 well crafted games for the price of only $25 is an amazing value, I have nearly 20 hours into it and have maybe only spent serious time in 1/5th of the games available and still have yet to try about 10 of them. I keep getting surprised by how each time I try a new game it is not only a fun and usually unique take on a concept that I haven't seen before, but that it is also a full fledged game sometimes being several hours long that probably could've been sold on it's own on steam for $10. And I haven't even tried the ~15 hour western themed jrpg yet. The fact that these games all tie into an overarching meta narrative on top of that with the fictional Ufosoft developer, and the progression you can see in the chronology of games going from the clunky Barbuta as game 1 to the much more polished games by the end, is just the bow that neatly ties this incredible package together. I will be enjoying many more hours of this great collection and applaud Mossmouth on the monumental achievement that is UFO 50.
_childDocuments_.name: UFO 50

_childDocuments_.review: Going into this collection, I thought it would be tailored to people who enjoy either wide varieties of genres and experiences, and/or people who enjoy retro games, but honestly speaking, the quality rock-solid design between almost all of these 50 titles make it an easy recommendation for anybody! It's been a long time since I've been this enraptured with a game, and the fact that after 50 hours I still find it hard to put down is a testament to the insane value of this package. Even if not all the games are to your liking, the games have plenty of replayability and challenge, so finding and playing the ones you personally enjoy will be enough to carry you through many hours of excitement with very little of the repetitive tasks you'd normally find from a game of this length.The music is also fantastic throughout, even down to the short catchy jingles you hear during "round start" in the more arcade-style titles! From atmospheric and gentle melodies found in Night Manor and Mooncat, to the catchy tunes of Pilot Quest and Warptank, I find myself wanting to come back to the games just for the music sometimes!Finally, the art direction is charming and of a very high quality throughout all the games. Limited colour palettes and recurring sprites in various games lend themselves to the idea that these are real classic games that were just lost in time, and are sure to put a smile on your face if you've ever played anything similar!It's shocking that a game this polished and enjoyable can release with the relatively small amount of fanfare that it has (not to say it's underrated of course, but I hope more people are able to find this game and experience it all for themselves)! The team at Mossmouth did a great job on this collection, and I hope my review may convince you to give it a chance, it's truly one of a kind!

name: DOOM 64
detailed_description: Originally released on Nintendo 64 in 1997, DOOM 64 is an action first-person shooter and a direct sequel to the events of DOOM II. In celebration of DOOM’s 25th anniversary, an enhanced version of DOOM 64 was released on PC and consoles in 2020 and can now be played here. Story Years have passed since you stopped Hell’s invasion of Earth. Quarantined for humanity’s safety, the UAC research facilities on Mars were abandoned and forgotten...until now. A signal from a degraded satellite suggests a single entity remains, and it has the power to resurrect the demons. As the only surviving marine who fought Hell’s forces, you are sent on a lone crusade to hunt down the Mother of Demons and stop a renewed demonic invasion. Features Released in 2020 to celebrate DOOM’s 25th anniversary, this enhanced version makes it even easier for players to enjoy the original game on modern platforms. Features include: Upgraded visuals Improved mouse and keyboard controls Gamepad/controller support Widescreen resolution support Native 60 FPS support More than 30 action-packed levels Additional “Lost Levels” continuing the story

_childDocuments_.review: I can't get Jim Sterling's "It's time to ♥♥♥♥ on Bethesda"-intro (which has a catchy music along a point) out my mind while writing this. Did somebody send a company-wide memo urging everybody to ♥♥♥♥ something up, no matter what? Bethesda finally has a game (mostly) without live service crap neither bugged to hell (no pun intended), but still can't stop being Bethesda. I am not even complaining about what feels like an hour of intro videos (which can be skipped with a bit of effort). Neither about News/Bethesda club on the main menu, which is already stretching it. But the Bethesda icon as a loading cursor in the otherwise old-school menu, coupled with the jarring Bethesda icon appearing amid the game when saving is too much. This is a classic! Everybody knows Doom is now owned by Bethesda and everybody is grateful for Doom 64 officially on PC. You don't need to shove yours into everyone's face!Speaking of being grateful, yes I am. With that whole "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on Bethesda" out of the way, damn is this game good!On the surface, it looks like Doom 1 & 2, but it's in fact a precursor to Doom 3. Meaning less open arenas, less enemy count overall (but unlike Doom 3, you keep your fast walking speed), more emphasis on the atmosphere. The dark, moody atmosphere coupled with the eery soundscape in place of rocking music creates a sense of horror crawling under your skin and staying there. Look, I get how the precursors were scary when playing them as a kid, but when viewed through the same lens as Doom 64 now, those are about as much horror as Resident Evil 6 is an action : superficially yes, but let's be real.Feel free to call me contrarian, but I prefer this one to Doom 3. I also prefer Doom 3 BFG over the original release as I'm into shooting games for mostly shooting and not flashlight management. Doom 64, more so than Doom 3 BFG, is thick on horror atmosphere but doesn't put it into the place of action. Similar to Doom 3 though, the game has ways to surprise you, to make you feel that sense of doom. The level & encounter design nudges you against rushing into rooms headfirst, there's less stuff to kill overall but more really unpleasant situations to get into, you're dealing with all this in the action manner of it's precursors making Doom 64 the go-to action horror game. Please don't get me wrong, Doom 3 is a good game and I'm replaying it on my Switch, not regretting having bought it twice for a single moment. In fact, it's corridors (contrary to arenas in the rest of the Doom series) are a good fit for the limp analog stick FPS gameplay experience.I rarely talk about visuals in my reviews and this is a port of a decades-old game, but the visual style is ageless. In fact, I prefer well-crafted sprites over common high-poly-no-artistry visuals any day of the week. Speaking of technicalities, it has mouselook, and mouselook is enabled by default. Speaking design, the supershotgun is delicious.All in all, worth a purchase. A fantastic game I finally get to enjoy with proper KBM controls. Yes, source ports have been in existence for dunno how long, but legally obtaining the game content hasn't been exactly feasible all those years and I salute Bethesda for releasing an official port of that gem!PS: Doom Eternal (and Doom '16) canonize Doom 64, in case you still need a reason to play it. Just sayin'...

Just kidding, I actually like you.

_childDocuments_.review: is an odd one. It was originally made by Midway for the Nintendo 64, and it's a darker, more atmospheric take in the series before DOOM 3 was actually a thing while having the fast paced action DOOM is known for. It has been forgotten for a while... up until now thanks to the release of DOOM ETERNAL. is your typical DOOM in terms of gameplay. You start out with your pistol and fists, you find more weapons as you play through the levels, you kill demons, you find key keycards, you can find secrets, it's nothing you're not used to if you played the first two. What is new however are the looks and sound. Midway went with a more unsettling look to the enemies, and the soundtrack is no heavy metal anymore. They went with a style that makes you feel alone, that you need to survive, and it works while maintaining what makes DOOM great. In general, the game looks decent for the time and hardware it was on, and it looks much better in the rerelease.The level design are also very DOOM, but they're also my biggest problem with game. Don't get me wrong, they're fun to explore, but many times I found myself getting confused/lost on what to do. The traps can also be a bit frustrating to deal with your first time, especially where at times they feel like they come out of nowhere without any hint (one section in Level 2 where you need to stand in yellow lights so you don't get crushed, for example). Again, the levels are still fun to play through, but the trial and error can be an issue.This port's optimization is absolutely fantastic. Sure, this is an old game, but I'm able to play this game at "1366x768 60Hz" resolution at 60FPS with very little problems on this old Windows 7 laptop. There's also many graphics options, like enabling Anti-Aliasing, V-Sync, and a filter to make the N64 graphics less pixelated. The game's also in widescreen, you can set the brightness, and the shimmering the N64 version had is gone. It controls well with the mouse and keyboard, and you can rebind any key to your liking. The scrolling is a bit weird, but it works and you can get used to it. This is a really solid game. It's still DOOM, and while the level design can be poor, it's still a great way to spend your time. As for the port, it's the best way to experience this game. For 5 dollars, that's a steal.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Premium classic Doom with the art style and sound design more reminiscent of the original Quake and with the level design being more sadistic than either of the two. The game is still run and gun but the overall vibe is much more horror focused than the majority of Doom with the other exception being Doom 3. The level design is some of the tightest in the classic Doom series with an emphasis on tight well thought out levels as opposed to the quite large levels of Doom 2 and there is an emphasis on traps and ambushes. Stellar game if you enjoy the classic Doom games and a must try for retro shooter enthusiast.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: underrated as hell, doom 64 was the last of the "classic"  styled doom games for a while and it went out with a unique entry. doom 64 is strange, its horror focus is bewildering at first but grows on you over time with a amazing art style and atmosphere that is perfectly invoked by the soundtrack. Unlike doom 3 however, which also tried for a more horror tone, doom 64 doesn't abandon or soften the iconic combat loop the franchise is know for. With tons of great levels packed to the bone with great traps and frantic monster battles, doom 64 still feels like doom, just a more surrealist variation on the series. It of course features the iconic Unmaker, a cut weapon from the original doom, a demon based laser rifle that has the unique distinction of being up gradable by finding 3 secret keys, in 3 secret levels. It can be a pain and confusing at points to acquire them, the gun more than makes up for it by becoming comically  overpowered. though it may have the occasional confusing and frustrating level, doom 64's pros majorly outweigh its cons and even handles elements from previous games better, doom 64 is a lost gem that is slowly getting the status it deserves as the bold, weird, and wonderful game that it is  8.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A dark and tight successor to DOOM II, this iteration tries to refine what made DOOM quintessentially DOOM and add things that were intended for, but never made it into DOOM or DOOM II. The scripting seems to be improved with certain functions not possible in DOOM used in these levels. The darker atmosphere and atmospheric tracks instead of metal make it a bit more forboding for some, but I found it lost some charm. Who doesn't like shooting a Cacodemon and seeing red green and blue guts everywhere? Many fans cite this as the best DOOM experience, and it's a little hard to fault them.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people dismiss DOOM 64 as a spin-off, since it was always assumed to be a DOOM port for the Nintendo 64. However, id Software actually developed an entirely new DOOM game from the ground up. It's the direct sequel to DOOM II. (While DOOM 64 is technically the 3rd game, it's not really comparable to DOOM 3 as the games are completely different experiences)Everything has changed:The only thing that hasn't changed is the gameplay, which is still the tried and true run-and-gun experience DOOM is known for. In the earlier levels, the maps and lighting could be better, but the second half of the campaign makes up for it, especially in Hell. The level design also includes much more puzzles this time around, the majority of which are solved by hitting switches around the map. While I normally dislike backtracking in DOOM, it's tolerable here because they spawn new enemies along the way to help you know where to go and keep things interesting. I think DOOM 64 is a much friendlier game for those who aren't used to Classic DOOM, as it's the final (official) iteration of the Classic DOOM experience.If you've played the original DOOM games and haven't tried out DOOM 64, you're really missing out. It's the literal DOOM 3, don't sleep on it.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say? The true successor to the original Doom throne. I own and played the original on the N64 back in the day and version is fantastic. More or less an identical experience to the original but higher resolution and much, much easier to see. Highly recommended if you're a fan of the original Doom legacy.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: After years of waiting we've finally received an official port of Doom 64!  Ever since I played this game on my N64 back in 2015 I knew I wanted it on PC.  This game is an absolutely phenomenal throwback to the style of FPS titles that were prevalent in the mid-90s.  The port of the game was handled very well as the developers did not tamper with the game's original rendition.  Obvious care was put into providing the best possible experience by including an absolutely flawless controller support.  This allows for the game to be played the way it was meant to be back in '97.  Boasting unique graphics and possessing a wonderfully ambient atmosphere, Doom 64 has stood the test of time.  I would highly recommend it to both Doom fans and retro gamers alike.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is my favorite old school Doom game. The atmosphere, level design, and gunplay are some of the best in the series. Also, since this is a good port, you don't have to bother with trying to set up a source version. Even though Doom 64 is a really good game, it still falls short in some areas. For instance, Doom 64 has the least amount of enemy interactions out of all of the old school Doom games. Due to this, the pacing is much slower than in Doom l and ll. Also, the lack of enemies makes Doom 64 pretty easy on the hardest difficulty. However, considering the N64 lacked power and dual analog sticks, I'm not sure if these can even be classified as problems. Overall, I had a fantastic time with Doom 64. If you want a slower-paced Doom game, this is a great buy.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Likely the most underrated and obscure entry in the doom series prior to this long overdue port. When I first heard about Doom 64 way back when, I assumed it was just a port of the original Doom for the Nintendo 64 and skipped it altogether. I was absolutely wrong. While it definitely shares the gameplay style of Doom and Doom II, it has its own original story and tries to introduce a little tinge of horror with some well executed moody lighting and a suitably haunting ambient soundtrack. It also sports new sounds and an all new visual style, featuring updated sprites for all the classic enemies and weapons along side some original creations.Doom 64 is a pretty respectable length, clocking in at 32 levels if you include the secret ones. I believe this edition also includes some extra "lost" levels as well which is a nice touch. The story of the game is a direct sequel to the events of Doom II, and if you played and paid attention to the background lore of Doom 2016 actually kind of explains the predicament the doom marine finds himself in at the beginning of that game. If you enjoy the gameplay of the other classic doom games I would highly recommend this entry as well, you should feel right at home.

_childDocuments_.review: W3D & Doom started the whole FPS craze.FPP - First Person PerspectiveFPS - First Person ShooterDoom clone - term that was used from '92 to '96 (release of Quake) that means the same as FPS, just doom was so groundbreaking that every other fps game was compared to it.All of FPS are FPP, but not all FPP are FPS.The alternative being third-person perspective -- or TPP -- which, technically speaking, should include any game where you're looking at the character you're controlling from the outside, but which, in practice, is usually used to describe games with an over-the-shoulder "follow cam" (as opposed to "isometric", top-down, side-view, and probably others).The FPS term wasn't widely used before release of Quake, before that they were all called "Doom Clones" or FPP. Doom was actually the first game that brought recognition to the FPS genre as something distinct (even though there are games that fit FPS description and predate doom about 19 years, Id themselves released at least 3 FPS games before doom - Hovertank 3D, Catacomb 3-D and Wolfenstein 3D)So if you want to be specific use FPS, if for example you want to talk about System Shock or Deus Ex use FPP as they're mix of FPS and RPG. And all games that came after doom and before quake can be called doom clones (heretic, hexen, duke nukem 3d, shadow warrior e.t.c.)There's also a subgenre of FPP that contains vehicular combat (i.e. descent series) that some consider to be FPS and some do not so in this case it's safer to use FPP.

_childDocuments_.review: After a bit of consideration, as was pointed out by a friend of mine in the comments, I might've been a bit too hard on this port. I think it was just all the new issues and inconveniences that this port brings rubbed me a little too much. As it stands, this port is the currently the only way for you to experience DOOM 64 on most game consoles without getting your hands on a ROM (which not many people have the luxury of being able to do so legally). So if you're just looking to play Doom64, then sure, go ahead and grab this port. I've changed my recommendation from no to yes, and I have left my original review below, unedited, since the things I say are still relevant, just maybe not the conclusion.This is one of those cases where I wish I could rate somewhere in between a yes or an no, but as it stands, if the question is "Should you spend your money on this?", I'm going to have to lean onto no, which really pains me to do. I'd also like to point out that this is not a review of DOOM 64 the game, but rather this port. DOOM 64 is a fantastic entry in the DOOM franchise with a unique atmosphere that really brings out the horror aspect of DOOM. A lot has been said about the game, and I recommend looking through those other reviews if you want to know more about the game than the port. I've played through the entire game before writing this review. My main issue with this port really just comes down to the fact that Doom64 EX exists. It's free, developed by the same lead programmer (Kaiser), and has a buttload more features, including mod support. I can understand that this port is trying to be more faithful to the original game, but when you're trying to set yourself apart from a free port, you need something to stand out. In the end, this is just a barebones port of the original game, which is a massive letdown considering that Nightdive Studios has done  work reviving other older titles, such as Turok and Strife... So why fall so short with this port? All this port really has of note is the addition of the Lost Levels, which exist solely to tie DOOM 64 to the new DOOM games (2016 and Eternal). The levels themselves, are ok... They're really just more of the same, down to the exact same final boss fight.One choice that baffles me is, in the spirit of keeping the game as pure as possible, that things that should definitely have been an option simply aren't there. I'm not referring to the lack of vertical mouselook or jumping, but the ability to toggle strobing lights. Instead of making the game optionally more accessible to people with epilepsy, Nightdive instead chose to just put a strobing lights warning during the game's boot sequence, consequentially barring people with epilepsy from playing certain levels in the game.Another thing that I found disappointing is that, again in the spirit of purity, issues that I had with the original N64 title are still present in this port. That includes but is not limited to:The port also comes with some new issues not present in the original game:While some of those issues can be fixed by messing with the game's files, it shouldn't be necessary. These issues are well known and have been complained about, but months later and no signs of any fixes...In the end, if you wish to play DOOM 64, I suggest you either play it on the original console (like I have) for the "authentic" experience, or play the Doom64 EX port instead which has many more features than the paid product. Purchasing this port will not support the original developers of the game (Midway Games), as the studio has been shut down long ago. If you wish to support NightDive (which you should, they do fantastic work), I would recommend you purchase Turok, Strife, or their upcoming System Shock games (including an official sequel!).
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Do I recommend this game? Yes and no. I'm up-voting this game because its a solid port with a few faults. The developer has made a decent port of the source material and that alone pushes it into recommended territory. The game itself is good but not great and I don't blame these developers for the original design. The game is like a partially completed Doom 2 wad with better graphics but then the interest or money ran out before they had completed all levels and monsters. Most of the levels are fine but the first two hours were a dismal experience of metallic copy-paste corridors and obscure switch hunts that made me consider refunding the game. It's get better 8 levels in and I found myself enjoying the hell maps. Six additional maps have been added to this version and they are challenging and fun.The game suffers from the same design faults as the original Doom. You should never let two weapons share ammo because it renders the less powerful one obsolete. I have never used the Doom pistol after obtaining the chain-gun and I did not use the pistol here either because it's just too weak. Doom 64 adds one upgradeable demonic laser gun half-way through which uses the same cell ammo as the plasma gun and BFG and effectively renders them both obsolete once you get it. It is too powerful, completely overshadowing the nerfed plasma gun, being able to kill the cyber demon or final boss in seconds. Compared to Doom 1 & 2, the plasma gun's rate of fire has been nerfed which makes it utterly unimpressive. Finally the poorly animated double-barreled shotgun is still too powerful and you will end up using it non-stop throughout the game.The game features new graphics for most monsters from Doom2. The revenants, arch-viles, chain-gunners and the Spider Mastermind are absent from the monster line-up and the game really suffers from it. I never thought I would actually miss these monsters but 10 hours into Doom 64 I am. There is one new monster, the dark Imp, and it is just a palette-swapped partially invisible imp with faster fireballs which isn't particularly impressing. There is a new end-boss monster but you only see it twice in the game so that doesn't really count. It could have been a decent mook in the normal levels and the final boss could have been something greater. All in all, the lack of monster variety hurts the game, I believe I killed more hell knights and barons of hell here than imps! The gameplay becomes a bit monotone with the same monsters all the time.The game's music ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sucks hard! The game tries to create a scary atmosphere by using oppressive ominous soundtracks with the sounds of babies crying in the dark. It sounds like a bunch of debased ASMR nonsense. The problem is that Doom has not and never will be a horror game! It is a game about killing demons with chainsaws, rocker launchers and double-barred shotguns! The pile of demon carcasses you leave behind means this is a horror game for the demons! I recommend you mute the game's music and put on something more appropriate in your music player of choice.All in all, I recommend this to people interested in Doom history and doom engine games. Play the original Doom games before you play this. If you like Doom 1, 2 and Plutonia/TNT then consider this. Everyone else can safely skip this game.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Really didnt expect to find a underrated gem here. While the game contrasts a lot with the more  kill em all attitude of the original two games, doom 64 felt pretty unique with its horror theme levels and creepy ambient music, it actually creeped me out a few times. Even while being pretty different, its still classic doom.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid port of an often overlooked treasure from DOOM's legacy. A different, but not entirely unfitting, take on the classic DOOM formula, 64 is a much more tense and atmospheric horror shooter than its predecessors, with an outstanding ambient soundtrack by Aubrey Hodges. In addition to the main 32 level campaign, this port, adds a brand new episode with even more new levels, which I found thoroughly enjoyable to play through.I've found very little off or questionable about this port from my boys at Nightdive, aside from a couple of very minor quirks. The default brightness was a tad high for me and messed with the original's moody darkness, but thankfully turning the overall brightness setting down all the way seems to get it about on-par with the original. And I find the time between booting the game up and being able to actually start playing to be just a tad too long, thanks largely to the lengthy company intros (which are thankfully skippable by just deleting the files from the directory) and the wait time for the game to check its connection to Bethesda's servers (thankfully, actually using a Bethesda account appears to be completely optional). Otherwise the port seems to be everything I could have hoped for! The controls seem well-adapted for keyboard and mouse, and are completely rebindable (even if the menu is a bit annoying about how it shows alternate inputs, by just shuffling between them). There's a decent handful of video customization options for enabling texture filtering and anti-aliasing, and increasing the FOV. And the mad lads, for no real reason other than posterity, have left the original game's password save system intact, despite adding proper save games. Completely unnecessary, and entirely appreciated for the novelty!The performance seems rock-solid, for me, and seems to be pretty well-optimized. Those minimum system requirements are  inflated. I have no trouble keeping a steady 60 at 1680x1050, on an old Core 2 Duo with 3 gb of RAM and a Radeon HD 7800. Your old toasters should have no trouble here!It might be tempting to let this release be overshadowed by Bethesda's criminal decision of locking it to Eternal's release date, but for real don't sleep on DOOM 64 - you'd be missing out! It's a solid port of an excellent game!
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Played this game for a very short time and I just have to say, this game is just great.This game just so smooth compared to the earlier DOOM games, and I haven't played muchDOOM nor am I a fan of it but after playing just a little, I could totally become a fan.This game is just a great with it's 144Hz compatibility, made everything feel much nicer and better.Would play for 3124 hours if I had the time.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing every classic doom game I can definitely say that this is my favorite out of all of them. Doom 64 is much more consistent in its quality than doom 1 or doom 2, where in those games the level quality seems to drop off after the first 2 episodes doom 64 has good quality levels throughout the entire game which is about 30 levels long.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this on the old Nintendo 64 in the past, as well as the modified version called "Brutal DOOM 64" which I downloaded for free from another website where you can download Brutal DOOM games from. However this edition on Steam gives you easier controls, especially the most convenient key bindings for satisfying gameplay, I didn't realize first when re-visiting the dark atmospheric world of DOOM 64 thanks to the dark and creepy soundtrack composed by Aubrey Hodges, how much this PC experience drew me in. This edition of DOOM 64 has the gameplay from the original N64 exclusive release as well as the lost levels I think, once you complete the game or maybe it's available once you start a new game? Anyways, It's a blast to play. I would definitely recommend to not just hardcore Doom fans, but anyone who likes retro shooters. I do like the 1993 Doom and Doom II also but Doom 64 is definitely alot of fun and it's only sad that this particular game did not receive a sequel after its 1997 release on the Nintendo 64.

The level design is terrific, and their are tons of different enemy types. And the final boss is one of the toughest ive ever fought in a video game. Overall a fantastic game 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 leans further into horror. Featuring tense atmosphere, pronounced use of lighting, and Aubrey Hodges' ambient soundtrack, as opposed to the typical metal, which leads to a creepy yet vivid listening experience. There's an emphasis on exploration and puzzle solving; more traps and hazards are used. The bestiary isn't as pronounced as Doom 2, but features horrific updates, and a new boss battle. Notably, the demonic weapon known as "The Unmaker" makes its' debut to even out odds. Updated visuals are put to good use with foreboding UAC bases, gothic citadels, altars of pain, and other such realms of suffering.Certain features didn't make the cut. The omission of some demons doesn't allow for the same variety in encounters, the shotgun and Super Shotgun reload animations are missing, The Doomguy face HUD is missing. Doom 64 stands out as a restricted yet evocative entry. As the wrapping point for Classic Doom, this DARK horse is worth a try.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is a stellar game, there's no doubt. But I couldn't put my finger on why I was finding it such a slog to get through until my most recent replay, and it's because it has such a dark atmosphere. It's a game of muted colours, shadowed hallways, and incredibly creepy ambient music. It's a potent mix that creates a deeply oppressive vibe, but it strips a lot of the raw fun that typified Doom 1 and 2. It's surprising that such a quiet and unsettling game was released solely on the N64 - a console known more for the light-hearted tone of its games more than anything else. But if you're looking for blistering speeds and raw energy, then that's where this game stands apart. For some that may be a good thing - it allies itself in that sense with Doom 3, a game I love. But I do find that, with the simpler visuals and gameplay, there is slightly more room for boredom to set in. You're not ripping through levels to empowering tunes, you're skulking through levels with an overwhelming sense of...well...doom. And the greys and browns that permeate the hallways lend their colour to the mood of the game, in sense. Doom 64 is very well made, but it's a marathon rather than a sprint.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This Doom game stands out from the other classic Doom games because of how unique this one is.The setting is a lot more dark and unsettling than previous Doom games and the music isn't much of head-banging metal tunes as it is Aubrey Hodge's horrifying ambient soundtrack.This game also stands out with it's lighting effects that I've honestly never seen anything like in another game, I can't actually describe how good the lighting looks so you should honestly just check it out for yourself.Only negatives are the lack of mouse look and the ridiculous amount of unskippable splash screens in the startup (Right click the game on Steam > Go to properties > Local Files > Browse Local Files > Delete movies folder)Overall this game stands out as one of the best Doom games and I'm glad its finally back in an official form.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, the best and worst thing about Doom 64 is that it's just more of the same. Alongside Doom and Doom II, this is just more levels with the same gameplay. But if it ain't broke, don't fix it. After you play those two classics, there's no reason not to check this one out too. It has slightly better graphics, but not by much, more detailed sprites mostly, other things like the weapons actually look a bit worse at times. Levels are somewhat more straightforward but do include some new wacky mechanics too. The aesthetics are darker and grittier and the banging metal soundtrack is replaced with chilling ambiance. Beyond that, it's the pinnacle of oldschool boomer shooter goodness as we all know and love it.I'm pretty hyped for when they finally release Dooms 4 through 63, can't wait. It is rather odd though that after all that, we are still just collecting keycards and navigating mazes. Hey, props to id for sticking to their guns I guess.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: You prefer the original Doom games to the new ones that came out recently (2016 and Eternal)? Then buy this, during sales is so cheap that you'd want to at least try it, a little bit on the easy side with mouse and keyboard since it was designed with the N64 controller in mind.If you have already played it on the N64 version and somehow miss how dark it was, just put the brightness on minimum, I'm serious it looks like how it was to me back then. Having said that I'm not a psychopath (maybe) and I'd leave it on the default value, maybe a tad bit less.Good level design, atmosphere due to the art style of both demons and props around levels, and the music that aims more towards ambient and noise stuff with a hint of demonic sounds, and the new set of levels give it new life and a reason to come back to it if you didn't already.So, a "must" for every "boomer shooter" fan to my eyes.

_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely LOVE this game and so glad to see a proper PC port released.If you haven't previously played it, know that DOOM 64 is very much unlike almost any other DOOM game released. Instead of the metal soundtrack and the frenetic pace, this game offers a different experience: The game is about atmosphere, navigating mazes, avoiding traps, and finding secrets. Of course there's plenty of action but it's overall a far more methodical game than any other entry in the series. It's somewhat similar in atmosphere and pace to a game like HeXen (also available on Steam).To give you an idea of the atmosphere, when I first played this on a Nintendo 64 as a little kid, I genuinely thought it was the scariest game ever. The mazes and puzzles run the gamut in terms of challenge, but are never too hard that you'll get hopelessly stuck (but expect to make a lot of use of your map). As a little kid, I beat the game without any guide or walkthrough (those were rare in the '90s anyway). But make no mistake, this game WILL CHALLENGE YOU.The one and only negative to this perfect port is the annoying developer/publisher videos when you start the game. Luckily you can easily bypass this by just deleting or renaming the movies folder in the install directory.It's worth mentioning that one improvement that the port has over the original is the brightness. Those of us who played the original on the Nintendo 64 will remember that the game was *extremely* dark. Even cranking up the brightness didn't help much, and we were playing on CRT monitors, so there wasn't all that much we could do. This version noticeably fixes the issue while retaining the dark atmosphere. Items like the "light amplification goggles" are still useful, but the screen is no longer so dark that you'll have to worry much about the brightness setting.TLDR: DOOM 64 is more of an atmospheric horror game, a unique experience that I remember fondly all these years after my childhood. The port is excellent and just like the way I remember the original.btw, the controls are great. I'm playing this on a regular xbox-style pc controller, and it's smooth and intuitive, maybe even better than the original N64-style controller. All the controller vibrations you'd expect are there (using the chainsaw, etc). Zero complaints.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 just drips with atmosphere.  The lighting, sound, textures, music, etc.  I'm happy to see it finally get an official release on the PC! So much nostalgia from playing this on the N64 years ago.Any fans of Doom I or II will adjust to this in no time.  The immediate visual changes you'll notice are the more detailed sprites, colored lighting, environmental effects such as fog and lightning, animated skies, and heavy use of darkness.  The levels are well crafted, it's basically if Quake and Doom had a baby.  The new Lost Levels were really fun as well.  I got mine for free with the pre-order of Doom Eternal, but at only $4.99, Doom 64 is practically a steal!

_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic port of a game I just think is okay. Don't expect stuff like full vertical mouse look or jumping or any of the extra features you usually get in other source ports; this is meant to be a faithful accurate release of the original game. It's better than the previous older port from the same creator, Doom64 EX, not just because of bugfixes, native controller support, various frame rate limits and interpolation settings, and DirectX 11/Vulkan support, but for me solely because the Nightdive port actually accurately replicates the texture filtering that was present on N64 that the game's art was designed around; the Nintendo 64 didn't just do plain bilinear filtering which smooths over everything like what you'll see in a lot of other source ports.As for the game itself, I think it's good but I don't really think it's . Maps tend to feel samey after a while, and while it's not quite Plutonia Experiment levels of being cruel, it's a tier or two below it. Doom 64  loves to booby trap everything for progression, usually resulting in rooms with insane numbers of bullet sponge enemies that aren't really hard to fight but instead just tedious. Puzzles can also get annoying because the game doesn't always follow consistent rules with stuff like switches; sometimes you can shoot them, sometimes you can't, and the game is never clear about which it'll be unless you waste ammo or time or both. The final boss is an atrocious frustrating nightmare unless you discover three secret levels and obtain collectibles in them that will upgrade the Unmaker, which can also still be missed and for some godforsaken reason can be The Lost Levels are good but very brief, and it's pretty obvious that they were made more recently by different people and not Midway. Some of the levels are a little too easy and the last map feels almost untested for how laughably easy you can cheese and break it compared to the rest of the game. They're a nice addition but they won't change anybody's mind on the game overall.Doom 64 has charm and will still be interesting to those who like the older Doom games; it's more of a true sequel to the older style of Doom games than Doom 3 is and it's great that it's been faithfully preserved by Nightdive for an absurdly cheap price, but I can only really recommend it to those fans. If you haven't played the older Doom games before, play Ultimate Doom and Doom 2 before this.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This is my second favorite Doom game in the series and I love (almost) everything about it. From the more grim/Gothic artstyle, to the ambiance, enemy design, and I liked the Unmaker (and the "what the #### is this" joke is kinda cute, had the game had more jokes it perhaps could've been more like Postal 1?) and the level design is great (mostly the og levels, the new "lost" levels are.... just rehashes of the already existing ones but it's fine), just wish opening the map would show how many kills, secrets and pick-ups we've got. It's not a flawless game (damn you Lost Souls and Pain Elementals) but it's worth it, especially since Doom 64 did manage to capture almost everything that ID wanted the original Doom to be.Edit: Finally got 64(.1) hours on this game, my opinion hasn't really changed all that much.

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 is a first-person science-fiction horror-themed shooter game developed by Midway Games for an enhanced version of the id-Tech 1 Engine, and re-released by Nightdive Studios via the Kex Engine. Taking place after the events of DOOM II, the player takes control of the battle-weary Doom Marine as he returns to the setting of the first game to exterminate a mysterious entity reviving previously slain demons.In a number of ways, the original DOOM was embedded deeper into the world of 90’s home computer gaming more than any other market. It was, at the time of its release, the most exacting 3D world in the entire gaming industry at large, when accounting for speed and screen-size. For a while, home consoles just couldn’t quite compete, despite a handful of earnest attempts. A wave of home console ports of DOOM populated the mid-to-late 90’s, with technical visionary and id Software co-founder John Carmack himself behind the wheel of at least one of them. Most of them couldn’t even light a candle to the original. Perhaps the greatest of these initial adaptations, however, was Midway Games’ remix and restoration of the previously id-helmed Atari Jaguar port for the technologically superior Sony Playstation. Featuring both DOOM and DOOM II in a single package, new audio-reverberation, an all-new score of CD-quality music, colored lighting, new sound effects, and a handful of totally original levels, the Playstation’s initial DOOM outing is a memorable one, and a profound enough update for the other John of id, John Romero, to call it the “best DOOM yet," at the time of its release. Even the Playstation’s DOOM, though, with all of its special effects, failed to live up to the PC original in a number of ways. It was missing entire swaths of the campaigns, most of the story intermission screens, and much of the more computationally impressive geometry originally found in the majority of its levels had to be sanded down.It wasn’t until two years later, in 1997, that home console players saw a DOOM release that was, for the most part, an unmitigated parallel and expansion of the experience that gaming PC owners had been enjoying for four years, with the Nintendo 64 release of DOOM 64. Unlike the Playstation version of DOOM, though, DOOM 64 is an entirely new campaign of exclusively original levels. It has its own storyline and its own artstyle, and its designers were free to alter various aspects of the game’s mechanics to suit its target platform better. Like the Playstation’s DOOM, it kept all of the eye-catching special effects that had made that port so appealing, and seized on them to create set-pieces and environments that would have been impossible in the 1993 home computer release of DOOM. The architecture and geometry of this new DOOM defer to a consistent artistic vision, one which takes full advantage of colored lights and radial fog to evoke a murky, lived in feeling, echoing the effect that the dynamic, diminished lighting of the original games used to have, but with a bolder, more extant visual maturity.Beyond just the visuals, DOOM 64 offers the most balanced combat experience in any of these classic-style DOOM games. Despite its smaller monster pool, every single encounter feels well choreographed. The Doom Marine feels both heavier and nimbler under the joystick than he did on a keyboard, and the ferocity with which the game pits intersecting arrays of moving projectiles at him makes the added precision necessary and satisfying. This heavier movement and the somewhat truncated monster variety marry to form a mobile and surprisingly sadistic campaign. But much of this sadism comes not from the snarling hoards, but from the riddling, vexing level design. Tricks and traps abound, alongside arcane puzzles whose solutions are obscured by dimly arbitrated movement and opaque sequences of switch-presses. The stop-and-go pace that classic DOOM has always had has never been as staccato as it is here, but the gripping, dreary musical accompaniment and dreamily austere visuals match the carnage with the confusion with ease.It's no exaggeration to say this is the first time a DOOM game has cared so consistently about presentation and mood. I recall an uncommonly effective series of events in DOOM 1's third episode, “Inferno”, when the player peers through a series of slits in the wall overlooking a courtyard of tortured souls nailed to crosses. As they step forward to survey this view, an ambush of battle-hungry foes springs out from behind them. It's a mean and nightmarish kind of trick, and every single level of DOOM 64 evokes the same philosophy as that moment. Creepy environmental set-dressing, playful psychological trickery and atmospheric mood-building all wrap around the core of DOOM’s gameplay. Future evolutions of the DOOM IP would take these same emotions and principles and use new advances in game design and technology to evoke them in new ways, from DOOM 3 onward to DOOM Eternal. DOOM 64 was the first to do so, using admittedly similar technology and game design to create an expertly massaged experience with more a refined focus towards particular reactions.The narrative, too, feels more directed and considered than those of the previous DOOM releases. From the haunting sound of babies’ cries underscoring the main menu, to the Doom Marine’s plaguing nightmares, referenced in the game's manual, every aspect of the presentation deals with themes of cycles and rebirth. The initial setup of the levels reinforce this, with the Doom Marine literally being made to walk the halls he's already thoroughly conquered, while “the familiarity of the situation” is commented on directly in one of the games’ text screens. Even the demons themselves, already returning foes of a kind, are said to be reconstructed tissue taken from the fallen carcasses that littered past killing-fields. Ultimately, the Marine's descent becomes an ascent and he himself is reborn by the end of the game. The character arc within this game mirrors that of the player themselves across the entire DOOM franchise, and framing it as a sequel is another instance of rebirth.Despite taking place after DOOM II, DOOM 64 isn't exactly a sequel to DOOM II. It's more like DOOM told through the lens of Quake's moody dreamscapes than a properly forward-moving evolution of DOOM II’s design. It's a surprising and cerebral adventure designed to thrill and dull the player into a uniquely jittery fugue state which can only really be understood through experiencing it. It pulls the player into a meditative zone, reactive and yet still thinking critically. Like Quake, it positions the player as someone somewhere between Daedalus and Theseus—both the master of the maze and the victim of its bloodthirsty secrets. In another sense, it transforms the player into the Minotaur, tumbling through underground shadows, hunting for the sounds of nearby intruders, and tapping loose bricks to reveal hidden passageways, until eventually comes the Cyberdemon, like a real minotaur, and the vicious spell is reset.By its climax, the campaign does what no title in this franchise had done before, and sends the player off with a satisfying and deeply foreshadowed confrontation, one whose setup had been deeply woven into the entire campaign before it. It feels, in this way, like the entire game is the culmination of DOOM’s impact up to that point, a refinement and enhancement of the tones, textures and impressions that DOOM had carved out for itself. It was also kind of the last calling card for this brand of software-rendered first-person action, which the industry, with Quake, had largely begun to age past. With that new age came new priorities. Future installments in the franchise would pull from the varying expressions of DOOM’s legacy, in their own ways. But none of them would ever truly marry horror with triumph as maliciously or as gorgeously as Midway Game’s DOOM 64.

_childDocuments_.review: I had to give up on this because the port is just too rough around the edges to be worth my time. During initial setup, I accidentally mapped Left Mouse to weapon 0 and therefore would automatically switch to chainsaw after each gunshot. Funny goof, my bad. Easy to fix, right?30+ minutes of troubleshooting proved otherwise. My first attempt to was to remap the Left Mouse to attack…but it was still assigned to that too (which leads to some interesting questions about if anyone needs macros to play Doom). Next I tried resetting mouse options, but that doesn't cover mapping. Then I tried mapping the Mouse Wheel as a potential replacement. Then I just tried mapping many random keys to hopefully use up too many slots and displace Left Mouse. Nope. Nope. Nope.I'm sure that I could go into the registry if I was sufficiently bent on playing this game, but it really shouldn't be this much work to undo a single mis-click. Combine that with the offensively long, unskippable series of splash screens, and I have no faith that the developers have respect for my time.

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 features the same objectives that have defined the series, and mostly the same awesome weapons. You have to go through dozens of levels, finding keys, shooting demons, pressing switches, and finding hidden weapons. Doom 64 is a memorable game that one can look fondly at years later. It's a great addition to the Doom series, however, don't expect modern controls or visual improvements. It's the same game with the same quirks as the original N64 version.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Thank you, Bethesda, for getting this game ported to PC otherwise I may have gone my entire life never playing it. Doom 64 is an underrated classic, and while it is different in many ways it is just as good as its brethren, Ultimate Doom and Doom 2. The level design is a little more simplistic and more squared compared to other classic Doom games but there are also some notable additions like colored lighting and scripted events that really enhance the levels. The new monster designs are interesting, though some of them are notably not as good as the classic designs. The game feels a little slower and more atmospheric and its a refreshing change of pace. The weapons feel as good as they should and the Unmakyr is a cool and quite overpowered addition to the weapon roster.Doom 64 is great and is worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: While there are some shortcomings that most likely come about from the restrictions of the N64 the game was designed for, Nightdive has performed art by creating such a fantastic port for DOOM 64.The level design compared to the previous DOOM installments is, overall, a great improvement, in part from experience and also from the advancements to the engine allowing for greater verticality and more dynamic environmental effects. The lighting and aesthetics of the game are impeccable and make the game really stand out for an N64 game. Dark, gothic, with a wide colour palette helps keep things feeling fresh, even when the same assets are reused. Shoutout to Aubrey Hodges for the one of the creepiest game OSTs I've heard in my entire life. Really damn good.Buy this game full price or on sale. Either way, experiencing the game is worth whatever cost you pay.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: only recommended if you're already a Doom fan. In which case, you'll appreciate it. If not, you're not missing anything. It's Doom. You've seen it before. I really wish Steam had an "It's a'ight" option with a sideways hand, because I didn't hate or seriously dislike this game, but neither did I love it. It's just that a lot of it is uninteresting, plain and simple. A bunch of the early levels are pretty drab, and the best levels of the game don't come in until roughly the last third. As you're nearing the end, the game throws you a lot of curveballs that will keep you guessing, not to mention some actually decent puzzles that may have you scratching your head. It's hard to recommend something that only gets fun in the end, but seeing as how it's a five dollar fully-functional port of a classic game, I feel bad about thumbing it down. That feels harsh. After all, I beat it, so there must be something to it.But that being said, I played on the hardest difficulty to keep the tension up, and I still found myself getting kinda bored of it halfway through. I felt compelled to finish it because I bought it. If you already like Doom, you'll find something to appreciate here with this classic Doom title. But if you're not a fan already and you stumble on this game, I say "move along", there's nothing special to it besides more Doom.Word to the wise, this game triggered some serious motion sickness for me at one point, keep a look out for that. Don't know why. I took my headphones off (switching to speakers) and upped the FOV, and that eliminated it. No idea what that was all about.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: imagine you're playing Doom 64, but you can actually see what the ♥♥♥♥ you're doing and don't need to use a aborted boomerang to play it.As usual with Nightdive, they've done an excellent job porting this two-and-a-half decade old game to modern systems with modern controls and video options. Technically, it runs flawlessly (as it should) and contains a wealth of visual upgrades such as antialiasing and higher resolutions. Control-wise, WASD keyboard and mouse is the standard here (although some default keybindings are weird: spacebar to sprint?!), as well as gamepad support. Not only that, but a secret episode of 6 extra levels has been included. It's not on the same level as the phenomenal Shadow Man Remastered, also ported by Nightdive Studios, which is probably the greatest remaster ever made, but there has been a huge effort put into this very polished release. As usual, the original feel of the game is preserved immaculately, but made far more accessible (read: not stuck on a long defunct console selling for $50 AUD minimum). The default pricing of $7.55 AUD is actually a bit of a lowball in my opinion. I'd happily pay $20 AUD for this.Onto the game itself, which was developed by Midway under supervision from id Software in 1997, as a Nintendo 64 exclusive. At the time it was praised for its atmosphere and gameplay but faulted for its lack of innovation and multiplayer; its contemporaries like Quake 2 and the Turok series were seen as more technologically advanced, with 3D models for enemies instead of sprites, more complex level geometry and more platforming abilities such as swimming. The lack of multiplayer was particularly odd, especially for Doom, the originator of the deathmatch, on a console swimming in splitscreen shooters. Goldeneye 64 released a year prior and is still remembered today for its 4-player action. I personally never had any interest in the game, having been far too young to buy it on release and never owning a 64, and with 64 emulation being very poor up until recently.In terms of gameplay, it's Doom to a T. Armed to the teeth with a wide variety of firearms, all returning from previous games in the series, you play through a linear set of levels, some hidden, dispatching hordes of a variety of distinct monsters. These monsters also return from previous entries, with some absences due to limited cartridge space, and some new additions that are mostly palette swaps, but which are nonetheless welcome. You'll find secret areas, dodge environmental traps such as crushers, push switches to reveal new pathways, and collect coloured card keys. Apart from some slightly more sophisticated level alteration, such as activating a large weight which breaks through the floor, it's the same old Doom.Really where it differentiates itself from its predecessors is the atmosphere, which will be familiar to those who have played Williams Entertainment's port of Doom for the PlayStation. Sound effects are entirely different, or reused in different ways, some better, others less so. Monsters have had their stats altered slightly, and their sprites are all entirely new, created from CG models. And of course the levels themselves are different, despite retaining the same themes and characteristics; you've still got tech bases and hellish temples, laid out in Doom's trademark abstract style. Coloured lighting returns from the PlayStation version, providing a distinct visual difference from its predecessors. The largest departure is the music, composed by Aubrey Hodges (also the composer of the PlayStation version). Here, other than the introduction cinematic and level end screens, the themes are entirely atmospheric and industrial, rather than the classic techno-metal we've come to expect from Bobby Prince. This is a double-edged sword for me. It succeeds brilliantly at providing an extremely tense and foreboding atmosphere, and combined with the new lighting which is overall far more moody and dark, immerses you in these grotesque environments. However, the original Doom and Doom II were also able to achieve this feeling when necessary, while still providing far more melodic, memorable and frankly far superior tracks. Listen to Bobby Prince's "Sinister" from Doom's Halls of the Damned (E2M6) level for example:  I understand music is especially subjective, so your mileage may vary, but I won't remember any of these tracks the moment I finish the game.Overall, it's more classic Doom, presented in a unique and sometimes fascinating way, finally freed of its exclusivity and available on modern platforms. As someone who has wanted an official* way to play this for a long time, I'm very happy with this release. It won't supersede Doom II: Hell on Earth as the pinnacle of the classic games for me, but it's an engaging and satisfying experience nonetheless.*I do not want to discount the amazing fan efforts that went into recreating and reverse engineering Doom 64 before this port was available. As usual, Doom fans are amazing and provided custom map sets and even whole recreations of Doom 64 far before its official re-release. In particular, Sam Villareal's Doom 64 TC and later Doom 64 EX were instrumental in contributing to the renewed interest in this game and I doubt this would even exist without his ingenuity and passion.

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 was released in 1997 for the Nintendo 64 Entertainment System. It was designed and distributed by Midway Home Entertainment, under license from id Software and features music and audio by the brilliant Aubrey Hodges, whom also created the music and audio for the Playstation and Sega Saturn Doom, Playstation Final Doom and Dreamcast Quake III ports.The game play resembles earlier Doom games, while also adding some more advanced features not found in the original Doom, namely in level design, such as an automap capable of displaying textured floors, cameras, gradient lighting, environmental traps, earthquakes and scripting. It wasn't very popular when it was released, primarily due to competing against (and being compared to) games like Turok: Dinosar Hunter and Goldeneye 007, but it managed to maintain a passionate (albeit small) cult following.Without diving into my own personal history with Doom 64 too much, it's arguably my favorite game ever. I still own my original copy of Doom 64 from 1997 and play it every few years. That said, my review is centered on the port itself, the "Lost Levels," and Doom 64's plot and established timeline, which most people (including Hugo Martin) seem to have wrong.The port runs on the Kex engine, which is loosely based on Doom 64 EX, which in turn, is a source port emulator built on Doom3D's code. While it isn't perfect, it is a mostly faithful recreation. It has a few bugs and other quirky behaviors not present in the original game, but they're largely subtle and only likely to be noticed by those that are intimately familiar with the original.It features some modern niceties such as higher video resolution options, and manages to maintain support for features present in the original Nintendo 64 version, like manual saving and password entry. However, it also introduces a number of annoyances not present in the original, such as an excessively long intro of developer movies (none of which were even really involved with the creation of the original game), Bethesda .net requirements, a "news" section with an animated arrow, and other unwanted garbage.The "Lost Levels" are new (albeit unremarkable) maps which add very little to the game. Several of them share more than a few similarities to Kaiser's "Outcast" maps or levels seen in other Doom games, such as Playstation Doom's "Redemption Denied" level and Doom 64's own "No Escape" level. Their existence is supposedly meant to be a bridge to Doom 2016 but instead, only serves to retcon Doom 64's entire plot and for no apparent reason, goes on to break Doom's actual established timeline.Doom 64's plot centers on the Doom Marine's exploits following Playstation Doom and Final Doom. In order, this is effectively: Ultimate Doom, Doom II: Hell on Earth, The Master Levels, Final Doom's TNT: Evilution and Final Doom's Plutonia.  With the demons having been eradicated and their invasion thwarted on all fronts, a planetary policy is established to seal and quarantine the UAC installations via apocalyptic levels of radiation. The bases are all considered lifeless and abandoned.Later, a dying and long forgotten relay satellite orbiting Phobos, activates and sends a final message to Earth. It is discovered that the Doom Marine had actually failed to completely kill one demon, which went on to rejuvenate itself and then, despite being in a crippled state, managed to systematically revive the demons, all while hiding in plain sight due to the high radiation levels. This single demon, which later becomes known as the "mother of all demons," serves as Doom 64's final boss.Being the only survivor of the "Doom" episodes with any combat experience, the Doom Marine is sent back into the fray to mercilessly exterminate the demons. During Doom 64, you learn that the demons had actually anticipated this and it was a lure to pull you back into hell. The game ends with the Doom Marine deciding to remain in hell to ensure no demon ever rises again.Canonically, it would have been at this point that the Doom Marine is pulled into the "Arena Eternal" by the Vadrigar, an angel-like race which the Khan Maykr seems to be based on, whereupon he manages to earn his armor and freedom. He returns to hell and following an unspecified amount of time, becomes trapped in the "Blood Keep," otherwise known as the Kadingir Sanctum.There is no "sister mother of all demons." The very idea of it conflicts with Doom 64 itself--which is, quite frankly, idiotic. Furthermore, it isn't even necessary for Doom 2016 to still make sense. Most laughable of all, Doom Eternal then proceeds to retcon Doom 64 (and by extension, this port) with the origin behind the Unmaker. To be fair, Doom Eternal also retcons basically every Doom game (including Doom 2016), as well as Quake III, and changes the name of the cyberdemon, but I've already reviewed that. Regardless, I'm giving this port a thumbs down.Instead, I highly recommend purchasing the original Doom 64 or alternatively, enjoying one of the many free options available for download on the internet and visiting Aubrey Hodges' bandcamp page, where you can spend your money and directly support him by purchasing the original or 20th Anniversary Extended Edition official Doom 64 soundtracks.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok where to start with this one???Well lets start with the GOOD points.DOOM 64 'aka the real DOOM 3' is noticeably different from Doom 1 and 2 and not just in its ascetics.Maps require much more back tracking. You'll be expected to 'think' from time to time. Not just mindlessly run around shooting. So if you get frustrated when a game requires you to rub your two dusty brain cells together from time to time, then you will not enjoy DOOM 64.Sprite work and textures are far superior to Doom 1 and 2 and the gradient lighting and fogging adds much more atmosphere to the game. Enhanced even further by the ambient sound track which adds a feeling of 'horror' to the game.Again, this is a matter of taste. If you love 'metal music' tracks then the ambient tracks of DOOM 64 will be lost on you. The 'BAD'Sadly a lack of some monsters. Most noticeably the Reverent'The lack of this monster leads to there being a lot of Baron/Knight spam. The game is a little short.As it had to be crammed into an 8meg Cartridge. Certainly could have done with a few more levels to make the experience feel more complete. Leaves you with a feeling that the devs did everything they could... with what they had. But would have loved to have done so much more. Conclusion.If you love Doom 1 and 2 and expect Doom 64 to be a rinse and repeat game with better graphics... you may well be disappointed. Because it's nothing like that. Best to avoid if your idea of 'thinking' is pressing a switch and looking around the very same room to see what it did lol. If you want a slightly slower paced Doom experience... with cleverly designed maps with more atmosphere... and dont start raging as soon as it's 'NOT LIKE DOOM 2!!!!' You will most likely enjoy it.
