_childDocuments_.review: So, Doom 64. To be honest, I'd probably give this a neutral review if I could, but between positive and negative, I’m leaning more towards negative. So why is that?Well, to start with the positives, it’s nice to see the ID tech 1 engine in its final form, with lots of fancy features that we didn’t see in the original DOOM games. It’s also nice that we got one last hurrah of classic-style DOOM before we moved on to DOOM 3. It’s also incredible that we’re finally able to play a DOOM game on PC that was until now (fan mods aside) locked to the Nintendo 64. Personally, I was very excited to learn that DOOM 64 wasn’t a simply yet another port of DOOM as the name might suggest, but a whole, brand-new DOOM game! But as to the game itself… There’s a lot I didn’t like about it. To start with what I see as the game’s biggest issue, the complete shift in focus as to how the levels are designed compared to the original DOOM games. A lot has been said about DOOM 64’s focus on puzzles and traps compared to the original, but in reality, 95% of these “puzzles” all involve hitting switches. Enter a new room but can’t see how this new room helps you progress in the level? Surprise! There’s a hidden switch you need to press! Most likely, on one of the many pillars in the room! But by far, the worst of these switch “puzzles” are the ones that involve hitting a switch which opens up a room God knows where, because it’s usually on the other side of the map and you can’t see or hear where this door is. So, your only choice is to hit the switch, then wander aimlessly around the level until you stumble upon an area that looks new. The game uses this “puzzle” CONSTANTLY, often multiple times in the same level. It creates a lot of backtracking, and it feels like blatant padding. People often complain about classic DOOM's levels being too maze-like, but the amount of wandering around and backtracking in DOOM 64 ends up creating similar levels of annoyance. Similarly, are the switch puzzles that also involve timing, where the door will close again if too much time has passed. While the original DOOM games used this type of switch puzzle too, it was only ever for secret areas, as opposed to DOOM 64 which uses them as part of progressing the level.As to the infamous traps, to be honest, they feel cheap at the best of times. You’d expect them to be punishment for failing or maybe getting greedy, but in many cases, you’re required to trigger them in order to progress the level. And a lot of them involve simply confining the player then spamming them with projectiles until a timer runs out. How much damage you wind up taking being a total roll of the dice. They are sorta neat, in that we never really saw anything like this in the original DOOM, but overall, they’re more annoying than anything else.Another big change that I’m not a fan of is a reduced focus on combat. There are now far fewer enemies compared to the hordes of demons in the original, with a much significantly larger percent of the level is now spent on wandering around. There’s only one point in the game that I can recall anything close to the scale that was in the original DOOM, and that’s literally in the last level just before the final boss battle.In terms of design and gameplay, I swear it looks like the DOOM 64 devs chose to focus on the weakest part of the original DOOM. That is, wandering around an empty level with no enemies to kill because you can’t find the thing you need to open the next part of the level. Another big change that I’m not a fan of is the presentation. Yes, the game is more technically-impressive compared to the original DOOM, but a lot of the design choices are a backwards step. While the modelling and detail on DOOM 64’s weapon sprites do look nice, (most of the time, an improvement over original DOOM’s weapon sprites), the animations and sounds make DOOM 64’s arsenal feel weak and puny compared to the originals. For example, original DOOM’s shotgun didn’t feel powerful just because it did a lot of damage, but because the animations and sounds sold its power. The firing animation showed it kicking like a mule, accompanied by a mighty “BOOM!” and crisp “KA-CHUCK!” as Doomguy pumped it. The animation depicting this action, of course, shows Doomguy fiercely slamming the pump back because this is a beast of a weapon that needs to be wrangled like a wild stallion! DOOM 64’s shotgun by comparison barely moves when it’s fired and pumped, and the sound it produces is more of a sad muffled fart than an explosion. It still takes down enemies just as well as the original, but it doesn’t “feel” powerful like the original shotgun. Pretty much all of DOOM 64’s weapons suffer from this issue, which makes me wonder if this truly was what the designers intended, or if it might have been a limitation imposed by the Nintendo 64. Weak muffled audio is definitely a common problem with the N64 at least. And speaking of the audio, it’s not great here either. While some of the sound effects are the same as the original DOOM, the ones they used for the replacements aren’t really improvements. For example, the health pickup is that generic sci-fi “VWOOM” sound effect that was used EVERYWHERE in movies and games from the late 90s. And while I respect their decision to use ambient music in service to enhancing DOOM 64’s dark atmosphere, it’s a tough act to follow considering how great original DOOM’s music was!But back to the new replacement sound effects, the new monster sounds are rather samey. It’s not like in the original DOOM where each monster (well, save for processed soldiers and shotgun guys) had their own, very distinctive sound associated with them that let the player know exactly who was around and what they’re currently doing. Also, for some baffling reason, they did reuse the “monster spotted player” effect from original DOOM, but it’s now used for “monster idling”. Not only does this make no sense (the monster stands around constantly roaring) but it’s needlessly confusing for players of the original DOOM.And on the topic of monsters, the new CGI sprites really don’t look great, with them often looking like they’re made from clay. Which is rather ironic, since a number of the monster sprites in original DOOM were digitized photos of actual clay models. The animation also looks stiff, and the monsters don't move very much. Which is again, ironic, since a number of original DOOM’s monster sprites were based on clay models. In conclusion, while DOOM 64 is based on classic DOOM’s DNA, which should make it an awesome game, the changes they decided to make hurt the game more than they improve it. And I don’t think that’s simply me as a “boomer shooter” pish-poshing because they changed stuff from how it was in classic DOOM. As I said at the beginning of my review, these changes feel like they were made by focusing on the weaker aspects of classic DOOM, which is the exact wrong way to go about improving on a game. Maybe if you’ve never played any of the original DOOM games and you were unaware of these differences, your experience with DOOM 64 might not be tarnished. I’ve heard the game is popular with people who never played any of the original games. If that’s you, by all means! Try the game out, you might love it! But fans of the original DOOM probably won’t be head-over-heels for DOOM 64. It’s worth playing for one final serving of a game that’s pretty similar to classic DOOM (I finished the game after all) but overall, I felt the game was a disappointment, that was far more steps backwards than it was forwards.

_childDocuments_.review: It isn't per se a bad game (it's not excellent either), however we are talking about the best video game saga of all time, so it's impossible to overlook some unforgivable errors on this horrendous port:- Terrible optimization. This is a game that was made two decades ago, and in spite of this it suffers from stuttering and some sluggishness. Besides, the pace being so slow compared to previous Doom entries doesn't help either.- Turning left/right feels weird. It isn't a smooth movement experience. You may experience motion sickness due to this, because it's as if the movement is delayed.- You can't look up/down. Purist players defend this decision by stating that some levels depend on your character not being able to look freely (i.e. some switches need to be shot from a certain balcony, for instance), but the level design should've been updated accordingly.- Terrible demon animations that should've been improved. In some cases these stiff animations produce an Uncertainty Valley effect, but here it only affects immersion, and they feel less threatening and a bit boring to fight, even on higher difficulties.- Until you get to the menu, you will have to wait almost a minute. Five logos (which in a recent patch you can skip, at least), a photosensitive warning, an animated introduction, and a "Start" button. It's too much.- The wait doesn't end there, as you'll have to wait a second after pressing every button in the menu. It should be an immediate response!- Dismal control configuration. The menu switches all the time and you have to change the key bindings keeping this in mind. Also, the key binding for Weapon 4 is broken, and it has never been fixed so far.It has been two years since this game was released on PC, and given how things look, apparently all these issues won't be addressed, so if you're a Doom fan looking to complete the Doom experience, you'll have to exercise some patience to deal with these annoying inconveniences.In one word, it's a poor and lazy port by Nightdive Studios, which inevitably leads to disappointment and, in some cases, frustration. I finished the game, but I decided I won't be coming back to find the secret levels, as I don't think the experience will be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Few franchises can boast Doom’s staying power, at least on PC. You’ve got your  (1993) and , both of which feel fun and fresh to play even today. On the other hand,  (2016) and  did for boomer shooters what  and  did for first-person horror walking simulators back in the day – meaning, everyone’s doing it now! Honestly, it seems like in whichever generation a couple of Doom games crop up, they can’t help but be massively influential and universally praised.Sure, there was a lull in there that lasted for, what, a decade? A bit more? But even , as polarizing as it was to cause it, was regarded as a success by critics and, if anything, a decent survival-horror experience by fans. Its departure from the fast, run-and-gun style of gameplay that boomer shooters are known for – and even more so in recent years – was disappointing to many, but honestly? I feel like Id Software did the right thing by not continuing down that road; not until they were prepared for some more innovation, at least.  Released back in 1997 and developed by the now-defunct Midway Games,  wasn’t just a port of the smash hit to Nintendo’s console, but somewhat of a re-imagining as well. Most notable – and this is what you’ll frequently see the game praised for – is the oppressive and claustrophobic atmosphere. No, you aren’t blasting demons with heavy metal music playing in the background. Instead, you’ve got an assortment of ambient tracks, made up of spooky-sounding strings, ominous chanting, and crying babies. Yes, really. Paired with a grittier take on  classic visuals, and gloomy lighting, it allows for the shooter to be played from an entirely different perspective where, in addition to running and gunning, you’ll be carefully crawling through maze-like levels, unnerved to your limits, checking every corner for enemies, where an Imp or a Hell Knight might be lying in wait.It’s amazing how big of a shift in perspective can be achieved with a different soundtrack and some tweaks to what are, essentially, the same assets from the previous titles in the franchise. Some of the enemies and weapons have gotten their sound effects reworked as well, with the new ones being a lot more appropriate. The Chaingun sounds beefy as all living hell, while the Imps no longer screech like a pissed-off donkey.-  😱So, with it being a re-imagining, you won’t be playing through the original lineup of  levels. Instead, you’re offered 31 completely new ones (not counting those unlocked through in-game secrets), taking you through both the heavily industrialized sci-fi bases as well as the labyrinthine depths of Hell. The enemy roster includes most of the enemies from the previous two games (as well as a few surprises that I won’t spoil) while excluding a couple from the second one. In all other things, it’s classic Doom to a fault.When  at its best, you’ll be inching through Hell’s hallways, taking in the ambiance and carefully listening for where danger might lurk; checking corners and bracing yourself every time you open a door. Or, in those areas that are a bit more open (and aren’t under-represented in the game by any means), you’ll be running around, performing the necessary ‘dance’ needed to best each enemy, dodging out of their attacks and swiftly cycling through your arsenal, picking the appropriate weapon from moment to moment as the ever-changing tides of battle force you to mix things up. Need to deal with a bunch of shotgun-wielding zombies before closing in? Gun ‘em down from afar with your Chaingun. Got a couple of hard hitters, like the Mancubus, thrown in there as well? Quickly get your rocket launcher out and blow ‘em up before they can do the same to you. Did a swarm of Lost Souls just spawn in behind you? Swap to your BFG and obliterate them with a single click. This is Doom as you and I know it and love it, even with the movement being somewhat clunky and getting you occasionally stuck on things.The problem is - we’ve been playing Doom for years. We aren’t some kid in the ‘90s who never got a chance to experience it previously because it was not released on their console of choice. We’ve already played the best it has to offer, and I don’t think a change in perspective, a new weapon, and a bunch of fresh, but mostly unremarkable maps are enough to not make  a bit redundant. Add on to that the fact of there being no modding support, and you’ve got yourself the most dated, albeit most faithful to the original experience, game in the series.  There are other things that frustrate me, but these might be either unreasonable to hold against a game this old or too much dependent upon personal preference; like the way sprites turn with the camera. What I wouldn’t give for some voxels, as it’d save me from having to look at Imp ass every time a dead one enters my field of view. Or how there’s no way to zoom out on the map, making it useless for finding your way around unless you just want to consult it regarding your immediate surroundings. Sure, you don’t need it to find your way around, but my guess is that I’d have saved plenty of time hunting for door switches if it was actually usable. And don’t get me started on some of the traps there are that can cause nearly unavoidable, cheap deaths. Pfft! Oh, and the Lost Soul? It’s not okay. It attacks too fast and the time of its pre-attack phase is like half a frame! We can’t keep pretending that it’s this one enemy that’s just annoying to deal with, but still cute in a certain ‘love to hate it’ kind of way. It is not okay!!! And the fact that it can deal damage even when it’s above you, where you can’t hit it, because each entity’s hitbox extends infinitely upwards? Ugh!  I felt like I was done by level 17, which is a bit more than halfway through a game that took me almost 20 hours to beat on the second-highest difficulty, ‘I Own Doom’ (because I do, it says so in my library). The repetitiveness of fighting the same enemies over and over while not changing up the level design philosophy that much had gotten to me. After all, I can’t hunt around forever for door switches, keys, and the doors those switches opened. It should also be kept in mind that it’s possible to mod the entirety of  into , with all the other quality-of-life benefits modding can provide, such as vertical mouse look (and voxels). So, maybe, unless you’re looking for a curated, “true-to-the-nineties” experience, or just want to showcase some achievements on your profile, then sit this one out? If you just want to play a classic Doom game, or just want more classic Doom, you can get that elsewhere.  I get that muddies my recommendation a little bit – but It’s still a recommendation, more so for the qualities  inherits from the previous Doom titles and then the way it applies its own charms to them, than those charms alone.

_childDocuments_.review: So - first of all. If your question is: Is this any good? The answer is a resounding: HELL YEAH!But first - the bad parts:- Intro:When you start it up there's just 45 (!) seconds of videos which you cannot skip. And that is before the actual intro which is 55 seconds that you can luckily skip. So, if I wanna play just for a short period of 10 minutes or so this wastes basically 10% of my time.EDIT: You can just kill the video folder which reduces the loading by a whooping 40 seconds down to 5!- :The very first thing I see after the intro is an error from . I haven't asked the game anything besides starting it and it already has a connection issue. I didn't even tell it to connect! What the hell?- Key bindings:I played like and hour or so and wondered why I was moving so slow when I considered myself running. Turns out - I wasn't running! To run you need to press space bar (instead of shift) and to use you press E (instead of shift). So - not even does it seem there's no way to easily get the original layout back, I also cannot change it to shift for running! And to top it of - the menu is so confusing because the display constantly toggles between current keyboard and current controller bindings, so it's extra hard to read what your keys are right now.EDIT: After starting it again a couple of times it finally seems to work. In case it doesn't for you - you can also manually set "speed" to lshift in the config file for the game.- Sometimes an enemy standing on a lower level can block you going down even if you cannot see. _childDocuments_.review: Back in 1997, DOOM 64 was surrounded by 2 blockbusters: Quake which was already rocking, and GoldenEye 007 which was a few months away. What exacerbated the competition more, was its repression due to N64's unpopularity and insubstantial capabilities; back then, this made people not batting an eye on the new sequel of DOOM—there is a reason for calling this game the DOOM game you've never played. As a matter of fact, it is the only DOOM game that was not developed by ID Software but was made under their supervision by Midway Studios. Nearly 23 years later, Nightdive Studios bought this relic into life for DOOM fans to rip and tear in HD.As a DOOM game, it stays loyal to the tradition by including a plot to fill the space. The entire story is presented through cool text on different slides between some levels after completing them; the game doesn't go far from the classic narration of stories in video games. In short, there are no twists or anything interesting that can capture the player's attentiveness. Anyway, who cares! It's a DOOM game, where your shotgun is the story and its bullets are the twists.Armed with a ruinous armament, all the player has to do is kill everything first and kill everything later. The customary is well-preserved in DOOM 64 by having the same mechanics as the originals. In terms of brutality, it stands on a higher stage compared to its predecessors. The Unmaker is a new weapon in DOOM 64 that fires laser beams and shares ammo with the BFG9000 and the Plasma Rifle. The weapon has 3 artifacts that the player can collect to unlock its full potential. Piece of advice, be sure to know the exact levels that have the artifacts, as if you miss an artifact, you have to go back to that level where you missed it to collect it and move on from that particular level again.The main theme of DOOM 64 levels lean toward being dark, atmospheric, and grim. It blindly follows the same route as the originals in terms of level design; in contrast, they only differ in the main theme. Low resources in the game are well-utilized by dispensing brilliant map designs in addition to adding distinguishing combos of strategically allocated enemies with bosses to plummet the boredom factor. There isn't a genuine level select option in the menu, but there is a hidden level called Hectic; after completing this level the proper way, a new option will unlock in the main menu of the game called the Features Menu. This option unlocks all the levels of the game, all maps, all weapons/ammo, and all cheats.The preponderance of replayability in DOOM 64 is in digging secrets, playing hidden maps, and finding Easter Eggs. In the re-release, Nightdive Studios included a set of missions called The Lost Levels; these levels act as a link between DOOM 64 and DOOM 2016. Including a multiplayer mode or any other new mode could've remarkably pumped up the replay value, especially that this is a repackage. An option of showcasing the player's progress within the game instead of the temporary one we get after completing a level would've been great. Lastly, I don't see any excuse for the limited save slots.True-hearted fans of DOOM 64 did their best through modding and emulating to bring it under the radar; their remarkable effort was enough for it to run on other platforms but was inadequate in optimizing it. Thanks to Nightdive Studios, DOOM 64 runs on modern hardware in HD like a cutting knife in a block of butter. A vital handicap in the original release is the dim lighting; the player can hardly see anything in certain areas of the game. In the re-release, the illumination is improved; however, the player may need to crank up the brightness in some parts of the game.I like the nostalgic control scheme of FPS classics, despite it being weird. For those who aren't familiar with this style, in brief, the vertical movement of the weapon is restrained, and the player must rely on the protagonist's movements to have the enemies in range. By words, this sounds arduous, but in action, it's a lot better. I can assuredly say that the controls are very fluid and perfectly abolish most of the drawbacks of the aforementioned control style. Sadly, navigation can get a bit irritating in tight situations, especially while doing timed, pitch-perfect platforming. I find the key-bindings option in the menu vexatious; the reason for this is the unification of gamepad and keyboard controls in the same menu.Due to N64 hardware limitations, the turning wheel got stuck in terms of visual aggrandizement. this lead to the diminution of DOOM 64 among the ambitious titles in that time. The irony is that nowadays, this serves the game quite well in terms of triggering a wistful smile by presenting retro graphics through HD display. The visual style in DOOM 64 sway away from being DOOM to being Quake; it has the foundation of DOOM and the tone of Quake—this may upset some fans. Fortunately, its gory and dark visuals serve its atmospheric setting.The sound design in DOOM 64 doesn't differ a lot from its predecessors but with minor enhancements like hearing empty shells hitting the ground after firing the shotgun despite the missing animations of reloading the super shotgun and cocking the ordinary one. Also, new enemies come with their unique sounds. To match the creepy environment and increase the bone-chilling factor, DOOM 64 soundtrack took a different path from the heavy metal style to a more ambient approach.The re-release of DOOM 64 is set to be a sterling example of experiencing the past in HD. After being free from the chains holding it in the Nintendo's exclusivity, it's a decent opportunity to have the complete collection and the total experience of the DOOM universe. Sadly, some aging wrinkles of DOOM 64 were hard to patch by Nightdive Studios. In summation, they did a splendid job!

_childDocuments_.review: As a general rule, the series DOOM has a fondness for Deathmatch, and I recall back in 1994, being in the Sixth Grade of Elementary School (where does all the time go), getting ripped apart by other more experienced gamers at Deathmatch. I eventually got better somewhat, and when Quake later came along, I tried my hands at Deathmatch via Quake, and found I was out of my element. As a result, while I'm fond of Deathmatch, I'm not fiercely devoted to Deathmatch, because I suck at Deathmatch. Now as a core fundamental of the series in general, how does Doom 64 get away with not having... Deathmatch?A minor history lesson before my review continues, is that DOOM 64 was developed by Midway Software in 1997, and released for the Nintendo 64. It wasn't that Midway decided "No Deathmatch allowed", it was hardware limitations and various software issues to work through during it's development phase. Coupled with Nintendo wanting a DOOM game for it's flagship console, Midway was hard pressed to deliver a product in a timely manner. Wonder why you don't see enemies like the Arch-Vile, the Chaingunner, or the Spider Mastermind? Tight production schedule. Interesting note, had DOOM 64 "2" been greenlit, Midway was absolutely dedicated to producing a Multiplayer aspect for that game, but poor sales of DOOM 64 shot down that idea.Cons about the game? Aside from the crippling lack of deathmatch, the game is very dark in certain levels, and you might be adjusting the brightness or gamma for said levels. As for paltry issues like graphics, I'm not going to downgrade the game for that issue. Again, the game was manufactured for the Nintendo 64, back in 1997, so if you want good graphics, may I recommend both DOOM 2016 and DOOM Eternal. You also might desire more from the Enemy's AI as compared to later DOOM games, but you might find monster infighting a life saver on higher difficulty modes when you're trying to conserve ammo.Pros about DOOM 64? You have most of the classic enemies out for your blood, cramped fighting in tight quarters, and some fairly awesome music for a DOOM game. It's not on level of Mick Gordon's work, but Aubrey Hodges made some fantastic dark ambient music for this soundtrack, and his music for DOOM and Final DOOM on the Playstation was equally haunting, if you're a fan of video game soundtracks, definitely buy his work on Bandcamp. One nice additional feature is the caveat of saving more often, as with the Nintendo 64, you had two ways of saving, via Passwords, or via a Memory Card. Could you save during the levels? No, and there was nothing more infuriating than being obliterated by Cyberdemons in the level "No Escape", and having to start the WHOLE LEVEL all over again. As a personal challenge, I try not to save often, but sometimes it just can't be helped.Rating for Doom 64? I'd give it a solid 8/10, and I can't give it a 10 in all fairness because of the lack of Deathmatch. Again, I don't lay the blame with Midway Software, it's sort of on Nintendo for being pushy, but it was a glorious chance for Id Software to have their flagship series on a Nintendo Console. Times have changed since 1997, but this game is better than ever. Buy it!

_childDocuments_.review: This is arguably the most atmospheric and genuinely creepy version of DOOM-- the stellar ambience & killer sound design earned it the nickname MOOD 64 back in the day. This port has the original campaigns in all their sprite-based glory and it runs extremely well, no frame dips or stuttering and there's no input lag at all. There's also a "lost" episode in addition to the originals and they are no joke on the highest difficulty setting so if you're looking to revisit a classic or try it out for the first time you should still find some novelty. In terms of difficulty: this is about on par with later DOOM II levels, though a big part of that is the more advanced scripting used-- there are some unconventional puzzles / mechanics that were never seen in the originals. On the highest default difficulty the challenge really ramps up after only a few levels and a big part of that is the sheer volume of hard mobs the game throws at you. There are quite a few tough maps in the original campaign but the lost levels are often significantly harder in general (the very first level is a good primer-- the whole campaign is roughly as tough), think Thy Flesh Consumed on UV but thankfully the pacing rarely gets quite as hectic-- this isn't Plutonia level hard but it's definitely not always easy.My only real complaint is that having some cut content re-added / finished (the Revenant, Archvile and heavy weapons guy were all scrapped in the original release because of space limitations on the Nintendo 64 cartridges) would have been perfect and really enhanced the original version. That and having some quality of life changes you come to expect on PC like mouse free-look would have been nice. That being said, this is the definitive official release and DOOM64 never looked or played better.It's not quite as refined as some modded projects but hey, it's an official port and is a perfect lead-in for DOOM 2016 / Eternal. It's also pretty cheap and legitimately gets you the WAD file if you want to look at some of the excellent PC DOOM64 mod projects.Solid 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: OK, first things first, yes it IS annoying that the game has 45 seconds of unskippable company logos every time it starts up, but if that's the ONLY reason you have to give it a negative review, you need to harden the [BLEEP] up because you're clearly too much of a [BLEEP] for this game anyway. (The same goes for it prompting you to log into a  account, which you can simply ignore. Grow up.)Anyway, this is the REAL Doom III. Now I unironically love the actual Doom 3 and think it totally holds up even today, but THIS is the real follow-up to Doom II: Hell On Earth. The original sprites have been redesigned and cleaned up, the graphics engine is better-looking than ever, the moody horror soundtrack creates a totally different tone to the frenetic rocking-out of the originals while still maintaining the pulse-racing violent blasting action, and the level design is simply SUPERB, with all-new tricks and traps filling the sprawling, open-ended levels with monsters lurking around every corner. The original N64 release was somewhat hampered by the control scheme and the graphics being a bit TOO murky to see properly, but this magnificent remastering has ironed out all the issues to result in quite possibly the best classic Doom game ever (let's face it, it certainly has the best final stage and end boss of the 3 original games, even if a fully-powered Unmaker renders it an anticlimax). The new expansion campaign is the cherry on top, with possibly the biggest and best levels of all.I actually think I may like Doom 64 slightly MORE than Doom 2016, which tended to confine its action to predetermined arena battling too much for my liking. I certainly played it more after I finally acquired both games at roughly the same time. It's a testament to how great the original Doom games were, and how they were able to launch an entire genre of gaming, with Doom 64 being the most-polished crowning jewel of the classic series. An absolute must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: Contrary to popular belief Doom 64 isn't an N64 port of the original Doom, this game is actually a full on sequel, taking place directly after the events of Doom 2 with a completely new campaign, so in a way Doom 64 is the true Doom 3. Doom 64 feels a lot like Doom 2, but with a complete graphics overhaul. Instead of the bright colorful look Doom 2 had, they went for more of a dark and gritty look, in some ways the game resembles Quake more than it does Doom to be honest. Gameplay is nearly identical to Doom 2 however but there is a new weapon added to the mix, an alternative to the BFG called the "Unmaker", and it's pretty fun to use.The soundtrack and general atmosphere is completely different too, there's no actual music within levels anymore, instead you'll be hearing creepy ambient tracks as you walk down dimly lit corridors, Doom 64 has an atmosphere that feels like something out of a horror game, and I kinda dig it. If you like Doom 2 chances are you'll like Doom 64 as well, there's also a brand new episode added in with this version of the game and I think it's worth picking up for that alone.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was made for the Nintendo 64 in the 90s.  Doom 64 takes place after the events of Doom 2, in which all the monsters you have previously killed have begun to rise once again because of the Mother Demon.  You fight through 28 maps in hell in order to kill the mother and stop the resurgence of demons.  The story is very simple and easy to follow which is great in my opinion.  The game play is extremely fast-paced and leaves little to no room for competent techniques or strategies.  The graphics for this game looks nice, but I personal don't like the overly detailed and grittier look of the maps and demons.  Overall, the game is simple to understand with fast-paced game play which leaves no room for mistakes to be made.  If I were to recommend this game to anyone, I would also prefer you play the Doom 1 and 2 beforehand, to get a sense of what you are getting into.

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty decent and no-frills port of Doom 64 for the PC. If you don't want to muck about trying to find a rom-dump of the original Nintendo 64 version to play one of the old faithful source ports (such as Doom 64 EX) then this is probably your best bet for experiencing the game.I would definitely recommend picking this title up if you enjoy retro shooters, especially at a mere 5 USD price tag, as it is unlike any of the other classic Doom games. The gunplay is still great, but the atmosphere and music are more horror-focused, along with some complex and puzzle-filled levels. I am a bit spoiled from Brutal Doom 64 (I can already hear the purists screeching) from all of the modern niceties (such as mouse look and auto-save at level start) and cut content it adds to the game, but the original still holds up well enough on its own.It should also be noted this port comes with a bonus mini-campaign (The Lost Levels) which tries to bridge this game's plot to Doom 2016, which is one of the more compelling reasons to spring for this offering over the old fan-made ports.

_childDocuments_.review: This port is just utter garbage.👎 High input latency. That alone makes it outright unplayable on my PC (and no, a Ryzen+RTX notebook is not too underpowered to play a 25 years old N64 game smoothly).👎 A series of annoying intro movies that don't skip by pressing any key or button. I know about "-skipmovies" or deleting the movie files but that's undocumented behavior. By default it's hostile towards the gamer.👎 YOU CAN'T UNBIND KEYS/BUTTONS! Sure, you can assign a new action to a key or button in the options but the existing one will not be cleared, meaning more and more actions will be stacked onto a single key.Prepare to edit "Saved Games\Nightdive Studios\DOOM 64\kexengine.cfg" in a text editor by hand like a cave man.👎 In-game localized keyboard layouts are respected, in the menus they are not. Don't even bother trying to figure out the difference beween US layout and your localized one because of the unbinding problem. Edit kexengine.cfg.👎 No modern texture filtering techniques, not even optionally. The original graphics were made with the N64's native resolution and CRT TVs in mind where the screen itself does interpolation work just through the way CRTs work. Low-res sprites and textures with bilinear filtering aged like fresh milk in the sun when viewing them on modern PC screens at HD resolutions.Luckily there is least an option to turn texture filtering off for a sharper, pixelated look that works way better with modern screens. I know modern texture filtering would be "not authentic to the original" but that argument can go were the sun doesn't shine. Intro movies, , etc. are "not authentic to the original" either and those made it in!👎 No way to use one of the many community-made source ports like GZDoom with this game to remedy the negatives stated above (at least at time of writing).Absolution and Brutal Doom 64 are mods for Doom 2, not for this. So yeah, if you want a better way to play Doom 64 on your PC, buy Doom 2 and follow one of the many guides how to replace this port with GZDoom + Doom 2 + Absolution or Brutal Doom 64 (I prefer the latter).The heartbreaking part about the port is that the game itself is amazing but the Bethesda/Nightdive release is not the way to experience it.Just don't buy this individually. If you got it as part of a bundle, follow a guide to replace this game with Brutal Doom 64 v2.5. At least you get Steam Overlay and playtime tracking.

_childDocuments_.review: I have no nostalgia for DOOM 64 and apart from watching some speedruns, i have no firsthand experience in the classic DOOM games. My review will be focused on if DOOM 64 is worth playing today for people who are completely new to the series. And my short answer is absolutely yes.While the DOOM series is kind of misrepresented as a mindless shooter on the internet, the thought provoking level designs that need thinking to progress makes me think quite the opposite for the series. DOOM 64 is a perfect example of show, don't tell. It never directly tells you what you have to do but levels hide clever indicators that guide you towards the right path. This results in a lot of "Eureka" moments that makes the player feel smart.There are 28 levels with varying degrees of quality. Some make total sense and feel fun to play while the others are literal mazes that are complete nightmares to navigate. Gameplay is as expected super solid. You can't look up and down which might seem like a problem for some but you get used to it very quickly. It also doesn't ammo starve you as much as the newer games which i actually think is the better approach depending on the difficulty. Apart from that i must mention the difficulty apart from the last boss was perfect. To expand the topic, the last boss is completely garbage. This would be the biggest con of DOOM 64. It's a sudden massive spike in difficulty and straight up an unfair fight. For the performance and the look of the game, i think the enhanced version does a great job at making it look and play modern. All in all, DOOM 64 is a solid retro shooter that every fan of the genre must at least give a shot. Though don't forget to take some breaks in between every couple of levels since the game can be a bit fatiguing.

_childDocuments_.review: i don't know why this game has such a stupid horror atmosphere that feels nothing like the original 2. in the first 2 there's badass music playing in the background and everything is taken surface level. you're just a badass dude killing demons for daisy's sake. in doom 64 even the music is just ambient horror sounds. visually it's mostly a downgrade from the original 2 in terms of environmental textures. even the actual character sprites themselves feel off with even those not feeling like they're the same monsters in the original 2 (this is especially the case with pinkys/demons). even the shotgun sucks since you can't even see it being loaded like in the original 2. it just bobs up and down. i don't like doom 64. maybe that'll change the more i play it, but after playing the first 2, it feels like a horror centric clone as opposed to a lore sequel, and i cant wait to move on to 2016 and eternal.u: after playing this game a bit more it has grown on me, but i'm still not a fan and think most of the things mentioned above  are still valid. additionally, as a linux gamer, the experience of playing this game in proton was much worse than the original 2 with constant crashing, or the game just outright refusing to launch. i still wouldnt recommend this game to people, but i'd play it if i had to (assuming it actually ended up working)u: after a lot more consideration and playtime my issue with this game stems from the artstyle and gameplay. DOOM 64 feels like a slog to go through level by level. part of that goes hand in hand with difficulty and level design. many of my points still do stand, but of there were a neutral option, i'd opt for that rather than outright no. i think it's about what you look for in a doom game.

_childDocuments_.review: It is definetly a game that any doom fan should try out and just anyone that likes boomer shooters, it's a "forgotten" doom game from an older console.Besides the main missions, you also have a bunch of secret missions as well as some "lost missions" which were maps that weren't originally released, but has now been included as extra.the general atmosphere of the game is more remniniscent of doom 3 than 1 or 2, which is quite noticeable in the soundtrack.It fits the dark and gloomy atmosphere, but you kinda start to miss the metal rifs that doom is so known for.This also translates into the gameplay, as it feels a bit slower, both in movement and weapon change, perhaps also in shooting, but i might be wrong on the last one.it has a lot more focus on puzzles and other types of switches and activations than the other games, which further makes it more unique.Missions overall are a bit hit or miss, but they're not terrible.it still feels like a classic doom game, in that you can still get quite lost in the maps despite having a map, and the infamous "you've activated a switch, what it activated we don't tell ya, so you have to find it yourself"It is a bit edgy in the writing, but it is whatever, you're here to shoot stuff, the story is secondary and rather forgetable.Definetly not better than the other doom games, but still an easy recommmend

_childDocuments_.review: Although I recently just got Doom 64, I do recommend it. Graphically, it's an interesting take on what came before and it does retain the classic Doom style in some ways. One thing to note if you're interested in playing it is that the system requirements are not entirely indicative of what's needed to play it, as you can play it with less that 8GB and it's only 90-ish megabytes to install. Since it's a recent port, it has features that make it run quite well on modern systems and the controls can be configured easily.EDIT: I finally started playing it seriously for the first time this week on Bring It On!, and it's just as good as any other of the old school Doom games but with moody lighting and music. The levels looked and felt good to play, except for a few confusing ones that came up here and there. Most of the gameplay from classic Doom is still there while still feeling like a different experience due to the lighting and the mostly new (new for 1997) textures and objects, etc. If you're not familiar with Doom 64, there are Demon Keys hidden in some levels that you definitely should find to power up the "demon deleter" or the "Unmaker" (Unmakyr, if you're familiar with Doom Eternal). This makes the end boss, the Mother Demon much easier. Though you can use the BFG as always if you didn't find the keys, it does enough damage to work. There was also a new episode made for the port by Kaiser, who at one point created an unofficial port of Doom 64 and developed the KEX engine framework that eventually led to this official port. "The Lost Levels" feel like they belong in Doom 64 and play just as well as the main campaign does, but you are required to find the Demon Keys in the final level in order to fight the Sister Resurrector. So you will have the fully-powered Unmaker to fight her with, and you can take out everything else in the level beforehand to make the boss fight less hectic. I have yet to try these out, but there are community-made expansions you can find for a fresh experience. The Unmaking is one of these, being a 40-map megawad. And there's Doom 64 Reloaded as well.But I'd say Doom 64 is well worth the price and more, and it's part of the canonical Doom timeline these days. (Doom, Doom 2, Doom 64, Doom 2016, and Doom Eternal are all canon)
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended! Great controls! No source port needed!I never played this when it originally came out for the Nintendo 64, even though I still have my N64. I wish I had gotten this game back then. I don't know why or how I ignored it, after all I played the Doom and Quake games during high school in the mid to late 90's. $5 for this is amazing! I think it's worth more than that. If you enjoyed the Doom and Quake games during the 90's, you should definitely check this out, if you haven't already. I've been re-playing the Doom classic games recently and this is the first of them that I don't have to recommend using a source port, granted you can still use Doom 64 EX with the .WAD you get from this. The game doesn't really have a soundtrack, mostly just ambiance. It's good, but the original Doom games had soundtracks or music playing, which was cool. I'm not incredibly disappointed though. I really like that this game performs well and the keyboard and mouse controls are smooth and right on. I modified the key bindings a bit as I was more used to the original controls (I like using Left Shift to run). This is great and I think any fan of the series would definitely like this. Also note that the game uses a password system, so you could input passwords and unlock cheats, other levels, and other features, so check out the guides section or Google Doom 64 cheats and passwords.

_childDocuments_.review: THE GOOD:The shooty-shooty-bang-bangGreat level designSometimes downright creepy musicGreat weaponsTHE BAD:"New" weapons and monsters are 99% re-skinsStory, as ever in old-skool DOOM, is non-existent and you get nowt but a single screen for your troubles upon completionTHE UGLY:Well...it's not a bad looking game as such, with somewhat crisper and more detailed sprites than the previous games. But NightDive Studios doesn't seem to have done anything in the way of upgrading the textures or image quality. This is a pretty bare-bones port, which is reflected in the lower price.OVERALL:I had a lot of fun with this. The game-play is pretty simple but very refined, and the level layouts can be pleasantly tricky. It's more of the same really, as the redesigned demons and weapons only add visual variety to the familiar mechanics.It can be tense, and the shooting and the gore is satisfying. One of the later levels has some of the most pant-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ music I think I've ever heard, it really is quite unsettling. It would have been perfect for the oppressive visual atmosphere of DOOM 3.  For the price it has a decent amount of content, so, all in all, I can recommend it for some enjoyably thoughtless mass slaughter.If you found this review to be helpful then why not check out my curator page here:

_childDocuments_.review: If you ever saw Doom 64 back in the day and overlooked it due to the countless ports of Doom on home consoles, guess again. Doom 64 is no mere port. It's frankly not a port at all. Doom 64 was a completely original game for the series that for over 20 years never made it's way to PC. At least not officially. Doom 64 retains the classic corridor shooting, demon infested, keycard grabbing goodness that you would see in Doom 1 and 2, with newer sprites to the enemies, colors that pop more, and an overall cleaner look to just about everything. and Nightdive managed to make it look even better. And also some great new features like Widescreen and even Ultrawide support, and jumping from the original hardcoded 35fps to now 60 frames per second for a much smoother experience. It also works great whether you're a keyboard warrior or want to keep it old school with a controller. Works amazing on the Steam Deck too. There's not much else to say here. If you've played Doom 1 or 2, this is going to feel right at home for you. For a crisp fiver this is an A+ port of the game that was originally never a port.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This is a cool game. It's Doom, after all. I love the atmosphere and unsettling sound design. I was legitimately frightened at times - and that doesn't happen to me often in games. It's neat to see how this game is a perfect bridge between the design and gameplay of the original Doom games and the later Doom 3.I will say, though, that I did NOT enjoy the so-called "Lost Levels" (very misleading, since they were developed decades after the OG game for this release). Features includes cheap/annoying enemy placement, confusing level layouts, lots of running around as you try to solve obtuse puzzles, WAY too many beefy enemies in tiny spaces, and more. There is a noticeable decrease in quality compared to the original campaign. I hate to say "they don't make 'em like they used to," but level design was pretty dope back in the day. I suppose it was somewhat worth it for the tiny bit of lore at the end.Anyway, the majority of the game is a blast, and you should definitely play it if you're a Doom fan. Plus, the price is super cheap. This was the only main Doom game I hadn't played yet, so it was well worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: People keep saying it's some sort of "forgotten cult classics" and stuff.You know - maybe there are reasons it is "forgotten". Don't get me wrong - it's still DooM and more DooM is always welcome. There are certain problems with 64 though. Pretty serious problems.Do you remember monsters from classic? Pixelated they were nonetheless hellishly elegant both in looks and animations. There was weight in all of their movements. Why-oh-why did they changed the design for 64? Say what you want - the game is ugly. Fight me on that, I dare you. The engine was upgraded, yes. Now it can do 3D bridges and colored lights. Skyboxes were redone. And with all these possibilities for God only knows why, 64 is dark, brown and look more like Quake 1 in terms of both color and level design. And not in a good way.Same goes to gameplay. 64 has some built-in scripting system that allows more tricks (yes and traps too). This is good, right? Well, yes. At the same time everything became slower. And I can't say it's a complement. They nerfed the BFG! Can you imagine that?As for the music and level design... Well, there are some undoubtedly cool moments in levels. Overall it's mostly "castles in water full of hellknights". Music... Someone on youtube commented one of the tracks for then upcoming Eternal as "It's just noise". 64's OST is noise. Literally. One could say it's atmospheric ambient. Yeah, on a technical level... Sort of. You know what? Quake 1 did the same trick and did it so much better.Why recommend then? There's a certain charm in 64. It's ugly, slow, basically has no music, castle themed but still charming for some reason. It's "forgotten classic" not because of the platfrom it was released on back in the days or unfitting name. It has problems. It's still DooM. And it would take extreme effort to really break the DooM formula.

_childDocuments_.review: So this was originally on the Nintendo 64, eh? Curious how well the hyper fast combat of oldschool DOOM translated to that console with the kind esoteric controller it has (still love that system regardless).Glad this game got a proper official port onto PC. Before people had to resort to N64 ROMhacks if they wanted to play it with a keyboard and mouse. Of course I didn't touch the original console version nor the ROMhacks, so my only impression of DOOM 64 is through this PC port. Gameplay wise it doesn't spew as many demons at you as DOOM and DOOM 2, which I think was due to the memory limit of the original console it ran on. Still felt fun despite that, and the difficulty felt right all the way through (Always play on Ultra-Violence). Enemy variety and behaviour is pretty much the same as previous classic DOOMs, but the Revenant, Cacodemon, and Archvile aren't present. There's the Specter version of the Imp though.What makes this version of DOOM unique in comparison to other versions of DOOM is not only the unique artstyle, soundscape, and level design, but also an original unlockable weapon called the Unmakyr (Replaces the BFG and makes an reappearance in DOOM Eternal) and a final boss named the Mother Demon. The Unmakyr can be upgraded throughout the game by finding Demon Keys hidden in various levels, eventually turning into a souped-up plasma gun. The Demon Keys also act as locks for the final boss level, making the fight slightly easier to get through, which I find to be lovely incentive to explore each level for secrets.Really enjoyed the unique artstyle and sound design of DOOM 64. It helped to make this game feel distinct from the other DOOMs. Level design is similar to DOOM and DOOM 2 in which everything could be made in its engine, but DOOM 64 made interesting use of enemy layout and rising and falling platforms not seen in the OGs. Gets my respect for that.Had a blast playing all 39 levels this re-release had to offer. Played it blind the first time without finding any Demon Keys, so the final boss was quite a pain to beat alongside the horde of demons that spawned alongside it. Had to look up a walkthrough to find them on my 2nd playthrough as well as the secret levels. So if you're looking to scratch that classic DOOM itch with new visuals and levels; this is it.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: The last classic Doom game, with a new art direction and a much more creepy tone. Gone is the fast tempo music to blast away hordes with. The new ambient and creepy sounding music really reels you into the scary nature of this game. Sadly with the limited power of the N64 there isn't as much variety as the other classic games, but it still is a very immersive experience. The difficulty is also toned down due in part to again the N64 not being able to handle as many entities on screen so that means less enemy numbers. But there are a few new tricks and content exclusive to this game that makes it stand out from the other classics, as well as a pretty interesting final boss fight.Using mods to upscale the game and graphics isn't required thankfully, as this is a newly released remaster of the original game. However, there are a few really good modded versions, such as Doom 64 CE, that I'd suggest installing for the extra maps and enhancements that really push this game to the limit. If you're planning on completing the game with all achievements, I'm not sure if using a modded version breaks/disables them, but I ran vanilla until finishing them just to be safe. Play the vanilla game and then come back with the modded game for the extra maps and content.64 is a nice transition into the modern doom games and it's definitely worth a look. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: An overlooked gem that is finally given another chance in the spotlight.  Dark, moody atmosphere, helped greatly by its ambient soundtrack; fantastic map designs with engine tricks not seen in previous commercial Doom games; and to top it off, a sense of polish that makes the game feel much better than its N64 incarnation.  Most say this is the REAL Doom 3, and after finally giving it a shot, I'm inclined to agree.  Highly recommended, especially if you're a Doom fan.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: What else can be said about arguably the most underrated Doom entry in it's highly influential & prolific franchise? Gotta love the added additions to it's arsenal, darkly atmospheric soundtrack, & completely addicting game-play. Missed this classic in it's original N64 glory but better late than never to play a certified classic.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best source port of DOOM 64 I have played.Story takes place after DOOM II (or Final DOOM if you count that as canon) and ties in to DOOM 2016.DOOM 64 itself is literally DOOM II put in a scarier aesthetic with more realistic graphics, revamped animations and sounds.One new weapon is introduced in this game:-Unmaker (you unlock through secret levels)Two new monsters:-Nightmare Imp (a transparent faster variant of a normal imp)-Mother Demon (Sister Resurrector in the bonus episode)There are a few demons missing in this game however but after you play the game, you realize that they didn't need to be there.Missing Demons being:-Arch-Vile-Revenant-Heavy Weapon Dude-Spider MastermindIf you love anything DOOM or always wanted to properly play DOOM 64 without the N64 console itself, I highly recommend this.Nightdive Studios did a wonderful job porting this game to modern audiences!
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the classic Doom games (Doom 1, Doom 2, Final Doom) you'll like this. Great conversion based on the Doom64EX version released for the PC. If you have Doom Builder 64 you can even make your own maps for this. Just be aware there's no vertical mouselook or jump, but that was never in the N64 version either. The keyboard mapping is a bit naff as well until you find the config file.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: It's not blatantly bad or anything like that, but it's a bit off in enough ways that it feels like an imitation of the real deal, which I suppose isn't surprising since it wasn't made by id. The most immediate striking difference is the drab colour palette and  musical style, which immediately reminds me of Quake. I wasn't a fan of that game's look and sound and I feel the same way here, the reason being that they're both going for a foreboding, dread inducing tone. That's fine on paper, but it's totally incongruous with the gameplay style here. This isn't a horror game. I don't care how much diarrhoea graphics and Trent Reznor's sonic ramblings you throw at it, it's fundamentally impossible to make a scary horror game where you play as an armed to the teeth Sonic the Hedgehog, and since it isn't scary, the tone ends up being boring instead. Credit where credit is due, I do appreciate most of the evolution of the sprite design here, particularly the imps and the chainsaw and chaingun.I also think that some of the level and puzzle design is questionable. At times there's a lack of clear cause and effect when you press buttons, there was one or two instances where I ended up solving a puzzle by accident and walked away not knowing what I even did right. There's also a few cheesy traps which more than anything feel like they're just wasting the player's time. The one at the end of level 16 stands out in my memory as being particularly BS. It's definitely a save-scum game if you don't want to be punished too harshly for being a first time player. The saving grace is that they got the run and gun shooting right, I don't really have anything to complain about there. I think this is the glue that holds things together here. Most of my playtime experience has been on the EX version before this came out, but this version does seem quite solid, running and looking great. tl;dr If you're a big doom fan it's at least worth trying, especially when it's deeply discounted and goes for next to nothing. You might like it, but don't get your hopes up about it being some hidden gem or secretly the best of the franchise or anything like that. It's mid at best.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 will guarantee you almost 64 more times you will lose your precious colorful keys on these boring, long and ill-infested demon-like levels. And you will probably never come back to those cursed things. Music is even worse than Trevor Reznik's Quake soundtrack. Unbalanced boss fights. You should get something nice like a necklace for all your pain, or maybe a flashlight for your one and only light source. Or just go back home and drink some wine. All your options are very clear.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 beholds some really crafty game design within that's just captivating in its overall elegant form. It relies on puzzles and backtracking and of course on the good ol' gory action that's just got DOOM marked on its forehead. It's slower paced than its predecessors, but that didn't go to the dogs for the quality of its gameplay, no sir. DOOM 64 is as solid as it can be for a good old fashioned action/shooter game that in a way still has the affinity to shake even the today's gaming standards.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A totally underrated and genuinely spooky entry into the franchise. The dark hallways and ambient, foreboding soundtrack that gives off an almost Silent Hill-esque atmosphere, mixed with the ever classic fast twitch Doom gameplay style makes this a one of a kind entry in this kind of genre. The new, PC exclusive add-on pack isn't bad either, but don't expect any new groundbreaking tricks, as it's more or less just an excuse to tie the classic series in with the newer game's canon.Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64, was my first Doom game and my introduction to the series. Not being much of a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥, I found it highly enjoyable. It's as simple as run and shoot. So purely on a gameplay level, you should definitely try it, it's great fun. Although, on normal difficulty it does not pose much of a challenge until like, the last 3 levels. Most demons are easily killable with a single shotgun blast. So with a few well timed quicksaves so you don't lose your weapons, the game is quite a breeze to playthrough. The last levels are a pain in the ass though (which explains why the achievement one recieves when completing the game is considered a rare achievement). All in all, great fun! Get it on sale, or get the Doom (2016) version on sale, I believe Doom64 comes with it.(Also very well ported, runs great on modern hardware)
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This is absolutely one of the best games ive EVER played!it plays great just like all of the other DOOM games!and this game id say is more unique then the others... it has a different feel to it... and you can tell because of the tone in music they chose!rather then having headbanging badass music... the music is creepy and ominous!the game tries do be more creepy then badass... and I think its a cool change! with the really dark environment and with the creepy music... it just makes you feel uneasy... and thats cool! _childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is a classic Nintendo 64 game that was never “officially” ported to PC (and other consoles) until now. Doom 64 is a follow up to Doom 2. It keeps the same classic Doom gameplay and it brings about some enhancements. Doom 64 has a completely new look and new graphics. It has much more of a creepy, horror look and feel to it. With regards to the music, they went a completely different direction with Doom 64. The previous Doom games (The Ultimate Doom, Doom 2, and Final Doom) had music that was upbeat and good. Doom 64’s music is completely different. The music in Doom 64 is just creepy ambiance music and sounds that are intended to add to the horror of the game. It does fit with the creepy look and feel of the game. Although some players may miss the upbeat music of the previous Doom games. One thing about this official port that some players may not like is that this port does not have mouselook (the player can’t look up or down). The developer said that the reason for this is because in the original Nintendo 64 game, the player couldn’t look up or down. And they wanted this official port to be as faithful to the original Nintendo 64 game as possible. This port has graphical enhancements, sound enhancements, and a higher framerate than the original Nintendo 64 game had. Also, this port comes with a brand new campaign with brand new levels (in addition to the main campaign). So you get the original levels and some new levels too. This official port of Doom 64 is probably the most faithful port of the original Nintendo 64 game that there ever will be. If you played Doom 64 on an actual Nintendo 64 console back in the day, and you want to play it again on PC, I definitely recommend this official port. Yes, there are other ports and mods of Doom 64 available for PC. And they’re good too. I would say that if you’re looking for the port that is the most faithful to the original Nintendo 64 game, I’d go with this one. Doom 64 is a good game and I definitely recommend it
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Kind of a disappointing game for me. As a big fan of DOOM and DOOM II, I was hoping this would essentially be a level pack in an updated version of the engine. Instead, there was a big shift in focus from fast-paced action to obtuse, slow-paced puzzle solving. The originals all had the occasional puzzle, especially if you're hunting for all the secrets, but nothing as frustrating as what DOOM 64 tosses you by the second level. Instead of running around at high speeds, ripping and tearing demons to clear the level and find the exit as fast as possible, you're stumbling around corners trying to avoid different traps so you can hit the right button to open a door *somewhere* on the other side of the map.To its credit, the game looks great, a neat midpoint between the original DOOM games and QUAKE, and the gunplay feels as a good as ever. I'll probably come back to this someday and give it another shot with adjusted expectations, but this is not the hit of DOOM I was needing.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: An overlooked classic that still really holds up. Even if you didn't get it for free with Eternal, it can be had for a song and is worth your time. If you are going to play with a mouse and keyboard, be aware that the game will feel much easier than it did back in the day with the N64 controller. Adjust the difficulty at least one notch over what you would normally play classic doom. Or go ahead and play a PC FPS in 2020 with a controller, I dare you.

_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: The combat mechanics in *Doom 64* feel outdated and clunky, lacking the precision and fluidity that modern players have come to expect. The controls are unwieldy, often making encounters with demons feel more like an exercise in frustration than an adrenaline-fueled battle. Many players have noted the sluggish movement and awkward weapon switching, which can turn a simple firefight into a chaotic mess of missed shots and unnecessary deaths. Instead of the tight, intuitive layouts that made previous *Doom* titles so engaging, *Doom 64* offers sprawling, confusing maps filled with convoluted mazes and obscure keys. You’ll spend more time running in circles trying to figure out where to go next than actually fighting monsters. It feels less like a challenge and more like a punishment for daring to explore. I can only imagine how many players have thrown their controllers in frustration after getting lost in these poorly designed levels. Rather than posing a genuine threat, foes often behave like mindless drones, charging at you with little strategy. The once-feared cacodemons and imps lose their terrifying edge, becoming laughable caricatures of their former selves. The difficulty curve swings wildly, with some encounters feeling far too easy while others seem arbitrarily punishing. Players have reported moments where it feels like the game is rigged against you, leaving you wondering if it’s a design choice or just poor execution. The shotgun, a staple of the series, sounds and feels weak, lacking the visceral punch that should accompany such an iconic weapon. When you blast an enemy at close range, you expect an explosive impact, not a feeble pop. Instead of exhilaration, you’re left with disappointment. If you dare to criticize this game, be prepared for a barrage of clown awards from the most fragile FPS fanboys you’ve ever encountered. It’s as if they’ve made it their life mission to defend this title, treating any critique as a personal affront. The irony is astounding—these individuals who preach about “free speech” and “different opinions” are the first to silence anyone who dares to challenge their nostalgia. labeled everything from “casual” to “fake gamer” for merely pointing out the glaring flaws in a game they hold dear. The level of denial and entitlement within this community is truly remarkable. They seem so trapped in their nostalgia that they can’t fathom that maybe—just maybe—*Doom 64* isn’t the masterpiece they remember. It feels like the developers relied on the *Doom* name to carry the game, rather than focusing on innovation or improvement. For a franchise that has consistently pushed boundaries, it’s disappointing to see a title that feels like it’s dragging its feet while the rest of the industry has sprinted ahead. It’s sad that many fans are stuck in the ‘90s, clinging to outdated mechanics and a flawed game, rather than embracing the evolution of gaming. If you’re looking for an FPS that actually holds up to modern standards, look elsewhere. This game is not only a frustrating experience but also comes with a fanbase so thin-skinned it could make a tissue factory jealous. I’ve heard it all before, and it only strengthens my belief that *Doom 64* is best left in the dusty archives of gaming history. Enjoy your nostalgia, but don’t pretend it’s more than what it is: a mediocre title that should have remained a forgotten relic of the ’90s.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: It's a classic. Puzzles to get through, steps to retrace, spawning hordes and weapon drops to help against those hordes. I grew up with the original DOOM trilogy as a child, all the spin-offs and alternate creature textures that came out for it were big deals in my life back then. I didn't end up playing DOOM 64 when it was new... but playing it now both takes me back and entertains new fancies. *I* am glad it popped up on Steam.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 is an absolutely outstanding game that could've been lost to the sands of time but thankfully wasn't.For years a lot of people had the misconception that this was just a port of DOOM to the Nintendo 64. Those people were wrong. DOOM 64 is an actual standalone game in the franchise. A proper sequel, not a mere port.This game ups the horror and ambience. It is, most of the time, a slower game than either 1 or 2. It focuses more on puzzle solving than the previous titles. But the action is still here and it's still amazing.And it's not just recycled content either... All-new graphics. A new weapon! Some new enemies! They even added a whole new 'campaign' to this remaster, the Lost Levels, which you unlock when you finish the main one.Honestly, while this may sound sacrilegious... I think DOOM 64 might be my favourite of the classic DOOM games. The only thing I like less is the soundtrack, it's more ambient and less rocking. It's still good mind you, it just lacks that oomph.Now, we all know that 64 will never dethrone 1 or 2, those games are absolutely eternal and have so many custom WADs made in the last 2 decades that you'll never play all of them. But if you're a fan of DOOM, or old FPS games in general, you owe it to yourself to try this out.Great remaster and the developers deserve our support for bringing it to us.RIP AND TEAR!

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself was a lot of fun. Personally, I feel like the music and atmosphere belonged in a different game. _childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: When reviewing a game like this you have to take in the time period, and the games that came out around that time. While Doom 64 holds up in its own right, it lacks a lot compared to modern FPS games, and even comparatively to other FPS games around this time. There is no vertical/diagonal aiming. To sprint you press the spacebar. There is no jumping. Doors don’t look like doors, and aren’t always obvious to the player. You have codes for levels that you’d have to enter to play that level (there are thankfully also saves, but they don’t show your time, so it’s hard to tell which one is the newest). Enemies are 2D while the environment is 3D; all of these things are odd and outdated, but I don’t think they detract as much as you’d think they would. It’s still Doom at the end of the day, and Doom is all about shooting and gore. In the same year, 1997, ‘GoldenEye 007’ came out, a game that had directional shooting, 3D enemies, 3D weapons, and was just in general leaps and bounds above Doom 64, on the same console. A year later, 1998, Half-Life came out, a game that defined what a campaign shooter would look like for the future to come. Half-Life had puzzles, voiced scenes, jumping, 3D everything, a showcase of many different environments, amazing graphics for its time, physics, platforming, seamless levels, and much more… Half-Life really puts a damper on a lot of games around its time period, and even after, so it’s a rough comparison, but one that gives ‘Doom 64’ no excuse for the supposed limitations. Now what does the game do well? Doom 64 has a surprisingly long campaign, with a decent amount of variety while maintaining the theme. It has a wide array of weapons, and a lot of varying puzzles. The game is dense in scope, and while it’s not crazy hard, I’d imagine on the hardest difficulty I’d quickly change my mind. Despite these positives, each positive comes with its own caveat. Its long campaign gets tiring and repetitive - this is doubled down by the fact that each mission itself isn’t that long, but most of your time spent is backtracking, making what is meant to be a fast paced shooter a headache at times. You have a lot of weapons, but because of the lack of directional aiming, weapon weight/drag/inertia, recoil, and other modern FPS mechanics, most weapons differ mainly in damage, with some differing in AOE. While it’s still good in its own right, it feels very dated, giving me mixed feelings. Is the game still enjoyable? Sure. Would I rather be playing a lot of other games? Yes.

_childDocuments_.review: unimposing enemies, really bad level design, poor music compared to the other doom games and an annoying unskipable bethesda logo in the beginning let me refund this crap. i played doom 1,2&3 with all expansions, but this one, where all other doom episodes failed, finally made me feel like being in hell; its sooooo not worth playing it. baphomet would be ashamed
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Often overlooked, as every review tends to mention, but it needs repeating. Doom 64 is a great package with a lot of fun re-interpretations of the classic Doom formula designed by a completely separate team. Immediately, the new sounds and sprites make the game feel fresh while also being very familiar.There are a lot of really cool ideas and stuff that was never possible on the earlier engine - not simply the coloured lighting but scripting and dynamic elements of the levels themselves. The "Lost Levels" making their first appearance in this remaster are particularly fun also and feel more designed around the dexterity afforded by mouse and keyboard controls.The main negative that comes to mind is that the campaign starts off a little samey, though it picks up especially around the first secret level and was a blast to get through. Make sure to save every so often because the designers can be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with the traps. While the level progressions may not be as solid as Doom 1 & 2 at times, with more backtracking to work out what a switch did than you'd probably expect, it never becomes a chore as you're usually then immediately thrown into a fun dance with some demons.Make sure you've got headphones on, or speakers turned up for the incredible soundscape and get ready to take in the atmosphere of what somehow feels like a blend of Doom and Quake. A great appendix to the Id library well worth a fan's time.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I passed on this with my N64 because I was a hardcore Doom PC player, and I saw the pictures and wrote it off as a weird port of the game I loved so much. That was apparently a mistake. I am so glad that I am playing this finally, and sorry that I dismissed it back in the day. I don't know how this handled on the 64, but I am playing it with my gamepad just fine. If you loved the original Doom, don't pass on 64  like I did. It is just more of what you loved about the original with a slightly different look.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: My first "classic fps" and man did I pick a good one. Really taking my time with it but I love the combat. I thought that no vertical aiming on the camera would bother me, but it actually improves the game in my opinion. I'm not great at aiming in general and taking away an entire axis has significantly improved my ability. This is quickly becoming one of my favorite games and I I can't wait to finish it and move on to DOOM ETERNAL!!!!!
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

Everything has been left intact from the original N64 version, but with modern controls and high screen resolutions. It even has brand new levels made by the champs at Night Dive Studios. What more could you want from a remaster? If you are a Doom fan and have never played this masterpiece before, you owe it to yourself to buy it ASAP.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is like an alternate universe version of classic Doom. You basically have the same weapons and monsters but all the sprites, sounds and textures are completely reworked. Instead of midi versions of metal songs you get a creepy ambient soundtrack. The level design is clever and the traps keep you on your toes. Because this came out in 1997 on a console dedicated for 3d graphics the devs were able to soup up the classic Doom engine and add stuff like colored lighting and higher resolution sprites. Overall a great entry to the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel graphically this is a huge step down from normal Doom (the new lighting is cool but all the sprites look drastically worse), and it's a bummer there are so many cut enemies.But the levels in Doom 64 are well-made. They have a better aesthetic than all of the stock maps in Doom 1 and 2, and they have a good balance of exploration and backtracking. Unfortunately, the levels keep doing one really annoying thing: buttons doing something somewhere without any hint as to what and where. This makes you go a chicken chase most times you press a button (not to mention the fact some buttons have a temporary effect, and some buttons can be shot, adding even more arbitrary variability to the mix).If someone were to port this level set over to Doom 2's engine while fixing all of the annoyances in the level design, this would be a great megawad. But even as it is, it's fun for anyone wanting an old-school shooter with old-school level design.
