_childDocuments_.review: After Doom released in 1993, every FPS game in the mid 90s tried to mimic it. Including it's sequel Doom 2. In fact the Doom IP was so popular, ID software allowed a game consisting of fan made Doom maps called Final Doom to be sold at Retail. (no this game was not a legit sequel to Doom 2). But in spite of this, after a couple years of Doom clones dominating the PC market, ID software released a game called Quake in 1996 and it changed everything despite having lots of parallels to Doom. Thanks to the game's Full 3D models and ground breaking online multiplayer mode, the old Doom gameplay became dated by comparison. However, in 1997 Williams software were given the green light to make their own original Doom game on consoles after the positive reception the Playstation version of Doom received from both fans and the original designer of Doom, John Ramero. This game would go on to become Doom 64. When Doom 64 came out in the spring of 1997 for the Nintendo 64, the  game completely under performed with low sales and lukewarm reviews. Due to being given an miss leading name, being released on a console known for full 3D games, being an M rated title with Satanic imagery on a system marketed towards kids, and the fact that the Doom franchise was just all around declining in popularity due to newer FPS titles like Quake, Goldeneye, and Turrok utilizing cutting edge technology. But in the early 2010s, that started to change. When younger generations started to develop an interest in the Doom series, they did research on Doom 64 thanks to the power of the internet, and discovered that this game was the actual sequel to Doom 2 as apposed ID's 2004 series reboot that was inappropriately named Doom 3. From there on out, this game got gradually more popular to the point where PC mods got released to loads of acclaim. And now we have reached a point where we can now play this game publicly and in a way that it was meant to be played. On a PC with a mouse and Keyboard. So how does the actual sequel to Doom 2 hold up now that's its being sold publicly? Lets see for our selves. Now I wont do a pros and cons segment here, because this is one of those rare games where what you like or don't like about it depends on what your personal tastes are. But What I will say is an objective positive of the game is that it plays exactly the same as the previous games... except that the mouse controls are vastly superior to Doom 1 and 2. And I found myself pulling off maneuvers that I could never pulled off in those games or this game's console version that matter. so it wins in the controls department. When it comes to the more subjective stuff I noticed that the level design is a lot more cryptic and puzzle oriented then the first two games, while it took me some time to adjust to this I eventually adapted to this no problem. Some may take a little longer then me, but I recommend to those people to give it a chance since it helps the game feel more uniqe unlike Doom 2 which played it too safe at times. It should also be mentioned that this game has a lot more secret levels then usual, in fact some of  them have these secret optional keys that power up the newest gun in this game, The Un-Maker, which will make the final boss easier the more you collect (think of them like the four sage temples from Zelda: Breath of the Wild). Hint: you'll need at least two of them to make  the final level a smooth fun ride. But the biggest difference between this game and the first two is the visuals and music. This game goes for  a more atmospheric and fear inducing tone, unlike Doom 1 and 2 which go for a more bright and colorful "YEAH, I'm gonna kill them all and love it" type of tone. The lighting is more realistic and dark, the music now goes for moody ambiance like the Quake 1 music by Trent Raznor as opposed to Doom 1 &2's music which mimics AC/DC, Alice in Chains, and Judas Priest, and the sprite models have been given complete re-designs. Most of which I'll admit look a lot more intimidating and 3 dimensional to the point where the old sprites  look more cartoony by comparison (except for the Mankibusses, and a couple of your guns). In fact  this was the only game I have ever played that managed to scare me through visuals and sound alone. Lastly, I should mention that while I do understand why some people didn't like this tone shift when it came to the PS1 version of Doom 1 & 2 due to the fact that the port was trying to take games that where designed with a different tone in mind and change the feel completely. However, This Game I feel is the right type of game to do something like this to. Mainly due to being an actual sequel That IS designed with this tone in mind, as well as the fact that one of the criticisms of Doom 2 is that it played things too similarly to the first game. So in a way, taking an approach like this is actually what the doctor ordered when it comes to making a sequel that raises the stakes. Overall, I can see why some people will see this as either the best or the worst of the original era Doom games. This games addresses the "playing it too safe" problem Doom 2 had to a T. And is once again one of those games where what you like or don't like about it depends on your personal tastes. As for me, I think all of these changes are for the best and are a welcome addition to this series. And for me, out of all the Doom sequels I have played, This is the best one. If your one of those people that have played this game and cant get into it due to the different tone and level design.I recommend that you keep giving it a shot, I promise that you'll eventually get into it. And If you grew up playing the original N64 version, get it anyway. There's lots of new additions for old players too. And the fact that the system requirements are not very high makes the reason to buy this all the more stronger. I give this game a 9.5 out of 10This is the perfect follow up to Doom 2 and I give it the title of being the REAL Doom 3. Going from Doom to  Doom 2 to This, makes for the perfect FPS trilogy in my eyes.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a little reluctant to try this but I'm glad I did. This is one of the most fluid and fun FPS games I've ever played. Even if I died (and I did a lot), I NEVER got truly frustrated, and instead felt encouraged to plan my attacks and git gud (hint: save often). I also enjoy the element of horror added to the game: Aubrey Hodges' score delivers an eerie, uncomfortable ambience while you search the labyrinthine tunnels of Hell and run into enemies. If you're looking for a great classic FPS you can't really go wrong with this game. It holds up VERY well despite being a 1990's game, with fair and balanced gameplay, an awesome array of weapons, creative enemies, and full of secrets to explore. And it's super cheap, too!

_childDocuments_.review: Far more fun than I expected. It starts out slow, but give it time. The ambiance builds nicely. The soundtrack really sells the unsettling dread vibe. The level design gets a little backtracky, and the puzzles a little obscure at times, but it is a fantastic Doom game, and an even more fantastic classic shooter. I just wish it had multiplayer.9/10 Will play again multiple times8/10 I recommend to the right friends
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I'll break this into two parts: 1. the port and 2. the game.As to 1: the port is great. Before Bethesda packaged this as a pre-order bonus for Doom Eternal, we had Doom64Exe, which was also great. There are a few texture glitches in the user uploaded source port that are not present here, or at least I didn't encounter them. We also get a few nice perks, including steam achievements and better controller support. Both Exe and this Bethesda port feature widescreen format and unlocked frame rates, neither of which are present on the original N64. Of course, the game still looks best the way it was intended: on an N64 cart through a CRT. As to 2: the game is good but not perfect. If you're like me, you might've thought Doom 64 was an N64 port of the original Doom. In fact, it is a totally unique game, designed by Midway Studios of all people. Officially, the game succeeds Doom II. However, there are a few notable steps back. The most obvious is the player animations have been pared down, likely due to cart limitations at the time. So, reloading is purely aural. Another is the removal of nearly half the cast of enemies, and most the new additions being mere re-skins of other enemies, again likely due to cart limitations. Thankfully, a majority of the non-returning enemies are Doom II's most annoying. Confusingly, they kept Pain Elementals, and somehow made them even an even greater nuisance. Overall, this is classic Doom: bloody, frenetic, kickass. In my opinion, it doesn't quite reach the levels of Ultimate Doom, but it certainly exceeds Doom II in terms of substantive gameplay scenarios. The levels are still quite open-ended, as in Ultimate Doom, but not as obscure as in Doom II. You shouldn't need a guide to experience most of what Doom 64 has to offer. In particular, the strength of this game is its atmospheric lighting, abstract level designs, and pacing. You will either love or hate the new enemy models, which were first 3D rendered before being turned into sprites. I love them. Where this game is at its worst is when it retains the ball-busting design philosophy of Doom II. Thankfully, much of the "unfair" levels have been relegated to secret areas. In a lot of ways, this feels like a true "Doom 3" insofar as it elaborates and expands the design space of classic Doom without abandoning the core tenets of early id game-making.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: It’s still good old DOOM 64: still the same standard 90s DOOM FPS gameplay, still the same ass-looking sprites and lighting, still the same sequel story that sets up the modern games, still the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ final boss that requires finding a bunch of secret levels to make it even remotely playable. That final boss aside, it’s pretty solid overall—the mouselook added in this version helps it a lot, and I forgot all the weird interesting ♥♥♥♥ it does with its level design. This version also has some new bonus levels; they’re overlong and uninteresting, but they don’t take anything away from the main game. Not as good as DOOMs 1 or 2, but still a fun time.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: More of a puzzle-oriented take on "DOOM" than its earlier installments, there's still plenty of mowing down demons to keep one's bloodlust satisfied. Gun switching is easy, traps littered throughout levels can catch you by surprise (those fireballs certainly come to mind), and Aubrey Hodges's soundtrack with its ambient noise and discordant, non-directional sensibility makes the atmosphere delightfully unsettling and foreboding. It's a far scarier experience than most other "DOOM" games I've played, especially with solid headphones.The big change from the original console version for the N64 (aside from some new levels and achievements) is the ability to save anywhere, which makes later levels far more manageable. As such, the exercise of actually getting through the game is more user-friendly.Aside from some poorly-implemented platforming, the only other notable negative is that the puzzles, while not "hard" in the sense of having the pieces in front of you and being difficult to figure out, are a bit aggravating. Most of the later levels will usually have one moment of not quite knowing where to go or what to do, and not in a way that feels appropriately challenging for a game like this. It's never enough to make you feel "lost," but you may find yourself smacking your head for not realizing you didn't see this one thing or do this one action."DOOM 64" is nevertheless a very fun game, one that satisfies the craving for early "DOOM" gameplay while also offering something intriguing enough on its own to justify giving it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, I was a fan of quake 2 on the N64 so playing this gave me a nostalgic vibe because the game shared that same creepy atmosphere with quake as the soundtrack is far more ambient than the classic doom bombastic soundtrack. I think my only issue I have is the reloading animations don't look as nice as regular doom, but that is just a nitpick because when you are shooting a lot of demons you probably wouldn't even notice it. The environment lighting in some levels is also very nice for a retro game. I would maybe give it a 8/10 worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Great re-release of this often overlooked game. A dramatically superior experience to playing the original N64 version. Only complaint I have is that the game was lacking in the audio department - there is hardly any music to speak of, and the 'ambient' tracks don't hold a candle to the original Doom games' music. I know this was the same in the original N64 version, I just figured maybe they would spruce it up a bit for this one.I think this is a great value at only 6-something dollars...
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: The true doom 3.the game is absolutely awesome, but not as good as doom 1 and 2.some sprites look bad, the soundtrack is meh, and the game as a whole is a little short (probably due to the restrictions of the nintendo 64 cartridge).the soundtrack is nothing like the other doom games (except doom 3),it makes it different than the rest, but id rather headbanging while killing demons than hearing babies crying. this doesn't make it bad though.also, who made the decision to release this game only for the nintendo 64 originally? it was pretty stupid.overall, pretty good sequel to doom 2.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: The Game:I think this is a fairly good Classic Doom style offering that does some tricks not possible in 1 & 2. (I.e Room over Room). Though it is fairly flawed. The atmosphere is what excels the best here, especially combined with the more abstract ambient ost. The level often feel larger than in the first 2 games. Theres some pretty clever puzzles.Though the game has some major flaws:Some levels require alot of backtracking and can be confusing on first playthrough. The enemy roster also is pretty small compared to Doom 2 (down to N64 cardridge size). You will see alot of Barons and Hell Knights due to this.Though alot of the returning Enemies are stronger (i.e Arachnotron, Imp). The game also has some evil ways to place them which Doom 1 & 2 sometimes failed.The Source Port:Theres some love put into the port. Theres alot of options to readjust controls, the game is now compatible with mouse and keyboard and achievment exist, albeit only few (not the case with 1 & 2s Unity remake).The game being remade from ground up means it also avoids alot of slowdown it had on original hardware.This also includes some QOL improvements like Quicksaves while the original game only had passwords, meaning you had to fully repeat a level as soon as you died.Lost Levels:The unity remake comes with a bonus episode of 5 maps, but they are honestly mostly pretty forgettable retreats of setpieces you already experienced, just at a larger scale. They are a bit harder than the main campaign but dont pose as much challenge as something like Thy Flesh Consumed did.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this game for WAY longer than 21 minutes on the Nintendo 64. But its been quite a few years since I've played it, and one thing I think Night Dive studios have done well is Remastering old games like Turok, Forsaken, and now Doom 64. They have completely overhauled the engine and cleaned it up quite a bit, they improved and upgraded the visuals and audio. Long gone is the extremely dark lighting which did make the original difficult to traverse. The only issue that I found is that the game favors the player more than the enemies, I'm not sure if is because of it being console born and then ported over. Aside form that this game is pretty solid and well worth the money they're asking for.So go buy it... NOW!!!
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: The level design can be a bit dickish at times, there are a few enemies missing from Doom 1 and 2, and the weapons/gameplay haven't changed much from the previous entry. However, it is still an enjoyable Doom experience and the atmosphere is much more ominous than its predecessors. If you can appreciate some classic Doom goodness, this is well worth playing especially considering how cheap it is.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Not much to say about this game, it's more good Doom. Cool levels, more horror-focused soundtrack, neat secret stages and a cryptic powerful new weapon, the Unmaker. If you're a fan of this kind of shooter, with barely any story but tons of satistfying action, or enjoyed the other classic Doom titles, can't go wrong at this price.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: The real DOOM 3. I played it a lot in my N64 as a kid (and I still have the original cartridge). It's a little different from the previous 2 games, it's more moody, with a "horror" atmosphere, but unlike Doom 3 it hasn't lost its speed and brutal combat. Some enemies from the previous games are absent (Archvile, Revenant, Chaingunner and Spider Demon) and it has a new enemy (Nightmare Imp, a stronger and faster version of a normal Imp), but what's done with the monsters that remain is awesome. The levels aren't much different from what you could expect from DOOM 1 and 2 I guess, but they do have a better sense of continuity. Also, there's a few new levels called "The Lost Levels", which are pretty fun and more challenging than the normal campaign. So, you like DOOM 1 and 2? Grab it, it's dirt cheap and it's an awesome DOOM game.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite of the classic Doom games, known for bringing a lot of new content to the table and exhibiting stellar and highly atmospheric level design, as well as having a dark ambient soundtrack in place of the usual heavy metal motifs and much harder gameplay (sometimes) than its predecessors. The port is a little obnoxious with its plethora of unskippable disclaimers and company logos dumped on you at startup à la the typical modern idsoft/Bethesda title but past that it's the exact same game with a fresh coat of paint, and unlike the previous Steam releases of classic Doom titles it doesn't run in a shoddy DOSbox emulator clone and actually feels like one of Doom's modern day source ports. I am one of the folks who very much likes its nickname, "The Real Doom 3". Definitely buy this if you've never had the chance to try it before, because now you do.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A classic Doom game, and a direct continuation to the story of Doom 2 brings back the faithful 90s gameplay that used to be only on the Nintendo 64. There are new enemies, new weapons, and a good challenge that takes you back.Fan of Doom or not, this is easily one of the best classics for a low price.

_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Sorry, I don't think this is a good game. Chances are you already know if you like it or not, but to me it feels like a Doom knock-off rather than a Doom game. I was 16 when this game originally came out in 97 and I didn't own an N64 because I already had a computer I played Doom games on. And believe me, I played the HELL out of Doom and Doom 2 on that thing. Played over dial-up, made maps, the whole thing. I don't even think I knew about Doom 64 until the 2010s. It seems to be a favorite among people of a certain age, maybe who were younger than me when it came out, I dunno. Maybe it's a nostalgia thing for them, maybe they had an N64 but no PC on which to play Doom and Doom 2? I dunno. All I can say is I just don't enjoy this game (yes I'm aware Steam doesn't show me having played it long, but I've played ports of it before). I know that the game is considered to be a sequel to Doom 2 or something, but I don't see why they threw out all the original Doom art. I'm sure they could have gotten the original sprites and textures and maybe even the engine from id, after-all they were already licensing the Doom name, so why not? I know a lot of this is just subjective, but I feel like the sprites in this game just look cheap (even with texture filtering off). There's something about the way they are pre-lit, the scaling and the color palette that I just find unpleasing. The animation speed and number of frames in the animations is off too. Watching an enemy I just killed slowly collapse to the floor in what seems to be too few animation frames is jarring and ugly. The wall textures are dull compared to the original Doom games and the lighting is bland and at times even harsh. I'm aware the game has colored lighting which is technically more advanced tech than Doom and Doom 2 but I don't really care. There's an overall lack of atmosphere to the game. The level layout feels really uninteresting compared to the brilliant maps that the older games were known for. Nothing about the weapons feels satisfying, the shotgun barely moves in your hand when you fire it, the sounds of weapons are underwhelming. The sprite scaling of the enemies is off, the zombies feel like they are 8 feet tall. I just don't get why they did this this way.I'm aware that this port on Steam isn't the greatest, but don't make the mistake of thinking I'm giving this game a bad review because of that. I'm not. I straight up just don't think it's a good game. If you do, good for you, enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: While I found this one slightly less replayable, this is a fantasic game, which takes a wholey new direction for the franchise (well, not wholey new, Doom on PS1 had kinda delved into this game's brand of atmosphere, but still). What's more, this game's level design is easily the most consistently high quality of the classic Doom games.For me, this is the real Doom 3.Also, fantastic job by the ever-brilliant Nightdive Studios porting it to PC and fixing this game's jarring lighting issues on the N64.(Formerly:great nightdive port of an amazing game. best classic doom game, don't @ me)
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A great, almost entirely faithful port of Doom 64, with a ton of love & care poured into it. Also includes new levels that tie Doom 64 directly into the new Doom and Doom Eternal canon.I cannot feign lack of bias when it comes to certain games. Doom 64 is one of them.To say I loved Doom 64 upon its release in 1997 would be an understatement. I lived in it. To the extent my then-feeble skills allowed, I mastered every level, every secret (even the ones we weren't meant to find, like the "I Suck At Making Maps" message hidden in some levels.)  I remember the first time I beat Hectic. It was one of the most satisfying moments I've experienced, before or since, in gaming. I was obsessed with this game.To understand why requires historical context. Doom 64 was the first game I played on my brand new Nintendo 64. I'd played the PC Dooms (though not on my own PC as I didn't have one at the time, which may also be why I loved 64) and was as affected by them as anyone.But far from the outlier orphan 64 was treated as by some PC gamers of the time (many of whom simply assumed it was a console port of the originals,) as both a diehard Nintendo and Doom fan this felt to me like a proper and natural follow up to those games. One which has haunted my memory ever since. Coming from those games into 64 felt amazing at the time. All the basic mechanical trappings of Doom, but with (for their time) much slicker graphics, a new weapon, shiny new enemy sprites, and bombastic sound design (for my money the super shotgun in 64 remains the most satisfying to date,) all set in a darker, decidedly more devious series of levels.The analog control and trigger of the N64 gamepad also aided my immersion. It may seem silly now to talk about immersion in a Doom game, but this was back when even Wolf 3D was still only 5 years old. FPSes as we know them today were new. They almost felt like virtual reality in an odd sense.Developed by Midway with supervision by Id, Doom 64 was recognizable as Doom, but had a style and a tone all its own. It was darker. The sound design was much creepier (a credit to Aubrey Hodges, who worked on the PS1 port's audio, to similar effect) and more ambient. Impressively improved graphics lent the game its fondly remembered atmosphere and sense of creeping dread. (Newcomers may not see it that way today, but at the time, this was a beautiful witch's brew of old fashioned sprite work, more dynamic lighting, higher fidelity textures, and an entirely new art style, all landing somewhere between the original Doom and its more advanced progeny Quake, which had arrived the previous year.)Doom 64 sought to confound returning players and Doom neophytes alike with a much greater emphasis on level design derived challenge. Lower enemy counts meant that even on higher difficulties where mob waves were impressively dense, the bulk of the danger came from devilish traps, spawn triggers, and quickly overwhelming players in tight quarters. To prevail, trial and error, experimentation, and learning what tools to use in each encounter were required, perhaps more than ever in a Doom game prior to Eternal, despite those statements being true of the entire series to some extent.I would venture to say that it's easy to see the design philosophy antecedent of Eternal in Doom 64. This makes a lot of sense, as Hugo Martin is on record as crediting 64 with being his favorite Doom, and the one that he felt was "always trying to mess with the player" the most.Whereas its predecessors invited fast run and gun orgies of slaughter, followed only after the fact by careful secret hunting and backtracking, every level in 64 oozed a sense of foreboding mystery; the feeling that something had gone horribly wrong, and that demonic secrets were waiting to be uncovered by those intrepid enough to overcome the hordes of hell and find them. And boy does the game ever reward you for trying to do so, with several secrets being both particularly unique in Doom history, and especially challenging to access. (Doing so back then, with no guide or internet, was one of the most fulfilling things I've experienced in any game.)Doom 64 forms part of a hallowed era in gaming and in life for me. A period during which I was old enough to truly appreciate the finer details and subtleties of games, but young and unjaded enough to experience wonder. The age of Super Mario 64, Suikoden, Ocarina of Time, Metal Gear Solid, Goldeneye 007, Turok, Quake, etc. And for me, a few forgotten gems such as Legend of Legaia and - yes - an odd, divisive, beautiful followup to Final Doom called Doom 64.We owe a great debt to Kaiser (Samuel Villareal) for his work in restoring Doom 64 in playable form for contemporary platforms. Several attempts at recreating Doom 64 exist. They include Doom 64 TC: The Absolution (which was Kaiser's earlier attempt at a less faithful total conversion of the game, with some additional content and modern bells and whistles) and Brutal Doom 64, among others.While TC/Absolution is still a perfectly playable and enjoyable version of the game, Kaiser was not satisfied with the lack of a truly faithful port. That led to Doom 64 EX, a true port of the game for modern PCs. Prior to this new, official release, EX was by far the most accurate version of the game available outside of the N64.However, with this official release, the holy grail has been all but perfectly achieved. This port is easily the most faithful to the game I was enthralled by 23 years ago. For a list of what's different between this release and EX, see: And for some general analysis, check out this interview:Kaiser et al at Nightdive cannot be commended highly enough for this port work. So much so, that it suffices to mention the few exceptions, rather than everything else bordering on perfect reproduction. They are:Health packs use different designs due to the Red Cross. Unofficial fix: The audio is fine but here are some inaccuracies. Unofficial fix: It's brighter (unless you lower both sliders and/or use a CRT display.)It's much easier thanks to saves and modern controls (though passwords still optionally exist.) Play on 'Watch Me Die' difficulty. Trust me.And that's it for differences. One of the most accurate ports of a game I've seen, and a love letter to a largely ignored installment in an iconic IP.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Like so many Doom titles, this one is pretty misleading. As I explained in my review of , this is not the 64th part of the nameless and silent Space Marine but, be careful, here it comes:Strictly speaking, the game is actually the third part, as it was developed for the Nintendo 64 by Midway Games in coordination with id Software, which was re-released by Bugthesda in March 2020, and the story takes place after Doom 2.So Doom 64 is actually the third part which would then make Doom 3 the fourth part, which isn't right either because Doom 3 is actually a reboot, which is what Doom (2016) also is and ok, let's just leave that alone...The game proved at the time that Doom can also flop, as it only caused many people to shrug their shoulders because the screenshots made people think that it was another version of Doom (1993), which included everything from a calculator to a toaster has been ported to pretty much everything. For others, the game with the “old-fashioned” 2-D enemies and the “retro game play” was simply too outdated.It wasn't until a few years later that an, albeit rather small, fan community built up around the game, which is probably due to Doom 64 EX, which was a very popular fan port of the game for the PC.The game was remastered by Nightdive Studios, who had made a name for themselves with remastered games like Forsaken, Blood: Fresh Supply or Turok and had done a good job of porting. The game runs on the Kex Engine with a stable refresh rate, although there are no other notable innovations and you can expect the same “mushy textures” and pixelated 2D sprites as in the original.Thanks to the higher resolutions, the image still looks pleasantly sharp and clean and you can adjust the optics a little better using an FOV slider, edge smoothing, V-Snyc and two brightness controls. In addition, the game now offers free key assignment and the ability to save freely, including quicksave and quickload. The classic level selection via code is still possible and so the porting plays cleanly and in my opinion is quite successful.Nothing has changed in terms of content and all the levels that existed in the original are there. But there is a small additional point that should not be ignored. There is a new chapter at the end that is supposed to build a kind of bridge to the new Doom offshoots with new levels and more story snippets.Doom 64 is a direct sequel to Doom 2 from 1994 and brings back the Marine, who once again has to shoot his way through a demon-infested station on Mars.So it plays just like the first two parts where you can't look up or down or jump. So you rush through the more than 30 levels at high speed, collect key cards, discover secrets and work your way to the exit where you slaughter tons of demons., if you're one of them too.The typical weapons are also back in this game and there is also a new energy weapon, the Unmaykr, which is also making its return in Doom Eternal.Sure, the game is about “old-fashioned” action, but that’s exactly why it’s so much fun.The fights and the stupid opponents aren't really the challenge in the old games. Rather, as in the first two parts, the challenge is to explore the labyrinth-like environment and not get lost. The levels here are quite small, but they are neatly nested and full of switches, teleporters, elevators and doors. Even if you have a good sense of direction, getting lost isn't difficult. If you press a switch, a passage opens somewhere, a platform goes down or a key card appears somewhere, where you can often only guess where exactly it was. It's certainly a bit out of date today, but in the 90s such level design was common practice, which you certainly can't blame the game for.Graphically, the game is still reminiscent of its two predecessors, but the engine did a lot more back then and Doom 64 offered a much better lighting model so that the environment was immersed in more colorful light. In addition, all 2-D enemies were replaced with more detailed ones and a texture filter smoothed the pixelated wall textures.The look and feel of the original Doom were omnipresent, which is why some Doom fans consider the game to be the “real Doom 3”.Doom 3 was just a complete reboot that had a completely different focus with tons of jump scares and dark levels.But that's another story that I'll tell you another time.✔ classic “good old” gameplay✔ technically perfect game✔ Graphics options and free key assignment✔ new chapter with new levels✔ free saving✔ old cheat codes still work✔ great soundtrack✔ many levels of difficulty✘ confusing level design✘ Hardly any graphical changes/improvements✘ no multiplayer mode✘ Played through quite quicklyRevised and reposted: November 26, 2023

_childDocuments_.review: It's Doom the way you remember it if you remember it with the nostalgia goggles cranked up to max.I don't recall playing this when it came out on the N64 or maybe I blocked it out due to the controllers and the graphics limitations.  Regardless, the base level FPS and challenging levels makes this purchase for $4.99 an absolute steal.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 is an absolute must play for DOOM and Retro Shooter fans alike! It is the most dark and gothic of the classic games and certainly hits hard in the atmosphere department with its amazing soundtrack comprised by Aubrey Hodges (He also did the soundtrack for DOOM PS1, Final DOOM PS1, Quake 64, and Quake II 64). The games levels are all excellent and filled to the brim with demons to slaughter and secrets to find. Most of the demon roster returns from DOOM II/Final Doom (excluding the Revenant and Arch-Ville) and all have had a make over for this iteration which helps make this one stand out a bit more when put next to it's predecessors. Secret Levels are also actually useful in this game as they house the hidden Demon Key's which are used to power up the new weapon to the arsenal, The Unmakyr! A weapon that makes the final boss an absolute joke when fully powered up!Overall I absolutely recommend!!!
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom's cybernetic heart beats with a rythm of science fiction. Future soldiers, high-tech weaponary and isolated installations on a far-flung world. It's blend that provides the key aesthetic for Doom: a fusion of metallic sci-fi with fleshy hellspawn. The satanic influences originate from Id's D&D sessions, where at the climax of the lengthy campaign the entire planet was overrun with demons. No longer constrained by the grid-based stone walls of Wolfenstein, Id's imagination could run riot: an indulgence of pure twisted fantasy. A departure from a loose historical basis: from 'heil Нitler' to 'hail Satan' Id have never been particularly afraid of controversial subjects. Still, the devil has all the best tunes - and a game like Doom needed a killer soundtrack. Id didn't have to look too far for inspiration: the tunes playing on their office stereo would provide ample material. Tracks evocative of Metallica, Slayer, Pantera, Judas Priest. True, they were lo-fi MIDI renditions but from first level to the last, Doom is chock full of trash riffs. Every inch the compelling experience: the world was ill prepared for a game like Doom. An amalgam of pop culture, it borrowed heavily from its era - but paid back the debt with interest. From influenced to influential and an impact that resonates today. A new genre forged, and gameplay choreography re-rehearsed countless times. Doom's success, invited others to follow in its footsteps. And why not? It's only natural. There is magic in Doom's heart. It's primitve, still raw and the essence of action beats throughout its chambers. Two decades later and it still kicks arse.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 is... well, basically it's just more DOOM. And it's hard to go wrong with that. However, the monsters have gotten cosmetic makeovers and the atmosphere overall is much more on the creepy side than the original two titles, from level design to music to everything else. No more banging melodies by Bobby Prince, with background music being minimalistic and ambient instead. It's hit or miss, but for me it was different and interesting, and it fit the overall tone of the game quite well.At it's pricepoint, I highly recommend DOOM 64 for any fans of the originals or old-school FPS titles in general. When the main complaint online appears to be the lack of option to enable jumping and vertical aiming in a DOOM game, you just know that there are no real problems to speak of with this port.A couple of pointers, though. Save a lot and often. This game will break your heart by slapping you with a falling floor trap right in front of a level end switch. And you will not be able to get up. Similar stuff happened on a few levels. Don't be the guy forced to pistol start a late game level or load up a few levels earlier.Also, Pain Elementals and Lost Souls are your new priorities. The Mother Demon has not fed them since the first slaughter, it appears. By the time you grunt from pain and turn 180 degrees to see what hit you, the Lost Soul has already had second or even third servings of your sorry ass. There's little to no pause in their attacks. And when you get a swarm.. you get the drift. Damn ravenous bastards.

_childDocuments_.review: It utterly baffles my intricate mind as to why one would express their free will in choosing this wretched jumble of code furtively disguising itself as a video game. To say that this game is a step backwards would be an understatement... Fact: Goldeneye allows the ability to look vertically, shockingly DOOM 64 does not. Yup, I'm being serious. You can only look left or right. Goldeneye is regarded as one of the most prestigious FPS games at the time, and a shining gem on the N64. It has local multiplayer that still drags in wistful gamers and gamerettes into its addictive grasp. There is no reason to play this game when Goldeneye exists... Fact.Not to mention the SNOOZER of a soundtrack... Next!

_childDocuments_.review: Although most of the challenge has been removed seeing as you're playing with good controls and a steady framerate (this port doesn't add a Nightmare difficulty either), this is still worthy of any Doom fan's time. Aubrey Hodges's creepy (and awesome) music adds to a creppy horror vibe not really found in 1 or 2.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A return to an amazing but mostly overlooked N64 era game. With Goldeneye 007, Turok, Quake, and the rising 3D FPS breed, this game looked like a reskinned version of the old classic, instead, we got a brand new game in the series, that despite the seemingly dated graphics and hard to grasp control, provided an intense and always appreciated FPS fix.Now, not only we can get to play it again, but with a new and really fun episode.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long-time fan of the iconic Doom series, I was thrilled to find  this hidden gem from the franchise. Having spent countless hours battling demons on Doom 1, 2 and 3 over the years, I eagerly dove into this reimaged edition, and I can confidently say that it exceeded all of my expectations.From the moment I launched the game, I was greeted with nostalgia-inducing visuals that seamlessly blended the classic atmosphere of the original with modern graphical enhancements. The dark and foreboding corridors of each level were brought to life in stunning detail, immersing me in a world teeming with danger and mystery.But it wasn't just the visuals that impressed me; the gameplay itself felt as smooth and satisfying as ever. The tight controls and fast-paced action that have defined the Doom series were present in full force, delivering adrenaline-fueled combat encounters that kept me on the edge of my seat. Whether I was mowing down hordes of demons with my trusty shotgun or navigating treacherous traps, every moment felt like a thrill ride.Of course, no Doom game would be complete without its signature arsenal of weapons, and Doom 64 PC Edition does not disappoint in this regard. From the iconic Super Shotgun to the devastating BFG 9000, each weapon felt powerful and distinct, giving me plenty of options for dispatching my demonic foes in creative ways.But perhaps the most impressive aspect of Doom 64 PC Edition is its level design. Each stage is expertly crafted, offering a perfect balance of exploration, puzzle-solving, and intense combat encounters. From sprawling industrial complexes to hellish infernos, every location felt unique and memorable, ensuring that I was always eager to see what the next level had in store.Overall, Doom 64 PC Edition is a masterful return to form for the classic franchise. With its gorgeous visuals, exhilarating gameplay, and expertly designed levels, it's a must-play for fans of the series old and new alike. Whether you're a veteran demon slayer or a newcomer looking to experience the roots of one of gaming's most beloved franchises, this game is sure to satisfy.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game overall and a fun version of DOOM - assuming you like circle-strafing wave after wave (after wave) of Barons. It's like the level designers couldn't remember how to place any of the other enemy types. BUT, word of warning: I've played Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II through to completion on Ultra Violence with no guide and using no save states - one 'life' for each level. Where if you die, you go back to the start and try again, and about three-quarters through DOOM 64 even I gave up on that and had to make the occasional checkpoint. Not because the combat or combat traps are hard (the part that *should* be challenging) but because of the designers' annoying penchant for disgusting, cheap traps that were never part of DOOM. Dart traps, lava pits that are inescapable should you fall into them (sacrilege) and ridiculous 'gun emplacements' in walls that spew rockets out when you can't even work out where they're coming from or what triggers them. These things may only be in a handful of levels, but they still rankle because they're not DOOM. Then there's the beyond silly last boss with skies full of Vore style homing rockets and Diablo fire stomps that launch you into the air. WTF. Yeah, those Midway guys should have just made DOOM II with new visuals and levels and left it at that! On the same note, I never fired the useless 'Unmaker' once after first trying it out.

_childDocuments_.review: The main selling point for this remaster is that Nightdive fixed the lighting. Ahem. Allow me to explain. Rumor has it that Midway San Diego developed and play-tested this game in near total darkness on the CRT monitors of the time. Problem with this approach is that the game, when played in your well lit living room was too dark to see anything. It wasn't unplayable by any means, and in a way it gave the game a pretty creepy mood. I still prefer the new lighting, it makes the game play better, especially on higher difficulties. With that out of the way, here are some other things to consider. The gameplay is identical to the original Doom and Doom 2. Any changes to the gameplay are minor, (its missing a couple of enemy types, and they added a new weapon.) Aesthetically it also bears striking similarities to the original Doom engine games, key differences here are the fully polygonal levels , and very N64 looking spritework (I've heard it called claymation looking.) In the sound department, it borrows heavily from the PS1 version of Doom in that it has a creepy ambient score by Aubrey Hodges. Unlike the PS1 version which was a recreation of the first two Doom games on a custom PS1 engine, Doom 64 has a completely unique level design which is more or less on par with levels designed by the original team at id Software. I should mention that this release has a new six level episode, which I have not played at the time of this review (from other reviews, it seems pretty good). The game is for all intents and purposes, a very well made level/texture pack for Doom. Not a bad package at all. A vocal minority of fans call Doom 64 "the real Doom 3." If I remember correctly, Doom 64 was the reason why Doom 3 turned out the way it did. While Doom 64 is an excellent game, it was dragged at the time of its release because it shipped a year after Quake, and months before Goldeneye, and looked dated as a result. The following year, some heavy hitters were released, SiN, Shogo: Mobile Armor Division, Unreal, Half Life, all cutting edge polygonal titles that put the final nail in the coffin for the "Doom clone" sub-genre. These were industry trends that really had nothing to do with Doom 64, but the game reviewer hacks of the time still dragged it. That's why Doom 3 was released a decade after Doom 2, and was a completely different gameplay style. Doom 64 really is the last of its kind, and the pinnacle of the OG Doom style. You should play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with a few annoying flaws in the port, but accurate and stable, and running on a good engine. Not very feature heavy but I don't think this port was ever meant to be advanced, it's vanilla by design.How to fix some annoyances:-skipping the intro:Set -skipintro in your launch options or an autorun file, you can now press esc to skip it (why is this not default behaviour?).-skipping the endless logo splashes:-move or delete the five OGVs in the movies folder.-keyboard movement controls feel sticky and unresponsive:set the dead zone in the contoller input settings to zero, for some reason this applies to keyboard inputs too (!) Also disable vsync and crank up your framerate cap for even smoother inputs.The console command g_unlockfeatures 1 enables the features menu with level warp and cheats if you don't want to do the ridiculous map01 easter egg to unlock it. Cheats disable achievements but level warp doesn't :).Enjoy, also screw pain elementals

_childDocuments_.review: All the goodness of the original N64 release without the N64. It's a very cool entry in the Doom series, and it's shocking it took as long as it did to get a PC release.For those that don't know what this game is, it was a version of the classic game, "Doom", made for the N64, but this was not a port. Doom 64 is its own full unique game with new lightning, more advanced usage of the Doom engine, new sprites and sounds, a new weapon, and many adjustments to old weapons (Usually for the better). The game does have some casualties due to the limitations of the N64's hardware, namely a lack of storage on the cartridge leading to several enemies being cut from Doom 2. But what you do get is over 30 levels of awesome Doom fun. This version of the game features the standard ability to save and load games, but the N64 release had a password system which is also still intact in this release.I'm going to say it right here that while Doom is a classic game that holds its own to this day and Doom 64 is an immensely fun and satisfying game for fans of the series, the star of this game is the atmosphere. The new lightning and art direction combined with the masterclass soundtrack leads to a much darker and more oppressive atmosphere. Doom 64 plays like any entry in the action packed series, but has the environment and sound design of a horror game. If you like old FPS this game is a no brainer, don't skip this unique entry.

_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who originally thought this was a port of the original game onto the N64, I never bothered picking up the cartridge or hunting it down, so I was surprised when I saw it had been brought to Steam. After doing some reading and finding out that this was not at all a port of the original but instead a standalone title, I waited for a sale to pick it up and I decided to fill the gap in my Doom knowledge. Doom 64 is a phenomenal entry that stands shoulder to shoulder with it's older brothers. The game has a bit more of a haunting atmosphere than the original two games (which may explain some of the direction of Doom 3 come to think of it), and the gameplay is a bit slower paced (slower movement, slower fire rates, etc). It took awhile to get used to the more slippery movement (everything feels like you're on ice skates, is this Source?), but once I stopped blowing myself up with rockets by trying to corner peek enemies I was bobbing and weaving around enemy attacks just like in the originals. Great sprite work, spooky music, thick atmosphere, difficult levels (I played on "Watch Me Die!"), and great gun play means this is an absolute worth while addition into the Doom canon. I can't imagine playing this on the hardest setting though with an N64 controller, that's an achievement outside of my ability. I waited for a sale so I wouldn't blame you for doing the same, however it's absolutely worth full price! Definitely recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Responsive, old-school Doom with the welcome return of the N64-only sprites.  The gameplay is great, but the port has some lag at times.  I don't know if this existed in the original N64 game, but either way, it's a problem.  Thankfully, it comes up only occasionally (maybe once or twice per level), but when a few hits can drastically kill your health pool, it matters.  Despite that, this game is highly recommended for any Doom fan, especially if you never experienced the original.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I love the DooM series, but I honestly can't recommend this entry. Outside of the bad ass intro war scene, the awesome ambient music, the brutal double chainsaw....this game is disappointing in almost every important way.Game play wise, you will be backtracking, switch hunting and figuring out what the button you just pressed did. You will be trying to figure out how to get to the next door MORE than actual combat. Almost every button you press will need you to search the whole level to see what changed to progress. Traps are cruel and unforgiving, and not devious and fun like the classic games, since the classic games still gave you a chance to survive. Not this game. You will be constantly quicksaving and quickloading, floors dropping from under you into lava, and spawning in a baron 2 feet away from you in a small room. MANY times enemies will spawn right in front of you in a boring fade-in effect, without any really interesting encounters or compositions of enemies. Your worst enemy is the lost soul, who moves the fastest in the game, and will attack you VERY quickly, melting your health in a blink of an eye. They arent fun to fight against due to their attack rate and movement speed.The new weapon, the unmaker, looks and sounds boring and uninspired. Ill admit I never bothered finding the secret emblems to power this weapon, so I never had it powered up. The game REQUIRES you to find secrets to power this weapon, and finding secrets werent fun at all. The final boss was completely boring and frustrating due to her homing rockets being almost the same speed as your run. The final bosses' design was uninspired as well, she just looked like a brown HR Giger alien.Monster designs are pretty decent, with the Pinky being the best looking remade monster, looking more beefier and demonic. The humans are boring and stiff looking, while the imps are alien looking, and the cyberdemon manages to look less intimidating than the classic design. All monsters retain very choppy animation and somehow look more stiff and uninspired compared to classic doom sprites.Running around these levels were boring and I just wanted to finish the game because it came with eternal. Play it, beat it once, uninstall it.4/10

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is not a terrible game, but there are too many issues that outweigh a recommendation. The levels are too long. If you thought the length of Doom II levels were bad, you are going to hate this game. The game is unfair. There are several areas that you absolutely cannot beat the first time without prior knowledge (particularly on the highest difficulty).The areas I'm referring to are a mixture. One consists of random spawns or door openings where you WILL immediately die if you didn't already have the proper weapon out. The other consists of cruel and random falling traps near the end of levels. It gets to the point that save-scumming isn't even scummy (coming from an Ultra-Violence, Doom I and II completion with no mid-level saves). I wanted to give this title some slack when considering older game design, but Doom I and II are even older titles, and they are free from my aforementioned criticism. It's truly a shame. I prefer the new textures and look of this game over classic Doom, it's a nice change of atmosphere, and it even has plenty of good moments. But if you aren't a  completionist of the Doom series, I advise to save some frustration.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A masterpiece of level design, atmosphere, and action. What stands out to most people's nostalgia and deserving of special mention is the score, which is more a series of disturbing ambient noise than actual music. 32 brand new levels + a new campaign to rip and tear through, and a new weapon! The old crew is back, all redesigned and looking for blood, crammed into a cute little 64-bit cartridge, now perfectly ported to PC for all true DOOMers to enjoy. DOOM 64 is a better game than DOOM II (yeah, I said it) and features plenty of custom special effects non-existent in its predecessors-- rooms over rooms, an animated plasma gun, and teleporting enemies, for instance. This is the third iteration of DOOM 64 I've played, and it preserves the negatives as well as the positives. (The minimap is useless.) A steal at five bucks.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I always dismissed Doom 64 as a bleak copy of the originals. But in the last couple years I've heard more and more people praise Doom 64 as a hidden gem. Now that I've finished it for the first time, I regret to inform you my initial impression was correct. I kind of get why people like this, because it has a unique tone among the Doom titles, and a few of the levels in the campaign are genuinely good. But on the whole, it's just worse than Doom 1 and 2. Enemies are worse, the weapons are worse, and many of the levels are either worse copies from Doom 1 & 2 or mediocre new ones.At its best Doom 64 feels like a hybrid of Heretic, Quake and Doom. It also has puzzles that hit the right balance of actually requiring brain activity, but not being too obscure. This is something you almost never see in modern FPS, and especially not in any other Doom game. Like I saw someone say Doom Eternal has puzzles. Can you really call them puzzles if they're so easy my brain didn't even register them as being puzzles?Despite me being unimpressed by Doom 64 on the whole, I'm still going to give a recommended. It's fine. You could do worse. It's a good game to play in the background if you've got a few hours of podcasts or audiobooks you want to listen to.

_childDocuments_.review: Back when I've played it on the N64 in the early 2000s, I didn't get far (obviously the controller was a massive handicap for me). A few years later, I've found out about "hectic", a secret level in DOOM 64. Then the first "fun" level I've played was "Cat and Mouse", I'll never forget my first reaction when the Cyberdemon jumpscared me by teleporting into my face and turning me into mashed meat.Overall, I'm grateful and happy that DOOM 64 is getting the love it deserves. Especially with the new "Lost Levels" campaign (I've beaten it on "Watch me die!" and it tore me a new one). The community is even giving their attention & TLC to DOOM 64 by breeding more life into a game that was unfortunately limited because of the N64's cartridge space. Such as reintroducing the missing monsters like the Arch-vile, Chaingun Guy, Spider Mastermind, and Revenant. As well, cut monsters and weapons like that two-headed canine and the beta version of the unmaker that is named "Experimental Laser Gun".  I strongly recommend this game to DOOM fans and for those who don't know much about DOOM 64 that want to get their first time experience. However, I still urge first time players to play the Original DOOM games like Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II.  Mods I recommend for DOOM 64 that I've played as of making this review:DOOM 64 CEDOOM 64 Super EX+

_childDocuments_.review: A different flavor of DoomIf you've played classic Doom 1 or 2, you'll have a reasonable idea of what to expect in general, so I'll focus on the differences. The remaster means that you get somewhat higher resolution graphics, a bunch of save slots, and better default keys, though it's still very much like the DOS games. The monsters and weapons mostly behave like what you'd expect, though there are a handful of new ones.Graphically, the monsters are if anything higher resolution, with an art style that skews more towards aliens than pure horror. Level design also emphasizes the sci-fi aspects, and does a lot with interesting lights, and rather more saturated colors. A Marathon comparison (or once you get out of the tech base, Heretic/Hexen) is somewhat tempting.Sound effects are mostly better, especially the weapons (though ambient monster sounds less so). The almost Quake-like ambient music definitely sets a different mood from the metal themes of the DOS versions, though perhaps clashes with the scenery.Level designs have lots of neat features in terms of interactions, scripted events, secrets, use of movement. etc, though are comparatively short and usually cramped. The former is presumably from N64 hardware limitations, but is in practice not really a drawback. They're still fun levels. The latter does restrict things quite a bit, limiting your ability to dodge and use cover until things open up in the later levels.In conclusion: if you want more Doom, this is a good choice.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 is often seen as one of the weirder DOOM games along with DOOM 3 because of how it doesn't focus as much on the action but rather more on the atmosphere and puzzle solving. It's got a darker more moody OST that can definitely give you the creeps at moments and some of the puzzles can be quite challenging even for a 23 year old game. The visual redesigns of enemies and environments have aged really well and in my personal opinion out of all of the DOOM games, this is the one that has aged the best. If you're more of a fan of atmospheric FPS games like Half Life and Quake, DOOM 64 will resonate with you more than some of the other old DOOM games.If there's one thing that I think I'll be left with years later after playing DOOM 64, it would definitely have to be the atmospheric environments. No other DOOM game achieves it quite so effectively (even DOOM 3 overdoes it with cheap jumpscares)Puzzlesolving is really fun! You can definitely tell that this was a focus as a lot of Nintendo fans generally enjoy games with puzzlesolving elements. I was especially impressed by a lot of the secret level challenges and a certain puzzle on Level 9, which involved obtaining a yellow key.I've always liked the designs of enemies in most DOOM games but I think of the old games, this one strikes a really nice balance of being faithful to the original designs, while also bringing them to a real 3D space. There are also 2 new enemies in the game (1 of which is a boss, so not sure it counts) The levels themselves are very different than DOOM 1 and 2, as they go for a more Quake-like gothic look, something which I've noticed echoes across in some of the DOOM Eternal levels (as I'm currently playing that too)This is the type of game I'd definitely go back to with how many different levels and challenges there are, even after clearing through mostly all of it. They're just that damn fun and even though I didn't play DOOM 64 back in the 90s, I can confirm I'll be having nostalgia for this game several years down the line and will be getting an itch to replay it. The secret and lost levels are especially fun and it's very cool that they have a mechanic tied in with the actual game, by letting you upgrade the new Unmaker weapon (though it does get quite OP by the end of the game once you have it fully upgrade. It practically shreds the final boss in seconds xD)So I know these old DOOM games never had much of a story to begin with but this game practically has none. The devs tried to tie it in with DOOM 2016 and DOOM Eternal with a final cutscene that was added in this remake and there's I believe one other line of text towards the final levels, but other than that there isn't much here. Even DOOM 1 and 2 had sort of an explanation at several stages throughout the game that kind of give a hint as to what's happening. You even had a map that you tread across that shows your path from level to level, but there's none of that here. AGAIN, it doesn't really matter, but I did want to mention for those of you reading this coming from the era of newer DOOM games that now have lore and more of a story.Though this DOOM game excels at puzzlesolving and atmosphere, it's weak point compared to other DOOM games is definitely the combat. Even at higher difficulties there aren't many enemies in the levels and you breeze through them fairly quickly, left with then solving the puzzle of discovering the secrets and the way to the exit. As I mentioned previously, it wasn't as much of an issue for me but I can see it being a problem for DOOM fans looking for intense fights in rooms filled with enemies, like in the other games in the franchise. I'd give this game a hard recommend especially for the price. I don't think you need to be a hardcore oldschool DOOM fan for this one, especially with the differences in its gameplay and design. With the current wave of retro 3d shooters like DUSK, this feels right at home! Also if you own DOOM Eternal and you get this on Steam, you get a cool skin ;) (It's currently as of writing this the only Steam DOOM release that has skins as DOOM 1 and 2 aren't integrated with the Bethesda account thingy)
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: First time I played this game was via a sourceport as a mod for DOOM II. And frankly, I don't see any reason to play this new version over that one. The sourceport version provided infinite possibilities for configuration and had awesome extra content. It also ran smoothly with zero issues.This version, on the other hand, is very limited in configuration, has unskippable intro videos, shoves  in your face and doesn't even allow a three-dimensional free look. Which, yeah, I get it, this is essentially a 2D game, and the original never had it. But the original, as well as Doom 1 and 2 were developed for controller and keyboard controls respectively. When playing with a mouse, it feels pretty weird not to be able to move your camera up and down. Besides, that feature just makes it easier to enjoy and admire the beauty of the environments. Why not add it as an option at least?To make things worse, this version has weird performance issues on Linux that are linked to input, apparently. Other users reported that they had to use a controller or remap the bindings, but I don't wanna do either of those things. And why should I, when there's a perfectly functioning sourceport version of this, which is free (if you own DOOM II)?Bottom line is, just play the sourceport version.Tbf though, if you wanna play with a controller, I guess this version lets you do that. But if you're gonna do that, why not just emulate the original N64 version? I guess, it is more convenient to just have this game in Steam with a one-click install, but that's the only advantage this version has.As for the game itself, it is fine. A lot of people say it's better than the first two, but I don't think so. Sure, it's more atmospheric and all, but it's also much slower with many puzzles and whatnot. And I don't think this kind of gameplay fits well with the mechanics of what was a fun run&gun shooter.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 was the last "classic" Doom game to release, and as such, I only played it after playing the others first.It's weird.That's the only way I know to describe it.Doom 64 is a very unique take on the Doom series. It has the same general play-style, but the atmosphere is totally different. This title is creepy, and I don't mean Doom 3 sci-fi creepy, I'm talking about old tombs, dark shadows, no music, but distant footsteps creepy. Everything from the design of the levels, to the look of the enemies, to the... soundtrack? Sure, let's call it a soundtrack. What you end up with is a delightfully spooky take on the classic Doom formula, while still maintaining the same run-and-gun style you've come to know and love across an entirely new, full length campaign.Now, that's not to say it's without flaws. The levels are smaller than what you are used to, and there is a lower amount and smaller variety of enemies. This is mostly due to the hardware limitations of the Nintendo 64. They did their best to make up for it with extra and more complicated puzzles, and they did a fine job, but it's still noticeable. The controls are also a little stiff, there is definitely a slight delay between when you fire and when the gun actually responds to you firing. It's slight and doesn't really affect game play much, but I found it to be a bit annoying all the same.Now, as for this particular version on Steam, this is probably the most true-to-the-source version you can get. Their main priority was to release a version on modern systems that would run at modern standards, but for all intents and purposes is the same game as the day it came out. As far as that's concerned, I really don't think they could of done a better job.So, would I recommend this? Well, I wouldn't recommend you start with this one if you've never played a Doom game before. But, if you've played the other classic Doom games first, enjoyed what you played, and are looking for more, you should definitely check this out! I personally didn't click with it the first time I tried playing it, but coming back to it for a second time... well, let's just say I finally saw the vision. ;)Doom 64 is a unique and remarkable experience for established Doom fans, and should be enjoyed as such. That's the endorsement it deserves....AND if you've played through this version, and are interested in checking out some community-created content for it, as well as some other neat quality-of-life improvements, check out the Doom 64 CE mod. I guarantee, you will not be disappointed!Thanks for reading my review, hope you found it entertaining and informative. _childDocuments_.review: Simply the best of the Old-style pseudo-3D Doom games. An underappreciated gem from an era when Level Design was the key mechanic. Perhaps slightly closer to Quake or Hexen in atmosphere, with a much heavier leaning in on Satanic imagery, with a more horror/foreboding feeling overall, it feels like the first Doom that took itself seriously, while not sacrificing any of its identity as seen in Doom 3. The sprite work holds up relatively well despite its age, and because of that aforementioned age, you can run this game on a walnut strapped to a 9V battery.This game also marks the first of only two appearances of the Unmaker(Unmaykr in DE), a weapon that leaves you asking a most preposterous but frightening question: Why did Satan need a gun?

_childDocuments_.review: Doom is one of my all-time favorite game series, as it is for many people. I’ve played just about every version across all the official platforms, and still play it today via source ports on PC. Heck, I even play the modern Doom and Doom Eternal and enjoy them both. I stood in line to get my original Doom shareware disks and to pre-order the full game at a local game shop when it was first released. Having been a fan of Wolfenstein 3D, Doom simply looked amazing, and it blew me away when I played through it the first time. ID Software become one of my favorite developers overnight, they were already pretty high up there thanks to Commander Keen and Wolf 3D.With Doom II, Final Doom, the add-ons, and countless wad packs (both official and user), it kept me hooked for a very long time, I even made some of my own levels. However, it was Doom 64 that really stood out in my mind as something special, something different, but still Doom. The overall look, feel, and sounds were Doom, but taken to a different level. It was the first time since the original Doom in 1993 that I was blown away by what they had done. Today, I still enjoy playing Doom 64 from time to time, and having it here on Steam gives me one more way to enjoy it. My only real complaint is the same as many others, the incorporation of  for no good reason other than to push it on, and advertise to, the end-user. I already had a Bethesda account, and I know Bethesda is the current publisher of the Doom franchise, but there is no valid reason to incorporate it into these old titles. Thankfully, you can skip it, but it shouldn’t have been included to begin with. Still, it’s Doom 64, the game is great, this version plays perfectly on my Windows 10 machine, and I am happy to own it.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is a very different but an original take on Classic Doom.  The maps are totally different from the PC-version and the overall visual style is more sinister. I couldn't stand Doom 64 back in the late 90's because of the different sounds and the ambient music, but later on I had a chance to experience the game again in the early 2000's, and I managed to look under the surface of the game.Then I realized what I had missed back in the late 90's. Doom 64 is a very solid Doom game, I've come to realize that the different sounds and the ambient music I used to hate so much decades ago are the very reason behind the unique feeling and the style of this game. Doom 64 also feels and plays very much like the other Classic Doom games, despite looking quite different from its predecessors. And yeah, I've grown to like the music and the sounds quite a lot over the years.Never judge a book by it's cover. Lesson learned.

_childDocuments_.review: Really glad Doom 64 is getting some long deserved love now.  It's Doom, but spooky.  Great level design (aside from a few questionable puzzles), STELLAR atmosphere and music, fun combat, and an aesthetic that still holds up, especially in its use of moody colored lighting.The port itself is great, and is more about bringing the original game up to par in areas like resolution, frame rate, FOV, etc than it is about adding modern effects or modifying the gameplay.  There's no bloom or fancy new lightmaps, because Doom 64 didn't have those.  There's no vertical look because Doom 64 didn't have it.  Weapon sprites will always be unfiltered because that's how they were on the N64.  It's quite playable by modern standards but keeps the original experience as intact as possible, which I really appreciate.This is a no brainer if you're a fan of the original Doom games, or really if you're just a fan of "boomer shooters" in general and appreciate a moodier creepier take on that style.

_childDocuments_.review: Not to discredit Doom 3 but this IS the canon Doom 3 that went under so many peoples' radar for so long due to it's N64 exclusivity. Nightdive knocked this one out of the park and are very much responsible for bringing this title into the light. Using their Kex Engine (much like Blood and other titles revamped by Nightdive) Doom 64 runs incredibly well on modern hardware and looks fantastic. Things you may notice if you've only played Doom 1 and 2, is the musical whiplash from the heavy metal soundtracks of the originals to the atmospheric gurgles and cries of Doom 64 (bar the intro theme), which lends itself to the horrific and moody design choice--similar Doom for the original Playstation.Another difference is the lack of some enemy types and addition of others, due to the memory limitations when this title was being developed for Doom 64. These include the Revenant, Archvile, Chaingunner, Spider Mastermind and the standalone Sergeant. Some weapon animations also lack extra frames with the hand, like the SSG and the shotgun, which excludes the reload animations.The level design feels much more complex and fun to explore, with secret levels to unlock 'Demon Keys' that can be used to upgrade the Unmaker. And there are security cameras that can be used to spy out areas with secrets or parts of a puzzle from a specific area.You now have a double-bladed chainsaw... nice! The blood can be changed to either red or green if you are a baby or the game makes you too squeamish.It was also a nice thing for Bethesda and ID to include this game as a pre-order bonus.If you love Doom, just do yourself a favour and play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 on PC is a long time coming. Having been initially released as an exclusive for – you guessed it - the Nintendo 64, PC gamers in 1997 must have felt a mix of emotions that their platform-defining showpiece was going console-exclusive. The original DOOM’s console ports were spotty to say the least, consistently being dragged down by abysmal performance on systems that weren’t designed to deal with the processing power required by DOOM. It wasn’t until DOOM on the PlayStation arrived in 1995 that console gamers could treat themselves to a respectable port, nearly 2 years after the original game released. From this perspective, DOOM 64 was likely met with scepticism, but also an opportunity to right some wrongs and salvage the series’ reputation within the console market. While DOOM took almost two years to produce an authentic console port, DOOM 64’s story is the exact opposite. It took six years for DOOM 64 to be ported to the PC, in the form of DOOM 64: Absolution in 2003. This unofficial source port consisted of level recreations within the original DOOM engine, but was the first chance PC gamers had to experience the magic of DOOM 64 outside of what would have been very slow emulation. Absolution was replaced by DOOM64 EX in 2008, still a recreation, but drawing from original data within the N64 cartridge. DOOM64: Retribution, released in 2016, was another popular port using the GZDoom engine, one of the most popular ports for running the original DOOM on modern systems. At this point, PC gamers had waited nearly 2 decades without an official release of DOOM 64. That is, until 2020. We’ve now been treated to an official 4K release running at up to 240FPS (or uncapped up to 1000FPS, if you desire). With controller support and added visual options such as anti-aliasing, was it worth the wait for first-time players?Simply put, DOOM 64 looks absolutely gorgeous. The visual makeover can be attributed to 2 new upgrades. First off, a stunning new colour palette had completely redefined the visual identity of 90s DOOM. No longer are we subject to battleship grey wall textures, but instead tinted reds, blues and yellows bounce off the environment creating a much more colourful look, all while retaining the horror feel through its dark moody lighting. Speaking of which, the games coloured lighting allows much more variance in how each room is presented creating clear visual landmarks through the use of colour. Out of the box, the game is a bit too dark – but this can be turned up with both environmental brightness, and overall screen brightness. I suggested turning the former up. While the game still plays in a 2.5D realm, many of the game’s objects are now rendered in polygonal 3D. What this means is, while many objects are still technically flat 2D images, and interact with the player as such, they are now presented visually in 3D. DOOM 64’s gameplay is near identical to previous entries. There’s no new innovations, no swimming, no vehicle sections, no third-person point of view, no jumping. Just like in 1993, you’re advancing through maze-like levels to flip switches and collect keycards. Surprisingly, this doesn’t feel like a chain to which DOOM 64 is held down on against its will. The core gameplay loop is still consistently enjoyable and it’s rare to encounter frustratingly obscure puzzles, although the odd switch on a particularly large map can still be a nuisance. Guns are still mainly the same, but have been rebalanced. The super shotgun is better than ever and makes quick work of nearly every enemy barring the cyberdemon, and most importantly feels satisfying to use. The chaingun is underpowered however, and is no longer the best option for quick crowd control. The rocket launcher is, as always, a bit of a liability with a consistent percentage chance to gib the player.The game is also completely robust. Not once in my 10 hours playtime did I encounter a single glitch, nor fell out of bounds or clip on the environment. FPS was locked the entire time, and the game’s data only takes up 82MB. The game features 32 levels + a bonus 6-level campaign, the latter of which is typically much harder with bigger levels than the original, and took me 10 hours to complete all in all.I would have preferred some more options within the menus. For example, there’s no way (as far as I could see) to auto-run. This means your finger is almost permanently locked down on the left trigger, in what seems like a really silly oversight. Other than that, I don’t have many complaints. Due to the (extremely) late release of DOOM 64, there’s basically no modding scene. This cuts the game’s lifespan substantially, and so there’s not much reason to play past completion beyond finding secrets and unlocking achievements. The recent DOOM 1 and 2 releases feature great in-game mod menus, which are completely gone in DOOM 64, leaving you with the great albeit limited official set of WADs. Overall, DOOM 64 is well-worth the £3.99 and I’d recommend it in a heartbeat for anyone who has enjoyed the original DOOM games. More of the same, but with a beautiful visual overhaul.
