_childDocuments_.review: The remaster of DOOM 64 is a fantastic reimagining of the classic 1997 first-person shooter. As a fan of the original game, I was thrilled to see that the remaster not only preserved the feel of the original game but also added some new features and enhancements.One of the standout features of the remaster is the updated graphics. The game's visuals have been given a major overhaul, with improved textures, lighting, and character models. Despite the updated graphics, the game still manages to retain the classic look and feel of the original game, and the new enhancements only serve to make the game even more immersive.Another great addition to the remaster is the inclusion of new levels. The original DOOM 64 had some of the best levels in the entire franchise, and the remaster takes things even further with new levels that are just as well-designed and challenging as the original ones. These new levels provide a fresh challenge for players who are already familiar with the game and make the remaster even more enjoyable for new players.The remaster also includes a range of quality-of-life improvements that make the game even more accessible and enjoyable to play. For example, players can now save their progress at any time, which makes it easier to pick up and play the game on the go. The game also includes new controls that are optimized for modern controllers, which makes the game even more intuitive and easy to play.Overall, the remaster of DOOM 64 is a fantastic update to an already classic game. With updated graphics, new levels, and quality-of-life improvements, the game manages to feel both fresh and familiar at the same time. If you're a fan of first-person shooters or the DOOM franchise, this game is definitely worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game. Retains the core combat Doom is known for, with a few changes that for the most part work in its favor. Textures are pretty and the ambient soundtrack sets the atmosphere well. A bit of key hunting, but it's mostly intuitive and no map overstays its welcome. Short and sweet campaign, doesn't stagnate toward the end, and the bonus "Lost Levels" that come with this version feel like a part of the base game rather than unfinished hackjobs tacked on needlessly.I have no real complaints. It's objectively a good game, but I'll outline the differences to the previous entries in the series I noticed, just so fans of classic Doom know what they're in for.• Player movespeed is slower. I think this is deliberate since the maps are mostly comprised of tight spaces.• Not as many enemy types. • Pain Elementals explode upon death and deal catastrophic damage if you're close, while still releasing Lost Souls.• Lost Souls seem to be more aggressive, and that combined with the Pain Elemental's death explosion makes getting close to one a death sentence. The saving grace is that they die in 1 normal shotgun blast. Personally I like how they work in this game, more deadly, but less annoying.• Mancubi shoot both cannons at once with the projectiles being adjacent to each other.• Arachnotrons shoot two projectiles simultaneously, which unlike the Mancubus', are close together and both slated to hit you if you don't move out of the way. They are extremely dangerous now, which I also like.• Spectres are actually hard to see now due to the overall darkness of the game, the shading and textures of the environment, and the partial invisibility effect looking different.• I think Cacodemon projectiles are a bit faster (not sure if placebo).• The orientation Cyberdemons shoot rockets from is different, and they lead some shots.• The BFG 9000 sees a major nerf, now killing 2-3 mid tier enemies in front of it at best. It's only situationally viable now, mainly for taking out Cyberdemons if you don't have an upgraded Unmaker, but even then requires way too many cells. • The Unmaker is an upgradable automatic cell-based weapon that, even in its weakest form, takes precedence over the Plasma Gun, which received a painful fire rate nerf, and from a gameplay standpoint probably shouldn't have been included. I'd say the BFG was made weaker because it'd trivialize fights, but this thing exists, so that's a moot point.• The Chaingun fires faster now. It's sick.Get it if you always wanted Doom to be spookier, but are allergic to Doom 3's full-on genre shift.

_childDocuments_.review: You'd be surprised how well this game has aged even without mods. The only thing lacking is the oomph in the weapons. These classic fps games have immersion levels at 100%. Not in a way that is "realistic" - but in a way that you feel you just got put in a world and you have to figure out a way to solve things. You don't get that feeling with modern games with "triggers", but oh well, at least we have nice graphics.Doom is a mindless shooter, some idiots say. The same idiots who never played the game and watched a gameplay clip where you see a nameless guy shooting demons. What they don't see is the maze-puzzle-like level design which you cannot beat unless you actually use your brain to memorize segments and have above average navigational skills - something lacking in current gen video games. Not to mention how the combat has a strategic element to it as well.Great game.  Def worth a buy. Recommend using a controller on this game. IF you don't have a controller, use only keyboard - just like classic Doom games  were designed for (unless you mod it). Because Doom 64 was developed for the Nintendo 64 console - which didn't even have a decent analog stick. So playing with the mouse n kb even on the highest difficulty is too easy and breaks the balance. And not being able to look up or down while using a mouse feels extremely weird too, so I recommend playing the game the way it was intended to be.As for the port, it's awesome. Unlocked framerates, FOV slider, ultrawide  - it's awesome. I hope they do the same with classic Doom 1 and 2.

_childDocuments_.review: took me by surprise. Growing up I never owned a Nintendo 64 (I was a PlayStation kid), so for years I operated under the belief that no such conversion of id’s classic first-person shooter had made its way onto Nintendo’s console. By the time I learned of its existence, my interest was best described as “indifferent”. I just casually assumed it was  all over again, not caring to dig any deeper into Midway Games’ title.What a putz.  is no mere remake of the original game, but a sequel to the events of . And, curiously enough, a more compelling and interesting game than id’s own , which followed some years later. You may boo and jeer me all you wish, but it’s true.For starters it’s a far creepier game than , creating a pervasive sense of quiet unease without ever laying it on too thick (there’s no ludicrous villainous laughter or any comical jump scares, for instance).We start our war against Hell’s relentless evil in a sealed UAC base, long since left dormant. Here the game echoes with traces of  dread and isolation, its horror far more acute than the original games. But then I never considered those games horror per se, and now, having played the entire series, I feel like only  and  can lay claim to being proper horrors titles.That’s not to say  is some kind of survival horror, though. It’s as action-packed and brutal as you’d expect from a  game, with a host of ghastly demons intent on pulverising you with balls of flames and sizzling orbs of energy. Unfortunately they’re not nearly as confounding as the game’s plethora of repetitive puzzles.Whilst I loved the bizarre and unsettling architecture of the world – especially Hell itself, with its great walls of fire and crackling violet thunderstorms raging above desolate sierras – they aren’t easy to navigate. You’re going to need to find keys to progress, but that involves pressing buttons to open doors and clear obstacles. The problem? It’s often a mystery as to where these doors are, meaning you’ll spend a lot of time racing around the map looking for whichever door has opened. It’s an in inelegant and frustrating piece of design.But beyond that you have a thoroughly enjoyable  game, brimming with atmosphere and the kind of gory, white-knuckle combat you’ve come to expect from the series. Sure, it was a little outdated even for the time, relying on the tried-and-true  formula, but I see little point in marking it down for that.It’s , and that formula was more than good – it was revolutionary. Kudos to Nightdive Studios for bringing it to PC, enabling players who missed out the first time to play it anew.

_childDocuments_.review: The level design in this game is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ past level 5. All the "puzzles" are really just convoluted mazes where the game tells you nothing about the environment while you bumble around the same 4 rooms for 10 minutes looking for the hidden switch on the same wall texture you've seen 70 other times, or looking to shoot the wall in just the right spot to open a random door 6 rooms over for 10 seconds. The combat isn't engaging, it's infuriating. You'll walk over the same spot you just passed and out of nowhere it will spawn 10 Barons of Hell and 6 Hell Knights and expect you to kill all of them without running out of ammo or dying. And that's just level 8! In level 9, they spawn you in between 4 Mancubi that are all shooting at you at different times, so you can hardly dodge them without luck, and even after you kill them, it spawns Hell Knights, Barons, Cacodemons, and Pain Elementals everywhere around you. You get one Soul Sphere, one Mega Armor, and one Invulnerability, along with some other minor pickups. That's it. The invulnerability just barely lasts long enough to kill the Barons with a rocket launcher or chainsaw, and you still have the Cacodemons, Mancubi, and Pain Elementals to deal with, not to mention the 30+ Lost Souls that have just been spawned by said Pain Elementals. It's a cluster♥♥♥♥, and that's putting it lightly. There's hardly any thought put into the combat, they just throw a handful of random enemies at you in some random formation and expect you to kill them. That's all it is. There is no effort put into the difficulty, strategy, or puzzles.It's fun for a 20 minute pass-time, but nothing more. Don't pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: A more fitting successor to Doom II than the slow, horror FPS Doom 3. Doom 64 has the fast gameplay of the first two games, with arguably more obscure key-hunting sequences. Enemy and weapon sprites are given a new coat of fresh paint. Level design can be occasionally frustrating, but the atmosphere is an achievement given the time this game was released. Maps are somewhat colorful yet unsettling due to the oppressive soundscape. Doom 64's OST is similar to Trent Reznor's OST for Quake, using things like droning sounds and  baby cries to create an unnerving feeling. Worth a playthrough for fans of retro FPS.

_childDocuments_.review: While often forgotten, Doom 64 is a solid and respectable entry in the doom franchise, and in my heart is the real Doom 3.  While the title could have been a wash and repeat of Doom and Doom 2 just scaled down for the 64, actual deviation was made to stand Doom 64 out from it's predecessors, with just as much changes to Doom 1 that Doom 2 had.  Weapon animations are minimal this go around, but the tweaks made to the known and existing enemies are neat and refreshing after playthroughs of vanilla Doom 1 and 2.   Map design is mostly solid, and is more vanilla Doom if you're looking for more Doom without getting into gzdoom and wads.  More environmental traps and 'puzzles' are in play with 64 than previous installments, however, and a few levels can feel like tedious switch hunts which isn't too different from other titles of this genre at the time.The port to PC runs flawless, and is certainly worth $5 if original doom is your thing and you haven't played 64 before.  (additionally, had no issues tabbing over to other programs and back on a multimonitor setup which is a huge plus)Only thing going against Doom 64 is it's soundtrack.  Attempts were made to deviate 64 and the soundtrack was one of them.  It goes for a more experimental and ambient deal to set the 'creepy' factor, and in the early darker levels (the better levels in the game tbh) it doesn't feel too out of place, but it's weird and it sucks. And when those weird 'creepy' ambient tracks are looped for a couple hours of gameplay, they start to get old and left me wanting just *something* else that didn't, well, suck.

You'renot likely to figure it out without a walkthrough unless you'rejust some kinda genius.I'd probably replay it, though. It still has a lotta good going for it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a day one owner of the Nintendo 64, and a huge Doom fan. But I don't think I realized back then that this version of Doom was unique. I must have assumed it was just the original game ported to N64.  Anyway, after all these decades, I played this game for the first time on Steam. It's a great addition to the Doom franchise. I can't believe I almost missed out on it. I also would have expected this to be a watered down version made for a younger audience, but no, this is more brutal and difficult than the original. It also has an eerie soundtrack that can be quite unnerving at times. Playing with Mouse/Keyboard is almost cheating as I'm sure this was way more challenging on the N64 controller, but I had a blast going through this game. To get 100% achievements you will almost certainly need to get some online help to find all the secrets, as they are hidden better in this game than any other Id Software title. It must have taken years to find them all back in the day.Tech-wise since I never played the original, I had to find some YouTube footage to compare. As expected this port is fantastic. It preserves the look and feel of the original, but adds support for modern hardware with high frame rates and high resolution and widescreen support. I give this an A+ and super glad it showed up on Steam and that I didn't skip it again.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have ever played original Doom games you what to expect from this game since this is basically an old school Doom game with a new coat of paint. I think the style suits the game fine, besides Mancubi that look like fat goblins that wobble around like they are drunk. Level design in Doom 64 is for the most part a pretty good and there are some rather creative set pieces and even few simple puzzles.  Still I think this game suffers from few annoying design choices.-Many levels require what is usually called "switch hunting". You flip a switch and then you have to figure out what it did. Sometimes it's not even possible to tell what is a switch.-The game has a habit of using really annoying traps such as lava pits without a way of getting out of them and walls that will suddenly fire a barrage of seeking missiles at you.-The game doesn't have proper music. Some people may find this atmospheric but I just found it to be really dull.-Finally the game absolutely loves to throw in enemies that just appear out of thin air to ambush the player. Sure teleporting enemies have always been a thing in Doom games but in other games there's a distinct audiovisual effect that helps player to react to them. In this game enemies just appear and it's not fun to be suddenly surrounded by Imps and Mancubi.If you are fan of old Doom games, or at least old school shooters, then this game might offer you at least some entertainment.

_childDocuments_.review: It's classic DOOM with an atmospheric horror twist. And honestly? I think it's up there with DOOM 1 and 2. I really love tonal switch up from blasting demons away to heavy metal, to trying to survive the horrors of hell. The gothic imagery is superb and the ambient, distorted soundtrack creates such an unsettling atmosphere. It's such a great tone for DOOM that I honestly don't know which I like more. Both are great.Gameplay is just as good as ever. Great weapon variety and the guns feel and sound so impactful. The new weapon; The Unmaker is absolutely devastating and with the Demon Key upgrades, it even makes the BFG seem underpowered. I also prefer a lot of the weapon designs in this game. Level design is mostly great. It feels more like DOOM 1 with it's endless corridors and tight spaces. But it also has DOOM 2's more open levels thrown in for good measure. One annoyance I did have was trying to find where to go. DOOM's levels have always been labyrinthine-y. But 64 has too many switch scattered about that aren't too clear on what they open. There's also traps which, unless you have the power of foresight. Will end up getting you in rather cheap ways. Enemy placement for the most part is fine. A few cheeky Hell Knights behind a door, but I've come to expect that from DOOM. I feel they do overdo it a bit with Hell Knights and Barons. It's like one of the most common enemy in the game and you get sick of fighting them in small spaces. The maps visually have this really nice progression in theme as you go through the game. It starts with the classic sci-fi Phobos base levels from DOOM 1 but goes more gothic and disturbing as you enter hell. As mentioned before, the game has some really amazing gothic imagery. DOOM has always had gargoyle faces on the walls, but 64 takes those few gargoyles and really goes in on that horror aesthetic. Coupled with the soundtrack creates such a creepy atmosphere. Enemies designs is just as good as DOOM 1/2's. The sprite work is incredibly done, with each enemy being very distinct from each other. Making it easier to track with enemy to priorities in fights. This to me is essential in a DOOM game and 64 does a great job. The designs themselves is honestly personal preference. They more or less follow the original designs but with some changes. Overall, I prefer 64's Imps, Pinkies and Cyber-Demon (Which is basically the same sprite but higher res) But a lot of the charm and character of a lot of Demons are lost to fit with the horror theme. Cacodemon and the Pain Elemental just don't do anything for me. A few enemies were changed for 64. There's a new Imp called a Nightmare Imp. Which is basically a more powerful Imp with some added Spectre in there. Mancubus now fire rockets instead of flameballs. And the Pain Elemental got the biggest (and most annoying) redesign by far. They don't resemble the DOOM 2 version at all and instead fire 2 Lost Souls at once. Lost Souls are also way more deadly, as they charge quicker and end up constantly hit you if you're not paying attention. Aside from that, every enemy more or less is the same. Also Chain Gunners, Arch-viles and the Spider Mastermind have been cut from the game. (And nothing of value was lost)TL;DR DOOM went through a goth phase and it was actually really, really good. If you like DOOM 1 and 2. There's no reason not to pick this one up.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't have an N64 growing up, and my friends who did, did not have this. I can't tell how close this is to the original, but this plays just like vanilla DOOM.The overall tone is darker and moodier. This is partially due to the low lighting and use of different colored lighting, but also thanks to the soundtrack provided by Aubrey Hodges. Where Bobby Prince Jr. provided thrash and metal-inspired tracks that gave DOOM a blistering pace, the soundtrack here makes you watch your back and fear what's around the corner. The engine used here can also do things that the original DOOM engine could not, such as arrow traps and a key that can randomize its position on the map.Due to time and storage constraints, the full bestiary is not available. Still, the devs made the most of what they had, and you will still deal with some relatively challenging situations, so you won't be bored.There are many that say that this was the "true" DOOM 3: Given that the gameplay is mostly the same and follows Doomguy from the first 2 games, I'd say they're right. With DOOM Eternal, it makes even further sense.If you are a fan of DOOM and played the original games, this is a perfectly good port.

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10Doom 64 is a great shooter on its own merits, but also as a companion piece to Doom. The atmosphere is wonderfully immersive and the combat physics work well enough. It isn't as crisp as Doom, but the environments are more varied and fully-realized, leading to a unique Doom experience while keeping its foundation intact.Doom 64 is fundamentally copy-pasted from Doom, but with some key differences. While movement and combat are still fluid and immersive, there is a certain blockiness to everything (specifically pertaining to weapon and monster animations, projectile mapping, and some chunky monster designs). Most of the monsters are derived from Doom's classic bestiary, and while some are more realized and menacing, others come off just a little goofier in execution (even if they're mechanically unchanged, largely).Level design and map layouts have the traditional abstract approaches. Secret-hunting and navigation is still fun, but modern players may find it irksome. Progression is still mainly built on find-the-key mechanics, but there are some interesting curveballs thrown in to keep players on their toes (items can now teleport in, and monsters can spawn from killing other monsters, separately from simply crossing linedefs). These unique maps make Doom 64 truly stand out.The only disappointment in the game is the sound design. Nearly everything sounds simultaneously muffled and echoed, which creates a sense of artificiality in the otherwise immersive world. Music is nice and unsettling, though, relying less on heavy metal riffs and more on ambient sounds of darkness and despair.Doom 64, while admittedly derivative of Doom, maintains an exceptional identity. It isn't the groundbreaking shooting experience that propelled first-person-shooters into the gaming stratosphere like Doom and Doom 2 did, but it deserves recognition nonetheless. Maybe it isn't perfect, but it stands on its own terms, and that's what matters.

_childDocuments_.review: I really really tried to enjoy this game, however, I got completely disappointed from it. Technically speaking it's not a bad game, but as a DOOM game is really mediocre in many ways (Personally) Let me explain this in a small summarise of everything. The whole ambience tries to give you a scary setting, but I honestly don't know how's that supposed to happen when at the same time gives you like 7 different weapons and you're essentially a unstoppable force. The music is almost gone for somehow? one of the most iconic things related to doom are its soundtracks, most of them violent and catchy, but here's just weird noises at the background (yes i know, there's plenty of them at the original ones, but it's just a part of the soundtrack, and not the whole of it) Considering this was released after and not before QUAKE, in terms of graphics is really disappointing (I'm aware that making anything work on a Nintendo 64 is no joke, and that's exactly my point, why?) the levels felt way too compressed, the enemies' sprites are way less menacing than before, and many animations were cut (even the super shotgun one is missing) and the levels are unnecessarily frustrating, in the first 2 games, the traps were supposed to be used to challenge those who wanted to look out for secrets, and here, they're literally everywhere, most of them unskippable, and at the other hand, most of the levels are just running mindlessly from point A to point B hoping to find what's the button doing when you press it. I really tried, but I didn't liked this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This Doom version offers richer graphics and new sprite monsters compared to the original DOS versions. It also has modified versions of the classic Doom weaponry.The game itself has many issues. Mouse steering didn't feel natural. Lost souls are on steroids and you can die easily from this already most annoying enemy. The levels are sometimes too dark. The biggest issue is with the map design. Many are maze like and you often have to backtrack the whole map when some switch opens a door on the other side.  Some puzzles are undo-able (e.g. the blue key in level 18) and one needs YouTube help for the solution. When you fall in pits you can restart the level since there is no way out.Overall I wasn't too happy with the game itself. Still glad that I could finally play this legendary Doom version. Thumb up is for Bethesda's effort to make this available on Steam for all fps fans.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished all 40 levels on the highest difficulty. It was amazing! But what it does, it does perfect.I haven't missed mouse aiming or jumping for a single second - it also played really smooth without crashes or lags. If you haven't played the original Doom 64 yet - go for it! You can't go wrong at that price. And if you already played it? Get it, too, because the 6 new lost episodes + 1 new fun level are really good.

_childDocuments_.review: Being a big fan of the original Doom games, 1 and 2 that is, I have to say Doom 64 doesn't really add anything.I guess it was interesting to see this ported version, out of curiosity, but yeah, I'd rather play the original game again, way better level design for one. (Get GZDoom)Did anyone notice how the intro movie seemed to suggest multiplayer Co-Op? Well, there's no Co-Op at all. Boo.The menus didn't quite know if they wanted to be mouse or keyboard-only sometimes, and those extra options Bethesda squeezed in there, did anyone use those?If you are a completionist Doom nerd, yeah sure, play it by all means, but if you like me treasure the old games, don't waste your money and time with this.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked DOOM 1 & 2, it's effectively more of that, but not quite as good in many aspects.The map design is mostly just ok. Has a lot of "Puzzles" that consist of constant trial and error running around the map like a headless chicken. Combine that with a lot of maze-like levels, it can become a chore on some maps. Enemy variety is mostly a mixture of DOOM 1 & 2, but mostly 1: it has the pain elemental, but no heavy gunner/revenant/arch-vile.The game lacks any music of note (mostly tries to go for an odd dark ambient set-up which doesn't really match the gameplay, or even the silly story text). Also, special note to the UnMaker weapon ; I know it's supposed to be a secret or late-game super-weapon, but it's either just worse than the plasma rifle, or (if you get the upgrades) blatantly better than both the plasma rifle and BFG, making weapon variety a bit odd since it is either unused, or causes two other weapons to be unused. _childDocuments_.review: is an excellent remaster of the unique Nintendo 64 game.  I've wanted to complete this game since I first tried it at a friends house a few decades ago, but the controller turned me off back then.  Now it's here on the PC with Mouse & Keyboard support! Included in this game are the original 25 Main Levels, 4 Secret Levels, and 3 Fun Levels.  It also comes with 6 challenging unreleased levels called , and 1 additional  .  Along with the great puzzles, and the new  weapon, there's a lot of content here to keep you occupied for 20+ hours!On the downside, you can't look up and down, nor is there any multiplayer, but neither of those were in the original game either, so it's not a deal-breaker. It's also easy to get snagged on wall outcroppings, making navigation a bit tricky in some hairy situations. Every time the game starts, or when you go to the  menu item, an error box pops up saying "", which was a bit annoying. Lastly, the intro movies take a while to play, and I had to add  to the game launch options to get the game to load faster.With that said though, the pros still outweigh the cons, and  is probably the best single-player experience out of all the classic DOOM games.  It's definitely worth playing, especially if you're a fan of , , , or the !

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely classic Doom but it feels like they improved a ton of things from the older games and managed to make a pretty satisfying 4 Hour experience. Although Nightdive was WAY too faithful with the port, leading to problems that will hurt the game's playability and longevity in the future for new generations of FPS players coming back to it.+One of the biggest improvements from the original N64 game is that the game had some of the most abysmal visibility issues on original hardware. The game was so pitch black and you couldn't see anything you might as well have had your eyes closed. It forced players to turn up the brightness on their TV to an absurd and inappropriate level. Now, the brightness has definitely been fixed. The game is finally visible and it's just dark enough so that it doesn't become a problem when looking at the screen and searching for enemies. This is by far the best part of the port.+The guns in 64 are much better mainly because they sound meatier and the impact of things like the shotgun and pistol are quite impressive. The game has the typical Doom Arsenal alongside a new weapon that shoots beams out of it. If you go through the secret levels you can upgrade it apparently, but I didn't know that until it was too late. Still, the weapons are a big step up from Ultimate Doom and Doom II, which is great because you want to see the game improve over every entry.+The atmosphere is also one of the biggest step ups from Ultimate Doom and Doom II. The game lacks the MIDI music and goes for more of a terrifying soundscape. In fact, I was so tense at points I literally jumped out of my seat when enemies attacked me from behind. Trust me, I pretty much screamed and almost fell out of my seat when that happened a couple times. Although, Doom is, and never will be a horror game. But this is the closest I think any of the original games aside from Doom 3 that is easily comparable to what we might call 'Horror'. It's really freaky.+There are some puzzles that can be a bit weird, but I figured all the cryptic ones out (The Yellow Key Jail) on my first try pretty much by accident. Some of the other puzzles involve hitting a combination of switches to unlock doors with the three keys you have gotten in the last chunk of the game and I felt so smart for figuring that out. The game feels rewarding for having you figure out these puzzles and it's never to the point where you have to look up a walkthrough.*In terms of the difficulty, I played on Normal Difficulty (Bring It On) and the game is mostly easy until the latter half of the game, mostly the final few levels. Although I don't think the game is really that difficult to begin with. The final boss provided a strong fight with hordes of enemies spawning. If you got stuff from the secret levels you can stop that from happening but I didn't know that. Thankfully, going right up into their faces with the rockets with the invincibility the game nicely gives you alongside the mega sphere helps a lot. The final boss took a couple tries but I do think it's doable. Just have to diagonal run from it's projectiles or hide behind some of the switches with your BFG or Rocket Launcher. If you run out, the double shotgun usually does the trick to finish it off. I'm pretty competent at FPS Games and have played so many this almost felt like a breeze. I would suggest if you're a veteran player to play on a harder difficulty (maybe not the hardest though).-A couple of problems though. One is that Nightdive was too faithful and decided not to add any QOL features like a level select or proper auto save at the beginning of each level. Instead you have this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ password system that should have been thrown out for how archaic it is. I don't know nothing about porting games or game development but I don't get why Nightdive doesn't just rearrange the code or program new things into it for these features considering the fact that they're essentially making a new version of the game for newer consoles and PC. It can be frustrating when you get cocky and don't think you need to save, then fall into a death trap and have to restart from a couple levels back because the game doesn't properly auto save your game. This drives me nuts in so many of these FPS Ports and Remasters from the 90's. Although that's just me talking out of my ass and having wishful thinking.-There's also a couple of VERY obnoxious visual effects in this game. Stuff like flashing lights and blinding brightness when you pick up power ups are very annoying and hurt my eyes when playing. BE AWARE if you have epilepsy, though these are mostly rare occasions when this happens.-Final Thoughts-Doom 64 is worth playing and it's dirt cheap. It's basically pennies when it goes on sale, but that asking price of CDN $6.49 is absolutely worth biting the bullet for. I wouldn't suggest this as your first FPS game if you're new to the genre, I would recommend something more along the lines of Modern Warfare 2007, Halo: Combat Evolved, Half-Life 2, or Doom 2016 (on an easier difficulty of course for all of them) if you want to get into this genre. Doom 64 has some stuff that is archaic and dated and some of the levels have big annoyances in them and the amount of Lost Souls was absurd and irritating, but the game itself for anyone who has played a decent amount of games in the genre, veterans wanting to pick up something that will reflect their tastes or people wanting to revisit it will want to get this. It's really good altogether.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly kind of think this game is the best of the classics (This game is the real Doom 3). Owing to the N64's limitations, the game is lacking some things from Doom 2, namely a few enemy variants and weapon animations, but the game makes good use of its relatively small (Less than Doom 2, more than 1) enemy variety and the level design, in my opinion, is consistently good and fun, something that I can't say in good conscience about the latter parts of Doom 2. The game runs extremely smooth (with the exception of two weapons that have animations which seem to be stuck at a lower framerate, but ultimately has no bearing on gameplay) and you can actually see what's going on since the brightness has been reworked a bit. It's more classic Doom, with sprite work and ambience that isn't really available in the games that preceeded it. The new levels that were added in this version are actually well designed and really fun as well.Do be advised that if you're accustomed to the additional features from Doom 64 EX, this version is pretty barebones in terms of gameplay options. However, with some finagling, you can make the WAD functional with EX, if you so choose. Complaints? I guess the baron's blood could've been changed to red. The unmaker and chainsaw have strangely choppy animations compared to every other weapon. The ability to freelook and remove autoaim would've been neat (with disabled achievements since it can affect progression on, like, 2 levels). But overall, I can't come up with any notable complaints that actually have significant bearing on my experience.I highly recommend this game on the grounds that the base game is great and you can legally own the WAD for use with other versions. It's great to see this once hidden gem finally receive the recognition it deserves. Just play it!

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start with the statement: I do not hate this game. In fact, I found it pretty entertaining. But mostly it is this weird thing I can barely comprehend. A bizarre anomaly in the structure of Doom reality. Like when you go to your girlfriend's parents for a christmas dinner and suddenly you are introduced to her crazy uncle who smokes two man size bags of weed and talks to a tree. It's interesting, but in the end you are left with just one question:Why? Why does this game exist and what was the thought process behind designing it? Why do developers make some decisions in that way, but not another?So, firstly let's skip some boring parts. This is a port of an N64 game from 1997. Porting was done by Nightdive using their KEX engine. It run flawlessly. I never experienced crashes, in very few instances there were frame drops. It has proper FOV adjustment — which could be a numerical number instead of a slider, but oh well, at least we have it. Despite being a console port mouse and keyboard controls are fine, never have an issue with it, however the mouse is little floaty, despite turning off v-sync, but it's not a deal breaker, you can easily adapt to it. So yeah, in this department all is fine.Idea behind the game is simple. You are a Doom marine, you kill demons. But instead of just porting the game from the PC, Midway — developer of this game, it wasn't made by ID software — decided to change everything. Levels, graphics, monsters, guns. The graphics were especially very improved. So is it a port or new game? Who knows, who cares, I have two barrels of super shotgun pointed in the nearest imp, I don’t have time to think about this.So yeah, now for meat and potatoes. I have several issues with this game.Firstly, D64 made the same mistakes that Doom3 did. It's trying to be something different than everyone expected. It's trying to be a horror game, but unlike D3, due to hardware and software limitations, and also incorrect design premise, fails completely. Hardware was n64 and lack of it computing power, which contributed to limited design capabilities; software was using ID1 engine to create unsettling atmosphere — engine to primitive to do a horror stuff; premise — well, you cannot expect from me to be scared when I have 100 rockets and bunch of shotgun shells in my inventory. And I am not saying it's a bad choice, it's just bizarre and in my opinion, not working properly. Because to achieve this feeling many aspects of core Doom gameplay was nerfed. Monsters are slower, there are fewer of them, Doomguy also moves slower, even when you are running. Enemy projectiles are so slow that it's almost laughable — I can stand and just see how imps fireball slowly… gently… flying towards me, like a butterfly. In another case I can easily dodge three hellknight while sipping tea, and they cannot hurt me. OG doom was never too hard — compared to, for example, Blood — but in this case I can count on one hand times when I died, and It was my first even playthrough in this game. You cannot scare me, devs, when I'm this unstoppable force of nature, spreading death everywhere I look. Especially when you throw at me pixelated, cartoonish monsters. Second, overall design. The strongest part of this game. Mostly. Graphics are improved, better resolution, better textures, more detailed. But it's on engine from 1993, developed on a console in 1997. Besides, even if I can see improvement, I also feel that all this is done mostly to levels, and it was achieved with a lot of sacrifice. Yeah, textures are better, there are a lot of clever tricks with lighting too, but thanks to this different aspect of the game suffers. Yeah, levels are prettier, but they are also much simpler than in OG games. It's just corridors, big square arenas, more corridors, stairs. Not much of different level geometry, not much of level complexity. When I stand before the door it is going to lead me to another corridor, and then to another big arena, and then another room, and then another corridor….. At some point game started to be more like arena shooters (Painkiller, Serious Sam) — you go to the room, monster jumps you, you kill them, then AND ONLY THEN switch appears, you pressed it, more monsters spawn (with no visual que, they just appears from thin air, thank God there is sound of it), after killing them doors opens, you proceed to next room where all this circus is repeated…   Thirdly, enemies. Another case of bizarre decisions. They have better sprites, but also they are more blurred compared to pixelated ones from Doom 1 and 2. And due to n64 limitations there are fewer of them. There are no Chain Gunners in D64, no Revenants, no Archvilles, not even a Spider Mastermind. The core monsters of Doom are gone. Some of you will cherish this, but they were always crucial in proper Doom experience, and a smaller roster of monsters made the game simpler, less engaging and easier. After the third room with only hellknights in a row I was starting to yawn — speaking of with. Game overused the poor knight to the point I started to feel sorry for those guys.And little more about monsters: There is no different model for shotgunner and pistol zombie. Why? Especially when you have two different types of imps, one normal, and one semitransparent and with faster projectiles? Design of enemies is hit or miss. Some are more unsettling, like pinky or pain elemental, some are just bland, like imps (just and alien with no mouths), some are ok, like zombie mans or Cyberdemon, or spiders, some just derpy — Hellknights/Barons, Cacodemons (cute tiny hands this one have, so precious!). I also liked the invisibility effect on specters — in more dark areas they really can jump on you when you are not prepared.  Next, weapons. And another: why? All previous arsenal is here. But again, in some instances devs cuts corners. There is no reloading animations when using shotgun and super shotgun. WHY? IT IS SO ICONIC PART OF DOOM, THAT RELOADING OF SUPER SHOTGUN, DON'T TAKE IT AWAY, PLEASE! Chaingun is much, much better in this game, same I can say with chainsaw — now it just melts every enemy. No pinky is a problem now, bwahahaha! Rocket launchers now have knockback. Again — why? As for Plasma and BFG — introducing the last weapon made them obsolete. No kidding, in the entire game there was one moment when I used the BFG. Because Unmaker exists, and you can grab one before Plasma and BFG. And this thing, even not upgraded, is OP. Too much OP I think. Only with one rune it literally melts everything, even Barons. With two no Cyberdemon was even a threat. It breaks a balance, monsters was not design to counter this kind of weapon. Thanks to Unmaker, the rest of the difficulty is thrown out of the window. Devs try to mitigate it by throwing less energy packs, but if you conserve ammo for stronger enemies only, you will be swimming in it.What else? There is no music. Only ambience. There are no cool midi metal riffs, no combat songs, only humming in the background. They probably did this to make the atmosphere more unsettling, but again, it's not working for me. I prefer shredding demons with a cool soundtrack. So, time for closure. It's a decent game. But mediocre Doom. More misses than hits. Changing pace and atmosphere was a bad decision. Doom is not a horror game, it's not working here nor in Doom3. And I think most people look at this game through the lens of nostalgia. “It was a cool game, because it was on n64, and it was a cool console when I was kiddo!” they say. Well, im scrub slav from central Europe who never owned a n64 or psx, or nes, or even a PS2 so maybe im less biased than you guys. Or I'm just rambling after too many shoots of Jack Daniels…

name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist
detailed_description: The Choices You Make, Make You. Growing up in humanity’s first extrasolar space colony means navigating a new world full of wonder, danger, and beauty. Explore the wilderness, study, fall in love, discover strange creatures, and deal with the consequences of your actions. Your choices will directly affect the lives of your friends and the fate of the colony. What kind of world will you help make? Will you survive to enjoy it? Why do you remember doing this before? Growing Up on an Alien Planet You have your whole life ahead of you. Will you spend it studying in school, or diving into the intriguing flora and fauna of this new world? Will you introduce space-age technology, or live in harmony with nature? Will you battle massive beasts, or nurture future generations? Realized in brilliant watercolor, the world of Vertumna is yours to explore. Your Pasts and Your Futures Matter Everything you learn and experience will make you and your colony stronger. You will thrive and you will make mistakes. These formative moments - your memories, decisions, and friendships - become collectible cards you carry with you. Each season brings new obstacles on Vertumna. The battle cards you earn from your experiences give you new options for overcoming these challenges, whether that is navigating relationships, learning new skills, exploring the planet, or staying alive. Every decision counts, during this life and the next. How Many Lives Will YOU Live? The cosmos is full of incredible mysteries, and your ability to remember your past lives is one of them. There are dozens of different endings to your story. How many lives will it take to save both your colony and the planet? Are you ready to wake up again? Features: Use memories of past lives to explore 800+ story events. Discover more than 250 battle cards as you grow up on an alien planet. Play your best hand in challenge encounters to ace your math test or escape from a wild snapbladder. Make friends, fight with your parents, go on dates, fall in love, and save the colony. 29 wildly different endings based on the choices you make each month. Pick from 25 colony jobs, like goofing off as a depot clerk, or surveying the valley. Grow into 15 skills, including bravery, toughness, organization, and empathy. Get to know 10 dateable characters, including dog-boys, aliens, hot politicians and stone cold killers.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked IwaTE quite a lot, but I think if I was attracted to men, I'd like it even more.  The fact is that artistically, all the men grow up to be extraordinarily attractive, and the women are mostly androgynous.Also worth noting: this game allows for complete pronoun customization (and independent of late teen masculine or feminine appearance), doesn't appear to have any kind of gender restriction on romances, and features non-binary characters, so if you find any of that problematic, and you probably will not enjoy this game.  Or maybe it would expand your horizons?  That'd be nice.The basic gameplay is what you'd expect from a life/dating sim: manage your time, raising a skill bar and improving your relationships with various people, with a fairly simplistic deckbuilding aspect: it's essentially "get the best poker hand" with a semi-customized deck.  It's marginally more complicated than that, but the bonuses for straights and flushes and x of a kind are where you get most of your points.  Once you select your task for a month, get some story, then play your cards.  You get perks for every 33 in a stat that either improves your card gameplay or unlocks new activities around the colony to raise related stats and improve your relationship with different colonists.The story is where IwaTE really shines; there are a TON of mysteries and stuff going on - you start off as a kid and the adults definitely don't tell you everything!  It's a gritty, tough exocolonist life; people you know WILL die (certainly one death is mandatory until a second playthrough).  I only managed to head off one impending disaster on my first playthrough, but was hit with so many other bad things.  I still grew up to become the chief engineer for the colony and felt pretty good about it, but it's still interesting to consider all the paths not taken; I'm sure there's a true end somewhere if you can save everybody if you can solve the food crisis or cure disease or improve colony defenses enough (but actually all of the above, plus a lot of other stuff!).Unlike many visual novels, though, rather than having a lot of very, very short "bad end" stubby branches to the storyline, something bad happens, but the colony just continues - a lot of time with fewer colonists or bleaker prospects ahead.  I really like this approach, and it feels like what I choose matters, instead of just populating a gallery with grim deaths and then immediately rolling them back, the colony feels like a real place, that keeps moving forward even as things get bad and worse instead of shunting you down a "correct" path after every mistake.  Some of the second playthrough choices already seem to allow you to go down a true bad end, too, so if you like schadenfreude, there's a place for you here too.  I definitely already had some plans for my second playthrough when I finished my first, but number three is going to be quite miserable for my colonists, I think.  Also, the idea that I'm considering a third playthrough after having just starting my second one, in spite of not having three partners I'm interested in should tell you just how much I like this game.Anyway, thumbs up for everybody, because it's a genuinely good story with an excellent approach to the visual novel space and simple but fun gameplay, but thumb way up if you're attracted to men, because that's definitely what the artist liked.

_childDocuments_.review: A visual novel / management sim with a hard(ish) sci-fi setting and lots of memorable characters. It is a delightfully well written, visually, and mechanically realized work of art that though definitely coming in part under the category of “dating sim” is not in fact “just” a dating sim.If what you’ve seen of it appeals to you, go buy it! It has lots of replayability which was obvious just from my first playthrough and you can easily many hours of enjoyment out of it. Though beware it will also tug at your heart.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stunned by this game. I applaud the writers for this insanely captivating story, amazing cast of characters, and all the twists and turns. The gameplay itself, the cardgame that determines your success or failures in different events is simple enough to figure out quickly but can be challenging at times, it has an option to avoid it entirely in favour of a coin toss mechanic which I personally have not used, but I suppose if you don't like the card game and simply wish to experience the story and leave a little more up to fate the option is there. The card game can feel a little easy at times but there is an option to increase the difficulty. Personally I felt the default difficulty hit a decent sweet spot. But the gameplay is simply a means to an end, this is a visual novel first and foremost and your decisions vastly impact the direction of the story and the replayability value is immense, so much so it's actually a mechanic in the game. Your first run will be messy and likely not turn out as you hoped, see it through to the end, your first playthrough will probably not have a satisfying ending but it certainly will be interesting. The game actively encourages you to try again knowing everything you've learned from your first playthrough. I played this game start to finish in a 14 hour burn and I'm eagerly looking forward to starting my second playthrough after I get some sleep!

_childDocuments_.review: A great story with many different available endings.  Highly replayable as you try to get different outcomes to events and endings to your story.  There is a card collecting system of sorts, in which cards you collect are actually important memories that you gain along your journey.  These cards are used in challenges in which you try to meet or beat a certain score to gain stats or otherwise overcome difficult situations.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, yes, yes, all of my yes. The characters are to die for, the art is gorgeous, the story has so many interesting moving parts all acting together. You can only influence so much of the story at a time, leading to events occurring that are simply out of your control. Plenty of wonder and tragedy and the bitter-sweet stuff in the middle. _childDocuments_.review: The first thing to know about this game is that you  save scum. The game wants you to do it and frankly you are missing out if you don't. There are game mechanics crafted around it, if you play all or most of your play-through 'straight' then you will have to replay the game to experience it. This game is comprised of three parts, visual novel/story choices, deck builder, and time management. All three are handled well here, and intermix. The story is handled really well and your choices definitely matter. One of the pitfalls games often do with "choices matter" is that they allow your actions to open up new paths, but they don't make your choices restrict others. I'm glad to say Exocolonist has the brass to do both. Characters will leave or enter the story due to your choices, not only that but you can only get certain choices depending on how you spend your time. A player that spends a lot of days studying versus one that spends a lot of time in combat training will simply not have the options of the other. You get micro choices in the moment with dialogue and actions, while you also make macro decisions over the years as you craft your character into what you want them to be. The deckbuilder fits right into this as your decisions on how you use your time changes what cards are in your deck, and succeeding or failing a game will have narrative impact. Making game mechanics intermingle so naturally is no easy feat, and its great that this is all on top of an engaging and interactive story. This game is a fair bit better than it has any right to be.

_childDocuments_.review: IWATE is pretty ambitious with its premise and promise of branching, choice-based gameplay, and for the most part it delivers. Characters are gorgeous and lovingly written, environments are believably designed and interesting to look at, worldbuilding is deep without bogging itself down and becoming excessive or pedantic, and the card collection based aspect of challenges is fun without being especially difficult or complex. An easily digestible stat building system delivered in a time management style vaguely reminiscent of Atlus's Persona titles (for lack of a better comparison) makes gameplay feel meaningful in the periods between narrative heavy segments, and the game features a rare 2D animated exploration element to simulate the wonder of exploring on an alien planet. While this feature is easily the weakest part of the game's structure, with events encounterable in the wild cycling through a set number of narrative snippets that wear down relatively quickly, it's still very refreshing for the genre, and performs its gameplay purpose admirably.The choice aspect promised on the steam page is definitely there, though, without spoiling much, I will say that I found the game's semi-secret ending to invalidate the importance of the player's involvement, just a bit. There are plenty of endings to be found here, and each can be granted further complexity depending on which relationships you chose to deepen over the course of your play time. There's even a customization feature that allows you to choose your starting skill levels and friendships prior to the initiation of the game's main story, though players who enjoy a roleplaying experience may glean more from this than more casual players, as it has little bearing on the story overall. The main character's appearance is also barely open to customization, with choice impact ranging from having short or long hair during the character's young adulthood. Your choices definitely do matter, but you might find yourself feeling like they don't following certain developments.All that said the story is still beautifully written; everything from the world building, to the prose, to the dialogue is natural and professionally done, so much so that you'll likely find yourself becoming more invested in the characters' narratives than you might expect. Each individual character is distinct and represents their own branching narratives and lore to explore; if you spend all your time interacting with Tang and Marz, for instance, you'll need to dedicate some time to a replay to unlock whatever developments are linked to Cal and Nem. There are plenty o secrets to unlock over the course of each playthrough, and replays and save scumming are heavily rewarded and acknowledged in-game. If you're a sci fi fan, you'll definitely love the game's light forays into speculative biology and tech, and the little hints of political drama are sure to be a ton of fun for people more into the human side of things. Nothing is as in-depth as what you'll find in a classic sci-fi novel, but it's plenty enough for a solid coming of age in space story. Just don't expect any galaxy spanning conflicts or interstellar warfare, and your expectations should be well in check.IWATE is definitely worth the price for any long time dating sim, visual novel, or sci fan fans as long as they're willing to temper their expectations based on the game's young adult presentation. It's worth more than a few replays, and the gameplay is interesting enough that the additional bits of branching story won't feel like the only thing justifying them. Buying on sale is best, but even if you can't, this is a wonderful title for a nice, cozy gaming session.

_childDocuments_.review: Adorable and occasionally (and realistically) grim; a lot more mature than the title might suggest. The artwork is gorgeous, even though it is at times a bit too "whimsical", which clashes just a bit with the more grounded and serious tone the game later takes. Writing overall is lovely, punchy and witty, with its main goal clearly being the flavourful, emotional characterization of the cast. Their all are very much imperfect, and what seemed adorable, or at most quaint, through the eyes of childish naivete might later develop into realistic character flaws. Character growth is not always for the better, that much is clear. Although the core mechanics of the game is card-based, it is not a hardcore deck-builder. Primarily, because there aren't too many direct ways to manipulate your deck, so moment-to-moment decision making during actual card challenges is more important. Tip: collect and don't forget to use consumable items.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game, It's a VN that's less on rails than traditional VNs that i've seen.  My first run took me about 12 hours, but I read quickly.  There is a fair amount of replayability in the game, but interestingly you don't need to start a new game to get most of the benefits.  Some points in the story let you use knowledge from your previous runs to change fate, or make things easier.  However, you can learn about something, and then just load back before the trigger and get the replay.  This does not cover everything though, some stuff needs more or less half a dedicated run to have access to on a subsequent run.Not a big fan of the exploration really, I would have honestly preferred it all be done via vignette than exploring the labyrinthine maps.Music is good, but pretty limited in amount.It's cute, and it's worth 25 usd, i got it for 20, and I'm not sure how much more i'll play of it, maybe another 2 runs?

I like the fact that theyre not build like traditional dating game characters (because its not a dating game, just a game that also has dating) and they CAN actually break up with you based on their preferences and your choices, in this sense they do feel very realistic, theyre shaped by the tragedies they live thru and the way they were tought to be and react. _childDocuments_.review: – Unique and interesting characters– Sometimes heartbreaking, beautiful story– Visual novel + RPG + deck builder gameplay– The most complex narrative-based game I’ve played with so many outcomes– Tons of replay value– So much gorgeous artwork– Overall a lovely game & a lovely story!This game is wonderful. I’m feeling a lot of feelings now that I’ve finished.Gameplay is relatively simple, in that all you have to do is talk to characters, make choices, choose an activity to do each month, and play some card games. But I’ve never played a narrative-based game this complex!It’s part visual novel, part RPG, part deck builder. There is a linear story, but it doesn’t work by having a storyline that branches every so often. There are 12 skill/personality stats, stress level, rebellion level, some hidden story stats, colony food, colony defense, and a bunch of relationships. All these things are constantly affecting or being affected by your choices. Some are easy to adjust (like getting a skill by going to class), some less so (like figuring out ways to build colony defense). There are also seemingly simple choices that can affect things in ways you won’t even realize at the time. Doing certain activities a lot or at the right times can also trigger events. But the real complexity comes from how all of these things work together. It’s really cool.This game also has soooooooooo much replay value and rewards you for replaying. There are so many characters to get to know, things to learn about the world, little events to see, and endings. And so many ways relationships and other things can differ within the endings. Special endings too. And the premise involves the player living many lives and having memories of past lives, so there are certain things you can only do once your character has certain memories.There reached a point in my first playthrough when I stopped having to really think about the decisions I was making and just sort of became my character. The way you’re with them from age 10 to 20, you really get to develop them and watch them grow, and I was surprised at how I found myself going with the flow and exploring life with them.And all the other characters! I loved getting to know them more and more in each playthrough. They’re imperfect, and I love them. They do sort of have one main defining characteristic, which can make them seem a bit flat at first, but most of them had more depth and I felt for them more once I got to know them. And they have cute or interesting or complicated relationships with each other, not just you. I very badly want an actual novel about them. Especially Dys 🥺❤️ So lonely and distanced from everyone, but also so passionate. And ok, sorta Vace too, because yes, he’s awful, but I love characters who actually admit to being wrong and try to be better (and his rudeness cracked me up sometimes).Now, the dating element. You can stick to friendship and the game is no less rich for it. You can even flirt without getting locked in, and you won’t be punished for flirting with everyone. If you accidentally end up dating someone or change your mind, you can break up, no hard feelings. (It is a little weird to break up and have the character be like, “Ok!” like they didn’t even care in the first place, but whatever.) If you are going to date though, don’t expect a dating sim because there’s no guaranteed HEA. There are 10 options (4 guys, 4 girls, 1 nonbinary person, and 1 alien who uses he/him pronouns but I’m not entirely sure he has a gender), plus an 11th you can get just in the epilogue. But… Some characters are not into committed exclusive relationships. Some end up dating other people if you take too long or don’t make the right choices. Some feel very strongly about having or not having kids. Some relationships don’t last in the epilogue, or something complicates them. There are some things I don’t love about this aspect (namely how awful the game makes you feel if you try to get with either of the two characters who are clearly supposed to be with each other), but it makes all the characters feel like they are their own people, rather than just existing to date the player.The story is interesting, but it’s also heartbreaking the first time. At least it was for me. But it does get better. Some of the bad things are preventable, you just have to figure out how. There’s a thought-provoking element to it all as well. Not just the obvious things in the story, like whether humans should colonize a new planet, but also things like how much of what happens in the lives of others is your responsibility?There’s a lot of cool lore and whatnot to discover too. Fascinating alien lifeforms and the history of the planet.– Gorgeous artwork, and so much of it. Backgrounds. Characters, including at various ages for many of them. Unlockable CGs throughout the game as you get to know different characters. Alien lifeforms. Art for each of the 29 endings. Art on all of the many cards you get. The graphics when you walk around and explore are cute too.– The music was unobtrusive and pleasant. Which I think is good for a game you’re going to play so many hours of.– The game lets you choose what pronouns and gendered words are used for the player character, with full customization. You can also choose appearance between masculine, feminine, and androgynous (it seems the only difference is hair length, and maybe a slight difference in outfit, but there’s a lot of art in the game, so that’s understandable). And you can change any of these things at  during the game.– Lots of diversity among both dateable and background characters! Canonically not-straight characters and relationships (and you can date characters of any gender regardless of your gender). Also characters who are trans, nonbinary, demisexual, polyamorous, POC, neurodivergent, and physically disabled. If you want to know more specifically (I don’t consider these spoilers, but some may prefer learning these things as they get to know the characters): *SPOILER*  *END SPOILER*– You can have pets! And they make an adorable little squeaky sound when you click on them.– You can have an unlimited number of saves, which is super helpful for planning ahead and doing strategic playthroughs when you’ve seen a lot already and just want to get the different careers and endings. Also if you just want to come back and look at the outcome of a different dialogue or small choice. The auto saves are great if you mess up a choice.Overall, it’s a beautiful game and a beautiful story. When you’re just about finished playing, I suggest doing one final “perfect” playthrough, whatever that means to you. I’m so glad I did. Just knowing all the outcomes separately didn’t have the same effect. I didn’t realize seeing it all together would touch me so much, but it really did!*Review can also be found on my blog (link in profile).*(May not include everything)– Can use mouse, keyboard (including one handed with either hand), combo of both, or controller.– Can change keys used.– Can turn off screen shake.– Can make menus bigger.– Trigger/content warnings available.– Can turn card-based games off (though it may cause you to lose some, I’m not sure how it works).– No TTS, not accessible for blind players or screen readers.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to give this a tentative recommendation.  I am not the target audience of a game like this, what with being a white CIS-gendered heterosexual Conservative Christian American male.  The very first thing this game did was try to convince me to stop playing by putting both pronouns and gender on a sliding scale, then introducing me to a cast of NPCs that included a transvestite and several obviously bi-curious 10 year olds.The game does not necessarily improve in that regard.  I outright avoided conversations with several male characters after it seemed like I was being shoehorned into romances with them just by trying to be their friends.  One character had two dads, and later in the game you had characters that were gender fluid or outright were furries with a nudist streak.  The plot seemed to revolve around that tired cliche of mankind being the real monsters, set against an anti-military establishment and pro-environmental backdrop.  One character later tries to convince everyone that money serves no purpose, and of course this character is one that literally contributes nothing to the survival of the colony. Despite all of this, I actually really enjoyed the game.  I got into a groove, and the game does a good job for most of it's playtime to keep things moving forward and feeling fresh.  I found myself wanting to play just one more month, and hours will pass because you do start to get invested in what you're trying to accomplish.  Game plays to me most similar to a dating sim, where the actual dating and relationships play second fiddle to the story and world-building. The game takes place over the course of 10 years of time between the main character's ages of 10-20.  Each year is broken into 13 months (on this alien planet), and each month you can choose a single action to do for the month (along with dialogues that don't necessarily take up an action).  These actions typically come with a challenge to complete, which is like a fantasy poker mini-game where the cards you have access to are based on the memories and experiences you've had so far in the game.There are a wide variety of actions for your character to perform, and each one develops skills and relationships with other characters, as well as presenting almost entirely unique plot developing scenes.  It's the strength of this developing plot that really makes the game addicting.  Early on the writers let us know that they had no qualms killing off kids and parents and that the stakes were high, so I felt invested in making choices that would best serve the colony.  When presented with plot choices, some options aren't available unless your skills are of a certain rank, so I buckled down and studied hard.  Balance that with exploration options and an attempt to solve the larger mystery of the planet and the years will start to fly by.I will say that the last third of the game seemed to drag down as I started maxing out skills and was uncertain where the plot was supposed to be taking me.  There seemed to be a story that I just couldn't access, and I wasn't sure what I needed to do to get that rolling.  As I finished my first playthrough, far too many loose threads were left unresolved, and not due to a lack of trying on my part.  The ending played out how the future of the colony ended up for me and for my primary romantic interest, but failed to elaborate on some fairly important plot elements that would seemingly be incredibly important.  I suppose I just didn't get far enough in those plotlines to see that resolution, but I'm a bit peeved the game came to a hard stop at the beginning of my 20th year.I do wish that the skills you develop in the game had more impact on certain story choices, or that the mini game itself was a bit more complex.  Drawing 6-7 cards and using five of them to make the best poker hand is frustrating.  You don't have a lot of control over your deck selection, with cards being added as events unfold, and limited opportunities to remove cards from your deck to streamline it.  Really wishing there was some more variety there.  I felt my inventory space was limited, as well, and I had a couple of pets but they didn't seem to do anything unless I "equipped" them, other than to follow me around on the map.Game offers itself up to replay, with the hint of major plot changes on a second iteration.  While I haven't played the game a second time, and don't have much desire to solely for that reason, I might return to it in a year or two for that experience.  If I can stomach the social justice propaganda that is shoved down my throat. Would actually consider playing a similar title by the developers as they've clearly got talent.  Perhaps something more RPG, where your character's skills and abilities come from memories and experiences, an RNG based challenge system that utilizes the skills you've developed, and retaining that heavy dating sim feel of developing relationships, perhaps a bit less linearly in a more complex system.  And with a quarter of the activism.

_childDocuments_.review: THIS IS NOT A COZY GAME! The content warnings should have tipped you off, but in case you're as oblivious as I am, you should know that this game gets emotionally brutal very quickly, and I am here for it.The first play through should definitely be done blind ( except for maybe taking a peak at the content warnings if you've got trauma you don't want revisited) so I'll try to be brief and generic. The story is very well crafted, and particularly shines in the sense that it made me feel like a teenage. Not just in the sense that I felt starry-eyed at all the possibilities that my future held and appreciative of the abundance of cartage in my joints, but also in the awkward sense of regretting the words that came out of my mouth and feeling guilty for not stopping things beyond my wisdom to control. It has some flaws. There are clearly a handful of storylines that are meant to be pursued, and they interact poorly if the player trys to swap between them. Especially late game, wandering into the beginning of a storyline can be downright comical in the context of what has already occurred. The 'game' portion of it is barely above mobil-game level of engagement, but it's no worse that say, rolling a 20 sided dice to deside whether a course of action will succeed or not. I also found that the reincarnation mechanic felt a little wasted, just by how much re-treading of the story occurred on my second playthrough. Despite its flaws, I do heartily recommend this game based on its touching and intense story.

_childDocuments_.review: With how excited I was after playing the demo, I'm happy to say that Exocolonist has lived up to and exceeded my every expectation and then some. The writing is stellar, the art is beautiful, the music (and silence!) are brilliant, the characters are complex, the story is compelling, the challenges are satisfying, and it's all so incredibly well paced.So many games have systems that fight with themselves, but it's a rare game indeed where every element is seamlessly interwoven into every other. Exocolonist pulls off this feat beautifully. Your every choice and action, how you plan ahead and spend your time, affects your relationships and skill progression and accumulated memories, which themselves help you overcome challenges and lead the story in different directions and open up an incredibly varied array of events.Your memories are a central theme too, with your character's experiences embodied as the very cards you use to overcome challenges, but also echoing across lifetimes. Just as you and your real-life human memories as a player lead you to want to try different things in another playthrough, your memories within the game from other lifetimes also provide new choices it would never have occurred to you to make through prophetic dreams, letting you take different actions without having spoiled them for you the first time through.And even the fact of your character having these dreams is woven into the story so well, from how your character feels about them to how others react to your actions. In other words, far from just an incentive to play again, the game feels like a whole meta-experience that spans multiple lifetimes. I've seen games try to pull off this kind of depth with parallel worlds or time travel shenanigans, but never have I seen a game succeed at it so spectacularly well! I love it.All the systems feel smoothly integrated like this. The in-game currency of Kudos reflects your standing with the other characters and the community, but also allows you to nanoprint gear which helps with challenges, or gifts to give to friends, or to change your deck in subtle ways. The card game looks simplistic in screenshots but feels so satisfying to play and never seems to become dull - even on easier challenges, there's always a motivation to try your best, whether it's to earn a bonus skill point or just an extra kudos for getting the best hand you can with what you were dealt. If it's too easy, you can set it to be harder, and if it's too hard, you can push through at the cost of stressing yourself out. And how you feel day to day, whether it's heroic or popular or depressed or stressed out all affects how effective you are at different things, which feeds back into the planning.Your level of stress limits how hard you can work and how much you can explore, encouraging you to take breaks which keeps the pacing nice and smooth. But the in-game breaks are themselves a pleasure. They don't just relieve stress, they result in all manner of interactions with other characters, bonding with your pets, unexpectedly learning new things and gaining skills, not to mention leaving you feeling amazing afterwards which makes you even more effective when you get back to it. And all this is tied back into the story and relationships too. The only regret is that you can't literally learn everything and spend time with everyone (at least within one lifetime!).And unlike many games with a diverse and varied cast like this, the characters all seem to have a lot of depth, especially as you all start to get older. I was certainly more attracted to 2 or 3 of them, but even those I was annoyed with initially grew on me, or I wanted to get to know them because of another character's interactions with them, or to nudge them into being a better person, or just to see what their deal is. So many games are filled with stereotypes or tropes or simplistic morality, but Exocolonist really takes it deep and gradually seeing more and more of this nuanced complexity really makes learning about the world and the characters a wonderful experience.The satisfaction of exploring really sparked my imagination too. In the demo, the area outside the colony that you can explore is certainly enjoyable but somewhat modest in size, but the moment I made it to a wider region I was amazed at how expansive it was and at all the different wildlife and encounters I came across. Not only was the scenery gorgeous and the music really enchanting, but it left me filled with curiosity each time I came across something. (And even here the things you find tie back into the other systems when you get back to the colony!) I'm barely into the first larger area and already the bestiary is many fold longer, and I even got to name a new species myself! It really feels like exploring an original new world with its own unique and complex and varied ecosystem.I'm truly enjoying this game and feel so eager to share it with others and to play more over the coming weeks and months. If you're at all on the fence about it, I highly recommend checking it out.

_childDocuments_.review: Exocolonist made a huge impact on me because it made me feel represented and gave me choices that resonated with how I want to interact with the world around me in both life and gaming. Thank you for your hard work and the beautiful product that you have created.
