_childDocuments_.review: About ten or so years ago, there was a dearth of stat-based, build-your-own adventure RPGs to supplement visual novel style play. A spiritual evolution of them, this game is probably the most aesthetically pleasing, varied, and rewarding of them, though it does keep a good amount of occasionally frustrating progress road blocks that can wreck a playthrough (If you wannabe a certain character's lover, you gotta' make like the Spice Girls and get with their friend). You play a child who grows up on an alien planet with a colony of humans trying to survive, and choosing to live how you see fit. While the character has one unified art style and only changes later in life, you can present and be called by binary and non-binary options (And if you want to be as anatomically impaired as a Ken Doll, go for it!). Your can give your path whatever head start you would like (Though super strength helps the other categories more than you'd think. A variety of other fields and paths require a minimum of physical abilities, and giving a double to stat boosts in that category minimizes the effort required to meet those standards). Your progress involves building stats and gathering cards from various life experiences . I'm not normally a card system person because random draws will punch you in the gut every chance it can, but it's poker style, which allows a lot of flexibility and ability to punch above your weight in meeting certain scores.To put this upfront, you will not be able to do everything you want the first playthrough. It is designed to be played multiple times, and the first time can be a melancholy experience. Every time you reach certain breakthroughs, you can far more easily access them on the next round and focus on something else. Or you can make people think you're crazy. The story is flexible, and learning new parts can even change it, depending on what you do with it. Like the older games, there can be hard roadblocks that require guides or ignoring most other things to get through them, but the game mostly gives you reasonable hints on what to do and where to go, and many times, the way through is trying something you haven't tried before.While its ilk leaned more heavily on the VN experience, this has a more varied experience. You can freely wander the colony, and eventually, explore the alien world if you so choose. The presentation is more of an illustrated storybook, and everything looks and moves very nicely. The game is accompanied by a pulsing and appropriately electric score. If I do have one quibble, there are certain cutscenes that would be nice to skip on session after the first run. The characters hit that sweet spot of sharing certain universal qualities that you can connect their types, but are individual enough to stand on their own. They are of various walks of life, sexualities, and attitudes, and exploring their complexities is fun, and helps inform the story. While some guides indicated that the fate of characters you have a relationship with will stay 99% the same on various endings, I have found much more variety depending on how everything else shakes out. Some characters are more flexible than others, however.Overall, it's an extremely successful game that's kind of a roguelite interactive novel. I'm not normally a fan of going through the same experience over and over, but I've gone through five full runs, and I'm trying to hammer out time for another, so......... I'd call that pretty good.

_childDocuments_.review: French existentialist Simone de Beauvoir argues in her 1947 book  that  that the personality and the core beliefs of each human individual is defined through their environment and their actions, and that the challenges that allow those personality-shaping events are the ones that truly test the scope of the limits between their limitations and potential, their past against their future, the comfort of familiarity against the fear of the unknown."I Was a Teenage Exocolonist" is a quiet meditation on this and other questions asked by de Beauvoir and her fellow existentialists, packaged stealthily in the wrappings of a Solarpunk-themed dating game.  Beneath the cotton candy colored environment of Vertumna and the egregiously tumblr-era character designs lies , one that manages to succeed at the challenge of remaining both replayable and emotionally impactful.  IWATE introduces the concepts of string theory, mortality, identity, collectivism, and on and on and on as each character you meet lives, grows, dies, lives again, and becomes a different person entirely.When asked about the passing of her lover, the famed philosopher Jean Paul Sartre, de Beauvoir simply said   Vertumna asks you to spend ten years with it before it lets you go, and readily welcomes you back again for the next loop of a cycle that continues on into infinity.  But each of those cycles of ten years creates a unique you, and the life you live with its people is truly splendid.ps: rex is best boy, even with the dumb tattoo, fight me.

_childDocuments_.review: Part visual novel, part deck builder IWaTE  is a real gem.The game play loop is simple but engaging, you pick an activity each month which may increase your skills, unlock side stories or otherwise progress the main story line. This will be accompanied by a test where you play cards from your deck to hit a total, poker style hands (straights, flushes etc) will earn extra points and many of the cards or tests will have additional modifiers. This has enough weight to keep things interesting and for deck building veterans there is a hard more.Both the cast and general story line are wonderfully executed and give a good feel for life on the frontier. Things can and will go wrong, characters can die and your actions will determine not just your own fate but that of the colony.The game is built to be re-playable and your own character will "remember" some decisions between games helping you avoid earlier pitfalls and discovering new routes through the story.  I'm only a few hours in at this point, I suspect a complete run will be around 6 ish but can see a lot of different ways things could have gone.

Well maybe two, first if you like story driven games, you like the feel of the design, and you can handle potentially difficult content, pick this game up. _childDocuments_.review: A fun raising sim/deckbuilder hybrid.Since most of this game is its dialogue, we would better talk about writing before anything else. The game's writing can be a bit on your face at times, but its so earnest and so caring for its ensemble of characters that it just comes across as cute - as if you were talking to a friend who is a bit too much into a fanfic they wrote. Even though there's little in the way of CGs and art what is there is very pretty to look at and helps with the overall tone of the writing. The worldbuilding is on the weaker side, and the meta-plot is sketchy, but the game's strength is its characters. The cast is very fleshed out, they all have quirks and fully fledged personalities. Most of them are adorable, and after playing I look fondly on every one of them.The deckbuilding/puzzle mechanic is a bit thin, but its a nice distraction and works to hide away the raw number checking of most raising sims, which can be a turnoff. At the end of the day you are still checking arbitrary numbers against arbitrary stat walls, but it feels like you are making decisions along the way. Its also quite flavourful in the way that your deck is your memories, and depending on who you are close to you will be playing with cards you get from hanging out with them.I was a Teenage Exocolonist is probably one of the best raising sims around right now. A great entry in the genre and overall a nice addition to the small corpus of games with actually decent writing.

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this? God, absolutely, I've already recommended it times to literally anyone who bothers listening to me about video games. Don't pay attention to my hours played, it is very low compared to the adoration I have for this game. Very, very low. I really need to play it more.Lets get down to this. Firstly, I love the art style, the art style was the main pull for me. While I'm willing to play a game with the appearance of something pulled out of the depths of the nineties, I have a soft spot for games with beautiful art styles. This is no exception. The art, all throughout, is aesthetically pleasing. But, no, the art style isn't the main selling point, there's so much meat to this game.You're met with a pronoun system when you're making your MC. Of course, you can go with set pronouns of she/her, he/him, and they/them, but no, they didn't stop there. What did those absolute madlads do? . I didn't use it, I was fine with using commonly used pronouns, I'm one of them they/them folks myself, but it made me incredibly happy to see the detail put into the pronoun ability.The characters are all lovable in their own ways and I got way too attached. Look, I'm a sucker for character diversity, from appearance to personality, and I Was A Teenage Exocolonist has a lot that I could ask for. I didn't expect the dogboy, but I'm not complaining, he was so adorable and then he got hot. Incredibly hot. That can be said about literally almost all of our peers in the game, though, like, oh my god?Anyway, away from my thirsting, even the non-romanceable characters are wonderful. From the start, my buried daddy issues hit me like a truck, and if that wasn't enough, my mommy issues came to light and hit me like a train. The mom and dad of this game are phenomenal and I would literally die for them. Even the non-important characters were memorable and I adore all of them. As somebody who is picky about character design, all of the character's designs are phenomenal and I want to shake hands with the artists and designers, and perhaps give them all forehead kisses because the artwork and the design are so wonderful. The story is good and compelling, this is coming from somebody who actively skips the story of any game they play. Yes, my girlfriend is occasionally distressed by it, particularly when I skip any Elder Scrolls plot, the amount of psychic damage that woman has taken from my antics should really be reimbursed. I lack the attention span for any complex story, I am maybe three-years-old at best, BUT this game managed to get my two-year-old brain to sit down and listen.Look, you've probably seen the screenshots. I sure hope you've seen the screenshots, what are you doing in the reviews if not? Weirdo. But, look, this game is primarily a written story, and I get that some people have the reading comprehension of a toddler, so if this isn't your cup of tea, it isn't. But, if you can at least TOLERATE games with a ton of reading, then I recommend you try.I won't say much on the story, I want you to explore that on your own, but let me tell you, you will NOT regret it. I'll let you hit me if you do regret it, but, like, I guarantee it's great.So, as said, it's primarily a written story. But! But!! But!!! Not all the time. That's what got me. I was like "♥♥♥♥♥ what?" when I first started playing. So, yeah, there's combat, you can fight things, but it's a card-based game fighting system. You have to get your card number higher than the goal, and it's pretty easy for  me. But, you can explore around, which is cool. The characters look super cute in the moving around style. I'll go talk to an adult Cal and he's, like, super cute in the art style, then I get hit in the face with how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hot he is when his actual picture comes up. Like, hot damn, none of these characters need to be that-Okay, I'm thirsting again, sorry.Anyway, you play a kid from 10-years-old to 20-years-old, and let me tell you, when my character went through puberty, I got some war flashbacks. You really start getting attached to your character and your peers, you also can go to school to level up your stats. Each of your stats is better for specific things, and there's a bunch of different endings. Also, you can romance your besties. Lets talk about that.The romances feel kind of... eh? The characters feel fleshed out, they have their own motivations, but the romance I went through felt a bit dull. I romanced Dys, our typical emo adventuring boy (not really, he's got more depth and I love him), and I sort of regret not dating the alien because APPARENTLY Dys accepts a polyamorous relationship with him. I am still upset about this turn of events because I have two hands and they're meant for my cute emo boyfriend and his hot alien boyfriend.But, anyway, the romances themselves were... I don't know? The build up was phenomenal, though, but... Thinking about it, that's okay. The romance doesn't need to be a big thing, especially when the build up was so good. Speaking from experience, when you've been best friends for a while, the transition from platonic to romantic doesn't feel big and extraordinary, and that's what I love about romancing the characters of I Was A Teenage Exocolonist.In a lot of media, the build up is intense, and the romance is full of passion, but in reality, that doesn't happen as often as it does in media. But from my own experiences, when you're already so close to someone, not much changes when you take the leap into a romantic relationship. I can't truly complain about the romances of IWATE because they felt realistic, and I'm just not too used to that in media.Look me in the eyes and ask me that again. Actually, please don't, eye contact makes me uncomfortable.$25 isn't bad for this game, actually, that's pretty low for this game. It has a ton of replayability, and the characters you get close to begin appearing on the menu screen. This game has parents who love you, a compelling storyline, memorable characters, and a horny dogboy that I can hug for friendship points.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend this game to others, but I hold a bitter attitude toward it personally. I genuinely tried my best to love this game. With pleasing aesthetics, intriguing stories, and a creative and attractive description of the future, the game had every advantage to be my Game of 2022.At that time, I was set back by a series of events and saw only the darkest days. Instead of attracting me with its imaginary future, it impressed me with its optimistic perspectives on the future. I was used to coming across one and other pieces of sci-fi where there were cool androids and social Darwinist structures. The logic just began with "We had a tough planet to deal with and "rebellious" people to control, so we certainly required blood and iron," which were not necessarily metaphors. And I just kept thinking, "Oh, here definitely goes a potential tragedy, and they will turn back to cruel futures soon." Still, the tiny colony exhibited its resilience and people stepped forward again from the past. They changed and grew, but not in the way those false prophets claimed, in which only the ruthless opportunists survived.I honestly didn't know what to feel about that. Everything in this game seemed way too gentle for me.  Though it was indifferent to say so, I just felt every event the game designed to make me sympathize with the characters was not really traumatizing enough. The characters in the game had complex backgrounds and met with challenging events, but they were all masters in dealing with pressure and never lacked support from others. I should admit I even felt a bit jealous about that. Their past was more temporary than an ever-bleeding wound, and none of the effects seemed permanent. Those events were also less devastating than I supposed. Other characters were also resilient and had their way of dealing with their problems. No one was really helpless here.The game is a masterpiece, but I can't feel the sense there personally. Nothing really tricky means the good ending isn't impressive enough. I'll recommend it anyway because I think these disadvantages are mainly personal, but I do have a conflict in my mind here.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll probably edit this review once I dive deeper into the game on subsequent playthroughs as that seems to be a major component of the experience, but I just had to make a review after my first playthrough. I finished this game about 3 days ago and can't get it out of my mind. I found this game by chance in 2022 during a Steam promotion for indie games while looking for a visual novel with romance/dating sim elements and ended up playing the demo. I'm forever grateful I stumbled on this game on that day. The characters and worldbuilding are just very well handled. Very few games actually take a serious approach to tackling a subject like someone growing up and experiencing adolescence over the course of years while also exploring their relationships with others and their environment. Actually writing compelling stories with the various potential friends/love interests is just astonishing to me. The handling of this kind of cast while also clearly establishing the passage of time and how their environment impacts them is just top-notch. You can tell the writers had tons of fun writing about all the various lore, fauna, etc. because they truly gave this entire world so much life. Even some background characters with minimal screen time became memorable parts of the experience and still stick with me. I have to applaud the devs for also being willing to tackle various tough topics both on large and smaller scales from stuff like different aspects of politics to things like domestic abuse. I can understand some being mixed on certain handlings of these things, but I appreciate there was a serious attempt to tackle these topics or issues with complete sincerity. I also have to appreciate the deck-building aspect which is one of the primary gameplay focuses outside the general visual novel/adventure game-esque segments. The deck-building I just adore because it's truly a case of being somewhat easy to learn, but hard to master and depending on how you play and choices you make, this can be either pretty good or bad. I also loved that the cards in the deck are based on memories from the main character's experiences. It was a great way of tying into core themes of the game itself while also talking about a broader subject regarding how experiences can help us overcome certain obstacles, but also letting go of certain memories can open opportunities for greater ones. Very few games make me emotional, but when I completed my first playthrough, I got very emotional. This game just presents itself so well that I couldn't help but seriously care about the characters and seeing how my choices impacted their lives really felt meaningful. Even 72+ hours after beating the game, I can't wait to dive back in and explore more aspects of these characters and this world I missed the first time while also learning from my first playthrough, just like the main character. This game truly feels one-of-a-kind as very few if any games have the same core components and execute it this well. This is one of the few cases where I would be completely open to the devs taking the core systems of this game and using them to make another game while maybe putting a twist on or re-contextualizing certain gameplay elements in a different kind of setting. This developer has earned my respect and adoration for the rest of my life.Small note: The soundtrack selection is stellar. "The Child You Were" by Frances Aravel is by far my favorite and a clear standout track. Such a great song choice for this game. Tying in the themes of that song into this game gives it a somber brilliance which really helped give the finality of a playthrough some emotional weight.

_childDocuments_.review: This has become one of my favourite games and I really recommend it. There is a lot of depth to the story, how you handle your relationships with others on the colony, the environment and politics. Even with the simple skills, cards and gifts system, how you choose to spend your time dramatically shapes the world around you. I also like the option of being able to read through my choices and get into the story or if I've seen it before or just want to chill was some music, I can scroll through the dialogue quickly and just concentrate on collecting and the card game. This game handles sex and gender so well, the non-binary options are so fluid and the ability to romance whoever is amazing.My only criticisms would be, making it easier to skip dialogue outside of clicking though each statement and more of a variation in gifts you can buy outside of cake, I can't imagine my friends appreciating my giving them random sticks and eggs I find on the ground, year after year. However, my biggest issue with the game is race. The two most sexualized characters, who have the most revealing clothing in the game are the darker skinned ones. Rex, is super openly sexual and also animalized like a dog, and Marz is at the start of the game is a materialistic, self-absorbed, overweight bully at the start of the game and by the end keeps most of her negative characteristics, but has this glow up where she just has the most revealing outfits. It wouldn't be that bad if other characters had this treatment, the only other character that reads as Black is Rhett the head of security, and he plays into a more positive trope, but at some point his physique despite his age is brought up. There's also Tangent and Dys, Asian coded twins, Tangent being into STEM and Dys being a socially awkward loner. It's just more racial tropes the game seems to gave fallen into despite handling gender and sexuality so beautifully.I still love this game and play it all the time and would highly recommend it to others. However, Marz's portrayal did give me really terrible callbacks to how people perceived me when I was a kid, and plays on my concerns on how people might see me as an adult. I bring this up, so others know what to expect when getting into this game, and that developers can be aware of how these subtle stereotypes can be repeated even with well intended storytelling.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a breath of fresh air, with a great story, a good cast of characters, and, considering it is a story-driven game, strong replayability due to the unique new-game plus features and diverging endings.  Story: Without giving much away, a group of biologically enhanced children are born on a spaceship in route to settling a new colony on an alien world.  The main character can build friendships that will affect their lives and the fate of the colony. The story is really fairly unique in terms of avoiding some of the most common sci-fi tropes (the closest sci-fi parallel I have personally read/watched would be Bios by Robert Wilson).  As you accumulate more playthroughs with more memories, your character can take actions they couldn't in previous playthroughs, making the storyline branch to some degree.The only cons that I can come up with is that the branching storylines on subsequent replays and epilogue stories while extensive also feel incomplete.  For example, one character that dies is non-savable despite any efforts, which seems odd on it's face.  Also, due to the friendship system being allowed to go up to 100 as fast as the player can, some fixed events seem out-of-character for some characters that overcome some of their flaws as you improve your friendship with them.  Also, the epilogue events sometimes feel like a bit of a stretch, for example Tangent's epilogue events seem as if the player's befriending them had little to no consequence.Overall, this was probably one of the games I enjoyed most in 2023.  With game writing as it is today, I'm not often struck with a sense of awe or excitement in games anymore.  While playing this I often felt this way.  As with some my favorite games where I find myself saying "one more level" or "one more turn", I often found myself saying "one more season" when I was about to quit playing.  If you love character-driven fantastical sci-fi, you will love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent choose-your-own-adventure-esque roleplaying game. The game mechanics are simple enough to not get in the way yet woven together well enough to keep them satisfying. _childDocuments_.review: I'm not normally prone to hyperbole, but I Was a Teenage Exocolonist genuinely is a modern classic. The quality of the writing, the complexity of the characters, the emotional investment, and the amazing replayability make this game stand out.Currently Exocolonist has nowhere near the profile or credit it deserves, and I would encourage anyone on the fence about whether this is likely to be their thing to give it a go. Please.Exocolonist is very much its own game, however it straddles a space somewhere between visual novel (VN), RPG and princess builders (such as Long Live the Queen and Volcano Princess).The risk of dropping a term like “visual novel” about a game such as this is that it risks creating the impression of click and read. I hate click and read, and most VNs leave me cold. I therefore use the term advisedly because it’s not like that at all. What the game is, instead, is heavily story driven with more reading than most people are likely used to.In Exocolonist you play as the main protagonist arriving on a new colony world. Your primary interactions are with other colony ship children who age together with you across seasons and years until you are 20 years old, at which point the game ends.Gameplay involves walking around different, smallish, maps interacting with other characters, building up skills and relationships, and revealing factoids about the other children, the new world you have colonised, and ultimately the adult world going on around you and their politics.Most events and interactions trigger stat increases across 12 broad categories. What areas you focus on can dramatically alter the events that you trigger and the skill checks you are able to pass across your journey.All main characters are potentially romanceable, although mostly in a pragmatic way – which is to say, most romance chains stay effectively platonic and the characters you romance maintain their own autonomy and quirks. The relationship outro also inevitably peters off into melancholy – for example distant characters stay distant, they drift away emotionally or get absorbed in their work, etc. Kind of like real life.Or you can completely skip all romance chains and focus on saving your colony from collapse, or investigating this strange new planet you have found yourself living on, or on a career, or (eventually) playing politics with the adults.It’s all very adult, and realistic, and emotionally impactful, but may feel a touch unsatisfying if your main goal in computer gaming is pure escapism.Other than walking around maps, training up stats, triggering events, and interacting with other characters the other main element of gamification here is the card system.As you experience the world you are rewarded with cards as a proxy for life’s experiences – such as [played] “Hide and Seek with Nougat”, “Harvesting Mushwood” and [learned] “Dys's Secret”. The cards have one of three different colors, corresponding to broad stat building themes, and a number. Later events as you age inevitably reward cards with higher values. To pass a skill check you need to arrange your cards into straights and runs.The card system was more than complex enough for me as it gives a wonderful sense of agency, without being overly onerous or punishing. The tests are inevitably a reasonably straightforward exercise in pair matching and light mental arithmetic.Finally, I absolutely despise replaying most games - one run though of a game is inevitably enough. Except in this case, where I have completed three full runs and started a fourth. (A full run takes around 7 hours.)Exocolonist has a wonderful ability to encourage replayability. In part, this is because it is so content-dense that it is literally impossible to experience more than a fraction of what the game has to offer on a single playthough. The game also, very smartly, acknowledges the conceit with references to past (and future) lives and an end of game admonishment to “do better next time”.There is, indeed, a lot of incentive to do better next time, in part because bad things happen in the game to nice people, and across multiple replays you can find ways to save them and to improve the colony's chances of success.Taking certain routes through the story can also unlock additional story lines and options in future playthroughs.If you haven’t worked this out already, I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Can be a tad grindy, as often management games like these are, but well worth your time. From the ability to create a character of many combinations of sex and gender, the choices with actual stakes in the story's progression, and an interesting take on the evolution of human culture and interaction, the game creates a story that is your own. It would be nice to customize your race but given the art requirements as characters are drawn sprites and not textured 3d models, I can understand why you have a fixed character.The card battling mini-game adds some variety to break up the story and conversations with NPCs but performing them over and over again starts getting a little long in the tooth, especially in the exploration portions outside the settlement. It would also be nice to be able to purchase the little items you can scavenge to use as gifts for the colonists as if you don't have enough bravery to go out exploring you're rather limited in obtaining them. It is also difficult to get rid of low end cards, so late game when you need to hit 100+ points in a challenge you'll still see 0 and 1 point cards in your draw.Part of the game is obviously trial and error as there is a New Game+ option. I'm looking forward to seeing a new story but at the same time I'm not excited about doing all the card battles again. There's an option to have it autoplay but challenges are resolved with a modified coin flip in that mode while I can play the battles to a win nearly every time. The story, art, both character and card, and creativity on display are all great. If you're a fan of management games, trainer games, or visual novels, you'll probably dig it. It's got the trappings of a cozy life sim but there are some really traumatic events so make sure to read the content warnings as while there's no visible gore, your choices will impact people in your colony in emotionally rough ways. I'm not ashamed to admit that I was rather upset several times during my first play through ( in a good way ). Music is mostly good, with some of the tracks feeling rather nice but a few I found to be a bit out of place. Thankfully there's a way to skip tracks you don't like.The card mini-game CAN get a little tedious but it's not a deal breaker by any stretch. Dunno if it'll scratch the itch for a hardcore deck building game fan but definitely would sate a casual's lust for card battles.Buy the game, give the dev some money. They earned it. You can tell the game is a labor of love. I'd love to see another installment and catch up with the descendants of my little colony.PS - Doggo himbo is the best boi. Give him all the hugs.

_childDocuments_.review: A newage teen drama with an interesting cast of characters, an exotic setting with well thought-out lore and plenty of high-stakes decisions for the player to make. There's romance, tension, and intrigue to be found in the crumbling space colony you try to build and even worse, not everyone will survive. For those interested in diversity and LGBT themes, you will find it in abundance here.My primary concern is how limited the ending system is, which was surprising given how much detail went into everything before it; it's almost a guarantee that you will be left wondering about someone's fate. Since the game is fully released and there likely won't be any major patches, I would lower my expectations when trying to find closure.

_childDocuments_.review: I only recently discovered this game and I have to say that I have immediately become obsessed.-Amazing Art-Amazing Audio and Music-Amazing Writing-Intuitive and Simple Navigation, UI, and GameplayThis game speaks volumes with it's stories. _childDocuments_.review: As other reviews have stated, do NOT wait for a sale. The devs deserve every penny they get for this game. In this game you play as, well, you, in a parallel universe where humanity has found another planet suitable for human life. You'll live a teenage life one month at a time starting from age 10, where every event is handled in the form of a quirky poker game, and your core memories are the cards. You have a bunch of skills that you can raise by playing this game of poker, and a ton of paths to take. Junction points, Life or death. Do you become an upstanding citizen of your colony, persuasive enough to take over as Governor, or do you live a life of danger, putting yourself on the frontlines. Or maybe you just want to chill with an adorable spider squid and a one-foot mouse like I did. It's all up to you.But if you do play this game, know that you will play it multiple times, because you have a friend who wants you to live your best life, and you have a secret power you will discover over the course of the game. Good luck, exocolonist!

_childDocuments_.review: On my second run, I saved Tammy's life, dutifully fed her cake every year, made my feelings for her known, and she still chose Cal over me. I can forgive her for breaking my heart, and I can forgive the game for enabling her, because I know there were ways I could have stopped their budding romance and claimed her for myself if I'd played my, ahem, cards right. Unfortunately, after finishing with those two separate characters, I found that I often still didn't know to do that.There are some great aspects of I Was a Teenage Exocolonist, and some of the disappointments in the first run are pretty easily rectified on subsequent attempts. Even so, both my runs had long periods of directionless wandering, and the endings my character got shoehorned into felt forced. As an overall narrative, it left for an inconsistent experience, with occasionally erratic pacing and a pretty abrupt conclusion once the teenage years came to an end.Then again, these could just be my specific conclusions based on the way I chose to play. After about 30 hours and those two different characters, I have no huge interest in going any further, so it's really up to the game to make its mark before that point. Even as it stands, there are a lot of positives here. The card challenges are fun, finding the optimal path for skill increases and perks is appropriately stimulating, and there are some very well-written scenes with surprisingly emotional moments. It's a memorable setting, and I generally liked the characters and wanted to make the strange alien world a better place. I appreciate the ambition of this undertaking, even if the execution isn't flawless.

_childDocuments_.review: To start off with, I cannot recommend this game enough. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly, there is not much for me to say that hasn’t already been said by other players in their own reviews. Also, if I wrote everything I had to say this would be an entire essay and I am unfortunately limited by the word count lol.The art is beautiful, both with the characters as well as out in the world when you get to move around, everything is top notch. Lots of pink and purples, but hey this is an alien planet, there is no better reason to go wild with the colors and designs!Music is great, it really feels otherworldly while having a kind of nostalgic feel to it that fits the sci-fi setting as well as the atmosphere they wanted the game to have.The story is straight forward, you live in a colony recently arrived on an alien planet trying to survive, but that is by design since the real magic happens with -how- you play. This game is a true and proper RPG, every choice you make matters and there is no true ending: there are good, bad, bittersweet, better than others, etc. and it is up to you which one you like best, what you would change, etc.The paths are never obvious, the game won’t tell you which choice is better or where you should head up next, it is all on you. The characters, oh the characters, I could write an essay for each character on just how great they are. Obviously everyone has their favorites and I personally have a soft spot for the twins. Every character here feels real and organic. They feel real, they have their own stories, they go through their own struggles and decisions, they have their strengths, weaknesses and best of all: they grow as they age. I don’t mean just design, I mean personality. They never stay with just a default personality the entire game, they learn and become wiser, their view changer either a little or completely because of their own experiences;some have to do with the player choices, but most do not, this is their life and you are not the center of it, you are part of it. The mean bully with an ego will not stay the same when they grow, the little cinnamon roll who wants everything to be nice and happy and is overall weak will show their strength just lies elsewhere (btw *chef’s kiss* with how they showed this), if  two characters dislike each other they might not stay disliking each other the entire game, same with if they like each other. Life is messy and gives you lessons which change your views and behavior, this game does a great job on showing this. These are your friends and they grow with you.Another thing I liked was the way friendships work. In many games I have played that have a friendship pointer if you want the character to be your friend or more you have to agree with everything they do or how they view the world, not here. These characters have their views but they also recognize that you have your own, even if you might not agree with each other chances are your points won’t go down, you’ll just get a response that says “I disagree with you and here is why… but I can see why you don’t see it like that”. It is a detail that I really like and it just adds more layers to the characters, your relationships romantic or not, feel -real-What I'm trying to say in very little words (which is hard): This is an amazing game and worth every penny

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game, and if you got to the point of reading reviews for it, you should probably play it. The graphic style is beautiful, the sci-fi is hard, and there is lots of replayability. The core card mechanic is okay, but once you get the hang of it, it gets trivial (at least on Normal). I played through the Exocolonist two times, one blind and one with a guide, and I enjoyed both playthroughs.There is one caveat that some of you might need to be aware of. The target audience of this game is clearly US, young, and at least somewhat woke.The characters and narrative are largely built around gender, professional and personal identity. History of the world has overpopulation and climate crises as its central issues. You might be a conservative person from another part of the world, as I am, and find some of the game naive or too in-the-face (fitting, really, for a game called 'I Was a Teenage Exocolonist'). Still, the game isn't propaganda, it's speculative sci-fi written from a particular worldview. If you can suspend your disbelief a bit, there is much fun to be had here for the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Five hours in and I'm hooked. Interesting decisions, just enough text, quick load times (Linux Mint on an SSD connected to a Steam Deck), and heavy subjects in the safety of a game.8.5 hours in, reminds me of The Quiet Year RPG, where players draw from a 52-card deck (divided into the four suits, as four seasons), look up the number on a table, and make a decision. The players take turns making and modifying the map (pencil or other colors, on paper), and the game ends during Winter when a Big Bad shows up.About 21 hours of playtime later: Finished my first life! That's enough for now, but it was a fun and thoughtful time. I appreciate the speculative-fiction side of the story. While I highly doubt we'll ever reach other solar systems, such stories are rich ground for considering how we might grow up more here on Earth.20241011 After detoxing from videogames, I don't recommend any games anymore. I do recommend collective action towards improving public welfare, rather than trying to amass as much as we can individually. Perhaps IWaTE is a gateway to new understanding for you, in which case consider launching from there into reading related books and finding people with whom you can learn and grow.

_childDocuments_.review: It's...okay. This is one of those times I wish Steam had a 'neutral' review option, because ultimately I'm conflicted on the game.There's a lot of effort put into the art style and general depiction of an alien planet, most of which land excellently. The core gameplay is decent as an idea, but ultimately ends up being tedious especially given the game wants you to replay it multiple times. And a major part of the problem is that it doesn't really engage very well with the whole groundhog day loop situation. There are some parts where you have influence over what's going to happen next, but it feels a bit too restrained. For a game that wants you to believe your choices matter and what you know from loop to loop matters, it ends up falling flat compared to other time travel or time loop fiction.It's a game with a lot of charm, a great art style and then a bunch of good ideas. But a lot of the good ideas end up badly executed and pull down the game as a whole. If they had focused around three or four core conceits and then really refined those to a sheen, I think the game would've been a classic. As is, my current opinion of the game falls on the side of 'A bit disappointing'. That said, I'll be keeping a lookout for their next game, whenever that might be.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance simple choice-consequence relation sim with a card mini-game sprinkled over. But the more you play it, the more you understand that there is so much more in it. So many complex details, so many complex choices that lead to sometimes catastrophic consequences. One thing though for some people - do understand that this game does really dive deeply into such topic as puberty, growing up in community where people live in total peace with LGBT, veganism, vegetarianism and genetic enhancements. And game makes Main Character, you obviously, take some hard choices sometimes as if to follow or not some of these paths as in choosing being true to your pacifist nature, being vegetarian or even having one or multiple relations with people of your/other or androgynous genders. But worry not, all these choices are yours to take and only yours. There are also endings for both people, who don't want to "hug Nature" and "be one with Nature". Another warning that should probably exist about this game is that you need to be aware of many 18+ themes in it - death of main characters, sexual innuendos, very graphic and detailed descriptions of some gross or horrific processes, animal cruelty/human cruelty and etc. Please, check CONTENT WARNING section before playing.And the art, it is just incredibly beautiful. Have to really say kudos to the designers of levels, characters and aliens. The music is also very good. Yeah, it does get repetitive at some point, but even then you may not notice it while playing as the music is not annoying or pushing on you, it is just a relaxing background.

_childDocuments_.review: absolutely stunning. genuinely, if people don't start looking at this game as a real best of 2022 contender, i might just get into utopia's blep tea contraband and start losing my mind. sometimes relaxing, sometimes surprising, sometimes viscerally tragic, and always true to itself, i was a teenage exocolonist deserves every bit of praise it's gotten and all the love it's yet to receive. every moment of this game was so incredibly and uniquely delightful in a way i haven't experienced in gaming before-- i've just finished my first playthrough, and i find myself oddly drawn to tears by it. very few stories i've read, let alone games i've played, come at their premise with such an amount of care: not just effort, but detail, and affection for it. there is so much love, here. the take on the nature of humanity that this story takes is heart-wrenchingly gorgeous, painful, joyful, hilarious, campy and fun and strange. it's an odd little thing, and unabashedly so. exactly as it should be. raising sol felt like raising my younger self, and even if you think you won't find anything here for you-- underneath and interwoven with the technicolor world and the fun mechanics and the politics and the most lovingly human (and sometimes nonhuman) characters i've ever seen-- this a story about growing up. as a narrative experience, it rivals (and then handily surpasses) any big studio game i have ever played, and does so with ease. i think where the story of iwatec succeeds, most of all, is in its discussion of loss. the human experience is full of it, in big and little ways. you're in a timeloop, so sometimes, naturally, you can stop the bad thing from happening. sometimes you can't. sometimes the best parts of iwatec are losing, terribly, inevitably, and piecing sol back together again after. a wonderful tale on what it means to be human. i don't think i know the answer, yet, but i'm about to wake up again and find out.

_childDocuments_.review: I really didn't know what to expect when I started playing this, but wow - this was so much better than I could've imagined. The narrative felt (for the most part) very reactive, which stood out against any other minor flaws the game might have had. Because of this, the role-playing part of this RPG was so rewarding and engaging. I crafted a character in my mind, and when I clearly wanted my character to be acting a certain way, the game read my mind and always had a narrative path ready for me to go down. The story was (to me) very touching, and I loved that they didn't shy away from the bad and the ugly of what this world would be like while still maintaining some of that childlike joy. I genuinely teared up at multiple parts, and was giddily grinning at others.A few major mechanics of the game had to grow on me, especially the deck-building, but I really felt like I got sucked into the game almost immediately. The attention to detail, the gorgeous illustration and art style, the careful balancing of difficulty as the years progress - a lot of passion and care clearly went into making a game, and it shows.My only real issue with the game is that after the careful hours I spent crafting my first run through, and finally getting the hang of the deck-building challenge mechanic, the ending of the game felt very rushed and anticlimactic. It wrapped up the loose ends, but I did feel like for my story's ending, there should've been more urgency and stress in the final moments.It's a game that practically is begging to be replayed at least a few times to unlock different ending, but more important, different stories throughout the 10 years the narrative spans. I can't wait to dive back in!!

_childDocuments_.review: Well my first playthrough of game took about 10 hours, second one where I was skimming the text I've already read took 8 because I wasn't active gift giver on first playthrough so missed lot of friend events, that combined with game having sort of "one more turn" effect means it ruined my sleeping rhytmn for two days :'D I've essentially seen just the standard and good ending and not any of the more tragic endings. so SPOILERS obviously.But yeah, visual, presentation and content wise this is excellent CYOA/visual novel. The timeloop/future vision aspect also brings nice stuff to replays, though it also applies on reloading save files. Bit of warning in that the content warning menu on title screen is very extensive and spoilery. Like the animal cruelty part straight up tells that a pet can die and how that situation comes to pass. I'm not sure if its case of warnings being extremely careful to tell everything that could offend someone or if its meant to also work as guide to avoid the said scenes happening. All in all, its not most immersive visual novel I've played(that's like Scarlet Hollow) since it still relies heavily on stuff like "give everyone regularly a gift to max their affinity to see their scenes"(with the later additions it feels like you have to give them liked gift every season on schedule :'D), though it does try clearly to be "realistic" regarding things like "♥♥♥♥ happens in life". I mean game is more or less lifesim of growing up as teenager on alien planet, while it kinda looks like dating sim and you can start relationship with any of fellow teenagers, there are quite few ones that just aren't interested in relationship beyond casual fling or that have deal breakers on some things with you so you break up during epilogue.(this in general is set in sexually open minded future, but I didn't test which characters are monogamy only and which ones allow polyamory, teenager wise two of them are in relationship with each other unless you break them up, other two are in abusive relationship unless you break them up, two go through casual flings, one is willing to be in open relationship with anyone and one doesn't get physically attracted until they are already emotionally attached. Rest of them I'm not sure of.)Story wise I have also some commentary: I do like that game tries to do the "both sides have reasonable point here", but I do feel like it still pretty heavily leans over the starting hippie community(that is what Stratos folks essentially are) colonists side of things. Like, yeah, they make sure that both sides have faults and good points and them being teenagers explains most of it(like the one usually nice character who is heavily pacifistic shows holier than thou attitude towards guards when they try to recruit him, but they did provoke him and they really should leave him alone(while they would have point about the "needing help with defending of colony", this being after Lum does the whole "and now everyone are considered to be conscripted" shenanigans), the Gardeners are hard to reason with jerks besides Sym, the most pro nature & anti human character is driven by lot of angst and self loathing, etc), but the "live in harmony with nature" ending is essentially happiest ending for every character you likely care about despite what it involves. Game does apparently imply though that the colonists don't have the most nuanced take on faults of Earth and humanity, but I don't feel like game does that exactly either regarding the environmental issues. Like yeah, purely in context of game the peace ending is reasonable compromise that doesn't involve war with planet or one side being wiped out and not every adult is happy with it. Overseer and Nocticulent's attitude makes sense considering what they are, but I'm still annoyed by attitude that sapience means some actions are inherently evil despite them being normal non sapient animal behaviour. Game doesn't imo end up pushing "humans bad" message, but it does still end up with less nuanced take on environmental stuff by the end even though it does try to be balanced.Oh and I assume the post credits new loop starting happens no matter ending, which feels bit of bummer when you've worked towards happiest possible ending :'D Make its kinda feel like world is stuck in loop even if that isn't the intention and its more of attempt at being immersive regarding new game plus sort of deal.

_childDocuments_.review: do not let the terrible terrible title fool you (like it fooled me for a good while - seriously 'i was a teenage exocolonist' does not sound like the sort of game i'd enjoy, it sounds like a sitcom). This game is a well written gem.I'm not a fan of the mechanics of the game (both the cards and the basic stat-grinding nature), but they fall to the background pretty quickly as you immerse yourself in the stories of the people around you. The card system can be easily turned off (though i haven't tested this yet), and while the stat-grinding can't (afaik) it provides excuses to provide cool scenes with which you interact with NPCs, see sides of them you normally wouldn't, so the stat grinding doesn't feel like wasted time.I grew to love the characters I interacted with, and even the ones I didn't interact with much I cared about, and I'm excited to play through again to learn more about the other characters.Additionally, oftentimes I ran into difficult choices, where I wasn't honestly sure what the right answer was, that shaped the future of the colony. Even when there is an 'obvious' right answer, sometimes it can be a difficult decision to make if it puts you in opposition with a character you care about. I love it!One major criticism I can levy against the game - other than that god-awful title - is that character relationships don't seem to interact much. I was friends with two siblings (Dys and Tang) who seemed to dislike each other, and I was expecting to either have some scenes where I mediated between them, or otherwise learn more about their relationship with each other, but mostly each character's story seems self-contained save for random scenes disconnected from their individual stories.(That said I have only played through the game once so far, so this may not be true of every character. Will update this if it turns out it's better for others).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a true gem. The storyline is incredibly engaging and I fell in love with all of the characters. My only wish is that there was more of a character customization because there's only so many gender combinations to go through to make each playthrough feel different. It would have been amazing if we could play as a child of the previous character, though I understand that wouldn't have fit the story. But even so, each playthrough felt very different and while a lot of the events repeat, it's amazing that there are options to skip through text you've already seen or even set the card battles to automatic. _childDocuments_.review: Truly a fascinating story.  I love the combination of card game with visual novel sort of storytelling.  The concept of the time loop allowing you to fix mistakes based on previous playthroughs is immensely satisfying.  And the fact that the game tells you in the spoilers section whether or not someone can be saved preventing you from overinvesting time into trying to save someone who can't be.  That being said it is also nice that just cause someone can be saved either in your first playthrough or with additional knowledge going into others doesn't mean it is going to be easy.  I also liked that given the game ends when you are 20, some of your romances fizzle out by the time of the epilogue.  Too often in these types of games you get "and they lived happily ever after", or worse it goes super bleak like "unfortunately they died shortly after" never any thing like "as time grew on you drifted apart" as is one of the potential romance endings in this game.  I love this, cause while I'm all for escapism, how often does a relationship started by teenagers actually last?That being said, it is worth noting this game is NOT for the faint of heart.  Game doesn't hesitate to pointlessly kill a prepubescent child within the first hour or so of the game.  Keyword is pointlessly, they strive to make great efforts to show that while any death, especially one of a child, is impactful it isn't always due to something like space vikings or whatever, it can literally be something like a toy short circuiting.  Thankfully that death can be undone as quickly as literally loading a prior save after it has happened, but it shows you that they aren't going to pull any punches.My only real complaint about the game is there is a lot of soapboxing during certain parts of the game.  While most things in it give you options some things are just presented as out and out wrong (without showing why, or in some cases literally showing the exact opposite leaving you confused as to the author's intent).  For example, the game goes to great lengths to show Capitalism as a negative force, and yet you still get "money" in the form of Kudos and there is a character who flat out says it doesn't make sense to give the same amout to someone who did nothing while someone else did all the work.The game also punishes you for staying neutral on too many things.  You more or less are forced to pick a side if you want a decent ending.  You leveled up your combat abilities as your focus because you liked the bonus it provided? Well I hope you weren't planning on talking anything out with the natives because if so you just earned yourself an everyone dies ending... This isn't necessarily a con as again you made that decision and you decided too late that it was a bad one.  Point is, that's another theme in this game is stick to your guns, and in some cases that is very much literal.TL;DR Game has its flaws no doubt, but it is definitely extremely enjoyable despite these.  Also similar to a rogue like game, a single playthrough isn't even a fraction of the full game.  I played through several times and still haven't seen all the endings.  Another nice caveat is the game remembers what youve encountered in other playthroughs even if you don't and is somewhat forgiving in that respect.  I appreciated the story, the inclusiveness, and the thought provoking side of the fact that almost no character is universally good or evil.  I also loved the fact you could save people you failed to in a prior playthrough, few things are as satisfying.9/10 GG

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely in my top 10 games of all time.The game's main function is the fact that you relive your live over and over. Without spoilers, I can can say it is done really well. With spoilers  The card game part isn't anything special. It's not especially difficult, my first playthrough I didn't lose a single card game challenge. The special part is the deck-building part. You have little control over what exactly goes into your deck, but they are determined by the memories you make and how you go about challenges. The art in the game is amazing. The character's portraits and sprites change as the years go bye. In some events the game gets rid of all the text and just displays a fullscreen image for several seconds for important events. The cards are all unique and distinguishable.The characters are all enjoyable and fun to get to know. At first glance, it seems like the characters each have one defining trait that makes up their character, something that often happens in other games. However, this game has probably the most in-depth and dynamic characters I've seen in a while. Characters change over the years, depending on what happens in the colony, who dies, and how you interact with them. They each have multiple endings to their own story, and will come upon some of them even without your help. Some of the romanceable characters will start dating throughout the story if you don't woo them first.All in all, the best life-sim game I've ever played, not a bad card game, amazing dating sim, and an emotional roller coaster.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not one to normally enjoy visual novels. Outside of niche elements in the genre, like Doki Doki and Disco Elysium, I find them to be boring. This one, however, sparked joy in me. Through the rudimentary life of a teenager on Earth's first exocolony (a colony outside our solar system), I experienced all the sadness and joy that life has to offer us. Exploration was interesting and fun. The card game is a simple, but needed addition. If more visual novels were this unique and engaging with fun and interesting minigames, I would certainly play more. It has single handedly made me take another look at the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good role-playing game where you play a child (who grows into a teenager) in a new colony on an alien planet. Lots of characters to meet, skills to specialise in, jobs to do and paths to choose. Text heavy but all the text is well written and the overall story has some twists and turns that keep you engaged. Usually in these sorts of games there's at least 1 bad mechanic but everything here works, the exploration is decent, the card mechanics are good, the dialog choices make sense. More than anything I was compelled to keep playing to the end to try my best to get a happy(ish) ending for my character and her partner. Lots of replay value too (no spoilers!). Feels finished and like a complete video game. If any of that sounds good, buy it!

_childDocuments_.review: "I Was a Teenage Exocolonist" is a visual novel game where you play a 10yo kid who is part of the first colony of humans on an alien planet! And who is also stuck in a time loop of reliving their teenage years until they can get their life right and save everyone!!You play until you're 20 years, and go through all sorts of struggles and successes in a coming-of-life-type story.... on an alien planet that's trying to kill you. The game gets pretty dark/has mature themes, but it's still really silly/light, as well as heartwrenching and emotionally satisfying. By the end of the game, you'll have loved and lost, and the core mechanic is to start all over again with memories of your past life to guide you, and just try to get it right this time. Super cool thing is the representation in the game!!!! There is so much representation for all sorts of marginalized communities, and the representation isn't a gimmick, it's just there to add to the characters!! I.e. I didn't know one of the characters was trans till my 3rd playthrough because it just never came up in the dialogue choices I made! And then it seemed so obvious in retrospect 😂 Like fr, there is representation for LGBTQIA, POCs, disabled people, polyam relationships, genderqueer people, etc etc. I've fallen in love with this game and can't stress how much it means to me. I know it might not be up everyone's alley but it's a BEAUTIFUL game and definitely smashed its way into my top favs of all times ❤️

_childDocuments_.review: The game shines when it comes to the creatures and and world building of the alien planet. The card puzzles were also fun and helped make leveling up more interesting. The art style is beautiful. However, the writing of the game and the story feels like it was made by people who spend a lot of time on tumblr and twitter. There's a lot of focus on how bad we are (or were as this game is not on Earth). The way you buy upgrades still felt like capitalism despite the game preaching against it. And despite our racist colonialist past being brought up, the colonists refuse to admit it counts with them too. I was disappointed with how it felt like trendy topics were brought up for brownie points with their audience, but those topics weren't truly challenged, including the morality of colonizing a new planet and the violence that comes with it. The characters felt bland. It felt like the focus was on creating an identity and sexuality catch 'em all rather than an engaging relationship system. The relationships and romance system felt shallow and for some characters they already have a built in partner. Being with them means breaking up their happy relationship. I think a more robust relationship system would have fixed this and given us more time to explore the characters and bond with them.Basically the areas that felt like sci-fi and the future shone, but everything else fell short. This is 2024 masquerading as the future while it explores trendy online discourse.If I sound salty it's because I expected to love this game but it left me disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist explores a decade of the lives of the first generation of children not born on Earth. While the genre of life sim games where you go about your life month to month raising personal stats and strengthening bonds is nothing new, I'm enraptured with the depth Exocolonist has to its systems and ideas. Sometimes it feels like choices are very telegraphed in games like this, that paths are direct linear routes without much leeway or wiggle room. Exocolonist can unfold into over 30 different endings, not even accounting for the different ways certain smaller storylines can end within a larger ending. It's easy to miss things, easy to have a bad outcome, but this a game that encourages you to carry on and, eventually, overcome. As the early game hints, there's more to this game than just a singular playthrough. This is a game really doesn't fully begin until you've beaten it that first time. From there it can unfold in various other ways as you try and grow and improve on what came before. The first thing I wanted to do when I saw the credits was start playing again right away, and that's exactly what the game wanted from me to. I can already see how much play time one can get out of Exocolonist just halfway through my second playthrough. While many things will obviously stay the same many more can change, either completely on purposely or entirely on accident. It's rare that I feel a game actually accurately represents just how much your choices matter in a game, but if anything Exocolonist undersells just how much agency you have in shaping things. The writing is interesting, which is of course integral in a game so heavy on the plot. Each of the characters you grow up with are quite interesting with personalities that shift and develop over the years. While some moments certainly feel tropey or even a bit on the nose, there's a sincerity to the writing in Exocolonist that cuts through any of those unsubtle moments. It helps that this is a game starring children growing into adults, you can't really blame a writer for making the puberty arc full of high strung emotions or for having the 14 year old kid with bright hair love the anime OVAs they found on the ship's medialogs. Moments of intensity or high emotion in the story work and land and I found myself generally invested throughout the length of my first playthrough and even more so starting my second. In particular if you are someone with an interest in exobiology, or generally enjoy the idea of fictional ecosystems and how humans might interact with them, this game is ripe with rather fleshed out worldbuilding and has a solid base on ecological concepts. While I don't think that Exocolonist is a game for everyone, I feel like it's an extremely easy sell to anyone remotely interested in what it has to offer. It also certainly helps that the game is abundantly queer friendly with perhaps the most robust custom pronoun/gendered terms options I've seen in a game. Generally a lot of games that veer into "dating sim" territories feel somewhat trashy if not outright exploitative. Exocolonist takes great lengths to avoid this while also adding nuance to its romance systems. I can't think of another dating sim where characters will start getting together on their own if you don't put yourself in the running for their hearts. Overall, this is one of those long rambling reviews where if you've actually made it to the end, we both know you're probably either bored at work, or are about to go buy this game. Either way: have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the few that has choked me up. I got more emotionally invested in this story than I have in almost any other game, book, movie, or show. The storytelling, world building, and illustrations are beautiful. Part of me doesn't want to do a second playthrough because I want the story from my first playthrough to live on forever in my mind in that state. This game is a masterpiece and worth every penny. My first playthrough took me about ~14 hours. I suspect that I will be able to easily get 2 more playthroughs with minimal content overlap and suspect that I will be able to get 5 playthroughs before the content overlap becomes an issue. There are a lot of possible endings though so there may be a lot more content then I suspect. If I had to complain about one thing, I would say that walking around the colony to looking for consumables and seeing if anyone has some new dialog event, gets a bit tedious at times, but it is a very minor point.In conclusion, this game is one of my top 3 all time favorite games to date, and my top story driven game. If you like story rich entertainment, you will be hard pressed to find a game or movie with a better story. This is a masterpiece with a ton of gameplay that will fully immerse you to the point that you will smile and get excited for the characters and also ache to be able to give them a hug and comfort them as you learn and influence their character aches.

_childDocuments_.review: This game pulled me into the world better than anything I have ever played. It is a fantastic journey that covers all aspects of the emotional range. The replay of the game is less satisfying than it could be which is in part down to how niche it can be to change major events. I understand the idea that somethings just aren't meant to be but it is upsetting if that happens to be the route you wanted but another route that somebody else might have enjoyed can work out perfectly.  My last point is more because I am addicted to the game than it was needed but I do wish there was more. I feel like the final stage of the game is less expanded and a bit more rushed than the earlier years due to the overwhelming amount of thing that can be tied up during this time compared to the earlier years.Right now I have had my mini vent about how this game is only 95% as good as it could be let me talk about why this game is a masterpiece. This game builds on the concept that bad events are gripping and that, because it is a game, the story does not need to end well all the time. This is not a new idea but when combined with its mature handling of sensitive, relatable and current topics, it allows for a world that you could see existing in the not so distant future even though it is set on another planet! It also goes without saying that the music and artwork are fantastic or the world really would not work as well as it does. The characters created are all unique and have really well developed personalities (well outside of repeat events like birthday gift giving which I feel like could be improved by having a new response each year). They also feel like a community that is developing together which you do have an effect on (again on the second play through this feels a little less true). At its core the game is a visual novel but the game play side makes it feel like a game as well which is hard to do without taking away from the speed at which the story develops. Not once did I feel like a year went by faster or slower than the others and the game always found a way to make that year interesting and memorable. I also didn't realise how hard it was to not be a murder when your life is at risk until I realised I was doing it. Last but not least the card game aspect is nice as it is complex enough to be interesting but easy enough to pickup that I don't actively want to turn it off or just fail (this was still true on the replay for me until I was basically just too strong for anything to be hard).So to sum it up buy this game if you want a great story, if you feel that the 8-10 hours you will get on the one run is not worth the price and you don't want to see how the game works behind the scenes (which you really will on a second play trough) then wait for a sale. Do not buy it if you want to have a happy escapism experience. If you want to get truly lost an in alternate reality then buy it. This game is in my top 10 of all time. Thank you Northway Games!

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic and engaging card/visual novel combination. The basic gameplay loop is to create a deck of "memory" cards. Remove older, less potent, memories, and seek newer, more effective, ones. With dating-sim/relationship aspects and time management it *feels* like a Persona game with different gameplay loop elements. If you like chill deck-builders, puzzle games, Persona-type visual novels, dating sims with puzzle elements, or just interesting stories, go for it!Edit: I am modifying this review to respond to the number of negative reviews complaining about the "Depressing" ending and first year. I would like to respond to that: Yeah, *chances are* you won't do the right things and get a depressing ending your first time  (I started a new game on my Switch - yes, I own this on two systems - and accidentally got almost a perfect playthrough  just by switching up my playstyle ). That's on purpose: That's the second act setback. The entire point of the game is to SPUR YOU ON because your first playthrough will probably be very depressing - if not, then just accept the ending and move on.That's just part of storytelling: The point of this game is experiencing  Just make your choices and move on. Choice paralysis doesn't have to be a thing because there is always another playthrough .

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to like about this game, especially during the early hours. However, it really, and I mean REALLY, screws the pooch when it comes to the ending and the whole "meta" business.IWaTE is essentially the Princess Maker. Every month you have to choose an activity and then test your stats against various challenges and story events that arise throughout your daily life. There's one important twist though - it's all a time loop, so some of your actions in previous playthroughs have an effect on your subsequent attempts at getting a better ending.Okay, sounds cool enough. BUT:1) Pretty much every challenge is tied to a "fun" little card mini game that repeats itself for hundreds (probably thousands) times per playthrough. Sure, you can opt into the "resolve card battles with RNG" option, but it's highly suboptimal, and the time wasted on this minigame quickly begins to add up.2) Building good relationships with characters requires a grind of Stardew Valley proportions, as you need to constantly run back and forth between people and spam them with gifts while keeping track of their birthdays.3) If you neglect your relationship with some characters and don't bother doing certain activities until late into the game, the narrative logic will break and start referring to the events that were resolved years ago or treat your MC like they are still twelve years old (when you were actually supposed to experience the aforementioned events).Getting the "golden" ending, which is the only one with any sort of closure or effort put into it, requires beating the game half a dozen times, but after completing IWaTE just once and reading a couple guides, I couldn't be bothered to go through all that grind and padding all over again.It's truly mind-boggling how the devs managed to botch a fairly interesting concept this much. Therefore, can't recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly fun little life-sim slash adventure!AFTER FIRST PLAYTHROUGH:A bit politically charged with the usual "capitalism bad" rhetoric. And I say this as a staunch old-school leftist. Communism didn't exactly solve pollution either. So, in real life, I see no reason to blame either ecopolitical stances when the problem is purely human, applying to every civilization. More growth, more consumption, more imbalance. IMHO But, that said, this is a game and devs are free to worldbuild how they wish, so I let it pass.The LGBTQI+ bits certainly give variety of players chance to relate to number of different characters, or even mold their character with traits with which the player identifies with most.That said, there are no minority demographics within the game setting, except maybe humans (more so the non-enhanced humans) themselves as the aboriginal lifeforms are still the majority on this plane where the game takes place. Apparently in this universe, humanity grew to accept most genders and orientations, and even embrace them in a large scale, yet still managed to ♥♥♥♥ Earth, because... capitalism(?). At least some characters ponder about this themselves, so it is not pure propaganda against conservatives.But these are minor meta-game issues that didn't bother me that much. Rather they were thought provoking if nothing else. The game itself is pretty enjoyable and really, my greatest issue was the lack of visual customization. My cis-woman (she/her) character still looked VERY masculine despite the game claiming this choice would alter character's looks to conform with the chosen identity. In this it failed, though I understand customization would've been a great task for a small studio of developers.

_childDocuments_.review: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist illustrates how well can RPGs and visual novels blend together, especially when written with care and finesse. It is spectacular in its variety, scope and re-playability potential—a merit Northway Games intentionally built upon. In other words, there are hundreds and hundreds of choices. No playthrough is ever the same.What I appreciated the most is that there is humanity within the characters. They evolve due to their occupation, your influence, global events or simply because they are growing up. Everyone has their good and bad moments, style, unique worldviews, insecurities and wishes—all of which is depicted in a colourful narrative rife with choices. It is thus very easy to become completely immersed and emotionally invested during a playthrough.I love to come back to this game. It is one of the best and most wholesome ones I have played.
