_childDocuments_.review: I would absolutely, wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of visual novels/Persona-style experiences. The story (which I won't be spoiling here) is deeply immersive and allows you to get invested much more than most games I've ever played. The characters are written so realistically and so well that I legitimately began to feel the same way about them as I do my actual friends.    It also gets bonus points for being inclusive and actually getting representation right. There are multiple non-white characters who are allowed to have personalities beyond being non-white as well as some major characters being LGBT+ who are actual people with flaws and strengths and three dimensionality which are both things I've seen disturbingly little of in media.   The art of this game is absolutely GORGEOUS to look at. The specific moments you can get highlighting the designs of each of the characters as well as the artwork are truly astounding and I could look at this game for days and still be able to find new details in the backgrounds or character designs, which are so full of personality and life that you can get a great sense of who each character is just by looking at them. Honestly, my only issue with the game is that the UI covers the artwork too quickly when you first see them and I wish that it would hold on them a little longer. This is rectified however, by the gallery menu, where you can look at the artworks you've unlocked without a block of blue showing up and covering half of it within five seconds.   The music in this game is phenomenal, it adds just the right amount of wonder and curiosity at the right moments and can make some instances feel truly magical. There was only one song I didn't like in the moment but that just because the audio mixing wasn't done right and it was far too loud for the tender moment it was placed in. The main menu theme is the highlight for me.   I also have to appreciate the fact that this is a "choices matter" game where your choices ACTUALLY MATTER. The things you do and don't do in the game have far-reaching consequences. Big events can    happen or be prevented depending on if you collected x amount of items while outside the colony or if you have enough friendship with one of the other colonists or picked one dialog option over another. If you don't have enough of one stat, you can't help one of your friends with a task and get a better ending.    The game overall juggles a number of ideas which, under different developers, might have fallen apart and crushed them. But Northway Games was able to hold it together in order to create what is, so far, my choice for best game of 2022. Outside of the singular grievance outlined in the section about the art, I genuinely cannot think of any area this game let me down in and as such, I would give this game a 10/10 and I can't wait to see what Northway makes next.   With all that being said, you should absolutely check out the content warnings (another very unique and much appreciated thing this game does) before you play the game, to ensure you can actually enjoy the experience. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly its rather depressing how little attention this game's gotten, cause it knows what it wants to be, and it does it amazingly. A VN that is charming, depressing, tense, sometimes all of the above.You control a 10 year old child that is on board a colony ship to colonize an alien planet. You start off with a great deal of freedom to build this character too, picking from their childhood friends, starting stats, sex/gender (there's an entire drop down list of pronoun stuff you can mess with to customize how people refer to you). After landing, you've got 10 years to increase stats, build relationships, and try to keep the fragile little colony from dying to the hostile planet. Where the game shines is the freedom to build your character as you want, while still making it feel like you can actually something even if their stats suggest they may not be able to. The main gameplay loop involves picking a task for each month, then you play a brief card game with an ever expanding deck of cards, which are earned by exploring and interacting with others. You have to make a hand high enough to equal or exceed the target score to get the best result in an event. Sometimes all that does is give you a skill point, other times it determines whether you succeed or fail, based on the context. If that sounds boring to you or you just want to play the story without messing with it, the game gives you the option to shut it off, or make it harder. I personally like the game, as each game takes maybe 30 seconds to a minute to finished based on how quickly you can process the cards you got, so it doesn't interrupt gameplay to an annoying degree.As for the story, its great too. It really feels like you are a child on a hostile planet, learning about it as you grow up. How you interact with the planet and the colony changes the outcome, including whether several characters live or die to see the end of the game. There are also enough events that occur throughout the game that it doesn't get stale. Just when you feel like you're getting the hang of things or the colony is about to become problem free, another issue arises. The game does deal with some dark themes, but the devs have a list of such events that you can look at before playing if you think it may be an issue to you. Basically the devs have really gone out of their way to make this game as inclusive as possible, which is a nice gesture on top of the games quality. One run of the game will take you about 11-12 hours roughly, each year takes maybe an hour to do. I won't spoil anything, but the game does have a system in place that allows you to get a bit more out of future runs each time you finish a game, which makes it all the more worthwhile to get to the end. If you like VNs, stat raising games, and/or a good story, pick the game up and give it a try. You won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is interesting because you can complete a life cycle in about 1 day of game play. The challenge is trying to save everyone you are supposed to save (and want to save) while still ensuring the colony is safe and thriving. There are a lot of different paths you can take, and each one emphasizes the value of a different aspect of life. Do you want to be creative, or tough? Have high reasoning skills or be good with animals? These values aren't always opposed to each other, but you do have to come to terms with the fact that you can't do EVERYTHING (at least not in one lifetime!) And of course, any review would be incomplete if it didn't discuss the fantastic representations of gender, sex, relationships, and family within this game. I saw someone comment that it was a WOKE game and I hope to god that Steam considers making WOKE a tag so that I can easily find more games that show such wide and beautiful acceptance of what it means to be human.

_childDocuments_.review: Ridiculously engaging VN! While it can be considered a dating sim, I think it does plot and friendships better. (More later.) Plot is amazing, characters are (mostly) likable and have growth! Epilogues are very detailed, the best in any game I've seen! Love the main gameplay draw, that you remember your past lives and can influence events in your next playthrough! Many different activities with unique scenes that help subsequent playthroughs feel fresh! You can have pets (and interact with them-not just eye candy!) Graphics are pretty, and I like that the seasons are part of the plot too, also not just eye candy! Card battles help add some variety.My main complaint is that some of the things you need to do (either for friendships or dating) can feel uncomfortable. There are a few characters that you need to break up to be able to date. There are a few characters that will break up with you in the epilogue no matter what. Hence why I'm hesitant to like this game as a dating sim. There's a character that starts off pretty toxic, and while there is growth if the friendship is high enough, to get that friendship up you have to pick options with violence towards creatures. In this same vein: there's a character that will always die, and for a game that's main draw is replaying to save characters, this feels bad.A smaller complaint, but it can feel repetitive/grindy on subsequent playthroughs. It does a good job of having enough content/adding content, but a lot of big character/plot scenes will repeat. I still recommend this VN and had a great time! I spent 64 hours on two playthroughs.

_childDocuments_.review: In this text based game you play as one of many children growing up on an alien planet, Earth's first space colony. The story follows the protagonist from age 10 to age 20 as you struggle to grow up, but also to survive. During each month you get to choose an activity to do and gain corresponding stats that unlock different dialogue choices. You can build your relations with the characters you grow up with and learn more about them by hanging out with them or giving them gifts. There are also card game challenges in which you use cards representing your memories to succeed in certain tasks.This game is masterfully written. Your choices truly impact the story and world around you, including your choice to ignore something. There is so much lore and things to learn, not just about this unexplored planet, but also the group you came there with and what led you to leave earth. The many paths you can take will twist and turn and intersect in different ways and the game is designed for you to replay it and explore! During your playthrough you can notice how the writing changes to reflect your character's growing worldview and vocabulary. The game explores the whimsy of childhood but also pretty quickly tackles heavy themes and have many gut wrenching moments as well as thoughtful scenes and messages. The characters are complex, multifaceted people that will grow alongside you and have their own arcs, even if you don't interact with them, making the world feel alive. You can eventually choose to romance characters but its worth noting that this is  a dating game. The relationships can be messy and lead to breakups depending on the character and your choices. Characters that are not dated can end up together or your actions can lead to another couple breaking up. But the relationships can of course also be incredibly sweet and heartwarming, its all a part of life! The presentation is absolutely gorgeous. The music, the character art and the backgrounds are all stunning, words can't give them justice. All characters are well designed and expressive and the fully illustrated scenes are always a treat. The UI is nice and simple with an in universe reason to exist and you can change its transparency and size according to your needs. The artwork on the cards is pretty as well but can feel a little out of place sometimes since they where all made by different guest artists but that doesn't subtract from the overall feel of the watercolor style and synthetic tunes.Character diversity is not a problem and the game is very inclusive. There is a broad range of people with different ethnicites, body types, mobility, gender and preferences, It never feels 'forced' or tokenized, everyone is just allowed to be their own people. You can choose, change and customize your gendered language at any time if you so wish, independent of appearance. Polyamory is possible with certain characters and you can date all the characters regardless of gender.The game is also well optimized with many options to increase performance. Even though its already pretty light since its a text based game, its nice to see! I played this on a laptop at times and it ran smooth there as well aside from some minor problems with the cloud sync. I Was A Teenage Exocolonist is a beautiful and heavy story game with card based mini-challenges, deep lore, well developed characters, inclusivity and a lovely soundtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game with gorgeous art, an interesting and diverse cast of characters, and a solid premise.I'm usually not a fan of time-management games, I get anxious about mis-managing my time early on leading to a bad end later, but Exocolonist's core concept and semi-rogue-lite setup means that that isn't really an issue, allowing you to explore all the way through the consequences of your choices.And you'll want to see those consequences. While you're usually more averting disasters than redirecting the entire path of the colony, getting to know different characters and learn different knowledge and skills about the world is engrossing thanks to the solid worldbuilding and strong character writing.All-in-all strongly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I was a QA tester on this game and have put hundreds of hours into it across multiple platforms. I was not asked to write this review and there was no expectation I would. I just genuinely adore this game.I Was a Teenage Exocolonist is a rare type of game that presents a narrative of both breadth and depth  and then allows players to explore that narrative through repeated groundhog's day scenario replays. There are over 600,000 words in the Exocolonist script, but you will only encounter maybe 1/8th of that script or so in any one playthrough. You control Sol (who you can name whatever you'd like), a man, woman, or non-binary character who grows from age 10 to age 20 over the course of the 10 years that a single playthrough of Exocolonist entails.You will decide what Sol does every single month during this 10 year period, including where they work, who they hang out with, and defining your version of Sol's opinions and beliefs through hundreds upon hundreds of dialogue choices. The game combines a Princess Maker style character progression system with a very compelling and emotional choice-rich narrative and card battles using cards which represent the many memories and choices your Sol has made. All of this together creates a surprisingly reactive system that encourages you to roleplay as a different Sol each time you replay. Through narrative choice you will be able to define everything from who Sol is attracted to and where they work down to the very granular level, such as whether or not Sol eats meat, what they think about the way the colony is run and which factions within the colony's web of characters Sol supports.And that's only the start! There are 10 dateable characters, each with their own story arcs that can end in any number of ways, and a vast array of secondary characters with their own arcs and often surprising backstories, many of which hold a further level of depth to them if you really go digging into everything this game has to offer. I could go on and on about the incredible aesthetic of the art in this game (I love Exo's future clothes!) and how fun it is to watch these characters grow physically alongside their narrative arcs, or gush about the emotional and stylish synth soundtrack, or Vertumna's incredibly vibrant ecosystem, but instead I want to talk about another reason why Exocolonist is always going to have a special place in my heart:Most sci fi depictions nowadays are bleak. Dystopias have become the norm in our cultural representations of the future, and for good reason, as our present day reality is itself quite the dystopia. I Was a Teenage Exocolonist does not follow this recent tradition. And that's not to say Exo's vision of the future is at all naive or happy go lucky, either. Instead it does something far greater and gives you a rich and conflicted future in which characters are free to express themselves and to live comfortably in that expression, but there are still those who would like to take away that freedom out of fear, malice, or misguided attempts to help others. Exocolonist's future is beautiful and scary and awe-inspiring and most important to me, it gives me hope. It thoughtfully presents a future different from those I've encountered before and then fills in that world with an incredible level of care and detail so that you can live in this world for as many groundhogs as you'd like.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR - Yes.  Absolutely Yes.  If you enjoy narrative-driven games and a replay cycle then you can and should enjoy this without issue.=====I did not know this game existed until I heard about it from a friend earlier this week.  They absolutely gushed about it and how amazing it was and all the cool things it did.  So on a whim I said "sure I'll give this a try."  That was two days ago and this has been the only thing I've been able to think about.I'll keep the synopsis brief because, as a narrative game, telling too much of the story is a spoiler: you're a kid born on a colony ship who crash-lands on your new homeworld and you have to survive, work hard, and grow up while going through the trials and tribulations that are common with striking into a new frontier.  You'll make memories, you'll suffer losses, but if you keep at it you'll make it to adulthood in one piece.  Hopefully.Speaking of memories, one of the core mechanics of this game is cards: this is as much a deckbuilding game as much as a visual novel and you get more cards by completing events that happen organically through the game: based on skill, relationships, jobs, and story events.  Some, like your youngest memories "giggling" and "crawling" can even be upgraded to be more powerful.  But the game doesn't punish you for not having a perfect deck: you can stress your way to victory or settle for a partial reward--not everything has to be completed perfectly.  If you LOVE card challenges you can add more difficulties, if you HATE card challenges you can even disable the whole system and leave it to some amount of chance.The other major mechanics are time and stress: the planet you live on has thirteen months per year and you spend 10 years living (ideally), doing one job per month to grow yourself as you see fit.  But you can't keep doing that job ad infinitum, you have to break and relax every once in a while to not burn out.  This puts time limits on certain events despite looking like you have all the time in the world, and when it comes due you better be ready to move on.Mechanics aside, the narrative is as much about your Friends' stories as much as your own and they are incredibly well-written.  Your peers grow up with you and you contribute to their lives as much as they contribute to yours.  You can even end up dating one or more of them, as per visual novel fare, though there are consequences for the story depending on how you progress.The game does have some uncomfortable subjects, some more intense than others, but the devs put a great deal of forethought into warning players and provided a list of everything that comes up that could be troubling, to the point that they also include specific spoilers.  It might be a bit much, but it's a good consideration on the part of the devs.The only real problem I have with the game is how it isn't quite clear how to complete certain events in the game and how opaque some of the things are.  The silver lining is that the devs intentionally built this game around a replay mechanic that flags things you've seen and done in prior playthroughs so you can make new outcomes that weren't originally available.There's plenty more to unpack, but I leave that for you to discover.  The bottom line is that I haven't seen a game this well-made in a long time, and I will now be following the devs to see what else they do.  I wholeheartedly recommend this to everyone, especially when it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Turns out this game was 22% of my total steam game-play for the year of 2023. I binged this game to the fullest, and even ended up writing an essay about it for my college English class. I ended up getting a 96 on the essay as well! The first most obvious charm of IWTE is the art and music. I loved the music on the soundtrack; it intertwines with the gorgeous and colorful art throughout every scene. It's very unique.Secondly, the game-play is quite smooth and easy access for all types of players. There's options to view possible triggers, as well as changing how your game actually works. You can turn off the card game and focus on the story, and you're able to skip through dialogue you've already seen. These features make it more re-playable than it already is, especially for people who might be achievement mining. People have different playing styles and levels, and this was definitely taken into mind.Thirdly, the characters and relationships! IWTE truly dives into the nuances of relationships, particularly the emotional and peculiar ones of teenagers. I love the fact that you can see other characters interact and see the depth to each personality. My only real qualms with the game have to do with some of the endings and the way they interact. I won't dive into the depths of it, but sometimes the endings feel unfinished when you understand the connections in the game. One catastrophic thing happens in one ending that can be ignored completely in another if you meet certain requirements. TLDR; Love this game after buying it out of pure curiosity. Very unique gameplay that make it replayable. Lovely to listen to and look at. Considering the team was not big at all, it's a seriously impressive game. Thank you for making this game. And if you're reading this review to see if you should get it: I think you should.

_childDocuments_.review: When it comes to the type of games designed for multiple playthroughs, especially narrative-heavy ones like this, I usually find myself so worn out by the end of my first playthrough, emotionally or physically or both, that I don't ever end up replaying it, or at least not for years. This is not the case with "Teenage Exocolonist". Instead, I find myself raring to give it another playthrough as soon as this week. Thanks to tons of diverging paths and a system that doesn't necessarily punish you for failing challenges, my curiosity and desire to dive deeper remains piqued.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a Teenage Exocolonist is a pretty decent narrative RPG with card-based battles. The game starts you out as a little kid born on a colony ship that has you eventually end up in a wormhole and crash on a nearby planet. It is then up to you to determine the choices that this planet & colony will navigate over the next 10 years of your life, ultimately ending at your 20th birthday. This game has 29 endings based on who you interact with over the course of the game such as who you level up with to become best friends or who you fall in love with. It also has choices that determine the end of the game based on what skills you specialize in whether it's medical, combat, engineering or others.My first play through of this game I ended up making a guy character and I heavily invested into the engineering skill eventually becoming a master in robotics & created a robot companion that follows me around. I then eventually got into a solid friendship with the loner Dys and eventually started dating his Sister Tanget. Which had me working together with her in later years. She eventually got so skilled in engineering that she developed a chemical bomb and one of the leaders of the colony convinced her to use it outside, which started a long term plague and killed all wildlife resetting the planet's ecosystem. However on my second playthrough, I made a female character & I ended up focusing entirely on combat & didn't focus on education at all. I even chose every rebellious option and when it came to the card battling system, I preferred to battle every monster that would attack the colony. In which I was able to prevent a bunch of characters deaths by being strong enough to defend against the monster attacks. I eventually befriended another athlete called Nem and we heavily played sportsball together in the colony when we were not fighting monsters. In which when I got to my 20th birthday, I ended up ending the game as a professional sportsball player and later a super supportive friend for Nem, who was going through domestic abuse. In which I become her guardian.With that being said, If your looking for a narrative heavy RPG about growing up as a kid or teenager while navigating relationships within a colony on a new planet, then this is your game. There's a lot replayability here within the game for multiple playthroughs. The game also allows you to be able to romance anyone and allows you to represent your sexuality in anyway you desire, which is great because it really allows you to have a more personable experience.In terms of the card battling system, the way that it's presented it's simple to understand and also simple to learn and even twink if you want it to be a harder difficulty. The way it works in terms of moving the story forward or simply introducing a new event or a choice makes sense when it comes to the battle system. The music for the game is also top notch and very enjoyable. Overall, I give the game a solid 7.5/10. I appreciate the narrative the developer is trying to tell within this game and I enjoy the relationship building and choices that are presented here.My only con with this game is I don't think this game is worth the full price of $25 unless your extremely into narrative RPG life sims. While I did have fun with this game, I only did two playthroughs in roughly 6 hours and that was enough of the game for me. Therefore if your like me and not really a huge fan of these games, I would only buy this on a major sale or wait for it to be heavily discounted. Once again I like the game, It's just the fact that playthroughs can go so fast in a short amount of hours. That you really have to be the kind of player who wants to explore every relationship dynamic to really feel like you got your money's worth. I think if your able to get this game at $10-$15, it's more justifiable,  Regardless, I recommend this game. Tons of people to friend or date. If I do another playthrough, I will probably try to romance the dog boy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was entertaining and alienating at the same time/space. You start playing as a 10-year old survivor of a colonial space-ship crash.  You get knocked out before the ship crashes, so while you're knocked out for several days, the adult castaways set up the essentials of your "exocolony" community. You play in cycles of months within seasons within 13-month years and success/fail progress is determined by a random card game, though you can disable that and opt out of a hard mode. Part of the gameplay premise is to reincarnate at the beginning of the game after a playthrough, perhaps changing strategy with the benefit of dream-like memory scraps from previous lives. This  part of the game's design plus the beautiful graphics is what intrigued me at first, but after my first play-through I don't feel like playing it again. I thought it would be science fiction but it's more of a fantasy game set it outer space. The colony is run by technocrats and there isn't any voting age achievement because there's no voting, your politics are limited to trying to influence the technocrats by one conversation each. You have 2 biological parents which seem not to be necessarily the norm, and they tell you at age 10 you should go figure things out by yourself so if you want, school's out FOREVER. There are visual-novel type conversations possible but sometimes your friends just keep saying the same thing over and over again so I started skipping them, likewise doing harvest-moon type gifts seemed to make no difference. There are some monsters and like a fantasy game they live outside the walls and invade once a year except your card game might beat them. The colonists deal with food shortages but everything else seems to be provided by uber-nanoprinting.  Children have the futuristic equivalent of a cell phone grafted into their palm at age 3 (they don't glow red at age 30 though) and that's the closest the game comes to having any religion. There is vague history about an ecological catastrophe on their motherplanet but other than one Star Trek pun about doctors there is no sense of history, or how the space ship was provided. Perhaps some guy built it in his barn on Krypton. During my first play-through, I managed to install the woman that does my nails as a new government, it was like having Gilligan's Island run by Ginger instead of the Professor. Everybody looked marvelous.

_childDocuments_.review: Although the storytelling behind Exo is competent and the gameplay enjoyable, the metagame is not for me. I enjoy playing games because I can win/get a good score with an understanding of the game and how it plays. Having to undergo multiple failures in order to get optimum outcomes is not what I come to games for. This game, for all that it clearly positions itself as accessible and progressive, demands to be played in a certain way for its artistic vision. Well, if I wanted to endure bleak outcomes in the hope of getting it right next time I'd just pay attention to my real life. Having to battle an inscrutably literal zero-sum game meta-system was only possible with guides diluted whatever joy the game brought and I still flubbed it. Had I known what this game required of me, I would not have purchased it. It's right for some, but not for meEdit: upon further playing to try and get some better outcomes for my peace of mind, I have discovered that no matter what you do Dys will commit suicide in ending cards and the narrative clearly approves of his decision. Had I known that,  as a person who has lost many people to suicide and is still struggling with active suicidality, I find this abhorrent. I know that the creators may not have thought about Dys's narrative arc in this fashion, but the way the ending cards are set up now it's pretty clear cut. From his name, to his backstory, to his obsession with death, culminating in rejecting his human life including a romanced Sol and reconciled Tangent right down to the injection of ambiguity with an animal observing the colony, everything about Dys's arc that remains constant throughout the meta-game indicates narrative approval of this fate. I sincerely hope the creators change this because it punched me in the gut when I realized I couldn't save Dys, obviously because I was projecting about myself. That really sucked.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a frustrating game that actively undermines the potential of the concept it is based on. The different lives you experience over and over again are supposed to play out differently as the player, and the main character, retain memories of past lives. The groundhog-day concept is difficult to pull off in visual novels, but Teenage Exocolonist fails to deliver on that front, as an observant reader will understand all hidden mechanics during the second playthrough - and as the illusion falls apart, all that's left is a major grind to unlock various combos of endings. Of which most are completely dull and merely reflect "who you spend most time with" and "what was your most frequent profession". And it's only the late endgame when the results of your choices make any meaningful difference on the story, as it's very much on rails for the overall 90% of time. Beyond the identical story across most of the in-game events, all that's left is a numbers game on where you put most of your points towards. The card game mechanic (which is more of a dynamic puzzle than a deckbuilder), although relatively unique and fairly complex despite such simple rules, failed to amuse me enough to get through all the rehashed content more than twice - and yes, I did get to some of the "best" endings in that time.Peculiarly, the game boasts LGBT-friendly features, and is widely acclaimed for featuring custom pronouns and independent gender and appearance sliders for your character - not toggles, each is a continuous spectrum that allows you to make the main character e.g. exactly 35% male, if you want; changeable at literally any time during the game. Very inclusive and welcoming! But it's just a farce, both sliders secretly snap to just three values, and their position literally never affects anything story-wise; to the ridiculous point where other character's sexual preferences follow whatever the player character looks like and considers themselves at the moment. I can't decide if that's an amusing reflection of a gender-inclusive utopia, or an insulting afterthought on the studio's part merely to appeal to queer audiences and capitalize on their enthusiasm.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, will ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ *destroy* you.Words cannot even begin to describe the pure emotional rollercoaster that is this game. I honestly cannot even stress that you *need* to buy this game. I haven't even beaten my *first* playthrough yet because this game ♥♥♥♥♥♥ me up so bad.This game is about growing up. Outside of your first class that you have to take, your parents tell you that at 10 years old, your life is in your hands. School is technically optional, but as long as you _contribute_ to the colony in some capacity, they will support you. This game takes place over 10 years, which is then broken into 13 months. Each time you do an "Activity" you effectively spend the month doing that and hanging with friends.And Time is both your greatest asset and weakness. As a year can disappear in the literal blink of eye, and the world will move on without you.This game is a CRPG, but its also a "dating" sim, and your choices matter. Who you end up spending time with will determine how your character develops in the game. I decided I wanted to play as a shy kid/teen, and largely neglected the needs of the colony. In doing so, I ended up getting certain character's killed because I didn't care or pay attention to what my people needed.And when you find out that your actions got someone killed...This game doesn't gut punch you. It _uppercuts you_ into the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ *Stratsophere* and rips your heart out. And because of this, I ended up being truly alone by my 17th birthday, and was legitimately feeling sick to my stomach over the choices I made to the point where I said to myself "I *need* to fix this." And this game makes you *care* about each and every one of the characters either consciously, or subconsciously.This brings me to the next part of this "Game" where your character has Object Permanence. Basically, your character retains knowledge of previous saved game states. These come in the forms of "Dreams" or "Nightmares." Which acts as a "reset" button functionally. This means that *some* of the deaths in this game *Could* be avoided. Or prevented entirely. And lemme tell you when you *Save* someone that you previously got killed, you will be sobbing tears of joy. Literally. When I saved certain characters I balled just as hard as I did when I saw them expire.And that brings us to, well *You.* It's *Your* life after all. For starters, this game offers you the choice of being whoever you want to be. You can pick which gender you want your character to be, or rather their appearance, between Male, Female, or Non-binary. You can also customize your character's pronouns. Whether you want He/Him, She/Her, or They/Them. And there is a *lot* of variety available. Basically for custom pronouns the game gives you every instance in which your pronouns will/could become relevant, and you may type in what you want the respective reply to be. I personally chose She/They as my character's pronouns just to see, and while *subsequent* playthroughs can make this a bit tedious, considering your choosing every instance in which you can be referred to, its not really *that* big of an issue.On top of that, the game has fairly good reprisentation all across the board. You have men, women, Non-binary, and trans characters that exist in the game, and every single character has their own pronouns that they are referrerd to as. This makes it easier because most of these characters *do* look rather androgynous, but in an attractive, and good way. Which, frankly speaking, had my bisexual panic going off all the time. Speaking of which, you can also engage in any relationship (once your 16/17), of any kind. You can be polyamorous, monogamous, or have open relationships with certain characters.All this to say, this game *will* make you cry. It can get...very dark at times, and though it might be a "T" rated game, it is one of the few that really pushes the envelope to a borderline M from such a cute, charming, innocent looking title. So, while it might be tempting to name your character "Trickydick69" with "Zoogle/Zayhos" pronouns, it does require a certain degree of seriousness. But you do you.If your a dollar/hr kind of gamer, then buy this game. Your average playthrough will be close to 20 hours by the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Deep story, world, science and characters that keep me coming back for more, with gameplay that ties very nicely in with the story. Or, as in my first playthrough, do a complete and uncharacteristic flip midthrough when a new character arrives that you desperately want to impress. I also like how the time twist ties into the overarching mystery and that I can bring some previous choices with me into the next playthroughs, makes every time I start a new game feel a little more interesting because I know certain things might happen differently this time around due to my and the character's knowledge from past playthroughs. It helps that I can skip the deck gameplay part entirely if I want to, but I don't really want to either since it means I get less rewards. But alas, this is a very minor complaint in the grand scheme of things!HIGHLY recommend this game, it will stay with me for a long time.

It's beautiful and exciting and scary and that's what exploring and discovery is all about.The characters are well written, acting their age and feeling shaped by their environment and growing in ways that are understandable but not stale. Their arcs as well are interesting to watch take shape, especially as you find ways to influence them. I genuinely felt attached, which is a rare for me.The story unfolds in interesting ways and I find I learn more the more I play which shapes my perspective of the characters and events, though I have a preferred outcome every time I play. It's compelling and, while it can be harsh, it never feels cruel. I always feel as if the events unfolding make sense rather than a direct punishment of my actions or inaction.The art and music is really enjoyable and, though I prefer a unified and consistent art style, it never bothered me when there were inconsistencies.The game play is fun and challenging at times, I like the card game mechanic, though sometimes I found it repetitive and tedious once I'd leveled up past a certain point or replayed the game. I thought choosing to skip the card challenges would mean I just automatically "won" them so I could focus on completing the story, but that is not in fact what happens. I found not actively playing the card game challenges left me very under leveled which made the game even harder rather than easier.Overall, well worth the time and money I've sunk into it.

_childDocuments_.review: A fabulous game, in every sense of the word.At its core, I Was a Teenage Exocolonist is a very solid life sim/visual novel with an (entirely optional) deckbuilding mechanic used to resolve challenges. Combined with the excellent writing, it's already an exemplary addition to the genre. Where the game pushes the boundaries of its genre into the sublime is through its "Groundhog Day" (or more accurately Groundhog Decade) central conceit. This takes the way most players play this sort of game - consulting walkthroughs or wikis on your second (or greater) playthrough to get the events/endings you want and avoid the ones you don't - and turns it into a game mechanic. The game remembers previous playthroughs and lets you use knowledge from those past lives to steer the fiction. Frankly, it's genius.The game isn't perfect. If anything, I wish the devs had leaned even harder into the Groundhog Day mechanic, since there are some situations your character will face that feel like they should be influenced by past lives, and I would have been happier if past lives also affected a character's starting stats and/or deck. Many mechanical rewards arrive so late in the game that they feel pointless. Very rarely, events will happen that don't make a ton of sense due to when they can happen in a character arc or the overall story. But these are minor things compared to the triumph this game turned out to be, and given the sheer depth and scope of content written into the game it's inevitable a few mix-ups would slip through the cracks.It's a real gem in the genre, and I look forward to seeing what the studio comes up with next.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, without a doubt, one of the best written story-forward games I've ever played. Each character is charming, each interaction is immensely entertaining. It's so easy to fall in love with. So easy to let it break your heart. Rigorous deckbuilder it is not, however, so don't expect the gameplay to be especially challenging. The real meat of the game came from long conversations with my friend over the motivations of our character under the weight of the many plot threads they found themself wound up in. Moments as simple as a character offering us a kiss became 40 minute long debates about our character's sense of self worth once placed into the context of the rest of their circumstances. There's a fantastic beating heart to this game; a loving philosophy. I never quite understood the hype around games like Undertale and people's feelings for it. I think this game brought me a little closer to that. I Was a Teenage Exocolonist is tragically obscure. We've been proselytising the game to anyone who will listen. Hopefully, if you play it, you will, too. There's a real magic here.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting visual novel with a unique take on the raising sim genre. You play as Solanaceae, Solana, Solane, or whatever you choose to call the player character. You can also choose to be male, female, or nonbinary. The game centers around a card game that can determine whether you pass certain skill checks, but I just skip it. Thanks for making that a choice, I find the card game boring. You, your family, and your childhood friends, among many others, are colonizing a foreign planet, which as it turns out, is pretty complicated! You can use the colony's resources to increase your stats, or go exploring the planet which also grants stat increases (you can explore outside the colony once you're old enough - unless of course you sneak out). That's all I'll tell you without spoiling anything. This game has a lot of ups and downs, but overall I felt that a lot of love was put into it. I enjoyed it!The good: The story and character designs are very interesting, it doesn't gloss past the dangers of space and colonizing foreign planets, polyamorous romance options, branching story paths, many different endings you can get, plenty of characters to make friends with/romance (don't always expect a happily ever after though), I'm glad for the content warnings since this game's story can get brutal at points, the game encourages multiple playthroughs through its storyline which makes it very replayableThe bad: I felt like the futuristic aspect kind of got hammered into your face at some points, the card game isn't very fun or interesting (though it can be skipped completely), why does everyone have ridiculous names like 'halitosis'? sorry but that was funny lol the teacher's name literally means bad breath

_childDocuments_.review: I may not be a 'teenage' player anymore, but god do I love this game!First Off, the graphics are phenomenal. All of the character and environment art are gorgeous, and the world building is just so well put together and thought out. Not to mention, the characters are 3 dimensional! Although they all have different augments, that is not their whole personality. A lot of media where characters have 'quirks' or 'powers', it gets very cliche and stereotypical. In this game all of the characters are very fleshed out!A feature that I really love is that there is save/load options. This game is incredibly based on the choices you make and you get the "best ending" there are a lot of requirements you have to reach. Being able to go back and change things or start from a certain point in so useful if you're trying to get a lot of different endings.The only feature that may sway people away is the card game mechanic. But, as someone who was wary of that at first, it is actually one of my favorite parts of the game! You gain cards based on memories and decisions that you make that effect your character. The card mechanic is fairly easy to figure out and understand, and there's also an option to turn it off if that's not for you! Overall, I think this game is gorgeous and underrated. It has definitely become one of my most cherished games I've ever played.Tang my beloved <3

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely mature in both subject matter and presentation, neat mechanics, and very interesting characters. I've made it two and a half years so far and I'm eager to see where this goes!EDIT: I have completed 1.5 playthroughs of this game and it keeps the quality up throughout. The story has a lot of interesting directions it can go, and I'm curious to see what I can accomplish on future playthroughs!I would say that my only criticism is that there's likely to be a lot of repetition on future playthroughs to get different endings and story scenarios. For example there is a specific scenario that I encountered in my first playthrough that was apparently very difficult and rare to stumble into naturally. I didn't know that, and simply backed out of it at the last second as it would give me an ending early, and I wanted to see where things went. The ending I got at the end of my first playthrough is probably the simplest "you did okay" ending, and apparently getting that initial early ending would set me up to make future playthroughs easier/ faster, whereas I just avoided it assuming it was a Yoko Taro "why would you do that" ending. Recreating that will take its own playthrough, and I really don't want to have to save scum to avoid falling into these pitfalls. Exploring the narrative is the point of the game, but that specific situation frustrated me, as now I'll have to recreate a very specific set of steps.

_childDocuments_.review: So a friend mentioned in passing about this game, they didn't own it nor did they know much about it but I looked into it and watched some of the gameplay videos on the store page and was interested. Though, I was struggling with the 20+ gbp price tag. Roll around September First 2022. Said friend gifts me the game, I knew I had to play it and play it I did. 6 hours of gameplay. 6 hours of one playthrough of a fantastic, changing story that gave me laughs, smiles, joy swiftly followed by gutpunches, heartbreak and genuinely pain. I'm an emotional person and I feel this may be best experienced if you are one too. It's worth the asking price. It's effectively a story book in which you make choices with an optional card game, which I personally played. I romanced Anemone, I became Military Hero, I made friends, lost one early and so young. (Triggering themes will be present, as someone with depression, it didn't trigger me but if you're more sensitive or are currently struggling, maybe skip for now.) I died in my early thirties, after my partner, with two children. I sobbed through the ending cutscene, it wasn't quite the Cyberpunk ending cutscenes but it was ♥♥♥♥♥♥ close. I highly recommend I Was a Teenage Exocolonist and I look forward to my next playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Your relationships with the characters are very controversial and there is nothing you can do about. Even with all the synchronicities, no matter how many reincarnations you take, you will always be alone in the end. I already got the "best ending", but I don't think I feel satisfied with how the story went with the characters alone. The catastrophes and corruption, I get all that. The devs are trying to make it somewhat "relatable" to real life which I don't hate but there are just some situations that does not happen to everyone and it's just hyperbolic. Pretty one everyone in this game will leave or even cheat on you in the end, which will a sour taste in your mouth. It's just not worth it.If you like childhood memories and wholesome moments, then try it. Though prepare to get bombarded with controversial relationships when you decide to form your social life for the main character. _childDocuments_.review: ✔️ Very nice story with colorful and interesting characters.✔️ Pretty artwork and music.✔️ Original and fun simple but efficient card-based gameplay.✔️ Quite a few possible choices with various outcomes.💭 The fact the game has been designed with multiple playthroughs in mind makes the first one a bit... weird? _childDocuments_.review: I've only played my first round of this game. A really important thing to remember about IWATE is its replayability, and though the main game only takes about 15-20 hours, you'll be playing it for far longer as you find different routes and invest in different skills each time. When games say choices matter, IWATE makes you feel like they truly do - regardless of how much impact they'll really have in the end. But, as always... you can try again in your next life.Each of these characters is so lovingly crafted. Even those who I didn't end up befriending were so full of life and personality, and I kept playing thinking "I know what I'm going to do next time". The way the game mechanics of making a new save and playing with the knowledge you have after a first experience is woven into the story is wonderful, even though I don't have the whole picture yet. Because you can only focus on so much at a time, IWATE forces you to replay from different angles and viewpoints you might never have considered.Nothing will beat the heartbreak of realising that I can't complete a challenge, and that it will probably result in someone's death.This world is vibrant and cruel, beautiful and unforgiving. IWATE may appear colourful and soft, but it deals with the effects of teenage trauma, how it feels to grow up, and bigger-picture threats; politics and ethics take a central stage in the latter half of the game, and it feels wonderfully grounded yet philosophical. It is not a graphic game, nor is it a lighthearted one. Do not go into this expecting an extreme on either end! There's a lot of sadness in its narrative, but a lot of happiness, too. _childDocuments_.review: "I Was a Teenage Exocolonist" is an entry in the somewhat niche genre of LifeSim games set on a distant alien world.For those unfamiliar, a LifeSim game is one in which you control a character over a period of their life (often during adolescence to young adulthood). Time passes in chunks (sometimes fixed, sometimes variable) during which you choose how the character spends their time or reacts to certain events. These choices feed back into your character in the form of stats and branching narratives that enable or disable future choices. At the end, the culmination of choices usually results in an epilogue that reflects what kind of choices you made during the time you controlled the character and how they play out years or even decades into the future. The genre encourages replayability because you can't take every choice at every branch and some choices ripple through years of a character's life, so trivial attempts to save/reload doesn't let you see everything.LifeSims are somewhat of a novelty as games because they struggle to find legs on their own. You might see them as a secondary mechanic in another game (like in the Persona series), but there are some entries that stand just on the appeal of the branching paths (Long Live the Queen). Usually a "pure" LifeSim game has simple pass/fail checks on narrative branches to lock out choices you don't have the skills for."I Was a Teenage Exocolonist" daringly attempts to lead with the LifeSim mechanic as the main hook, supplementing it a deckbuilding mechanic where most challenges see you drawing a hand of cards and attempting to assemble the highest scoring combination of 5 cards from the ones drawn. From an initial deck of cards, new memories are added when you build relationships with characters, overcome obstacles, or face adversity, tying your success in the challenges back to what you have done throughout the story. Score is calculated based on the face value of the card (usually 1-8 but some even higher), plus combo points for sets of matching colors, numbers, or sequences. Many cards also have additional effects that modify either themself or other cards. Didn't get quite the hand you needed? Collectibles can be spent to change the cards or just draw more in hopes of a better outcome. Taken in a whole, the challenge resolution mechanic is a surprisingly robust and engaging system and tying it to the narrative element helps the two create a feedback loop.Once you complete your play through of the game (probably 15 hours for your first one), you have a chance to start over, knowing more about how the game works and ready to try something different. But not only do you know more, your character also remembers some things from the other life. They are haunted by memories of alternate futures, and having been there you now open up chances to alter the story further by acting on information that wasn't available the first time you encountered a situation. Can you find a path through the keeps everyone alive and happy? Is that even the best outcome? Join us on Vertumna and find out.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is truly fantastic. I'm not sure how I came across it, but the reviews and description were good enough to sell me on it. After playing two complete playthroughs, I wanted to come back and share my thoughts:The narrative and writing are as good as any AAA game out there, IMO. Your interactions and relationships develop naturally and feel authentic, and your choices have real and meaningful impact in your character's world. On top of this, the game does an excellent job of realistically covering the changes and challenges one faces as they grow up in their teens. The is coupled with deck-building and rpg gameplay elements that are both fun and help to shape the experience of your character as they age. The game's art reminds me of Wyldermyth's: A colorful, well-executed, charming, and cheerful pseudo-3D style that fits the theme, even during some of the darker moments of the story. Clearly a lot of thought and love was put into the designs of each of the characters as they age, as well as the flora and fauna you encounter throughout your adventures. The music is also similarly fitting and well composed, and is good enough to make me consider getting the soundtrack, something that only a few games (e.g. Transistor, Bastion) have succeeded in getting me to do before.If you've played Sleeper Citizen or Wyldermyth and enjoyed them, or if any of the above sounds awesome to you, I'd highly recommend giving this game a try.

_childDocuments_.review: The cheerful aesthetic of the GUI, art style and character designs had me thinking this game would be a full meal of wholesome with a side of romance and a sprinkle of action. I was blown away by what I actually got. Don't get me wrong - it does check all of those boxes. There's a lot of sweetness and optimism in here without it becoming saccharine. But you can FAIL in this game, and fail HARD. There are severe and irreversible consequences for playing poorly (if you're worried about that, I believe some aspects of gameplay can be turned off or at least made incredibly easy) and for ignoring deadlines. Your fave character liking you a little less is the least of your worries - you should be more concerned about getting them killed. Or getting YOU killed.As a VN/RPG, it is, of course, highly replayable. But a lot of VN's I've played do this thing where a new route is just the same sequence of events from a slightly different perspective, depending on which characters you're interested in hanging out with, and maybe you get a 'true' or 'secret' route at the end where you get to fix everything at once. In Exocolonist, using the information you've carried over from every run after the first can be used to deliberately shape the story. Characters can be saved that otherwise would have died. Relationships can be mended instead of broken. The story itself evolves as you repeat it, over and over. And there is no 'true' ending here, only the endings that you prefer.It's also a solid work of original sci-fi. By which I mean, it explores the tropes of the genre and the implications of advanced technologies, future cultures, evolving ways of living, what have you. Science-fiction, not just science-flavoured.10/10, greatly enjoyed having my expectations subverted. WIsh I could forget the plot faster so I can play it again.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you enjoyed stories about  a crew of abuse survivors at the bottom of the ocean trying to work at an energy plant or a group of genetically modified astronauts drifting towards some highly intelligent and conscious-less danger which will leave no one intact? Well then, how about growing up  stranded in a small colony on an unfamiliar and unfriendly planet with nowhere to go? Knowing you've been failed in many ways by those, who brought you there, yet trying to squeeze any opportunity to make things  for you and those who've been there together with you. This is a dark, claustrophobic and terrifying story carefully wrapped into a teenage visual novel drama with all the love, fondness and attention to littlest details. And speaking of teenage drama, this game also gets it surprisingly brilliant, making one feel an entire spectrum of human emotion and crying the eyes out of compassion. Whatever you're looking for: either a (somewhat) heartwarming story of growing up on another planet with romance, taming unicorns and stuff, or a grim dystopia that will break your heart, you'll find every aspect executed masterfully and with great care.Another little soothing thing for this old lady's heart is accurate and down to earth autistic representation, that feels real compared to a bioengineered superhero like Siri.Cannot recommend this game enough.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. The setting and cast of characters are refreshingly spun vibrant takes on classic tropes. Well-written dialogue, plenty of different paths and hidden twists to experience. Good for replay for a story-focused game. The amount of choices has been really engaging and immersive, and Your choices help shape everything from who your character is to your friend's lives and the fate of your colony.My only criticism is that there is a lot of allure to try so many new activities, but spreading out your progress between your skills too terribly much is discouraged as it might limit you later. There are 12 skills (4, physical, 4 mental, 4 social), which is otherwise really cool, but often you will encounter an event/dialogue option with a skill score requirement. I suggest saving your game often, as your decisions, big and small, will sometimes matter a lot, and there are bonuses to be earned for making the right calls in events and in challenges. Challenges take the form of a fun card game in which you use your characters memories as cards, with opportunities to collect different memory cards throughout your story based on your decisions. Memory cards can be cut from your memory deck through forgetting them during certain activities, so your character ends up forgetting a lot of their earlier memories  as most of us do.

_childDocuments_.review: This has been one of the more engaging stories I've played. The plot strings are intriguing and interesting and placed to tug my curiosity along to the point that I KNOW I'm going to play through again, and the mechanic that encourages additional playthrough has already gotten me thinking about what I would do differently on the next game but not regretting what I chose now in any fashion. The choices feel realistic for what my character can do, and anything I can't is filed away in my thoughts for the next time around.Edited to add that, they are very straightforward and open about the content warnings. The emotional impact of this game can be pretty intense, especially if you had a rougher childhood. There's a big button in the menu, and when you start it even emphasizes that they have it. If you have trouble with unhappy situations or endings (and it doesn't encourage you to go back and start a new game to try to fix it, which is one of the big themes of the entire storyline) then this may not be a game for you. New playthroughs have new options, which is one of the things that's drawing ME back to play again once I finish my current play.As for the technicals, I've not had any bugs of any sort to cause crashes. The game runs beautifully, and is beautiful on it's own. The artwork is wonderful and sets the tone, the character designs are impressive in the depth of representation and presentation. I was pleasantly surprised at the constant use of 'they', and everything is just so equal in terms of representation! And it's presented as if it's a normal thing, which it is, but still noteworthy in this particular day and age. I really appreciate the fact that I get the name of the song thats playing and who wrote it when I bring up the main menu, and that the artist names are presented in a way that I can actually see them! Its just...overall such a good setup, I'm hard pressed to think of anything really negative to say! If you're not a fan of card style puzzles, they have a way to not worry about it. If you are, they have a way to make it really challenging!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautiful and refreshingly nuanced portrait of a the teenage experience. The story is exceptionally well written, and the characters are distinct, diverse, and charming. There are so many ways the story can unfold, and the designers took a lot of care to make them all feel worthwhile. Even negative outcomes feel supported, which always made me feel like I was in good hands.To get the most out of this game, you must be comfortable playing through the same story multiple times (sort of like Nier: Automata). This can feel like a tall order, since each playthrough can take upwards of ten hours, and the cardplay feels a bit like a chore after you've seen it many times over. I recommend creating regular save points so you can choose to replay particular segments rather than starting from the beginning each time—but there are many things the game has to offer that require starting fresh.I was able to experience a lot in three playthroughs (with the help of a guide on the last). There's definitely more to see, but I consider my time complete. I think that's the real trick; set your own goals and play at your own pace. There's a lot of really beautiful stuff in here.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy the writing in the game, and my first playthrough felt really good. The overall plot is interesting and you get drawn into the world pretty easily.the problems start coming with subsequent playthroughs. This might just be that my first playthrough was actually quite successful, in terms of the worst possible outcomes to the best. Spoilers aheadThe core gimmick here is that you're stuck in a sort of time loop, and memories from your previous playthroughs give you new options and make it easier to get a good outcome in the game. Ultimately these changes are actually fairly minor in terms of the main plot, mostly serving to make things you could have achieved in your first run through other means easier.Pretty quickly, especially if you made an effort to befriend everyone in the colony, you'll reach a point where there's not much else to see in the game, and you'll reach that point long before you unlock the different endings. Some of the 'hidden' parts of the game aren't nearly as well hidden as they seem to think they are. Combined with the gameplay consisting of a card minigame and clicking through menus to train your stats, new playthroughs take a long time for very little new content.This kills a lot of the replay value, which is ironic for a game with a core premise involving a time loop. It's still worth playing, I got around 20 hours from two playthroughs (steam playtime is including leaving the game open for a few hours) but I'm already feeling like I've scooped out most of the content the game has to offer having only achieved three endings (I reloaded after the 'hidden' one to get an actual ending on my first playthrough).

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely love this game. The art work is breathtaking, the characters are realistic, and so are the the choices you get to choose between. I have played this game over and over again, through different skill sets, jobs, and partner choices and I can say that the amount of detail put into the story is just so immense. Some people could call it tedious, but to me it felt real. I would redo lives only to find little details like who you talk to that month could completely change the whole story line, it's great. I also really enjoy the "mini" card game, which is actually optional for those who don't, even after playing the game for hours. Some people say it was repetitive, but I don't agree as different choices meant different cards that you are dealt in the mini game, which is also such a great representation of the character's life. The amount of romancable characters in this game is also very high compared to others, and even with so many all the characters are so beautifully thought out and portrayed. Even the less personable ones like Tangent and Vace have their own (very hidden and easily overlooked) lovable sides and your choices matter so heavily in their stories, that is if you ever even decide on taking their routes. I became so obsessed with this game that I set out to unlock all the achievements and actually got me into achievement hunting. It's all just so satisfying and I wouldn't hesitate to spend my money on this game just for the fact that I would be supporting the creators. I even purchased the soundtrack and art book when I never do for other games. I spent many days with this game in my wish list and I soooo regret it now. If you are trying to decide between this game and another game by scrolling through reviews, choose this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Alrighty, my first ever review for a game and this one absolutely deserves it. There's lovable characters, characters that are easy to hate, relatable characters, cool alien life that you can keep as pets, an amazing art style, a thrilling story, and the sci-fi exocolonist life you can dream of. Some aspects of this game are very full of care, and I heavily recommend reading the content warnings before playing. The story is crafted so beautifully to incorporate some harsher topics relevant to the story, and less-plot-relevant things can be missed if you feel a bit of ick reading about them. Each character is unique in their own ways, and each one will shape your views of the world you're playing in (and maybe the real world too!) _childDocuments_.review: it's a really beautiful game that i think does a really great job of tackling adolescence and how people become themselves and coming to grapple with the circumstances they were born into. i get shades of The Dispossessed when i'm playing it and i think the game does a good job of exploring a lot of the interesting ethical questions of colonization.one of the tempting conclusions in a lot of science fiction is to assume that colonizing planets without people is kind of a freebie and isn't worth further interrogation, even when the environment might threaten our survival, but Exocolonist neatly cuts that knot by representing several characters who don't place humans at the top of a natural hierarchy. it's even easier to do that when humans are the newcomers! the first generation of a colony, with their reasons for being there, have to determine what it means to live their principles and to what extent those principles should balance with survival or prosperity.the characters have real preferences and the game is largely respective of their agency, the lengths you have to go to change what other people want can make you feel downright sociopathic but it's refreshing to feel like other characters want a relationship to be on their terms as well.i think the game does ask a lot of the player, the first playthrough strongly implies that you should probably do a few more and has more than a few punches to the gut, but once you know your way around you can start finding a lot of interesting corners in the story. after a couple of playthroughs, there's an option to skip text you've already seen, and i'd suggest enabling that.

_childDocuments_.review: Real talk, this game has a lot of great qualities but I believe there's one central element to it that might make-or-break the game for you. Exocolonist has a time limit and A LOT of invisible triggers. It's purposefully designed to be replayed a lot - maybe even dozens of times. You probably won't see or "achieve" much in a single playthrough, and while there's always something new to find on subsequent playthroughs, there's also a lot of repetition. To me that felt grindy and sometimes frustrating, especially since the triggers can be extremely hard to find. But if you like chill games and don't mind replaying a short game, then Exocolonist might be for you! It's a charming and thoughtful game about growing up, managing your time and bonding with people.

It's nothing too complicated but if this is unappealing you do have the option to turn this off.Go into the game as blind as you can and you'll have a much more pleasant experience on your initial playthrough.The game does have some potentially distressing content, however the main menu has a content warning button that spells out for you what to expect in this regard, which is a nice safety feature for those concerned.

"I can save you!" I declare, sobbing at the screen. "I can save everyone!" Well, everyone except maybe for Vace. I mean. No one really likes you, sugar. You're kind of a ♥♥♥♥♥. The very month the game got released? This game is FANTASTIC. Please do give it a go if you can. MAYHAPS
