_childDocuments_.review: I think this game rocks, because it fits my gaming style in many ways. It won't work for lots of other gamers and that's fair. This is quite a niche game, and hopefully people can read reviews like mine and move on if it's not a fit for them.I am a true lover of the sandbox survival base-building genre and I am happy to support any game that moves that genre forward, however imperfectly. I can chop trees and pick rocks for hours if it means I can build an awesome base and craft my way up to OPness, even if it would be way more practical to get by with less. I don't get bored easily and I mainly want a beautiful simulated world that's mine in which I can make my mark. I understand creating a massive open world in which the player has this much agency is a big challenge for game development and it's hard to have the funding to take the time necessary to not release it with growing pains. Yes, the full release is closer to an early access in its quality, but these guys did it differently. They gave us eight sessions of beta game play for preorders in which you could return the game at any time even if you had played hundreds of hours. I prefer this model to early access in which you only get two hours to refund and have to trust a promise. Those of us who did the beta know what we are getting into. While it's still a diamond in the rough, the dev team have been extremely responsive and done a ton of work along the way.My two favorite things about the approach this game is taking are the very reasons many players might hate it:First, it is effing hard. You have to shelter from violent storms, but the weather will tear your thatch or wood shack to pieces if you can't run around with your repair hammer fast enough as pieces are torn from your building parts. It has the most beautiful fire mechanic I've seen and lightning storms take every opportunity to burn down everything you've achieved. Early game, the predators will wreck you and the spawn mechanics don't play fair. When you die, and you will die, you face a massive xp debt and any diseases and wounds, of which there are many types, will persist after death. If you are the type to rage quit, don't play this. I  personally laugh at each disaster and love the challenge to overcome then. When I eventually prevail it gives it so much more meaning. So know who you are, be warned, and choose wisely.Second, in the main game, you don't get to keep anything. It is "session based", meaning each time you drop down to the world you may have days or a month, but your gear, your base, and everything you've gathered will be wiped. It's basically a survival rogue-lite. You keep your levels and the rewards can provide some small upgrades for next time. For a hardcore survival gamer like me, early game is the best part and I relish being forced to do it over and over again. You may say what's the point and that probably means this isn't for you. But I always found a server gets a bit stale once I've finished my awesome base, besides the fact that they always get laggy after that, so wipes are inevitable eventually. This tears that bandaid off, and I'm ok with that since it's really the act of building and crafting that I love the most. It reminds me of the Dada art movement in which the destruction of the art was as much a part of the art as the artwork itself. (Btw, there are some small maps in which you can keep your builds forever)I have a beast of a PC (3090, 5900x, 32GB). I can run this on epic with rtx global illumination at about 90fps and it looks gorgeous. Feedback from my friends who have played this makes it pretty clear that unless you have a 20 series card or above, performance won't be great. I think their recommended specs are pretty honest about this. That said there are some basic things people can do to help with their fps that the devs would do well to communicate better. For example turning your fov up to 100 from the default 80 can give you as much as 20fps more. Also there's a slider in the settings to turn up the vram usage to what your card can handle, which really helps with performance. I've heard people with 3080s complaining they couldn't get good performance, so better access to info like this could really help.I know this is long, but one last bit that this game struggles with is communication of the lore. It has a very involved backstory which explains why it makes perfect sense that you are running around in a space suit in a forest. They've done some really good live acted docudramas on their youtube channel that explain it. However most people aren't aware of it and just think it doesn't make sense. It would behoove RocketWerkz to convey this better. The other part of the lore and the future promise of this game is that the forest is just the beginning. It was part of a failed terraforming to make the planet earthlike, but not all of it is like that. Each season of this game promises to get more formidably alien, moving well beyond the initial stone tools in the forest into futuristic gear in hostile otherworldy environments. There are so many crazy places they can take it and I'm down for the ride.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated review 2.25.22! My original review was not to recommend this game based on numerous issues with both the functionality of the game and the QoL of the player, as well as what felt like missing content. There are also much needed changes to really make this game a more well-rounded, immersive experience, but that being said, here are my original recommendations and what has been changed so far, and why I changed my review to recommend this game!Original Recommended fixes and what's been done: 1) I don't think the farming/grinding needs to decrease, as that's part of the fun (if there's a reason for it). The time spent actually completing an objective once you're done with farming and grinding should increase to make all of it actually worth it. - This has been a constant review and update process for the developers, and so far it's been going in the right direction, although not resolved yet. With their commitment that they're still reviewing this aspect, paired with what they've updated so far, I'm comfortable waiting to see how this pans out!2)Work on bugs instead of releasing more repetitive prospects. - This started happening! So many bug fixes so far! Yes, there are still quite a few, but they don't feel so immersion-breaking or game crashing.3)Implement the quality of life changes that were recommended in the beta weekends that don't impact the gameplay or difficulty. - HUGE improvements in this area in the Week 11 and Week 12 content. This has really made the game all around MUCH more enjoyable, including some of the previous aspects that were considered to be very tedious.4) Make the tech tree items more relevant, and reduce the cost of higher tier items. - The developers have committed to improving this as well, so also looking forward to these updates! The minor changes to the cost of higher tier items helped, but they're still not viable or feasible for like 90%+ of the missions. 5) Add talent points to use in the solo branch, independent of the regular branch. - This was done in the week 12 update!6) Give the animals more AI. Add more flora and fauna diversity. - Still waiting on this as well. There were some minor improvements made here where animals will now react to sounds differently and don't get stuck on a rock or tree, and they no longer hear or see through stone walls of your shelter (unless they're right next to you outside), but I consider this as still in progress...7) Add more lore! - Still waiting patiently for this!

It essentially feels like a continuation of the beta weekends, but with some more plants, mobs, the whole map to visit, 4th tier unlocked, and the station features available. Apart from that, the basic feel and issues are pretty much the same.I think my primary pro's and cons can be summed up as follows:+ A fair bit of freedom in how you approach stuff, and how you build your hide-outs+ A rather varied skill tree, with options in how you play, though I main the resource gathering due to the 'restart restart restart'-nature of the game- The melee 'experience' is flat-out garbage. Flat ground dodging is a trick of the mind and you might as well just face-tank and hope you kill whatever it is before you get turned inside out... Or you simply exploit the terrain and hope the AI don't just run up anyway. If an enemy gets to start the attack animation and you're in range, you get hit.- I already grew slightly weary of the restart-nature during the beta weekends, and it hasn't improved for me. Whilst interesting in a way, I just don't really like how you have to restart your entire tech build-up every single new run, outside of Outpost mode, as if the planet nuked itself, and reset the environment in its entirety.A friend bought the game for me to get me to play it, and frankly? If he hadn't, I wouldn't be playing it.Near 100h playtime update:Most of it was spent gathering resources, levelling up, building outposts, and then finding out the mission was pathetic and I could've just bloody sped through it within an hour or so, even with my non-speedrun build.That pretty much sums up my experience so far. Not sure about the later missions, but the early ones? It's essentially flat-out pointless to waste time on a nice hideout, and you're better off getting some basic gear, and then just run off to do whatever menial task they came up with... at times on practically the other side of the map. Because of course it's way too much effort to land closer to the objective, or, heavens forbid, letting the player know what they have to do half-way across the map beforehand, and instead have them trundle over there to get an update that should've been in the briefing.Looks-wise, Icarus is pretty decent. Still some issues here and there, but it's fine.Story-wise, it's... not brilliant. The basic premise is that terraforming went bo-bo, air's poisonous (not devoid of oxygen, like some reviews seem to think; the planet-side life adapted to it), and stuff's all fubar. However, shiny stuff was found, so now the big megacorps are paying for scrubs to go down there and do stuff. So off you go, wearing your fancy suit that will allow you to survive planet-side, and do things like not dying from poisonous air, breathing underwater, and getting pneumonia from dampness inside caves... wait what? Gameplay-wise, the main issue I still have with the game, apart from bears with mountain climbing gear and the garbage melee combat, is the extraction mechanic.Because of course it makes sense for you to toss out any and all non-exotic gear, and do it all over again the next time around... not.I frankly really think they should rework that aspect. I'm fine with not being able to  bring back entire workbenches, a full house, and maybe a warehouse or two in ingots, as that would be rather silly.However, I genuinely do not see a reason we can't bring a small selection of normal tools and gear back with us, to bring to a next mission.We can stuff a mammoth's tusk in that pod, or stacks of exotic ores, and exotic equipment is fine, yet for 'reasons', not even a small titanium knife can go back.I might try the outpost a bit more, but frankly? I'm rather tired of the normal missions.

I stumbled upon a bear, unprepared for the encounter, I ran. I ran and ran and jumped over rocks and through some trees and even off a fairly short cliff side. I ran long enough and through enough obstacles that eventually I was like, "Surely I've lost him or he's lost interest. Let's take a look behind me." I turn around (while still moving forward) and my face is inside the bear's mouth... This was with a few points in Movement Speed and food buffs... Moral of the story? Kill them before they kill you and aim for the face. Also, the kill cam was an amazing, albeit guilt inducing, addition. Death cry + the amazing physics simulator make it feel... real lol.If you're an open world survival player, this is your game.

_childDocuments_.review: It falls short. Graphics are poorly optimized and gameplay isn't thought out. Story content says the air is trying to kill you, but space suits with a closed O2 system can allow you to get an infection from the air in the cave. You need oxygen mined from rocks, on a planet that supports earth life and creatures and plants because reasons. You even have a line from a character saying your suit should be able to filter out anything harmful, and obviously, it doesn't.Missions are quick, but all progress in the area is gone after you leave. I get that's supposed to be how it is, but it makes building or crafting anything above "stone quality" pointless. After playing since beta, I've found most missions can be done with a bow crafted from twigs and a knife from some rocks, high tier gear isn't required and is more of a pain due to the high cost and poor design. And with the workshop in the space station, now you don't even need to craft during the mission, just grab the gear from the station and go. The talent and tech trees are a mess. You can only get something like 1/15th of the total talents available in the game, and not even enough to fill out one talent tree. You have to debate on a 1% or 2% buff, on a talent that may or may not be a broken mechanic. Most of the maps are empty, and mission objectives are far too spread out for the short timers that missions have. The game doesn't do a good job of encouraging crafting as it does running from point A to B, then back. And since most missions can be done with just stone level gear, it turns out to be a really big running simulator."Outposts" can provide a spot to build, but, that's about it. The area is extremely limited and Outposts don't contribute to the gameplay at all, there isn't a point to them apart from just building - they don't contribute to missions, gear taken on missions, or even XP (since you get 75% less XP in outposts).Animal AI is terrible, and needs a ton of work along with the related combat mechanics. I shouldn't have to cheese fights just to get by, and the fact that I can annoys me.This game isn't a full release and needs some serious work before I'll consider playing it again.

_childDocuments_.review: As a certified Open World Survival Craft enjoyer, this is a good one.  It is pleasing to look at and exist within, and it is quite intuitive for the most part.  It also does an excellent job of rewarding players for the various jobs you can do.  In my case, I'm getting just as much XP farming and crafting as my buddy did hunting and mining.Gameplay incentives are a strong point here.  We face frequent wind storms in our area and wood structures take damage at the height of the storms, but stone structures have a buff towards wind resistance.  The perk trees have incentives for practically every way you could want to play.  Example, you can take buffs towards cooking food, or you can take buffs that enhance eating uncooked food- leading to the point that you can even eat spoiled food and gain buffs from it. There are some minor issues with placing building parts (ex. parts getting placed under the map), and there is some jankiness to the physics (ex. trees entering orbit after falling onto a rock, animals clipping through walls).  One design flaw on the annoying side I have encountered is that this game is pretty brutal when it comes to mining large stones specifically.  Oxite nodes will "break" when you reach the 20 or 15% mark for the deposit but stone will not, so you must physically mine the entire thing down to the last atom if you need to clear stone out of your space.Additionally, it is extremely tedious to place a large amount of buildables (ex. Crop Plots) down because 1) they don't stack and 2) hotbar slots don't automatically remember and refill with the buildable you just placed down.  So you must either fill your entire hotbar with buildables to get them down quickly, or you are stuck opening the inventory and clicking each one individually to deploy them all.  The only reason I've gone into depth on these problems is because there are lots of other quality of life features in the game already, so I am hopeful these things can be addressed.I will also throw it out there that older hardware definitely struggles with this game.  If you meet the recommended specs, it is a beautiful game, among the most beautiful in the genre.  If you don't meet the recommended specs, it's like a nearsightedness simulator.Overall I'm enjoying it a lot more than I'm not.  It takes elements from lots of other games in the genre that you'll find familiar (Ark, Rust), while adding unique twists and rewards in ways that others do not.  And since it is 1-8 player co-op, you never have to worry about your creations being griefed offline.   Things would have to really fall apart in the late game for my initial impressions to change drastically.  It is an easy recommendation if you're already a fan of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★☆☆☆☆ (1.5/5) [demo only]𝐼𝐶𝐴𝑅𝑈𝑆, a game with a dearth of verisimilitude coupled with rather lacklustre models,  rote, wooden animations, and the promise of a rather mindless slog of gathering to navigate recipe trees from point zero in an overpopulated, grossly timeworn genre.  The net result?  It feels dull and lifeless, and it doesn't help that the premise beggars belief.  The powers-that-be sent me off in a rocket, wrapped me in a self-contained environment suit, but didn't have enough resources to include a steel axe, nor any other basic tools?  No, I'm just not buying it.  I didn't last an hour prior to stopping, my eyelids were heavy and the game did very little to make me want to keep them open, other than getting the obligatory initial-level achievements, which still felt like it took too long (there's never a raging, homicidal bear around to kill you when you're ready to die to get the achievement). Even 50% off base price feels too high for this kind of game - although if you're really into survival, and/or building (the footage has some impressive-looking structures) it might be worth your time at half off - I wouldn't go for it for less than 80% markdown.  It may not be a bad game, but for me it had no hook - nothing to get excited about continuing to play.

_childDocuments_.review: While this game is pretty, has well thought out options for visual aspects and realistic challenges, it is a dull repetitive time sponge, and not in the good, get lost in game for hours way...Everything just takes too long, without enough variety to make it interesting while levelling or accumulating resources. Which wouldn't be so bad, if they gave people the option to turn up XP gains or something similar, if they don't want to spend their short lives trapped in a mundane slog towards no sense of achievement.The problem with such a labour camp of a game is that eventually it becomes paralysing, because you invest so much time unlocking the XP or gathering the resources, you end up disappointed with whatever you unlock, rather than excited, leading you to not want to spend your gains, and eventually not bother getting them at all. There's loads of stuff that just doesn't make sense too, like advanced tech that can't do the prior level so you can have a fancy base, but your bio-fuel cooker can't just cook some meat. Or tech that's dependant on other tech which it doesn't have any mechanism for telling you. In fact there seem to be a number of almost completely redundant tech trees, which is what makes the progress so hollow. It's not like you actually need much of it and it doesn't add anything except extra work. Then there's the expense of the higher tier stuff... I mean surely higher spec tech would make life easier, not mean you have to do even more of the same mundane running back and forth for resources?It's a shame, this game has a lot going for it, just not fun or satisfaction. Once you have the means to defend yourself, not even excitement. The realism stuff with fires etc, was so promising... it's like they forgot it's a game. There needs to be an improved inter-relationship between the XP, the perks, the tech tree and the game... some kind of parallel progression, and some more thought put into the tech progression, so that each tier can stand almost alone. The seeds of all of these points are in there, but the balance needs work still.

_childDocuments_.review: Icarus is a fun game with a very large blueprint and talent tree which keeps you striving to work and improve.  The progression through these trees is good and the work required to unlock tech and talents is reasonable and fun.  I enjoy the missions but you have to build a base and crafting bench, etc. for each mission and this is fun for quite a while but it started to wear on me.  I would make a unique base for each mission to make it fun.The dialog and voice actor is not good at all, I turned the narration volume off and started ignoring the captions, they are useless and disturbing.  I'm really tired of sophisticated space outfits being run by cringe goofballs that want to make a joke out of everything.  The dialog and narration should be professional, sophisticated, and high-quality.The instability issues are real, I dealt with them but I was able to fix them with hardware changes.  The minimum-required graphics card is Nvidia GTX 1060 6GB.  I attempted to play the game with a GTX 1060 3GB and can confirm it is unplayable with this card.  I upgraded to an RTX 4070 and I was getting a complete black-screen, power-off PC crash while playing.  I upgraded my power supply from 860 watt to 1,000 watt and I haven't had that problem again.The base building and hunting is very fun, the weapons work great.  You can make massive, high-tech bases.  There is no exploration, there is nothing to find.  The world is still fun to traverse, there are mounts you can tame for faster travel.  There are multiple biomes to see with different creatures, both passive and dangerous.Icarus is a great game, I highly recommend it.  There is an update every week, they are currently on week 149.  This is very impressive, I imagine that is a lot of hard work.  Thank you for reading, feel free to ask questions.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy Icarus for what it is. Session-based PvE survival.Yes, your "progress" in your current session is wiped after you complete the mission and go back into orbit. The biggest thing that you take with you as a player is knowledge. For example, learning how to optimize your start so that you progress through the early stages faster and faster, remembering where to find the various caves for mining, and getting used to dealing with threats from wildlife and the planet itself. Each new drop you undertake won't feel very different for a while, but once you break into new biomes you have to learn to deal with the new challenges they present. Pros: Beautiful environments and storms, base building / planning is enjoyable, devs who address issues and clearly care about the product they've created, I have a friend who is afraid of bears (endless entertainment)Cons: Can be a bit choppy at times & can't carry a light in your off-handPlay this game with friends, work together and build your talent trees to complement each other, don't set your house on fire.

_childDocuments_.review: Icarus is a difficult, open world survival game with RPG style skill trees. You'll need to plan ahead for the weather, what gear to bring, and what fauna you'll face. Death is impactful. Missions are often lengthy marathons. The basic loop is to explore the landing zone, build a shelter, complete the objective, and extract. Between missions you'll spend your currency on persistent gear to assist with the next mission. However, the slow-paced struggle against nature makes it a very immersive experience with outstanding sound design and above-average graphics.Icarus suffered from a rocky launch. Since release there has been a tremendous amount of optimization, and nowadays it runs smooth on a decent machine. Furthermore the developers put out a content patch roughly once a week; new items, new missions, overhauled systems etc. The version history is evidence enough that the developers are actively improving their product-- a rare thing in today's early access hellscape.As far as downsides: there isn't a great variety of enemies, some of the missions can feel repetitive, and you'll need to rebuild after each mission. To be fair, the primary struggle is versus the environment and creature variety has steadily improved. However, it's still limited and it can feel tedious slaying your hundredth wolf. As far as mission variety and engagement, it seems like they're improving and taking more chances with the New Frontiers expansion. Hopefully this innovation will spill over into the base game. Finally, with the Hypatia updates, *most* missions can be launched without returning to space and starting over, even allowing you to keep some of your crafted gear. Overall it seems like despite the rough launch, development is on the right track.tl;dr Icarus is an underrated gem that was review bombed initially, but has dramatically improved and continues to improve. Performance and graphics is decent to good. Get it if you're interested in an immersive and grounded survival experience against a hostile environment. Skip it if you need immediate action and frequent rewards to stay interested.

_childDocuments_.review: Icarus offers a fresh take on survival and base-building. The game allows you to play in a number of ways with more or less persistency of the buildings and equipment you craft during your missions, and give you loads of skills and tech to unlock as you progress your character. It is also, unfortunately, a game where the developers seem to not care about or respect the players’ time spent to achieve anything. Your typical mission starts with “go to drop-zone to get further info”. In most cases, the follow-up is a simple grocery list of supplies you are requested to supply to complete the mission. While these types of missions are not uncommon in survival games, Icarus manages to make it extra tedious by making sure you will travel across the map several times to first find out what exactly is requested before you even have a clue what kind and how many of a material is required to finish a mission. You then get to decide if you want to make a temporary base in that area, grinding for additional recourse on top of the requested, or travel all the way back to wherever you might have a base already. On top of this, some missions will have you travel to several rockets in one or more zones, to supply with arbitrary resources not necessarily common in that specific environment, further bloating the tedious travelling back and forth in the game.While I understand Icarus is about survival and exploration, and the travel across the map thus serves as a form of “survival”, this particular form of quest design seems to only serve the purpose of artificially prolonging a game that can already be very long, especially if you do individual missions rather than open world game mode, which is rather unfortunate in my opinion. Enemies in the form of wildlife offer little challenge even early on, especially if you have a mount available, and even apex predators like bears or cougars can be handled by either moving right behind their line of sight as you travel, or simply attacking them up high from a safe position like a rock they can’t climb or destroy.However, despite the unnecessary long time you will spend travelling around in Icarus, I do think the game is worth picking up (at least on sale). Base building and equipment to unlock makes the (relatively easy) grind worth to explore the game in its open world mode in my opinion, and I hope the devs will focus more on QOL updates, quest types, unlockables, and game mechanics rather than adding yet another outpost map in the future to further improve on an already promising concept for a survival game.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Very pretty game with a notable exception. The water and nature both look incredible and really let you enjoy the world while you are building and surviving. -there is plenty to look forward to while you are leveling your character and there are plenty of neat gadgets that you look forward to using.-the storm system is fun and the nights are super dark, which both allow you really spend time in your homes. I was worried that the rabbits would be too fast to hit, but I was headshotting wolves in no time. I love the bow. -hunger system and dehydration are handled well, though the expiration rate of food doesn't make much sense as its not tracked seperately within a stack. Cons:-Super buggy and unfinished. From having to have an 'unstuck' button in the menu to constantly seeing wood that you chop or deer that you kill clip through the floor of the world to disapear into the abyss, the game could really benefit from some TLC. I wouldn't even call it missing polish, just basic functionality.-Character models are ugly. Really doesn't match with the rest of the world because of how pretty it is. ITs not that bad, just out of place when compared with the rest of the world. -The leveling system is very slow and hard to enjoy, it would be better if there perks points where a little more easy to come by, but you have to spend the majority of two level ups of perks on getting your first articles of clothing. It takes about five to learn how to build things and you are long onto a better tier by that point. A way to fix this might be to make lower perks somehow cost less or to sperate the perk points by tier, but that might be confusing to players. -Animal spawns are sometimes right on top of you, which is frustrating when you are trying to hunt. Its basically like the game is just dumping stuff in your lap. -Servers can be buggy, which can make if so you can't play with your character until its fixed. _childDocuments_.review: A survival game I've been waiting for. I recommend this game for those who are looking for a sci-fi themed survival game that balances challenges/ stakes/ and an enjoyable chill experience. imo, Icarus is like 7 days to die mixed with astroneer, big game hunter, and arc. But, without dinos and zombies.Icarus provides the core cooperative survival experience that too many games miss; a gambit of challenges that can be completed solo or with your friends. There are enough stakes to keep players going for hours, but not so much that you'd look back at your last week and say, "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. All that time... gone.."Similar to Valhalla, Icarus does have some room to grow. Mods could help improve QoL elements like quickly splitting and moving items in inventory. But the punishment for a player death isn't nearly as harsh; and, if you are playing with your friends they can divert on a special rescue mission to get you back into the game without suffering an xp debt.Icarus seems to be more demanding on your video card than New World. Or any other game of late for that matter. I think 32GB of RAM should be considered for the best experience. I'm running on an Asus 'TUF GAMING' laptop with:- Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-8750H CPU @ 2.20GHz   2.21 GHz- 16.0 GB RAM- 64-bit operating system, x64-based processor- Windows 10 HomeI'd like a feature that allows players to reset their talent points to better accommodate solo players' and improve a dynamic group from one mission / environment to another. I hear this is in works so thumbs up from me there.The kill cam on feature for long range arrow kills can be entertaining, even epic. But I think the allure wears off after a couple days. I would like an option to either elect to turn off kill cams; or, I would like a sliding bar in settings that adjusts the min distance for kill cams to be pull me away from the action.At the time of writing this, the AI can be cheesed too. Chopping down a few trees can work as an obstacle that bears and wolves seem to struggle with. Grizzly bears seem to have a single avoidable attack if you pay attention, but, it isn't anywhere close to Dark Souls level of difficulty. I feel like wolves' hit boxes may need a little tweeking too.Server connection this past week after launch has been spotty at times in the evening (US CST) and I don't think the dev team have done as much as they could to communicate the server status and maintenance needs to players in-game. But the serves DO reliably save your progress. So, the impact is fairly mitigated; all things considered.The dev team has a lot more planned for Icarus.The driving story and core features of the game are flexible enough to do just about anything with this game.Even a battle royal, imo. Overall, I would say the game is a solid 8 to 8.6  out of 10. If I had a better machine to run on max settings, I might be willing to say 8.5 to 9 out of 10. But, I am running the game with very conservative settings to make it playable. So I am likely missing out.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a long haul for me when it comes to Icarus.More than probably any other survival-sandbox game, I have had a love/hate relationship, in equal parts, with the world of Icarus.As I recall, I pre-purchased this title back sometime in November of '21. This allowed a friend and I to take part in the Beta Weekends program that ran for several weeks prior to actual release. I am pretty sure it was released as full retail but it was arguably still in very early access condition.Since game mechanics were still being implemented it would have been defined as an alpha phase game.It was harsh, unforgiving, but strangely addictive.Many hours of hard work could be totally wiped out by a poorly placed torch, a random lightning strike, or the retro-engines of a coop buddy randomly being given a trajectory to enter the map that targeted directly at your camp.Wolves could chew through multiple layers of stone construction in as little as 60 seconds.You find yourself frequently faced with situations where you either rage-quit or simply roll over laughing hilariously at the unexpected.It's can be that kind of harsh.But fun!Since I stay pretty busy with a small cadre of gaming friends who are mostly from my generation, (I am currently approaching 62 very soon.) so after release I decided that I would keep the game and check back in every so often to see how things were going with it's development. I own server hardware from which my little band of old farts play various survival-sandbox games and such as our interests lead us. Time marches on...Now it is fast approaching Halloween for 2023 and I notice that I have around 258 hours of play under my belt from which I can form an opinion. Steam is reminding me again that I should offer up a review... so here I am.The game is quite fetching, with a lot of natural mountain splendor, open desert vistas, and frozen wastes.There are now enough play options and locations available from which to work feverishly on gathering resources while the local wildlife attempts to gnaw your ass off at every opportunity.Why does the suspiciously "alligator-esque" looking crocodile seem to find me far more appealing as a dinner entree than the pretty pony, with tusks, that also wants a piece of my sweet-meats?If you kill something, you had better dress it out in a flat-ass hurry, or hope it's small enough to throw over your shoulders and carry with you. If not, in less than 30 seconds, other denizens will come running like you rang a dinner bell.It can quickly get out of control and you find yourself needing waders to slog your way out of the corpse pile of now dead predators you unintentionally attracted.If... you survive.Players are allowed to set up camp practically anywhere.Caves are interesting, but the current mechanic is terribly janky, thoroughly breaking any semblance of believable immersion from outside weather conditions that insist on following you into the depths of the underworld in an unpredictable fashion. You can literally perish from heat stroke while suffering from frostbite inside caves that act as passageways between different biomes. The caverns seem to "want" to have their own biome but just can't manage to enforce it throughout with any dependable consistancy.Being in a cave large enough to allow you to build a completely enclosed structure is just about your only chance against those subterranean sandstorms.Beasts of burden have been added recently. A much needed addition to the game.Now, if I could just convince my buffalo that "defensive" mode means it should defend itself if attacked, not go off full-Rambo at the merest sight of a possible predator in the distance.Normally pets follow at a distance, unless they are going psycho-aggressive on a perceived intruder or if you are stopping to dress out a fresh kill. At that point they will amble over, stomp it to ensure it is dead, and then proceed to stand on the carcass in an attempt to prevent you from claiming your kill."Look fart-stain, you either get off my dinner or I am going to introduce you to my 'boom-stick' and make an entree substitution."I think you all get the idea... this title is a little gem under a considerable bit of early access crustiness.There is something to love in here, but it needs some elbow grease to make that sparkle visible.

_childDocuments_.review: Icarus is an interesting idea wrapped in a mediocre execution with poor worldbuilding and an incomplete and grindy gameplay loop. The concept of a persistent character in an ephemeral session-based expedition is an interesting take on the Survival Crafting genre. However, it leaves you feeling like you accomplish little over time as the world doesn't evolve with you. When your session timer expires, the mark you left on the world disappears forever, and if you fail to make your shuttle, so do you, making much or all of your progress disappear with it. The developer's choice to use a hand-crafted 8km square map makes the scenery incredibly beautiful and very scenic but ends up feeling like you're playing a Survival Crafting version of Sliders. Where every drop you return to the same lake, in the same valley, in a new parallel dimension untouched by human hands. It becomes very repetitive and boring once you learn the map. You and your crew are the only prospectors you ever encounter, no remnants of older attempts or failed missions.  It's a bit surreal and very immersion-breaking. A game like this desperately calls for some amount of procedural map generation or at least procedural map assembly akin to Scrap Mechanic, otherwise the level of replayability becomes fairly limited.The gameplay logic level is artificially punishing "because it’s survival" rather than using consistent logic and well-thought-out gameplay. Good, creative, or logical solutions are often punished instead of praised and most of the mechanics used to force you into a playstyle are very artificially punishing rather than creatively guiding. For example, you can get randomly infected with pneumonia by simply being in a 20-foot deep cave for 30 seconds despite being in a sealed environment suit with an air supply. Aggressive wildlife can tear through brick and mortar or solid wood logs with ease in seconds and they hate both you and your base for simply existing. Storms are so violent that they regularly cause severe damage to thatch, wood, or stone alike, frequently felling trees at a rate far faster than they could possibly regrow in the environment. Animals however seem relatively immune to the storms and will frolic around during them unless they get struck by a tree or lightning bolt. None of the animals fear fire. Frequently during playthroughs, bears and wolves spawned inside or below your base despite them not having any possible way to get in. Some decisions like night(and often day in the shade) being completely unplayable due to being almost pitch black, skipping the night requiring a bedroll which requires both a fire and an inordinate amount of materials unavailable in the early game, and storms requiring you to basically sit in your house with a hammer and fire whacker for sometimes lengthy amounts of time lead to the game feeling more like a chore than an enjoyable experience. The lack of tangible progress your character makes from session to session doesn’t leave a good taste in your mouth. Your character advances by gaining talents which are mostly just simple stat gains and through blueprints which give you more things you can build. The catch with blueprints is most require you to build lower-tier stuff before you can build upper tier. Once you learn stone, you still have to build a wood or thatch building to house your stonemason workbench before you can build it. Icarus is in desperate need of customization sliders for difficulty, mission parameters, and for the love of god put in gamma correction. It’s tuned far too easy for the truly hardcore crowd who desire a never-ending pain and punishment yet far to difficult for the more casual crowd who end up beating their head against the wall caused by the poor mechanics and illogical gameplay. In attempting to prescribe a single difficulty level for everyone both camps are a bit alienated and the gameplay suffers as a result.The lore is mostly a bunch of pseudo-scientific nonsense cobbled together without any consistency to explain away bad gameplay decisions focusing more on the fiction than the science. The game relies on the premise of a terraforming job gone bad to explain why we’re basically on earth with really bad weather but a smattering of earthlike animals. It's supposedly an environment with sufficiently low oxygen to not support human life but easily support apex predators like bears and wolves. Trees or wood will catch fire in seconds and spread as if in a pure oxygen environment. Storms form in seconds without warning, pass in a minute or two, and vanish shortly after. To explain away the space age caveman, the prospectors, of which the player is one, apparently sold or spent everything they had to go to an unexplored planet in search of "exotic matter" without any tools, knowledge, or preparation. Thus they must craft stone tools out of what's handy and relearn ~6000 years of human advancement in a few months.The various biomes are boring and incredibly uninteresting, adding new difficulty mechanics because they add difficulty rather than the difficulty deriving from the environment itself. Bosses are just reskinned buffed versions of existing critters and often the best and only way to take them on is to cheese them. The game truly struggles with knowing what it wants to be. It suggests base building but adds repetitive severe weather and magical animals to discourage base use plus makes key resources required for those bases both scarce and highly necessary requiring constant relocation.  The Nomadic lifestyle on the other hand requires you to carry multiple workbenches and furnaces in your pocket, deploying yourself in caves suspending disbelief significantly, and creating a seemingly undesirable meta.The game just doesn’t know what it wants to be other than punishing. Most of the mechanics make limited if any sense and just seem thrown together because it sounded like a good idea somewhere else rather than a well-thought-out and cohesive mix for THIS game. For as much as everyone dunks on Dean Hall for "abandoning"DayZ he has a valid excuse. However this game is 100% his brainchild and true legacy, so far I personally am not that impressed.Pros- Very pretty graphics for the genre IF your hardware can support it.- Session-based survival with roguelike progression is an interesting premise albeit with a flawed implementation.Cons- Limited content for a Full price game, should have launched as Early Access.- Punitive measures to prevent/discourage logical play.- Incredibly Grindy gameplay without much sense of progression- Entire experience is poorly balanced and lacking a feeling of purpose.- Inconsistent gameplay decisions and design. --- Massive Rocks are minable but the terrain is not.--- Require a sealed environment suit with oxygen due to exotics yet eat and drink local food.--- Environmental Suit with Oxygen is required but airborne diseases are easy to catch.- Animal AI appears omniscient and vindictively aggressive.- Graphical Glitches galore & numerous clipping issues.- Solo play despite being a "primary gameplay goal" is poorly thought out.--- Solo death penalty is punitive. Multiplayer revival is "free".--- Solo tree is not really designed to balance the loss of multiplayer perks.--- Game is incredibly stingy with Talent & Tech points and has an unnecessarily large and spread-out tech tree.- Game Clock is poorly thought out. --- Mission timer is real-time and not related to the gameplay. It keeps ticking no matter what even when the Gameworld is offline and paused.--- Sleep magically makes it light out but no actual time passes. Storms, mobs, torches, crafting, mission timer, etc are unaffected.  - Biomes are boring and mostly lifeless.- Storms are boring and grindy, basically leading to whack-a-mole gameplay for 5 minutes.- Game lighting, while beautiful, makes daytime tree shade too dark and night a complete waste of time in early and mid-game.

_childDocuments_.review: So, after 30 hours of playing the game solo, I have to say it's not overly friendly to solo players. It's a lot harder dealing with some boss-like wildlife on your own. Being under-prepared often leads to a death loop unless you spend time building weapons such as firearms, which can take hours. You cannot keep your items after leaving the planet, which means you have a constant groundhog day type loop every mission, starting all over again each time. This makes me not want to spend hours crafting the more complex items. What's the point? It's all lost on the next mission. If they could add a game mode that makes the solo player buffed to do more damage or cause the high-level enemies to be more balanced, then it might be a little more enjoyable. Also, keeping a stash on the planet would be good. It could be a container similar to where you find the mission scanners. Adding this option would allow some of my hours of crafting and gathering worth it for the next mission. Making these changes would give a faster start for a solo player as it takes so long to prepare all this stuff. Yes, you can buy items off-mission using credits earned from missions, but these missions pay so little for the time it takes to complete them. It just feels like too much of a grind. I like the survival elements, and it's an excellent concept. I will continue to play and hope they make some favourable changes to the solo game.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely one of the more fun survival house builders i've played. Alot of gripe with this game boils down to the slow progression, which honestly I enjoy alot. Alot of survival games are to quick to introduce you to new systems, and new upgrades that completely waste over the lower tier items that you work hard to get, where as icarus provides a slower progression to make you appreciate each unlock, slowly working towards the next goal. If you enjoy games like Enshrouded or Valheim, i think you'll find something here to really appreciate.Besides what I enjoy about the game, there are some issues I have with more minor issues when it comes to progression and balancing. As of writing this now, currently polar bear hitboxes are very broken, and will connect with you even if you are meters behind them. There also seems to be issues with the hitbox of bears heads being noticeably smaller than what it appears they should be. To go back on what i've said a little with the balancing of progression, I definitely think the armor in the tech tree should only take up 1 point per set, as how it currently is, you have to level up at least twice, and invest all tech points received in order to unlock a single armor set. I think similarly this could also pertain to tool sets of the varying ore type. Certain skills i think should also be a given, for instance highlighting thrown knives, or shot arrows/bolts. I also think the skill in regards to automatically collecting wood of chopped trees should be default. There have been to many times to count where ill chop down trees, only to stuggle to find the wood beneath the brush. That, or the wood physics cause the wood to fly off to kingdom come, or clip beneath the map. While this isn't a major issue, it's still something that could be tweaked.All in all i think this is a really fun game, and i'm excited to see how the devs expand on the groundwork they have laid out. It's important to note the game also features a feedback system for reporting bugs within the pause menu, which is certainly a commendable addition, and shows, to me atleast, that they take user feedback with heavy consideration.

_childDocuments_.review: Difficult review to write.  After 60ish hours, my overall impression is simply one of wasted potential.  Visually the game is stunning, and the survival elements are diverting.  I enjoyed hunting, building, managing oxygen. I wanted to enjoy exploring (including learning new biomes), and I thought the concept for the setting oozed potential.    However, as others have pointed out, this game is astonishingly empty.  All the systems work, but It's early early early access from a content perspective.  There's an unlock treadmill, where as you gain levels you unlock recipes which give you new survival tools and materials.  Unfortunately, all the tools feel the same - upgrading a stone knife thru bone, iron, steel, etc doesn't change the way it functions, and doesn't feel more fun to use (in any way).  Contrast that with a game like The Forest, where each new discovered tool has different animations, opens up new gameplay, can be customized, etc.  Talents are much the same - at first they seem like deep and interesting trees, but then you realize that, while they do affect gameplay, they do so in very subtle ways and a character who has invested in say 'survival' has access to the same gameplay loops, and feels  as one who's invested in 'combat', 'mining' etc.  I mentioned above that the game is beautiful, and it is.  Sadly, it's also lifeless.  There are half a dozen animal species per biome that spawn, you'll see them over and over and over.  They have very limited behaviors, they will run from you/run at you (predators will walk/run directly at you, always), they'll rest, they'll drink, they'll graze or they'll wander aimlessly.  There are no non-interactive animals - no birds, bugs, bees, flies, nothing that makes the world feel alive.  I contrast this with games like Subnautica, where marine life does it thing all around you as you explore, survive, build.  You don't immediately notice this absence, because you're probably very focused on gathering to build a shelter, but when you're on your second or third mission walking kilometers between objectives, you start to notice just how lonesome Icarus is.  You never feel like you're planning an expedition across unknown territory to get something new, necessary, rare.  As another point of comparison there, Valheim has way more resource diversity and exploration payoff than Icarus does, and Valheim has a procedural map!   Last thing I'll express as a disappointment is the storyline (or lack thereof).  So much potential!  The premise of the orbital station and the poor grunts wildcatting on the hostile surface is brilliant.  There are hints of interesting factions and concepts throughout the mission briefings.  But the missions themselves use [b}none[/b] of this material.  You never come across a failed prospector base, you never interact in a meaningful way with unique creatures (couple of bosses that you kill), and there's no mystery in the setting whatsoever.  Aliens?  Haven't seen any 60 hours in, other than cave worms and mission specific poison plants.  The map is persistent, which seems like it should be cool (learnings from one mission can be useful in the future), but within each biome (forest, desert, snow), everything is exactly.the.same.everywhere.  There's just so little variation from place to place, that there's very little payoff in travelling.  This review probably sounds angry or hyperbolic - sorry about that, I'm trying to express the prevailing emotions of playing the game, with some detail.  I wanted to love this game, and I applaud the devs for taking a risk with the concept.   It mines gameplay concepts and settings that I typically greatly enjoy.  Right now though, my take is that it's a time-waster, there's not enough payoff to the experiences.  I'm not sure if it will improve over time either - there's a great survival platform in place, but for this to become something I would enjoy playing, they need to build a game and a story on top of it, and it doesn't seem to me like they will have the customer attention time to do so.

_childDocuments_.review: Good survival game.  Scratches a lot of itches.  Feels like Ark and Rust, just single player and friends only.  Always found it hard to stick with those latter games, but this let's me play at my own pace and you don't really feel the time restrictions on the missions.  If I had to critique the game it would have to be the punishing EXP system.  Dying in this game is not balanced what so ever.  If you die with hardly any exp accrued, then it's nbd.  However if you die with even just a single point of exp left before the next level up, you lose it all.  It's such a punishing way of doing things that it's very frustrating to die.  Makes it not worth exploring anything until you pretty have the highest tier gear.  If instead of losing all exp, if was capped at percentages, it would be a lot better.  If we instead lost some kind of fraction every time we die, then it wouldn't matter how far into our current level we progress, it would always be consistent exp and would scale over all levels.  So after X amount of deaths we would lose all our exp which is a lot more reasonable and not so punishing and anti exploration and anti risk taking, instead of 1 and done.

_childDocuments_.review: The people in the game are so technologically advanced that they can go to space and land on an alien planet but still they use a stone pickax and build their houses out of wood. JUST BRILLIANT... AIN'T IT!!!!It’s basically a dollar store Ark but without Dinosaurs.Both me and my wife’s boyfriend have been playing this from launch (on his account) and the game then is nothing compared to the game now. Sure it has its faults here and there but overall the experience is highly enjoyable and constant updates keep this game changing more and more for the better. No matter what anyone says, the thing that makes this game different from other survival games is the missions. In this mode of play you drop onto the planet and start from scratch. Every time. You can decide how much you want to prepare for the mission or if you want to risk going fast with little to no prep. It's got a good risk reward gameplay mechanic. But you need to be ok restarting every time. I LOVE making a new base. I realized that I always loved starting from scratch in my survival games so this game speaks to me. If you enjoyed how hard ARK was when you first loaded in then you should enjoy the mission style of this game.If you want to play on the standard survival modes there's not a lot to set it apart from other survival games though.I started playing with friends and now I play solo all the time. There's even a solo talent tree that kicks in if you are alone. So you're given advantage to play alone. It's really nice. I like logging on and playing a mission over the course of a few play sessions and then being done for a while.The other thing that makes this game unique is the meta progression of currencies you earn for doing missions which let you buy equipment to drop with. That progression which makes subsequent missions easier is a lot of fun.If you stick to the missions, you'll have a clear purpose, as every map has plenty of them. But if you prefer open world - it's a sandbox, so only you decide for how long you would be able to come up with ideas about what to do today. If you enjoy the game, and the process, take your time (mission timer is there of course). Build up and play as you see fit. If you like the missions and want to "complete" the game, go hard. Most missions can be done with rudimentary tools, etc.Open world is fun for experimenting with builds. If you liked legos as a kid, you will like building in this game. I loved the missions and the whole grind of it all, but I also have had a fun time in open world building bases in the middle of lakes, on cliff sides and wherever else looks fun. In the end this is a game you can play in your own way. It’s up to you and up to your skill and  patience. I've played everything from ARK to Minecraft to SCUM in the survival genre, and honestly this is one of the best in my opinion. If you enjoy this type of game, it seems to me that it took some of the better parts of most survival games and made them one game. Again I personally think this game is one of the better survival games to have come out in a while. If remotely interested I encourage you to try it out and I hope you get to experience it in your own way.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Starting out this game has potential. The first few hours are enjoyable as you learn what to do and how to survive, but after that, the game loses all enjoyment. Anything that could potentially be fun and enjoyable is completely ruined by horrible game mechanics and design. There is a robust crafting and building system, that is completely useless. The grind to even get to the point where crafting higher up assets makes it not worth the time and effort. Most missions feel as though they were copy pasted, and boring. The idea of 'difficulty' is  completely broken. Regardless of how hard a mission says it is, you can in almost every circumstance just run the objectives, and then when you have completed the mission, you get to run all the way back to your ship so you can leave and have everything you worked on completely wiped.Why there is no "Mission complete pull me out" mechanic is beyond me. To add difficulty? To make it harder? All it does is create a severe annoyance, and is an absolute waste of time.Once you complete a mission, there is no reason to remain unless you want to grind out mining the exotics so you can unlock more gear. Fun fun. Leveling up is basically just creating a stack of arrows and grinding out killing animals which, considering there is not really a variety of animals, is just not fun and boring. I think the most upsetting part of this game is that the devs have created a handcrafted world, one where they could create all kinds of missions, always new, never knowing really what the next mission is going to have you do, but that is simply not the case. Each mission pretty much follows this same path:Spawn => Run to Objective => Do this thing at objective(s) (normally 5 minutes or less of work) => Mission complete => Run back to ship and leaveAfter 50 or so hours of playing this game I have summarized it into a few key descriptive words. - Hiking Simulator- Grind Fest- Unbalanced- Not Fun

_childDocuments_.review: Icarus is a relatively simple to understand survival craft game, that has variety in how its played. The building is very nice, the sound effects are nice, the world is beautiful (Olympus and the new DLC Prometheus), and the crafting is pretty in depth. The game is not without it's faults, however. There are occasional bugs and/or frame drops, but the devs are hard at work with weekly content drops and bug fixes. So if you encounter a problem, odds are it will be be fixed within a week or two. With that said I have not encountered any major bugs or crashes so far at almost 73 hours. My time has been spent exclusively in the open world mode, and I have yet to even try the mission based mode that the game originated as. But from what I've heard from others some of the early missions serve as a tutorial of sorts to help introduce new players  to this games mechanics for those interested. All in all, I would recommend this game to any fan of base building and survival games.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good survival game, one of the best I've played. I have about 20 hours in and still feel like I've just started out. Pretty cool twist with this one. You can go down to Icarus to do either missions (which are timed) or you can play open world, or you can play outposts which has lower exp gain but no enemies and no harsh storms. I have not played outposts as yet. The weather/storms not only effect your well being but they can destroy your shelter as well if it is only made from wood or thatch. Your dwelling can also catch fire if struck by lighting. I've seen some pretty good forest fires now. The enemies I've encountered so far have been wolfs, bears, komodo dragons and such. I have even seen a polar bear but took the long way around him. If you meet a bear in early game it's pretty much death for you. Also there are deer to hunt as well as rabbit and fish. You can also eat berries and carrots and such. So overall pretty good game going on here, if you like survival, craft, base building thing this one is a must.

_childDocuments_.review: I have very mixed feelings about this game. On one hand, the graphics are amazing, the world is interesting, and the skill system can be very fun and immersive. However, the game also has huge balancing issues, repetitive and boring missions, and game breaking bugs.If you are thinking of playing this game solo, I would recommend you don't. This game punishes solo players harshly for death the same way they punish people playing with others. The amount of useless crafting tech in the crafting tree makes it actually annoying to spend points (as you have to sift through all of the completely useless tech to find the ones you need). The higher tier the item, the more ridiculous and absurd the materials asked for are (especially considering you might have to travel far away to collect resources, only to get encumbered and still not have enough). Not to mention that none of it matters once you complete the mission.As for the missions, they too are a pain. They are incredibly samey and require you to start from scratch each time (despite aforementioned material issues). The missions end up getting boring real fast, which makes you not want to play the game.On top of these issues, are the incredibly annoying and frustrating game breaking bugs. Bugs that actually make the game impossible to play (such as not being able to craft anything despite having the resources to do so). What makes these bugs worse is that they can appear hours into you playing a mission. And it's not like you can wait for them to be fixed, because guess what the missions are timed irl. So while you sit there waiting for them to fix it, your mission is well on its way to expiring.TLDR: I would not recommend this game in it's current state. Which is very unfortunate, because I genuinely think this game has a ton of potential. But it seems like the devs are more interested in adding bogus content than fixing preexisting issues. For example, the issue with costly high tier items has been a known complaint for months. But it still has not been dealt with. I do hope that one day I can change this review for the better.

_childDocuments_.review: Chapter One: The Story Icarus is a hardcore survival game about prospectors sent on various missions to perform different activities on an alien planet (which looks suspiciously similar to Earth). There is no backstory explaining who sent these characters or why. Is it a greedy corporation? Or is Earth simply running out of resources, forcing the human race to seek new ones to survive? The basic premise is that humanity is trying to terraform the planet Icarus to make it resemble Earth. However, something goes wrong and problems arise, as with every big plan, there's chaos theory, which says, "You can't predict complex systems." We learned that from Dr. Ian Malcolm in Jurassic Park. And that’s essentially the story— the rest is up to you. Chapter Two: Graphics and Presentation The graphics in this game are somewhat decent but have their flaws. One major issue is with the color palette—some colors appear too bleached and don't pop out as they should. Texture popping is also a frequent problem, even with 12GB of VRAM. The world is rich in flora, but there are very few creatures inhabiting this otherwise lush environment. The intro cinematic is captivating and will catch your attention. However, it doesn’t provide any story elements or hints about what the game is about, other than showcasing crafting. You see various tools and objects spliced together in a cool montage, but it’s nothing too special and somewhat forgettable. The animation is fluid and pleasant to look at, as you’d expect from a game powered by Unreal Engine. Chapter Three: Music and Sound The music is almost absent, and the intro tune consists of strange ambient drones that lack any particular theme (not even close to the ambient brilliance of Star Trek). The sound design, however, is absolutely astonishing—one of the best in the last decade. The sound of storms is disturbingly realistic, and the clank of the pickaxe hitting stone or trees is incredibly satisfying. This is the best part of the game. Chapter Four: Gameplay and Mechanics Leveling - Achieved by exploring, crafting, hunting, and gathering resources. Progression - Divided into many elements—perk points, solo points, crafting points, credits, and exotics (more on that later). Crafting - In Icarus, crafting is very straightforward—you get the recipe, gather the raw materials, and craft in seconds. It’s as simple as that. Loot - This is where the biggest problem lies, and the main reason why I’m giving the game a low rating. When you go on a mission, you gather all sorts of loot—raw materials, crafted items, and more. However, all your hard work is pointless because you won’t keep your loot, no matter what. When you finish a mission and return to your ship, all of your loot is deleted. Yes, you can “kiss your loot goodbye,” because for some extremely weird reason, you are not allowed to carry any items you gather during your mission on the planet Icarus. However, there is a catch. You are allowed to carry specific items that are only crafted in your base station (or whatever it’s called). This is a horrible idea because crafting any of these items costs an insane amount of credits/exotics. Because the game is buggy as hell, I often had to start the same mission over and over again, only to receive no rewards at the end due to a game-breaking bug. I spent a good amount of time in the game, jumping from mission to mission, doing the same thing repeatedly—build a stone axe/pickaxe, build a shelter, go somewhere, and then...oops, it’s bugged. That’s it. In all the gameplay time I’ve spent, I was never able to finish a single mission due to horrible bugs and terrible game design decisions. Conclusion Icarus is a game with amazing potential. It features a rich crafting system, a complex and unique character progression system, and an immersive, realistic atmosphere. However, the game falls short in several areas: Horrible gameplay bugs Weak multiplayer experience Lack of any item storage Repetitive missions Bad optimization Disjointed storyline Empty and dull world No real enemies or foes (just animals like wolves, bears, wild boars, and something like horses?) Stupid and nonsensical loot and storage system—you cannot carry any looted items from mission to mission with your ship, even though you have cargo space. The only items you can carry over from mission to mission are special ones  Infuriating building mechanics Poor optimization and frame drops Tons of bugs in the missions I give this game a 3/10. Things to Make It Better: Being able to carry a small amount of items between missions would be amazing. Fix the game bugs. Optimize the game to run better (I currently experience FPS drops on an Intel i9 12th gen, 64GB RAM, RTX 3060). Add more mission variety. Lower the prices of workshop items in the space station. Introduce more character customization options.

_childDocuments_.review: Icarus, developed by RocketWerkz, presents players with an extraordinary survival adventure set on a distant and hostile alien planet. As a fan of survival games, I was immediately intrigued by the premise of Icarus and its unique twist on the genre. Tasked with colonizing and extracting valuable resources from this alien world, I embarked on a thrilling journey of exploration, resource management, and strategic decision-making. Let's dive into the captivating world of Icarus and discover why it stands out as an exceptional title in the survival genre.Icarus delivers a visually stunning and immersive alien planet, meticulously designed with rich and diverse biomes. From dense forests to frozen tundras and scorching deserts, each region feels distinct and teeming with unique flora and fauna. The attention to detail in the environmental design creates a sense of wonder and discovery as you navigate the planet's treacherous landscapes. Combined with atmospheric sound effects and a haunting soundtrack, Icarus effectively immerses players in its otherworldly setting.Surviving in Icarus requires careful planning, resource gathering, and adapting to the harsh conditions of the alien planet. The game's survival mechanics, including hunger, thirst, temperature, and oxygen management, add a layer of complexity and urgency to gameplay. Players must strategize and prioritize their actions, balancing the need for food, water, and shelter while exploring and exploiting the planet's resources. The constant struggle for survival creates a palpable sense of tension and keeps players engaged.Icarus offers a dynamic and open-ended gameplay experience. Players can choose from a variety of missions, each with its own objectives and challenges. The game allows for both solo play and cooperative multiplayer, where you can collaborate with friends to tackle the planet's dangers and build a thriving colony. As you progress, you unlock new technologies, skills, and equipment, enabling you to explore further and take on more ambitious missions. The sense of progression and the ever-expanding possibilities keep the gameplay fresh and exciting.Crafting plays a vital role in Icarus, as you gather resources and create essential tools, equipment, and structures. The game features an intricate crafting system that allows for the creation of customized items and structures tailored to your needs. Constructing a well-designed base becomes crucial for survival and progress, providing shelter, storage, and crafting stations. The freedom to design and expand your base fosters creativity and strategic thinking, making each player's colony a unique reflection of their playstyle.Icarus incorporates strategic decision-making, where choices have consequences that impact the outcome of your missions and the development of your colony. Balancing risk and reward becomes vital as you face environmental hazards, aggressive creatures, and limited resources. Choosing which missions to undertake, which resources to prioritize, and how to allocate your time and workforce adds depth and complexity to the gameplay experience, offering a satisfying sense of agency and responsibility.Icarus stands out as a thrilling and immersive survival adventure that challenges players to conquer an alien world. With its immersive environments, challenging survival mechanics, intricate crafting and base building, and strategic decision-making, the game offers a rich and engaging experience. Whether you're exploring the diverse biomes, facing off against formidable creatures, or working together with friends to build a thriving colony, Icarus presents an intriguing blend of survival, strategy, and exploration that will captivate fans of the genre. Prepare to embark on a gripping journey among the stars and test your skills in the face of the unknown.

They might try to add new features, address bug changes, fixes talk about future updates they are looking. The time of me writing this, they just made update 33 for "week 33" so they've been on a roll, this isn't a promise that they will and are only on week 4. They are going strong. I've also finally learned the strategy for fighting bears and I have a small army of horses that fight for me. The open world mode is a big improvement. You still need to do prospects to get items you can use on your load out but the prospects are still insanely buggy. The bugs are well documented and the developers have chosen to focus on new content instead. I want to like this game and I keep doing new prospects but when you're four hours in and it bugs out and you can't complete it, it's quite infuriating. Solo is still rough since no one can revive you. They did break the solo points out into a separate tree which was a good idea. Lastly, the building talents need to be rethought. It took 1.3 hours. 1.29 hours of  that was running through the map for 60 seconds, walking for 10 to let stamina recharge, rinse repeat. Hold F the entire time so you can fill up that million XP bar at an average of 15 XP per thing you grab. Try to avoid wolves. Get to the waypoints, run far away and stealth so that when they drop really difficult animals on top of you, you don't die. If you do die, hit alt-F4 and reload so you don't have to waste even more time to do a corpse run. Finish all the way points. Run for 8 minutes, realize you've taken a wrong turn and there's no way through, run back for 8 minutes. Regret ever purchasing the game. _childDocuments_.review: Immersive, challenging, beautiful. I've been hoping for a persistent survival game for a while and this really hits the spot. The Good: There's a LOT to do, find, build, develop, and discover. The Beta offered a taste but the full game is much more expansive -- the added variety with vegetation is very welcome, and the spaces that were assumedly safe before now have a few surprises. The leveling gives you something to strive for, and the rewards feel balanced. Playing with friends is extremely fun.The Not-so-Good: Playing alone is oppressively difficult. If you decide to go Solo, you'll take a few lessons in patience and futility when you're about to level up and get suddenly attacked, only to lose all of your XP. A solution to this could be a leveled XP deficit after death, instead of the entire level of XP. It's difficult to see your friends even when you're standing next to them - at the risk of breaking a bit of immersion, maybe an onscreen HUD element could show you where your teammates are? Other minor complaints are that forest fires don't generate light, the talent points for base stats typically only go up to 15% which feels like nothing, and a few of the game mechanics (such as the Improvement Tool) are complicated to the point that an in-game journal/instruction manual would be very beneficial. Overall this is an excellent one I've been excited to play for months, and it very much lives up to expectations. Can't wait to continue exploring and also to eventually construct the exotic "Dong".

I see where the devs are going for tho, having a very detailed survival experience is what it's about so at the cost of getting 60fps average which is perfectly fine except for bad pop-ins and watching the shadows literally come into existence, this game is really fun watching your house just get struck by lightning is so hilarious and scrambling to put it out is just so fun. I know also about some bugs and to be clear they are not game breaking the arrow on the bow bugs out, the bow and arrow keeping zoom FOV when swapping weapons, trees can hurt you when walking on them, medium shadows let you see in the back of caves, I mean the list goes on but not forever, but in all fairness this game is perfect. I run on a Intel i5 9400f 16GB ram GTX 1660 SUPER and the game runs at 55-60 fps consistently. People tend to forget how taxing shadows are and blame poor optimization and blame the devs for their game design and to be honest I feel like most of these reviews are not rated correctly if they stop and think about how demanding this game really is. My advice do not play on max shadows and you will have a really good 60fps experience, one last thing I would like to note is that the stutter are there but not bad in an open world game you should expect to be stutters, just wait and let the devs fix it.  8/10                                    [EDIT]~ The servers are fine I had no problems yet with me and my buddy.
