_childDocuments_.review: That's how I would describe this game. Let's break that down for a moment. The base management part of this game is definitely where the XCOM influence is felt the most. You'll see that most commonly in the reviews. The overworld also has a progressive difficulty scale that increases daily which is similar.However, where this differs from XCOM, is the psyche of your marines and how stress-build up affects their psyche definitely reminds me of Darkest Dungeon. The biggest influence of A:DD's Gameplay is clearly inspired by .  If you've never played Red Solstice it's a Tactical RTS/Action RPG that was  called "SWAT". If any of this is ringing any bells then you have a good idea of what to expect.This game is  Be aware that this game will punish you repeatedly for tactical mistakes or being impatient. You have to  do your best to remain calm and plan ahead while you navigate increasingly maze-like structures and basements. While you can 'slow time', your moment-to-moment decisions will mean the difference between squad-wipe and small victories. I know because... I've had both happen in the same mission on separate playthroughs when I chose to do  different things. For some people that will be a huge turn-off - but if you're like me, that adrenaline high is extremely addicting.You also have to deal with an in-mission "Alien Awareness" gauge that means the more gung-ho  you choose to be, the more the Aliens are going to punish you.  You are awarded for striking a delicate balance between stealth and decisive gunfighting.Despite my wholehearted recommendation of this game it is not perfect. , the writing, and the voice acting. Super, super cringe-worthy. Fortunately the flimsy story held together by Elmer's glue and toothpicks doesn't fall apart enough to make me stay away. It merely serves as a vehicle to move the gameplay along. One massive XCOM feature I wish they had also done in this game is the randomly-generated missions. I would honestly like this more if it was like XCOM and I just had an infested planet that I had to free from the clutches of the aliens via randomly generated missions and levels. It would be even better if I had a separate mode where I could just bypass the story entirely.  If your main reason for gaming is narratives and well-written characters then this is not the game for you.TL;DR - Bottom line, if you like Aliens/Xenos and enjoy difficulty... .Another solid entry into the Xenoverse. I'd put this behind only Alien Isolation and AVP 2010. I really enjoyed Fireteam Elite too but this game is way better. It's an extremely creative use of the Aliens license and I hope to see more of this franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically XCOM in the Alien universe, except combat is in real time instead of turn-based.  You assemble a squad of marines and guide them through missions, which can take multiple deployments to finish.  Marines need to heal/recover between missions so you'll need at least two squads to rotate between.  Marines can be customized my choosing 1 of 2 classes for each marine, with 5 classes available total, and you can choose perks and weapons, some of which are class-specific.  You can do things that you saw in Aliens, like weld doors shut to create a safe room, set up auto turrets and hack terminals.  The game is basically attempting to emulate the movie experience in every way possible.  If that sounds fun to you, you'll probably like the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've heard a lot of people describe this game as Aliens: Xcom. That's incorrect. This is Aliens: Darkest Dungeon.I'd describe the gameplay as a mix between Darkest Dungeon and classic Resident Evil - a tense, resource management-based dungeon crawl through lengthy missions that can go wrong at any moment. Combat is best avoided, not only because it drains your health, ammo, and stress meters, but because it gradually increases the aggressiveness of the aliens until they start sending massive waves of attackers and minibosses at you. This creates wonderfully anxiety-inducing gameplay that perfectly mimics the feeling of all those tense moments in James Cameron's Aliens. I can't praise this game's mechanics enough for how perfectly they evoke the feeling of playing out an Aliens movie in real time. Beeps on your motion scanner give you goosebumps. Patrolling drones make you hold your breath. Onslaughts make you panic and trip over yourself to weld doors shut and set up sentry guns. It's an engrossing thriller from start to finish.There are only a couple of things that hold Dark Descent back. One is the state of polish. It was pretty obviously rushed to release before it was ready, resulting in quite a few bugs and minor gameplay annoyances that really shouldn't be there. Fortunately most of the major issues seem to have been shored up at the time of writing this review. I only ran into two hard crashes during my ~30 hour playthrough, and all the other bugs I encountered were purely cosmetic.The second thing that hamstrings the game a little is the story. It's not aggressively bad or anything, just incredibly middling and predictable, with generic characters who yell because there has to be drama and plot threads you're asked to care about without establishing any emotional investment. The opening hour is honestly a slog to get through with its combination of tutorial hand-holding and intrusive cutscenes. There are a couple of other missions like this towards the end, but fortunately the vast majority of the playtime is pure gameplay.This is the kind of game I'd absolutely love to see done in a more open style, with freeform missions and randomised elements rather than a scripted narrative. All the best missions in Dark Descent are the open-ended ones with lots of side objectives. The core systems produce a heck of a lot of emergent gameplay based on how the hive reacts to your marines, and the scripted sequences feel fairly lacklustre by comparison. The mechanics here are probably the most original and engaging ones an Aliens title has ever seen. There's a ton of creativity that went into the ebb and flow of the core gameplay loop. It's just a little unfortunate that it was crammed into the mould of a generic Aliens narrative and rushed out the door rather than playing to its strengths.Assuming you manage to dodge the worst of the bugs, this is a very refreshing 8/10 for me that could've been an easy 10 with a bit more polish and a different approach to its storytelling. If you love Aliens, you'll probably adore this.

_childDocuments_.review: A:DD is a real-time boardgame (if you have played Free League Alien RPG this feels like a game-version of it) with solid story, some new implementations with expanded lore added (Seegson, weapon designs, enemies, etc), yet it feels as a core Alien(s) setting with powerful, authentic atmosphere. Very challenging and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ unnerving. Last time I felt like this was when playing Alien: Isolation. Light base management akin to X-Com, good class progression with 5 options and additional bonuses/perks. You can clear the mission in one in-game day/drop or retreat to the base if situation becomes critical or too risky and return with fresh marines with most of the level progress remaining (aliens break welded doors during your absence, apparently. static motion trackers and all ungathered loot remains). Can return to previous missions to explore or finish some special targets. Scarce resources generally. You can stockpile the technical stuff, meds, sentry guns to have more for next missions/drops or craft them before mission if you have spare resources. Game is quite demanding hardware wise, but it looks incredible and delivers the sense of presence even though it generally has an isometric/top view (you can use follow camera with lowered angle as much as you like, too). Huge hand crafted levels (a lot to explore and find adventure in - primary and secondary objectives, bonus resources, lore, hunt for survivors, too), CUSTOM difficulty settings (love the devs for this!), challenging gameplay (sometimes warranted, sometimes not - cluster♥♥♥♥ is one step away). There are no manual saves in the game only rare auto saves - self-welded rooms, floor changes in elevator, main story events, day changes on the base. The tension you get before getting to the next save strengthens the atmosphere. Getting a rest to alleviate stress levels on your marines does the same for you :) TIP: ammo > stress > health > hunt difficulty stage.Will mention some things that really got to me and this is the main - If squad moves together and you cannot move separate soldiers, then when one soldier notices a target, the sniper should be able to acquire this target without player trying to squeeze some absurd movement angle to get the sniper to see the target in time to get the shot off. This is really bothering me for a silent/stealth approach. You will experience situation where you mow down groups of aliens without them reaching you and sometimes a drone will "neo" his way to you, tail slash 3 marines and explode in acid on death with everyone screaming (% hit chance calculation). This makes you feel on edge in any engagement. When aliens search for you (when visually detected or after fights), quicker the next tier of mission difficulty approaches with additional events happening - hordes, bosses, etc. You have to evaluate when to engage, where and maybe to choose to retreat to ARC (APC scout variant for 2 crew, 4 marines) to the base and continue to progress on the next in-game day. ARC can be used to travel across the mission zone and mow down targets with it's high caliber guns, drive them over if lucky. Or call it to specific spots to cover your squad. It's a set location, mobile indestructible turret. Drive to complex North part in ARC, disembark, get through the building and while coming up to the East entrance call for ARC to get to it asap. That's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool!Then some bugs happen like some stats aren't being displayed correctly on the base screens (like accuracy and bravery), but are correct in the mission. You cannot adjust the details of characters on pre-mission launch screen, have to go back to barracks to spend points - really annoying waste of time. Music in missions is superbly fitting, on base it's half-muted, non-looping mess.Main characters fit in the cartoonish style, rest look goofy, thankfully you don't see them in detail during the missions.Physics / ragdoll animations aren't good, people fly around sometimes, aliens die in weird poses. Very rarely a marine gets stuck somewhere during the mission - if this happens in a bad spot, it will warrant a re-load of last auto-save. There's a good glossary of mechanics and decent tutorial. I strongly suggest to start the game on Medium enemy health (or even Low) and rest of settings having as Low if you wish to explore. It will not be easy by any margin! Especially the first time. If you wanna storm through with higher challenge go for all Medium settings. You will have to sacrifice unless you're super lucky or extremely patient. You can go hardcore with one auto-save on pre-mission launch :) Great game - great value for it's price/quality/content. Get it if you like tactical games with character/resource management and it's a must if you're Alien(s) fan. Worth it even just for the looks, atmosphere and tension.

In Aliens: Dark Descent, command a squad of hardened Colonial Marines to stop a terrifying Xenomorph outbreak on Moon Lethe. Lead your soldiers in real-time combat against iconic Xenomorphs, rogue operatives from the insatiable Weyland-Yutani Corporation, and a host of horrifying creatures new to the Alien franchise. name: Wizard with a Gun
detailed_description: Better Together Take your co-op wizardry to arcane new heights in Better Together, a free content update for Wizard with a Gun that brings, at long last, four-player co-op! Journey to the Shatter with up to three fellow Gunmancers in your crew, choosing from four new preset difficulty levels. Or create your own custom difficulty mode, tweaking variables to make the game harder or easier. Wizard with a Gun has never been more accessible—or more challenging. Back at the Tower, unlock the Library—a new building—to unearth fascinating lore about the Shatter, Chaos, and the many other mysteries of Wizard With a Gun’s fractured world. Rebuild the Voidskimmer sky ship with materials gathered by hunting down rare bounty enemies. Then open the doorway to the Oculus and experience the thrilling conclusion to the main story of Wizard with a Gun. Brace yourself for a fresh, challenging experience where greater firepower brings greater rewards. So grab your posse, mount up, and get ready to battle Wizard With a Gun’s most dangerous challenges to date! Bounty of Guns New enemies invade the Shatter! Hunt down and dispatch these scoundrels with an expanded arsenal in Bounty of Guns, a free content expansion for Wizard with a Gun. As you scour through the increasingly dangerous Shatter, pick up lucrative Bounties to earn special rewards. But beware, they come with increasingly difficult challenges. Your new foes move faster, hit harder, and possess special attacks. Defeat them to fulfill the Bounties, then claim your reward from the Bounty Mechana and unlock extraordinary new weapons. An expanded arsenal of weapons awaits you in Bounty of Guns, with more than 50 new guns, including new weapon types such as a minigun, mortar, and a two-handed SMG, each with unique properties, powders, and uses. Store your newly acquired arms and show them off on Gun Mounts, a new piece of furniture for your Tower. The Bounty of Guns update also introduces four new mini-bosses, each unique to their own biome, while Ambush Events randomly trigger as you explore the Overworld. Good luck, gunslingers. You'll need it. About the Game Wizard with a Gun is an online cooperative sandbox survival game set in a magical wilderness wrought with dangerous creatures and arcane mysteries. Embark on a journey alone or with a friend to collect, craft, and outfit your wizard however you see fit as you explore the unknown. Carefully design weapons, bullets, and furnishings for your tower home but try not to burn it all down as the magic you wield escalates beyond your control... Magical Weapon Customization Collect resources from the world and craft unique enchanted ammunition for your arsenal of guns. Combine elements for intended or suprising effects that alter the shot, blast radius, bullet trail, and even the status of the creature in your crosshairs Customized Whimsical Wizards Create a dazzling wardrobe for your magic wielder from robes and hats to armor and accessories - functional and fashionable in a way that's sure to impress. Randomly Generated Biomes Explore and uncover new sections of the world filled with deserts, swamps, tundra, and prairies - all loosely floating together through space and time after the world was fractured. Unleash cosmic power from the safety of your tower to reset the world and emerge once again to find a new layout to once familiar lands. Cooperative Adventuring Survive alone or with a wizard friend in online cooperative play to combine resources, magic, and creativity in your tower building. Or just watch it all burn down together - the choice is yours. Systemic Gameplay Experiment with new spell combinations and find out how they affect enemies and the world around you the hard way. Creative arrangements can lead to powerful creations that overwhelm your foes while untethered amalgamations can be a recipe for disaster!

_childDocuments_.review: As of today, June 14th, 2024, Galvanic Games are officially disbanding, and Wizard with a Gun will no longer receive official content updates. This is quite the difficult pill to swallow for many, myself included. I was really hoping that WWaG could be a huge success akin to Don't Starve or Terraria, but it looks like things got cut short.To be completely honest, I'm not entirely surprised by this announcement though. The game had so much potential, but it always seemed to be struggling to live up to all of it. I knew launch week was rough, with the game still feeling like Early Access and opening a day early, but I didn't think it would come to this so soon...While the content the game had was by and large quite phenomenal, it was simply over too quickly for most people at it's price point. Perhaps paid DLC could've kept it afloat a while longer, but there were simply too many issues with the base game on launch (lack of unique guns, no concrete ending, too few bullet types, missing multiplayer) that a paid DLC had to be delayed in order to fix. If the game had simply initially released in Early Access I believe many of these issues could've been prevented, and this ultimately fate be avoided entirely. But what's done is done, and I'm sad to see it go regardless. I hope that all of the developers whose passion was so apparent can find work and remain in the industry, even if not part of Galvanic.I'd like to think that someday WWaG will return, but it's a small hope. If a good modding scene could be established perhaps the game could be revived in some sort of community-guided state similar to Starbound. Perhaps some years down the line WWaG may receive some form of spiritual successor, and at least keep the concept alive. But as it stands, it seems unlikely that WWaG will receive official content anymore. I know this fate is one that befalls many indie games, but it's nonetheless hard to see happen to such a passionate and unique title.All of that said, I still would recommend the game to any potential buyers. While the initial launch was indeed rather rough, Galvanic made great strides in fixing the original issues with the game, and I can now confidently say that while the game never reached the heights of games like Terraria or Don't Starve, it is nonetheless an excellent product as it is. The music and art direction are both phenomenal, and the gameplay loop of killing, crafting, and arming yourself with new weapons and spells is indeed very fun. While it is a tragedy in itself that we will never receive the highly anticipated Breath and Bone update, the game itself is fun and engaging, and I'd highly recommend it to anyone.Farewell, Galvanic. While I wish things had turned out differently, please know that you've created something quite special to a great many people. Good luck in your future endeavors, and may you always look back fondly on your time with us within the Shatter.

_childDocuments_.review: You are not so much a "wizard with a gun" as much as "You have status effect bullets on 4 repeating guns". This game is a lot of small number increases, you don't get a new rifle, you get a rifle with -.1 reload time and +.3 range. You don't get a magic hat that lets you teleport, you get bullets you have to produce over and over to teleport, instead your magic hat gives you +50 health.Bullets have a decent range of uses, but fire bullet 1 and fire bullet 2 just enable you to hurt higher level enemies, it doesn't add anything crazy or unique. The game focuses on setting up 2 bullets in the same gun and swapping using them. "Use poison bullets to use sepsis bullets", but the issue is "coat something in oil bullets and light it on fire" is basically the same as the poison combo.The game can also be grindy at times, You want a mark 1 glove that decreases cooldowns? Go get 10 tea, which requires a total of 20 mushrooms and just as many herbs. You want to refill on that speed tea? Go to area 1 to collect mushrooms while everything dies in 1 hit. You want more fell stone for whatever reason? Time to return to area 2. You want to up the numbers on bullets? Well you need to wait for eyeball monsters to spawn since you can't find any portals.Then you get your base supplies, and look into mark 2 cooldown gloves. Oh sorry they don't exist, the first gloves are called "Reduce Gun Cooldowns I", but there is no 2. But maybe i can interest you in "more fire damage" or "More max health" or "more electrical damage", The most interesting gear upgrade for any of your armor is "increase dodge roll distance", and that really encapsulates the issue i have. Upgrades are number increases, not wizard stuff.I never felt like a wizard, i felt like hour 1 and hour 5 were functionally the same, minus a new bullet type or new biome. If this game had melee weapons (like a hammer with a shotgun shell for a head) or interesting abilities beyond "but this bullet does THIS damage type", i would be more invested in beating the game, but a friend and i hit zone 3 and decided we saw enough. Also, if you could just craft bullets once and grab resupplies, and the game was focused more on base building, or exploration (with more events and enemies, there is like single digit enemy types in a biome) i'd be a lot happier. But right now it's grinding for number increases and to restock the supplies you use to get those number increases.

_childDocuments_.review: It hurts to write this as a Don't Recommend, but I set this game down feeling frustrated. I have two main gripes that both pretty seriously impact the experience.The largest sin first, is Inventory Management. It's a crafting game, and managing limited inventory is a center point of the game. You go out on runs into a ruined world and scavenge reality for materials that you use to build and upgrade, but your backpack only has so much space. At face value, that sounds okay, but the execution is honestly just *bad*. For starters, I was playing 2 player with a friend, and we'd both have full packs with more than half the time remaining on the clock. After we hit mid game, we never once ran out of time because we always ran out of backpack space first, and it felt like we needed everything in there.But I could forgive that if it weren't for the god-awful management system awaiting you back at the base. A chest has about the same inventory space as you, so you need a ton of them, and a crafting bench can only pull resources from a chest if its within 3-4 spaces (Not sure of the exact distance, but it's pretty short.) There are... 8? different elemental crafting benches in the game, a reload station, potion crafting, smelter for metal, clothing station. The crafting benches are 2x2, and the chests have such a finite storage, that you need to have a chest for each bench, and *manually* sort out what materials are needed for what benches.Now, this wouldn't be such a problem if it weren't compounded by the fact that many materials are needed in multiple places. Leaves for one, are needed at the Reload station (for charm bullets) potion crafting (for HP brews) and biology research. Spell tomes are needed literally everywhere (They're the primary meta-progression for unlocking things) as well as Eyes of Chaos (tier 2 rarity unlocker). Iron is needed loads of places, as is wood, and... you get the picture. I spend as much time shuffling things around chests as I do actually playing the game, and Inventory Management Sim is not a fun game to play.The second big issue I have with the game is the Gameplay. It's called Wizard with a gun. You have the gun, but you won't really do any wizard stuff, ever. Every gun has 2 chambers, each can be loaded with an elemental bullet, and each chamber can have it's own enchantment, and there's different guns for different styles (Rifle, pistol, smg, shotgun, the usual suspects.) But that's the extent of your 'magic'. Everything else is magic flavored construction. You don't learn any actual spells. No healing spells. No combat spells. No buff spells. Not once will you cast a spell the entire game, unless you consider 'i shoot bullet' to be a spell. It just... feels like a let down. The sick animations and funky characters, all of that is only skin deep.At the end of the day, the only thing you'll do in combat is shoot guns, and all you'll do out of combat is manually sort your loot. There's other crafter shooters that do their job better.

_childDocuments_.review: I kept putting off making a review for this game since I really WANT to like it, I had really high hopes for it and they were inevitably crushed.The trailer was amazing it captured what I really wanted this game to be, wizards with guns that instead of casting spells, shoot with rifles and instead of having mana, they have bullets. It felt REALLY cool and that is why I was so excited.Come launch day, I buy the game, I play, I get introduced to the lore, I like it, everything is great.I beat the first "major" boss, I beat the second "major" boss and suddenly, I am bored after a couple of days.To start, here are the good things:Now, for the not so great things:In the end, I want to try to not be too harsh and say that maybe the game is not bad. If you like it, you like it. But I also cannot recommend this knowing first, that there are so many better roguelikes out there, second, even disregarding the idea of other roguelike games, that this does not do well on the most important things that it should.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good concept and a fair execution but it's a bit hollow. If this was advertised as an early access release and/or was a good 5-10 cheaper it would be fine. The game loop is cool and the death penalty hits the sweet spot of encouraging risky exploration while also giving it a decent weight.  I will definitely be changing my review in the future if things become more stable and fixed. I don't think it's an awful game, but I just don't think the game is a worthy purchase at the moment.Multiplayer is quite a bit unstable with frequent disconnects and it's only available for up to 2 players. The survival craft and decoration aspects seem to exist only to fulfill a checklist and aren't that strong outside of that (decor is plentiful, but it's very limited in what can be done with it). A lot of materials used for upgrades are relatively universal and similar in every tier. The novelty of harvesting metal with an electric weapon to get charged metal wears off pretty quick and becomes pretty dull very quickly, and its similar with each weapon type. This is exacerbated by the main resource for upgrades being killing particular enemies regardless of weapon typing. Enemies are diverse and cool for the most part, but the dodging and evading feels really inconsistent which leads to the controls feeling pretty clunky.I feel like it's a case of two systems coming together in a way that obstructs instead of enhancing.P.S.A pet peeve of mine is how some upgrades have both a positive and negative aspect, but the game only describes the positive ones and isn't clear what gets affected by the positive benefits. For instance, after testing with the carbine, increased area of effect has a massive penalty to rate of fire. Additionally, increased area of effect doesn't affect certain weapon effects like the summon ground bullet (and still gives it negative penalties).

_childDocuments_.review: Horrible. Very disappointed with the game.The gameplay itself isn't anything to write home about - it's modded Don't Starve. You have a dodge roll and a gun. There's not a single enemy with an interesting mechanic in this game, they all either just shoot at you or charge at you. There's exactly one boss I felt had thought put into it - the sniper that runs away from you and sets the arena on fire forcing you to think about positioning. The "final boss", if you could even call it that, is a joke. It's literally just a big enemy with big lasers that dies uncerimoniously. Of course, the most enticing part of the gameplay is the magic behind the guns, right? Well, that's not very interesting either. Yeah, you can mix and match, but there isn't really much build variety. You're basically just doing the same thing - damage - but in different flavors and with different levels of convoluted. You could oil your enemy and set them on fire and let the DOT do its thing, or you could just freeze them and use Lightning Strike to deal a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of damage. You could use debuffs, or you could just freeze them and use Lightning Strike. You could use different guns, or you could also just use the shotgun. The game is easy and forgiving, staying up close to an enemy isn't a threat. YOU are the threat in that scenario.The progression in this game is basically Starbound but somehow even more boring. In Starbound, you go to planet 1, mine ore 1, make backpack 1, that lets you go to planet 2, on which you mine ore 2, make backpack 2, and so on. In this game, you get resource tier 1, defeat boss 1, move onto the next biome. Prepare to farm the same resource dozens of times just to upgrade your equipment. The story is told through dialogues from NPCs and lore you can find scattered across the world. The worldbuilding is really cool and the characters are interesting, I did enjoy this part of the game. The art direction is stellar, the game has a clear style and it looks fantastic. It has an identity and a striking image. The music is kinda forgettable for the most part, but has some great tracks that I do listen to from time to time outside the game.Aaaaand here comes the kicker - there isn't much of a game. In 10-15 hours you can see everything. By everything I do mean everything, including upgrading your equipment and doing a bit of base-building... And let's not forget that they're already putting in DLCs with cosmetics. Sure, they're just cosmetics, but why are you putting in microtransactions when your game is basically half finished? There's not much to do besides just getting to the highest tier of damage or putting 100 chairs in your tower, and sure, it's a sandbox game, but there isn't much sand in this box to begin with.Get it on sale. Don't expect much.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been following this game for a few years and was looking forward to the gameplay from what the trailers showed. Taking my time in single player I was able to get all the gears within 12 hours, which basically means that I've done everything there is to do unless I want to achievement hunt.For what I paid, I feel like 12 hours is fair, and I don't regret my purchase, but the gameplay is just... . The Don't Starve inspiration is on full display, with the game claiming to be a sandbox, but the timer counting down that you need to keep adding to in order to play in the overworld feels severely limiting.The combat is very barebones. Yes, you can vary your playstyle with the bullets you craft, but it's just  I only died once, and that was to a boss.I'm not interested in decorating my base, personally, which is a big thing in the game. Others will enjoy it, and that's fine, but for me it's not fun.The lore is somewhat interesting, though a bit hard to piece together from the scattered texts you'll find. _childDocuments_.review: the game has charm and potential, the main driving/sale point of it is the art design front and center, as you will read in other reviews, the vibes that come out of this game are so interesting, but there's not much to enjoy after the first few hours of wonder wear off. the music and visuals sure are nice but the "meat and potatoes" simply aren't there to sustain it;it feels astoundingly rushed and clunky, with lot of cut corners, the more egregious one being the absurd variety of guns in your arsenal - 4, a revolver, a carbine, an smg and a shotgun. alongside with that, there aren't any FUN WACKY WOWZERS™ bullets that will amaze you into giving it another run, nor any of the enemies possess any resistences/weaknesses or seeming any differences that push you towards experimenting;the core gameplay loop is grindy, repetitive and unrewarding, even though the game sort of drives you to trying elemental combinations by dandling the upgrades in your face, the bore that is sitting through a menu - that is very unclear in several aspects (the bullet details before unlocking them, for one) - end up pushing me away from my tried and tested combination;one would think that, in a world where there is magic and automatas abound, a thing as simple as inventory/resource management would be a thing of the past, but apparently not, so be prepared for a sea of chests and a lot of back and forth between crafting stations;all in all, it feels more like a bad copy of don't starve than an homage to enter the gungeon and other decent roguelikes

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Tedious, repetitive, clunky and WAY too easy, but oozes with style and offers tons of shootin' and lootin' fun.After farming way too much and obtaining 100% of achievements, I can say the following. The game is undercooked. There are no two ways about it. Odd and downright bad design decisions aplenty. 1. Slow movement speed everywhere, even at home base — even with the lategame 45% buff. 2. Clunky mobility: you absolutely have to be able to squeeze between diagonal gaps and slide towards edges of obstacles when running directly into them. I died only once over the course of 32 hours, and it was because of the noise on the screen coupled with the game's god awful movement. 3. Bad stash system: why would you have three tiers of chests, lol?4. Guns don't matter. I played with four SMGs loaded with eight different bullet types from second region onward, and never felt like a blunderbuss or a carbine would've suited a bullet type better.5. Bullet types don't matter (for the most part). The bullet system is both overcooked and undercooked. The only reason to have multiple bullet setups is that utility bullets (the OP stuff) have cooldowns and enemies get a brief period of immunity to some of the utility effects (for example, you can't chain-freeze an enemy, but you can freeze, then stun, then stasis them). Fire is just worse poison. Anti-chaos bullets are barely better against chaos than other bullet types. Lightning is OP for resource farming. Charming bullets are too situational.6. Bloated but kinda superficial system of outfit buffs. Your mask has a slot for an enchantment, but there are no mask enchantments in the game. Wat. Also, different gear enchantments only offer an illusion of choice, as there's always the clear best option.7. Bloated loot system: each type of resource has four equivalents in different tiers, but you never know how much of each resource you'll need so you end up farming everything and inevitably end up collecting way too much of several things. Which is sort of accounted for, because you can turn anything into universally useful "arcana," but then it turns out that you need some of those lower-tier resources down the line. It's hell.8. Bad lore. This one I can forgive. Torchlight 2 had an absolutely laughable "story," and it's still one of the best games I've ever played. Seems like the same thing happened here.9. Odd choice to put the gunsmith in the overworld. You can't craft the higher-tier guns yourself. So it goes like this: you farm higher-tier resources, return to base, empty your inventory, reroll the overworld, go into the overworld to check with the gunsmith how much of each resource is needed per new gun, return to base, pick up the necessary resources, reroll the overworld, go into the overworld to craft your new guns, return to base, craft the bullets and powders for your new guns.10. The base area is way too big, and decorating isn't fun or appealing.11. Music is forgettable. None of the tracks stand out, and you won't be humming anything off the soundtrack  while making morning coffee.There are other issues like typos and minor complaints, but those are probably my biggest ones. So why am I recommending this game? Well, the simple reason is that it's still really fun. Other reviews say that the gun play is boring, but I found it quite the opposite. Gun play was by far the game's biggest strength. It's still a little clunky with k+m, but the sheer variety of effects on the screen is a delight to play around with and experience. Also, unlike most games, here you can apply all special effects (well, save for charming, duh) to bosses! You can freeze a lowly level 1 automaton AND you can freeze the final boss. I love it. More games should do it. The looting feels nice too. I'd say, give it a go. Freeze and lightning were super fun to play with. In the end credits, they promise more content in future updates. There will most likely be adjustments to gameplay, and I expect that most of my gameplay-related complaints will get solved. I'm glad I bought the game. Now I'm looking forward to version 1.1 and will do another run when it's out.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a universal negative review, it's a great idea with some problems. Read the positive reviews for the good parts, I'm going to be listing my issues with it. A lot of this could be fixed in future updates with re-balancing or similar, so I'm sure this is will lose relevance in time.The loop is similar to Crashlands, if you have played that. At the moment, this an okay podcast game, but it's not something I'm happy giving my full attention to.The advancement isn't rewarding. Even with experimenting, I find myself going back to the same loadout despite not really wanting to run the same thing over and over again. The upgrades tend to be very specific to what you're using, so 95% of the things I've unlocked I don't use after trying them out and experimenting. There's a bunch of options in theory, but they're just not all viable. It also kind of sucks when you want something you think sounds cool, unlock it, and it just falls flat. In many ways, the mainline combat abilities are way too similar, and there isn't the variety in enemy abilities to really require other loadouts. Fancy debuffs and combos don't get you anywhere near as far as just raw damage output.Advancement is gated behind specific common items that appear in certain areas, but once you get to that area, it's easy to rapidly unlock everything you want. This may sound cool, but it means you get a bunch of advancement all at once then sit around for awhile, semi-stagnant. It takes away the thrill of going for something; I discovered that you could use combinations of abilities to harvest different drops, but then found out that what I'm grinding for is a super common drop in literally my next run. Enemies slowly get more bullet-spongey, and then you get a new resource and the problem goes away. Repeat.Combat is either trivial, or running away. It really is entirely about damage output. You can either put down enough mobs fast enough where you are, or you can't. Mobility, tanking, support, dps - there really aren't multiple playstyles, at least that I've found. Damage output is the only metric. The graphics also make it difficult to figure out where enemies are, what's going to damage you, what is open space versus blocked, and so on. Everything is over-themed with the same color palate to the point of being unreadable. Whether you are hitting terrain or an enemy, an identical health bar is going to pop up and they're going to be the same color as everything else. So with a pack of mobs, you really have no clue what you're hitting or even where you are, exactly. In the middle of combat, standing in a pool of poison looks like standing on grass.Experimenting with loadout is also expensive, from a player-time perspective. Changing what is equipped on a gun means clearing out what you have from it, and losing all those resources. So if you get or unlock something early, it doesn't really matter because you can't afford to experiment with it until later when you're an area where that material is a common drop and it's dirt cheap. But at that point, you're already on to something else. I can understand expensive unlocks, I can understand expensive consumables, but what I can't understand is why experimentation and re-equipping yourself is expensive. There's no gameplay there, why does it take resources?All of this is kinda going towards one thing and one thing only - it's not worth doing anything except advancing the main story. Don't bother unlocking things, don't bother grinding, because all will be opened up trivially if you just advance. And advancing that is incredibly easy. Rather than unlocking upgrades to allow you to tackle harder bosses, the bosses seem to... unlock upgrades? It's a bit cart-before-the-horse, and run after run it's the same thing.

_childDocuments_.review: Some fun, fresh ideas for a roguelike.  I always like it when there's a storyline explanation for the "roguelike" elements and this one has a nice one.Seems like some interesting possibilities for the spell system but i'm several hours in and it seems pretty pointless.  I've yet to really care that deeply about the more advanced spell combos (eg douse an enemy in oil, then set them on fire).  Seems cool but usually is overkill, just blasting with fire/poison/lightning is enough.Additionally, even if i wanted to explore the spell combos, the game doesn't really give you enough materials to explore them all.  Sure you can farm the mats specific to that spell, but ultimately there's a couple base materials that are needed for all upgrades, and that tends to be the limiting factor.  So maybe there's some fun to be had with a wider variety of spells but 1) I don't get enough materials to explore them and 2) I don't feel like I really need to, the base spells have been fine for blasting through everything.  I think I've died twice in several hours of playing: once due to a new boss fight setup and another just because I wasn't paying attention and was in an inventory screen or something.So they've made it unnecessarily difficult to explore the only interesting part of the game.  The gunplay?  Totally generic.  Nothing compared to the variety of weaponplay you get in a game like Hades.  Variety of enemies?  Basically none.  I've been through the first two zones and they're all pretty interchangeable.  Dash, stomp, shoot.  Again, look at Hades and then look at this.  QoL?  These games all have the same base crafting/inventory mechanics, and so many of them go through the same loop: get obvious player feedback after release and then release simple QoL changes over the course of a few months.  Let us stack items into ALL nearby chests! Let us craft using materials in nearby chests! (see: Terraria or Grounded)  Let us upgrade existing chests and move chests while things are still in it, and for GODS SAKE let us open a chest while another player is in it (see v rising).  This isn't 1997 Diablo 1, you should be able to preventing item duping in a multiplayer game without hurting the player experience.So, mildly entertaining, some really interesting novel ideas, great idea to mix these genres, and I feel like they did 98% of the work to make a great game then just didn't really think deeply about what makes actual interesting gameplay (see: Ship of Fools for another game that seriously forgot this step).

_childDocuments_.review: I received this game from the PAX West 2023 booth, which was awesome as Devolver always does a great PAX booth.I like this game, it's charming and has some fairly robust and potentially interesting systems in place. However, I cannot recommend it. While the system's that make this game's core are interesting, they're just far too clunky with arbitrary and sometimes outdated implementation. The game has resource gathering, researching, crafting, and building. The gathering is as you expect, break a thing, item drops, grab item, store item. It's fine. Could be better, but that can be said about most "survival" games.The research is just, like, god -- there are just countless things to research in this game. You research how to make a bullet type, then you research a research table to research higher tiers of that bullet type. There are bullets to heal things, bullets to charm things, bullets to pacify things. Then there tiers like Healing Bullet 1 that can be upgraded six times -- but not to Healing Bullet 2, no, that's a different bullet that can also be upgraded six times. Why? This just feels like a skill tree that is attached to a building instead of a menu. Oh yeah, forgot to mention, after you research the research tables you have to build the research tables in order to research your research.The crafting suffers from inventory management, small storage containers, and a lack of a universal ingredient pool in your home base. Standard for "survival games" but still not good. Just let the player store everything in their home base and let anything built in the home base have access to those items -- no matter where it is built or where the item is stored within the base. It is not enjoyable to run between chests trying to figure out where you put that one rare resource for that one thing you were going to do later after you got that other rare resource. Building is fine other than that it doesn't offer any real practical benefit. You have to build every one of your crafting and research stations -- and there are loads. Fine, whatever, I already griped about that above. The other things you can build are things like various wall types and decorations. Actually, scratch that, the walls offer no real functional benefit unless you want to cheese enemies, they might as well fall under the decoration category. As a reminder, I like this game, it's just not a game I can recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently at about 4 hours. Beat the first boss, about 3 or 4 cogs before the second "world" boss. Watched some YouTube reviews and other steam reviews to compare how I feel about Wizard w/ a Gun.Lots of complaints about the 5 min timer before chaos overwhelms. Many people complaining about crafting and inventory management. Other complaints about overall difficulty and slow progression/game play.My take:So far, I love wizard w/ a gun. All the complaints made are valid when i watch videos. All of the videos I've seen for day 1 full release videos are using a controller instead of keyboard mouse. Due to this, intuitively aiming is more difficult and quickly shift-clicking/ctrl-clicking helps a ton with inventory management.As far as difficulty, it's a nice medium. I feel as though it is a little easier than I would want currently, but that is because I created solid synergies with my guns. All videos I have seen of day 1 reviews had just weird ammo mix ups that don't make much sense at all.Tip: put oil w/ fire, lightning w/ stun bullet, and the freeze bullet with the cold bullet. (To me this is obvious, but after watching videos... i dont have much faith in some of those reviewers) Having 3 different guns also helps alot with ammo supplies and using the right tool for the problem. Guns have their own allotment of ammo. Meaning if I have 4 revolvers, they all have their own ammunition pools and do not share ammunition with others. This is a great thing and enables you to bring in PLENTY of ammo after getting your second gun approx. 10-15 min after the tutorial.Timer:5 minutes isn't much time. It goes by quick. Get in, get out. It's a slight extraction shooter. But, if you kill a chaos spawn you get +30sec to the timer, and if you kill a larger chaos spawner you'll get 3+ minutes to the timer. This is plenty enough to fill up your inventory, get out and start crafting/upgrading.Timer end:Really, it's not that difficult. If you keep moving in a line towards the exit when the timer hits 0:00 you will be plenty fine 9/10 times. On top of this, the mechanic needs to stay specifically for farming arcane.Crafting/inventory management:If you are somewhat organized it is easy to know where all of your stuff is. Also, chests connect to any crafting station if they are touching. For the people that complain about how slow the smelter is. Put a second one down. Some of these complaints are so extremely invalid, because when people played vanilla minecraft 10+ years ago, they didn't complain about how slow that smelter went. They just put a second one down. I also feel the crafting is very rewarding and is amazingly balanced between cog/main story progression and craftability/obtainability of resources. When you first enter a biome expect to grind resources for a trip or two, upgrade your ammo and skills then go burn down the world. "Potions/consumables" are also extremely cheap to craft and use. One healing soup only costs 2 leaves, which takes 3-6 bullets to get with the revolver. 1 wood crafts 100 rnds of basic revolver ammo. I believe 3 or 6 basic revolver ammo will cut down a small tree, giving you 1-3 wood. Just numbers to help you understand there isn't much grind for the resources, but you do have to prioritize them. Visuals: greatAudio: greatSoundtrack: honestly Kind-of mid.Shooting and burning everything down with huge trails of fire, 10/10.Gameplay loop:Enter biome. Spend 1 or 2 trips obtaining the biome resources. Upgrade ammo/skills. Kill. Kill. Kill. Get cog. Kill kill kill. Upgrade more. Kill kill kill. More cogs. Kill kill kill. Upgrade, kill world boss. Repeat.Monkey brain enjoy.TLDR: good game. Good difficulty. Wouldn't recommend playing with a controller. Gameplay loop is solid if you're fine with getting resources, crafting/upgrading, killing, collecting cogs, big boss and repeat. Overall very well polished and a creative game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game just came out so this review is subject to change. Personally, I do not recommend it right now. The player character customization is super cute tho. I'm living for the Final Fantasy Black Mage picrew vibes.Tl;dr: This game feels like it needed a few more months of polish in some key places.Overworld + combat doesn't feel great and it feels monotonous to progress. Base and resource management felt like it was wasting my time even more.I think combat + movement tweaks, changes to the upgrade economy, and QOL improvements could fix it all. Long:The overworld exploration (slow codex scanning for recipes and lore) and boss hunting (gathering Gears from minibosses to get closer to the Area Bosses per expedition) feel a little monotonous, even with the urgency of the 5+ minute timer until the expedition gets more dangerous with Chaos enemies and ground tiles being destroyed. The combat (dodges + gun feel) doesn't feel good enough to make up for the monotony. Movement is slow, even with the 5% movement speed boost I have upgraded my shoes with. No enemies have really felt particularly interesting or threatening, I haven't died yet.So, onto the base building. This is what is killing me. Spell/weapon crafting + research felt like it was wasting my time with the poor storage management experience. You have a hub area where you place furniture and utility objects. Crafting stations, research stations, etc. There are 8 distinct spell research stations for different schools of gunmancy. There is a bullet crafting bench, a potion crafting bench, a cauldron, an evaporator for purifying liquids, a composter, normal and lightning furnaces, and several other smaller crafting stations. This is just too much when storage is not universal. Your inventory is 21 slots. Small chests  are 18 slots, and medium chests are 24. These chests take up 1x1 tiles of space. Crafting and research stations take up 2x2. Chests can supply stored resources to crafting and resource stations if they are on one of 8 adjacent blocks. Because of the size of these crafting stations, at most you can have 4 of them adjacent to a chest. It looks ugly and is clunky to use, often causing the wrong thing to be selected on M+K. On top of that, it isn't even that much of a benefit because research and crafting stations use mostly the same resources. So you've gonna have to either split your resources between all of your crafting station chests unnecessarily, or you'll check a recipe (and probably tag it as an objective so you don't forget what it needs, which is a good feature!) and then go grab the stuff from whatever storage you have it in and walk back. Even with these crafting stations that can grab resources! It's just needlessly time consuming and necessitates annoying micromanagement of inventory and expanded storage. Augh!I hope I can update this review with good news some time soon. Shrug.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish steam allowed for more neutral ratings. So, my boyfriend and I played this game together and after we finished, we decided this game was pretty good, but somewhat of a mixed bag. I'm grateful I decided to play this game with him for a lot of reasons, but regardless, there were flaws that became more apparent to both of us as we went on. I understand the initial mixed rating now because this game would've been nearly impossible to finish alone.To communicate my thoughts more clearly, I’ll be listing my thoughts in a list of pros and cons.Pros:-The art and animations are lovely. The world is really well crafted, and you can tell there was a lot of passion poured into the look and feel of this game. The way your character moves feels really satisfying, with the pace being particularly noteworthy. While the lore of the world is a little inconsistent and requires a lot of reading, I found everything we discovered to be fascinating and enjoyed crafting theories on everything.-The general mechanics are pretty fun, albeit a little repetitive (more on that in the cons section). This game, outside of a few parts, also felt like a fair challenge and it did feel like upgrades stuck.- The enemy diversity really helps elevate this game. While a lot of the characters were reskins and had similar attacks, it didn’t feel that way because of the unique designs and animations. The sound design of character reactions and attacks were really satisfying too. You could feel the anticipation and the attack of many characters movements, and it made dodging and focusing feel very rewarding.-The time loop function was honestly pretty fun. I’ve played a few time loop games at this point and I liked how that feature wasn't very frustrating outside of making explorations have a time limit of like 7 minutes in game. While it did make some of the dialogue pretty repetitive and made the characters a bit underdeveloped (which is disappointing when you’re trying to make your audience feel connected to certain characters) it’s not like the game forces you to interact with the characters and sit through the same dialogue over and over again, which is often an issue I have with time loop games (even the ones I like). I also enjoy how the actions you do over the course of the game feel like they matter, especially at the end when you fight the final boss. It was a game that successfully used time looping without making you loose progress or developments, which is something that I really like and appreciate.-I liked how, if you so desire, you can change the look of your character to different outfits. While the only options are the skins that you were presented at the beginning of the game, I was very appreciative of the fact that you were given the option to diversify your clothing after building a clothing station. -I liked the ground laying gun! While you need a lot of resources for it and it can be a little slow moving, setting down more places to move felt satisfying to me.-I enjoyed the music of this game.Cons:-The gameplay gets really repetitive over time. The fact that there are no spell casting options, nor any minigames to spice up the gameplay makes the lack of getting new abilities all the more apparent. While the actual gameplay loop is pretty fun, it gets old pretty fast when there’s nothing else to do outside of shooting and scanning stuff. The scanning was kinda a chore, given how interruptible it is. There isn’t really even a leveling up system outside of clothe charming and bullet crafting and even then, those have their own flaws. There wasn’t any sort of signal to show that you were really progressing outside of character dialogue. While I understand that adding certain mechanics is much harder to implement than people make it out to be, it still would have been nice to have.-There were multiple sessions my boyfriend and I would have to stop what we were doing to resource hunt. Resource hunting was such a grind because there was a 50/50 chance that the resources we needed would even drop. The crafting process also was not very fun. You often would have to just wait around with no other options for an item to finish being refined at a table so you could craft some bullets you needed.-A lot of the bullets were not useful. While there were a few that were effective in certain areas (i.e. the frost bullets in the desert) the majority of bullets were not useful. The only truly effective bullets were the fire bullets, making our only incentive to research the fire bullets as much as possible so we could realistically fight the enemies. The only reason any other bullets were researched was because I decided to try them.- I wanted to charm my clothes with different abilities, but you can only charm an item with one charm and the majority of the charms were not useful, leaving me to stick to health charms because they were the only useful charms for me.-There were several areas that were straight up unfun/unfair. The desert immediately comes to mind for me. The enemies are insanely unbalanced and there are a million of them. A single hit from a lot of enemies in the desert area would half your health, making the sheer number of them impossible to fight. There were several times that there were so many enemies the game would lag, causing your characters to barely move and get hit. We started taking long routes to avoid enemies so we could survive/finish on time. The desert almost felt tacked on, like the devs felt like the game was too short/not hard enough so they made this unbalanced area that is unavoidable because it requires resources you need.-If it wasn’t for multiplayer, I would have easily been soft locked in multiple areas causing me to have to restart the game. Chaos enemies completely destroy and erase the ground around you when you fight them. You need a lot of resources for your ground layer gun to build your way to places, and I wasn’t aware of this at the beginning of the game. There were several points my boyfriend or I were stuck on a single block and either had to hope the enemy would come back to hopefully destroy the block and respawn us back onto the map, or wait until your partner could come and save you.-The final boss and ending were both anticlimactic in many ways. The fight that directly proceeded it was incredibly difficult. Considering we finished the final boss in less than 10 minutes, whereas the previous one required a lot of stopping to resource grind and try again, it made it easy to notice. Which sucks because the actual design and phases of the level were the most satisfying at that level, and yet it was so easy to defeat in comparison to basic enemies. -There are 2 endings, and the first one was disappointing. It’s not clear what you’re supposed to do to get the good ending when not doing a wiki search (you have to golden bounty hunt then charm former bosses). I wish that the history between your character and the other characters was explored. It was a little disappointing to not see, but ultimately not a deal breaker.I know I’ve listed a lot of lengthy cons here, but I really do have a lot of respect for this game. The reason I listed the flaws was because I really enjoyed the game overall and would love to see it improve. Unfortunately, I don’t think that’s an option now that the company that made it went under. I was lucky I got to spend my time playing it with my boyfriend and it was a really good bonding experience. I think it really helped us spend quality time to get to know each other. I’m really grateful Galvanic Games was able to add the better together feature before their untimely disbandment. While this game absolutely could have been fixed with a few more patches and I would have loved to see a local co-op option, I think everyone can agree that for what this game is, it’s pretty solid and the studio did not deserve to go out in the way that it did.  Best of luck out there team!

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I didn't enjoy myself that much while playing Wizard with a Gun. The game does feel like it was rushed or lacking in certain areas, like the basebuilding. Which is hardly even there at all. The most you can do is pretty it up with decorations but there's not a whole lot of room to build on. Spells are pretty lackluster in what you have, since synergies are hardly a thing you even have to bother with. Poison seems to just be the best option for damage, and all the other options are kind of useless. Fire especially is more of a detriment, which is a huge shame as an avid arsonist.Also the game is just incredibly easy with no real difficulty scaling? Your gear gets better but the enemies hardly feel like they evolve with your gear. My friend and I were very surprised that the final boss was just out in the open world, and had like 3 moves. Not to mention it dying very quickly and easily, which left us underwhelmed.That's not to say that this game is all middling. The art is great and very charming, and the sound design was really good for the most part. I greatly enjoy when the music changes depending on your situation i.e. a low pass filter being applied as you get cold in the snow biome. I'm also a big fan of just being able to change your character's outfit at all times and having cosmetics be unlocked the more you progress.I do wish that steam had a mixed option for recommendations instead of yes/no, but for the time being I'm leaving my recommendation as a no considering the game left us in a state of ''That's it?''Hopefully this is remedied in the future with more updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, don't expect a Don't Starve with a weapon, this isn't the game, don't be fooled.Wizard With a Gun is a Roguelike survival game, your deaths only make you perfect your techniques even more.It is possible to craft four different types of weapons, but its difference lies in its ammo, where we started with a simple ammo made of wood, but over time we discovered the vast arsenal of spells and ammo manipulation. There is a huge variety of ammo to be crafted, including fire, ice, poison, lightning, thunder, oil, ammo to calm wildlife to become an ally, healing and resurrection ammo and many others, in addition, it is also It is possible to craft a variety of consumable potions.Its world consists of a small starting area, where we can collect some basic resources to progress, and as we advance, the world expands to new biomes with new challenges. The world is randomly generated, but some elements will always spawn in certain locations (NPC's for example).I really liked the game because I love about wizard/sorcery themed games, I also really enjoy the Rougelike style of play.In my opinion, it's a good game, but it's worth highlighting its negative points and its short playing time, which can frustrate certain players.

_childDocuments_.review: After beating this game, I can say that it's honestly not worth it. The premise is interesting, but the gameplay is boring and repetitive. The guns and spells aren't very interesting and there's very little synergy. You'll end up using the same 2-4 spells pretty much the entire game. The "terrain" is destructible but this just means that rocks and trees and other things will block your bullets making fighting in certain areas a headache at best and downright infuriating at worst. The game is insanely easy in that you can get through the game by stacking lightning strike bullets on carbines and 1-2 shots most enemies making pretty much every other bullet and gun pointless. Dying doesn't really happen, but when it does it's absolutely punishing. You lose all of your inventory and your run ends if solo. If playing with another person, and they die, there's a 10 second window in which you can revive them and in order to revive them you have to stand on top of them and hold a button down for nearly 20 seconds, which is impossible to do when enemies are constantly shooting you and interrupting your revive cast. There is a revive bullet, which I never bothered to use since we only died once while playing so maybe that's better, but still. You are constantly having to manage your inventory because of all of the crafting materials for the different bullets and such. There is so much cross-over in crafting mats between bullets, upgrades, potions, and construction that all require the same mats so it's a neverending grind to ensure you have enough of something to craft what you need. My favorite part of a lot of these games is building and decorating the base, but the game pretty much forces you to use materials for everything else and basically makes the base building an endgame activity.There's more I can say, but I've probably said enough and nobody is going to read this far anyway. You are better off spending your money on something else.

_childDocuments_.review: Wizard with a Gun isn't one of the best games I've ever played, but it did enough cool stuff with weapon modification, art design and music, that I'd easily recommend it to someone looking for a coop game with a decent amount of depth. You're stuck in an infinite timeloop where you gather materials and upgrade yourself and your arsenal. The base-building aspect isn't too time consuming, and you can clear the whole thing with a friend in under 20 hours.It was interesting enough for me to want to see a more refined sequel or expansion down the road, but due to the closure of Galvanic Games, I don't think that's going to happen. Best of luck to the former devs in their future endeavors, wish it had gone differently.

_childDocuments_.review: I had been waiting for Wizard with a gun to come out for the last year when i saw it was teased. My mind immediately went to Don't Starve together but with guns and I couldn't be more excited. Unfortunately it fell short of my expectations.Wizard with a gun plays more like a short twin stick shooter with some very small rpg elements. For most of the game i found myself using the same 3 elemental bullets and the combinations the game present you with see completely pointless when those bullets just out damage everything. This game needed more stress towards elemental weaknesses, enemies maybe even immune to certain types. However this is part of the games shortcomings, it gives you options but there is always a clear best option. Combat besides the point, the game itself has no survival elements besides the repeated "ticking down of the clock", which i found myself not scared about at all as the enemies you encounter slowly trickle in even after long periods of time in a loop. Wizard with a gun has its charm as a game of its own, but it left me wishing it had more depth and utilized the more interesting bullet combinations you can make.

_childDocuments_.review: It really feels like this game was supposed to be something bigger than it currently is. The mechanics in the game step all over their own feet with how conflicting they are. It plays kinda like an extraction shooter or roguelite with metaprogression where the emphasis is on shooting enemies with ridiculous spells but it has elements of base building, inventory management, and the remnants of a Don't Starve style survival game that really just get in the way of that and make it feel really tedious.The only buildings you'd want to build in the actual map where the action takes place besides maybe walls and floors are the ammo loading station and potion crafting station which just feels clunky to do. You'd probably not want to build walls anyway because fighting enemies in open space is easier and you home base never gets attacked so there's no reason to have walls at all and boss fights take place in entirely separate arenas. Furnace type crafting stations take a lot of time to transform ingredients into ones you need so you either sit around and wait or go into the overworld so that it's done by the time you come back. Inventory management sucks and even if the crafting stations have some QoL (they pull from the chests placed beside them automatically) it just gets in the way of advancing your tech tree so you can get stronger and go out into the overworld again. The consumables system looks like it was supposed to be more complex but instead we have various heal over time items and one or two buffs plus some anti-weather potions.Supposedly the most fun part of this game would be the gun building; it's in the title. Gun building is actually really shallow. You have lots of ammo types that deal various elemental effects and you can attach multiple buffs to the ammo so they do things like go faster, do more damage, have AoE, etc... but it's not really as interesting as you'd hope and the novelty wears off quickly.This is a game that feels like it either doesn't know what it wants to be or was rushed out the door too fast to truly take shape and I really hope it improves with updates over time but it's hard for me to see that happening when this is the framework they have to work with.

_childDocuments_.review: Not bad, but WAY too short for this asking price. I've beaten it in 13 hours and I wasn't speeding either, I honestly feel ripped off.There are other problems too:*The game feels unfinished and it's not optimized properly - it stutters and drops frames constantly. *The final fight and the ending were so anticlimactic I actually laughed when the credits rolled. *There's a lot of room for improvement when it comes to QOL features. *Some interactions don't work, like for example I've never seen an order bullet crit, even with crit chance powder x3.*Game's too easy for a rougelite. _childDocuments_.review: Hello. My first serious review because I really, really looked forward to this game and it hit a lot of the points/aesthetics I am looking for in games these days. I do recommend giving it a chance if you like a chill time, casting spells and being a rootin' tootin' shootin' wizard. If you're looking for a challenge however, and you have a lot of video game literacy, you're probably better off looking elsewhere.This game is a tad too easy (which is FINE) and I tore through most of it so quickly I became afraid that I wasn't going to be able to relish it fully (I guess that's what 2nd playthrus are for). I wish that there was a difficulty slider. There's a mid game area where you can watch a bunch of effects cascade into each other and things can get pretty dangerous but that was something I could easily manage still.I think this game is probably a lot more fun in co-op, i played alone for the most part, where you could probably create a lot of crazy effects whereas i stood behind my shotgun and just used the same couple of bullets for the entire play through. There's a lack of impact I feel when it comes to bullets and effects and it just boils down to what kind of wizard you want to be or what play style you like (something you'll probably decide on pretty early on in the game.)Overall, it's a fun little clicky time management shooter. I think this game has a lot of potential and could become something more. I'm excited to see if the devs will take this game even further.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a decently fun game. You repeatedly enter a dungeon and as you defeat bosses, the map gets bigger each time you go in. When you return back to your base you can upgrade your bullets and research new ones with materials you gathered in the dungeon. You can also put modifiers on bullets such as homing or leaving a fire trail.Combat was somewhat simple. All you really do to fight is shoot them with different bullets. Most enemies have very simple attack patterns. A large majority just have a charge attack where they project a line and then charge down that line.The final boss was a bit underwhelming but still good.Story was absent and lacking. I don't remember at all or maybe the game didn't even tell us why we were fighting the chaos.The crafting and inventory management in this is game is a bit unfun. Your different crafting stations, which you have like 20 of, can pull from nearby chests. This is a great feature and I greatly appreciate it but it has a range of 3 blocks or something. That means that you'll never be able to have all of your stations pull from the same set of chests since there's so many different ones. If they're gonna include the pull from chests feature why not just go the distance and make it so you can pull from anywhere in your base?I also hate how inconsistent things stack. Some have a max stack of 20, some 99, some go above 99. You can decorate your base which is pretty cool. I would have probably done a bit more of it if it weren't for the fact it requires precious materials you use to research and craft bullets.Overall it's a solid game. Kind of short depending on how you play. Its good but I would recommend waiting for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The closure of Galvanic Games is an important lesson to all developers on how a strong aesthetic and marketing campaign cannot save a shallow game from impending failure. It does well in capturing the atmosphere of an untamed, savage land destined for ruin, and there are a great number of tools with the potential to bring out unique gameplay, but it fails to create any meaningful experiences for the game's presence to last.This game commits the sin of being so average to the point that it is simply unmemorable. For a game that encourages some form of exploration, the progression of your weaponry is very linear, and the crafting mechanic is nothing special to talk about. It does nothing to innovate on its simple enemy attack patterns. There is little incentive to swap much between different gun elements in second-to-second gameplay when each zone is themed on a certain element with an obvious immunity, without trying to mix different types of enemies together.There is supposedly some narrative explanation to the world's happenings, but I cannot comment on this as it is presented in the least interesting manner possible, laid across huge walls of pure text that few would bother to skim past and even get the slightest clue.It's an uninteresting game loop of collecting enough time gears so that you can eventually reach the zone's boss and break up the monotony for a while, before going back on the time gear hunt. There isn't really much else to do besides bounties, which are admittedly the features which I've had the most fun in this game. It sends you out to defeat a normal enemy with buffed stats, range, and an additional random ability, and rewards you with a unique gun outside of the game's linear progression. It's not anything particularly special, but they're the only engagement spikes in the game besides bosses.The way the game functions is that there are 2 worlds. One of them is your home world that acts as your base where your crafting stations and chests will persist, while the other is the apocalyptic world that procedural-generates and resets every time you enter it, based on your current progression. You have limited time in the apocalyptic world until hostile creatures start to spawn unendingly with the power to eat away from the world's flooring. It sounds threatening, but it ends up simply being an opportunity to endlessly farm those enemies for resources until you're spent, without any hard limit or superboss to provide urgency.Speaking of which, part of what makes your actions less meaningful in this game is the fact that your base is completely isolated from the apocalyptic world where all the enemies and resources are, without any threats or looming dangers. Granted, you can also craft temporary facilities in the apocalyptic world to prolong your self-sufficiency, but long trips end up being meaningless as you are hard-capped to only collecting a limited number of time gears before you have to return and reset that world. It embraces a very passive gameplay style without any opportunities to go beyond the given path.One more thing. For some reason, this game is horribly optimized and is prone to severe lag as you progress and open more areas in that one apocalyptic world, especially in multiplayer. I suspect this is due to entities not unloading when off-screen.Overall, this game is a waste of time, in a mediocre fashion. If you need a fast-paced twinstick shooter in an apocalyptic setting, go play Nuclear Throne. If you want a hostile procedural-generated survival game with a focus on resource management and combat, play Don't Starve Together instead.
