_childDocuments_.review: Right now, on November 2020, this game has the worst reviews a game can have. Why? Those reviews will make you think this game belongs with Big Rigs, Daikatana or Superman 64, but the game is certainly not abysmal. The disastrous release created a tsunami of bad reviews for many reasons: the outrage for feeling ripped off, having idealized the original too much (and believe me, you had to idealize the first game to love it. I know it because I was one of those players!)... Now, the reputation of this game is probably harmed forever, but believe me, it's a very solid 7/10 game, nicely done and very playable. I don't know if it will ever be judged fairly after this, but believe me,  it's not that bad as they say.This release had a lot of bugs at launch but hey, try to release a game during COVID while working from home and see how it turns out. They actually did a very good job in creating the game itself, but it needed more testing and bug-fixing. Way more. Anyway, I have played it to completion getting 100% of the achievements using the Level Select trick to avoid extra playthroughs (about that: sadly, the difficulty achievements don't stack. *That* was a bad decision, developers). And there's no doubt that the game is very playable right now because a big section of the game is based on stealth and it works as intented. Have you ever played a game with ill-conceived and badly executed stealth insta-fail sections? It can be the worst thing in gaming, next to escort missions. But here, they pulled it off, so that's how you see they knew what they were doing.The graphics look great to me, finding a good balance between realistic and cartoony, IMHO. Other people think they look too realistic (well, they actually say "this remake has no cell-shading!, which is not factually correct), but if you want plain, simplistic graphics, you can always go back to the original. Loading times in this remake are instantaneous (a quality-of-life feature we all loved in Super Meat Boy and Hotline Miami but that you can't find in many FPS. In fact, I only remember the also-recent Ghostrunner right now), and that's really nice. The game just sends everything back to the checkpoint point and spawns everything back in the blink of an eye after you click "Continue". It mostly works (well, only once in 20 hours I got sent beneath the ground, falling to my death in the digital void beneath the map), trying to set you a little bit above the ground with a nice "drop in" effect. Again: maybe when you read this you are already used to the absence of load times in your cool PS5 or Xbox Series X, but believe me, every FPS player hated to wait for minutes until the game was ready again. That was the standard back then. So yes, this game has great features, and reviews should mention that.So everything looks just how I remembered it (memories are deceitful: I have just watched some videos of the original Gamecube-era game and it looks terribly blocky and simplistic), and the cool-as-heck dynamic music and voice-over (with David Duchovny as the English-language lead, Daniel Beretta as the French lead, Ramón Langa as the Spanish lead, etc.) are exactly the same, sounding great. What's not to enjoy? XIII is a nice old-school shooter with lots of style and content (it's quite long and varied), they did a great job and I think it deserves to be played. I enjoyed these 20 hours, and I know that I will play it again.

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome back, agent! "XIII" (2020) aims to revive the cult classic from 2003 with a fresh coat of cel-shaded paint and updated gameplay. Unfortunately, this remake struggles to balance nostalgia with modern expectations, delivering a mixed experience that’s as intriguing as it is frustrating.The game’s aesthetic is its standout feature. The cel-shaded graphics give XIII a unique, comic book-like style, staying true to the original's roots. The visual design is playful and vibrant, evoking the feel of a graphic novel coming to life. However, this charm is often overshadowed by technical issues. Bugs, glitches, and inconsistent frame rates can pull you out of the immersion, reminding you that this isn’t quite the polished update fans had hoped for.You step into the shoes of XIII, an amnesiac super-soldier accused of assassinating the President. The storyline remains compelling, with conspiracy theories and espionage woven into the narrative. Voice acting is generally solid, but some performances lack the punch needed to elevate the drama, leaving certain moments feeling flat.Gameplay tries to modernize the classic first-person shooter mechanics, but it’s a mixed bag. Gunplay feels satisfying when it works, but clunky controls and AI issues can turn intense firefights into frustrating endeavors. Stealth sections offer a nice change of pace, yet they too suffer from inconsistent enemy behavior, making some segments feel like a chore.Sound design is a hit and miss. The soundtrack captures the retro vibe, complementing the comic book aesthetic perfectly. However, audio bugs can disrupt the experience, with some sounds cutting out or misfiring at crucial moments.In the end, "XIII" (2020) is a nostalgic trip marred by technical setbacks. It’s a game with a lot of heart but lacking in execution. For fans of the original, it might still hold some appeal, but new players may find its charm buried under a heap of frustrating flaws. Approach with caution, agent—you might need more than a few retries to see this mission through.

_childDocuments_.review: A remake of the beloved original 2003 version by Ubisoft Paris (now humbly called XIII - Classic).It had a rough start on its way to provide a worthy modern successor, when overambitious goals met a tight deadline and limited development resources at the developer PlayMagic.Luckily, Microids (the publisher), despite the disastrous reviews, still contracted another team, Tower Five, to address a lot of issues and even though it's not a perfect superior version of the classic one due to the large band-aiding, it's perfectly playable and the multiplayer is stable and has smooth gameplay.Unfortunately though, this is the only treatment done, bringing the minimum of playability that is expected for any game, inclusive a different graphic style that is closer to the original, but still has its drawbacks.The single player, when it comes to the general gameplay, now does smoothly, but lacks a few cutscenes, means someone experiencing the XIII story for the first time would be thrown into a new environment without knowing their actual purpose at that place. Likewise, other details are missing (like being able to shoot down the chopper on Brighton Beach).The multiplayer, while providing an incredibly smooth gameplay thanks to the foundational overhaul of the player controls, it severly lacks of maps, modes, customization features.The  is literally a matchmaking service with zero options. The only mode is "XIII kills", an up to 13 player large deathmatch session. The maps, player name and skin are picked randomly. But it doesn't matter anymore since the matchmaking is broken. It's unknown whether the service itself is still functional or if it only struggles at achieving a match within a smaller playerbase. It was more or less reliable when the update rolled out and many players wanted to try it out, but obviously the number declined and several recent tests with fellow users actively trying to join a game together haven't succeeded since.The  is an existing option from the initial remake version. This one has not received any updates and is completely different to the online multiplayer. It provides three maps to choose from as well as deathmatch and team deathmatch with a max of 4 players of which each one is required to provide a game controller. You might come to the idea of using Steam's Remote Play Together in order to bypass the broken online service, but given the latency in this mode (and the awkward splitscreen view) it's anything but an enjoyable option.It's great that Microids contracted another development studio to remedy the most severe flaws, but it's the bare minimum you'd expect from any game, yet they called it a day for good, not caring about the still heavily blank multiplayer that would play great and attract players if it had actual working online servers, a leaderboard and the features from the original.

_childDocuments_.review: 39,99€ seems a lot for this, considering that some people even own the original game and it's state on release (at least they made release day..) . I've bought the old XIII twice now, now on steam and once back then in CD Form "2003-Style" and I loved it! It was one of my fondest multiplayer experiences from back in the day and I loved the story, too.I then recently played it again, the Steam version, but didn't enjoy it quite as much. I seem to have forgotten many bad moments of the 2003 XIII in the past 17 years. The hit reg was horrible back then, plus the saving mechanics were all 100% manual, no autosaves. nothing was done automatically. Then there's the max distance of weapons, weird controls and horrible resolution and graphics (WE'RE SO SPOILED NOWADAYS!!). That being said, it was still a great game, and I had fun, but I wanted the remaster!!Now it came, it launched and honestly it ain't that bad, but it COULD have done sooooo much better and for what got delivered NOW the price seems kinda high. Maybe it will become decent after a few patches? Right now, only the single player campaign is enjoyable, as you can kinda get past the odd-stuff, like most prominently the extremely easy difficulty of the game and the lousy NPC-AI. I played on the 2nd hardest difficulty, thinking it would be hard. It was not. I died precisely when I meant to, that one exact time, 50% through the campaign. The original XIII has better AI! And that is not a joke. The damage inflicted by enemies on the HARDEST difficulty is so minimal.. the only thing that does damage is the rocket launcher, that thing "could" potentially kill you. Plus the NPCs barely move unless they get alerted and want to run to an alarm. Back in the old XIII, you didn't "just" finish a level on the hardest difficulty. It was a walk in the park, the new park!!The multiplayer feels horrible.. I don't even want to put time and effort into it at this moment. It needs a lot of patching!The only positive things to be said:Good graphics overhaul, looks good. Needs optimisation, though.Still fun, although too easy. Story is still good. There's waaay more enemies to fight now. Games has collectibles and achievements, autosaves and a new mission select for those who might care. Then there's the better feel to weapons and better hit reg in single player. You can finally shoot at enemies with pistols and rifles over 30m away from you! (It's kinda broken and makes the game easy, especially if you can aim like me). The gunplay and movement actually feel good, it's a start!!! :)Soo final statement:-Fixed some aspects of the old XIII-Created MANY new problems-Needs fixes, big patchesWhat has the be said: Patience! It might go somewhere.. there's still hope for a postive multiplayer experience in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: XIII:~~~ President Sheridan has been assassinated and the American people can’t believe what just happened. The entire country is gobsmacked! Who would want to kill the well-beloved President? Well, holding the office of Leader of the Free World has its . . . how can we put it . . . deadly downside.  As the FBI tries to figure out who is behind the assassination, you wake up somewhere on a beach with a dreadful headache, and you don’t seem to recall who you are or what happened to you.  The only hint you have is the tattoo on your upper left Pectoral muscle and that everyone is after you. That’s a good start, shall we say?! Good luck to you XIII!XIII (2020) is a remake if the iconic (2003) action/first person shooter game. This version was developed by PlayMagic and Published by Microids on the Steam platform on 11th of November 2020. The game is also available on PS4, Xbox One and Nintendo Switch.Before I start this review, I would like to mention that I am a very big fan of XIII; I purchased the original game in 2003 on it’s release day and also purchased the game (XIII Classic) when it hit the Steam store a few months back. I also vividly remember the bugs that the 2003 game had, and the first big one was at the bank level where the game crashed over and over again. Those days, we didn’t have Steam or other platforms with automatic updates, and it took a couple of months to have a decent patch. Nonetheless, I stuck by the game and I am glad I did!This version consists of a campaign of 16 levels which you can play in one of four levels of difficulty, and a multiplayer mode which I couldn’t access. The multiplayer mode seems to have three maps and you can play a deathmatch or a team deathmatch. What I really like in this version is that the developers were faithful to the plot, the graphic style (which is now better) and all the weapons of the original. Each level has a few collectibles to acquire, in the form of dossiers and golden statuettes, which are cleverly hidden somewhere around the level; so make sure you explore every corner to find them. I actually finished the game in the normal difficulty mode and started another game on the next level of difficulty, and I must say the game should have been pushed back due to the sheer number of issues I encountered. In regards to the audio, it seemed to work fine until I reached the Kellownee Lake stage, when the audio started having some sort of a fit . . . it was all over the joint! The weapons started to shudder and in the middle of it I heard footsteps and god knows what else was in there. I had to shut down the game and restart it.  This occurred randomly several times. The frame rate dropped on and off, which is also frustrating to say the least. In terms of weapons, well, I had my fair share of frustrations especially when I couldn’t reload my gun or when I needed to sneak my way through and use my knives to kill enemies (I had a bad case of superglue fingers on the steel blade!). To be honest, it didn’t matter too much, as the enemy’s AI kept performing some sort of dance before attacking me (still trying to figure out if it was the Tango or the Lambada)! In any case, I had enough time to swap weapons. It is such a shame because the original was a great game and I have no doubt the developers will fix these issues as fast as they can. But I must say that I was bitterly disappointed, and it might have been better to push back the release date to fix these major issues prior to the launch. Despite this, I still believe XIII (2020) will improve with each update to give us what we deserve from this great title. What I really appreciate from Microids is the fact that they have posted an apology and are listening to the community, and I commend them for that. Yes, the pandemic might have created delays, but you surely knew these issues when you released the game.Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Nice graphics+	Good soundtrack+	Faithful to the original in terms of level designs, weapons and plot+	AchievementsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	No trading cards as yet-	Plenty of bugs (Audio, frame rates, weapons to mention a few)Who killed President Sheridan? And who are you? You’ll find out in XIII! 5/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: Being a fan of the original XIII, I really want to recommend the remake. In some ways, it's like a love letter to the classic game. The graphics are refined and crisp, some quality-of-life improvements have been made, fun additions like collectibles have been added, and splitscreen multiplayer is now an option. However, the glitches and missing content are too prominent for me to overlook. This really needed more development time to iron out its issues, and while the September 2022 update improved some aspects of the remake, not enough has been done to make the game worth buying.XIII's story is the same as in the original game, so I won't bother going through it again. The same voice acting, levels, and characters return for the remake. Collectible documents and character trophies expand on the central conspiracy and the factions involved in the game, encouraging players to search for more answers. The remake handles the storyline just fine. However, one of the biggest missed opportunities is that the original game's cliffhanger ending remains unresolved...except now there isn't even a hint at a continuation. This could have been a chance to resolve that mystery and bring the plot to a conclusion, but it sadly wasn't touched upon.Some parts of XIII have been improved, while others are weirdly lacking. Combat generally feels more responsive. All of XIII's abilities are available from the start, meaning that you won't randomly gain improved sniping abilities midway through the game. You can aim down weapon sights to improve accuracy. The dual pistols now fire whenever you pull the trigger instead of their strange two-round burst from the original game. Some underused weapons from the classic version now appear in additional levels, like the double barrel shotgun and Uzi. Stealth is more forgiving than in the original. A small portion of your health can now regenerate if it goes too low.At the same time, features from the classic version of XIII are absent. Weapons like the Shotgun, Harpoon Gun, and Bazooka now lack their alt-fire melee attacks. Multiplayer is missing several modes and bot support. Some smaller details that made the gameplay rewarding, like shooting down the first level's helicopter to cut off reinforcements later on, are not included. The complete Golden Guns bonus from the deluxe edition of the remake is unavailable...though, for some reason, enabling and disabling that setting can give the M16 its golden skin. If the files are already in the game, why not add them to the pre-order bonus or unlock them for use by everyone else?Then there are the bugs. Man, oh man, are there a  of bugs in this remake. Some are harmless and humorous (female corpses flopping away when you set them down, the Pistol being held at a different angle when carrying someone and dual-wielding, enemy bodies getting wedged into doors). Others are distracting (the Shotgun reload sounds often being off-sync, the dual-wielded Pistol's slide being locked back until it is reloaded, silenced gunshots coming from the unsilenced second Pistol). There are more than a few that can hinder your experience (Dual Uzi reloads being bugged and failing to give the correct ammo, collectibles appearing in levels after you have obtained them, knives sometimes locking up and failing to be throwable). All of these issues combined with glaring spelling mistakes and tips referencing missing features (like the Shotgun melee attack) make the remake seem shoddy and poorly handled.In spite of these issues, I had fun with the XIII remake! It's more playable now than it was on release. I had to lower the resolution from 1920x1080 to 1600x900 for it to run well, but only a few levels (like the Bank) had framerate issues after that. The gameplay and secret-hunting elements are a blast when they work. The story still has a lot of intrigue and mystery to it. The art design is also charming and provides a good mix of cel-shading and more cartoonish character designs. It's one of the rare games that I enjoyed enough to go for 100% completion.That doesn't take away from the XIII remake being a bad game, though. I really wanted to enjoy it, so I ended up doing just that thanks to my own biases. If you're an average FPS player or a fan of the XIII comics, I would stick to XIII - Classic instead of the remake. The original still delivers a solid gaming experience and comes at a much lower price. I can't recommend the remake until more of its bugs are fixed. It would be nice to see more of its missing content restored, but having its glitches fixed should be the main priority of the developers now. The September 2022 update was a step in the right direction - now I hope that they keep the momentum going and turn the remake into the polished experience that it deserved to be.

_childDocuments_.review: XIII is a remake of a classic, first-person shooter that I already reviewed so I wont repeat myself here again, instead I will talk about what changed, the good and the bad.This time we can sprint and aim down sights with all weapons which is great. Healing is just a simple button press or hold. When I first saw the graphics I wasnt really into it but after playing through the game I started to like the different look and now I prefer it, the game is prettier to me especially the lightning, looking back at the original, im happy with how the game looks.With that being said, this game still has and probably forever will have plenty of bugs. Let me try list some:( my first playthrough was on hard difficulty and I had small number of issues but during the second playthrough on easy - for achievements - I encountered more problems, it got to a point where I couldnt progress so I switched to hard difficulty again and it was fine, I dont know why or how does difficulty create bugs but oh well )- enemies sometimes behave in a weird way, they freeze completely, stare into the ground or straight up ignore you ( you can still kill them but they wont react, making stealth sections not stealthy )- models bug out, arms get stretched, heads are see through- sound turns off when shooting- weapons dont reload half the time even though the animation plays- enemies seem to be also deaf to gunfire ( on easy difficulty )- you can get stuck in textures or straight up fall through them all the way down to the abyss which is just flat grey space- enemies float above ground- dialogue still plays even if you kill whoever is talking- friendly npcs love to stand still in one place and then teleport instead of walking/running- headshots show one picture three times- everyone looks emotionless which is awkward during serious cutscenes- lifeguard lady at the start can roll her eyes to the back of her head which is creepy- comic book text on alarms keeps playing even after restarting, making it look like alarm is activated when it isnt- enemies ignore hits from objects like chairs and brooms - death animations dont exist, everyone just kinda freezes and leans on the floorTheres probably more but this is enough to see that it just didnt work out. While im glad someone decided to remaster this game, it obviously went south and now all I can do I warn others to stay away from this mess.If you want to experience the story, play the original.

_childDocuments_.review: "Mr. Rowland? It's been such long time!" Unlike others, I've experienced no issues with the audio. Sounds come from the original version from 2003, which I actually don't mind.I have finished first 3 missions and i'm just gonna state issues that hit me right in the face. I have played it on the highest difficulty.- The animation of the lifeguard lady is terrible. Her face looks like she comes from some kind of Japanese cartoon. Until you see her white-then red eyeballs turning around until pupils show. That's some horror stuff right there.- When I killed the first guy with Kalashnikov, I could not pick the weapon up. I had to take another one, that was comfortably prepared for me a step further.- When I jumped into the water, I was suprised I can't hold any weapon in my hands; the inventory showed them locked. So I have swum above the water line. The weapons were no longer locked, yet I couldn't equip them.Also the transition between below the water and above it made me think my GFX card is having a stroke.- With the weirdest lighting I've ever seen, the teller behing the counter in the Winslow Bank looks like a ghost.- In the reminiscence in the bank safe, if you step into the Jones' path, she will start pushing you around, making you crouch and jump uncontrollably. What an odd experience.- Everyone needs to be hit with 2 chairs in order to "sleep". Sometimes with 3, who knows how aiming with furniture works. One bottle is enough, though.- Oddly, every bank security team member has 4 bullets in his .44.- Every single enemy has the same animation for being hit and for dying as well. If you score a headshot, the enemy takes his time to reminiscence about all his life choices, about his failed attempt for lacrosse career, about that time his now-ex-girlfriend wanted a baby and he rather left her alone with her dog and remembers he forgot to feed the dog on the 2nd of July 1997. Feels sad and somewhat angry. Then he slowly  gets back to the present, realises that he got shot in the head, lists all the gods he knows, choose one and say a prayer in his mind. Then he snaps back to reality, realising he's taking good hour before dying from headshot and throws his body against the floor immediately. Yes, that's how long it takes any enemy to die from a bullet in the head.- And the "best" for the last part. The horrendous AI. Remember, I played on the highest difficulty. Its description says "You're not supposed to make it." or something like that. Yep, I'm not gonna make it. Sane. Because I've never seen something so terrible. The description and tutorial tips say the AI is sharp and reacts to dead bodies. Sharp as a bowling ball and their reaction is audible "Hmm?". That's all.The AI just stands there, looking at you, pretending they are a flower pot. The "?" above their head occasionally changes colour.The AI is able to storm into the room it heard gun shots from and perplexedly run around you trying to figure out what does that dead body means.You can run towards AI from 50 meters, they will just point their gun at you and take 3 steps back, letting you punch them into oblivion with your bare hands.And the ultimate, godlike move to confuse the AI: closing a door.TL;DRDon't even look how they've massacred our boy.

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the original game, I cannot reasonably recommend buying this remake in its current condition, even through I've only played the first level. This won't be a review per-se, but a summary of the problems that immediately arose in less than half an hour.The level played out like the developers didn't run any proper degree of QA on the game. Although the game would seem like the animations of the cutscenes are on point, they are a bit buggy. The gameplay itself didn't feel right at all, with the audio balance being a complete mess, there being times when I had no idea I was being shot, let alone shot at, and with the reloads bugging out a few times, playing out but not actually reloading the gun. I'm also not completely sure of if you're meant to have the full weapon selection available like the first game or not, but having a Wheel with eight slots for things to go in, but being only able to hold two weapons is deeply confusing me to the point where I can't tell if it's a design decision or a bug.Outside of that though, there's no FOV slider whatsoever, although I feel like what it runs at is adequate, but still not ideal. Not only that, but if you bought the game expecting the same multiplayer with bots that the first game had, you'll be shut down. It's local-only, and there's no bots at all. You can't even load a map on your own.So as of right now, I'd suggest just buying the original game, and use the Steam Guides to get that running at 1080p and with a playable FoV, and hold off on this remake until this review is amended when (and if) it's patched.

_childDocuments_.review: Was looking forward to this remake, played the original on the PS2 when I was a baby, and played it on PC a month prior.So many things to talk about that are wrong about this game within 1.2 hours of gameplay I've encountered.Visuals:I actually don't mind how the game looks, besides when it goes into the flashback scripted sequences. I actually think the game looks really nice, though a bit dated on tech. The animations however just ruin all of that glimmer with random cut-outs and just odd choices. Gun animations feel like they're trying too hard to be over-the-top, which in the original game, it had a subtle comic feel to them. The character animations are not bad, but needs more variation, like in the original game. Enemies seems to have similar animations that doesn't match the kind of damage they've taken, unless you use a shotgun at time, which they go flying back a little bit.Gameplay: So you can't carry all of the weapons like in the original game. Can't carry a AK and an M16 anymore. Shooting enemies do stagger when shot, but it still doesn't feel right no matter what weapon you use, but what's the point of shooting everyone with all the neat looking weapons when I can just kill an entire room of enemies with a headshot with the starting pistol.The stealth doesn't work like the original game. It use to just be a sight-based bare-bones stealth, where you just knockout or kill enemies without being seen and hide bodies, and it did have a some thrill to it. Trying to land blows in this game is a hit or miss chance, and I've died multiple times in the Winslow Bank area because of weird bugs like that.There are other bugs with the gameplay, like how areas are not completely reset when you restart from the last checkpoint, some scripted sequences, like the bridge section in third mission can lock-up mid animation etc etcI've seen small game developers create such great games, so I don't see that as an excuse.This game really needs a lot of polishing and fixing up to do. Really disappointed how this game was just released like that. Refund while you can, or be hopeful they will fix this game with updates, otherwise I'm not gonna touch this game again. However I will keep it installed, just to check if any updates have improved the game.

_childDocuments_.review: The President of the United States of America has been assassinated. You wake up on a desolate strip of New England beach. The near-fatal impact of a bullet has left your head pounding, and your memory erased. What's more, the number "XIII" has been mysteriously tattooed on your chest, while your pocket holds a key to a New York City bank box. Head swimming in amnesia, you struggle to your feet only to encounter more assailants intent on finishing the job. To your shock, you handle the hitmen with the killing skills of a professional - before heading to the bank in search of any shred of information about your lost identity and your involvement in the President's murder. What lies ahead is a deadly quest not only into your shadowy past, but America's darkest corridors of power. [Ubi Soft]

name: Going Under
detailed_description: Going Under is a satirical dungeon crawler about exploring the cursed ruins of failed tech startups. As an unpaid intern in the dystopian city of Neo-Cascadia, you’ll wield office junk as weaponry as you make your way through the offbeat procedural dungeons beneath your company campus. The Future is Wack Failed businesses no longer just cease to exist--they sink beneath the earth, and their employees are cursed to wander the halls for eternity as monsters. It’s your duty to put these monsters out of their misery and repossess their assets--so that your boss can afford a new car, or something. Not All Heroes Get Paychecks Battle through the remains of failed startups themed off of gig workers, dating sites, and cryptocurrency. Uncover the true motives of your employer, a carbonated drink startup known as Fizzle, and their parent company, a subscription box manufacturer with an army of helpful shipping drones. Make friends with your co-workers! Hire a freelance goblin! Date a slime! Invest in crypto! Set a rideshare on fire! Fight Flexibly In the dungeons of Going Under, almost everything can be used as a weapon, from laptops to brooms to body pillows. Proper weapons can be found as well, but even they can break at a moment’s notice if you aren’t careful. Playing cautiously and picking the right weapon for the situation are musts if you intend on surviving your internship. Horrible Bosses And you thought your boss was a monster. At the bottom of the dungeons lurk the founders of the cursed startups, getting rich off of investments while their employees fight amongst themselves. Defeat them and return to the surface with their enchanted relics to empower the company you work for. Get Paid in Experience As you explore, you’ll encounter powerful Skills that change the way you play. Learn them at the Cafe and they’ll show up in future runs. Use a Skill often enough, and you’ll get it “endorsed” and available to start your expeditions with. Combine multiple Skills for crazy synergies, and you’ll be cleaning house in no time. A World of Characters Complete Tasks for your co-workers to gain Clout with them and unlock their unique bonuses. Learn more about Neo-Cascadia, the origins of Fizzle, and how the drone shipping empire known as Cubicle came to dominate the city. Can you save your company and yourself from going under for good?

_childDocuments_.review: The combat in this game feels remarkably similar to My Time at Portia (which isn't a combat-focused game).  I wouldn't really compare it to Hades because it isn't nearly as smooth and you don't really build up a "godly" combination of powers like you do in Hades/Risk of Rain.I think the appeal is more from the jokes told in the conversations and the atmosphere of the dungeons.  I think the combat is a bit clunky and can be difficult to aim but at least if you are used to i-frame dodging think it's not too difficult to beat everything in the game.  Instead of learning how to avoid attacks, I think it's easier to just hit spacebar at the right time and keep smashing them.  I found it way more difficult to figure out how to avoid attacks, especially for the "final" boss.I'll probably check back in after 100% achievements but I can say about 8.8 hours in that the achievements so far seem very doable in a reasonably short amount of time.  I doubt it'll take up to 100 hours like Hades did to reach 100% achievements (which is a relief).Edit: In retrospect after beating the Imposter mode for the first time, this game is a bit too grindy for me.  It feels so repetitive that it's hard to stay focused to remain at full health and the Rolodex achievement is too frustrating because cards come so rarely and some enemies bounce around too easily without any sort of aiming mechanism for the Rolodex cards.

Needing to get new weapons every other room or sometimes every room is really annoying and when a weapon does break you don't auto equip another weapon you're carrying is dunce level bad design.  Not showing any time of durability rating is weird when that's one of the things you'll constantly be worried about.A better camera and some polish to a few aspects of the combat would have meant a world of difference here.

The game offers up some very good challenges but does a great way of leveling that with a huge amount of passive skills that you unlock and use as you play. _childDocuments_.review: Going Under is one of my favorite rogue-like games, and I play a lot of rogue-likes (check my library). The best thing about this game throughout all the hours I have played is the satisfying, fun combat and the amazing characters that I would want to know (and already know. I'm looking at you Swomp). If you want an easy chart, here it is:Pros-Great character chemistry and story-Tons of items and weapons-Great combat with weapons that break, heightening the frantic nature of fighting goblins. (It feels like Breath of the Wild combat)-Distinct dungeons with different enemies-Jackie embodies the working spiritNeutral (Personal thoughts)-By end game (for me would be about 11-13 hours in), the other characters ran out of general things to say. I had played so many runs that this was inevitable, but you will hit a wall where runs will be your focus to see the credits-I ended up having a lot of similar runs because of certain items being dropped more often than others. This may only be my instance but YEET and Thunder Cloud were in every other run when I have a large percentage of the 100+ items unlocked.-Some of my later runs in the games would bug with the luxury car app and I would phase through enemies until the car ran out. (Some characters get stuck in geometry and ragdoll out, but I found these instances funny. I was never soft locked.)Cons-Not that many bosses (though each one is a highlight of the game)That might be it for cons, but I'll update it if I find something on my second play through. Overall, I really liked this game. The story was well paced and I loved the characters. I would love more content, but it is absolutely worth buying right now if you like this style of game.Original review at 4.9 hours:This is a really fun game where you fight failed startup company goblins and talk to coworkers that are a bit uncanny in how familiar they are. It's worth playing for the characters alone.

_childDocuments_.review: The art style is good, the story is neat.  The gameplay and mechanics aren't there to back it up.  Going under is a pretty shallow game.  I would describe it as a disposable weapon based beat-em-up.   Not much good as a roguelike or roguelite though.  The game gets boring fast.  A lot of novel ideas, but weapons are too disposable and can only have one upgrade. So everything feel lack luster and no items really stand out. _childDocuments_.review: It's a roguelike that plays like powerstone or breath of the wild. There's a great story to it, sure. There's great perks to help round out your build, sure. There's Mentors that help you change the way you approach each dungeon sure.However, what really matters is that you're going in a dungeon, grabbing anything not nailed down, and smacking monsters with said items until they give up the loot. Weapons break constantly but each room is just stuffed with things to hit people with. Keyboards, Monitors, Motivational t shirts fired from canons, skuls of your enemies, coffee pots, if it's not nailed to the wall, it's free game to smack someone with.You are going to be doing a whole lot of smacking of enemies. It's chaotic, it's lovely, and yup, great story all the way through. Highly recommended, and to the devs: I can't wait to see your second game.

It's one of those games that the developers put much thought and care in, and it's palpable. Something you don't expect from a game like this is the insane amount of attention to detail the creators put in every single corner of the game. There are so many little things about it which made me smile, like how your character drops whatever item she was holding and starts playing on her phone when you go afk, or how a massive metal ball appears chained to your foot whenever you are in debt. _childDocuments_.review: Going Under does a great job of bringing its satire and personality into its rogue-lite elements.  Even though the exploited intern isn’t a newly relatable tragedy to dissect, the game’s continuous and unexpected references to it as well as modern work life and the oxymoronic habits of technology conglomerates kept the occasional rogue-lite mundanity at bay. However, whether the pop culture gags will hold up well over time is something that remains to be seen.A favorite example of this thematic/gameplay dynamic is how the “student debt” curse creates a heavy ball and chain that restricts your movement. The concept of having a pinned skill is another clever addition that aligns with the interning premise. Roguey games often have a few busted skills that every run is basically leading up to, so picking one preferred power to start out with seems like a good compromise. It’s worth noting that the music is pretty catchy too (although the final boss theme drove me nuts).Switching between several breakable weapons was jarring at first, but as the rhythm of the game began to settle in, planning around the impermanent tools and understanding the properties of each one became quite rewarding. Nothing is there to directly teach you the technical details of weapon types, but I’d rather be confused than bored in this context. A few skill descriptions could be a little clearer though. I’m looking at you, Yeet.While their assistance can be pretty useful, the mentors’ sub-quests were usually bizarre, highly situational, and opposed to ‘main’ progress. Going out of the way to progress them a bit felt tedious, didn’t lead to any noticeable story changes, and was probably unnecessary. With the right luck, you might not even need those unlockable bonuses since Going Under can be inconsistently easy.While it’s not particularly strong as far as rogue-lites go, the strangely unique gameplay serves the comedy nicely. Just the concept of a rogue-lite (difficult, endless, and unpredictable with fragments of continuous progress) is an apt allegory for building a career. Every time the randomness or unpredictable physics deceived me, there were a dozen cheeky details that kept me engaged until the end. Since you can’t tell the same jokes forever, it’s for the best that Going Under can be reasonably short.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is an incredible experience, which I would highly recommend. Witty, smartly written commentary on Late-Stage Neo-Liberal Capitalism, with the added bonus of having a script that clearly draws from lived experiences of those within the games industry. The characters are recognisable archetypes, with more depth than expected, which is a delight to discover, and conversations with them are just as engaging as the (very excellent) combat. Music and sound design create an evocative mood, and every hit feels juicy and responsive. Fairly forgiving early on, giving even a new player to Roguelikes/lights (like myself) ample time to adjust, Other mechanical adjustments solve a lot of other little frustrations without making things too easy (such as rolling over an object picks it up if your inventory is empty. Overall, though, an excellent time, well thought through, and a joy all the way through. ♥ Looking forward to completing it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been going through my backlog of games after putting it off for so long and I didn't have too high hopes for most of them but I gotta say I was really surprised just how fun this game is! Usually roguelites I've played in the past are pretty difficult and a pain to get into but this one is different. It's very beginner friendly and ramps up the difficulty fairly and steadily. Runs only take about 15 minutes so it's easy to play for a bit and take a break. The combat is fairly simple but satisfying enough to not get boring, weapons break really fast so you have to utilize whatever object you find in a room as your weapons. The game is basically a big parody on modern times and big companies and as such the game has mimicked the alegria art we all know and hate. But I have to say the way this game does it is actually charming, I really do like how the art looks. The writing and humor is millennial-esque because again it's a parody of modern times so that's what you're stuck with, just be thankful it's not zoomer humor. And as cringey as that type of humor and lingo is, the way the game utilizes it is in a mostly self aware manner so it doesn't get too unbearable or anything; even though I did groan at a couple lines. A game I really didn't have much expectations for and it actually charmed me in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: I couldn't get into this game at all. Going Under was tediously difficult from the tutorial. The levels, even "procedurally generated", were more or less the same (even between dungeons). The humor felt forced, bland, and far too on the nose (we get it, you're poking fun at startups and corporate culture). The color scheme is obnoxious and makes me feel like a pez dispenser choked on some cotton candy. Combat requires quick reflexes but the controls are unintuitive and clunky.I'm not trying to be mean. I really wanted to enjoy this game. The idea of a non-fantasy dungeon crawler seemed like it'd be a fresh take on an old genre, but nothing in this game piqued my interest. Apparently, I'm in the minority. But I'm uninstalling this one. I like challenging games, but there is nothing in this game which is pushing me to overcome the hurdle of the challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly I wish I could give this a recommend. As you can see I've put a bit of time into the game, completed the main game and am onto the endgame content. I enjoyed it, but for being roguelike, it lacks replayability. Not due to game mechanics or lack of variation, but fundamental, game breaking, run ending, bugs. Bugs that have not yet, nor does it look like they will ever be, fixed.Looking at the positives:Great game. Love the look, the characters and the story. Controls are fairly tight and game mechanics are fun and interesting. Music is great and love the art.Negatives:THE BUGS. Coming back to the game after a few months of not playing it, and trying to beat the final game mode I have easily lost 20%-30% of my runs to bugs. Cameras rotating and not stopping, mechanics breaking (items doing nothing, items having infinite ammo or uses or items having unintended effects). My last run (and why I will probably stop playing this game) when fighting the final boss during her transformation scene I broke. My character stopped moving, I couldn't do anything but pause the game.If you read this far, honestly if its cheap and on sale, its a fun time waster. BUT DO NOT expect to 100% the game, you will die from the bugs just as much as the enemies.

_childDocuments_.review: BIG NOTE: it supports ultrawide straight out of the box. do not be fooled by the demo!!!!! prereq to LOVING this game: + worked in any office any where in the world in the past 10 yearsthis game hits hard.+ hella ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ relatable with incredible writing+ it is filled to the brim with humor, memes and a fresh new take on dungeon crawling, bringing LIFE to a typically one-dimensional genre. + the aesthetic with psychedelic colors are clearly inspired by the the ubiquitous vector illustrations found on stock websites describing the many abstract energies businesses love to pretend to have (like TEAMWORK)+ it vibes off the startup unicorn bubble of the past couple decades but the cynical observations of everyday working life are S P O T  O N for anyone who has ever lived a life as part of any office environment + i have actually never experienced a game of more solid game design in recent years; it doesn't stagnante you when you fail runs and actually lets you progress in the game plotwise through non-linear experience of in-game events and dialogue. it redesigns experiences based on choices (try skipping the cutscene from the beginning in a new game and see for yourself!!!). even the dialogue screens are innovatively framed. i ADMIRE it from a design standpoint. this is...a game...with insane personality and playability. i hope it goes big. i am snobby as all hell when it comes to video games and this one is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely art direction, pretty decent music, and some pretty chaotic gameplay (in a good way).Some games do not have a super fun weapon durability system, but this is the exception. Every combat is a mess of grabbing whatever office supplies are closest to you, breaking them over the head of some poor ogre, and then trying to find a new item to smash into bits over someone's body. It's really fun.The game's parody of a corporate art style is simultaneously spot on, while still having more character than any corporation out there. The characters themselves are pretty neat, and having different characters with different backgrounds is a great idea for a game that's aiming at a lot of social commentary.Going Under succeeds on pretty much every level, and while it might not have the *best* jokes, or the *best* combat, or the *best* music, it is above average in every single category at once. Definitely worth the 20 euro.

_childDocuments_.review: Such an amazing rogue-lite, it's a shame it got overshadowed by Hades.Having played both games I can say with 100% confidence that they are both worth your time.The experiences they offer are completely different despite being part of the same genre.Going Under offers a unique take on rogue-lite, where weapons have durability and break.It's full of good writing and humor! It might be a short game (I finished the main story and all the quests within 16h of playtime) but it doesn't need to be big to be good.You can definitely feel the passion that went into this project, and I loved the story.Gameplay-wise the game is brutal and challenging at times, especially in the beginning, but once you get the hang of it, it's really a matter of whether or not you got the right setup (just like most rogue-lite).In Going Under you can pick up various weapons that are part of the environment or dropped by enemies. This ranges from thrash than you are supposed to throw at enemies, water guns, clubs, maces, spears, etc.While in the dungeons you can also find Skills which are basically powerups, stuff like Increased Crit, your weapons get bigger, objects you throw light up on fire, etc. (all of them have awesome names btw).Picking up the same skill on different runs gives you experience with said skill, and eventually, you can choose to start a run with (you can only start the run with 1 skill tho).There are also apps to be found within the dungeons, which grant you one-time-only powers, like transforming into a rainbow car for a few seconds or healing 1 heart.Finally, the various NPCs give you quests and are completing said quests to equip them as mentors. Completing more quests for the same NPCs levels them up, grating you more benefits from equipping them. These range from gaining more money to getting monsters to join your party in the dungeon, etc.I loved this game and I'm looking forward to the post-game content now!

_childDocuments_.review: If this game could have taken its first half and doubled its length or completely eliminated the unremarkable second half of the game, then this would have been an easy recommend.  Minor spoilers following:The opening up to the mid-point of this game is incredible: the setting, the art style, the characters you meet, the writing - all well done and overall charming.  The humor is varied, from explicit to subtle, but it never feels cheesy or cringey.  However, with any rouge-like, the gameplay is the bread and butter.  And here, the bread wasn't fully baked and the butter was over-melted and made everything a bit soggy.  What do I mean?  The combat feels like Katamari Damacy physics in a rougelike Zelda format.  Initially, this isn't bad - working your way through the first 3 dungeons is an enjoyable time as you make mental notes of different weapons, enemy cues, and power-up combinations along the way.  The enemies are wacky parodies and you get a feel for how to weave in and out.  However, the dodging and animation cancelling feels off, but everything is doable.  The fourth dungeon is an amazing take on the the rougelike genre itself within its own game - straight 'clear the enemies' objective, grab a weapon or powerup, move on, keep going, it gets harder, fight the boss, win.Then the second half of the game opens.  This is where the game ultimately becomes a rehashed and lackluster shadow of its first half.  All the NPC dialogue that was enjoyable between runs?  Eliminated.  The clumsy dodging, odd animation cancelling, and Katamari Damacy physics?  Frustrating and unwelcome against quick enemies who have now become damage sponges.  The dungeons are remixes of the first 3, but boredom, tediousness, and a lack of NPC interaction makes the world feel utterly dead.  Your coworkers simply stare at you between runs instead of having quirky dialogue that breaks up your attempts.  Clearing out the remixed dungeons in the second half wasn't a matter of them being hard, but dodging being 'janky' for lack of a better term.  Gameplay never sank into frustration, just boredom.The only thing I could perceive as fixing these issues is having a fixed camera angle and/or pulling the camera back.  Too often, especially in the later stages, the action was too chaotic to have any reasonable chance of dodging everything.  This is mostly in latter mob rooms; boss battles did not suffer from this - boss battles were extremely fair tests of skill.I absolutely enjoyed my first 4 or so hours of this game.  But the second half has soured the taste and ruined the meal for me.  However, I am looking forward to Aggro Crab's future work as they seem to respond extremely well to criticism and have made improvements to the game after its initial setbacks.

_childDocuments_.review: - Gameplay is.. strange. It has some good ideas, and is alright, but repetitive and doesn't quite seem to know what it wants to be. I found myself getting bored really quick, even if the music is nice.- The game has an interesting aesthetic and style which is executed /terribly/. Going Under wants to be some sort of parody/critique of the overly sanitized tech startup capitalist environment, BUT; it's characters and writing are very evidently written by someone who is a PART of the thing they're supposedly parodying, every character is super tenderqueer and behaves obnoxiously "wholesomely." _childDocuments_.review: Feels incredibly shallow and uninteresting to me. Gives me more of a itch.io concept game vibe than an actual fleshed out experience. None of the humor or jokes really landed for me, though not due to me not understanding them, they just felt ham-fisted in fitting every zoomer and silicon valley reference they could. It just left me feel like I was slogging through walls of text that added nothing to the experience and often felt unresponsive when button-mashing to try and push through it quicker.The combat felt alright I guess though the weapons don't really give you a sense of anything other than power level which becomes irrelevant when they all have different swing types and speeds and they seemed to blow up or break randomly without any sort of intuitive reasons to why. The item hits all sort of felt like wet noodles to me, without any sort of visceral (I don't know if that's the proper term) feedback to hitting an enemy or making contact with powerful and larger weapons with longer swing timers. Throwing an item gives you a guide line that is seemingly meaningless to how far you'll actually throw or what kind of trajectory the item will have and with every item felt so slow that the enemies would just mosey up to you completely avoiding it and hit you before you could finish and most of the rooms weren't even big enough for the throw to work properly.The power-ups or artifacts or whatever they're called also presented a problem for me in that they are intentionally obscure opting to use flavor text for the actual description which didn't really add much to the experience other than obscurity for obscurities sake.The rogue-lite parts of permanent progression only seemed to be being able to pre-equip a power up if you played enough with it and having a mentor that did something like gave you slightly more money by choosing them after unlocking them through a task.At the end of the day, nothing is fundamentally wrong with the game, as in I didn't run into any crashes or technical issues and everything seemed to function as they designers intended, I just really disliked the game and after 30 mins I'm tapping out with no motivation to play it again especially if you compare it to the responsiveness and depth that similarly priced games in the roguelike genre have to offer, this just really isn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: i really wanted to like this game, but there's a lot that's dragged it down for me at just about every level, some things are just personal preference, and some just feel like core issues.The art style is fun, and a bit satirical of current design trends in apps, UI and things like how commercials like handling cartoony people, but... because it's in those trends, it can feel a bit lifeless because for me? it feels like i'm about to descend into corporate speak, or something.the writing is okay, at first! but she never has anything of value to say, just sorta is like "capitalism, am i right?"since there's so much emphasis on mentors/these guys in general, i kind of want to think of it as a situation like hades, where death lets you converse with these characters between times of gameplay, but it started to feel less like something i was doing for fun, and more that i felt like i had to- and the spacing of the characters is random, with me running around to find that one person who is just out of frame...and honestly, this is my own opinion, but the music can be... really bad- it feels exactly what you would imagine this sort of game to sound like, and i can't really explain how that's disappointing to me- and the winkydink music is probably the worst, for me- it's deterred me from continuing to fight the different dungeons.and the fighting can range from kind of fun to tedious and annoying- throwing is useless, i only do it to get rid of weapons, dodging feels awkward and slow- focusing also doesn't feel natural, with it choosing people that sometimes were across the room. movement also feels strange and floaty, like im putting in a ton of work to move around and hit- the most fun i had was with the joblin boss, but he was so insanely easy that i beat him on my first try, while the difficulty spike to the other dungeons feels too harsh for me to try to follow up on.the upgrades don't... feel like they do much of anything, and the apps feel too weak to use, save for the hp recovery one- it feels like just about everything is too much of a risk to use, and i end up using the same items over and over, which gets boring...i really really wanted to like this game, but when even the positives have some caveats to them, it's hard to keep playing

However, the latter half of the game falls off a bit in my opinion. The amount of story and dialogue becomes almost non-existent compared to the first half of the game, and literally no new mechanics or unlocks are introduced whatsoever. The game just becomes more significantly more difficult, but provides no rewards or tools to help you with your journey. You would still be using the same weapons, skills and mentor perks you used for the first half of the game, and it got quite tedious near the end of the game.I don't really understand why the difficulty ramps up as much as it does. The game is not mechanically deep enough to justify it, and it also heavily based on RNG. This made the game incredibly frustrating to complete and reach the end of the story.Despite all this, I still recommend at least checking out the first half of the game. _childDocuments_.review: Legitimately one of the funniest games I've ever played - anyone who's spent time working in an office (especially a younger startup) will find the story and characters painfully relatable. Ray and Marv are basically every boss I've ever had.The gameplay is a really fluid combination of roguelike dungeon crawling progression with Breath of the Wild style weapon management and Soulslike combat mechanics with armor frames and invincible dodge rolls (there's also some hillarious references to souls bosses which I won't spoil so you can laugh at them yourself). It's challenging but always feels fair and the bosses are well designed and fun fights.Enemy variety can get a little samey sometimes and I wish the weapons and powerups were a bit better balanced - there are lots of situations where you don't really have a meaningful choice over what to pick up because there's one option that's clearly better than the rest. That said the ways powerups and weapons combine and interact lead to wildly different playstyles across runs (as a good roguelike should) which help keep the game feeling fresh even once you've seen every enemy type. Overall an extremely solid first game from a young studio that I can't recommend enough and I'm really looking forward to what Aggro Crab does next.

_childDocuments_.review: ~Game finished and all achievements acquired at the time of this review~Pros:-Hilarious satirical dialogue most can relate to in some way.-Movement and striking is very fluid and responsive.-Very large variety of skills and weapons in the game to acquire.-Music is outstanding and probably will be very overlooked!-Intuitive and unique quest system to unlock "Mentor" perks.-You can pet a wiener dog named Eclaire.Cons:-Progression permanently locks you out of older dungeons.-No replay value after the final encounter outside of just unlocking remaining skills.-Enemy ability to stun-lock you into taking successive hits can get absurd and frustrating.-Dungeon runs are far too short (took about 10-12 minutes or so on average).-Needs more than 3 base dungeons (not including the special 1 off encounter areas).Overall I find myself hard pressed to not recommend this game because frankly it was just an absolute pleasure to play through.  Every new experience had me chuckling to myself and it was quite relaxing despite successive failures.  I will say this; if you come into this expecting a typical rogue-like gameplay loop...YOU WILL BE DISAPPOINTED.  Do not go into this expecting a Dead Cells/Undermine length run that will slowly power creep your base character for hundreds of enjoyable hours.  While that is the case in this game too you will find reaching those caps will not take very long at all.  I took my sweet time and manage to fully unlock all skills and fully complete the game, both the achievements and bosses in about 21 hours give or take.If you want to pick up this game and truly enjoy it.  Just know going in that it is a more linear rogue-like with a distinctive ending point in my eyes.  It is absolutely fantastic don't get me wrong but I would love to see some content added for those of us who would like to push the envelope and be truly challenged by a game, as so many seeking rogue-like titles are also looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely holds its own against Spelunky 2 and Hades and plenty of other brilliant roguelites released this year, and that's about all you need to know.But, I really enjoy this game, so alright. I'll write a couple more words of praise.Going Under has great combat. I played BOTW on an emulator for a bit. I really disliked how weapons would break so fast. It's kinda similar here. But I love it here. I think it's a case of there never being a shortage of weapons around and the game being based on small rooms rather than one big, explorable area. Also not having to deal with inventory management. That's probably the biggest factor. But yeah, here keeping an eye on how intact your weapons are adds to the fun and hectic feeling of the combat rather than it feeling like a chore as it did to me in BOTW. Also, the whole using random furniture to attack people thing? Reminds me of Indiana Jones and the Emperor's Tomb, and any game that manages to remind me of that one is gonna earn my love right away. Just saying.Going Under has a great visual style. It manages to parody (or maybe just pay homage?) to corporate graphic design and illustration trends, and it feels absolutely spot-on, while also outshining the vast majority of art you see used for those kinds of purposes. Just brilliant character designs and visual gags. I also enjoy that some of the abilities change your player model.Going Under has a great narrative structure. It's kinda similar to Hades, actually. There isn't any chatter when you pick up upgrades or any abilities to give gifts to characters (that I know of at this point), but just like in Hades, death never feels annoying because returning to the hub area and getting to chat with your coworkers is fun.Going Under also (so far) seems like it's a breath of fresh air in the roguelike genre in that it seems... okay with you getting to see most of what's on offer pretty quickly and not requiring literal hundreds of hours to be beaten. I might be talking outta my butt (and I might edit this part of the review in the future). In my current playtime, I've manage to arrive at what seems to be a final boss fight, maybe? I haven't beaten it, and based on the achievements, I assume there are probably more challenges ahead, but yeah. So far it felt a lot more forgiving than many other games in the genre, while still being challenging and interesting. If you're usually the type to swear off roguelikes, consider giving this one a shot anyway.I think that's about it. Look, just buy this. It's great and the devs have a fantastic sense of humor.

_childDocuments_.review: A swell little roguelite. It's no Hades, but it's neat and competent enough to grab and keep one's attention.It's very tongue-in-cheek, and it's also very, uh, zeitgeisty. This may not sit well with some, I imagine, but personally I'm enjoying the game's style and writing just fine.Metaprogression feels surprisingly mild, so while the game does provide certain ways to permanently improve your character, they aren't numerous, and they have to be earned. Going Under is meant to be challenging, something that's directly stated when you're starting a new game, but a customizable assist mode is available (can be tinkered with whenever).Combat revolves around weapons having durability, meaning you are always looking for not just better equipment, but equipment in general. I'm generally not a fan of such systems, but what Going Under has going for it doesn't feel awfully restrictive to me. It helps that there are plenty of respectable "midrange" weapons, while junk can always be utilized as throwable weaponry.Overall, a perfectly solid game that's easy to enjoy and appreciate.

_childDocuments_.review: This is very much a thumbs in the middle review, very slightly tilting upward.Going Under is a cutely presented and occasionally amusing office spoof. It shines in its presentation and entertaining character interactions. The wide variety of thematically-appropriate weapons, some with quite clever twists (eg a ream of paper which becomes smaller and reduces in damage with each hit), make for interesting variety. There are a good range of skills, some which make for different strategies.Unfortunately, the gameplay is weak. Combat is too hectic, especially in more difficult stages, for such floaty controls and inconsistent mechanics (particularly in respect of cancelling enemy attacks). The invulnerability window after getting hit is just too short for a game where you can wind up surrounded by enemies in a cramped and visually busy environment - it's too easy to lose a huge chunk of health in a few seconds. While these problems can be glossed over in the early portion of the game, as it's not especially challenging, they are overwhelming in the second half when the difficulty spikes. They are compounded by the limited return for runs.Much as I enjoyed aspects of the game, it got too frustrating by the end. I slightly recommend it just because it's a bit different and was fun for a few hours, but with a strong caveat that it quickly wears thin.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm seemingly halfway through, I am absolutely in love with this game. The humour is perfect for me, it's topical for modern day twenty somethings. The music is stellar, I love what they've done putting so many twists on the corpo tunes, and the ART, oh my god, the ART! Art is often the last thing I'm focused on in games, when you put the 3 core facets in front of me (gameplay, art, sound). The first thing about this game that drew me in was the reclamation of the corpo artstyle, and how much amazing personality they give that style. The character designs are super endearing, monsters are varied and clever, and animations are perfect for each personality. It's hard for me to fully explain, but the way this game feels is so comfortable. There are a few games in history where I just feel comfortable in their hub worlds, namely Super Mario Sunshine, A Hat in Time, Splatoon 1, and now, Going Under joins that small group of games where I just feel at home. Everything about it, from the stage design of the hub world, to the music, the decorations, the level of detail inside and outside, and the population of these characters... I'm totally enchanted in a way I can't describe. I'm not quite done and I anticipate many more great hours with this game, and I want to give a full proper review later. As it stands, though, this is already a game I wish I grabbed on launch, at full price, had I known aggrocrab was so talented. This game makes me want to pick up game development. I'm a composer, but this makes me want to learn how to 3d model, how to animate, how to code. Everything about this game makes me wanna learn how to make something this cool. Thanks aggrocrab, hope to meet you guys at PAX one day :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a weak thumbs up. It is with great hesitancy that I give this game a thumbs up. I both appreciate and despise that the combat system is like Zelda: Breath of the Wild (BOTW). The fact that weapons have finite durability is actually quite fun. It's a great feeling pummeling some enemies with a hockey stick, having the stick break, and then having to dive roll into a battle fan to continue pummeling the enemies. In this sense, I really enjoy the frantic nature of the combat. However, since the combat feels like BOTW, it feels like a worse version of a combat system that I'm well-versed in. The game simultaneously feels both tight and slippery in its controls. The game does not usually expect precise dodging (in the cases of e.g. boss fights and individual enemy attacks), but it does start throwing you into situations where it is near impossible to avoid damage without the access to precision dodging. In later levels, the enemies will swarm you in such a way that avoiding damage (due to the enemies newfound super armor) comes down to hoping that there is not too much debris in the way of rolling into a safer location. Also, the roll is inconsistent. Sometimes it does what is expected, other times it randomly gets caught on the hurtbox of an enemy or some debris.I really wanted to love this game, but it just feels worse to play than the other action roguelikes that I own. The art is great, the tongue-in-cheek dialogue is charming, and the concept of the combat  are all strong points. However, the game fails to deliver in the game feel of its combat, which is the focus of most of your time while playing.Buy the game if it's cheap, but don't expect to put it on the same shelf as Slay the Spire, Enter the Gungeon, Spelunky, or any of the other great roguelikes on the market.

The characters are cute, but is this a story game or a dungeon game? If it were a Banjo-Kazooie type I could understand. However the dungeons aren't so static/easy as a linear puzzle stage. You can't make me excited to go back to the dungeon after a failed attempt and say 'but you can't go back yet! first you need a cutscene, and then go to the hub, talk to people to find out they had nothing important to say instead of giving you a quest like last time even though they have an prompt bubble over their head, then take a look around at all the stuff you cant interact with either now or maybe ever and then you can go find the level you actually wanted to go back to!" It feels like a waste of time and like the game wants to shove its theme in your face instead of letting you enjoy it and discover things at your own pace. I really like the creativity of the game. _childDocuments_.review: Overall: C-Rogue-likes are an incredibly crowded genre, especially in the indie scene. Making any indie game stand out is difficult but all the more so when you have to compete in such an overpopulated arena. When I saw such positive buzz online about the game and its developer, I put it on my radar. Unfortunately, being in such a crowded field means there are plenty of comparisons and Going Under cannot compete with any of the heavy-hitters of the genre.   Visually the game’s a mixed bag. The genuinely wonderful 2D character art stands in sharp contrast to the 3D visuals of the majority of the game. Models aren’t just simple but they feel like they lack polish. In combat sections, it becomes easy to ignore so let’s do just that. To be completely fair, this game was made by a small team and this was their first game as a studio so problems with visual fidelity can mostly be set aside.  Unfortunately, the visuals aren’t the only aspect lacking. The gameplay feels tired. By the end of the game, I had to force myself to keep playing just so I could say I have finished it and could fairly give my thoughts on it. Dungeons have random layouts, as is standard with rogue-likes. They don’t matter. At all. Because of how levels are structured, random room order doesn’t make a difference since you will be required to visit every room which isn’t a shop. The layout of each floor might as well be a straight line for all the difference it makes. Each dungeon also has a very limited number of room layouts and since you need to see so many per run, it becomes tedious quite quickly. Further compounding the issue, to beat the game each dungeon has to be cleared twice (with one being on hard mode). The hard-mode dungeons have changes in aesthetics but they feel almost entirely the same.  Monotony is sort of a theme in this game. Weapons might have a different number or coat of paint but all fall into just 4 major types. Since weapons also break frequently, you will always find yourself with a loadout with nothing but that dungeon’s basic 4 or 5 damage item. Even the upgrades lack any noticeable punch. Most change things so slightly they might not even be there. One of the game’s best upgrades makes the more powerful 2-handed weapons swing like 1-handed which provides a noticeable power boost but makes the game’s weapons feel even more homogenized.  The game’s humor around hustle and grind culture and the toxic aspects of the American workplace works well enough. Nothing too crazy but the characters did constantly provide entertainment to the point I was disappointed when they ran out of things to say before I finished the game.  I hope you fine more enjoyment from this title than I did. I tried my best to enjoy myself but I just didn’t have much fun. If you are thinking this might be for you, I’d only recommend it to fans of action rogue-like games who have burned through the big names  like Hades, Enter the Gungeon, and The Binding of Isaac.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a diamond in the rough. Modern, at times hilariously dystopian, and with a strong emphasis on never giving up, it's a roguelike that will surprise and charm you with every twist and turn. It's colourful and sweet and I really enjoyed it. Potential spoilers ahead as I pick this game apart;You play as Jacqueline, a fresh college graduate eager to take her first (unpaid) step into the world of corporate advertising! Unfortunately, she doesn't get very far before being asked to deal with the goblins - sorry, Joblins - in the basement.If that gives you any idea of what this game is like, good. It stays like that. The whole way through. This game will absolutely challenge you to your limits and keep you on your toes, but treats failing as a natural step, and just like any good roguelike, you're making progress with every run on the dungeons. The controls are good, and while I will be the first to admit I was not great at this game, it has solid enough controls that they fall very close to that sweet spot of 'easy to learn, hard to master'. Speaking of dungeons - the theming. Wow. Just WOW. The creativity, especially with the characters and setting, were incredible. The story is not quite at that level, but it doesn't need to be. It's strong enough to carry these characters and the setting, and that's enough for me. My favourite was Winkydink, but Joblin and Styxcoin were equally strong. I spent about 20 hours on my completed file, and I unlocked almost all the skills available to the player in that time, as well as finishing all the internships the characters give you. I didn't touch Impostor Mode or Overtime Mode - the extra content provided by the Working From Home Update - but if you're looking for a challenge after the main story, that's where you'll find it. TLDR - Great game, not quite as polished as the triple-A developers yet but they definitely made a winner with their first game. Going Under is fun, sarcastic, and genuine, and I really enjoyed playing it. If you like Roguelikes at all, you'll really like the fresh perspective that Going Under has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: With at least 10 hours of gameplay to complete in my experience, Going Under offers up plenty of content and inherent replay value by random generation, and the constant desire for one more run. As someone who has been playing Risk of Rain 2 non-stop as of late, but has been looking for something a little different to scratch that itch, I’ve finally found a new game to invest in.The gameplay alone is solid enough to be worthwhile, but what really makes the title shine is the story, characters, and writing. Even some twists and turns you may not expect, both in lore and gameplay, as time goes on. If I had any complaints, it’d simply be wanting more dungeons. The game isn’t lacking in content, it’s just so good that I’m left wanting more regardless. Of course, the future is full of possibilities, so maybe down the line we’ll see more to come.Either way, I highly recommend this game, to anyone who loves rogue-lites and hates tech-bro culture.And even if the genre isn’t normally your thing, the easy-to-pick-up, challenging-to-master style of gameplay in Going Under may offer an excellent launchpad into the genre. And, topping it all off, a customizable assist mode is available to those who want to play but would otherwise be barred by the game’s difficulty. A very welcome feature I hope to see in more and more games going forward! Game good, please support these devs.
