_childDocuments_.review: This game nails its setting, its characters and its plot. The music is fitting, and the progression is unique. However, the gameplay itself is Not That Good, for reasons ill get way in depth over, but its not a complete deal breaker. The controls of this game work when the game is easy. Unfortunately, towards the second half of the game, it starts asking more of the player than the controls can provide, and the game goes from easy to bullsh*t. This mainly stems from the fact that every action is non cancellable. Started an attack animation and noticed an enemy starting theirs? Too bad, nothing you can do about it (this is on top of most of the weapons having long wind up animations). Again, this is fine when the game is easy, as enemy numbers and aggression are low. But as soon as those go up, it starts to feel like youre a dark souls 2 character being dropped into bloodborne.The lock on mechanic is also basically useless most of the time. Its main role is to help with lining up targets for thrown objects and thrusting attacks. Neither of these attacks are worth using. The throwing action feels especially weak, as you are not throwing AT them, you are throwing TOWARD them, with a predefined arc, meaning even when locking on you can are either too far away or too close, as it travels in an arc over their heads There are a wide selection of weapons in this game, most of them being unique to each area, with many different animation sets. Unfortunately, only about 3 per area are actually any good. If a weapon does not have an sweeping attack, ie, thrusting weapons, its not worth picking up, as on top of having no crowd control, it wont have increased damage to compensate.This is extremely frustrating in the second half of the game, as on top of getting more enemies, with more health, with higher aggression, the game gives you less good weapons. Many times you will find yourself walking into a room, seeing 7 enemies and a bunch of cardboard boxes, pencils and junk items. And on top of that, theres weapon durability, meaning on the rare chance you DO find a weapon you actually want to use, it lasts exactly half an encounter.The durability in this game feels like its balanced around the first iteration of the areas. The enemies arent too tanky and theres enough weapons lying around that you would want to use that it makes the game fun. Youre constantly cycling through weapons, its chaotic and fun. Unfortunately that second act happens, and it turns to frantic and frustrating. As mentioned, In the second act, the weapon pool gets scaled to favour the crappier side, with weapons that have the same durability against more enemies that have become more tankier. Its frustrating to be halfway through a fight, finding yourself with all the weapons you started with broken, and left running around the room praying that theres something that isnt a thrusting weapon or a junk item. In short, the accessibility/assist options could have helped to fix this, with options to change player health, enemy damage, invincibility frames and durability. Unfortunately, it can feel like a putting a cast over a light graze.I opted to turn on the durability assist, as i was getting too frustrated with the system. I could have stuck it out, i already beat one of the three areas without it, but i wasnt having any fun doing so. Unfortunately , instead of being a slider, it was a toggle, and it jacked up the durability way too far for me. So now the durability went from frustrating and frantic to nonexistent and braindead. For an assist menu that opens up with "everyone has fun in their own way", its quite odd that im not able to tailor the experience been not enough and too much Minor things that i either took issue with or think that adding them could make the game better, in no particular order - There needs to be some sort of outline or indicator for the player for when they are behind or under something, as it is extremely easy to get lost in the frame - One of rays perks needed to be "pin 2 skills", it just makes too much sense to not have that - While holding a blank card, highlight enemies that we have not yet added to the rolodex. - Let us pick up the card if we miss an enemy, its super annoying to have it disappear into nothingness- Let us toggle something so that the only perks that show up in the level are ones we have yet to endorse, not a fan of having that be left up to chance - The marv fight is not good. This is a boss that feels like the only reason why you would ever use the lock on mechanic, and yet the lock on goes away every time he teleports, please let the lock on stick onto him - Why would you make it so that the floating objects in on the way to the marv fight block you, its lame - The styxcoin event never feels long enough- some of the mentor challenges just dont show up half the time. there was multiple times where i went through a dungeon and the the game forgot to spawn the mission room, unsure if intentional- please give swamp a higher chance of stealing the game console, having to rely on the rng sucked- weapons take durability damage when hit, but hitting weapons is the only way to get them off a high shelf. this is lame- the fists suck to use, even with the power up. on top of having no damage they dont even stun the enemy. i know youre supposed to pick up stuff, but come on Keep in mind tho, that despite how negative this review was, i still mostly recommend giving it a go

_childDocuments_.review: A modern office drama combined with a simple yet fun roguelike, Going Under lets you live the life of a college graduate desperately trying to get an unpaid internship in the hopes of someday having a paying position with health insurance. It all starts off with having to clear some goblins out of the basement, then you have to crush the hopes and dreams of cryptominers and horny people. Things get kicked up a notch when your company gets bought out by Not-Amazon. The cast of characters are all varied in personality and make the journey all that much more enjoyable.Albeit a little buggy (I've mostly had some camera issues that were solved with alt tabbing out and in), the game is well worth the price tag for the laughs and hours of gameplay. For an extra challenge, an optional dungeon rush mode unlocks about halfway through. If you like jokes about work (not to be confused with workplace humor), have ever dreamed about bashing a coworker's head in with their keyboard, or just enjoy quirky roguelikes, I highly recommend giving this a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I've worked in startups before and the writing, humor, and satire here is really charming and at times, kind of insightfully poignant. Its also chock full of tech world easter eggs and I think people working in that industry will appreciate the inside jokes.The gameplay is pretty stimulating, forcing you to equip and re-equip items on the fly and switch between weapons in different combat scenarios. Weapons break easily but practically everything in the office environment can be used as a weapon and it can be kind of fun just going around wrecking everythingWhen it comes to criticism I'd say that the gameplay can be a little shallow. The game experience itself is over pretty fast and I found myself using the same weapons and strategies after a while. Towards the end I started getting to a point where I would no longer get flavor text between runs. I also wouldn't mind seeing these characters interact with each other in a daily standup every so often. The writing is the best part of this game so I wish there was just more of itOne last thing I will say is that for some reason, I can't shake a certain melancholic feeling at certain scenes. This game ended up being pretty prophetic in terms of how technology would negatively affect our lives in the future. _childDocuments_.review: Protip: Don't be afraid to turn on assist mode. I was nervous to, thinking it might break my save and disable achievements or something. (It's hard to find any information on it, but if you just...just click it once, it explains everything.) Anyway, Going Under drew me in with its art style and writing when it first came out -- and Aggro Crab seem like legitimately cool developers based on how they dealt with trolls and dorky gamergate kids. It's a good game, but I was left disappointed by the gameplay.I enjoyed the first fourth of the game or so -- before you get to the True Founder dungeons. It was repetitive to a degree, but it didn't wear out its welcome quite yet. After you beat that chunk, however, the difficulty spikes through the roof. (Note: You'll find lots of complaints about this online, it turns out. The good news is a recent update lets you go back to replay the easier levels if you need to grind without stressing out.) It doesn't, unfortunately, spike in such a way as to reflect clever souls-like design principles, but rather because the combat is a bit clunky, the hit boxes questionable, some enemies are just not balanced well at all. A lot of the second and third acts of the game rely on RNG more than anything, which I found *so boring*, and led to my time being inflated by just hours upon hours of grinding the same dungeons over and over, leveling up mentors, &c. It doesn't help that all the dungeons are recycled with added difficulty, so you're only left with three total dungeons overall -- one of which (Styxcoin) I felt was notably worse in design than the other two.The final battles are full of so much screen shaking and endless hordes of enemies it was impossible to tell what the heck was going on and I was left dodgerolling and hoping for the best. This was the point I gave up and turned on assist mode; I wish I turned it on much earlier.Most grinding is to level up skills (of which there is a literal plethora) and your mentorship relationships, which provide extra bonuses. The high number of skills keeps things interesting, though a hefty chunk of them are not helpful. Only Swomp's mentorship is, imho, worth pursuing. (It's also the biggest pain in the butt, RNG-reliant to max out.) Three of the five are borderline worthless, and I am kicking myself a bit for wasting the time it took to max them out.I think this game really shines most in the aesthetic and the script. Having worked in and with the tech industry, the perspective and jabs on that culture and its obsession with buzzwords is just too on-point and clever not to admire. Who hasn't stood by muttering no, don't, stop, you don't know what you're asking for, while air-headed managers fall prey to the latest business fad like work culture mindfulness or slapping neural networks on frickin' everything? The digs at the frequent misuse and misunderstanding of machine learning and AI particularly killed me; they were too accurate. Sigh. The script was fantastic, it's just too bad the gameplay was such a chore long before I hit the ending, making this *barely* get a recommend from me. Definitely into it enough to follow Aggro Crab in the future, tho.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under quickly became one of my favorite games. The gameplay, art, and writing all weaves together nicely around a unique setting based on a hellish job market inspired by present-day, making it oddly relatable despite all the absurdity happening. The gameplay has you constantly adapting to your surroundings, as all the furniture and appliances in the room are weapons to take and break. The combat features many lil' quirks and interactions that make the improvised office fights more fun and chaotic.The aesthetic is simple and colorful, and generally makes something nice and charming out of an otherwise sterile corporate artstyle. The animations are lively and full of personality that add to the game's flavor. There are innumerable visual gags and thematically appropriate puns hidden in plain sight, and the character interactions got me looking forward to all the dialogues that'd pop up in-between runs. The plot is also more than I expected for this kind of game.The main caveat is that the camera takes a bit getting used to for this 3D dungeon crawler, but that becomes second nature relatively quickly. Overall, this game is definitely worth the investment.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent little rogue-lite with great satire and not serious gameplay.Pros:Combat feels good and dodge rolling is very responsive.Using throwable junk is an interesting combat system that adds to the weapons breakage formula.Runs are not long at all, with most being 20-30 minsSatire is great. If you are familiar with startup culture and silicon valley tech companies you'll enjoy it.Game is a good length.Mentor abilities are interesting and add a lot of replayabilityCons:Due to the physics based gameplay, items and enemies will sometimes knock you down and keep hitting you. It's entirely possible to lose a run just from being hitstunned into a corner.Mentor quests are a great idea but they fall flat when they require specific dungeons. I beat the first dungeon on my first try which meant I had to keep going back in for many many quests.The difficulty also felt wildly inconsistent. I beat the first 3 dungeons all within 3 attempts (2 on my first try!) and 2 of the second set within 3 attempts. And then one took me like 12 tries.There are too many skills for the length of the game. You would need to grind to unlock them all. I unlocked 66/99 in my run and that was after buying them every time I could. Why would I want to grind for skills post game?End of floor fights felt... pointless? There are no bosses aside from the final one in each dungeon so why bother making a special arena room.Probably the most damning thing about the game is that the first 3 dungeons are recycled to form the second 3. To be fair, they are ramped up in difficulty and have unique bosses, rooms and enemies. One of the game's strongest points is it's theming though and you have to redo 3 levels with the same theme as last time.The game's second to last dungeon has around 8 rooms filled with the same 2 enemy types that are massively tanky. If you fail the boss you have to do this over. The rooms and enemies never change.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played my fair share of soulslikes, but I don't think I've played one so unique and so creative as "Going Under". It is also a beat 'em up, a dungeon crawler and a roguelite, all while being visually arresting, funny and satirical about today's companies. It's a game that evokes different ideas and succeeds at them all, without ever feeling aimless.This game is so many things... where do I even begin with? For starters, I would say this game isn't much of a RPG; it's a roguelite first and foremost. Death means starting over again, but it gives you the opportunity to buy perks and improve your chances at each run. Still, there are no character stats, no leveling up. This doesn't disqualify the game as a soulslike, due to its lock-on mechanic and dodging. I will admit I didn't make much use of the lock-on, since my approach to combat was much more based on getting closer to my enemies and then button smash rather than the more tactical combat from "Dark Souls". But by God, I dodged a lot in this game, which is a central characteristic from the games by FromSoftware. In combat, multiple enemies will come at you at once, so dodging and moving are key for combat.As you crawl into dungeons, the game really shows its beat 'em up colours. Almost everything around you is a weapon, and can be used against your enemies. You can only carry three weapons at anytime, but some larger objects can only be used when they're at your hands, meaning you can't store them. Some weapons may come with buffed attack speed, damage or critical hit chance. Weapons naturally are of limited use and eventually break; there will be times when environments around you will be scarce of weapons, but so often one will be hanging in a wall nearby. Also, if you have no weapon at hands, dodging at an object will automatically make your character take it, which may have been a way from developers to avoid having your character be unarmed in a fight, but I would constantly grab useless items. Yes: they're here too.Dungeons in this game are randomly generated, meaning that a run will never be precisely like another. However, they'll always be divided in different floors, and as you move to a floor, you can't go back. Once you get to a room with enemies, you can only leave it by disposing them all; some rooms have these optional battles that, if you accept them and perform well, can grant you nice items. There'll also be specific rooms with shops, printers and perks. In shops, you trade the money you made for weapons, perks and health: pretty basic stuff. Printers - and this is when things get interesting - give you this blank paper that does massive damage, can only be used once, and that can convert enemies (even bosses) into cards, which go to your card collection. My problem with these printers, however, is that you can only take one paper from one of them, meaning that if you waste it, you're screwed.Perks are these buffs that grant you some extra power for that run only. Once you use that perk enough, you'll unlock it and be able to start a run with that power. But that's not all: it gets complicated. Before that, you need to buy these perks at the hub area, so they'll be available to be found in dungeons. And there's a different currency for that, called "cubits", which can also be found in dungeons. Whereas you can't take regular money with you back to the hub area (since it can only be used in dungeons anyway), cubits are used to buy these perks in the overworld, as well as card paper. Some are game changers, and when combined, can pretty much guarantee you a successful run. Still on the matter of perks, you'll also find at dungeons rooms with this vampire-like character offering a negative perk: it will affect you for some battles before dissipating, but you'll gain access to three items of interest, so it's up to you to judge if it's a worthy sacrifice.From time to time, you'll come across secret rooms that are not in your HUD map, and they may contain powerful weapons. There'll always be a boss at the end of your run, and once you defeat them for the first time and take their prizes, your basic health capacity increases permanently.Then there are the mentors. God, I love them as a mechanic and as characters. The mentors will give you side quests, which are really these Rebellion-like challenges in which you're requested to dispose of enemies in specific ways, or do runs without buffs, or not get hurt for so long. At some points, mentors may ask you to eliminate enemies that will appear at dungeons in special rooms. But the absolute worse is when they ask you to buy them things in the shops: it may look simple, but these items will be specific to one shop at a specific floor only, and once you move on, even when you get the necessary cash, you can't buy it. For that, you need to make use of tricks that, fortunately, you can pull off. As you complete such tasks, mentors will grant you interesting advantages, such as shoplifting, or starting the run with a food box.And then there are the apps, which can grant you momentary buffs such as high speed, health recovery, invincibility and so on. If you have a certain mentor selected, apps will be replaced by soda cans, and the difference is that while apps are powers for you, cans generate these blasts that affect nearby enemies in different ways, and I personally preferred doing runs with soda cans. The high variety of weapons, perks, apps, soda cans and mentors allows players to try different playstyles and techniques, so if you feel like you have already found your style, it doesn't hurt to leave your comfort zone and try something different - maybe you'll find something that suits you even better.There are three dungeons in the game, plus two special levels. I can't reveal anything more without spoiling, but suffice to say, there will be a moment when you go through them again, but with different, harder enemies. Dungeons have these little nuances that differentiate them from each other, but they play more or less the same. One of them even has its own currency, just to make matters more complicated! In the end, "Going Under" is not extensive, but more of a game in which you play the same levels in different ways. And no: it doesn't get tiresome.This is very much a game for completionists. Everything about it feels like it was designed for players to keep coming back for all the side quests, perks, cards and achievements. It's a game that, with its very addicting combat, feels so compelling to play that you want more from it. It indeed got the "Work From Home" update, which added a new challenge, but unfortunatley it's incredibly repetitive and grindy, and a major sore point. The game also features what it refers to as an "assist mode", which is to say it gives players options to customise the game's difficulty. So here's a HUGE difference between it and the works from Hidetaka Miyazaki.Last but certainly not least, the presentation, and its biting satire of modern corporatism. The characters, the visuals, everything is evocative of today's companies. Dialogues - which are presented as text messages - are delightful and don't at all feel like tanking the flow of the game. The characters are all stereotypes who seem straight from "Silicon Valley", and they're so enjoyable that I connected with them and their little dramas - I wish I could romance Jackie with Swomp, seriously. In fact, the whole thing looks like it could be a colaboration between Paul Verhoeven, J.G. Quintel and Alex HirschIn the end, "Going Under" is a bright, funny and addicting game from all the involved. It feels like a passion project though and through, and the future for Aggro Crab is bright if this was their debut.

_childDocuments_.review: A pleasant surprise, and a damn good time considering how much I normally despise this style of dungeon crawler. Going Under has a lot of good stuff going for it. The art style is unique and colorful, the combat is very hectic and requires a lot of improvisation thanks to a BOTW style weapon system, and pretty much every skill results in a significant game play change. It's not as in-depth as something like Binding of Issac or Enter the Gungeon, but the 3 worlds and relatively low amount of items in comparison to those games didn't get boring at all during the game's relatively short campaign. It's much more of a bite-sized rogue lite, which is perhaps one of the reasons I enjoyed it so much. Progression in Going Under is rapid as hell, often resulting in multiple unlocks from each run. The game is very happy to dish out currency for unlockables as well, which makes each run actually feel worthwhile. The only area where Going Under hits some speedbumps is with the Mentor unlocks, which are essentially character abilities that get unlocked through specific mission objectives. The only problem is that these objectives rely on some pretty hefty RNG a lot of the time, and will have you confused as to how to proceed. You will be lucky if you have more than one mentor fully leveled up by the time the credits roll, which is a shame because a lot of the abilities seem like a lot of fun.Going Under has all the workings of a great rogue-lite and then some. The combat is punchy and satisfying, (most) enemies are balanced, and the boss fights are a ton of fun to complete. The game avoids a lot of frustration that I feel from other rogue lites by having runs last usually a max of 15 minutes, and progression that would normally 10 hours in other games here takes 2. It does cheapen the thrill of the unlocks occasionally, but you also have a much more tightly packaged and designed game that feels rewarding to play and is addicting as all hell. I can't remember the last time I completed a game in 2 days, let alone one so far outside of my comfort zone.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Dungeon Crawler!At first glance this game didn’t look like much from the steam page, but I was pleasantly surprised once playing.The plot is modern and different from any other theme I’ve seen in this genre. It’s very hip heh…The characters have a fun stereotypical design, and the dialogues are easily digestible. I wouldn’t say dialogues had anything special about them other than it fit the theme of what they were going for with each character really well. Still, something I appreciated when playing.I loved the music in this game being something like a mix between lo-fi and futuristic chillwave I guess?? Either way, it has a very nice soundtrack to have on while fighting your way through these dungeons and talking to people. I usually play these games and watch something on the side, but the music kept me engaged and vibin.The combat is probably where the game is good but not as good as other dungeon crawlers I’ve played. Personally, like combat that feels like you are hitting your enemies and I did not get that feeling when playing this. However, the weapons felt very creative in relation to what dungeon you were in and had good variability to them.At first, I thought the game was a bit too easy but as with many other DCs, it got harder when progressing. I would recommend it for both casual and experienced players.	The visuals are stunning making me want to eat my monitor. Everything is very bouncy and marshmallowey. The locations had fun details that fit the stereotypes I think they were going for, and NPCs fits their theme making me think that developers put a lot of thought into it.All and all I would say for those looking for a satisfying and fun dungeon crawler with great visuals and an intriguing story, this is the one for you!

_childDocuments_.review: 07.08.2021.Game #170You know what I hate? Getting an internship job at a new company and from day one someone telling me to kill monsters under the company floor. That really sucks. I mean, come on! I applied for the marketing department and they are telling me to go downstairs, grab whatever I could find, and whack monsters until there aren’t any left? What am I supposed to whack them with? Laptops, potted plants, fake swords? That’s basically Going Under and the above description pretty much describes the game, except for the part where I say that I hate it, because I love this game.In this game you go into randomly generated dungeons where you fight monsters, collect power ups, different weapons and eventually beat a boss at the end. It’s very similar to most rouge-likes such as The Binding of Isaac  or Enter the Gungeon  but not as deep. The biggest difference here is that you do everything from a third person view and have full control of your camera wherever you go. While we’ve seen a lot of whacky rogue-likes with wacky weapons, I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game where you use almost all office supplies for combat. Mugs, pencils, potted plants, protractors, mining picks (for bitcoin mining, obviously), laptops, you name it.Each dungeon is making fun of a certain company culture and each dungeon feels a little different than the last. In one dungeon for example, you fight against bitcoin miners and in another against job trolls. It’s both funny and endearing. Most importantly, the game is fun.From what I described above, you’d think that combat would be chaotic. While it can get a bit messy with too many enemies I almost never had a situation where I didn’t feel in control. Moving and using weapons is very responsive and very simple. While you may be tempted to grab the biggest thing in the room and whack enemies with it, many weapons break easily so you are forced to swap between them quite often. Not as frustrating as Zelda: Breath of the Wild but it still makes you think twice before picking a weapon for the next room. Also, each weapon has weight and physics. It’s take twice as much to swing a heavy weapon than a small pencil. Each weapon can also be thrown at enemies which is a great strategy when a weapon is about to break. You can also dodge roll, which works really well.You can also use fire to burn enemies, power ups to make some encounters easier, buy things from the dungeon shops… I mean, for a joke game like this, this is a very deep rouge-like.From the presentation, I thought this was going to be a walk in the park, but no. This game can be really hard, just like any good rogue-like. It took me quite a few runs to reach the end of my first dungeon but it never felt like the game wanted to screw me over. Sure, the game can be hard at times but it’s one of those cases where, the more you play the more you learn.  I adore the way Going Under looks. It’s so colorful. I’m a sucker for games with bright colors and this just makes me hopeful for the future. Why do all games nowadays have to be dark and gloomy? Why don’t we have more silly games that make fun of startup companies? Combine this with a simple yet catchy theme with each dungeon and you’ve got yourself a rouge-like that’s really eye-catching. As of writing this, I haven’t really played this game too much but I know that I’ll be back for more. Yeah, sometimes I really need a quick run of a dungeon and I think Going Under is going to do just nicely. I’m looking forward to seeing more of its parody on modern companies.Next game: A Golden Wake

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could leave a mixed review, but I'd rather give this game a thumbs up than a thumbs down because of the things that it does right.The characters, art style and dialogue are very good, its a successful parody that at no point feels preachy or bitter, it pokes good fun of corporate culture through the dialogue and art style.My main issue comes from the second half of the game, where the difficulty just gets cranked up way too high and the combat doesn't support that.Most weapons you use don't give you enough time to dodge, coupled with the problem that some enemies don't flinch even when you are using heavy weapons that take way too long to swing and can be interrupted mid-swing along with the fact that weapons can break. _childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a third-person roguelite developed by Aggro Crab, and their first game at that. Roguelites have become a bit of an oversaturated market over the past few years, but I think Going Under definitely sets itself apart from the crowd.Interestingly enough, the fundamental gameplay was probably my least favorite part of Going Under. Not to say that it's bad. Keep in mind this is coming from someone with a ton of experience in roguelites, so I'm comparing Going Under to the best of the genre in terms of pure gameplay (i.e Dead Cells, Hades).The basic gameplay is pretty simple. You pick up weapons you find in the dungeon and use them to fight a wide range of enemies. There's a durability system, meaning your weapons break after enough use. Thankfully, you can store up to 3 at a time. I'm not a fan of durability systems in games but I think it works very well in a roguelite. It forces you to use weapons you might normally not use, which helps add variety to runs as well as getting good with all sorts of weapons. There's a targeting system to focus on a specific enemy, which is super useful. It's very similar to Z-targeting from the 3D Zelda games. You can also throw weapons at enemies, which I didn't find particularly useful most of the time, but is a nice option anyway. While I wasn't huge on the basic gameplay, the systems present within the game are all fantastic.The skills in Going Under aren't as fun as some other roguelites. Don't expect to find some completely broken combination that will let you easily steamroll the game ala Isaac. They are, however, still fun and provide the player with a good deal of choice. Each floor has a guaranteed skill room, which has 2 skills. You choose 1. This gives the player some degree of choice as to how they want to play their run. Even after completing the game, I still haven't unlocked all of the skills, so there's definitely a good variety present. Once you use a skill enough, you can endorse it, which means you can start a run with that skill already learned. This is really great in my opinion, removing some of the luck from a run and allowing the player to start the run on their terms. Big fan of this, wish more roguelites did stuff like it.All the characters in the game (barr Marv and Avie) have a mentorship you can progress through. Basically, you talk to them, get missions, and complete them to progress through the mentorship. There are 4 levels to each mentorship, and each level has a unique perk that gives you an advantage. I love how each mentorship is strongly tied to the character (i.e Ray is hugely irresponsible and gives you the Company Card, etc.). Just like the endorsement system, this gives the player a lot of control over how they play each individual run. It can be very fun to try them all out as each mentorship is distinct.Going Under features multiple, short dungeons to choose from as you progress through the game. There are 3 main dungeons, and each has 4 floors, with the final floor containing the boss of the dungeon. They each have a unique theme (as they're each based around a fictional company) with different enemies, events, shopkeepers and bosses. The dungeons you explore are very linear. There isn't any real exploration to do on each floor of the dungeon you're going through. The most I've found after around 12 hours in the game were some hidden rooms and a few branching paths. This linearity isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it's something to take note of. It makes each run decently quick, but can definitely impact the replayability. Thankfully, in the most recent major update, the devs added Impostor Mode, which lets you go through all of the dungeons at once, much more like a conventional roguelite. Definitely a good choice to add.The story and characters are what made me really love Going Under. They're genuinely fantastic. The basic premise is that you, Jackie Fiasco, are an intern at Fizzle, a subsidiary of Cubicle (which is basically Amazon). Unfortunately, you're forced to go through a bunch of dungeons instead of marketing work. Thanks Marv. I'll leave the rest for you to find out!The characters are all a lot of fun. You really understand each character and we're they're coming from. Fern's genuine love of his work. Tappi's frustration with her inability to reign in Ray. Kara's hatred of her job and indifference to the fate of the company. Swomps.... swomp-ness. Ray's privileged and carefree nature. Marv's indifference to your situation. The character writing is something to commend. Every conversation in the game is pretty great. One of the reasons I like the mentorship system so much is because you learn more about each character and their personality as you progress through their tasks. Going Under is super, super satirical. A lot of dialogue focuses on satirising working in the modern day, and particularly startups. The game is pretty much a metaphor for working as an intern at a startup. Except instead of doing menial unrelated jobs in the workplace, you're going through dungeons and murdering monsters. It's made super  clear that Ray and Marv aren't paying attention to what the people working in Fizzle actually want. Tappi is constantly frustrated at Ray refusing to stay on budget. Marv often makes promises to the team (especially Jackie) that he clearly never intended to fulfill. A lot of the game's satire is focused on how poorly workers are treated in modern day corporate spaces. One of Ray's missions is literally to bust a Joblin union. The team essentially gets replaced by Avie, a super-advanced AI. Ray and Marv's refusal to pay attention to their team makes it clear that Fizzle is doomed to fail. It's clear that everyone (barr Swomp, I guess?) is overworked and underappreciated.Jackie is a great protagonist to deliver a lot of laughs. She often plays the straight man, and it's very easy to relate to her struggles. She's just someone fresh out of college looking to get a start in the corporate workplace. Her conversations with Marv are all funny, but a bit sad. Jackie just wants to get some real experience, dammit!That being said, I would be remissed if I talked about the humor of the game without mentioning Swomp. Every line Swomp says is f*cking hilarious. Maybe my sense of humor is just really dumb, but he's so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ funny. He talks in all lowercase, uses crappy grammar (i.e saying "ur") and is just a super carefree, chill dude. His missions are so, so funny. Just completely stupid sh*t, like running over a car with a car, or buying a dank gaming rig (actual words used in game). He often refers to Jackie as "beb".I seriously recommend completing his mentorship, because his business card is probably the funniest thing in the game.Going Under is really unique and fun visually. I love the polygonal artstyle, and how bright everything is. Each dungeon has unique theming and colour palettes, and each enemy looks distinct. The character design is fantastic, you can pretty much understand the basics of each character from their vignettes in conversation. The enemies all look unique and separate from each other. The design of Fizzle office is pretty much an ideal hub world. All great stuff.The music is genuinely splendid. Love, love, love it. Whatever tone the game is going for, the music complements it brilliantly. The mundane but slightly upbeat tune that plays in the Fizzle office. The unique themes of each dungeon (especially Joblin, can't get that track out of my head). The epic boss battle songs. It's all so, so great.If you read through this whole thing, congrats. I wrote it all and I could barely do it.  I hope this review convinced you of the merits of Going Under.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a top-down roguelite dungeon-crawler set in a fantasy city called Neo-Cascadia. As Jackie, a newly-graduated intern, fortunately receives the marketing job offer at the famous beverage company Fizzle. However, the "job" does not seem to be what she expects: weird marketing plans, irrelevant budget usage, and worst of all, dungeon-crawling?! Battling joblins, skeletons, and demons is definitely far from marketing. Players will help Jackie conquer different dungeons of failed companies, as well as unmasked the beautiful facade of Cubicle. This is the roguelite game I've played that hits home. It's satiric approach of corporate greed, underappreciated employees and misplaced intern mock the reality of our society. A consistent and coherent story seasoned with tons of mockup names of real-life company and business phrases really makes the game charming and joyful. I highly recommend everyone trying Going Under out. The focus on story makes up for lack of variety in terms of room spawn, and the fast pace and short runs are great feature for people looking to experience the beauty of roguelite.A combination of Deadrising and Breath of The Wild is the accurate summary of Going Under's weapon system. Everything you see in the office/dungeon is a potential weapon for your survival, and there are tons of items to weaponized: from typical furniture to office appliances; from classic swords and hammers to that body pillow which is too embarrassing to show. Beware! These "weapons" break easily, so make sure to have something you can bash the mobs with nearby. Besides interesting weapon system, the game also introduces various perks as Kiosks, which can shape your combat style. Helping yeet things faster and more accurate, or disguise yourself so you can avoid combat, you name it. My favorite so far, is baby Jackie with beef-up arms and a spinning saw blade around her waist. How terrifying to see a tiny person running full speed at you, swinging a moai like a piece of plastic.The npcs in Going Under is a perfect replication of a typical company: an overlooking entrepreneur, encouraging but manipulative manager, a depressed accountant, an engineer who hates her job as an engineer, a weird scientist, and an out-of-loop guy. These npcs feels alive with their special interaction with Jackie the clueless intern, though most of the time complaining. They also offer different tiers of side quests you can complete during the run. While most of them are simple tasks, some have leave me interesting memories. Like Kara tier 2 quest: walking Eclaire through B3. The leash actually binds your movement. As a result, you need to time your dodge well and make the best of your maneuvers. This side quest adds a lair of difficulty in this rather easy roguelite game.This game is oozing satire from head to toe. The opening cutscene is a mockup tech demo concept video. The overall art style is Alegria Motion but wackier. The dungeons in nothing short of fun. The Joblins are contractors and freelancers that help promote caffeine; The Styxcoin is the embodiment of the digital-mining cryptocurrency - they literally put "mining" and "crypto-" into this dungeons theme; The Winkydink is straightforward ridiculing those dating apps all over the place, including emojis sexually-spamming through the character. And you cannot miss this. Remember that guy who brags about his Lamborghini and "knowledge", he is in this game too, as a vampire!While I do say that the focus on the story makes up for lack of room variation, this is still a glaring issue in terms of roguelite games. Even though I consider Going Under to be a short roguelite game exploration-wise, I still think the room spawn become easily repetitive after 3 to 5 runs. To be fair, the devs do design three challenges unique to each dungeon, but there are still more rooms to be desire. After all, the funny joke and satire can only go so far. I suggest adding some kind of racing challenge: the room is full of environmental hazards, and the player needs to go through it either to progress or obtain a super strong item. Basically, adding more "high risk, high reward" situation to spice up the run.

_childDocuments_.review: Good:-Visual appealing ranging from it's colorful and fluid art style-Has a funny sense of humor with its writing, terminologies, and references-Friendly rogue-like with a balance of intrinsic and extrinsic progression-Lots of weapons and power-ups that encourages experimentation with different play styles-Combat is fun, fast-pace, and challengingBad:-RNG can greatly affect runs (especially on imposter mode)-Descriptions for some skills are unclear due to its comedic writing-Character dialogue might be a turn-off since some text are paragraphs longFor me, I would say the strongest points of this game are its art style and combat. The alegria art style suits this game since it revolves around advertising and business. It's an art style used by most modern tech companies since vibrant colors and fluid shapes are visually appealing. Ironically, it's one of the reasons I bought this game. The combat has a lot of depth as there are many weapons and power-ups that can be acquired which can encourage experimentation with different play styles. This game has a good balance of extrinsic and intrinsic progression. Players are able to increase their max HP and gain new skills to use in future runs. However, intrinsic skill such as adapting to RNG, dodging attacks, and patience is also needed to do well in Going Under since the game gets more challenging and chaotic overtime. A few main issues I have are the RNG and the descriptions of the skills. RNG can greatly affect runs especially on imposter mode where you can't start with a mentor or starting skill. Some runs can be good while others can feel unfair. As for the skill descriptions, some are confusing to understand due to the game trying to be comedic and witty. The least the devs could've done was be more detailed on what certain skills do. But despite my complaints, I think Going Under is a very fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: You know what's worse than playing a bad game? Playing a game that starts being awesome and then suddenly changes mid-way, turning into something that you do not enjoy anymore and leaves you bewildered as to why such a change was necessary.Going Under is one of those games. A game that starts very well, managing to use its narrative features to gloss over its shortcomings and reel the players in, but fails to keep itself going and starts focusing on the wrong things as well.Going Under is an enjoyable critique of current work culture dressed up as a game. The game's events happen in a world very similar to ours, with mega corporations that grow with each passing day, taking smaller companies and startups as their own and then doing whatever the hell they want with them. You start the game in the shoes of an unpaid intern named Jackie, who is assigned to an already struggling startup to do marketing, and gets entangled in a whole lot of stuff instead.It's actually amazing how well this game handles work-related topics in our current world. The whole story and all of the dialogues are cleverly written commentaries of various topics such as corporate greed, workplace culture, startups, artificial intelligence and even overuse of the technology. In fact, some of the story events literally depict what we have seen happening around us and in bigger corporations in recent years.And the game delivers these commentaries through clever jokes, well-done references and easter eggs, fine humor and a cast of likeable & colorful characters, with occasional drama to make you really feel what the main character's co-workers are going through. All of the characters you will see in this game have distinct personalities and mannerisms, to the point you can't help but constantly get reminded of real people who are currently working at a corporation or running it. Hell, some of these characters and what they told me even reminded me of people who are around me and are not even working a corporate job.When it comes to easter eggs, Going Under has one of the best instances of hiding them or giving subtle nods. The game literally puts the easter eggs in front of your face but unless you are paying attention, you won't be able to identify them. And the things the game references with its easter eggs are wild, from other video games to actual people and even viral internet things that you would never expect seeing them in a game like this.And the game needed such well-done narrative presentation, as the gameplay does not have any charms of its own to encourage players to carry on.Despite what people are saying on this game's store page, I firmly believe Going Under is not a rogue-lite. This game is a beat'em up at its core, with rogue-lite elements sprinkled in to inject some variety to the gameplay. And honestly, they're not enough.The meat of the gameplay consists of arriving at a dungeon and going through multiple rooms that are randomly put together by the game, each either containing enemies to fight, showing a specific optional task to do or offering you to pick up potentially helpful powerups and skills in forms of special rooms and shops. Your goal is to get to the ending room and fight a final wave of enemies for the first three floors of the dungeon, and then face the boss and beat them on the 4th floor. But you won't have access to weapons from the get-go; You have to pick up items that are scattered around the room and use them as weapons, and them maybe switch them with the actual weapons the enemies drop; either to get a better weapon or switch your currently damaged weapon before it breaks mid-combat.However, contrary to what you might think, the combat is not fun. Despite the game offering the mentorship system (unlocking passive skills in exchange for mission completion), curses (temporary debuffs in exchange for items) and a boatload of skills to unlock, the combat is still very underdeveloped and the novelty of the whole thing quickly wears off. Because what you do through all of the available dungeons is literally the same thing and the optional missions sometimes are more infuriating & time-consuming rather than being challenging. That's why the narrative presentation is so strong. The game simply uses the story and the witty commentary to make you want to carry on with the gameplay.The game does this for the first 4-6 hours, at which point you will finally feel the gameplay fatigue kicking in, with the story being unable to stop it. By this point in time, you have reached the mid-point of the game, awaiting the second half of the adventure to begin. But while you expect the game to reveal its next big thing and add something new to the gameplay, it just does something completely different, dramatically decreasing the value of the game in the process.The second half of Going Under features one of the most severe quality nosedives I have ever seen in a video game. And I do not mean it has ♥♥♥♥ quality. The game just starts focusing on doing the opposite of what it was already doing, completely forgetting how it kept the experience going for so long.Upon starting the second half of the game, you'll see a series of dramatic story events and then the quality of the game sharply drops afterwards. At this moment, the game completely stops being fun; because it changes its focus from what works for it to what doesn't work. If the first half of the game focused on carrying the gameplay through narrative, the second half tries to carry the narrative through gameplay by removing all of the story and dialogues, and locking them behind gameplay progression. There won't be any optional conversations with the NPCs or story cutscenes until the very end. If you want to see more of the story, you have to beat all of the dungeons again and reach the final boss. And that is without mentioning the difficulty spike you'll be facing.In the second half of the game, you will be forced to run through harder versions of all of the past dungeons and bosses in order to access more story content and reach the ending. In each encounter, the game will throw more enemies at you with significantly increased health and more armor points, turning them into literal damage sponges. Meanwhile, you'll be using the very same set of abilities that you've been using since the start of the game. This makes the game unnecessarily hard and in the case of the second dungeon, even unfair & poorly designed. And that's where everything falls apart, because as I mentioned before, the gameplay gets incredibly stale after a while and it's the narrative and commentary that drives the players forward in the first half of the game. So, by switching the driving factor and not adding anything of value to it, the game completely loses its appeal.And even if you power through and try to finish the game with all of the gameplay issues and frequent bugs (like curses becoming permanent, item descriptions getting messed up, optional missions becoming unbeatable, and more) your reward is a disappointing final boss and a lackluster ending, with the story being completely unable to salvage them. By this point I was completely burnt out and didn't even bother with the optional game mode the game offers you. Because honestly... I didn't want more of the same gameplay I was playing until that point.Starts great as a charming & enjoyable game with clever commentary on corporations and work culture, then the quality sharply nosedives upon getting to the second half, changing the game for the worse.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Just wow.This is by far the best rougelike I've ever played by a lightyear. Most rougelikes are just cheap and quickly made video games to give someone a lot of mileage from a moderate bank of assets via remixing and challenging progressive gameplay.This, on the other hand. Is ART.It has a fun and cute artstyle, the world and characters are bursting with charm, the amazingly deep-rooted understanding of pop-culture of 3 generations is so one-of-a-kind here. Every single aspect of game development is nailed here.The themes and underlying message of this game are so on point it hurts. And it's just so well-handled.And the finale just slaps so hard. It's rare to see a game stick a landing so hard.But onto gameplay.This one of the most accessible rougelike I know of. I didn't see the options till after I beat the game but wow, it's cool that even a more casual audience can enjoy the story!It's also refreshing to play a game in this genre where learning, patience, and skill are rewarded and can carry you without needing the luck of a "good run". Usually devs make cheap or unfair enemies/levels to further pad out the genre, not here.The loop is fun, the curses are more fair than they should be IMO, and the mentor missions really mix up how you play some dungeons. The progression of skills and mentorship are very rewarding and satisfying. The second half of the game is pretty brutal, but never gets to the point of frustrating.I beat this game feeling inspired and happy. And if I could I would give the entire dev team a standing ovation for this incredible game. If you like action games and rougelikes, you owe it to yourself to play this gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under? More like Going Underrated! - A vibrant, colourful aesthetic. - Amusing dialogue often full of corporate humour, pop culture references, or general silliness which, quite frankly, is right up my alley. - Charming, loveable NPC colleagues each with their own personalities. - A large variety of melee and ranged weapons to use against your enemies, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. Each weapon also has a 'charge' attack that behaves differently, e.g. small swords perform an AoE spin vs a sledgehammer which does a slow, high-damage overhead attack vs a spear doing a leap attack, etc. - Roughly 100 or so perks to collect with various synergies. You can also select one to begin with once you have found it a few times during gameplay which is nice. - Various limited-use consumables to collect with varying effects, e.g. an 'app' that repairs and randomly buffs your equipped weapon, or cans of soft drink that cast elemental novas that apply status effects to enemies. - Occasional secret rooms with special weapons and enemies. - Various risk and reward mechanics to keep you on your toes, e.g. take a debuff for X rooms, but get a few perks/weapons as compensation or kill an optional wave of enemies for a chance at a box containing strong items, etc. - A great soundtrack that fits the areas. - A 'mentoring' system where you can complete challenges to gain passive improvements and can select between the different groups of improvements, e.g. one mentor focuses on improving apps, another on item boxes and money, etc. - An optional 'assist' system where you can enable certain crutches if you find the game too hard, e.g. more health, more item durability, etc. I think this is a nice feature for the more casual audience. - Completing the rolodex (beastiary) can be rather challenging. You can only add an entry if you last-hit an opponent with a special blank card item. You can usually only get 1-2 of these per run and they are a one use item, so it can take some time to obtain this if you don't time things right/miss/die before you are able to use it. Pro tip: make sure you have the 'focus' key pressed when using the card! If you intend to get all the achievements, then this shouldn't be too much trouble as you will have completed enough runs to get this by the end. - Changing your weapons is a core part of the game. They only have a limited durability and will break after extended use, forcing the player to find new ones which keeps things fresh. I can see some players might find this to be annoying. On an attack where a weapon would break however, the attack will deal double damage which I find surprisingly satisfying. - Certain items bounce around to an annoying degree, e.g. if you open a crate and a jobwich (healing item) pops out, you usually have to spend time chasing after it as it bounces around the room. - Particular room/enemy combinations can be quite difficult to deal with initially, e.g. fast/AoE monsters in a small room. This becomes easier to deal with as you get familiar with the game however. - Enemy corpses sometimes wig out and fly around the room.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a satirical dungeon crawler that takes you on a journey through the dark and twisted world of failed tech startups. With its unique concept, sharp humour and engaging gameplay, this game is sure to keep you entertained. But be warned, the procedurally generated dungeons, rogue-lite elements, and button-mashing combat might not be for everyone. The game's concept of using failed tech startups as dungeons is both original and thought-provoking. Players take on the role of an unpaid intern, Jackie Fiasco, who must explore these procedurally generated dungeons to defeat the monsters that have taken over. The game is set in a dystopian version of Seattle, where the startup culture has gone too far and has resulted in the creation of monstrous dungeons. You will encounter a variety of comedic characters and situations throughout the game, and the humour is often self-referential and satirical. The game pokes fun at the tech industry in an entertaining and thought-provoking way. It's like the developers have been reading my twitter feed.The art style is like playing in a cartoon world filled with vibrant colours and unique design elements. You'll feel like you're in a dream, a very weird dream. The game's dungeons are procedurally generated, meaning each playthrough is different, like a choose your own adventure book but with more monsters and fewer illustrations.The gameplay of Going Under is based on a combination of action and RPG elements. Players can use a variety of weapons and abilities to fight monsters, and they can also collect money and other items that can be used to upgrade their character. The game also includes a rogue-lite element, where players will have to restart the game after death, but some progress will be carried over, which provides a lot of replayability and encourages players to explore and experiment with different playstyles. It's like a real-life unpaid internship, but with less coffee runs and more monsters. And don't worry, you'll respawn and be able to keep some items and abilities, just like in real life.In conclusion, Going Under is an excellent game that is sure to provide hours of entertainment for players of all ages. The game's unique concept, humorous writing, and colourful art style make it stand out from other dungeon-crawler games. The game's procedural generation, rogue-lite elements, and replayability make it a game that is worth playing multiple times. Overall, Going Under is a game that I recommend, especially towards the younger generation. However, this is byfar the least enjoyable rougelike i have played out from Dead Cells, Risk of Rain 1 and 2

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a really fun action-rpg I'd describe as something like 2D Zelda meets Enter The Gungeon, with a dash of Breath of the Wild. It benefits from a really fun, simple approach to combat, based on using and discarding breakable weapons throughout procedural dungeons. The weapon breaking system works better here than in BOTW, as the dungeons are full of all kinds of junk and weapons to beat up your enemies with, and the chaos of breaking weapons and scrounging up new ones on the fly adds to the combat. Macrogame progression-- that is, getting stronger over the course of runs-- is handled via  acquiring and mastering skills, and advancing mentorships with the cast. Each mentor has different perks and requires you to complete quests in the various dungeons to level them up. This allows you to tailor your runs to your playstyle.If you enjoy a good action-roguelike, this one is quite lovely.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for June 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before July 6th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.This is a Dungeon Crawler slash Roguelite with a corporate environment theme.  You play a young intern who is hired to work in the marketing department, but ends up going into the basement to slay monsters, in your Amazon-inspired office.  Going Under had me laughing quite a bit, perhaps that’s because I’ve spent too much time in Corporate America or I recognize what most of these scenes and characters are supposed to be.  I don’t know if this will translate to everyone, but I still got a lot of chuckles out of this game.The gameplay is as solid as the writing.  This is a typical rogue-lite but focuses on a Breath of the Wild style durability system, but in the case of a rogue-lite where you’re constantly moving rooms and locations, that is a pretty solid system, and it keeps players from favoring a specific item.  Each dungeon also has a different selection of tools, so there’s no one strategy to win the game. Pick this up if you like Roguelites, clever writing, or like this art style.  There’s something funny about knocking an enemy out of a car to drive it around yourself, or fighting goons who use moving dollies to smack you around.  Maybe it’s just me, but I couldn’t get enough of this game. The fact that weapons break, often lead me to be more cautious as well as jump in at the enemy with different tools (including  furniture). And I believe if it was never for that, I would have never found myself using all of the said tools nor finding ways of synergizing with everything else that I have. The player also gets the opportunity to acquire skills, which often have one think of different ways to approach a new encounter (or function as funny little gags, or better yet - both), because the skills the player can get usually don't function as normal stat buffs (if they do, they may have some catch to it).    All of the things mentioned above, always kept me on my toes, but also provided me with some fun time.   I feel like the visuals, music and dialogs blend in seamlessly with one another and really establish the mood that developers were going for.   I enjoyed this all the way through.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic little roguelike that combines an action RPG with the kleptomania of party balls in Smash Bros, and carries with it some hilariously witty and absolutely  writing about Silicon Valley and Seattle startup culture.The challenge level is set to be challenging but not insanely so, around the level of Hades or Hand of Fate 2, without making it insurmountable due to level- or collection-gated progression. Successful first runs are possible (albeit very difficult), the control scheme is very tight and fluid, enemy attacks are heavily telegraphed, and failure is generally caused by a war of attrition that feels fair instead of from cheap or unexplained mechanics.That said, the game does stumble in a few places (and not just from slipping on spilled coffee in the middle of a run). Items occasionally (but rarely) clip through other objects or the floor, certain text boxes do not line up with their effects in Impostor mode (the more roguelike of roguelike mode), and there are cases where the AI simply cannot deal with certain mechanics and stand there to take a beating. In particular, I was able to stunlock a significant story boss by using a single ability to deal damage while dodge rolling, and their otherwise brilliant AI script could not handle it and stood there doing nothing (please fix this!). Other similar broken interactions between items and abilities exist (albeit very rarely), though they felt appropriately niche and amusing when I exploited or succumbed to them.But frankly, these are forgivable in an otherwise fantastic game from a small development team, and while they're notable, they feel like nitpicks against how much fun I had playing this. As this is their first game, I'm looking forward to seeing what Aggro Crab does next.

_childDocuments_.review: So. After 13 long hours (or what some might call a long work day), I've finally beaten Going Under. Was it worth it?Absolutely.This is a charming and funny game for anyone who enjoys roguelikes. Take on corporate Neo-America as an unpaid intern doing near-slave labor. But, you know, slaying monsters and clearing dungeons instead of endlessly fetching coffee and making copies. If you take the time to pay attention, this game will NOT stop poking fun at the corporate workplace, mindset, lifestyle, and so on. If you've ever worked corporate, you won't stop laughing. And hell, even if you haven't, you'll laugh up a storm! I know I did!The difficulty is just right, which is hard for a roguelike. There's some luck involved, for sure, but once you learn key skills like resource management, effective dodging, battle tactics, and careful skill selection, you'll work your way up to being unstoppable. I personally enjoy the mentor and key skill mechanic, as it allows you to prepare for a dungeon crawl with your own strategy. It also rewards you, even if you don't clear the dungeon on that go. The only time I had an issue with difficulty was in the final boss. Without spoiling it...it's not the best programmed section. I often had to endure weapons falling through the floor, or off the stage at times. And it occasionally doesn't play fair, as it's VERY easy to get combo hit to death if you get unlucky. The combo hit issue is present throughout the game, but it became a lot harder at the final boss. But if you're ever struggling, you can always turn on assist mode. But I never found myself needing to use it, even with the final boss.It's also gorgeous. Poking fun at the corporate artstyle is a great choice, especially since they flavor it to make it interesting. Every dungeon has its own general color theme, too, which helps things feel fresh and alive. I never found myself getting bored on my repeated tries to clear a boss.My only real downside that I have yet to mention is the card mechanic. While you can go out of your way to use a blank card on an enemy to get their business card, which unlocks a profile...there's honestly not much reason to do it outside of completion. I wish it provided some form of bonus, though I understand the game wouldn't want to go overboard.Overall, a fantastic game. Would not complain about seeing a sequel of some form. Even if the place is going under, there's a lot to go back to.

_childDocuments_.review: I figured I'd be a bit more indepth than I usually am with steam reviews because I have a lot to say about the game.So first off, the game is fun and I do enjoy it. The combat is simple but fun if a tad janky at times, the enemies are all easy to understand and have good tells for their attacks, and there's a very simple joy in beating a goblin over the head with a cactus rather than something more practical like a sword. There's four dungeons in total from what I've seen, with three floors and a fourth boss floor for the first three and... I'll get to the fourth dungeon, but it's real bad.Visually the game is very pleasing, with some great character designs for both the main characters and the dungeon inhabitants. There's some amazing visual comedy on display here as well, which more than makes up for the game's lack of any real comedy in its writing.Yeah, I won't sugercoat it; the humor in this game is not great. There's a severe overreliance on memes and forced attempts at being quirky that can get rather annoying due to the game trying extremely hard to be 'relatable'. It's basically "How do you do fellow kids" in video game form. Which sucks because when the game isn't trying to be funny, it manages to have some genuinely heartfelt and meaningful moments. This isn't to say the jokes never land, some of them are well executed, but memes are not punchlines and the game's writing won't age particularly well as a result.Also worth mentioning is that the music is good; special mention goes to the Styxcoin boss theme, it's a bop.Now, about that fourth dungeon. It uh... it's basically just a series of rooms where you fight enemies from across the game rather than a new dungeon with new mechanics and enemies, which would have been infinitely more preferable. Maybe there's a fifth one in the second half.Which... did you really have to take the Ghouls N Ghosts route and make the second half a harder rehash of the first half? Something tells me I'm not gonna enjoy it.The game is still good and fun though and I do reccommend it; I just think it could do with a bit more work in some crucial areas.3.75/5

_childDocuments_.review: Quick disclaimer: although steam says i only played for 4 hours i actually played for 13,I just don't have internet all the time. Going Under has been one of the biggest gambles ive made buying a game. i first saw this game on twitter and was hooked on the concept as a whole but when i played the demo for the first time i really didnt like the combat, i couldnt get a hang of the controls and i was really unsure if i should buy the game. Fortunately i did end up buying it and this game is absolutely amazing. I think i had to just get used to the combat format but after the first 15 minutes of play i was loving every second after. Going under is a fun rouge like beat em up with a engaging world, story and combat with wonderful music, characters and dialogue. essentially everything is fun and packs a punch.I'm going to be hyper vague and brief about the story because this story and the humour cant be spoiled. essentially you play as an unpaid intern at a company in a future where capitalist endeavour has spiralled out of control causing all sorts of mayhem. if you haven't guessed the game is always taking a jab at current views on all aspects of work and business and it shows it off so well you never feel like its a serious critique even when it definitely is. combat is the main aspect of the game, and it shines all the time. Before when i said i didn't enjoy the demo i think it was because i wasnt expecting the enemies to be so difficult for a demo. Dont get me wrong, each enemy goes down in a few hits but when you first start the game you can feel overwhelmed with the variety of things you can use as weapons (essentially everything), overwhelmed by the fairly smart AI that can stunlock you and surround you with no mercy, overwhelmed at the buffs that are super under explained and overwhelmed by how unprepared you are for the game. it will take a  run or two to understand the mechanics and a few more to really begin mastering each of the three very unique dungeons. After a while youll know which dungeon you like best, which buffs are the best for your play style and how to tackle each enemy with ease.  its a wild ride and i never wanted to get off. the other aspects of the game are just as good, music is smooth, fun and playful and will never be a distraction or forgettable,  just perfect. characters are really fun to interact with and completing their quests are rewarding and achievable. and Aggro Crab as a whole are cool as hell top props for making such a sick game.in the end i would 100% recomend this amazing game no matter what.

_childDocuments_.review: OK, which Going Under intern tripped and fell headlong into the "publish" button only one week removed from Hades? That's almost "Suikoden 2 releasing right before and immediately getting steamrolled by Final Fantasy VIII in North America" levels of unfortunate timing.Although Going Under is not quite the Suikoden 2 to Hades' FFVIII, it sure is a delightful little game. The dungeon crawlin' action starts off rough and -- after you've gotten used to the dodge timing, weapon types, and the various perks and boons -- honestly peaks at a middle-of-the-road "acceptably goofy." However, the writing is extremely sharp and funny right off the bat. Genuinely some of the funniest, silliest (and, on frequent occasion, most incisive) writing I've seen in a video game in a while. Paired with the charm of the world and the (mostly non-punishing, which is a plus to someone like me who sucks at 'legit' roguelikes) one-more-run-based structure, it all adds up to a highly worthwhile package.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like the Dead Rising series, but the brutal difficulty, the constant time pressure on quests, and above all the bleak humour of the zombie apocalypse turned me off.  What I liked most about Dead Rising was the idea that you would be constantly salvaging weapons from your surroundings and using them to defeat the enemies around you.  Even if you prepare yourself with a full inventory, eventually your weapons break or run out of ammo and you need to find more.This game does that, but with the Hades-esque room-by-room progression through a dungeon.  Each run is more bite-size than Hades, which is different (not better or worse).  Getting new skills each run and either maximizing their use or (more frequently with me) being pleasantly surprised when one triggers to my benefit, learning to fight enemies and dodge their attack patterns, figuring out which weapons are good and how each weapon swings or shoots, all feel good.  Well, mostly -- I still have fights where enemies will attack faster than I expect, and suddenly a single room feels impossible to get through without losing half my health because I'm being shot at from three different angles, but those are few and far enough between that they primarily add a sense of danger and spice to runs in general.  There's a feeling of skill, moreover.  Attacks take time and you can't cancel them out with a dodge, particularly attacks with heavy weapons.  You can't just button mash -- you have to read enemy body language and consciously queue up only as many attacks as you think you'll land.  It feels rewarding to get into this flow.I was prepared to dislike, or just tolerate, the writing of this game for two reasons.  First, because a game about Living Under Late Capitalism, even as a satire, strikes me conceptually as depressing rather than funny.  (I am admittedly a sensitive soul.)  Secondly, because I got here through playing the (edited to correct:) Veewo / Team 17 game Neon Abyss, a 2D shooter roguelite, and while I find that game fun to play, the writing is hacky, overly referential, and not really important to the game anyway.  I wasn't sure what Aggro Crab might bring to the table that was different.In that sense, I was pleasantly surprised.  Meeting your co-workers in this game, and getting to know the distinct voice of each, is rewarding.  After each run, much like in Hades but in a less complex way (it's hard to avoid the comparison here), you return to the hubworld (Fizzle Beverages' office) and are given the opportunity to check in with your co-workers and supervisors, as well as add new skills to the pool that will appear in the dungeon.  Each co-worker feels like a well-defined character, even with the cartoony, slightly caricatured tone that Going Under takes: Marv is the archetypal middle manager, smoothing over but not resolving problems.  Tappi the accountant has surprising nuance in her cheerful appearance hiding her inner conflict, and Swomp feels like a very real slice of easy-going minimum-wage nihilism.  Even Jackie, the main character, has a likeable personality (my feeling is that it's tough to make a protagonist feel both heroic and interesting).  My greatest complaint is that, after what feels like too short a time, you run out of conversations to have with anyone in the game.  They become idle-animation models, nothing more -- no more conversations to have.  Then again, when your greatest complaint is "the writing ends after a while," that says something about its quality while it was there.I like the story, which I've just completed, beginning to end.  Good news, though: Once you finish the story, there's another mode to keep you engaged in achieving more without just repeating things you've already done!  (The developers compare this to Hades' escalating scale of difficulty through the Heat system.  Look, it's an influential game.)  I like the gameplay quite a bit, so I appreciate there being more to discover as opposed to just 100%-ing the list of skills, business cards, and so on.If you like roguelites, chaotic but controllable combat, the joy of discovering something new and often silly in the next room, and like your games colourful and vibrant, Going Under should do it for you.  (And if you aren't sure, well, there's a demo!)

_childDocuments_.review: I have something to tell you all that is very important. A game that isn't turn-based is NOT a roguelike. A roguelike is a game that PLAYS LIKE ROGUE. _childDocuments_.review: Very conditional recommendation from me, I wish there was a "mixed" option for reviews. I like the presentation of Going Under, and believe it is the best aspect of the game. The art style, writing, and music are all truly excellent. However, the more you play it, the more frustrating it becomes. It's already a pretty difficult game with weapon durability (which I loathe), an extremely short hit invulnerability time (you absolutely will get locked somewhere and get hit multiple times, the base dodge roll is also really bad), and a pitifully low starting HP pool. But the worst part is the endgame, where you have nothing left to unlock, are forced to replay harder versions of the same dungeons, and then playing the game feels like a chore instead of fun. Some people will be able to look past this, and see the greatness of the game, but I do think the designers could have done certain aspects better. Here's hoping their next game, "Another Crab's Treasure," will use the lessons they learned from this.7/10, it's (mostly) good.
