_childDocuments_.review: Use your sick days,  is a great 3D rogue-lite and satire of contemporary work culture that’ll keep you locked-in for hours at a time. You play as Jackie, an unpaid intern who’s told to go into the literal depths of failed start-ups to kill monsters (employees) and claim their magical business items.There are three separate dungeons to attempt, each with their own themes, enemies, and boss encounters. Like any rogue-like, each run will have you encounter different randomly-generated floors—of which there are 3, plus a boss floor, for any dungeon—helping to keep each run fresh.The combat in  is simple on its surface, but allows for a fair bit of fun when you start layering on skills you obtain and different weapons you pick up on a run. Almost every object in the game can be picked up by the player, and this isn’t limited to conventional weapons. You can pick up pencils, reams of paper, staplers (which you can use as staple ), as well as swords, bones, maces, pickaxes, and lots more. Each object falls into one of a few weapon types. Longer weapons, like brooms and spears, have a long narrow reach, pencils and other similarly shaped weapons stab short and fast like daggers, and larger weapons like the mace or dolley can dish out heavy, slower swings.You can also  anything you pick up, and you better believe each of these categories have different throw mechanics too.Now, it might conjure up uncomfortable memories of , but all of these weapons can break, and that’s a good thing. Whereas ’s weapon-breaking paired poorly with long treks with the wilderness and a persistent inventory, ’s weapon-breaking feels so right. Weapons in this game break , so you’ll have to be constantly picking up new ones littered throughout the level, changing up how you approach any given encounter. They of course break all of the time while you’re fighting, so get ready for a lot of frantically looking for something to wack the dolley-wielding goblin before they wack you.Death will force you to reattempt the dungeon you were in from the beginning, and it’s in this hub world that you’ll be experiencing much of the story, which I enjoyed a great deal. It takes constant jabs at capitalistic work culture, which is funny and kind of sad at the same time. Each character has unique noises to accompany their dialogue, a la  or , and simple but expressive 2D drawings to go with it. In fact, the whole visual style of the game is minimalist, an obvious parallel to many corporate logos and branding. The player character Jackie is basically just some sausage limbs attached to some circles. It’s appropriate thematically and a joy to look at.I’m a huge fan of the soundtrack, with the 2nd Joblin theme and the Joblin Boss theme being my favorites. They’re upbeat and catchy, and I find myself bobbing my head a bit to the beat while I’m in that dungeon.A small thing I take issue with is the inability to rebind your controller inputs. I would’ve liked to switch the button I had dodge on, but it wasn’t too hard to get over, only taking a short readjustment period every time I booted the game up.Aggro Crab has done an excellent job with their debut game. It’s wonderfully made, and I can’t wait to see what’s next. The only big mistake they made was releasing it a little over a week after , the gold-standard for rogue-likes.I highly recommend it, especially if you’re a fan of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of my favourite games of all time.I've explored some rouge-likes before, and Going Under has a fresh take on it by surrounding the game in a pretty immersive narrative about the struggles of start-up culture. The 3ish different dungeons, the characters, the dialog, and the story made me wanna continue every time.The game is designed to be a bit hard, you go through a couple of randomly generated dungeons until you reach the boss floor. You pick up almost anything you see lying around and hack and slash monsters until they break. The way having weapons is designed makes your gameplay different, dynamic, and fluid. Your item management is what's engaging, not necessarily what weapon combos you have.The more strategical part of the game is having skills. You can pick up skills twice every floor: one in a shop and a choice between two in a room. This allows for some zany strategy that scales well as you go later on in the game. The RNG of skills is my biggest gripe however, since some skills just kind of suck loool.When I finished the game, it was really fulfilling, I was able to see how the characters you fell in love with wrap up their story of being in a crappy start-up. I felt like the time I invested really paid off. And the dialog you have with your enemies was really good commentary on the culture too haha. After the Work From Home update came,  that's where I really grinded. With the game play I mentioned before, you can really test your micromanagement of items and your character while strategizing what skills you choose or not choose.tl;dr Pros- fun rouge-like with a fulfilling narrative- micromanagment of weapons usage and skill strategies is very engaging- funny, witty, colourful world and characters- post-story grind of Imposter mode if that's more your thingCons- there are some bugs that i had to restart the game but since it's a rouge-like it wasnt the worst thing to happen- a little too rng when you get meh vs really good skills

_childDocuments_.review: I have finally finished the main game (haven't beaten Impostor mode, nor have I finished the Rolodex. But I'm close!), so I feel comfortable doing a thorough review.Pros:+ Great story and writing, enjoyable characters, and very entertaining jokes.+ A pitch-perfect satire of startup culture, mega corporations, and the hell of being an intern.+ Very wide assortment of weapons, enemies, skills, and tasks to achieve.+ Terrific soundtrack!+ Great initial gameplay loop---I really felt hooked on it after only a couple dungeon runs.Cons:- Only 3 main dungeons, so you'll be seeing a lot of the same enemies and weapons, despite there being a good variety to begin with. Without spoiling, there is a point in the game where you return to the dungeons to find some stronger, different enemies, but for the most part they're variations on ones you've seen before.- The combat system is pretty basic---everything has good weight and animation, but you really see a variety of 4 weapon types.- Sometimes hit detection feels iffy, especially during chaotic moments onscreen.- Generally, did not use certain mentors because they didn't seem to provide a good enough bonus.- To the above point, I think the game encourages adopting your own playstyle and sticking to it, to its detriment. I would experiment sometimes with different mentor/skill combos, but I never found them to be as effective as what I usually did.Conclusion:This game is worth playing for the story and writing alone, but it also boasts a fleshed out (and challenging!) roguelike system with very addictive dungeon crawling loops. Though it may get a bit repetitive, especially as enemies are concerned, I spent a good 23 hours trying to get as many skills, mentors, and business cards as I can---and I intend to keep going after this! I'm excited to check out Aggro Crab's next game and I look forward to seeing what they do in the future!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under was quite a refreshing experience for me. It is an interesting twist to the rogue-like genre with tons of personality and charm.First off, let's start with the obvious: the artsyle is amazing. I love how they used a 'graphic design' approach to everything (UIs, companies' logos and visual identity, character design...), and then made it 3D, achieving a high degree of designery flavour that gives the game a lot of charm. The tech company vibes are on point and definitely give Going Under a distinctive flavour among other recent indie game releases. The music and sound design also fit that friendly-looking corporate theme completing the startup-esque experience quite accurately.As for how the game deals with its story and message, you should not expect a deep narrative with lots of social commentary or lore. Going Under does throw in some criticism and satire to the modern entrepreneur environment, but it is done in a humorous, lightweight manner. It does throw a punch here and there with some dialogue lines from time to time, but it always tries to do it in a not-so-serious way.Gameplay-wise I must say I had a ton of fun playing through it, and I'm sure I will keep playing a bit more. The controls are buttery smooth, the combat is fluid and very straight-forward (though rather deep if you take your time to learn all of its potential) and the Tasks give you constant new challenges and twists to how you approach the dungeons helping them stay fresh for quite a decent amount of time. And speaking of tasks, you should definitely take your time pursuing them in the first half of the game, otherwise the second half will become a very steep difficulty spike for you. It has an interesting approach to managing dungeons, progression and content by mixing everything up and adding in some new things, but if you are still in a very early state for your character and power-ups you will suffer a lot. Fortunately Going Under comes with some very cool accessibility options for you to tweak in case you just want to have simple fun at some point.I just hope they keep adding content via DLCs in the future, because that could increase the game's playtime quite a lot. They already have all the ingredients in place, so I'll be keeping an eye on future developer's updates.Totally recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: A neon drenched sugar coated cartoon comedy rogue like with a heart of rainbow.According to the store page tags, this is an action roguelike dungeon crawler beat 'em up.  I'd say that's a fairly accurate description.  We play heroic intern Jackie Fiasco, and it is her job to descend into the subterranean levels deep beneath her new office to confront and defeat the nasties that dwell there.  This involves travelling into "dungeons" beating up lots of crazy characters, and slowly unlocking new perks and skills which can then be utilised in subsequent runs.The story is filled with humour, existentialism and some socio-political commentary.  It is a pastiche of our crazy consumerist times, told through the eyes of a downtrodden and mildly jaded young woman, just starting out on her career path.  A protagonist that most of us will be able to identify and sympathise with.  We've all had those days where we feel like work is hell, and that we are just little cogs working for the giant corporate machine; selling our souls for a pittance.  What better catharsis than smacking up some jerk manager in a garish dungeon?!A hyper stylised, brightly coloured aesthetic makes this eye catching and fun to look at.  The screen literally fizzes and pops, and there is never a dull lull.  The character designs for both the protagonists and the antagonists are quirky, but cohesive and really help to build a world that makes contextual sense.  Level design is clever and succinct.  You can tell everything you need to know about a dungeon within a couple of rooms.  The overall art direction is absolutely outstanding.  Company logos are clever, the co workers are diverse, levels are varied, even the menus and title screen are all designed so that any individual element will be instantly recognisable as belonging to the game.  I'm sure it's a kind of irony that there is such perfect brand synergy on display here.The sound design is equally good.  Combat sounds are just perfect.  Enemies signpost attacks with vocal cues.  Things explode nicely and impacts are sufficiently weighty.  Each character has a specific sound when they speak (no needless full vocal tracks here) and it's amazing how such simple effects can really capture the essence of a character.  Special mention must go to King Felix's original soundtrack.  The music is a blend of styles, but there's an overall vapourwave, electro chill vibe that I really enjoy.  It's also the first instance I ever remember of a soundtrack making me laugh.  There is one specific track which plays in the Winkydink (think Tinder for demons) offices which is just so raunchy as to be hilarious.  Standing ovation for that alone.Gameplay follows the standard format for these games.  Go to dungeon.  Defeat many enemies over a number of floors.  Gain skills from combat and from shops.  Face off against boss.  Defeat boss and get McGuffin.  Return to hub world.  Purchase more skills with loot from dungeons.  Next time you visit dungeon, these new skills will appear at random.  It's a tried and tested format, but the combat is pretty tight for such a goofy looking game.  And don't be fooled by the cartoony looks, this game is challenging.  My first run didn't last very long.  Still, as you unlock more skills, you begin to stand a slightly better chance.  Once a skill has been used enough times, it becomes endorsed and can be activated before a run.  However, only one endorsed skill can be activated prior to a run.  More will be available on the run, but they are random.  It is rare that you will feel overpowered.Another aspect is that each of your co-workers will set you tasks to fulfil on dungeon runs.  Kill so many of enemy x, get object y, discover thing z etc.  Complete enough of these tasks and your colleagues will become your mentors.  Selecting a mentor unlocks permanent perks such as a packed lunch, or better items in the shops.Boss battles are fun and again have great design.  They can be pretty tense and especially the last few battles are particularly tough.  I think I finished with one tiny sliver of health left, but boy did that victory feel well deserved.  My victory was Jackie's victory and vice versa.  Art imitates life on this one.If you do pick it up, definitely try to complete it.  I played for nearly 22 hours, but had I played in a couple of longer haul sessions, it may not have lasted as long.  As is often the case in this style of game, the longer you play, the more you enter into the flow state.  Time away from the game will result in a steep fresh challenge on return.  This is no bad thing.  It never feels unfair, and your skilled play is justly rewarded.What a delightful time I had with this one.  Sure the beats are all pretty familiar, but it's just packaged so well that it is much stronger than the sum of it's parts.  I highly recommend to fans of the genre, and to those who like a little poignant humour that pokes fun at the society we Western devils have come to rely on.Fizzy.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a parody game throwing shade on the entire Silicon Valley startup culture where you, as a brand new (unpaid) intern, are assigned to smash your way through remnants of other failed startups, defeat the ghosts of workers past, dismiss the zombie CEO (i.e. beat him up) and acquire their secret sauce (read: intellectual property) so your current employer, Fizzle (a nutritional/sports drink company) can use it. If that sounds too complicated... it's a 2.5D smash-em-up where you fight various enemies on screen, clear each room, and keep clearing levels until you defeat the end boss... I mean zombie CEO. The graphics are low-poly and stylized the fighting physics are good, some tactics are called for, and add some extra between mission interaction (with your co-workers) with the same sense of parody and you have a parody game. While you can fight with your fists alone, you really should pick up weapons ASAP, as well as pick up any object in the room and even throw them as improvised weapons, from computer keyboard to ban-hammer, from mugs and office crossbow, there are plenty of weapons available. Even the giant red stapler.  You can sometimes take on bonus jobs, which gives you a special reward box. Beating the end boss also gains you a reward box. As you wander through the "dungeon", you will find occasional cafes (where you can buy items, skills, or heal, and you only have X number of hearts). You can also come across storage rooms where you can pick one of two skills to improve your resume. But the obvious objective is to beat your way down to the boss, and beat him. That will trigger an evaluation (which also triggers if you fell during your quest). Between forays into the dungeon, you talk to your coworkers, who may give you extra requests while in the dungeon, which if you complete, unlocks him or her as your "mentor" with bonuses. Using the skills will lead to an endorsement, which levels up the skill as well. You can also install some apps which enables finding more bonus items The game definitely is not easy, so much so you can turn on "Assist" mode to make the game easier by giving you advantages, as well a penalize your enemies. And the game *is* hard. So if you just want to enjoy the humor feel free to turn on the Assist (or should it be "intern assistance program"?)The opponents are not that hard, but the bosses can be challenging. Fortunately, their attacks are well telegraphed. So if you just pay attention and dodge in time they are quite survivable. All in all, if you understand startup culture and the humor here, the beat-em-up is just a bonus.

_childDocuments_.review: Executed with spirit but sadly not with an equal amount of competence.Going Under is one of the best-written games I've played in a while, it's extremely charming on all layers, from enemy designs to dialogue to music, and you'll very quickly *want* to like it unless you're some sort of heartless ghoul.This is why it's a sad fact that the actual game under the charming exterior just isn't good enough to consistently like. The issues are a combination of minor things that pile on to make the tougher end-game areas unfun, but they're two-fold:Firstly, poor information. A lot of power-ups just don't concisely explain what they do when picked up and used. If there's someone who can figure out the effects of every can of Fizzle and every App without visiting a wiki, I'll eat my own shoes. Hell, even some of the perks are kind of vague about their effects. I also still have no idea how the dating challenges work.Secondly, the visuals that give the game a lot of charm are kind of poorly served by the gameplay purposes they're put to. The big blocky designs don't work well with cramped arenas and tons of effects(both active and graphical) that make it hard to tell exactly what's going on half the time. For the kind of gameplay intended, either a simpler style with less flair or larger arenas with more space for the chosen style would've done a lot to make it more easy to parse at a glance.Lastly, poor random generation. About half the game's perks, weapons and mentor effects are either useless or clearly very vastly outclassed by others, so you are very much at the mercy of whether the game designs to spawn a room composed of 90% trap tiles(walls AND floor) and a dozen armored enemies which you have to defeat with a folding chair, or a room containing several high-powered weapons, no traps and a single enemy.In short, I really like what Aggro Crab does in terms of writing and presentation, but unless they take some serious lessons in *gameplay* design, I'll pass on their future games unless they're dating sims or turn-based.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game more. It has a fun style to it, and the dialogue is witty without being over-the top. I like the setting, and when I found a succulent plant I could pick up labelled 'Potted Succ' I felt I was guaranteed to have at least a slightly good time.The actual act of playing this game, however, is very obtuse, and the controls feel weirdly clunky in a way I can't quite articulate. Certainly the 'pick up weapons that break after a while' is a hit or miss gimmick, and it fell on the 'miss' side for me... every time I found a cool weapon I wanted to use, it was gone within a room or two, leaving me feeling empty-handed and helpless. Even the act of hitting enemies felt unsatisfying, like they weren't responding to my hits at all, and the dash has minimal i-frames with a lengthy recovery period. I wish I had more good things to say about this game, but the third time I came back to it I got thrown into a giant unskippable chunk of dialogue. Then I was reminded that I've been getting meta currency the game still hasn't told me how to spend. Every time I die, I think to myself "yeah, I guess, but I'm not really sure what I could have done differently". It just doesn't feel satisfying to control or play. Possibly there is a really great game underneath here, but all the style and personality in the world can't make up for bad gamefeel. In this day and age I find it is sometimes the case that giant parts of a game will change wholesale after enough feedback from consumers, but I wouldn't recommend holding my breath for that. For now, if the idea of clunky core mechanics and the weapon switch gimmick don't sound fun to you, I would recommend avoiding this despite its lovely writing and art.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the satirical sense of humor in this game!  If you love this kind of humor, buy this game and play it!The rogue-lite elements are done well in this game.  I love the how the system of skills and mentors work.  If you pick up a particular skill enough times, you can have it as a "pinned skill" and choose to start with it at the beginning of each new  run.  Mentors provide you support in one form or another to provide you perks such as "free" items at shops.  Each mentor can be leveled up to provide even more perks.Dungeons are randomly spawned with different layouts and items to go in it.  The available dungeons in this game are uniquely themed and distinct.  Most of the items in the dungeon can be used as weapons.  It's fun to be able to use items in an office-themed environment to beat up monsters in this game.I don't think the combat is perfect.  It's fine during the first half of the game when there isn't many monsters spawning but when the second half of the game begins, the difficulty spikes way up.  I feel like this is because of how cluttered some the dungeon rooms can be when they're generated and the amount of monsters that are spawned.  When you're in a small/cluttered space with tons of monsters, it just feels unfair because you can't dodge or get away from all the incoming attacks.I can still recommend this game even with what I've mentioned in the previous paragraph.  The graphics, colors, rogue-lite elements and humor all come together to make an entertaining experience.  Edit: Update with "The Big Run" is out, it's got replay value now.

_childDocuments_.review: Can you believe they turned being an unpaid marketing intern into a fun game? Me neither. There's not much marketing to do here though, the game sells itself!Anyways, the game, yeah - it's a roguelite, you go trough randomized dungeon and beat up enemies and collect random upgrades. This one is action-centric like many other topdown roguelites - apart from bashing enemies you get to dodge their attacks a lot. Another important bit is that you have a limited inventory and everything breaks fast. While there are some "proper" weapons including extremely rare and powerful ones, there's a big focus on using improv weapons like staplers, furniture, and eggplant emojis. Yeah. There's means to power up weapons, extend their longlastingness, etc, but you have to prepare for the fact none of them will last. Also there are bossfights and progression of unlocks, but that's staple roguelite stuff. I think gameplay is fine and fun but better highlight is story and setting - something you would never expect from a roguelite is that it's a satire. Of startup culture. It doesn't say absolutely nothing new, but it's all wrapped in a good comedy and ties with the gameplay which is quite an accomplishment! It is amazing how hard this satire aspect permeates the game - like the game's art style is like a 3D rendition of that art style startups and major companies love, with goofy misshapen people of all sorts, all flat and simple. Except while the particular style is usually considered pretty soulless, there's plenty of heart put in this game's renditions. The sound is on point too.One major criticism I have is that the game's second half after you complete three dungeons and beat a major boss is rather disappointing - you retread the dungeons again, but with a major increase in difficulty and some few additions. Personally at that point, if you struggle or feel bored of retreading (makes sense, it's a roguelite), I recommend going to main menu and cranking Assist Mode to the max because the proper finale after retread is very much worth your time if you appreciated the story and character bits of the game. Nonetheless the part between fourth boss and finale is genuinely the weakest part of the game that feels too hard and adds too little.I dunno who exactly to recommend it to, like exact audience - too much grinding for narrative-centric players and kinda lacking in depth and content for roguelite fans - but I guess it's a really good roguelite for people who find most roguelites too long and unmotivating, while still appreciating the premise?

_childDocuments_.review: Editing this to reflect my change of opinion. I had a bug that made some of the content impossible to complete, but seeking out the Discord gave me a solution that fixed the bug.That's one of the game's 2 problems. There's a few bugs, most of them are small and kinda funny. Only one (permanent curses) was large and negative enough to impact the game.The other problem is that without the assist turned up, weapons break too fast. BotW pulled off breaking weapons by giving you huge pockets, ranged weapons, shields, and a way to freeze enemies if you needed a breather. This game gives you 3 weapon slots, plus your pathetic fists as a backup if you can't find a weapon. It's more frustrating than challenging.The game has many positive aspects too. The dialogue is hilarious and very well-written, the characters are likable and interesting, the weapon variety is great, combat is not too simple and not too complex, and the atmosphere of job culture is nailed perfectly. Even after I was frustrated with the game I found myself wanting to play it again.I don't feel like the writers knew how to make good, satisfying endings. Both the main game and the side story have disappointing ones that make you wonder if they're trying to leave it open for a sequel. No real closure or sense of accomplishment.Overall though, it's a game that's so fun I kept wanting to play, even when I shouldn't. A really good game sucks you in and steals time from other parts of your life. This one did that.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw a Let's Play of this game and was instantly curious. The humor was right up my alley and I liked the art style. Three hours later, and this might be the best $20 I've spent on Steam in a long time! Rouge-Like dungeon crawlers are typically not my style. But the humor was enough to keep me playing. They've managed to capture the look and feel of Corporate America right down to witty satire. Maybe it's because I'm also in Marketing, but this game hit on all the right notes for me.Instead of being frustrated when I died, I immediately went to talk to coworkers and did it all again. Each try felt like a new day at the office. It's quite brilliant how they've managed to capture the theme perfectly in the gameplay and aesthetic. Not only is the gameplay loop addicting, you'll unlock more dungeons as you progress.There's a nice balance of quests and progression in the story to make each death rewarding when you return to the office. Combat is easy to pick up as well and weapons are littered throughout dungeons. A mechanic I hate in Zelda BOTW (weapons breaking) actually works perfectly in this game. With there being so many weapons in a single room, you never feel like you are at a loss when it happens or scrambling to find a new one. This game surprised me a lot. But in the best way possible. I'm getting that dopamine hit of "one more try" that rouge-likes are known for. It's fun to finally feel that myself.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a love letter to our soulless, lifeless and contradictory experience of corporate life. It's also a roguelike with great writing, cool art style and a messy combat.If you've ever worked in an office or startup, the setting and characters of Going Under will certainly feel familiar to you. Surprisingly this game has a lot of cool dialogue between various characters, that feel over the top and funny. The game makes fun of so many stereotypes and corporate lingo and there are even scenes where the personality of these characters clash, just like in real life. The artstyle mimics the popular design of many-many startups and creates a cohesive and unique visual identity. It's incredibly well done.The game has multiple dungeons and offers a really active combat experience. Your weapons degrade over time so finding and picking up new ones or improvising something else is essential. This elevates the combat a lot, since I never felt like I found a meta weapon and the game was always pushing me to try new things. There is a wide array of passive abilities you can unlock, most are not that impressive on their own, but once you have a large number of these you can become almost unstoppable. The combat is honestly really fun and chaotic and even if you get hit it's not the end of world, since you can buy back health every once a while. There is a surprisingly large number of weapons and other items you can use, some come with special abilities too. The enemies are varied, but their attack pattern is quite simplistic. You have to look for their telegraph and dodge accordingly or rush them down and stun lock them. This is were the first issue emerges, sometimes enemy telegraphs only last a few frames and are impossible to react to. In late game areas, the game just increases the enemy count, which would be fine, except the environments are quite small and cramped with detail, meaning it's really hard to make out what exactly is happening when you have 2 allies and multiple enemies of various sizes trying to attack you. The player character gets lost in the visual clutter too often.The combat becomes too chaotic and too hard understand, and enemies can hit through each other potentially hitting you multiple times before you can even react to the first hit. I think the devs probably realized this, since one late game section takes place in a much bigger area and crowd control works really well there.Going Under has a lot of content, but just like with every roguelike, at some point it will feel like work, (which is funnily enough the exact thing the game criticizes) and that's the point I lose all my motivation.  In this game that moment arrived quite late, so that's pretty great.I would recommend Going Under not just for its unique combat, but for it's story and general aesthetic.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot going for it. The story is exceptional, the characters are fun, the roguelike elements stay fresh for a long time, you have lots of customization, lots of different ways to play, great sound design, it's all wonderful.The gameplay is just one step short of amazing though. It also has a lot going for it! The boss designs are interesting and are very interesting. There are a good amount of different enemies across the various biomes you'll run into. But there's an essential clunkiness to the combat that makes things much harder. Your attacks have a pretty hefy windup with most weapons, and while enemies do telegraph their attacks well, the density of enemies in rooms and the long follow-up animations most weapons have, locking you out of dodge-rolling, makes it very easy to take a lot of damage if you don't play very very safe.Now I've played through the game and beaten it, but I will say that this essential clunkyness did add some frustration. It's a game that makes you want to wade into combat and skillfully weave through enemies, like say, Hades, which it takes a lot of good notes from in style, but because of how unwieldly it is to fight, you really can't do that. Your dodge roll is too short and long-cooldown, while getting stopped by enemies, and your attacks are far too slow.Still, overall, a very fun game. Would recommend if you're a fan of other top-down action roguelike (or roguelite, if you insist), type games.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under manages to upcycle the refuse of our everyday routines; its a Big Art Attack of 2-hour commutes, stolen tips and that one pinball machine your boss bought to make a chill room after he laid off three of your coworkers during a global pandemic. It’s one of the most honest investigations of existential digitisation and corporate greed ever made in videogame form. It addresses the farce of employment with creativity and humour, two things no malignant narcissist with a modest cash injection could ever take from us.

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★★Going Under is a game that sold me on its charm and kept me with its depth and its story. A surprisingly short experience with comparable replay value to games other games in its same genre. Going Under takes a similar approach to Hades, where your reward for playing the game isn’t strictly getting more powerful each run but instead leans heavily into developing relationships with your coworkers and moving forward a very engaging and poignant story. I found myself shocked with how impactful the contents of this game were with how short the narrative experience was. Going Under also exists in an incredibly unique design space, its visuals are unique and eye catching, but its design problem “what if there was a dungeon crawler where you play as an intern, set in the body of failed tech start ups, set dressed in a corporate Alegria art style” is something that I have never seen before, nor knew I wanted. Going Under’s Alegria charm doesn’t just stop at its premise though, between the “smart” weapons that track enemies, the incredibly creative puns/concepts behind each of its dungeons, having your coworkers “mentor” you to give you passives on each run, and the hilarious variety in its enemy/weapon/“app” this game was in all ways surprising and fresh. I find the rogue-like genre space to be completely over saturated with fantasy/sci-fi design, and this game was a refreshingly ballsy move away from it.Going Under is a must have experience from an upcoming studio that took an incredibly new and fresh take on a genre that has become over saturated with sameness.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the protestations of far too many game studios recently trying to deny this, it turns out that video games can be really good at political and social commentary. What makes this even more fascinating is that there doesn’t even seem to be a limit to the ways that this can be achieved; we can have gritty shooters like Spec Ops: The Line expressing the horrors of war, and that can rub shoulders with something like Flower; a beautiful exploration game that explores the idea of environmentalism. Yet, despite knowing this, Going Under’s mix of styles still came as somewhat as a surprise to me - a comedic roguelike that both comments on and parodies the sheer absurdities surrounding internships and the start-up world. Um, ok? It’s probably best to take a step back at this point and explain a little more of what’s going on here; You play as a marketing intern in the hottest new drinks company, Fizzle. Yet, like many internships in the real world, it soon transpires that you won’t be doing much of what’s listed in the job description. Instead, you’re tasked with killing the monsters crawling up from the dungeons of the failed start ups that have preceded you – such as a cryptocurreny company full of (literal) skeleton miners. All the while you also have to assist your co-workers, including the ambitious yet clueless company owner, a boss who forces everyone around him to work harder while doing very little themselves, and many other stereotypes anyone who has ever found themselves in a similar job situation will immediately recognise.  Even with explanation I admit it’s a strange concept, and you may be thinking at this point that Going Under is being rather on the nose with its criticism about such industries. And… Well, you’d be right. But even though it may be trying to make a point, it does it in such a light hearted and jovial way it’s nigh on impossible not to be charmed by it all. There are just so many superb little jokes or jabs dotted throughout the experience - for instance, buy things you can’t afford, and your debt takes the form of a literal ball and chain, slowing you down. In another example, leaving your controls alone sees the main character toss everything aside and start lazing around on their phone in a matter of seconds. There’s even a brilliant nod to a classic YouTube advertisement many will remember, where it’s not the Lamborghini in the garage the owner is proud of, it’s his vast wealth of knaaawwwledge on the bookshelves behind him. The constant good-natured teasing and sly observations are honestly perhaps the greatest part of the game, and they’re certainly things that never failed to bring a smile to my face.  All the charm in the world, however, means nothing unless there’s a decent dose of gameplay backing things up. In Going Under this takes the form of running through randomly generated dungeons, grabbing whatever lies around the place to pulverise the monsters that are determined to make your career a short one. These weapons range from the expected, such as swords and maces, to the odd, like body pillows and potted plants. Couple this up with a healthy selection of skills from the ever-growing unlock pool, a large chunk of dodging and weaving through attacks, and the obligatory challenging boss fight - all pretty much staples of the genre. It’s entertaining stuff, for the most part – there's a certain glee to be taken from trashing up each room, tossing things in frenzy at your foes. Yet while the core appeal never truly falters, sadly there’s a ton of little issues all over the place which cause the overall gameplay mechanics to truly stumble in their paces.For example; you have the ability to change your attacks and lock on to foes, but both of these slow you down a considerable amount. As it turns out, this is a big no-no in a world where enemy attacks are rapid and constant, and movement is a key skill in not being overwhelmed. Therefore you soon realise your effective repertoire when it comes to seeking success is essentially whittled down to running and slashing. Skills suffer a similar fate – some are effective in every situation and others have extremely limited implementation, so many will never see much use unless you have no other option but to take them. Even weapons are blighted by the same plight – you’ll soon realise most are garbage or simply too slow to use (without the right skills, at least), so you soon learn to avoid these and as a result endlessly pick up the same stuff. Weapon degradation and destruction does help to mitigate this final point, but there were very few situations where I found myself left with a massive shortage of good gear. And yeah, I get it – there’s always the ability to self-impose challenge upon yourself, and exploration should always be encouraged. It’s just a shame large chunks of what's on offer here don’t really have a practical use beyond that, and instead seem to be sidelined as mere curios. Another problem comes from the game’s erratic difficulty. It never gets truly insane or soul crushing (I completed the story in a little under ten hours, which if anything is short for a roguelike) but it does feel like it jumps all over the place. The first half of the game, for instance, is straightforward once you’re used to the mechanics. Hit the second half, however, and suddenly the challenge level shoots way up, with any sort of success requiring a good deal of focus. These jumps in difficulty even affect individual rooms, where one can have a single lowly minion to easily turn into paste in a wide open area, only for the next to have exceedingly powerful enemies cramped into a small space. There’s also the recently added imposter mode, which I’ve only dabbled in, but seems to require insane amounts of precision to succeed in – and that’s before that mode’s exclusive difficulty modifiers kick in. Experiences may vary - you may struggle and others may storm through – but it never feels like a truly streamlined appearance. Such cracks in the quality extend to the last thing that needs to be touched upon, and that’s the visual style. Glancing at a single screenshot is all you need to spot the game’s unique flair, and it’s certainly used well to create a world that’s extremely fun and engaging to be part of. Two issues come part and parcel with this, though. The first, I admit, is a miniscule one; all the text initially is presented with an odd blurred and distorted effect surrounding it, which to me was so incredibly off-putting it actually made me feel oddly unwell. Thankfully this is only a minor annoyance, as there’s an option in the settings to turn this off - and I highly recommend you do so. The second issue, however, is a far bigger problem. You see, the bright colour palette and sheer plethora of visual effects that start filling the screen when a fight really gets going are good enough to look at in a vacuum, but couple that with combat that often requires your close attention and it often becomes difficult to tell what’s happening. It can only take one major visual distraction to whittle off a major chunk of your health, and for that to happen due to something that feels out of your control is incredibly disheartening. It’s the one thing that let little spikes of anger seep their way into my general enjoyment of the game, and that’s a real shame.Overall, though, Going Under may not like the polish or substance that really makes it stand out as a must play, but by no means does this make it a complete write off. There’s a lot here to enjoy and appreciate, and let’s be honest - any game that lets you smash computer monitors over a zombie’s head must have something going for it. It’s worth playing (although there’s a small part of me that would suggest perhaps waiting for a sale before doing so), and certainly not one that deserves to be thrown on the scrapheap.

_childDocuments_.review: for more reviews like this.I'm very conflicted about this game because I want to love it, I really do. The art style, the music, the whole theme of it. It's all unique and very nicely well done. There's so many little details such as the lofi music mode in your room, the little nods to corporate business structure, and the parodies that each of the 3 dungeons are themed after. The aesthetic of this game if fantastic. They really did nail every aspect of it. Unfortunately the developers failed on the most important part of an action game. THE COMBAT IS A MESS. Your dodges leave you vulnerable and the way the rooms and dungeons are set up, there's explosives, and traps, and hazards filling every room on top of 4-5 enemies and you simply do not have the necessary space or dodging abilities to properly avoid damage. There's also virtually no hit invincibility period so if you get cornered, your run's done. The dungeons are simply not laid out properly for the movement options the game gives you. It's a shame because this game could have been truly fantastic but there's just so many games that have combat systems that work so much better that it's hard to recommend this game over those.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. It's a pretty well done roguelike with very active/hectic combat and a lot of fun upgrades to unlock. The coolest part is definetly that the upgrades change your character's visuals in a similar vein to Binding of Isaac (though a lot less grotesque). The art is neat, the models are cute and the music is good and unique (In my experience, at least). There are some things that pull it down though. 92% of the time everything works perfectly, but the game does not handle unforeseen circumstances well at all (such as: perk-linked companions perma-dying in certain scenarios, allies breaking bosses by attacking mid-cutscene...), which can lead to frustrating moments. Impostor mode also has a tendency to get a bit confused when you buy the same mentor twice in a row. None of these are deal-breakers, but they did dampen the experience whenever they appeared.If I were to score this game, I'd give it a 4/5. It's good fun, and the plot surprised me in good ways. Worth picking up if you want a 3D roguelike with a bit more color than it's peers.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been on my radar since Iron Pineapple, the youtuber, featured it in his series 'Steam Dumpster Diving.' Since seeing it, I've been infatuated with the satirical corporate aesthetic and I just wanna make it clear that the atmosphere, settings and characters make for a very good little piece of commentary. Granted, it isn't hard to put across the message of "corporatism and consumerism bad," but this game does it in such a charming way. Lots of points here. While I do generally enjoy the combat, I do find it to be a little janky. Keep in mind I've only now beaten the first dungeon but I'm very experienced in other rogue and souls-like games, so I feel like there is room for improving the flow of combat in the game. The combat is fun but feels a little tedious, with the dodge roll being janky and often leading to stun-locks by enemies who all attack at once. Now if the game is indeed going for souls-like I think this is spot-on, the issue is that the rooms are so small and everything moves so fast, that I feel the player doesn't really have time to make a plan of how they want to approach the room. Overall the combat isn't bad per se, it's just a little unfair at times. All in all a very solid and memorable game, will defo be finishing this one. 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sat here at 1:30 AM forcing myself to stop playing this game and go to bed. It's got its hooks in me, and I can't help but be endlessly amused by the meta-textual significance of that feeling. The game is a satire of the addictive, self-destructive nature of the modern social/media/technology landscape, and it has that woven so deeply within its DNA that the actual visceral experience of playing it evokes the same complex cocktail of emotions brought on by engaging with said landscape.It's obvious in the visual presentation: a clear parody of the minimal, block colour Alegria style that is the current trend in social media graphics. But where those illustrations are flat, uninspired, and often lifeless, Going Under manages to inject the style with vibrancy, personality, and charm. And there's a subtle but profound attention to detail in the design here: for instance, particle effects are depicted as bubbles and sparkles, which fits naturally with the business your character works under. The logo of The Cubicle - the mega-conglomerate to whom your employer is a subsidiary - is innocent enough, but gently suggests an eye, gazing out, watching every move.The game is FULL of this sort of thing, from the most overt jokes (an enemy designed much like Mario's Chain Chomp, simply called "Block Chain"), to the subtler (a sign on the wall of the 'Fizzle' - soft drink/meal replacement company - headquarters: "make your dreams fizzle!"), to the subtler still (commentary on cryptocurrency, the gig economy, online "swipe" dating, the crunch crisis, dude-bro venture capitalists, Tai Lopez in his garage, the list goes on), this is a truly complete, encompassing parody piece. And I love it so much for that.And if it was just that, that would be fantastic. But it's also a weighty, chunky third person action game, that is satisfying in that tactile "feel it in your bones" kind of way. And it's tough too, in a way that makes me ache to explore the game's systems and master it all. It implements a full contingent of tried and tested rogue-like mechanics: perks, active items, weapon cycling, "curses", bosses, shopfronts, meta-run upgrades, etc. And it does all of this solidly, but in many of these iterates dramatically on convention. I love the Breath of the Wild style weapon breaking system; in fact, I think it works better in this game than in that. I think that the small scale, fast paced combat effectively distils that mechanic into its purest form, eliminating its downsides and strengthening its upsides.And, as stated before, the artistic presentation of all of these elements isn't just a "media corporation" sheen. The references, terminology and themes are all up-to-date and relevant, and are not just skin-deep. And I find myself, as with other games that make these kinds of points (check out the game Deep Rock Galactic if you want more like this), amused and somewhat disquieted by how the game's progression systems are a kind of pastiche of real-life "gamified" applications, which I suppose brings it all full circle. It's apparent to me that this is an intentional part of the point here, and I find it disquieting because I can feel myself buying into it. The numbers crawling up, the arbitrary progress points, the artifice of upwards mobility, all of it satisfying the reward centre of my brain, just as it does when real-life corporations use the same tricks. And so I buy into it, just as I and everyone on some level buy into the hyper-capitalist ultra-consumerist world that we live in. And that's a hard lump to swallow completely, but this game draws these kinds of complex, introspective conclusions because it evokes complex and introspective emotions. Even the weapon breaking mechanic can be read as a comment on the consumptive, destructive results of the culture we live in.At the time of writing this, I've only played the game for 3.9 hours. But I do believe this game is something really special. It manages to do what only the greatest games do: use a holistic combination of gameplay, mechanics, feedback, visuals, writing, and tone to achieve ludonarrative cohesion and deliver a reflective commentary on pertinent themes with breadth and depth.If any of that sounds like a good time to you, buy this game now.Thanks for reading

_childDocuments_.review: A charming, delightful, and surprisingly deep game - both in mechanics, and writing.I expected a short, silly adventure - but fell in love with the varied gameplay, inspired design, drool-inducing graphics, and bombastic fights. As a lover of souls-games, I was not anticipating I would be impressed or so fully engaged by simple controls and silly physics - but there is a shocking amount of creativity and skill required to push your way through the game's disparate challenges. Learning the intricacies of the 'elemental' weapons actually felt intriguing and useful - not just a silly gimmick or graphical flourish.As for the theme-ing, never have I seen such a delicate and well executed balance between cynical satire, and sincere comedy. The eye-rolling lambast of modern work is cutting, but never becomes grating or depressing, and characters that appear as flat-jokes will later reveal nuance and charm. The game is (thankfully) light on cutscenes and dialogue, so every line feels well placed and intentional.A masterful work - far more fun than I expected, lasting far longer than I would have thought, and worth far more than what they are charging. Easy reccomend!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I wanted to like more than I did. The art style and writing stuck out to me in footage, and they're honestly the best aspects of Going Under. The characters and environments have a colorful, simplistic look which pairs well with the narrative about the dysfunctional workings of big corporations. Dialogue in the game is consistently funny; interacting with your goofy co-workers makes returning to the main hub a fun break between runs. Unfortunately, Going Under really just doesn't deliver on the roguelike side of things. While combat seems enjoyable at first, it's dragged down by a lot of small issues that really add up. In general, your character's movement is sluggish and clashes with the frantic, crowded scenarios that the game throws you into. It feels like the game wants you to play aggressively, constantly breaking items and maneuvering around enemies, but you often find the most success from playing cautiously. Because health items are shockingly scarce, taking minor instances of damage can be incredibly punishing over the span of a run. The game's difficulty isn't helped by how little room there is for synergy building and resource management. Many items have borderline useless effects that clog your runs with bloat. They may not be very exciting, but having more flat stat buffs would really benefit the game; anything to make you feel like you're actually getting stronger. Without digging too far into balancing, there are far too many moments that make you think "Why was this designed this way? Doesn't this seem like a useless addition? Couldn't this have been fixed with a small numerical change?"Going Under is a perfectly functional game, but it's ultimately more enjoyable to watch than it is to play. I think the developers are capable of making something really great, but their efforts here unfortunately fell short. I believe the most enjoyable way of experiencing this game is turning on the assist options so you can speed through the main story and get the most out of great visual and audio presentation.

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★★ stars"Going Under" is an unexpected gem that completely took me by surprise. Recommended by a sibling, I dove in without any prior research and emerged with a newfound appreciation for dungeon crawlers and roguelike games. The game breathes new life into the genre, offering a fresh, innovative take that kept me captivated.What sets "Going Under" apart is its exceptional storyline, which masterfully blends humor with a poignant critique of corporate America. Its randomly generated dungeons ensure that each run feels new and challenging, pushing players to their limits while also encouraging them to keep trying. The variety of weapons is a highlight, turning everyday office items into tools of dungeon exploration.The difficulty is well-balanced; challenging enough to be engaging without being frustrating. The game smartly incorporates power-ups and permanent buffs, allowing for strategic customization of each run. Additionally, the inclusion of NPC co-workers who provide assistance adds a layer of depth and strategy, making each attempt unique."Going Under" excels in creating tense, edge-of-your-seat gameplay, where success feels rewarding and each run is a roll of the dice with the RNG gods. Whether purchased at full price or found on sale, this game is a must-own for fans of dungeon crawlers and roguelikes alike. Its unique blend of story, gameplay, and challenge makes it an essential addition to your library.Thanks for reading my ted talk! _childDocuments_.review: I like Aggro Crab as a company and hate to give this a negative review, but I have to be honest and say that the gameplay in this game just isn't up to the standards set by other roguelikes. It's slow, clumsy, not especially responsive nor even the slightest bit satisfying. There's very little weight to the attacks, weapons break in literal seconds (at least early on) and the fun factor just isn't there. And, while this is more of a personal preference, the character models in-game are EXTREMELY off-putting. They remind me of those creepy little mascots Kroger grocery stores have taken to using, with their tiny, perfectly round heads and featureless, tubular appendages, and I absolutely hate everything about them. What makes all of this so disappointing is that I adore the atmosphere of this game and everything attached to it. I love the character art and design (basically everything about them except their actual models during gameplay), I love the music and the overall art direction with its bright colors and cheeky references, and I love the very idea of battling corporate hoards through the ruins of failed tech start-ups. The story actually seemed like it had potential to keep me interested, at least for a while, and the sound design while not perfect or mind-blowing, was more than good enough for what Aggro Crab was trying to accomplish. It's a wonderful idea overall, but the execution of the gameplay is the most important part, and it's where the game blatantly falls on its face. I plan on keeping an eye on this studio in the future regardless, and while this game may not be for me, I think others will certainly find enough enjoyment in Going Under to keep them coming back for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a great roguelike with an excellent combat system. If you're a fan of Breath of the Wild or Control's combat system, you'll feel like Going Under is everything you've ever wanted from those games' combat encounter and more. You'll be swinging, yeeting, breaking, looting weapons left right and center, true mastery can make you feel like an unstoppable joblin-slaying intern, managing your weapon resources like a DOOM game.While the main focus of the game is its combat, the art is vibrant and unique; and the writing is on point and genuinely funny, you can really see and read the love the devs have for this game and I can't wait to see what Aggro Crab is going to make in the future.With that being said, I truly believe everyone should give Going Under a try. Even if you're new to the roguelike genre, there's a lot of accessibility options and you can turn those on and off at any time. So what are you waiting for? Grab a folding chair and a filing cabinet, it's time to go under!

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best games so far this decade for this price point. Game currently has some crashing issues and camera flickering bug but those have been announced by the devs as known issues being fixed, once those have been fixed the game is easily a contender for game of the year. Overall extremely well-polished game that has the best balance of difficulty for a single player that keeps you playing even after finishing the game to challenge yourself to get even better. I don't usually bother with single player games for the simple fact of it being a matter of 1 playthrough of ~10 hours (sometimes less or more) and it's repetitive onward, the exception is this game has a much more generous price than it should (imo), while offering every run to be completely different from the other by a fair margin. It's also not a bad game for those who are fans of speedrunning, although rng would be a factor it's still a well balanced game that the differences of good-bad rng will still give you some competent weapons as long as you manage them effectively. I plan on getting a 50 or so hours worth of playtime out of this game before I expect getting bored slowly.

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun rouge-like that has a fun art style, fun combat, and some pretty good writing that although can sometimes be a little cringy, is a lot of the times pretty funny and isn't that overbearing with its commentary on the toxic working conditions of tech companies.It's soundtrack is also incredibly good and fits the silly aesthetic of the game.The game has it's flaws with the absence of a warning for a big difficulty spike that occurs after defeating a certain boss, a throwing mechanic that is usually a waste of your time, and a dodge roll that is a little underwhelming. When you do hit the difficulty spike though I feel the game gets way better and becomes a lot more challenging and makes you think more about some skills that I though at first were pretty useless but proved to be very helpful with the ramped difficulty (Example: one skill has a chance to charm the last enemy left in a room, which when enemies are pretty weak in the easier mode they are underwhelming wit their damage output. Once there are a lot more difficult enemies though, you can strategize to kill off the easier enemies first to leave you with a chance of charming a pretty helpful and powerful enemy while also now not having to fight that strong enemy anymore). The difficulty spike also changes the dungeons in so many ways and it made the game a lot more fresh and fun to play!Despite those problems however, I think this game's variety and game loop is very enjoyable and makes it a worthwhile purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: A cute and funny action game where you play an intern at a startup that has to clear out the dungeons of other failed startups underneath her company. Combat plays out room by room like the original Legend of Zelda or Binding of Isaac, and you equip yourself with the office junk and weapons when you can find them. However, the core gameplay loop of going through a dungeon run, getting incremental upgrades of your abilities, and repeating is one that I'm just worn out on. I also found the maps cluttered, with the junk constantly getting the way of movement and making it difficult to maneuver in fights. If you like this Hades-esque genre of games and are not sick of them yet you'll probably like it, but it's not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a cute little roguelike with a great unique style that for some reason hasn't popped off like other roguelikes.Going Under is as standard as standard can be with the roguelike formula. Enter dungeons, find varying items and weapons to defeat increasingly stronger enemies until you reach the boss. Thats all very standard in the genre, but where Going Under differs is in its very unique style. This game looks, plays, and sounds fantastic, with this hipster indie company office vibe you'd find in something like GTA5 as a side mission. You start each time at the office, where you can talk to and accept side objectives from the cast of pretty damn funny characters, aswell as spend currency on unlocking new perks and items to find in your next dive in the one of several dungeons.The combat is essentially a beat'em up with dead rising style weapons, If you see it, its most likely a weapon. Chairs, plants, keyboards, spears, swords, pencils, the list goes on and on. The game actually feels alot like Zelda Breath of the wild with its weapon durability and ragdolling enemies, even the first enemies you fight are goblins. One issue i had however, is the combat isnt the best in general, rolling doesn't give you many I-frames and its very easy to be stun locked on the larger enemy's attacks, and the combat just doesnt have the same feeling of mastering it like Hades or Enter the gungeon do for examples. Its not bad combat, just lacking.Going Under is in desperate need of getting its name out they're, its a solid game with alot of potential, but is very easily overshadowed by larger names like Hades. $20 is very fair, and more content is on the way, buy it now to support the devs or wait for a sale if your hesitant.

_childDocuments_.review: There's only one real nongameplay or story issue i have with the game thus far, when i boot it up and talk to an npc. the game lags for the first conversation.Other then that and the difficulty spikes. the game is fun, for sure.Let's start with the basics. Roguelikes have bad difficulty curves, usually, this one is still not perfect, as there's a few spikes that make sense storywise, but still aren't as fun to deal with inside gameplay. The gameplay is very basic in theory, so it's easy to learn it. But it's difficult in the same way a sport is difficult. The few fundamentals you have to rely on (dodging, weapon management, health management, positioning, hazard/gimmick adaptability) become fleshed out in the best way. Let's just talk about one, and then you can imagine the others.Dodging enemies is a basic thing, but because environments change from room to room, and because you're dismantling the room (cover objects- like tables, hazard objects- like red video game containers), the game becomes less repetition and more decisionmaking. This becomes more complex as you gain abilities that use room props as weapons, cover gets destroyed, enemies with projectiles are introduced, then spawned in groups, bosses generate enemies that are also forcing you to dodge in certain ways.All of these things, they fluidly interact with the basic dodge roll you are given. The few but unique and satisfying upgrades you can find within runs do not BREAK the mechanic or fundamental. They only give the mechanic more wiggle room, and more player choice gets added to the decisionmaking.A roll upgrade may give your rolls a status effect, you can hit enemies and set them on fire with it, making you roll INTO the enemies. The fundamentals of this game all are like this, very basic to understand, very hard to separate, but most importantly, never complex enough to overwhelm the player with rube goldberg number status chains.this is because the writing is supposed to, and is definitely first for why you should play the game.The best way to represent the writing in a roguelike is through respawning and interacting with the story each loop. At least. that's what it seems like recently developers are doing.The approach isn't perfect for a long narrative, or a highly complex game of thrones style plot, but it works for narratives about repeating themes. Like for hades, futility, willpower, meaningless struggle, and how drama and lessons come from failure and success.In Going Under, the tone and comedy tells itself via repetition, how the insanity of tech startup culture becomes more obvious, the more you understand the personalities of people who exist within that culture.The worst boss isn't a bad boss because he's making one decision that hurts employees, it's the mindset that drives everyone up a wall. It's so much more funny to see the consistently horrible decisions, BECAUSE he is telling you about his grind, and his idea guys, and why beating up union workers is cool. The comedy comes from the absurdity being consistency.It's so on the nose, and so brutal, because it uses repetition. Artistically. I LOVE the vision and the tone.The art style, the absurdist, nihilist sarcasm, the killer soundtrack, the writing, the game design is all there.The only issue i have IS the difficulty spikes being so jarring. Spoilers on where.The first half is alright, easy to grasp, kinda tough, but it's a good balance.Then the special dungeon hits, and it feels kinda like there isn't a curve at all, until the boss swiss cheeses you with a dark souls fight. Then the difficulty spike 2.The revamped dungeons are WAY harder, TOO much harder. I don't hate it, I don't want an easy mode, I just feel like the power ups feel less impactful. This feels like the game chucked me off a cliff, if i wasn't familiar with this from isaac, gungeon, spelunky. I would have dropped the game.Tbf, it isn't easy in the beginning, and the game does wait for the sucker punch until the second half.But, that's my only REAL gripe with the game. So overall. I love it.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under has an interesting opener, as a breakable weapons, dungeon exploring, beat em up. However while the general tone and humour is spot on, the game mechanics themselves lead to disaster as time goes on.For one thing the actual combat, it's fast paced and frenetic, but certain features lead themselves to making the experience feel tilted against you. The dodge action being the worst offender. The dodge is easy to manage while you have open room and can focus on a target, but when clutter starts inevitably building up and more enemies start attacking it ends up being a rather large detriment. It doesn't go past enemies or objects meaning you often end up stuck on terrain and it has an alarming rate of sending you no distance on the side dodge, since it follows the camera, so enemies can quickly get you during the non invulnerable frame. Picking up items automatically during the dodge may seem useful, until you accidentally pick up something on fire, or something about to explode. Lastly you can't cancel attacks with a dodge, so unless you play extremely conservatively it won't be able to be used when you actually need it.Hit stun is also a problem in that with so many enemies you might feel like trying to hit and run would be useful, except enemies enrage after being hit enough times becoming immune and certain enemies never get stunned outside of electric damage. It means when you get swarmed there's basically few outlets to run and this comes up more frequently in the imposter mode, where healing is scarce and you're denied end of act skills and beginning boons. It's also frustrating when hit stun applies to you, especially when knocked down as the mercy invincibility is just short enough to stand you up to get knocked down again.Finally some skill combinations can doom you down the line because of poor implementation, the slow down on dodge seems fun until you realise it just means when you encounter a boss it just stacks all its attacks into an impossible frenzy (Looking at you Hu$tleBone$), larger strength and size also means larger hitbox, and setting things on fire is great until they get up close and personal and set you on fire too.The camera and item pick up distinction also starts getting aggravating as time goes on. The camera has a view of things from a tilted down perspective, but when objects start blocking the view or you're backed into a corner it is incredibly difficult to actually see what's going on. Then because items inevitably break, you might need to grab another, but if there's a lot of items around (and trust me, it gets messy later) then you'll often end up unable to pick up the one you actually need in the heat of battle. Pick up and make do is fine on occasion, but when it comes down to a 50/50 between a plant pot and the weapon I need to kill something I far too often end up with the plant pot because it is just bigger.Finally there's too many run ending bugs, the three most common I keep encountering are as follows:1. Curses don't expire - Can happen randomly during a run and it makes it so much harder than it needs to be. Pretty much dooms an imposter run too. Worst offenders are the debt and first person curses for this.2. Camera spin after leaving first person - This one means you can't see as the camera spins wildly out of control, it's run ending and nauseating to boot.3. Locked in one direction - With the way weapon mechanics work you aren't always going to be guaranteed an item that works well no matter which way you swing it. Also locks dodges down to a 4 way path.There are others but they come up far less frequently.Basically I would sum it up as follows:It's fun for a while, finishing the story is enough to walk away with an ok experience.If you are getting it, get it on sale, and don't feel pressured to do any more than the base experience or you may just end up frustrated with the total package.

_childDocuments_.review: Some games are made with so much heart that it shines into every aspect of its design. This is one such game. If you live in Silicon Valley or any such tech bubble, you owe it to yourself to play this game because the humor is on-point. (Heck, even if you don't, there's a lot of humor one can unpack simply from being online or having worked in an office before.) That's not just the jokes, but everything: The enemies, the abilities, the concepts behind the dungeons, and the slapstick nature of it all.It all comes together and fits the atmosphere of the corporate workplace, namely in how it replicates the upbeat oppressiveness of new-age capitalism. Other details that add to this atmosphere include the art style, the bumping soundtrack, the specialized loading screens for each dungeon, the dialog system resembling messenger. It's so cohesively, consistently good. I could get lost in it and I'm sure I've forgotten some things too.The game-play itself is kind of am odd mix. You can see the user tags for that, but honestly, I'd describe it as most similar to a roguelite "Breath of the Wild" with constantly throwing and breaking weapons, but it fitting the experience much more with your limited space and surroundings. It's fast, frenetic, and chaotic, leading often to getting mobbed in small rooms. There's a sharp difficulty spike partway through the game as well, so if it seems too easy at first, that might be because it sort of is. They take the training wheels off later. Though I also feel obliged to mention, the game is a bit short with only three primary dungeons. Eh, it can't be helped with how small the team was on this game.If it seems like even remotely your type of thing, I encourage you to give it a try. Heck, there's even a free demo, and a good one at that! You won't get the same density of humor from the demo, but trust me, it's there. It's incredible to me that a small studio is able to produce a game of this quality. On their first try, too!To borrow a term from the game itself, in a sense, this whole thing seems like it was "an object made of pure despair" for the state of corporate capitalism. But they've really done well in making it into something so cool and I'm glad I got to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an outstanding game for so many reasons. The gameplay is fun, surprisingly deep, the characters are full of personality, the soundtrack is absolutely amazing and catchy (one of the few I've actually listened to outside of the game). I hope the devs will one day add more content in the future.Hopefully if there's enough support then they can add extra levels (there are currently 3 dungeon types, each with a unique theme and aesthetic). It's hilarious how many ways they've managed to lean into the start up theme, whether it's item names, enemy types, etc.There's a great attention to detail and depth they added in a number of ways. One of my favorite discoveries is a perk you can get which allows you to purchase items that you normally can't afford. If you do this, however, you are burdened with debt for the amount that you couldn't pay for. This comes in the form of a ball and chain that attaches to you and slows you down. The higher the debt, the bigger the ball = the slower you move, but this shrinks as you defeat combat encounters. This is already more depth than many games would offer, but you can also use that ball and chain as a weapon (albeit slow).Another example is a dungeon that is a failed cryptocurrency startup. Instead of spending money normally like in the other dungeons, you can (and in some cases must) convert your cash to cryptocurrency to purchase items. Just one of the many creative details included in the game.If you enjoy the roguelike genre at all, absolutely check this game out. And encourage the devs to revisit it and add more content!

_childDocuments_.review: I just wrapped up Going Under (as in, saw the credits, I still have a mode to investigate) and I might be inclined to say I enjoyed it more than Hades overall. Hmm. A few things I love about it:The theme isn’t just a wrapper; it bleeds into pretty much every aspect of the game, from its structure and concepts, to its enemies, weapons and skills (even the ‘Working From Home’ update is a genius marriage of our current real-life predicament, an in-game scenario and the new mode itself). The writing is very sharp and witty, Aggro Crab-stabbing at capitalism, the tech industry, consumerism, corporate culture, automation, exploitative labour and various other related topics, all with some serious flare, creativity, humour and heart. How it balances all that tonally is very impressive. I thought Atomicrops’ puns and wordplay were good but Going Under’s is nuts.The gameplay loop isn’t as immediate or addictive as Hades, but that’s fine because, damn, Hades was dangerous. The combat is loose and has more in common with Zelda’s L/Z-targeting and Power Stone’s room-wrecking chaos. Weapons break frequently so you’re constantly having to improvise and grab what you can, thrashing and throwing stuff as you go. It can be absolute carnage, but in the best way.The big thing for me is the structure and length of Going Under. Each failed tech startup is its own distinctively themed dungeon, with unique enemies, weapons and bosses, and they each take around 30 minutes to complete. As you hit different milestones, the story develops and escalates, new skills get added to the pool, the dungeons and bosses change, all while you’ve got the different mentor objectives to juggle and complete. All these layers keep things interesting and the big finale/showdown is the cherry on top--it's so good!It took me about 25 hours to do my first run on Hades and another 25 or so to roll the credits. I’d be lying if I said it maintained its momentum throughout that time. Your last run isn’t wildly different to your first run. Hades was one of my games of the year but I was honestly glad to finally wrap it up.It’s taken me 25 hours to roll the credits on Going Under (your mileage may vary) and I’ve had such a great time from start to finish. There’s variety and plenty of surprises here so I didn’t burn out. I actually finished wanting more, which is the best feeling to end a game with. There’s an ‘Imposter Mode’ which is a gauntlet of sorts so I’m keen to try that out now. ‘Imposter’ as in ‘imposter syndrome’ and you access it via the mirror in your tiny company flat. It’s a very clever game.The presentation is impeccable too, skewering the popular 'Corporate Memphis' aesthetic perfectly. It’s chunky, bright and bold and the graphic design pops and transitions beautifully. The soundtrack is also fantastic.Edit: there's a generous demo for this that's well worth checking out if you're unsure.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you want to play a worse Hades where you're a jaded millennial who can't find steady work? You should probably keep walking then, because this isn't worth it. Although the characters are written well and the deliberately soul-crushing corporate memphis artstyle is well-realized, the game itself is shallow and repetitive with limited metaprogression to offer escalation or differentiation between runs but without the depth to allow such a flat difficulty curve to be interesting. There's a lot of charm here, but when that charm is largely predicated on very specific existential horror derived from the fight for survival in a neo-corporate hellscape that's far too on-the-nose for a recreational activity while I'm actively on the clock for one of the companies being lampooned, it's just a notch too far when the gameplay itself just isn't up to scratch.
