_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is an okay game, which is a fair thing to say for a game that will last you around 10 hours if you're just aiming to finish it without maxing out mentorship or grabbing EVERY power up in the game. The characters were cute and amusing. The Dungeon crawling, although a bit short and strange difficulty spikes, was fun and quick enough for me to keep my attention and continue through without much trouble. My only real complaints are:1. The ending of the game wasn't all that rewarding and felt like a so-so ending. Not bad, but not great...2.  The dodge roll to me is weirdly too short to be too helpful.  Sometimes I would dodge roll away from an enemy only to be still take a hit just because I was too close to where I was.   3. The response time was also weird,  sometimes, the dodge roll wouldn't respond fast enough and I took a pointless hit that an enemy telegraphed several seconds ago. 4.  The final boss is kinda bland.  You just have survive several monster waves and fight the real boss, but if you get hit once, than the boss knocks you away and regenerates all the health it lost, forcing you to fight it again and try to get to the next phase of the fight.This just felt like extra padding for time and a weak attempt at difficulty. I wish the fight was more unique.  I'm just thankful there was some health items during the last fight, otherwise I definetley would've died.Besides those gripes, the game was fun, and worth the purchase. If I had to give a fair rank, I would put it at 6.8 / 10.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh my god, I absolutely ADORED this game.Wouldn't have even discovered it if not for finding the soundtrack on Spotify (the music is stellar btw, go support the composer feasley if you want), and I'm so glad I didn't miss it in the flood of roguelites this year.The art style is charmingly simplistic with expressive character portraits, the gameplay is fun regardless of your skill level, and the story was genuinely engaging instead of being fluff around the edges. Oh, and there's enough puns to feed a minimum wage worker for years.The tasty lil' snippets of dialogue and character interactions show that the creators were clearly run through the rougher parts of the industry, so all the more respect to them for being able to make something positive and enjoyable out of it.Two things before you buy though, because they might bother some of the game's more hardcore prospective audience:1: Be prepared for a few bugs, maybe even ones that'll end a run. Most of the game's performance was 10/10 and I saw very few recurring bugs, but sometimes you'll get a run where every bug rears its ugly head at once until the geometry itself is out to get you. I got stuck in focus mode a few times while unable to attack, one run ended with me being flung through the ceiling while driving a car and slowly losing 5 hearts until I fell back into the map, and one attempt at the final boss turned me into a statue who couldn't make inputs or take damage.2: Impostor Mode is HARD. If you're an achievement grinder, be prepared to sink some serious time into the increasing difficulty tiers, as well as abandoning more reckless playstyles in favor of delicate ones. The best comparison is Risk of Rain 2's Eclipse modes, where you have increasingly detrimental debuffs slapped onto you over the course of a much longer dungeon crawl. Not quite Tainted Lazarus levels of pain (if ya know, I feel for ya), but you'll have quite the challenge to chew on nonetheless.To be clear, neither of those reasons should scare you away from the game, especially since a small dev team can't possibly do flawless stress tests on every aspect of their creation. I still 100% recommend it, and thank you to everyone who worked on it! Looking forward to see what you do in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great fun. I would totally recommend this game to absolutely anyone. _childDocuments_.review: If you aren't someone who's worked at a startup or in a corporate environment, Going Under is a competent and colorful roguelite, that may seem to make a few odd decisions.If you *have* worked in a larger corporation or at a startup (I've done both), this game becomes something special. Everything about the game shines when you see how they've taken aspects of modern white collar work culture and adapted to every part of the game. For intance:- The character art is based on simplified, inoffensive HR-inspired cartoon human shapes- The skills you get during a run are all based on phrases and personality traits you may have heard in an office environment, but adapted to in-game mechanics- The different environments representing failed startups are well-realized satire of familiar startups and businesses that actually exist, with the additional twist of working in a sort of 'monster' enemy type in each one that is unique- The other characters that can act as your mentor feel like fairly standard office personality archetypes: the jaded software developer, the overly-passionate creative, the anxiety-ridden accountant, and the platitude-filled shallow dudebro CEO as examples.- Some of the dialogue in the game gave me flashbacks to real interactions I've had; subtle gas-lighting about performance, not doing the job you were hired for, seeing someone above you say or do something you can't wrap your head around but know you have to accept to not rock the boat...it was actually surreal at times playing this game.- weapons in levels feeling like they are based on either great puns or cringy startup office toys.The game starts off pretty easy but ramps up in difficulty after you get a few wins. Luckily your 'coworkers' can be assigned as mentors and you can do quests for them to get more benefits (like starting levels with allies, more item drops, special shops, etc). Gameplay is fast and frantic, as weapons break quickly and most rooms have quite a few enemies along with a lot of office furniture.I still can't believe how relevant this game is. I know it's design inspirations may limit who finds it compelling, but if you are familiar with the tech work grind and enjoy roguelites in general, please give this game a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't like this game (reasons below), BUT if you are a massive fan of the roguelike genre and need something new, I could see it being worth to pick this up just to experience its more unique mechanics.For a more casual fan like me though, I really felt like the combat started to feel clunky after the mid-game difficulty spike. The enemy spam, tightly packed rooms, and fast character movement seem to indicate that the devs want you to be aggressive and fast paced, but its quite easy for enemies to chip away at your health. So you have to be overly defensive, which imo just doesn't really work well either, especially after the difficulty spike.Since you have to manage your camera its not uncommon for projectiles or enemies to come flying at you from off screen before you can react. Enemies move telegraphing is also pretty hard to read when they are all crowded up and you have to manage your camera - on top of explosions and other effects that obscure your vision.I honestly didn't feel like there were many interesting stand out skills either. So most of my runs ended up feeling very similar because unlike a game like Binding of Isaac where you have like 8+ floors, you only have 3 floors + a boss floor here, so not many chances to get super crazy item effect combos. Especially since in hard mode health drops when completing rooms is extremely rare. I've gone through whole dungeons without getting a single one regularly, this means unless you play perfectly you have to spend your money on health instead of upgrades when you go to the shop.The ability to get buffs through leveling up your mentors was pretty cool, and the endorse mechanic (which lets you start your run with a skill of your choice if you use said skill enough) was as well. But ultimately I just got frustrated with this game and didn't want to finish it.For more detail, consider checking out my full video on it!

_childDocuments_.review: A well made short and sweet roguelike that leaves you wishing for more, and delivers like a monkeys paw.The controls are simple and the camera doesn't get in your way whatsoever which is a surprise considering how busy every room is. There is so many different items to unlock that it took over twice the length of the game to get them. Certain combinations let you do different builds and depending on what you got the last few levels are going to be really easy or really hard. Enemies have fair "tells" and ways to dodge their attacks, and bosses are difficult but fair, it gets harder as you progress, the same enemies get upgraded and no longer can be stunned. Curses are handled much better than other roguelikes, they aren't run-ending like other games like Binding Of Isaac, they are a temporary challenge with rewards should you survive. The best part about this game is that you can recover from a bad run easily, and there are multiple paths to take for fighting and retaining HP. You have apps that can summon more weapons, give you health, have every object in a room attack your enemies. The store, you can steal from and get discounts on. Fizzle drinks that do who knows what. You can base an entire run around any of these not all inclusive ways of getting upgrades, health, and surviving, or you can combine or switch between them depending on what you get. There is a LOT of perkbuilding here and tons of fun combos that can help you and hurt you.The story is cute and relatable as someone who has worked in a corporate environment before, they got the personality types down to a T. The art direction is fantastic for each of the 3 worlds you explore, it's consistent and clever, as long as you dont look too closely. It starts off as an obvious parody of the corporate art style but kind of forgets about that and throws in whatever's colorful and cel shaded. The music is surprisingly good as well, it changes between rooms slightly and remixes the track when you've reached the harder difficulty. The art direction, and naming scheme of items and places are extremely clever, make for interesting enemies, and items and bring a groan at the wordplay.The weapons are cleverly designed and you are forced to use everything in your environment to hit people with due to the durability mechanic. You have to learn the fighting style of each weapon and not get married to a select few since they'll be gone in 2-3 fights. Better or upgraded weapons add something for you to be on the look out for and using sparingly when needed, there is quite a bit of resource management involved.This game is fair, and mostly balanced towards the player if anything, but there are two enemies that are NOT fair, because you cannot dodge their attacks. The upgraded chain chomp, and the hands. Both have attacks that cannot be interrupted and they almost constantly attack. The chain chomp has virtually no way to avoid taking at least 1 damage from. This is really only an issue in the challenge mode which is already broken though.This is one of the few games I have seen with a zig-zag shaped learning curve. It took me around 40 hours to beat the main game and I ended up getting what I thought was reasonably good at it. After trying the challenge mode, I realized not only was I not good at the game, but the challenge mode was broken. The challenge mode is broken because all curses never lift. The first person curse IS a run killer because it never lifts. This is a glitch that people have posted about in the forums and has been ignored. I couldn't get past it because of the glitch because taking curses really did help you a lot so much they weren't really a risk to take since they lifted in 3-5 rooms. After a long time of struggling I finally learned to beat the FIRST LEVEL of the challenge mode without curses, and the second, and finally the third had a new challenge involving curses which fixed the glitch for the harder levels thankfully. I hadn't felt that frustration in a long time, the game took off the baby gloves and I had to relearn everything that the main story taught me, the game hadn't gotten harder it had just required more endurance. While it wasn't intentional by the developer it was interesting to experience a huge skill wall.A challenging colorful game with deep gameplay mechanics and tons of build opportunities. Just be weary of the challenge mode. PLEASE FIX THE CHALLENGE MODE!I finally 100% this game after 135 hours. I actually went back and played the base game after completing the challenge mode and it's trivially easy now that all the chains are gone. I didn't love the RNG grinding especially after seeing that better weapons were more common in the regular mode, I felt like I had overcome an insurmountable task beating it. The game itself was against me, sometimes glitching out and forcing me to end a run. I beat it. Looking back on it I think the reason I kept coming back to this game in the challenge mode was that each new compounding "rule" presented, changed the way I had to think about the game, it became almost a puzzle game with things like order of room clearing, whether or not to even pick up a powerup and in which order, and finding some really specific mechanics to give me every edge over the game. I enjoyed having to scramble to win under increasingly menacing game mechanics. The game itself is not really meant to be played at some of the higher difficulties because there are some mechanics that are just plain unfair, like: There's about a 30% chance that hitting the enemy in the middle of its attack will not cancel the attack. It's hard to rely on anything to your advantage, mimicking the corporate environment. Maybe hard work does pay off? ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is just about the best game I've ever played. From the top-notch writing to the excellent progression, I've been hooked on it since I started playing. As someone with hundreds of hours in Binding of Issac and Risk of Rain 2, I can say with confidence that Going Under not only delivers an exceptional rogue-lite experience, it elevates the entire genre with its unique spin on combat and content progression.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is funny and cute, and is fun for the first 1/3 of the game. Then.... without spoiling anything, things change. The music gets worse everywhere, the levels look uglier, and even the title screen gets a downgrade. But the real killer is the difficulty spike. I've mastered Dark Souls, place consistently on leaderboards for 20XX and have a 66 win streak in Hades, and I have no damn idea how I'm supposed to progress any further. There are large enemies with attacks that come out instantly, can't be avoided, can't be staggered, have huge range, and come in groups of two with a bunch of backup. The camera is also awful. The devs came really close, then just... forgot to playtest the last part completely.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is pretty fun for an indie roguelite, a genre that I'm not on the best of terms with.The combat is decently varied if a bit button-mashy, and the breath of the wild-esque weapon breakage is at least unique even if I'm still not sure if I like or hate it.The story is a less-than-subtle critique of hyper-corporatism and the struggle of the young jobseeker, and the graphics emulating that ugly, disgusting artstyle they all use is a very nice touch.Unlike most roguelites, a run only consists of a few levels in one world rather than needing to go through the entire game every death, which makes it perfect for short gameplay sessions.I'm not a fan of the character questlines that rely on luck to complete, and the difficulty spike with the second set of worlds is a bit on the  high side, not to mention that some perks don't have any description of what they actually do. But all in all the experience is an enjoyable one, even if it isn't groundbreaking or mindblowing.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a gift from my colleague and fellow intellect, Occamsnailfile, whose opinions I sometimes seek and always respect.  She was right.  Get this game.  It stands in stark contrast to anything else I've been playing over the last few weeks, and I've wielded a foam thumbs up to beat up anybody who disagrees with my opinion.  Don't try me, it does huge damage.Anyway, threats aside, this is a roguelike.   It follows the tropes of roguelikes quite closely.  You will assail a randomly-generated dungeon, you will likely die a lot,  You will gain character skills, and you will learn how the game works over time, and you will get better.This one brings a bit of whimsy and light-hearted humour to the genre.  The art style is striking, the game is kind of silly, and the humour is subtle and sly.    (Seriously, I laughed like an idiot at "low-hanging fruit".  That's class.)Some of my friends don't like roguelikes, and I get it, it can be frustrating to bounce off the same content repeatedly.  But this one keeps it short and punchy; my longest run was only 20 minutes, but my average run time is much shorter, and there's all kinds of between-mission interactions setting the tone of the world.It's a charming game.  And, as the respected intellect Occamsnailfile notes, the difficulty can be adjusted if you grow weary of smashing your face against a roguelike wall and want to just get through the game.That said, as of this writing, I've beaten two dungeons as of this review.  I know there's much more to it after that, but it feels surmountable, as opposed to Heroes of Hammerwatch which just felt like a mountainous slog.So anyway, get this if you need quick shots of action gaming.  It's brunch-sized gaming; long enough to feel substantial, short enough you can do other things with your day.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under - A Vibrant, Dungeon Crawling Delight - In Going Under you play as Jacqueline, an unpaid intern at a start up success called Fizzle, a company that manufactures soft drinks which are also a meal replacement because let's be real who has time to eat these days, it's all about convenience! Upon joining the company you quickly discover that the depths of your building, accessed via a series of slides, are filled with bizarre creatures living in the remains of previous failed tech start up companies who all need to be dealt with swiftly and efficiently. So before you're even able to settle in to your brand new job in the marketing department you're tasked with seeking out the boss at the end of each of these dungeons and putting an end to them in a timely manner. Thus begins your journey into Going Under, head down into the failed tech start ups, battle your way through the sprawling dungeon using whatever you can get your hands on to survive and attempt to overthrow the maniacal boss who waits at the end. Simple.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if I can recommend this game.Depth wise the game runs its core gimmick dry in a few hours. The dungeons are boring and lose their charm after the third or forth time being in them. The combat isn't compelling enough to keep me interested, there isn't enough ways perks and items synergize with eachother to justify continued playthroughs. Of all the mentors only like two of them have interesting potentials for builds.It really pains me to give this game a negative review, it started out *so* strong and it does genuinely have a lot to say and a really funny sense of humour. But I just can't be bothered to sit here and work through runs of this game over and over when there isn't anything here to work with.The wink wink nudge nudge humor of the game stops being funny when the dungeons stop making sense and just become weird and gimmicky. The apps are barely useful and there isn't enough of them, the perks are more often then not completely useless and theres no real way to cleverly synergize fun builds for a run. You are following the dreaded issue that plagues a lot of roguelikes which is that you're just kind of hoping the RNG rolls the way you need and gives you a run that doesn't suck balls.Combat just becomes a frustrating floaty mess, constantly getting stuck on geometry trying to side hop is not interesting, and as interesting a gimmick it is to have anything you pick up be a weapon, in reality like a handful of the stuff you can pick up in a dungeon can actually be useful. The rest of the stuff is liable to get you killed if you try use it.Overall its a disappointing experience, this game had me so hard in the first few hours but its quickly become a chore to even play the thing. I just don't care enough to see what else the game has to offer and given how much praise the game is getting its very unlikely we're gonna see the combat and dungeon overhauls the game really needs to live up to the potential it has.

_childDocuments_.review: Unpaid internship in the form of a dungeon crawling roguelite, where every level is a different abandoned office/business.Lot's of charm in this one, your basic gameplay flow is trying to get to the bottoms of each of the new offices you unlock - and defeating their boss. Your weps are.. improvised! See a stapler? Pick it up and start shooting staples. See a laptop? Now it's a melee wep!You can throw weps, too - they have statuses( liek shock, freeze, burn, etc ) some are ranged weps ( like water guns, or a fire extinguisher ) and you can hold 3 weps at any time ( weps also have durability, so they will often break, forcing you to scramble for a new wep in the heat of combat, sometimes ) in addition to weps, you also have phone apps - which basically serve as a consumable item - some shock enemies, some put you in a rainbow car of death, some heal, some give you shop discounts - there's a bunch of em. in addition to those additions, you have co-workers that offer you missions in the offices, and once you complete them - you can take that co-worker as a mentor, which offers you benefits in the runs. Do more missions, level them up, get better perks from your mentors. in addition to the addition of the additions, you have all your various perks ( stuf you expect in any roguelite ) liek makign your melee stronger, adding a chance to infclit status, super sizing all your weps, etc ) and the more you use them, the more experienc you earn for them - once you complete the bar, you can " pin " the perk, which allows you to start with it. I'm loving the game so far, the runs are fast, colorful - nd every new office has a theme, all the weps change and the enemies change, and there's gimmicks, too.the first office you enter, JOblin - is your un of the mill entry level in a roguelite = it's just gonna show you the ropes.the 2nd one is a cryptomining office, and you fight literal miners, complete with minecarts, and lil missions to harvest as much crytpocoin as you can ( called Styx here ) The writing is siblime, the characters all have plenty of charm to them ( and the squiggle vision animaiton for them in portraits is petty cute. ) I'm not sure if there's more than 3 offices atm - but I'm afraid that's all there is. Not to say the game is light on content, I just wanted to see how far and wacky the devs got with the new levels. one level is for a dating app, and you literally can use a bodypillow as a wep.It's got a good sense of humour to it, might not be the most hardcore roguelite out there, but it's a fun romp.TL;DR - fun style, charming writing mixed with a roguelite that uses a dead rising style combat system.absolutely reccomend.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely game with a unique theme. Haven't played a satirical game in a while, if at all! It is easily the most unique theme I’ve seen among rogue-like games, and brings attention to American corporate & startup culture with some pretty good humour and awesome characters. Even the art style has that corporate non-opinionated look, though they make it work in interesting ways and it hasn’t really grated on me. Also the music ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slaps, I love it so much! It’s in line with the different “dungeons” you visit, and I honestly vibe to them outside the game at times.Fizzle Beverages where Jacqueline, the MC, is assigned as a marketing intern is a newly acquired subsidiary of Cubicle, which is basically Amazon in 30-40 years.  You get to visit defunct subsidiaries such as an overworked contracting company, a “handsy” dating app, and a hype-fueled ♥♥♥♥-coin firm.The characters are really fun to listen to. You have the jaded programmer, the improooover / self-help CEO, the distraught accountant, the dreaming creative, the overbearing project manager, and the chill dude. Of course, these characters are archetypes, but their interactions really make the game shine, whether in getting at least a little attached to them, or revealing the dynamics of the workplace in the conflicts that keep unfolding between them as the plot progresses. You also get to do tasks for them in the dungeons, which adds some longevity to the game. You get to do tasks for these characters, such as “Go steal from the pizza party,” “Go bust the union forming in Joblin,” “Go find the golden cucumber in WinkyDink” etc. etc. These are fun, they are in line with the characters that give these tasks, and they fill up mentorships which lets you take a bunch of unique skills from a character to spice up your dungeon runs. The tasks, since they have you revisit the dungeons, also pair well with the Rolodex feature which has you finding a special card weapon to use it on enemies and get their business cards to fill up your bestiary / rolodex. I got pretty caught up in this Rolodex collection challenge and kept repeating content since the dungeons were pretty fun, the skills I kept gaining as I went on were interesting, and there was the occasional secret room. Also they have some humorous descriptions at times. The procedural content and the variety between runs was not really top of the line, but I kept coming back because the dungeons were unique between themselves. Each one has completely different types challenge rooms, enemy types, themes, and even currencies! Joblin is more standard, Winkydink introduces charm mechanics, and Styxcoin is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ chaotic and has a speculative cryptocurrency investment system. They introduce different weapons and even mechanics too, with WinkyDink heavy on fire & frost for example. The mentorships you gain and the fact that you can pin up to one endorsed skill (use the skill a couple times to take it with you at the start) as you go into a dungeon also lets you control your experience a bit and spices up the runs further, while also adding long term progression. The real progression is in unlocking more and more powerful skills which you can then find in the dungeons though.The combat is... alright. It really starts to shine in the late game after the ending, but I’ll get to that. As far as the base game goes, your weapons break quite fast, you can throw stuff, you have a dodge roll (but no stamina so its not a souls-like! :P), a shop, etc. etc. So far so good. What breaks up the fairly standard combat here and takes it to something more fun is the skills, mentorships that give rest rooms, apps, status effect inducing beverages, as well as the curses you can take on, the different weapons you can find etc. It’s not perfect by any means, and some enemy animations have odd wind-ups, the rooms are sometimes cramped and you get hit multiple times without being able to do much, etc etc. but by no means is it unfair. The fairness does come from most rooms and especially bosses in the early  game being easy though, so yeah... Some enemy types  are quite lethal at least, and combined with the occasional deathly room, the game keeps being challenging, especially when the difficulty ramps up in the later mid and post-late game. The game literally has a sword named “The Cornercutter.” I love this game. I think especially when it came out, it really lacked the variety and long-term progression a game like this needs to keep people coming back though. The Working From Home update has tried to fix that, and I started playing the game after that update, which introduced the rolodex that kept me engaged, a bunch of new skills, and the Impostor Mode. I have talked quite a bit about the “base” game which I imagine has been a lot of people’s experience with Going Under. This game used to be a 10-15 hour long, solid, imaginitive, if a bit combat-wise stale journey, but this new update has tried to carry the game to a whole new level. The reason why I engaged with the Rolodex grind was because of the new skills, secret rooms, weapons etc. that I kept finding, a lot of which came with the update.In the late game, especially in my Impostor Mode runs, I suddenly found myself being able to do creative combos as I picked up skills & weapons. There is the commonly found combo of upscaling a rare weapon, since upscaling also resets the durability, making it possible to use it for a long time and making the weapon stupid big. There is also the interesting combo of having a slime ally when you get hit spawn, or any charm ability, paired with the skill that has your allies lose HP instead of you. There is the ability that increases fire damage, as well as the one that charms enemies on fire, paired with the skill that lets you put enemies on fire by focusing on them occasionally or the one that ignites your thrown items. There is the skill that gives you 2x more money but makes you lose it faster, paired with the skill that has you hit for more the more money you have (I think it scales up to 2 times). There is other combos too, some I have found, and probably quite a few I haven’t. Of course you pick up a bunch of different skills in a run, so often you can complement these combos you create with different skills. Quite a few are helpful all the time, especially the ones that give a minion or shock enemies occasionally, increase survivability etc. etc.The game seems to have gotten a bunch of these great skills with the Working From Home update which brought in the late game Impostor Mode, the Rolodex grind (good kind of grind for me though), secrets, more curses etc, and I assume even some of the really rare weapons I came across like once or twice in 40 hours. So the game has these build variety inducing things largely after the “base” game finishes, and we get into the 10-15+ hour mark which I assume how long it took for people to finish the game. Unless you are like me, fell in love with the theme, and proceeded to grind the Rolodex entries in dungeons you already completed before finishing the game :PUnfortunately the game suffers from a host of bugs at this point of longevity. I encountered none in the base game, but the Impostor Mode and the new skills are so heavily littered with them that I started to  come across a game breaking bug once every 2-3 runs.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with some bugs that still need buffing. I played through the entire story over the course of 2 days and had a great time. I spent the rest of my time trying to beat the challenge mode 'imposter mode' and had a huge bug. Without spoiling anything, I got to the challenge boss who then glitched when it reached half health making the game unbeatable. I couldn't damage it and it couldn't damage me but we just kept going. Normally not a problem, if not for the fact that the most difficult dungeons in the game precede this boss so it left a bad taste in my mouth on an otherwise impeccable game. In fact, this game is so good that my only concern the entire rest of the time I was playing it was 'oh man I hope there's more content here.' The visuals, music, and gameplay all feel great and create a cohesive world that successfully parodies startup culture.  Personally, I'd highly recommend this game with an 8 out of 10. Everything that's on the table really comes across as a labor of love, and the game places a high emphasis on quality over quantity. The 2 points are being taken off because:1. The bug I mentioned really pulled me out of the experience. That was the most drastic example, but there were others (for example companions spawning into walls in another critical boss fight making them irrelevant.2. I said quality over quantity and I meant it. For a Rogue-lite there isn't a ton of replayability beyond the really solid base experience. The item catalog is small and items don't synergize in interesting ways. There are maybe 6 separate worlds that get recycled. In spite of those points this is still a fantastic game to start off anyone's 2021 and there are moments that will have you bellowing with laughter at your screen. The question is, once your hooked how are you going to feel 10 hours later when you hit that wall?

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a rogue-lite dungeon crawler where you can use almost every object in the game as a weapon. Beating up a bunch of monsters with a laptop or a fire extinguisher is so much fun, and because each object only lasts a few hits you need to switch weapon regularly. Another great idea are the mentors: by completing specific tasks for them they give you unique perks. You can also install "apps" that temporary give you benefits, and like most rogue-lite's you'll find random skills that you need to unlock by killing enemies.While I had a few hours of fun with this game, I've retired after beating all 3 dungeon types. After that, you are required to beat all 3 dungeons again but with stronger enemies and different bosses. The unique rooms in every dungeon are already very limited, so it felt like playing a game you just finished again from the beginning on higher difficulty level to me. What I played was definitely worth it tho.

_childDocuments_.review: People would benefit from more games like this. This game starts off with Jackie, a newly hired intern at Fizzle a company that was recently acquired by a huge corporation named Cubicle. Yes, this is an adventure based on life working on the corporate ladder. Jackie applied for marketing at Fizzle but is instructed to instead perform clean-up duty by defeating all the monsters! This story is refreshing! Yet, in its way, it can be very relatable. The story has you growing closer to the characters around you as you get to know them at work. The fact that the characters embody the craziness of an actual workplace is itself very impressive and fun. I won't spoil too much but I will say that the monsters are perfectly themed and designed. These characters...have character...and that is great to see!The atmosphere of the game is simple but colorful. It very much looks like an Indie game that does its best for what it has. I think the creators pulled it off very well even though it could be described as "cellphone game graphics". Like many other Indie developers, the characters are best expressed during conversations with visual art avatars rather than the avatars you see during gameplay. Each character does come alive and become more like actual co-workers the more often you speak with them. Plus the environments of the dungeons are hilarious and perfectly fit for the themes of the enemies.Ironically, I would say the gameplay in itself is the weakest standpoint in this game. That is not to say that the gameplay is bad, it is fun to hit your enemies with a tennis racket or computer monitor, but rather that it is very simple and has been done many times before. So the gameplay is simple, but is ironically tricky, making you likely to add "assists" to your profile to finish the game. It's great that you can modify the difficulty, and I would recommend it so you don't get burnt out on replaying the dungeons. I say this because I don't want people to quit this game mid-play through! The end is worth experiencing!Overall, the gameplay itself isn't what makes this game stand out but rather the unique storytelling and characters. This game would be a perfect gift for someone who just got a new job or promotion! People would benefit from more games like this.Score: 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Set within Neo-Cascadia, Going Under sees you working for a carbonated drink brand called Fizzle, owned by shipping giants Cubicle. You play as Jackie, an unpaid marketing intern arriving for her first day and within minutes of getting there, monsters appear within Fizzle’s building. Adapting to this unexpected situation quite swiftly, Jackie is pressured into defeating more baddies by her manager, Marv, leading us to an unwinnable first dungeon before being introduced to her new co-workers: Swomp, Kara, Fern, Tappi and Fizzle’s CEO, Ray. It becomes clear this wasn’t the internship she was previously advertised, and soon enough, she gets co-opted into further fights.At the heart of any satire is a political message, and behind this colourful visual presentation, Going Under communicates its own message with consistency. Parodying Amazon via Cubicle, it tackles mind-numbing corporate culture, capitalism’s worst excesses and a jaded workforce forced to participate in a broken system. It treads into other subjects with less focus, including modern-day privacy concerns and the trading of civil liberties for convenience. This is all backed by a strong sense of humour – though it's an admittedly niche one as it sometimes relies on memes, one example being how the exit screen states “Noo don’t leave, you’re so productive haha”. Those who enjoy these jokes will love it but that humour soon becomes dated.Within Going Under, failed start-ups don’t disappear; they get banished to the underworld, cursed to remain there for all eternity as wandering monsters. It’s a harsh punishment for failure and these ruined companies become your foes. There are three procedurally generated dungeons in total, so no two playthroughs are ever the same, and each start-up spans across four floors, comprising of gig economy recruiters, cryptocurrency and dating app employees. Waiting at the end of each dungeon is the respective CEO, bringing a literal definition to "boss" fights. Whether you’ve chosen traditional weaponry like a Warhammer to office supplies including the humble stapler, anything you find can be used as a weapon in this game.Combat is simple, giving a basic attack whose strength varies depending on your selected weapon and a dodge roll for defence. Attacks can be charged for greater damage, too, also letting you throw items about, but each weapon has limited durability, so you must regularly switch things up. Skills can also be gathered throughout each dungeon run and these add buffs such as increased health, proficiency in two-handed weapons or dropping bombs when dodging. They don’t stick with you upon leaving, but using them gains experience and if Jackie becomes proficient in them, she can enter dungeons with one skill already equipped. Upon gaining a smartphone, apps can be randomly found, and these have their own perks like ordering in new weapons, creating a dummy Jackie to fool enemies, and more.It’s easy to learn and by mixing together skills and apps, combat holds a surprising level of depth, helped by a good variety of enemies so it never feels repetitive. The only downside is throwing items, which can prove rather cumbersome in terms of aiming – but that’s honestly quite minor. Once defeated, enemies drop money (plus the occasional sandwich) and each floor holds an underground shop to purchase items from, providing boosts like food for health refills, extra heart containers or new skills. You can also earn Cubits, a separate currency that sticks with you once you leave a dungeon and that can buy further skills back in the office.Dungeons are quite challenging, so take what help you can get and you’ll need to make good use of that dodge roll to survive. There aren’t difficulty levels, but if you find yourself struggling, Going Under includes assist options which grant extra lives, higher weapon durability, lower enemy health and more, making it a more accessible experience. Optional challenges also emerge once per floor, tasking you with missions like “Defeat the enemies quickly” or “Mine Styxcoin”. Your performance is ranked out of five stars, rewarding you with various item crates that depend on your score. The "Hauntrepreneur" offers his own challenges too; it doesn't cost coins but makes life harder in exchange for skills, such as causing enemies to explode upon their defeat.Outside of Marv, each Fizzle employee becomes Jackie’s mentor, making for quite a clash in personalities; they ask her to carry out various tasks inside dungeons. Usually, these are simple requests like “defeat X amount of enemies with a particular weapon”, but some offer special challenges, including crashing a demon pizza party and walking Kara’s dog. Upon completion, your colleague relationship levels-up and that offers increasingly beneficial perks, such as Ray’s company credit card or monster allies to assist you. Only one co-worker can be selected at a time though, so choose carefully. This essentially amounts to side missions and not only does it bring some good character development, it adds a level of replayability which means that the game remains interesting.Going Under makes for an excellent debut from Aggro Crab. Though the humour won’t be to everyone’s taste, it brings us a corporate satire which hits closer to home than most, and by doing so consistently, never feels ham-fisted in its execution. This isn’t the longest experience you can find on Switch – taking around 10 hours to fully complete including side tasks – but it provides an entertaining story, and one that’s filled with great combat and high replayability. Keeping you hooked until the end, this dungeon crawler comes with a modest recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those maybes. If you only play through for the story and can find this on sale, pick it up. It's a charming core, but when you try to do everything the game has to offer, it changes from enjoyable to downright awful. Pros- Fun commentary on corpo environments and their bland art and buzzwords- Good gameplay concepts- Entertaining references that don't feel forcedIt exists- Weapon durability (rare instance of me not hating this)- Soundtrack (it's ok, styxcoin has way too many skips, the rest is fairly forgettable)- Characters (they aren't bad, but aren't something all that interesting either)Cons.- All of impostor mode. The devs played Slay the Spire and tried to copy the ramping challenges of elite mode. They failed. Slay the Spire hinders, Impostor mode demands more perfection than the game is willing to offer. That feeds into:- The game doesn't function well enough to expect as much out of the player as it does. Max level Impostor expects you to overcome having 3 hearts with no upgrades available, you take damage picking up skills, and all bosses do double damage. Difficult, but I like a challenge. Problem is:- Enemy tells. They break. They don't exist. They do both. They swing, and the lingering hitbox smacks you a full second after. - Mechanics explanations. I still don't know how mentors work in Impostor mode. Sometimes they stack, sometimes they don't. Sometimes they just don't do the effect they list (you still paid for em though! yay!). Did you charm that enemy? Will it stop attacking you? Who knows!I like difficult games. Difficult FAIR games. This ain't it, chief. It's a well-design package containing a dark mess of a disappointment. Once I was hooked, I was in too deep to drop it, and the last 10-15 hours spent on 100% completion have been an unenjoyable nightmare.

_childDocuments_.review: I reaaally wanted to like this game. I love the art direction, music, character design, and unique premise, but the actual gameplay feels clunky and unfinished. The speed that weapons break makes comparing or strategizing around them either a nonstop chore, or too ephemeral to form any attachment to or excitement about. They're also just too similar in how they play, especially with the lack of level or enemy variety to take advantage of their differences.The camera requires too much attention for a relatively fast-paced game. You have to react to enemy "tells" that often aren't even on screen because the camera isn't in the right position. Needing to constantly switch between using the face buttons and right stick for camera control on top of paying attention to item management and enemy tells & positioning is a lot to pay attention to and quickly becomes overwhelming.It looks like there's only 3 short dungeons that all feel like reskins of the same square, rectangle, and slightly bigger square? The pacing between combat rooms and upgrade/shop rooms also feels off to me, like a single combat is enough to get into the flow, just to have that flow broken by deciding between upgrades or which weapon I want to use for the next 5 seconds instead of spending more time actually using those rewards. (In contrast, I think downwell is a great example of a game with a similar minimalist roguelike approach that gets this balance right.)I didn't feel a meaningful sense of progression from level to level or with each upgrade in the way I'd expect from a roguelike. The short repetitive dungeons don't create a sense of exploration or varied challenge I'd expect from a roguelike.  The constantly breaking/rotating weapons are too short-lived to invest in and don't lend themselves to interesting synergies or playstyles.I think the game had a ton of potential but feels like a half-baked compromise between ideas, just a pivot or two away from becoming something really incredible.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel misled. A cartoony game with bright colors, explosions, surprisingly fun combat, masks a lot of very adult themes that I'm very frustrated about. There is nothing in the main product screen that shows there's something like this in the game. There is an entire level dedicated to implied sexual encounters, references to being groped, and sexual innuendo, including sex dungeons with beds, large mirrors and "whips". I get the jokes and the satirization. I personally don't want anything like that in a game. In a game that I thought was just going to be about satirizing the work and office experience, the fairly direct innuendo is very bothersome and unnecessary to me.The gameplay itself is great - fun, varied, and fairly refreshing combat with well designed bosses. Interacting with each character, save perhaps Marv, is an absolute joy. Is the game fun? Yes. Can I recommend it for the gameplay? Yes. But I personally hate when a beautiful looking, clean, brightly colored action game contains suggestive themes when the game is not even remotely advertised to include such things. To me, that's false advertising, and for that, I do not recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a charming, tongue and cheek, neon joy to play.I am not someone who likes dungeon crawlers. In fact, I would say I downright dislike them. I usually find them frustrating, stressful, and at times, boring. It was the only genre of game that graphics and a good story couldn't save... Until Going Under. From the moment I started, to the exposition, to the tutorial, Going Under really held my attention. Whether it was the hilariously written dialogue and dry humor, the interesting level design, the fun combat, the story, the curious and well written characters, or the beautiful soundtrack; I was entranced. It didn't matter if I died right at the beginning of each dungeon because I'm terrible -- this game was fun and it honestly took a lot of stress of the bad day I was having. This game managed to reach out to an audience that wasn't their niche and managed to pull them in. If you're into satirical, cute games: this is your game. If you're into kick ass dungeon crawlers: this is your game. If you enjoy games that're good, guess what, this is your game. I sincerely cannot suggest this game more and I can't wait to see what the team comes up with next.

_childDocuments_.review: Though the combat and core loop design is perhaps a bit simplistic, the presentation is extremely charming and relatable. Surprisingly well written dialogue for a roguelike, and I've laughed out loud more times than I care to admit.However there's a big half-way hurdle that comes with a design issue. There are challenges to obtain upgrades that ask you to do certain things, and if you don't do them as they pop up, it will be harder to do it later when you're struggling without those upgrades, as the game only lets you access harder dungeons at the half way point and blocks off access to the easier equivalents. Completionists won't run into the same issues that casual players do. For example, I ignored 'Only punch 10 enemies', and when the game's halfway point occurs, all the enemies have more HP and appear in more difficult group compositions and you can't go back, making it harder to obtain this and other challenges. Without keeping the easier versions of the dungeons open, I would call this a bit of a design oversight, but it is my only real complaint.I just got out of a 7 year job in tech and a few characters say some VERY relatable things. Overall, I like the presentation too much to let a progression complaint hold me back from a positive review, but I would recommend going into this for you to do every challenge as it arises, before progressing through the dungeons.AlsoYEET!

_childDocuments_.review: Hilarious and charming theme, narrative, and style, but ultimately the game has a clunky and claustrophobic core loop.  I wanted to keep playing sheerly for the charm, but that alone was not rewarding enough to justify grinding through the repetitive and frankly aggravating combat.I tried playing both with controller  with keyboard + mouse; with the easy mode handicap disabled  enabled, and I honestly do not believe the ♥♥♥♥♥ is with the controls, nor the starting HP, nor how long the invincibility periods last, etcetera.  Offering options and handicaps with these things only band-aids the real problems with the combat loop.  I understand the game is intended to be challenging, but I don't believe that's a strong enough defense for just how under-polished the combat loop (which is supposed to be this game's most core loop) feels.In my opinion, the most fundamental issues are with the play space and actors themselves.  This includes room dimensions, clutter, interactables, enemies (and their pathing/AI), and the player's own basic spatial capabilities, signifiers, and feedback.  You can't fix these things with math adjustments or offsets.  These issues needed to be identified and iterated on quite early in development, unfortunately, because so much else builds off of this core loop.It's just a real shame, because the art direction and overall narrative of the game was so polished and compelling... but yeah, I'm not going to be playing this one through, and I'm sad to say my opinion of AggroCrab has been knocked down one peg.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderfully fresh take on roguelike dungeon crawlers with a really fun art style and good combat mechanics. There's a lot to like, but a couple of things some may dislike. I personally find it to be pretty fun to jump into for a few hours at a time, and was actually pleasantly surprised to find a relatively fleshed out narrative; so it doesn't just feel like another hack n slash with thrown together purpose.Pros:- Really diverse weapons, skills, and enemies.- Lots of character progression via unlocks with fun side missions and interesting challenges (reach end of dungeon without using a skill, for example)- A narrative that feels thought through but not forced or overly predictable. Pretty uncommon for games like these.- Lots of replayability. This is standard for a roguelike but worth mentioning.- You can win a lot of fights but you almost never feel overpowered, even in one-on-one situations. This is a really great balance they managed to achieve.Cons:These are all nitpicks. The game is great, but this is mostly a message to devs if y'all are interested in some tweaking for a better experience (IMO):- Weapon durability is annoyingly low. The game is centered around constantly finding new things to use, and that's a really nice dynamic, but there are CLEAR winners and losers (a plastic knife? why bother?) and it just seems like there's just too much weapon searching. This is occasionally fun, but as the game gets harder and more enemies are thrown your way, it becomes almost impossible to manage this (see below). It almost seems like durability should scale up a bit with game difficulty to keep pace, and also generally be tweaked a tiny bit to allow weapons to last for 2-3 rooms instead of 1-2.- Weapons can be damaged by you hitting them while on the ground. With this and the above, it's very common to pick up a weapon that only has 1-2 hits left in it because you accidentally smashed it when it got in the way of a fight ...or even worse, hit it when trying to knock it off a bookshelf and now it's busted before anyone touched it. Seems like "weapons", like, clear weapons (maces, axes, sticks, but not monitors laptops chairs etc), should not lose durability outside of being used. Or maybe there should be separate "destructibility" (times the item was hit by something) and "durability" (times this item was used to hit something) stats.- In "Act 2" of the game, enemies become significantly more challenging with zero change in your ability to fight them. They basically warn you about this, and generally increasing difficulty is fine, but I honestly think it needs a bit more tweaking. There are many cases, especially in large mob rooms where items are flying left and right around you, where you have basically no opportunity to fight and will end up taking damage no matter what.- Explode-y things tend to explode way too fast. Burritos, dynamite etc have an extremely short fuse, which is only bad because they tend to explode when you kill someone holding them. If you're mid swing, next to one of these things, you basically have zero chance in dodging-- and this means when you kill one of these enemies at close range, you will take damage.- Ranged weapons are hard to use, and "targeting" doesn't make it better. You will often lock on to a seemingly random enemy because you happened to turn to the right. I almost never use targeting for this reason, which means I often never choose ranged weapons (or throwing), and that feels like a huge loss.- Finally: no keybinds. I will often straight up refund a game if I can't customize controls (we don't all have the same keyboards!) but I give it a pass because at least the buttons here are fairly simple. That said, please add keybinds, there are a handful of pretty awkward buttons that hinder my ability to play the game.Anyway, I really love this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Good soundtrack, fun gameplay, deceptively challenging - honestly really good satire and humour as well. But the unexpected main draw for me is that this feels a lot like Spiral Knights. I honestly doubt that the people who made this game even played Spiral Knights, but for somebody who has a lot of nostalgia for the atmosphere of that game, Going Under feels like an oddball spiritual successor. Very happy I found this!
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: Its a fun game, Good play to take out our Frustrations. Especially when your both applying for jobs and studying in real life. Does have its downsides... Like the clunkyness of the game play... leading to a harsh difficulty spike later on in the game when everything moves fast and hit hard. But, those are actually kinda relative to irl? You know when your knees start hurting.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: Such a shame that this game didn't get more attention! It has a great premise that's well-executed (each dungeon really makes sense and manages to stay fresh throughout), strong writing, themes that really resonate and make you think about modern society (technology, companies in general not just startups, dealing with coworkers, the dangers of AI, privacy violations), amazing soundtrack with varied tracks that really suit the area/scene, interesting mechanics, and overall a really fun vibe. It can be kind of janky at times--sometimes items in a room vibrate on entry or are halfway through the floor, and there are too many ways for allied monsters to accidentally kill themselves and any allies near them (WHY DO THEY JUST STAND IN THE FIRE??)--but that actually added to the charm for me most of the time. Like oh of course this Joblin is trying to attack the harmless roomba even after the room is cleared, let's just hope he doesn't somehow start a fire...It's a challenging game but you can turn on "assist mode" to adjust the difficulty to your liking based on multiple aspects.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: I suck at these kinds of games; but, you see, I still had a good time with this game--nay, a GREAT time!! It was a very good time, and it has driven me to find that i actually like these kinds of games (kinda, i just need to get better). Overall, the story is great, the items are interesting, and combat is fun. 10/10!

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a very tongue-in-cheek styled rouge-lite game with a fresh (and honestly relatable) premise. The concept of going DOWN multiple start UP companies is pretty genius, and I really enjoy the added small details, like how every single reoccurring character has their own manner of "texting" which pretty cleverly conveys how real world people tend to speak differently, as in, dialects and accents and the such. That alone helps make the characters themselves more memorable and likable as a result.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: Love the style of this game. Fun setting and characters with good music. The combat is very frustrating at times though. I've been put in countless rooms which just felt unfair and was guaranteed to take hits due to small rooms with multiple big enemies. The dodge is too slow to start after an attack and the invulnerability is too short after getting hit. You end up getting knocked down and take multiple hits just trying to get back up. There are skills to alleviate these problems but they should really be a part of the core mechanics to make it based more on player skill rather than RNG. I felt more claustrophobic than in Binding of Isaac. Even locking on to enemies is horribly random.I really wanted to continue with Imposter Mode and almost got the first win on my second attempt but was just not having a good time on the subsequent tries so have decided to stop. I do recommend playing this especially for the main story. I just feel like with improved combat this could be a much more enjoyable experience and would have kept me playing for much longer.

_childDocuments_.review: Didn't see a Metaverse reference. 11/10. But jokes aside, I wanna thank the youtuber IronPineapple for making a video on this game in Steam Dumpster Diving series, otherwise I wouldn't have find this gem of a game. The developers did a great job of showing their creativity by making a world by mocking corporations.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is one of the best rouglelites I've ever played. From the very start you can see the love and care that has been poured in to every corner of it. The gameplay is unique and fun with you constantly changing between a ton of fun and hilarious weapons. The story is surprisingly captivating with twists and turns making it a wonderful experience. I can't recommend this game enough, even if the genre isn't your favourite this game is well worth playing!

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game after seeing some gameplay and thinking it looked like a good time. I was right! The story, the graphics, the gameplay and the OST are all great. I've never played any roguelikes before so I had a bit of a learning curve, but leveling up the mentors and skills kept me coming back. I love the emphasis on using items and breaking them too; it's very fun.Overall, definitely recommend even if you're a newcomer to roguelikes.

_childDocuments_.review: Was not fun for me.May be fun for you, may be I am not the target audience, but after a couple hours I quit.It's an action game requiring skilled reflexes (not a complete dealbreaker, I like Souls games), but 1. There doesn't seem to be any incremental progress. Your character doesn't increase stats or anything so if you are struggling it's not going to gradually get betterand more importantly2. There is NO CONTROLLER SUPPORT and the keyboard/mouse controls are ABSOLUTE a**. The control scheme is something that would be usable in a slower paced game but here is just infuriating.Also it looks like s***. It looks like s*** very intentionally as an interesting and completely unique stylistic gimmick, but after the first five minutes the "wow that's clever" wears off and you're left with something that's just aggravating to look at.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-Going Under is a serviceable roguelight hack n slash w/ a really unique premise and lots of great characters.  The setting is terrific, the writing is hilarious, the meta progression is solid, but the gameplay feels like a one dimensional beat em up at times.  I think this is a fun enough game to recommend, but I do feel like it doesn't quite live up to it's potential.Consensus:-Middle of the Road Game (Tier 4 and makes up 25% of my reviews).  Snag this on a 50% discount and I think you'll get solid value.  I wish that the core combat was a bit more diverse, but it still offers a good time for at least a few hrs.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: This is very much a roguelike in the current fashion. You buy upgrades with meta-currency that can then be found in a run, and you buy them with run-currency in stores in each run. You can also equip abilities from "mentors" that can level up as you do quests for them in the dungeons.The characters are written in an exaggerated but relatable way, and the whole thing is very cute. As a certified Tech Person, a lot of their bickering looks very familiar. The way they satirize our modern corporate tech dystopia is a bit on the nose, but you can't say they're wrong.The moment-to-moment combat is actually better than I expected. The roll and the tables in particular make space control interesting, and the challenge ramps up fast enough that experienced action gamers won't get bored. You can adjust your reach and speed with both weapon choice and power-ups.I really enjoyed my time with it, even though I didn't 100% it.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under has cute character design, chill music, and a great sense of humor complementing dungeon crawling rougelike beat 'em up gameplay. I got this during the sale when it was $10 and it's been great fun for the price. There are also gameplay modifiers you can tweak to adjust the experience to your liking if you find it too difficult to progress.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: I really recommend this one, a big stream of fresh air in the genre. I'ts not the longest roguelite you will ever play, but it has more than enough content for the price, and the gameplay and aesthetics are top notch. Furthermore, at this time there has been an update that adds a traditional roguelite mode and an Slay the Spire's-like ascension mode. Tons of more and rebalanced content. If you are a fan of roguelites this one is one of those that's worth of joining your (surely) big collection
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: This amazing roguelike made me laugh out loud on multiple occasions. It is such a pitch perfect jab at startup culture that I feel like I *know* these ridiculous coworkers and this horrible boss. It's brilliant and hilarious and *this is what it's like to work in these environments*.What I think makes this game extra special is that my mom's name is Jacqueline too. I grew up on her stories from her time working in local government in the 90s. And they were every bit as ridiculous as portrayed in Going Under. In a strange way, playing this game makes me feel more connected to those stories.My only gripe is that the controls just seem... off. Dodge roll on (A) is such a weird choice that my fingers constantly have to readjust when playing other games.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: the vibes are cool and the core loop kept me coming back, but the details give it a unique . there are rough edges, but listen: turns out it's hard to make a decent multi-platform commercial video game under neoliberal capitalism with limited time, budget and staff,  still give the people involved adequate support instead of replacing them when they burn out with underpaid industry newcomers.don't expect super critical political analysis or super radical agitprop: it's a bittersweet comedy with heart and a specific sensibility (the graphic design is especially accurate). if you have experience with this particular kind of bullsh*t, you will spill your drink at least once, and by the end you might feel inspired to take some sort of action. another world is possible, solidarity forever <3
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game. The art, music, humor are all great. They nail that modern corpoart style, the characters are all likeable and funny, and the writing is witty.That all said, the gameplay isn't great. It doesn't seem to be balanced well and isn't very tight. A lot of the skills you earn I actually regret buying because they just clog up the pool with junk. Many of the apps seem barely useful. For a roguelite it's so shallow. I really wish this was a linear single player game. As it is, there's not enough depth and I don't feel like there's enough here to keep me coming back. I want to complete the story but the dungeons are starting to feel like a slog.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: I would've liked my first-ever game review to be a positive one. Especially for a game I genuinely enjoyed the first 70-odd hours in. But that would mean it wasn't a buggy mess that didn't cause me to do my first-ever rage uninstall. I get the appeal of unfair games, I do. But this game breaks the confided of unfairness and simply lands in broken territory. though this is only after the main events come to an end and you get to imposter mode, the experience of playing that mode has left a sour taste for the whole game in my mouth. As many others have mentioned, the curses that won't go away or just their effects lingering ruin a run. The *unique* camera becomes something you must fight with on later floors when each tiny room is crammed with enemies. The focus feature becomes useless in my opinion, either being finicky to target your desired enemy or just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you over with blind spots. But not so useless you can breeze by without it and not getting your ass kicked at you fail wildly at the enemy only to hit the air between while you yourself have the hitbox of an elephant.TD;LR: A fun game that has been forgotten, leading to a very unfun, unfair late-game experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing Going Under. It was a perfect satire of modern day corporate work life. The comedy and writing was very well done. The music and game play was very addictive as well.Surprisingly, this was the first game that I preferred mouse and keyboard over a controller. I just didn't think the scheme was efficient. There are some other issues that I think could be improved upon. The major one is the lock on system, and how if you kill a monster while locking on, it does not lock on to the next target. The dodge mechanic could use a little fine tuning as well.Overall, I think this game was great. If this is the first game that this studio has made, I am more than eager to play the next they develop.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: This game is an excellent first game from a new studio and is rather refreshing for a roguelike due to its charm, humor, overall presentation, and simplicity.  In general, it’s not too difficult, which I see as a positive.  Overall, it’s a good game that I may come back to from time to time, and I would recommend it for most players.---------------Now, for the detail.  To start, I would HIGHLY recommend using a controller with the game.  I’ve read other reviews and noted that several had trouble with the keyboard controls.  I am in that boat.  Admittedly, I’m not the best with keyboard, but the difference between the two is night and day.  Given how fast the enemies can move, having more precise input for movement is a life saver (literally).  Save yourself some trouble and just use a controller (don’t be stubborn like me!)The humor is satirical in nature, poking fun at everything from startups, hustle culture, crypto, and the like.  Further, the characters are cute, and I enjoyed talking to each and every one of them (I got sad when I exhausted the dialogue).  Story is simplistic, but it gets the job done ;)  I found myself relating to many of the jokes, as someone who was also once an unpaid intern at a poorly run company…Gameplay wise, it’s overall solid, and has a rather engaging formula.  There are some minor drawbacks, such as visual and audio glitches, but nothing game breaking.  The largest issue with general gameplay are the abilities – in order to unlock the higher level abilities, you have to unlock all of the lower level ones.  This is usually okay, except there’s no way to DISABLE those lower-level abilities, including those you would never want to use.  Thus, as you progress, it gets harder and harder to get abilities you want consistently on each run.  I think it would be great if they incorporated a system that allowed you unlock a feature to disable certain abilities, but it looks like this game isn’t being updated in terms of content.Biggest issue with the game: THE DIFFICULTY SPIKE.  Overall, this game is not super difficult.  As I was playing through the first section of the game, I was thinking to myself “You know, this would be a great game to use to introduce people to rogue like/lite games!”  Then I hit midgame.  I can no longer say this.  Due to the midgame difficulty, this is not beginner friendly, in my opinion.The midgame bosses are FAR more difficult than even the final two bosses.  I’m not sure why they went with this choice, maybe to pad for gameplay time, but it was beyond frustrating.  My old controller broke, and I literally bought a new controller to beat this game, as I found the keyboard controls lacking (I was planning on buying a new one anyway, but still…)  With a bit of persistence, the midgame bosses are not impossible, but I can see that they might make some people drop the game.  (In fact, you can actually tell from the steam achievement percentages!  Yes, there’s a drop off).  While you can grind to get upgrades to help with those bosses, they (in my opinion) are far more difficult than they should be.  This is my main issue with the game.But, even with that, I still think the game is worth giving a shot.  It’s some of the most fun I’ve had in a game from this genre in a LONG time, and I’m excited to see what else this company creates!Overall score: 8.5/10 (points detracted primarily from the difficulty spike, the ability issue, and minor glitches)

_childDocuments_.review: Safe to say I really like this game if I'm looking at another dozen or so hours to get the final trophies.Going Under is a 3rd person action rogue-like where you go through procedurally generated dungeons over and over, slowly getting more powerful to make it easier to bash and beat goblins and skeletons and demons oh my. Now, this is a well-trod path that a lot of popular games have done before so does Going Under do enough to stand out?Most definitely.You play Jackie Fiasco, an unpaid intern in a megacorp run Pacific Northwest, starting her first day at Fizzle; a new startup making a carbonated beverage to replace breakfast, lunch and dinner. Unfortunately, as you see a goblin steal some office supplies, your new boss sends you into the dungeons to defeat the employees of failed startups that hide underground. There's more to it than that; it tells a simple plot and story but does an incredibly good job at satirically poking fun at techbro culture, modern office crap and capitalist conglomerates. It's often not subtle but bluntly derisive in all the right funny ways. Jackie and her coworkers are actually pretty amusing and engaging characters and anyone who has worked a dead-end awful job is going to repeatedly feel pangs of sympathy for what they have to go through. The characters, the world, the dungeons are all really well done so that everything feels part of this well-designed whole that keeps you in the game. It's just absolutely charming.The gameplay is your standard 3rd person action game; lock on, dodge roll, swing your weapon. The thing is, your weapons are office supplies. Staplers, laptops, goblin swords...well, maybe not all office supplies. And the trick is, everything breaks after a number of hits. So you have to be on the ball and changing weapons constantly, using what you can find which adds a layer of strategy and chaos to the combat. There's enough weapon variety in how they work and how many enemies attack/do other stuff that a lot of combat is gonna play out differently. It's easy enough to learn but can get super chaotic as you progress. Mostly because of your abilities.The two points of progress in the game are: skills and mentors. Skills are things you can find or buy in the dungeon that let you do stuff like drop bombs when you roll, wield two-handed weapons with one hand, and way more crazy stuff like set enemies on fire with a glance. Use a skill enough and you can endorse it, letting you equip it before you enter a dungeon (only one though). Mentors are coworkers who give you advantages in dungeons. You can do sidequest tasks for them to level them up and improve what they can do for you, and honestly the things they do change how you'll tackle a dungeon completely. One of them makes enemies drop more cash and allows you to buy mid-combat deliveries, another unlocks cans of soda that drop from enemies which do AoE attacks and set fire or slow time or electrocute. There's a real lot of variety.So the gameplay loop is, try to reach the bottom of the dungeon, collecting skills and using whatever you can find, then dying (or winning) and going back in to do it all over again. Which asks, as is often the most important question, is the loop fun? Well, I'll tell you after I grind out this last Overtime 5 run. I would say that the main success of this game is that the gameplay loop succeeds wonderfully. I always wanted to go back and get farther or use a new skill I unlocked or even try to fill my rolodex of enemies. It really sucked in my time. Both narratively, to see where things were going or to have more amusing conversations with my coworkers, or because I got so close to winning and needed to go again. It's fully satisfying up to the end, where it has a surprisingly fantastic end sequence and final boss fight that got me completely hyped.The main weakness of the game is that it's a small team making a pretty well polished, put together game. As a result the variety and time investment is less than say a Binding of Isaac or Hades. There are only 3 dungeons (...sort of, I'll let you find that one out), maybe 6 or 7 enemy types per dungeon, a smaller soundtrack, etc. Though the soundtrack has some absolute bangers on it. So temper your expectations that this isn't gonna be some 80 hour epic content sink. I don't personally think that's a weakness but some people might compare it to higher budget or games by industry vets which I think is a bit lopsided.I would 100% endorse this game at full price. I enjoyed my entire time with it, pushing on even past the end to try and trophy hunt which I've only ever done with Binding of Isaac. Which is pretty high praise honestly.

The devs have already given a roadmap with a new dungeon being released in q1 or q2 this year. I would just be warned that this is a good game now, and hopefully will be great in the future with more content.

_childDocuments_.review: The best story/setting of any rougelike I have played. It doesn't keep me saying one more run just because like risk of rain 2 does, but the progression of unlocking skills, mentorships, and progressing the story is wicked satisfying and keeps me coming back. Plus I actually laugh at the jokes in this game, which feels like a pretty rare thing to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a roguelite-inspired dungeon crawler about exploring the cursed ruins of failed tech startups. You’ll wield office junk as weapons as you battle your way through the forsaken office complexes. Stab a demon with a thumbtack one moment, run over a goblin with a smart car the next–your options in combat are constantly changing.
