That means that every side quest helps you with the main quest sort of.I also liked the setting. A world where humans have not yet mastered the wilderness.All in all a real gem :)
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is a text-based RPG in a world where nature is dominant over humans, who live in the shadow of horrifying monsters and herds that punish aggressive deforestation with slaughter. Sent to explore a remote peninsula that has attracted the attention of merchants from one of the land's few cities, you have 40 days to clear the trails, make allies, uncover lost secrets, and find your missing predecessor. All the while, you have to worry about the needs of survival in a frontier where everything wants to kill and no one is really interested in helping out. At first.The game seamlessly transitions from managing basic resources needed for survival to delving into a complex web of interlocking rivalries, friendships, and interests in a tribal frontier. It's easy to die or miss something important, but thankfully you can save and reload at will. There's a lot of reading, so bear that in mind, but it's well worth it, easily the best $5 I've spent on a game in years.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden has been one of my favorite games this year. Almost like a single-player DnD adventure game with a wonderful mix of character building, combat, and exploration. At some locations you need to type in actions that you want to do in that location. I've heard that some people struggle with these more open-ended prompts, but I've found that an open mind and a couple tries are enough to solve them. I love the exploration style in this game and how the map style doesn't clutter the locations too much. One problem I've had is that I never seem to have enough money or food, even with fish traps (yes, plural), foraging, and selling every bit of antler, horn, and pelt I can get my hands on.  A fair warning, however, this game is very text-based and if you skim through the lore you'll likely miss a clue for the quests. I've had some problems with the quests in Gale Rocks as the mini-tasks for the villagers are not put under quests and if you need to look back at them you have to scroll up into the archive, which gets deleted after a certain point. The quest information is organized in massive paragraphs in chronological order, which is honestly kind of painful to read and makes it difficult to look back at any info you forgot.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this experience.  It was the first text based RPG that I've ever committed to finishing, and I wasn't disappointed.  The development of the characters that you meet on your journey as a Roadwarden is really satisfying.  During my play through there were decisions that had to be made, and I was so invested in the story, I could actually feel the weight of those decisions.  Reading through the dialog, and investigating further through some of the areas of the game felt rewarding.  I will probably play it again with the other classes.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Life on the Peninsula can be summed up in one word: challenging.From the very beginning, I knew this journey would be difficult. At the same time, I was both right and wrong. Right, because indeed, life here is difficult. Wrong, because the extent of this difficulty was so great that I was forced to redefine the meaning of this word for myself. What I used to call "difficult" before is very different from what I now call "difficult".I have faced many trials and made many difficult decisions here. The decisions, dangers, secrets, people, and leaders are so numerous that the 40 days I had to fulfill my mission felt like a single week.Life here is plural. Numerous villages and people need help, work, items, messages, protection, and even people seeking revenge... wherever I went, my mind never ceased to find objectives and challenges to fulfill.A major challenge was prioritizing whom to help and where to go. These were the shortest 40 days of my life. Time seemed extremely limited here: the Peninsula is vast, and the wilderness is untamed and brutal - many days were lost on these treacherous roads.Every soul in this place has their own goals, needs, frustrations, and individual difficulties, and they struggle fiercely to secure what they believe is best for them.It was my job to explore as much of this Peninsula as possible, while simultaneously ensuring the road was safer for myself and everyone else. All of this while I faced my own difficulties: being attacked by wild beasts, struggling to find safe shelter, and striving hard to keep both my pocket and stomach full.Autumn has finally arrived. And with its arrival, I begin my departure. Today, I embark on my journey back to the Cities, proud of my accomplishments here, yet frustrated by my inability to do more.My impact on the Peninsula was real - I know that. But I have but the strenght of just one man. Clearly, I failed to do everything I promised, which weighs heavily on my shoulders as I leave. This weight is alleviated because I also directly and indirectly improved many lives with my work in this place. While I saved entire villages, at the same time, I abandoned others completely to their own  luck.I bring back to the Cities everything I have learned about this place, its people, their difficulties, and - perhaps the most important for the Cities - the wealth that can be found here.Roadwarden has a LOT of content. It's definitely worth playing and even replaying the game. It's highly unlikely that you'll complete 100% of the game's content on your first playthrough. There are many details that, depending on the priority and order you complete each individual mission, take more time to discover. Having known such details earlier could be a huge time-saver for you, leaving you with more time for adventuring on the Peninsula.The game is immersive, and the atmospheric music/sound effects are good and help a lot on the immersion. In the first few days, I felt an uncomfortable repetitiveness in the music, but that quickly passed once I uncovered and opened up new routes for exploration.Personally, I give this game an 8/10 rating. It's a narrative-driven game, which may not appeal to everyone. If you're not willing to read (and read A LOT), narrative games may not be your thing (and that's okay, if you don't enjoy it, refund it).My biggest issue with this game was the feeling of being poor, extremely poor.Narratively, it makes a lot of sense, considering your character's mission is to explore a place facing many hardships. The help and services you provide are hard and demanding, and the payment for your work - in most cases - does not meet the effort you input.And as you face all the hardships of this place, all while paying for shelter, food, and services - this all combined quickly drains your pockets. With an empty pocket, you need to work. By working, you can't explore. Without exploring, you can't fulfill your mission and uncover the various secrets and stories of this game.That said, I highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Game is truly amazing, really immersive, the story keeps you grounded makes you wonder whats gonna happen nextThe relation between cities are great too, you can do whatever you want with it.The mystery of the previous roadwarden is what kept me going!Some part of the game actually feels like DnD, including the story, atmosphere and the gameplay mechanics. Truly one the best Text - Based RPG ive ever played
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal. If you only plan on playing through once, and want to be sure you see pretty much everything, be sure to play on casual--I really took my time, got to meet everyone, and committed hard to getting the ending I wanted, and it took about 110 in-game days, while the default difficulty restricts you to 40.From what I see, I was extremely slow compared to others, but I feel very happy that I played it the way that I did. Keep a little notepad by your side, grab a bevvy of choice, and be prepared to read a ton.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game for 7 hours straight.You're a Roadwarden, someone who keeps the roads free from monsters, obstacles, and highwaymen, while building relations with the locals and relaying messages between towns. Your primary task after being sent to the Dragonwoods by the capital is to track down the previous Roadwarden named Asterion. You get to build relationships with the characters (which is sometimes helped by your chosen faith - mine was pagan. Go druids!) and slowly uncover the land's secrets. You get to meet a reclused sorceress who may or may not have an addiction problem, a bear of a woman who owns an inn, a vain and cunning (but sincere once you gain her trust) mayor who is deeply connected to a tragic incident that befell a local town years and years ago, several monks, a lot of druids, a male version of Poison Ivy, a lotta undead (burn 'em or not, up to you), and if you're lucky - a unicorn.There's tons of little aspects to the game like dragonbones (turned into shillings. I'm not kidding), timed quests, whether you're a fighter or pacifist, class perks, unique inventory items (that bait you into selling them only to regret doing so later on because oh ♥♥♥♥, they're important), how each town thinks of one another, bed-and-breakfast which slowly becomes free (if you're dedicated to establishing good reputation), influence on your character's worldview, and more.Creeks was my favourite town by a long shot. I'm not sure if the Roadwarden can choose where to settle down yet but I'm settling down in Creeks. It was also interesting how no one had seen a horse before save for mine. The capital, Hovlovan, vaguely reminded me of King's Landing though some dialogue options seem to help you flesh out/choose how you want it to be like. Trust is a great factor to learn more information in the game as well as get better endings (and achievements).This is the first time I've played a text RPG like this. I honestly didn't expect it to be so well done. At first I thought it might be like D&D, but no, the story is pretty centered though there's a lot to unpack. it's like a little CYOA because of how varied the endings each character and town get - it all depends on what you choose to do and not do with the information you have. The story, gameplay, and characters successfully kept me at it even until my eyes were begging me to go rest. I'm going to play another round of this to unlock the other achievements, mainly find . Cheers. 8.9/10Update: I did it! I moved into Creeks! Got an achievement for it too. Still unable to unlock Bed Connoisseur though
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: If you like text-based adventures/interactive fiction, this is probably a good game to choose. There is definitely more to it than a few other text-based games I've played - I especially enjoyed doing the puzzles, though the ones that require text-input can be a little tedious as you have to be quite specific. Naturally, this game has a LOT of reading, so keep that in mind. You also have to be really good at time/resource management, so a great game to play if you're one of those people in RPGs that never uses items 'just in case you need it for later'. Also, if you like The Witcher games, you might also like this - not in terms of gameplay but there is a very similar atmosphere to this game. Overall, I very much enjoyed playing this.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: As someone that had never touched a text-based RPG before Roadwarden was, for me, an all new experience and one I will likely never forget. Though I wish I could, just to experience it fresh again.The sombre music and charming visual style would be enough for me to recommend this to others. Hell, I even voted this as my best soundtrack of 2022 as it is one that, despite having finished the game a short while ago, I keep coming back to just to listen. Yet to compliment the sound and style of this game there is an equally compelling story. Suspicious locals, occult activity, and classic bandits, all staples of any solid fantasy world, are just a handful of obstacles you will encounter whilst unravelling the mysteries of the wild peninsula you are tasked with exploring and securing after the former Roadwarden abandoned their post.From the gruff owner of Pelt to the carefree folk of Creeks there are plenty of interesting people to interact with, learn about and even befriend, and yet, despite this definite presence of others, the tone of this game is one of solitude. Being the titular Roadwarden you have no choice but to move on eventually to aid other folks and continue your work.Be it the vivid descriptors and charming dialogues or the many mysteries of the land, something will keep you coming back (if you somehow manage to not binge it all in a couple of sessions as I did).A long and somewhat meandering review admittedly but all to say one simple thing: This game was an absolute delight to experience and I hope that it gets more attention than it already has.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Oh man, I cried. I think this is the first review I've ever left but I enjoyed this game so much I just have to share.The story, characters, setting are all beautifully written. First game in a long long while where I knew each of my decisions would matter in both the short and long run. The lovely pixel art scenes add way more than I thought they would to such a text heavy game.There were a few point I wish I had saved beforehand so I could see how they would change the ending but I'll have to put that aside for another time as each full play through is quite a time commitment. I fell asleep thinking about this dang game during my whole first play through, I hope the developers are able to make more worlds and stories like this one because I'll absolutely be playing anything they put out after this. Amazingly done.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure if others would agree with my use of the word "Cozy" here since the game does involve tension and life or death stakes, but that is the vibe I get playing this game: I feel cozy leaning back in my chair, sipping my coffee while I immerse myself in the beautiful art and atmospheric sounds and music. _childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is a fascinating game. It is dripping with atmosphere and has an incredible soundtrack. Before this I hadn't played a game that so thoroughly assessed my ability to read, comprehend, and recall information. I made choices in this game that added up to real consequences that had potentially devastating outcomes. I played on the normal difficulty with no modifications and felt challenged. Even if you play on the easiest difficulty with every advantage you'll get sucked into the story and start counting every coin and ration with fervent care. Do yourself the favor, buy the game, turn off the lights, put some headphones on and lose yourself in the woods.From a friend who watched me play through the whole game: The story is incredible. Every decision you make matters and has a profound effect.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on a whim and was pleasantly surprised, couldn't help but binge through it in 10 hours straight - very much like a good book you just can't put down and end up reading way past your bedtime. _childDocuments_.review: "We have nae to give and do ne wish to trade with outsiders."Roadwarden presents itself rather straightforwardly. You are a roadwarden, a person hired to manage roads in an isolated peninsula, a stranger to the people who inhabit it and as such, are very often rebuked by the townspeople when you barge into their homes and begin asking questions. You will not have the trust of people you speak to initially and it takes time, work and much conversation for people to open up to you. The game also lets you starkly know that you will return back to the city of Hovlavan within 40 days and use your time carefully. However, there is a great deal to explore, many past events and relationships to discover and the fate of the peninsula to decide. The game is engaging and doesn't hold your hand, forcing you to choose what you wish to accomplish within 40 days. It constantly remind you that you are only an outsider and you won't have your way in a grand fashion as you have with many other RPG games, and are just the messenger before the flood gates open. There are a few complaints I have; Old Pagos and the white marshes really felt underwhelming in terms of the interactions you can have and the number of villagers present to interact with. There are some other choices which could have been fleshed out far more, namely .  However, overall, this game is a gem and I recommend it for people who enjoy text based adventures relying on imagination. I do hope for a DLC to expand on the peninsula or even a second game where the player can play a more centred role and interact far more deeply with characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful rendered text adventure filling you with the wistful melancholy of the long road working to bring some semblance of peace to a disconnected wilderness. The granularity of the weight of your decisions and what this spells for the Peninsula drew my straight in and connected me with the land and its people, concerned for them and the land I had come to hope to help rather than hurt.

_childDocuments_.review: A low-key fantasy "road movie" in the form of an illustrated text-based RPG. Crafted with love, lore, and exquisite storytelling.Games like Roadwarden heavily rely on a compelling story. Fortunately, this aspect of the game is what makes it worth playing. Levitating between fantasy adventure and detective mystery, it features rich worldbuilding, dry humor, captivating characters, and well-versed descriptions (to be fair, there were errata and text inconsistencies; overall, the story is very well-written). I would probably read this as a book, but having it as a game where you can influence the outcome is even more satisfying. In a nutshell, it is a "visual novel" designed for those who still fondly remember text-based RPGs and text quests.The world of Roadwarden reminds me of the Witcher universe. Maybe because the author is also from Poland? Or, because it is hard to imagine a fantasy setting without being influenced by Sapkowski or Tolkien? Probably both. It is more down-to-earth (not down-to-Middle-earth, heh), though, with no superheroes or supervillains. That makes the lore more credible and distinctive than usual.The RPG aspect is also convincing with this one. Choosing starting traits and beliefs influences how an effective playthrough looks like. I replayed the game several times to see how that would work; the results satisfied me because every playthrough turned out to be a little different despite having more or less the same core progression.The morals and raised questions felt subtle and nonjudgmental, even when they touched on topics like environment, religion, politics, etc. Of course, you can influence how plot twists resolve and what happens to the Peninsula. Despite this, the game ending ensures that any outcome is OK and will have "something positive" and "something negative" in different proportions and for conflicting parties/causes.Music deserves mentioning. The main piece complements the narrative and its sepia-toned illustrations, maintaining the melancholia very nicely.Lastly, a few words about playing Roadwarden on Steam Deck: the experience is not as smooth as, let's say, Disco Elysium, though the game is perfectly playable as it is. The text is readable; controls are clunky (you must use a pointer most of the time) but manageable. Overall, it is an excellent game.

"I go left", "I open the door", "I continue".Great, wonderful, "I exit game"

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of the best gaming experiences I've had in recent years. An old school text adventure that's deep enough to make you really feel like your choices matter. I've uncovered ancient secrets, made and lost friends, fought bloody battles and gotten embroiled in complicated political intrigue... and that was just my first play through. The character creation options are just enough to make you feel like a unique person without having to get bogged down with character sheets and the like. At points I found myself genuinely moved by the story and you can't ask for much more than that from a narrative driven game. Spoiler Warning...When you first leave the camp instead of heading west to the inn, head east to the little stone building, inside look for the trapdoor. there's a box in there with a health potion which you can give to the trader in Howler's Dell (West of the inn and then north of the ruins). Pretend I left it there for you, safe travels Roadwarden.

_childDocuments_.review: Grimdark people pleasing simulator. Your role is ultimately to play politics between a bunch of factions that have not-always-friendly relations with each other, and the game does a great job of putting you in this role. Sometimes those politics involves doing things that are Objectively Good, and sometimes people will complain even when you are doing things that are Objectively Good. Other times you have to bend the truth a little to achieve your ultimate goal (colonialism). Just like real politics!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. You're not the chosen one, you're just a person with a horse and a job to do. Depending on what class/religion you choose, your view of the world completely changes, and you get differing opportunities as well. Playing as a Pagan Warrior or as a Mage Wright-Worshipper will give you very different playthroughs. The dialogue is rich, and the characters are diverse and have motivations and worldviews that make them feel like real people. 10/10, just play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent text based narrative game.-Great worldbuilding with fresh, interesting and coherent fantasy elements.-Solid writing throughout.-Strong sense of freedom and player agency.-Lots of places to discover and explore; three dimensional characters to meet; complex factions to approach; deep secrets and mysteries to uncover; monsters to fight or fear.-Constant decision making, from character creation/progression to money/equipment/time management, combat, political relationships. So many choices and actions will shape the experience differntly.-Impressive balance between time limitations of the objectives and scale of the game: all the freedom and opportunities clash with the time constraints in a thrilling and thoughtful way, especially towards the end where every minute and tiny choice counts; and you start seeing the weight of your failures and anchievements.-Small gameplay choices that enhance interactivity and immersion.A surprisingly strong, novel, smartly designed, "ambitious in a good way" narrative experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful game. I'm in awe of how much is packed into just one playthrough, never mind the different ways you could play it over again. The music is gorgeous, the visuals are so detailed. I adore how small changes could happen and they're still represented in the image you're given. This is the perfect type of game for someone who loves having a bunch of quests where you can tick them off one by one, but it still gives you a healthy dose of decision-making so it doesn't feel stale. Also, there are so many mentions of gay couples, poly people, trans and nonbinary people! In this world it's clear they're just as normal and abundant as cishet people.So pleased with this game, and so excited to play it over again. I think my only sadness came from not having the option to date anyone (that I could find), but it's not like this game was advertised to have that option anywhere - so really, not the game's fault.

_childDocuments_.review: its a great role-playing game, while you can save-scum its more interesting if you don't, as the game has very few "fail-states". Roadwarden rewards you richly with great story telling whether you succeed or fail your tale is your own. *spoiler*[scroll past new roadwardens  as this is an account of my first day]- my first day I travelled east at the first crossroads. I ignored multiple warning signs painted in blood and took the dangerous path through the forest. My character, a fighter was no coward, and was eager to prove himself up for the job. I came face to face with a beast twice my size. It tore my gambleson to shreds but I manage to cleave its head from its body in a display of mastery and desperation. alone, afraid and very much now aware of the danger I pressed on, too late to turn back. I happened upon bandits, while I sense some sort of sanctuary from the forest, they greeted me with bruises, threats, insults and issued demands of me or else. They allowed me to leave after I gave into their demands with my ego bruised I continued down the path. A shell of my proud self with clothes and armour to match. when I hit a crossroad, the sun was setting and with the night I knew danger was close, the crossroad's signs would offer comfort to most but I was illiterate having been a soldier my whole life. I had to choose and I picked to wrong path, nighttime was upon me. Luckily, I was saved by a wondering light who help me find the nearest city bruised, clawed, bloody and very much no longer the man  I was when I entered to forest, they dragged me to the nearest inn each stair thumping my limb body. I woke up to the sun greeting me, covered in bandages and a changed outlook on life.

_childDocuments_.review: [Preface] I heavily suggest choosing the Casual game mode. A time limit adds a bit of challenge, but if you wish to explore every nook and cranny of the peninsula, you will find yourself cursing the passage of the season. A timed mode is more applicable to those who have seen what is available and know how to navigate the game. Easily one of the best games I've played. Your chosen quest at the beginning of the game isn't a binding contract; you can seek to fulfill it or you can choose directly against it. Your identity, while exerting certain influence, does not gate you from certain choices or outcomes; at worst, you'll have to put a little more effort in. There is an onslaught of decisions with dire consequences, but judgement is never thrust upon the player. You can savescum or you can live with the consequences to your actions. At first, you'll be totally mystified by the world you're in, grappling with strange vocabulary, attempting to decipher the words of the locals, each group speaking in their own heavy accent, expertly portrayed through text. As time goes on, the veil lifts, and you find yourself among a greatly flawed populace. Some are greedy, some are liars, and some are addicts; their first impressions collapse and you're left with people of imperfect action and worldview. Petty squabbles amplify, yet are increasingly seen as fruitless. This coalesces into a theme-defining moment which whisks away one's soul, effortlessly demolishing any image of the peninsula one has so confidently concocted over their journey. It leaves the player, again, with the question they have asked from the beginning: what am I to do?

_childDocuments_.review: Commits the classic adventure game blunder of requiring a B.S. in Moon Logic to figure out some quests -Dolmen wants you to type 'trapdoor' instead of 'hidden door', 'fake door', 'hidden passage', 'secret passage', 'secret door', or even 'keyhole'. -A spear is needed to make a quest less dangerous. You can recklessly fight a mob across the map, and if you "win" you get a spear (why would you do that? The game repeatedly drives home the point that unnecessary risks can be lethal and you don't know what you're going to get until you've already done it), or lie to someone to get it in time for the quest (you have no knowledge that you'd get a spear that way, and the game implies that your reputation is important, thereby discouraging lying)Uses Pokemon "open world" design, where it looks open, but most of the paths except for the pre-determined one are either hard locked (come back later when the shiggus diggus leaves) or soft locked behind requirements so expensive that it makes zero sense for the player (doing a dangerous encounter exhausts you to the point you have to rest a few days before you can venture forth again, or you spend all of your money on something not worthwhile.)The general time limit on the game is incredibly stupid. It encourages the player to "solve" the game instead of experiencing the open world naturally.That being said, there are quite a few likable characters (nobody trusting you initially gets tedious), the world is decently fleshed out and presents a novel scenario, although if I squint really hard I can see this game being The Witcher fanfic (roadwardens are treated an awful lot like Geralt in Witcher 3). But once you see the man behind the curtain, typically if you die and savescum and play around with different choices, the game falls apart.Overall, I wouldn't recommend to most people, especially not those on the fence about adventure-choice gamesAs an aside, what's up with all of these RPG games with glowing overwhelmingly positive reviews being a mixed bag of turds and truffles? I swear it's getting worse.

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is a text-based RPG where developers decided to focus on the depth and originality of their story more than anything else. It paid off as it is one of the most engaging world-building made in quite some time. At the crossroads of a  book and a novel, Roadwarden is an excellent game at a great price tag.In Roadwarden, you are the new… Roadwarden, as soon as you arrive on the , you can see this gloomy, wild and dangerous world that will make your mission difficult. The City’s merchant guild is sending you to open trade routes; you will also need to explore the world, try to soothe it as best as you can, tame the wild monsters, and why not figure out what happened to the previous Roadwarden while you are at it.The gameplay revolves around large blocks of text and some contextual elements that will help you throughout your decision-making process. From the get-go, you will see that everything revolves around the writing, including the art design of pixel graphics accompanying each piece of text to engrave an image of the world in your mind. Extra panels will remind you who the characters are, the places you visited, the quests you have or even a bestiary. Roadwarden makes sure all the context you have discovered so far is in your archives and easily accessible.Throughout the exciting dialogues you will have; Roadwarden is letting you dream of this world, of your character, and you can easily replay the actions in your head due to the excellent quality of the writing. You will wonder what would have happened if you had handled this situation differently, said something different, or taken a different approach. As such, you can replay the game to experience it fully. With three different difficulty levels, Roadwarden can be either forgiving or pretty challenging; you will decide this for yourself.Something that stood out is the freedom offered to you; the way you will conduct yourself is your own, and while the game lets you pick between three starting classes, your background story is yours to make, and so are your actions. Each decision will allow the plot to evolve and remind you that your choices matter.Patrol the roads, protect towns, fight monsters, explore dark caverns, take bribes, negotiate, and accumulate wealth. Please do whatever you feel like; it is up to you. Of course, your health, nourishment levels and armour quality are essential for you to balance as they will provide bonuses or negatively impact you on your journey.Sadly, I experienced tiny bugs such as my mouse cursor highlighting the text I didn’t pick or some text lagging to appear and having me skip it by mistake. Nothing game-breaking, but assuming it would have happened at a different time, it could have been highly punishing and frustrating. Though needless to say, the pros far outweigh the cons.Usually, my experience with text-based RPG is with mixed feelings; games featuring heavy writing often fail to make you dream the world or let your mind wander. Roadwarden doesn’t have that issue. As you play and follow the story, you will have no problems visualizing all the action in your mind and at your own pace. We also need to credit the music; while discreet, it perfectly fits the game and ambience.In the end, I had a fantastic time playing Roadwarden, and it is one of the most engaging world-building made in quite some time. At the crossroads of a  book and a novel, Roadwarden is an excellent game at a great price tag. If you liked this review, you can check my curating page for other games you may like.

_childDocuments_.review: From start to finish, I could see why this game was compared to The Witcher.However, Roadwarden tells its own story through a familiar tone. This fantasy world was such a breath of fresh air, while keeping its descriptions nice and simple, not dragging out the descriptions to leave some room for imagination.The choices are plentiful, with unpredictable outcomes and characters beaming with life and opinions, leaving no room to please everyone if you truly play by the way you feel, not to please everyone.Anyone looking for a fantastic, almost soothing journey, I HIGHLY recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Simply incredible. After Golden Treasure and Citizen Sleeper, I was sure there's no way that 2022 would have another great text adventure ready for me. _childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden offers a world that is at once charming and merciless. Most of your time is spent as a political actor of sorts, trying to win the favor (or begrudging acceptance) of various villages and factions throughout the peninsula, which ends up being an excellent way to combine narrative and gameplay-centric sources of tension for the player. Instead of feeling like a book that was jammed into an .exe file to boost sales, as so many narrative games do, the decision-making and resource management feels very natural, like an homage to TTRPGs on the narrative side, or to old-school text adventures on the challenge side. Even if this game were more of an executable book than a game, the writing is strong enough that it still would have stood out. The world feels truly alive, and the various competing interests and hidden motives of each actor make for an intriguing experience in its own right.If you like narrative-heavy games, and want something that invokes the feeling of curling up with a cozy fantasy novel, this game was made specifically for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Really something special. A resource-based, story-and-choice-driven RPG similar to Disco Elysium, Fallen London, Citizen Sleeper, or (without the ship combat) Sunless Sea or Sunless Skies. You have 40 days as the new Roadwarden (like a more responsible witcher) in a frontier area to scope it out on behalf of a colonizing merchant guild, help out people, find what happened to your predecessor, ally with various factions against one another or your employers - the web of decisions and possible story threads to pick at is bewildering, and you won't have time (unless you are a strict min/maxer) to do it all. So your playthrough feels very personal. Haven't felt this great about a story-and-choice-driven RPG since Citizen Sleeper. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a strong, well-written, expanded, stylised CYOA-novel. Nothing more and nothing less. It will appeal to fans of games like Sunless Sea where strong narrative beats and the fun of exploration wins out over graphics or engaging minute-to-minute gameplay. Try the demo if you are in doubt.I will say that the developer promise of "30+ hours" is probably exaggerated for anyone with a decent reading speed. I completed my first playthrough in around 12 hours of gameplay, seeing probably 90% of gameplay by reloading at key points to play different branches. I think the average player with an average playthrough can expect around 10 hours, which is fine for the price point, but temper your expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: Since this is a visual novel-like game, I expected some good writing, which is lacking in modern games. But the game meets you with California-style writing, where no matter of setting, the characters speak and act like modern days college kids and things like mix gendered military units are more common than nowadays. I do not mind this, it is just already too much of this on the market, and sometimes you actually want something that feels creepy-authentic.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A short charming choose-your-own-adventure story where you roleplay as a roadwarden, which generally consists of patrolling around a circular loop of a rural peninsula to keep the roads safe, and running errands for various people from nearby settlements, along with the more specific task of finding your missing predecessor, and securing cooperative deals with the local settlements for your big city employers.The game involves a lot of reading, which is perfectly fine as the writing is enjoyable, and functional – gathering information is important for directions to points of interest, interactions with people/creatures you’ve yet have to meet. It also has fallout/fallout 2 style epilogues to show your impact upon the world at the end, which is nice. Not all choices are impactful, quite a lot of them are flavorful, but still enjoyable as it allows you to express who you are and sculpt the world according to your tastesGameplay consists of picking one of the provided text options, and occasionally typing out something specific to do – it’s a choose-your-own-adventure story.You pick one out of three classes early in the game, each with unique equipment, skillset, and situational options/dialogue choices There’s a bit of resource management involving managing food supplies to keep your stomach full, managing your health/vitality, keeping your light armor intact, and keeping your appearances presentable. There’s also some light inventory management involving your tools and equipment.There is an adjustable time limit when you start the game, but the middle settings provide you more than enough time to finish everything to do on the first blind playthrough, unless you are wasting a lot of time or really bad at time management.The save/load system is very handy and conveniently implemented, with enough compulsive saves you have a lot of freedom to experiment in explorations and encounters, without worrying about ruining a run and needing to restart.

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden paints a compelling, vivid world, and its characters hint at depths that, as a mere traveler, you know you'll never fully understand. It's definitely the best cRPG I've experienced so far (maybe a few Choice of Games games come close to being this memorable), and it's mostly text-based.I could criticize it for a few ways it can be a little obscure (for example, the mystery of the dolmen was mildly annoying, for me), but mostly the adventure treats you reasonably fairly and there are usually multiple solutions to problems. It also mostly seems not to judge your ethical decisions other than in how characters respond to them.It does a great job balancing your relative powerlessness and aloneness with the substantial impact you can make. The sheer number of weird beasts and their descriptions and habits is gobsmacking, and often the advice from the experienced huntress is "run away" or "if you encounter them, you're at their mercy." Also, I'm not sure if I've played another character before who can't read - that was interesting.Overall, it's really satisfying. It gives you some goals, but also asks for you to make your own goals. Highly recommend to anyone who doesn't mind reading carefully, especially to people who are interested in being game masters. The writing isn't too flowery and isn't too sparse - it services the story very effectively alongside the simple (yet pleasing to look at) art and the excellent soundtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful text-based adventure paired with lovely pixel graphics in a fantastic frontier setting, where the monsters and wiilderness retaliates against too rapid human expansion.I would write a lengthy review but since this is so story-heavy, the only thing I want to say is that the writing is superb. If you want a game with a story you can immerse yourself in, this is perfect.

_childDocuments_.review: I normally don't manage to stick with text-based games for very long, but this this game plays a unique magic trick that had me deeply engaged with the story the whole way through. Even though the game is -on an extremely basic level- almost exclusively pointless descriptions in text form and tedious micromanagement, all of it feels so meaningful to me personally. So *real*.'The game never stops inviting you to reflect on the mechanics of the world and the happenings within it. You get to decide whether you see your mount (and by extension animals in general) as a dear friend or a barely-tamed monster. After travelling with it for a while, you are asked to consider what color it is. Whatever you choose, you will be provided with some history and superstition related to that breed of horse. This prevents you from abstracting away the experience of riding horse into pressing the 'I want to go here'-button. One night, you are prompted to share your thoughts about what you think the moon is. (A creature? A rock in space? An eye?) By forcing you to have an opinion about the world, you are made to feel like a part of it in a way I haven't seen done before.I can greatly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys getting absolutely lost in even the most minute details of a fantasy world, to anyone who enjoys piecing together a world's history and internal politics, and to anyone who enjoys a game that requires you to take notes - but kindly takes those notes for you.

_childDocuments_.review: The smallest choices have the strangest impacts. Roadwarden is an incredible visual novel. I just can't say more than that, because that's the soul of it. Anything else would be inadequate. It takes an interesting look at community, tribalism, colonialism, the effects of economic domination and systems of reliance.... but mostly it's about being a roadwarden. And that's mostly about not getting killed and eaten! Among other things! Your personal agency is literally unmatched. Your choices are more far reaching than you think, and little action is wasted for an inquisitive mind. If you like puzzles, politics, earning peoples' trust, uncovering secrets, and weighing your safety against exploring just ONE MORE dark tile on the map... you'll like this game. I LOVE this game. A couple of minor annoyances/ quirks:The 'save' menu is separate from the quicksave/quickloads visible from your main UI screen. That's a function of it being made in ren'py, so it's not exactly unexpected. It's just easy to miss during the course of regular play. If you want to take advantage of multiple save slots for exploring branching narratives (and you can save at literally ANY point of dialogue), hit escape and go to save. I would recommend NOT save scumming as much as possible for your first playthrough. The writing is hilarious, poignant, and unexpected. Just trust it and see where your actions take you. But yeah. Save files. They exist. Second, the muted colors can be a bit hard on the eyes. I wish this game had some alternative color schemes for reading, since there is a LOT of it, but it's beautiful and matches the artwork, giving everything a very "legends and myths" type feeling. Something about those sepia tones just make you think of a story, told so many times over with the details changing.. There are two font options, one a pixel font and the other a serif, though I found both a little hard to read at some points. You can get a good look at your options from the game trailer though, so you won't be surprised. Finally, you can make notes!!! IN GAME!!! And you will use it!! Or else!!! Type- er- write! Your thoughts into your journal for easy reference later, when you're trying to remember that person who so-and-so told you about... er.. at that place.. uhh...Listen. Just trust me. You're gonna need it.10/10 Penicillin shmenicillin. We don't need that, we've got healing potions!

_childDocuments_.review: A simple and beautiful game with a surprising amount of complexity! I loved the dynamics between the tribes and the characters in them! Above all though, this is a game about finding your own purpose and meaning in the struggle to survive and make a better world for yourself or others. For example, your character's religious outlook is entirely dependent on what you choose, but also what choices you make.  Different characters react differently based on the beliefs you have, which is so rare and cool for a game. For me I fell in love the land and the strange differences between it and our own. It was a lovely experience of difficult and meaning moral choices but above all I fell in love with is strange and surprisingly detailed little world. I am looking forward to what this dev does next!All in all heartily recommend if you like text based story RPGs at all, what a great experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Hi, if you've seen some of my other reviews you might be puzzled by this choice. Let me reassure you that this is worth every penny. Let me say stuff about the art direction/music first; it is unique, and I mean that with sincerity. It's got a clear goal of what the developer was trying to convey both visually but auditory as well. The music is top notch. I'm very happy to hear the developer's final update post included information to listen to it and credit the authors. The art while simple is comfy and while paints a picture also allows you to interpret or imagine it in a sense. The cozy hearth in the inn near the start vs the ruins you could sort of fix up. All dusty and covered in bugs. Not to mention what may come at night.The game operates on the simple text based adventure system I wish we had more of. This game is not just a throwback but a re-imagining of that genre. It has a plethora of options out the gate in different scenarios depending on your character background or skills or even kit. That bottle you didn't buy? Well because if you had it and some base alchemy knowledge you could make some useful potions. That fishing basket? You just got yourself a meal free of charge or some extra coin for no work or risk.The premise of the story is also full of moral consequences and physical consequences. Will you save the random man in the forest who's injured or ride along? Would you help the old lady and her sons at the lake? Will you clear out the goblins in a nearby ruin or leave them as they are too much for now? Perhaps you wish to seek a new faith or destroy that of other's in a crusade of a sense?After all you are here to report on the progress of the Island in 40 days (game has awesome tweaking feature; can set to 999 days). The status of settlements, their woes and fortunes, your own experiences as well. It has natives and they have their own faith like anyone else.I truly recommend you this game. It's simple yet makes you think, hard but in a fun way, interesting and cozy. Please make sure to review it as it really helps these solo devs/small teams. Good luck Warden.

_childDocuments_.review: I did pretty good on my first playthrough and survived to the end! You have 40 days to pull all of the loose threads you can find in the peninsula. _childDocuments_.review: is one of the most delightful world's I have ever had the esteemed pleasure of playing. It deserves a thousand compliments for its story, mysteries, adventure, world-building, intrigue, characters, and so much more. Playing as the titular role of Roadwarden, you are to explore the Northern Peninsula with the intentions of establishing trade relations with your home city of Hovlavan. You have 40 days to accomplish all you can and return home. A piece of the game I cannot get enough of is the fact  Everything about your character and your home town of Hovlavan is designed by you as you play the game, with NPCs asking you occasional questions of what it's like in the cities. This small detail is one of my favorite parts of the game because as you yourself learn more about this world and its system, you make a true and deep connection to your character. There are many missions to accomplish, and the game makes completing those missions so rewarding. Every quest is its own saga-length adventure, I can hardly recount all that I've accomplished in my 40 days. After this review I am certainly going to play the game again; while I know some of the world's secrets now, there are many quests I never finished in time. And I am eager to see a whole new side of the game by playing as a different class. Perhaps I will be a Mage this time around.I have never before written as long of a review, because I have never before had so much to say about a title. TLDR, It is simply one of the most intriguing and rewarding worlds I have ever experienced. And I'm so glad that there is enough mystery to play through it again.

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is a gamified Choose Your Own Adventure book, tarred and feathered with sepia and pixels. The old school aesthetic combined with RPG system mechanics lured me in, then I got hooked by the low fantasy worldbuilding that's beautifully complimented with weighty roleplaying consequences. You're placed in the boots of a freshly trained, and soon to be overworked, civil servant on horseback armed with an axe and a customer service oriented focus. The primary objective is to uncover why contact was lost with the previous Roadwarden, who was assigned to patrol a peninsula at the unmapped edges of the kingdom's frontier.Class choice significantly changes your available approaches to problem solving, and a 'personal quest' of sorts is selected to provide another narrative angle with its own benefits and pitfalls. There's 40 days on the clock to accomplish your goals before the region locks down for the winter, so avoid becoming like the bodied players in the negative reviews and manage your time wisely whilst roaming the untamed wilds. Don't hyper focus on a single region, act like the militant postal service you're equipped to be and macromanage your neighborhood route. Engage in local politics, accept Jesus Christ into your heart, condone necromancy, consider the social ramifications that misdemeanor and felony aren't in this fantasy lexicon yet, then die violently because a bunch of flesh eating gibbons induced a full body stroke with magical screams. Spoiling any of the characters or plot points would be a great injustice, but know that this meat's dripping with flavor. Just as a note-- using a fighter with no guides, I finished up everything my heart desired with a whole week remaining, and my play was definitely not super optimal 100% of the time.Definitely try to make the most out of your first go-- it might be because I'm not the typical visual novel player, but for me, this is one of those titles that can only truly be experienced once since prior game knowledge invalidates much of the mystery and intrigue. My only real complaint, and I'm gonna be really vague to not spoil anything, is that there are some potential forced sequences where the player may be given the impression that a particular plot point can only be resolved a certain way, however, the game's epilogue does allow the player autonomy to choose a different outcome as long as the proper conditions are met. There could have been a better way for the game's systems to account for a player's potential shifting motives but, ultimately, it isn't a huge deal. Just put some faith in the system.By the way, game is woke AF and would be on that Steam woke content blacklist if its moderators could read.

_childDocuments_.review: Video games have always been a huge part of my life. As I've gotten older I find it harder and harder to get totally absorbed by them like I did when I was a kid. I'll pick up games for a few hours and then get bored and never touch them again.Roadwarden is one of those rare titles I play once a year, maybe once every few years, that reignites my passion for video games and makes me feel like a kid again. Undertale, hyper light drifter, hollow knight, rimworld, disco elysium, celeste; roadwarden deserves to be mentioned in the same breath.The compelling but simple mechanics are a testament to the timeless genius of traditional D&D tabletop elements. The writing is inspired (good video game writing? what the ♥♥♥♥?), the sepia pixelated art-style is immediately impressive, and the OST is start-to-finish bangers.The main draw is that (much like DE) information about the world is doled out slowly and methodically with a few major twists and turns. At the beginning of the game the peninsula feels massive and unexplored, harboring a near infinite variety of strange beasts and magical oddities. As you progress the map quickly begins to feel smaller until every nook has been searched, every creature slain and every NPC dialogue option exhausted. The illusion of infinite depth cracks and you see the game for what it is.8-10 hours of near perfection for $10. For me the game is a 10 because anything that feels a bit unpolished only contributes to the intimate indie feeling and my only legitimate complaint is that there isn't more of it.

_childDocuments_.review: A short but awesome and well-written adventure that will keep you glued to the screen.Roadwarden creates a world that constantly makes you feel like you're just a member of it and not the classic overpowered hero of many other RPGs, and yet never punishes you for your mistakes so harshly that recovery is impossible. You can feel comfortable taking risks knowing that, even without reloading a previous save, you can always bounce back. You are also always rewarded for just being yourself. There is no "meta" way to win the game; do what you think is right for you or the character you're roleplaying and you will get somewhere interesting. Perhaps not where you planned, but no path you can take is dull or uninteresting. In addition, the game is chock full of choices that really only matter for the player: small gestures that reveal what kind of person you would be if you were thrust in that situation. How you greet others, or interact with your horse. These small choices don't carry consequences for the game's progression (usually), but make you feel more connected to the world.And the world is very peculiar and interesting. By focusing on such a small territory, the developers filled it to the brim with secrets and interesting facts to discover. At the end of the game, I discovered that I really cared about it and the people that lived there.I would heartily recommed Roadwarden to anyone looking for a relaxed and complex adventure that's a bit different from the usual. Such a lovely game.

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden does a brilliant job at evoking the immersion and beauty of text-based RPGs of ages past.The character customisation may be lacklustre, but it's in the dialogue and available actions that the freedom of role-playing truly shines!Worthy of mention is the worldbuilding, gorgeous and insightful stories that weave the lore of the world with its people and the actions you take.Ultimately, I found myself replaying Roadwarden and quick-saving often due to how enthralled I was with its storytelling and narrative design.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game. Lots of reading, so if you didn't learn to read, or are one of those whiny butts who writes "there's tooooo much reading, mommy!", then this is NOT the game for you. Don't buy the thing, then whine about it having too much reading in your negative review. There are plenty of games for brainless people on the market. This is not one of them.You play a road-warden, obviously. It is your job to try to keep the roads safe. You're trying to find-out what happened to your predecessor. There are plenty of fights and areas to explore. This is an old text-based game renewed for play on modern computers.

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed my first two playthroughs. In one, I played as a somewhat religious warrior who helped the peninsula but didn't fulfill some of my duties. In the other, I became a scholar turned hero, and embodied a successful roadwarden.Initially, I was concerned that the 40-day standard time limit is too short to ♥♥♥♥ around and find out, and that it would limit my exploration, but once I understood the game mechanics from my first playthrough, this wasn't an issue.If there were to be a sequel, I would suggest some minor improvements and additions, such as romance options, character portraits (retain this art style), and timed events. Overall, Roadwarden is a near-perfect game.Update: On my third playthrough as a scumbag wizard.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This is it, finally - a combination of the best of a novel and a game! And I only had to search for years! Something about Choice Of games always bugged me, maybe because they felt formulaic and young adult, like an editor was checking boxes on relationships, family issues, magic (always magic) and character growth. Those are all in Roadwarden, but here they feel natural, revealed by investigation and social interaction. Many fantasy novels read worse. This is the perfect mix of maturity and adventure, and it offers wonderful little tools to affect a melancholy-but-hopeful world. And all it requires is patience.Oh and pick a good name for your horse. It's a good horse.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Oddly specific audience I am reaching out to here, if reading books is tiring for you for whatever reason, but reading big strings of text in things like video games, comic books, or fanfiction is relaxing, boy howdy do I have the game for you. In all honesty, this game is a lot of text, but the dialogue is so interesting and steeped in that good almost hard to find in new stuff, truly classic fantasy genre aspect. And it has a lot of qualities unique to the game to balance it out! One of my all time favorite games, I find myself wanting to replay it over a long stretch of time again and really take my time with it. If you want to find an odd cozy comfort with an easy to identify with and understand fantasy setting, and do some good ol fashioned text rpg type gameplay, you will adore roadwarden.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden has a deep and beautiful world filled with very interesting and human characters.To start with the Cons:-The classes are fairly unbalanced with the best easily being -One particular character resource feels useless. Even if this isn't the case it's impossible for you to see the the pros of investing into it or the cons of ignoring it. It basically is like a trap for you to waste time and resources on.-A few dangerous encounters could be more telegraphed. There are some indicators of danger but certain encounters are deadly with very little warning and can sometimes feel unfair.-That's it. Pros: -Very deep and human characters with interesting goals, conflicts and relationships. Building connections feels rewarding whether you are creating enemies due to moral differences or forming allies for discounts and reinforcements.-A beautiful and immersive fantasy world that houses rich lore and fascinating creatures. You find yourself thrown into a world with many different cultures and practices and how each of these cultures deal with the horrors of the world, from necromancy, to spiritual guides or just pure optimism. Each area feels unique with how you can engage with them and how they will engage with you.-Meaningful and impactful choices, some of which with immediate ramifications. Almost every dialogue option feels important whether you are unraveling secrets, challenging someone's moral compass, or engaging with the world. Every choice you make or don't make, whether you lie or tell the truth, all accumulates to an ending unique to you. -Gorgeous soundtrack and art. The backgrounds give you a solid understanding of your environment while the text fills you in on the details. The ambiance and music fully immerse you into the game until you don't realise that hours have passed.-Interesting puzzles and engaging quests. The game is fantastic at giving you clues and pieces of a puzzle that can come from many different sources. The resolutions to questlines and main quests feel rewarding and earned. The choices you make and the knowledge you gather accumulates to whether you fail or succeed grand conflicts.Seriously, stop looking for a reason not to try the game there is a free demo and glowing reviews. The only issues I have are nitpicks. Classes feel unique and challenging encounters make the world seem hostile and dangerous. The real criticisms are in the positive reviews and unfortunately, there are too many people in the negative reviews who are scared of gay characters and powerful women.

_childDocuments_.review: A strange mix of death stranding set in the witcher world. You will be helping villages, learning their history, collecting new and sometimes magical gear, occasionally you will be fighting various creatures, as you seek to improve a ruthless land. If any of this sounds appealing to you, and you can stomach text based games (with visuals), get this game. You will not regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the Demo extensively, going through each of the three Class options and exploring what I could within the Demo's time limit of a few in-game Days. I had a lot of fun exploring the different options each Class brought to the game.Now that the full game has released, I decided to pick the Scribe Class, as it appeared fairly useful in the Demo. There are three difficulty settings, the easiest of which completely eliminates the full game's time limit of 40 in-game days. The hardest difficulty cuts this to 30. The UI is gorgeous, and the text can either be displayed as an old-school pixel font or a more elegant modern font. Everything is pretty intuitive, and it won't take more than a minute to navigate the entirety of the menus. The Journal option is SUPER in-depth, and a must for referencing names and places to NPCs. The ambient guitar music needs mentioning: it's not very repetitive, and it's actually quite soothing. You'll be hearing a lot of it, but with different tunes--occasionally some drums for battle, or bells/chimes for more pensive areas. It's a Choose Your Own Adventure game, with a lot of modern Quality of Life features (quick save/quick load, a fantastic repository of knowledge a few clicks away, an enormous Glossary for any lore-based terms, etc). I was told that this game has about 30 hours of gameplay, and I can believe it--especially if you play as the other two Classes, and the mechanics between the Mage, Scribe, and Fighter all vary greatly. I definitely recommend Roadwarden, especially for $10.EDIT: With some extra time to think about it, I wanted to add some things:There are some sections of the game where you will need to type out an answer to a prompt (I alluded to this feature at the end of my third paragraph). For example, you can ask an innkeeper for some gossip on characters you've met, or you may be in a strange room and the game will ask you to name what you look at. For the former, you can reference your Journal and look at Character names and type them into the prompt. For the latter, you'll need to use some detective skills and describe where in the room you'd like to look. It isn't always so simple: you can mention names to the innkeeper that aren't in your Journal yet that you only heard in passing, for example. The prompts want specific answers, but are relatively forgiving (a funny example is when a character asked me if I knew where they were from, and I had misspelled the name of their village... They corrected me, but said I was "close enough." I thought that was clever). In addition, I overlooked a key aspect of the game: the graphics themselves. It's all pixel art--a lot of greens, browns, yellows, greys... But the detail of the art is stunning. Coupled with the text, you can tell exactly what's going on in the landscape you see before you. It's also incredibly satisfying to reveal parts of the otherwise black map. There's a true sense of exploration here--neither you nor your character have any clue what you have gotten yourselves into, and it's nice to have some evidence of your progress after a particularly grueling day. There are also plenty of shortcuts you can create or discover, which will make your travels much more efficient: very important, if you're playing the normal or hard difficulty. This is kind of fun, so I'll come back to this when I keep finding important things to note. Still loving it! Try the demo!

My experience of this wilderness mirrored that of the main character, as I ventured into a scary and unknown land but slowly came to know it and was eventually confidently crossing even the most dangerous areas. I didn't find it quite as brutally difficult as I expected - in fact, most of the time my failures were only met with minor consequences that I could deal with relatively quickly, but I still greatly enjoyed it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like somebody took some of the best choose-your-own-adventure novels from my childhood (Lone Wolf) and made it into a Steam game. It works very, very well. _childDocuments_.review: Flipping excellent. Some of the best writing I've seen in this medium, scratches an itch I never knew I had. Only gripe is some strangely colloquial phrasing at times that feels at odds with the setting. Plus a very very slight bit of continuity error regarding a certain fisherman (though the narrative is generally excellent with this otherwise). _childDocuments_.review: Such a beautiful and immersive game. All elements - characters, writing, world-building, pacing, pixel art - are absolutely stunningly done. I played through twice fully with two different backgrounds to see the ways your choices change the gameplay and outcomes, then did a super quick run through with the third to do some final interactions I wanted, and I was really pleased with the way your decisions are altered in small ways from the decisions you make (and, importantly, the backgrounds offer lots of flavor changes and worldbuilding opportunities but no styles of play are limited by the choice). Super fun, absolutely worth the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I found this to be an enjoyable game. It's certainly not for everyone, the vast majority of gameplay is just reading and making choices. I find it hard to get into fantasy most of the time, but this had a decent enough mix of fantasy and reality that I found it mostly immersive. The overall plot was interesting and you get to interact with a lot of different characters with varying backgrounds and religions. It definitely scratched the "adventurer" itch. My personal ending was pretty much a downer across the board, even though I felt like I made pretty good decisions overall. Not sure how many different endings there are. In any case, I wouldn't change my choices and I wouldn't play through it again, but it was a lot of fun in that first play through.If you enjoy text-rich narrative games, you will want to check it out.

_childDocuments_.review: What an experience!I think in a way I played this game at the perfect moment in my life. As I tried to become a better DM in our weekly tabletop RPG campaign I was thinking about fictional worlds, the structure of stories, and how characters interact with each other and the player a lot lately. Then I played the fantastically written Roadwarden. A game that would best be described as a chimaera with the head of a visual novel, the body of an RPG, and the legs of a text adventure. In the beginning, the game lulled me with its beautifully atmospheric pixel art and its equally fitting melancholic music. But it wasn't long before I was fascinated by its world. A rough world, where survival isn't a given and death lurks around every corner. Where every little hamlet, every path through this land had to be painfully carved out of the wilderness and relentlessly protected against the wild beasts (one of which is humanity itself). But the aspect that really made me fall in love with this game was how it handled the player's involvement in this world and the web of relationships the player has to navigate. I never felt railroaded, always in control. There was no clear direction to take, not even a clear goal. And so it felt more like a real world, like a real life I was living. I was trying to improve things, yes. But ultimately I was just a small cog in this machine that will keep on running long after I finished the game. Every decision I made was mine. Every path I took belonged to me. Every friendship I made along the way was personal. In the end, there isn't the best way to play this game. Not the right decision to make. Not the correct path to take. Every player's story will differ, no outcome will be the same. It was my story and my story alone. Never has a story in a game felt so personal to me.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic homage to the old text-based adventures. The soundtrack is absolutely fantastic as well. There is a ton of replayability value as well- the different ways you can build your character, the many random encounters, and the way you can choose to handle quests can all make one playthrough completely different from another. Highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought the writing was overly verbose and difficult to tell what is important what isn't.Also difficult to gauge how much of a problem something could become or what the outcome might be of a certain situation.Combat isn't interesting. You might end up dying in one hit, you might end up losing nothing at all. For exaple: you charge at a bunch of goblins, kill one .... And then run away? I'm feeling fairly confident but apparently my character isn't. Then there's the why-part. Why am I doing this? You get to choose your own goal to some extent but it didn't quite motivate me to move on. You run into certain situations along the way which automatically turn into quests. Why? I guess it's because you're a roadwarden and you feel a need to stick your nose in everyone's business but why should I care?

It's more focused on resource management, but I feel like it's one of the only games in a while that made me break out a pencil and paper and write down things that I needed to remember when out patrolling the roads. It reminds me also of old school D&D. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write reviews, but this game is truly phenomenal. Harkening back to the classic "Quest for Glory", you choose an archetype (fighter, mage, or alchemist) and go about solving quests as the "Roadwarden", basically a sheriff/adventurer/messengerboy. "Where's the old roadwarden? What happened to this ruined city? Why are the other villages feuding? Oh, and by the way, figure out how to rope all of these settlements into our trade route."The gameplay is quite similar to a choose-your-own-adventure book with great narrative and flavorful descriptions. Thematic stringed soundtrack, RNG combat aided/hindered by your choice of inventory/armor/etc gives this game a plethora of branching options. And your dialogue choices feel alive/impactful. I've got to admit: during the epilogue, I was tearing up at some of the writing. Can't recommend the game enough. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is a narrative RPG about understanding and changing (or deciding not to change) a wilderness and its inhabitants. It pairs lovely writing, minimalist art and excellent music together with a really rich RPG system that is packed with branches and responsive characters, rather than dice rolls and statistics. The game almost feels at home alongside games like Outer Wilds or Her Story, because it emphasises information and player knowledge so strongly. I loved every moment with the game, and it's really worth dipping into.

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden has a few small frustrations, but with a generous system for saving and exploring all it has to offer, the game provides a world with life, people, history, and culture like no other. You will love, hate, feel betrayed, betray, and by your choices, your instincts, your perception, and your wits, you alone will determine if a noble land is marred forever by sin and regret, lies and betrayal, fear and ignorance, and greed and gluttony -- or if the road of hope is discovered and preserved,by the Roadwarden.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of Disco Elysium, give this game a try. Unlike Disco Elysium, it is almost entirely text-based, except for maps and your inventory, but it offers an equally compelling story, characters, and challenges. You might also enjoy Roadwarden if you like the Divinity: Original Sin, Pathfinder, and Pillars of Eternity games.A little bit about the game: You get to pick a class from three choices: fighter, mage, or scholar. I really enjoyed playing a scholar on my first playthrough. If you play on standard difficulty or higher, you have a limited number of days to complete your overarching mission, so the game also involves a lot of strategy regarding how you spend your time and resources (e.g., food, money, health).My first few hours into the game, I found myself frustrated that my character was low on friends, money, and food, but once I read some advice online about making a little money from  (both available very early on), I started to get a hang of things. I ended up getting really engrossed and completed the game in a couple of days. In the end, I felt happy with my character progression and the outcomes of my decisions. I think the game has a lot of replay potential, and I am sure I will pick it up again. It's well worth the $10.99 at full-price.

_childDocuments_.review: Very well written and immersive text-RPG. If you're like me you will find yourself caring for the land and its people and do everything in your your power develop it, clear and protect the roads, improving communications and trade. The atmosphere and writing is very good and discovering the different towns, their story, culture and inhabitants gave me the same feeling as reading a good fantasy novel as a teen. The game is visibly a labour of love and the universe is very well thought out. I definitely recommend it.
