_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden provides a core RPG experience and a very good one at that. You can already see the mechanics of the game by looking at videos or reading other reviews. Here I'll try to focus on what makes Roadwarden uniquely good.If you're the kind of person who maybe likes things like levelling up, skill trees, inventory management, party management, but understand that these things are not critical or core to what makes an RPG, then there's a good chance you will enjoy this game. The only other question is your tolerance for reading.Note that this game still has satisfying and good inventory management! It's neither the primary draw nor the secret sauce of the game...Roadwarden rewards the player for entering the role of a roadwarden managing the Nameless Peninsula. You are rewarded for paying attention and for making guesses and deductions based on in-world information.Most RPGs are so bad at setting up the world and making it feel rooted and consistent, that I've been conditioned to automatically do some casual level of meta-gaming. While playing Roadwarden, I unthinkingly looked up on the wiki where can I sell furs and metal for the most coin. But then I realized, that Roadwarden is a game where I don't need to do that. Because if I consider what I know about the settlements -- where hunters are, what kind of wildlife exists in that area, what is their access to metals -- then I can easily deduce how prices would vary.A lot of things are like that in Roadwarden -- you can make reasonable assumptions and not get screwed over. And this is largely due to the healthy amount of respect for consistency and richness of setting that this game has.Instead of feeling like you need to meta-game in order to not waste your time, you end up wanting to take responsibility for your decisions, because it's so rewarding to make them, even when things don't work out perfectly. It validates your preferences and your understanding of the world. This is the hallmark of a good, core RPG experience. Roadwarden looks modest but stands at a zenith in this regard.At the end of the game, I found myself tearing up and I was surprised I got that attached. That attachment was fostered by how the game managed to make the Nameless Peninsula come to life. From detailing humble flora, to detailing the weird mix of familiar and alien fauna; from describing the activities and life of each village, to creating complex interlocking interests and conflicts between those villages. I was sad my journey was over because this world had captivated my imagination.The game is not as flexible or as reactive to your decisions as it might seem. It does do some intelligent smoke and mirrors. It appears deeper by some amount of obfuscation of the numeric values behind the mechanics. But the balance is tastefully struck and appropriate for the kind of game that Roadwarden is.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: An acquired taste, Roadwarden is not going to be for everyone - and not just because it's text-based.It took a surprising amount of time for me to warm to this game - something I hadn't expected as an experienced RPGer who's played many a text-based RPG (including the old school MUDs from the 90s).--  --Roadwarden delivers what it promises on the tin, and offers up rich world-building, story-building and character-development, plus role-playing opportunities in spades.The text is often copious but, if you're a reader, it's nothing you can't get used to. (The ability to skim read will probably help a lot though).Once you find your groove, it's genuinely exciting and easy to immerse yourself in Roadwarden's world. There's no lack of things to do - wild creatures to vanquish, knowledge to discover, ages-old mysteries to solve, fish to trap, bargains to strike, and entire villages of people to win over. There's also so much to do that one playthrough is nowhere near enough to achieve everything you'll no doubt  to do once you really get started, so replay value is high.--  -- Unfortunately and unexpectedly, it took me quite a while to find my groove in this game. I trace this back to some of Roadwarden's decisions around gameplay and mechanics.For instance, your character has a maximum of 4 HP ('vitality'), which are depleted through combat, hard work or, strangely enough for a roadwarden, sleeping in the rough. This means just having one rough night's sleep is enough to have you teetering on the edge of death and unable to fight or work. You also spend quite a bit of time and money making sure your belly is always full since, if you're hungry, you suffer in-game penalties. This was probably my only real complaint about Roadwarden since the hunger mechanism added little to the story or the gaming experience. Instead, it took up far too much headspace than it was worth in terms of ensuring your character was always in good enough condition not to suffer debuffs.Also, unlike classic RPGs, the weapons, armor and combat systems aren't well-formed. You have one gambeson and one battle axe, and that's pretty much it for the whole game (unless you spring some coins on a crossbow to fight flying creatures). The foes you fight in the wild have no visible level or HP, so there's no way for you to make informed decisions about when to fight and when to flee. All combat in Roadwarden feels like swinging your axe in the dark and hoping for the best.All the above meant it took me about 15 in-game days to find a good balance and actually start enjoying everything that Roadwarden has to offer, which - admittedly - is a lot.Unfortunately, the slow start together with the game's time cap (40 in-game days on 'normal' difficulty) meant my game was suddenly and sadly cut short before I could see things satisfyingly play out. --  -- Roadwarden is not without its shortcomings, but it is a promising little game. I say 'promising' because I have yet to finish and experience it properly - and by all accounts it seems there is much more to experience.Will I come back to Roadwarden? Maybe. The game is good enough to make me want to come back. But its shortcomings are also just annoying enough for me to consider booting up a different game in my library instead.Rating: 7/10---** EDIT: I did end up coming back to Roadwarden, playing it on story mode the second time around - with no in-game time cap. This made a genuine difference in my enjoyment of the game and I'm glad I had another try at it. I'd highly recommend playing it this way. It's still worth noting that Roadwarden doesn't offer the 'classic' detailed mechanics of ye olde RPGs, so approach it with an open mind. **EDITED RATING: 7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. What a treasure. Roadwarden is a robust, text heavy adventure RPG unlike any I can recall having played. The closest recent experience I can compare it to would be Disco Elysium or Citizen Sleeper, though less like Disco primarily for the absence of an isometric UI, favoring instead a fairly simple renpy-esque design. The premise is fairly simple, and I won't give away too much as the world is a huge part of the beauty of this game (and discovering / exploring / drinking in that world): you are a kind of mixture of an adventurer, guard and mercenary, the titular Roadwarden. You have been sent to an untamed land in the north to fulfil the duties of a Roadwarden, namely to guard the rural portions of the Empire of this world which are too vast to be secured through patrols of the army. This world contains an abundance of dangerous flora and fauna, and while many may have familiar names they are in almost all ways uniquely redesigned in this world. You move through the world guided by simple static images accompanied by lovingly crafted robust writing that fills your mind with the details and images of this world. Immersive is the word that comes to mind most insistently for me when it comes to the flavor of this game, I truly felt like I was living in this world while I played this game. Choices range from complex to simple, mundane to fantastic, and from guaranteed to chancy (though your true odds are hidden except by discerning the context, randomness indicated only by the presence of an unclarified symbol of a six sided die). Choices are a driving feature of this game. With the time allotted in a standard session (though you can turn that time limit off) I don't think it's possible to do everything in one play through. That's even more the case because some choices are exclusive: there are a variety of decisions you make about your  character at the start, for instance, that heavily influence the nature of your playthrough. Further, almost anytime you meet someone new you can decide the verbal and non-verbal 'tone' of your interaction from five choices, in theory altering the initial character of your relationship with nearly anyone. While many of the 'quests' might be repeated between playthroughs, many have a variety of possible outcomes. If you love to feel like your choices matter, I feel you ought to be very satisfied with this game. I just finished my first playthrough and it was delightful. I really can't give more glowing praise to it, with only a couple of asterisks:First, it is text-heavy. Big time. If you aren't a reader, or if the quality of a game's writing isn't enough to make you enjoy a text-heavy experience, you may sadly need to take a pass on this one. Secondly, and this might be totally me specific but...the name of the studio, Moral Anxiety studios, couldn't be more accurate. Sometimes I don't have the mental fortitude to boot the game up because the immersion is so intense and the burden of so many of the choices so visceral that I just don't have the heart for it. Its a hard world in so many ways, and with things as they are in our own real world, heavy games are not always what I want to boot up. That said, the game is underscored heavily by a funny kind of optimism. The characters feel very believable. There are only a few (honestly, maybe just one) characters I might accuse of being evil; generally, they float around neutral in a way that feels very believable and authentic. Most people, in my experience, aren't good or evil in clear terms - they are just who they are, good and bad. Do with all that what you will.Long review summed: 9.5 / 10; a treasure for the right player who can look past a writing heavy UI.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a great story and amazing worldbuilding. The combination of the setting and interactions with characters really comes together to make you feel alone and out of your depth in a dangerous, alien place. It can be unforgiving at times, and you are often given hard choices that affect your survival and the fate of others, and you may be pushed to act recklessly due to lack of resources or time. I feel like I have to do another run to uncover some of the secrets I had to leave behind.Altogether it's a very rich, compelling story filled with desperation and loneliness, can't wait to see what's next for this dev.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a great text-based adventure game (though with enough of a pixeley art style and soundtrack to give the game some wonderful atmosphere). The forest peninsula you find yourself the warden of is dark and full of terrors. As one of the few people willing to venture beyond the walls of the region's small towns and hamlets, your every word and action carry significant weight for the denizens of the region. Assist the townsfolk by completing quests, follow their intrigues, uncover their secrets, but also earn their trust and reap the rewards. Combat is both difficult and dangerous, but creatures can often be outmaneuvered or outwitted with the right knowledge and preparation. In addition, the ability to save multiple files and load them freely prevents a great deal of frustration. That said, given that most of the combat encounters are pre-scripted rather than random, by the time you have upgraded your equipment and found yourself a few epic artifacts, you will no longer have a real need for them. Still, it feels nice growing stronger in such a hostile wilderness. The main story is engaging and compelling, and will likely take more than one run to fully experience. While the three different class types each offer unique gameplay, dialogue, and combat mechanics, there is not much more value in replaying the game once you have completed all of the major questlines. By the end of the game though, you can use the relationships you've developed to shape the future of the peninsula. Using your influence to open the region to the City's merchant guilds, looking after the various "best interests" of the townsfolk, or following your faith to cleanse your rivals and advance the power of certain groups over others. While the game leaves you wishing there was more, it is perhaps the mark of a good adventure that ends if only a little bit too soon. Quite possibly the best five bucks I've ever spent on a game, and if they ever release a DLC or sequel I would get it in a heartbeat.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I write this review because I really do believe that this game deserves way more exposure. Roadwarden is the definition of a hidden gem. A heavily narrative driven game, the atmosphere created by its amazing writing and a great soundtrack is extremely captivating. Decisions matter, build up, and intersect each other in so many ways. Additional plus that there's three classes you can play as that add unique choices and systems to the game which adds to its replayability. If the store page remotely interests you, try the demo out! Sold me completely. Strong 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I dont play many text based games, but I have played this one through twice now. What a beautiful, brutal, aching, and inspiring world this creator has made. The world building drew me in immediately and the strong character writing kept me going. I felt like all the characters had their own perspective and none were weighed down by out-dated gendered ideas. The women could be aggressive, evil, brutal. The men just as kind and emotional as anyone else. A truly beautiful story with an incredible soundtrack to back it up. Even the pixel art felt so in-tune with the aesthetic of the whole piece.A beautiful work of art.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game - austere and brutal, thematic and flexible in its mechanics and story design. Highly recommended for those who like a deep RPG experience. A few things for the Devs:- it would be helpful if names, dialogue, objects, and key words were highlighted in the text like place names are. As a skimmer, I often found myself missing key information - the lack of a hint system is quite punishing and took the steam out of the game for me. It doesn't need to be explicit. In an example, if I'm trying to get someone to trust me a line suggesting 'they might trust me if I offer them X' would be extremely helpful and make me feel I can make progress. If I'm to solve a puzzle I appreciate a clear view of the puzzle I need to solve. This systems presence could be an optional mode of the game for users less interested in a long term grind and more interested in exploring the wonderful story this game offers - the user entry "what do you look for" sections would benefit from a great deal more guidance, as I found the lack of steering really difficult to overcome and I ended up ignoring those sections, probably to the detriment of story opportunities- the lack of active quest logs with waypoints and instructions makes coming back to the game after a time away a real chore; reading back through all the logs is a big taskThanks!

_childDocuments_.review: Something rare and special. This game reminds one of the old "Choose your adventure" books, where disaster feels constantly at your door. _childDocuments_.review: I would give this game an easy 9/10Positives:Great price for the size of the game. A single playthrough in normal difficulty will take around 15-25 hours, and there is some level of replayability if you want to find other endings and with a different class.Amazing OST, it really fits the atmosphere and was very enjoyableIt can be very rewarding for the more observant players, as there will be some events or interactions where you can really mess up and lock yourself out of interesting storylines if you weren't paying attention.Active dev in the community forumA VERY wide diversity of endings, not just for the main character but for side characters, locations and storylines.Easily one of the best games I've ever played, I'll be sure to be on the lookout for games in this style or by this developer in the future.Negatives:You'll probably have to save-scum a bit at one point or another. Either you'll run into a big cat and lose all your life, hunger and armor or you'll make a trip somewhere only to realize that the trip was useless and you've lost half a day, or you'll fail a quest because now you can't get to were you neeeded to be in time. Without a bit of save-scumming your first playthrough will have some very annoying parts, and you'll probably have to play the game again to get a resolution to all the main storylines. Obviously save-scumming isn't the end of the world and it's a nice way to change the difficulty, but if you end up abusing it too much it really takes away a lot from the story.The diversity in the game can be a little excessive at times considering the setting. There are gay, lesbian and bisexuals individuals, a polyamorous couple and even a nonbinary person. If this were Cyberpunk 2077 or a game in a setting where that makes more sense then it won't break your suspension of disbelief, but in a game that has a very medieval setting it absolutely takes you out of the setting. Maybe if it were addressed directly or involved in the story, e.g. the main religion in the game opposes these beliefs but the pagans are accepting of them (so it becomes another plot point in the game) or vice versa, it would be less noticeable and wouldn't break the player's immersion, but as it stands it did end up doing that a lot. However, the way that diversity was added was the correct way. Instead of it being something that you immediately discover about a person (which can end up feeling like forced inclusivity with no purpose other than pandering), their diverse sexual preferences were usually something you'll only discover after talking to them for a bit, and the way it was mentioned was very natural and logical and did not feel forced. So maybe the setting wasn't the best for this kind of inclusivity and it could have been integrated into the story to make it more reasonable, but at least it never felt very forced, just a bit jarring at times.The pace falls a little bit halfway through the game and it occasionally feels like a little bit of a struggle to continue, but it picks back up. Or maybe I only felt that because I completed it in two sessions so I just got tired halfway through, who knows.Occasionally you will make decisions that seem very small but will actually completely affect the ending that you get, which can be a little unexpected. This one is less of a con and more of an in-between, as it leads to interesting and unexpected endings but can sometimes lock you out of desired endings simply because of a small decision that you made much earlier on.

_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing storybook game! Dive into a unique fantasy world whose engaging and nuanced characters encourage you to learn more about the world through dialogue and moral choices. You have to balance limited resources, money, favors and even personal appearance while travelling the roads of the land. Choose to fight and kill monsters, spare their lives to reduce their reprisals or even go hunting for loot in the unforgiving woods. All in all an amazing game that I enjoyed thoroughly. The story puts you in the place of a Roadwarden trying to bring about a new age to the countryside through the sponsoring and protection from "the big city" to the south. Pursue mysteries, help locals, be a violent jerk or a sensitive friend of the forest. If you like reading, fantasy, choice based rpgs, pixel art and some choice music you will love this game!

(also, there are several mechanics i'm taking note of as some of the objectives and setup for this game run somewhat parallel to a project of my own but besides that) I think this game is really fun, it has a lot of heart and it's clear the developers put in the time to make something challenging, engaging and immersive.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden feels like a cozy tabletop RPG session with one player (you!) and one very ambitious dungeon master. Placing players in the dusty boots of a Roadwarden, which is basically a hybrid park ranger/highway patrolman, the game lavishes you with rich descriptions of a living, dangerous world where survival is paramount and a single misstep can mean doom. Every choice feels weighty and important, and your decisions also go far in shaping the world in many unexpected ways. This game also provides one final stroke of brilliance by allowing your character to choose their motivations early on. With the railroading nature of most CRPG plots, this simple addition seems so obvious in hindsight but is usually entirely overlooked. If you're missing a tabletop group in your life, Roadwarden goes far in filling that gap. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

Fantastic sound design as well (both music and ambient effects) that pulls you in. I was continually surprised by the depth and quality of lore, story, and characters.  Writing is first-rate.  Encountered a couple of trivial bugs that did not detract from enjoyment at all. _childDocuments_.review: This game has amazing writing but falls flat when it comes to freedom to play the game how you want to play it; It's a fairly linear map progression and the order in which you encounter People/Beasts seems to be predetermined ruining the sense of an open world. In my almost 2 hours playing I created 3 characters both getting them to the 2nd crossroads hoping that there was some sort of randomness or sense of variety in the game, alas it was the same 3 runs with the very similar 3 dialogs with everyone you encounter and finding the same items in the same places. It seems the only "random" aspect of the game are the small moments where there are dice throws to determine outcome but even those are preset to be in certain areas and at certain times.I really came into this game wanting to love it and I did enjoy the writing but if you're looking for an open ended adventure with a sense of replay-ability and open-endedness this isn't the game for you. I'll be waiting for Adventure mode in Dwarf Fortress to come out and have a truly open world adventure, until then I'm getting a refund as I don't find this game's game play loop to be what I was hoping it would be as it presented to be  something close to D&D but it's too linear for that.

_childDocuments_.review: Some may say the text-based RPG genre is dead. Some would be wrong. Roadwarden is proof that, with a compelling story, immersive world, and endless choices, even a genre as old as the classic text-based adventure can be compelling. Of course, it has extensive help from the gorgeous pixel art graphics, which makes Roadwarden a treat to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This...is an  game.  As the description states, it's text-based; a lot of that is the sort of see-a-lot-of-text-and-select-a-choice you'll see in visual novels or choose your own adventure or dialogue choices in a standard RPG, but on top of that are exploration, combat rolls, and occasional text-entry.The main loop is a lot of travel and exploration trade and dealing with people and events.  When dealing with some things, the text prompt gets added - some towns and locations allow/force you to look for things based on text entry rather than choosing from a menu.  What you're looking for can be something visible in the little map shown on your screen (the bushes you can see over there), something that should obviously be present (a trader in the town you just reached), or something mentioned in a quest or dialogue.  That makes it harder to 'find' things than just noticing a new menu option appearing - so you have to pay attention!  There are even a few 'combat encounters' that can be drastically affected by a text entry reaction.The setting is... not grimdark, but on an obvious deathworld, where people can't just do what they want, and Nature actively fights back.  I wanted to type 'humanity', there, but it's not clear that you're actively  with humans, or even that your character is human - there are various mentions for various characters of fur, purple skin, or gills.  There's not a lot of description of  how alien the people of the world are, but it's made obvious it's an alien world and an alien people.So far I've been quite impressed with what I've seen of the people and the plot - there's not a lot that's just  to you, so you've got to  it.  The immediate impression you get of a character is  always correct; not everyone is as nice or as nasty as they immediately seem, and there are  floating around in the villages that you may not even find - though you'll certainly want to look.Villages and certain characters can be befriended or angered by your actions, which can affect the quests/jobs available to you, the price of goods, and the options available for interaction.  Items that are too expensive to afford at first may become far cheaper if you successfully befriend the shopkeeper, and quest rewards aren't necessarily just money or items.Quite enjoying this title so far- the questing and exploration and interactions are far more than I've come to expect from most implementations of the engine being used, and it's already been well worth the sticker price.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Well, as I play games based on what catches my eye I gave ROADWARDEN a try. This game is so well made i had to gave it a thumb up.This game is rich in terms of decisionmaking and characters complexity. I really felt the consequences of my choices. I think that's rare nowadays. It is worth to note that if you don't like reading you should not play this. The walls of text are just showing one after another which lets's your imagination do the work of GPU. The main and sub stories are not simple ones so you have to make hard decisions with little knowledge on a subject sometimes which is nice.  Worth to note that acoustic part is awesome in my opinion. I recommend this especially for those who wants something different than mainstream games. Really refreshing game to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Exceptionally written, beautifully crafted. I enjoyed the bits of medieval history and sociology that were incorporated into the story - such as two-phase sleep, which I've never seen incorporated into a video game story before. Roadwarden's world is so finely crafted that it gives you the impression it continues to exist outside of your observation of it. As you meet people, observe (and fight) monsters, and visit new places you'll slowly piece together how the little villages and societies of Roadwarden function. The thrill of that discovery is a feeling that persists through the entire game. It also has my favorite party-based exploration event since Mass Effect 2's suicide mission.

_childDocuments_.review: Its been hours since I completed my 3rd playthrough yet this game is still ALL I can think about. I am SO incredibly enamored and obsessed with Roadwarden, I love everything about it!!! The writing, worldbuilding, mechanics, art, soundtrack, meaningful choices... all perfectly tuned to create a deeply immersive experience that I desperately wish to relive again for the first time. _childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I completed my first playthrough of Roadwarden in around 12 hours, on the Normal difficulty, which has a time limit of 40 in-game days. Normally, games with time limits give me anxiety that makes it difficult to complete them. Roadwarden's time limit never gave me anxiety - it gave me a sense of purpose.You see, in most RPGs, it's sensible to snatch up every quest you can, pick at every loose thread, ask every character every question available at any given time. In Roadwarden, you are encouraged to and rewarded for prioritizing your goals - and the game leaves it up to you to decide what your goals really are. With only 40 days to explore the peninsula and meet its inhabitants, there is simply not enough time to do everything for everyone. It's a beautiful change of pace from the average RPG, and its world is masterfully presented through a combination of text and lush pixel art. If you like fantasy stories and/or visual novels, Roadwarden is a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had been on my radar for quite some time during it's development since the aesthetic of Roadwardens from Warhammer Fantasy always appealed to me. _childDocuments_.review: It's a very nice slow text based game. Fair warning though, it's very slow paced with little combat, with stats mostly being gained or lost from more menial things like getting a bad night's rest. Most time spent is you walking the outer forest paths to meet the villages and pass news between them. It's a very specific story for a specific audience, if the idea of just being a person walking around in the woods helping out any random people you see doesn't appeal to you then maybe skip this game. I've also often heard the setting being compared to the Witcher, particularly the books.For a review on the basic game mechanics, I'd say it's pretty solid as far as text based adventures go. The game very rarely asks you to input specific words, and most of the time the answers to those situations are pretty obvious if you're paying attention, with one exception being a certain spider. Otherwise the game generally presents you with a wide array of options that never felt too restrictive. The game also has 4(5 if playing as the mage) stats that change how events play out. As a general rule, being full on food and health helps you be strong, appearance will generally save you time because people will be more likely to give you/progress quests when you first meet them, and armor stops the other stats from going down as often. Just vaguely try to keep all the numbers up and you'll be fine. The game also has 3 classes, Warrior Mage and Scholar. The game recommends warrior at first, but they all have somewhat similar capabilities in general life. The warrior starts with better gear and has strength based abilities while at high health, the mage has a magic pool to use on stuff but has a few input issues which are annoying, and the scholar can gather potions and herbs and can read which comes in vaguely helpful at random times.The game has 3 difficulties, but I'd only recommend the hardest for challenge runs after you've beaten the game once. The other 2 mostly decide whether or not the day limit will be active, which is a bit of a point of contention. Personally, I like the idea of the 40 day limit because i'm a weird person who thinks that endings that don't answer all the questions are cool, but if you're not good at rpgs and tend to do things slowly, or want to see all the quests and not get any bad endings then that's what the easy mode is for.Oh, and this game has a lot of transcribed accents. I dinnae think it much a problem, but ye may ne care for it

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore this game. You can tell there's been a lot of love poured into it and as someone who usually struggles with holding attention while reading I must admit the writing is very engaging and keeps you intrigued at all times. The pixel art and the soundtrack are lovely and together with the interesting story form a truly deeply immersive and atmospheric experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is a text based attempt to make an RPG.While the interface and a world backstory is quite good, the other parts are not so much.I'd like to recommend it but every part of the game is spoiled in some way. E.G.:- The world setting is quite interesting, but it is filled out with characters that can not exist there at all. They're probably made just to meet the current US agenda. Which it terrible for RPG in general and especially for a text-based one.- Player is provided with two ways of progressing by collecting information, but those conflict with each other and both has a poor implementation. And that is core mechanics of the game.- There are a lot of choices, but only few of them has consequences.Other than that the core and an idea of the game was really good.It has a good visuals, different ambient sounds for locations, a nice simplified character representation and other small things. That is a shame something with such potential was spoiled that hard mostly by netflix editors.

_childDocuments_.review: The wall is still standing. There are no wolves around, no stench of blood. Good signs.	This should be the place I've been looking for. I was supposed to meet with a group of soldiers, but I hear no voices, no sounds of labor.	The gate is ajar, the camp isn't safe. It may keep out the goblins and pebblesrs, though not the beast folk, nor trolls. Night is drawing near.	Fara breathes heavily, she's had a long day.	I dismount her, my heavy boots hit the ground. Pain of the long ride catches up with me. I stretch out, bringing my back and legs some comfort. 	All I want now is a table , a decent chair, a nice mug of mead and some warm stew.	With any luck, my axe won't be needed here.	If this is a military encampment, it doesn't look the part. Plenty of wasted space, and the fire pit is cold.	Two soldiers are sitting at a table, they appear tired and disheartened. They look in different directions, paying no attention to one another. One of them is holding a cup.	As I approach, it takes them a few breaths to glance in my direction. The first soldier greets me with a wave of his hand. There are bags under his eyes, his beard is unkempt. Despite his simple shirt, he's wearing durable, decent boots.	A mace, with a head covered in iron hangs at his side, though he doesn't reach for it.	I look at the second solder, and just like me, she's wearing a gambeson. It fits her a bit loose, as if she took it off a corpse. Her head is shaven, perhaps protection from lice. Her eyes weary, yet kind. She smiles at me.	Considering the detachment was sent here half a year ago, these two certainly look the part. Though there should be more of them. Eight, I believe I was told. 	"It's nice to see an unarmed traveler in this forsaken ♥♥♥♥ hole, makes me just a tiny bit hopeful." The bearded man says in a strong, yet timid voice. "You'll be staying the night with us, I guess?"	"We're soldiers, he and I." adds the armored woman. Her posture switches from half asleep to relaxed.  "We'll do our best to keep the camp safe, if you were to take the first watch, it would be a huge help. Travelers ought to help each other, wouldn't you say?"	I think for a moment, to fully rest, I'd need a good nights sleep. Reluctantly I agree.	"Fantastic!" she rubs her hands together. "I don't remember the last time I had more than half a nights sleep. The hours before midnight should be the calmest. Just wake us up if anything happens".	The man flashes me a wide smile, "It's easy to wake us up, just yell." then takes a drink from his mug.	"I was hoping to meet with your sergeant, could we talk for a bit?"	The woman lets out a loud sigh, dusts off her gambeson, and steps towards me. She pays little attention to the sword at her side. 	"We most definitely can, you and I, though holding this rank is still somewhat new to me. Are you a messenger? Did you lose your mount?" Observing me with curiosity. "Or are you looking for help?"	"I'm your new roadwarden, my horse is tied up outside." I reply.	"Really?!" The solder in the shirt leans forward. "That explains how you arrived here in one piece, and all by yourself."	"Better bring your horse inside the palisade." adds the sergeant. "We have no hay, but I bet it dreams of dropping its saddle." A long pause. "I'm Tulia by the way." 	She reaches out her hand. "Haleth." I reply. 	Her grasp is confident, the shake is slight. "Just keep your horse away from the tent." She steps away. "We don't need to smell it's dung."	"Ah, there's one issue." The soldier in the shirt rises to his feet. "We've no tent to spare, you'll have to use a blanket or something." 	"I should get accustomed to sleeping on the ground anyway." I reply. 	I walk through the gate. Fara looks around and snorts anxiously.	Not many humans could ride a horse. She's not only taller than I am, she's also bulky, and as heavy as she's strong. I can get into the saddle within a single breath. Most people wouldn't know where to even begin. From every side, she's a wall of flesh.	Horses were brought to The Dragonwood from the conquest in the South. They can trot for a long time, though won't outrun some of the local monsters. My palfrey needs me to survive, though, without her, I too would be lost.  	She's my only companion here. I want her to feel at ease.	Fara takes a few steps towards me, scolding me with another snort. I scratch the bottom of her neck, with strength and confidence, just the way she likes it.	Humans see useful animals, and even pets, as monsters in disguise. Getting emotionally attached to them is believed to lead humans to their doom. 	I know horses need companionship.	I speak gently and lead her to the fire pit. Removing the saddle makes her nicker with relief. I take a couple of minuets to examine her back, just in case. While the riding equipment is not that heavy for such a strong animal, with enough time it starts to chafe. 	I wish she had something better to eat than this shabby grass. I should look for an inn.	I need to unpack.	I haven't brought that many things, and I lost one of the sacks while fleeing the Crimson Corps Eaters. Worst of all, I have no rope left, maybe the soldiers could spare one. Shouldn't cost more than a dragon bone.	Aside from the travel set, I own a few valuable possessions, essentials for my trade.	I spent my life's savings on decent combat equipment. A fine gambeson, an axe made of steel and a reliable crossbow with bolts.	I unpack and inspect my belongings. My water skin isn't pierced and the spare clothes are still here. Just in case, I take a look at my wooden bowl and mug, my cape, tinder box, bandages, food rations, knife... nothing special or too cumbersome.	From time to time my routine helps me avoid mistakes, this doesn't always make it any more exciting. 	I return to the soldiers, who are sitting at the table again. They are observing my horse and chatting between themselves. My stomach growls at the sight of them eating out of wooden bowls.	One more bowl was put at a previously unused end of the table. I can sit down on a tree log.	I join them and take a look at the meal. 	It is cold gruel, the meal eaten in times of hardship. This specific bowl is filled with water, hog millet, some strange looking cereals and blueberries.	Welcoming me with a meal, even a humble one, is beyond their duty. Soldiers live with and for their companions, constantly on the move from one part of the realm to another, making sacrifices to protect their group as they face dozens of hideous creatures. Their lives are filled with discipline, hardship and camaraderie.	Roadwardens, on the other hand, learn how to work by themselves. We seldom engage in open combat. Patrolling the same roads for years on end. We help the settlements stay in touch, maintain commerce, settle down, and forge friendships. When there are no laws to follow, we use our own judgment.	Different responsibilities, different lifestyles.	I eat quickly, not focusing on the taste, then speak with Tulia.	She looks focused and is choosing her words carefully. Looking away when gathering her thoughts.	"I'm afraid I can tell you less than I would like and less than I should." Nodding toward the other soldier. "As you can see, there's not a lot of us left. At the beginning of summer there were eight of us, including our previous sergeant. Five are dead, one has run away in tears."	"We're also strangers in this land." adds her companion.	I smile. "Any piece of information may help me do my job."	The man leans forward, his legs shake nervously. He sounds like a kid asking a bard to sing on more tale, tell a joke, or do a magic trick. Whatever it takes to escape from boredom. His untrimmed beard hides a much younger face than I originally thought. 10 of 10 so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden takes a fairly interesting premise and implements a mechanically competent game about it, but is fatally dragged down by wordlbuilding that's in practice fundamentally uninteresting and moderately unpleasant to inhabit.On a technical level, the game is impressive. If it weren't for the familiar save menu I would have no idea this was derived from a standard RPG engine, and its writing and art are really consistent with their tone and aesthetic. There were only a couple spots where the mechanics got in the way of the game, and I particularly praise Roadwarden for only having a couple examples of the classic RPG problem of selecting a reasonable prompt resulting in an insane course of action - no, when I said to make some space I did not mean you should blindly step back toward the growling you heard behind you.The only consistently bad mechanic were the bits where it asks you to manually query a text box. These were always a bit frustrating, frequently missed obvious potential inputs, and in a couple places were maddeningly obstructive. For some reason the big spider in front of the bandit camp has one of these, and it wouldn't accept any of the reasonable courses of action I tried - fight, look closer, go around, distract, nothing. No idea what the issue with that one is.Roadwarden also has a setting with a fairly interesting base premise. Medieval humanity, but the wilds are harsh and aggressive, full of beasts. If any settlement cuts too far into the woods, a tide of monsters will be roused to anger, and everyone gets their torso atomized by unicorns. Neat idea!The problem is in the execution of this - the world turns out to be basically the same as reality, except there's some magic around and everyone's kind of an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ [meaniepants]. On the worldbuilding side of things, it's just weird that there's no response to this new aspect. The cities have some form of walls around them, but nobody is trying to develop solutions or defenses to the monsters. There are no specialists who train to kill them, no movement promising to eradicate and tame the woods for good, nobody theorizing a way to mitigate this issue, no real exploration of the smattering of different opinions people have about humanity's relationship to the wilds. The more fatal problem is the second half - everyone in the game is kind of a shallow jerk. I made it through a ten-hour playthrough without finding a single character I was invested in. Nobody with big dreams, only a couple people that were nice to talk to. People charge a fortune for everything - the important secrets or services seriously require the majority of the cash in the game, you can probably buy like 1.5 of them, maybe two if you buy nothing else. Beyond selling, nobody's willing to tell you anything? People are so tight-lipped and standoffish it genuinely stretched my suspension of disbelief. Seriously? There's not a single person on this entire peninsula that will tell me what happened to that town, except for the one innkeeper that wants to charge the equivalent of two months of room and board for the info? Nobody mentioned the tribe that lives off to the east and keeps to themselves when I was asking about the major settlements of the area? It feels less like a realistic part of the setting and more like the developer reaching out from behind the scenes to gag the setting because it would be too easy otherwise.I ran out of time after uncovering what seems to be the main mysteries of the game, and just went home because there wasn't really a financial path forward and I didn't care about these people. Got a postgame report that the merchants guild decided not to expand north, every faction either died under a horde of undead or barely held on, and I felt nothing.I went to start another run, to see if I could figure out the grand mysteries of my predecessor on the secret island or awakening the spirit of the forest to cure a plague or figuring out what the deal with those bandits was or learning what happened to that town... but while I was selecting the difficulty for it I just stopped and took stock. Why bother? I don't actually care about any of it, really. I'm not invested, in any of these people or places or groups. Hell I'm not even invested in Leto's wellbeing, the game really feels like it should be a roguelike but the one time I died (killed from full health and armor in one hit without any real recourse, thanks for that by the way) the game just lets you restart that one encounter and continue on your way. The game claims to be about razor's-edge survival in the savage wilderness but the moment actual stakes rear their head it automatically savescums for you. The only real failure state is the time limit - the game would actually be much more engaging if it was as lethal as it claimed to be and reset the run when you died, letting you get a little better each time as you gradually uncover the mysteries of the peninsula and work toward a successful run.There's a critical lack of dynamism in the world here. The only group that wants to change things are the merchants that sent you north to scout, and you only talk to them, briefly, once. No people or factions with great dreams or aspirations, nobody that even wants to get along. I mean, get this - for most details about the civilization you come from to the South, y'know the only source of change in this setting, when you're asked about them you have a full range of options to essentially make up that bit of the setting on the spot. When the most important aspect of your setting is so nothing that its details and relationships to other elements can accommodate a full range of different and even contradictory options with no impact on the broader setting, that's... I don't even know what that is. Not a sign of interesting worldbuilding, that's for sure.Why would I want to keep playing a game that's just like real life but worse? Humans aren't like this in real life, the universal and inexplicably ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ [meaniepantsness] is a bigger obstacle than the monsters, and there's no aspect of the game that makes me curious or interested. For a fantasy game, I can't think of a more fundamental condemnation.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface this with by saying that I struggle to focus on reading for extended periods of time. That said; I have played this text-based adventure for hours at a time and hung on (almost) every second of it.Its such a fascinating world, and you can clearly see its inspirations in its sleeve. _childDocuments_.review: While I'm normally hesitant to get into text-based adventures, I thought this one was absolutely fantastic. The writing was engaging and the world felt deep and rich. All of the characters and communities felt real and distinct from each other, and the game gave a great sense of the deep history and complicated relationships within them. Add to boot, the art that is present in this game is excellentGameplay wise, it was a joy just to explore this world and see what challenges and rewards were around every corner. I liked that you really had to plant our your days and your tasks to try to get the most of it, and I loved how exploring and exploiting various parts of the games made other parts easier.Overall, the game is excellent. I would love to see a similar style of game but playing out over a much longer time period, so we can see the effects of our actions really change the world. Excited to see what's next from this developer!

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love this game. If you're looking for an extremely unique text based adventure with beautiful pixel art to match, this is the game you're looking for. Just finished my very first full play through as a mage, and I'm left wanting more. Every village is unique and interesting, every quest line is immersive and truly makes you feel as if you are in the shoes of the Roadwarden. My only criticism is that the text based search feature can often leave you confused as to what to do. I would love to see a sequel where you play as a different Roadwarden in the future. Thank you for reading.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid fan of fantasy, Roadwarden truly delivers, maybe not in the mainstream idea of your high fantasy story where you progress through the game until you fight or become a god.  Instead roadwarden’s world presents you a subtle yet realistic take on a wild and untamed Archipielago with characters struggling to survive and settle, each with interconnecting stories, motivations and a past for you to discover all while never stripping you from your own deductions until you discover the truth, or not. While simplistic and bare-bones as it is, Roadwarden sticks to its strengths and does them real good. To some it might seem just like a glorified choose your own story book. But damn it’s a good one. Truly incredible, really does make you feel like batman 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: What an addicting fun role-playing game! It's mostly text based, but choose your own adventure style has never been better. A lot of reading here, so if that's not your thing you might want to skip this one. The story is richly in-depth and gripping at times. The graphics, music and ambiance adds a lot of fluff and flavor to the game. The text is very descriptive and the choices you make actually matter and make a difference. This gem of a game kind of reminds me of the old solo role-playing adventure paperback books I used to play when I was younger. I used to really like the ones that you had to keep track of stuff on paper, like items and skills. This game also has that and your journal keeps track of everything, including quests, people and places etc.  I can tell there was a lot of work that was put into this game, and the journey is excellently crafted. I haven't got to the end of the game yet, but I have died a few times. A great adventure is to be had here! Have fun and enjoy the experience! Just writing this review makes me want to play it some more. I might start over and try a different type of class, not sure yet. 10/10 - Tell em' Large Marge sent ya! Hahahahaha!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I had no idea what to expect playing a game like this, but after putting more than 200 hours into Disco Elysium on the old Steam account I called mine before I decided to give it all up and become Golden Hat Mick, I was pretty confident Roadwarden would be a worthwhile journey in the early days of my new gaming identity. I was wrong — it was way better than merely worthwhile. It shattered those humble expectations, crushed them as if they were a fragile human shell in the hands of an enraged frightape.After five playthroughs and just over 80 hours, I've managed to uncover a good chunk of what this game has to offer, and I can confidently state that it's a world more gamers need to experience. Whatever is lacking in the graphical element is easily replaced by competent sound design and sufficient geography artwork to stay connected to the environment. This is largely a text-based experience, but presentation quality is superb, and I don't mind reading, especially prose as polished as Roadwarden's.Each of the major locations is unique, its characters memorable, and the impact you as the roadwarden can have on the final outcome is significant. You won't get far in your first investigation unless you're playing on the easiest setting, and if you're like me, you'll be eager to jump right back in and start anew regardless. Even now, after having finally finished a satisfying run that cleared my lengthy quest list, not everything went how I planned, and I forgot to tie up at least one loose end. And echoing thoughts of others, the ending narrative never feels quite as satisfying as it should.That's a small matter, however. Credit to Moral Anxiety Studios on a fantastic adventure. I hope for further content down the road, if not in Roadwarden, then in other creations. I'm a full believer in the talents of this small-but-promising studio, and I'll be following their progress closely. As for me, I don't think I can stop my visual novel momentum at this point. I've already got my eye on several other titles like this one, and I'll be mixing plenty of them in along whatever winding path that gaming takes me.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is essentially a text based rpg where you role play a roadwarden who naturally travels the roads of the land delivering messages, fighting mosnters, doing odd jobs, etc. This game has no real time combat, only dice rolls. I bring that up because for many people that may be a deal breaker. However, if you are ok with a completely text based game this is an amazing experience. Perhaps what I enjoy the most about roadwarden is that the world doesn't spell everything out for you. You're forced to pay attention to the information you gather from npc's or the world in order to understand what is going on and make your own inferences whether they be wrong or right. For the right person this results in an extremely immersive experience. Throughout the game you will travel the roads completing quests for the various villages and villagers which in turn increases their trust in you as their roadwarden. Once you get in good with a village/villager they may be willing to share more information about themselves or the world around you, not to mention they may toss a few draon bones your way. (money) Which you can use to upgrade your gear or maybe buy a room at a fancy inn for the night. basically what we have here is an old school rpg done right that has a very interesting world with many things to do and places to see. Its a very fun time and i have no complaints.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: The first couple hours were a bit slow and I thought about returning the game. But I'm glad I didn't because this is a gem. The most impressive thing is its tone - melancholy yet optimistic, exciting yet serene. It's just feels good playing this game. Beautiful, layered world in a simple yet deep package. At the end I felt a little sad, like the end of a wonderful journey and wonderful story. A pleasure to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fantastic adventure that is well written, thoughtful, and FUN. If you're a fan of choose your own adventure, or old school point and click adventures then this will definitely be one for you.Characters in the game are diverse, memorable, and well written. The quests range from simple to complex and even at the end I was finding hidden lore and loot. I was hooked from the beginning and scoured every nook and cranny I could find, yet still finished the game with only half the achievements. Already I'm tempted to play through again and make different choices to see what else I can uncover. All in all, it's a fun game for those who like to read, puzzle out things, and discover what the game has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hidden gem I hope heralds many more such games. The story is beautiful and haunting, your choices have immense depth and unexpected consequences, and the characters you meet feel like they actually live in this terrible world you find yourself in. There are no heroes, but maybe you can one person's life a little easier, to push back the seemingly inevitable entropy, if only for a little while.You'll have to manage not to starve to death first.Quick tip - this is heavily "old style" RPG of ye olden days, so have a notepad handy and take good notes.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This game's understated art style and music allow the audience's focus to settle onto the writing, which evocatively describes a harsh but intriguing world. Even more impressive is that unlike so many visual novels, ROADWARDEN is only very rarely overwritten and barely ever does lore dumps for the sake of lore dumps. Everything you learn about people, places or creatures does end up having a practical purpose in-game. Learning one village's backstory helps you make appropriate offerings to them when you first meet. Learning about the ecology of the setting's monsters helps you make better tactical decisions in combat. The game's RPG elements are also brilliant, and a welcome addition to the VN formula. There is a surprising diversity of builds or strategies to pursue, especially for such a mechanically light game.Roadwarden is a beautiful narrative game and many of its details and questions will linger in your mind for a long time after playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played very far, but I love it so much, already. There's so much *character* in the writing, and the orange/sepia graphics calls me back to my youth (I only wish there were an option to turn it green, in case I wanted more of an Apple IIe vibe than my old 286). Every NPC I've met was characterized well and the lore is very interesting. The world as portrayed is grimy and I'm here for it 100%. And the music! If you think you might like it, just get it. I don't think you'll regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: New Vegas but you get to be an actual trailblazer and help to tame the wilds. Old ruins are included. Although AFAIK you won't get a chance to screw everyone as royally as the Courier did at the Divide, for better or worse.The Witcher but more down-to-earth and less horny (except for one place).Death Stranding but with the actual people instead of basement-dwelling vtubers.Choice of Magic but with more graphics and a bit less replayability (argueable).Most importantly, its a role-playing game but with actual roles to play, world to immerse in and characters to care about. _childDocuments_.review: Very solid game, with a few caveats. After having completed Roadwarden on its middle "standard" difficulty, I'd highly recommend playing on easy/casual. Standard doesn't change much except add a 40 day time limit to your game, something I personally hated.Easy recommend if you're okay with reading a lot. Pixel art is gorgeous and goes great with the presentation, soundtrack is great though the limited track selection did start to grate towards the end of my playthrough. Very interesting world built entirely through dialogue in a way that feels natural.Really my only complaint is the time limit. It sucks, and I ran into it hard at the end of my playthrough, rushing through the last couple quests I wanted to complete and running out of time anyway. Time pressure in the game is otherwise almost non-existent and the time limit feels tacked on to add some kind of urgency to a game that is otherwise pretty relaxed. This feels strongly like a game that wants you to take your time and really dig into it, and the time limit feels so completely at odds with the rest of the game that I have to wonder why it was included. It genuinely feels like it ruined my playthrough and retroactively soured a lot of my time with the game, and if I'd had the option to turn it off in the final stretch I would have done so without a second thought.Despite this really long rant about what a pain the time limit is, I strongly recommend Roadwarden. Despite selling itself as a dark fantasy game it neatly dodges many of dark fantasy's pitfalls, presenting a world that, while harsh and unforgiving, has bright spots of humanity that are a real joy to explore and interact with.

_childDocuments_.review: "Roadwarden" is a narrative-driven RPG set in a post-apocalyptic world where the player takes on the role of a Roadwarden, a member of an organization tasked with protecting travelers and maintaining order on the roads. It’s a game that blends narrative-driven gameplay with a rich, immersive post-apocalyptic world. The game is reminiscent of classic text-driven games like "ZORK" and MUDs which are near and dear to many old gamer’s heart. Roadwarden successfully captures the spirit of those old-school games while also offering modern gaming features and mechanics.The game features a branching narrative with multiple endings, where the player's choices and actions have consequences on the story and the world around them. The game also has a unique combat system that blends turn-based and real-time elements, where the player must manage their resources and make strategic decisions in order to survive.One of the standout elements of "Roadwarden" is its immersive world-building. The game's post-apocalyptic setting is rich with lore and backstory, and the player is given the opportunity to explore and uncover the mysteries of this world through their interactions with characters and the environment. The game's art style and soundtrack also contribute to the immersive experience, creating a moody and atmospheric world that draws the player in.Another strength of "Roadwarden" is its emphasis on choice and consequence. The game presents the player with moral dilemmas and complex situations, where there is no clear right or wrong answer. The choices the player makes not only affect the outcome of the story but also impact the world and the characters around them. This creates a sense of agency and ownership over the player's experience, making each playthrough feel unique and personalized.The game's combat system is also noteworthy. It combines turn-based and real-time elements, creating a strategic and dynamic experience that requires the player to make quick decisions and adapt to changing circumstances. The game's resource management mechanics, such as limited ammunition and fuel, add an extra layer of challenge and tension to the combat encounters.However, there are also some potential drawbacks to "Roadwarden". The game's narrative-driven focus may not appeal to players who prefer more action-oriented games or those who prefer a more open-ended experience. Additionally, the game's reliance on player choice and consequence may also result in some players feeling overwhelmed or frustrated by the complexity of the decision-making process.In conclusion, "Roadwarden" is a fantastic computer game that successfully captures the spirit of the old classic text-driven games us old gamers enjoyed over 30 years ago while offering some modern gaming features and mechanics. The game's emphasis on player choice and consequence, its immersive post-apocalyptic world, and its innovative combat system make it a standout in the RPG genre. Fans of classic text-driven games and curious modern RPGs alike should definitely give "Roadwarden" a look.

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden sits at 'overwhelmingly positive', so this review represents the minority report. There's good here, but also plenty not-so-good, and the result is a middling story, middling characters, middling RPG, and a middling adventure that simply wastes too much time. The proper way to play this game is by spamming quicksave and refusing to accept any negative outcomes when gambling, fighting, conversing or traveling, which says something about the overall design. The game desperately needs quality-of-life improvements; for example, a magical camouflage tent that lets you sleep wherever you wish without decimating your health and giving you socially crippling morning breath. Truly, at some point the day/night travel suffering needs to stop. Within a few hours, the gameplay resembles a poor sod driving in endless circles on the i285 loop around Atlanta, going round and round desperately trying to eke a few new sentences from the same old locations and characters, reading the same descriptions and repeating the same interactions ad nauseam. (To be fair, there is a setting to disable the descriptions--use it.) When the game finally presented me with an exit, I took it, though my job wasn't finished (I was long past caring), and what proceeded was an admirably exhaustive summary of what subsequently happened from the point of my early retirement until the heat death of the universe. (I might have been skimming.)As to replay value, there are three character classes to choose from, but a bowling ball strike to the groin would be preferable to slogging through this yet one more time for a few minor differences. Let the credits roll and then hit uninstall.In summary, dear gamer, if we may assume that our self-destructive dopamine habits haven't yet rendered our attention span to that of a Mayfly, you would be better served by turning off the computer and heading to the library (or, if you must, the online Project Gutenberg). Seriously, go read a book instead: Richer plot, deeper characters, and blessedly free from endless backtracking, numbing repetition, and scrounging coins. The end, cue the heat death of the universe.

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is not a game, it's an e-book that's been dumped on Steam masquerading as a game.  As a visual/interactive novel, this doesn't feature any notable gameplay, it's just a lot of clicking through badly written dialogue that would never have been accepted or published in print, which poses the question, "How did something this badly written end up on Steam?".  When someone hoping to become an author is unable to get published in print, they spend $100 and dump their high school fan-fiction onto Steam, under the guise of a game.  This e-book was slapped together with the godawfully bad RenPy Visual Novel/E-Book construction kit, so just like no professional writing took place here, no professional game development took place either, it's just a product of filling out templates in the construction kit.This E-book features Choose-Your-Own-Adventure elements where you make some decisions that don't do anything to change the fact this is just an E-Book.  Nobody finished reading a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure book and said "Boy, what a great game I just played!".   Because E-books aren't games.  And neither is this.In fairness the developer did spend a bit more time with Ren'Py than your typical asset flipper fanfic writer does, as you get a few more of Ren'Pys very shallow pool of functionality available like a couple of meaningless stats and a meaningless inventory system (that could have just been tracked internally with the Ren'Py CYOA stuff going on), so at best one might be kind and compare this to a Steve Jackson Fighting Fantasy book, but then that would be insulting to Steve Jackson, he was successful. Visual novels/e-books are tedious at best... imagine the best novel you ever read, be that Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy or 2001: A Space Odyssey or Twilight (if you have terrible taste in literature), but then translate that to a format where the words dribble out and you have to click your mouse every time you wanted to read the next sentence, instead of just turning the pages. You'd think it was garbage.Now imagine that experience, but with much worse writing (because if these guys could write professionally, they'd be published authors and this would be on shelves in bookstores, and they wouldn't have to pay Valve $100 to self-publish this on Steam), and you have your average Steam e-book.From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the E-book is extremely low as a result.While there are options to change the resolution for the E-Book, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the E-Book, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for readers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Roadwarden has the ridiculous price of $11 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games (real games, not E-books).  This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.  Given you can get better quality books and comics for free online or from public libraries, or from bookstores for a fraction of the price of this "game".  Steam isn't a comic book store, neither is it Netflix, it's for games.  Your gaming rig is not a Kindle.  It's impossible for me to recommend things to PC gamers that aren't really games.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute gem of the game. Having finished my second play through (of at least 3 or 4 more to come) I can say that I have enjoyed the experience this game provides quite a significant amount more than most Triple-A titles released within the last 5 years minimum. (EXTREMELY light spoilers ahead for gameplay effects)The experience this game provides puts you directly into the mind and soul of an adventurer who has the odds stacked against them, yet prevails. Travel the lands, encountering nightmarish scenarios that batter and bruise you, and send you limping back to the nearest tavern or town, aching for a brew and some place just to be able to lay your weary head for a night. Your encounters only provide you with experience and skills that you can use in your next encounter with all of the secret bonuses you get to rolls as you play the game that come and feel very natural for the kind of person your character is.You also are able to gain tangible knowledge that not only affect secret chance-based rolls in the background, but open up entirely new scenarios between yourself and the creatures that prowl the mysterious Peninsula, as well as the people who inhabit it. Talk to the locals, figure out secrets and knowledge only certain people have, unravel mysteries and intrigue, slay/drive off the creatures who inhabit the land, or attempt to make your peace and subdue them through nonviolence; however you want your character to act you usually have that option.Roadwarden is a game meant to be played on the normal difficulty, which is under a time limit that will take, on average, 5-10 hours to complete. There *IS* a story-mode where the time limit is a non-factor and encounters are easier, but that takes away from the experience that is Roadwarden. Some people find the time limit to be too stressful or a detriment to the experience, but the reality is that the world and area that Roadwarden is set in are exactly that: Almost insurmountably stressful and dangerous. However, as you travel and make decisions, your choices have a tangible impact on the world around you, significantly reducing that stress and danger through one method, or another. Travel times between well known places decrease as you solve problems plaguing the land and make allies, traveling during certain weather conditions either benefit or harm your chances at certain actions or traveling, but you can reduce the impact that random events have on the world through your own actions.The game is not without flaw, of course, but they are so few and far between that they won't bother most people. To give an example, there are certain areas where you have to type out when looking for specific things or people, and searching for relevant information can be somewhat difficult or not entirely accurate, but if you spend the time to think critically, you should be able to figure it out. Another example being that solutions to a few certain problems are *quite* vague, but as long as you're open to exploring and leaving almost no stone unturned, you should figure them out eventually, and if need be, come back on your next play through with that knowledge already in hand and bust out these problems with little issue. These problems, as stated, don't come up often and don't detract from the overall excellent experience.Overall, Roadwarden lends itself well to avid readers and explorers. You will stumble, you will fail, but you will learn to prosper. Roadwarden lends itself, as well, to something important for a game so short: Replayability. Your first play through, you will likely mess up. You may not even get what could be considered a "Good Ending." As you learn from your first play through, however, if you're anything like me, you will become determined to change the outcome. You will play through again, and possibly more than a few more times, using your previous knowledge on how to handle problems and interact with the people of the North to quicken your goals and unravel more and more of the mystery that surrounds the entire peninsula.Verdict: 93/100

Best game i have played in a long while

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good little game that desperately needs another coat of polish. The core mechanics are quite good, the storytelling is mostly excellent, and the scope is pretty much perfect. I enjoyed my time with it, and I do recommend it. However. The translation/localization has many errors, some large enough to completely derail a scene or confuse what's actually going on. Sometimes it's not even a translation issue, just a piece of the description being completely left out. The game mechanics are also poorly explained, and I found myself getting screwed over in the beginning because of the lack of transparency. I was also quite saddened overall by the depressing tone of the story. You can do some good and make some friends, bu the game has sooo many more opportunities to be selfish or destructive. And casting a shadow over everything is the fact that you're working for a colonial hegemony that would like nothing more than to spread its rule over this rural land that you're now responsible for. Added to the number of rude, mean, cruel, and sometimes evil NPCs that populate the game, it does become hard to feel good about your overall impact. All that said, when the prose, characterizations, and storytelling isn't being hampered by lack of polish it is very absorbing. The characters are all distinct and fully fleshed, and the peninsula has a life all of its own. The world, monsters, religions, accents - so many things bring it to life. Put that on top of some very solid mechanics (once you understand them) and overall I am glad I played the game.

I still ended up making mistakes but it was a very enjoyable experience for both playthroughs.Spoilers:
