_childDocuments_.review: Great game if you love text based adventure/roleplay game. Tho I wish men and women didn't feel identical to men. There's a mechanic at some points in the game where you have to type what you're looking/asking for, great stuff In my opinion, there's just the right amount of it, enough to get accustomed to the gimmick but not too much of it that it becomes annoying, really gave me morrowind vibes.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent adventure RPG that will run you 10-15 hours on a first go.  Anyone who enjoys survival games and text heavy RPGs will find a lot to love in this game.You are a Roadwarden and your job is to not just survive, but thrive in the dangerous frontier filled with monsters and sparsely populated, highly agitated, utterly distrusting local settlements with all sorts of historical, cultural, and personal baggage.  And you will be operating under a time limit, harkening back to Fallout 1's well liked search for the Vault water chip replacement, and does so with just enough wiggle room that you should be able to pull it all off with 5-10 days to spare if you figure out how to do things well.  And even still, you won't be able to do everything so the directions of focus you choose will determine how far you make it down certain paths.  And there's likely outcomes that can be very different if you progress faster.As for the narrative, the story is presented excellently.  The writing is significant but not overwrought that it feels like it's overstaying and overstating things.  Quest design is fairly open ended and often most solutions you can think of are on the table which means you should think before you do something.  Just because you CAN doesn't mean you SHOULD.  And credit to the game, it does not care if you decide to abuse quick saves or not.  It's not worried about holding your feet to the fire.  Experiment to your heart's content and enjoy the twisting and weaving component of the game's structure.All in all, it's worth any RPG fan's attention.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing text based game. The story features many choices, options and solutions. There are many actors to side with or against. I have yet to finish the story but the way all settlements connect to the main story and each other is great. Highly recommend this game. Can't wait to play the next game by these developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic text-based RPG that hooks you in almost immediately with its mysteries and story line. I think something that doesn't get enough praise is how good the soundtrack is! It perfectly matches the vibe of what is happening and is just such a great pairing to an already superb fantasy world. But it's worth noting that this game is almost entirely based on reading and if that's not really your thing then you probably won't like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Engrossing. The game starts in motion, with nary a character creation screen, but just as rapidly as you learn about the world, you'll make choices that define your character. Like a good tabletop RPG, the world feels completely open, but presents you with enough tantalising threads to pull on that by the end, you'll be wondering about all the paths you didn't take and wishing you had just one more day.

_childDocuments_.review: i thought the game was excellent. it's a medieval/roman disco elysium fantasy clone. disco elysium's still better obviously but this is worth it even with the full $20 price tagjust cause a game has a lot of text doesn't mean it has a good story. sometimes the game goes on a little bit longer than it should, and perhaps the last 1/4 of the game could have used a bit more polishing. but generally speaking you feel like you're a small cog in a larger world that hums along with you but you still make an impact on itbut those are minor complaints. it doesn't have much replayability... but in my opinion that doesn't mean it's a bad game. some stories are meant to end.  not every game needs to be rimworld or dwarf fortress where you can play endlessly forever

_childDocuments_.review: I had no idea what I was getting into when I picked this up, but I'm so glad I did. I feel quite attached to this fictional piece of land.Great writing and world building. Gaining the trust of the characters you meet is difficult, and I kept having to weigh how a decision I made with one person or tribe would affect my relationship with another. No Skyrim style "do everything in one playthrough" questing here; your choices  close some doors and open some others. Hell, if you play on normal or restricted mode, even where you choose to rest will do that.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is a wonderfully written experience, that combines a sandbox experience on the Peninsula with a whole lot of stories. Memorable characters written with a lot of consideration and moral complexity are the heart of the story, if you want to call it that. The throughline, the goal you choose at the beginning gives a lot of form to the experience and can make it quite replayable, though some of the writing may become a bit less lively with the second reading.The music also deserves a lot of praise, lending itself perfectly to the ambient and giving the whole game a calm and relaxing feel, while helping with the general mood of the locations.In terms of gameplay roadwarden is unlike many modern video games, being a text based adventure with a low amount of dice rolls in certain situations. The most gameplay you get is by either choosing an option of answer to a situation or typing what you are looking/ asking for. Personally that was more than enough for me, though you should expect any type of grand modern RPG battles. The biggest strength is the writing and being able to enjoy that is maybe the most important part about enjoying the entire experience.There is a good argument to be made, that the game has a certain Witcheresque feel, especially in the writing of the characters and their morally complex lives and backstories, which have made me fall in love with multiple locations and people over the course of the game, truly wishing the best for their own journeys. Even minor characters get a lot of attention in little things and very much deserve a mention.Lastly the visuals. When I say, that the game looks beautiful, it evokes a lot of wrong ideas. Mostly you can see a small map of the area on your left, the text boxes in the middle and your stats on the right, all held in a sepia pixelart. No character gets a picture, instead relying on the narration, which works quite beautifully. The maps however are made with great love and attention to detail, while the general look gives place to a lot of the mood of the game.In short: This game is a great investment for anyone who enjoys a good read and a deep and engaging story and world, which is thought through and full of engaging characters. I personally enjoyed the hell out of it and will surely play another route to engage with some other parts of the story I could currently not reach.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been an absolutely fantastic surprise for me. I thought it looked like a cute little story-based game that I could play on my Steam Deck, in-between matches in other games, etc., but it turned out to be so much more.The storytelling, atmosphere, world-building, and just overall feel of this game will completely suck you in. I got so hooked I "finished" it straight through, putting in something like 20 hours in 2 days - even playing remotely during downtime at work. Not completely satisfied with my ending and decisions, I immediately jump back in and played through it again. I've now completed it 3 times, and I think I'm finally ready to put it down for awhile: though I'll probably feel the itch to play it some more soon.Overall the game is just really fun. You definitely get an immense sense that your decisions are important, not just to you as the player, but to the entire world that you are playing in. It feels like a much better (no shade to them, I love them) version of the Telltale games. The simplistic graphics really fit the world and game style perfectly, providing just enough to get a sense of things while allowing the player to fill in the world with their imagination. Like a book, but with just enough assistance to make sure you understand the descriptions (especially with directions) well.I'm in love with the universe/world of Roadwarden, and can't wait for the next thing from this developer. I'm even considering setting my next DND campaign here. It would be an excellent backdrop for one.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is the sort of game I have been looking for my entire life. It just scratches that 'itch' that other games can't seem to fully reach. The game itself is something similar to other Choose your own adventure games in a way, but the added art and music make it a truly wonderful experience. I've played plenty of games that are text based and have RPG esq vibes to them but this one was the only one that had me immersed for the entire journey. I haven't been able to finish this beauty of a game because I'm just too afraid for it to come to an end. The world seems to come alive as your journal is filled out with the common folks words of advice or thoughts. Your goals are tied with the people you talk to and the information they give you, though the information often feels somewhat vague this just makes the experience better as you find yourself sleuthing through what you think is real and important compared to what isn't. I wish there were more games like Roadwarden out there in the world and I truly believe that this Dev has created something truly amazing. I hope there is some sort of sequel or similar styled game that Moral Anxiety studios works on in the future but if Roadwarden was all they had in store, I would be more than content with this quality piece of work. Thank you guys for making such a lovely game!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic text adventure game with great writing that really sucked me in. While the focus of the game is definitely on the story, the survival mechanics are worked in really smoothly and help with immersion. Only real complaint I have is that I wish you could have a bit more control over the ending - I tried to do maximum good, but things seemed to backfire a bit arbitrarily in the ending slides. But, only a minor complaint and I recommend this game heartily!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent roleplay focused CRPG full of interesting characters. Definitely recommended for those who enjoy the less tactical elements of TTRPGs.The pixel art is lovely, and while I wished there was character art earlier in my playthrough, the writing was so evocative that I didn't miss it once the story sucked me in.I wish there was a little more to the story as I felt like I uncovered most of the mysteries in my first playthrough, making it less enticing to play through a second time. Despite this, because of how many choices one makes in the game that are incredibly impactful I will likely play through a second time.I feel like I played fairly efficiently and I still got 14 hours out of my first playthrough, so it's very much worth the price if you're worried about how long you'll get to play without replaying.

_childDocuments_.review:
A brave stranger putting your life on the line to make a difference in this grim fantasy world. While most people would never risk a solitary journey through the wilder parts of the land, you willingly accept the struggle. You guard travellers, connect isolated villages, support merchants, and repel attacking creatures, bandits, or even undead.

A powerful merchant guild has called on your services, sending you on a journey into the unknown planes of a mysterious peninsula in the hopes to expand the guild's influence even further.

Explore this world and gather as much information as possible to reveal the secrets surrounding the area. It's a dangerous task, but an equally respectable one.

Roadwarden is an illustrated text-based RPG that uses isometric pixel art and combines mechanics borrowed from RPGs, Visual Novels, adventure games, and interactive fiction, such as inventory puzzles, dialogue choices, character abilities and progression, hit points. simple survival mechanics. or quests restricted by in-game time.

name: Nebuchadnezzar
detailed_description: Nebuchadnezzar is a classic isometric city builder game inviting players to experience the mysterious history and culture of ancient Mesopotamia. In the campaign, players get to rule over influential historical cities filled with magnificent monuments. Discord Join the Nebuchadnezzar community on the official DIscord server. Share your cities, ideas, suggestions with other players and the developers. Gameplay Build your city while you oversee the manufacturing of different agriculture and goods for your population. Solve problems, prevent population loss, trade with other cities, handle foreign relationships, take care of varying population classes and employee types across various industries and services, and many more. Nebuchadnezzar’s gameplay is geared towards all types of players: from beginners of the genre to experienced strategists. Campaign Nebuchadnezzar’s main campaign contains more than a dozen historical missions covering the colonization of ancient lands to the conquest of Babylon by Persians in the 6th Century bc. Each mission summons a different time period in Ancient Mesopotamian history, providing comprehensive historical experience. Players must carry out tasks important to the specific time and place of each mission, including the construction of historical monuments. Monuments During the campaign players will not only build complex ancient monuments, but design them too. Nebuchadnezzar features an in-game monument editor giving players complete control over their buildings. From structural design to color scheme to final details: it’s in the hands of the player. Will you recreate history or make history? It’s up to you. Mods & Localization Nebuchadnezzar was created with mods and localization in mind. Expand your experience with the full support of mods from new buildings, new goods, production chains, and even new maps, missions, and campaigns. It is almost entirely moddable. Localizing mods will also not be a problem. You can create mods in multiple languages and/or add languages to existing ones. This applies to the base game as well.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're as old as I am, you may remember a series of games that came out in the late 90s and early 2000s. Caesar 3, Pharaoh, Zeus and Emperor were all very good city builder games made by Impressions and published by Sierra. Balanced around the "walker" mechanic where goods would be distributed a bit randomly as these delivery folks would turn randomly right or left at intersections to distribute goods. Made in a bright, colorful, cartoonish style, these games allowed the player to build some truly beautiful ancient cities while madly trying to keep all the plates spinning. Because if your goods didn't get delivered, people would move out, houses would degrade and the dreaded cascade failure was always in the back of the players' minds. Sadly, Impressions was forced to release too many of these games too closely together and they all largely played the same. Caesar 3 in 1998, Pharaoh in 1999, the expansion to Pharaoh in 2000, Zeus in 2000, it's expansion (Poseidon) in 2001 and Emperor in 2002. They flooded the very market they created and the last couple of games didn't sell that well. Impressions closed 2 years after the release of Emperor.Since then, a number of games have tried to recapture the magic of these games. Lethis, Hearthland, Children of the Nile and a few others all tried their own spin on this sub-genre of city builders but none really recaptured the magic of the originals. Until now, that is. Since Pharaoh was just re-released, now's a good time to look at Nebuchadnezzar (Neb) since it's succeeded where others have failed.For the sake of space, just a brief rundown of the mechanics. It's a city builder with supply chains. You build the supply chains (they're usually pretty simple) and focus on getting these goods to your residents via warehouses and markets. Walkers distribute the goods, keeping your people happy and eventually upgrading their housing. You'll also deal with illnesses, fires, appeasing the Gods, trade (this is a very large component in Neb), building monuments, city defense while making your city efficient and appealing.Really, he main difference between this and the old Impression's games is that walkers pathing isn't random in Neb. You assign the pathing route for your walkers and they do what you tell them to. This takes a bit of the randomness that you'd get in the Impressions' games (they used roadblocks eventually to do something similar) but you have enough going on with getting your goods efficiently moved around the map to not have to worry about the randomness. The early reviews of this game weren't exactly great. Features that should have been included weren't and the maps were far too small. Give serious props to the devs, who have continued to work on the game and the latest 1.4 patch dramatically expanded the size of the maps. The game doesn't feel like you're trying to cram as much into a tiny area as you can to meet the winning conditions. Now you can spread out and create something you're more proud of. They've also added combat (haven't experienced this yet), colorblind modes, walls, Gods, festivals, decorations, fire, crime, sickness, better information, taxes, wages and more. This game was released far, far too early. But unlike most games that are thrown out the door and abandoned, the devs have made Neb into a really great title. It's also been rock-solid for me with nary a bug in sight.So what I like about Neb are the same things I liked about Caesar 3 and the rest of them. The challenge of spinning plates to keep my populace happy. Meeting goals. Appeasing Gods. Building cool and colorful cities. What made the core of those games so great is here. So what don't I like?- Music is a little dull. It's period appropriate but not interesting or ear-catching.- Voices when you click on your little peeps are awful. Really awful. Good thing that I don't click on my peeps much and don't have to hear it. - You're going to approach most maps the same way, so you will end up doing the same thing in each scenario with only some differences (as game play mechanics are introduced or map difficulties are overcome).- The last, and most significant, issue for me is a winning condition called prestige. In essence, it forces to you trade with nearby cities in order to boost your "prestige score" which is often the last winning condition. It's a bad game play mechanic because it feels very artificial and unnecessary - why do we need to have "500 prestige" when I have 100k gold, all of the people to meet the winning conditions and a temple that would make the Egyptians jealous? It's just very annoying.But if you're looking for a city-builder experience and want to try to recapture the magic in those old Impressions' titles, look no further. I'm interested in trying the new Pharaoh remake but frankly I'm not in any hurry because Nebuchadnezzar is worthy of being ranked up there with the very best of the Impressions' classic games.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Although it definitely looks like one of the old Impressions Games, the main source of inspiration when it comes to the bulk of the  gameplay mechanics is clearly Anno. Which isn't to say it's a bad game - in fact, I think it's excellent - it's just that you need to have your expectations tempered when trying this game out. If you come at it with the expectation to scratch your Impressions Games itch, it's going to leave you wanting, and it's going to seem either simplistic (in parts) or overly complex (in parts).Since the focus is shifted from providing your peoples with amenities (in the form of entertainment, religion or cultural buildings) it it has to be placed on something else, and in this case the focus is almost exclusively in the . That's the real meat and potatoes of this game: building up your production chain and making sure your markets are stocked up with the necessary goods your houses require to level up. The logistical challenge of providing resources from one end of the map to the other is the real game, actually leveling up your houses is almost an afterthought since you don't have to provide them with , just delivering  is enough. This production-chain-management core is good, really good, if you're into that sort of thing. You need to handle all sorts of facets, including but not limited to: making sure your buildings are in range of each other, making sure you have enough warehouse space for both resources and goods, make sure your markets have a good path laid out (which you have to manually place), make sure that your resource buildings produce enough of their resource to keep your workshop constantly stocked etc. The math is fairly clear and straightforward, and the game has a nice overview where you can see exactly how much of something you're producing, and how much of it your current population required. With a little bit of simple math, you can plan out your city well in advance. If, on the other hand, you expect the walkers to just figure stuff out by themselves (f.ex. in Caesar a farm will automatically stock the closest granary that accepts that food and a market supplier will automatically pick up food at the closest granary that has that foodstuff available) while you try to build your city so that you can maximize coverage through smart path layout, this isn't quite the game for you. The city you build looks a little lifeless and same-y when you're done because of the aforementioned lack of amenity buildings. Kinda every block of houses ends up looking the same since there's almost no variety to building  city versus building  city.Monuments are clearly inspired by Pharaoh/Zeus/Emperor and they're a nice addition to the game, but in the end it's still more of the same: make sure you build your resource buildings, workshops, warehouses and caravan houses in such a way that the monument receives all the resources and goods it needs to be completed. It's not bad, but it plays the exact same as building a city except the end result is a nice looking pyramid or whatever. All in all, though, I think if you look at this game as if it's an Anno clone, you'll end up having a lot more fun with it than if you expect it to be something it's not.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar could bring you back to the 90s when Caesar and Pharaoh, and some other city building games, were something new for the first PC gamer generation. Yes, we spent quite some time on those games:-) This game could warm up your heart with some nostalgia but a good alternative for the younger generation too. But this one, while looks like a city builder, not exactly a city builder, it is more like a lovechild of a city builder and factorio/dyson sphere. Creating supply and production chains, and then deliver each consumer good to the doorstep of the houses require some patience and planning.Now let’s take a peek on the details:I really don’t remember when was the last time when I saw such flawless gameplay in a game, around its release time. The developers clearly cared a lot about this game. No pathing errors, citizens doing their job properly… I'm not saying that this game doesn't have any bugs at all, but during my 24h gameplay I did not find any. It is actually a nice feeling after my previously played new release where i got overwhelmed by different, game breaking mechanisms multiple times, just in a few hours. High five to passionate developers:-)The campaign and the missions felt very easy at the beginning. That changed on mission 5 when the “tutorial” finished. Suddenly it started to be really hard. New buildings, citizen types and resources are introduced with every single mission so Nebuchadnezzar stays interesting and refreshing while playing the new maps. The difficulty went up significantly by the increasing population and prestige requirements on each part of the campaign. After some, a good pre planning of your city was essential to qualify for the requirements of the completion.You can build your own world wonder. That is during the gameplay, not in some editor. Set up the construction site and once the building materials are flowing in just build it up from the selectable building objects and in any color you want.Starting each campaign mission from zero felt a bit boring until I progressed to a more complex city where the new buildings or resources were already required. There is an advanced start for the missions, but because of the map size a proper city development is required if you want to fulfill the requirements, so it is much easier when started with a clear map.There is only one campaign and nothing else. The scenarios menu has some promise for extra content later, but a custom game mode would be more than essential for these kinds of games in 2021.Not encountered ANY bugs + deep, complex city building and resource management mechanisms. This game is worth playing if you love the genre.Then check out my short, 12mins long video(no ads, not monetized, hobby channel):Perfection time: ~40h+, this could depend heavily on how much time you spend with creating your own monument or just by trying to build better cities. Since 1.2 the game has some challenging achievements, and as the game feels quite unbalanced now, even on easy difficulty, those are quite hard and time consuming.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Ouff, this is a tough one.See, on one hand i admire the energy they put into shaping this game as an attempt to make it a great city building title.It takes inspiration from Pharao and other "Impression" Games of that time.But thats basically it, an inspired attempt.Basic things like crime and fire, typical social aspects, were only implemented far later.And even with those basic mechanics its still far behind the standard of the games you know in this genre.There is no military branch, no defenses, let alone city walls.One of the iconic features, the temples that you can build the way you want, dont serve any purpose besides giving a good look and "prestige points".They now, more than a year later, are getting to the point where they will fix that flaw and implement gods and festivals.And yet and again, even with that, its still just barely at the same level of these 20+ year old games that made it far better.All Nebuchadnezzar does, is getting me into the mood to shut it down and instead play Emperor or Caesar.They were far superior, in both sandbox/scenario and campaign, in features, mechanics and depth.The only thing Nebuchadnezzar manages to do better, is providing modern resolutions and UI.But even the presentation of the city is lacking.The only people you see moving are your carriers. You are not seeing people in buildings, or on courts, there arent any leisure buildings that have an animation going on when they become active.You know, like Caesar having large buildings like schools, the forum etc, that had little people sitting there and doing things or artists doing their craft?You wont see these details here although it technically should be more advanced.Nebuchadnezzar has a hard time catching up with a genre standard from more than two decades ago and thats just embarrassing in a way.I am still somewhat ok with buying it for the campaign, even though the story presentation is lacking and there isnt enough depth to it (you cant for example choose a military or economic campaign as in caesar).But only because it was on sale and only because it received post-launch support.My hope now is, that they will drastically improve the game further and add proper diplomacy and military.Right now there isnt much to do after you beat the campaign.The scenarios dont receive any options to tweak your experience with or gain more depth.Load up Emperor Rise of the Middle Kingdom and you will find that scenarios give you plenty to do besides just building and puzzleing.It also has some weird issues.Loading up the game takes several minutes (yeah really) on high end specs. It should basically just be demanding on the RAM, yet loading it up takes so freaking long that people voiced that issue on the forum.Other than that i noticed that they scrapped some songs that were present in the beta and were actually really good, only to be replaced with some generic music.Only an occasional track manages to catch the theme and i wished they brought back the beta songs.Nebuchadnezzar is a somewhat ok-ish city builder, but not only far behind the genre standard but also other current iterations like Anno 1800.In that sense the only positive thing i could say about it is the theme they picked as its underrepresented and i love it.Besides that?Lacking, far too lacking.Certainly lacking too much to recommend it at full price.If its at around 13€, sure, worth a look.And maybe it will someday form into a good city builder.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Very sadly, I ended up uninstalling and requesting a refund. There is the base of a great game here, but unfortunately it's just not yet ready. Their is far too much content missing to be considered a full release. Chiefly their is only a single campaign of a dozen missions, with half of them being tutorial missions.No military.No religion.No entertainment.No crime.No taxes or upkeep.No building fires.No building collapses.No natural disasters.Small maps.It isn't all bad. They allow you to specify hauler paths giving you control over the distribution of goods, however it adds a significant amount of micromanagement as you must specify a path for every single good, at every single market.This game's primary focus is more a logistics puzzle game than anything else. You have to figure out how to set up all the production chains in a very limited amount of space and get it distributed to all the citizens.If that was the goal, that's fine, but the developers made a big error in making their game so heavily similar to the Impression Games titles for which in reality there is very little in common.

_childDocuments_.review: I think many people reading this review will fondly remember the old Impressions Games titles (Caesar III, Pharaoh).  Nebuchadnezzar is very much a spiritual successor, but with some excellent quality of life changes for today--like global employment, a robust warehouse/caravan system, and even a growing Steam Workshop presence.  It does my heart good to see the team continuing to push out some of the community's most-wanted features: gods, entertainment, disease, fire, crime, and now the upcoming warfare update.  I have no doubt that this game will become the quintessential experience for anyone looking to relieve late-90s city builders.

Its fairly simplistic and besides just moving things between warehouses and some requests.  There isn't anything that feels rewarding when I complete the tasks or missions. _childDocuments_.review: I used to play a lot of Pharaoh and Zeus as a kid.I discovered Nebuchadnezzar and Sargon DLC in 2023 when I really needed something new to take a break from multiplayer games I also play but got tired of, I have already finished both campaigns and I really liked this game and in my opinion this game is much better than Pharaoh because of additional features I will mention below (but I also understand some people may actually dislike the game for them).Pros:+ Workforce is global so you do not have to worry that much about placing workers's houses+ You set up merchant routes manually so they really go where you want them to go+ You use caravans to transfers goods between warehouses on long distance so production feels faster because the building worker has shorter routes to follow and can carry more resources+ 3 types of fully customizable monuments - missions provide you with a template ones but you can build your own and building something new every time is really fun (pyramids are just boring ziggurats and in addition to ziggurat you can also build a palace and hanging gardens depending on a mission you play or construct them all in a freeplay mode)+ There are many gods from different pantheons to worship and they provide you with different kind of bonuses - you can switch them freely to suit your current needs (only the one god who is a city patron is unchangeable), new gods are discovered by starting a trade with another city+ Festivals are present but happen less often so you do not have to remember about them all time+ Multiple missions in Sargon DLC happen on the same map, so you can develop your cities longer but also have to plan ahead their developmentCons: (well, mostly a wishlist of things to update)- Campaings feel a little too short, even with Sargon DLC- I have a feeling that maps are too small because at the end of almost every mission there was barely any free space left- Gods' bonuses could be even more impactful- Sometimes when deleting roads you have to reconfirm caravans route- Battles should receive some additional love like cavalry/chariots bonus vs infantry - now we have only flanking damege bonus- I understand you cannot produce ivory but importing wood every mission quickly gets annoying because you cannot cut down these palms growing on the map yourself... there is no lumberjack building in gameBut still this is a really good and enjoyable game for all Mesopotamia and city-building game lovers!

_childDocuments_.review: This game copy-pasting every single mechanic from "Pharaoh and Cleopatra" and to be honest, at the moment they have implemented less than half of the content from the reference game. For example here is the list of features you won't find here:- Military activity (weaponsmith, army management, hostile encounters)- Taxes- Religion and events related to gods- Crime- EntertainmentI believe that one day Nebuchadnezzar will finish his task of copying "Pharaoh and Cleopatra", but now I would not recommend buying this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar is a glorious strategy game, heavily inspired by Pharaoh, Caesar and likewise old city builder games. And I must say, I was skeptical at first, as I've already seen failed attempts at bringing those games back to their full glory, I was very surprised to see Nebuchadnezzar truly becoming spiritual successor of those.Now, there are some things that may affect your opinion about this title, depending on how much you compare it to its over 20 years old competitors. As of patch 1.3, there are for example no military aspects in the game, which I don't consider as some crucial aspect affecting my review, but it's a valid concern that you may find more content in original games. Personally I don't attempt to compare it as a clone, but standalone game, and as a standalone game inspired by Pharaoh and alike, the game is truly a very satisfying experience and I'm glad that I managed to grab it in Humble Bundle, which was a steal.In comparison with Pharaoh or Ceasar, Nebuchadnezzar is much simpler game. For example, you no longer have to worry much about distance from houses to work places, as your citizens apparently can teleport at work right away. House-planning aspect was also simplified, as you no longer need to min-max roads and exact placement just to ensure that your bazaar workers manage to give food to everybody. At the same time you still have to take into account the usual mess, whether that will be production buildings, storage, transportation, delivery and everything in-between. However, since everything is vastly toned down, the game should also be a satisfying experience for more casual players, rather than being constantly pressured about supply chains.I really liked the campaign, which very similar to Pharaoh, guides us through history of ancient Mesopotamia. There are like 13 missions total, which took me more or less 45 hours total taking into account some slacking off, and that's plenty. Every following mission features some new mechanic, production chain, or additional logic which needs to be implemented in order to finish it. It was pretty satisfying to finish whole of it.What else I can say, if you liked Pharaoh, Ceasar, or similar games, Nebuchadnezzar will definitely be along your alley. If you expect from it die-hard experience, you might get disappointed, but even that is configurable with selection of difficulty, so I'd say you should be good to go. For people that somehow skipped those marvelous city builders released more than 20 years ago, I'd still recommend this title if you enjoy city builders in general, and you're covered in case you'd still want more afterwards.I can heavily recommend this title. Maybe it's not a masterpiece that keeps me awake at night, but it's a very solid production that I had a lot of fun with, as can be seen with the amount of hours clocked. As a mid-to-hardcore strategy fan, I'm satisfied.---If you liked my review, you can find more of them on  and on my .

_childDocuments_.review: The game needs significant work to be compared to Caesar II and Pharaoh. Lots of mechanics like stockpiling are not enabled making trading/accumulation very hard. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a step up from the old Sierra city-building series, but at the same time greatly differs in playstyle. There is a much greater emphasis on logistics, which can be good or bad depending on how micromanage-y you like your citybuilders to be.I found the game to be relatively unforgiving, especially on the later missions. A little inefficiency can spell doom for your city, which means that building optimally is almost always the only option you have. Particularly when risks can and will still trigger negative events; even when you flood the city with copious city watch posts and firehouses, making sure that the risk levels are very close to 0, thieves and strikes still happen regardless. This isn't good especially when thieves literally empty whole warehouses without warning, potentially causing a cascading failure of your city due to unmet housing demands.Ultimately, I found myself building cities that are more or less the same. City block of peasants, city block of middle-class, city block of rich around a big temple dedicated to reduced upper class consumption. Each city ended up being a cluster of three small cities, each with its own wealth class. Blocks were uniform, essentially following the same floor plan as the game punishes you for deviating from optimal patterns. It's a sterile experience towards the end of the game.In summary, I'd suggest this as a very mild recommend. It's a flawed experience, but it does satisfy the itch of playing something more than the old citybuilders.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game with much potential, yet it fails in many aspects, getting VERY BORING after fews days.First, the good: aesthetics are great, nice details, pretty HUD, music ok.Then the bad: > Amount of non-essential weekly updates constantly breaking mods, turning saving games unusable. Steam updates are inevitable, so it would be cool if updates were scheduled or if most popular mods were added to the game as optional settings.> One key feature that many old games had was roadblocks, they were used to keep workers inside certain route. It was specially useful to keep guards, firemen, healers inside that route.This game doesn't have this feature, and you can't set a route to those workers neither, so you gotta keep adding more and more firemen and you still getting fires because they keep wandering around instead of going to places at increasing risk. Same applies for healers, you can only have ONE healer per healer building, so you need plenty of real estate to add 5 of those buildings in different spots of your city close to the houses and only hope they will care about it.> Also, in old games, the brick roads increased speed of those foot workers, I guess this game does not have that. So brick roads are only vanity, which is historically inaccurate. We didn't develop roads because they were pretty, but because we got faster with a flat surface to transport people and goods around, comparing with bumpy muddy roads.> The lack of citizens walking around makes the city look sterile and dull, at some point it will look like a huge lockdown with only essential workers on it. It takes out the life and soul of ancient cities, as they were essentially pedestrians. > No people visiting monuments, no one using the parks, no guards walking over the city walls. City is sterile as it gets. > Houses get "riskier" to fire and diseases right after they upgrade, because now they "lack" essential products to keep that upgrade, and you don't have an option to hold that upgrade until they have enough of those products served to that house and then allow new residents.That means you get a massive fluctuation of residents coming and going from this yo-yo effect of houses upgrading/downgrading sharply, plus the fires and diseases you get. Very annoying.At some point, the game starts to get very uninteresting after so much babysitting, I won't be playing again.I won't even bother to buy the expansion.Suggestions:> Instead of getting market workers doing routes and houses getting downgraded because they didn't get the last bread, add citizens to the game and make them go by foot to the nearest market instead of expecting it getting doordashed. Caesar IV had this feature. So instead of adding 3 markets close to each other to have enough workers to deliver goods and set opposite routes different merchants of same product to make sure all houses will be evenly supplied, we could just build markets close to houses and make sure they will be supplied properly.> High unemployment rates should affect happiness and to be compensated with events, festivals and amusement, where the player needs to spend bread or money. There's no real penalty for high unemployment.> Add floods, wild animals that kill people, natural disasters, plagues destroying crops, anything to make game more interesting! It could be random or consequence of an angry god. Nature in this game is way too tame and sterile, crazy boring.> Make construction of canals around noble homes increase appeal, and make it essential to be able to have gardens around, water was luxury back then and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon used several canals and pools. Make the use of water more than just agricultural!TL;DR: This is a logistics game pretending to be a city builder, the constant babysitting takes the joy away as you spend hours fixing butterfly-effect events that could be prevented if game had better mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty disappointing. You're not building a city, you're building a silent collection of buildings. There are no people walking around, going about their lives, there is no ambient noise or feeling that this city of yours is actually lived in, and though on the surface it might look like one of the old Pharoah/Caesar style games, it's just a lifeless clone.Remember how in the older city building games you could literally feel your city? How you could click on any of the people living in it, who would be happy to tell their thoughts? How you were constantly listening to the background noise of the city itself? The exchange of money and goods, laughter, music, pottery breaking, drinks being poured? How it was full of little details that made your city actually FEEL like a city, and that these details only grew the larger and more complex that city got?Well from what I can tell, there's none of that here. The only time people walk around is when they have a specific job to do. They don't say anything, there's no ambient noise, there's no citizens walking around the residential districts doing their jobs. It's just buildings. Buildings that sit there and look pretty, and eerily absent of any form of life or occupation. The only time you see anyone in your city is when there's something a worker needs to do - like take resources from a production facility to a warehouse, or plant seeds for crops. You can even see it in the screenshots. The cities you build look pretty, but are completely empty. This isn't the next Impressions Games' City Builder. It could be, but right now it isn't. It's just an imitation of one, a city-building skin stretched over a bare-bones skeleton with no meat.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a citybuilder in the same vein as the Impression titles (ie Pharaoh, Emperor, Zeus, Caesar) - give this a skip. There is no risk of hazards, invasions, taxes, crime. The only thing you need to manage is food and resources and making stuff to keep your citizens happy. I feel like they put a lot of effort in to the monument building aspect of the game and it just isnt fun. Too few missions. Only thirteen or so. None of them particularly endearing or challenging. The game also has no soul. Unlike the Impression titles that have these epic storylines, there is no narrator and the opening texts are just some boring factoids about Mesopotamia. In fact I have to say the script is terrible. All in all, it feels like the creators gave up half way on this game and released it. It doesn't feel complete.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick review of Version 1.1 before 1.2 hits: I'm a longtime city builder fan. I've spent most of the last few years playing Anno games, although I played Caesar 3 and Zeus back in the day. Taking GamerZakh's advice and buying the game last week, I am finding Nebuchadnezzar to be a very fun and compelling game, heavily focused on logistics. In that respect, it is similar to the Anno franchise, but without the multi-island overhead and enemy AI that I find to be overwhelming in the late game. Nebuchadnezzar is much more relaxing, with great music and a nice aesthetic, making it easy to admire your city and ponder the puzzle in front of you. I'm looking forward to the Version 1.2 events adding more character to my cities, even if it might make the game a little looser than I'm currently enjoying. There have been some complaints here about the lack of armies, but personally I don't miss them. As far as I'm concerned, no city builder has done a great job with armies. However, if the developers are working on adding them, I hope they take their time. I'm willing to pay for DLC from this point.

_childDocuments_.review: A nice comeback to the city building genre. It's not a strict Sierra games clone, but a slightly refreshed approach. The small size of the maps is the main difficulty here. The game has been given regular updates and the devs seem to be listening to the community, so I believe there's plenty of new content coming.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: It is a puzzle-like city-building game where you start by constructing simple houses, farms, and bakeries. Then you supply the houses through markets so they get upgraded and fit more people. Then you build villas, ceramic workshops, brickworks, breweries, etc, and supply them with clay, barley, and more. Then you build residences, copper workshops, libraries, administrators' buildings, supply them with copper, ceramics, papyrus, etc etc etc, all the way to lawyers' offices and observatoriesYes, it is precisely what you are looking for. A bit heavier on the logistic side of things thoughNot really. Not overly easy though, you still have to pay attention to supply chains if you don't want to see a mass exodus from your cityIt's of high quality in every aspect. The graphics is pretty and readable, the UI is your friend and the sound is good. However, certain game mechanics could be more impactfulPlaying Nebuchadnezzar feels like navigating a beautifully illustrated children's history book, with a decent actual game behind it. Although no book would showcase the vital importance of a fresh water source for a cityMission design in the main campaign is rather meh. You are expanding your city to a specific size and then proceeding to a next mission, which mirrors the previous one with a larger goal size and additional buildings available. It's more like exteeeeeeended tutorialAdditionally, the game primarily revolves around logistics, with the social and political aspects of managing an ancient city taking a back seat. I missed the edicts, laws, and happiness mechanics, and so might youIt is a solid  game, well-crafted but lacking in content. Still recommended for anyone who likes city-building It's slightly better with the DLC, but the fun part is still Sandbox

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the old isometric city builders such as Caesar III or Pharaoh, I was really looking forward to this resurrection of once great game genre. Knowing that a team of just two people were behind this, my expectations were not high. The game, however, is something else. At first glance, it really looks and feels like those isometric games. The graphics is genuinely great (and by that I also mean the architecture, style of buildings etc.), the music is great (although the occasional piano does seem a lil' out of place here). It doesn’t play like that, though: the maps are very restrictive by terrain and size, and you’ll be very much struggling for every square you can get. There is almost no freedom to build as the requirements to complete a mission are harsh as they are. This is a very deterministic game – you build what you have to build and once it is built, it stays that way. Citizens, once set up, also distribute via that route. This is great addition as I often struggled in the old games when people started distributing on another pathway. However, it all feels more like a logistics puzzle than a city-building game, I can’t get much joy by playing it.+ graphics, style, architecture, looks+ music, ambience+ attempt at an old isometric city-builder+ setting up of distribution routes+ very detailed history lessons- maps are too small- absence of random events, such as fire, crime, etc.- people move so fast at even the slowest setting, which is quite disturbing to my tastes- no army, no city defenses- too few house levels and the related amenities for their development- very restrictive and limited overallEDIT after completing the game: the last three misssions offer somewhat bigger maps, so this improves the gameplay a lot, though the previous things still apply.EDIT as of 21 January 2022, Patch 1.2, which brings risks of fire, crime, disease and riots.The newly added risks make the game slightly more difficult, though you can mitigate the risks by setting lower taxes and higher wages (apart from the obvious construction of fire stations, guard posts, healers and hospitals).+ the most important improvement of this patch might seem miniscule at first, but helps a huge deal in your city layout: you can now select whether a particular caravan is to load or drop their goods in a warehouse, instead of having a warehouse purely either for loading or for dropping a particular type of goods – this means you can now have just one storage for both incoming and outbound goods of the same type.. something which wasn't possible before!+ you can now increase/decrease the rates of wages and taxes+ newly added scenarios with huge maps.. these maps let you properly build a big city... and don't feel like a logistical puzzle anymore (as is the case with most of the campaign)+ there is more coming in the next patch (gods, religion, festivals), so I must give a thumb up for the devs' love for the game and for the new additions to come

_childDocuments_.review: If you played the Impressions Games (Caesar III, Pharaoh, Zeus, Emperor) and liked that kind of resource management sim, you will know what to expect. While not 100% the same, this game is its own take on that style of game. If you haven't played those games, then know that this is a city builder but it is not like SimCity. It is much closer to Stronghold. It is quite mirco-heavy. You will need to manage production chains, import/export goods, make your various classes of houses get those goods from markets, in order to sustain your pop. Building a city is hard. You can easily screw up your logistical arrangement and watch a whole supply chain fall apart. You will now know how the pandemic screwed up real life supply chains so badly.  Maybe this sounds insane. But, a lot of quality of life features, like a chart that just tells you how much you make of what and how much you consume of it, makes this game very noob friendly. Also, unlike SimCity, building a big, sprawling city is hard. It's an engaging challenge that requires careful planning. It turns out ancient city build is not so much a drag and drop experience. And in this way you really get a sense for the life of your city. Each worker, each market, each fisherman, better reflects an eco-system, an ecology you have come to know, love, and understand in an intricate way. I love it for that reason most of all; it is my own mechanical work of art and a look at a kind of visible labor system so often hidden by our modern world.

_childDocuments_.review: Pharaoh and Emperor Rise of the Middle Kingdom nostalgia galore. Improves several game systems from those games, and provides a very enjoyable experience.There's no combat, religion, entertainment, fire & crime, but it makes up with a more complicated tech tree, 3 classes of citizens and a few new mechanics. I especially liked the caravans, the docks and how the missions were challenging in how you had to approach them (relying on certain imports, which you unlocked after getting more reputation). The art is great and the music is catchy (although limited in number of tracks).The downside was that classes are interdependent, and one slight mistake of getting in the red on money and being low on basic food/pottery will cause a domino effect to bring the whole city down. This makes it challenging, but I felt the lack of the "disable specific industry" that I remember from the Sierra city builders that this burrows from.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for March 2022. If you are interested in the game and it's before April 5th, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A challenging resource manager.There are a lot of games where players take control of a city and have to build it up, generate resources and there are few wrong moves.  You just keep following the whims of the people and avoid making obvious mistakes.  Nebuchadnezzar isn’t that.  While a lot of the game is resource management, this game feels more challenging and often feels like it’s on the edge of a knife.  A wrong move may have a cascading effect destroying your entire city, rather than just being inefficient.Players will learn how to avoid these wrong moves over time, but a large amount of it is micromanagement of your resources.  If you have too much of A or Not enough of B, suddenly some buildings might regress, but then that will also cause you to have fewer workers, which means even fewer resources, and before long everything is at a standstill.   It’s an interesting but challenging proposition. Pick this up if you’re interested in a more challenging city-builder.  If you played Pharaoh or Caesar this is very similar to that, and the graphics are good, but those are also twenty-year-old titles so I’m not sure how many people there are that are familiar with those titles.  God, I’m dating myself on those references. If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: I recently tried Pharaoh, remembering how I enjoyed Caesar 3 when I was younger, but was immediately turned off by the dated graphics and poor UI (by modern standards).  The recently released Pharaoh remake has poor reviews, so where was I to turn for this style of game?Nebuchadnezzar is the modernized version of Pharaoh that I was looking for.  It follows the story of ancient Mesopotamia, where you must build larger cities and more impressive monuments to reach successively more difficult objectives across many missions.The graphics are simple, but easy on the eyes.  The UI has been updated with all the modern goodness I wanted.  You can scroll with WASD, speed and slow the game both with buttons on the UI and with hotkeys, pause with a press of the spacebar, all the standard features we have come to expect from modern games.  This while keeping the spirit and charm of its predecessors.Also, your service buildings allow you to specify what route their workers will take, meaning that unlike previous games you don't have to build in any special patterns to cope with randomized routes occasionally leaving some of your buildings without service.Exactly what I was looking for, this is where to find the best spiritual successor to Pharaoh.

_childDocuments_.review: It isn't Pharaoh 2 and that's completely fine, because this game goes a slightly different direction in terms of gameplay. It's much closer to Dyson Sphere Program, where you optimize your output to try and pump out the most optimal amount of goods with often limited space and trying to get certain goods because your mission goal is largely responsible for what you build ie. working class houses need water at level 2, but villas of the upper class don't need water at level 2. It's more a production chain builder and city builder than it is a city simulation, which I think is what people expected when they saw this. But there are a fair amount of buildings (62) that keep the game fresh through its relatively grindy campaign. Unfortunately no RNG that ♥♥♥♥♥ you over also means that once you've built something it will last and work from the first cycle as is. At that point your only real need is money to not fail the mission, but trading makes earning that very trivial.What it also could improve on is the feedback. Like having a very quick animation and a more satisfying sound when demolishing or putting things down or hitting certain buttons on the UI would definitely improve the experience. There's also the the messages about workers leaving, which can be very annoying. Warehouses can only load or unload caravans, but not both (might make it too easy). The editor also seems a bit clunky with no brush sizes or procedural generated tree brushes.It's overall a good game. It's just not a sequel to Pharaoh 2, which apparently people kept hoping for this was for some reason.

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant take on the city builder. Plays a lot how I remember especially Emperor: Rise of the middle kingdom and the Caesar series, but with modern high resolution graphics and user interface.You build simple houses, livestock farms, wheat farms and bakeries. Then supply the houses with the goods via markets, and they can upgrade to fit more people. Rinse repeat with a sprinkle of (good) headache to get the watering canals working, a lot of manual setup of warehouse goods and transport between said warehouses, and route planning for market workers. There is also a neat trade system with other cities.I am just enjoying the puzzle piece setup of the cities on easy mode so far, and are about 7 missions into the campaign, with no rush. _childDocuments_.review: Since its release Nebuchadnezzar  has been quickly progressing towards becoming a proper successor to the Impressions Games city-builders of the 1990s and in some ways has already significantly improved upon the genre. The game is still in development, but it has already seen a series of fundamental changes over the course of only a year and is likely to see more. It is worth buying in its current state, but wanting to wait for the full game is fair.  Unlike Pharaoh, Caesar III, and Emperor:Rise of the Middle Kingdom,  Nebuchadnezzar is being developed post-release by small studio. Released in early 2021, it finished the year with the additions of fire, crime, disease, religion, festivals, some voice acting, and several reworks. As of early 2022 the game does not have features of those old games like military, politics, culture, and in general still lacks a lot of polish. The game is still in need of more voice acting, sounds, and animations to match the quality of those old games. However, the regularity of updates suggests that there is little reason to doubt that some of these missing features will be added as the games development progresses. This game may even see expansions and be a framework for other city building games about other largely unexplored historical eras if it is successful. Nebuchadnezzar is still having features added, but in some ways has improved upon Impressions Games city builders. The most noticeable change is the change to how walkers work. Walkers bring resources, manpower and infrastructure to buildings that they pass by and in the old games the only control the player had over them was how they built their roads. Impressions Game’s cities were designed around the pathing of walkers, but in Nebuchadnezzar the player has complete control over the pathing of their walkers. This gives the player many more opportunities to optimize and customize their cities. Other great features include,  customized monuments, three classes to manage, mod support via Steam, non-campaign maps, Steam achievements, multiple crops with one farm, control over how much labor each building can access, better detailed graphs/charts to manage your city, and more. Nebuchadnezzar is a must-have if you are a fan of the old Impressions Games city builders and probably the best game to buy if you want an entry into the genre of historical city builders where you upgrade your city by providing consumer goods and services. Hopefully this game results in a revival of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Many of us loved the Impressions ancient-time building sims. Building a pyramid in Pharoh, a large temple in Zeus, or a Colosseum in Caesar 3 was great fun. Now at least three games took this blueprint and try to make a modern game with it. There is  Builders of Egypt (demo already available), there is Pharaoh: A New Era (planned for 2021) and there is Nebuchadnezzar. And maybe some more I don't know.So, what about Nebuchadnezzar? It is a city builder with a focus on the economy. Build houses, and new settlers come running the same second, then build some production buildings to keep them happy. Don't forget that every building needs to be connected to a road, those lazy bums will not walk one meter across grass. They also don't like to walk long distances, so build your (pre-)industrial buildings close together. Lots of micro-management is required to keep your population happy and to finish the missions. Apart from managing the economy, you also have to build monuments with surplus ressources.So, is it a masterpiece? Nope, I don't think so. Micro-managing an ancient economy is nice, but there is not too much else to do. Ancient city builder. A nice warm-up for Pharaoh: A New Era or Builders of Egypt.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good, and propose an unusual focus on logistics.At this moment, fire/sickness/crime are included, as well as commerce; and is fairly balanced right now (Sept 2021).The team behind the game delivers regular updates, so I bet the game will be even better in a few months.I advise you to ignore all reviews from the first half of 2021, as people were moaning about things that are now fixed, or released:_Random events are implemented, and will be complemented in a future update_The constraints of the small maps is actually part of the game difficulty: you have to plan your city well_People having issues with warehouses, travel distance, etc: again, this is part of the logistics challenge_You have to trade goods to make money, which is the natural next step of managing your city logistics. Right now, there are still some issues / things to improve:_"People are leaving" pop-ups. This is annoying, and I would like to be able to disable it, because sometimes I just accept the population swings_What could be interesting would be a building to transform the land: remove rocks from the soil, smooth the coastline / riverside, etc (it could use the same mechanics as the temple, long and heavy on resources, or a more simple one like the irrigation one). It would ease the game for some people, and would feel more realistic._The pollution containment by plants is not clear enough._I would like very much to be able to enable / disable several buildings at once.A small advice if you are struggling to get over the beggining of your city and go bankrupt before being able to export goods:You have to use almost all your starting money to build the skelleton of your city, with also the minimum required to export basic things (a port, fishing decks, a few pottery manufactures, etc). Look at your commercial map, and focus the first partners available. Then, unpause the game, and there you can go bankrupt without much problems, because as long as you have the necessary buildings, all you have to do is to balance the workforce until you reach equilibrium.Once you have 1 trade going with your first commercial partner, money won't be a problem anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have played Caesar\Pharaoh\Zeus: Master of Olympus this is pretty much that, but with another country design,region appropriate features and few small differences. So in case you liked above mentioned and not much adverse to Babylon architecture\flair (personally not a big fan of it btw) this game is right up your alley.This is very traditional city builder that requires pretty strict resource, production and placement management, as tutorial rightly says - available land is one of the most precious things in game. There are typical material and goods making chains along with necessity of working logistic and distribution planing while not forgetting about health\law enforcement\fire prevention. Same as before society is separated in classes, so your populace would need different type of homes for each of them and better variety of available resources and services to develop those houses to accommodate larger amount of people. Actually do not remember for certain about how diplomacy\trade was implemented in other games - here you get a bunch of other cities in region depending on map\campaign mission you play which would like to trade with you after settlement reached enough prestige for them and you give a gift. Follow-up presents would increase your relationship gauge till certain point, reducing tax for both import and export, which is quite useful, as trade is primary means for getting funds, as your town taxes would be lower than salary till late stage developed city. Also establishing trade relations allows you to add god of that city to your pantheon.Speaking of gods - they provide passive bonus and "active" one that is spread by building shrines, number of which is limited by your relationship with the deity. Raising it is done via holding festivals that'd spend chosen resources and assigning temples to particular god to slow down relationship decrease, which happens with time and speed of which would increase the higher worship lvl is. So you'd have to hold festivals regularly and in case of worshipping several gods, to bear decrease speed more lavish celebrations are a necessity. It is possible to have 4 gods influence in your city, with main god being vital concern constantly, as you cannot change it and in case worship level falls below minimum, could suffer divine wrath. 3 minor gods could be switched anytime by choosing others from available pantheon and as mentioned before - you could add more via trade with other cities and their worship, unlike prime god would never fall below minimum.Game also has wars... which feel kinda tacked on, though the fighting itself is actually less primitive than in other games of genre, where it's just straight auto-combat with sole possibility of commanding troop to move somewhere. Still, here fighting is still very simplistic - fight is just three by two field for each army, where you have frontline for melee\siege and rear for ranged with right\left flank and center columns. defeating any flank would allow melee in those columns to get big attack bonus against center and prevent opponent from moving melee troops to that column from now on. It's still auto-combat thought, where damage is done in turns - first turn ranged from one participant shoot melee in same column, next is ranged from other participant, after that same goes with melee. Before each engagement and after melee turn, you could move your troops between columns and rear\front. Side that loses all troops or loses melee center is defeated, in case of fight with walls, besides center, wall has to be breached with siege equipment too. Losing battle if you're the attacked does not necessary mean all your army is dead, you could even still have all your regiments, but with small number of survivors. Armies require their own branch of economy, which diverts resources and manpower from city development and does not provide much in return. Thankfully people in regiments are not subtracted from total workforce even when killed in battle, but you'd still need available population of appropriate society class to recruit. Also in order for them to function, other resources would be necessary both regular and specific military goods, which would ofc need separate from normal production chain. And obviously logistic and distribution is still a thing for above mentioned too. Thankfully  . They'd be mandatory in DLC though. If you attack enemy city and win the battle - you get a choice to receive a tribute from them in form of some amount of one of resources they'd normally trade you, you just don't have to pay for it now. However, relationship with them would always be smth to watch out for, since it'd depend on your military power and in case it drops below certain amount you're have war with them again. Considering that your total military might impact on relationship is spread among all your tributaries - it's necessary to either have really overpowering army or integrate them. Integrated places would no longer provide free resources (still can trade) but instead would give few troops to reinforce your army in battle and never rebel, while having great relationship.Btw, DLC has its own feature (besides minor stuff like voiced plot and dialogs) - there are mission sets, where what you built in previous mission of same set transfers to next one. So If you already made megalopolis with strong economy, each subsequent mission from same set might only require few minor actions to win and continue on to next.Visually it's not much different from Caesar, still 2d, but nicely drawn and optimised for big resolutions. Audio is ok, made so it'd not erode your brain on long building sprees. UI is one thing that was definitely improved to make it more comfortable and user friendly compared from earlier titles.

_childDocuments_.review: As a person who had logged hours of hours of time in the old Impressions Games city-building series of the late 1990's to early 2000's, this game will give you vibes of days gone by. It's 2-D interface will easily get your attention. Like Impressions Games, Nepos Games have put in a lot of time into research of the history, music, daily-life of Ancient Mesopotamia. It almost makes you feel like you're making history while playing this game. Here's what I like and what I would like to see improved. PROS:-Impressions Games-esque style of interface -Being able to customize monuments-Soundtrack-True city planning when it comes to where to put residential and where to put industry.CONS:-The mechanics are a little bit off putting when it comes to the distribution and logistics of goods.-Not being able to trade earlier in the tutorial missions in the campaign. Mission #4 is quite the challenge when you're not able to set tax rates.-No threats, no fire, no chances of buildings collapsing, no military aspectI'm still giving this game a recommended because it's constantly being updated and hopefully the developers will add more in the future. If you're a fan of the Impressions Games series you owe it to yourself to at least give this title a try. If you're new to the city-building genre and want to have a challenge then you should give a look into the genre's storied past. At the time of this review the game is currently at version 1.1.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to give this a positive review. It plays like Pharaoh but it leaves out the annoying stuff like fire, collapsing buildings, army, and praising gods every few minutes to make sure they don't burn down your storage yards (I'm looking at you Ptah). It even adds a nice copy and paste building features.The problem is that this game introduces more issues and challenges that frankly shouldn't be there:- A limit on how far regular workers will take their goods. You have your farm (more on that in a sec) and you can control how many people work at that farm. However the guy that takes the goods from the farm wont take them very far to get to a storage yard. This means you have to have intermediate storage yards and set up a caravan system just so you can move goods from your farm storage yard to the bakery storage yard. Then you need another caravan to take goods form the bakery storage yard to the store storage yard to dish them out to the houses. This happens for every single product. Yes you might be lucky and be able to have your bakery near your farm but you still need to move that an additional step. In Pharaoh all you had was a bloke who said "I need to take these goods across the city, it'll take all day" but that's it.- Farms need a massive amount of space. Farms work by building one main building, which needs road access, then you build individual plots around the farm, but then you most likely need to irrigate it so you use irrigation ditches. By the time you are done you barely have any space left.- Income is very difficult and slow. The way to make money is either through taxes or exporting goods. Nice and simple. However, you can't actually start taxing people until you've given them a constant supply of 2 goods. If you aren't getting quite enough one of product then the houses will downgrade and lose you money, making it harder to build more production building for that product. Exporting goods is a way of getting income, however setting up trade routes is a pain as each city wants a different thing before they will even talk to you. Then you have to make sure you dont sell too much that you will starve your own citizens, and then you have to make sure the goods are near a storage yard near the dock with another caravan.Some players might enjoy the challenges this game makes, unfortunately I am not one of them. I love city building games but this game needs a lot more balancing for me to return to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This is reminiscent of games like Pharaoh, Cleopatra, Emperor: Rise of the Middle Kingdom, Zeus, and Poseidon. So far it's been a great deal of fun and I'd recommend it to anyone who likes the above games.However, there are two issues that need addressing:1. They need to edit their English dialogue for grammar. There are some wrong tenses and missing words.2. More importantly, the first mission in the tutorial to deal with clay and standard houses needs to be reworked. I had to restart the mission twice and eventually lower the difficulty to easy because the tutorial forces you to place farms and a warehouse in specific spots. The issue is that, unless those buildings are moved, there is no way to irrigate some land for the clay pit. If you don't have ceramics, then there is no way to complete the level as ceramics and water are necessary for the standard houses.This game has great potential and just needs a few tweaks and play-ability checks before it's perfect.
