_childDocuments_.review: I don't think this very often but this is a beautiful game. The way the tutorial walked me through made me feel good. It wasn't overwhelming, and strangely I found myself grateful for the guide himself. He was there long enough to explain things, wasn't too demanding or hands on, felt mature and alive, and left after their job was done.I bought this because it resembled the Pharaoh series, but that was also what made me somewhat hesitant. I was not looking forward to having to laboriously manage my city, but instead what I found was that it took the more frustrating parts of Pharaoh, ( namely the buggy logistics and choppiness ) and instead of just abstracting it away with an AI it turned it into something very enjoyable which made it fun. I appreciated the standardizing of units and subdividing them into groups of 4, and the citizen/worker management. It felt like I didn't have to micro-mange as much and could focus more on planning and development, and this felt good. The systems felt smooth and adding the right-click menu for fast buildings was great.The music is flowing and continuous and kept me feeling engaged, and the tone of it was very appropriate. The historical descriptions were also great, and follows much of the same theme as the other series. I loved the artwork on the map, especially the trade map. I loved seeing the land of the middle east, and seeing the detailed green along the rivers and coastlines. I only played up to the final tutorial mission, but so far I really like what I see and would recommend it just based on that. Good job!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Well I wanted to like this game, I played much Ceasar 2, 3, and some Pharaoh back when I was a kid. Even some of the newer rome city simulators like Imperium.The game most feels like Ceasar 2 the most. But my problem with the game is how restrictive it is.-Much of the coast is jagged not allowing you to build fishing ships/irrigation (water in irrigation dosn't travel very far)-Many of the buildings have very strict range of how far the workers are willing to travel to drop off goods/deliver goods.-These restrictions cause many of your cities to looks very blocky and square as you can see in the screenshots. Not organic at all.-Should add a slider for workers to each workplace. Instread of restricting it to 30/30 or 18/18. Maybe let us put 12 water deliverers, 15 pottery, 20 bread, 9 milk.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions: Carefully, even lovingly made homage to Caesar III, Pharaoh, etc... that misses some of the key things that made them fun and satisfying.It's not a bad game, but it has taken more organic, automated, flowing and relaxed systems from the originals and replaced them with overcomplicated yet lifeless, time-consuming alternatives.  Only some walkers can be clicked, and have incredibly bland comments delivered without passion, with varying volumes and audio qualities, mostly in incongruous accents. I think I actually preferred it when I thought you couldn't click walkers at all, rather than merely some of them.The towns don't feel populated by wildly bouncing little lifeforms anymore, just meaningless (and equally basic, over 20 years later) animations flickering - ignored - between buildings. This feels like Caesar for people who didn't enjoy the chaotic ant-nest vibe, but wanted more economic/logistical detail and control.Lastly, while the Monument customisation system is a very impressive evolution, there's no sense of watching it grow. You merely wait for haulers to drop off bricks (but don't really see this process meaningfully visualised in terms of the immense quantities involved), then you rapidly click in all your components and click 'done', except it's already done.There's no sense of watching your wonder slowly grow under the hands of a hundred eager artisans... It's just slammed down by the player.Ultimately this serves as a great example of flaws with the game as a whole. It's an Impressions historic citybuilder without the charm or the sense of being.. alive, and this reduces the satisfaction the game offers considerably.I can't call it a bad game at all, especially not with only a few hours playing - I do recommend it to those who enjoy citybuilders, so this is a thumbs up with caveats.If you've not; go and play Caesar III and Pharaoh, maybe Zeus.If you have, go and play Children of the Nile.If you're still hungry, come back and try out Nebuchadnezzar.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: The best parts of Pharaoh and Zeus. Employment is automatically filled by unemployed citizens, the houses give very clear and defined requirements for levelling up, and an unusual but (at the time of writing) not unpleasant warehouse system.One of the most interesting new features (again, 4 levels in at the time of writing) is the fact that walkers have manually set routes. This eliminates the need for roadblocks, because they have a specific route to follow to go to and from their building.The other most interesting feature, although not at all to my luddite tastes, is that you can design the monuments you build, from the ground up. There is also a template version of each monument, which is great for people like me who abhor designing things. I just suck at it, but for the rest of humanity, I'm really happy for yall.I'm really enjoying it so far, and the tutorial gentleman, Gil, is very well written. The music is nice, as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: [Playing in June 2021 - v1.1 ]The game is alright. It's maybe more of a puzzle/logistics game than a traditional city builder. Buildings can only collect and distribute resources over a short distance. Better group things together ;)You need to layout production somewhat efficiently and put homes not too far away, knowing that buildings won't catch fire (until the next update that adds fire).It's a fairly different style than Pharaoh. (Doesn't mean it's bad, just don't expect to organise your city the same way)At the moment there is no fire/collapse/crime, no religion, and no war. (It's just been announced that disasters will come with v1.2 soon). Don't go thinking that the game is easy though, it is pretty hard ;)The game is relatively low on content, but there is more than enough to play (now).I have 20-30 hours actively playing and I have not completed the campaign (edit: finished after 40 hours).Update v1.1 added multiple buildings and game mechanics, then patch v1.1.3 made much needed balance adjustments. I can't imagine what it was like before these, the game was basically empty and impossibly difficult/annoying. You can safely ignore ALL negative reviews before May 2021 ;)MY ADVICE:- If you are open minded and want to try something new and challenging, you can buy.- If you want a clone of Pharaoh/Caesar, it's nowhere as complete or as polished right now, it's fair to wait.- Expect future updates to drastically alter the gameplay. (I don't think they can add fire or war without serious change).
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Not on the same level of quality and replayability as Caesar III or Pharaoh, personally, but 90% of the time it certainly feels like an honest Impressions Games tribute. I do enjoy how you can customise your monuments and adopt foreign gods, however it's rather lacking on the warfare and diplomacy side - I found it exceptionally easy to befriend the entire ancient world through trading with them, honouring their requests (all of which are very cheap) and giving the occasional gift; once it snowballs it's barely even a worry. The lack of "on-the-map" warfare with 3d units was also a disappointment. Hopefully these are things that can be improved down the line.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the old Impressions games, you'll like this. Just don't try and compare them.The old impressions games cost $40 in 1999 which is $65 in today's money. If I'd paid $65 for this game, I'd be angry and upset. This game cost me $18. That is VALUE for money in terms of the price paid and what you get. The negative reviews are a little silly. I am very, very happy the developers made this because I've been waiting for a game like this for some time.  I am enjoying this game a lot and it is really well done. I haven't encountered any bugs or glitches or crashes which is great.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up playing the caesar/pharaoh/zues series and i was excited to see someone taking up the mantle.  However Nebuchadnezzar is not able to measure up.It lacks character and feels very basic. Granted i am not fully into the campaign but the story missions are slowly paced and have goals that take quite a long time to accomplish. That coupled with a very bare bones economy mean that you can leave the game running and walk away with no risk.I want to like this game but after playing 7 missions i just want to come back to zues and pharaoh. Perhaps with some mods or content patches this game will be great but as of right now id give it a 5/10 its not bad its also just not good.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is a great game, and a real gem from a small development team. Do not be put off by others who say this doesn't meet the expectations of the old Sierra city builders like Pharaoh and Caesar. True that this doesn't have the same depth or breadth (understandable given the size and scope of development), but it has good gameplay, charm and integrity. It does play more like Anno than a true city builder, managing supply and demand and trade, but the chains are pretty simple and are introduced one by one. I think it has just the right level of complexity for a relaxing experience - I didn't feel the need to find optimal strategies or online help. The art style is consistent and clean, and the audio is top notch. The ability to customise your own wonders is a nice touch and adds some creative elements.It took me about 30 hours to finish the campaign which was a good deal for £20 or so that I paid for it. Not every game needs to have reams of DLC or live service content - I think this is a great little game to play over a holiday. I look forward to more from these creators.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: So, played the old Impressions citybuilders and wondering if this is for you?You will likely enjoy this game if, in your experience:- As your cities scaled you found the warehouse controls woefully inadequate, wondering why you couldn't set up explicit routing between warehouses and granaries so you could get proper goods distributions- Once you understood the walker mechanic you were frustrated by the need to carefully build everything around it, invalidating what would otherwise be perfectly viable road layouts in real life, or things like large open plazas- In general you just felt the desire to be able to let your city run without the fear of the random number generator dealing you a bad roll- You liked seeing how efficient you could be with your space and your industriesYou may not however, if:- You felt like the warehouse controls were just fine and tweaking them wasn't one of the things you enjoyed doing- You saw the nondeterminism more as your city behaving organically- You enjoyed actually watching your monuments being constructed- The production chains and exploring them wasn't one of the game's highlights in your opinionIn general I would describe this game as the result of someone playing Pharaoh and wondering why it was that they couldn't be more granular with their economy when they ran up against limitations with the goods transfer system between warehouses or the walker system.  Granted, the ability to fine-tune these things in Nebuchadnezzar comes with, you know, actually having to specify how everything works, but personally I find it satisfying when you've got your space utilized properly and your houses well-supplied, and it's nice to just watch the city functioning.Being able to customize the monuments is a very nice touch, although I do wish there were a way to see them actually get built.  The monument buildings themselves are pretty cool.  There is a pretty wide variety of decorative roads, statues, and gardens you can use to enhance the look of your city and build custom plazas.I can see where some people might think the tutorial levels are a bit, uh, steep, although personally I didn't think they were too bad.Something of a fresh direction for the genre.  Keep in mind when deciding whether or not to purchase that this steers heavily in the direction of a true logistics-focused game rather than the old model of a citybuilder built on RNG and partially-obscured mechanics.  This comes with micromanagement that some may not enjoy, but for those who enjoy building and fine-tuning a production and distribution system against the backdrop of Mesopotamian cities, it's very enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: As I read the epilogue of Nebuchadnezzar, which tells us about the sad disappearance of the last truly mesopotamian civilization in the 6th century BC, I couldn't help but figure everything that we still nowadays have, use and live with, that date back to the times of Ur, Uruk, Nineveh, Babylon, Eridu, Akkad and the others. They say the way we count the days in a week as well as the hours, the writing, all come from the Mesopotamian. I felt like a part of me came from there, and felt nostalgia for times long gone, which I have never known.This epilogue was a perfect conclusion to a superb game, that brought me all the way back to when I started playing video games and launched, for the first time, the almighty Pharaoh from Impression Games. Many early critics of the game regretted its unfinished state and its lack of features. As someone who played a now very largely improved version of the game, I can say with confidence that the game feels complete, barring the military aspect, which I personnaly dont really mind, for this type of games lends itself anyway not the best to military strategy and battles, but rather to precise micro and macroeconomic management.And this is where this game clearly shines, and, in my humble opinion, even outshines the games from Impression Games. The working of the supply chains - clearly the center of your attention - is well thought out, and can be adjusted to your liking. This gets nerve-wracking when your city gets bigger (#Babylon and your 50.000 inhabitants) and forces you to plan very carefully your city, and to make sure the supply lines of your most basic ressources are (very) well served. This is the aspect that makes the difference, on the micro as well as on the macro level.Beside that, money is mostly tight, so you'll have to balance your imports and exports, your workforce and your taxes with utmost care, to make you always keep a little surplus. Only when your city is fully developed will you have room for more exports (or, at that time, just ginormous amounts of taxes from these lavish residences.And now, we're told a DLC is near, which will add the military aspect to the game, while introducing a whole new fully-fledged campaign centered round Sargon the conqueror.What more can we ask? For a game that only costs 20 bucks?Verdict: 11/10, would almost collapse the whole city of Nineveh because of a little mistake in the milk supply chain all over again.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: You know Caesar 3 from 1998 ? Or Pharaoh from 1999 ? Nebuchadnezzar is a very decent mix of those two games and there mechanics and a really good new representative to the city building genre.btw. the last 4-5 major updates improved the game immensely.10 months ago Nebuchadnezzar was a 5/10 at most, now it's easily a 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: A Caesarlike citybuilding game where you develop your build houses and agriculture and industry, trying to meet your citizen's needs so that their residences upgrade and your city flourishes. Enjoyable at first but as the game grows more difficult, the size of the maps and the restrictions on what can be built where make the game feel frustratingly cramped, along with incessant barrages of notifications about fire hazards or health risks that don't seem to abate regardless of how many healers or firefighters you build.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A very decent spiritual descendant of the old specific genre of Sierra/Tilted Mill city-builder games like Caesar, Pharaoh, Zeus, Emperor... More focused on the hands- on economy managament than all of the aforementioned games, you have to manually set up almost everything and the most of the negative comments seem to spur from that experience. I can't see it as a negative thing, i don't want my management games overly automated. In my opinion, it's worth the money and time for the die-hard fans of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I completely understand why some old school city builders may thumb their nose  at this game.   It is a bit simplified compared to Caesar 3 and such, and lacks some of the polish.   Personally speaking though, I'm having a blast with Nebuchadnezzar.   There have been a few games as of late that just remake  or directly copy some of the classics, trying to cash in on a shallow shell of a past classic.  This is not in that category at all.   Clearly a labor of love built from the ground up and still growing.   Honestly to me this may be the best intro to the genre that exists, being slightly simplified makes it much easier to wrap your mind around before jumping into a crueler experience like Caesar 3.    I hope a few  more dlcs really build this thing out into a monster of a game, but even as is it is well worth your time!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Sorry, but no. Games by Impression (that this one is obviously inspired by - inspired so much that you could call it a clone or a reskin) were my childhood and I revisit them frequently. So when a modern game promised to hit the same vibe and amtosphere, I was excited. Only to be incredibly disappointed, so much, in fact, that I felt the need to write a review, which I don't do normally.This game is incredibly bland and dry, it's drier than the desert that you have to build your cities in (except this time you can't add some irrigation). There's no flavour of atmosphere that even 15-20-year old games of this type had. No dialogue by the villagers, limited ambient sounds, boredom-inducing mission briefings, samey buildings in the monotonous landscape. Even Pharaoh+Cleopatra that also had you building cities in an unhospitable desert was more fun.There's no poilce, fires, military buildings, culture, gods and religions, the monuments (from what I've heard) are built instantaneously as soon as the goods are delivered. You just plop some production buildings, houses, micro-manage some routes/ranges (which is a new addition, and, frankly, a frustrating one) and just watch the numbers grow in your almost-dead town.Not to mention there's no freeplay scenarios, the campaign is short and repititive and the devs are already planning to put out DLCs for the military system etc.I will refund this but I might revisit it in a few years, if there's going to be improvements (which I doubt since the core of the game would remain the same).
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: While inspired by the classic Impressions city building games, it would be inaccurate to say Nebuchadnezzar is just a reskin of Pharaoh. The game has its own mechanics that are distinctive such as the beautifully worded caravanserai or the planned market/bazaar walking routes (as opposed to the annoying random wandering of sellers in the Impressions games that required the use of roadblocks). There are a ton of resources in the game and the tiered housing levels have an interesting intertwined dependence on how these resources can be collected. I'm interested to see how much the developers will push the potential of the game, because if done right, this game will be VERY good. They have yet to add critical components like unemployment penalties, warfare units, defensive structures, or any interaction with divine figures. Things like crime, fires, and political instability are not present either. Luckily, the developers seem passionate about the project, and it is nice to see how much they are continually adding to the game. It would be nice if the map sizes could be bigger, and if more buildings had sounds or animations to make the city feel more vibrant and alive. They should add native wildlife to roam the map. There is a distinct lack of large beautification structures. I find the texture of the sand and water to be a bit too bland. The trading ships and fishing ships are too close in size and it is weird that you can't click on them. The world map with trading cities needs more dynamism (maybe add names of the rules and give some indication of their philosophy or personality). It would be nice to indicate which cities on the map are the most powerful and influential instead of simply just unlocking trade routes by a prestige scale. I agree with others reviews that the citizens walk too fast, it's oddly distracting.A way for this game to be distinct would be to add in more elements of what made Mesopotamia unique, like farming (which the game has already) or their ground-breaking use of astronomy. One Idea is to perhaps add nighttime animations or modes, this could be a way for the game to tie into the important gods of the time (An, Enlil, and EnkiI) which were observed by the Mesopotamian cultures' fascination with the night sky. There should at least be more astronomical structures or elements.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I was very excited about a new game the likes of Zeus and Poseidon but this one just needs a few more features before it can be played. The biggest being that you need to be able to turn specific industries on and off to be able to manage the loss of inhabitants. The balance of the game is circular because the lower houses depend on the people who live in the larger houses to provide goods to them. So if one industry suffers in any way, everyone moves out and there is no coming back from that.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game when it first came out and it was enjoyable, but a bit bland and I stopped playing pretty quickly. I revisited the game just a few days before the DLC dropped (didn't even realise it was coming) and the tweaks and changes since release have been great!If you liked the Impressions city builders, this would be right up your alley.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I was pretty disappointed with this game around launch, but as a result of the patches released by a developer that knows how to embrace constructive feedback, Nebuchadnezzar has turned into one of my favorite city builders - up there with Pharaoh and Caesar III. Patch 1.1 remove almost all of my complaints from the game by expanding the map sizes, adding freeplay scenarios, and adding new buildings to the supply chains. Patch 1.2 is an excellent iteration that expands on the systems in place and adds many new gameplay features such as fire, crime, and new visualization layers. Just a fantastic game to lose hours to as you set up complex trade routes and manufacturing chains.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: If you're like me, this game caught your eye because of its resemblance to Pharaoh. If that's what you're after, I would have no fear: Nebuchadnezzar is both strongly evocative of Pharaoh, and different enough from it to make it its own game.The central challenge comes from careful placement of buildings to optimise your space, and to make sure your production chains flow smoothly from raw materials to industry to homes (or to export). You can plan walker routes, and the way that resources are distributed is more or less deterministic (unlike Pharaoh where there was a lot of randomness to account for). This means you have fine-grained control over what resources end up where, and a lot of the game is working out how exactly how those mechanics work so you can plan around them. I'm only on the fifth mission but I can tell this is going to be a tough but rewarding task.Yes, the Pharaoh influence is everywhere, from the design of the mission briefings, to the animation of the immigrants, to the mechanics of the production chain. Even though the nature of the challenge is a little different, the theme of what you're trying to do is the same: organise your city properly, manage your economy to keep yourself in the black, and grow until you reach the mission objective.Being able to customise monuments is nice, though personally I find it slightly gimmicky. If you enjoy learning about ancient history and how civilisation got started there's also a hefty dose of background between each mission, which gives good context. The UI has some rough edges: copying walker routes is not very intuitive, the city trading screen has a confusing layout, and the production statistics could be a bit clearer; but these are minor problems and overall it's impressively polished for a brand new game.All in all, looking like an excellent game so far and I'm pleased with my purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished tutorial and one more mission and i am realy sick of micromanaging warehouses and logistics chain, this whole mechanics should have been thrown away in the middle of development, because it is really killing the game flow. Final nail at least for me is spiraling failure effect - you make a mistake and people leave, now you are unable to fix mistakes because you do not have people to fix the mistake.Generally it is not better than its predecessors which is sad. And these old games like Ceasar and Pharaoh unfortunately feels really dated.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Not in it's current condition!This feels like a very sad rip-off of "Emperor - Rise of the Middle Kingdom" which I still play occasionally.However:- In no particular order:-It takes at least twice as long to load as any game I have ever played including "The Sims 3" which is so long that the developers provided a mini game to play while you wait!  Nebuchadnezzar does this without providing a fraction of the game content expected with long loading times.The graphics, navigation and game set up are not as good as Emperor, now 20 years old.  Surely in that time there ought to be improvement.The game play is frankly irritating.  It is almost impossible to provide enough requirements to the houses with available workers.  Goods delivery is frankly a mess, though, I do like the ability to move goods using caravans.  The irrigation system is not realistic. - You seem to require large numbers of unmanned pumps!  So, what provides the power in this ancient era?  Prayer, possibly! (I suggest the developers go take a look at the irrigation in Emperor.)Maps are bland to the point of being boring and the very slight visual difference between rocky and arable land makes deciding where to place fields a chore.  What is it with the huge pollution from essential service items such as the healer (10 squares in every direction - reducing to 8 if you surround with decoration items.)   Placing far away (example behind farms) makes them extremely ineffective while close to where needed upsets the workers.The essential service staff really need patrol routes not the blunt instrument of they go where they wish - up to a not easily recognised point.  Placing a second facility, which you eventually must do can have very unpredictable consequences!  Walled residential areas could solve this.It does not seem logical to me, more like a chore, to have to place farm tiles separately for each farm building. But then, I am used to placing multiple farms then laying the fields in a single operation!Why can't I select, using a single click, to shut down or reactivate an entire industry.  Seasonal workers, as in real life, should be able to switch quickly when their industry is dormant.  (Apple pickers simply do not get paid 12 months of the year in exchange for a few weeks harvest - do they?) For example, and this is from Emperor, Silk growers tend and harvest their crop in the spring and summer then I switch immediately to weaving for the winter.  Essential for balancing the books in the early part of the game.The game, as delivered, runs too fast in normal speed, this can be adjusted it you feel confident to edit the .ini file.  I chose to half the original speed.Warehouse default is accept everything.  Why?  It took me a while to find it, but, you can change this to accept nothing until the user selects the desired product(s).Auto save every minute is frankly excessive again a little exploration and this can be changedI could rattle on, but, I think the point is made.  This game needs work - lots of it and in almost every element - before it needs more DLC!The historical blurb is long the instruction help falls short of satisfactory (D-).  I certainly will not be paying for voice history blurb DLC.   I am now off to play a few stress free and fun rounds of Emperor! :)
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve bought Nebuchadnezzar because of its atmosphere, naivety and its system requirements, along with its inviting low price: only 20 bucks.Most of the games, nowadays, are nothing but a 'good looking' crap, I’m afraid. And they ask, on average, €40 (~48 USD) for it. We must buy a new PC every 6 months only to fulfil the new game's recommended requirements, that just don’t worth it.Nebuchadnezzar runs smoothly on my i5-5300U CPU @ 2,3GHz, and i've never had a CTD till now.Being Nepos Games an Indi game’s producer, I wasn’t expecting a superb game. But I was pleasantly surprised, because I realized that Nebuchadnezzar has its own character and any comparison with the good old Impressions Games is absolutely unfair.It has no random walkers, no roadblocks and no lazy cartpushers. You can design the path of practically any character on the game and even listen what they have to say on their individual voiceover. Even the pictured civilization (Babylon) came as a surprise because it hasn’t never been explored as a citybuilding game before.I’ve great expectations on Nepos (small) team: i wish them the utmost success for them to grow and still surprise us with new improved features, DLC or even their new project concerning the Persians, Indus Valley civilizations or even the Pre-Columbian American Civilizations, for example.If you are expecting war/military features you must wait for the next great update. However, the game presently is worth every buck I’ve spent on it.I do recommend Nebuchadnezzar because it overcame all my expectations and I do trust Nepos will present us a continuous improved game in a short time.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A great & compact love letter to old city builders, but not amazing. If you enjoyed Caesar 3 and Zeus, you'll definitely like this game. For 20 Euro, this is a bargain.I wish the game had more content and that extracting more raw material was possible such as wood, ivory. It's also not the biggest game in terms of content, but for the low price it's still definitely priceworthy and the campaign and gameplay is definitely more complex than Zeus for instance.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I want to give this game a recommendation. I want to. I want to. I want to. I love the time period. I love the place. I love the history. I want to love this game so badly. But...even at its "released" stage, it's incomplete. They only JUST added fire, gods and taxes? Are you kidding me? Come back in a year or two, and maybe there will be a full game here worthy of your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some good mechanics but it's very repetitive and ends up being a bit boring.I'm on mission 11 and since mission 1 everything is the same, each mission they add a new level of depth in the house's levels to achieve but that's about it. Once you start a trade with another city you can't really lose anymore.This game is complex but too easy at the same time. Why is it complex ? Because you micro manage everything, from the bread seller to the milk seller... you build tons of warehouses everywhere and manage ressources to try to get houses to level up. That's about it.You never get attacked, you don't get demands from the higher ups that could make you lose, just demands that you can ignore from other cities trading with you. The game doesn't feel challenging at all. It's just a ressource management game. You can play for hours without losing, there are no time limits when you build a city, you could spend a thousand years building your city and still win the scenario.

_childDocuments_.review: I have had this game since EA and I had no idea how brilliant it was until I had the time to really sink my teeth into it.  Truly made by someone who LOVED the Sierra games of old and HATED all the same things about it as the rest of us.  The only one I ever played was Emperor: Rise of the Middle Kingdom.  I didn't like any of the others because ERMK was my first, last to be made, and best of all of them.  Now that you understand my perspective, I will talk about my opinion of Nebuchadnezzar which from here on I will refer to as "Chad" because ♥♥♥♥ that red-squiggly-line-for-miles-eyesore of a title.  I wouldn't have the name changed for anything though.  TL;DR--CON: Be prepared to figure a lot of things out for yourself, the guide is ♥♥♥♥♥.  Ambient noise is kinda annoying.TL;DR--PRO: possibly historically informative, beautiful, subtle soundtrack, volume controls customizable, DIY monuments.PRO:EDIT:  well balanced.Amazing logic.Can design every detail of your monuments.Beautiful artwork, below average graphics.Seperate volume controls for music and ambient.  History.  Take it in, soak it up.  Incidentally learning about ancient history through a game made by someone who clearly loves the subject is unbelievably satisfying.  I liked that about ERMK too.  If you don't care, you don't have to read it and you can easily access the info again if you want to read it later.  *SIDE NOTE:  I have no idea how accurate it is as I am NOT knowledgable about ancient history, so if you read[red] that book, I have no idea what you will think of the game.  Buy it, try it, give it the rating it deserves for being a game (not a history lesson) then deliver your notes below.  That way you don't have to tank a game's reputation just because you needed to go online and flex.  There is a mature way to flex, where you gain respect WITHOUT having to take it away from someone else!  If you INSIST on being a sorry P.O.S. you can always refund it anyway........sorry, I'm dealing with a lot of repressed rage, but therapy is going well!Music is relaxing and stays in the background where it belongs.Anyhoo...the QoL differences is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 10/10.  I'm dropping the F-bomb alot in this review to convey just how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ IMPRESSED I am.  Not that my opinion is anything to you, but I figure if you are still reading then you are at least entertained.  CON:  In-game guide doesn't bother explaing most of the amazing QoL improvements and they are NOT easy to figure out (I'm hoping to write my own guide some time soon).  Maybe devs figured it was obvious to younger gens?  Who knows.  Thank you for reading my entire opinion.  I hope it wasn't boring and was helpful.  P.S.  I didn't recommend this game until now because it always took 9 years to load the game.  But since then the dev added another pretty loading screen for me to stare at while I contemplate my existential dread.

_childDocuments_.review: For what it offers, the game should cost 4€ , if that even.The game feels like a tech demo.The most annoying part is that there's no option to transport goods between warehouses, you must do spreadsheets to make sure every production building is within a tile of a warehouse which is within a tile coverage of a market  in tiny-sized maps filled with land obstructions. Every other city builder from 1999 has this feature where you just request/empty a warehouse and another one picks it up. Not this 20 euro game.The theme potential is amazing however this game is merely a tech demo not an actual game.Half of the functional features that makes it feel like running a city builder are missing.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: For the fans of Caesar and Pharaoh this is the game, but it falls short of the complexity and detail of those titles. It still needs  work, I would have liked to see more animation, the buildings are very static, especially residences and more sounds. Scenario mode is missing also, so there is only the campaign for now. I would consider the game early access in its current state. _childDocuments_.review: I loved the classics Zeus, Emperor and Pharaoh so much and while this clearly expands on those classics it does it in an overly complicated, finicky and extensive micro-management style that some people may like but I couldn't get into, because I'm not capable enough to actually manage all the moving parts here. not bad, but just not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: When I was 5 years old playing Pharaoh I couldn't understand why the gods kept punishing my poor cities and why nobody wanted to live there. Now I have a chance to redeem myself with Nebuchadnezzar. Up until this point I am having a very satisfactory experience, blemished by a few caveats. Will recommend for potential, although right now it feels like Nebuchadnezzar's vision is off. The game is somewhere between a punishing city builder like Banished and a casual builder like Planet Coaster but doesn't hit the mark either of them left me.And, as someone who makes music, I have to say the soundtrack is seriously amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I waited for v1.2 to buy and i'm very happy with my choice.  This feels like a really rounded game with a refreshing twist on the city builder genre. Gameplay is great.  I'm addicted at the moment.  I'm excited to see what updates come next. I would love to see the user experience fleshed out some more with more voice acting, ambient sound, artwork, music + historical content. _childDocuments_.review: This is not a city builder; this is an Annoish-inspired puzzler with some city-building elements. If that's not what you're looking for, don't bother. Regardless, it's an unique blend of gameplay mechanics and pretty good at what it does - for the most part. Considering that, I think you should at least try it if you're interested in the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Despite being a lifelong fan of the Impressions games and highly anticipating Nebuchadnezzar's release, I waited to buy this after I heard cautious reviews at launch. In short, I think the game is a fantastic successor to (though not surpassing) these citybuilders. The game does demand greater focus on issues of resource management, but I disagree with the review that characterizes this game as more Anno than Pharaoh; it's a little more Anno than its inspirations, but it's still unquestionably and primarily a familiar love letter to Impressions Games. Here are my responses to concerns brought up in other reviews:* "The logistics are so annoying; you have to set paths for walkers!": In my experience, this concern is an over-blown nitpick. The system of setting walker paths (for markets, etc) actually improves over earlier games' solutions to the walker issue (roadblocks galore and standard housing rectangles)* "There's no religion/fire/etc!": yes the game is lacking some of the features which Impressions-era fans will miss, yes, but the developer has already shown a commitment both to bug patches and free feature patches, so I think these will be added.* "The tone is off": the gameplay feels "right" to me, but my biggest issue with the game is its narrative framing: while Pharaoh/Zeus scenario intros were narrated and made the player feel like a participant (an actual leader) in the era, Nebuchadnezzar's intros are quite dry and academic, lacking the personality of the earlier games. The in-game tutorial attempts to be "in-universe", but isn't a very significant part of the game. This is the biggest area of improvement for the game in my opinion, as someone who became interested in history and mythology as a kid from the engaging narratives in, say, The Peloponnesian War campaign in Zeus and the encyclopedic, historical information attached to the Temple of Bast (etc) in Pharaoh.If you were on the fence like me, give the game a try and support these developers who clearly love those old Impressions games as much as you do.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: (loved Siera games, still play them sometimes).I really wanted to like this game despite some annoying mechanics (like, I don't know who decided that managing warehouses would be fun), disbalanced economy, etc. What really killed this game for me and made me delete it was, of course, the city siege screen. Just wow
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed previous games of this genre (Impression-style city builders), but i gotta say this one is the worst I've played so far.I really wanted to like it on the basis of its beautiful setting, good looking sprite-work and nice soundtrack but some of the mechanics are completely baffling.My biggest gripe by far, is that events while based on manageable probabilities - are completely unavoidable, and without a large population of unemployed to take up the slack or large stockpiles of spare required goods can fairly easily induce a cascading failure.Curiously, this game has partially replaced the familiar 'road block' with the tedium of manually defined patrol routes - mind - this is only for some service buildings. Eventually you will encounter the frustrating scenario of an important structure reaching near-certainty of spontaneous combustion while the nearest fire warden f*cks off into the desert.If like me you enjoy playing these sorts of games on high speed with planning and constructing being done during long pauses - then prepare for the unavoidable and never ending procession of suddenly burning buildings, thieves with bottomless pockets emptying entire f*cking warehouses, and sudden outbreaks of Covid19 *DESPITE* the fact that a quarter of your workforce is employed in the exact buildings that supposedly remedy these issues.I want to reiterate however that the setting, sprites, and soundtrack are top notch, and i respect that the developers are trying to innovate within the confines of the genre - its just i cant bring myself to put up with this games sh*t while i'm attempting to relax.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar is a  puzzle game, in which you are required to optimize your space as much as possible. In small cities and the first few campaign missions this is fun, however in larger cities it quickly becomes tedious to build warehouse after warehouse and to draw every merchant's path separately.There is also the occasional weirdness in how the game works. You can build an irrigation system originating from a river or lake, at the same time you can build a well anywhere but no irrigation canals to or from it. Firefighters never extinguish fires. Unemployment is somehow portrayed as a good thing. Shrines have a tiny area of influence (just like most buildings). If you disable a ware from being stored in a certain warehouse, the remaining wares of this type have to be deleted to be removed, merchants will no longer pick them up.The game has the potential to be a fun city builder with a rather exotic setting for the genre, but as it is right now I would not even recommend it as a puzzle game.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This game was actually fun until the later levels, at which point it becomes clear just how much of a house of cards anything is, and how absolutely awful experience it is to recover when it goes down. My 22000 population city went down to 4000. Why? Because some bakers living literally next to a police station decided to riot and it sent everything down into a death spiral. How to mitigate this? Screw yourself, you don't. You just have to recover. And it's *very* slow, painful micromanagement, where you turn off buildings one by one, try to get people back into your city without law enforcement (can't have that when all your middle class called it quits in the death spiral). I would compare the experience into a traffic jam simulator, except you get to watch the traffic jam from a bird's eye perspective. It is about as fun as stabbing those barbed needles used for felting in your eyesockets and up your urethra. And the time it takes to unscramble itself is longer than actually restarting the map from the beginning and completing it. Desperately needs some kind of prioritization system or ability to turn off entire industries while waiting to recover.EDIT: Managed to fix it, got back to 24k population. Took 5 hours total, which was longer than I had played that map at that point. Then my clay tablet factory burned down, despite having 3 firestations right next to it, and it happened again. Back to 4k pop.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I just wanted to recommend this game as I think it deserves more than the recent mixed reviews.This game builds upon the formula of Caesar and Pharaoh, but it innovates enough to be worth playing even for Impression Games veterans. Additionally, the developers have expanded the campaign maps, making city construction more enjoyable and less like a puzzle to be solved. The visuals are somewhat monotonous when compared to Pharaoh, but if you're patient, you can stylize the city to a great extent, especially given that you can set up worker routes which enable diverse housing block patterns within the same map.Finally, just to give you an idea of this game's quality, my personal ranking is: Pharaoh, Caesar 3 (Augustus), Nebuchadnezzar, Caesar 3 (unmodded), Emperor, and Zeus.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: While it looks like an evolution of the old isometric games like Zeus/Poseidon, it is very, very barebones. The game lacks charm very much. No citizens or workers *ever* talk. There is no voiceover, and there is not even written sentences. It's overall pretty bleak.On the positive, it is an evolution on the old systems - you can now define walker routes by yourself, which is great, and control the exact way the warehouses and ware distribution in the city works. Overall, I wouldn't recommend the game in it's current state at all. Zeus/Poseidon is still a far better game. Maybe in a year it will get close, but I doubt there will be much work put into making the cities more lively.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game, I would definitely recommend it.-Ignore reviews saying it is a statistic game or not like the old sierra games. They obviously played on release and the game did come out very plain and basic. New updates have improved the game.-Follows the same city building mechanics that most sierra games had.-Has some tedious mechanics like caravanserai and irrigation canals. A lot of micromanagement compared to other titles.-Very complex but straight forward game play. Mods make it easier and logical.-It is lacking features like military that will come in patch 1.4. Needs more features other than that.-Paying wages, wages used for goods, taxing your citizens = Lose 50% of your yearly estimated returns. Does not make any economical sense.-Campaign is all about rushing to trade so you do not go broke.-Campaign is kind of boring and not very hard. -Events are very lame. EJ: Zeus: Master of Olympus had gods attacking your city, other cities raiding your cities or allies, gods sending their minions to kill you, earthquakes or volcanoes. In Nebuchadnezzar, there are only trade requests, fire, sickness and unrest as events, which are just random events that happen and you cannot stop them. Also very basic and boring.-No sounds makes the game feel lackluster.-Worst feature is workers range. Has to be the stupidest thing implemented in this game as workers will not go to the nearest stockpile if it is out of range but, is willing to go around the map to a stockpile that is in range but will take 10x longer to get there. Range should be based on kilometers it would take the worker to get to destination.Has a lot of negatives in my opinion but it is still a great city builder. Not as great as Zeus: Master of Olympus but still a great game and I hope the new updates flesh it out more.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: You will suffer a bronze-age systems collapse on every map. Good luck. Nebuchadnezzar is a hardcore city-building puzzle game that will make you rip your hair out in frustration. Not for the faint of heart. Balancing production, consumption, and trade becomes increasingly complex as you attempt to juggle more resources/goods. Your amazing city is really just a house of cards and can collapse into slums and abandonment in mere minutes if the logistical puzzle is not perfectly balanced.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very fun I played it for 14 hours straight, and then 7 hours after I woke up.  But every time one industry has a hiccup, then everything turns to crap. Everything in this game seems to hinge on one thing. All you need is one thing to go wrong and your entire system collapses. The moment you think everything is stable and place one thing down. BAM! Instant collapse. Don't have fish? Guess what, you don't have beer, clothing, jewelry, meat, furniture, and anything else that the housing that relied on that one frigging item made. There is no grace period, so to speak. The instant the housing reaches zero of any one thing they're gone. Instant collapse.Not only that, but but just try to balance the books. It is near impossible without trade. Removed everything I could to a skeleton crew and still the taxes did not cover the wage payments. After I got trade started, I turned taxes off and set the wages to max. This was when everyone started rioting, buildings started constantly burning down, crime started happening everywhere, disease plagued the city. This is what lowering the taxes and raising the wages was supposed to prevent. None of this was happening until I did this. Yes, I made sure I didn't have it reversed.Everything going smooth? No problems? WRONG! Haven't changed one thing just admiring my build and everything starts collapsing for no apparent reason. Checked all the housing, and they have everything they need but the people are fleeing the city in droves.Really seems like the issues had no real cause. Like it were just some sort of glitch. I tried to push past it and figure out a solution, but nothing seemed to work. I never do this, but I Finally said screw this F&#K*NG game and rage quit.  Yes, it really was rage inducing. Wanna be Miffed Off at insanity? Play this game.  It was fun at the times when I wasn't screaming at the monitor. I might try it again later from scratch, but right now, NOPE!

_childDocuments_.review: I never thought that I would ever find a game that compared with my old Sierra favourites like Caesar, Pharaoh, Zeus, etc, but this one really does fit the bill. I have just completed the 10th of the 12 campaign missions and although they get progressively more difficult to achieve the challenge to complete each one is impossible to ignore. Over 60 hours of game play already and I have still have 2 more missions and scenarios to play so in my opinion that's money really well spent. Highly recommend this game especially for those who played the games I mentioned previously and for others that haven't. However be patient and stick with it as you might find it a bit tricky to achieve all the targets (prestige especially) at first. Excellent game, go try it!

I'm not stupid (I'm pretty sure), but after three tries, I'm done attempting to skirt whatever the game wants me to do, which is to irrigate 82 tiles with only three irrigation pumps when those only supply enough water for the one field, and one pasture, which in this case is is a third of what I need... which isn't near any my goals. How do I do this? Make me feel dumb when you show me how.Might come back to sandbox it, but otherwise not impressed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a waste of time. One single mistake during city building causes your city to die. One disease, one fire, one of anything causes you to lose since the economy is balanced on a knife's edge. Prestige system is terrible, not explained well and all around ♥♥♥♥. City watch is useless, you need countless of them around houses, warehouses, farms, produciton buildings, you basically won't have enough workers for them. Water pump is enough for like 7 canal tiles which means you will be spamming them all over the place. No road blocks is just ridiculous. _childDocuments_.review: A nice love letter to old school city builders, if you’ve been a fan of Impressions Games, you’ll almost certainly enjoy this one.Compared to those it’s definitely a bit heavier on the logistic side of things, but in return it’s very transparent in terms of what each building produces and has a detailed breakdown of production, consumption and surplus, which makes managing larger cities a lot smoother.I’m not entirely sold on the newly introduced military system, which feels a bit micromanagy, but I’m in general not a big fan of that specific aspect of city builders, so I’m not going to be the most suited to judging it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're trying this, chances are you're a fan of Pharaoh and looking for a similar type game.  After the first 6 levels I'm enjoying it immensely.  What I love best is the ability to set routes for some of the buildings (bazaar, wells, priests. etc).  This eliminates that stupid walker mechanic that requires you to set roadblocks everywhere you don't want them to go or they'll wonder off into the wild, blue yonder.  Yes, there are a few other buildings that you cannot set a route (firemen, healers, city watch), so you can't control where they go, but it hasn't caused any problems as far as I've seen.  There are many other features I feel that have improved upon the mechanics established by games such as Pharaoh.  We'll see how if the game can continue to hold interest after continued playings, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the closest any game has come to recapturing the old Impressions City builders (Pharaoh, Zeus, Emperor, Caesar etc).This type of city-builder game focuses very heavily on production and distribution of goods to supply your population, where a mistake in logistics management can cause the whole city to come crashing down. If you're expecting something more like a SimCity or Cities: Skylines, you might end up frustrated with the strong presence of logistics management aspects and harsh penalties for making mistakes in that department.This game will likely appeal most to fans of the old Impressions city builders (of which it seems to be a spiritual successor), or other city builders with a strong focus on logistics such as Anno or maybe the Settlers.It isn't exactly the same as the Impressions games, though. Some features such as warfare or religion are missing. On the other hand, the features that are there feel like (IMHO) they have been overall improved from the old games, with better customizability and quality of life.PROS (as compared to the Impressions games)-You have direct control over the paths taken by market and service walkers, removing the need for unrealistic-looking closed road loops and allowing much greater flexibility when laying out your city.-You can control how much labour an individual industry/agriculture/etc building uses, and how much of that labour is used for goods haulers vs actual producers (e.g. a building further from a warehouse may need an extra hauler to ensure constant supply), giving you a bit more flexibility.-Improved system for warehouses and the flow of goods between them. Warehouses themselves now cost no labour and no longer have their own haulers. Instead there is a new type of building (the caravanserai), dedicated to moving goods from warehouse A to warehouse B as per your configuration.-Monument buildings are extremely customizable, and can be designed by a tile-based system (There is also still the option to build the monument from a template if you don't feel like designing a custom one)-Trade is a bit more dynamic, as the prices of goods vary depending on your prestige and relationship with the city you're trading with-3 different classes of labourers, each needed for different jobs, giving a bit of extra depth. (This is similar to the concept of elite housing but taken a few steps further)CONS (as compared to the Impressions games)-No military mechanics or other diplomatic interaction besides trade and requests-No religion mechanics where the gods need to be kept satisfied-Campaign missions lack variety. Each mission essentially unlocks another tier of housing and tells you to build a slightly larger capital city than in the previous mission. In the older games there might have been some other missions spliced in that are more oriented for building a smaller town geared for trade, military or producing a lot of a specific resource, rather than always building a large capital.-The very limited speed and distance of basic haulers from buildings, and the corresponding need to rely heavily on caravanserais, takes some time to get used to.Also as of this writing there aren't yet any crime/fire/disease features but those are confirmed for release in the 1.2 patch in September 2021.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Maps are really small, making city building frustrating. Balancing finances is counter-intuitive and thus painfully difficult to do. The range for resource transferring is WAY too low and honestly shouldn't exist at all.Overall the game is just ridiculously restrictive, it drains it of all of the fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: To make it short, if you want to chill playing a puzzle like, retro, city builder, give this game a try.If you played Caesar III back in the days, liked it and want to play something that looks like it, you may like Nebuchadnezzar. Note that a lot of city mechanics are simpler (as of update 1.1, no fire, no disease, no god wrath or plagues, etc.). You must choose the market merchant pathing in Nebuchadnezzar, so house levels don't drop due to some random factor, which is nice. I didn't see any military thing either which is also a good point for me as I don't like it in this kind of games.Edit: 50+ hours, last mission done, damn I had a great time! Still recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I expected I'd be getting an improved Pharaoh/Cleopatra, but Nebuchadnezzar that came out more than twenty years after those is nowhere near their level. The mechanics are very bare bones, there is no pressure, no upkeep, so everything is about just waiting long enough. There really is no sense of progression as you always start on the same-ish very bland map, build the same stuff and then just wait till you tick your objectives. The production chains are not very interesting, the logistic micromanagement doesn't really bring anything, your city doesn't feel very lively and there simply isn't anything interesting going on.

_childDocuments_.review: SHORT: I definitely recommend the product! No question about that! I have been waiting for something similar for years and overall I was not disappointed. BUT! Very importantly, the game is far from perfect and I have a few comments, especially for the developers.LONG: The game is in dire need of walls. Whether there is war in the game or not (I think it is better that there is not), without walls there are just no Mesopotamian cities, so characteristic were the walls not only surrounding the cities but also within the cities (the temple complexes and palaces were surrounded by their own walls, they were small cities within the city!)The game's trading system is horribly presented, even with the help of tutorials, it's not clear exactly how it works. I would consult a UX specialist to review this because in its current state it is confusing and frustrating.The way the markets work is unnecessarily overcomplicated. It doesn't make a game more complex to have to enter the distribution routes of traders one by one, it just makes it annoying. Within a certain range, I would make this feature work by itself. Managing caravans will still cause enough problems, but I can swallow that. The optimization of the game is just terrible. I'm sorry to say that. No matter how good your computer is, the game will always load millennia when you start it. Not just a few minutes, oh, no, but what seems like an infinite amount of time. No joke, I went to brew a coffee and the game was still loaded when I came back. This must be due to poor file-handling there can be no other reason. Something needs to be done about this because more than once I specifically preferred not to even start the game because I had 20-30 minutes to play, but if 10+ minutes of that is loading, it's just not worth it.Still, all in all, this is a great game with a lot of work, research, heart, and soul behind it. It shows in every pixel. As a game developer myself, I know how much work it is for a small team. That's why I want my criticism to be taken constructively by the developers, even if they don't take all my advice. I enjoy the game tremendously, and there is not much that separates it from being a true classic in my eyes. I really hope - indeed I know - that the game will be polished a lot more by the devs so that I will happily return to it year after year.PS: The music is amazing!

_childDocuments_.review: Okay game overall, and if you like the genre, this one might give you some chill time for some time. However, not recommended for the ones not familiar with the genre. I got stuck in 4th tutorial (hence the low playtime). In this game first 5 missions of the campaign are considered as (are also designed as) tutorial. Problem with 4th tutorial is that some of the game mechanics are locked (that will be introduced in 5th tutorial , probably), results with impossible funding management of the city and the the inevitable bankruptcy. One of the 2 income mechanics (and the main one) is locked for this mission (to introduce in 5th tutorial) whereas the 2nd income mechanic does not even provide a sustainable financial setting, let alone profiting.I like micro-managing. But I don't like micro-managing with some mechanics of the game locked away. Problem is: The game (its mechanics, features, settings etc.) is designed as a whole (theoretically). Locking away some mechanics of the game without adapting other parts will cause problems, as with 4th tutorial here.4th mission is doable, yes. If you "rush" one of the objectives with certain steps, or if you plan "long-term", like really "long term" and make certain steps for it, with just cheating or modding etc. But this is a tutorial, let the player have a chill playthrough for the tutorials. This is an elemental design flaw (just my opinion) that put me away from the game

_childDocuments_.review: I played the whole campaign and enjoyed the overall experience. Would buy again.I particularly liked:- That you have very good control over which goods go where, although it's quite heavy on micromanagement, but everything runs very smoothly.- Setting (I love ancient Mesopotamia).- Music (very fitting and relaxing)- Gameplay feels like a hybrid between Anno and Pharaoh. It builds on existing concepts, but is a very refreshing experience.There are a few things that could be improved:- The overall storytelling and how it is integrated in the campaign. You essentially get to read a piece of history and then play a a map, but it has little to no relation to what is going on at that point in history. The campaign maps are all very similar, but essentially incremental. It doesn't feel like a campaign, but it's a consecutive expansion of features/goods/building/upgrades.- Historical accuracy is quite lacking. Are we not going to mention the Late Bronze Age Collapse at all? :D  No decline in civilization around 1200BC? Nothing? - Obscurity about a building's status: some issues in buildings cause an icon to spawn over it, but it's not enough. With the heavy micromanagement (you have to set up what goes where), it would be useful if warehouses and caravanserais had icons indicating what goods they are set up to store/transport. Or when a production building has no resource or full stock, there could also be an icon to indicate that. Could also add a visual indicator how many employees a building currently has. - Overall balancing, especially regarding money. In some missions, you are set up to go broke before you are even able to open trade to make some profit, but once you do, you can basically ignore money. And upgraded houses pay more taxes than they earn wages. Really? Is that how economy works?- Production chains feel a little cookie-cutter. - Huge temples, but very small local reach. - Please allow me to open more than one window. Setting up goods transport across the city can a real pain because you have to go back and forth several times between warehouse and caravanserai.- There are some bugs, too.

_childDocuments_.review: Well... I want to like this game, but insofar it has a defect that many similar games have: all phases feel like a 'puzzle', meaning, you kinda have to solve the one, correct way of finishing the phase. There map blockers (hills) where you can't buldoze or build anything, and they seem placed in such a manner that you have to 'figure out' the correct way to place your buildings, otherwise, you end up without space or access to water or enough room to pass both a road and a cannal. I don't like this system. Strategy games are there to let you do things 'your way', and either succeed or fail. If a map is construed in such a way that it has a propper way to be 'beaten', well, that empoverishes the game. I tryed to check the game's full potential for now, but there are no random or custom scenarios, or sandbox maps. They inform us that those are on the way, but ultil then, my review has to be bleek like this.

_childDocuments_.review: This style of city-builder has always been my favourite, with just the right level of management for my taste - relatively small areas with a lot of close logistics work, rather than the wider, more distant-from-the-people remit of something like Civ. Nebuchadnezzar does a great job of recreating the feel of the old isometric games, but with a lot of improvements to the way things run that makes it far less frustrating to play. It's still a somewhat simplistic game, with new features being added in updates, but what's there is solid and engaging. My only gripe is the overreliance on trade - once copper is available as a resource, the early game becomes a mad rush to gain access to the trade partner who can supply it so that you can stabilise your whining middle classes. Mines have been added, but not in the campaign. Overall though this is a really solid game, one I easily lose myself in for hours and can see myself doing so again and again in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: English review here, česká recenze níže.So, first of all, it is necessary to realize that the whole game is practically done by 2 guys from Prague. Respect!It's a tribute to classic city building simulators. It is closest to Pharaoh from Sierra (desert environment, farm irrigation). Is the game size comparable to AA or AAA titles? No. Is it a fun game for tens of hours? Sure!To this day, I sometimes play Ceasar 3 or Pharaoh. Nebuchadnezzar brings the original environment of ancient Mesopotamia, improved graphics and expanded logistics options. The game is built on the right settings of logistics and production chains. I like it. On the contrary to the old games, it lacks culture, festivals, gods (shut be added in the new update) and warfare. I don't miss war in Nebuchadnezzar, although fighting Hannibal's elephants in Caesar 3 was satisfying 😊.I have currently played 33 hours and completed 10 missions on normal difficulty. I only know version 1.2.11. I have read in older reviews observations that are no longer valid. So keep an eye on the changes, the authors are improving the game.The game is very logistics-oriented. I had to leave some missions (I ran out of money or my production collapsed) and I succeeded up to 2-3x attempts. And that's grea, its a challenge!Personally, I don't like building temples, but I understand that someone else will like it. The maps didn't seem small to me, I take it as part of the task of saving space. The game is accompanied by nice music, menu and icons are intuitive.Pros:• The original environment of ancient Mesopotamia• It's a challenge (difficulty makes you think, plan and optimize)• The campaign teaches you gradually the increasingly complex mechanisms• You will feel nostalgia if you like Ceaser 3 or PharaohConc:• Playing is a little bit repetitive – you have to build each city in the same order• Still just a few mechanisms (perhaps the next update will improve)• I dont understand the system of healers and firefighters (it would make more sense if the route could also be set up as at retailers, etc.)ČESKY:Je potřeba si uvědomit, že celou hru dělají 2 chlápci z Prahy. Respekt!Je to pocta klasickým simulátorům. Nejblíže to má k Pharaoh od Sierry (poušť, zavlažování farem). Je to velikostí hry srovnatelné s AA nebo AAA tituly? Ne. Je to zábavná hra na desítky hodin pro nostalgiky? Jasně! Dodnes občas hraju Ceasar 3 nebo Pharaoh. Nebuchadnezzar přináší originální prostředí starověké Mezopotámie, vylepšenou grafiku a rozšířené možnosti logistiky. Hra je na správném nastavení logistiky a výrobních řetězců postavena. Za mě je to plus. Naopak proti starým hrám ji chybí kultura, festivaly, bohové (má být doplněno v novém updatu) a válčení. Mě válčení v Nebuchadnezzarovi nechybí, i když bojovat proti Hannibalovým slonům v Caesarovi 3 bylo uspokojující 😊.Aktuálně jsem odehrál 33 hodin a splnil 10 misí na normální obtížnost. Znám pouze verzi 1.2.11. Četl jsem ve starších recenzích postřehy, které už neplatí. Tak sledujte změny, autoři hru postupně vylepšují.Hra je hodně orientována na logistiku (kam správně co přivést). Některé mise jsem musel opustit (došlo zlato, zkolabovala mi výroba) a povedly se mi až na 2-3x pokus. A to je dobře! Stavění chrámů mě osobně moc nebaví, ale chápu, že někdo jiný se v tom třeba vyžije. Mapy mi malé nepřišly, beru to jako součást úkolu, že se musí šetřit místem. Hru doprovází pěkná hudba, ovládání je intuitivní.Výhody:Originální prostředí starověké MezopotámieJe to výzva (náročnost vás nutí přemýšlet, plánovat a optimalizovat)Kampaň vás plynule a pozvolně učí stále složitějším mechanismůmNostalgie (pokud máte rádi Ceaser 3 a Pharaoh)Nevýhody:Opakované hraní působí repetetivně – každé město musíte stavět ve stejném pořadíStále málo mechanismů (snad zlepší příští update)Nechápu systém dosahu healerů a firefighterů (dávalo by větší smysl, kdyby šla také nastavit trasa jako u prodejců zboží atd.)

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately a bad take on the old classic games like Caesar, Pharaoh and Zeus.I really wanted to like this game, and tried to power through the campaign at least.But i now give up at scenario 8, it simply became so much not fun.There is so much in the game that is just blah, but i try to list some of the worst in my opinion.- The logistics system with the warehouse, ports, and caravans is just badly implemented in the game.  And there should be better tools available to micromanage distribution.- The way firefighters, healers and town watch moves around  is really bad. They seemingly just roam about at random and   when they reach a building where they reset the risk counter to 0 they turn around and go to another building far away   and resets that and so on. They will leave all other buildings in the area alone even when they are at high risk.- And fires, disease outbreaks and burglaries will happen even with no buildings over minimal risk in the overlay- And the huge temples which you only need loads  of bricks to build.............Except if you really need to scratch the old Impression Games itch i would not recommend buying this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Impression games for a long time. Well this game doest realy play like them. It's a mix between Anno and Caeasar and co. If you want a real spiritual successor I think you will be disapointed. However, it is pretty interesting in itself. The beggining is REALY easy. difficulty increase gradually. The challenge comes from managing the production chain and the lack of space (may be cheesed if you know what you're doing). I have finished it (the last mission is challenging enough) so I can say that for a first game it is not bad. I would recommend for people liking gestion and managing commerce and industry. Again it is NOT a clone of the old Impression games, if this is what you want you WILL be disapointed. Come with an open mind and wait until le 5th or 6th mission to see some sort of challenge.  I'd like to see more (and maybe a little more colorfull :DD brown gets tiring after a while).

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of old school sierra isometric city-builders then you'll probably love this game as much as I do. The logistics and balancing your economy and production is deep and rewarding when you get to higher housing levels. In this one you tell the vendors where to go and distribute goods, no more road blocks. So you can plan your city out any way you want, it will be as efficient as the lay out you choose. The historical and culture aspect here is great too, it will really get you into mesopotamian history. A few things I would love to see are the ability to shift click the green flag for caravan/market routes and apply to everyone instead of having to click every single one everytime to sync up. Also the military aspect is lacking, I get it, it's a city builder first, but end game is stale without some action, and let's be real, 3/4 of history from that part of the globe and time period was war, lots and lots of war. Even if things were broken back in the pharaoh/caesar days I think everyone agrees seeing sentries on your walls and defending your ACTUAL city was really cool, not some menu with blocks. A night cycle set on a timer would be amazing too to make it feel alive. All in all, great game, scratches that itch, but I really hope there's a combat overhaul at some point.

_childDocuments_.review: The game takes over five minutes to startup everytime. It then takes around two minutes to load a scenario. This really breaks it for me...Now about the actual game:The game itself has a great story with lots of historical details which are definitely very interesting. The mechanics start getting a bit boring after a while, it does seem a bit similar to Caesar or Pharaoh but for me personally some aspects of micro-management make it a bit tedious, I understand these are the mechanics of the game (having to design the routes for every market so goods get properly distributed amongst all houses, same with transfering goods between warehouses via the caravansarai...). It´s good for 2-3 hours, but after that it just gets boring to play a new scenario and having to design the same district over and over again.Overall a beautiful game, great setting, great script/story, definitely give it a try and see if it´s your style (and if loading times are decent for you, I´ve seen it´s a common problem). But in the long-run I couldn´t get into it.

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up playing city building games and used to think to myself, today's games with the high specs are great, but i wish they would make games like they used to (Caesar 3, Pharaoh etc) . My prayers have been answered !I'm only a couple hours in and have yet to experience everything this game has to offer,  but so far I think this is a very good game, they have clearly gone for the same idea as the classic city builders, but with a touch of updated mechanics. I especially like how you can direct routes for your workers, where in the old impression games it would be a pain making sure all your goods were evenly distributed.  There are one or two things i would still like added, for example watching buildings be constructed (the only construction i'm aware of is the default temple, customs temples just appear once you place them). However with the current updates that have and are still to come I'm sure these things will be taken into consideration.Overall, would i recommend this game from what I've played so far? yes. This game seems to have a lot of potential, and as previously stated, with the updates coming through i can only see this game getting better and better
