_childDocuments_.review: It has been too long since I have played a game like this. So excuse me if I am not very objective in saying how much I have missed this gaming experience and how much Nebuchadnezzar has scratched this itch.I loved the art style and music after the first trailer and after building a few cities I adore them.I just wish the UI was a bit larger on 1440p since I don't play on 4K and can't use the option for 4K UI.As for the gameplay it's totally addictive and gave be just the right mix of complexity, provided by the 3 different citizen classes and the 35+ resources / goods, 6 services to manage, and simplicity because production chains are just two goods long.The manual monument building, section by section, and prop by prop is a true novelty in this genre and makes sure that each new city is crowned by a unique monument I built.Trade is a puzzle of imports and exports, different but always fun to solve on each new map.The campaign is the only way to play in the current version of the game, and while there is no dedicated sandbox the last few missions are on huge maps, with lots of money so they feel like a sandbox game.Some will argued that there is no challenge because there is no plague, fire, destruction, armies, angry Gods or whatever else but I didn't miss those gameplay mechanics one bit as I was too busy enjoying the process of city building, monument building, production and consumption balancing, upgrading 3 citizens classes homes, which all required different goods and services to level up.The overlays for each of these where a big help and the manual placement of distribution paths gave me total control which made the cities success completely dependent on my own skill. This can get tidious in a major city as there are hundreds of these to place and replace but to me that is the definition of fun in a game like this. I just can't wait to see all the mods people will make for this game and add new campaigns, scenarios, maps, monuments, goods, production chains, buildings and who knows maybe even more services and game mechanics. Oh endless joy !The game is totally stable btw not one CTD or any game breaking bug so far.

_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I love all of the games that this game is based on. Pharaoh, Caesar, basically all of the Impressions Games line. And I was really excited for this. I bought it the first day that it came out and have been playing through, but right now I can't recommend this game as anywhere near the level of what I was hoping for. It is not intuitive and even with a walk through the distribution system is seriously annoying. I want to manage a city, not micro-manage it. Setting routes is nice, huge advance in game play, but these routes don't have any automatic re-route in the case of a restructure. It's nice that a little exclamation mark shows up over the building you've effected, but it would be nice if there was a mix of auto-routing and ability to customize. Even in a smallish, but getting bigger city, keeping up with reroutes and restructure is kind of annoying. Understanding the warehouse system is also a bit of a to-do. They've basically complicated a system that is mostly fine as an automated thing. Basically the idea was really awesome, being able to micro-manage when something isn't working (stupid water carriers), or when you want something specific is super cool. However having zero AI automation is basically swinging way too far in the other direction. It takes a lot of the fun parts of the games this was based on an whittles them down to nearly non-existent. Additionally the introduction of building range makes it so you more or less block all types of the same building together, leading to a really boring looking city and very narrow structure of play. I think that in the effort to distinguish themselves they created a game that is definitely unique and memorable, but in a lot of ways that are not ideal. It's hard though, to walk a line of nostalgia and individuality, especially when you are competing with some absolute cult classic games.I have 2 more hours to play before I have to decide if I want to return the game, but honestly I will likely keep the game in the hopes that updates are made and things become more big type fun, and less micro-management play.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: People seriously won't walk a block to the market to prevent themselves from starving? Everything must be Doordashed. It makes this game 100% a route management and placement optimization game at a precision level. Some folks might like that as it's more of a puzzle game but I don't really find it appealing in a city management game myself.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I like This game.  A long time ago I played many hours of Pharaoh and Cleopatra. In some ways this is similar. But the differences are in some ways better. In P&C the movement of all the walkers was randomly generated. This this game you define in a simple manner where you want your traders to walk, thus guaranteeing that if you have supplies in your shops they will supply to the houses. In P&C you had to more carefully construct the road system and road blocks to ensure supply of goods. This system is better in my opinion.I also very much like the right mouse button option. When pressed you can select 5 options, Delete objects, build road, build irrigation ditch, build warehouse, build the last object you created which isn't one of the of the previous 4. If right mouse click on an object you also get a menu which allows you to delete it, copy it, delete multiple, copy + which allows you to copy the object as presently configured. For example if you copy a clay pit with the non default number of employees it will allow you to create a similar configured copy of the one you right clicked on.So the right click options are great time savers.The shear scale of the maps are impressive.The learning curve and tutorials are set up at a good pace. You learn just enough in each of the scenarios to learn a lot but not get over whelmed.There are three different social classes in this game. The classes have their own kind of housing and different levels and also need different supplied commodities.  Carefully managing these different classes is one of the main challenges of the game. The trading with other cities is easy to understand, and is a necessary part of the game.There is a lot to learn and a lot of fun doing it on all the different maps. I haven't gotten to the warfare yet. but I am looking forward t it.There is a campaign, which is what I am working through right now. but there also stand alone scenarios also.I'm having a lot of fun playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A good classic city builder in what many other have described as a Pharaoh/Empire rise of the middle kingdom like game.  Nebuchadnezzar for such an odd name does justice to the games that have come before it with better systems, UI, and looking at future updates more content and features (with the exception of military as of now). I was surprised as how quick the tutorial but it was filled with good enough info to get started, the campaign seems decent in length and there is freeplay maps that you can choose from.  The added fire, sickness, and crime update fixes what most of the initial launch worry was about however I think these could be expanded upon with droughts and and famines, maybe even floods to really bring it home. The building doesn't have "walling" to separate districts but does opt for you to decorate around wealth higher class citizens and also asks that you keep industry away due to pollution.  The decoration list is decent with different status and paths that all match the aesthetic.  While im on the subject of art the game looks visually good, buildings are easy to see their economic state as well as being easy to identify.  Some animations could be added to foliage or fields but you can still see fields grow and get harvested, fish jump through the rivers, etc. To cut it short the game is good, 20 USD gives you pretty much a complete game with room for expansion, the devs seem eager to keep building off of it and with time it can only get better. Worth the pick up.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: If you had played and liked Pharaoh from Sierra back in the days then you would like this one as well. Similar but enhanced mechanics to my taste.I have been enjoying the campaign so far. It is not too easy so that you feel the achievement when you complete a level. On top of that I loved the detailed information it provides regarding the history of the ancient civilization.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: As addicting as Pharaoh, it a few ways different and in many ways better. It misses a few features but nothing that would cause you to skip this one. Many reviews complain that it tries to copy Pharaoh while failing at it. I strongly disagree, it has it's own ideas and they provide different puzzles like handling logistics with goods.Keep up with updates, things like taxes and wages, scenarios were already implemented.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I recently played this game and found it to be pretty cool. However, I think it could use more depth and content to make it even better. The logistics system is new and interesting, but it would be helpful to have a wiki or some other resource to help players in general. I also found it strange that we have to import wood planks instead of being able to cut down trees ourselves. The graphics are nice, but I think the game could benefit from some additional weather effects like sand storms and insect infestations. the soundtrack is really cool and sets an atmospheric mood for the game. I also think some annoying character would be cool when playing throughout the scenario game mode, and the character will say some stuff for example when you have a riot going on somewhere or when you have plague happening in the city or when people are starting to leave the city, it would be cool touch and make the game more alive. Overall, I would give this game a 7/10 rating.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I'm kind of sorry, but I can not recomend that game. Even if I really want to, because it is remarkable how the programmers tried to make a good game. I'm a huge fan of old school city builders like "Ceasar III". This game is NOT like this. This game is just more like a complex puzzle. It is not possible to play relaxed and build a working city. It is more like that you need to puzzle detailed things and balance stuff. But not in a cool way it is quickly very anoying. Even the military (like "Pharaoh" or "Ceasar") is not implemented. Maybe it will change, but for now at this price it is unfortenately not worth it. Only if you obsessed with freaking complex puzzleing, this game could be some thing for you. In any other case: Don't buy it for more than about maybe 3–5€.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, labour of love. Great depth. Beautiful Atmosphere.I love this game to bits. It improves on the Impression games and i really wonder if the remake of Pharaoh will be this good.(Yeah this game is miles ahead of the travesty that is New Era)This game has intelligent solutions for problems  the old Impression games had.If you like those, then this is the evolution of the genre it needed.Fantastic game.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: The Pharaoh remake can't come fast enough. Some of the mechanics added in this game make no sense. Pollution, really? Buildings need to have a slightly longer range. Caravans are nice but I shouldn't need them to walk some clay 3 blocks down.I need to stockpile 4 warehouses worth of goods in order to bribe a city to start trading with me. I'm fine with it having a cost but 4 warehouses have a large footprint that I need to accommodate in my city. Why not just ask for money instead? Or let me send partial "gifts" to these cities until i cover what they want to start trading with me.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A nice game with some interesting concepts, runs well and is quite pretty.Unfortunately, that's it. It's like playing Pharaoh or Caesar with a modern overhaul mod.It's got some logistics going on which might appeal to some, and the wonder design is nifty.At the moment though, there's not enough new or exciting for me to recommend it.One might as well play ye good olde Caesar 2.I might come back when there's some additional content, background noise (cities feel... empty, despite the amount of things going on), research trees etc.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: From the early reviews I was worried that this game will be too shallow and uninteresting, but it turned out to be just right for me to relax after work when I don't have the brainpower to play something like Anno 1800.+ intuitive controls+ comprehensive tutorial+ just the right amount of complexity+ music that sets the mood perfectly+ free post-launch updates that introduced more features- could do with just one more level of zoom and graphic fidelity- only some workers can be clicked and tracked and their voice acting is hilariously bad :DOverall much more than I expected, totally get this game on sale if you like relaxed city builders ^^
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: The Caesar III experience you like. Money may not become a problem, but space will. Smart city planning and worker allocation make this an interesting and beautiful addition to the genre. Less spontaneous breaking buildings, more tools for min-maxing more your production. You will find yourself asking "Am I willing to build slums for extra workforce I can't feed?" when you miss the challenge of Caesar III and Pharao, which got lost with Zeus and Emperor. if you wish to build as large and wide as you want.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar is a modern successor of games like Pharaoh or Zeus. The user interface is extremely polished and streamlined, so much better than the games that inspired it. And I love that the focus is on the logistics and building side of things, without having to be worried all the time about nasty things like fires or malaria. Additionally, you are in complete control of your workers and caravans, as you can set exact path for each of them they should follow, instead of relying on the awkward roadblocks. The feature of designing your own monuments is pretty cool, too. Add to it great graphics, inspiring sound track, slick tutorial, modding support, and you have a package that will please many. Definitely recommended!Edit: the developers are very active and brought us new features, such as wages and taxes, or crime, fires, and diseases. Fortunately, they did it just right, so these are welcome additions which do not detract from the logistics aspect of the game. Looking forward to see what next is coming - we were promised festivals and deities. Nice!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game a while back but barely played past the first mission, the game felt a bit empty and soulless. HOWEVER, after a few patches, an expansion and a lot of love and work, this is a worthy part of the Caesar / Pharaoh / Zeus family. I am really enjoying the game and struggling through the campaign. But we'll get there...
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: this game is all about moving goods A to B and B to C. The city building is a lot like Anno where every city looks the same to a certain extent. Really good if you like production chains, exporting/importing goods, and providing needs to residents. I haven't gotten to multi-input production chains yet but eager to implement those.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Very unfinished game. Once you balance out the city you can leave the game there running, your city will never turn turmoil.Lack of features, Campaign becomes repetitive and boring after 2-3 missions.There is only one aspect of the game that was solved nicely is the "walker-path-edit" system.Graphics are beautiful, although buildings could have different sprites, they look very homogeneous next to each other.The music nicely blends to the theme.After 20+ years as a successor of the grand caesar3 and pharaoh I think this is really not enough. I recommend to wait at least 1 year until you'd but it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Overall really like this game but it is heavily focused on (micro)managing the economy. There appear to be no real consequences for any behavior other than not planning out your caravan routes properly. More diplomacy etc. would be nice. Or keeping your people happy beyond fulfilling their basic needs. There is lots of room for fun improvements. The game looks beautiful and is very atmospheric.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Still a long way to go to become a worthy successor of Impression's games but the devs are constantly improving it. Right now the issue i have is with economy, especially that taxation is fixed property tax, and wage can't be changed, i'd like to include income tax, as well as ability to change wages and taxes just like in Pharaoh.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: So, i have played this game for around 18 hours (including some menu idel time).I really want to like this game. It reminds me of back when i played Emperor as it has some of the same mechanics and the same visual feel with some extra features.However the gameplay is lacking. Instead of using Emperor's "Workers travel random paths", you can now set checkpoints for workers to travel. The first thought is "isn't that a good think? doesn't it just take away some silly micromanagement?", and yes it does that, but that also removes kind of the only hard gameplay.What remains is to just do the same thing in each level, over and over again, and a lot of time waiting for temples to finish building.If you are looking for some easy achivement points you can get while being afk, go for it, otherwise i would look at some of the better city builders that are out there
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Since, I am an old fan of these old games series like Pharaoh, Ceasar, and Empire. I really have a high hope of this game and I am glad that I found this little gem.One new big main mechanic in this game is the worker slots in each building. You can lower your production efficiency for lower upkeep, and  you can choose to either employ more worker for better efficiency or more transporter for better logistic, and this is fun, very fun, it's allow me to create my own play style.The other mechanics are there, such as production chain, local market supply, trade with neighborhood, risk prevention, social class. There is no war or military aspect in game, which is a little disappoint, however the developer just start to implement religion and gods aspect to the game. So there is still hope for a perfect game.The achievement is quite challenging but still possible. The campaign got a good time length. Overall, I really enjoy this game so much.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: It's technically sound, but compared to other contenders in the genre pretty simple and boring; To me at least it's pretty much the same as Aven Colony. Looks great on paper. Simply not worth the time in the end.It has great graphics that capture the old school vibe pretty well and in the limited time I didn't encounter any bugs. The warehouse/market system however is tidious, and the population fluctuation probably looks very good on paper but with the randomness of the goods deliveries makes for a very annoying time.I really, really want to like it. If only because I like the art style and setting, and if you really want to play a pharao/cleopatra something revival, you will probably be okay. It's definitely not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: No sandbox, no dice.Imagine your favorite Impressions builder and then dumb the walkers down significantly and you will have this game. Walkers don't have a range, you have to set their paths. That was the beauty of the old Impressions games; you build the building and its walkers would find what they need... just make sure you build it in range.Also, if the dev is going to deactivate beta keys, I should get a clean slate on playtime and achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I haven't played much yet but it seems like a decent Zeus/Emperor like game. I can't get past one issue....it seems like the pedestrians and workers are unclickable and do not make any sounds or comments. One of my favorite things to do in Zeus was to hear the people talk about what was going on, hear the gods comment on everything, hear the workers talk about their job, etc. Having this missing really takes away from the game for me. Hopefully in the future some voice acting will be added but for now I can't recommend it.Maybe that's me being picky, but damn does it feel lifeless without it and I've only played for less than half an hour.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved Pharaoh, Ceaser, or Emperor: Rise of the Middle Kingdom, you'll love this. They took the core gameplay and modernized it. Instead of the unreliable walker system, you get to manually plot routes for services provides while industry is automated. And theres no terrible combat! Take ur time, build an empire, and enjoy the beautiful artwork.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: There are just things in this that doesn't make sense.1) When you build a farm, you need to have either bakeries or storage close. Instead of being able to direct the transport worker ON THE FARM to were goods needs to go. So trying to maximise farms with bakeries you cant have bakeries just outside the limit of the farm, even though they are right next to the other bakeries that the transport worker can deliver to. Crist its frustrating to plan.2) There is a map view where the trees and everything is removed so you can plan out what to build where. Nice... but no. Because when you place down buildings they are removed from view as well, which means you cant see where you placed farms and fields. so you have to switch back and forth between this view and normal view. It also doesn't show how much area the other farms can lay claim to via fields. So this view just isn't good enough. If you are trying to min/max things to any degree, this is really frustrating.3) The farms doesn't seem to display the number of fields possible in its area. Also you seem to be able to hire more farmers than the farms max possible allowed fields, which is a bit weird.4) Then there is time. Time vs travel vs goods doesn't seem to match anything realistic/meaningfull. If your farm produces enough for x amout of people. It will still take several years to get the goods all the way to those people so that they can level up their homes. This is sort of a minor thing. but it still breaks any emergence with regards to time passing.The game is good looking and building is okay and the gameplay feeling really seems to mimik the good old games of this type. (from the little below 2 hours that i played)But there just seems to be so many of the small details about gameplay (like described above) that just isn't thought through. Its not like they have to invent a completely different way of doing things. Cause when it comes to distributing goods to villagers, they have excactly what is needed for all the production and everything. You can plan distributing routes.This game really seems to have a lot of potential and a really good feel with UI. But there are just to many things that i feel should have been done differently to make sense.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with its own take of the city builders of old. Can be frustrating at times, but I found that the case with the old games too, so either way go for it.Don't listen to the moaning myrtles about load times - good chance it's your Windows Defender or other antivirus (which you 80% probably don't need in 2024), check if whitelisting the game helps.Works perfectly on Linux as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I consider myself quite a fan of the old Sierra Games, Pharaoh on the top of my mind an heart. Nebuchadnezzar really hits the target on delivering a somewhat modernized experience of old Pharaoh. "Modernized" stands for a lot of QoL changes, like the fact that you dont have the annoying walker "recruiter" on buildings that forces you to have slums on your city.That being said, it is not Pharaoh: it's its own game, and thus there are some differences: If you are expecting a Pharaoh clone this is not it - for instance there is still no military (someone described the game as a "warehouse storage simulation game with monuments" and I think I love it). That being said, the dev team is really reachable and they are adding new stuff quite often, so we may see some of that stuff at some point.TL;DR: If you want a modernized - fun and constantly updated version of old Pharaoh without being old Pharaoh, this is your game!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I've played it for a couple of hours. Sadly I can't recommend it.Yes, its a fun game. And yes It's beautiful and does evoke the feeling of Sierra's old city builders (Pharaoh etc)However. This game does have a flaw that is touched on in some other reviews.As your city grows, the logistics system bogs everything down and makes the game not-fun.The limited range for markets, warehouses etc, the need to individually plan out each and every markets distribution routes for each and every individual seller, and the use of caravans to transport goods from industrial areas to residential, can make your game quite frustrating and boring. The fact you can only gain gold (needed to build) through trade, which requires a bit of investing to get access to, can mean you will and can very quickly get stuck. Which is exasperated by the logistics system which you have to tweak and refresh each time a new building is placed or road. The lack of a deity system, fire, police or structural engineering systems. The lack of military scenario/play. The lack of walker comments/talking etc. These all make the game feel unfinished, unpolished and sadly a little dry.While visually the game can be stunning, it can be dry.I'll re-review it after a few patches, but for now I'd recommend saving your money till maybe 3 to 5 patches down the line, or any major updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think it is worth getting, at least until it supports freeplay/scenarios/random map. Currently only campaign is available, and it is not great either. It fills padded - the only difference between 5th and 6th mission is access to single building and one residential upgrade tier. You are doing exactly the same every time.But what really drives me crazy is the map itself. Not only it is small (by design, as the only challenge in game is limited space), but you can't scroll beyond it for even a pixel - whole screen has always be filled with it. That means UI elements are  covering the map, preventing you from building on some squares. Another weird thing about the map - it is "diamond shaped" - the road grid and map edges are rotated 45 degrees.The monument building is also weird. I had plenty of spare workers and warehouses full of bricks but no one was actually delivering them to building site. At least not with sensible speed. Do I need to assign more workers? There isn't any way to do it.Anyway, unless I missed something, it is much simpler than Caesar or Pharaon, so keep that in mind.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Voice-over lines for walkers have been added, giving some much-needed flavor! Good job, devs!Original review follows:This game lacks charm; there's no sugar-coating that. You can't examine walkers. There's no building-specific ambiance. Your citizens feel more like lifeless logistics robots than actual people.That being said, the logistical problems the game presents are actually fun to solve, and the core gameplay loop of figuring out your production chains - while dry - presents interesting challenges. The difficulty and complexity also ramps up in a sensible way.I do wish the game were a bit more immersive, to make it feel more like a city-builder than a things-mover. Still, it's been interesting and fun enough to merit a lukewarm recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great. It scratches both my city builder and automation itch nicely. There is so much thought put into every facet of the game.I really look forward to see what the modding community will do as the mod support seems to be quite good. The game features combat mission, but there is always a peaceful option if that is not your cup of tea. I was pretty sure I'd skip the combat, but is a clever little turnbased strategy minigame and the vassal system adds a small extra layer to each combat map. Now it's time for me to try my hand at the DLC
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Worthy successor to Impressions Games Series.I really enjoyed playing the Impressions Games like Pharaoh when i was younger. It was easily my favorite game series. Sadly these games were discontinued and the entire formula disappeared. I still replay the games once every 3-4 years or so. So i was happy to finally see a game with the same formula as those ancient games by now. While they are tough shoes to fill and the game ultimately falls a little short from being on the level of my favorite Pharoah it is definutely a great successor and an excellent game to try for those who love the genre.The game does lack a little bit of the unique atmosphere a game like Pharoah had. For me the voice over / music / mission intro was what really got you into the various missions and that is missing in this game. Having said that they have history lessons about the relevant time period in mesopotamian history instead which is also really interesting.The missions do lack a bit of a challenge as well after a certain time. The lack of war, unique events or even invading gods (haha) make it that if you got the city running profitably its usually just waiting for the monuments to finish (this takes rather long even at fastest speed) and expanding your city to have the necessary housing requirements. I am not sure it has great replayability like the Impressions Games do because of that. Having said that the developer is still actively developing the game as well as making more missions.The game maintains quite a few of the old concepts of the classic games but also has a lot of modernizations, which in general work really well:I am a big fan of the waypoint system for service providers. Its what i always thought i would have done to get rid of those pesky roadblocks and it works excellent in this game.The caravan system is another great innovation which fits well with the setting. You control where the goods go. Very important. I think we all remember these cart pushers pushing goods all around the city in the old games!I also really like the trade / dock system the game has. You situate a ton of warehouses next to the dock on the watershore and also add a lot of production buildings next to it. Having more than one dock in the later missions works really well. No horror scenarios here like in that old Heliopolis (?) mission i Pharaoh with the 4 islands! I often imported a good like copper in one dock area. Had the copper jewelers turn it into the finished product. The caravan then takes it to the villas to deposit it in the warehouse where the market people pick em up. Any exces jewelry the caravan people would then deposit in a warehouse near a second dock to export. In general a big fan of this system.Then there is the custom monuments. Another great innovation. Personally i have to say that i just went with the default ones to see what they would look like but on subsequent playthroughs it can be fun to mess around with this.I did customize the look of my beautification / aesthetics. While the amount of gardens / statues / fancy roads at your disposal is fairly low you can customize the colors giving every map a unique feel. Lots of opportunities for creativity in making beautiful cities in this one.All in all its a great game and a worthy successor to the Impressions Games. At the moment it ultimately falls a little short but the game is made by a much smaller team and still in active development! Some great innovations / modernizations have been made and work well. I would highly recommend trying this game if you miss the old classics in this genre like me. I am curious to see what the game will look like in a couple years as well if they improve on the couple things that arent perfect yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Great citybuilder reminiscent of the old Impressions games like Caesar, Pharaoh, Zeus and Middle Kingdom! It's not completely there yet, but its close. A few more systems to finetune worker and goods allocation would be nice as well as a bit more variation in maps and gameplay objectives. Nonetheless a good homage to a near dead genre. And the more games we get in this genre the better!Highly recommended for those who love the genre!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Game is interesting enough until you get to second tier production chains and there it falters. I like that you can set up routes for sellers; The haulers don't seem to want to walk further than next door. The catchment areas seem be random with no consistency. The plebes (peasants, whatev), bless their lazy, flabby little hearts, won't walk 3 blocks to the market? UI is counter-intuitive and unnecessarily complex (clicking on the building SHOULD highlight the catchment areas. Period.  They've added an extra step which is time-consuming and unnecessary). _childDocuments_.review: Rather than write up a review, I'll post the question I got asked on our local forum about the game and my answer.Q: Are you finding that this game is pretty much a clone of the Caesar/Pharoah games, but in a prettier package, or are there any strategic or gameplay differences? I don't really remember enough about those older games to say if it is a clone or not, but it seems to elicit the same feel I remember from those games. Nebuchadnezzar has strategic elements with regard to trading with other cities and with the upcoming 1.4 version there will be military requirements, but pretty much it is everything happening on the one map, like the old games. Not to say that there isn't a lot happening on that map, there is. Each new campaign mission (I'm on my seventh now) unlocks new buildings and other aspects. Planning is very important, but if you goof up where you, say, put your bakeries, you can move them without too much effort. There are more plates spinning with each new mission, but the game doesn't have a frantic feel to it like some other city builders do. I seem to remember that this was the way I felt about Caesar and Pharaoh.Also, and this is important to me, there isn't the "death spiral" aspect you get in Banished or in the more recent Timberborn, where if you fail to plan properly almost everyone dies and it takes forever to get the city back on track. In Nebuchadnezzar if, for instance, you get busy with other things and neglect that you've run out of bread and your houses start reverting to a lower stage, some portion of the population leaves but you still have plenty of folks. You'll need to shift around some workers and deactivate some currently unneeded buildings so the remaining population can concentrate on getting bread production back on track. But it's not a catastrophe.In a way, it's rather like the more recent Anno series, like Anno 1800, but all the gameplay takes place on a single island rather than multiple ones. You don't need to build ships for trade, just set up a port, provide resources there and other cities sent their ships to buy and sell. Things like providing resources to the workers requires "walkers" rather than just being in range of a market like in Anno 1800 but like Anno a worker living in any residence can work at any facility in the city, no worrying about means of getting there like Cities: Skyline or the Tropico series.In a way, you could say for familiarity purposes that it is like playing Anno 1800 on a larger island with most of the resources present. There aren't the bells and whistles of Anno 1800, no semi-animated characters talking to you or pop-up missions requiring you to look all over the island for loose pigs, but there is very solid gameplay in Nebuchadnezzar. The in-game help is quite good and although it doesn't have the mouse-over pop-ups like Crusader Kings III it isn't too hard to find out most of what you are looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar is an excellent city builder that I can't stop playing.This game positions itself at the halfway point between the classic Impressions city builders like Caesar 3 and Pharaoh, and the Anno series, while introducing some novel and interesting ideas of it's own. At this point in it's life cycle, Nebuchadnezzar has risen from a promising but flawed game into a real gem, and I highly recommend it to fans of the genre.The game features a walkers based resource and service distribution system like the Impressions classics, but in a reimagined way that offers more control over the paths they take. In this way Nebuchadnezzar eliminates the need for roadblocks and other ways of forcing walkers to behave the way you want, instead allowing you to manually set their routes. This lets you build a wider variety of housing block layouts, and offers more ways of controlling the flow of resources and optimization.Nebuchadnezzar has tiered resources and citizens in the style of the Anno series, requiring you to progress through different levels of production and housing and set up distribution networks in order to meet the needs of your population. The challenge of managing production and distribution of various goods while maintaining a steady workforce from the different classes of citizens is very enjoyable, and the campaign maps offer further challenge by setting different constraints and goals for you to accomplish, such as limited space for building and farming and the need to import certain goods you are unable to produce which differs from map to map.The religious system allows you to pick and choose between various gods, which offer passive bonuses to economy, population and industry which can be increased by holding festivals that consume various resources from your stockpiles. By allowing you to choose between a wide variety of different gods and their bonuses, Nebuchadnezzar lets you customize your gameplay to suit your strategy and specific needs, which is really nice to see in a game like this.The new military system provides further challenges, and the campaign missions that feature the military can be optionally played in peaceful mode instead which adds to campaign replayability. The system itself is simple but enjoyable, with some tactical depth and new resources to manage, import and produce which need to then be distributed to your army. The added complexity of this addition provides further challenges to missions, and adds to the depth of the game as a whole.The game is not without it's flaws. Voice acting is limited and in many cases seems unprofessional, and I suspect the developers used fans and amateurs rather than professional voice actors for most of the voice lines in the game. The audio quality is often sub par for many voice lines, and feel a little out of place in an otherwise very polished experience.For the Adventures of Sargon DLC campaign the devs also used AI voice emulation to provide much of the voice acting, and while it is nice that so much of the DLC features voiced dialogue this too feels rough and out of place.Some features from the games that inspired Nebuchadnezzar are also missing, such as the ability to place random decorations (though individual tree and park decoration tiles do feature slight variations so they don't look exactly the same), are missing, most notably when placing decorative roads, and a flat mode feature to gain a better overview of your city for building placement without having to resort to constantly rotate the map to look behind large buildings.These are minor issues though, and don't detract from this otherwise excellent game.Nebuchadnezzar is a great game. It borrows from classics of the genre, and offers enough new features to stand out among them. While the game started out rough it has recieved numerous updates and additions that have made it into a truly great city builder that I can't recommend enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar isn't exactly like the old Impressions Games (e.g. Caesar, Pharaoh, Zeus). It is almost solely focused on building optimized supply and delivery chains in a space-efficient manner.Gone are the mechanics which used to be more of a chore - collapsing structures, fires, disease, and random pathing of walkers. You can now control exactly where your market workers walk!On the flip side, campaign missions are fairly dry (get X amount of population, prestige, and build X monuments), instead of Impressions Games' missions which had elements of war, different climates, terrain challenges, and trading challenges. This is the biggest downside of the game, IMO.Most of the game revolves around providing enough resources to your three tiers of workers in order to keep houses populated. Each tier of worker (peasant, tradesmen, and aristocracy) has different roles, just like in Zeus. However, it's more intricate as there is close interplay between tiers, such as tradesmen being needed to produce a product to upgrade your peasants to the final tier. If your rate of production minus inefficiencies due to logistics falls below the rate of ingestion for each worker tier, be prepared to watch an avalanche of population exodus across all worker tiers, especially if it's a fundamental resource.Long story short, it's a fun logistical optimization game, but I felt like there needed to be more mechanical dimensions to the game (such as the ones listed above that are in Impressions Games) in order to feel like a worthy successor. Still recommended though. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is refreshing in a lot of aspects. It brings its own flavour on the genre, which makes it different from the traditional games of the 90s but similar in the good ways. The positive signs here are as follow:- You will get a total new experience thanks to the specfici "skin" of the game. You will embark in campaigns and scenarios during the Mesopotamian era including historical background.- The population tier is affecting also your industry, this means that you will have to balance your populaiton between each tier.- Those tiers are necessary between themselves. To evolve Peasantry, you will need Townfolks. This means that tiers are inter-dependent. This brings a whole new dimension of planning and balancing your city to make it sustain each part of the population.- You can create Monuments, Temples and Palaces are fully customizable, you can achieve so much wonderful marvels.- You have the whole baseline features of any citybuilding (walker management, industries, good distribution, commerce and so on and so forth).Imagine that this game was developped by 2 persons, they are friendly and accessible and listen to the community, patch regularly the game in case of bugs and issues and have a roadmap to deploy new content along the way.I would encourage any lover of the genre to support the developers and buy this game. You will spend hours in it easily and enjoy them. In the long term, you will benefit from new content. I am confident to say that eventually, this game will sit amongst the others as a reference in the genre.

Are you looking for hours of building, maximizing routes and pondering whether to plant wheat or barley? This is for you.Do you want scenery, drop dead graphics? This isn't for you. _childDocuments_.review: Great spiritual successor to franchises like Caesar, Emperor: Rise of the Middle Kingdom, Pharaoh, and other iso-city management games. You have everything you expect from a game that looks and feels a lot like Caesar: production chains, managing the needs of the different classes of citizens, and trade, all while having to do so on maps that offer challenges when it comes to irrigation and available space. The caravan system makes managing all of this really easy and intuitive as well. It's still in early access so improvements are on the way. I think some fine tuning in the economy (it's very easy to get into death spirals when one resources starts to run low). I also think the caravan system can benefit from a "assign caravans to routes" rather than a custom route for each one. There are quite a few instances where you have to run multiple lines through a town to make sure everyone has access to the goods that they need. 8/10, great game to scratch that Caesar itch but you don't want to play in Rome again.

_childDocuments_.review: To save anyone else from the same disappointment I had: This is _NOT_ a city builder game. It's a collection of 12 structured campaign missions. I only played three of them before requesting a refund but they essentially provide you with a checklist of buildings to place, you place them at the start then fast forward time until the mission completes. The maps are also very, very tiny.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Check out my .Nebuchadnezzar is an exceptionally polished and fun game to play, and moves the subgenre of the Impressions city builders from pure city builders to logistics planning and simulation. While it only has a single campaign and no sandbox mode, it offers a lot in terms of gameplay, especially if you find that period of history interesting.The only drawbacks I had were some uninspired campaign missions that were essentially reach x number of y, and that trade was a nuisance in that other cities would regularly demand items for no reward other than preventing a loss of reputation.Other than that, I can highly recommend this game, as it is clearly built by inspired devs and the game is essentially bug-free, a rarity in this market.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Rise of the Middle kingdom is still my favorite. It feels really good to have a perfect flow of goods. I think this is a good #2 on that subject (better in my opinion than the Caesar games and all other known franchises of 25 years ago). Well worth the play if you miss playing those kind of games. Not sure what newcomers to this genre will think of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, relaxing logistics game. Its absolutely worth buying IF that is all you are looking for. Its not much of a city builder, there is no combat system, and the main way you could lose is if you run out of money, which can be easily generated once you set up your first trade with another city. The logistics part is a lot of fun though, and it steadily ramps up over the campaign.Also, there is no replayability value, as you only get to play with the ~12 campaign missions, with no random map generation so if you want more out of it, then maybe you can wait for some workshop content.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely best city-builder available right now, I don't remember when it was the last time I enjoyed any game so much. It probably won't appeal to everyone, but for any fan of a peaceful city builder and deep management - a must. Great mechanics, great attention to details, great visuals and audio design, great balance, great gameplay overall.The game is not perfect and I hope devs will add some useful features and cool scenarios. But until then - thank you very much for bringing the genre to life. Looking forward to your next project.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: You can look down on Nebuchadnezzar as stripping out some of the features from the old impressions games or you can focus on what this addition to the genre does well. - More than twice the resources as Caesar 3 (35 in total)- Almost three times as many resource chains as Caesar 3 where you turn one thing into another- A succinct 30 hour campaign that doesn't drag on past its welcome- Three different types of citizens to manage and upgrade with different needs- A reworked walker system for more player control- A customizable monument system for those with a better artistic sense- And a modern setup for newer computers where you wont have to mess with .ini files or mods to get it running.- All for less than one third the price of the old impressions games when they first came out? I loved the short time I put into the game for what it is instead of criticizing nebuchadnezzar for things it isn't trying to do, and that's an experience I would recommend for any long time fan of the city building genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: There are some good things about this game and I will explain why I don't recommend it. Graphics are fine. I dont expect anything more so it satisfies. But at the same time it is not important because graphic is not something important in this type of genre. Building temple is a good idea and I really liked it. Caravensarais are nice. Tutorial is quite nice. It is fun and explaining everything pretty clear.However, I cant think of anything else which makes this game different. Still, this is still not a big problem. The big problem is that the map is extremely, extremely small. Maybe it gets larger later on but I finished the tutorial and stuck in the 6th mission. It is not hard by the way. It is totally doable with what is given in the map. But it is painful. Not like dark souls. I felt like an accountant who just waits for the shift to be over. Agriculture is painful. There is no place for farming (which make sense). But what doesn't make sense is that when I build 2 grain farms almost one fourth of my map becomes unusable. Why? Really why? Why the map is that small? I said the idea of building a temple is good. It is... However, just a temple takes a huuuuuuuge amount of space. Again it makes sense when we think that temples are huge. Sure! But why the map is that small? Why there is only and only 1 place I can build a dock? (There is 1 more in the 6 mission. But you cant use that dock if you build there beacuse you cant put a warehouse.)Ah yess.. Warehouses. Again why are they so small and so big? Why they can take only 36 goods? If you put 20 fishes and 16 breads, you cant put anything more. But these warehouses are big too. They take a huge space as well. So if you try to be a bit generous and put 1 more warehouse then you supposed to then everything gets difficult. One other thing is that your city can collapse in a matter of seconds. For example I forgot to change the maximum number of bread a warehouse can take. So, no one could put milk in it. Therefore, everyone in the city left. Just like that in couple of seconds. So there was no one to work in the fisheries. Because of that all the people in villas left as well. At the end I had  only 2-3 hundred people while I had almost 3000 people 30 seconds ago. To be honest fixing these things and then constantly checking if everything is fine is painful not fun.I was excited for this game but it is not really up to my expectations. If you "need" to play a city builder game sure give it a try. It is not expensive. But frankly, I believe this game could be a huge deal if we were at 2001. However we are not.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I was hungry for a builder but what I found was a puzzle game.I think the game design on this one is super flawed, to the point where this feels more punishing than it should be. it's disgustingly hard even on easy, particularly about income. annoying popup messages, UI and clunky infratructure handling. There is some beautiful art in there to be sure and from an aesthetics view, it is getting Pharaoh vibes, but it unfortunately feels like worse than those games even though they came out 20 years ago.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Huge letdown for me.I expected a relaxing city building game that gives me the old Pharao vibes. This certainly isn't it.1. There is no "free play"-mode where you can build your own city freely but only missions with a predefined goal. Once you reach the goal, mission is over. You can continue to play but you never unlock more buildings. What the actual ****. Who creates a city building game with no free play mode??? I don't know that's like creating a shooter and not adding any weapons it feels like the most common-sense thing to do doesn't it?!2. The game  limits your creativity because it doesn't give you enough space to build. Maps in general are terribly small for no apparent reason, but whats even worse, maps are intentionally build in a way to 'challenge' you. For example there is no terraforming (why?) and then they add mountains that can't be removed to limit you from building water channels and other structures. You don#t get a 'map' you get get a maze of unbuildable terrain and you kind of have to figure out the correct way to place all your buildings. Terrible design decision, makes it feel like some sort of puzzle game.3. Buildings have a rediculously low range/working area. It's a real chore to set up production chains, again, as I said before it feels like a puzzle game. Did I mention they give you a laughable amount of fertile land?4. You have to  set paths for  trader that sells a good at  market in your city . WAT. Who came up with that idea?! I will now refund this game, it's certainly not worth 20€. Go play 20 year old Paraoh instead, seriosly I play city building games a lot an this isn't anywhere near the top 20. So angry right now.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, having enjoyed Ceasar 3 and the entire impression serries.But where the game had fun, this game has you looking at graphs a lot more and just... Not having fun. I spent most of the time fighting with the production menu and waiting to see when it would accurately reflect my base game then I did designing a fun city or enjoying myself, and didn't get far passed the tutorial due to spending the whole time on "E" high speed mode just waiting for ♥♥♥♥ to happen.Not to mention the most annoying crap like needing to individually shut down industry if a worker shortage happens and having to manually assign over workers to certain things - which is fine when you have like 6 industries but boring when you have 100. The game is far more of a hassle then it is an enjoyment.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Have literally been waiting YEARS for this game to come out and it does not disappoint. It's close enough to the old Pharaoh to be recognizable but with improvements to game play which are great. The few times I came across something that didn't seem to work I managed to figure out what I was doing wrong.  I can't wait to see how it develops. More Please!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: For a brand new game, this has an exceptional level of polish.  It has been a very reminiscant day, reminding me of the likes of Pharaoh and Ceaser, but with the gameplay perfected, and the whole game modernised.  I thoroughly look forward to more and will watch the developers with great interest.  Well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: *** I got a preview copy of the game but bought a key immediately after release to really support the devs***If you played older Impression games, this is the ultimate modern game for you. It isn't the same - let's clear that right out of the gate. Also - ancient mesopotamia? What a great setting!The game is much more logistics oriented and you need to make sure everything runs smoothly and effectively. You don't need to place police, firemen etc. - you need to make sure your markets are sufficently supplied, your walkers are walking efficent routes, your workforce is in the right places...Trading is pretty much the same, nicely done, good interface - overall very nicely done!Missions are interesting, map design is superb - you always need most of the map, so you have to plan accordingly and there isn't much place for mistakes... That's even better than most missions in older games.There is no military but I can't see it as a bad thing overall...Should I say something in the end, it would be that if you like city building, ancient Mesopotamia and wish to support a group of fine, hard working devs - this is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: It's good for the price, and quite similar to old classics like Caesar 3 and Pharoah.All the mechanics you'd expect from a game like this are mostly in it, such as overlays for desirability. An improvement is custom routing for street-walkers.It can be hard, I had to reset mission 3 about 3 times due to running out of money. You can only make money through trade so far and only get that laterSpace is a premium for I guess balance as it mentions space being "the most valuable thing" so you feel boxxed in to a degree. You might have a jagged coastline in a mission so only 1 space for a dockThe game's supply chain system is its biggest weak point. The caravan system (of getting goods long distance between warehouses) is confusing and I had to fiddle with buttons for a long while and observe to actually get a successful transfer of goodsA few bugs, that do impact gameplay so far, such as irrigation ditches that wont extend fertility In the Akkad mission (southern shore). Also possibly a bug or I'm not getting the system but one where bazaar merchants will claim "No resources" despite a full warehouse right next to themNote all that is in the game so far is the singleplayer campaign. There is a scenarios option but no scenarios with the game shipped. I wonder if there is a scenario editor or map maker with the game as that is what the scenario system hints at?
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: The game is nice, I liked it very much, but seems repetitive and the only real difficulty is the map size. You play a campaign mission a couple hours to realize that you ran out of space because you didnt planed your city and resources 4 hours ahead, and thats just in normal difficulty. If devs wants to be unforgiving with the map size, then they need to add, at the very least, a plan feature, like in oxygen not included, where you can lay your grand design beforehand.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Everything that makes impressions games' city builders great with a focus on logistics. Distribution of goods is defined by the player. The balancing act of keeping your houses topped off and using resources for trade and buildings is challenging when you must expand to take care of other objectives. The game is as complete package as can be without it being fully open source: modding and scenario editing are available and extensive.The negatives are that the sanitation and safety aspects are a little out of your control and wonders are less impressive but i've yet to complete the campaign. Easily one of the best bangs for your buck if you like historical city builders.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: oooofffff. What a HUGE disappointment this game is. Graphics are not that good, but much worse is the gameplay. I love games like Caesar 3 and 4 for example, but the gameplay of this game does not make sense, at all. I expected much more. The tutorials are very very hard to follow, the actions you have to perform do not make sense at all GUI is very user unfriendly. So my conclusion is: Mesopotamian city building, great idea, extremely poorly executed. I asked for a refund. Simply not even fun to play. It looks like a completely failed attempt to rebuild caesar 4 in Mesoptamia.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This is an ambitious and good-looking historical city builder that has obviously been shown a lot of love by the devs, and should be fun to play, but isn't. The risk mechanic ruins this game for me, over and above the unusually demanding level of micromanagement required. All the overlays and statisics are opaque  and bare bones, but the risk overlays in particular are incomprehensible in relation to what is going on, and tell you nothing. Police, fire and healers walk all over the map without any way for you to control them or direct them, regardless of where the buildings are placed, unless you spam service buildings everywhere. I am a veteran player of all the Impressions city builders, and was really looking forward to this game. It still is playable, and even enjoyable at times, but the flaws make it very frustrating. Instead of the addictive gameplay one expects, you very soon tire of literally putting out fires, not to mention quelling riots and strikes that seem to respond to nothing the player does to mitigate them. I would give this three out of five stars, solely because of the risk dynamic.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Reminds me of  Caesar and Pharaoh.   Needs some tweaking on how to identify placement of clay pits and other water based industries and maybe so routing work for caravans but so far it is pretty good.  I am just now about to build a monument for the first time so will revisit review after a few more hours of game play.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy this game, even though it is still in its starting phase it brings back a great feeling. The music is beautiful and I spend almost more time reading and researching about the detailed historic explanations before the missions than actually in the game - and not because it is too quick, but because it is very interesting.There is great potential and even though there is a bit limited content at the moment I don't regret a single penny spent on this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun city builder, I like the setting choice, the art design, and the music is pretty nice. The city building mechanics are pretty much a more streamlined version of Zeus, walkers can be directed through routes meaning that roads aren't cluttered by roadblocks, production buildings can store a minimal amount of goods and directly send them to markets which slightly lowers the amount of storehouse spam in the game. Mechanics that could be completely ignored in Zeus like invasions and unrest were cut out. The player is given a lot more room to worry about the more interesting parts of logistics and I appreciate that. The amount of content in the game is limited, but optimising logistics is pretty great if that's what you're into.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I love Pharaoh and Cesar and got this game on day 1 thinking it was not early access but it is early access there will need to be a fair few updates and patches. For example the Campaign is more a tutorial and there is no sandbox mode or scenarios yet. The tutorial or in game guide does not fully explain how to work the custom monument feature. I don't find the layout for checking your resource balances intuitive. It is a bit of a boring table with a few numbers. If you spend long enough looking at it you will understand it but not fun or interesting. The game is a bit OTT on efficiency (maybe it needs balancing better). I love efficient layouts and stuff but the game does it a bit too much for me and it sucks the fun/freedom out of it. For example, a new system where every farm or industry can only deliver goods to storage yards 4 or so, tiles away is too limiting. I would love the range to be a more just to give a little flexibility and fun when building. The irrigation wells can only fill a few tiles of irrigation ditch so you end up spamming wells and using the bare minimum/most efficient irrigation ditch layout. I would say worst of all the maps are crazy small and you end up building right to the map edge where it becomes a pain to see what you have built without rotating all the time because something is covering the buildings in the corners and edges. In fact the maps are so small you cant build a city without focusing on efficiency only.Plus there are a few bugs i am getting only with this game for example it always loads on my secondary monitor so i have to unplug the secondary, load the game then plug it back it. Easy work around but a pain. Also if I rotate the map alot the game crashesI will keep it and see if it gets better. Im
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

You must set up trade routes for every single good through buildings, calculate everything, buildings have specific ranges. It's basicaly Anno but you do not have the magical warehouses. Thank you for creating this amazing game of one of the civilizations that was missing.PS: Perhapps you could look to the Americas in the future? I long for growing crops in them Inca mountain farms.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played the first 4 missions. As a fan of the Zeus + Poseidon series I'm really enjoying this so far.I'll update my review once I accumulate more hours of play.Quick Notes (Work in Progress):Pros:Something I appreciate is a comprehensive and digestible tutorial.This game does a good job of teaching you the mechanics without boring you with endless walls of text.Cons:It keeps starting in my secondary monitor on a multiple monitor setup. **** This was patched today, there is now a settingI REALLY wish you could zoom in just one or two more levels.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Aww, it's really too bad ;( I was hoping for a new Caesar itch-scratcher with this one...The awesome stuff:1) The music2) The beautiful artwork in the loading screensThat's about it for the first hour, and that's not good enough. What I'm missing:1) No free rotation (there's just 4 compass directions and boring isometric view).2) Zooming. Even though the tutorial says you can zoom, none of the zoom options do anything, I just stay in satellite orbit view, and the land and city just looks light brown with no details.3) Good looking graphics... This looks kind of like early SimCity's, but in higher res because 4K. I get that this is not a multi million $$$$ investment or anything, but it's just not pulling me in enough.A minor gripe: the tutorial text is way too verbose. Like, entire unnecessary sentences. If there's a button "end tutorial", there doesn't also need to be a long-winded sentence informing the player that they can, if they so choose, finalize the tutorial by finding the button for ending the tutorial. (See what I mean? :) )So yeah... This does not scratch any itches, in fact it creates more itches. Maybe I'm hoping for too much here, but I would really like a city builder that doesn't make me want to replay 20 year old city builders like Caesar 4, that had more and better functionality and much, MUCH more charm-factor in the UI, graphics and voices (even though that was not a great game).Too bad, Seeing the review ratio I had really hoped for more... Maybe it's actually a great city builder game in terms of city mechanics, but as (to me) this feels more like a sandbox engine demo, it doesn't pull me in to the point where I quickly start to enjoy that gameplay. Not like all the old games did anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games you'd love to love, but it just has too many flaws. First of all it shouldn't be hard to release game in 2021 without having minor updates which adds walls or fires. Second of all it also shouldn't be hard to have fluent controls in this type of game in 2021. I understand these mechanics that would smooth the gameplay were harder to implement 20+ years ago, but now there shouldn't be excuses. Camera is awful and maps too small. Often you have to build farms or whatever to spots you can barely see. Third of all the atmosphere is lame. It doesn't feel like you're operating city. It feels like all houses are in separate universes. I didn't want a literal copy of Emperor or Pharaoh or something. I wanted a well made economy strategy city builder in the spirit of those games. And even Emperor had more things when it was released. This is not a bad game really but I wouldn't buy it again if I knew better.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. Enough remaining of Pharoh to be familiar but different enough to stand on it's own. Obviously there are some things that I would have changed in the design (Increase irrigation pump function am I right?) but there is nothing serious to knock. If you are a fan of the 2d city designer, this is well worth the get!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: So, is it Pharaoh in Babylonia? Yes.Is there a certain lifelessness in your towns due to the absence of walkers, like the Steam reviews are saying? Yes, they're right. I don't think that walkers need to fulfill any function necessarily like they did in Pharaoh, the game works a bit differently in that respect which is not bad because the Pharaoh system definitely had issues (looking at you, market seller that randomly stops going left for 1 year and lets the houses on the left side of the market degrade into huts), but it would be really nice to see the people walk around, even if just for decorative purposes. I hope they'll add that eventually.Still worth it? Sure. I mean, it's Pharaoh in Babylonia, is there any other "Pharaoh in Babylonia" game that you can compare it too? No, so go and get it. Worth every €.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely great game, silky smooth logical intuitive practical interface, with all numbers quantities clearly stated. If you're missing something you can tell why immediately. Love the graphics, clean and gorgeous. An absolute must for anyone remotely interested in a city builder, and a great intro to the genre if you've never played.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game that gives me the vibes of Sierra classics like the Pharaoh and Caesar series.  My only complaint is that it often takes a very long time to boot up which makes it hard to enjoy when I have a limited time to play (thus, the reason for my low play time, I had to move on for now but I'll come back to it)
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar offers the classic isometric, resource-management game, which we got to know from Pharaoh and Ceaser. Much of the gameplay is similar, but it's simplicity (in essence) makes it very good and it keeps it entertaining. The way the campaign is done, allows the player to continue learning new things in a progressive way. The campaing offers two types of victory (military or presitge), giving more flexibility for the player. The combat is a bit mediocore, but I guess that was never the main focus of this game. I really like the statistical overview the game shows you, allowing you to optimize the production chains  of your cities  vs. the consumption of your civilians. I can't tell if the old games had this before, but for me makes a huge difference in how to organize your city. The manual distribution of your goods (via caravans) can be (a bit) laboursome, but It will also allow you to optimize your producion chains even more. I really like this puzzle. The 3 difficulty options are very nice; it will allow you to make the campaign more challenging if you want to.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Opinion: 6.5/10 This game has some potential. It's somewhat like Anno 2000 BC would be. I found the management of supply chains tiresome, as others have mentioned, stockpiles have practically no range so half of your city is a matrix of stockpile buildings and overall ... felt a little lackluster (I felt like "Why am I playing this and not Anno 1800" ).It's not a bad game, it's just not exceptional either. (Tough I have to commend the tutorial, it was quite nice to have one that is not overly restricting and actually quite helpful )If you are a sucker for the era and art design, then go for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly fails to learn any of the lessons of two decades of city building games that came after Pharoah and earlier games of the same genre. Lacks the modern sensibilities of games like 'Grand Ages Rome,' or even 'Sumerians.'I realize this 'failure to learn,' is actually an artistic choice, I just don't think it is a good one.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible. It has huge potential. But first things first. I'm a huge fan of Sierra's Pharoh and I'm confident this game will be a worthy successor.This game has no bugs I couldn't find any in 55h of gaming. This is incredible since the whole game was written by one developer supported by 2 game designer, art and music designer (5 people in total).First missions are easy but the further you go it gets harder. The balance of the game is really good, and it is always possible to recover from city collapse (although tons of clicking will be required to close production and later to reopen it). Not many things can wreck your great city, the city won't burn, you won't be robbed by unemployed citizens, there is no military mechanics etc. but given the games price and it's quality it still provides a lot of entertainment and I'm pretty sure developers will extend it.

Once gained, you expand your town with the new one, build a bit more of what you have and wait until complete.Yeah. _childDocuments_.review: Great, very much like old Impressions Games / Sierra historical city builder games (Pharaoh, Caesar, Zeus etc.) but not exactly like them, it is more like some a modern restart, if you enjoyed the overall mood, art style, overall polish, city building / production gameplay, music of these games then Nebuchadnezzar is for you. It is fairly similar to the old Sierra games with some things of its own like monument building which allow a bit more customization than before and some game mechanisms like you can add/remove different type of workers in building, the game also rely heavily on fixing production issues and transport / import / export / optimization of supply chain / roads. It is refreshing to see yet another game like this in a different time period, the time period is well chosen. The UX could be better i guess but it also has some quick shortcut that make it ok.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A spiritual successor to Impressions Game's city building series, which included: Caesar, Pharaoh, Zeus: Master of Olympus and Emperor: Rise of the Middle Kingdom.I recommend it to anyone who loved the isometric city building series like I did back in the 90's.I nominated this for the'Sit Back & Relax' award, 2021.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I am writing under the strong impression of my first gaming addiction: Pharaoh, from 1999. At that time I was about 12 years old and was looking for the game. Contrary to what many would think, however, it is not just a childhood memory; I still play this classic from time to time.That was also the reason I bought Nebuchadnezzar. It exuded that pharaoh flair in the trailers. Now you can think what you like about the games of that time, but they have aged gracefully. Although Nebuchadnezzar offers the game in 4k, the animations and "details" are rather blurry. For me, the speed at which the houses rise felt too fast. This may have been an (intentional) effect of the tutorial. The logistics could become exciting in the later campaigns, but didn't really convince me until the introduction of the caravan. The fact that the workers of the market can be planned with a route is certainly more advanced than placing a barge at that time, but I didn't understand the depth. As a feature, it was too shallow to add any depth to the game, so it seemed more like a necessity that you had to deal with. I played the game until the fourth campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: When I've fondly remembered the old Sierra city-builder games over the last 15 years, wishing they made them like they used to, this is the game I imagined.First off, it just  great. It manages to combine the nostalgia of  and  with the extra breathing space of modern UI, controls, and menu design. It's clear that the art has been done with a lot of love and attention to detail. The music is professional, atmospheric, and varied enough that it doesn't feel repetitive after several hours of play. The ambient sound design is almost perfectly immersive (I did catch one market crier hawking his wares in English, but I can forgive that - it's not like there are many sound libraries of people speaking ancient Sumerian). It's also great to see ancient Mesopotamia get some love, and downright cool to design your own temple or palace complex, even if the monument interface could do with some quality-of-life improvements.My biggest gripe: I feel like it could have been made clearer that this isn't yet a feature-complete game. As of writing (19th Feb 2021), the only playable mode is a campaign, so there's no sandbox mode (although the devs have just announced it will be in an upcoming update, and there's an everything-unlocked scenario mod in the Workshop that does the job for now). Scenario mode is available, but there are no dev-made scenarios yet, only what you can find on the Workshop.That said, the campaign is fun to play through, with a well-thought-out tutorial that strikes a decent balance between holding your hand and getting out of your way. The pacing might be a tad slow for some - at times I felt impatient to get to the higher-tier buildings and industries - but I never stopped enjoying myself. Even if you don't have all the toys yet, it's still damn satisfying when you get things humming along just right, industries well-balanced and all your Mesopotamish citizens happy with your rule.Praise Marduk!
