_childDocuments_.review: Very polished, very well balanced! Finished the last mission after 45 hours, was totally addicted and it was just over when I started having enough of it.It's like a new version of the old city builders (Zeus, Pharao...).If you want to compare it to the Anno games: in this game (I won't even try to write the name) you basically do the things, that happen pretty much by themselves in Anno. You micro-manage where all the goods go exactly. While in Anno you just put houses into the range of a market, here you tell the traders exactly what route to take. Be aware that sometimes this feels a bit tedious!And unlike in Anno you don't build one huge world for 50 hours+, it's 13 separate levels that get bigger and bigger. And that is great! You keep getting a fresh start and can improve upon your previous mistakes that you carried through to the end. When I finished the last level it felt like I had mastered it. Very satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m a huge fan of the classic city builders (Caesar III is a personal fav of mine), so Nebuchadnezzar was definitely something I had to check out.This is not a full-blown strategy game with warfare, diplomacy, and the like. Rather, it’s more of a straight city builder with a heavy emphasis on building and expanding, one developed by a two-man team at that. Despite that though, there is a surprising amount of depth here, both in the building and management elements. Having now played the game for over a dozen hours, I’ve grown to enjoy this little indie city builder.If it wasn’t already obvious, Nebuchadnezzar goes for that same isometric viewpoint that the classics did, albeit with the ability to rotate. The graphics follow suit and are generally low-res across the board (which becomes very apparent when you zoom all the way in). Granted, this is likely by design and it never felt off-putting. The music is comparable, nothing too great there – but not bad.As this is a 2021 release, Nebuchadnezzar also brings some modern upgrades. Most notable would be its support of higher resolutions up to ultrawide 4K. My only problem there is that the UI cannot be freely scaled. There is an option to enable a 4K UI, but nothing if you just want to adjust it a little bit – the game could really use a UI scale slider. The entire experience is also capped at 60 fps, which was a bit disappointing to see, but at least it was a stable 60 fps.Most of my time was spent in the campaign mode, which itself is made up of a bunch of loosely connected scenarios. The goals usually involved reaching a certain population, prestige, or smaller stuff like having a set number of a certain building. There is a nice learning curve in that you’re only introduced to a few new goods and buildings with each scenario, giving you time to get acquainted with them before repeating the process with the next.By the end of the game there is a ton of stuff to juggle, including multiple social classes that can only work specific jobs, a dozen or so different buildings needed to craft certain goods, and an involved house upgrade mechanic that will have you setting up a ton of different worker paths in order to get goods where they need to go. As I said before – there’s a surprising amount of complexity here. Despite this, it doesn’t go overboard and the core loop is very satisfying once you get the hang of things.It has a similar feel to something like Factorio or Satisfactory, where you spend all this time setting up harvesting and manufacturing of one good, just for that to open up paths for you do to the same with even more goods. It never gets old seeing this small village become this massive web of buildings, farms, and workers travelling all over.As there is no warfare, crime, or disasters of any sort, the challenge is instead shifted to how well you can optimize and make effective use of the space provided. You can just slap down some buildings, connect them together, and call it a day, but there’s a lot of fun to be had in coming up with the most efficient farm layouts, the shortest possible pathing for distributing goods, and the most profitable trades with other cities. This just so happens to be my favorite thing to do in city builders, so I felt right at home here in Nebuchadnezzar.I believe the biggest flaw people are going to find with the game comes in the form of its lasting appeal. Once you’ve completed the campaign and scenarios, there really isn’t much in the way of replay value. At least, not from the base game itself. I say that because there is a mod manager and, with time, I could easily see the game becoming more robust through all the different stuff people add to it.There’s also the issue of quality of life – and let’s just say that Nebuchadnezzar has some room to improve there. Being able to copy-paste routes across different merchants would be my most-wanted feature, but it would also be nice to be able to delete bridges over canals without actually deleting the canal along with it. Minor stuff for sure, but improvements to be made nonetheless.As a fan of classic city-builders like Caesar and Pharaoh, there’s a lot to like here. There’s the polished and satisfying core game loop, the heavy emphasis on building and expansion, and even the more unique stuff like the house upgrade system. Sure, it’s not a challenging game and could still use some quality of life improvements, but it’s a fun experience overall and impressive given that it comes from just two people. If you’re a fan of such city builders, it’s worth a look.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: This is another builder game where the developers want hard core players to automatically love and learn their product. I've seen this since the late 1980s.TLDR if you are a casual player who loves semi-historical god games you may want to give it a pass.The onboarding tutorial starts off ok. Build a farm. Ok.But the next level tutorial gives you no feedback on why you are failing. Presumably this is the forced social community aspect which has become endemic, while completely ignoring casual players aren't looking to be forced to go online.If at this point you are rolling your eyes, please parachute out. The rest of this review is for casual players who like god games. Starting from Settlers to the first Nile game. Let's not even get into Civ who mastered the casual AND advanced player genre.The game devs aren't going to tell you why your milk farm delivers to the warehouse to the market just fine while the farm/bakery you built in Tut1 now fails in Tut2. Roads? Yes all there. Distance? Who knows? Go blunder a bit. It's a fun learning experience for your unproven as yet to be beloved product. And if they don't want to read your mind? Screw them.It just goes on from here. There is not enough player feedback. That's the entire problem.I paid $16 US for a peek into what should be my favorite genre for 30 years. But I'm not impressed. Heck Settlers in the 1980s understood this. Pick your reason: arrogant developers, or underfunded developers who don't understand market buy in... means they can go off and do wonderful things.What I saw instead was just another well intended "let's do everything game" that flounders because it doesn't do much of anything, does not appeal to the casual player to build up product market share, arrogantly assumes what is not obvious into the minds of the developer means the players is stupid or unwilling to create an ecosystem to cover for the developers' false assumptions.Recommendations? Yeah the most obvious. The UI should show exactly what is needed. Don't be coy, don't be arrogant because your intended market is not telepathic. If you think your market has to be as clever as you as to read your mind maybe consider bringing in people who like people.This could be a good game but like many such recent offerings they get the basic game mechanics down but go to market to soon. And doom their product. Just stop already, do the hard work to make the product accessible.Or just sell it to mom and your three dear friends.

_childDocuments_.review: I was apprehensive to play the game at release due to an apparent lack of depth, having said that, Nebuchadnezzar has been greatly enhanced since then.Nebuchadnezzar seeks to emulate the old Sierra games, mainly drawing inspiration from Pharaoh and Caesar (3), and does a  good job of combining the intricacies of each title. That's not to say Nebuchadnezzar is simply the "best of Sierra Studios" though. While the game is quite similar to the aforementioned titles, it manages to carve out it's own identity in the genre by simplifying certain aspects (or even outright omitting them), while simultaneously expanding upon others. While I did claim some mechanics are "simplified", its more accurate to say that they're deceptively simplified in order to place emphasis on others. For example, the distance between housing and any sort of work is irrelevant. Peasants can live and work in total opposite corners of the map with no issue. In part due to the house/work relationship, road placement becomes less crucial as you no longer need to formulate the perfect path for jobs. That being said, the placement of buildings and roads still matters greatly once you understand what the main aspect of Nebuchadnezzar is: logistics. Sure, it might not matter where a wheat farm and house are located, but what does matter is how, or rather, where you're going to store that wheat in relation to the farm. After you've stored the wheat, it's turned into bread. But where do the bakeries go? Where is bread stored? Where does it get transported (if needed) so it can then get distributed to your citizens. Oh, and after that, where do you place the markets in order to distribute the food, how many merchants do you use, and what path(s) do you give each one? The process continues with over 2 dozen different resources alongside a multitude of services (religion, healthcare, crime, etc.) all feeding into one another. Nebuchadnezzar doesn't actually place so much emphasis on building a city, but rather building and maintaining an ever-growing distribution chain where your goal is to maximize efficiency, and minimize any points of failure.And as far omittals, the only noteworthy example is the total lack of any militaristic features. However, that's actually being added in the forthcoming update. Speaking of, updates (both major and minor) have been coming at a steady pace ever since release.  Its a good game, but as it stands, I don't think Nebuchadnezzar is quite the same caliber as the games it seeks to imitate. But with the quality and frequency of updates so far, it has the potential to not only reach those heights, but even eclipse them.

_childDocuments_.review: From the detailed background information about the different cultures in ancient Mesopotamia, one might think 'finally an ancient city simulation game which gets history right'. Short answer: Not so much. As a seasoned ACOUP reader, the first thing one notices is how peaceful the cities of the game generally are. From my understanding of history, cities were administrative centers used to extract resources from the surrounding countryside by violence or threats of violence. So the first thing one would assume a city to have would be soldiers. As there are likely to be other would-be extractors around, the second thing one would assume a city to have are defensive structures, at least a palisade wall around the granary. Instead, external threats are absent, and the eventual city guard mostly deals with the occasional criminal and certainly does not seem to collect taxes from farmers at spearpoint. Agriculture is only slightly less ridiculous. Okay, the irrigation system idea is neat. However, irrigation pumps only cost a fixed amount and then run forever, for free. The practical limits on irrigation are the amount of straight sections of the river/lake coasts (which are also needed for fishing and harbors) where pumps can be build. Land comes functionally in just three flavors: inaccessible, grassland (irrigated or naturally wet) and desert. For both pastures and horticulture, you need grassland. This seems totally ahistorical to me: wheat is obviously a much better way to use good land, while pastoralism is important because it allows the utilization of marginal land. Fun fact: if there is a single thing one might think to be in abundant supply in Mesopotamia (which includes modern Iraq), it would be desert land. In the game however, while waterfront real estate is probably the most limited resource, overall accessible space is often also rather limited. I would have assumed that the vast majority of people are subsistence farmers from whom a tiny amount of surplus is extracted to feed the city folks. Instead, it is very possible to have most of the lower class unemployed without anyone starving. On the other hand, the populations appetite for ceramics is truly insatiable. For every three people working the fields, bakeries and goat farms, expect two working clay into pots. I guess that eventually the Greeks will discover that you can actually reuse pots instead of using new ones all the time. There are no mills. Both the bakeries and the kilns operate without fuel, powered by sunlight, magma or power of will.The overall economy is weird. From the start, it is currency-based. You pay your employees fixed wages, slavery doesn't exist. Anyone living in houses with suitable amenities pays taxes, irregardless of employment. How do the unemployed make money? Unknown. Prostitution, freelance software programming, synthesizing gold from thin air. In the first few levels, the housing level is limited, so you will probably only make a surplus by trading with other cities, which are willing to overpay for your ceramics. Non-wage labor, which I would have assumed to make up the bulk of labor (e.g. subsistence farming, in-house cloth production) is completely absent. Buildings are made out of two materials. The gigantic monuments are made out of bricks, every other building is made out of money. Most of the game is actually about managing logistics. While employees can teleport from their homes to their place of work, transporting goods by haulers is subject to strict union regulations based on the maximum norm of the vector difference of the position of the two buildings in question, regardless of the actual walking distance. To transport goods further, you need warehouses which can be connected by caravans. The placement of some industry buildings is reasonably governed by land use considerations. For other industry buildings, transport efficiency can be improved if a hauler can directly move goods (e.g. grain) from a producer (farm) to a consumer (bakery) instead of the producer->warehouse=>warehouse->consumer chain which involves two haulers and one caravan. Any goods in warehouses are also directly available to fulfill requests of other cities. In my head canon, this is because some Rimworld escapees crash-landed in Mesopotamia and taught the Sumerians how to construct orbital trade beacons. Every citizen of ancient Mesopotamia has an Amazon Prime membership and thus is unwilling to walk (or teleport) to wells (did I mention that Sumerian well drilling tech is superb: you can build a well miles from any wetlands, and it will just work) or markets to fetch daily life goods. Instead, markets are basically delivery centers employing people who will delivery the goods directly to their customers. These are also unionized and the maximum distance between their waypoints and the delivery center is limited. However, if the shortest road connecting two waypoints takes them out of that area, they will happily provide houses along the road with goods as well. Also, distance does not matter because they do not actually haul goods from the delivery center to the houses, but instead carry a portable consumer good teleportation unit to teleport the goods from the markets directly to the doorstep. Giving these unfavorable contracts, it is little wonder that they refuse to carry more than one type of consumer good at a time. Copper working is a thing in the game -- we are not in the stone age any more, after all. Of course, the only use of copper is to sate the upper classes hunger for copper  jewellery -- basically the NFTs of ancient Sumer. Never mind that by 2000 BCE, they ought to have long discovered bronze and used it for both tools and weapons.Just beyond the border of the map, countless ageless gender-fluid people of all classes camp in the desert, waiting to move into your city should they find suitable conditions. And that is where they will return quietly when the conditions of life take a turn for the worse: "Maggy, no priest has visited us in a year. Pack your stuff, we are moving out into the desert again." The parts of the game that are not directly logistics are mostly related to keeping a sufficient workforce supplied. Personally, I think that too much detail is lost when you go from simulating individual citizens (e.g. Dwarf Fortress, Rimworld, Tropico), which have home, job, skills, philosophy, politics, relatives and so on to aggregate statistics only: "You have 1224 peon level jobs. Your city has 986 peon class citizens. 248 peon-level jobs are unoccupied." Unlike Sim City, Nebuchadnezzar does not even have the excuse that they have to many citizens to simulate, as the amount of people is artificially inflated anyhow: A residential building might house 70 people, while a bakery might employ 75 (in convenient groups of 25) -- not to shabby for a preindustrial civilization. Just divide by ~25, make the bakery have three employees and the house have three (working-age) citizens, and you can suddenly give them actual identities. There are some educational games in which the game mechanics are actually tied to the setting. Kerbal is definitely one for teaching spaceflight 101. If ACOUP is to believed, the Paradox games are rather good for teaching history. Nebuchadnezzar will teach you whatever you read in the info boxes (which seems plausible to me as a layperson), plus the fact that irrigation is kind of a big deal. If you enjoy logistics/planning heavy games, but can't be bothered to get into Factorio, Nebuchadnezzar might be okay for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I hope Nebuchadnezzar gets more love in the form of content; what you get today, as a "feature complete" game is a resource management puzzle rather than a city builder.  Each scenario map pits you with a challenging layout of unbuildable terrain, jagged rivers and little overall map size for fertile tile growth.  It's your task to build some housing blocks that can receive the necessary goods from your production chains, in the little available space provided to you; money comes only in the form of trade with other cities (and you can only sell/buy specified goods each map; so if you're overproducing milk? Too bad).And, well, that's the game in a nutshell.  It's fun, but it's not really fair to compare to Caesar, Zeus or Pharaoh; these games had additional layers (many!) of complexity.  You would hire prefects for theft protection, well water carriers to fight fires, you would require medicines and have health care, you would set up taxing agents for tax income from your plebs, colosseums and other entertainment buildings for joy, etc.  None of that is here in Nebuchadnezzar.  You simply provide goods to your citizens, and that's that.If you're looking for a Caesar, Zeus or Pharaoh style game in modern times, you're probably looking for Anno or Path of Progress.  Nebuchadnezzar is not a bad game by any means and I recommend it, Nebuchadnezzar simply took a different path but leads you to believe it's a Sierra game of old, when it's not.  It is a resource management puzzle game, and for that, it's at least a very good one.

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar is an ancient-style city builder similar to a couple of other older city builders like Pharaoh, where you attempt to build up an ancient Mesopotamian city and meet certain requirements to finish scenarios.The problem is that the tutorial mode is very broken. The first mission asks you to stockpile bread and wheat, which are part of the same supply chain: wheat gets harvested and turned into bread. It does this by having you build a wheat field (which plants and harvests wheat once a year) and then build two bakeries (which turn wheat into bread and operate 24/7/365 unless told specifically not to). Once you do this, the game goes "Oh, it's fine, just let the simulation run and it'll eventually complete on its own."The problem is that the scenario will never actually complete if you do that, because the bakeries will grab all the wheat and start cranking out bread and you'll never reach a point where you have enough wheat stockpiled. In my case, I managed to just turn the bakeries off and finished that part of the tutorial that way... even though the game never actually told me how you do that.A lot of the problem is that the game does the Paradox thing where it has a wiki and provides you links to the wiki for everything.. which is bad game design. Wikis do not excuse a bad tutorial. Then I get to the second scenario, which involves making bread and milk and then distributing them through a market to the residential areas. The goal is to get the residential areas to level up by giving them enough bread and milk via the market. Again, I ran into a problem: the game goes "Just let the sim run and all the houses will eventually level up, and then the tutorial will end."Unfortunately, that's not true either. The actual scenario goal is to reach a certain population and have a certain number of leveled-up houses.. which never happened for me. I let the sim run at 12x speed for like ten minutes and nothing. I'm not even sure it's possible to reach that population level with the houses the game starts you with. The second tutorial was just.. bad. I couldn't get past it no matter how many farms and houses I had - I tripled the number of houses and had four farms doing nothing but making wheat and another four doing nothing but making milk and still couldn't get the goal to complete. There's also a lot of very questionable mechanics that are extremely janky, if not bugged. As an example, wheat farms need to have fields manually placed around them, but also need a road connection directly to the farm building. If you place fields all around it, you can block the road from connecting and then have to manually demolish the fields to put a road in. What I don't quite understand is why I'd ever want a farm with less than maximum fields (since as far as I can tell, fields don't cost anything) or why the farm building doesn't have a road automatically attached to it so that you can't render the entire thing useless by surrounding it completely with fields.. or better, have a road connecting to the fields themselves count as a road connection.Overall, I'd say avoid this until they fix it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar is reminiscent of Pharaoh, while adding some much needed improvements. I loved Pharaoh; however, I would always become frustrated being unable to truly control the walkers' pathways--in Nebuchadnezzar you are allowed to do just that which makes for easier management and distribution. The game itself is beautiful and the music is wonderful (except for the song with a piano--don't quite remember that instrument being found in Ancient Mesopotamia). The developers definitely wanted to make the game more challenging: the maps are small and require strategic planning and forethought to build your city. As another reviewer put it, though, this might be challenging but it limits the player's creative expression and doesn't allow for major expansion or very large cities. If there is one thing I could request it would be to see the gods and goddesses walking around the city like in Zeus, Poseidon, and Emperor, but possibly the developers wanted to keep more in line with Pharaoh.

_childDocuments_.review: Very pretty looking and impressive work for a team of two people, but unfortunately it's a pass.There is just too much focus on micromanaging logistics over actual city building. And citizens expect food delivered to their house door, and would rather do the long trek to leave the city, starving, instead of fetching it around the corner.This feels less like playing as a powerful ruler and more like managing a stone age Just Eat. _childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed this game way more than I expected! I remember that initially on launch there were some rough reviews, but it's great to see that developers kept adding to the game and it seems like they've managed to create the definitive Impressions Games-style city builder.The tutorials could've been a bit expanded, I've been confused by a couple of mechanics. But after checking two 10 minute videos on youtube I got the hang of things.I love the economical and logistical tightrope you need to walk in order to grow and expand your city, with challenges (like trading, diseases, fire, gods) being thrown at you. I wish more city builders were as reactive to your choices as this game.Warfare is another recent addition to the game. I was a little intimidated by starting a campaign with warfare goals. It didn't have a dedicated tutorial, but it was quite easy to figure out. It's definitely not what you expect it to be, however it is an interesting additional system on top of other things that you need to manage when building your city. It's not mandatory to the game, you can turn warfare off it you want, but it's adds an interesting challenge to the mix. I've yet to go in-depth with it, but first impressions are pretty positive.Either way it's a great game! Great job devs for sticking to your vision and listening to the community where it was appropriate.Update: After finishing the final mission, I can say that I've loved it! The educational part of it was also amazing and fun to read, especially the one after the final mission. I would say that warfare missions are way harder than regular ones. But if you learn to optimize your city (there are some great Steam guides) you'll manage just fine.The difficulty scales gradually throughout campagin, with the later levels being the most challenging, and it was very satisfying to complete those, even though it took me up to 2 days to work through them.

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar really should be called nebu-chad-nezzar :)A wonderful game and a worthy tribute to the classic we all love (I assume that's why you're here)A short breakdown to the similarities and differences to pharaoh:Overall, the resemblance is obvious: A city-building game set in an ancient era. Many of the game's core mechanics come straight from pharaoh: You build a city, tend to its citizens and build up an economy that provides stability in this symbiotic circle of people, economy and state. The campaign introduces you mission by mission to the mechanics of the game, starting with a small village that's self-sufficient but is very simple in functionality and variety of goods. You then get introduced to irrigation, the gods, monuments, trading, diplomacy, warfare... all the stuff we know from pharaoh. Where nebuchadnezzar shines though, are a lot of welcome, nicely made improvements:______________________________________________________________PathfindingPharaohs horrendous flaw was that of its horrible AI. You had to structure your roads in a particular way to make sure that providers would walk the path where they would do their service, and not have the bazaar lady running around in an industrial zone, while your poor citizens would starve to death. What nebuchadnezzar did is provide an easy way to set actual routes for providers. Each provider building comes with haulers, who grab resources from nearby warehouses. Furthermore, each building has a number of slots which can be filled with eighter providers or haulers. You can also choose which provider distributes which wares, resulting in high customisability, but also a higher learning curve in finding the best setup for your supply chain.Other service providers such as firemen or healers simply head out and check buildings by sorts of in-built logic you have no control over. There is some attention required from time to time, as your growing city will require more and more service providers to keep risks in check, but so far, when something happened, it was really my fault for not paying attention, instead of a flaw in the game's pathfinding mechanics. ______________________________________________________________The godsUnlike in Pharaoh, deities are not the resentful pricks who condemn your city to pain and suffering unless you have built 3 temples, a monument, 10 shrines and keep providing a sacrifice to them once per year sodom and gommorah would be proud of. In Nebuchadnezzar, 10 years may pass and you haven't bothered building any religious facilities whatsoever, which is when you will get the notification that your main deity is a bit sad that you haven't called in a while, and therefore your clay miners reduce their productivity by 4%. Festivals are also not something you have to be bothered all the time, which is quite the relief when you just need to skip time until certain conditions are met. Once a festival is planned, it starts immediately (which is also observable in your city),  and you cannot hold another one (meaning you don't have to worry about it) for quite a while. An honourable mention is also that you may customise your festivals: The goods to be consumed, a bigger variety defining the size of the festival, and addressing it to up to 3 deities simultaneously. ______________________________________________________________MonumentsA huge funbrake in Pharaoh was for me the mind-numbing long times it took to build monuments. While they are still a somewhat resource-demanding and basically time-consuming issue in Nebuchadnezzar, you can quicken the process by throwing more resources per minute at it, and since that is also a price to pay, it doesn't take away from the satisfaction.The system to build your own monument is lovely. There are certain conditions you must meet, to not cheat your victory by building a shack and calling it a temple, and if that isn't your pair of shoes, you can still pick a premade blueprint.______________________________________________________________Economy and balancingThe overall feel of the game is more demanding than Pharaoh, but that is also the fun in it. The new possibilities with routes, logistics and distribution make building your city an engaging and incredibly satisfying experience. There is a whole new learning curve to be tackled in this game, and I had so many moments where I found new ways to make my economic  systems even better. Managing your city will be a constant challenge: In order to generate money, you will have to start trading with other cities, which means less resources for the population. ______________________________________________________________Trading and diplomacyWhile trading is pretty much the same as in Pharaoh, they have refined it with some nice little additions, as well as adding diplomatic functions. Whereas your kingdom rating would raise in Pharaoh for completing requests, you now tend relationships with each individual city. As you become friends, you also can demand favours from them and send gifts to improve relationships. On the world map, you also see the military strength of each city, and eventually, you want to declare war on them.____________________________________________________________WarfareWhereas in Pharaoh you've built an army for more or less defensive or diplomatic reasons, Nebuchadnezzar allows you to send your troops out and conquer other cities. While you do not actually control captured cities yourself (they will send tributes in form of wares), it still adds another strategic layer to the game. Combat is depicted in a rather barebones tactical map, where you move your troops in fixed fields forward or sideways. It's obviously not total war CA level of combat, but it's certainly a lot more engaging than what Pharaoh did, not to mention Pharaoh: A new era.______________________________________________________________PresentationThis game is a work of art. The map, the animations, artworks and UI all work together marvellously in pulling you into this wonderful world of old. The music is beautifully composed and of a flawless quality, and hits the tone of the game deadeye. Buildings are clustered with visual detail, and pretty much everything is animated that needs to be: Industrial buildings show the workers doing their job (IF they do so), barracks are gradually filled with soldiers, markets change their colours to represent the goods they distribute. The plazas and gardens we know from Pharaoh make a return. And here's one little critique: While I love how you can design your plazas yourself by not only handpicking from a broad variety of designs but by also setting colour schemes, it is a chore to place whole districts that way, piece by piece, unless you use one design solely. Unfortunately, it is the same with gardens: There is no option to just pull a square and have it filled randomly, it's either one design on the whole place, or handpicking field by field. A style editor and distributor would have been lovely.Another point of critique may be the voiceovers: I doubt the mesopotamians spoke with such a stark british accent. But honestly, as far as I know, Nepos Games is a small studio with just one game released, and when compared with the rest of the game's presentation, this really is not even worth the mention.______________________________________________________________Famous last wordsAs you might have noticed if you have read this whole review, I am genuinely stunned by this game. It is one of those miracles in the indie gaming industry, the standard only a few meet. If you liked Pharaoh, get this game. It is a brilliant, highly polished gem, and belongs in the masterclass of modern gaming development. If you are displeased by the current gaming industry, get this game. It is a love letter to quality in graphics, difficulty balancing, and player experience, and quite frankly to gamers :)

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often play city planners but thought I'd give this one a try. So far I think it's pretty good. All the planning is fun though  there are some bits of tedium I don't want to really be bothered with and that comes down to manually planning market routes. I'd much rather have service buildings automatically service all other reachable buildings within a radius instead of creating paths for individual workers.  My other one big gripe is that there isn't enough information (or it's hidden somewhere) about how much a building produces/consumes. How many open slots there are for employment etc... give me more numbers and graphs! But like I said it's pretty ok.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I've played Caesar 3 and 4 extensively and it's almost immediately apparent to me that this game takes much inspiration from that series.This is a very well-crafted game that gives you a fairly high-level of freedom in how you approach each challenge and go for building the biggest city you can.  As of this writing, the game probably still has more patches and additions incoming but what I've played so far is quite engaging and I would recommend it for anyone who loves city-builder games.  My favorite aspect of this game has to be the fact that you can build various monuments free-form and you can shape the structure however you please, the game giving you a great deal of freedom in how you create it.  The only limit there, is the space in your city, how fast you can get the building materials to the site... and your imagination.I will give one word of warning though: this game has a very extensive resource system and as such, the game has a bit of a learning curve so if you're new to this sort of game, it's probably best to take it slow and play through the campaign, which will introduce the various aspects of the game, one at a time.  Trying to build a free-play city could end up leaving you feeling overwhelmed.Other than that though, this game is shaping-up to be an irreplaceable experience where you can create cities and monuments that are truly yours.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A refreshment towards city-building and management. Nebuchadnezzar unlike it's Pharoah, Emperor and Caesar III predecessors brings a little bit more to the table in terms of planning and cautiousness when expanding. This game lives up to the potential I always miss in newer city building titles. Which is the fact that you can easily rush after a certain milestone has been passed in most city building games.I personally really like what they've done with the genre for once, they've made scaling not only resource wise, but also in terms of complexity. It does not come down to "plopping down" a structure and call it a day. Routing has to be done and not only that one has to consider efficiency to be a key aspect in planning for expansion, but also further down the road. Which is really something for those that like a challenge or for the more seasoned city builder fanatic. For those that TL;DR:Why this game might be something for you?:- Complex city planning & management- Nostalgia: (Caesar III, Emperor & Pharoah vibes)- Nice artwork and design- Campaign & tutorial- Sandbox mode- Steam Workshop- Building your own temples
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: First I wasn't so sure about the game because I felt there was some kind of 'trade rush', but I have to add that there has been some balancing within the game mechanics. I like it now.Once you've set up the base logistics and society strata, some nice mid-game challenges can be taken on to keep it more interesting than just the city-building aspect. Build temples, wage wars, direct your religious development, functional decoration...The campaign gives a good aim as well. Missions don't feel limiting; they rather encourage your creativity to apply your game's knowledge in new ways.As for the nostalgic isometric style: well that's a no-brainer if you've seen or played this genre in the nineties. I love it.By the way the voice acting is hilarious. I think that wasn't intended but if it was: good one :P
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very much a continuation of the Impression games, only with about 20 years of players experience pushing the difficulty A LOT, if you're a (Zeus, Pharaoh, Caesar III, etc) veteran this is the update and challenge you've been waiting for, but for newcomers I'd reccomend an Impression game first to properly learn the way these games work, probably Caesar III.This is a very well made, very true to its core philosophy game that is a genuine achievement.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fun of the Pharaoh, Caesar, and Zeus/Poseidon games, you will love this! It's a more in depth version of the classic city builder genre, adding more flavour through custom temples, logistical management, and fleshed out religion. Although the game is still being developed by two indie devs, I have high hopes for the potential in this game. Definitely recommend it for anyone looking for a challenging city builder.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Great city builder with a short campaign like 12 levels or so. The sandbox mode is my favorite as I get to build w/e I want. There are a few great workshop mods to keep this game interesting, but not enough to have replay value. I just managed to get all the achievements and lost interest already. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This might not be the city-building game many people would expect, but as a nostalgic fan of Pharaoh, it is right up my alley and what I was hoping it would be. Having played Pharaoh as a kid and revisiting it as an adult, things I remembered loving about the game and things I realized weren't so great when I started replaying recently quickly became apparent. Seeing the different places and time periods Impressions delved into, I was disappointed to see that Mesopotamia didn't get done. Cut to me finding this gem.One of the main things I actually enjoy is how it isn't finished yet, it seems like things are being reviewed and perfected before going so far that baser mechanics can't be fixed. What's there now, to me, works very well and makes for a great foundation to add things to, perhaps even cool things Pharaoh didn't have. Even so, I'm still having a blast with what's there now.Another big thing I like is how missions aren't time-sensitive, unlike most of the missions in Pharaoh. I like being able to take my time designing and planning for the future, so this was a big plus in my casual-gamer book.Of course, you can't have a game that takes place in Ancient Mesopotamia without war mechanics, but I'm glad the developers put it off to focus on economy aspects. Resource management was one of my favorite things about Pharaoh, so I'm happy to see it play the primary role here. I'm a super casual gamer, so my thoughts on this should definitely be taken with a grain of salt.And finally, although I could sing its praises a lot longer, I have to applaud the customization mechanic. One of my disappointments with Pharaoh was not being able to at least choose the color schemes of city décor. Not only can you do this in Nebuchadnezzar, but you can even design the layout of giant temples! Super epic.All in all, fabulous game, and big thanks to the developers for bringing a great idea to life. Hopefully, with the great historical background provided before missions, this could be a game to use in schools to give kids an idea of what cities were like back then. I was introduced to Pharaoh in elementary history class and have since been a history buff, so I'd love to see it be a way to inspire kids to delve into this stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This appears to be an updated version of the old Impressions Games city-builders two to three decades ago, with an ancient Mesopotamian setting. Some of its features are unique, such as being able to customise your own monuments & decorations. The goods delivery mechanics also differ from Impressions' games, being much more customisable instead of the old formula 'deliver from A to B', though it may catch old Impressions veterans wrong-footed. Similarly, for a history aficionado, the campaign info is interesting to read, allowing you to learn how Mesopotamia came about as the world's first civilization.The downside is that some elements are not well-fleshed out, and the unique goods delivery mechanic tends to lean towards micromanagement if one is not savvy enough. Particularly irritating though, is the map editor. In comparison to Impressions' editors for Caesar III, Pharaoh Cleopatra, Zeus/Poseidon, and Emperor RoTK, actually creating a map is shockingly difficult, particularly for non-programmers. Instead of the simple 'load a new map & design as you see fit', you have to read Nebuchadnezzar's wiki to actually learn step-by-step how to do so. The consolation is that the game's developer is open to community modding, making things more enjoyable.It's only been over a year since Nebuchadnezzar's release, so I'll not be too quick to judge. For the time being, I'd say it's somewhat fleshed out. Perhaps this review may change when I revisit the game a year or two from now.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very nice and has very similar mechanics to the classic Impression Games series (Pharaoh, Zeus, Caesar...), but with some new twitches that allow for an even better management experience of ressource production and distribution. A perfect dose of difficulty and pleasure: hard enough to keep you awake, but not a constant pain. I truly recommend this game to those who like city building adventures and thank the developers for such a good job.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved both Caesar 2 and the Pharoah/Cleopatra series from years ago, this game combines some of the best elements of both and resolves some of the worst elements to boot (like the fact that you can actually route your market salespeople, water carriers, etc. instead of having to set stop signs and hope that they randomly walk past all your houses to provide for your people.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: It has a lot of similarities to the Impressions Games city builders like Pharaoh, but I would say it requires more careful pre-planning of the city layout than in those older games. The transporters that carry goods between buildings and storage areas have a quite limited range so you have to manually set up caravans that can carry goods any distance around the city. Frequently you produce one thing in one area of the city, then you manually set a caravan route to bring it nearer to a residential area so it can be distributed. If that sounds like too much micromanagement then this isn't the game for you, but personally I still enjoyed the nostalgia of replaying those old-school city builders.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar feels like Impression's Games city builders' engineer cousin. That is, almost everything is represented with clear numbers and player has incredible amounts of control over everything in the city. This control can be welcoming but it also pushes tons of management to player. Neb's mechanics are also much more gamey feeling compared to its spiritual predesessors, with details like different population classes having their own good types.As veteran of Impression's games, I found the game good but somewhat spiritless. But I would still suggest it for people who are hungry for more city builders.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I would wait for a sale, but I would definitely also recommend this game, the mechanics of the game is easy enough to understand, and it's clear that a lot of love has been put into the game the way everything is very nicely stylised. Also, I really enjoy the period this is set, so this might constitute a biased review.tldr: On first impressions alone, a 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A game with a wonderful atmosphere that I get lost in. The music is hauntingly beautiful and the puzzle is engaging.It is similar to the old classic isometric citybuilders, like Caesar 3 and Pharaoh, but also different. There are many small quality of life updates that makes the experience smoother, and some mechanical changes that makes for a different experience.Like with most things, it is not for everybody. I personally enjoy the focus on logistic and the spatial puzzle of working with tight delivery/work ranges. The ability to set the routes for many service walkers means I can experiment with crazy road layouts to make intricate aristocrat neighbourhoods or messy worker neighbourhoods that still works.But it is not a game with constant external pressure, so will not appeal to those who crave that from their games.I wouldn't mind more variety in the missions, or more depth to the diplomacy between cities (which might come with 1.4). But the devs seem to have a clear idea of the game they want to make, which is commendable. I've now played almost 50 hours on Steam and GoG combined, and don't see me wanting to stop anytime soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: an old-school management game, very enjoyable and made with love (I appreciate the mesopotamian theme: historically convincing, and reminding of management games origins - i. e. "The Sumerian Game"/"Hamurabi" ). I am looking forward to warfare update!Two small observations: 1) sometimes I would like to see the full map, without menus, in order to place better the buildings. Is it possible?2) a suggestion: add a slavery management. Perhaps it is not "politically correct", but it is historically most accurate and it could be a meaningful innovation (it had been proposed also for the Caesar games series).
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Great modern take on classic city-builders in the vein of Caesar 3 and Emperor:RotM, getting rid of the more annoying aspects of these games (job walker system, anyone?) and sprucing the games up for a more modern standard with pleasant yet stylized graphics and UIDefinitely a game you must try out if you enjoyed playing those games in the past (or present), while newcomers to the genre are better off waiting for a discount - to someone without the "nostalgia" factor, this is still a solid city-builder, but one that can wait until its 10-15$
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: An ancient city builder where you manage some of the first cities to appear in history, you'll have to plan the foundations for giving people houses, ensuring their needs are met, keeping the finances afloat, building monuments to the gods, so on and so forth!You jump into a scenario and begin working towards the goals for said scenario. You can pause the game whenever you want, increase the game speed, and even turbo it to go even faster. The background audio works fine to give you a relaxing feeling while the little peasants run around doing their tasks and errands.I found that the tutorial for the game was decent enough to explain what I needed to do but not overly overbearing. Some elements of the game could be improved a bit though as even with the tutorial I needed to get some help to overcome the forth and fifth missions of the game (which were the 2nd last and last missions to 'have' the tutorials). The UI was okay for the most part but definitely contributed to hindering me in learning the game.The main value in this game is all about designing cities how you want too. You pursue how a city develops, who it becomes friends with, and what will be accomplished. Overall I believe this to be a fun little city builder to kill time with; possibly too much as you move to achieve whatever goals you have.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A fun little ancient city builder, the main problem I have with it is the camera.  It feels like in an effort to not have "black space" outside the map, you can't build in the corners, which is frustrating.  otherwise its really great!I'd probably advise waiting for a sale, just because 20$ is a bit of a steep price for this.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game. It's addictive and requires careful planning. The game (depending on the setting) allows you to demolish stuff and get all resources back meaning you can try different designs & tactics without being punished which is a great positive because the game is all about trial & error, making the most of the space you have. It's a good modern iteration of the old classics such as Caesar, Pharaoh, etc. The music & atmosphere is relaxed, the game has enough depth to keep you going and generally it's just good.BUT. Don't expect this game to be perfect. For a first attempt it's a really strong one and really, most flaws could be patched in time but here are some of my main annoyances:- the maps are always small meaning you have to already be aware of where to build your residences right from the start. All trade routs need to converge on residences since that's where you "spend" them. This limits your freedom quite a bit but on the other hand, without the small size, the game would become too easy since you'd be able to have virtually unlimited resources.- the game can become rather repetitive - you always have to build up in a certain order and some of it feels like grinding. After a dozen maps you'll be able to fluently design the trade hierarchy and it's not really taxing at all. - there are no limited resources - every resource can be grown infinitely at pretty much any place (except for fish). It means the only real element on a map that counts, is access to water since this is vital for trade, fish & irrigation. Other than that, build wherever you want without any limitation. Clay pits can be placed everywhere and not just on clay ground for example.- trade is too random: depending on what other cities will accept you can either make an easy fortune buying copper and selling jewelry or you'll be scratching your head because you can only sell fish or other low-cost goods that take up too much space on the map to be worthwhile. It would be better if the economics were more fluid and prices fluctuated.- It's a good idea that you can't get some goods unless you import them but it feels as if that mechanic isn't fully explored.- building a temple is not very transparent - it's clumsy & awkward and I generally just use the pre-designed temple- warehouses will accept every good by default - this should be the opposite. Too often I've placed a warehouse and before I have a chance  to pick an item, the carrier started filling it with a random resource I don't want there- the system for setting up walk paths for bringing goods to homes is a mess - please improve it.- police & fire brigade doesn't work as it should - I notice they don't walk up to buildings within range that need "inspection". I often get fires right next to a fire station - how does that make sense? Please make these officers put their focus on buildings that have become high risk.- the warehouses are far too small. 32 units is peanuts and half the work is struggling with how warehouses are within range of workshops while still being able to handle the output. I think they should double the capacity of the warehouses. Also, if you set certain goods to no longer be accepted, you should get a question whether they should be removed from said warehouse.- prestige is boring and makes levels longer than they need to be. You can reach every goal but have to sit there letting the game run for half an hour longer just to hit your prestige level. I mean if the game requires 1000 of a certain population, why demand prestige that means you really need 2000 population (because population and quality of  the dwellings is the main way to get prestige). This feels unbalanced- You have multiple types of road that cost different amounts but there's actually NO practical difference. Why not make it affect walking speed? A dust road vs a quality paved road would make a huge difference in real life. Instead the ONLY difference is prestige. Please fix this because it means 90% of roads should just be dust roads with the current system. I mean, why pay more otherwise?
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Well its a great looking and has some good potential but it need some work specially in the economic game play. For example you'll never find aristocrats in workshops and in this game they make you wait too long for certain game play mainly the arrival of aristocrats to work in shops. I think they need to research the word aristocrats they mistaken with craftsman who worked shops and provided the aristocracy with jewelry and good . The aristocrats were rulers not workers, and this is the problem with this game. you can't get some good used by workers but made by aristocrats?? This is the main problem . The editor is not for the laymen its for programmers , so they need to take a look at Caesar 3 editor, user friendly and well balanced. Is it worth it. wait after its problems are resolved. But its very engaging even as it is.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This city builder has an excellent tutorial and is set in an historical setting with a campaign.  I like the fact that this game has set goals for achievement.  Another very important feature missing from several other games of this type is a system for setting the paths for citizens providing services which makes it much easier to provide services to all that need them.This game is still being regularly updated.  It has an easy to use GUI as well.  This game is an excellent choice for those that enjoy city building games and I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Finally gave up on this.  As I was playing, I found myself cursing it more than praising it.  Too many concepts, rules, and procedures are just not explained well enough to be able to enjoy the game.   The tutorial, which should have covered these things, started out well enough, walking you through many of the more basic mechanics; but once it got to the more advanced subjects such as trade, religion, and prestige, the devs just threw up their hands and said, "you can do these things, but we're not going to go into any details in the tutorial"... what a cop out.An additional frustration is the hauler AI.  They seem to fixate on the closest warehouse to the point where they will not deliver any goods further away (but still within range) to the market... Extremely poor design.I was really looking forward to playing this... what a disappointment it turned out to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar is a great game with a similar look to the classics.Due to the relatively small maps, it becomes more of a puzzle game than a sandbox game, which might be off-putting for some, but it did not bother me. What botheres me is the initial loading time till you get to the loading screen is absurd for such a game.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Review version = [Version 1.3]Currently the game is features complete enough for me to recommend it. It play quite like the old Impression game, but with much more focus on space and logistic planning.  If you enjoy Zeus and Emperor you should be familiar to what this game will offer you.So was it fun? I would say kindna? The game is much harder than Pharaoh and Zeus at normal difficulty, and it play more like a puzzle game where you has to figure out the optimal city-layout to achieve the map's objective. I enjoy that aspect of the game a lot. However, I do not like how small the housing upgrade there is in the game. In Pharaoh your house will upgrade a level for every 1 'item' you provide to it. However in Nebuchadnezzar your house will upgrade at every 2 'items' provided. In the end your house only has 4-5 level of developments for each type of house. As a person who took ton of joy from upgrading house in Impression game I found this wanting.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay: All in all a good game; maybe not excellent, but imho well worth a play if you bought it on sale. The initial guide popups help you understand the mechanics very quickly,  and everything flows decently from there. Sometimes you want some minor information/description on some building you never used and can't find what you are looking for, but that mostly resolves itself once you get to play with the building a bit. Gameplay wise all the info is in easy to find places.Graphics: Do the job well. Nothing groundbreaking, but they do have a bit of charm.Audio: It's there and is mostly a pleasany backdrop.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from Master of Olympus Zeus which still stands the test of time to this day this game does plenty of things better. No more healers and guards wondering around hoping that they arrive at the location you wish them to go, since they quite smartly go where they are needed. It also looks pretty/good enough for modern title in this vein. Market people go where you tell them to go and you can set up routes for your cartmen to carry stuff around. I found the UI a bit confusing at start, but once you get used to it it makes sense and works. Took me a while to understand the trading view.  Playing with the religions in this game is, eh whatever. They give you buffs if you remember the gods, honestly I forget them more often than not. I also didn't like the fact that the distance between a trading port and a warehouse is so small, It makes trading fidly in my honest opinion. Same with the Markets and farms. They have to be really close to the warehouse. Too close to my liking. In Olympus you could see when for example your wineries are filled with grapes, and filled with wine. If grapes or wine were not moving you could instantly tell it just by looking at it which is super handy. In here you need to click at the individual farm/refinery to see if they have the resources they need, or if they are not delivering to warehouse. It's a nitpick, but since making resources flow from one place to another is such a big part of the game I find this really annoying.But honestly. The biggest gripe with the game I personally have is just how clinical it is. There is humor no where to be found and your cities feel really empty. Even though it's pretty it's not interesting to watch. I wish I could "Meh" a game on steam. It's not a bad game per se, and I think you can find enjoyment in here if you like this type of game and have played the classics like Caesar, Zeus and Pharaoh too much. I haven't played this game too much, but I don't think my opinion can change much since I disagree with the style. I think Nepos Games have shown their love for the game with patches and I commend them for it.If you don't mind the clinical take you might like this game better than I did. If you are unsure wait for sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Great for anyone who loved the Sierra city builders with some unique twists like the caravan system. The game is mostly about warehouse and supply chain management, more so than Anno eg. The developers obviously put a lot of love into the game and it has improved greatly since release, with further updates coming in the near future.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Player from Emperor.1. Map alone too much restrictions, small, obstacles, pump not placeable, terrain not modifiable or reroute/re-sit  structure automatically.2. Ui need to improve, "needs", can be simplified into 4 bars at once, hover one to one to verify which is low supply is annoy. Building temple level selection is confuse by eye + arrow.3.
