_childDocuments_.review: I love X-Com and tactics games, I've tried so many but none really hit the mark how I felt playing X-Com the first time until playing this game. It has stuff you are familiar with like overwatch, upgrading your Knights, base building and management, cover system, melee and ranged attacks etc. If you like tactics games but all the cutesy anime ones turned you off, then this game is definately a good choice.Each level is a good size. They take a little, but not overly long and not too short. There are plenty of side missions to do where you can get XP for your Knights, recruit new knights, find new gear and they all have little stories in them too. The art design and aesthetic is really good. It's like a mix between a Dark Souls aesthetic, and Crusader King's. Like a mix between fantasy and real medieval stuff. The narrative itself is really cool. Arthurian Legend but it's definitely not a simple heroes vs villains idea. Your main character is Mordred, not Arthur. Much darker and morally ambigious than most Arthurian Legend takes so far. Plus you get to see alot of characters from these stories if you are familiar with them, E.g. it was pretty cool when I stumbled on Uther Pendragon's and Igraine's tomb.Controls are good. I use W,A,S,D but mouse clicks Diablo style work too for running around stages, then once in combat phase it turns into X-Com style controls which all work as expected with no issues at all for me. It isn't like X-Com where movements are all grid based. Yun run around the maps like Diablo, then when you encounter enemies it turns to a X-Com style combat phase. I think this is far, far better because you arent constantly using turns like in X-Com to get around the map and waste turns when theres nothing around. It's just far more efficient and no time wasting. Alot of different enemy types with strengths, weaknesses etc. Ranged, magic, melee. Status stuff like fire, poison, hexes etc. Theres armor, HP and Vitality which seems a little odd at first but pretty much armor works as expected, HP is Hit Points, and vitality starts to reduce when HP is gone, and is where the risk of things like injuries or death start to rise. It's a bit like Darkest Dungeon.It has performed pretty well for me and I don't have a super high end PC. My little RX580 has run it well with mostly high settings, but just texture and shadows turned to medium for a few extra frames. I'm pretty much always around 60fps for most part. The fog seems to cause the most frame drops for whatever reason. The install size is really large, around 120GB and I suspect it may be very high res textures because I can't see where all else the size is coming from. If it is the textures, separating into a high-res texture pack would be good to save space since I'm running in 1080p anyway.Overall recommend alot, particularly if you like tactics and X-Com games and looking for something more serious and not the anime stuff. Even more so if you have an interest in Arthurian Legend, or if not, you can learn it here. There's good character bio's that explain alot.

_childDocuments_.review: King Arthur: Knight's Tale is a turn-based tactical game set in the mystical realm of Avalon from Arthurian legend. The combat is reminiscent of a more melee-focused version of XCOM, with a smattering of XCOM's base management. You play as the Sir Mordred who awakens in Avalon after he and King Arthur have slain each other on the battlefield. Mordred claims Avalon's dark reflection of Camelot, and it's Knghts of the Round Table, as his own, and places Avalon under his protection. It's up to you whether he rules as a just and rightful king or a greedy tyrant.The core tactical game-play is extremely strong and once you get the hang of how the armor, hit points, movement and damage systems work, overcoming the challenge is quite rewarding. Additionally, leveling up your knights is full of interesting choices and adds a great layer of strategy to the game. These factors alone are enough for the game to get a recommendation from me.  The base management is fine, not as in-depth or critical to your success as XCOM but still an important aspect of the game.My only complaints about the game are: - Infrequent, but noticeable bugs. -  Occasional late-game combat encounters that use unfair systems that the player hasn't been prepared for, such as having enemy reinforcements show up with no warning mid-turn leaving your knights that have already acted out of position and vulnerable. Fortunately,  this is uncommon and you can reload if turns out ruinous.- The knights themselves have fairly one-dimensional personalities and their interesting dialog is pretty much exhausted after the mission in which you recruit them.The game is visually interesting with its depictions of the knights and it's dark fantasy setting of Avalon. I found the story a bit hard to follow, and was never clear on what Avalon is and what it's rules are. Is it a faraway island in the ocean? Is it some sort of Faerie Realm? Is it the Afterlife? If so, why is it populated with peasants working the fields and how do it's inhabitants die?But these are relatively minor nitpicks. If you like Arthurian legend, dark fantasy, and tactical combat, King Arthur, Knight's Tale is a great way to kill 60+ hours.

_childDocuments_.review: King Arthur: Knight's Tale has been an incredible experience so far. It's deep tactical battles remind me of stellar games like XCOM, Battletech, or AOW: Planetfall. With only 4-5 units under your control, it makes each move you take a wonderful puzzle where you are trying to balance offense while not putting putting your knights in a place where they'll take too much damage. I love the innovation of a separate bar for Hit Points which can be replenished relatively easily with potions, campfires, or the end of a mission vs a bar for Vitality which can only be slowly regained by missing future missions. Armor is also an excellent mechanic as it progressively gets stripped away during missions. This steadily increases the tension during missions until you finally get the relief of seeing the Victory screen.Like the other games I mentioned, Knight's Tale also has rewarding systems for obtaining and optimizing gear for your knights, skill trees to make your knights more powerful over time, and a base-building system as you build the capabilities of Camelot up to better service your knights. You are constantly making strategic trade-offs in all these areas to best utilize limited resources.  I'm about 80 hours in and my knights are level 6-8, so I have plenty of game to go. I started out on Hard, then at level 5, bumped it up to very hard and this has been the perfect level to punish me for every mistake while allowing me to progress if I use every move and resource well.Overall, Knight's Tale is my Game of the Year so far!

_childDocuments_.review: This is an exceptionally crafted game that is clearly well-loved by the developers. It's the first game I've bought in a long time that had me truly engrossed. It's a captivating world with a very tightly built combat/character builder system driving a unique strategy experience.It's hard to describe the game, though -- and I think a lot of negative reviews involve player misconception/player expectation colliding with what I've come to recognize as Neocore's off-meta style of game development/design. Neocore has their own in-house engine, their own completely in-house set of assets, and their own in-house approach to creating a gameplay experience. They almost completely forgo the best practices of streamlined/attention-absorbing gameplay design, almost always build a kind of baroque cathedral of math and numbers into your gear and skill progression (which makes them deep and rewarding but also bizarre at times), and almost always make somewhat quaint or quirky design choices -- in King Arthur, for example, all your characters are left-handed, for whatever reason. The result is usually a game that feels lovingly hand-crafted and kind of compellingly oddball, but is also often funky or janky too. They're not an "indie" studio with a discernibly indie style, but they're not a AAA studio either. It's just...Neocore.I personally think it's great, and they're one of my favorite studios. They have a few IPs they clearly deeply cherish -- the King Arthur/Avalon setting is one of them (their earliest games were set in this same setting, and with King Arthur: Knight's Tale they've returned to it with a fresh take). The other two are Van Helsing and Warhammer 40K -- and I've put hundreds of hours into those games too.All that to say, I think this game is well-worth the price, and well-worth your time. I've played through the game on most of the different morality quadrants (which give different missions and knights) on Very Hard and Hard -- don't believe reviewers saying it's too hard or gets boring -- it just doesn't. There's plenty you could pick at -- the characters having a few lines of dialogue they repeat quite often during missions, some missions have randomly massive spikes in difficulty, the inability to change the cosmetics of your characters. But I don't know -- I love this game, and don't think I'd like it as much if they'd made it feel like a AAA title with AAA levels of same-y polish and same-y features. It's a rough-cut gem, I guess. A few final notes: The DLCs feel a lot more like "supporter perks" than like DLCs -- they're just challenge modes. But they're also priced accordingly, and I have no complaints about that. The "endgame" is a bit nuts -- just a huge spike in difficulty. You've been warned!

_childDocuments_.review: Purchased this game on a Sale, only 15 hours in but enjoying it a lot.Difficulty- x/10I haven't yet played the game at higher difficulties, but most games in this genre are more difficult than average. However, King Arthur: Knight's Tale is an exception to this rule, as "Normal" feels like "Casual" difficulty.That said,  there are many difficulties to choose from, so I'm sure the game gets plenty punishing. However I do wish the descriptions on the difficulties were more appropriate, as "Hard" should be described as "For players already familiar with the genre". This game would be a good introductory game to the genre, as the "Normal" difficulty is extremely forgiving.Gameplay & Mechanics- 8/10.Love these types of Tactics games, although this one runs easier than others I have played.The mechanics are engaging and interesting, every choice feels like it matters, whether in dialogue, choosing what to do with your units, or choosing what to do with your Gold and Resources.Skill Trees are great and pretty well balanced, at least from what I have experienced by leveling up the first several Knights.There are some bugs in the maps, WASD movement is slightly buggy, and sometimes you can sneak around intended combat-initiation zones and walk into enemies who won't respond to your existence.The loot call-outs are clutch, several times now, when I would have missed something due to the camera angle, my companions informed me of some loot. Some of the lines used, though, are a bit misplaced. I know they probably just wanted to splice some already-recorded lines and use them for call-outs, but there are some weird ones, from "BY GOD!", to "I was hoping for something more" when you get a Relic item from a container, to misread lines like "GARBAGE...........or real loot this time?"Visuals, Setting & Mood- 7/10. Great dark atmosphere, maps feel "just right" in terms of size and how much there is to do. Secret locations are relatively easy to find but reward you for going off the path.The colors are a bit washed out, especially for a setting that is already dark, foggy, and gloomy. Colors become indistinguishable from each other, and the shades of grey are too similar. I had to turn contrast and vibrance way up to get more clarity out of the image. The exposure is also faded. Fine for the visual style but could be more crisp instead of foggy and dreamy.Soundtrack / Music- 7/10. Fitting soundtrack, nothing that will stick with me for ages to come, but atmospheric and a pleasure to listen to, nonetheless. Even though the same tracks play often, they don't seem to get old, but instead it's the type of track you begin to habitually vibe to. That's a sign of a good composition.Sound Balance- 6/10. Overall nice, and there are options to adjust balance, but the Voices are edited to be extremely bassy, which is OK as a style, but means you effectively never want to use the "Bass Boost" EQ in the Options because, while it sounds great on the music, it sounds awful on the voices.Also, the heavily edited bassy voices of the Males contrast greatly with the Females, so you similarly never want to use the "High Boost" EQ, as it makes Females sound crunchy and airy. Not to mention, some of the Females are much louder, probably due to how compressed the Male voices are.Voice Acting- 6/10. This is a weird one, because there are some great voices, and some really bad ones. Some, like the Hedge Knight, sound like they're basically AI. Enemy targets that have voiced lines sound like they had the wrong idea of what the line was supposed to be before they read it; the direction is off. Overall amateurish. Fortunately, the Narrator and Morded's voices, along with a handful of others that drive the main plot, are good.Writing- 7/10. Grammar errors or other writing mistakes are quite common, including in voiceover lines. However, the overall plot is a very fun role-reversal concept between Arthur and Mordred. The choices and morality are a very engaging part of the game.However, there's a lot of pseudo-religious themes that may be a nuisance to some. The game is entirely fantasy, obviously, but they very loosely use Christian themes irreverently that would be seen as outrageous if it targeted a religion that took this more seriously.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting RPG that plays like a XCOM game. Knight's Tale you play as Sir Mordred who has been brought back to life by the Lady of the Lake to hunt down and kill King Arthur. You'll recruit many knights along your journey who each have their own skills and abilities. You'll even be able to recruit classic knights from the King Arthur lore such as Sir Lancelot or the Black Knight if you make certain decisions during your play-through.I had a blast with the main story-line, things got pretty hard towards the end of the game. You have a main base of operations in Castle Camelot, you'll be tasked to rebuild it giving you choices on what to rebuild to aid your quest for King Arthur. You'll find many weapons and armor to aid your knights in battle. Combat plays like a game of XCOM where each character how their own turn to make decisions on their movement and attacks. The enemy will have their turn as well, so planning is key to survival. I learned a lot of King Arthur's lore and found it interesting, the story was well written too.But I had a few issues during the end game, which they released as free DLC later one. It feels unbalanced and even on normal difficulty if you didn't find the right equipment, pick the right skills or class of knights, the end game is nearly impossible to play and you'll end up lowering the difficulty to survive. Instead of proper balancing of the end-game sections they just threw so many enemies expecting your four man crew to survive. It just felt lazy when the main game was well polished. Thankfully its not required to experience the main story, but it does add story elements that would be interesting to explore.Overall its a great game, and I couldn't recommend it enough. Even with the lazy end-game sections. It is worth a try if you like turn-based tactical games with RPG elements.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Knight's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Great game.  Fun turn-based combat, super atmospheric grim-dark setting, decent story and some fun rpg elements with skill tree's and gear.These devs also made the excellent Warhammer 40K Inquisitor and this game has similar bones (isometric view which allows for rotating and zooming).  Like Inquisitor, the game is a series of missions in which each begins you on the edge of a new map. You have key objectives but are free to explore the map as you please and there is typically some extra loot to be had if you do.A huge bonus for me (kids, family, busy life) is you can save at any point (eg half way through a mission).Well worth the money, my understanding is there is a ton of content (I'm 14 hours in and I think I'm 1/4 the way through).Well worth it, A+
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Knight's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: It had a rocky start, but it's grown on me quite a bit. Movement at times feels clunky and click-move seems the most viable with Q and E for rotation, whereas the WASD aspect fails greatly. Camera tracking is not very intuitive and the choice for camera angle just feels off. The dialogue leaves a bit to be desired in some areas, whereas in others it truly shines. It feels all together schizophrenic and I love it. I can't help but laugh at how poorly written and voice acted some scenes are, yet others are downright inspiring.The 120 GB is primarily used for ground textures and mapping but for the life of me I can't tell why.Where the game really shines though is the combat. Yes, it's buggy sometimes. Yes, one of your party can get stuck in combat start and be unusable throughout - save frequently. Once you work through those though, it's grand. Very much the "medieval XCOM" and the variation and combinations of each champion's skills lend to that. I haven't lost a champion, yet - but I fear the investment into and loss of said champion will be near heartbreaking.After the first act, I'm hooked. It's up there with other favorite tactical turn based for me. Keep an eye on this one, it was worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. While it is not open world and you're not entirely free to roam as you'd like, the story progression is always forward, even in side missions. I do wish there was a little less random to the crafting system, as sometimes you end up investing precious material into things that end up being fairly useless to your build. Combat is simple but deep - each character has some unique features to it, even within their given class. Specific skills and traits are often found dispersed among the skill tree in that each class seems familiar, but still has a flavor to them that you want to explore.And while I enjoy unlocking features in Camalot and sending out nights on their missions, I really wish there was a better way to rotate into service. Right now it seems there's just a very rare tome that allows you to move an aspiring knight you might have unlocked to your roster. Meanwhile I'm stuck with a bunch of knights I'm not really all that interested in. Particularly since I see a better skill set for my team than what I have before me. I do like the moral system - where you can unlock features and potential new knights by making some choices in either tyrant or righteous direction, or old religion or Christ. BUT, while this allows me to get new characters to use, I find the limitation of aspiring heroes being for the most part entirely locked out, because my roster (again) is full, with almost no ability to move them around. Yes, there should be a penalty for moving someone from roster to aspiring hero list; such as potential hit to loyalty, but as of not I keep unlocking lots of very interesting guys, and they're simply just blocked by this terrible feature. And as my main team increase in levels, all those other really interesting heroes are locked at whatever level I unlocked them in, making a potential use in the short run, more or less pointless. This game has been out long enough for someone to consider changing that system.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best tactical games I’ve ever played. Great visuals, solid voice acting, quite good story and most importantly engaging combat and interesting classes. Have you ever read a book or watched a film and felt immediately sad afterwards knowing that you experienced something great but now it’s over? That’s exactly how I feel about this game. After completing the main story on two morality paths (Rightful/Old Faith vs Tyrannical/Christian) I felt a bit defeated as I wanted to continue with the main character. The endgame missions have been added later, but I would rather have another story act or two.My personal wishlist for patch improvements and additional content:-	The game has six classes but allows to take only four characters on a mission. This is too restrictive and hurts experimentation. Please increase it to five through story unlock (act completion reward?), meta progression or just in campaign settings.-	The same applies to the number of active heroes you can have – it’s limited to 12. You might think that’s a lot, but already by mid-game you will have more than that. Increase it to 16-20 (through meta progression?)-	Some of building unlocks are just bland and deserve a second pass. Make me want that unlock – adding +5% hp doesn’t excite me.-	Court titles at the round table should give something more than just +loyalty. The same can be said about laws and decrees of the round table. Some are OK (exchange of resources), others are meh-	a meta progression of sorts, encouraging replayability of the main story-	faction DLC packs allowing you to play as Picts, Seelie, Unseelie and maybe as the Lost.-	completing a main story unlocks minor story campaigns for heroes you didn’t choose (Balin/Balan, Merlin, Gawain, Faerie Knight) or exiled (Tewelyn) in your playthrough-	finally, a modding workshop would ensure that this game would never run of content and remained a king (get it?) for a very long time

_childDocuments_.review: If you want to go thru the story and only face challenges on bosses then play "Normal" difficulty. Hard is where you really feel the weight of the game. The atmosphere and design really captures  the dark setting and feels for the time this story takes place. Controls can be a bit finicky if you try to force them. So if you are using Mouse to select boxes ensure you've rotated the camera as models will some times stop you from clicking the box you intended. The game plays well and its nice that tho it gives you choices they all seem to fit the character. Your choice aren't polar opposites in how they are presented. Which i think it great. Its nice to see the character being arrogant and rough even when making "Good" choices rather than just being a  full 180 from what the story presents him as. I do wish there were some more customize able choices with knights as you'll find yourself setting skills as you unlock new tiers. As the new tiers seem to have skills that push knights down specific builds which means some early investments aren't optimal. But there is fun in just making something work.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish you could give a 'neutral' review.  It's 'okay' but there are much better tactics games out there.  There are few classes, with enough skill points to get all desirable skills, which basically mean 4 cookie-cutter characters (they try to have small variation per individual, but it's inconsequential).  Combats gets very stale and repetitive rather fast, and even the campaign overstays its welcome.  I was 'done' around lvl 15, and I slugged through to end of campaign at lvl 21. The idea that anyone would want to play an endless 'endgame' after that boggles my mind, to to each their own.  On the plus side, game is stable with few bugs, art is good if you like tainted grail type fantasy, story and characters are up to par for the genre.  Itemization is stat only (items visual never change) but decent with ok progression and interesting powers/combos.  Not a bad game, but limited, repetitive and grindy.  Sort of a take it or leave it kind of deal.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid tactical RPG with a cool boardgame vibe. Each mission feels like a quick, satisfying challenge you can knock out in one sitting. The combat is strategic and varied without being overly complicated, thanks to the diverse characters you can play with. The game’s systems are easy to grasp—no drowning in walls of text here—and the base-building adds just enough depth to keep things interesting.The story does the job but isn’t super deep, and the camera controls can be a bit clunky. Still, even though it doesn’t excel in any one area, the game as a whole is greater than the sum of its parts. If you’re into strategy games that are fun and easy to get into, this one’s worth a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: I love fantasy RPG, this one is additionally pretty dark which is good as well :)Despite cons I find this game enjoying and worth buying, below are the pros and cons I found in the game:Pros- Combat, despite some unsatisfying feature is generally satisfying - Good character's levelling system- Supported by GeForce Now- I'd love more "big battles" like 20 vs 20, it was great and I definitely miss something like this in X-COM- Mode after completing campaignCons:- There were some bugs after launch which made game unplayable -> already fixed- World's textures are sometimes unreadable for me- I'm missing neutral / rightful /christian arcanist characters (basically all of them are tyrant / old faith)- level of combat difficulty vary as hell (some fights very easy, some very hard)- polish translation although generally good, sometimes fails horribly :P- some parts of combat were not well thought -> ice is not negating fire and vice versa for example -> I would expect the same combos as in Dragon Age.- I have impression, that side quests have no impact on the game (plot)- Some "cut scenes" can't be skiped- In endgame mode, I completed every mission, killed the boss etc. and actually nothing happens -> no summary, no end credits, no "thank you for playing" etc.

_childDocuments_.review: All games have elements of other games, but despite similarities to other games such as X-com or a taste of Darkest Dungeon, this is really it's own game in the turn based combat / RPG genre. Even which heroes to use for each mission changes not only with skills and strategy but with the results of previous missions potentially leaving them injured. _childDocuments_.review: Roguelite mode isn't roguelite at all. It's not even ironman. You can just brick your save beyond repair by making a decision you didn't know was a bad one. Bricking meaning, you will be on a defeat loop that just doesn't end.Many options within the game lack transparency, constant clarification from devs on how basic systems work through their discord is required because it isn't actually explained anywhere within the game. The game has pretty poor performance for system that are specced outside the top 20% it seems.There's an entire exploration layer to the map that feels like the devs really don't want you to explore.Some balance things are just kind of bizarre. For example, bleed and poison mechanics will feature in a lot of character builds with characters sometimes being specialized beyond repair towards them but half of the enemies you encounter just ignore these mechanics.Tons of strange bugs that are more goofy than anything else. A damsel in distress will cry out in a feminine voice that men are about to rape her, only for her voice to change from female to male after rescuing her, as an example.Writing isn't great. Characters make repetitive comments towards one another without any banter. You won't be surprised by anything that happens in this game from a story standpoint.They are working on it right now, and while I enjoy some things about the game, it's a bit of a slog. It feels like a continuation of early access with how much polish it still needs.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good:When i first saw this game i passed it off when it came out, mostly on the fact that this game was based on Arthurian legend. Im not a big fan or really a fan at all of the myths that come out of Arthurian legend, but i found myself more and more interested this year about it, mostly brought on by the excellent film the Green Knight. My fear is that they would have just shown a very black and white world like most of the legends are made out to be, but i was wrong. Theirs so much mythos in this world, that many times i spent time outside of the game to research some of the things in the game. You will probably see a lot of familer characters that you have seen before in other media, and getting to play these characters is actually kinda cool, but maybe im just a nerd. Worldbuilding is also great, with tons and tons of myth's built into the characters, the places that you visit, religion, and the enemies that you face. The integration of the mythology is the best part of the storytelling and the plot. I also do really like the overall look of the game, its very bleak and i think it fits the whole medieval style perfectly, though i do wish people were overall more dirty looking knights and bandits dont have any grime on them. Combat is just great and super addicting, they put you in alot of situations that force the player to be strategic. This is because theirs just so many modifiers to how you can play/plan out a mission. Their are mutiple classes and everyclass is pretty unique, with so many classes it is so fun planning out and trying different compositions of heroes. The rpg parts of the game are actually very good, the items you get have some streagty because you have to think about who should have a certain item based on its traits, sometimes i would spend like 20 minutes sorting out my items. The skills are also great tons of skills have great skill expression, some skills are just point and click while others require your team to combo their skills so that they can setup for other classes to use their skills. I also really like how skills have passive perks so that you can upgrade them, but its not just a simple upgrade like more damage! or longer range!, most of the time they actually change the skill entirely. Ontop of all of that theres also passive skills that give buffs to your character that are very specific but when used smartly it greatly improves your team. MehThe plot is good in some parts, i feel the pacing is pretty poor, some parts of the story gain much more time then others.  Expessally the start of the game where it feels like your fighting the same enemies for so long and other times it feels like you barley get to fight some enemies before the plot point ends.  Some of the writing is great, while some points feel too expository. Their is also a morality system that has 4 choices tied to it your religion choices Christianity or Old Faith, and your morality choices Bad and Good. You chose one of the 4 and gain a point for that choice, those points go to upgrades and unlocking new characters for one of the 4 choices. I liked this system in the terms of unlocking new stuff, because it integrates the story choices directly into the gameplay. But when it ties into the writing im not a huge fan, since because of how the system is designed to gain the most out of the choices you have to stick to one religion and one morality, and because of that it feels like most of the choices is just you picking the icon rather than actually making a choice. Still it wasnot a huge issue but it defiantly took away from the writing and people might be more frustrated then me.  Sidemissions also exist within the game and unlock based on your choices, some are really good and explore some of the characters from the mythos, while others just feel really rushed and poorly planned out, with little story and annoying gimmicky battles. Voice acting in some spots is amazing, Mordred is amazingly voice acted while some of the main cast has similar acting. But the majority of the characters lack voice direction even some of the mains just sound kinda stale, like the actor is just reading from the script with no personality.Balance of the game is also very hit or miss. I played on hard and some of the levels are not designed around it. Some of the sidequests have tons and tons of character spamming, while this is not that much of and issue when you understand how to fight these enemies when you first start out and your learning its very hard and since your charaters arenot leveled up to the standard theres issues with balancing. Speaking of balance some of the classes are very broken and some are underpowered, mages are very very broken because they stack cooldown removing and massive AOE spells that also deal damage, apply CC, and apply burning, which leads me into burning which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bonkers, it can deal up to 50 damage every turn which enemies at the end game have 150+ hp. Archers are very useful early game but fall of very hard lategame due to them being single target. Some characters have unique skills that just suck while others have unique skills that are so busted that it makes the characters that are the same class feel useless. Some enemies have unique skills and some of them feel just unfair for example 2 enemies have an ability to make themself invincible the 2nd of those also when using the skill becomes intargatable while also when he dies he explodes freezing anyone close. How the ♥♥♥♥ are this guys going to be harder than most of the bosses in the game and who the hell had fun playing against these enemies. The Bad:I hated the music, found it to be boring and the same tracks played way to often during battles, so i turned it off, maybe it was good but i just hate it when games have long battles and the same track plays on and on. Game runs pretty poorly i had to put it on medium for my pc to stop sounding like a jet engine it crashed once because of memory overload something that has never happened with any game so far on this pc. The ending is kinda terrible tbh, the boss battle is poorly made and too easy and you barley interact with the enemy before you kill him which sucks because the build up is great but it just falls flat.Overall this game was very surprising to me as someone who was not really interested in the setting. Gameplay is very fun and addicting, but some of the balance and difficulty can be very frustrating, rpg mechanics are very good and allows for ton of gameplay choices, that opens the door for more strategy in fights. Plot is slow but has alot of great moments, exploring the world of Arthurian legends is awesome but requires patience with the expository storytelling, characters are the best part of the story and it is awesome playing them. Ending is bad and the game dosnot run that well. In the end King Arthur: Knight's Tale is a worthwhile purchase for anyone who likes turnbased tactics since the gameplay itself carries the game even through the story is just meh, I really enjoyed it despite the jankyness, 8.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: 65 hours in, yet to complete the game and still have fun. If you like turn based strategy rpg games, you'll like this, more emphasis on the combat and strategy then role playing. One of the aspects of this game I appreciate is the lack of RNG (like Blackguard) you always hit, just with reduced damage from say cover or armor, similarly spells always "hit" as well, just with reduced effects (possibly entirely) with resists. The religion/morality system adds a good amount of replay-ability along with giving you role play choices to make and unique knights to recruit. The knight themselves also feel unique due to having different skills to level at varying levels. I'm not versed in King Arthur lore but the story and the lore behind is compelling.They added a great deal of new post game content as well as the great main campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: With a huge supporting cast of knights and sorcerers, and only 12 seats at your Round Table, there are plenty of hard choices to make on your quest to save Camelot. Some knights will align best with the righteous, others with tyrants, while others still might not share your love for the Old Gods. Then there are those who revel in blood magic and fey ritual. Those are the knights I took in.I keep waiting for the mid-game slog that is so pervasive in every other squad-based tactics game, but it just hasn't happened yet. In fact, this game just keeps getting better! The only negative that I've encountered is the uncalled-for 122GB installation size. Seriously, I have no idea why it's so massive; I've only seen 3 cinematics in my 32 hours. Regardless, this is my favorite squad-based tactics game since XCOM:Enemy Within.King Arthur's combat seems a mix of Final Fantasy Tactics and XCOM, with base building (and injury treating) reminiscent of Darkest Dungeon. If you liked any of those games, this one will be a treat.

Lower your expectations and you might enjoy this if you like turn-based combat.It was enjoyable until the endgame which had a significant difficulity spike. On some missions the game just throws so many enemies at you at once that it was impossible on my chosen diff and on other missions it was way too easy and boring. This was a problem during the main campaign, but not as bad. Some characters were OP and some didn't work at all for me so I mostly played with the same builds/characters which got boring towards the end. After listening to 'What are we waiting for' being said by multiple characters I controlled for the 100th time in the last 20 minutes I was just about to throw my keyboard at the wall, but fortunately the game ended.Huge upside for me was the ability to speed up combat on both my and enemy turns. _childDocuments_.review: This game is so good I'm writing my first review. The combat mechanics are polished. The ability trees are fun and well thought out, opening up new dynamics with progression and meaningful boosts to obtained abilities. New/interesting enemies are introduced often enough to keep things fresh. The story is well written.With that said, I'm not a fan of the injury + vitality mechanic. I skirted it by playing on normal difficulty and only suffered injuries a couple times in late game, so it wasn't a big hindrance, but I'd love to play on hard without these mechanics. I think it would work better with one mechanic or the other, but injuries and vitality healing that have to be resolved in two different buildings (multiple missions missed) is obnoxious. The dialogue can be a bit cheesy, and the voice acting is hit or miss. There were a few short-lived side characters with excellent voice acting, but many with awful acting. But I was able to overlook this for the most part considering how much fun I was having playing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is generally good - the "surprise twist on Arthurian lore" isn't that surprising as every postmodern fable - from the book "Grendel" to the movie Shrek - takes the approach of "the guy you formerly thought was a bad guy is simply misunderstood (while the guy you thought was the good guy is actually evil!).  Nonetheless it's competent, with no forced diversity or other signs of modernity - though there are more one-liners than I would like (the English voice acting ranges from good to mediocre). The biggest issue for me so far is something they don't spell out at the outset - namely that if you don't recruit enough knights, the game becomes a slog. When you encounter a knight, they make it easy for you to alienate or execute the guy, and even award "good guy points" for carrying out a righteous execution. So I naturally took that course. I only alienated one knight and executed another, but it made the whole game become a slog, as every level you pretty much get two of your party wounded, and without backup knights, you have to keep sending wounded knights back out into the battlefield. I might even start over because of this (I don't like toggling difficulty in the middle of a game - it feels like defeat). So yeah...at the start you should make an effort to recruit every knight you can, lest you be stuck in the same situation.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a lot better then I expected. It is a "combat focused" turn based game with light RPG elements. It has similarities to battle brothers, x-com, darkest dungeon. In certain ways it does some things even better then those popular games, but it falls short in the replayability those games are known for.The foundation of the combat is very very good. The armor/hp is well implemented, There are a lot of interesting abilities and I liked how this game moved away from percentage hit chances. Each individual knight you can recruit has unique art, voice, and skill sets which give them more depth compared to the characters of above mentioned games.I liked the graphics and atmosphere of the game.The itemization is not amazing but it is not bad for this type of game, and going back to town/building up your base is fine. There is not much replayability, in that the experience is linear. You are forced to proceed with the storyline. There is no room to level up/gear up doing random missions, you much choose the hand crafted missions (which aren't bad for a playthrough) but dont give you that feeling of gearing/leveling up which fights you choose like those other game do so well.. The only reason to replay the campaign is to try playing with different knights(which can be fun) but it dosen't have a true roguelike replayability. Despite being able to have up to 12 knights in your roster, you are heavily incentivized to level and gear a single 4 man group with maybe 1 alternate. In these style of games having wipes can be entertaining and trying to rebuild from that is part of the fun. This game dosen't really allow much room for that despite giving you the illusion of that. Overall I enjoyed the game but what would make this game go to the next level(to go from 60 hours played to 1000 hours played on peoples profiles) is if they truly implemented a roguelike mode anolagous to the aftermentioned games. The foundation is there.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a jewel. Of course it will not appeal to you if you like your games fast and easy, but if you are into games like XCom, Jagged Alliance or even Panzer General you will love this. To the superficial it may seem repetitive, but it's actually hugely varied. What I love most is how the very same mission may go from nigh impossible to a piece of cake depending on which heroes you bring to it, and how even the very same battle can go from hellish hard to pretty easy depending on the side from which you approach it. Tactical depth at its finest.Which does not mean there is no room for improvement. Dialogue sometimes matters, but often is just there as a fill-up. The management section is underwhelming. Interaction between characters could have been richer and more humorous.What I would most like to see in future games from the same studio is concurrent missions. Instead of one mission per week where you send 4 heroes out of 12, maybe even with a pausable real time management level, several threats at once, so forcing you to split forces. Single missions of course still turn based. So you have to decide who to send where, assessing the threat level on info that may be more or less accurate depending, for example, on buildings you have made. The missions could also stray from the fixed 4 limit. Some could limit you at two or even a single hero, other could allow you up to eight.  The roster could be expanded beyond 12, and If short on available heroes you could maybe hire one-time mercenaries to assist you.Just some ideas. But if you do not yet own this game and love tactical turn based games, rush to get it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game, played 10 hours in the first day I got it, so I'm pretty hooked, can't tell if it will last long but at least 20 hours will be enjoyable to me !The dark Arthurian background and the story are quite good, the dialogues and events are well done, and I like the combat system, RPG progression, skills and lootThe game is overall quite close to WH40K Chaos gate, replace the space cruiser by the Camelot castle, and the Grey Knight Order by the Knights of the Round Table, et voila !Battles are quite easy in Normal at least, but yet you need to think to avoid getting injured, which incurs severe penalties and off-time for the wounded, it's more doing it perfectly than simply winning in the end, given that a "mission" is a chain of 6 to 10 battles (maybe more later). As there's no healing magic (only potions) you can just rest 3-4 times to regain some HP or armor in a mission, so you need to be careful not being too badly hurtThe art and sound design are very nice, the models and animations too, but the 3D maps much less so, everything is so washed out in a greygreenish hue it's rather ugly, and technically it looks old as if done in the 2010s... Well not a big deal for me (I've started playing PC games in VGA 320x200 lol), but it's not the game best aspectThe UI is ok but sometimes pretty clunky as well. It's more of an A or AA  game but not a AAA one, and the price tag is maybe a little high, but it's really enjoyable

_childDocuments_.review: King Arthur: Knight's Tale was (for me) a very enjoyable gaming experience. It has fairly beautiful cutscenes, the artstyle itself is gothic, gritty and very atmosperic. The characters are varied and, after you find ones you like, enjoyable companions to bring a smile or some banter to your dark, gloomy exploration of tombs, forests, ritual sites, even different planes.Unlocking the champions and figuring out which ones you might prefere is imo an interesting part of the game and unlocking/playing each of their own mini-stories can be fairly intriguing. Some of the skills and classes only attain real usability in late-game but you can always reset skills and try out if another combination might make more sense as to your preference. There are several differing ranged and melee units and each character can be built slighly different and/or set up differently despite having the same class on paper. As some commenters mentioned, the game  get somewhat grindy, but if/when you have found yourself a set party you can always focus on just those - leveling + gearing up only them won't be overly exhaustive then.The difficulty levels of some fights can change greatly depending of the units you take with you and how well rounded their skillsets are - legendary gear and relics can be big gamechangers here.So, if you love complex and engaging battles X-Com or Divinity style, enjoy atmospheric levels and a grumpy (or hilarious rather) main character you'll spend quite a few hours with this beautiful game :)

_childDocuments_.review: This title does exactly what it says on the tin. Interesting premise -and a clever "refresh" on a well known setting-. A story which, so far, remains engaging. Tactical combat with meaningful choices. "Strategic layer" that is a bit basic but does what it's meant to. Interesting RPG progressions. A few ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but nothing that significantly detracts from the whole - potentially room for improvement (e.g. creating really meaningful incentives for using different heroes). Technically speaking the title seems reasonably robust. Very (too) large storage requirement, which has already been flagged for action from the developers. A couple of glitches and a single CTD, about 20 hours in. All said and done, a better offering, right out of the gate, than many "AAA" titles these days. Food for thought.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: an absolute fantastic game, perhaps my favourite iteration of turn-based combat ever.Longer version:Gameplay: Out of combat:Top tier, light settlement management (buildings/upgrades for them), assigning your knights to different passive boost duties,  browsing some merchants, nothing too grandeous here, just smooth basic stuff.The meat, aka the missions and combat:Dozens and dozens of handcrafted, beautiful maps with a handful or two of encounters in each with plenty to discover for those who like to search every nook and cranny. This is the appetizer for an incredibly enjoyable turn-based combat, with plenty of depth, options and fun mechanics. Each knight you recruit adhers to one of 6 base-classes, but they are all unique, with special skills that are layered differently, some dip to abilities that members of their class don't usually get, all that, so variety for different build/group setups is astonishing and toying with them is tons of fun. Actual combat has a decent bunch of innovation to it, simplified description would be: A) Armour prevents damage according ot the value. Armor piercing attacks deal some of their damage through it, while armor breaking attacks eat a chunk of it away. Classes in heavy armour can generally recover it with varying levels of efficiency, for medium/light it's more challenging.B) Damage goes through and taxes the Health of the target, this is "safe" damage that is still easy to recover, most classes have some skills to recover this in combat to an extent and there are the potions we all love to manage as well.C) After Health has been diminished character starts to take Vitality damage. This leads to injuries and is difficult and/or expensive to recover, mostly only done at the settlement and recovering both actual Vitality and injuries both takes time or a big chunk of gold.Each map has you navigate your way through multiple encounters, so you get to juggle the armor/health pools of people while using the campfires you find to choose between either recovering some health or armour for all characters. At least personally I really enjoyed the pacing of it, every map felt like an adventure.Actual fighting has a robust AP(Action Point) -system, reminiscent of the original 90's X-Com, and with the variety of abilities and plethora of enemy types you encounter with multitude of different character builds at your disposal this might very well be my favourite combat to date. I do greatly prefer turn-based combat so I'm very biased on that, but for anyone not downright allergic to it I'd say you are in for a good time.Story/Characters (Spoiier-free)Main story won't win any innovation awards, but neither does it annoy at any point and it has plenty of good peaks that are cool to experience. Overall, while the narrative isn't original by any means, the amount of handwritten content is massive, each mission in the main campaign be it sidequest or part of the main quest will have a unique map(few locations are revisited, but the encounters and events in them will be vastly different), and there are a lot of them so while it won't leave you wondering about the meaning of life or tear-eyed you'll like enjoy the overall experience.Characters are a bit more mixed thing, though not really due to any fault by the developers, more so because of the way the game is built. Basically main character is realized very well, and the characters that participate in the primary story arc have some meat in their bones, but the sheer number of knights, all unique all with their own VA's for their own story missions and random quips while adventuring prevents them from going too in-depth with any of them. It won't have as memorable companions as the more traditional rpgs, but they are still each a personality with unique build options and due to the emergent narrative nature of the game some of them will end up becoming dear to you through the journey.Technical Side:Beautiful, with downright impressive amount of unique, hand-crafted map layouts, the knights have great animations and unique models (which is somewhat of an accomplishment with most of them being, well, armoured knights), enemies are generally cool and realized well. Music/Sounds/VA's: Music is between good to great with some absolutely beautiful tracks saved for well chosen moments/missions. Combat sounds combatty, nothing special but nothing that feels off either. VA's are between mediocre to great, averaging on the side of good or better. The few poorer performances were for temporary side characters/NPCs and they are few and far between, most are pleasant to listen to. Main characters VA is spot on, damn good even.Had an absolute blast, can't recommend this enough.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty mixed game that is way too repetitive for its own good.The protagonist of the game is Mordred. After killing King Arthur, the latter cursed the land and now everyone in Avalon is either running around as a brigand or an undead. Mordred is brought back by the Lady of the Lake to kill the variety of evil monsters King Arthur's soul has been twisted into. Along the way, Mordred recruits a variety of characters from Arthurian legend to help him while rebuilding Camelot.The gameplay of this game can be summed up in one word: SLOG. You select a team of knights to go on a mission. The missions are largely redundant; you go to a crypt or some burnt out ruin, fight a handful of encounters, open up a few chests to acquire gold or gear, and complete the mission. Your characters have armor (which wears down over time) that mitigates damage, but your characters have two health resources: hit points and vitality. Hit points are replenished to their maximum after each mission, but lost vitality does not regenerate unless you put the respective character in Camelot's infirmary to heal over time. Mordred's Round Table can have up to a dozen active members at a time, but there are 30 different characters that you can recruit over the game's progression. Some characters, like the Black Knight and Queen Boudicca, are absolute powerhouses, while others like Sir Ywain and Sir Damas are pretty worthless. The encounters in this game are tedious and redundant, especially at the beginning, where you fight undead. Tons and tons and tons of undead. To make it worse, the undead in this game have an effect where they will reanimate themselves after 3 turns if their remains are not destroyed, adding to the tedium of this game. Every objective is the same - grind down the enemy's vitality to 0. "Here's a bunch of bad guys, kill them to advance" is virtually every victory condition for almost every mission, main and side, in this game.The environment and terrain for these combat encounters do not help either, as they are completely static, always taken place on a flat surface that may or may not have a few pillars of cover at most. The crypts and ruins you are sometimes required to delve into look as if the assets were copypasted - corridor, chamber, corridor, chamber. The outside environments are a consistent mixture of gray and brown with swampy, fog-filled bogs. Between these boring missions you return to Camelot, where you click through boring "base management" and boring lordly decisions. Camelot's management screen looks like it was made in a very early build of the game and the developers decided not to change or improve it. You will be treated to ugly fonts etched on ugly windows, of which there are many. Equipment management is abysmal, as nearly every icon shares the same sword or cuirass icon. You have to actually highlight the item with your cursor to see what class it corellates to and how it will change stats - and by change stats, I mean it's yet another game where it's a matter of "Green numbers = good". Mordred is also required to make decisions on the realm, and what he chooses will affect his morality chart, which ranges from Christian and Pagan on the X axis, and Rightful and Tyrant on the Y axis. These determine which heroes you can eventually recruit, in addition to seemingly trivial bonuses, but after a while you will stop bothering to read these moral dilemmas and just pick the option to boost the morality you want. Sometimes this will irritate various heroes in your arsenal (i.e. building a church may anger your Pagan-following heroes) and if their "loyalty" gets low they will take penalties in combat, but that's it. They don't defect, they don't express their outrage at your leadership. In fact, the interactions with your vassals and followers is virtually nonexistent. Your hear the thumping of your armor as you run to-and-fro on a mission's map, and one of your party members may make a quip about Avalon's state of affairs, which is only followed by more awkward silence. It's a lack of interaction that adds on to an egregiously dreary setting.This game is, unfortunately, one of those games that people seem to power through just to see the ending because it becomes repetitive and unenjoyable. This game is long - probably too long. With the way the game's leveling progression pans out, you are essentially required to do every side mission - partially due to leveling up your main squad, partially to progress your other knights' training at Camelot in-between missions, and partially due to recruiting certain heroes that are flat out superior.Overall, I would give this game a 5/10. For every good aspect this game has, it's overshadowed by two negative aspects. But if you're interested in playing it, wait until it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing turn based strategy game. I've yet to come across a game in this genre that is this polished. I'm not finished so i'm unsure about what the replayability looks like but this game certainly is better than the XCOM series...and it's from an indie studio.XCOM is really mostly all I can compare it to but here it is:- No hit rating probability BS where you can miss a 99% shot like in XCOM (extremely frustrating).- Relevant to the above, they have total health split between HP and vitality where HP replenishes after each combat automatically while when HPis depleted you take vitality damage which DOES requires further 'resting'. This is a nice alternative giving that all attacks will hit outside of dodge probability.- Armor is far more meaningful in this game which does add to the two mentioned above- Far more items and gear to kit out your soldiers- More in depth skill trees to tailor your play- Being able to see the line of sight of each unit on squares before moving to them- Having additional side objectives within main mission and side quest that are not a copy/paste of just a few options- No time based mission BS (I like to play very methodically so I dislike being rushed)- You are able to free roam in between encounters in every missions trying to find treasures and perhaps side objectives- There are no randomly generated soldiers as all are predetermined with name and class. This is a negative for some but for me a positive as it gave greater meaning to each person which also extends to special missions and interactions they have in certain missions and side quests.Just my thoughts.

_childDocuments_.review: Have been completely hooked on this game since I first started playing it.The dark theme, and alternate story line are actually very well done. Graphics match the theme - it is dark. Voice acting is also really well done.Thoroughly enjoy the turn-based combat, but it scales pretty quickly, so you definitely need to invest in skills for your knights that help deal with crowds/multiple enemies.  You also need long-range knights who can take out their archers/mages - otherwise you are going to hit a wall really quickly.The Action Point system takes a bit to adjust to - although if you have played something like Divinity you will pick it up qucikly.The armour/HP/vitality system actually works pretty well, and means you need to think through your actions and how to position your characters rather than just charging headlong into a hack and slash. The backstab mechanic is a bit frustrating but once you know how it works you need to be aware of that in positioning your front line.Mobility is key. Each campaign mission has an objective, and once you finish that you can move on. This sometimes means you can make a straight trade of XP/gold/items from sub-quests or side missions vs just completing the main objective. Given rest points are limited in each map, and vitaility, injuries are things you cant deal with during a campaign (must be at Camelot) it definitely adds a challenging dimension and means you do need to think through whether you really take that fight or not (on harder difficulties).The ability to customise your knights and their abilities is good. It does feel a little "sameish" between knights of the same type (e.g. all champions seem to have very similar skills - maybe just in a different order, or start with different ones when you pick them up), but there is a really good variety of knights available as you progress which makes this less of an issue. The way combat works you really do need to have your knights focus their skills into certain paths rather than be generalists, and that means they dont all end up the same. (which is great).The morality system also means that different knights are available based on the decisions you make, and the further you move down one path the less you can utilise knights of an opposing persuasion - means you have to make choices - but "them is the breaks".The equipment/relics you pick up as you go have some variety - but I am finding that is perhaps the least interesting aspect  in terms of the variety of things you find.Out of the box, if you are not familiar with this sort of game you are going to struggle. There really isn't a lot of tutorial/guidance and no real hints on what buildings to focus on for Camelot or skills to develop for you knights. I would therefore highly recommend a couple of YouTube videos to get you up to speed - Slandered Gaming and FextraLife are two channels that will help you out with some of the game basics. I would also suggest a newbie cranks the difficulty down to "Story" initially so you can get a handle on the way combat mechanics and other things work before cranking the dial back up.Overall a very good game worth the investment.

_childDocuments_.review: I am hesitant to not recommend this game, because there's a lot to like, but here's what I don't:- Recruiting knights really is the driving force behind the game, and it's fun, but after they stop showing up, the game loses steam fast. Also, once you add them to your party they become a generic grunt with little to no further development beyond skills in battle. If there was some sort of dialogue system, maybe events to build camaraderie, something, anything more than just a portrait with a handful of voice lines... - Why on earth are knights that you dismiss gone forever? It makes NO sense! The whole point of the story is rebuilding a kingdom to save the freaking world from certain doom- You don't think they would prioritize that over literally everything else?  So what? Put them in the garrison or send them out to help others. Anything is more plausible than permanent banishment... I know it was done for replay value and to force hard choices, but it's just that: forced. You can spend half the game getting your morality to a point just for a recruit, then say sorry pack your bags and don't come back I already have two vanguards and don't need another. It's not a good mechanic and I will stand by that.- The battles got repetitious sooner than I had hoped, mainly because the environments you fight in are almost always just flat rooms and clearings with some scattered obstacles. It's very rare for there to be any kind of elevation or hazards in play. So if you are a veteran of games like Xcom, Divinity or Solasta, you will find it lacking.- This game isn't very well optimized, especially for older systems (my GPU is four years old, shame on me), and there are persistent bugs like floors disappearing if you tweak the wrong setting to try and  improve FPS, which is mostly a fruitless endeavor. There's this baked in motion blur and grainy volumetric fog that make everything muddy and icky, though maybe that was the point.I really like the character designs, music and morality system, but I put over 50 hours into this game and even though I am near the end of the story, I don't know if I'm going back in.

_childDocuments_.review: Some other reviewer summed it up nicely - this game deserves a neutral rating, but as there is no such thing available, I will go with negative. It ticks all the boxes for a player like me - party based, turn based, you have unique skill trees for the heroes and the skills are mostly nice and combine well, you can upgrade your base, upgrade weapons and armor, there is a morality system with two scales giving different bonuses, there is loyalty scale on your companions as well. So on paper the game looks great.But in reality the playthrough still felt repetitive and uninspiring. In almost all encounters, you get similar map with several chests and several groups of enemies. Their skills and defences do not differ that much once you have played several missions so very soon each mission feels like the previous ones. There is very little outside of battle so if I have to sum up the game, it is something like that - buy/upgrade/heal in the castle, pass an unispired copy paste mini event (either click a button to send a companion to do a job or just pick the right choice based on your morality), go to the next boring repetitive mission (and then repeat). Although there is morality, the game does not push you to make any tough choices, you just pick a type based on the bonuses that it gives you and stick with it (I even stopped reading at some point and just clicked the button that matched my morality choice).Honestly, the only reason why I managed to finish the main story is because I was listening to audio books on the background.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually play squad based tactical games (Ex. XCOM) that utilize firearms. I hesitate to play similar games where the combat is primarily melee because, in my opinion, they lack combat depth (height advantage, cover destruction, etc.). However, King Arthur: Knight's Tale (KAKT) is an exception and rivals similar games in the genre, such as Expeditions: Rome. Good:- Combat mechanics- VFX- SFXAbove Average:- Graphics- Voice ActingAverage:- Strategy Layer (Base management, overworld events, etc.)- Map VarietyPoor:- Performance on some maps - Inventory Management designPersonal Gripe:- Difficulty settings: Early in the game, enemy group size increases from about 8 to about 10-17. You will still encounter about 4-5 groups of enemies per mission. On normal, enemies deal low damage and your knights will easily survive as long as you are not careless. On hard, enemies receive a substantial damage and health boost (about double damage and 1.75x health). Knights with high armor values and who are oriented towards the attacking enemy (you do not receive increased damage if oriented towards an enemy) will still lose a large amount of health and armor. The enemy damage and health boosts, along with the large amount of enemies present, leaves no room for play mistakes. A few play mistakes, which would usually cost a knight some health or armor loss on normal, will cause your knight to be severely injured or killed on hard. I expect to be punished for play mistakes but the difficulty gap between normal and hard is too significant. I would recommend that the developers lessen the enemies' health and damage boosts or lessen the amount of enemies present. KAKT is good game for the price and one of the few games in the genre that excels in multiple aspects. With a little improvement, KAKT could become a great game.

Killing each camp, barely taken any damage. Final encounter (again: SIDE mission) a huge beast, so many armor symbols I cannot count it, massive HP, summons a bunch of other giants which stun, aoe etc., even has a potion that heals HP AND armor! Srsly who made the balancing in this game? Or did you just hit “randomize all”? So, you are forced to do missions to improve your chars this or the other way. This is the game breaking problem: you have basically no idea what awaits you in the mission. Once inside, you can't leave, only reset the mission. You also cannot change difficulty, equipment or chars. Meaning you are TRAPPED IN THE MISSION. Which ultimately means, you might end up in a mission which you cannot finish because the balancing is ♥♥♥♥ and this ends the game for you. _childDocuments_.review: It's...OK. I'll recommend it for tactical RPG enthusiasts, and enthusiasts only. It's not a bad game - it's generally well made, and has all your bells and whistles, you know; kingdom management, morality chart, the works - and I found the take on Arthurian lore unique. But...I quickly found myself getting bored and not really looking forward to the next battles in each map. They just became so tedious, because the core gameplay is very limited and conservative in scope. The game wants to be tactical, but I found it more or less a very straightforward RPG-ish experience, and the gameplay to more of just hack and slash rather than taking into account positioning, turns, environmental factors. Yeah, these elements exist, but they make a very small impact on the overall game experience. Like many games in these crossover genres they open up later on, but I found myself not really caring for the core gameplay. Hell, Final Fantasy Tactics offers a more varied and rewarding experience and this was a game made over 20 years ago. Like, come on guys. Is this all there is to the gameplay? A few interesting class skills? Focus down enemies one by one? A few meaningful abilities on each unit? Snore. Perhaps I'm spoiled by Expeditions Rome's gameplay (which offers a superior tactical experience tbh). I found myself sighing to myself and complaining... "not another zombie level", or "not another brigand level." Additionally, I found the art design to rather drab; greys, browns, and blacks. Must we copy the color schemes of boring modern movies too? In real life, Medieval settings were actually much more colorful than what is portrayed in modern media. The writing is also bad, with some real cringy dialogue choices. Overall I would only recommend this to hardcore tactical RPG fans.

_childDocuments_.review: Yep, that's right, despite the title, in this game you take on the role of the anti-hero Sir Mordred! A very refreshing twist on Arthurian legend. Even more so when you factor in this is dark fantasy, so undead, magic and all manner of beasties come in to play.I found it great to approach this new tale from an unusual angle. Mordred is exactly the weapons grade bellend you want him to be. A towering defender full of one liners, snappy comebacks and scathing putdowns.A presence so terrifying, that even the members of the court and table of Camelot quietly accept his contempt as he gathers them under his command.The game itself plays out in series of missions, that are essentially skirmishes with a goal or parameters that must be met to achieve victory. These missions push along the story as well as providing the necessary XP and loot to progress and build out Mordred and your party.While loot and XP are gained as you combat and explore the mission locations, neither can be applied to party members until the mission is over and you are preparing for the next. This "intermission" is also a chance to apply your morality points. A kind of Paragon system based on decisions you make out in the game world. These place you somewhere between Tyrant and Rightful for your actions and Christian and Old gods for your allegiance. Points spent here can be used to unlock modifiers, abilities, buffs and followers. (for example: if you level Righteous to 13 you unlock the Pious Prick Lancelot)Progression is really well designed, more like an RPG or MMO's set of skills, abilities and modifiers with extensive and varied customization. Loot is likewise diverse and spread among the now obligatory common, uncommon, rare, legendary tiers; some locked to specific classes. Tooltips are, for the most part, clear and helpful and with a little bit of planning it's relatively easy and extremely satisfying to build out a character that synergizes skills with equipment loadout. This synergy can be further explored between party members and there is a certain Divinity feel during combat when this is exploited.Combat in Knight's Tale feels more Xcom like than Divinity though however and there is always the risk or permanent injury or death for your party members. I did find myself genuinely invested in my party's welfare. The well scripted back and forth and excellent voice acting had a big part to play in this I'm sure.The combat is everything you'd expect from a tactical RPG, AP, abilities, situational positioning etc. etc. A tutorial you have played a hundred times no doubt. But while Knight's Tales doesn't really do anything new in this respect, it does it very well. Combat moves along at a good pace, abilities are well thought out, easy to use and the area of battle is easy to navigate and clear to interpret.Knights Tale builds atmosphere really well. While it doesn't have the most jaw dropping aesthetics, it does a good job in painting a picture of dark despair and foreboding, a muted colour palette of monotone and grays remind you that this is no Bugsnax adventure, this is "Serious Business". Environments have been built by using photoscanned environments and complemented by high-quality mocap animation, then rendered inside a modern PBR engine utilizing DirectX 12 to support strong, atmospheric effects.Audio is again top notch, as I already mentioned the voice acting is on point. Particularly with fantasy games, its very easy to go HAM over the top or conversely fall short and seem like shy nerd mumblings. Here however the voices, dialogue and conversations are all very well created and add immeasurably to the over atmosphere and immersion. Sound effects add weight and gravitas to actions and abilities; while the background music is the sweeping choral ooohs and aaaahs you would expect from a game with this title.All in all this is an excellent title and very enjoyable even in Early Access. I'm someone who has never really quite clicked with the tactical turn based genre, but I do love an RPG. Knight's Tale takes aspects of other fantasy genres to make itself accessible and enjoyable to a broader range of players and that's a great achievement.

_childDocuments_.review: + grim atmosphere+ quality combat system + a choice of different ways of developing the group's based on morals and beliefs+ relatively many types of enemies- progress brings only a little new to gameplay- weapons and equipment with random stats available in shops and lootThe move King Arthur surprisingly lets us play as his nemesis Mordred, who is revived by the Lady of the Lake to save Avalon from King Arthur tainted existence. Depending on whether he leans towards good or evil and the old faith or Christianity, Mordred gains different companions on his way, who have similar parameters. And then it depends on the player to match a group of compatible heroes, because if their loyalty to Mordred is the highest, then they have the best qualities. Fights take place on pre-generated maps of individual missions with mostly 4 of heroes, the possibilities of healing or repairing damaged armor are relatively limited within the mission, and damage to vitality can lead to permanent injuries or death. There are 5 basic hero classes, but their development trees are implemented slightly differently within each character.Each character can be improved with equipment, using consumable items or permanent improvements through special challenges.Combat is high-quality, built on the AP system, contains various combos and synergies, and the range of enemies is just as wide.The atmosphere is dark, the graphics and the sound underline it.Difficulty is optional, I personally chose normal in combination with roguelite (one save), when the game was relatively easy.It's a bit frustrating that the number of hireable characters is higher than the castle's capacity, and therefore not all available characters can be hired and player have to choose whom dismiss for good, when he choose someone else.Overall, I consider the game to be a very successful in turn based genre this year, but I enjoyed Chaos Gate: Demonhunters a little bit more.

_childDocuments_.review: After 40 hours in, I have had no critical crashes or bugs.  I can say that the game is fairly resource-hungry, as many others have pointed out.For those who like the Arthurian legends, the developers did a tremendous job of putting a grimdark spin on many of the legends!  The storytelling in the side quests and main quest are interesting to me from that perspective, and it was a fun game. The combat/management is similar to xcom. As a plus (in my opinion) there is no researching technologies like Xcom, but instead, your decisions in quests impact your morality/faith, which in turn leads to unlocking new buffs/unique knights etc.  I like this system.The game also feels very long in terms of content, so I feel that it is good entertainment:cost ratio. Looking forward to future iterations of the game and polish.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy the King Arthur theme in all genres, books, games, films including all the lore so buying games like this will always  happen. I think it is only fair to be honest straight from the outset, it is a very short early access game which is quite expensive for the content you will receive so you should only consider this if you are looking to support the Devs or like me as I mentioned previously this is something that really interests me so supporting the Devs in completing this game is worth my investment. The game plays with exploration opened in a liner world with combat entering in to a X-Com esque environment. There is thoughtful tactics which brings tension during each battle. The RPG element is enjoyable and you can see even with this limited amount of content that every action will have a consequence. A few options which would be great if implemented, Looting of dead bodies, minor skill upgrades clearer to see in the character page, armour and weapon changes shown on characters. Overall, I enjoyed the experience and am looking forward to watching the game develop, I just hope that more content is released prior to the game going in full release to avoid others from refunding and not returning without seeing the final version.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is reaaally good, especially if you love the Arthurian legend and knights in shiny armour. The story is a bit dark but good, the characters are very good, graphics are excellent (I love those shiny armours and the 3D-models are very detailed and realistic).
