_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't leave reviews on games but Coral Island is the exception. Though I have only played it for about a week, I have completed almost the whole year and am heading soon into winter. Things I have noticed is that The character customization is great but it could be better, since the game has a salon and option for different clothing styles, we should have the option for different hairstyles, clothing styles, and even dresses. I have noticed this game does not have dresses for full-body outfits but overhauls which are great because it's the main game aesthetic but I think a dress or two for those festival days could go a long way. The NPCs also do not currently change their outfits during the seasons, though I believe this is a known bug and will be corrected in the next release. Sam's shop after completing his quest also being one of them. I also noticed that It's a little difficult to tell if you've completed a quest enough to trigger a cut scene. Some quest could be done but no cut scene will trigger, other than waiting for content to be released. I think the devs need to add a tutorial, for planting and mining and cleaning up the ocean. I had to figure out how to plant trees and it took quite a long time so maybe a letter or even a how-to would help. I love the game it's very fun, but also the romance is a little lacking. Ben is always missing from the map, I can never find him. Pablo will check in on you but doesn't really ask you any big questions or on dates to locations. And the mermaids are not even on the list of characters you can romance. Speaking of that a lot of the shrines are hard to figure out, the forest shrine says to place an offering to a tree, but what tree, where is it? And place what? The monkey shrine seems like some type of offering/puzzle but you can't move the tree stump at all. The monkey shop has a few items that do not work when paid for, and cleaning the ocean does not get rid of the black sludge. I know this quest can not be finished but in early access, I think it should, because a lot of the cleanup is done, and all the shrines are lit so why do we still see the oil spill around the island? Plus the bug where the toolbar gets stuck is very annoying. All and all I love playing the game, and I can't wait until more content comes out and the dev's fix the bugs. I hope this feedback helps. I also think the player character needs some art options so they can have their own art pop up when speaking to characters. I also wouldn't mind voice actors as well if that is something the devs are thinking of doing in the future for the text. I had a lot of fun in the game just designing my farm and house, maybe adding something like a ping for someone's birthday, or notice for special days not consider'd festivals because when grinding it's hard to remember and longer days even with the fifty percent added that would help. I love playing and can not wait until the next release.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game so much. It is really beautiful and I'm really enjoying the story. I'm impressed by how big the map feels, there's a big variety of activities and locations to explore. I really love how many other people are in the town to interact with, too. Really feels like you're escaping away to an ideal little world. I'm really excited to see what else gets added in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most fun, enjoyable game I've played in a long time.  There is something for everyone, farming, diving, crafting, cooking, combat, foraging, exploring, livestock, pets, friendships and relationships.  As of writing this, I have over 50 hours in my first game with so much left to do.  If you like Stardew Valley, you will love Coral Island.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: Game is good. I was fiddling with some options while I was playing, it was around 20 o'clock in the game, and I activated some things, and the game restarted, so I lost all my progress in that day. That design choice (which actually isn't, they just didn't implemented the alternative options menu for ingame) is beyond stupid and I can't recommend a game that has any trap that could make you lose progress.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: So far, this game is amazing. It has a lot of normal "farming sim" features such as crops, animals, gathering etc.  I wasn't sure if I would like the graphics when I first saw the game, but I started liking them pretty quickly. What makes the game amazing to me is the depth of character development and interactions, the level of detail put into things like gathering and crop selection, and the general theme of the story/town. As of writing this, the developers have been releasing content fairly quickly in my own perception, with a major update at least every 6 months. At 66 hours I have completed most of the content, and raised my "relationship score" with most of the characters to around 4 to 6 out of 10. I usually get into the game a lot, play it for weeks until I finish the current content, and take a break until they come out with more.TLDR: very well done farming sim game, more on the relaxing side instead of being challenging, with well-done QoL and gameplay
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game and has a lot of potential.  Sadly there are just too many bugs and crashes at this point for me to give it a recommend. Maybe come back in a year and it'll be worth it, but right now I'd say don't buy just yet.  A lot of people have put 50-100+ hours into this game and then, because of a bug or crash, they can't access their file or they lose it altogether.  It's just a little risky at this point.  They have a discord if you'd like more knowledge of peoples experiences.  Their "Coral-crash-report" and "Coral-bug-report" get new reports every other hour if not every hour.  They are working really hard to try and fix things and so I commend them for that, but sadly it's always the same problems.  If they actually fix the problems, I would love to come back to this review and change it to a more positive one.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: Things to love:The diversity of dateable characters and body types.Setting gametime speed to something a little slower for a cozier experience.The various quest/storylines.The exceptional art.The myriad ways to decorate your farm, really making it yours.Things that may need improvement:Some optimization - NPC's will occasionally call you "Player" rather than your name, rocks in the mines appear inside walls, beasts in the mines will spawn inside rock formations effectively "burying" them where they can attack you, but you can't hit them until you've removed the rocks hiding them.I know the devs are still working on the game, and it will continue to improve.  But as of right now, for me, a solid 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: Undoubtedly released too early, with missing content and elements of the game feeling very far from finished. This game does, however, have that cosy feeling that you will be familiar with from other similar types of game, but encompasses this in a sense of style and personality of it's own.I would dearly have loved for the developers to have held this game back in Early Access for longer, but I can't deny that I have had a lot of fun during EA and through to '1.0', and hope that this game continues to be worked on with new content for a long time.My perspective will be influenced by the fact I bought this game in Early Access, knew what I was signing up for, and have had fun along the way. For new people considering buying, unfortunately you will need to decide whether a 1.0 release that still feels like Early Access is worth the risk.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: Obviously I play farming sims because of my deep passion for sustainable agriculture, the socio-economic intricacies of destination towns that rely on tourism for business, and a vested interest in healing the impacts on a marine ecosystem due to destructive energy practices.And not because the blacksmith told me that my outfit looks amazing.Why do you ask?
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely fantastic game, even though it's still in development. If you're missing covid era nostalgia, then this is the game for you. There's so much to do, and as someone who could never get immersed into stardew valley, I'd say coral island is going to be one of the greatest farming sims out there. Thank you, devs, for your hard work :D
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: I've sunk countless hours into farming sim games of all kinds, beginning all the way back with GBA Harvest Moon series, an experience that I can say with pretty high certainty is shared among fellow Indonesians who are also into farming sims (this game's developers included). For most Indonesians, HM is *the* reference point when talking about farming sims, much more so than Stardew Valley or any other later iteration of the genre. It's not even close; *all* Indonesian news and reviews of Coral Island that I have seen unanimously compared the game to HM series instead of SDV. Thus, when I read English reviews saying that the game is mostly an SDV copy, it's actually pretty funny because SDV itself was intentionally made as an HM clone with more content and an improved gameplay experience. The same can be said of Coral Island, and I'm not complaining.Most of the base game mechanics in Coral Island are shared with HM and SDV, but there are lots of additional content even in the current early access state. You may farm, mine, fish, scavenge items, raise animals, make offerings, donate to museums, celebrate festivals, all of the things you can also do in many similar games. However, it also has a unique environmentalist flair with the ocean trash collection and recycling mechanics, as well as extensive arrays of plants, animals, and items to farm/raise/fish/catch (though some will not be available until future updates). Not to mention the diverse NPCs to interact and develop relationships with.Art style-wise, it's not particularly groundbreaking, but the mixture of 3D models and 2D illustrations in this fits perfectly. I like that the game doesn't go for chibi-like aesthetics and gives a more realistic proportion (though still cartoonish) to the 3D models. The landscapes of the land and the ocean are done beautifully, and I really love the shiny, wet rendering of the town during rainy days. The music can be better but at least it's comfortable enough to listen to.For all its similarities with other farming sims, Coral Island is still a charming game with its own personality. Do give it a chance if you love farming sims in general, or have been wanting to play one but don't quite like HM/SOS and SDV aesthetics.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: GAMEPLAY:Plays like a 3D, heavily modded Stardew Valley. Exactly like Stardew Valley. I supported this game through kickstarter. i did not know it was going to be an exact copy of STARDEW VALLEY. The main plot is the same (big corporation comes into to ruin the natural beauty) except tweaked to fit the location.I've only seen one festival but it was exactly the same as Stardew Valley (luau with a potluck soup)Edit: I have played another festival and it was very original and I commend the developers for their creativity. The secondary plot is the same; you donate items to bundles to unlock new areas and restore the community. The mining system operates the same way, the NPC gifting and hearts system works the same. The house upgrades operate the same wayThere's a small ape that sells you stuff in an abandoned house in the woods, just like in Stardew Valley, and hes named "Concerned Monkey"I know a lot of people say "oh all farming sims are like that" yes. i understand that. however, that does not mean that every farming sim is a copy of the last popular one that came out.There is a difference between being inspired by a game and copying a game.Stardew Valley did not copy Harvest Moon, it was inspired by it. Coral Island has copied from Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing; plot-for-plot, mechanic-for-mechanicWhen I back a project for $45 I expect it to not cheaply plagiarize from a game I have already sunk 1.5k hours into. This game has the potential to be great. I like it's diverse cast of characters, and the diving aspect is grand. However the obvious copying has made me incredibly disappointed in this game so far.##########################################################################COMPUTER DEMAND;I don't know anything about computers. At all. However, I do know that this game should not eat up that much memory.I can't have any other application open while playing this game. Discord? NO. Steam? NO. Google so I can refer to the wiki? ABSOLUTELY NOT. This is the only game I have ever encountered this kind of memory demand with. I had this computer built so I could play games like ARK: Survival Evolved on max graphicsThis little farming sim should not break my computer the way it does##########################################################################As I continue to play the game and as i gets updated I will put more information here and/or correct my original opinion. Edit #1. I've played a few more of the festivals and it was something new, and I very much enjoyed it. A lot of people say that all farming games are like this. Yeah the vibes are similar, but as i stated before, when I spend $45 on a game I expect it to have a unique and interesting plot. This does not, so I'm very disappointed in it.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game.I see a lot of comments that basically say this is ripping off stardew valley, but while I see where they’re coming from on some points, I don’t really agree.For every similarity (that’s not shared by 90% of the genre) they seem to have arrived at a similar result from a different direction. Enough that I didn’t even notice until reading through the reviews. It also helps that I love the visuals of the game, the gameplay feels pretty smooth, the story is compelling, I can slow the game speed so I don’t get so anxious in my perfectionist heart that I’m not spending my time/stamina well enough, I enjoy interacting with every character I’ve met, the fishing mini game doesn’t make me want to throw things, and there are decidedly unique aspects to the game, including the animals, the festivals, cleaning up the ocean, and the storylines relating to the caverns and the ocean (if you’ve managed to avoid spoilers so far, I’m not taking that away from you).At the moment my only frustration is troubles with cooking, and I think it may be a bug that will be squished in a future update.Many thanks to humble games for making, if not my ideal game (that would be far to much work and not nearly profitable enough), then closer than I ever thought I’d see.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: Doesn't matter if it's clone of Stardew valley. It's just a nice game I really want to play.There is some huge gap in difficulties of catching bugs or fish and the monsters in cavern are very easy, but the rest of game touches my heart. I want to come back to this game and collect everything I can, I would like to have some more of this. Maybe some extra celebrations on next year's of playing. Some more giving back from citizens, some challanhe to get their hearts. This game has a lot of potential and makes you use your imagination and say "I WANT MORE".So yes. I want more of this.

Wish there was controller support for the playstation controllers and not x-box but I am just happy I can use a controller. _childDocuments_.review: Well there's a lot about this game,  i feel like it needed a bit more time in EA or should say it feels like it still is in EA...the placing of objects on your farm is ackward as 1/2 the times the placing box ends up enderneath your character make it illegal placement for anything you can't normally walk on... this almost makes basic farming more cumbersome then it should be for being a part of the basic game.The game is cute and has a lot of good elements, but not having a good fine tuned base gameplay of the game makes doing the every day parts more like a chore then fun interactive element (unlike other games in the genre from the My time games and games like stardew valley, and harvest moon games.)
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: Game is fantastic. It's VERY similar to Stardew valley, like borderline a clone. But has a few elements from other games the same players love like Animal Crossing and My time in sandrock/portia. You can tell its early access; some things are missing like music during cut scenes and content walls, etc. There is also some polishing that needs to be done, some lag, skipping moving. Maybe its just me, but catching bugs feels like hitting a sniper shot and not a "mini game". That’s all I really have to complain about though. The map is fantastic, the characters are fantastic, the game play is solid and it has all the qualities I love in games like these. If you are good waiting for some content and optimization, 100% pick it up.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: I'm loving this game so far! After playing Stardew Valley too many times, it was nice to jump into a different farm game. Love the art style, the controls, the interesting characters, and game mechanics, especially diving! This game also feels very lore heavy, which I LOVE. My only real complaint would be that the movement speed is so slow, and with the size of the world I spend a lot of time mashing the spacebar to dash around- exploring the map would be more fun if it didn't feel like it takes all day to get from point A to B. Can't wait to see how this game progresses, I can't get enough of this art style and am hoping for more customization in the future <3EDIT: I take back the speed complaint. I just realized you can level up your sprint speed!!
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: i really want to love this game. I like the game play loop and it looks beautiful but not only is it unfinished but the characters are just so bland and boring. it boasts a huge romance roster but there's allot of characters who just aren't finished and the ones that are don't even remotely peek my interest. this is the first time in a game like this where i really don't want to romance anyone (which is the main reason i play these games.) a big gripe i have with the characters is that you'll have random cut scenes that are pointless and don't develop the them AT ALL. In stardew when you got a cut scene it revealed something about a character so you could get to know them and warm up to them. only a few of the cut scenes do that and even those are just not well done. just as an example, there's a short one where this dude and his kid are on the beach looking at crabs. he tells the kid to not scare them and the kid says ok. THAT'S IT. like, what was the point of interrupting my mad dash to the store that's gonna close in 10 seconds? It didn't develop the characters at all. Just pointless filler. with such little depth to the characters i am just sooo tempted every time to skip scenes which is something i never do.another gripe is when the characters say the most redundant things. i had one tell me 'planting trees is good for the environment' my guy, who talks like that? why are you telling me this? and this particular character almost every encounter with them was like this but they did have a few bits of interesting dialog and even some of their cut scenes so far were kinda good and relatable. so i do feel like it's possible for them to be better but i'm just constantly thrown off when a character starts speaking like an automated robot. TLDR: the characters have little to no depth and it's very hard to really like them. gameplay loop is fun and there's allot to do. game is unfinished. looks very beautiful. Do not recommend mainly because it's unfinished.

_childDocuments_.review: I've waited for this game for SO long and I should say it is worth the wait! YOU SHOULD EXPECT THIS. Even with limits, here's so much to do just like most farming sim games. This is a perfect blend of Stardew and Animal Crossing, in my opinion. also idk what is in the water but everyone is ridiculously hot and it's so unfair.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely ADORE this game BUT it has lots of issues... The first 30 or so hours WERE great fun and everything worked well but after that I'm finding lots of bugs. Specifically with festivals and the ocean once I meet the Merfolk which is a major piece of the game. I purposefully waited until it was no longer in the early access stage hoping that all the issues would be worked out but that's not the case.I'm going to take a break from playing and hopefully they will have patches to fix the current issues soon. Again I LOVE the game but am disappointed with the fact that it needs a lot more testing and doesn't seem ready yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: I have thoroughly enjoyed this game. I started playing it with the Early Access option, and while it is disheartening that I was unable to continue from my original save it was nice that my money came over to the new save file so I don't feel like I am starting over completely. In regards to game play, it is similar to Stardew Valley but in comparison I enjoy this one a lot more. I like the options of mining or cleaning the ocean, the dialogue with the characters already feels unique and I just love the style it is in. For me, I love this game and it can be seen by how many hours I have put in so far. I see myself playing it, and I like that I can put in 30 minutes or a few hours and still feel like I am making a dent regardless.
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: I needed to update my review, because this game is so important and I am so happy I gave it a chance. Even though it's still in early access, there is so much to do. I love the diving and bug catching aspects especially, but the farming, mining, fishing, and ranching have fabulous mechanics as well, even in early access. The characters are well thought out and I adore them already. Not to mention, the story line already addresses major current issues and brings the attention those issues need in a beautiful way. I can't wait for the special events to be finished and fully playable. If you enjoy wholesome games such as Animal Crossings: New Horizons or Stardew Valley, I highly recommend giving this game a chance. It's only going to get better from here, and I can't wait to see it completed!
_childDocuments_.name: Coral Island

_childDocuments_.review: Coral Island is a vibrant and laid-back reimagining of farm sim games. Be who you want and experience enchanting island living at your own pace—live off the land, nurture animals, build relationships with a diverse cast of townsfolk, and make the world around you a more vital and harmonious place.

name: Crusader Kings III
detailed_description: Chapter III available now! Starter Edition About the Game Your legacy awaits. Choose your noble house and lead your dynasty to greatness in a Middle Ages epic that spans generations. War is but one of many tools to establish your reign, as real strategy requires expert diplomatic skill, mastery of your realm, and true cunning . Crusader Kings III continues the popular series made by Paradox Development Studio, featuring the widely acclaimed marriage of immersive grand strategy and deep, dramatic medieval roleplaying. Take command of your house and expand your dynasty through a meticulously researched Middle Ages. Begin in 867 or 1066 and claim lands, titles, and vassals to secure a realm worthy of your royal blood. Your death is only a footnote as your lineage continues with new playable heirs, either planned… or not. Discover a sprawling simulated world teeming with peasants and knights, courtiers, spies, knaves and jesters, and secret love affairs. An extensive cast of historical characters can be romanced, betrayed, executed, or subtly influenced. Explore a vast medieval map stretching from the snowswept Nordic lands to the Horn of Africa, and the British Isles in the west to the exotic riches of Burma in the east. Claim, conquer, and rule thousands of unique counties, duchies, kingdoms, and empires. Each character is larger than life, with traits and lifestyle choices determining their actions and schemes. Prompt fear and dread as you rule with an iron fist, or inspire your subjects with magnanimous deeds. Genetics can be passed along to your children, be it the gift of genius or crippling stupidity. Groom your heir with the appropriate guardians or educate them yourself. If found wanting, marry them off or despatch them through other means. Customize your ruler and noble house, from appearance to attributes, and create a monarch worthy of all their inherited virtues and vices. Govern an ever-evolving realm and grant titles to whom you see fit - or usurp your liege to claim their crown as your own. Be wary of rivals, from restless serfs to revengeful concubines. The shadows stir frequently, and danger lurks around every darkened corner. Recruit agents and other unsavory elements to undermine, blackmail, or murder those who stand in your path. Or be inspired by the bard and ballad, and seduce your way to power and influence. Blood will flow. Assemble men-at-arms units and powerful knights. Manage your battlefield tactics and armies. Raid and plunder nearby lands or hire mercenaries and Holy Orders for your major conflicts. Be a pious king to invite the religious powers to your side, or design your own faith as you battle between everlasting fame or eternal damnation. Bring novel innovations to your culture and construct mighty castles and bastions to increase the wealth, prestige, and security of your realm. The paths to follow are limitless: experience thousands of dynamic events and life-altering decisions tailored to each and every conceivable situation and character. There are countless ways of securing and keeping your place in the history books.

_childDocuments_.review: An unexpectedly pleasant and vast improvement on CK2. That was something I didn't expect to be saying. Every system has been improved and most reimagined in a way that makes the enter experience more enjoyable. This is far more than a graphic update.With that said, however, if you have 100s of hours clocked into CK2, you may find the game a little, empty. The number of events and activities seems far more limited than CK2, probably because many more will be coming in expansions.
_childDocuments_.name: Crusader Kings III

_childDocuments_.review: Strategy games usually suck when they launch until they get polished with DLCs, this is not the case.The game is awesome. It will be milked with DLCs in the future for sure just like CK2, but for the current price and what they offer, the game is soooooo worth it.The best thing is if this is your first CK game, then you made the right choice. It is easy for beginners and very deep for advanced players. The perfect balance!

He was married to Czech princess (for alliance), his sister was married of russian prince (for alliance). When I died, vassals rebelled, cause that incestous adulter had absolute zero opinion and respect. 10/10 Love this game

_childDocuments_.review: Somewhere beneath the surface lurks a great idea of game. Sadly, it is buried deeply under the usual warmongering tradition of the X4 games. I wish I could do more in the CK3, but... Every time I read the patch notes, I see more schemes and intrigues nerfed - and warmongering buffed. You can have one single murder attempt per few years - yet you can have as many wars as you wish. And most confusingly, wars are magnitude cheaper than intrigues. ... Alas, it could have been a different (a more interesting?) game.P.S. "Don't recommend" just to be a devil's advocate.
_childDocuments_.name: Crusader Kings III

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to preface by saying I have over 1100 hours in Crusader Kings II and that game is held by me in high regard, despite some AI shortcomings.I've bought, even pre-ordered the Royal Edition of the game on the blossom of faint hope that miracles do happen. The first few hours even gave me enthusiasm for this game due to a much more pleasant scheming system, the ability to soulmate-scheme your wife most of all; interesting approach to warfare and army quality, albeit I wish they kept the flanks system in; feudal contracts as a step-up from CKII Realm Laws... seemed, honestly, that miracles do happen.Then Mr. Emergent Narrative (Henrik Fåhraeus) waltzed into my game and asked for a refund on my hopes for this game (just as I have asked Steam for a refund on the game itself). It began with the "attach to army" button, which was very useful is CKII and allowed a la Darkest Hour control of your AI ally armies, being gone. It continued with my AI allies being utterly incompetent in warfare - with walking off a "20 days to go" siege that would have granted us a lot of war score, practically won the war, even (I won the war in the end no problem, so this isn't trying to pass off responsibility for lack of success), with refusing to join battles being 51% won - and thus missing out on increasing enemy casualties, with many more things I didn't stick around to find out.Crusader Kings III, more like DLC Isn't Free, and while the many expansions will successfully tackle all the small issues I was willing to not be so upset about, there's no $15 fix for the AI. J*han deserves not a single cent of yours.
_childDocuments_.name: Crusader Kings III

_childDocuments_.review: At the outset, if you're not into 4K simulation games with a very steep learning curve, this is plainly not the game for you. If you are, read on.Anyone who enjoyed the Vikings TV series knows that blood-soaked warfare is only half the battle. The other half is waged within the ruler's own court. And here you get to role-play your realm's besieged ruler - so long as you can keep him or her alive. Subtle court management and murderous intrigue is just what Crusader Kings excels at. The RPG elements are top-notch and impressively varied, with a vast array of cultures to choose from across Europe and Asia. This is backed up with truly great character artwork which faultlessly charts your character's development and inevitable decay.And as a simulation of Feudal governance, CK3 is really unmatched - something even those great historical Total War titles always abbreviated. Here, your throne sits within a taught web of feudal rights and obligations you have crafted to control your ambitious vassals and allies.Your greatest challenge is a reoccurring crisis of succession occurring every time your player-character-ruler dies. That's when you really learn the hard way what all those quaint royal titles actually meant. Now, as the inheriting ruler, you battle to re-unite a kingdom divided amongst it's hereditary claimants - all the time trying to subdue your powerful vassals now sceptical of your inexperience. There are certainly wars to be fought out there on the campaign map. But this is where CKs is far less impressive - offering just the most bare-bones battle mechanic. Foreign policy depth also is still lacking, with very sparse options for interacting with other kingdoms. Nevertheless, Paradox is a very DLC-focused developer. So you can expect to see many of these gaps filled in the future.SUMMARY:CK3 is complex but very well-crafted in all that it sets out to do - less so in other areas. This is a great game for those who want to play-for-keeps in the snake pit of a feudal court.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings III, is an improvement on the predecessor CK2 in almost all aspects. It comes with most of the content that the CK2 DLC added already built-in. However, some of the more super-natural features are not currently included. Modding –There is already an active modding community allowing you to tailor your game to improve your experience or just to mess around with some silly features.DLC – I am hoping that the future DLC will work in the same way of CK2. During the development of CK2 a free content patch was always added for all players and hopefully this is continued going forward. Difficulty –As with the last game you can change the difficulty settings to suit your skill level, but I feel that CK3 is much easier to learn for new players than CK2 it clearly shows why you can or cannot do certain actions.New features –The skill tree system for characters makes the game much more interesting as you really need to focus on character development to get the most out of their reign. Whilst they benefit from different trees depending on their childhood development.Renown, the new dynasty renown system makes it benefital to have a powerful family instead of just killing of all the members who may oppose you, meaning you can benefit from the potential risk, allowing you to balance out the pros and cons. Using renown, you can get bonuses for all members of your household which makes a big difference in the long run.Piety & Prestige, this used to mean very little other than other characters opinions but now they have a much bigger impact on what you are able to do, only a famous king can declare for major wars without reason. Stress system – This system means that you must make decisions based on the characters traits otherwise you will cause them stress which can in turn lead to them ending their own life. So, you can no-longer just make the same choices each-time without negative effects.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game where no two realms are exactly alike and you have to handle the fluidity of your domain and vassals with the same care to famillial ties, religion, culture, and personal grudges as with foreign leaders who are all on the lookout for an easy war/murder. The systems that constitute your realm are at a perfect level of complexity so as to not hinder the new player who wants to pay little attention to them while at the same time offering the experienced player new avenues for world domination down unconventional paths. For example, there is little the new player can do with the intrigue system in this game other than kill various threats to the realm, kidnap people, and torture them. However, an experienced intrigue player can take these basic tools and shape the outcome of entire dynasties. Truly a great game that is somewhat held back by the AI in all honesty. I wish that the government system was more fleshed out with more laws and potentially some level of trade system as well (yes, yes I know that feudal rulers rarely traded with each other directly, but to say that trade did not constitute a significant factor in people's lives, and especially in the life of royalty, in medieval Europe and Asia would be a lie), but overall the game is in a great state right now with only few complaints that the developers themselves have addressed and hopefully will fix. Buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: As of early 2021:Overall it's decent, but it will not spoil you, especially if you had experience with final stage of CK II.Cons:- It's just somewhat heavy on gpu.- Lots of interface utilities gone in flames or redone with varying degree of success- Snowballing all over again - large bullies are unlikely to get beaten themselves (especially true for empires) and so it goes until large sections of map get dominated by blobs.- Needs rebalancing also in other, less obvious areas (i.e. where one lifestyle focus makes it significantly easier to get dynasty perks)- Personal traits - it's just pain that you get in basic scenario just 3 traits. It bluntly kills any hopes of balancing out pros and cons of various features and with sins/virtues system getting wrong ones just stacks a bit too much.- Compared to late CK II lack or crippling of some personal involvements such as religious groups.Pros:- Overall clearly much more generic, extensible system (contrary to many features of CK II). Better hopes of future rebalancing and modding prospects.- Very nice, highly customizable religion system (with it's minor balancing flaws however)- More interesting and tactical army-type management.- Technologies bring real benefits and system of acquiring them has got it's "personal" aspect.- Sane and elaborate personal relations system.- Interesting hooks and favours system.- Specific feudal contracts with all vassal lords in addition to crown laws.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game where I'm on the edge of thumbs down but will keep playing. This is because the learning curve and slow starts are probably going to turn off almost everyone not a very dedicated fan of this sort of game. I am looking at this game as a sim or RPG rather than a strategy game given the ability to switch kingdoms, but that won't be readily apparent to everyone.Pros- Lots of historical context.- A world full of people you can interact with, not just rulers.- Dynasties instead of immortal rulers means you mix up game style.- Map covers essentially all of Europe and Asia and a good chunk of Africa.- Ability to switch realm you're playing opens up options to play with a narrative rather than competitive focus.- Game emphasis is not about total domination.Cons- Lousy UI - too much clicking around. Particularly challenging in managing intrigue, diplomacy, and interacting with the wealth of other characters in the game.- Slow game starts despite launching into an established, explored world. Gold cheats can help here.- Too many actions take too long in game years. Some intrigue options take silly amounts of time.- Limit on intrigues active at a time is too low, at least when starting.- Military management is not intuitive and weak even once you start to figure it out.- Bugs of course. Worst seen so far was my 3800 strong army somehow becoming an 800 strong army while enemy's numbers went up when combat started. Instead of being ~ 3800:2200, it was ~ 800:2600.f there is a game mechanic such as an ambush happened, there was nothing I could see that told me.Wishes (other than fixing the cons)- Mode to play as a non-ruler or otherwise start much smaller.It feels like there is a rich mine of complexity, but the poor UI and slow game starts make this a huge time investment. This feels like it is mixing its metaphors between historical diplomacy, real time strategy, and 4x far too much and it results in glacial play that keeps you busy crawling through screens with the result that it feels grindy.The UI is a fun killer because this is a game that is trying to make diplomacy and intrigue paramount, yet so much of the information and actions are buried behind multiple layers of menus and screens that I feel like I'm going on pause or slowing the game down way more often than I need to just to get to do the same tasks over and over again. This is exacerbated by inconsistent handling of ui elements where some widgets on the map screen move to stay in view when you bring up a side window, but others don't. The ones that get hidden seem too often to be the ones I need to keep an eye on if the game isn't on pause. The game also explains concepts poorly and so you're never quite sure if that -87 relationship with one of your vassals means anything or not. UI is also terrible around armies and map view in general. You have to click just the right spot too often. For armies, it seems like click the feet b/c it's the map location, not the little man that is the hot spot. For your capital, it can be a little hard to get the right click to get the city instead of your character details. Raising armies takes serious getting used to and it can be really easy to really screw up once you get beyond a handful of territories. I'm still not sure if I'm actually drawing properly on the strength of my vassals in a war.Game starts are slow and there's no meaningful way I've discovered to change that other than just start from the tutorial and that limits you to Ireland 1066. It feels like it is trying to be a 4x so you have to build up and skill up your kingdom before you can do a whole lot. It seems like most kingdoms I've started with are in a position to immediately conquer a few neighbors, but then you'd be overextended immediately. As such, it seems like you're in for 2 hours of turning turtle to build up before you really start playing the game aggressively. Sometimes I enjoy that, but often I just want an accelerated start. Even for some playable kingdoms that are bigger when you start, I feel you need to turtle too much to start. With this being a game that operates around dynasties rather than immortal rulers, the poor explanation of game mechanics and the incredible amount of game time many of the diplomacy/intrigue actions seem to take, you can often see a ruler dying before they do a whole lot. That is important because only the current ruler is your player character, so watching relationships get changed because of succession and needing to basically restart some threads can be painful.  That's only partly realistic. If your successor is your ward , you should have better (not complete) influence than you do. That's where the limited number of intrigues you can support at a time and the incredible length of time they take become the problem. Which all adds up to unfortunately meaning cheat codes are probably in my future so as to tweak game play.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll keep it short: When you liked CK2, you will love CK3.When you are new to this game (series): It's by far one of the most complex games I've ever seen. Sometimes I pause the game for hours and just look around on the world, figuring out what is going on, finding angles to interfere with politics, and I still have the feeling that there is so much more depth that I cannot grasp.And that's also a reason why this game might not be for everyone: This game isn't primarily about building and improving cities and raising armies and leading wars. This game has so many aspects, so many mechanisms, and when you really want to build empires you won't come far with war alone.This game is great for people who are more patient and who like to think ahead. And when you don't plan carefully, each transition from your current character to you heir has the potential to destroy everything you have built so far. So while this can be the best game for you, it also can be the worst game for you, when you don't like that sort of gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I love CK2 a lot and have almost 2k hours in it but I can recognize it's flaws, some of which were improved upon greatly in CK3. I cannot say it is a worthy successor, however, primarily because for every feature improved upon, they have stripped another that made CK2 more fun. There's so little flavour in CK3 I thought I had contracted COVID-19. There are ridiculous restrictions for declaring wars, especially religious ones, the UI is clunky and annoying (I could get to everything important much easier and quicker in CK2), cool features that we paid for in DLC such as searching for a smith to create your own unique house relics are gone. For Christs' sake you cannot even rename your children without a mod that disables ironman. This game is more barebones than CK2 without mods. Do not be fooled by this game's more appealing visuals, you can spend $50 on this or get CK2 for FREE, buy the great DLC's such as Way of Life, Reaper's due, Holy Fury and have a much better experience. CK3 in it's current state is a repetitive, clunky mess. Paradox clearly just want to resell 8 years worth of DLC to us and for that reason I just cannot recommend this game. I want to reiterate I am not simply nostalgic for CK2, I know it's far from perfect and I was very excited for CK3 to release but to find so many missing features it became clear what Paradox's intentions were and I want to make it clear to anyone looking to buy this game that you can find more replayability in CK2 with just 2 DLC than this entire $50 game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm on the fence about giving this game a thumbs up mostly because it feels 'shallow' at times. One of my biggest issues is the death rates of knights. Another is the frequency of pillages and raids. Once the technology becomes available, everyone and their grandmother takes up the torch and raids the nearest town - this can be done seemingly without repercussions (Unless you have an army to prevent the aggressors). But then, unless it is a decisive trounce to fend off your land, you're faced (or at least I was) with knights and marshals falling off like flies.As an avid EU4 fan (an outsider looking in at the CK series), I knew this game was supposed to be more rooted in character development versus the entirety of a nation (Though, you do that as well essentially). But, i can't say I find the character development that deep and interesting. Schemes only go so far, and your diplomatic measures with other nations are extremely limited without certain family trees. Marry your kid here, and your other kid there - get an alliance - make sure your kids have kids and fill the court - perhaps murder your kin to take his/her title - and so on.However, I'm still a novice and looking over different ways to play - as well as watching some gamers play it - perhaps I'll learn a bit more... and Paradox may add more features to their notoriously unpolished releases.All of that said, the game has its moments, and I can't give it a thumbs down until I truly know a bit more about the events and mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: I got my buddy to pick this game up, we made characters for our first campaign and we played it on easy so we could figure the whole thing out as I hadnt played in some time. Fast forward and I became the King of Scotland mean while, he's having a hell of a go in Ireland. Things are going good, until my king dies in a trial-by-combat, then his son (who I didnt like) gets killed too. So, the real Heir of Scotland takes over and things are going great for my kingdom. Im tossing my buddy gold to help him out here and there and he takes a couple counties in Ireland and its picking up for him. His main king is still alive at an astounding 72.My army is requested to war to secure a the rightful throne for another who swears fielty to me, my buddy is a vassal to me for protection and its all good. I help win the war for this NPC and he swears fealty to me. After the war, two of my brothers are mysteriously murdered and I think nothing of it, "probably one of the other nations near me doing it." We get off the game for the night.Today, I snap my buddy and I tell him my plans, "Hey Bro, I think the goal is for my army to push into Ireland and take it over, then I will just grant you titles and such so you can own that land and have me as a liege." I get a snap from him back later in the day saying. "Yeah, but for that to happen I would want less taxes and levies & I will STOP ASSASSINATING YOUR BLOODLINE."Im completely shocked, cant believe my buddy was responsible for my brothers deaths, then he hits me with, "oh, and one of your kids may be a bastard." So I hit him back with, well...."I guess I have to rid an entire bloodline now and potentially execute one of the 'heirs' to the throne."TL;DR: Play this game with friends, it seems overwhelming at first but power through and take the time to learn because betrayal and espionage is fun and there are some crazy moments within the game that will be awesome memories for you to share with your friends. 10/10 recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: Revised Review as of September 13th 2020Crusader Kings 3 is a game that, in few cases, improved upon its predecessor but in more cases is a direct downgrade. Although I cant really judge whether or not the design decisions which were made to make the game more accessible were effective (sales and reviews would indicate yes) as I have a lot of time spent on Paradox's previous games, it seems, in certain ways, they even managed to fail at that task since, for some unknown reason, hovering over decisions in game you cannot take will only tell  you that you dont fulfill its requirements. How anyone thought it was a good idea to not tell you what to do to take a decision is seriously beyond me. However that is only a minor annoyance and I hope paradox will fix this in a future patch. The new UI of CK3 is much more cleaner and modern looking than that of CK2, which one you prefer is a matter of taste, however the new UI has some serious problems with scaling. While the messages on the right of the screen can take up almost half of your screen with mostly unimportant messages, the "Stress" bar is a very tiny bar next to the character is barely noticable.The already mentioned Stress system was added as a way to force the player to play more according to a characters traits, but this is seldomly an issue and I have not yet managed to above stress level 2 without trying. Similarly the new Dread-meter, which scares your vassals into not rebelling against you is almost never an issue since you will always have enough prisoners, that you can execute to keep your Dread at 100 without even taking tyranny maluses. This is only exacerbated by the religious mechanics (you can execute almost any wrong faith characters without tyranny maluses) through which it will happen way too often that nobles in Europe will convert to Bogomilism etc. leaving Europe to look like modern art with all the colours splattered around at the end of a campaign.Another 2 mechanics that were added were the character skill trees, which I think are a bit gamey but nothing in comparison to CK2s societies, artefacts and bloodlines and the dynasty skill tree which arguably has some rather stupid bonuses like a higher life expectancy. It is especially frustration when you are trying to save up for a high level dynasty perk but then your charcter dies and for some reason some random count becomes dynasty head for a few months and spends that renown you saved up tp buy some perk you didnt even want.However probably the worst changes in the game lie within the military mechanics. At first it seems like it was improved upon from the predecessor, since not even smaller armies can win battles, since other factors, like amount of knights, will play more of a role in deciding the outcome of a battle than in CK2. However the game seems to think that those play a way larger role than they actually do, since I have already experienced 7k stacks trying to actively engage my 40k doomstack. The biggest problem, and I dont know how this ever made it into a release version is the ability to spawn all of your troops within any province you control within 2 months. That means if you play in Scandinavia and somehow gain a single landlocked county in the Levant you will immediately by able to teleport your troops there. This makes it so that having a scattered realm does not matter at all and, since it seems like the AI always spawns their troops in their capital, every human player will have a massive advantage. The only downside you now have is that it will take a while longer for your troops to gather after disbanding them, this, I think, scales not according to the distance from the capital or something but only by your army size and when the penalty is actualy big enough to have an impact, you will have so many troops that the game is not a challenge anymore anyways. Another controversial addition to the military system was the possibility of just turning your troops into ships by paying a bit of money (ironically EU4 mocks this mechanic in the Civilization series). This mechanic might be fine with limitations however it is possible to to just create ships for your troops wherever you want, with how many troops you want, be it friendly, neutral or hostile territory and be it a forrested province or the Sinai peninsula.In CK3 you will almost always find that most AI rulers have alliances which is definetly welcome since that was a very rare occurence in CK2 and would easily give the player an upper hand. However the issue of "blobbing" has become very bad with the AI, for the Byzantines especially, which almost renders crusades useless as they will control the entire Levant sooner or later anyways.The HRE however will almost always be complete chaos with rulers leaving and being reabsorbed by it.Now the aforementioned Byzantines are a complete mess. Paradox probably  decided to just have them as feudal and make them work properly with the next DLC, which is not excusable given the importance of the Byzantines during the games timeframe, intsead it was decided to give more provinces to Tibet and remove provinces from Ireland in a game called Crusader Kings.The game still have some minor issues, such a a lack of Regents or factions being able to press claimants that will make land pass from your domain despite having high crown authority which should forbid such a thing, but these issues are relatively undisruptive of usual gameplay.Finally it must be said the CK3 is definetly not a bad game and it is also not an unfun game but i would not recommed people to buy it since CK2 is the better game in many regards and the DLC are often on sale or even being given away for free. _childDocuments_.review: I want this game to be better than it is.The main game play is a bit of a slog. It's like playing a solo board game like Dominion or Diplomacy, with random events that pop up as though drawing cards from a deck. I could see how this would be a fun game in multiplayer but as a single-player experience it's disappointing. The warfare mechanics are also somewhat clumsy and I've found that the UI in general is counter-intuitive--it's very easy to trigger a screen drag when I want to select and move an army.In general the game is plagued with minor usability issues and bugs that mar the overall experience.The worst part of the game is that the frequent updates don't seem to guarantee backward compatibility. If you're 20 hours into a playthrough and you get an update you'll also get a warning saying that the saved game might crash since it was saved on a previous version--oh, well?   I will likely revisit this game when it's closer to the end of its development cycle and all the DLC is published and on deep discount at Steam, but for me right now this doesn't live up to the hype. Seriously wait until this game is finished.

_childDocuments_.review: overall, very smooth, and impressive game. somehow only 2GB, not sure how that works but anyways.obviously if you compare both CK2 and CK3 side by side, CK3 is lacking alot of content. But that is to be expected, with the appropriate DLC's it has the ability to become better than CK2. Paradox has put alot of effort into making the game more user friendly, so the UI and mechanics are dumbed down from the previous game, i believe this actually improves gameplay and entertainment, but to an experienced players standpoint, you will then be able to see the holes it has when compared to CK2. A few quirks in the game that annoy me: obviously 4 hours is nothing but long enough for a few family members to go by. 1) vikings are OP and colonise everywhere: unless you're in india you will probably be invaded or be a duchy away from a viking colony. kinda annoying. 2) you will have an amazing start.....but as soon as your character dies, you'll want to end your game. not only is there bull crap succession, but the only way, to only have your heir to be granted all your titles and "crownlands" is primogeniture (elective is a gamble...not worth taking).....and you cant get that until really late game.....as in 1300+3) Tech/ ideas: its kinda stupid, you research ideas that give you bonuses, buildings, and decisions. there are trees, tribal, early medieval and so on to late medieval. the ideas in each tree are locked behind years. so you cannot start early medieval until late 900s for instance, and to actually progress to the next stage you need to of researched a certain percentage of total ideas in the previous tree.......oh did i not mention....you probably wont do your own research either. you CULTURAL HEAD is the one doing all the research for your entire culture, great if you play as a king or powerful duke, ♥♥♥♥ for a count. and it depends on the cultural heads learning skill, so if youre cultural head is a low learning for 3 generations, the entire world will be so far ahead of you its not funny. 4) you cant name your grandchildren.......so when your children come of age and have children (your grandkids) of their own, those kids will get the weird auto generated names of the culture. 5) the pope calls crusades in early 900s, one of mine, i switched to the vikings since they were giving me a problem and it lasted 100+ years.......not fun. 6)raiding places like paris or contantinople or rome isnt really fun anymore, before youd get events but now its just a regular raid. And most of the time my 1500 strong raiding party would be completely ignored by the 5000 man strong army of the king of francia. 7) when you muster your armies, they dont come from each part of you lands, instead you place a mustering flag in your territory, (legit anywhere) and your armies will automatically muster there, sometimes it takes a month if your armies are large, but it makes it kinda broken. i held one county in france and mustered my entire army IN FRANCE. no boat required. Now for some cool stuff1) CHARACTER TECH TREES....... its amazing, its like a skill tree in an mmo, so fun and so powerful. but youll never get them all, so focus on one, but make sure you branch out to others when needed, the learning tree has a health line for instance, and the intrigue tree has a seducing line. in time of need these can be helpful, but try and pre plan. it still takes time to select the focus and gain skill points to that specific tree. youll get about 15 skill points per life on average i think. 2) no nay micro....personally was never a fan of the navy, now you just pay a one time payment for your army and off they go, normally around 40 gold for a 3000 man army. 3) Mercs are now a one time payment, you pay about 150 gold for about 1000 men. then they stay with you for 2 years. no upkeep. makes it pretty cool......but the ai likes them too so be careful. 4)  Realm laws, from which you governed your vassals tax or levies is now an individual contract between you and each vassal, makes it more personal. though you will most of the time need hooks....5) which brings me here, intrigue is super important now, hooks you get on a character allow you to force them to do things, for instance, a hook on a vassal, will let you take his land or edit his Feudal contract, on the pope will allow you to request any claim you want. and so forth. nice improvement personally. 6) personal armies, taking a book from the retinues page. but they arnt constantly mustered. but they still need upkeep though its quite small, 0.4 gold. you can create 'Man at Arms' your own more professional portion of your army, on top of your levies, Bowman, light footman, onagers, light horsemen. upgradable in size, gives you a bonus in battle. so as you can tell, alot of problems and missing content from CK2, but alot of new mechanics and improvements as well. its playable with mods (primogeniture mod from start in particular), will make you wanna rip your hair out after your first character dies, but can be quite fun, luckily celibacy is only 2 points in the learning tree, and can be abandoned and retaken after unlocking. honestly, id say wait until a few dlcs come out, or about a year until they fix the annoying parts and add the character creation (will be a free update) but if you cant wait, you can play it now it is a fun game, just quirky at times. cheers.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me be clear that I enjoy Crusader Kings 3 and intend to keep playing it - but that's as someone who is already trapped down the well of Paradox's grand strategy titles. I'm a fan of this sort of thing, but wouldn't recommend it at this price point for someone who isn't already.CK3, more than its predecessor, is really a hybrid title of two kinds of gameplay. The more traditional element is a grand-strategy "paint the map" style game where you acquire new territory through conquest and strategic marriages. This is backed up by a really solid set of co-dependent culture, religion and "de-jure title" (whether London should be held by the King of England or not) systems. The second system is a role-playing experience where you guide a particular character, with their own traits, relationships and foibles through their life as a mediaeval noble, taking over their heir in turn. You're encouraged to act in concert with their personality traits, as acting against them (e.g. a just character torturing prisoners) will cause stress, which can in turn cause "mental breaks" and other negative effects. This is supported by a really robust character animation system and UI that helps you parse and remember all of the interpersonal relationships that are going on and is a massive accessibility step up from CK2.Many people who dislike CK3 seem to do so because of the way these two systems interfere with each other (they don't want roleplaying elements to distract from their world conquest), but I couldn't disagree more. In principle, different ruler personalities really shape up the strategic game over the course of a long campaign: I might pursue a campaign of keeping my lords in check through love and loyalty with one character, and then cow them into line with the next.The problem though is that neither system is really deep enough to reward long term play. Strategically, once you have an independent empire title, the game may as well end as there is really no restraint (e.g. CK2's coalition mechanic) stopping a semi-sensible player owning all of Europe by the 1400s. On my very first game (and really not as very experienced CK2 player), I was immediately deposed as the king of Hungary (good!), but then managed to usurp the Holy Roman Empire and refound the Roman Empire almost by accident within the next 150 years. On the roleplaying side of things, there just isn't enough diversity of events for a 60+-hour campaign, and you'll settle into a reliable routine of feasts, hunts and pilgrimages with the same handful of variations. If you acquire a mental break, this will almost always act as a minor stat debuff that gets you a new "expend resource to reduce stress" button (e.g. reducing prestige by secluding yourself away for a while). There is just not enough variation in events to make this world feel alive for a meaningful roleplaying perspective.This would all be somewhat fine were it not for Paradox' somewhat mickey-taking DLC policy: in line with EU4 and CK2, you will eventually need to buy multiple reasonably expensive DLCs for what is already a reasonably expensive game to bring it up to scratch for what is the intended experience (Paradox has a bad habit of introducing important systems to games that are only really playable with DLC - looking at you, EU4 development).With all that in mind, I wouldn't recommend CK3 to the average person on the street.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played a LOT of EU4, this game is another gem. It's like EU4 if you played as a family rather than a country. You guide your dynasty through the timeline and try to do better each time. It's a pretty complicated game, but I found the tutorial to be pretty helpful. After restarting following a mishap I was able to conquer a huge empire for my dynasty and become the most powerful country on earth, it was very satisfying.A major difference between this game and Europa is that it's much easier to make it big as smaller families in this. I played as a small Balkan state and was able to create two giant crusader states for my dynasty, establishing major Christian influence in the east. It would have been much harder to do that (at least with my skill level) in EU4. The game has lots of roleplay potential, given that each character has different stats, traits, and genetics. You can breed super people if you want, you can also marry people to get the best alliances or prestige gain. Very intricate. If you breed with relatives too much you end up inbred and vulnerable to negative genetic mutations.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the best in the row of Crusader Kings, it is true that they (true to Paradox business strategy) have pulled out a lot of content, only to trickle it back ever so slightly in overpriced expansions over the next couple of years and if CK 2 is any indication, there will be a ton of these in the years to come.But they have managed to add one crucial game mechanic that was not in the earlier iterations, and that is stress, the effect of which means that if you act according to your personality, will get rewarded, if you act against it, you get stressfull (which can have a serious effect on your character). _childDocuments_.review: So just to start off, I am a bit of a Paradox fan so this may be a little biased.  Crusader Kings III, like the other Crusader Kings games is less of a grand strategy game and more of a role playing game.  Don't get me wrong, there is still a whole grand strategy game here, but (at least for me and my friends) it's more of being a sadistic dude from the 9th century AD, creating an empire out of some silly tribes and then getting even more froggy from there.  There are four areas I normally would look at in a game.  Gameplay, Visuals, Performance (PC Performance with my mid tier that acts like a potato at times), and then the Company.  Gameplay - The gameplay is very fun.  It goes as I mentioned earlier as it is both a grand strategy and a role playing game.  It can be hard to get into the game as far as learning all of the mechanics and such, but that comes with time.  Plus, as far as UI for learning those mechanics, this is probably one of the best games as far as a UI Paradox has put out.  It can feel intimidating to even try half the stuff you can do in this game but is very rewarding once you see the progress you've made.  Even if your goals are more internal and and less about taking all of the land in the world, you can play pretty much your own game in a game.  Tons to do and almost unlimited replay ability.  Visuals - If you haven't seen the pictures from the steam page or haven't seen the game on YouTube, it's a top-down style of game.  I feel the visuals have been improved since the last CK title.  The people look well modeled, the map looks very nice both up close and when you zoom out to see the whole of Europe, North Africa, Middle East, and Western Asia.  It's not very explosive with intense rendering and effects but what it does have feels refined and well put together.  Performance - This game runs well even if you haven't made a computer that would be used at NASA.  I run the game on a fairly mid tier gaming pc with an I7 cpu and a 1050 ti gpu with the best graphics settings no problem.  It's not a super gpu intensive game though you do need to process a fair amount of things going on all at once.  My friends who have less into their specs don't complain either.  It can stutter for me once in a while but it's like when something extreme has happened like the Holy Roman Empire fragments into like 100 little states trying to take what they can.  Generally, the game runs well with no issues.  Company - The reason I include company in my reviews is because you can tell a company's intent in the game and identify problems immediately (EA).  Paradox is fairly good at keeping business and game making apart.  They also let you use all of the DLC that the host uses even if you don't personally own it yourself which is awesome.  Paradox has released games like Hearts of Iron, Stellaris, and many more great games of the same genre.Conclusion - This game is a must have if you like early medieval to late medieval games, grand strategy, and immersive role playing games.  It is so much fun conquering the world as the only Sadist who follows Satan that ever ruled England (because did I mention you can create your own ruler).  It is super fun meming and playing the game legit.  I couldn't recommend this game more.  5/5 stars easily.

_childDocuments_.review: A delicious cake with a generous helping of bull***t icing. Seriously, this is my grand strategy dream game turned into reality, but at some point in the materialization process it picked up a fetish for self-sabotage. I can't list everything, but here are some ideas for improving it:War Coordination and Crusades       -  While it has gotten better, your AI allies will still gladly march to their death or sit in the next county over while your own forces are being slaughtered. They only join if they see you trying to engage the enemy but they'll rarely be in range and it isn't always practical to meet your foes if, say, they're defending a mountain stronghold. Crusades are these issues x100. My solution would be to let players opt to control any allied armies so long a the army's liege is not engaged in another war.New DLC to flesh out more cultures and government types. No more minigames       - Royal Court and Iberia added minigames which, while having cool elements like actually having to mediate between vassals or big land grabs during the opportunity phase of the Iberian struggle, are mostly gimmicks. The Iberian Struggle mechanic is held back by arbitrary resolution conditions and the fact that it doesn't fundamentally change anything about the game: I can just declare war or assassinate people as normal. Likewise holding court is usually more of a risk than it's worth. Basically, these dlc added intricate mechanics which you're better of ignoring instead of new ways to play (imperial mechanics; new and more fleshed-out government types like nomads, clans, republics, and theocracies;Rework events so that there are positive outcomes      - Currently, some event only exist to hurt you. There's one where you have to choose between three horrible traits to give your heir and every other court event boils down to hurting your relationship with a powerful vassal. It's okay for negative outcomes to be on the menu, but you should be able to choose between desirable and undesirable outcome according to the challenges associated with each. For example it seems like teaching your heir to be fickle might the *easy* thing to do, but really you will always want them to be diligent and even if it comes with added parenting stress. Maybe you should have to choose between the easier but weak-willed decision and the desirable but more challenging one.impose a time limit on "reduce crown authority" and other factions       - Your vassals will constantly try to reduce your authority and might threaten rebellion to do so. Even if you submit to their demands, they will be back the very next week to do it againDecrease the mandatory Council time for vassals with hooks on you       - If a vassal has a hook on you, they can put themselves and their terrible stats on your council for 25 years. Let's tone that down to 10 or even 15Cap stress build up from random events       - Depending on your character traits, a single random event can give you 250 stress, put you at the highest stress level, and leave you on death's door at a moment's notice. RNG is part of the game's formula but because there's no counter-play to this they should tone it down and cap stress gain from random events at 100 stress.cap event pop-ups    the late game can become unplayable with the sheer number of events and random interactions (feast invitations, gifts, diplomatic incidents, etc) that occur every few secondsfix "adopt feudalism"      - In its current rendition, there's no reason you'd ever want to play a tribal empire into the feudal age unless you conquer an area that's already feudal. This is because feudalism (for no real reason) doubles all your court expenses, shrinks your military, undermines you authority, and obliterates your economy. Again, this is a problem that exists because of a lack of counter-plays you can make.  The tribal economy isn't equipped to prepare you for the transition and because you're tribal your people are apparently too stupid to invent anything so you can't get the feudal buildings you'll need to maintain your ecohonestly, just let me choose my heir      - I understand why they want to limit you by locking primogeniture behind technology, but just make me spend some prestige to choose to which heir I want, even if their siblings try to murder them. It seems to me that breaking a (succession) law should be possible but come with consequencesmake reformations and revivals easier        - I'm pretty sure Martin Luther didn't have to accumulate 8000 piety and control three holy sites to kick off the Reformation, so ease up on the requirements a bit. Especially for reviving Hellensim which takes like 40,000 piety and can only be done through obsessive min-maxingLet players choose gift amount        - If I just need to improve my relationship by a little, let me gift just a few gold. I don't need to give my vassal 150 gold to get 83 favor, sometimes I only want 25 favorAI rework      - stop the shy, compassionate, and forgiving courtiers from killing each other out of boredom. Stop my landed heirs from marrying hideous, STI-infected, barren women they found in a dumpsterChange Ironman and achievements       - Don't lock every achievement behind Ironman. This is a strange conceit of Paradox games but I think people should be rewarded for playing regardless of whether they're using saves or not. I think removing some achievements from Ironman would reward new players who really shoudn't be jumping into Ironman yet let me search for artifacts by name. Likewise make AI stop requesting your artifacts every 5 seconds and make it easier to request or outright purchase artifacts from other rulers.        - For example, Muslim rulers get almost nothing from most Christian artifacts so they should be more willing to part with them. I once restored the Roman Empire as an Orthodox Christian and declared a massive war against the Persians just to recover the authentic Crown of Thorns. I did this because I bored and wanted another prestigious item for my court. but I should have preferred to just pay the guy 1000 gold for the artifact he didn't even want or benefit fromwhen commissioning an artifact, let me choose who to dedicate it to.        - The player should get to choose who to improve their relationship with, not RNGrework personal schemes      - personal events often require you to choose one of three option based on the recipient's personality. Some of these are straightforward but some have no correspondence to their traits at all and it's just a roll of the dice. Either make these more clear, remove them, or let me choose a neutral "skip this" option (which only a couple of these have)Provide an interface that lets you see who will get your titles upon your death.       - Currently, you have to either look at each title individually or mouse over your heirs to see who gets what but it only shows three or four titles so if the list is long you won't see everything. This can cause catastrophic mistakes like when my last game was ruined because, even though my daughter was my designated heir, she didn't get any land when I died because France only allows Male succession. This meant my second cousin got all my land and court artifacts while my amazing Empress had absolutely nothing and was unable to retrieve the title

_childDocuments_.review: There is obviously confusion as to what amounts to grand strategy. If you define grand strategy as being an impersonable and characterless country/nation that send legions into combat for the entirety of the game, then maybe this game isn't for you. If you think the Civ franchise with it's empty diplomacy and number driven gameplay loop is grand strategy, then maybe this game isn't for you.If you like a game that incorporates who your character is as a person into your own grand designs, a game that forces you to look generations ahead and decide what land you want, what people you hate, and what religion and world you want to create, then maybe this game IS for you. If you want a game that see's you balance internal and external forces, your family, and just random chance, then this game is for you. If this isn't grand strategy, then how do you explain the exploits I undertook within an hour of playing?Start as a French count with my brother as a neighboring count. I am in second in line to inherit my brother's lands if he and his daughter die. I see an opportunity for growth!Call him into a war as my ally against a different count, trying to take that count's landsIntentionally lose the battle to get him captured and imprisoned by the count we were attackingAbduct his daughter through scheming (she was next in line to inherit, one spot above me)Have my brother assassinated while in the rival count's prison by bribing and blackmailing his courtiers to help meBehead my own niece in a public executionAnd viola, I inherit the lands, boosting my size by 200%. My starting character had the trait "treachorous" so it makes sense from a narrative and RPG point of view as well (something CIV tries to achieve but usually fails). He revelled in these actions!Since then, Ive been a loyal servant to the crown through 3 generations of characters, each of which was different than the last. After biding my time and building castles and cities with my stewardship focused character, I'm finally big enough and powerful enough to stab my liege in the back and take france for myself. It's taken at least 10 hours to get to this point, and all I am is a duke so far. If that isn't grand strategy, I'm not sure what is.The grand strategy is most apparent when you don't start the game off as an emperor or king, but instead start low and claw your way up. The lower in rank you start, the more grand strategy is involved. The higher in rank you start, the more RPG elements replace grand strategy. But at no point does the strategy aspect fall away from the game. Anyone who says otherwise is likely dissuaded from a lifetime of other games spoonfeeding them instructions about what they should do next. You set your own goals in this game.
