_childDocuments_.review: The Crusader Kings series could be accurately said to be well-beloved by its fans, part of its lovable nature comes from its ability to put you in situations you had never thought you'd be in, and to say things you had never thought you would say. For example, in my playthrough, of Crusader Kings 3, I uttered the sentence "My daugher cheated on her brother with me." There is also the time I had intimate relations with the pope, and I didn't even buy him dinner.But let's get to the meat and potatoes of this review, shall we? Crusader Kings 3 has a way of writing an entire  that desperately needs to be made into a film. I found myself admiring the world that I had a part in creating, I also found myself screaming like a mad man when my soldiers entered into battle, like a football fan might cheer on his team from the comfort of his own couch to somehow encourage them to get a touchdown.  was just so challenging, so fun and so rewarding. At the same time, I was surprised to see how many scenarios could be potentially crafted, just from the religion mechanics which adds to the  factor, although it's in this same category that there's an elephant in the room to address.CK3 (Crusader Kings 3) by its nature, doesn't have a predetermined story or plot. However, that isn't to say that it lacks any story at all, CK3 quite literally makes stories as you play. There are wars happening all around you, family dynasties rising and falling, there's intrigue and diplomacy. In my particular playthrough, I found myself forming an empire in Africa, with numerous kings as my vassals. On multiple occasions I found myself examining the various kingdoms of my realm, digging through the title's history, like an archaeologist at a dig site. I couldn't have possibly observed every single kingdom in my playthrough, and so I was piecing together the pieces of the puzzle, trying to find out which child inherited which kingdom from which parent, and from which war they lost the throne to their challenger. I witnessed a foreign kingdom, the kingdom of Ireland be formed under Irish rule, then taken over by the Norse, then liberated, and then once again conquered, that time by the French.If you are a lover of history, as I am, this game would be an absolute blast for you.Decimating enemy armies rarely feels this great. I saved many a great holy war from defeat, and I've my fair share of turning points in wars. It's almost like witnessing your own version of Gettysburg, the battle where you just know, THIS is the deciding battle, the enemy will never be able to recover from it.The best battles to witness, in my opinion, are the ones that you barely win by the skin of your teeth. You start cheering your soldiers on, you start cursing the enemy, you start swearing vengeance upon them and their entire family should they succeed. And when the battle ends in your favor, you start praising the god of whichever religion you might be playing as.What caught my eye most of all during my playthrough, were the religion mechanics. I loved the way they were done. Though I don't believe they are entirely unique, as there was a DLC in Crusader Kings 2 that allowed you to reform your religion and pick various beliefs that benefit you in some way. However, this being my first time exposed to modular religions, it was amazing. I created a nudist warrior cult, where women would command the armies, out of an African pagan religion. Now over the course of my game, I noticed too, that the religion mechanics need to be tweaked in various ways. For one, you can create a thereotically infinite number of Holy Orders to fight for your religion, however, while it was said that they were fighting in our great holy wars called upon by our head of faith, I never saw them fighting for the holy land. The Holy Orders would also rent out your castles and cities to be used as headquarters, however they would never build in them or improve them in any war, though that didn't seem to have an effect on how many holy warriors you could hire, I do wonder if it didn't have any impact at all. Certainly if they upgraded their baronies, they could've at least gotten more money to buy more baronies, which does affect their overall numbers.Furthermore, fighting and winning great holy wars in and of itself, I feel like needs to be reworked. When you win a great holy war, your religion loses fervor, which seems to be a representation of how much your believers are willing to fight, or crusade for the holy land. However, when your fervor is low, heresies start popping up. So what ended up happening, is after we win a great holy war, people would start converting to our old religion. Which doesn't make sense to me, it feels like if anything, the fact that we won our great holy war should be indication of our religion being the one true religion.Although, on the matter of replayability as a whole, one things need to be addressed. Typically, in Paradox games, different nations have different bonuses to give them an edge in a particular area. For instance, in Europa Universalis 4, the English get a bunch of bonuses to their navy, which reflects their history, Britannia rules the waves, afterall. There are exceptions like Victoria 2, and Stellaris, though Stellaris is an entirely fictional universe. However, one might reasonably assume that CK3 would have these historical bonuses for different cultures.It does seem as though that is the plan for this game. The Northern Lords DLC gives the Norse two whole dynasty legacy trees to complete that are unique to them. In effect, making their gameplay unique in some way. However, with the game being so new, you don't have that for every culture. Now, various cultures may have a different set of challenges. The Catholics in Europe are probably going to be more developed than kingdoms in Africa or Tibet for example. And there are minor differences in cultures, for instance, the North African cultures get their own unique cultural fascination, the Germans also have their own, as well as the Indians.However, these cultural fascinations don't add up to a lot of diversity in their gameplay. Now with religion being so modular, I believe you could have multiple playthroughs that are unique in their own way. For instance, you may choose to have a warmongering religion, as I did, or you could pick beliefs that would make your gameplay more peaceful, and choose to build your empire taller rather than wider. But if you are expecting to be able to have a truly unique gameplay experience as, say, the French that reflects something about their history, and then play as the Persians and have something totally different, you may want to wait a few years and see what's changed then, before making the decision to buy the game.CK3 was my absolute favorite Paradox game to play, and for that I am going to give it a 10/10. It is what I want Paradox to achieve with all their series. I love the direction they're going in, I love the point from which they started. There were times when I had been playing CK3 non-stop the entire week, to get this review out, and I felt burnt out, but then the game roped me back in with a challenging war and I found myself rekindling the love I have for Paradox games. Overall a 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Unlike most reviews I'm seeing, I never played either of the previous CK titles. I'm a 4X strategy fan that heard nothing but good things about this game in the lead up to release. Now I feel a bit like the child in the Emperor's New Clothes. Really? This game is getting amazing reviews?I mistakenly thought this was a military strategy game with lots of "flavor". Unfortunately, actually managing a war is so unsatisfying, that flavor is all that's left. You can have incredibly detailed relationships between the characters, but to what end when combat is just two stacks with numbers that gradually reduce. There's no tactics or multiple units to manipulate, just literally "click here and increase turn speed until it's over". I expected to orient my knights and archers, to use cavalry to outflank formations. Instead combat has all the excitement of launching an attack in Risk, watching troop counts getting whittled down by dice rolls.So, no, this game isn't for me. I do not recommend it to anyone looking for a game like Civ, where you manage an empire and military. It feels- honestly?- like a text version of the Sims set in the Middle Ages where you use a map to navigate from one dialogue to the next. I might recommend this to fans of other story generators, like Dwarf Fortress, Rimworld, or Stellaris, but even in those cases there was an underlying game type that the story centered around: survival base-building or 4x (though Stellaris' combat also bored me). For the life of me, I can't figure out what the core of this game is supposed to be, because I've never experienced a video game where war and combat were so boring.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to get into Crusader Kings 2 years ago but despite my desire to get into it, trying to figure out what to do or getting the UI to make sense to me was extremely difficult and eventually I shamefully gave up.  When I heard that Crusader Kings 3 was coming out and that changes had been made to the formula to make it a bit more intelligible and having watched a few YouTubers play, I decided to cough up my money one more time to see if I could grok it. 212 hours of playtime a month later I can safely say Paradox absolutely nailed it. I'm obsessed. I have bored my spouse to tears calling them over to show them my gargantuan Holy Roman Empire. I've minmaxed my dynasty to become handsome genius thick gigachads whose freakishly strong genetics have spread across the globe. I have relentlessly dabbed on the Pope by conquering Rome and then chasing him across the globe to conquer any other lands he dares to settle in just because in my first try at playing the game, he beat my army by hiring 100000000 mercenaries and I wanted revenge. I am having a stupid amount of fun. I almost feel confident enough to start playing Ironman difficulty!The Issues tab is very helpful in guiding new players in figuring out what to do and the redesigned UI feels a lot more intuitive to me personally, as someone who couldn't figure out CK2. I still need to have the CK3 wiki open on the second monitor, but that's par for the course for any game that's knowledge intensive. Also, numbers and details on the screen are much easier for me to read/parse than CK2 which is very nice because I like to be able to see what I'm doing without switching to a different pair of glasses and sitting two inches from the screen. These are all positive changes.If you've never played Crusader Kings but you've always been interested in playing it but never made the leap, this is the time to make the plunge. In terms of hours of enjoyment vs cost this is hands down the best purchase I've made on Steam. I might even buy the DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: King Zbra's Wild Ride - A True Rogue Rating!Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5) Crusader Kings 3 is like the medieval soap opera you never knew you needed, and it's absolutely bananas in the best possible way! If King Zbra were here to write a review, he'd probably give it a solid five out of five warhorses, but since he's busy winning more wars, I'll settle for a Rogue Rating of five out of five crowns.King Zbra, by the way, is a character you'd kill to be, pun absolutely intended. He's won so many wars that even his court jester is starting to think he's a bit of an overachiever. In fact, King Zbra once declared war on a rainy day just because he thought the weather was conspiring against him. That's the kind of lunacy you can expect from Crusader Kings 3.The game is a delightful mix of political shenanigans, family drama, and horse-based conquests. If you've ever dreamed of ruling a kingdom while juggling a family tree that looks like a tangled spaghetti monster, this is the game for you. Just remember to marry off your cousin to that distant relative in a far-off land for some sweet alliance points. Who cares if it's a bit awkward at family reunions?The diplomacy system in Crusader Kings 3 is more complicated than trying to explain quantum physics to a chicken, but it's also more rewarding than discovering your long-lost uncle was actually the Pope. The possibilities are endless, and you'll be bribing, seducing, and assassinating your way to greatness faster than you can say, "Wait, that's my horse!"Graphics-wise, this game is like an illuminated manuscript come to life. The character portraits are so detailed that you can practically see the stress lines on your rival's face as you scheme to take their kingdom. And the map? It's like Google Maps for the Middle Ages, complete with fog of war and undiscovered lands. You'll spend hours just staring at it, planning your next move like the master tactician you are.Now, I should mention that Crusader Kings 3 does have a bit of a learning curve. It's not for the faint of heart or the easily discouraged. But once you get the hang of it, you'll be backstabbing your way to glory with the best of them.In summary, Crusader Kings 3 is a rollercoaster ride through medieval madness, and King Zbra would be proud to call it his favorite pastime between wars. If you're looking for a game that lets you unleash your inner rogue, this one's a must-play. Just be prepared for more political drama than a royal reality TV show, and remember, marrying your horse probably won't win you any alliances. Probably.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings 3 is a game where you can grow an empire, watch is prosper, only to die from an infection and watch your empire dissolve, because you have not a clue how the inheritance system works. Mobbing your rivals by exposing their family to the world. If you can‘t kill your enemy, you can still destroy them tomorrow.Learn the languages in the medival world, only to talk to your people in others gibberish. Stealing stuff form your landlord or other kings and lord, with the cause to show these objects in your own throne roomMarry your sister. Divorce your sister because she‘s too old.Marry her daugther instead. Turn your family tree into a family circle, and watch your dynasty burn to the ground as your children catch every chromosome known to man.And your doctor who can treat you by lossing your leg and arm, can also trim your facial hair like the good old days in the middle ages.You play as a single person you picked or created from the world map, who is then forced to live though your terrible decisions.The point of this game are the characters, which behave as uncontrollable agents of chaos that act and react to everything you do, often in the most unpredictable, illogical and insane way possible. In other words, they act exactly like humans. Ultimately, you‘ll play this for the journey not the outcome and the stories you create in the process are unique to your experience. In this game there is no reason to explain you their mechanics.Instead, let me share you a story!Once i played as the lord of Thomond in southern Ireland. After my first wifes dies of entirely „natural causes“ I fought, „convinced“ and sleeped with other lords and ladies to give me their land on the island and so. I created the Kingdom of Ireland in the 11th century. We joined the crusades as bystanders, only to get paid by the church to make my own Crusade. On the moment of the Irish Crusade in the 13th century, we set sail to the westafrican kingdoms and tribes to conquer them and raise the Irish Flag. Once we secure the amount of land, Ireland needs we annex them and hold them to the end of the game.And thats the story how Ireland became a colonial power in the middle ages.I hope you enjoyed reading this essay as much as I enjoyed writing it. After playing this game for so long, i finally find out the game‘s purpose. The primary goal of CK3 and perhabs life itself isn‘t about living a good or bad life. It‘s about living an interesting life and inevitably to die an interesting death, so vou can loudly proclaim on your death bed “Thank God, I didn‘t waste it on a boring life.“ Once you‘re dead and buried, you won‘t be a footnote in history. You‘ll be an interesting footnote in history. Take and do whatever you please in this life, because eventually it ends. And life can take anything and everything away from you. Except your stories, so better make them interesting, because we‘re all heading towards the same destination.I enjoy CK3. I think it‘s very interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not so much of "This game is bad" review, as "This game is worse than its predecessor"; I like Crusader Kings 2 and have logged a lot of hours in it. Unfortunately it had a bunch of issues that were not fixed or were made worse in Crusader Kings 3, but if you don't own Crusader Kings 2 Crusader Kings 3 is not a game you should necessarily avoid; if there was a thumbs sideways option I would probably pick that.I have listed the main things I dislike about it, and if they don't bother you it is probably worth a purchase:I think the game has some promise, but the game is dominated by the vassal mechanic - You have to have vassals after your country reaches a (small) size, and they then spend their entire lives doing nothing but trying to revolt, or waiting to do it again; the people who have sworn fealty to you (including people who are given lands to rule by you who immediately turn around and hate their benefactor, so replacing the vassals doesn't do much for the harmony of the realm) just really don't want to be a part of your country, and after I have a few kingdoms and an emperor title I find myself spending nearly all my time and money on beating up my vassals who throw a rebellion during the rebellion during the rebellion during the rebellion, and it really doesn't make any sense, and it certainly isn't fun. I think a large part of the problem is how upset they get about having too many provinces and/or duchies, which really doesn't work well - you die, your heir isn't quite as good at management as you used to be, so now your choice is between giving away provinces you should be able to manage (later), or everybody wanting your new character to die.I feel like Paradox made the vassals even worse than in Crusader Kings 2 where babysitting them took up most of the time, but at least they could be managed, and I rarely had to handle more than 2 simultaneous revolts.I would like to see more interactions with the vassals to help build up the country, manouvering for support, both within and outside the country, more ways to create alliances than through marriage, etc, and less focus on the constant pointless civil wars. I would also like to see the other countries be more aggressive than they are; right now with few exceptions the only wars I am in are civil wars or offensive wars I start in between them.I also think the advisor mechanic scales really poorly as the country grows, and I find it very unrealistic and frustrating that it is impossible to hire additional people who can help govern your empire.I hope that these issues will improve over time, and I look forward to changing my review to a glowing one after they do.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming into CK3 as a longtime CK2 and EUIV player, I was slightly concerned about the content and playability of CK3. After all, CK2 in its initial stage was very limited, and it was through the course of very many DLCs that fleshed out CK2 to what it is today. CK3, being brand new, and (rightfully) with no expansions, felt like it would be in danger of being a pale imitation of its predecessor. However, now with over 40 hours in CK3, I can safely say this game lives up to everything that CK2 brought to the field and more! The UI is much, much more intuitive and new player-friendly. Furthermore, content that was added over a long period of time through expansions/DLCs like India and Tibet are in the game right off the bat and immediately playable! There are also many new, welcome mechanics, at least for people like me who like to roleplay their dynastic legacies or 'jump ship' so as to speak. Let me explain!To start myself off in CK3, I decided to go with an old favourite, the Magyars. Leading the fore as Almos, I led the Magyars to migrate into the Carpathian Basin, snatching it from Bulgaria. Following this, I attempted to conquer enough lands to reform the Taltoist faith, but combined pressure from the Carolingian Kingdoms and the Byzantine Empire led to the death of Almos and poured cold water over my dreams of reformed Taltoism. As Almos's son, Arpad, I turned Catholic, and used 'holy war' as an excuse to conquer all my heathen neighbours despite being pagan just years ago. With Hungary formed and its borders secure, Arpad finally passes on. As the 3rd-generation King Szonuk, I noticed Bavaria was no longer in the hands of the Karlings, thereby breaking their tripartite alliance. I bide my time, building prestige, formed alliances with West Francia and the Byzantine Empire, and proceeded to invade and conquer Bavaria, creating the Austro-Hungarian Empire centuries before its supposed to exist. As Szonuk dies and my 4th-generation Arpad II takes the throne, I notice I am, in fact, able to claim the West Francian throne for my mother. So I invade my former allies without further ado and put dear mum on the throne. As my mother passes on and the throne of West Francia comes to my greedy little hands, the Austro-Hungarian Empire has surpassed even Charlemagne, and stretches from France to Hungary. My son, Szonuk II, through careful eugenics, is a genius, and my grandson, Arpad III, a HERCULEAN genius! Nothing can stand in our way now!But wait. A killer roams the castle. I am shocked and horrified to discover my herculean genius grandson dead. Dead before he even has a chance to fulfil his glorious legacy. I vow to find the killer myself. Clearly, it must be a Karling loyalist, or maybe even a Byzantine spy trying to undermine my power. As I investigate, I get ever closer to the truth... and then receive a letter, from none other than the killer! The killer says they have been living under my nose this whole time, and that the truth will only bring me pain. I push on nonetheless... I must know the truth! And when I confront the killer... its...... My son, Szonuk II! Why?! How?! it's your own son! My grandson! I am aggrieved. I disinherit him and put him in jail immediately. My successor changes to one of my other, more virtuous, less kinslayer-inclined sons. As I ponder what to do with my insane genius kinslayer of a son, the Pope's messenger arrives. A crusade, he declares, is to be launched into Jerusalem. Being the pious Emperor that I am, I of course, agree. To my surprise, my son qualifies as a beneficiary of the crusade, due to being disinherited. Hm. So be it. I free him from jail, force my son to be in the frontlines as a knight, and send him off to lead the imperial armies and hopefully die a virtuous death despite living as a sinner. The crusade against the Abbasids goes swimmingly. Too swimmingly. In a twist of fate, my sinful son becomes monarch of the holiest kingdom, Jerusalem itself. Well. So be it. He'll probably die defending the holy city once the Abbasids recover and launch their counter-assault. I have no inclination to help him. So, I click past the notifications, and...... I accidentally click "I wonder what kind of King he'll be?" And now all of a sudden I'm the kinslaying villain disinherited by the Emperor, and sent to be king of a forsaken holy kingdom that i have no chance of holding. With a single demesne, with all my vassals and everybody in my family hating me because I'm a kinslaying nutjob. FFFFF-Just as I consider ragequitting, I figure... Hang on, this might be the most interesting character to roleplay as yet. A kinslaying, lunatic-genius exiled from home and sent to die fighting for the cross to atone for himself. So I lean into it. I become the most insanely fanatical holy king ever. My first order of business is to imprison and revoke the titles of all my vassals from the contributing houses of the crusade. Now my demesne is full and my coffers are slowly filling up. Then, I befriend the Byzantine Emperor, bribing him with huge amounts of gold, most of it given to me by the Pope despite my lunacy due to my renowned piety (thank you, Your Holiness!) and swaying him with my evil charisma. I see that he has three sons. I marry my daughter (thank god I didn't kill YOU too) to the youngest matrilineally. Now we have an alliance. With the aid of the Byzantines I survive in the land of the infidels, and slowly expand by absorbing the smaller Islamic emirates around me, never lifting a finger and simply burning prestige to let the Byzantines do their thing and wipe out my enemies. Following this, I systematically kill off the very helpful Emperor's older sons. The first murder goes unnoticed. The second, unfortunately, is traced back to me. The Byzantine Emperor is very understandably heartbroken and furious with me. So I assassinate him too. Now my son-in-law is Byzantine Emperor, and he hates me for killing off basically his entire direct family. Sure, understandable. I check my daughter and see she already has two sons born to our house. Cackling madly all the way and out of my mind with stress, I commit suicide. Now I am my daughter. Over the years, I watch as my husband drinks himself to death, leaving the Byzantine Empire to my oldest son, who I groom into another herculean genius. By the time I pass on and play as my son, the Herculean Genius, Hungarian Catholic, Byzantine Emperor and King of Jerusalem Szonuk III, I look to the west and see our ancestral legacy, instead of imploding like I thought, has remained intact, and blossomed towards England and Scandinavia as well. As I look at the sea of Arpadys covering the map, I vaguely realize I've recreated the Western and Eastern Roman Empires. What can I say except 10/10 game.

_childDocuments_.review: CK2 with all DLC is a blast, and surprisingly CK3 manages to top even that! Pros: Beautiful aesthetics, use of dynamic music to reflect calmness/murder discovery/war makes events feel more engaging (CK2 just played through a soundtrack instead which missed out on this neat trick), character focus trees are actually quite fun to work through and allow the player to do more with lifestyle focuses (going intrigue focus and being able to kidnap the Pope after a while is always a good laugh in this game). Additional features like dynasty renown and legacies also help to make CK3 feel like a refreshing sequel. Tutorial is actually very helpful for once in a Paradox game so new players can get stuck in quicker!Cons: Some things still need a bit of tweaking or fleshing out. For example, the ability to change to any religion as long as you have the piety cost seems a bit farfetched to me but it's not a big deal. Expect expensive DLCs coming soon most likely!For new players looking to get into grand strategy, this is probably one of the best titles to get started with! For older players concerned with Paradox's recent performance with HOI4/I:R, if you like CK2 then grab this, it is definitely better than CK2 and set to improve even more.

_childDocuments_.review: I see this as more of a "first impressions review," as there are so many aspects of the game that I have yet to fully experience.  Overall, I would say this game is a noticeable improvement over its predecessor.  I have seen a few reviews that feel it is inferior (mostly due to the lack of content/addons that CK2 had in its final state).  However, many features that were not added until later in CK2 are already implemented, such as custom titles and improved religions.  Sure, it may not have a full ruler designer yet, or many other CK2 dlc features, but what it does currently have is done well and intuitively.  I haven't done much with exploring all the features yet, but I really feel some similarities to other games, with the "innovations" being similar to culture & technology from Civ6, as well as the dynamic character expressions that also could even be compared to a Sims game to an extent.  Like in the Sims or Civ6, characters really express themselves after a major event, and the wide variety of expressions may not seem that significant but I really enjoyed it.  The new "portraits" are amazing with much more life and variety.  Some new features that I was impressed with was creating custom religions (really fun to use this as another layer in how you want to influence a realm or group of people, and also quite similar to how it is handled in Civ6), as well as how dynasties and bloodlines are now handled.  Now it's much easier to see your lineage from both sides (paternal and maternal), as you may even get notifications when some distant cousin does something or is in danger.  You also have greater control and freedom over your dynasty and how it develops through history (by gathering renown, you can adopt new enhancements over time).  Sure, it may be fair to say that it still feels a little "empty" without some features that you might be used to from CK2, but what it does have is done very well, with more depth and not as much of a static, lifeless portrait feel as CK2.  Hopefully it will only get better over time.  Would highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: While early on it lacked the depth CK2 accumulated through the sheer number of DLCs and mods the second game received, CK3 is a phenomenal blend of strategy and personal intrigue. I love how the game uses stress to encourage you to play the way your character's personality would indicate, while still allowing you to act out of character - struggling against your nature to do what's best for your dynasty/realm. Because of this, I think this game may be worth a shot even if you're not traditionally a fan of grand strategy. If you're a fan of political intrigue, there could be enough here to keep you engaged. My brother is not a fan of strategy at all, but as a Game of Thrones fan, he was able to sink hours into this game.While I haven't kept up with the DLC and updates, the new free additions that have come along with the new DLC have looked great. I think legitimacy does a good job of rewarding lawful play styles and adds some fun emergent gameplay - no more marrying random beautiful peasants. Plagues look like they have potential to bring mortality rates up to be more in line with what one would expect historically. I've heard people say that these mechanics need balancing but I can't comment on this as I've not spent much time with them yet.Overall: I recommend this to fans of strategy games and more broadly to fans of political intrigue.

_childDocuments_.review: A potentially magnificent game and standout outstanding story engine completely undone by lazy systems. Paradox has a long history of injecting difficulty into their games to compensate for lackluster AI and CK:3 is sadly no different. Any time you begin to stabilize yourself, make progress or generally bypass the games pre-determined progression path, you'll find an obstacle where there simply wasn't one, or in most cases, a cascade of "bad luck" rolls and failures coincidentally placed and manufactured on spot to give the impression of "challenge". A war with a neighbor (even ally) will break out overnight, a vassal who's been loyal to your family for generations will suddenly spearhead a revolution, all your children will die months apart from a grab bag of causes, the pope suddenly excommunicates your arch-catholic utopia...Wait for mods to catch up or a sale, not worth the time or money investment as is.Update 1.1:Held out for the devs to launch their mega-patch of corrections. Everything above still stands but now has long persistent performance stuttering and less effective AI that actually gets buffs and has persistent knowledge of the map through FOW, fundamentally making any war a complete gut wrenching chore. Fighting the AI is effectively like trying to catch a cat that fell in the tub, fleeing in the optimum path nano seconds after you click, and with their new clairvoyance will do so the instant you begin moving towards them from a continent away. That is of course unless they have a substantial advantage, and then losing them is like John Connor trying to shake a T-1000.But the AI can't change your children's heritage retroactively, or solve all it's problems with seduction anymore; So there's that.

The biggest problem is the combat AI in my experience, more noticeably so during crusades, every crusade I've been on so far has always ended the same way for the Christians, they get absolutely obliterated, yes they aren't meant to be easy, but the reason they never succeed is that the AI sieges down a holding, gets onto a boat, moves to another and rinse and repeat, they bankrupt themselves and never seem to take any battles and only try to retreat usually leaving parts of their army behind to slowly get destroyed one by one as they couldn't make it to the boats in time with the rest of the army. I've probably played around 50 hours ish on the Xbox store so I'm not just struggling to get to grips with the game, I can quite easily take a count to an emperor, but unfortunately it's also mostly down the bad and overlooked problems with the game. I do enjoy this game a lot, but not for full price, the game even is missing a simple attach army button which would solve a lot of issues when you aren't the primary participant, during a war where you're the war leader, your allies typically stick to you like glue, if you go into a battle and probably have a bad likelihood of success, they will still follow you into the battle because they are trusting your judgement, that's good, but when you are an ally or secondary participant, wars lose their fun. In CK2 the embark and disembark issue wasn't really a thing I ever noticed and having over 600 hours on that game I can say wars seemed a lot more polished in that game. If they fix the army AI, the game will be 10x more enjoyable for me.

_childDocuments_.review: The Crusader Kings series has always been about playing the hand you're dealt. Not even the most well-laid plan survives contact with reality. It's not Starcraft, it's not Civilization. The CK games have never been games that were about minmaxing or optimizing strats' - and while CK2 retained some of that DNA from Europa Universalis, CK3 has become its own beast.This is a story generator and a role-playing game. CK3 encourages putting yourself into your character's head and acting accordingly. This is helped by a smoother UI, a generally improved AI and absolutely gorgeous graphics and sound design. If you are looking for a strategic challenge as a player, this is not the game you're looking for. If you want to see your *character* struggle with what life throws at them, it absolutely is.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit 2022.6.30There has been some new updates and the game is much better than before. pro- AI armies' marching logic is now less evasive- AI faction seems to declare war more reasonable.con- Each faction's profesional men at arms still don't rely on buildings like barrack to unlock, and they will still magicly appear here and there. Seriously, the game need to bind those units to buildings. Changing from NR to R, because I no longer expect developers to fix the condition I mentioned above.========================Edit 2021/12/16The dev seems have changed a little the army teleporting mechanic, so the warring part of the game is now at least acceptable, that if you disband your army in north africa and instantly rally them again in britania, your army won't magicly been teleported from north africa to britania.But other campaign warring mechanic are still bad:- Your personal army(men-at-arm) don't have a Barrack to stay, they still live in some magical plane.- You can't merge your men-at-arm units of the same type. So I have 1/8 Archers, when I die, my son inherit my 1/8 Archer, but he won't be able to merge his own 2/8 Archer with my legacy 1/8, he will have to fire my legacy 1/8 archer and then pay gold to hire a new 1/8 for the 2/8 archer he brought.-------------------------Original Review--------------------------------------------------------------------The Role-Play part of the franchise is still perfectly presented in this title with improved character appearances in 3D. So, if you don't mind other aspect of the game for being simplified, then this game is still very recommend for you. Plus, in battle, the counters between different types of men-at-arms are also making the combat even more enjoyable.But for me, the Warfare part in general and the Settlement Management part of this game are overwhelmed with frustration.CK3 introduced a Rally Point feature that allows you to gather your troops in nearly any region inside of your realm, so far so good, because this new rally method get rid of the repetitive "select all & drag". But this causes a new problem: in CK3, men-at-arms are no longer recruited via the construction of martial infrastructures, but were created in a panel that doesn't  have a stationary location. This leads to your elite troops been able to "teleport" inside your realm with no delay at all as long as you can have them disband first. This problem breaks the immersion so hard and making the planning in between wars needless.And since the buildings no longer provide men-at-arms for your army, Paradox decides to let them increases the stats of those elite troops instead. It makes the benefits from military buildings for both your vassals and those foreign rulers been reduced to minimal. Most of time they builds buildings they don't need that much as the few extra levies these buildings provides can be easily crushed by your well combined men-at-arms force. So, this design decision makes upgrading a building no longer that meaningful, I would rather save the money for creating teleport-ready men-at-arms or for hiring mercenaries than to grab a few hundreds more levies. The only good result it leads to is that you no longer lost special units after adopting a new culture, but is it worthy?

_childDocuments_.review: THE KING IS DEAD, LONG LIVE THE KING!I am absolutely loving my time playing CK3, The character portraits are so much better and bring so much more variety to characters and the diseases are really gross (Good thing there is an option to disable that in the settings for those who are squeamish).Don’t listen to the people saying CK2 is better, as it is unfair to compare a game that has had 7+ years of development and continued support, to a newly released game.Hooks and Secrets are a really cool new feature that makes scheming far more interesting and dynamic. The new religion system also adds a whole lot more granularity to religions and allows far more unique religions to be portrayed in the game. (CK3 has around ~99 religions in total since last time the Devs mentioned an exact number, which is over double the amount of religions in CK2).The game is also quite bug free and runs really smoothly (as long as you meet the requirements). The games graphics look amazing as well and the map is gorgeous and with Baronies represented on the map, (however not playable still) the map as far more granularity for movement and the new terrain bonuses that interact with the new Men-at-Arms system (which replaces the old retinue system from CK2) means that battles can be far more tactical as you need to take into account terrain.The game also has a far, far better tutorial and with the new tool tips in tool tips system and built in encyclopedia, it is far easier for you to get into the game and learn how to play. The game is also better at displaying opportunities you may want to do, such as claims you can press and where you are in a succession, so you know who to murder to become the new heir. While the game may seem easier than CK2 which can put off old players, I think it has the same difficulty, it is just better at telling you what is happening.I give Crusader Kings 3 10/10, it has a lot of potential for more flavor and I am excited to see what they bring to CK3 in the future. I say it is well worth the purchaseEDIT: With the release of 1.2 of the game, I will leave a small edition to the review, OMG, the Ruler Designer is awesome, the absolute monstrous rulers you can create with it is insane. I also love how you can make them as op as you want and can still play with them, rather then in CK2 where you couldn't play the character if they were over the point limit.The Game is still definitely a massive thumbs up from me.

_childDocuments_.review: I played a lot of CK2, and a lot of CK3 when it came out, but the DLC's since release have been totally uninteresting and so has CK3 in general. As I see it, the problem is that there isn't enough game here. There's the strategy side of the game, and that side of the game is totally unchallenging. Then there's the roleplaying side of the game, which is deeply repetitive. And neither side serves the other in a meaningful way. Roleplaying isn't an exercise in being given a poorly optimized character and playing anyway, but that seems to be the definition they want me to accept. What I mean is this: if you need to pivot your gameplay from a focus on wealth and development to a focus on subterfuge and match-making, your hands are basically tied. You may be able to plan long-term to raise your next heir appropriately, but you can't really respond to changing external challenges quickly enough that you can predict what kind of ruler you'll need by the time your current one expires. So you metagame. Or you just give up on mechanics and try to lean in to the massive text walls meant to immerse you, but if I wanted to read a novel, I'd read one with a meaningful plot. Life is already tedious, arbitrary, repetitive, and meaningless, and I play video games to escape that. And that's why I've stopped playing CK3 and don't imagine I'll start again. Some people may enjoy laughing at the game for entertainment value, but I'm not one of them.

_childDocuments_.review: Like Crusader Kings II, just with another I.More seriously though, Crusader Kings 3 is an excellent successor to CK2. Although it doesn't quite have all the content that CK2 has in its final version, CK3 is still nonetheless a great improvement upon the previous game. Trying to comment on everything that has changed will probably be too long, but some very noticeable improvements are the changes to the map (now much more like the translucent map from Imperator), the improved lifestyle options and events leading to a greater element of character role playing, and the reworking of decisions and schemes.There are nonetheless a few weaknesses to the game, and some things that could be improved upon are the way wars work, what with the ability for armies to march all over neutral territory, and the ability to just bypass castles without taking or at least putting them under siege cuts out a lot of the strategy in regards to positioning and seems rather unrealistic (a system similar to the forts in Imperator might be good). Also, the UI seems a bit odd, with it somewhat less intuitive than CK2, although that may just be a case of getting used to the new one. Oh and the game obviously isn't compete and requires DLC to be so, but that's nothing new from the publisher, although the base game still provides many hours of game play and is certainly worth the price.Overall, the game is certainly well worth getting, and a seemingly worthy successor to CK2.Crusader Kings 2 is dead, long live Crusader Kings 3!

_childDocuments_.review: The problem with Steam reviews is I can only give thumbs up or thumbs down and no "thumbs in the middle", because this is a "thumbs in the middle" game, at least at launch. Knowing Paradox, it'll be a 10/10 given enough free updates alongside staggering expensive amounts of paid DLC. But this review is a review of the game at launch. Keep that in mind.This game has the look, feel and intent of its predecessor, CK2, but lacks all of character that made that game so unique. My primary example is that hiring a court physician in this game means picking between an expensive but skilled candidate or a cheap unskilled candidate. When you get ill they either make you more or less healthy based on their learning skill and their disposition towards you. In CK2 hiring a court physician meant sending someone to scour the realm for the nearest blind man who is consumed by alcoholism and is also a lunatic. That or a mystic who has absolutely no medical knowledge, but who assures you the spirits of his ancestors are sure rubbing a cat against your spine will somehow cure your cancer. You just don't get that in CK3.You get some similar events in CK3 such as the "my spouse is cheating on me" event but it never seems to carry the same about of juice. When I read it I never feel as betrayed as I might have in CK2. It doesn't seem to carry as much weight because, at least in my experience, no amount of them cheating on me will lower their disposition of me and I'll still be able to use them to pump out heirs upon heirs. I mean I could imprison her. But why? There's literally no benefit. I could gain a strong hook. But why? She's not landed. She's not a vassal. It doesn't benefit me? If my wife in CK2 cheated on me, our heirs would be born bastards and I'd have to spend time consistently legitimising them (if she even liked me enough to sleep with me) unless I either killed/divorced her to remarry, or killed her lover. I've had three spouses incestuously cheat on me in CK3 and there's never been the feeling of lasting consequence.This is all what I mean when I say CK3 has those things that the previous game had, but with none of the character - with less of the heart, of the juicy, juicy drama. I mean I'm not going to pretend CK2 isn't a "paint the map your faction's colour" type of game, but the amount of variation between the events occurring in your characters personal life, between your conquests, which literally varied from adopting a dog to becoming bloody immortal, elevated the game above your typical game of snowball conquest. In CK3 more emphasis is put on the conquest; On the map painting. While the roleplay is still there, and admittedly excellently done in some places such as the skill trees and stress system relating to your character's personality, it just isn't as impactful as it was in CK2. Well, in terms of impacting gameplay it IS more impactful because your personality dictates how your character makes decisions and perks literally give you bonuses, but it doesn't feel impactful in the sense that it rarely merits a responce from me. In CK2 some random events make me go "OH ♥♥♥♥", like when I duel someone with far inferior combat prowess than me, but they either cheat the fight or take me down with them using their superior intrigue.While I don't think this means the game is that bad, it does make the game worse than CK2 in my opinion, because painting the map my colour was always a secondary objective to sleeping with every countess in England, to building a great wonder, to hording treasures, to writing a magnum opus, to literally giving birth to the anti-christ, none of which are things in CK3 that contributed to making CK2 so great. For me, Crusader Kings has always been about the roleplay and crafting personal story, whcih seems to have been swapped her for crafting the story of your nation.It's a matter of preference; If you enjoyed the conquest side of CK2 then you'll love CK3. If you were hoping for the same amount of warped humour, character, heart and juicy drama as CK2 then you'll be disappointed. Roleplay here isn't impossible by a long shot, as it can have it's moments, but it does take more of a backseat role in some regards. As such I give the game a thumbs down... Even though it definetly deserves a "thumbs in the middle".

_childDocuments_.review: My pick for game of the year.  Pdx has done it with this one, a true masterpiece and a worthy successor to Ck2.  There's just so many great things about this game, it's hard to know where to begin:GAMEPLAY:  10/10Probably the best life simulator I have ever played, in an awesome setting--the middle ages.  The gameplay in this continues to improve upon the model of prior Ck games, where you live the lives of a dynasty spanning up to 600 years.  This RPG and strategic mix makes Ck truly unique and I have yet to see it in any other game. GRAPHICS:  9/10I was doubtful of the 3D models when news of the game first broke, but they work, really well.  They add more life to the characters and interactions.  Torture someone in your dungeon, and watch them cower in fear.  Lose one or both eyes, catch bubonic plague, or be a drunkard, and see your face and body reflect that.   The map and troop models are beautiful, and build on the prior Ck games. MUSIC/SOUND:  9/10Waldetoft has done it again; he's managed to compose music so great you get lost in your characters in their time, without sounding too repetitive.  And it's perfectly epic when momentous occasions happen.  Only reason I don't give it a 10 is I wish there were more songs, and I'm also missing the execution sounds from Ck2.REPLAYABILITY:  10/10Again, one of the best of any games I've played.  There is no end to what you can do with your characters in this game.  You can be good, evil, or a mixture of both and everything in between.  Differing religions, cultures, and legacies add flavor to every place.  Over thirty hours in and I'm more excited to play than when I started.  I can't remember a game doing that for me in a very long time.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings 3 is quite possibly the best game Paradox has released. Not only is CK3 an amazing gameplay, role playing experience, it's excellent UI and high level of polish lend itself to CK3 being one of the greatest Grand Strategy Games ever made. (And no, I'm not exaggerating). Pros:- Intuitive and excellent UI.- Engaging gameplay mechanics that fairly balance player freedom within an ever changing medieval world. - Much improved battle and retinue system. - Religions and the religious systems are much more enjoyable and unique. - Cultural differences feel varied (though further development wouldn't hurt). - You can do some very "interesting" things with your character and family....Cons:- Some minor balance issues - Repetitive events, however, I am sure with every update this will become less of an issue. Conclusion:If you love role playing games, or grand strategy then this is the game for you, especially if CK2 felt too complex and expensive to get into. Cannot recommend enough.The recent updates (1.1 and 1.2) continue to improve CK3 and I am very much looking forward to the future of this game. It is certainly looking very bright!

_childDocuments_.review: Massive wars? Check. Political intrigue? Check. Building an immense empire that lasts the test of time? Check, and check.As a history buff, CK3 checks all the boxes and scratches that itch for more strategic gameplay many fans of the RTS genre crave. Gone are the frantic unit-spamming battlefields of Age of Empires, and the overly complex micromanagement of Civilization. Instead, CK3 replaces everything with a streamlined experience that borrows the best from everywhere. To top it all off, there's a noticeable element of realism. Sure, you can march your troops all the way from the shores of Portugal to the Tibetan Steppes, conquering every land in between. But the larger your realm grows, the more unwieldy it becomes to manage, and the less content your vassals become. It's almost as if forcing disparate groups with distinct cultures and religions to unite under one banner is kinda difficult to maintain (looking at You Alexander the Great)!One of the most surprising takes on your typical RTS, CK3 is more about establishing your line of succession than growing your kingdom. Yeah, you can launch wars to conquer the globe, but that's all secondary to creating a lasting dynasty.One of the game's best features is the staggering amount of choices you have in how to play. Fight, plot or marry your way to victory. How you choose to forge your family's legend is up to you. That being said, for all of CK3's positives, there are still a few pitfalls. Sometimes, the game just decides it's time to destroy everything you love. Don't be surprised if your entire family gets assassinated after a rough succession 40 hours into a very successful playthrough. The worst feeling in the world is marveling at the absolutely massive empire you've built one moment, only to have your character die from the black death in the next without any warning. Lands and thrones change hands frequently, and maintaining your grip on power is a bloodthirsty business. Be prepared to experience a few game overs before you finally hit your stride.But if you can brave your way through all the frustration, you'll find CK3 has hundreds of hours of tantalizing gameplay to offer you. I would recommend it to all students of history and fans of RTS alike.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game, but, to be honest, it's quite a soft recommendation. Crusader Kings 2 is my most played game. I spent countless hours having fun in it. I've already spent over 120 hours playing this one, and I've had fun. Compared to CK2, I find this game much more playable. I'm not sure I'd say it's easier, but it's certainly a smoother playing experience. The objectives your character should be aiming for are much more obvious, and it's a lot easier to do things like fabricating claims. I think the game is very playable, and quite arcadey, in this respect.Unfortunately, I also think this game lacks a LOT of the things that made CK2 great. Granted, many of those things came in the form of DLC, but still, I don't think this game improves on anything enough to be worth buying if you own and love CK2.I suppose my review boils down to this:I do recommend this game. It is a lot of fun and you can whittle away the hours playing it quite nicely. However, when compared to CK2, it lacks a LOT of content, a LOT of depth, and it's missing the spark that CK2 has. CK3 adds 3d character models to replace CK2's portraits, but these models seem lifeless. Where a portrait in CK2 was a glimpse into what a deep character would have looked like, CK3's models feel like caricatures. The art is nice, but they pull silly poses, and all the characters in CK3 are predictable and boring. Everyone feels the same. Or, rather, it feels like there is three or four characters perpetuated over and over again. Because of this, when you play CK3 you will play roughly 3-6 characters before realising you're repeating yourself, and the game very quickly loses any charm it had.Every mechanic in this game is like a shallow but pretty version of a system in CK2.I wholeheartedly recommend this game to someone who is quite a casual gamer, who wants something smoother, easier to get in to, and with less depth. If you want a deeper experience, then I recommend CK2 instead. The characters in CK2 feel living, and because of that, the world feels living. You never know what is going to happen. It's like a simulation of a medieval world. This game is like a bundle of relatively fun minigames. It's fun, but it's missing the heart and soul that made CK2 so good.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings III is an amazing experience, so long as you understand what you're getting in for from the offset. Whereas CKII was a deep strategy game with some fun roleplay elements, CKIII is a deep roleplaying game with some interesting strategy elements. This isn't to say that CKIII isn't a good strategy game, or that it's inferior to the predecessor. The warfare aspect of the game has been vastly improved, religion and culture have much more depth, and the internal politics shine brighter than ever. But most of the massive improvements have been made in the terms of the character building element of the game. Between inter-character events, expanded traits, and a variety of new interactions, there's tons of new ways to play out each individual character in tons of new ways. Combined with a new user interface that makes the game dozens of times easier and more convenient to actually interact with, CKIII is just about the best historical medieval roleplaying you can get currently.Unfortunately, the new focus on roleplaying does mean that some of the deeper strategy mechanics have been left by the wayside. The government structure mechanics from CKII are notably absent, as are the trade mechanics and pandemics. Although none of these destroy the core experience of CK (i.e. being the adulterous murder hobo we all have buried deep inside), they do stand out, especially if you enjoyed developing weird strategies using those mechanics in the previous game. Most of these have been discussed as additions during later updates and DLC though, so keep up with news for the game if you're a bit on the fence. Which leads lastly to the other big downside of CKIII, the fact that it has Paradox's controversial DLC strategy. Although I don't think the DLC have been that bad, and work well in further developing the game's world, it still stands that they're an additional cost on top of a fairly pricy game. Between second party sites like Humble Bundle having the DLC at more reasonable prices, and the amount of content released for free, I wouldn't say the price is a super massive hurdle, but it might drive you away if you're already unsure of the best fit for the game. CKIII absolutely isn't the perfect strategy game, but it fills an interesting niche that few if any other games are currently trying to fill. While that lack of competition allows Paradox to be weird with their monetization, the game itself is a solid one, and well worth giving a try.

_childDocuments_.review: CK3 is out and it is a gem. With vast UI and accessibility tweaks, a revamped military system, 3D models for every character, plus countless quality of life improvements, Crusader Kings 3 has laid the groundwork for a phenomenal sequel to a beloved and enduring franchise. Paradox has handled the development and launch with grace, steering away from their previous title's rocky entry with Imperator: Rome. It is important for new and old players in the CK franchise to know that CK3 as it is right now is a fleshed out BASE GAME. Religions are all playable, governments (while streamlined since CK2) are all playable as well. You do not need a DLC to play in India, or anywhere on the map for that matter. Many lessons were learned from CK2. I feel confident and excited in CK3, and look forward to the expansions and updates that will make this solid and wonderful entry in the CK franchise into another timeless gem.

It's taking them years to add basic features of the last game like message settings. Other QoL features fromt he last game are nowhere to be seen, like directing your AI allies. Do not mistake my hours in this game as an endorsement. By this time I had double the amount of hours in CK2 and completed several more campaigns. I have tried to enjoy it so much. I LOVE CK2. It's my favourite game of all time. This game pales in comparison. At the same number of years of development as CK2, CK2 was already releasing their Horse Lords DLC. Most of its best DLC had been released. Most CK3 DLC are bad or at best mediocre. This game has a lot going for it which should make it an upgrade to CK2. The visuals are much better and the 3D characters are very immersive. The religion and culture mechanics are better than CK2 for the most part, though catholicism is missing basic CK2 feature to this day. The travel mechanics are really nice and the map is the biggest and best version of any CK map. But most of the other mechanics are outright bad. The vast majority of the events are trivial, poorly written, many ahistoric, nonsensical, or filled with horrible "humour" and they are the focus of every DLC and all the Dev time.  They also have a ton of events that are basically constantly spamming you with mundane worthless information or choices. Warfare is dumbed down and worse than CK2 and actually intentionally implemented ahistorical "fodder" levies that are actually a detriment to use. There's no trade mechanics, though CK2's were limited. Dealing with vassals is much easier than in CK2 and you have much fewer laws and levers to work with. Some systems like the new muslim government form don't even interact properly with older government systems around the rest of the game. The game is very easy once you get to tier king ranks, which is trivial enough in itself, because you can just put all your smaller vassals under a single duke (or king if you're an emperor) and then only deal with that single vassal which will usually love you for giving them all your vassals. Once you understand the game, failing is just a matter of RNG and there is A LOT of RNG in this game and the vast majority of the time it is simply bad for the player. A lot of the later part sof the game is just the process of mitigating RNG. Buy CK2.

_childDocuments_.review: CK3 basically improves upon everything CK2 had. The Characters feel much more in depth and unique even if patterns seem to repeat after a while. Gameplay is less interrupted with constant message pop-up windows which was the most annoying part of CK2.That being said, I really don't like the new way of magically summoning your armies out of thin air and instantly anywhere you have a holding, even though they tuned that down in 1.2 by making it impossible to levy more than the maximum capacity of the region (which is the least thing that can be done to make actual sense of that mechanic). The second thing is the complete removal of ships. Now, again, armies magically create them when they need to cross seas, only costing a little bit of time and money. I have no doubt this will be added back in an expansion but that feels low, really low.Besides that, I enjoyed pretty much everything else the game has to offer. They kept and improved mechanics that were good, created new very interesting ones such as "hooks", and got rid of bad ones, because that's what a good sequel should do instead of keeping every possible mechanic from the previous entry just to please fans. They took what was relevant and expanded upon it.As to cut content from the previous game's expansions, to me the most important ones are there except The Republic. Because, to be honest, even if I had all DLCs from CK2, I personnaly never really played nor liked Jade Dragon, Rajas of India or Horse Lords, and Sunset invasion was more of a meme expansion, fun once and never played again. As I said, the only one I miss is the Republic and even there, I actually think the idea was there but the mechanics never really did it for me, so I would really love to see a new take on an expansion focusing on this.I also was quite concerned before release given the terrible empty shell of a "game" that was Imperator: Rome and was so relieved when I started playing CK3. I actually have no problem at a game being a base for numerous DLCs to come if the actual base game already has a lot to offer and is solid, which is definitely the case here. This is completely different than Imperator because this one was broken at its core, with awful mechanics, CK3's mechanics aren't, they work really well.In conclusion, I strongly recommend Crusader Kings III since day one. It's a very strong base for what is definitely a game I'm gonna be playing for years to come. Hell, my first playthrough has already been close to 100 hours and I wasn't even done with it!

_childDocuments_.review: After playing 1500 hours of CK2, I'm pretty disapointed by this sequel as it stands now, would definitely not recommend buying in it's current state.LOTS of features are missing from the previous game (less succesions, no societies/orders, no papal influence system, no artifacts, much less events and event chains, can't chose a specific starting date only a few bookmarks, less intrigues and plots)Some mechanics have basically been streamlined into oblivion even though they were relevant.I can understand wanting to make the game more accessible, but having to manage boats and their cost, being able to raise only specific vassals' troop (in order for exemple to avoid annoying potential trouble makers), having different troops raise in their home region, all made sense to the game and added a layer of micromanagement. It took some time to get used to and learn to use effectively, but once you did, it worked just fine.With less mechanics and content, this game feels bland and soulless compared to its predecessor.The AI is terrible, and doesn't really have a clue what it's doing, whether it be at managing its troop, its dynasty or its realm.UI definitely needs some improvement, map is sometimes hard to read, information is sometimes hard to find, some buttons are weirdly placed and pop up windows are way too large, sometimes you want to be able to browse the map and character panels while you process what to do about events, but it's pretty hard considering the pop up just takes most of the screen.Couple positives things to note though, Characters all have gorgeous full sized protraits and detailed backgrounds, visually very pleasing.Battles are more better with more factors to take into account And the stress system, does make a characters life a bit more interesting and unique, as taking actions against a character's personality will incure stress which can have various repercussion later down the line.Overall, there are some good ideas in this game, but too much content is missing and it seems Paradox got confused and thought streamlining just meant dumb down as much as possible....I would recommend giving this game another year or so and taking it after it's gotten a couple of expensions and a price cut.I'm confident it will be a solid game sometime in the future, but that's just not it right now.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings III is a triumph for Paradox Interactive and I recommend it for two major reasons:1. Both role-playing and strategic decision-making are expertly balanced within the game. Whether it's the personal struggles of an shy alcoholic ruler at a grand feast, a furious vassal ready to conspire against their liege in a murder plot, or regional religious warfare plunging Iberia into yet another needless slaughter, CK3 allows the player to simulate the realities of medieval life, from the mundane to the exceptional.2. Given the two starting dates (867 and 1066), the range of historic starting characters and customizable ahistoric characters, constant free updates and paid DLC, and well-loved community modding scene, CK3 provides players with endless opportunities for engagement in this fantastic medieval sandbox.With any recommendations come caveats and here are the following words of caution.1. Crusader Kings III is a Paradox game and tied to anything from this developer is additional paid content. For many, like myself, this is worthwhile and adds a lot to the game, but for others with limited incomes, they may rightly get the impression that they are missing out.2. CK3 is not as oriented towards "map-painting" as other Paradox titles. Historically, this makes a lot of sense as medieval life was very localized (with some notable exceptions), but it might lead to some initial frustration for those seeking to recreate the Roman Empire. My advice is to take pleasure in the little things and learn to embrace failure, just like life. :)

There’s definitely a learning curve if you’ve never played games like this, but learning is the fun part. I’ve created characters and totally wrecked their dynasties, just for the fun of it. When I play as a King, I can’t help but get a thrill out of how many kids the Queen can produce for me, and on the flip side when I play as a Queen, it’s amazing to see how many heirs she can produce. Culture and Faith are hugely improved from ck2, and the dev team has added an amazing amount of player choice, depth and customization into mechanics that acted purely as flavor in ck2. I am excited to see how this game further develops and am looking forward to trying out the landless DLC coming out later this year

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Answer? CK3 is an absolutely amazing game and if you like roleplay, strategy, and history you should grab it.Longer Answer? I spent about 60ish hours playing the original Crusader Kings. Then I spent well over 2k hours playing Crusader Kings 2. I bought every DLC and some of the cosmetic packs for CK2. I absolutely adored that game. BUT CK2 was quite hard to get into. The UI was clunky, the information you needed to play hidden, and it just had an extremely steep learning curve.  I should know, a few of my tutorial videos on CK2 are still watched today, and after CK2 became free to play I got a lot of people commenting on videos or coming into my stream asking how to do things. Why? Because it just wasn't easy to understand anything and the tutorial was a hot mess.CK3 is an entirely different story. The UI is EXTREMELY far from clunky (though it does need a few tweaks, as I've said in a recent video, but they're all fairly minor). There are amazing tooltips inside of tooltips, making the knowledge needed to play the game very easy to access. There's also a great gamepedia in the game for quick access to information.Now, that's all about learning the game. But what about playing it?The entire CK experience is so much richer. The character events are much more detailed, and the responses you can pick are just so much more meaningful and entertaining. The 3D portraits add a lot of life to the game, making you genuinely care about the characters. The new Way of Life trees bring a lot of things to the surface that were hidden before. The combat is quite streamlined, as is building your army to suit your needs.  The fact that you can convert to any religion at any time, or change your religion as long as you have the piety is quite brilliant.  The new Dynasty system really makes the fact this game is built around playing a family, not a nation, so much more visible.Basically, the developers of CK3 took everything that worked in CK2 and made it better. And then they took everything that didn't work and either made it work, or entirely tossed it out for the release. I know many of us are hoping for the return of Merchant Republics and Nomads in the future. But, you have to admit, those governments had some severe issues and limitations in CK2. So, my hope is that if/when they come to CK3 they'll be just as marvelous as the governments currently in the game.Full disclosure, my game key was given to me by Paradox Interactive, but my words and opinions are my own.

_childDocuments_.review: The year is 1176. I am playing as Alberto, King of Italy and Tuscany, and holder of many other titles. Events are progressing well. I am well on my way to my ultimate goal of creating the Empire of Italia, bringing Italy, Corsica, Sardinia and Croatia under my heel. As Alberto I have used my stewardship ability to build up the power of my realm to rival the Papacy, my next target. I fully intend to pass on a legacy to my son and heir, Sinibaldo, a promising child of many talents.It was my occasional practice to grant titles to my children. This always carries the danger of them falling victim to some battlefield accident, but I sleep better knowing those titles are in the hands of close family. Sinibaldo has his own dukedom and is waging war on my vassal Duke Ugo, who is not a family member but who is a true ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The war does not go well for Sinibaldo and he becomes a prisoner of Duke Ugo. An unfortunate event, but surely he will simply be ransomed and we will all move on with our lives.But several months later I get the shocking news: Sinibaldo has been executed! My only son, struck down at the tender age of 14 by the vile Duke Ugo--how can this be? I am enraged. In the heat of passion I move to revoke Duke Ugo's title, but he rises up in rebellion against me. The impudence! As I rally my troops the true extent of my mistake becomes clear--my other powerful vassals have also rebelled. With growing desperation I realize there is no path to victory. My last army is destroyed and I lose the war, my kingdoms stripped away, I am deposed.I lean back in my chair and think about the rash idiocy of my actions. My son dead, my titles gone. I now have to play as my daughter and heir Benedetta, an eleven year old girl. It is time, I think, to pull the plug on this game.But what of Duke Ugo? Can he be allowed to go on, after the vile murder of my son? No, I must bend every effort to see him brought down. And so I forge on.As Alberto I had paid little attention to my daughter. Her guardian was some knight or other, and under her tutelage she had become rowdy, a warrior in a world of men who would never accept her as an equal. This, I thought, did not bode well.As Benedetta my reign was immediately disturbed as the vassals of Tuscany formed a faction to remove me as Queen. But wait, this faction wanted to install a new king in place, none other than my own father, Alberto! I suddenly realized that as his only child, unless he fathered another male heir I would inherit his titles upon his death and once again the kingdoms of Italy and Tuscany would be part of the same realm. And so when the faction presented its demands I simply capitulated. Alberto was now King of Tuscany and I was Queen of Italy.Yet my power was still not enough to challenge the evil Duke Ugo. To keep him close I appointed him my steward, but I also sent my spymaster to dig up dirt in his court.Years passed. I got married, had children, quashed several rebellions, organized my realm and bided my time. When a Crusade was launched I led my troops against the infidels attacking my cousin King Mario of Jerusalem, returning in triumph and finally impressing even the most retrograde of my male vassals. The waifish eleven year old girl had become a warrior Queen.But Ugo continued to plague me. As my steward he was often in my presence, always there to remind me of his evil treachery. I hosted a feast and there he was again, even trying to strike up a friendship! I coldly refused him, and he became my rival. The stress of dealing with him was almost unbearable.And then the miracle--my expert spymaster had uncovered gold. Duke Ugo was a deviant!This changed everything. I now had the key to bringing down my brother's murderer. But it must be done carefully--Ugo was still powerful, and I could not take him down as long as he and the other vassals of my realm opposed me. So I only blackmailed him, getting a strong hook that I would use to ensure his loyalty while I consolidated my position.In 1211 I received news of my father's death. After the messenger left my chambers, I went to the family shrine and knelt in prayer, vowing to my father's spirit that his son, my brother, would finally be avenged.More years passed. As both kingdoms were now mine, I slowly amassed enough gold and troops to take on my entire realm. A careful campaign of pacification had made my vassals compliant.It is the year 1218, and time to put my plan into action. I expose Duke Ugo's deviancy. He is now a criminal. As my father did twenty years before, I revoke his title, and again, he rises up in rebellion, but this time no one will stand with him. My troops outnumber his four to one. With laughable ease I storm his palace and win victory. My knights drag him out and throw him down in the mud before me.I arrest him and throw him in the dungeon. I revoke all of his titles and grant them to a distant toddler cousin. Years of emotional stress are wiped away in an instant--Ugo, my rival, murderer of my brother is now mine to do with as I will. Shall I torture him? Execute him? Shall I simply leave him there to rot in filth and misery? I ponder this choice, and the sweetness of vengeance.

_childDocuments_.review: He was a bear, but not quite. He had the fur, the claws, the teeth, but also the eyes, the voice, the mind of a man. A man who had lost everything. His job, his home, his future. His wife, who hated him. His children, who feared him.He had nothing left. Nothing but his computer, his game, his escape. He played Crusader Kings 3, a game where he could be human.But his wife would not let him have even that. She yelled at him, she cursed him, she provoked him. She made him suffer, rage, snap.And he did. He snapped. He killed her. He killed her with his claws, his teeth, his anger. He killed her, and he felt nothing. Nothing but relief, satisfaction, peace. He went back to his computer, his game, his escape.He went back, and he played. He played, and he forgot. He forgot his wife, his children, his life. He forgot his bear, his man, his hybrid.He forgot, and he was happy. Or so he thought.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to really, REALLY play this before sitting down and putting thoughts to paper...or digital bulletin boards, whatever. This game is excellent, but not in the way you might expect. One of my favourite Reddit comments I read about Skyrim's popularity chalked it up to being a very-simple "baby's first Elder Scrolls." Quaint. Cute. And very accurate, but moreso on WHY. The UI in Skyrim is much easier to read, manage, and get into, especially with a controller, and all the quests are simple to start, but deep as you go along. It fits great, and is excellent for newcomers and longtime fans.This is exactly how I would stack up Crusader Kings 3 to the previous entry. Crusader Kings 2 is great to watch pros play and make stories of on YouTube, but for the life of me I could not figure it out. I'm a hardcore Europa Universalis 4 fan (not as hardcore as SOME of you, but getting there), but the mechanics just did not work for me and I found the text hard to read.Oh boy they took notes. From the first second you boot up this game, it holds your hand. It says, "Try this" or "Do this" or whatever and gets you going. And then you can just right-click and tell it to shut the heck up because you've got this. Then everything breaks down and you go back to handholding until you get it right. Definitely the game for newcomers to see why we like these sorts of games, and definitely a lot of fun. If you're a big fan of all the features from 2, it is WILDLY scaled back, so be ready for that. I think Paradox took a big step-back in quality with their Rome game that just felt like an EU4 mod, but this is the real-deal $50 USD-worth strategy game.My hope is you're reading this because you've been drumming your fingers waiting on a sale or whatever, but trust me, you'll get your value out of it. Even if you're not a fan, it helps you become one. Good luck to all of you, and have a phenomenal day.

_childDocuments_.review: So much easier to get into than CK2.
