_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings is one of the greatest strategy games of all time, and the new version does it justice. It DOES incorporate most of the DLC from CK2 and improves it -- at least the good ones, not necessarily the silly ones like Aztec invasion ha ha.If you feel like all strategy games lack longterm playability, and just aren't intelligent or interesting enough, Paradox is definitely on the forefront of producing strategy games that are the right balance of complex but not monotonously detailed. CK differs from Europa Universalis in that it's about the medieval period, it's more about personal rule than nation-states. As such, you can suffer a disease and lose your dynasty suddenly. Or you can suddenly inherit a massive kingdom due to the same. You can amass a kingdom but loose the support of your own feudal lords and lose your kingdom. It's a lot more random than Europa, but that also adds more color, personality, and intrigue.It improves on CK2. The most annoying and time-wasting features are streamlined, the vassal management feels more like human relationships. I see some reviews w/ players complaining, but that's because they eliminated a few cheap workarounds you could do to your vassals to gain power. These workarounds were annoyingly time-wasting and the game is vastly improved without them! There is so much less clicking on each and every character in a big list to blah blah whatever.The lifestyle perk now adds many bonuses in that area for your character, unlocking new skills and interactions. It's a much better system. I've heard players complain it incentivizes sticking to a lifestyle to unlock the higher bonuses. That's why they call it a "lifestyle". Once again, they've made the game more realistic and human!If you like turn-based strategy, definitely play this! After 5 hrs, I was like, "this is the same as CK2, they messed it up"... after 10 I was like "holy crap no! this is better and whatever DLC and mods come out will only build from here!"

The game looks good, it feels good and it is fun for probably 10 hours. Then you realize that CK3 does not feature something you could call an "AI". Your opponents are braindead. They cannot use most of the tools that are given to the player. There is no "strategy" involved, you don't need elaborate plans or ingenious tactics because the AI will be THAT stupid that you could let your cat walk over your keyboard for 20 minutes and STILL win the campaign!And I'm not even kidding or exaggerating here. You can start as the lowest count in the worst part of the world and STILL succeed because the AI simply has absolutely no clue whatsoever. Examples are legion so I cannot list them all but mainly legacy management, realm prosperity, marriage logic (dont get me even started on this on) and on top of it all the horrendus warfare logic. AI cannot win a war. It simply cannot. I'd rather play chess against a braindead pidgeon in the park before I start another campaign. Sorry, Paradox if the fanbois are too blinded to tell you the truth but this one has nothing to do with "strategy" as it is more  historical SIMS.

I'm sure that the game will improve and will be much better in a few months, but today it is a huge disappointment to have paid 75 euros for a game that you have to put in the "fridge" and wait to play inside a few months when it has been corrected. It is, of course, not what is expected of Paradox after many years of the launch of CK2. Graphics improvements, animated characters, etc. are not bad but it is not what those of us who play these types of games need more. We need possibilities for roleplay as the main reason to play. Among other things, how is it possible to launch CK3 without a character editor that allows you to create your own character or dynasty? Where are many of the functionalities of CK2? Definitely, if you liked CK2, my recommendation is not to buy the game and wait for future versions. PS: The map of the Iberian Peninsula is wrong, with Astorga, Sarria and Villablino changed places.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game with the plague system turned on. If you turn it off, at the start of your game, then this game is pretty amazing and fun. The issue with the plague system isn't that it creates a new challenge - instead the options and ways a ruler would have counteract the plague are extremely limited and make you feel like you have no recourse unless you're in a feudal goverment. TLDR: the game gives very limited and unrealistic ways to deal with a fairly aggressive mechanic. So turn it off and this game is fun. Turn it on, and unless you're feudal, you feel helpless and it makes the game feel bad. Examples: A barony is infected. You can't send your physician or any medical team to try to counteract it. You can't have a wise person or hedge hermit go and try to cure it. You can't isolate the barony or county. You can't station troops to limit people from leaving the county. You can't simple kill off a town. You can't close borders, you can only isolate yourself or your ruling family. We're given the option to have our physicians research but they can't directly research the current plague or malaise in an effort to discover a cure. We can't increase the diet or change the sanitation of a barony or land unless it's a tradition.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an amazing disappointment. I cannot recommend it to anyone. Crusader Kings 3 is best described as a puddle the size of an ocean; it lacks depth, immersion, and meaningful content. Oh, it's full of mechanics, sure, but these mechanics are boring and uninteresting. There is no real drive to conquer - you don't get any real sense of accomplishment. There are no deep systems to interact with, only some levers to pull to make one number go up and another go down. It is literally unplayable without mods, as you will be drawn into the same boring loop over and over. I have around 1,800 hours in CK2 at the time of writing; at least 150 of my hours in CK3 come from working on a variety of mods, all of which I can no longer motivate myself to work on due to the base game being so boring and poorly developed. They have insulted the fanbase that built this game through unending love of CK2 by giving us a truly unfinished, halfbaked, poorly thought out product, and then trying to sell us back the best qualities of CK2 through overpriced garbage DLCs. 100 events as a DLC? Really? I hope people learn from this. We need to stop supporting developers and publishers that treat their playerbase so poorly.UPDATE: This game is now actually pretty enjoyable... WHEN IT WORKS. I play on Linux. I will always be using Linux. When ran natively - the game is supposed to have native linux support - the game constantly crashes due to horrific graphical errors regardless of which version is used. When using Proton, it runs fine, but will crash at random for seemingly no reason wiping your progress to the last save or autosave. Absolutely unacceptable!!!

_childDocuments_.review: People protest this isn't as complex, deep, layered and content-filled as CKII, and that's fair, it's not. But it's a lot better than CKII was at release, it's much more new-player friendly, and I have full faith in Paradox that their following expansions will bring all that juicy depth that over seven years of support and development gave CKII with time. Yes, Crusades can be very difficult to win, as disjointed swarms of tiny Christian armies flock to attack waiting hordes of Muslims with months to prepare for the crusade's arrival. For anyone protesting the ahistorical nature of a coordinated attack and a feeble and late defence, see the First Crusade. 4th Crusade and onwards the above makes complete sense, but perhaps a toned down first crusade response, toned up Jihad and latter crusade response would be nice. It's early days. Yes, without secret societies, artifacts and diverse government types the game can get a bit samey after 150-200 years. Playing with mates helps, and again, a more open UI makes for better new player experience, but it does lack that depth. Give it time. For me, CKIII is a worthy successor and well worth the price, and will only get better with age.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This game is amazing, I still hold that opinion, but the DLC policy will always be horrible and this is another nail that we're being made to bear. I really can't believe I'm leaving a bad review on this game. I love CK3 to death. I got into CK2 just before they announced CK3, and fell in love with CK3 just the same. What Paradox is doing, however, is...honestly the same ♥♥♥♥ they always do: milk their games to the last dime. And we, the consumers, just deal with it like we usually do. We buy dlc constantly, and yet the dlcs that paradox keeps putting out are getting more expensive for less content. Them doubling the price is just the same ♥♥♥♥ different color.None of these flavorpacks are worth doubling their price. Not a single one. The biggest argument you can make is for the northern lords pack, but even then it doesn't have enough content to justify 13 dollars. Fate of Iberia adds new interesting mechanics to the game, but right now its only for Iberia, and I assume we will be paying 13 dollars each and every time their going to add this mechanic to a region, if they add more at all. Then there's Royal Court. I was interested in royal court I won't lie. It seems like an interesting thing to add, what with the new 3D models and artifacts coming back. In reality, though, it added something that was honestly useless to the game. How many people actually click hold court? If you do you either do it for "immersion" or simply because your a masochist who loves getting random negative events 9/10 times. Royal court ended up not adding that much useful features for 30 whole dollars.Now Paradox wants to release a stupid event pack that is "100 events" for what will probably be, if we're lucky, a split between good and bad events evenly. For what is probably still going to be 13 dollars.

_childDocuments_.review: (Overall I recommend as a game to play, but there are issues i do list later on, i will update this as things change and I gain more experience playing.) The game runs smooth at a constant 60fps and I haven't encountered any major or minor technical glitches. The map style is really good looking, from an art pov the game looks great. Music direction, great. UI? Smooth, mostly fine and feels a bit more engaged than CK2 overall with a few clunky boxes here and there but nothing game-breaking. I like the religious systems and the hook system, lifestyle system is a bit bland and I would have liked to see ambitions still be a part of the game. Combat is nice and overall much clearer.Big Problems:- My biggest gripe is the level of detail contained in the game compared to CK2, whilst counties have been divided into subsequent baronies, bishoprics etc, on a bigger (and PLAYABLE) scale the detail has been reduced, despite them advertising the map as being much higher in detail, it doesn't translate well into gameplay. For example - playing as the count of Lancashire in CK2 in 1066 was possible, and you could start small and make moves to develop from there. In CK3? Nope, you play as the duke of Mercia who controls a large portion of England, and there is no option to play as the count. There are less counts overall and less opportunities to play from a rise to power pov, too many big named starts. - Map modes: How did this get overlooked? Only 6 options with the main default being to terrain/realm view? really? No diplomatic map for example, no opinion map, again a reduction in detail. - CB claims: CB claims are far too easy to acquire now, oftentimes in CK2 you could be waiting ages to fabricate and push a claim, CK3 has pushed it to the other extreme, just wait for the timer to ping and bam. Also, there are problems with random claims coming in too often  (eg Ireland in 867, every chief has a claim on you from the off).- Timer gameplay: Feels almost a bit like a mobile-game with the number of timers present: Whether it's fabricating, swaying etc. It's still chance based, but it does often feel like i'm simply waiting for a clock to run down. - The character finder has been nerfed totally, whilst the reasons for this make sense in terms of historical accuracy/distance to other rulers, the actual interface itself has been butchered. Instead of being able to search for people to invite to court in an efficient way, you are reliant on guests turning up in your court with the right skills lest a council member dies or you want to improve things. Same issue with arrange marriage options. It feels like paradox simply ruined a system with nothing solid to put in it's place other than the hook system, it feels like a lot of the reductions in these parts of the game are just a way to shoehorn in the new intrigue mechanics which end up feeling tedious as it's essentially doing the same thing but having to go through some character before getting what you want.  Small Annoyances:- When selecting any character to play, there is no option to re-select the date at the game rules screen without going back through the main menu/loading and deleting saves again.- Timers on decisions seem too long, and there are less available. - No option to save game rule preferences/profiles, you have to change them every time you start a new game. - UI can sometimes be annoying when going through several menus to find something, only to want something else and having to click off and start again entirely: e.g character finder.

_childDocuments_.review: I deliberately did not leave a review for the base game for quite a while, understanding perhaps that the game was still in early days and that future updates and patches would likely fill up some of the gaping holes present in the game. I liked the base game as a good platform for them to add on to - the graphics are superb, new traditions and skills are a fresh new way to play, religion changes are good, but the game was still deeply lacking. It's been two years now and we're nowhere near CK2's level of polish. Some of you might think that isn't fair, that it's a separate game - but I'd argue that it's a direct sequel, and should improve upon its predecessor, but CK3 has yet to do that.Even worse, - something no man alive or dead thought was possible. This is the main reason for this review.Their 'content packs' which add a few new mechanics and traditions to certain areas of the world, such as one for Scandinavia and one for Spain, are overpriced and do nothing to address the massive gaping content holes in the game (i.e. lack of any government apart from Feudal and Tribal, which means practically every playthrough will be the same regardless of where you are in the world - you either start feudal, or you start as tribal and then become feudal. No, 'clans' are too lacklustre to count). Their only major DLC, Royal Court, was an extreme flop due to the outright absurd price and lack of depth to justify said pricetag. It glued one half-baked mechanic onto the boringly flat game. So, two flavour packs and a major expansion in with no major fleshed out improvements, what do they decide to do? Release a DLC that is entirely a text file for new relationship events. No new assets, no new mechanics. And still, according to reviews, they mess that up. But this is a problem for Paradox - people don't like their new DLC that they spent no time at all on! What should they do to fix this? Well, they had a genius solution - rather than update the DLC with new content to actually justify making it worth paying for, they instead decided to . They also put out a statement saying that this price change will "...reflect the overall value of this kind of content moving forward". That's Paradox speak for 'We realised later on that we could charge double and you clowns would still pay for it, so we will be charging exorbitant rates in the future as well for the same garbage!"Even their dev diaries that should be allaying concerns with the game seem strangely 'plastic' to me, praising their latest DLC's as successes with lots of positive feedback, when they have mostly negative reviews on steam. All signs point towards this being insidiously expensive for you going forwards, and will take years before it is anywhere near being even a shadow of its older brother, CK2. It's fundamentally a good game to get into if you're new to the genre and have the money to spend, but for fans of the genre I am concerned as to the direction it's going.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr at bottomSo off the bat, no, this game doesn't have as many features as CK II. If you're expecting it to be as fully fleshed out as an almost 9 year old game that received constant updates and DLC, you're not realistically setting your expectations. What this game *is*, however, is still fantastic. It's dropped a lot of the tedium of CK II while expounding on what made its predecessor interesting. It looks better, plays better, and feels much better. A big thing that drove away people from CK II was the randomness of it all, but there is certainly much more strategy here than before, and players are given a larger amount of control over their dynasties while still being encouraged to play characters differently thanks to the stress system. Returning gameplay systems from CK II are also *much* more interconnected and intuitive - a symptom of many of those systems being added progressively. Here, everything is cohesive and has its function. Maps are also more interesting, and characters will act in much more meaningful, different ways. My biggest criticism right now is that it's lacking in the events departments, government types, and gameplay in different regions will need to be fleshed out in the future. But for a Paradox release, this game is probably in the best state of any of their more recent releases (especially in the performance department). A worthy addition, and well worth the wait. Pros - Looks great, characters look unique and it's no longer just kid>young adult>adult>oldMassive mod potentialCohesive and interconnected gameplay systems that make sense/aren't overly game-eyNPC characters actually act differentEncourages players to actually play characters differentlyPerforms well technicallyOverall a very solid base game with lots of content to exploreCons - Regions need more meaningful differences and unique eventsLet me hover my mouse over a tooltip once I open itUI can be a little counter intuitive at timesThere needs to be meaningful differences between government types and more ways to manage a realm, Byzantines and reformed Viking pagans should *not* be operating the same wayI would also love to have great works back, the feeling of building something monumental added weight to my empiresOverall 9/10, back to kicking the Saxons out of the Isles I go ~

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a finger grade than Yes / No on these reviews. I got my money's worth, but now I'm uninstalling this game in disgust, determined to never play it again. This is one of those games that draws you in and keeps you hooked by promising so much; and then the more time you spend with it the more you realize that most of those promises were false.There's a good core here which all Paradox games share. The game shines in the first few decades or even the first couple of centuries of your dynasty. And then it collapses under its own weight. The same two and a half repetitive 'random' events. Idiotic faction system. Harebrained AI rulers. AI completely takes over gameplay, ties your hands, and instead of taking your dynasty where you want it to go the game drags you back into constantly firefighting the same tiresome external events over and over and over and over again. There are too many systems and no hint of late-game balance. Every successful dynasty, no matter the path you choose, devolves into the same late-game slodge. It's literally the 'suffering from success' meme. Too many vassals, too many cultures and religions, too many claims, and a whack a mole of rebellions and invasions and propping up moronic vassals. To be fair, there's also the other late-game slodge: start off slow, expand at a snail's pace, and manage the crap out of your tiny realm, in which case the slodge is staring at your screen as the decades zip by until you dare make your next tiny move.Sure, it's 'realistic' and even maybe 'historically accurate'. But is it fun? Is it rewarding? Absolutely not. Cleaning out latrines and shoveling crap in the stables is also realistic, and was definitely an important everyday part of medieval life. But would that be fun to put in the game? This is was CKIII does. You start off with a small realm and a couple of latrines and one stables, so you only have to realistically shovel crap every once in a while. But as you grow, the number of latrines and stables in your realm grows exponentially, and soon enough your entire gameplay is getting bombarded with 'your latrine in Magdeburg is full sire', 'stables in Split are 97% full sire', and you're just constantly emptying one latrine after another instead of, you know, marching on Jerusalem.

BUILD YOUR SHADOW ASSASSIN Craft your weapons and armors and upgrade your elite warrior with a wide variety of abilities and shadow powers. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a stealth game that tries to be metal gear, splinter cell, and ghost of tsushima but manages to fail at all of them all at once.Pros:- Its a stealth game, hide in bushes, assassinate while trying not to get caught. If that's your cup of tea this game is for you- Stealth is manageable and your character is rather mobile for a stealth game making him feel like a shadow spirit walking in and out with little a whisper- Designs and art are rather charming and not bad to look at- Customisation is there and not bad- Multiplayer is also there and can be quite fun with good friendsCons:- While this is a stealth game it felt like it was a game about speed running your way through every level as even on higher difficulty I was literally finishing levels in sometimes five minutes or less.- Enemy AI is trash, often glitching and spotting you from 100km away or not spotting you at all, or simply glitching in a state of awareness and permanently being stuck looking in a corner screaming about someone being dead.- Speaking of which there is no downside to killing versus knocking out apart from knocking out take longer which for this game was just painful. + there is very little downside to simply running around slashing anyone in your way as blood doesn't trigger enemies and it's way more convenient.- Level maps are repeated which is fine, however some maps were used up to 4-5 times and with little variation beyond more enemies that seemed to be dropped like someone was blindfolded in garry's mod with their left click taped down.- Item's are rather useless and I rarely if ever used them as they bring very small benefit beyond healing and emergency smoke grenades once and a while.- Not only can levels be completed rather quickly, but there are apparently 51 of them! which would be fine if they were there own zone with well thought out dynamic to get around. But considering this is the fifth time I am in the mine to collect/assassinate/destroy/meet a contact/ or destroy a couple boxes became quite boring after the first 20 times I had to do it, and especially tedious when they are used as padding between the main story missions.- Speaking of the story is complex and makes little to no sense, it seems there is lore here but even other people who played the previous game say the lore in THIS GAME doesn't make any sense. In addition very little is explained as to what or who people are or why any of the story is transpiring.- The HUB area which while pretty was another form of padding making me run up to a temple to get a small bit of dialogue, a pat on the shoulder from the leader before I am sent back to the bulletin board for another mission. It's also good to note this is mostly to hang out with your friends and buy items however my friends and I started trying to speed run these sections as they became absolutely monotonous very quickly.- Single player is present however many times during the game I felt that certain areas were meant to be tackled as a team and not to waste anymore time I simply did my best to sprint through them- In addition while the game says "Skill based combat" think some of the new assassin creed games but infinitely worse as players can only handle around 1 -2 enemies at a time not because of skill or speed, but because enemies have an absolutely absurd stamina bar that the game doesn't really provide skill to counter and main attacks only take slivers while they take large chunks out of yours. But wait I hear you say, "Isn't this a stealth game?" why yes it is, and while that would be appropriate for a pure stealth game unfortunately they added a mission completion bar based on how many fights you got in like splinter cell.- while there is a skill tree I barely if ever bought skills as 90% I didn't use beyond the passives, upgraded whisper, and the multi kill- Personal pet peeve, but considering your charging 40$ for this and you are repeating several levels, bugs, the story is incomprehensible, and there isn't that much content seriously put's a damper on recommending friends to purchase this game.So to conclude is Aragami 2 a bad game, no. for certain people or a good group of friends it can be a passable experience however considering all the issues it would need a few things before I could recommend this to anyone.- Shrink the campaign, if you need 20 missions to tell the story then make it 20 and make them good instead of adding 30+ filler episodes especially when the filler is all on the same maps with slightly different objectives. (they can be added, but keep them optional to get xp or items instead of slowing the entire story to a crawl)- Overhaul your combat system to where it is passable (ie add more combat based abilities or tweaking combat to handle more enemies) or don't have it at all with it there mostly for escaping and creating distance.- And make the lore understandable, I didn't play the first game and if I can't even figure out why my character is in this fight beyond ThAT GUy bAd then it needs some work.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a sequel. Combat, gameplay and how stages are made as well as mission objectives and the way missions are set in a completely differently and anyone coming into the game expecting it to be a sequel is bound to be disappointed but I welcome discussion.However and its own way it is incredible. The combat brings a new element to the game where it’s not an instant death but gives you a chance to test your skill for your life. The skill ceiling is higher than the first well it can be very forgiving in the first game in this you have two deaths then you can restart the level. Individually each level is a mixed bag it can be easy or hard or anywhere in between but you have to take a new approach to each one for every level you just can't run in or do a certain stealth path you have to look at what's happening around you and adapt.The movement it's much better in the first game and has been improved dramatically you can build up speed by running and falling do long jumps and double jumps having to consider whether you want speed or to go far you can take everything at your own pace or speed run. The shadow leap no longer makes it as a get out of jail free card, you have to know when and how to use it as well as your other abilities you have to think of them as not your abilities like in the first game which were separate from your movement and gameplay but in this game they compliment them and allow you to take out enemies from a distance distract them, turn them against themselves or send them to sleep.there are negatives like some levels feeling stale or overused and the mountains of bugs but the developers are working tirelessly to fix them but one thing is the story it's nothing to write home about and the game can be a bit boring at times but picks up.I personally feel that customization was a welcome change and I loved in the end game to change my load out and playing with other people overall I think if you're coming into the game expecting a sequel you'll be disappointed but if you're looking for a good game you'll be pleasantly surprised

_childDocuments_.review: is a game that improves on various gameplay elements of its predecessor, but sacrifices its tone, charm and unique nature in the process. The enjoyable teleportation mechanic has been replaced with one that offers less freedom, the clear sense of progression was ditched in favour of repetitive filler, and the focused narrative has become a wider and far less concise affair.  Judged as an independent game and not against the virtues of its predecessor,  is a decent game at best, and an absolute drag at worst.Beyond the tutorial, our story starts with the Aragami, our protagonist, being killed and thus discovering that he can respawn.  When he does, he finds himself in Kakurega Village, a place populated by other Aragami who immediately start giving him jobs to do.  Being an entity seemingly lacking independent thought or desire, our protagonist then proceeds to perform every theft, assassination and scouting mission asked of him without question. The motivation for all of this is that, apparently, the Aragami suffer a curse that grants them their abilities, but slowly consumes their minds.  If you're a fan of the first  title, you've probably noticed that everything I just said clashes with the entire plot of said game.  It seems that  is not so much a sequel as a re-imagining, and the protagonist's appearance and the general theme of his abilities are the only meaningful connections between the two.  This would not necessarily be a bad thing if the new story were grander and more fleshed out, but it was not to be.The first game featured a relatively simple and narrow plot in which the Aragami was a shadow spirit called to assist his summoner by defeating her enemies and enabling her rescue from the forces of the light.  With that, we had a simple light vs. dark theme facilitating and being reinforced by gameplay mechanics. This story was not an especially deep one, but it provided a clear setting and a simple premise that saw players continually progress through new areas with a clear goal in sight, encountering and overcoming new obstacles along the way.  Such a sense of progression or theme is completely absent in , dropped in favour of something larger but with little depth.  Kakurega Village acts as a hub for the player to return to between missions, and offers limited services such as a vendor for the game's new consumable items, including health potions.  The main function of the village, however, is to house the NPCs that continually give the player missions.  The nature of said missions is the game's biggest problem by far.  To begin with, players move between several areas, completing simple objectives such as assassinating a target or stealing an item. These objectives are broadly the same as those featured in the first  title and are quite enjoyable the first time.  You may be tempted to take your time, plotting your path and making use of your stealth abilities and the host of new combat items such as stun grenades and poisoned needles.However, if you found yourself in this same place again, heading for the same building as last time but for a  different objective, would you want to put so much dedication into it again?  What about the third time?  What about the fifth?  Content is endlessly reused, with very little challenge or variety added in the process.  Some new enemies appear, but this changes nothing about how you'll play the game, and I rarely felt it necessary to use the majority of my abilities or items.  New locations do appear now and again, but you'll always end up coming back to the same old places from the start of the game – places that often look very similar, to boot.  The objectives you'll be taking on in these places hardly change, either.  This constant revisiting of old content slows the story's progression to a crawl, and it's painfully obvious when a plot point exists solely to make the player do more of it. At over eight hours into the game, I found myself in the same place, doing more or less the same thing that I was doing at one hour into the game, and with no noteworthy challenge or mechanics to make it different.  It was at this point that I decided I was done with the game, and to write this review.  I normally like to finish the games that I review, but moments of interest are so few and far between that I am simply too bored to continue.Something that bothered me when playing the first game was the Aragami's inability to scale low walls or climb ledges.  addresses this by adding not only ledge-grabbing and climbing, but a double-jump and mid-air dash as well.  When combined with the reworked teleportation ability that allows one to instantly move to a nearby ledge, it's possible to traverse terrain at significant speed – something that quickly becomes very useful when ploughing through the filler content.If one doesn't feel like avoiding enemies, the game does have a combat system, though it is more likely to cause the player's death than an enemy's.  This is not because the combat itself is particularly difficult, but because the game tries to force players into combat mode when an enemy attacks, snapping the camera to the enemy and severely inhibiting the player's movement.  Combine this with the enemies' ability to seemingly teleport to and strike a player who is attempting to flee, and there's cause for much frustration.  If one does stick to a stealthy approach, however, the gameplay is solid. Running the game on its max settings, I got a consistent 60fps with no drops.  Bugs were minimal, with just a few minor issues that did not impact gameplay in any meaningful way.  I did, however, discover some baffling design decisions; namely a complete lack of keybind options or a pause function – even for singleplayer.While  graphics are a technical step-up from the first game, they still look rather dated and no longer have a stylised flair to mask the fact.  Though this game does have some nice-looking areas, I think the original looks better.  Smaller visual elements such as animations, meanwhile, have been improved and generally look quite good.Upon arriving in Kakurega Village, one may notice a beautiful track playing in the background; it's the highlight of the game's soundtrack, which is of high quality and lovely to listen to, for a while.  Unfortunately, its tracks seem to be few in number, and they quickly get old.  The rest of the game's sound effects are of decent quality, and there's little to complain about on that front. While  would not qualify as a worthy sequel to its beloved predecessor, it would pass as a decent and relatively enjoyable stealth game if it were not burdened with a weak story and unnecessary filler that drags the experience down into the mud.  If played in co-op and/or in short stints, the game is serviceable, but it meanders far too much to hold my interest.  This makes me sad.

_childDocuments_.review: This has to be one of the worst games I've ever played, incredible downgrade from the first Aragami. Everything about this game is bad, the graphics have been downgraded and the game looks boring and bland. The best thing about aragami 1 was it's mission / map design, each mission felt very different and had it's own sort of vibe, in Aragami 2 all the missions feel the same the maps are just a piece of land with a bunch of buildings. _childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2~~~~~~~~~After the immense success of the first Aragami game, Aragami 2 aims to bank on the critically-acclaimed experience of the first title and take it to new levels. Aragami 2’s story takes place about a century or so after the first game’s timeline. This time around you are going against the Akatsuchi Empire, a fierce invading force that aims to take over the land of The Aragami clan, known as Kurotsuba.Plot: You play as the Aragami ninja, who after a selfless heroic battle against the Akatsuchi Empire, gets pinned down and cursed by the enemy and barely manages to escape the clutches of the Akatsuchi Empire. He finds a safe haven in a nearby village ruled by a peace-loving clan. After battling the curse he manages to control it and as one of the few Aragami capable of using Shadow Essence to their advantage, it is up to you to fight off the Akatsuchi Empire.Free your people and defend this new village that you call home.Gameplay: Aragami 2 in short is a linear, story-driven game with mission-based format where you take up contracts for eliminations, information gathering, stealing items of interest, and rescue ops.You take the control of Aragami, a ninja who uses Shadow Essence to his advantage. After each successful interaction with villagers and clan elders, you are provided with missions and contracts.Each of these missions/contracts takes place in the Rashomon Valley over and over again within a limited number of locations with minor changes to the locations' layouts. It was a constant battle between the ultra-linear story structure and repetitive mission locations, versus the genuinely fun stealth gameplay. In the end, the gameplay managed to keep me occupied for a good amount of time.As mentioned, you get to play the same types of mission over and over again with minor storyboard changes and different map layouts within the same locations, constantly backstabbing the same rusty old enemy AI. The only saving grace, Combat: Aragami 2 just drops you off at your starting positions and gives you full control over the playable area.And my god this system is so good, there are literally no restrictions; you can do whatever you want as long as you get the job done. You can go full jungle fight scene Rambo, no F…s given. A brutal mixture of a nimble ninja sneaking past his enemies to Rambo, backstabbing 3 enemies in a row and running away while the rest of the enemy goons come after you.This time around you get some consumable/throwable items in the game to enhance your combat effectiveness and get creative with items such as the Shuriken, Amnesia Needles, Potions, smoke screens, and more. Throw in some experience-based supernatural abilities to unlock, and you’ve got yourself an ultimate shadow-dashing, high jumping, wall-climbing killing machine. Sadly, everything is not perfect here, and three major downsides bring down this awesome combat section – 1. Parry: Yeah the parry doesn’t work as intended. Drains stamina too fast leaving me defenseless, damaged, and dead. 2. Enemy AI: Just horrible, in every single mission certain enemies will randomly start walking in the wrong direction, randomly ignore a buddy being killed in front of him, randomly start throwing fireballs without detection and so much more. 3. Auto-locking- My god this feature is a load of hot trash! Whose idea was it to put auto-locking in a stealth game? And for what purpose? Every time I died, I swear to God it was caused by this faulty auto-lock system.I killed an enemy and was detected. Okay cool, as I’m trying to run away from the enemy, this stupid system auto-locks on him and slows me down, causing an animation chain reaction where I lose all defenses. World design: Aragami 2 is supposed to take place 100 years after the first one, but visually and artistically both look the same to me. This time around the maps are much bigger, giving the players a big leg to stretch their muscles. The map layouts across each mission were really good, although I wished they had implemented more unique locations rather than changing up the map layouts for each mission. Visually there’s a lot left to be desired as well. Expected a bit more charm and sparkle. Music and sound effects: What Aragami 2 really gets right is its background music. It’s really good and very relaxing, suitable for a stealth game for sure. I demand more of such music in the upcoming updates and DLCs. The same goes for the sound effects; very good sync with the combat and parkour throughout the game, especially the blasting spray of blood coming out of the enemies as I stabbed them repeatedly; that was nice. Positive: + Linear story + Fun stealth gameplay + No holds barred, just get the job done+ Mission rating system without a leaderboard! + Strong, balanced tree of abilities + Balanced and useful throwable/consumable items+ Decent amount of character customization + CO-OP PvE support Negatives: - Minor animations issues - One-way mirror map layout wall, with holes- Problematic Auto-lock feature - Dumb and rusty enemy AI - Repetitive missions - Story structure could’ve been improvedNo holds barred Stealth action; just get the job done! Anything goes in the fight against the Akatsuchi Empire. 7/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: The original, but you actually feel like a ninja assassin.Don't get me wrong, 1 was great and I loved it; lots of cool moments where you pull off a chain of expertly-timed eliminations, but I always felt like I was just objectively weaker than everything else if I didn't have the teleport. In 2, I never feel like that. The way I play is nearly identical, but it just FEELS better to do. Also, if I feel like it, I can just go sick-o mode and run into a level, foghorn blaring, which we absolutely couldn't do in 1.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Over-ambition has been, and will unfortunately continue to be the end of many.It's abundantly clear that Lince Works gave Aragami 2 everything they had, and then some; however, the height of their aspirations soared far over the stars. Such a distance proved far too hefty, as we would come to discover over two years ago.This is far from a bad game. There are some aspects of it that I find myself truly fond of, such as its very free movement system, whereas there are many others that feel incomplete, clunky, or forgotten, with the main story being the most obvious example. Even so, these comparatively janky segments of the game are rarely intrusive, nor worth making a fuss over if you're simply looking for a by-the-books stealth experience. It's easy to ascertain Lince Works intent when looking closely upon these half-baked parts of the game, and see where they were coming from.Having finally completed everything both Aragami titles have to offer in convincing fashion, it's hard not to feel pity for the recently defunct developer. Making a product with a quality that ranges from great to meh doesn't earn the creators such a saddening fate, in my opinion.Hopefully the many talented individuals who helped make this game, and its predecessor a reality are able to lend their aforementioned skills elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Completed the game in ~25 hours, 41/44 achievements (will hunt remaining ones bit later).Starts awesome but gets boring & repetetive quickly.Out of 51 missions game has to offer I enjoyed doing first 6-8, then nothing interesting up to mission 40, and then the last one (although it's the same as #40)Missions are on the same reused locations (there are ~10 of them and each has 3-6 missions) with the same reused tasks (kill target, capture target, destroy materials, gather materials).This game could be so much more :(Still enjoyed playing it!
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: I have not played all the way through this game but I do want to write a quick review for people that played the first Aragami. This games mechanics are not at all similar to the first one. Story seems fine but they have changed a lot. The first Aragami you had to sneak around and not get caught. In this game you can block, dodge, and parry. If you are looking to experience the first Aragami again this is not that. With all that being said this game is not bad but it is different.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: What I love :- The OST is surprisingly nice.- The stealth and assassination mechanics are much smoother than the first instalment. - 3 players co-op instead of 2- The addition of a skill tree and equipment with stats makes for much more diverse builds- Subsequent updates that added classic mode and such adds replayability and is a nice comeback to Aragami 1 mechanics- The story is nothing special, but it holds up.- The ability to chose your assassin dripWhat I dislike :- Some bugs here and there can be annoying- As some pointed out, it is repetitive, but that was to be expected- I wish there were some more mission typesOverall :Aragami 2 is a good stealth assassination game, best played with friends, but can be enjoyed alone. I recommend going for hard or classic mode. Don't buy this expecting a true sequel to Aragami 1, it isn't. It's certainly more modern, maybe to a fault sometimes, but I enjoyed it thoroughly and went for all achievements because it was really fun. Speedrunning this has been a blast.8/10★★★★★★★★☆☆
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished the game as of yet, but from what I've seen so far, I can recommend the game.I was a huge Shinobido and Tenchu fan and this game feels like the closest we've got to that on PC at the moment.You have a HUB where you come back after every mission and upgrade your character and purchase different items, then you go back to the board to accept a new mission. The missions take place in mini open maps, just like Shinobido did back then, so that was a huge plus for me.Gameplay now feels more in line with Tenchu than the first Aragami when it comes to how agile you are. Which I really enjoyed.I did encounter some bugs, but I'm sure they'll get ironed out as some patches come out.So far I've only played singleplayer so I can't comment on co-op. I will update this review after I finished the game to make it more in depth.Lastly I wanted to say thanks for bringing a game in this genre to Steam. Since there aren't many Tenchu/Shinobido like games on PC, it's nice to have this.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: coming from a person who has played both games, i would say this is a pleasant upgrade compared to the original. the original had a gripping story and stealth was its key feature. the first game was janky yet it had heart to it. the second, albeit still having some bugs but from the hours i have played and is still playing, i have not come across a bug that has ruined my experience with the game. the movements are fluid and the actual gameplay makes you feel like an actual ninja of the shadows. it still has the heart of the first game, yet has done better and even upgraded most of its earlier mechanics in all regards.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Right, now that I've completed the game, I can update my review. In short - the game is a VAST downgrade from the previous installment. In long terms? Here's a list.FIRST THE PROS (cuz its short af)-CO-OP play-more sneaky beaky gameplay-the skill tree is quite interesting and especially helpful for the stealth side of the game. Some skills are a tad too powerful, but that's related more so your skills-some of the maps are well-designed and aesthetically pleasing-the new enemy class variety is a strong upgrade from the previous game-the apparel you unlock at the shop bears a cool design, most notably the Oni setNOW COME THE CONS-the AI is very terribly designed. They will sometimes just detect you from across the map (and I mean that literally. It happened on multiple occasions), detect bodies hidden in grass, pathfind THROUGH walls, sometimes they hear from far away while other times you can perform a knock out mere meters away and they won't even turn their head-the aforementioned skill tree has some useless additions, too! The combat skills shouldn't exist - this is a game focused on stealth. Why can we have a melee brawl and survive it like it was nothing? - and some of those combat skills are pretty mediocre at best-your utility arsenal (kunais, grenades, etc.) is mostly irrelevant. Realistically speaking, the only weapons you need to remember bringing in are the sonic and smoke grenades, and needles. The rest is either combat-oriented (and again - the first game was all about stealth. Why ignore that fact in this game?), or just there to collect dust-and while on the topic of the shop. The essences you randomly get have such little impact on the game, you might as well remove them. Hell, some just straight up make you weaker-you are forced to dash at the beginning of every sprint, which is a damn big problem if you don't have a specific skill unlocked. One dash and you're 30% depleted on your stamina. Now take in account that shadow leaps and mid-air dashes all consume a hefty chunk of stamina, and you'll quickly realise how slow the game isin the first half-the parkour is SUPER buggy, especially on later levels. Last few hours of my play time consisted of my enemies fazing through walls, me fazing through walls, or bodies I had thrown fazing through walls. And if you're not fazing, then the simple movement mechanics like dash jumping causing you to grab onto the ledge instead of simply flying over (or the much more common 'forced into a cover lean instead of just walking around the corner), will irritate you throughout the whole game. Some objects also can't be teleported to/climbed on top of/jumped over because of their T H I C C collision boxes-speaking of the environment - most of the maps are very lackluster in their design. For such an expensive game I was expecting a damn golden gem, not... whatever we got. Seriously, the forest map should not exist, nor should the very big city-the first game was all about sticking to the shadows and night time raids, this game is all about broad daylight assassinations and enemies ignoring the menacing shadow figure right above their heads. Why the hell was such a massive and illogical change necessary?-the standard enemy class (the one that is littered everywhere) is laughably deaf and/or blind, so that's pretty lame. On the other hand, however, you have the resurrected undead enemies! Undead will hear and spot you from much further off, and the ninja class basically has wall hacks. Too bad their pathfinding is the worst in the entire game-now, I'm not saying the story of the first game was some god-sent blessing from the heaven's - beautiful, poetic, engaging, yadi yada - but this basically doesn't have a story. It's all told you line dialogue you WILL skip through, the occasional cutscene is somehow worse quality than the first (just my opinion. you can have yours, while I have mine), and the general progression of the missions is just "Huh?"-the last mission. Not just some nitty gritty detail, but I mean the mission as a whole. The map is somewhat poorly designed and buggy, the AI bugs out and doesn't move when resurrected, the fight cutscene was so horrible in more ways than one, and just that the 'fight' itself feels frustrating or boring-hidden achievements. Yep, this game has 'em. And that's not a bad thing in of itself, more so that EVERY achievement but the "Complete chapter X" is hidden. Quite annoyingOverall, terrible game for such a steep price tag. Linceworks, ya'll made an amazing first game, then butchered this game so hard, the studio shut down. Rip
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game does not hold up to the original by any means. I stopped playing the game for a year or so after launch because NPCs would glitch through walls when alerted and instantly detect me. When I came back, the same issue occurred. They also added "classic mode" which I though would've brought back the old controls of Aragami 1, but somehow it seemed even worse than the normal controls. The first Aragami was such a solid and fun game. I don't know what happened with this title but it seems hardly solid and questionably fun. Definitely a big let down. The customization is really cool though so I guess it has that going for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: I love ninjas and stealth games so my opinion's biased but this is one of the best games I've played in a long time. You know the way Sekiro was a souls-like with some stealth mechanics? This is the converse - a stealth game with souls-like combat. Nice, fluid movement system, fun combat and the familiar satisfying stealth kills. The stylised visuals whilst hardly 'next generation' are still very cool, too.I'm not too bothered by the relatively simplistic enemy AI myself. Any game which hasn't been developed with a AAA budget has to compromise somewhere. Buy it, and hopefully they'll do another sequel which'll be the Witcher 3 of ninja stealth games.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: I can definitely say it's a fair bit weaker compared to the first installment as far as single player is concerned.You can no longer teleport to any shadow. The Shadow Dash system has been reworked into something akin to Sekiro, where there are some specific ledges you can grapple onto. It's not bad, it's just much more restrictive compared to the original. No idea why they tried fixing what worked perfectly already. The enemy AI has not been improved at all. No peripheral vision, simple patrol paths.I think the main draw of this game is being able to play with friends and have fun together.The soundtrack and the environmental visuals are definitely great, no complaints here.The game lacks the polish of the original, particularly in the animation and responsiveness departments, but I'm sure it would be a really fun co-op experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: THIS GAME IS PERFECT!I enjoyed the concept of Aragami1 but Aragami2 is everything I wanted in a game such as this. Coming from a background of dark stealth games: Tenchu, Dishonored, Shinobido, Sekiro; Aragami2 is now a solid part of this severely underrepresented theme.Pros: Fluid combat, movement and stealth systems. The shadow dashing feels very natural and weighty, and comes across as a well implemented blink/ grapplehook mechanic you'd find in Dishonored or Sekiro.The stealth kills have a decent variation to them depending on how you approach it. You don't have to kill but I'd rather.The ranking system feels fair and has good variation based on how you prefer to play.Level design: there are multiple ways in which you can approach the mission, there's a lot of freedom in this game. It feels really good.Sound design is nice, it glides well with the locations and dynamic moments so it all comes together as naturally as a film would.Combat: Some people say it's clunky but I'd argue that it's on par with Sekiro in terms of fun and flexibility. So far, after playing a few missions and entering into combat a few times the parry system feels great. Just time your block right and knock them off balance until their stamina is depleted so you can perform a fatality (or finishing blow).cons:Optimisation. Somehow despite the low res textures there's still some chunkyness happening on my pretty high end system. It's ok though it doesn't detract from the game itself so much.Bugs: Don't carry a body and then attempt to vault a fence.Limbs: Enemy limbs seem to stay intact :(Blood: Needs more ridiculous blood spray, the spatter itself is fine, there's so much of it and it's hilarious. Much like Tenchu 1 really. It's amusing and feels good :)
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the first one, it wasn't perfect but the story and the mechanics were working nicely. I played both with a friend. When we started the game, we noticed a few collision bugs and enemy seeing us while being at cover for no reasons but we continued to play in stealth as much as possible up to a point when it was just so annoying that we started rushing the game (after mission 40) to finish it and get rid of it.List of negative aspects we have encountered:- bugs of collision (could be a classic in a lot of games),- being seen by enemies while being undercover,- enemies almost always one shooting in hard mode,- repetitive levels with just different collectibles get old very quick,- the story is just flat in comparison of the first game,- dying for no reasons while passing through the environment (I mean seriously ??),- trying to teleport enemies, ending teleported to the enemy place instead...I could go on for long, have they really tested the game ??It's clearly bad for this price. We tried to like it as we did for the first but the game didn't want us to do so.If you don't mind bugs of this extent go for it but I clearly think that it's not worth it, I can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Better than the first one, but still janky - clunky and buggy.I quit first Aragami when stepping into water killed the shadow ninja and failed the mission.I quit Aragami 2 when at end of a mission, dropping from height turned out to be a "defeat".After decades of Assassin's Creed and Dishonored games to learn from, this was...sad.But mostly it was other bugs, poor performance and general jankiness.A shame the company dissolved, they seemed on the right track to make Aragami a worthy evolution of the idea.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably an unpopular opinion for the fans of the first game, but I very much enjoyed the change of pace in this sequel. The movement feels more natural, quick and fluid, and the new mechanics and powers are very satisfying to use. The AI has improved a bit as well, although still pretty dumb, but that doesn't ruin the experience at all. The story has been decent so far, but I might update this review once I get to the end of the game. If you're looking for something like the original game, this is  it. In the first game, stealth was absolute key in order to complete the levels, but in this one you have more freedom to create different playstyles. You can go full berserk (or "oni", if you will) and just engage in melee combat with every enemy you find (which I wouldn't recommend, but I'll get back to this later), be a pacifist and not kill any enemies, be an agile ghost that can complete the level without even touching a single enemy etc. The progression through the ability tree (where you can unlock new "shadow powers" and "passive abilities") is quite slow compared to the first game, since you level up slowly and only get  ability point per level up to spend on the ability tree, with every shadow power costing 2 points and every passive ability costing 1 point, but all of that is probably because Aragami 2 is much lengthier and the progression has to make up for that.The melee combat is just awful, with unresponsive controls, glitchy animations and just a general overload when facing more than one enemy at once, since the targetting system doesn't work like the industry standard and you have to press it too many times for it to target the enemy you want.The stealth system has seen a major upgrade from the original game, adding many new enjoyable possibilities. I don't really have anything to say about it, it's just great!This might be a bit biased since I already loved the art style and graphics from the first game, but the graphics have definitely improved a lot. The game looks beautiful! The lighting looks pretty and realistic, the shadows look great and work great for stealth gameplay. The textures and the visual effects look stunning as well.The animations during gameplay are fluid and satisfying to see. Although there are a few bugs here and there, they don't impact too much on the experience. I do have a major complaint about animations during non-cutscene dialogues, though: they look pretty bad, I think the developers could have polished the facial animations and such a lot more.Nothing extraordinary, but they bring you a nice and classic Japanese vibe. Generally enjoyable, with high quality audio.I don't regret preordering the game, since I've had a fun experience so far. I've seen people who refunded it due to it not being at all like the first Aragami, gameplay-wise, so bear that in mind before buying it if you're a fan of the original. For me, this game is a great choice if you're looking for something in the stealth genre, it certainly delivers that. If I had to give the game a score, it would be . Not excellent, not extraordinary, but a great, fun and enjoyable experience. Forgot to mention that, on launch, the game lacks rebindable keys, which is stupid, to say the least, since that should be industry standard by now. I forgive the developers, though, since they've taken notice to this issue and have announced a beta branch with this feature that's coming very soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: The last thing I want to do is compare Aragami 1 and 2 as they are both very different and very good in their own way. However from reading the other reviews people they seem to be quite disappointed.Things i liked:- While Aragami 1 was more shadow based, hopping from shadow to shadow, staying in darkness. Aragami 2 is more free in terms of you are able to teleport practically anywhere giving you more freedom and choices rather than deciding which shadow to choose which I think is a nice addition.- Movement is also very fluid. You can move so quickly at times and it just feels really smooth.- Great customization to make your Aragami truly yours.- Satisfying assassination animations.- RPG upgrade points, some really nice upgrades to help you battle through levels.- Story is well thought out. Very different from the prequel.What could be improved about the game:- Being able to change key binds- Minor Bugs like continuously rolling while carrying someone (Can be fixed with a quick Crouch) and falling through the map at times which doesn't matter since you get re spawned where you last touched the ground with 0 cost to score.- And not being able to pick up items if you move your camera too far in one direction ( keep looking at it until its gone)- AI could use a tweak as right now it feels like its on easy mode, pretty good for a casual play through although not a real challenge.- You can be dangling right above an enemy, having them practically kissing your toes and they wont know you are there.- While the movement is free, it also feels very restricted. You can only shadow leap to a ledge that you can dangle from. (Aragami 1 you were able to teleport with an arrow that indicated you will be placed at the top of the wall or ledge)I recommend - 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about the game but all of the negatives I feel come from my love of the first game and expecting this game to build off of that instead of completely ditching a lot of what I loved. However, I still recommend the game as it's still fun and scratches the itch from the first game.For some reason, Lince Works decided to ditch shadow creation and teleportation and have made shadows in general a non-mechanic. This is genuinely disappointing to me since that was a huge part of why the first game was as enjoyable as it was. That isn't to say the new movement isn't fun but it could be improved to feel as fluid as the first game.The combat is really nothing special. It's very basic and overall still best to evade it, like the first game. I don't know if this was intentional or not.The AI is still... something. It's not bad but it is predictable. One of the first upgrades you can get just straight up tells you the path the AI follows. This isn't a negative as it does help a lot with planning your attack and routes.I understand Lince Works is a small studio still and I appreciate what they've made. It's fun for me even if it shed a lot of what I enjoyed from the first game. At least those mechanics were placed with other fun abilities.Other than this, my gripes are small and pet peeves at most.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Aragami, you'll probably like this too. It feels quite similar to the original, but shaken up enough to be new. They managed to make a new story, with new gameplay elements while keeping the aspects of what made the original great. I definitely recommend it, especially if you have a couple friends to play with.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: For a sequel, this might as well be a standalone game. It deviates a lot from the original, but not in a bad way. The movement is much more quick compared to the more methodical and patient playstyle of the original. The only common link between the two games is the fact both games are about the aragami, but even then, the second game basically threw out all the established lore from the first game out the window. Gameplay is mostly smooth, there are a few bugs currently like vaulting over objects and going through walls/ceilings, other weird clipping, etc. but most of- if not all- of these bugs will hopefully be fixed eventually. Theres also some areas where you cant climb up a ledge even though you should be able to, but there are very few of those kinds of areas, so I dont even remember where they are honestly. Biggest change between the original is the replacement of essence with stamina, and not being able to teleport between shadows, but most skills from the original have pretty much returned, aside from shinen (or maybe theres a bomb-like item unlocked later in the game, idk yet) and banmoku. Other skills like kurosuna and the kunai have become items instead, with limited uses per level but no cooldown, meanwhile the shadow creature kill has become an ability that is on cooldown instead of being a second, riskier kill option like in the first game. Good change imo, as the shadow kill was very low-risk most of the time because of the patrol routes of the guards. However, the new alternative 'kill' option is to knock the enemy out. I'm assuming the intention is if you choose to play pacifist, but knocking an enemy out is basically the same as killing, so thats boring and makes going pacifist feel the same as playing the game normally but pressing E to knock the enemy out instead of Lclick to kill.Only interesting use for knocking an enemy out as opposed to killing is to counter priests. They detect if an enemy that they're connected to is killed, but not if theyre knocked out. I'd say thats an interesting and smart use, but the priests are usually placed somewhere where they're alone, or only one enemy is patrolling, so they dont have the chance to send a guard nearby towards the enemy you just killed, and they themselves can't leave their post. Im hoping a mobile version of the priest with a sword will be introduced later in the game that'll track you down, but I've no clue.The game is unnecessarily long though. There are 14(?) or so maps which are very large, but you return to these maps over and over again for new objectives and missions, with enemies having new patrol routes. Due to the map's large size though, you're restricted to specific parts of the map, so its not as repetitive as you'd think, but its still fairly tedious at times. I would complain more but the movement and combat is pretty satisfying and solid, that its not a complete chore to do the levels.Finally, the animations are a bit janky at times, like, the aragami stabbing and the guard reacting sometimes dont sync up, usually the guard lags behind after the aragami stabs him, and also Lady Miyoshi's hair. The hair at the front of her head clips into her face, especially during the cutscene you meet her, because that just makes her look goofy as ♥♥♥♥, but then on the other hand, the hair on the back of her head is stiff and doesnt have the same flowing physics as the hair on the front of her face. Her whole model looks stupid, but luckily I barely have to see her so thats good. Overall great game 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 is a great stealth game, however I would strongly recommend playing it on classic mode only as the shadow mechanics are much more like the first game and make for a much better stealth experience. The story is pretty uncompelling and there's a lot of recycled areas, granted with enough changes in each that you'll need to rethink your strategy a bit. The biggest problem with Aragami 2 though is that too many resources were invested into the combat when the game really doesn't need it. The first Aragami feels like more of a pure stealth experience, but the added mobility, more reliable shadow leaping to ledges, a better range of tools and abilities, and being able to move bodies are all very welcome changes in Aragami 2. My hope is that the developers will combine the best stealth elements of the first two games and bring them into Aragami 3.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not nearly done with the game, but at this rate, I'm excited to delve further into it. Don't let the mixed reviews scare you off, this is still a lovely game. The main critique that I (and many others) have is that this second game loses some of its "Light against Shadow" concept by making it more similar to a normal ninja game, but personally, I don't mind it much. The story is still interesting, it still goes into a theme of a supernatural ninja, and you are still being rewarded for playing stealthy over becoming a blood-lusting killer. The stealthier you play, the higher your Rank (S being the highest for a level), so the easier you will unlock abilities. For me, the game still holds the charm of feeling like "the big bad boogeyman that strikes from the dark" that the first one had, but improves on it even more by giving your Aragami a chance of combat when being spotted. You aren't simply struck down anymore, you can fight back against a small enemy group, and the ability to use items you can unlock through collectibles for your own benefit is quite enjoyable too. And the amount of customization possible makes your character truly "yours", unlike the first game, where there was only about 4 clothes, here you have many more outfits to unlock, mix and use for yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: It's fun, but it's not an Aragami sequel.One of the few times where being a sequel does the game no favor. For anyone who's played the Sly Cooper series, think of Aragami 2 as the difference between Sly 1 and Sly 2. However, unlike Sly, wherein the 2nd game largely built upon the first in all aspects, including the stealth mechanics, while drastically overhauling many of the core systems of the first game, Aragami 2 does not. If anything, it goes backwards in stealth while giving the player more direct combat capabilities. While it's a fun game, save for a few bugs, it is definitely not an Aragami sequel and your expectations going in should be as such. If the first Argami game was a stealth game, Aragami 2 feels more like an Action-RPG with better than average stealth mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: I had already played the first one when i played this. I think this one is imo slightly better than the first one. The shadow abilities are better than the first game. This one doesn't rely as much on stealth but its still a lot of fun. The classic mode also is great for people who liked the stuff in the first game. Shame that the studio closed they put a lot of work into this.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun game to play cooperatively, I essentially 100% completed the game collecting all the achievements and collectibles. While very fun, the game is extremely buggy. I encountered a number of game breaking bugs which forced me to retry a level. Like the final boss being frozen and uninteractible after assassinating him. Or literally being unable to purchase certain collectibles from the store even though I unlocked it because it wouldn't show up in the shop.I originally was concerned about the controls and playstyle being radically different from the 1st, but playing through the entire game in classic mode I felt it was quite comfortable minus the initial shock of not being able to create shadows.I recommend it but be warned this game is incredibly buggy.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Very good! I get that some don't like the shadow mechanics being changed, but this game is pure Aragami but better in virtually every way, imo. Still only just shy of 4 hours in, but the missions I have done have been completed using stealth, even a ghost rating on the third one, so the game has not been made an action rpg as one review said. Only gripe I have is that there is a little delay between an assassination and the prompt to carry the body to cover, leaving you very vulnerable for too long. Performance is great, no bugs so far and the music and graphics are fantastic. Waiting on this one for a while and it was worth the wait...solid purchase for me!
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: A good game with mixed execution, and one I highly recommend doing with a friend or two. Otherwise... Eh?I played Aragami 1, and I like their straight forward approach to stealth. Unfortunately, this doesn't scale very well with their enemy types. The AI and enemies are, to be frank, too dumb. This sequel also provided an option for open combat, letting you get into a sword fight with the enemies. Doing so is dumb though. The combat system is too simplified for any kind of depth, it gets quite bad with 2 or more enemies, and it straight up fails in multiplayer. But variety is the spice of life. If you want to go combat, perhaps different and better weapons might help? Stronger metal armor to weather blows and really get into the thick of it? NOPE. Everything is cosmetic, and thus pretty pointless. Colors are there, but you are hanging out in the dark most of the time, so they are pretty meh.I mean, seriously, the CONFLAGRATION BLADE doesn't IGNITE. I'VE KILLED ENEMIES WITH FLAMING SWORDS, WHY ISNT MY SWORD FLAMING?! Overall, recommended with friends. Otherwise, don't.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: You can clearly tell that Aragami 2 tried to improve the formula of Aragami, but lost itself in the process.Animations are less stiff (mostly) and character has much more mobility with dashes, jumps and double jumps. Also, hand-to-hand combat is also an option if an enemy spots and detects you. You can even survive 1v2 with correctly executed parry and blocks. All skills have their own separate cooldowns, which enables some good combos if you get to use them in quick succession. But this alone didn't bring the game and series to another level. Storytelling is worse than it was in Aragami. And even in the first game it was sub-par at best. You do missions, talk with the same several characters between the missions and that's it. Chapters end abruptly. Rinse and repeat.There are a lot of missions in this game. Like 51 or so. After 10 or so the game becomes excruciatingly repetitive and boring. Most missions have very simple objectives like - collect 3 things of something. Talk to an NPC and find him an item or two. Or just bring an unconscious npc to the map portal. All these objectives get very repetitive the longer you play. There are 10 areas in this game and some missions take place in the same area 4 or 5 times. replaying the same areas just with a bit different objectives and a bit different enemy placement is far from being fun. At first I tried to kill all/most enemies, but I soon realized that I'm just wasting my time and I began to speedrun the objectives and sneak around most enemies. This way I could finish levels in 10-15 minutes instead of 30-40.Skill progression is slow and skill unlocking is way to grindy. In the first game you could unlock most/best skills early on if you were collecting (not so) hidden scrolls. While in this one you have to play for a very long time just to get to more interesting and powerful skills.. If you aren't playing on the hard difficulty - you'll unlock more powerful skills way after the mid-game (you get like half a level from a mission completion if you play on normal difficulty). Which is a shame in my opinion. This is probably the biggest reason why this game gets so repetitive only after a few hours.There are a lot of bugs too. If you carry a corpse and try to put it somewhere in the corner - you get teleported into an open area where like 4 enemies can see you (insta-death). Sometimes your character can sink through terrain into the void. There are a lot of animation bugs too.Aragami 2 should have had much better and more interesting objectives, more interesting enemies and better skills progression. Sadly, I can't recommend it.

My honest opinion, it's a nice and steady pace that I enjoy, and you may enjoy it also. Lince Works has made another amazing game if you ask me. I can't wait to see what they make next!I'm so glad to have this game now!! I've been waiting for this since I got 100% on the first one. As soon as I saw this I had to pre-ordered this and eagerly wait for it to be available, like a kid on Christmas. But, all the giddiness aside, I love this series. And this game is so great! The soundtrack is absolutely amazing and beautiful. Pretty sure I've listened to it more than I have played the game right now.
