_childDocuments_.review: After having played the game for a bit (3 hours as of writing), I'd say it's a decent game.Some reason, the graphics seemed a little much for my graphics card (AMD 6900XT) which was confusing for me because triple-A title games are rather smooth. It seemed to be loading a lot of assets that weren't even on screen when looking around. At least that's my assumption as when I pointed the camera straight down, my frames would shoot back up to 100+ and remain constant. Might be a mis-configuration on my part though, always a possibility. Speaking of graphics configuration, this game doesn't really give all that much granularity in graphics configuration. Not that it's really a bad thing (some games have way too many options, causing most players to just ignore the graphics section entirely), but I wasn't able to tweak the game to run  smooth enough for my liking without going into my driver settings. Again, might just be my setup. Must have been my configuration as the next day, I played for a bit longer and haven't noticed the inconsistency. Please disregard the above paragraph!The story, from what I've played so far, seemed a bit "meh". The first game got me pulled in within the first few minutes, especially with giving enough mystery to be interesting but not too much that I have more questions than answers. This one, on the other hand, seemed to take more of the idea of "Okay, so we got this really cool ninja guy, but he finds a community and helps them out a lot." While it fits in many sorts of games (i.e. Assassin's Creed III, Black Flag, etc.), I just don't feel like it fits in an Aragami game, especially considering the first game where the player is a lone wolf, and the game is designed around that entire idea. Just didn't sit right with me; but again, just my opinion here.Okay, this is just me nit-picking, but I feel my immersion instantly broken when I see characters moving around unnaturally. Walking up stairs in a linear path (feet not connecting on the steps) as well as motions not matching up with solid objects (hands moving through sword hilts and other various items hanging off the body), they just kinda take the magic out of the game a bit for me.Okay, so the first Aragami game I absolutely loved because of its rather unique mechanics of jumping between shadows and refilling energy with the darkness. And with the story behind the protagonist's power (revealed at the end of the game -- no spoilers) went and provided a rather interesting twist. On top of this, the game itself was a rather unforgiving; it was a challenging stealth game that had a  emphasis on stealth over everything else.This one, however, seems to focus a little more on mobility, aggression, and combat with an underlying idea of stealth in the background. Of course, I'm not far enough into the game (yet) to figure out where the shadow powers come from, but I already feel like it's just gone in the wrong direction by having a whole community of shadow people -- I guess this goes back to the story section a little, but having these shadow people be lone wolves is really what  these characters feel a lot more real and brings a whole lot more life to the story.Either way, I feel like the game itself has lost quite a bit of its glamour when it comes to actual mechanics, as it feels a lot more like something you'd find in Assassin's Creed, but slightly clunkier, less refined mechanics (as compared to, say, Odyssey -- not to say Odyssey was had clunkiness either, just relatively  jank from what I've experienced).As for the ledge-teleporting, I wouldn't mind it so much if I could explicitly select which ledge I want to jump to. Having the game auto-select which ledge I was able to jump to got me caught more times than I'd light to admit, which was especially frustrating when I was going for a zero-kill, pure stealth run. And it wouldn't have been all that frustrating if during those runs, there were checkpoints. I couldn't tell you how many times I replayed a single level just to  on the zero-kill run and go on a total-annihilation run (which, by the way, was much more successful in the end) because I got so frustrated at the pacifist methods I'd take, just to be caught by something so small and have to restart. All this to say: .I haven't tested the multiplayer aspect of this game as I don't have any friends who are into stealth games and I don't really like playing in public lobbies either. Not sure how it all works, but I'm sure that if there were issues, the devs probably fixed it / are working on patches for it.This was mentioned a bit here and there in other reviews, but I just wanted to also mention it myself. The lighting in this game is  to get right as it helps set the entire tone of the game. The first Aragami game was set at night time throughout the entire thing (I believe the entire game was supposed to take place in one night). Sure, it got a little boring, seeing the same old tones of "Oh, this is moonlight! Oh this is shaded moonlight! Oh, this is a fire, this is a light..." etc. However, that inherently brought a more somber, serious tone to the game and added to the ambiance immensely. Aragami 2, however, seems to bring a lot more orange, yellow, and green tones throughout the game. Sure, it makes things a little easier on the eyes for the player, but at the same time, it seems just way too bright to put the player in a place where a literal shadow demon spirit ninja thing is slicing up soldiers right after a five PM supper. Doesn't make too much sense to me, and I noticed that I wasn't really as immersed into the game, the mechanics, and everything -- thus taking me out of the story and not really enjoying the game as much as I did the first one. That being said, the music itself was really good, I absolutely enjoyed listening to it as I was creeping around rooms and open spaces.Oh, that's another thing. The mechanics that were in the first game allowed you to create shadows and teleport to them as a means to kind-of hop, skip, and jump between one place to another. This game doesn't. It not only made me feel like the area was bigger, but also made me feel like most of the ground was just lava, and that I can't walk anywhere.Just to reiterate, I don't think this is a  game. I actually think it's a rather decent game by itself, if it were separated from the Aragami name entirely. Keep the character, Kuzai looks cool asf. Also, keep the music, I absolutely love the tone it sets. But the game, honestly, doesn't feel like it should be called Aragami, especially if it needs to live up to the legacy of the first game.I put a thumbs down on this review only because there's no three-star option. I cannot really recommend this game over the first one for people who were looking for a similar stealth experience that the first one provided. However, if you're a fan of Warframe, Assassin's Creed, and maybe heard of the first Aragami game (or played it and thought it was too challenging), I'd say this is a rather decent game. It's not as challenging, but it definitely is demanding... and it's just about as frustrating as Ghostrunner, except it's slower-paced (depending on your style) and more tactical.I like the game and see myself playing it fully through -- at the very least to get my money's worth. However, if there's going to be an Aragami 3 that's just more of this, I think I'll pass.Thanks for reading, hope this review helped in some way.

_childDocuments_.review: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice is a 2019 action-adventure game developed by FromSoftware. It was released in Japan by FromSoftware and internationally by Activision for the PlayStation 4, Windows and Xbox One in March 2019 and for Stadia in October 2020.Sekiro follows a shinobi known as Wolf, who attempts to take revenge on a samurai clan that imprisoned him and kidnapped his lord. The gameplay is focused on stealth, exploration, and combat, with a particular emphasis on boss battles. It takes place in a fictionalized Japan during the Sengoku period and makes strong references to Buddhist mythology and philosophy. Lead director Hidetaka Miyazaki wanted to create a new intellectual property (IP) that marked a departure from their Dark Souls series, looking at games such as Tenchu for inspiration.Sekiro received acclaim from critics, who praised its gameplay and setting and compared it favorably to FromSoftware's past work, although opinions on its difficulty were mixed. It won several year-end awards, including the Game Award for Game of the Year, and has sold over ten million units as of September 2023.During the late Sengoku period, the Ashina clan, led by Kensei Isshin Ashina, seizes a land rich in divine favor, including a foreign deity dubbed the Divine Dragon which can grant immortality through a bloodline dubbed the "Dragon's Heritage" and through the Rejuvenating waters and its mukade-infested Sediment. During this time, a nameless orphan is adopted by the wandering shinobi Owl, who names the boy "Wolf" and trains him in his ways. As Wolf grows up, Owl entrusts him with safeguarding the young lord Kuro, the last of the Dragon's Heritage line.Two decades later, the now-elderly Isshin is on his deathbed and the weakened Ashina is besieged by the forces of the Interior Ministry to finish the unification of Japan. Desperate to save his clan, Isshin's adoptive grandson, Genichiro, seeks Kuro to use his blood to create an immortal army. Disagreeing with his grandson's methods, Isshin has his private physician, Emma, warn Wolf so the two can flee. However, Genichiro confronts them and defeats Wolf in a duel, severing his left arm and capturing Kuro. Wolf is saved by a man called the Sculptor, who gifts him a prosthetic arm. To rescue Kuro, Wolf assaults Ashina Castle, where he meets Isshin and is given a new name: "Sekiro". Optionally, Sekiro can revisit his past; three years ago, Kuro's home was raided by bandits led by the shinobi Lady Butterfly, leading to Owl's apparent death. While Sekiro defeated Lady Butterfly, he was fatally stabbed by an unknown assailant and only survived after Kuro shared his blood with him.Sekiro again duels Genichiro and defeats him this time. However, he survives due to having used the Sediment to gain corrupted immortality and escapes. Afterward, Kuro refuses to flee and instead wants Sekiro to perform the Immortal Severance ritual on him, which would result in his death and eliminate the Dragon's Heritage. Sekiro reluctantly agrees and sets out to collect the necessary materials for the ritual, including a weapon that can kill immortals known as the Mortal Blade from the Divine Child, the last survivor of experiments with the Rejuvenating Waters. After collecting most of the ritual elements, Sekiro is confronted by Owl, who faked his death in pursuit of the Dragon's Heritage and revealed to be the one who stabbed him three years ago. If Sekiro renounces his loyalty to Kuro on Owl's orders, he fights and kills first Emma and then Isshin while Owl kills Genichiro. However, Sekiro then becomes corrupted by bloodlust and kills Owl as well while Kuro watches in horror, leading to the "Shura" ending.If Sekiro refuses, he kills Owl in combat and enters the divine realm to recover the final ingredient for the ritual from the Divine Dragon itself. Upon returning to the mortal realm, Sekiro discovers that Isshin has passed away while Ashina is under attack by the Ministry. Fighting through the chaos, Sekiro eventually finds Kuro under attack by Genichiro, who has retrieved another Mortal Blade. Upon defeat, Genichiro sacrifices himself in a ritual that revives Isshin in his prime so he might restore Ashina, a wish that his grandfather attempts to honor despite disagreeing with it. After killing Isshin, depending on the items gathered, three endings are available:- In the "Immortal Severance" ending, Sekiro performs the ritual as instructed, killing Kuro and making himself mortal again. Afterward, like the Sculptor before him, Sekiro spends his remaining days carving Buddha statues while keeping his prosthetic to pass on to someone else one day.- In the "Purification" ending, Sekiro performs an alternate ritual worked out with Emma's aid which has Sekiro sacrificing himself while freeing Kuro of the Dragon's Heritage. Afterward, Kuro prays at Sekiro's grave with Emma before departing these lands.- In the "Return" ending, Sekiro collaborates with the Divine Child to make her a vessel for the Divine Dragon's power. After defeating Isshin, Sekiro takes the dying Kuro to the Divine Child, who absorbs him into herself. The Divine Child and Sekiro then leave on a journey to return the Dragon's Heritage to its home in the West.Development of Sekiro began in late 2015 following the completion of Bloodborne's downloadable content, The Old Hunters. It was directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, who had previously worked on the Dark Souls series and Bloodborne. Sekiro draws inspiration from the Tenchu series of stealth-action games developed by Acquire and published by FromSoftware. The team initially considered developing the game as a sequel to Tenchu; however, it quickly outgrew the concept. Miyazaki intended the combat changes to capture the feel of "swords clashing", with fighters trying to create an opening to deliver the fatal strike. He and the team also created the game to be an entirely single-player experience, as they believed multiplayer to have limitations they wanted to avoid. Despite the game taking place during the Sengoku period of real-world Japanese history, no historical people or locations are featured in the game.The game was revealed via a teaser trailer at the Game Awards 2017 in December, showing the tagline "Shadows Die Twice". The game's full title was revealed to be Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice during Microsoft's press conference at E3 2018. The game was published by Activision worldwide, with FromSoftware self-publishing it in Japan and Cube Game publishing in the Asia-Pacific region. Sekiro's soundtrack was composed by Yuka Kitamura, with some contributions from Noriyuki Asakura. The game was released for PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One on 22 March 2019. A collectors edition was also released the same day and included a steelbook case, a figurine of the protagonist, an art book, a physical map of the game's world, a download code for the soundtrack, and in-game coin replicas. A port for Stadia was released in late 2020. On 31 October 2020, a free update was released that added new content to the game, such as new cosmetics for Wolf and a boss rush game mode.The word "sekirō" (隻狼) is a contraction of "sekiwan no ōkami" (隻腕の狼), which translates as "one-armed wolf." The subtitle "Shadows Die Twice" was initially meant to be used as a slogan for the teaser trailer until Activision requested it be kept for the final name.

_childDocuments_.review: I have since completed the game and rewritten my entire review.The review assumes you've played through Aragami 1.There are extremely minor spoilers in the story and pacing section. They are not hidden.Aragami 2 is a step away from the mechanics of the first game, bringing it more in-line with traditional stealth games. While I myself was fine with the change, if you played Aragami 1 for it's 'Stay In The Shadows' gameplay mechanic, Aragami 2 has done away with it completely in favour of a more streamlined stamina bar that regenerates anywhere.Movement is probably the best change that Aragami 2 changed. Verticality is much more accessible, movement is fast and gets you from Point A to Point B. The Blink has been replaced with Shadow Leap which only works on ledges/specific jump-points instead of being able to be aimed directly. It works for the most part, occasionally sending you to a wrong point when there are multiple points tightly packed.EDIT: So the shadow leap seems pretty inspired by Sekiro's Shinobi Grapple [], I only found this out now since I recently bought Sekiro. The circle fills in depending on how close you are to the grapple point and when filled, can be leaped to. Level design is considerably different. Aragami 1 was linear; you would go from Point A to Point B in a streamlined fashion whilst occasionally looping around an area to do multiple objectives before proceeding []. Aragami 2 instead has a handful of much bigger maps that are sectioned off for specific missions, and can be played more open-endedly, approaching the objectives from any angle you choose. The maps are very well detailed and are a visual treat, not to mention just exploring them is fun. As there only a handful of maps, the game repeats them a few times. To that end, you actually have a hub world to reside in now, where you can upgrade your skills, items, change your colours, talk to citizens.....and that's kinda it. Not too much to do at the hub-world other than progress the plot or to buy things. Not to say it's useless, though. Just doesn't have too much to justify hanging out in it [].Multiplayer is clearly more risky than Singeplayer in terms of both bugs and gameplay. Multiplayer is where a lot more funky bugs show up, and not to mention desync issues. Gameplay wise, it's another person that can make a mistake during stealth. Though it's still lots of fun, and I don't regret any time spent just laughing at the bugs with friends in call.The graphics are a step up, but I'm conflicted about comparing it to Aragami 1. Aragami 1's graphics felt like they were designed with the art director in mind, and the characters blend nicely into the setting. Aragami 2's Aragami[s] can all look very out of place [], because it feels like the Aragami and the art direction don't mix well. While it isn't an issue, it's noticeable.Briefly touching on character customisation, a step foward, but a small step at the same time. Aragami 2 features customisation of the Aragami's Head, Chest, Legs and Sword, but firstly, are locked until rather late-game, and secondly require you to find the damn blueprint first. For what it is, though, the all look stunning, as impractical as some may be [] for the setting. Also, rather annoyingly, the Toggle Light feature from the first game is absent.Combat isn't 'Press Left Mouse' anymore! I mean, it still is, but now there's actual substance. In Aragami 1, when you were spotted, it was basically over; enemies would rush to you in droves, they'd parry your attack and then instantly kill you. Now, you have a proper healthbar and combat system, meaning even if the enemy/enemies attack you, you can still emerge victorious. You can now parry the enemy's attacks for a window, but in general the fights can last a while. It's still not incredibly well in your favour to go about rampaging enemies head-on, but now you actually stand a fighting chance.Difficulty is fine. Only problem is that enemies can't seem to look up or down and their AI bugs out sometimes. Note that enemies do indeed look up if they're already locked onto you. Run/Defend, choice is yours. Bugs are everywhere, but they are being fixed, with some minor exceptions here and there. It was horrible at launch, though! Have a lot of pictures- I digress. Bugs thankfully don't really affect the gameplay as much as it used to, but don't hold your breath.The big downside of this game is the pacing of content and story. There are a total of 51 missions in Aragami 2, and the issue is about 1/3 of those are repeated missions. The story takes forever to actually pick up and 'The Big Bad' is only revealed late-game. While the reveal being that late doesn't pose much of an issue, the real problem is that there's almost little to no buildup to it! With regards to content, there's a lot of cool ideas that also suffer from being more mid-late-game problems. The game teases a fair few concepts here and there, like unblockable attacks and specific mission parameters, but the latter is used so infrequently it almost feels like an afterthought. As a side note, the only mention of Aragami 1 I could find was in the legacy attire, though seeing as the game takes place 100 years after Aragami 1, it doesn't really bug me.Characters do really feel a bit shallow. I did find difficulty in being properly invested in the characters and story. Almost none of them are properly likeable and memorable. The voice acting can't be commented on because it's not  voice acting, just mumbles here and there that sound vaguely like Japanese. Some words are intelligible, but as it's all intentional, I can't fault it.Music and sound design? Absolutely stellar. The hub-world theme is great, and I admit that I have a few tracks saved on my phone for playing. The sounds are clear and identifiable; it lets you know when you've been spotted and plays a stinger whenever you kill/KO someone. The sword SFX is a tad serviceable, but it conveys what it needs to i.e sword go swing. I do really like this game and it's art. But the story is slow, some missions are genuinely tedious, and it could definitely use a bit more QoL improvements for certain things. I'll still recommend the game, but just be prepared for a little annoyance here and there. Game's fine enough.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a sequel to Aragami 1, look elsewhere.While Aragami 1 was all about shadows, the main movement-related shadow mechanics have been removed in Aragami 2: teleporting is limited to ledges only unless the player chooses the Classic difficulty. Neither teleporting to the ceiling/walls (shadow surfaces) nor creating shadows is possible.However, movement in general feels more "free" because sprint speed seems faster and the player can jump. There is also "Shadow Leap" which helps to cover long distances (with the included risk of being glitched underground).Aragami 2 offers hand-to-hand combat with parrying, but it feels very clumsy and buggy and is best avoided completely whenever possible (which is most of the game, outside of maybe 1-2 missions).I found the length of the game (51 missions) way too long and the gameplay repeating. Most missions include finding something or someone, and there are no markers until the player gets very close, so most of the time is spent wandering around and wondering where in the ♥♥♥♥ the objective.The story seems to happen in a completely different universe and I did not notice any references outside of there being a Legacy Armor set. I cannot compare the story to that of Aragami 1, because frankly, I don't remember ♥♥♥♥ about the first one - though the main (only) female character was better in the first game.There are also a few albeit frequent bugs where vaulting over an obstacle sometimes results in the player falling through the map. Teleporting (while running?) also sometimes teleports the player backward, out of bounds, with no way back to the mission area, forcing a restart.In summary, do not expect a sequel to Aragami 1 and just treat it as a standalone game. It is a bit long, somewhat buggy, and the combat sucks.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, the game can be a pretty fun and fast paced stealth sim but less than halfway through the missions all bleed together due to an underwhelming map pool and boringly repetitive troop placements. The story is bland, mostly because it only exists in the hub world and you don't really *feel* the impact your missions have.Most egregiously the game is a buggy mess. The amount of times I've had to restart a mission because I've gotten stuck inside the terrain, been seen because I clipped through an object or, my personal favorite, been unable to kill a quest target because they "died" but didn't die (don't take warp strike. If your kill is in any way interrupted it'll put whoever you targeted in permanent stasis. I'll admit that the cause of this bug is user error, but it shouldn't exist regardless)And honestly, I despise this game as a followup to Aragami because it feels absolutely nothing like the first game. Unique HUD that was on your character in the first game is completely gone, and so is the ability to teleport via shadows (sorta. Technically you can take it as an alternate game difficulty but it's a buggy mess since the game wasn't designed with shadows in mind)I genuinely want to love this game. It has a lot of heart, and it starts off strong but... The longer I play, the more I just want to play the first game again. It's sad.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely beautiful. I was a huge fan of the original Aragami, so i was very pleased to see updated movement and parkour added! _childDocuments_.review: I first heard about this game from a friend of mine who is super into stealth games in general, and I wasn't super interested until she mentioned there was multiplayer so I was like you know what? Let's give it a try, and boy was it worth it.This game deserves so much more attention, definitely one of the better stealth games out there. While the multiplayer can be buggy, it didn't take away from the experience in the slightest. However, I do have two problems with this game.#1: The abilities feel a bit unbalanced. For example; there is one ability you can get that pretty much allows you to roll directly in front of enemies and not be spotted (There is no cooldown for rolling, just stamina).#2: This game needs much more content. All in all this game would have taken about 6-10 hours if we were not going for 100% completion.That being said, this game is still very worth it and I fully recommend it to anyone looking for a solid stealth game.

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVE this game, it's scratching the same movement game itch that popped up after I played Ultrakill, and while it may not be as fast paced, the movement is freeing in comparison to a lot of games in the stealth game genre, and utilizing the movement it provides you with give *me* the same feeling of catharsis. I'm not sure however if I can recommend it at full price, at least unless you're almost certain this is up your alley. It's something that I feel like appeals to my very niche requirement for a movement based stealth game with medals/ranks tied to whether you either don't kill *anyone* or kill *everyone.* *I* find this very engaging, and I plan to play it far longer than the 12-13 hours I've played it so far, but I planned to pass it up for the $35 price tag and while *I* may feel like that's a decent pricepoint for what *I* can get out of it, I don't think it's worth it to the average gamer. Grab it on sale, it's absolutely worth it for like 15-25 bucks.

_childDocuments_.review: My feelings regarding this game are a little complicated. I beat the first game just a night before starting this one and really enjoyed it, the stealth gameplay of it and absolutely having to be sneaky really appealed to me, and as did the art and setting. This game is not that game, but that doesn't mean it's bad, just different. This game is closer in style to Assassin's Creed or Shadow of Mordor than Aragami or Tenchu. It is super fun, Aragami is tense and methodical, this game is fast and punchy. Where it does stumble and fail however is the repetition, there are 51 missions in the game, and only a small handful of maps. Worst of all many of those missions are the definition of filler and should have been optional, but missions that boil down to (find 6 sacks of food) are somehow a main quest, and are the majority of them. Listen, if you want fun stealth gameplay that awards being sneaky, a fast and great parkour/traversal system, great artstyle, and a lot of content and can handle some repetition this is a worthy investment as there is a lot of content, but towards the end of this game it did feel like a chore for me. In the end I would recommend it, but with those important caveats above.

I 100% recommend this game to anyone who are interested in ninja games and that goes for aragami 1 as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechanically and visually superior to the predecessor, but as with a sequel that is expected.I am not too good of a writer, so I wouldn't be able to tell if the story is any better or anything.But if you played Aragami 1, you'll likely enjoy Aragami 2 since it is everything you've come to know but recognizably superior. Plus, it is co-op. Who doesn't love a good co-op game? My favorite addition over the previous game is that there are guards that refuse to leave their posts, so you have to play AROUND them if you intend on sneaking everywhere. I like this game; I do, but this game is not fun enough to play 51 missions of; I am on 25 and barely able to finish because I am getting bored stiff. It makes me wonder, "Who wants to play for another 25 missions?" This is one of very few games that I have to muster the energy to open because there is no fun in playing it. Even with tranquilizer needles, sonic grenades, mesmerize, wraith, and dark flame, there are simply too many guards late into the game. It has gotten to a point that fighting them head-on is no longer desirable, and the joy that can be garnered from this game is not worth it and is hard to support. I began to realize the reason the game is designed like this is because it was meant to be played cooperatively, but if you desire some assistance, they essentially have to have beaten the game before because otherwise you are forced to play catch up. Honestly, with the shenanigans you get up to as an Aragami, it makes sense that whoever is in charge just said, "♥♥♥♥ it, put guards everywhere." Hard to recommend a game so painfully boring. I wanted to complete this game to give it a fair trial but maybe another time.

_childDocuments_.review: Steam really needs a neutral option for recommending games.  I played through this game co-op with a friend of mine and overall I would say we had a good time and the game was worth but, but my god I can't ignore the various bugs that just insisted on screwing up our experience.  As a stealth game it performs alright, nothing revolutionary but not bad.The main problems come from two big issues.  The first is the bugs that cause the game to just randomly not perform correctly, and i'm not even talking the desync between host / co-op partner.  Sometimes you use abilities and they just fail.  Throw your sword at a guy and teleport to him to execute him instantly? nah instead you just did an uncontrollable regular swipe and now he and everyone in range sees you and is pissed.  Trying to distract a guard with your whisper ability? sometimes it just goes on cooldown and nothing else.  Turn invisible to get in close to a guy and give him the stabbing? Invisibility just decides it isn't working today.   The fact that the skills can so regularly break is frustrating at best, and actively killed our play some nights simply because we got too fed up with a given stage.  Then there are the items.  You gather a pitiful flow of money through the game which can be used primarily on cosmetics and dyes for your outfit, but also for modifiers runes and consumable equipments (throwing knives, damage amps, healing items)  But they are all worthless.  The rune effects are lackluster at best.  Attack boosts when fully stacked won't give you a breakpoint to even kill an enemy one swing faster, and defense is pointless thanks to stun locking by some later mob.  The only rune effects that 'do' anything are essentially stamina recharge so you can run around more.  The consumable equipment is even worse, costing exorbitant prices per usage.  To kill an enemy at range requires a kunai, of which you can only hold 3, and they cost 200 gold per.  Problem is even at late game most stages are only worth around 600-800 gold.  So you can blow your payment for the mission to kill 3 people.  In stages with upwards of 60-70 enemies.  Or you can buy things like portals to warp back to town quicker at the end of the mission.  That will run you 900 gold to buy, keeping in mind you won't even make that much.  For this game to really earn a recommend, it desperately needs the bugs to be fixed, nearly 3 months on and this is just not acceptable.  Second, for the sake of the game just being at all satisfying or fun, the consumable items need a serious look at.  If I spent a boatload of money but the items were restocked every stage and I could screw around with em? sure that could be fun.  If the items were dirt cheap and using them was just a minor fee, I could accept it.  But the idea that you blow nearly 2 stages worth of funds to accomplish nothing? That is just a bad joke.  It's a shame really, I pushed a friend of mine to get this game because of how much I enjoyed the first Aragami and the fact that this game was so.... frustrating more often than fun is just really not a good feel for the game.  It wasn't out right offensively bad, so I wouldn't say folks who like stealth games should not get it, but if you aren't explicitly a fan of the style of game, I would never recommend this to most of my friends.

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor to the original Aragami. _childDocuments_.review: Keep in mind that I've played this game on xbox game pass. However, the game was removed today. I saw the 50% sale, and I picked the game up on steam. When I played the game pass version, I loved it. The game borrows HEAVILY from Assassin's Creed. But I don't see a problem with it. It's an indie company taking what they love about a certain game, and putting a fun spin on it in their own game. Every movement mechanic makes sense and I love just bouncing around in the hub world. Aragami 1 is a game that I love, but I believe that it's to slow to really make me feel like a badass. But Aragami 2 on the other hand, oh man. You just feel like a sneaky ninja taking down enemies while you shadow leap around the place. I also love the combat in this game, Aragami 1 didn't have a combat system and Assassin's Creed combat is just spamming mouse 1 until someone attacks you and you counter-attack to kill them instantly. Aragami 2 has a good combat system because it's really difficult to fight multiple enemies at once, but you will win most duels without a single hit. It doesn't overstay it's welcome but it feels so damn good to use.So, my verdict?The game is good. Would I pay 40$ for it? Not really. However, if this game is on sale, it belongs in your library. ESPECIALLY if you like stealth games and Assassin's Creed games.

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 is basically built on the concept of quantity before quality, it's a long game, yes, but you will feel like you've seen everything within the first 10 hours.Now how should I begin? Aragami 2 is definetly nothing close to Aragami 1. I preferred Aragami 1 in almost every aspect to be real with you. Aragami 2 throws away established lore of this universe, but is in its core still a stealth game. The aesthetic is still the same, but everything else has been changed, even though some things didn't have to be deleted. I think the story is far worse in this one, the combat is very clunky, the game is unpolished, rushed and too long.Aragami 1's unique design of putting the UI on the character is missing, its very cool looking stealth kills are mostly sped up or missing, but it doesn't feel as cool, because the Aragami just teleports its sword back into the sword holder thingy. They got rid of the teleporting and instead of encouraging active exploration you end up having a level system that you wont be able to finish 'til the end of the game. Cosmetics and color settings are nice tho.Aragami 2 is semi-open world, meaning that it isn't as linear as Aragami 1. Most parts of the map have multiple districts, which is why you won't be able to see them combined later. This semi-open world isn't memorable, most of the time you know where you are when you're in the level. Furthermore, this semi-open world comes with the flaw that they're forced to reuse the map again and again and again. The game is 51 missions long and at some point you dont see anything new. It's just supply mission after supply mission and I prefer Aragami 1's linear approach, each chapter had a different level with multiple parts to it.The worst parts of this semi-open world is the removal of checkpoints. You get 2 lives. Aragami 1 had checkpoints with no lives. There's a good chance that you try to finish a mission and then suddenly there's a boss, so you end up dying and have to redo the COMPLETE mission. This is terribly frustrating, especially when you consider that nowadays lives are considered old game design. How come Aragami 1 has a more modern approach than Aragami 2?The fighting system is a joke. I expected it. It's just parry a few times and then you get a few hits until the enemy dies. Now don't get me wrong, implementing a fighting system is a nice idea! Sadly, this fighting system only works against 1-2 enemies. You easily get overwhelmed and end up realizing that it isn't worth to fight in this game, it just drags everything down. Swinging your sword and instant kills are on the same button too, so if an enemy is suddenly out of reach you might end up attacking nothing and the enemy spots you. Enemy variety only gets fixed in the late game btw.The story basically ♥♥♥♥♥ on established facts and rules of the Aragami universe. The Nisshoku are mentioned once and never again. I don't think you need to make a direct continuation, but disregarding everything we know about Aragami and then mentioning a clan from Aragami 1 is confusing and makes no sense. The characters in this game are nothing more than just a bunch of 3D models with no soul. The game always mentions that a war is going on and that your characters are helping you, but everything happens off-screen. Rarely are they truly useful and not some words in a textbox. Out of 51 missions maybe 12 of them are story related, most of the time you just collect stuff, the leader says "good job" and the next supply mission starts. You never grow attached to the characters, even though the game tries to, but I can't remember most names. The villains showed up at the 15 hour mark, but never are they a real threat. I cant remember most names, everything seems so unnecessary. I cant grow attached to characters if there is a story mission every 4 hours. I don't feel like im a part of anything. I also want to mention that the 2 only characters who show their faces have no face animation. They talk without any movement and don't even express emotions. How can I take this seriously, especially after Aragami Nightfall that had the SAME problem? Are you just lazy, Lince?Aragami 2's biggest flaw (the quantity) is also noticable when it comes to abilities and items. You have 10 different items and 30 variations of them. You have around 20 abilities and 3/4 are passive abilities that automatically happen and are simple boosted stats. I never changed my approach because the game offers you only around 10 interesting items you might end up having fun with. Even Aragami 1 was better in terms of abilities, I dont want the game to do everything for me as I watch. Let me double kill and choose my target instead of automatically choosing one for me!The only thing I like about this game is the movement, it's way faster than Aragami 1 and doing parkour is fun if there wasn't a stamina mechanic.To sum it up:Aragami 2 is not even worthy to be called a proper Aragami game. I'd rather call Aragami: Nightfall "Aragami 2" than this mess.

_childDocuments_.review: While an improvement on Aragami, Aragami 2 doesn't make enough changes or upgrades to appreciably make it worth your time if you are a stealth fan. It pales in comparison to Shadows of Mordor in every way (animations, story, voice acting, breadth of combat options, open world, visual fidelity, not to mention nemesis system), and if fantasy/LOTR isn't your thing Sekiro is set in feudal Japan. Not to mention the HITMAN games all having a lot more options and just plain fun. Or we can talk the Metal Gear franchise roots, or old-school Thief if you want great gameplay and the graphics don't bother you. Even Styx and Deathloop have more charm than Aragami does out the gate, despite their flaws you can have quite a bit of fun with them. All-in-all, not mad, just disappointed and was really hoping the devs had stepped up their game. 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game  because I wanted to play a co op stealth game with my partner. I played the first game and thought the story was fairly interesting, but what I enjoy more is the setting and characters. Although it's an entirely different style of game play from Aragami 1, I have really enjoyed this game so far. It has its bugs and glitches, and some errors have lead to a bit of downtime, but the developer seems to be working on them as they get reported and they are doing their best. While it's not as complex as some of the AAA stealth games, it feels like a throwback to games like Tenchu and especially with a partner, there are plenty of ways to defeat enemies using a combination of the right timing and tools and sometimes just luck. Frankly, some of the things possible are just cool, and chaining kills together is really fun. The movement feels really fun too, especially at later levels when you regenerate stamina faster. Character customisation is pretty decent, and mixing and matching armour types and dyes can lead to some unique looks, even with only male bodies. The costumes have a lot of character and I especially enjoy the way things glow in the shadows. Let's hope they add some female armours and perhaps some more diverse locations in future updates and DLC. That would be all that's missing for me at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: UPD: The game added the second "gamemode" which made the game play much like the first one. It helped a ton and now it feels more playable and true to the original. Although the size of the location makes it much harder and unkillable enemies are still annoying, it is a massive improvement. Soma controlls still feel clunky though, but it might just be my inexperienceAfter spending 5 hours in the game, I had a certain negative impression, which you can read further. And, although the game itself is not bad, its main disadvantages, for me personally, outweigh the pros.Let's start with the pros. The graphics really got better, the game became more pleasant to watch. Having the ability to hang on ledges is just as nice. Different types of missions add variability to the game, which also pleasantly surprised. The system with the purchase of skins, that is, cosmetic equipment through in-game resources is pleasant, but not for me, although I see some advantages in it, for example, the selection of my own "look" in the game. Functional equipment (runes and consumable items) is new, and so far they look interesting, but there is also a big question about their use, which I will touch on below. The starting location is very nice and gives you the opportunity to just jump and practice the controls. Plus the interactivity with the NPC complements it. It's nice to see that the mission is given 2 chances, perhaps the biggest plus of the game at the moment, and the presence of HP allows you to make more mistakes. Having improved skills allows you to greatly customize the gameplay, which is also a big plus.As for the cons. The plot, so far, seemed weak to me compared to the main game, but this may change, so this can not be considered as a point. Where the main problems turned out to be is in controlls. For the first 5 hours of the game, Shift and Shadow Jump (f) are simply shortened compared to the first game. If in the first part the player had the opportunity to really jump across the entire map, on the edge of shadows, then in the second game you are limited to a short shift and ledges, windows, etc. (which takes away from the feeling of a shadow ninja. And although I didn't get to the later upgrades, I suspect that the ability to jump in the shadows of objects will not appear, and even if it does, the beginning of the game is very upsetting without it). In addition, bouncing off the wall sometimes does not work, or the controls are not intuitive. Often, hanging on the windows, instead of jumping away, I jumped inside the building. Later I realized how to "jump away" correctly, but it is extremely inconvenient on the keyboard and mouse. Stealth kills (executes), due to the fact that the combat system was added, were also cut off and now it is possible to kill from stealth only if there is a red circle around the target, which does not work on the principle of the proximity of the enemy to the character, but because of the camera angle (at least that was the impression)?? Murders from around the corner especially suffer from this problem, since the character sometimes just "peeled off" from the wall or could not "stick" to it, which was also very annoying. Bags of money were spawned in locations that could not be reached without being noticed, at least without some skills. The wheel of abilities and items are on the same button, which is why you often use the wrong thing (it would be better to either separate them, or give the opportunity to take only one type of items on a mission and record it on one button). And the items themselves seem very expensive to me (especially when they are used 90% by accident), although perhaps I have not gone far enough and the problem with the prices of items will be corrected. Also, some of the protrusions are simply not working, although they look like they are.In general, as I have already said, the game is not bad, but the control problems that I have encountered in the game at the moment are very frustrating. The most terrible moment was when I had to move the stunned target to the portal, I went down to the bottom of the map by accident and it turned out that I had to throw the target over a hole in the map (there was water there). Slightly wrong angle - my target fell into the water and the entire run (40 minutes without detection with all the murders) was reset)) After that, I closed the game and walked away from it for a few hours. In the stealth-action genre, controls are very important, and in this game it upset me a little, plus the "vibe" itself, the feeling of the game is very different from what I imagined and expected from the original Aragami. The main mechanics of the game were simply removed from the game. Therefore, as a fan of the first game and to the same people as me, who loved the first part and are thinking wether to buy it or not - I suggest you don't, you will probably be disappointed. Fans of the Assassins Creed series will like it more.

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 is a better looking but far-worse sequel to a truly classic stealth game marred by and bogged down in confusing design decisions. And that kinda sucks. I want to preface what I'm about to say by saying that  It was a wonderful stealth game. Playing through the campaign with my friend was great. The levels were wonderful puzzles where stealth was the key, the abilities were interesting and impactful, and the enemies felt powerful. Points where they are deserved, Aragami 2 improves on a lot of my complaints from the first game, and I'm still enjoying the experience. The game looks wonderful, has a lot more detailed environments and characters and reuses assets less often. The story is easier to follow where the first game could get a little tangled. And of course, the animations. Aragami 1 looked kinda awkward, but the animations filled their role. The Sequel has some excellent animation. And the added movement options feel wonderful to use. We even get true cover options and tall grass to hide in. But that's where it stops. We ran into issues from minute 1. As soon as my friend and I finished the tutorial, we tried and failed to connect, he had some issues between his network an the servers that prevented him from accessing the game. After an hour of him fumbling around while i jumped around the ninja village, we posted in the dev discord and gave up on it for the night until we could fix it. while he was trying to figure that out, I found a half dozen or so places where i could fall through the geometry of the world—one of which resulted in a soft lock. Another idiosyncrasy caused me to repeatedly vault over a rock until i released the sprint key at which point you'd fall into the water and respawn. I also found a way to get passed this boundary and while it's funny to run under water for a bit, the rest of the bugs in this game aren't as silly. Two days after, we were able to get it working. His network blocks any connection to Russia for reasons and disabling that allowed him to connect. Which is weird. What could possibly needed to route from Russia when we're US east? regardless, we get to play. Aragami 2 is just not as compelling as Aragami 1. A large part of this comes down to worse level desgin; the guard placement and paths feel a little too easy to work past, and there are seemingly a lot of paths that aren't really even guarded. This is exasperated by the fact that maps get reused, blocking off some areas and changing up guard locations depending on the mission. We played through the first level on normal and the second on classic and stuck with classic. The shadow system has been gutted and it's kinda sad. No longer are we phasing through gates and levels are often much brighter which messes with the mood. Light is no longer dangerous, so that's one less tool in the level designer's toolbox. The other major issue is the combat.Honestly, I think the default left mouse sums up the change from 1 that I think could have ruined the game for me In Aragami 1, the left mouse button lets you create shadow the targeted location that could be used to hide in, teleport to, or use for abilities. In Aragami 2, the left mouse button is the attack button. This difference colors the entire game.If you didn't play one. Every single guard could 1 hit you at range by throwing a fast-moving blade of light from their sword at you. It honestly feels like they tracked you longer and farther in that game as well. They were . It was very much a stay hidden or die game, which made you feel like a badass every time you got the stealth kill. Even bosses which required multiple hits were still about finding your way in to hit them from stealth and then getting away again. Essentially, there wasn't combat. In 2, you can just fight them if you like. Thankfully it's not as obnoxious as assassin's creed's "parry, kill, repeat" style of combat. facing your enemy head on is still not good plan, but getting discovered is basically a non factor. You can mostly just run away because most of them have to hit you with their sword, while a handful use fireballs that are less accurate and slower moving than . The only times I was really in danger were if the guard i whispered decided to hop the wall i was hiding behind instead of walking around it or i accidentally got the attention of the sorcerers and the fireball hit me threw it and this completely robbed the tense feeling that 1 did so well. Another big difference is how the abilities are limited. Aragami 1 used a charge system while 2 uses a recharge timer. If you have ever played a game focused around stealth and tense slow movement, you know which makes more sense.If you play on classic, it's closer to what 1 was, but the guards are still easy to just run away from even if they do usually one hit you (I survived managed to survive a direct hit fireball with a sliver of health for some reason during one mission). That said, playing this mode doesn't bring back the full mechanics from 1, and I miss shadow summoning.The thing that actually ruined the game for me was a bug. I actually didn't see any of the weird boundary or fall through bugs in the levels, which was nice. This bug we—well, at least  ran into came after unlocking a second action through items or active skills. only I, being the second player, ran into this bug, but it ruins a large portion of the game. If i had multiple powers and items—which is available as early as level 2 or maybe 3—I could only use one of them. I'm still not totally sure on the effect. i noticed it first after unlocking the blacksmith and single use items. I discovered I could only use the vitality potion and could no longer access whisper, the first power. I also had the shuriken that I couldn't use. I originally thought it might have just been an item bug and ignored it because the items ended up being pretty unnecessary anyways. I used a single potion after accidentally falling off a high point. But unlocking the invisibility made it clear when i tried to whisper and turned invisible. To clarify, I could still select the other abilities, but attempting to activate them changed my power to whichever one was taking precedence and using that instead if applicable, so i could only have access to 1 ability.All The Small Things

_childDocuments_.review: Look, it's a 6/10; if you can live with the incredibly infuriating game-breaking bugs there's fun to be had. If they repair the serious issues, it'll be an 8-9/10. The game isn't complex enough to have a lot of moving parts so the things that have gone wrong are seriously fundamental to what you're doing.The game has a ton of glitches and bugs that are incredibly punishing in the stealth/never-get-caught genre. It's about 80-90% of the way to a polished, finished game, and if they fix the single most imporant bug (I'm not holding my breath; seems to be a fundamental part of the game) it'll actually be fun. How they took a step back from Aragami 1 (or even 1990s Playstation 1 games it's based on) I can't understand.The good: Animations are a little better. Leaping around into shadows and ledges like a ninja is still tons of fun. Multiplayer assassins is great fun. Skill progression is more dynamic and integrated into playing the game.The bad: Hoo boy.1, When you sneak up behind an enemy or near enough to one on a ledge, *most* of the time you get an instant stealth kill reticle which lets you execute your enemy. Some enemies just wont trigger, in which case they'll see you and set off an alarm (or stab you in the head *and* set off an alarm). This is essentially game-breaking as no matter how well you play, probably 1-3 times per mission enemies just wont die instantly no matter how well you play. As this is ***THE FUNDAMENTAL MECHANIC UPON WHICH THE ENTIRE GAME IS BUILT***, screwing this one up is unforgivable. Examples: you're hanging off a ledge, you lure an enemy over, you can't kill him and he alerts. You're hiding by a wall, an enemy walks by, the reticle doesn't trigger, and you wildly slash your sword initiating combat. Etc.2. Hidden bodies of enemies will sometimes just be visible through walls or grass to patrolling guards. Enemy alert AI seems buggy in this way. Congrats, you just went down a rank because some enemy saw his dead bro through 200 feet of cliff face.3. Some enemies that are meant to be lured by your essential/core skill "Whisper" wont respond to it. Guards of a certain type aren't supposed to respond to it, but patrolling guards are meant to and some are just missing the code to react correctly.4. Carrying a body and triggering the "leap over barrier" animation triggers an infinite, wall-breaking airborn floating glitch that is hard to break out of and often means a forced level reset. I'm terrified of low walls because of this. I have seen the void (and once rolled through an entire castle only to land in a pack of very angry fire guards).5. There is, for exactly no reason, a multi-second delay between murdering an enemy and picking the enemy's body up. After you kill an enemy the "E" prompt pops up to pick it up... you then have to wait about 1.5-2.5 seconds before hitting "E" does anything. Badly coded, quality-of-life issue.6. Stealth range (vision cones, sound range) is never well explained.7. Fall damage. What. In a ninja platformer there's fall damage for some reason.The reason I'm not confident these issues will be resolved is that they seem really close to the essential, root coding of the game and I doubt there are easy fixes here. In a genre where you're generally going for a perfect score, having seriously problematic issues like bug 1 above diminishes the fun by a good 50%.

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the first installment, I'm puzzled by the sharp criticism surrounding this game. While the controls have shifted away from the original, resembling more of ninja stealth classics like the Tenchu series, it seems tailor-made to appeal to fans. Simultaneously, it retains elements from the first Aragami, resulting in a faster and more dynamic gameplay experience.You can play this game using both a controller or a keyboard, accommodating various player preferences. Additionally, the inclusion of the Classic Mode specifically caters to fans of Aragami 1, offering a mode closely resembling the first game's control scheme across all levels.However, the absence of a level editor, a feature present in the first game, is a noticeable drawback. Overall, it's regrettable that the studio faced financial troubles, as I would have loved to see further iterations of the Aragami series.Rating: Despite the changes in controls and the absence of a level editor, Aragami 2 offers an engaging experience that blends elements from its predecessor while introducing new dynamics. It's a worthy addition for stealth game enthusiasts and fans of the original Aragami, despite missing certain features.

_childDocuments_.review: It is generally expected that a sequel has some resemblance to the game that came before it, and even make some improvements. Aragami 2 fails on at least one of those objectives. It is so far removed from the original, it might as well have been a reboot, though as best as I can tell, it was not. Regardless, getting into the meat and potatoes of this review, the  feels very generic compared to the original, as they completely butchered everything that made Aragami unique. Though the amount of  is vastly improved over the original. Meanwhile, the  is halfway decent, but it fails to make up for the remainder of the price tag.For a game where you play as, what can best be described as a shadow ninja, shadows don't really play a huge part in this. That is the single biggest criticism to be made of this game. Whereas shadows played such an integral part to the core gameplay of the original so much so that one of the earliest ability you got in the original, was the ability to make shadows, now shadows are so insignificant. Shadows play the exact same role that they do in every stealth game, that being that you can hide a little bit better in the shadows, but even that minor effect is taken away by the addition of tall grass which hides you better, and is in abundance on every stage. Furthermore, whereas in the original you had to regain shadow essence by sticking to the shadows, in the sequel it seems as though shadow essence is just a part of you. Your abilities no longer draw from any kind of pool of essence, they just go on cool down when you use them.The A.I. is relatively stupid as well, they might as well be saying "Must've been the wind" they give up searching for the player relatively fast. On one occasion I was spotted by a ranged enemy and he threw a fireball in the complete opposite direction of where he last saw me. The variety of enemies basically amounts to some enemies being stationary, and some having patrol paths. Furthermore, one of the A.I. behaviors that seems to have been removed in the sequel, is guards alerting other guards when they see a body, or the player. If there's some type of alarm system nearby, they will try to alert others. But in the original game, if a guard saw a body, he would just yell out to the other guards.The addition of a combat system, while being new, it's completely unnecessary and goes against the very idea of this being a stealth game. Why the developers felt a need to include a combat system in the sequel is unknown to me. I can't imagine who would buy this game wanting to explore the combat system.The one positive thing I can say about the gameplay, is that you have a lot of freedom of movement, You definitely feel like a ninja playing this game. For $10 that might be a sufficient experience. But for $30, I need more added to the gameplay.The one major improvement that was made over the original was the amount of game there is to play here. I completed the game in roughly 20 hours, whereas the original base game can be completed in 7 hours, with DLC included it goes up to 10 hours. Furthermore, the missions you find yourself going on are quite varied compared to the original. One mission you might be tasked with assassinating a target, another you might be gathering supplies or intel. And there are some missions where you're rescuing or kidnapping someone. This amount of content is definitely a vast improvement over the original.Here is another aspect where the sequel underperforms compared to the original. Overall, looking back on it, the story isn't that bad, but it fails to keep your interest as you're playing. I feel that one part of it is the amount of characters you're being introduced to as you play. Whereas in the original you had just 1 character you were in contact with, and the story was being explained through both her and flashbacks, in the sequel there's at least 3 main characters, and you don't really form an attachment with any of them.Beyond that, the sequel often conflicts with what you learn about Aragami in the orignal. For instance, an Aragami, being made of shadows, it disintegrates in the sunlight. Hence why in the original the story takes place all in 1 night. But in the sequel, there's multiple missions which take place in broad daylight. You almost begin to wonder why this game is a sequel to Aragami when it doesn't seem to follow any of the previously established rules for what an Aragami is.While the content is there, the gameplay just isn't. The only reason you might play Aragami 2 is to feel like a ninja. But beyond that there's so many other games within the stealth genre that are more unique in their gameplay. It's just hard to justify spending $30 on Aragami 2. You don't get much value from the story, the unique gameplay of the original didn't carry over, the one saving grace is the variety and amount of missions.  But that isn't enough to justify the price.Overall I would give this game a 5/10, if it went on sale for $20, I maybe could see that value being justified, but nowhere near $30.

_childDocuments_.review: This game made me confused as to what year this was. It's obviously brand new, but the game design is straight out of the early 00s. The enemy AI is laughable, as are their patrol routines. They walk in two lines, patrol in a square, or stand in a single place without moving. They have no peripheral vision and are insanely stupid. It's almost like going up against the Chuck E Cheez band. They get around this by covering the levels in dozens and dozens of enemies, but this game is still extremely easy no matter what. Unless you try to fight things, at least. The combat is horrible. The game automatically locks on to the first enemy to attack you, which makes crowd control and getting away clunky as hell. The camera also shakes like crazy when swords clash. It's just purely awful. You're supposed to lower your enemy's stamina like Sekiro, but it feels like the lowest-rent knockoff imaginable. The missions themselves are all basically copy-pasted to death. There are 11 maps and you'll either be eavesdropping on enemies, stealing things, or killing enemies. There are 51 missions and most of them feel interchangeable. Only a few are actual story missions. The game is reasonably fun for the first 30 minutes or so, but I started getting sick of it quickly. It feels so insanely padded for no good reason. It's purely a quantity over quality thing. On top of that, the game's mechanics are unreliable. Assassinations don't work reliably unless you patiently wait for the prompt to appear. If you're trying to speedrun, you'll end up simply slashing at foes and alerting them to your presence instead of assassinating them. It's a crapshoot as to what happens when you actually aim for speed. The movement is solid and I really like the air dash, but the inputs for all sorts of things just don't feel all that great, as if there's a disconnect between you and the character.The game will also randomly decide you're not crouching anymore, so prepare to get spotted when your Aragami starts standing up for no reason. You can unlock skills and many are useful. Reducing stamina cost and adding invisibility upon dashing basically breaks the game, so you can just dash your way through missions without even being careful. One ability is supposed to assassinate a second enemy when you assassinate someone, but I could almost never get it to work. This is a really disappointing game with a lot of dated, unreliable mechanics that often don't work as they should.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the incredibly rare games that I will keep coming back to. Having played through and beaten it 3 times now with three different play-styles and 100%'d both the achievements and collectibles, I don't think I could recommend this game enough and it saddens me to think the studio that made this went under.If you're in the mood for one of the few stealth games that doesn't punish or chastise you for killing people in the video game, and especially if you're in the mood for a ninja themed game that isn't ball-crushingly hard, Aragami 2 is pure, clean, fun.The only negative things I have to say about this game are:1. The way the mission rewards work. You get XP and Gold for equipment you may want the most when you complete a mission for the first time. After that, subsequent play-throughs of the same mission on the same Difficulty reward you with HALF the XP and Gold. This -REALLY- incentivizes you to not only do it perfectly the first time but to play on the max difficulty for the max reward. Granted you absolutely do NOT have to Min-Max your rewards like that to get everything in the game and I understand it's to prevent grinding for things early. I don't ever really use my gear anyway so it gathers dust 9/10ths of the time.2. Inconsistent enemy detection. Enemies in this game can both see and hear you. If you knock out or kill somebody too close, they WILL hear it, turn around, and now you have to either immediately deal with them or suffer a "Player Detected" penalty. Sometimes though, this seems wildly inconsistent depending on the action that results in the kill/knock out. Killing someone from inside tall grass is apparently quieter than if you'd just snuck up behind them and killed them that way. I could understand how falling assassinations/knock-outs would be louder though. Something I do love about this game is the timer is rather lenient for how long you have to deal with them before it penalizes you. My only other gripe with this is if you -KILL- somebody it should not count against you UNLESS multiple people find you. Dead men tell no tales, usually.The other problem, and I do understand some enemies have better perceptions than others (Like the dreaded ranged enemies that can spot you practically from across the map) is that their perception seems wildly inconsistent. Sometimes guards are practically blind. Sometimes guards have super hearing. On some maps some guards are stuck looking up which makes most of your ninja ♥♥♥♥ impossible 'cause they'll just spot you anyway unless you're invisible. 60% of the time it works EVERY TIME. The game by far and large is great but once the AI starts breaking down or gaining telepathy and just seeing you when they rightly absolutely should not? Infuriating.3. And finally, this game can get buggy at times. Particularly toward the end. The AI behaving erratically on one mission. Teleporting off into the void only to be teleported back where you where. Enemies spotting you in tall grass which just shouldn't happen, that's literally the point of it. I have seen an enemy try to climb a ledge onto a water fountain, get deleted from this life, and count as a kill. Again, the game works beautifully 80-90% of the time but once it starts to fail it's like a cascading effect that can make the game infuriatingly unplayable.A lot of these are minor gripes that don't effect the game most of the time but when they do it is noticeable.I 'S' ranked all the missions save for 1 or 2 missions I 'A' ranked furiously just to come back almost immediately after and 'S' rank them out of spite. The next two play-throughs I 'S' ranked every single mission in a row. Granted with many restarts but it restarts almost instantly and the only thing stopping you is your frustration versus your patience. This game is -NOT- hard in my experience.Just remember, shinobi... Patience is a virtue.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game. I beat Aragami 1 and was kinda obsessed with it. This is an ambitious addition to the series, but it holds up pretty well and does a good job of delivering new stuff. It is slightly jankier than the first one as there are way more functions for your character, but it's not really a big deal. There's certain things that bugged me like when in the FIRST cutscene that you see your character, the sword is clipping through their hood. Like dude, come on. But the movement, stealth, problem solving, and customization is very fun in this game. You can create builds for your character. That's great. I would definitely recommend this to most people who would want to be a shadow ninja. It nails that feeling arguably more than the first one, in my opinion. The story is kinda like, eh whatever, to me personally. You might like it though. I enjoyed the first one more and kinda wish it built on the world of the first one - which kinda brings me to my next point - it's more of a soft reboot. It has virtually nothing to do with the original story and the gameplay style is a bit different, but they added a "Classic Mode" however, if you wish to play everything like the first one. If you enjoyed Aragami, you will likely enjoy Aragami 2, maybe even more. With classic mode, you are bound to have a pretty good time and I personally enjoy the new gameplay style just as much. Tl;dr: Game good, shadow ninja cool.

Sometimes the geometry of the levels gets ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the game will instead of allowing you to hide behind feneces and such because there is an incline behind the thing you are trying to hide behind, force you over them right into the hands of the enemies on the other side. hell ive been spotted killing someone by a guy on the other side of the map. _childDocuments_.review: Seriously disappointed with the sequel as i loved the first one and was excited when they announced sequel for this game.The gameplay is quite repetitive with no new variety the missions are basically assassinate  a person, get supplies, steal some stuff etc and it will get boring after sometime. The combat is horrible, its like Sekiro except it's nowhere near it. Its clunky unsatisfying and its also filled with bugs. Unlike its predecessor Aragami 2 doesn't have its core feature which was to stay in the shadow, you can just go move freely even without staying in the shadow. The AI are really predictable and unchallenging at times. The pros are basically the visuals are better than the first one, the stealth kills are quick and satisfying, and also thank the devs for the  jump ability, Also the armor sets are pretty cool not gonna lieOverall the sequel to this amazing game is below expectations thanks to its repetitive missions, the clunky combat and the bland story. It has some game breaking bugs (they might've fixed it by now), the core component of the game which made it special is gone and made it uninteresting. I really wanted to like this game but my brain made me come back to my after a few more missions.Rating - 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good stealth action game, not gonna lie. A lot of improvements from the first part, a lot more skills to level up, customisation, free movement and more ways to kill enemies. Definitely worth a try, especially if you have a coop partner.Small update about the game.65 houts in, I've got all the achievements, finished all missions in both "hard" and "classic" modes, got all possible medals, have done pretty much everything the game has to offer. I think I have few more cosmetics and colors to buy, but I have no desire to play the game because there is pretty much nothing more to do. I've seen the message from the devs that this is it, the game is in it's final state so there will be no more content, especially the endgame one.Now for the multiplayer.I might pick the game up once I'll have a friend to play it with or convince any of my relatives to play it, but that's another story.Even though there is a multiplayer menu in the game, it makes me think it was designed in all possible ways to prevent you from playing it. All the servers are always sorted by regions and not in a normal way, but in the way that shows one region at a time. As for me, I live on a "border" between two regions - EU and Turkey, so I have to cycle through those to find myself a partner to play. Cycling through regions comes with a few seconds lag, in which the game tries to update a lobby list for that region, but the next problem is pretty dumb - regions aren't sorted by their location on the world map, so even though EU and Turkey are close together IRL, they're on the opposite sides of region list inside the game, so you have EU - US East - US West - few more regions - Turkey - Australia - few more regions - Japan - EU again, so I have to sit and manually scroll through those with few seconds of delay each time just to see that nobody is playing in needed region. Not that big of a deal, but just an annoying little thing you have to overcome each time you want to play multiplayer.Also, this game was made with third-party-programms usage in mind (for example discord or some chat messengers), because the only way you can communicate with other player (besides actions like attacking, crouching and jumping) is through pings, that can't express anything more than general direction, which is not enough at all. You can't explain to a random partner which kind of approach you are doing (no kills at all or killing everyone, no detections or it doesn't matter to you), which leads either to a lot of restarts or frustration with thoughts that you'll have to play the same mission one more time because your partner can't understand the task.Here are some examples on what am I talking about:1. I've played most of the missions before playing in coop, but was replaying those in order to get all the medals. My random coop partner started killing every enemy immediately, and I understood that my no kills medal was screwed, so had to complete few missions with him (because I've wanted to play some coop to see how fun it is) and redo all of those missions with no kills.2. Opposite example, now I had to kill everyone without being seen, but another random guy was stunning enemies and hiding them in bushes. I've decided to go further into the level and kill everyone just to return and finish his job later on, but he kept being detected and dying, even though each mission has 1 extra life, he ruined the same mission 6 times for me (didn't want to kick him because coop is quite a rare experience and I've played hours before someone joined to me).In conclusion, coop is one hell of a mess that requires discord on background, which is sad because I generally don't like talking to random people in coop games and prefer to play without voicechat.Those are just a few details for anyone who is concerned about such things, but overall the game is pretty good and worth it's money.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a proper review, but I really do feel like it needs to be said that while the first is inspired by traditional stealth games, this game is EXTREMELY Tenchu Z inspired. Tenchu Z was the co-op mission based Tenchu spinoff with a similar structure.When this game came out, it was blasted from on high by people who didn't really understand what this game was trying to be. "Decaffinated Sekiro" is a quote from one of the positive reviews right now that sort of describes how Tenchu actually is.Sekiro, actually was a Tenchu reboot really early in development before FromSoft ditched the idea and made a new world, because FromSoft were the Japanese publishers of Tenchu and developed many of the later spinoffs. This is actually a possible reason FromSoft publshed Sekiro through Activision, because they previously published Wrath of Heaven.I understand this isn't a proper sequel to the original, and it's very different, but this game is very much built on a different blueprint. Shame the studio went broke, both of their games are good, but there is a strong bias towards this game because it's so different from the first. Tenchu fans really like this game for a reason, it is pretty on-point with Tenchu, and just as brutal as that series.This game was on Games Pass for a while and I'd tried it there before, I got the Steam version later from a bundle.If you like the first game though, go and grab Ereban Shadow Legacy, it's not perfect, but it is like the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 is a weird one here is why:Stealth mechanics and enemy types are really good, collectibles are fun to collect (you actually get something from them, like dyes or new armor set) levels are nicely done and there are like 7 missions in 1 level that progressively unlock more and more of the map so you constantly play on the same mission but with minor changes.You can play up to 4 player co-op and you can play stealth or just rushing in, its your choice (there are various builds that you can make) i didnt play co-op but from videos i seen its just total anihilation of the enemy npcs and its easy win.There are a lot of powers and skills that can make you OP and make it fun too.Huge minus is enemy clans (Nobu, Tsubuyaku and Akatsuchi, not a spoiler) they just  appear in game after you progress and these clans have same enemies but with different color so its just lame recollor. Cinematics and conversations are really boring and except for the end, the game has so boring story that i even think that there is no story till the end lol. Your character gets stuck often which is annoying, especially when you want to suprise an enemy and then you slide a hill and he sees you.But overall i had a great time playing this and i fully recommend it, just not for full price, wait till sales comes out.
