_childDocuments_.review: The Aragami series holds a dear place to my heart as it is one of the very first games my partner &I ever played together. We were ecstatic when we saw Aragami 2 was out & purchased it without hesitation. I've played the game for a total of a few hours now & there are definitely some pros & cons in this game.This game doesn't follow the story of the first Aragami game & I'm OK with that because it felt like the first Aragami game's story was told & not much more could be built up on it. However, I'm not sure what it is about this story, but I am significantly less invested in the story than I was in the first game. I'm honestly more excited about the action/gameplay than I am the story. Some of the things I love about this game is there is a little more character customization. In the original Aragami, the only thing you could change was your mask & the color of your outfit; that was it. In this game, you can choose from different masks, tops, bottoms, & swords. However, even though all of these pieces are merely aesthetic, the game still requires you to rack up gold in order to make some of them. If they were all cheap, it wouldn't be a big deal, but I don't feel I should need to rack up 3500 gold just so I can purchase black dye when blue, yellow, & green dyes are around 300 gold each.There are a lot of glitches in this game & I REALLY hope the devs fix them. There's a glitch where I will fall through ceilings after pulling myself up onto a rooftop. My partner & I have seen issues where one of us will have duplicate NPCs & they will actually attack & kill you even when the other person can't see them. The NPCs area also really buggy; sometimes insta-kill won't pop up even when you're above them & it causes us to become detected because the game apparently never sensed we were in the right position to perform an aerial kill. One big gripe I have about this game is the inability to map controls to specific keys/buttons. I tried playing this game on mouse/keyboard & it was god awful, but it wouldn't have been if we just had the ability to map the keys for ourselves. This forces me to play the game with a controller, which is fine, but is not as smooth as mouse & keyboard. I also do not like the controls when hanging on walls/rooftops. You either have to press a button to drop down or pull yourself up; there is no ability to just jump away from the ledge & the jump button is mapped to the pull yourself up button, so if you wanted to attempt to jump, you couldn't anyway. That might sound minor, but when you play the game, the ability to simply jump away from a walk in a NINJA STEALTH GAME would be really beneficial to the gameplay, but instead it makes it a little bit more difficult to play. Ultimately, I live for the action & that's what I have fun with in this game. I don't think this game is bad by any means, but I think there is significant room for improvement. I would really love to recommend this game, but in it's current state, I really cannot recommend it at full price. I would wait for it to go on sale in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: This is barely a positive recommendation as I found it pretty fun at times, but annoyingly painful to play at other times. It is not  2. This game feels very different losing what made Aragami great and adding only mediocre new game mechanics. Yes, jumping, vaulting, dashing mid air, and hanging from walls are welcome additions, but the completely new combat is not super polished. Fighting one enemy is perfectly fine, but add multiple and the jarring camera movements and limited gameplay makes it annoying. The removal of gaining power from the shadows and dashing to shadows was the worst mistake they made. Hard mode makes it annoyingly hard to escape if you are caught. Its almost impossible to simply just run away as the enemies teleport directly on to you and one hit you every time. When you add on the annoying auto lock with the combat system, its extremely annoying and clunky feeling. And only on certain maps is it physically possible to escape due to the possible shadow leaps. Speaking of maps, the repetition of the same maps is so lazy and makes each level blend together making every mission feel the same. I also think the crouched moving animation is weirdly bad. If you enjoyed Aragami, I can't say that you will enjoy Aragami 2. Despite all of this, the stealth in the game is still very fun and feels good. If you are looking for a decent stealth ninja game with a variety of fun abilities, then yes, buy Aragami 2 when its on sale. But if you have played through and liked Aragami and want a second installment, then be a little more cautious.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is janky. It's got some weird animation glitches, occasional graphical hiccups and it's not the most visually impressive game out there, and every now and then the control scheme can fail you if you're not 100% precise in your movements.It's also the most fun I've ever had with a co-op stealth game. While it may not have the polish or reputation of Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, it has the same thrilling joy of coordinated, ghostly slaughter. When playing alongside a friend, with whom you're on the same wavelength, utilizing your skills and abilities in tandem, there's few games I've played as rewarding as Aragami 2.It's worth noting that it's a pretty significant departure from the gameplay and story of the original. Mechanically it's much more high-mobility, and instead of encouraging more deliberate, stealthy approaches favors a more high risk-high reward approach. Additionally, unlike the first game where you're almost certainly instantly dead if spotted at all, Aragami 2 gives you the tools to actually stand your ground and fight, allowing you to kill your way out of a mistake rather than returning to the previous checkpoint. Still, you're much deadlier when attacking from the shadows, and it's easy to get overwhelmed once spotted as enemies will call for help, so there's still plenty of incentive to play smart rather than simply playing aggressively.If, like me, you've been searching for a spiritual successor to Chaos Theory, it's finally here. Easily the best gaming purchase I've made in quite some time.

_childDocuments_.review: (Summary at the bottom as well as my score for the game.)Aragami 2 feels so pointless, the first game had a pretty definitive conclusion, and this one seems to exist to cash in on and take advantage of the people who loved the first game like myself. The story is there, kind of the only thing I can say about it since I really didn't care about anything that happened in the story and only begrudgingly progressed through it because of how much I enjoyed the first game. The characters aren't memorable, even after just now finishing the game, I couldn't tell you any of their names or anything they did beyond assigning me missions. However, the most disappointing aspect of the game is the game play loop.There are 51 missions in Aragami 2. That may seem like a lot of potential for variety; however, this game seemingly took the Wolfenstein Young Blood approach to level design. You go to the same areas constantly, fighting the same enemies with the same spawn placements with the same music for the overwhelming majority of the game, and much like Young Blood, it's tedious and boring. This gets repetitive almost immediately, I think I got 2 hours into the game before it became unbearable and it took me almost 11 hours to beat this game. I started on Normal, but the AI is incredibly finicky on Normal and will spot you almost immediately, and besides Aragami 1, I don't usually play stealth games, so I found the experience to be a bit more tolerable on Easy. Doesn't help that the AI cheats and can often times spot you through walls, while hiding in grass, and even when you're invisible.There's only a handful of different mission types as well (Kill x amount of thing, eliminate this target, carry thing to teleporter, 3 missions where you auto fail if you get caught OR kill something, find random item, and listen to people talking to name a few, probably missed 1 or 2 others). It feels like the game was rushed since even late into the game, think it's missions 46 and 50 both take place in the exact same area, both require you to find 7 of the exact same item which is in the exact same place in both missions, only difference is that mission 50 also has you kill 4 Necromancers (and not to mention half of the last 10 missions in the game have the objective to kill Necromancers). You fight the same exact enemies the entire game as well, until mission 40 where undead versions of the same enemies appear. The only major difference is that they'll spot you much quicker, kill you in like 2 or 3 hits, but they don't notice dead bodies, so you can just power through them if you got a lot of stealth upgrades in the skill tree. As you progress you'll get new enemy types, but everything dies in 1 hit if you stealth kill them, and they all have a similar movement pattern, so even with 3 or 4 different enemy types, it only feels like there's 2 in the game. Ground troops or archer/look outs. Even being spotted doesn't feel punishing. In Aragami 1, if you get spotted, or if a body is found, the enemy that spots you and/or the body, they'll alert the other guards and every enemy in the map will be fully alert and hunting you down. In Aragami 2, since the maps are so huge, you can litter bodies everywhere, and even if a guard notices, they won't alert other enemies, they'll just be more alert for a couple of moments.There's also a hub world where you can upgrade skills at the Dojo via skill tree and there's an armory that let's you "craft" (you just buy stuff, but the game calls it crafting) items, armor, and runes. While the skill tree is fine, the armory is a bit on the useless side since only a handful of items are worth taking, the armor is just cosmetic, and the runes are underwhelming to the point where I didn't use them at all during my play through of the game and it went fairly smoothly.The game play is different than the first, it's like a poorman's Sekiro Shadows Die Twice. The new melee combat system just doesn't feel good to use, and fighting more than 1 enemy at a time isn't worth the hassle. You're better off playing this game like it's Aragami 1, but because M1 melee attacks now, if you turn off V-Sync, the assassinations barely work. It'll flash across the screen constantly, or often times not show up at all even if you're walking behind an enemy that doesn't notice you and it lead to my first half of the play through being really frustrating because I'd get caught due to instances that weren't my fault. The movement in the game does feel pretty good, especially later in the game when you get different upgrades that let you move with even more stamina and stealth, but the decent movement doesn't save this game from feeling stale because it's way too long. There's no reason there should be 51 missions, even half of that would be too much. Additionally, since the maps are so big now, there's these obnoxious invisible walls that completely break the immersion that the first game nailed. Aragami 2 is so unpolished! You'd think that since this game is made on Unity (like the first game) the developers would have an idea how the engine works since Lince Works had no problem nailing Aragami 1, but it's laughable how many visual bugs and glitches you'll find in this game. Anytime there's a cutscene with a character that has hair, their hair will clip through their face and clothes constantly. If the character has a weapon, it'll constantly go through them as well; even long clothes just constantly clip through characters. It looks really bad and breaks the immersion even further since the levels you play in the game hardly feel like they exist in an actual place as well.Ultimately, I'd give Aragmi 2 a 4/10.While the movement can be fun at times  the tedious repeating levels and mission objectives absolutely slaughter what could've been a fantastic game. Unfortunately, I feel that I have to not recommend this game. 35 dollars is way too expensive, and even with the on sale price going down to 17.49, I'd highly recommend using your money to get Aragami 1 if you want to play a game in this style. With a default price of 20 and currently on sale for 4, Aragami 1 offers a much more well rounded experience. Better story, better level design, better stealth, and better game play. Best thing I can say after finishing Aragami 2 is good riddance.

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 is a Stealth-oriented action game & a decent sequel that took the risk of changing it's overall formula from it's predecessor. You control a special type of ninja warrior with the ability to "resurrect" & you aid a village afflicted by a supernatural curse that makes it's hosts to slowly lose their personalities , memories and eventually their faces. So you try to find a way to lift this curse while defending the village from invaders & the shadow army.  Kakurega Village will be your HUB/Home base , from which you'll take quests from it's inhabitants, craft/buy weapons, outfits & consumables, unlock characters, abilities & runes that enhance them & completing tasks/ from the billboard to further progress the story. All these gave me strong Monster Hunter world vibes in terms of how you organize your char and their stuff before embarking on missions.  Gameplay wise, you can either conceal in the shadows and find tactical approaches to reach your given tasks, one hit killing or knocking out the enemies & hiding their bodies to not alert caution, or you can go the traditional Rambo wayand comforting em face to face. Combat in that aspect, feels like your typical light soulslike , with a few attack sequences , guarding / parrying & dodging while managing your stamina bar.  Special skills come to play as well , with either enshrouding darkness to reduce vision in a area, enhancing your weapons,teleport kills, creating shadow decoys and much more. In comparison to the 1st one, this one feels better in some aspects and worse in others.Movement feels heavier in a good sense, instead of teleporting in between shadows you gotta decide more tactically how to approach to remain unnoticed, the combat feels a bit better overall and imo this feels more like Tenchu than the previous one. Lastly , i encountered a few bugs , such as throwing bodies and them ignoring walls or terrain, a few off-sliding animations during execution cinematics but nothing deal breaking so far. It's not a breath taking or amazing experience , but it's an enjoyable one, especially if you're into Stealth adventures and Ninja's.

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 is fairly different from its predecessor. It's faster-paced and uses a replayable mission system with varying difficulty. I know some people would say that makes this one inferior, but I don't think that's a fair assessment of it; the first one filled a particular niche, while this one is a little more mainstream in its style. This, of course, turns off some of the original players. I also started with Aragami 1, and I see these two games in the same way I see Dishonored 1 & 2: each is different, each has strengths the other lacks. If you're going into this as an Aragami 1 player, keep that in mind.They also more recently added a "classic mode"  that tries to mirror the original game, which you can use at any time.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 is much more fast paced than the first game, and less punishing in stealth. Fighting is an option now, though not necessarily always the best one. Overall I am really enjoying the changes from the first game, and classic mode is a great way to have your cake and eat it too for the people that preferred the stealth style of the first game, while still benefiting from the fluidity of the 2nd. This is some of the most fun I've had with a stealth game in years. Also, the soundtrack. The first games soundtrack was so good I used to boot up the main menu to cure headaches, and this games soundtrack may surpass that.

_childDocuments_.review: The game plays a lot like the old Tenchu series, but it still keeps a lot of what makes it its own game. Shadow powers, an intriguing story, engaging atmosphere, a neat combat system, and some character customization. That being said the combat is not always easy. Granted a lot of people are butthurt about losing the easy travel shadow teleportation, probably because they have no patience. There are some edgy bugs but nothing game breaking. If you've been looking for a good ninja game its a good buy, if you're skeptical wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Another UPDATE: None of these things matter anymore. The studio has shut down and that of course means no more updates. It's a good game and if you like the sneaky-stabby type of gameplay it offers, you should definitelly get it. Don't bother with feedback tho, the great people behind the Aragami series are no longer there to hear you and fix the issues. RIP Linceworks, you folks made many of my evenings a lot more enjoyable. You won't be forgotten.UPDATE: Most of the bugs have been fixed. The game is much more enjoyable now. The animations are more fluent, your sword no longer disapears from your hand, you no longer glitch through textures, the combat is a little less ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and I no longer think that no dubbing is a bad thing in this case. The game would lose a lot of it's feel, if it got dubbed to other languages. Despite that I still have a few complaints: - There still are some spots on maps, where you can see through the textures (for example when you go out of the spawn location on the last mission and look on the rocks to your left)- IF YOU STUN TSUBAYAKA BY EXPLODING A LIGHT NEAR HIM, HE WILL FALL TO THE GROUND AND DISAPEAR MAKING IT IMPOSSIBLE TO FINISH THE MISSION- The bossfight is also a tad bit dissapointing, because you can just kill the boss by sneak killing him 3 times.- The resolutions of textures needs to be upped a little bit, I can see the individual pixels on some of the faces and ornaments (mostly clothing is the problem)- The fights in cutscene are sometimes not dynamic enough. I recommend making the movements of characters a little faster.Other than that everything is fine. Still recomend playing this with a friend for the best experiance, but it is WAY better than it was. I am looking foraward to the next game by Lince Works and am on track to getting all achievments.LOOK HERE FOR MY PREVIOUS OPINION ON THE GAME + WHAT I ENJOY ABOUT IT (most of the bugs are now fixed):For one, the game is not bad, as me recomending it sugests, I also don't think that it being different from the original is terrible either, nor does anythig blast me into space :).The good sides:+ The change of pace is refreshing.+ The missions are well done+ The multiplayer is fun (make sure to have good internet)+ The secrets are well hidden+ Customization is awesome+ Story line is interesting + The music is amazing!+ Abilities are sick!+ There are way more anymations ... Bad sides:- ... but often bug out- The fighting mechanic is often total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥- u hit someone, u get stuck, u die, or you try to kill an enemy and get killed yourself, because ALL OF THE ENEMIES CALL ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ON YOUR LAST HIT, CAUSE WHY NOT, it will always be 2 attacks at the end of their stamina, from which, one is guaranteed to inflict damage on you.- THE AMOUNT OF BUGS ACTUALLY RIVALS CYBERPUNK 2077 and here's a quick list acumulated in about 5 hours of playtime- some times killing an enemie will make you unable to move until you dash; in multiplayer enemies can become resistant to ALL damage from you, and your friend will have to kill that enemy instead; your sword can LITERALLY DISAPPEAR from your hand (you attack, but inflict no damage); the AI can  magically decide, that they are just gonna walk into eachother, a wall, or you, sometimes ruining your stelth run, or swarming you with 5 more enemies; in multiplayer, the loading screen can glitch, making one player's screen black, and not doing anything but that, resulting in a mandatory restart of the game (and likelly a lobby restart as well)- The shadows have gotten a huge downgrade, only useful for hiding  from enemies- The blood feels sometimes too cartoon-ish- No dubbing- NO RAGDOLLSIn conclusion, It's a good game, that needs some fixes, which are possible to make (add more frames to animations, repair bugs and combat). _childDocuments_.review: 🏯 First of all, the top reviews aren't updated and people are too harsh on this indie (still one of the best ninja stealth games that you can now play with friends!) The style has changed, but the design & atmosphere are still fascinating. The plot remained small, smooth and appropriate to the setting, but the gameplay was stretched (this is where more isn't better). Many missions are quite monotonous, as they are designed for co-op (locations are repeated, and there aren't enough bosses for variety). But the only real problem (since the classic gameplay was returned as an additional difficulty) is the “Unity clumsiness”, which creates minor bugs that can sometimes ruin half-hour missions that you wanted to get through undetected or without killing anyone. Various secrets help unlock more customization items, the arsenal is gradually expanding so there's plenty of replay value. The game isn't even close to bad, but yes, the first one was perceived better.

_childDocuments_.review: Hear me out. It's not bad. It's no Aragami 1 mind you, but it's not bad if you separate this game from the first one.The addition of the "classic mode" saved this game for me. Before the addition of this mode the game was honestly not very enjoyable and really was lackluster in its delivery. I only play in Classic, therefore my review will revolve around this game mode specifically.I feel as though this game is more of an "introductory" stealth game, which when it is compared to its predecessor. It's rather hand-holdy and is much more forgiving than the first game and gives more power to the player (which following the first feels very out of place). Certain mechanics are now missing such as light harming you, and shadows are only used for re-gen of powers making them less of an importance and more of a bonus additive. However, with the addition of the classic mode, teleporting to shadows becomes the only way to utilize your teleport over terrain (minus to rooftop sides and building ledges) making the game feel more like the first in this aspect. It definitely brought more of the original feel of the game back for me when this option was available.Combat in this game is poorly optimized and very janky. They attempt to teach you in the beginning how to do it correctly, but throughout the game it ends up being a very glitchy one sided experience often resulting in your death due to glitchy mechanics and weird button inputs. Classic mode once again resolved this issue for me due to the fact that combat is still available but is severely punished with the implementation of the OG Aragami mechanic of "one shot one kill". Meaning that you do have the option to fight should you need to, but one hit will kill you and force you to start over (and you will get hit due to the poor fighting mechanics). Therefore in classic mode, stealth becomes all the more imperative due to it being more of a punishment than the ability to actually kill your attacker in a 1v1 fight.The levels do get a bit on the redundant side, especially since the first game had you going to different places throughout the game. Personally, this wasn't really a big con for me, I didn't really mid it all that much. Would some more level diversity been a little better? Yeah, was it a deal breaker for me? Not really. I also really didn't mind the hub world either. I really liked the music in this area so I wasn't really upset or bothered about it being a thing. The one thing I really was upset about was the story itself. I would have loved a continuation from the first game into this one. I was really looking forward to playing Aragami again and learning more about the character that I became attached to in the first game, however, the story-line in this game is legitimately all over the place and has nothing to do with what was established in the first game about the Aragami. That was a bit on the confusing side to me, as suddenly the entire lore was changed from what we had learned in the first game. We're no longer playing the first guy, but some other guy who's now an Aragami because he's cursed. While the story isn't "bad" per say it was a huge derailment from the established line of story from the first game which honestly left me feeling some sort of way. This story-line almost felt too "Naruto-y" to me which gave it that cliche Sasuke angst feel. This ultimately made the story really hard to connect to and had me tuning out half of what was going on throughout the story-line because it just felt so discombobulated and far removed from the first story-line. Did I hate it? No. Did it keep my attention? Not really. Did I still play the game? Yes.All in all, it's not bad but not amazing either. Do I still play it to satisfy a certain fast paced stealth itch? You bet. Is it as good as the first one? No. Is it worth $34.99....not really. I'd say if you're curious, go get the first game. Play it through with a friend and have a great time. Then come to this game when it's on sale. Personally I'd say this game is probably worth about $15 as it does have some love an care obviously put into it and it's not a hot dumpster fire disaster, but I'd not really pay over $20 for it. TLDR: Good game, not as good as the first. Janky combat. Classic Mode made game better. Wait for game to go on sale before playing.   6.3/10

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, this game is not the exact same as first game, but releasing the exact same game but with upgraded graphics is lazy and boring.Aragami 1 was a slow-paced and more or less tactical stealth game with a pretty annoying coop with barely any respawns Aragami 2 however, is has a much more casual, fast-paced gameplay, with parkour and freedom of movement, where being busted no longer meaning game over, instead allowing you to correct your mistakes and fight off an enemy that you've alerted, which also allows a fun, engaging, challenging non-stealth playstyle. The game still has great challenge and depth to it, it's still very challenging to try and be 100% stealthy+pacifist/demon. Level design is great, levels are big and barely restrict any movement, yet no level has those weird empty spots with nothing in them, instead they're filled with collectibles, enemies or objectives.Want to also say about the games perfomance, the game at launch has stable fps, next to no bugs that I've encoutered, doesn't force an online connection 24/7, with a fair price, which is rare for modern games to have.

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 takes the concept of Ninja stealth to the next level of Ninja stealth. That didn't sounded right was it?What i want to say is that this game is the underdog of indie games right now imo, the game looked down on due to the amount of bugs and graphic issues which i kinda agree. If you are really looking for the best stealth experience, i cannot word it enough of how much i recommend Aragami 2 as the best choice of both financial budget, PC game budget and... budget?The game is pretty easy to learn and master but sometimes there are moments that DOES make you think that this part was poorly made, but then you realiz how much accurate the stealth really is.Pros: -Fast-paced stealth and the reaction time you need just like a ninja, you have every tool of a true ninja to approach the enemies in various of different ways that you cannot imagine.-Three different playstyles with each having it's own talent and rune build which i find pretty impressive-Crossplay which is not something many games add these days.-Creative customize options and the return of [REDACTED] attire.-Lore weak but yet really touching story and sometimes actually makes you wanna drop tears.-Three player Co-Op is out of question, it's the best experience i ever had for a Ninja stealth game with a multiplayer. The game is extremely fun with friends, i cannot describe the perfection.-Intelligent and really challenging enemies, they actually act as a human and not a pure dumbass, and some enemies have different abilities and make your experience really challenging, by the way, did you know that they can climb walls?-Ninja, just Ninja. the way you can travel through the map or design your character is extremely creative.-The game is extremely long and offers ours of playtime, with the gameplay and the beautiful environment, this game never gets old since you also have to revisit the locations several times. Cons:-Bug fest, but it will be fixed soo.-Unachievable Medals because of problems with... coding?-Some location extra closes the doors to secrets so you actually have to load the right level in that location for the door to unlock.-Items get extremely expensive at one point. -NPC's mouths wont move when talking during cutscene.In short, I recommend Aragami 2 to every stealth fan, it may not be as good as games like Batman Arkham series, but sometimes it just offers something that i never saw in any other stealth game, which is what is making the game so unique that i will come back to the game once i finished it for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for Aragami 2, especially after enjoying the first game, but unfortunately, it falls short on multiple fronts. The stealth mechanics, which were the core strength of the original, feel clunky and unreliable. Enemy AI is inconsistent, often swinging from comically oblivious to unrealistically perceptive without any logical progression. The story is forgettable and lacks the engaging narrative that drew me in before. Character development is almost non-existent, making it hard to care about the protagonist or their mission. Additionally, the graphics, while slightly improved, still look dated compared to current standards, and the level design feels repetitive and uninspired.Multiplayer mode, which could have been a redeeming feature, is plagued by connectivity issues and lag, making it more frustrating than fun. Overall, Aragami 2 is a step back from its predecessor and fails to deliver a satisfying stealth action experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying currently i have about 7 hours in the game by the time i write this review, which means i have a neat grasp of the game and i will judge the game both as its own game and as a sequel to the first Aragami.As its own game, this is a fantastic stealth game where movement is smooth, there's a wide variety of gadgets that can be used for different playstyles and how you approach things, a clean HUD and UI, customization where you can make your character look like an assassin or a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bare chested monkey, and animations that are clean and quick.As a sequel to Aragami, its a bit complicated. The devs certainly have improved some things like how movement makes you feel like a ninja instead of a slow snail that needs teleportation to catch up to enemies while sneaking. The game has also added combat that is "passable", its certainly not the best but that's the point, as its supposed to be a last resort option instead of immediately giving you a game over in the first game. Customization has also improved by separating armor sets into four pieces (Headgear, Chestgear, Pants, Katana). The level design and AI has also changed due to the movement changing and how the dev's aim for bigger maps instead of linear levels like in the first game.Now here's the bad part about it being a sequel to Aragami, some stuff HAS indeed improved, but at what cost? Aragami 2 stripping away its identity as a sequel to Aragami. The shadow teleportation mechanic in the first game has been removed and has been replaced with a more simpler teleportation where you can teleport to ledges and you can roll to become shadow. Now some people say that this is a bad thing while i'm pretty fine with it, as the shadow teleportation wouldn't work due to the fact that movement has vastly improved over the first game and how shadows are less important in the second game. Speaking of shadows, you heard me right, shadows are widely less important in here, that shadow essence bar? removed for a stamina bar. Although i would put a reason being how lore wise that you're not the same Aragami as you were in the first game and blah blah blah, i would guarantee that you give ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about lore, but the actual reason was again, due to the movement being overhauled. Lince Works didn't have the skill and manpower at the time to create a movement system so they made the shadow teleportation in the first game so there's more movement with the use of the ability.I can go on and on but its better if i make a checklist of the pros and cons of the gamePros/Things that i liked about the game:-Movement has been overhauled-Animations are quicker than the first game-The game has RPG elements such as a skill tree that doesn't allow you to unlock every skill so to make co-op more interesting, and runic charms that you can imbue onto armor sets that give buffs and nerfs-Customization is waaay better than the first game-The game is longer than the first game-Clean HUD and UI-The soundtrack in the game is a banger-Banmoku has been removed for "Shadow vision", which is basically Eagle vision from AC-Maps are bigger and better and mixed in with the movement, will make traversing through it a breeze-Kurosu (the bird in the first game) is removed and now you can just use shadow vision to highlight where you're supposed to go, what your objective is, and where enemies are-How abilities are used is different from the first game as now there's a cooldown instead of running out of abilities-Consumables exist as you can heal yourself, throw shurikens to damage enemies during combat, smokescreen the area around you to blind enemies and cloak yourself, and more-A hub area-More enemy varieties-AI can now navigate through the maps so its harder for you to escape-An option to kill or to knock people out for genocide and pacifist runs-Enemies are woken up when they're asleep so to give an actual reason to knock people out instead of immediately killing peopleCons/Things that i didn't like about the game:-The story is "there", it certainly exists but not even a decent story to keep you engaged-They removed things from the first Aragami for better or for worse-There are too many levels (50) and too little maps (10), it will get repetitive-Shadows are less important as the only use for them is to make your character glow in the dark (like in the first game) and making enemies spot you slower when you are in shadow-Combat is dull but its a necessary dull as combat isn't the point-No checkpoints as the bigger map size would be difficult to implement it, no quicksaves too. BUT you get two lives in each mission so you have one more chance to press onward before you have to start over from scratch-Medals return from the first game but aren't as important and harder to get as there's more enemies and armor sets are gained from blueprints instead of medals-AI and enemies are sometimes questionable, sometimes there's enemies who wont leave their post, which is more realistic but gets annoying as you cant lure them in, and sometimes civilians (enemies who you cant kill/run away to alert real enemies) will just continuously run into wallsAnd a third section: Things that i didn't like about the game BUT will be fixed in later patches/dev's have acknowledged them and will be rolled in the next patch:-You cant stop the game when pausing it-Co-Op has issues such as delays, lag, etc, but its only the first week so no wonder theres a bunch of bugs-Bugs, you are likely to encounter one or two but its not as bad as most triple A games at this point, and its nothing game breaking like soft locking or crashing the game, just some minor ones-You can't remap controlsIn SummaryYou will not find a worthy successor to Aragami here, but you will find an awesome stealth game made by passionate devs who wanted to make a great ninja game. It can be summed up that Aragami 2 is the "true" Aragami experience as this was the game that they wanted to make and that they would have made when they were making Aragami 1 if they had the power to actually make it.As its own stealth game, i would rate it an 8/10As a sequel to Aragami, i would rate it a 7/10I'd buy it if it was under $20 bucks, i got it for $10, so its definitely worth the money. And all i'm gonna say, don't listen to the people that have below 1 hour in the game and complaining about the smallest things in the game and giving it a negative review. Listen to the ones that actually have feedback about the game and an actual reason that they cant recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to preface this review by saying I am a huge Tenchu fan. In particular Tenchu: Stealth Assassin's, and Tenchu: Wrath of Heaven. Tenchu is the game series that got me into the stealth genre, which opened the door for games like MGS, Splinter Cell, Dishonored, etc.   Over the course of the past few decades we've had games like Ninja Gaiden which brought a more combat and magic oriented focus over the stealth approach. While this is a popular gaming style it did not scratch the itch for stealth that the previously mentioned Tenchu games delivered. Mark of the Ninja brought it's own flavor and style of stealth into the side scrolling 2D and was an excellent title, but it lacked the open level design that only 3 dimensional games can offer.   When the first Aragami released it granted players a unique way of navigating the 3D maps. Using the shadows to leap from one shadow area to the next, both horizontally and vertically. There was no jumping in the original game. Combat was also shunned in favor of a more pure stealth approach offering players ways of both assassinating or ghosting levels without killing or being spotted.   Enter Aragami 2. The biggest deviation from the original game was the necessity of having to use the shadows to navigate, that is no longer the case. Instead, in Aragami 2 there is a dedicated jump button in conjunction with Shadow Leap (think grappling hook from the Tenchu games) that allows players to jump and dash around the games environment, regardless of whether there is a shadow present or not.    The combat has also drastically improved, whereas in the original Aragami combat was a death sentence. In Aragami 2 the game offers a more robust combat experience by comparison. Parrying, light attacks, heavy attacks, along with specific tools and powers to help augment the player if they want to engage in combat rather than having to flee. It is still far from having great combat encounters though, but at least the option is there for players that want to actively fight rather than escape when the occasion arises.  The game offers character customization in a variety of ways too. From armor sets that can be mixed and matched to various swords.  They even have an assortment of dyes to color your character with as well. The game provides runes which can be purchased via the blacksmith vendor in Kakurega Village (which is like your home area in between missions). These allow to further customize your character by augmenting your stats like stealth, armor, stamina, attack, etc. There is also a variety of tools and potions at your disposal before each mission that you can purchase and stock up on.  There are a total of 50+ missions in Aragami 2, however maps are revisited repeatedly which can get repetitive by the end of the game. The mission objectives do get tougher though as the game progresses into it's later stages, challenging the player not to be detected and to not kill anyone. This is obtainable by the abilities you gain as you level through the ability tree. There is a good selection of abilities to add to your growing array of skills to allow you to approach mission objectives in the best way that suits you.  Overall the story was cool. Nothing mind blowing but I enjoy this type of setting and way of story telling for this particular type of game. I had a lot of fun playing Aragami 2 and it brought back a lot of fond memories of playing the older Tenchu games while also simultaneously forging new ones for this game.   I would highly recommend it to anyone looking for a ninja stealth game that is trying to "scratch that itch" of older Tenchu titles. In summary, the best way I could describe Aragami 2 is like Tenchu with shadow powers. Not to take anything away from this game. I think the developers did an outstanding job with the atmosphere and the music too is spot on. I am currently working on finishing up collectibles and maybe even try my hand at the hard difficulty.   That reminds me, the devs have even added a "classic" mode, which allows the player to play Aragami 2 similarly to the original game. Sticking to the shadows and shadow leaping via the shadows. It just goes to show that the developers have listened to player feedback and incorporated a feature that the fans asked for. I think that is noteworthy & worth mentioning in this day and age when a lot of requests fall on deaf ears.   In any event, it's been a fun ride and I hope to see an Aragami 3 in the works down the line.

_childDocuments_.review: ----------------------------------Missed potential but appreciated what I gotPick it up on a sale, It's lacking the substance for full price.Achievement Hunting Difficulty:  Easy as balls, just be thorough and try a couple skills in your playthrough--------------------------------------------------------------------Aragami 2 gives you the choice to play as violently as you wish and does it's best to make combat based players viable. You'll quickly find however that playing a vengeful spirit isn't as efficient or as fun it would seem.Why spend the extra 10 - 20 minutes making sure everyone is dead on one of the larger maps so that when you win you get an arbitrary performance rating and the same XP that an efficient pacifist run would offer in less time?Now if you were to tell me that my playstyle had plot rammifications, NOOOOWWWW we're talking.Suddenly going through the effort to be a Ghost or a Demon is significant.You'd think the political parties you thwart would take countermeasures against the literal one mofo ruining their fun but no. They're content with regular guard routes and static observe posts.In fact, some missions require you to do a genocide run - making the illusion of player agency even more superfluous.Now when I say they "Do their best to make combat playstyles viable" I refer to the Essence System. Basically a buff that detracts from another skill. You can make yourself dish out more damage at the expense of stealth but in all honesty, you can break their LOS and just instant kill a guy and suddenly you realise you dont even need to touch this system beyond getting the achievement to apply one.I could pick from a few nails but I'll close this coffin with this:Returning to an old map with new areas unlocked and filling them with vague instructions and dumb objectives is what really hammered the tedium in for me."Aragami, I need you to make the journey to the capital city of some bastards messin' with our ♥♥♥♥ so you can cut the rope on 12 regular alarms, then travel back home so we can send you to another familiar place because we realised we needed to collect something from there - but hey the black wall of denying exploration has been lifted in an area so there is 25% more map for you to explore"I mean c'mon whats goin' on?------------------------------------------------------------------Sure. There is a thrill in navigating maps & moots efficiently, Unlocking cooler cosmetics tickles my brain & parrying anything gives me the false impression I would be just as good at it in Sekiro.I think with the introduction of some smaller details to flesh out the core systems and this would have been gold:- Throw in some spicy acrobatics when jumping/ long jumping. - Perhaps other weapons beyond swords exist in the Aragami world - What if the final boss .- What if the AI reacted to your typical strategies? EG:  "Oh, you use Darkflame to knock us out alot" - insert counter-measure.I very much am thankful that Lince Games is pushing through with expanding the Aragami franchise. I only wish that what we got in this sequel had more substance. I realise it's easy to ask for more without acknowledging the true scale of a task But I also believe every creative sets out to the do their best work, and Lince can do better.I wonder how Lince Games will use the lessons learned in making Aragami 1 & 2 in their next work

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked some of the changes made: the movement feels more fluid, there are more traversal options, combat is pretty fun and rewarding, and the option of lethal or non-lethal takedowns is a welcome change. The aesthetics are still on point for the setting, and the soundtrack is fitting and adds to the atmosphere. I don't mind the leveling system or that skills have a cooldown now and are no longer limited per se. Crafting and dying apparel is nice as it allows you to better customize your look (you can mix and match from different sets, and you have a helmet, upper body, lower body and sword slots). The hub area is a decent addition, as it offers a brief respite and allows you to interact with certain NPCs. Also, shadows and light are no longer as crucial as in the first entry in the series, which may rub some of the fans of the original the wrong way, but for me, it's not really an issue. Haven't noticed many bugs (fell through the map at one point and had to restart the mission, but otherwise nothing that game-breaking).The biggest problem with the story is that it's incredibly long, and it overstays its welcome. There are a few levels that get reused multiple times with the exact same layout and enemy positioning. Most of the quests in the main story are just fetch quests and are dull/uninspired; they could've been omitted or just be optional content to farm gold or find blueprints. Maybe playing co-op would alleviate some of the repetition and boredom, but the game is still flawed, and the campaign should've been much shorter (similar to the first game).Can't really recommend this one, as it feels like an exercise in frustration most of the time, and completing all missions/finishing the story is a chore.

_childDocuments_.review: This game brings it to the point when one thinks of "quantity over quality". Technically, the game is really good. The mechanics work, and while it may seem now more generic than the first Aragami game, I think a lot has improved and gives much more freedom to the player how to advance and what playstyle to pursue. Also, this gives a lot of replay values to the missions. That brings us to the elephant in the room: the missions. Most of them, apart from very few, are just mindlessly set on ever repeating maps. Go here, go there, grab that item, kill a target, save/kidnap a target... It gets repeated over and over again with almost no storytelling at all. This happens mainly in the hub area. I can see why they did this: the devs wanted to bolster the multiplayer part, and the way to do this, when not everyone wants to follow the story or skip cutscenes, is to do missions without any story to them. But it is just so boring to play through them. Even with changing maps, it feels like the same routine over and over again. Nothing really to discover, it just feels so bland. So instead of having over 50 missions that are totally forgettable, I would have preferred a dozen very well designed. Well, if you have nothing else to do and just want to throw some time away, you can just play a mission every evening (no save function inside a mission!), maybe you have some fun. But certainly this went into the wrong direction for me.

_childDocuments_.review: So listen. I just came off playing the first Aragami, and hated it for various reasons.Aragami 2 basically does away with MOST of these things.The movement is fluid, the executions snappy, your character isn't super slow, doesn't die in a hit, there's actual "combat", although it's mostly button mashing, then parry, then kill, you can CARRY bodies. Just like that. Yay. Enemies don't endlessly respawn, etc. etc. The CORE GAMEPLAY is really fun ... it's NOT like Aragami, which is why hardcore fans of that game will hate it.There is a "classic" mode now in the game, which makes the game more like the first one, but it's still vastly improved, and I'd actually play that, because of its more methodical approach.Now, why the down vote then? Because everything else about this game is lacklustre ... Shadows are almost meaningless unless you play in Classic. Enemies are almost meaningless, because you can easily drop aggro and just kill them from above a few seconds later. Carrying bodies is great, but rather useless, because enemies discovering a body isn't really that big of a deal or threat.The upgrade tree feels rather boring, maybe not because of the upgrades, but because of the rest of the game built around it. Which is the biggest point of critique: There's just nothing to it. Instead of an epic adventure all you do is run around in an empty hub area, accepting "missions" that all take place in rather the same environment with enemies placed almost randomly throughout, and rinse-repeating that process. Either solo or in MP. MP is probably fun if you have someone to really play with.As a solo all you got is the rather good stealth combat system, although one might argue there's not enough stealth in this game if you're not playing the hardest difficulty or classic, I guess. But that doesn't carry a game, especially not when you do fail a mission after dying twice and have to restart it, only to mark 3 crates of supplies again.What Aragami 2 needed was actually just the improved classic mode following a set of UNIQUE missions with different settings. You can make them sandboxy and give the player full control how they want to approach a situation, but you a) shouldn't punish them for trying something out and failing (check points are a thing you know!!!), and b) make them do grindy, repetitive missions.In essence Aragami 2 made one giant leap forwards, to me, at least, but then 3 steps back. And for almost double the price of the original I can't recommend it I'm afraid. Give us an actually good story mode, some tweaked combat and abilities, perhaps, good level design, and a bigger focus on actual shadow mechanics, and this game would be an easy recommendation.The funny thing is that this reminds me of Sekiro as in younger cousin who wants to be Sekiro, but fails at everything that made Sekiro excellent. Minus any actually engaging combat mechanics, but the rooftop stealth grappling into attack/parry loop is noticeable. So, Sekiro is a better stealth game than an actual stealth game, which just makes me sad.

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow feels like a downgrade visually and mechanically from the original.The original's shadow mechanics created this interesting gameplay loop where you could use shadows created by the environment or yourself for advanced mobility and setups, but this game feels like a disassociation from that in favor of promoting co-op and more aggressive gameplay.While not inherently a bad thing, the fact that the original game started off as this almost stealth-exclusive experience that gave you a very basic idea of what could otherwise be evolved into something greater, this "sequel" decides to do nothing innovative other than reformulating the entire concept into something worse than its original.Animations and textures are mediocre (even on high settings, as far as I could tell) and the story is so shoehorned into your face that it's difficult to appreciate anything the game is actually trying to say. There are so many 5 minute long cutscenes in the first 30 minutes that it feels like I'm watching an extremely mediocre movie moreso than playing a game.Just play the original Aragami. It's not perfect, but it's better than this.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, gameplay.Why is there fall damage in this fast paced action-stealth game?Why do every cutscene have characters clipping either with other characters, or themselves?Why are there obvious seams in the geometry, and also in characters that appear in cutscenes? Why is there a piece of equipment, that changes the main character's skin tone from undead to not-dead?Why are there stairs when guards who investigate suspicious activity will climb cliffs to arrive at their destination?Why is the difficulty of the game only escalated when it introduces a tier of enemy that can spot you across the map?Why does the game break the pacing with very long cutscenes that either do not continue the plot, or give some sort of context for the player's actions?Why are there 3 defence items when 1 would do and the second and third upgrades are both 'more aoe'?Why is almost every interaction labelled 'eavesdrop' or 'observe' even when you are actually talking, investigating, or writing?Why are there mandatory stealth missions in this 3-player co-op game?Why are the mandatory stealth missions in this stealth game so late in the game?Why do you have the ability to take people down non-lethally when taking them down lethally is more effective and leaving them alive is a risk to yourself?Why is non-lethal takedowns and option in a game where you are instructed, and indeed forced to, kill to complete the mission?Why is there one mission where after a long and arduous battle you are instructed to jump down a pit; and if you fail  to grab a ledge you instantly die from fall damage? See earlier question about fall damage.These questions I have no answers for. I hope when the developers was reviewing if their design decisions were conductive to fun gameplay they had sufficient answers to these questions.Secondly, some constructive criticism of the story:Stories usually have a beginning, a middle, and an end. Each part creating the conditions required for starting the next. For example: Your family has a magic sword that is the only way to defeat the bad guy, the bad guy shows up and hides the sword and does bad things that give you a motivation to defeat the bad guy. You find the sword, and by having the sword the bad guy targets you for more bad things. The story concludes with defeating the bad guy. That's a very simple story. Aragami 2's story is not that concise, yet has even less substance.Story threads that could have been cut include the child being returned to the mother leading into the mother exiling herself leading into the mother coming back to eat the soul(?) of the child and then the child having a nap. The story thread where the clan elder is dishonoured by being bad at his job, despite it not being his fault that things went awry, attempting to kill himself, failing, and then acting as if nothing had happened. The part where they return 1\10th of the souls back to the aragami, realising it is not the 10\10ths they need, and then abandoning the plan altogether rather than repeating it 9 more times. The story thread where you are tasked to track down a powerful artist(?) whom you then imprison and continue to do nothing with. None of these story threads advance the plot, or resolve some other plot element. All of them are superfluous as none of them lead anywhere.A generally good writing tip is also to make it so that your characters do not have amnesia. Characters with amensia might seem like a great idea to suddenly reveal sweeping plot changes, but are in fact counter-productive to your story. If a character knew exactly what they had to do but simply could not remember until some random point in the future; that means every action taken up until that point was a waste of effort; they could simply have waited until the character remembered and saved themselves a lot of effort. It is also generally a good idea to employ the writing technique known as 'setup and payoff', the less said the better. Presenting a character and then telling the player that they are in fact a big deal explicitly by stating it in the text, moments before the character does something tremendous, is simply bad writing. It is more bad than doing the same, and then discarding the characters because they never mattered in the first place. This game is guilty of both.In short, do not write a story if you do not master the basic storytelling techniques you might find at a highschool level. I recommend in future to read a primer, or watching any movie, or reading any book, ahead of time to give some inspiration for structure. Also, making the final boss Darth Maul is a bad idea. If this was supposed to be funny, the intent was not clear; though the reaction certainly was. In short I would recommend to be mindful of "cause and effect" when writing.TL;DR-This game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bad.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing Aragami back in 2016. i loved the story and had so much fun both playing it solo and with my friend. Now Aragami has returned better than ever AND I ADORE THE CUSTOMIZATION. At the time of this review there are some small bugs and glitches, but don't let that scare you off. this game has a good story line and plenty of customization. your missions are done in a few different levels with different layouts to do your stealthy killing(or knocking out :D), but if you prefer the "not so stealthy approach" then go for it!Customization in the game has been done in a way that i personally like a lot, your armor is divided into 4 pieces (that can be earned and found throughout the game) but these are purely cosmetic and give no benefits other than looking awesome, the 4 pieces are as following- Mask- chest-piece- pants/leg-piece- swordIt is possible to dye your armor as well, each dye needs to be purchased once and can then be applied to all cosmetic pieces.Compared to the first game you now don't rely on the shadows to regenerate your abilities (no more constant sneaking, such a blessing) and your stamina is shown under a health bar. this is a big change compared to the first game in which a cape was used to show your energy and you had no option to attack enemies out in the open as a tactical approach because you would die instantly.There are plenty of maps in the game. Going through the story, you won't notice it that easily but you eventually repeat the same maps over and over. At the moment this is no problem for me, but i have a feeling that endgame this might have people not enjoy the game as much as they are right now. Then again, this is simply a small thing i noticed but honestly do not mind. I'm used to these kind of things because I've played a lot of RPG's in my life.Multiplayer is a little bit wonky if i say so myself and needs some work, crossplay is an option but for that to work you need to use a specific workaround if you are in different regions (EU/US), if you are in the same region you can easily join through the public lobby system on both console to steam and vice versa. The multiplayer system is simple, you can create a public or private lobby or join a public lobby through the in-game  tab, joining private lobbies is done by receiving an inviteAt the time of this review, rebinding your hotkeys is not possible, this was at the beginning of the game the first thing I wanted to do, but after getting used to the layout anyways, i paid it no mind. This is a small "ease of access" thing that most games have, however .The workaround is only available if you play with 3 people at once and is done as follows: we have player A(EU steam), player B(US steam) and player C(US XBOX).If player B hosts, player A joins via the steam invite sent by player B. Player C can join via public lobby menu

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game on Jan. 4th and as such many of the bugs stated in other reviews have since been fixed. There are still bugs, but it's usually nothing game breaking. The biggest issue is that contextual actions will sometimes not work correctly, or stealth hitboxes will not line up correctly. Meaning, you sometimes sneak right up behind someone and press 'assassinate' but instead your character does a normal sword swing which will allow the enemy to detect you and reveal you everyone around, very annoying, but not the end of the world. If you take things slow, these issues dont usually happen. Aside from the technical side of things, the game is very fun. I got roughly 30 hours of normal gameplay out of it, but that may be reduced to 20 hours if you really rush through each mission. At max, you may get around 40-45 hours out of it if you do every optional challenge for every mission, although you don't get anything for doing so. The stealth, abilities, combat, customization, and rpg elements are all fantastic and well done. The movement system in particular makes for a very fluid and fast-paced experience should you want it to be. The entire game can be played in co-op with up to 3 players total, and overall it reminds me a lot of the WolfPack co-op mode in Assassin's Creed 4 Black Flag. Communication is key to not getting spotted, or you can just run in, katanas out with your friends and basically play what equates to a multiplayer Sekiro with lighter combat mechanics. The story....is eh, but not really a big focus over the gameplay, you even get an achievement for skipping any cutscene you skip first. Overall, pretty damn good game. Lot's of flexibility with light replayability and a good time with friends. If you're a fan of older assassin's creed titles or just looking for something to tide you over after playing Sekiro, then I'd say this is great bang for your buck. I hope Lince Works releases additional content for this game. I could see free or paid dlc taking this game very far. As it stands, there is little to do in-game after finishing it, but there could certainly be any number of additions that give players something to do. Maybe a stealth pvp mode, or randomly generated dungeons, with new enemy variety, and possibly more bosses. All to unlock more cosmetics, runes, or items to broaden your abilities.

name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles
detailed_description: Immerse yourself in a dramatic yet charming and witty world of evidence-gathering, deduction and courtroom battles with this double-pack of the adventures of rookie lawyer Ryunosuke. Set in late 19th century Japan and England, each title features five murder-mystery episodes filled with all the drama, laughs, twists, and “turnabouts” you’ve come to expect from the legally labyrinthine legacy of Ace Attorney. Join Ryunosuke Naruhodo, ancestor of series mainstay Phoenix Wright, as he attempts to uncover the secrets behind an international criminal conspiracy and solve a hauntingly baffling cold case, while tackling a series of tricky trials along the way. Dozens of hours of attorney action awaits you! In the course of each case, you’ll speak to witnesses, examine evidence and clues, and attempt to deduce the dastardly intent behind the crime before proceeding to the courtroom. In court, you will hear testimonies, cross-examine witnesses, and present evidence. And of course, it wouldn’t be an Ace Attorney game if you couldn’t shout “OBJECTION!” when you know you’ve got the facts and evidence needed to contradict the prosecution’s claims and prove your client’s innocence. The game includes a convenient assistance feature in case you hit a dead end in your investigation, so even if this is your first Ace Attorney game, you can get into your amateur sleuthing adventures with ease! Will you be able to crack these clever cases? The game is afoot! NOTE: This game can be played with English audio or with Japanese audio and English subtitles.

It's the Ace Attorney that's so beloved but with a Victorian flair. This game is an easy recommend for anybody with familiarity with the series or just an enjoyment of murder mysteries or logic based puzzle games. _childDocuments_.review: slow start, but once you get onto Resolve you're in for one of the best Ace Attorney games.plot: very very good. 1-2 and 1-4 are a little below average but every other case is very good, even for ace attorney standards. the ending to the first game feels a little unsatisfying at first but everything is explained in Resolve, so don't worry! plot twists are amazing, the mystery behind each murder is very well written. i'll hold back from writing any more on this before i spoil anything because it's best experienced going in blind!characters: the best cast in the series. you'll fall in love with the detectives, prosecutor, assistant, protagonist, defendants and culprits. even the judge, jury and random suspects have great characterisation. if you play games for the characters this is for you.music: great! fully orchestrated, sounds "epic". not the chiptune sort of style you might be used to from the Trilogy but the composers handled the new style very well.setting: i really love the setting. it feels exactly like my perception of what victorian england should feel like.animation: the best in the series. there are only a few cutscenes but they're good. the characters' animations however are amazing, i really hope they put this sort of detail into ace attorney 7! animations alone will make you fall in love with certain characters ;)investigation game-play: the weak part of the game imo. can be slow - the pacing isn't great. if you're patient and like reading/character interactions then you might not mind it. there are no psyche-locks/logic but it's okay. the "move" screen gives you hints for where to go if you're stuck.game-play: pretty great.sometimes multiple witnesses take the stand at once, and the jury system is cool (at first, but i feel it had more potential and eventually felt overused). evidence presentation and pressing are entertaining and fair. the difficulty is pretty high for the series (definitely harder than AA1/danganronpa/investigations) but i liked that. would still be fine for beginners if you're up for a challenge, though! _childDocuments_.review: I have played all the Ace Attorney games officially available in english: The original trilogy via DS emulator, Apollo Justice, Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice on the 3DS, and Ace Attorney Investigations 1 also on a DS emulator. When TGAA was announced to have no plans of localization I was sad, but having it finally available now on PC makes it no less of a wonderful experience. Of this writing I have just finished TGAAC, the first half of the stories included in the steam release.What I find fascinating is how intricately crafted TGAA is, even when compared to its former games. All the games have 5 cases, and often the cases are isolated from each other, with some cases being completely unrelated to the overarching theme. TGAA has dense and layered stories both within each chapter, and that builds off previous chapters, the finale being the most notable example. Previous titles often had long and confusing investigation sections that were less interesting that the courtroom battles, TGAA condenses investigations and also adds a new mechanic that allows for looking for and deducing contradictions outside of the courtroom setting. All the games primarily deal with 'finding contradictions'. Other games had mechanics that used supernatural elements like the psyche locks, the mood matrix, and the divination seances. TGAA supplants the 'finding contradictions' gameplay by including multiple characters on the witness stand, as well as the jury. While I've enjoyed all the gameplay in the series, having mechanics less reliant on supernatural things and being more grounded on reason and arguments made it even more enjoyable for me. Going backwards in time for the setting allowed for some interesting changes. The other games almost all have Phoenix Wright, Maya, Apollo, Athena, or Miles Edgeworth. Breaking off from the established setting allows for a lot of new things to be done narratively. I understand why it must have been seen as a challenge to localize this game for a western audience. The themes of cultures and societal roles plays a large part in this specific story. There are a few unexplored questions at the end of the first game that I imagine are answered in the second, I imagine that the two games are ideally meant to be experienced together, much like how the original trilogy ended up being.Character designs and animations are excellent, music is excellent, story is amazing. The puzzles are not difficult - there is often much buildup and anticipation before the game requires input by the player, which hints at what needs to be chosen, and input is not required often. What is enjoyable about the series is the deliberately nuanced unraveling of a finely crafted scenario. It has taken me a long time to read this far, but I'm looking forward to reading the second half of Chronicles.I will make the Empire of Britain and the Empire of Japan my enemy to protect Gina.

_childDocuments_.review: I started with The Great Ace Attorney 2 when I began this game, having already bought the first game on my phone and played the fan translation. I was tempted at first to write an early review just for that in the mean time, because in my eyes even the first game is worth the price of this; it's a fantastic entry in the series that more than holds its own, and uses its nature as a spin-off and a fresh slate of characters in all sorts of ways to surprise newcomers to the series. Shu Takumi is the mastermind of Ace Attorney, and the game sees him back in full sprint; there are very few low moments, and every character is as colorful and lovable as you would expect. Its soundtrack is the best in the series by an unfathomable margin in my opinion, full of rich, bombastic orchestral tracks that I'm still not quite as tired of as I thought after two years of repeatedly going back to them, much in the same vein as Professor Layton vs Ace Attorney's (Shu's previous return to the series, no less) music. The comparisons extend to the courtroom as well, with the return of the multi-witness mechanics and the inclusion of new ones that work extremely well, like the addition of a jury that has to be convinced as well (but also give vital information of their own during the closing arguments, in which you have to convince them to turn the tides of their verdict one by one in order to keep the trial going). It's fun, it's refreshing, and it's good; I might not put it among the ranks of Trials & Tribulations or Investigations 2, but it's more than worth playing even by itself.But I held back until now, because I did want to see what the second game had to offer first. I realize that mystery franchises are often the hardest to write sequels for, simply due to diminishing ideas for creative whodunnits, and went in with an open mind -- if nothing else, at least I knew the first game was rock solid. I've played every other game in this series, I should probably add for context here; even spin-offs like Professor Layton vs Ace Attorney (which I adored, personally, despite its flaws) and the extremely good fan translation of Ace Attorney Investigations 2. I say this now because The Great Ace Attorney 2 is, in my humble opinion, far better than any game in the series before it. It is a masterpiece, and if it ends up being the last AA game we get then I'm content to end it on such an absurdly high note. It takes a relatively slow start and continually ramps up the intrigue until it's practically spiraling out of control, plunging you into a web of lies that spans both games in so many ways that it's almost hard to consider them two separate titles, rather than the question and answer arcs of the same story. It's backed up by another brilliant soundtrack, and while 2 reuses quite a bit of music from the first game in revisited locations it still manages to have a full two discs' worth of its own equally incredible tracks. What it all adds up to is the most excitement I've ever felt playing this series; it builds up more hype than any game about courtroom lawyers has any right to do. Early on it occasionally stumbles, sometimes letting you figure something out long before you can present it, but once it hits its stride it never loses it, carrying you along for the last dozen or so hours to its conclusion whether you're fully prepared or not. In that regard, it should be noted that both of these games are quite long, even for the series. My own playtime isn't really accurate, given that I only played 2 on Steam, but they're both easily 30 hours each if you dig in and enjoy the environmental flavor texts and such; they're both five-chapter games, and all of them range from a bit longer to notably longer than the average. If you're a fan of the series this game is a must-play, and the only reason I'd ask anyone new to the series to play another one first is because the rest of the series, as good as it is, might seem a bit lacking after seeing everything this game has to offer. Because these aren't just another Ace Attorney game; this is 'The Great' Ace Attorney, and it fully earns that title.

_childDocuments_.review: The eight Harry Potter movies total over 19 hours. The six extended versions of the Hobbit and Lord of the Rings movies all together are 20 hours. All eleven Star Wars movies put together are 25 hours.So this first "Great Ace Attorney" game has no right to clock in at 30 hours (according to  it somehow took me 39 hours - maybe I left it paused for a while?).Don't get me wrong; there are five cases here, and some of them are rather good. (I personally liked cases 1, 3, and 5, but felt that 2 and 4 were disappointing wastes of time.) The problem is that they are . So very much text to wade through; the characters have leisurely side-conversations at length about every little thing. Yes, I know this is so that the player might not notice that small facts mentioned here and there might become important in a case later, but still. For a completely linear game where all you can do is get through all the text from start to finish, I could have spent my time better than by sitting here for 30+ hours watching Sholmes being daffy, Iris being precocious, and Susato being guarded. Time and time again I thought I was finally on the way to seeing a case wrap up, but no; there would be a curveball thrown, Naruhodo would again find himself on the verge of losing, and the entire case would be run through again from a slightly different point-of-view.I've played several of the Ace Attorney games and have really enjoyed them; my favorite parts are the courtroom scenes where I get to analyze statements, compare them with evidence, and find contradictions in them. So I was disappointed that so much of this game occurs outside a courtroom. (I think episode 2 doesn't even have a courtroom in it at all.) There are plenty of places where a plot point is visible hours before the characters start mentioning it in dialogue, and that's always frustrating. It also has a few leaps of logic that don't really make sense, and a few places where to make progress you need to present a non-obvious item at a non-obvious point during witness questioning, so having a walkthrough to refer to is a must. says that Great Ace Attorney 2 is even longer than this one by four hours, so even though it'll doubtlessly bring answers to the questions left open in the first game, there really are more fun things to do with my time.I miss the days when an Ace Attorney game took around 20 hours. I think that's a much more reasonable length: all of the turnabout without all of the fluff.

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor - or, rather, prequel - to the iconic Ace Attorney series. With a steampunk Victorian setting, it represents a lot of firsts for the franchise, including being the entry that finally convinced the localizers to entirely stop pretending the Phoenix Wright is from California. Honestly, though, the whole 'period piece' setup is a bit of a bait-and-switch - at first, it seems to promise a move away from all the forensic and technical evidence you have to contend with in the more modern games, since you're now operating in a time before DNA-testing, surveillance-cameras and Luminol, at a time when fingerprint identification is still considered a revolutionary new technology used in only a small number of court-systems... not including the British or Japanese one that you get to wrestle with. So, a greater focus on witness-statements and more primitive-yet-ingenious trickery.Buuuuuut then the game introduces you to Steampunk Sher... ahem, HERLOCK SHOLMES, and his Dr. Watson stand-in, who together proceed to invent Steampunk DNA Testing, Steampunk Luminol, Steampunk Surveillance Cameras, and so on. Not that it stops there, even, since they're soon busting out stuff that qualifies as sci-fi even TODAY, which cannot help but feel somewhat ludicrous. But then, this isn't a series that's ever taken itself overly seriously, despite the dead-serious subject matter it often works with - murder, betrayal, emotional trauma and so on.Still, the game DOES have some new entertainments to offer, such as joining Herlock Sholmes in a 'dance of deduction', or going toe-to-toe with the British Jury-System of the time. Certainly a worthwhile outing for any old fan of the Ace Attorney series - and also a treat for any 'Wrightworth'-shippers, I'd imagine, considering how very  the ancestors of Phoenix Wright and Miles Edgeworth are shown to be. Why, just in the second case of the first game, we see them sharing a cabin for a loooooong sea-journey, and get strong hints that Steampunk Phoenix Wright is in the closet... or at least the wardrobe!
