_childDocuments_.review: The game is afoot! and so is my learned friend    One of the best games I have played in a while. This is my second Ace Attorney game played (after the trilogies) and while the trilogies are my all-time favourite so far just for the sheer nostalgia and special place in my heart, this game was battling to be my favourite. ( I am currently finished with the first game and onto the second) Gameplay-wise, this does top the trilogies. It was marvelously interactive, I found the "Dance of Deduction" to be one of the most fun I've ever had playing an Ace attorney game. it made me feel like I am doing something rather than pressing A and RB occasionally while the character did all the thinking for me. I LOVE going back into the evidence and spinning it around, and it not pointing out what I have to do to find it.     However, I also like that it's a little easier to understand. It is by no means simple! but I have to look up what to do less, which I appreciate. The story is easier to follow with many plot twists, though they don't seem unreasonable. But, by far my favourite aspect is the CHARACTERS! Susato is such a lovable helper, Herlock is probably my favourite (I just love his effortless likeability) and Naruhodo is a great main character! He can't compare with Phoenix, but at the same time, it's different. He's cute and cool in his regards. I love the scenery, and the dialogue is amazing! I play it in English, they portray the accents well. I also play it in the Japanese dialogue, and they do great there! The graphics are phenomenal and the idle animations are so cute. I LOVE the jury minigame, and the pursue mechanic is also so nice. I do miss the pysche-locks, the lumisol, and other mechanics of the trilogy but gameplay-wise, this game blows it out of the park! Anyways, 10/10 game

_childDocuments_.review: The Phoenix games only came out as good as they did because of hardware limitations.Lift, those and the word count jumps by 90% but still conveys the same amount of information.The cast is extremely dry this time around, the few wacky characters that are present can't properly bounce off anything because of that, resulting in them just being annoying.The new jury system is a interesting idea, but it never reaches the same impact it had when it was first introduced when it seemed like a dynamic system. The jury exam is sadly linear and will always happen at the same time, a criticism of the system would usually be that it detracts from the Prosecution (the rival character), but since he is so boring this time around, the jury is quite welcome.The trials are interconnected in this one, leading to some great late game cases, what is not great is that the setup cases often feel unsatisfying or unresolved because they have to build up the final.I just don't believe in investing so much time until a game gets good.Too much of what made Ace Attorney so enjoyable is just not present in this title.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is the first international release of two previously Japan-exclusive Ace Attorney prequels helmed by series creator Shu Takumi. These games are on a fundamental level quite familiar to fans of the series in terms of both gameplay and narrative and aesthetic tropes, but the setting is now primarily Victorian London. They also prominently feature characters and names from the classic Sherlock Holmes stories, but as some aspects of those stories are still under copyright in the United States, these games remained Japan-exclusive until 2021 and arrived internationally with some tweaks to circumvent those legal issues. It's a shame that they took so long to get here, though, since these are both very excellent games and among the best in their series, and all the better thanks the remastered visuals and excellent localization. The two games are effectively two halves of a larger story, with heavily overlapping casts of characters and identical gameplay. Many of these characters fall into familiar Ace Attorney archetypes, but most of those put their own spins on their predecessors that help them stand out, and that's to say nothing of highly entertaining "original" characters like Herlock, Gina, and Soseki. This game also introduces several mechanics that build upon the series' existing gameplay and feel like they're worth transplanting to the mainline series. The biggest highlights of these are the Dance of Deduction segments that help break up the traditional point-and-click system of investigation segments by incorporating the deductive elements of the courtroom segments, even if they're usually stretched out excessively long. The new jury system and the changes to the cross-examination system, both within the courtroom trial segments, are also very welcome.The Great Ace Attorney: Adventures serves as an introduction to this new version of Ace Attorney, but it's definitely the shakier of the two. The first two cases are tutorials of the courtroom and investigation gameplay respectively, and only the final trial manages to have a proper Ace Attorney-style victory without asterisks. On the other hand, this contributes to the protagonist's character arc that ultimately satisfies, and the odd-numbered cases are all highlights. Particularly, the pacing of the first case does a great job at building up to the protagonist's first declaration of "Objection!" Still, Adventures ultimately leaves large number of dangling plot threads to be resolved (no pun intended) in the sequel.The Great Ace Attorney 2: Resolve fires on all cylinders even in comparison to Adventures. The game is consistently excellent from start to finish, with the opening case being the weakest only in comparison. Besides having played the first game being more or less necessary, this game's most questionable choice is the odd chronology of the game. The first case focuses on a different protagonist than the rest of either game, the second is a flashback to an unseen case set immediately after the first game's fourth case, and the fourth and fifth "cases" are actually one single case spread across two chapters. Still, it executes all of this superbly, with even the "filler" cases being up there among the series' best. That's to say nothing of how this entry manages to tie together nearly every dangling plot thread left from the first game in an extremely satisfying way, culminating in a spectacular climax.The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is an easy recommendation to just about anyone with an inkling of an interest in Ace Attorney, be they completely new to the series, fans who fondly remember the Phoenix Wright Trilogy, or even fans burned by the more recent mainline games. I eagerly await to see what Capcom has next in store for the Ace Attorney series.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a duology of The Great Ace Attorney Adventures originally released in 2015 and The Great Ace Attorney Resolve originally released in 2017. It is a spin-off to the mainline series featuring Ryunosuke Naruhodo, ancestor of Ryuichi Naruhodo or better known in the west as Phoenix Wright. If you're new to the Ace Attorney Series this is a great place to start. The episodes of the game all connect into an overarching story; each case you solve gives you a piece of the puzzle and builds up towards the final episode. The final episode is stellar and makes the journey through the previous episodes worthwhile despite some of the episodes being rather slow to get through. The antagonist of the whole story is pretty predictable but the journey getting there and the why was fun to experience. The game portrays Britain at the height of its power really well and gives a lot of characterisation of the relationship between Britain and Japan. There is a lot of text to read through so be prepared. All of the main recurring characters are well portrayed and memorable. Just like the other Ace Attorney games there's plenty of quirky and fun characters to enjoy.Ryunosuke Naruhodo is a nervous rookie of law but grows through the episodes where he has doubts about what his goal should be when he defends his clients, whether he should believe in them, do whats right for them or seek the truth.Herlock Sholmes the great detective is active in the game with his logic and reasoning spectacular and although he may act weird and dumb at times he's actually far smarter than he leads on making him a reliable ally in times of need. Kazuma Asogi is a Japanese student of law given a mission by the Japanese Government with the goal of changing the climate of law and justice in his home country. He is Ryunosuke's best friend.Susato is a reliable judicial assistant that is able to give Ryunosuke the push and support he needs when he feels like there is no way forward, her father plays an important role and she at times questions what her father really knows causing her to choose her own path.Barok Van Zieks is the main prosecutor you face against and he is often able to force Ryunosuke into a corner right from the outset, making the accused seem like the true culprit. He has an interconnected history with the overarching story of the game. The game follows the formula of Investigation sections and courtroom sections. In the investigative sections you examine objects and characters to find evidence or information relating towards the case and build up weapons to use for the courtroom sections. In between these investigative sections are Sholmes' Logic and Reasoning Spectacular where you will have to correct Sholmes deductions to make sense of the situation at the given time. Using the powers of observation, you can correct and deduce additional information which is one of Ryunosuke's strong points.During the courtroom sections you cross examine witness testimonies and present evidence to show inconsistencies in their testimony, this game unlike previous entries features multiple witnesses at the stand, so you are able to confer and compare their testimonies on the spot with each other. This is a pretty cool way to include more characters at once rather than sitting through just 1 person at a time. At times when you are backed into a corner by the prosecution the Jury gives their vote and you subsequently have to do a Summation Examination, very similar to a cross examination and pit their statements together to overturn their decision and keep the trial going. By the end of each case you are given a small hint as to what the overall story is about and there's never a large gap between cases creating a good sense continuity while playing.While there is a ton of text to read and go through, these gameplay sections were never too difficult to figure out and it only got really difficult, understandably towards the end. Each episode could vary between a 5hr-12hr each, so best to take your time going through this one.The 3D models and environments were great and it was always easy to identify any evidence or objects of interest. Each character has their quirky movements such as Ryunosuke's bullet sweat, Susato takedown, Sholmes cap flick and Van Zieks destroying of expensive wine. The environments represented how Britain looks fairly well though it leaves out quite a few major landmarks we know of today.Soundtrack is great, many enjoyable themes and its easy to recognise each characters theme when they get their moments. There's a very clear leitmotif especially in Kazuma's theme that invokes a sense of courage to pave the way forward. The pursuit theme is pretty fun and gives you a heroic feel when you figure out the inconsistency. Investigation theme is pretty sick too, really makes you feel like you're a great detective yourself looking for clues. The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a solid entry into the series giving a full complete story, leaving no mystery unsolved and paving the way for the future. There could very well a sequel in the future if they wanted to make one. This game is definitely worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased this game simply because of how amazing the first Great Ace Attorney was. I had played it with a fan translation, and was amazed at how good of a game it was despite it being such a late installment in the series. It introduced so many new things that made it feel so fresh. The cases were great, the characters were hilarious, and the prospect of a direct sequel/part 2 got me quite excited.So, as for Resolve, it was everything I hoped it would be. The story runs so deep. Every case is connected to the final showdown in some way. I found myself looking back at cases not only from Resolve, but from Adventures as well, to connect the dots. There were so many twists and turns, and I love it. It had me second-guessing so many times, which is great for an Ace Attorney game. The predictability of other installments in the series was not nearly as present here. I found there to be quite a few challenging parts, which was quite refreshing. The final case was absolutely spectacular, with so many shocking revelations. I really felt that the final case was possibly the best case in the entire series. If not, it is at least Top 3. It was expertly put together and I do not think I could have enjoyed it any more.I do not want to say too much to spoil the game, so I will leave it at that. If you are looking for a fresh installment to the Ace Attorney series, especially in the area of theme, I would absolutely recommend this game. Both Adventures and Resolve are excellent games and are some of the best. I hope that there may be another installment to this particular series. I would love to see van Zieks, Holmes, Iris, and Gina again.Oh, and Drebber's animations had me laughing so hard.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of the Ace Attorney series, I was quite interested and excited in this series now that it was being localized. Though I would technically "recommend" this collection, that comes with a huge heaping tablespoon of salt as well.I'm not going to sugarcoat it; the first game in this collection/story is BORING. Like, really boring, and super slow. All of the characters feel incredibly one-dimensional. Dialogue is tedious and drawn out to a mind-numbing degree. Many characters (especially Herlock Sholmes) are just idiotic way beyond the degree that would be entertaining. The Herlock Sholmes deduction "minigames" are incredibly slow and repetitive, make the character look even more incompetent, and more often than not just waste the player's time due to how pointlessly easy they are. Despite sporting slow and tedious dialogue, the game ironically also has a serious issue with pacing and rushing through key moments of the story; the few investigations that the story does have are crammed into a single day, which leads to awkward overly detailed investigations of places with seemingly no relevance to the issue at hand. Since trials also only last a single day, every important story beat is crammed back to back which leads up to a feeling that the game will pause for a brief reprieve only for the entire case to just conclude abruptly. The first game has a couple of interesting moments, but it really does get drowned out by the 30+ hours of tedium and the overall insipidness of the story.The second game in the collection (and the conclusion to this duology) however, is AMAZING. The individual cases are much faster paced and exciting - with much more complex characters and its' stories interwoven together to make a really satisfying final picture. A large number of the cases in the second game would honestly rank among my favorite Ace Attorney cases of all time - they're that good. Ideally, I'd just recommend skipping the first game to enjoy the second game, however...In reality, the biggest problem with this series is that the first game does nothing but set up the metaphorical dominoes of the story (a slow and tedious process), while the second game spends the entire time knocking those dominoes down; this is why it's so exciting and memorable. Basically, the first game crawls so that the second game can sprint. Unfortunately, the second game is going to lose all of it's impact without seeing the first half of the story.Personally, I think the second game's merits vastly outweigh the issues of the first game. Keep in mind though, that means trudging through 30+ long and boring hours before you can get to the 30 great and exciting hours. If that kind of commitment seems excessive, I'd recommend passing on the whole collection. Otherwise, I'd still highly recommend it - especially to existing Ace Attorney fans.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write reviews often, but I feel this game(s) definitely deserve it.The stories told over the course of both games are in my opinion the best in the series, often ending on a more somber and realistic notes than in other installments. All storylines are resolved by the end of the second game, culminating in the grand finale, that's on par with "Rise from the Ashes" or "Farewell, My Turnabout". The music is the best in the series so far, fitting to every character, every location, and of course every part of the trial.The cases were very well written, often making pretty solid twists and playing with players' expectations. I could't really find any "weak" cases, I thoroughly enjoyed all of them.My only issues with the game were that sometimes during the trial you have to present an item that fits your narrative, but doesn't actually prove anything, so you'd probably just miss it. Also the game may occasionaly crash (but autosave mitigates it well, and it wasn't a major problem).Overall I believe it's one of the greatest (IF not the greatest!) games of the series, which makes it even more infuriating that this gem remains so underrated. From what I've heard this duology was supposed to be a trilogy, but because the first part wasn't very popular in Japan they've scrapped that idea, and waited 4 years (or 6 if we count from the first game) with English localisation for both games. Which was a crime more heinous than the ones in games.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played every game in the Ace Attorney series. After Dual Destinies and Spirit of justice, I was dismayed at the stark decline in quality of the series and not hopeful for it's future, despite it being among my favorite video game series. As it turns out, a change of setting and the return of the legendary original series director Shu Takumi is exactly what the series needed. These games do a fantastic job of telling a complete and expertly-woven story with fantastic characters while also providing the thought-provoking and exciting gameplay and witty, intelligent dialogue the series is known for. I never thought any Ace Attorney game could surpass the prowess of the original, but upon completion it is clear to me that The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is the best game in the series. I was initially worried that, with how complicated and interconnected of a story it weaves in the first 9 cases, the game would not be able to wrap everything up in a satisfying conclusion in the final case, but I was proven wrong in a spectacular manner, and the game's final chapter feels like not only the culmination of the story of Ryunosuke Naruhodo and all the people he meets on his long journey, but also the culmination of a 20-year-old franchise that has innovated and defined it's own genre of puzzle-solving visual novel. As far as specific mechanics go, this game introduces many brand new ideas to the court system and the investigation segments alike, such as the jury examinations, witness pursuit (though I feel that this particular mechanic is a bit underused), and the incredibly fun and vibrant Great Deductions. It is very refreshing after the cluttered and obligatory mechanics of the most recent preceding Ace Attorney games. Also to help combat the staleness that had begun to plague the series, this game has a completely new cast of characters and constantly builds and expands its immersive setting. There are a slew of historical references and references to The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes that keep the world interesting far beyond the surface level.Overall, if you enjoy Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney Trilogy, this game is basically a must-have. It feels like the magnum opus of the Ace Attorney series, in which the developers and writers have finally perfected the core gameplay/formula while simultaneously defying every expectation a long-time fan would have going into it. I'm not sure what's in store for the future of this series, but The Great Ace Attorney will be very difficult to live up to. It's a once-in-a-lifetime kind of game and a fantastic ride from start to finish, and I implore anyone who may be interested to try it for themselves.

_childDocuments_.review: is the complete duology made from the two games  and , both visual novels developed and published by CAPCOM.It follows the adventures of Ryuuichi Naruhodo's (Phoenix Wright's) ancestor, Ryunosuke Naruhodo, as he, by a weird twist of fate, ends up becoming a practising defence lawyer in the late 19th century London.My favourite character from this game is (yes, he's based on a real person). Because of this, all subheaders in this review will be four-word alliterations. (I've tried to underline the most significant word for the subheader. Don't be too hard on me, I tried my best.)I'll also be referring to "the original trilogy" in this review, by which I mean the Phoenix Wright games.I'll not speak much on the story, but one thing right of the bat: Every case ties into the overarching plot. There are no "filler" cases like in the original trilogy. Yes, even the tutorial cases have some significance.In typical Ace Attorney fashion, many cases are ridiculously convoluted but the momentum of the courtroom drama tends to make you forget about it, which is good of course. They're not meant to hold under heavy scrutiny, they're roller coaster rides that you go on for the thrill.This game respects its setting though. Most of the time. For example:In one case, a friend of Ryunosuke's develops a chemical compound that makes blood change color depending on "whose it is". My initial response was "surely a 19th century court won't accept that as evidence", and it didn't! Coming from the final case of the original trilogy, this surprised me in a good way.As previously mentioned, this is a visual novel. Most of this game is spent reading. There are a few things in place to spice it up however.This game is divided into 10 episodes (5 each for GAA and GAA2), and with the exception of 3 episodes, they have the same structure: one or more investigation phases and one or more trial phases.In the investigation phase you talk to people and investigate the crime scene to build your case for the trial phase. While this part may seem free-roam, it's actually pretty heavily on rails, and the game will not move on to the trial without you having all the evidence you need (thank goodness).To break up the investigation phase this game has the Logic and Reasoning Spectacular (also known as the Dance of Deduction) minigame where Ryunosuke helps the character Herlock Sholmes figure out some sort of truth using the environment and evidence. This is a fun visual spectacle if nothing else.In the trial phase you listen to formal witness testimony and point out contradictions in their statements using evidence. You can press their statements to reveal new information or alter their testimony.Unlike earlier Ace Attorney entries, multiple witnesses can be in the stand at the same time. Another witness may react to the currently speaking witness' statement, which you can then pursue to gather even more information.Also new to this entry is the Summation Examination game, in which you try to convince the jury (who have all voted your client guilty) why they should allow the trial to continue. This involves selecting two different jurors and pitting them against each other for some reason, usually because their statements contradict.The original Ace Attorney trilogy comprised of the first visual novels I ever read. I've since read a lot of different ones, and I've realised that Ace Attorney can be quite inconvenient to maneuver at times.I'll go over a few good and bad things:Even with "skip read text" on, the text goes by so slow. The reason for this is because Ace Attorney games alter text speed and pauses to give an impression of how the speaker is saying their lines. It's not worth it. There is also no skip button, a feature found in even the oldest visual novels out there.This is at its worst during Herlock Sholmes' deductions, which take FOREVER to get through. They first have you read through his deduction, then you have to go through them AGAIN to correct his mistakes.This game's soundtrack is stellar. It uses significantly more classic instruments compared to the original trilogy's more electronic soundtrack, which is fitting considering the game's setting.I'm particularily partial to the Cross-Examination theme, which I consider the best in the series. Compare the  version, which is played during most witness testimony to the  version, which is usually played during the final critical testimony you have to work with.There are many more good ones, but I'll put  as my last example. It really reminds me of a puzzle.Steam Achievements for this title are tied to in-game "accolades". Some are gotten by just playing, for others you need to do certain things during your playthrough. The window of opportunity for some of there are as short as one dialog box, and if you miss one you have to either reload a save or start the episode all over again. Because of the aformentioned lack of skip mode, this is beyond tedious and I'll never see myself doing it. Use a guide if you desperately want all accolades in one go.There are a few surprises thrown in, which are more likely to get you if you're an old fan.There's for example a moment where you have to , even though you have  that you can do so. You instead have to realise you have to do it based on other factors. This was great! I personally wished you had to use the new courtroom mechanics more, and in even more unorthodox ways. It may have sounded like a lot of negatives, but this is a really good visual novel aside from the things I've mentioned. It clearly respects itself and its characters more than, say, Spirit of Justice. It's also a step in the right direction for the future of Ace Attorney (if there is still a future that is).I love Phoenix, Edgeworth and Maya as much as the next guy, but this visual novel is a prime example of what this series needed: new characters and new stories.If you've never read a visual novel before this is a  entry point to the medium. It has more gameplay than normal visual novels, so you'll be eased into the experience! You'll also not miss the normal visual novel conveniences like skip mode and the text scrolling issue I've mentioned.For returning fans I say: This game is for you. It's new, it's fresh, and it's Ace Attorney.

_childDocuments_.review: What a truly marvelous game and experience it was.I waited until I finished both before I would leave a review and 63 hours later here we are!So the pretense, as a huge Ace Attorney fan I was excited for more in the series and at first had skepticism on whether or not this would live up to my expectations of it being great so I tempered them. I won't make this an extremely long review but will point out what I did enjoy and didn't enjoy. The music, the story, and the setting was such a beautiful package for this duology. I do agree with people's sentiment that the first game by itself unfortunately doesn't hold much water and it's alright at best do to the overall story just ending abruptly and feeling like you never really got a chance to understand everything at play.The bright side though, is that the second game is a masterpiece of it's own. Essentially the first game more or less sets up the story to be explored and resolved in the second game. It's a long journey that feels exhausting to the point of wanting to just give up and drop the game after the first one but the payoff is worth it. Luckily this game sells as a package with both the first and second game so you can experience both of them but I must advise to really push through to the second game and it's slow start to get to what I and I believe some other fans would concur as one of the best games in the entire series. If I would to compare to Original Ace Attorney Trilogy, I would say I prefer the Great Ace Attorney Chronicles over the Trilogy just because I am slightly biased the setting of Britain, detectives etc but also because as a whole package Chronicles really nails it on the head. With Trilogy I felt it was easy to enjoy certain aspects of some things while disliking others but it was always hard to say as a whole the game felt like a masterpiece of sorts. With Chronicles, it felt like they took everything they learned from Trilogy and made it that much better. The entire package from the music to the setting, characters etc were all just wonderful and made for a great experience that I will always remember. I do hope one day we get a third installment in this chronicle as it truly deserves one. Overall If you're a fan of Ace Attorney in general, or maybe detective stories/investigations I recommend you give this game a shot even if you're not a big fan of visual novels. I personally don't care for many myself but felt glued to this game, and previous experience of the Original Trilogy is not needed to understand or play this game.Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, awful PC port...Ever since the original release of Dai Gyakuten Saiban, I've been dreaming of having a chance to play, what can arguably be considered some of the best Ace Attorney games in the franchise. Now finally... 6 years after the original release of Dai Gyakuten Saiban and 4 years after the release of Dai Gyakuten Saiban 2, I finally got to play them... Words cant describe how happy and satisfied I feel having been able to enjoy these games by myself.-The PC port has some issues-Let's begin with the elephant in the room... Now, it's pretty clear that these are just the mobile versions of both games ported to PC. Even though playable, it's quite clear that these games were not designed to be played on a PC. Exit game... Where is it??? Seriously, not having an option to exit the game in the main menu was already a pretty bad sign. The only way to exit the game is through the options, which honestly isn't where an average gamer would look for it. Exit game is typically located in the main menu, this is honestly something that should be fixed as soon as possible in my opinion.It's very easy to see how muddy the textures look and how models clip through each other on higher resolutions. Anti-aliasing needs some serious improvements and the game needs more options for the players to finetune the game for their computers, there are only 4 customisable options in the game: Resolution, Windowed/Borderless, AntiAliasing On/Off and V-Sync On/Off.  That's right, the graphics are not customisable, you're not able to tune the frame-rate... Just very barebones settings in general.The frame-rate is locked to 30 by the way, this includes all the main menu animations and this frame cap is there seemingly for no reason whatsoever. And before you say that it's normal to be locked at 30fps, I have to disagree since even the Nintendo Switch version runs  at 60fps. Luckily there is an amazing mod to fix the frame-rate alongside some other issues:  And the audio... God, how did Capcom mess this up so bad? Luckily there is also an amazing mod to fix the soundtrack:  I do use both of these mods myself, but I have to say that these issues shouldn't have been there to begin with. If you don't want to deal with all this garbage, I would honestly recommend buying the Nintendo Switch version instead if you already own the console. And please Capcom, for the love of god... Fix the PC version ASAP, I honestly expected better from a 39,99€ game.-Localisation: The Good-Episode 1 The Great Departure is the way Ace Attorney games should be localised. Just the fact that you allowed us to play this game with the Japanese dub instead of the English dub was already a huge step in the right direction. Honestly, that is the way I would love to enjoy the mainline entries in this franchise, give us the option to play the games with the original dub, original character names and Japanese elements.I know I may just be beating a dead horse here by mentioning Ace Attorney Investigations 2, but honestly, I would love to play both Investigations 1 and 2 with a similar localisation seen in Episode 1 The Great Departure. Hell, I would love to play every game in the franchise with that kind of a localisation. Perhaps something worth attempting in a future entry?-Localisation: The Bad-Now... I have to express that I am disappointed about some characters having their names changed. Now just to be clear, I am not referring to Herlock Sholmes here. I am referring to characters that didn't really have any copyright issue behind their change of name such as: 'Mitrov Stroganov' being renamed to 'Bif Strogenov' , 'Benjamin Dobinbough' being renamed to 'Albert Harebrayne' and most disappointing of all... 'Haori Murasame' being renamed to 'Rei Membami'Some of the changes were completely understandable, but honestly there were a lot of names that should not have been altered to begin with, unfortunately the localisation team went too far with the changes... Again.-Herlock Sholmes-I know that some people have an issue with the fact that Sherlock Holmes was renamed to Herlock Sholmes and Watson into Wilson. However, this happens to be the only way we're able to enjoy these games in the west. It's not Capcom's fault that Sherlock Holmes has such awful copyright issues. If you want to complain to someone about this, complain to Conan Doyle Estate, since Capcom really didn't have a choice here.-DGS1-An absolute master piece, I loved every moment of it. I honestly don't really have bad things to mention about this one. Perhaps my only complaint would be the lack of a task list during the investigation sections of the game. The characters were fun and unique, all culprits had solid motivations that even made you somewhat sympathetic of their fate.-DGS2-I have to say that, DGS2 had a lot to live up to as a sequel to DGS1 and it is clear to see that it was aiming to be even more ambitious than it's predecessor. However, there were a few downsides to the scale of the game. For example, the lack of animated cutscenes was somewhat disappointing as they really contributed to the overall feel of the first game. However, the pros really outweigh the cons in this sequel. It had a significantly better story overall, having more twists and being darker than its prequel. It introduced plenty of new characters and expanded the soundtrack. -Conclusion-Whether you're new to the franchise or a long time fan of the Ace Attorney games, this is something you absolutely have to play and enjoy for yourself as this is one of a kind masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: This courtroom text adventure game in late 19th century Japan and British have a lot of features, even with the previous Ace Attorney works are very different. With the detailed character costumes and backgrounds, the strong sense of history and atmosphere, the majestic music, and excellent characterization, along with the game's detailed 3D character animation, players can experience an unprecedented adventure. In the plot, The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles presents a layer-by-layer, cocooning type of plot development, each chapter of the story is closely linked, and ambiguous, no chapter is meaningless, and in the final unraveling of all the mystery, the feeling of shock and excitement brought to the player is unprecedented in any text adventure game.The reviews of The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles tend to be polarized, and not without reason. The progression of the plot brings with it an overwhelming lack of tension in the first and middle stages of the game. The design of many of the cases in the game seems rather undisciplined, neither interesting nor deep... The Great Ace Attorney: Adventure, as the first half of the game, though the development of the subsequent plot paved a lot of ambushes, the design of the plot and puzzles makes it less interesting and often difficult to motivate players to continue playing. The climax of the game comes too late, whether the player can persist to this point is a huge problem. At the same time, the Steam version of the game globally locks 30 frames, and can not set the Japanese voice is also a very huge drawback, and very damaging to the player's gaming experience.The quality of The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is actually not that bad. But this can only be concluded after you have experienced the entire game in its entirety... And I think this is actually the biggest drawback of this game because the ability to keep the player until the climax of the plot is the biggest pain point of this work. If you are very patient, love the Ace Attorney series, and love the suspenseful story of players, then The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles will not let you down. If you do not have any of the above elements, perhaps The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles will not give you a memorable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, The Great Ace Attorney. This duology of games with it's endearing cast of characters and very gripping story has sold me fully. As a longer-time fan of the Ace Attorney franchise I had heard mixed opinions on this game and was hesitant to try it out - but to me The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is well worth the price. Getting the obvious out of the way first: Yes, TGAA has trouble with its pacing, especially the first game. The first two cases are extremely slow paced, which for a visual novel can be detrimental as engagement will suffer for it. While it does pick up from there, the rest of the first game and a lot of the second game still have a pacing issue, most notable in the filler cases. It is very noticable that this was initially meant to be a single game, which was too lengthy and thus split into two. The first game in the duology got the short end of the stick in terms of engaging cases and story, sadly. There's little to say in its defence here - this was an avoidable issue and can definitely turn people away from the game.Another point of warning is that the game deals with some heavy topics in the racism/sexism that Ryunosuke and Susato often encounter in their time in England. While I personally think it good that the game does not shy away from addressing these issues and instead have the Japanese law duo fight and overcome these prejudices, it can understandably be a turnoff for some. Luckily, though, The Great Ace Attorney also does a lot of things right. To begin with: the characters. The main cast consisting of Ryunosuke, Susato and Herlock Sholmes are all very different in character and mesh pretty well together. Ryunosuke's general unknowingness stands in sharp contrast to Susato, who is well-versed in general knowledge. And Sholmes' character is wholly chaotic in the best way. He's almost always entertaining in some form, whether that is through his curious methods of deducing or his general inability to act like a normal person, whenever he's on screen it usually brings me great amusement. And that's just the main three; many of the rest of the cast also have a lot to love. Ranging from the intimidating Barok van Zieks and Lord Stronghart to the adorable Iris Wilson - there's only a few of the recurring characters who I didn't feel at least something positive for. The interactions of them with the main cast and with each other add a lot to the worldbuilding. None of the recurring cast feels like they were there just because a character was required for the story. The story itself is the most important part of a visual novel, and these games deliver. The story, importantly, feels cohesive despite its pacing issues. The games have a lot of dark undertones and the story takes itself really seriously. For a genre where the story is heavily important, that's good! A main reason for me to keep wanting to play this game for long sessions is to see where the story would go from there. To me it was not a predictable storyline and when the story concluded and all was revealed - everything makes sense. The twist reveals are logical, the motives line up and the conclusion is very satisfying. The climax is honestly my favourite part of the duology and it left a very strong impact. Though I must say that I love every single bit from the third case of the second game all the way until the very end: these to me are some of the strongest cases the series has to offer. Another point in favor is the soundtrack. This games music shines the most in its character themes, whether that's Susato's soothing song, Sholmes' almost-serious detective theme, Barok's intimidating theme that really sells his accordingly intimidating character or Iris' whimsical vibe with its upbeat tones that fit her cheerful nature to a tee; when a character has their own theme it is without exception a great exposition of their character. The court and area themes do not disappoint either, the moderato/allegro cross-examination themes keep these sections engaging while the suspense themes rise the tension as they should. And that's not even having mentioned the Dance of Deduction themes - wonderful pieces of music only adding to why I love that mechanic so much.Speaking of which: this game adds a few mechanics onto the standard Ace Attorney formula. Already having mentioned the Dance of Deduction, I'll start with that: these are short sections that break up the investigation segments with a logic minigame of sorts. In these sections, Ryunosuke and Susato try to make sense of whatever ridiculous nonsense Sholmes has cooked up this time in order to reveal new information. They are generally pretty simple but they serve their purpose well and the charming animations help sell this mechanic. The second and third mechanics take place during the court sections. One is to have multiple witnesses at once, where they can react to each other's statements which reveals new information. The other makes use of the jury system, where Ryunosuke has to convince the jury of his client's innocence by finding contradictions in their reasoning. These mechanics serve to add a little extra depth to the court sections, which for me is appreciated. It makes you feel like you're actually making progress whenever one of these shows up, helpful because of the general lenghtiness of the court sections. In conclusion, this game to me is definitely worth the investment. The second Great Ace Attorney game is my favorite game ever made, though I tried to be as objective as possible writing this review. This duology is not perfect, but if you're okay with playing a slower-paced game I 100% recommend it. One of the franchises highs, for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: Having finished the game on Android devices a few weeks ago, I highly recommend this game now. The story is great and in-game mechanism is very interesting. The 'turning around' elements are now more structural and embedded within the whole story in a rather subtle and symbolic way. It's no longer the forced 'turn around' as in Ace Attorney 1, 2, 3. It's also great to see how the game discuss the themes of ethnic racism and internationalism in that fictional yet realistic early 1900s. It's inspiring and sometimes consoling to read between lines about how in the game the Brits and the Japanese find common grounds as human beings.That said, lacking any Eastern Asian language (e.g. CJK) is rather disappointing. I understand that it's Japanese students studying in the UK, so they ofc speak English. Still, it's a pity that young people in Eastern Asia countries, especially those that still lack a just legal system, cannot play and experience the story in a language that connects more with them. I wish one day Capcom would supplement this release with proper Eastern Asian languages.Also, it's 2021 and still there's no high definition texture. It's a shame, really.对中文或日文用户来说，可以购买此游戏，然后自己找国内汉化组过去的汉化版本在电脑上玩。此版故事和机制都很不错。然而可惜没有中文或日文等语言，使我等东亚学生不得以更亲近的语言游玩并感同身受。其他评价可阅读以上英文不想（主要是不想再写一遍）。

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a fantastic duology and albeit flawed a brilliant experience to play through.I played the first game all the way back in summer 2021 and finally got around to playing the sequel in March of 2023: And while my memory was a bit hazy, I cannot stress enough that the characters are so memorable that picking up 1.5 years later was no issue. As soon as someone came on screen I immediately remembered them, and that just is peak character writing to me.Things to consider:The biggest issue that I have with especially the first game is the excruciating slow pace. And the issue to me doesn't necessarily lie in the slow storytelling, it's more that the game often gives you clues so early that you figure out what's going on before most of the characters can. While that eliminates the tedium of the mainline games where I remember often being stumped, not knowing how to continue, GAA takes it a bit too much into the easy direction. GAA feels much more like a courtroom drama and less like detective games, which means you pretty much always know the culprit from the get-go and instead of piecing together what happened it's much more like: "alright, we know the destination, but how do we get there and out of the current conundrum".As soon as I understood that I had a much better experience, leaned back for the ride, and enjoyed everything the game was throwing at me.Especially the second game goes hard. It culminates in a grand finale that to my satisfaction was able to tie up literally every single loose end. It doesn't leave any question unanswered and gives all the characters closure. I haven't felt that good about finishing a story in a while.One other thing that stood out to me was the brilliant localisation. The team that translated these games went above and beyond. I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys visual novels or the mainline series. The second game for sure has catapulted itself into my top favourite entries of the franchise, and I will remember the characters of the duology fondly.

The deductions and corrections system is somewhat reminiscent of the "testimony / press" system of old, but WAY more tedious. You have to play out each and every dialog line a second time, with the full overdramatic animations and TONS AND TONS OF FINGER SNAPPING. It's just dreadful. Takes forever to get through, instead of just being able to cycle through the dialog lines quickly to get to the one you want to correct (like pressing on dialog in the original Ace Attorney trilogy).The third case was the final nail in the coffin for me because they introduced a character who just snaps his fingers as a character trait, on top of the filler dialog just droning on and on.The only way I could recommend this is: "if you liked the original Ace Attorney trilogy but wish it was slower paced and even more dramatic, with tons of filler dialog, and you love the sound and animation of finger snaps, this is the duology for you".

_childDocuments_.review: Everything is be 95% spoiler free other than mentions of some names.Overall it's pretty much your ace attorney experience with new characters, so if you've been playing ace attorney, it's gonna be a very familiar gameplay. This game is definitely more for Ace Attorney fans, but still playable for new players.Score: 8.5/10Gameplay mechanics:- Introduction to pursuing other witness' testimony felt slightly fresh although in the end it's very clear on what you have to do except maybe once on chapter 1.5. However I do feel like due to the tendency of player to immediately pursue another witness, they could have just made it that we could get clues when we actually decide to NOT pursue the other witness.- Judicial Assessment is another new thing in Ace Attorney Series. At first I was quite scared that if I actually pressed on certain testimony, I would actually get a quick guilty verdict for the defendants, but in the end it's just the same thing as Cross Examination, just toward the jury.- Sholmes Deduction Spectacular... or something. A mini-game for investigation, just like Pearl's magatama or Edgeworth's game with connecting clues. However I do feel like... having to listen to Sholmes (stupid) deductions and have it repeated again when we correct it feels even more.... tiring.- Personally I like the trials more than the investigations, but at the very least the game gives you hints if you haven't finished looking for everything yet (Thanks to Susato or Iris). But of course, there's no mention of what the clue is or what you need to present to the person.- The game is very forgiving when you do mistakes. 5 chances, refreshed after every trial part. Unlike some parts in normal Ace Attorney series, you get a life bar and it will be depleted each time you do something wrong, however there are times when the game would do major or critical damage if you would do something wrong in the normal game. Although you can just save and load the game, I feel that it made your decision to really be accurate and you must not miss at all. GAA doesn't have that at all and you're free to make mistakes if you want to and I kind of... feel that it's a bit of a miss.Character (Art, Character, Voice)- It has always been something with Ace Attorney character designs where the defense will always have wide eyes and the prosecutors having sharp eyes. I guess they're always trying to give the same 'Bright Eyed, Phoenix Wright'-like defense lawyer as protagonist. But then again given by the surname Naruhodo, the protagonist is literally the ancestor of Phoenix Wright, japanese wise. But also all prosecutors in ace attorney have always been hot, one way or another.- Maybe it's just me missing Detective Gumshoe but there's not many big and bulky character except 1.2 and  2.5. However they do have diversity of character designs, mostly from the witnesses.- Name changes still happen for english adaptations (aside from the obvious Herlock) but does not do much for the game experience (other than the obvious sholmes)- I'm only playing with English voice so I'm not sure how it sounds in Japanese, but I do feel like the 'Objection' part, at least doesn't leave as much impression as the old Ace Attorney games where Phoenix would just literally scream the word. Van Zieks' 'Objection', though does suit him very well but that might be me being biased. Judging from the videos I've seen on YouTube, they probably sound better (Especially with van Zieks being voiced by Tsuda Kenjiro)- Character breakdown after they do something wrong, especially the culprit's final breakdown after they've been exposed has always been something that most players are looking for, however perhaps due to the usage of 3D models, they're very limited on what they can do along with the expressions compared to their previous games with character sprites and animations all drawn by hand. Although the best Culrpit breakdowns do happen in 1.1 and 2.5, for me personally.- They try to put different British accents in the game so it is quite good for the diversity, although it might be a bit of a problem for those who might not understand them or even uses English as their second language.- If it's not obvious, I love Lord van Zieks, thank you very much.Sound and Music- Perhaps due to trying to match with the Britain's music back in the 19th century, the music feels quite lackluster compared to the previous games with more.. upbeat and perhaps retro sounding (which is considered modern compared to the ones in GAA)- There's no option to adjust the volume of music, voice, and sound effect. Only on or off. I wish there's a liberty for the player to adjust them to taste- They do keep the same sound effects from their older games like the shocking sound when someone says Objections or Hold It, the twinkling sound when someone realizes something, the sound when someone is shocked, and even the judge's gravel sound. It makes it even more nostalgic with the familiarityStory (No spoiler, just opinions):- The game is split into two parts. I personally find the second part to be better as things start to be in place.- Personally the best case which makes things fall into place so well is still 2.2 where I have no trouble in fitting the pieces together. It also has a good ending for not only the defendant, but also the culprit, I suppose.- Just like your usual Ace Attorney game, there will be times when you feel really stuck and you're not sure which exactly evidence to present even when I know which part of the testimony to pick. For me it was 2.3 right near the end, and 2.5 somewhere in the middle which was where I had to consult to a guide.- A lot of part of the story during the investigation really made me feel bored not gonna lie. I had everything on auto (except 2.4 and 2.5) but I guess it's because it's an unvoiced visual novel other than a few scenes and things like 'OBJECTION'Others:- I love van Zieks so much. He's actually much smarter than most prosecutors I've encountered in previous Ace Attorney games. I love his design and I sympathize him.- WTF, Herlock and No ♥♥♥♥, Herlock.-  Always. And I mean ALWAYS show your defence lawyer badge to everyone during investigation. For funsies. You might not know what you'll get (spoiler: a certain steam achievement)- I wish Wagahai would make more appearance in the game. But I guess she's replaced by the appearance of Toby in part 2 as she loses her significance to the story.- As usual, the game has one route only. Me personally I would be van Zieks' side because dude definitely needs a friend like wtf- 'YES!' is so weird. I don't know why they put it in the game, mostly in 1.1. But I suppose Naruhodo was still a greenhorn.- They actually put some inside jokes for Ace Attorney fans as easter eggs. I find them endearing.TL;DR. Your usual Ace Attorney game with new characters. Not my most favorite Ace Attorney game, but enjoyable nevertheless. Van Zieks I can be your brother yes.Score: 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: After many years of waiting, we finally have The Great Ace Attorney available officially in English. I honestly thought we’d never see the day, but I am definitely not complaining now that they’re finally here!The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a collection of two games: The Great Ace Attorney: Adventures and The Great Ace Attorney: Resolve. These two games are spin-offs of the main Ace Attorney series and take place in the Meiji era (late 1800s to early 1900s) rather than the near-future. The two were first released on the 3DS in 2015 and 2017 and were never released outside of Japan. As such, this is the first time we are seeing them officially in English in any form.These games are basically full-blown visual novels with some light gameplay additions thrown in. The vast majority of your time will be spent simply reading text, but the gameplay elements that are here are pretty cool – letting you take part in investigations, presenting evidence in court, pressing witnesses for information, and generally just being able to move around and interact with the game world.The Great Ace Attorney takes this gameplay up a notch compared to the original games. The same core “investigate for evidence, find contradictions, present evidence” system is all there, but now you have a jury to worry about and you’ll need to swing their opninions in your favor by pitting their own words against each other. It’s like a regular cross-examination, but with an additional layer and it was pretty cool in practice.In general though, the gameplay here is still not too complex, but a nice step up from what I was used to with the main games and it gives the story that touch of interaction that it needs to keep you involved.The first case is a bit slow to get going, but once it does, it really hooked me. In fact, that was pretty much every case after that point. They each follow that same steady rise in pacing as they go on and get more and more complex. What you think happened at first is never quite right and the twists and such are both ridiculous, yet feel right at home in this series and some of them really caught me off guard with how well executed they were.The third case in particular takes a very interesting turn towards the end that is quite unlike any other case across the entire series. It exemplifies all that I like about these games: pacing that rises and falls naturally with each development, characters that actually have... character, and mysteries that are somehow 10x more complicated than they look. Each case is a journey in itself and I’m happy that these two games were able to maintain that same level of quality from the main series.The games also manage to have all of these serious cases and crimes to solve, but never lose that lighthearted feeling. There’s the ridiculous character quirks, the dumb one-liners, and I really love how this series is able to make references to itself even when its not necessary. I laughed out loud when I found out who the first prosecutor was – because of course they had to make him the same as the one from the main series but bill him as an ancestor.It’s the little touches like this that really give the series its unique feel and I know some may say this makes it hard to take seriously, but the story can get serious when it wants – it just knows when to do so and can actually manage that balance there.You can expect around 60-80 hours for the two games combined. The second game is longer than the first, but they’re both fairly meaty visual novels and are comparable in length to the recent Ace Attorney Trilogy release despite that one containing three games instead of just two.The collection is hard locked to 30 fps but does support higher resolutions. I played them on both 1440p and 4K and the 3D models and such look great and I didn’t have any technical issues there. Control-wise, the collection plays fine on both controller and keyboard and mouse – the latter of which is rebindable.Simply put, The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is the best visual novel release of the year. It takes all of the series’ strengths, throws it into a new and interesting setting, and delivers an Ace Attorney experience quite unlike any other. On-point writing, excellent comedic balance, gameplay that is actually interesting – it’s got pretty much everything and is an easy recommendation for fans or even newcomers to the series.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: This duology manages to strike a great gust of fresh air into the franchise, elevating the series to even greater heights than the original trilogy managed to achieve all that time ago.  The extra focus given to developing grounded, believable character relationships shines especially brightly here, leaving you feeling far more attached to the narrative and cast as a whole; it undoubtedly makes every well-earned revelation even more impactful than you'd expect from the series so far. I think the series could be a great entry point for new fans, too. Don't feel like you have to play all the other games to give these two a try: you can easily approach these as if they're a soft 'reboot' of Ace Attorney as a whole. Something, truthfully, the mainline games have been crying out for for some time. I'll be looking forward to a third game, if it ever arrives!

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney? More like the Greatest Ace Attorney!I've played all mainline Ace Attorney games (except the AA6 which I will play when it releases on PC in January 2024) and the Layton crossover so I would consider myself as a fan of the franchise. The Great Ace Attorney is not a mainline entry into the Ace Attorney and should be perceived as a spin-off to the franchise, even though the game is directed by Shu Takumi, the creator of the franchise as a whole, who approached this spin-off in a more liberal way, meaning bigger changes to the franchise’s core mechanics. The game consists of 10 chapters varying in length and after finishing the third I was already completely sold on it being the best Ace Attorney game I’ve ever played. One thing I always disliked about original Ace Attorney games is the lack of an overarching story, something which the Layton crossover introduced, and one that complemented the concept of Ace Attorney brilliantly making each case feel more important and meaningful. So, I was delighted that this over 70 hours long game wasn’t just cases tied loosely together, but consisting of one overarching story that unfolds over the course of the game. The investigation parts were the weakest parts of each Ace Attorney game. This is also true for The Great Ace Attorney, although the investigations that happen latter in the timeline were enjoyable, the introduction of “Sholmes’s Logic and Reasoning Spectacular” really helped the otherwise slower and blander parts of the game by involving you in the gameplay in a really fun way.The trials also profit greatly by the creative liberty made possible by this not being a mainline Ace Attorney game. The reintroduction of multiple-witness testimony first introduced in the Layton crossover was a great addition and while the summation examination seem a bit forced at times, I really liked how they played into the course of the trial.The Great Ace Attorney is a great entry to the franchise, one that everyone who even remotely enjoyed one of the more popular Phoenix Wright games should definitely give a shot, you will not regret it for one bit.

_childDocuments_.review: An exceptional AA game. Yes, game, because despite the 2 titles in this collection they're better understood as two halves of the same game. A great conclusion buoyed by the usual highs of the AA franchise: exceptional writing, criminal cases that border on the insane and strong characters. The setting and scenario really strengthens the game and the casual period-accurate racism gives the game a lot of flavor. The game is structured in a way that the finale, seeded from the very beginning, builds to one of the best in the series, likely since AA3's legendary slow-motion final objection.That having been said, there are some drawbacks. Because of the way the game is paced and structured, there is very little comparative payoff for cornering someone, at least in the first half of the game's cases. You don't get the usual AA satisfaction of seeing someone melt down on the witness stand until quite late in the game; this is all for plot reasons, but it also makes the first half of the game less satisfying. The game also takes way too long to get going. The prologue case is fine, but once the intrepid rookie lawyer decides to actually travel to Britain and the course of the game's plot is set in motion, the game spends way too long introducing its characters, setting up its mysteries and new mechanics. Of this the most egregious is the Sholmes 'Course Correction' mechanic; the sequences are both way too simple in practice and take too long to play out, leading to them generally feeling like unnecessary padding.But what are you reading this for? If you're an AA fan, you already know this is a must-play. Newcomers to the franchise, I suggest looking to complete the earlier games in the series before you tackle this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the original Ace Attorney trilogy so I decided to pick up this duology as well. I'm SO GLAD I made that choice, because not only do these hold up to the OG trilogy, but in my opinion they FAR surpass them. (TLDR at the bottom) The writing is really good - fantastic story throughout the two games' storyline, with intricate elements to each and every case and a very compelling overarching plot that is SO SATISFYING to finally solve in the end. The mystery is never too easy or too hard - the original trilogy of games was a bit weaker in that regard, and often I had to resort to online guides. Here, nothing is immediately obvious or given away, but it's not so frustratingly hard that it borders on illogical, so it's a genuine delight figuring out the mysteries that have been laid out for you to unravel in every case. The cases also all felt like realistically plausible events, which is also a large improvement to the OGs. Every member of the main cast is likeable in some way, and I found myself extremely fond of almost everyone by the end. They're all multidimensional and really feel like real people (even the more ridiculous/eccentric ones. shoutout to Herlock Sholmes. love that man), and that attachment to the characters made me enjoy playing through their story all the more. Even the one-off characters manage to be interesting, and unlike the original trilogy, none of them are so ridiculously frustrating to deal with, or just plain annoying, that it takes the fun out of the game (i.e. Moe the clown). The animation was something I thought was going to be off-putting or strange at first, as I was used to the charming but effective limited 2D animation style of the OG trilogy, but it absolutely surpassed my expectations. The 3D animations allow for some cool effects that weren't possible in the 2D version. The animation may not be the high quality you can see in other games these days, but I think it's quite charming and works well with the game's style.The backgrounds are all very pretty and detailed, and the GUI has a cool aesthetic that very much fits the setting of the game and helps to immerse you in the 19th century feeling. I also quite like the occasional anime-like 2D animation scenes and the narrated prologue sequences, which work with the rest of the game quite well too. Typical Ace Attorney duality of investigation and courtroom sections, both of which are engaging and fun to play. There's some expansions from the OG trilogy to both sections - the investigation sections have one "Dance of Deduction" sequence per episode, which areinteresting both visual- and gameplay-wise, and I think they're a really good minigame to help break up the long visual novel investigation sequences (also they're funny and endear the characters to me even more. they are simply a little bit silly <3). The courtroom sections, meanwhile, now have summation examinations, add another component to the courtroom gameplay, giving the whole thing some more variety and keeping you engaged even through hours of gameplay taking place in the same courtroom.Also, as mentioned above, there are a couple of anime-style animated sequences, and almost every case is preceded by a narrated prologue sequence in the style of a Sherlock Holmes story, which is different from the rest of the game but a charming touch as well. GOD. THE SOUNDTRACK. The two composers for these games really did a FANTASTIC job, and I could honestly write entire musical analysis essays about their outstanding work here. Rather than sticking to synth tracks like the OG trilogy, these games have fully orchestrated music, and while at first that seems like something you'd need to get used to, it not only fits the aesthetic of the game much better than synth sounds would, but also pays off in the form of letting you hear some absolute BANGERS, as well as pieces that really tug on the heartstrings and make the game so much more impactful.The courtroom soundtrack sticks to the usual Ace Attorney formula, having set themes for the defendant's antechamber and "court is in session", a moderato and an allegro version of a cross-examination theme, a bare-bones "suspense" theme, an "objection" and a "pursuit" theme, and so on. These also remain largely consistent across both games, with the notable exception of .Outside the courtroom, we also follow the formula of having an "investigation" theme, as well as different character themes. These are all really well done, with a lot of them being really catchy, and all of them very memorable. Kazuma's theme is my absolute favourite, not only because it's a really good piece of music by itself, but also because of Overall, an absolutely outstanding OST. Definitely one of the strongest parts of these games. Most of the game isn't voice acted, as is typical for Ace Attorney games, and sticks to the visual novel formula of text boxes with scrolling text. However, there IS occasional voice acting, and in my opinion it's really well used! I played the game with English audio, so my primary experience is with the dubbed voice acting, but I did also have a listen to the Japanese version, and I have to say I think all the voice actors did a fantastic job. I especially like Susato's English voice acting, and Van Zieks is very well done in both versions. Overall a nice touch! The "Special Contents" menu offers some fun additional content that I quite liked making my way through while taking a break from playing the actual story! I like that the achievements menu has a checklist for the multi-parters, and the unused music, concept art, bonus voice lines and extra mini-episodes are all very cool to look through! Fascinating story, interesting and likeable characters, engaging visuals, fun gameplay, BRILLIANT soundtrack, good voice acting, and neat extra content - an absolutely fantastic set of games that is 100% worth the money. Cannot recommend enough. <3
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: This Series Should've Ended A Long Time AgoWhen i first read Shu Takumi would return to direct the next AA games on 3DS i was very excited only to be disappointed later when it turned out to be Japan exclusives. Well, here are the two AA games in one package and man... I'm even more disappointed with these two games than i was with Dual Destinies. These are probably the worst games i've played out of the whole series! Both GAA1 and GAA2 are are mostly the same in terms of music, graphics and gameplay so i will be summing down both games in this review. The story takes place in the late 1890's and our new protaganist is Ryunosuke Naruhodo, ancestor of Phoenix Wright and who also happens to be a law student. Ryunosuke travels to Great Britain to further his studies and meets Herlock Sholmes. I'm glad Capcom USA wasn't able to change the setting to LA again this time, but how is this going to connect with the English localization of the mainline series? I guess it won't, also did we really need yet another family member of Phoenix? This really just undermines his character as some lawyer prodigy but, fan service i guess.The visuals are really good, probably the best the series has ever looked in HD and in 60fps with some patches. The animations are very smooth and nice to look at. They have definitely improved but they're so repetitive that it gets annoying at how many times we see the characters have the same reactions. There is some partial voice acting but most of the game is just text. The sound effects are mostly the same as older games and the music is nothing worthwile it's mostly generic Japanese and British scores.The pacing is so slow and boring, you have to read so much before you can move on to the next chapter and the developers were aware since they game added an auto continue mechanic so you won't fall asleep. Deduction is a new gameplay element by explaining the crime scene with logic and reasoning and by contradicting our new idiot detective, Herlock Sholmes. This guy is incredibly annoying, he ruins the tension of the case just by being goofy all the time like why does everything needs overly comedic these days? I usually stop caring about finding out the culprit as soon as Sholmes starts hiding and dancing around the crime scene. The long awaited multiple witnesses and jury gameplay mechanic hinted in Apollo Justice has finally made it into the series and it sucks HARDDDD... The whole point of a court trial is to convince the judge, or in this game's case, six jurys, that your client is innocent. You would think that the jury would need to be convinced in real time as in unscripted gameplay, you're supposed to show the right evidence at the right time to make your case more convincing or make mistakes and the jury will doubt your defendant for guilty. If more jurys believe your arguments the higher chance of you winning, if less then you lose... But if it's noting like this, then what would be the point of having more judges if the gameplay is practically the same as having one judge? Well, that's exactly what it is, the f**king same as previous games... It doesn't matter how many mistakes you make the whole trial stays scripted and you have to convince all jury for you to win so there is no real tension nor difference with just one judge or one hundred judges... Like what is the point of this new mechanic just to show more relevant characters in court? This was supposed to appear in Dual Destinies until Takumi decided not to direct that game because Capcom screwed up his vision with Apollo Justice. I'm sad to say DD turned out to be the better game than both Great Ace Attorney.In conclusion, this franchise is over, Shu Takumi had a great run with the original trilogy and Apollo and i'm sure the franchise would've stayed strong had Takumi not left the series to the B team of Capcom. (which did a great job with Investigations 1&2 and AA6) Sure, Ace Attorney 7 will come along and sell a couple of units and the series will be dead again for a while but i won't be there to support this crap anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a spin off/prequel to the well known series many of us love.Now, obviously, it's a little difficult to not go spoiler heavy but here we go.The 144 hours on this game are not representative of the actual duration of the 2 games.I would say around 40 hours seem rather fair.These 2 games have a very heavy emphasis on long term story telling.All 8 cases are deeply interconnected, although you won't see it immediately, obviously.That type of story telling usually comes with a downside and an upside, and this one is very obvious.The pluses -Long term storytelling with big payoffs.-Overall good characters-Completely ditching the bad mechanics of the last few installments, like visions through the dead or technological bs that destroyed immersion and credibility.-Prosecutor is a pretty good one, as per usual to be honestThe minuses-First game suffers heavily from the storytelling while the second reaps all the rewards-The Jury mechanic, while used properly at times feels somewhat underexploited on most cases-Cannot be played sporadically, you've got swallow both games in a row, otherwise you might forget very important details-Soundtrack feels a little under the rest of the sagaOverall I had a great time but the first game really felt slow and boring, the second on the other hand is just going at an absolutely perfect rhytm.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing spin-off to the Ace Attorney series that's also great for first-timers to the series, going with new mechanics introduced in Professor Layton x Ace Attorney and taking it beyond.Double/triple witnesses, a jury system, a MUCH better exploration system that warns you if you missed something or if you should focus on exploring a certain scene instead, a completely new character roster, fleshed out animations improving a lot on what the 3DS games did, and a system that allows you to simply enjoy the story and read it as a visual novel instead of doing any gameplay sections if you're here for the writing and the characters.Loved the cases, the new OST, the new characters, the new animations. The price is a bit steep, but for two superbly written games with a lot of content (each taking ~10 hours to complete), I believe it's justified.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who greatly enjoyed the original trilogy, The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles has lived up and surpassed its heritage in almost every way. The stakes were higher, the characters have further development, the mechanics were more complicated, and the game felt more tightly woven together.The original trilogy had a tendency to focus too much on individual episodes and left the plot scrambling for an overall meaning (JFA is the worst offender of this). The same weaknesses can be found in this game (especially for some of the middle cases) but is easier to swallow thanks to the extreme mystery presented.There are several plot points that are gradually built upon the course of the two games that come together in an extremely pleasing way.  and  are still my favorite cases in the series, but  and  from this game are right behind them. Would highly recommend this game for fans of the series. I would consider it a must play.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Once you get through the incredibly slow, and even a bit intimidating, opening cases, you're in for what think is one of the richest stories in the entire franchise, ESPECIALLY once you reach Resolve.It's humorous, charming, but knows when it's time to be serious, all while having extra emphasis on the mystery aspect, when compared to other installments.Can I recommend this to new AA fans? Not really. Can I recommend it to fans who are familiar with the formula of AA? Abso-freaking-lutely.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played many Ace Attorney games and I can definitely say that I've enjoyed these 2 the most. It is the pinnacle of the series and the way it wraps everything up at the end while still making every character well written and making you intrigued until the end. I do admit that GAA (DGS) cases 1-1 and 1-2 are both a bit boring in comparison but it'll all be worth it. The cast of these games were amazing to witness and I'm kinda sad it's over.The localisation does seem to remove a lot of the discrimination to a point that it may have lose some meaning. I played DGS1 basically entirely through Scarlet Study on the 3DS before it got officially translated and I can see why they toned down some parts of the text. That being said, the localisation team did a very good job translating and making the characters really feel Victorian. I genuinely thought I wasn't fluent in English (I'm native lol) until I had to search up some words that were said to be archaic nowadays. _childDocuments_.review: Once again a great adventure game in the Ace Attorney series. You can play with Japanese sound/speech if you want, but subtitles are in English. The PC port is solid with some minor issues. You cannot control the various sound volumes; you only select on/off.
