_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles really does a lot of things well, so if you are interested in Mystery Solving Games this game is a must buy.Pros:+The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles does a really good job at giving its main characters a in-depth personality. It focuses really well on their main characteristics and during the course of the game also gives them some depth to their personality.+I myself really enjoyed the "Logic and Reasoning Spectacular" with Sholmes. I felt that they were really refreshing during the Investigation Parts of the game.+The Story is really great and the Cases all have some Connection to each other, and are not just some random cases.+The Soundtrack is absolutely amazing and everything fits the mood the Music tries to set.+You get 2 games for the price of 1Cons:-Some Chapters can feel kind of stretched out, especially the Investigation Parts can take really long.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes!I've played through all the Ace Attourney ports on the app store, and am a big fan of the series. I love these games, and I've been looking forward to chronicles finally coming to european players. The Ace Attourney series is a mix between visual novel and detective game. It's memorable for its goofy characters, slapstick humor, and story arcs that span several cases.I think this game takes everything I enjoy with the series and puts it neatly into one package. I think it's the most polished and consistent attourney game I've played. I especially like the care that was put into the music, I think it makes a big difference. And the characters are done so well! They are memorable, lovable, and goofy - to the point where they almost seem to form the substance of the game.What usally dissapoints me with these games is that the intended audience is someone who has never played ace attourney, and so every game starts off frustratingly easy. This game had a difficulty curve that progressed into the second game, which I appreciated.Some moments felt very tedious in the game, like the deduction acts - although visually fun, I thought they were a little tedious and simple. The testimony has a gimmick that could have made interesting gameplay, if it didn't hit the player over the head with it with a big alert. The cases were good, but ultimately, It's not Ace Attourney to me unless you're stumped sometimes and get the hammer and verbal abuse and such and such, and I didn't get that feeling until the second game.Otherwise, I can't find too much in this game that's objectionableI hope you get this game and that you like it as much as I didSee you in court~~

_childDocuments_.review: A great take on the AA games, The Great Ace Attorney follows the same trial formula with some new twists. It breaks up the investigation and trial sections neatly, adding a breath of fresh air, along with some nice quality of life improvements. It follows a fun cast of characters who keep things entertaining-- including the legendary Herlock Sholmes!From Japan to England, rookie defense lawyer Ryunosuke Naruhodo's cases range from simple to anything but. You'll have a great time yelling OBJECTION! and enjoying the old fashioned English dialects from the colourful characters you'll attempt to wrangle into submission. Fans of the original AA games will have a blast revisiting the courtroom, while new players will get to start entirely fresh with new characters, sleek play concepts, wonderful art, a developing storyline, and a beautiful soundtrack.If you're looking for a game without much gameplay required, then Great Ace Attorney is a wonderful way to chill out and play with little spoons needed. I enjoyed it a lot!

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles consists of two games that tell a single story over 10 cases. If you ask almost any Ace Attorney fan, they'd say this is the peak Ace Attorney experience. While I don’t entirely agree, I will say it’s a REALLY good game. The story is compelling, but the pacing is painfully slow.The first case is particularly frustrating. It’s ridiculous—they try to introduce all the main Japanese characters and set up a mystery that doesn’t pay off until the latter part of the second game. At the same time, it tries to balance a wacky Ace Attorney vibe with a more serious tone, all while stretching on for 4 hours in the courtroom without any investigation. So, you have to commit 4 hours to a game you haven’t even formed an opinion on yet and don’t fully understand the mechanics of. It’s absurd.But that’s not all—the game piles on mysteries that won’t be resolved until the second game. The first game needs closure, but the ongoing story is only really continued in cases 3 and 5, which isn’t enough to tell a big story. As a result, case 5 drags on for 10 hours. The second game, however, improves significantly after the first case, and you really start to appreciate the storytelling and characters. You begin to understand the atmosphere, the humor (though the original trilogy is funnier), the tight overarching plot, the insanely good soundtrack (probably the best in the franchise, in my opinion), and the incredibly likable characters. This game made me sympathize with a character who was complicit with a serial killer, which is a bit unsettling but a testament to the quality of the writing.But none of that even matters—this game has Herlock Sholmes, and he’s the most epic thing on the planet. I recommend this game to everyone.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Ace Attorney is one of my favourite series of all time, so I was excited to pick up a new title. Unfortunately, The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles has none of the charm of its predecessors. As of the moment of writing this review, I haven't even been able to bring myself to finish it.The whole game feels tedious with very little payoff. The dialogue drags on, there are very few challenges or surprises compared to prior games, and many of the characters are written as charmingly eccentric but just come over as annoying.I'll probably go back and finish this later, because I hate leaving games incomplete, but I really wouldn't recommend buying this if you've played other Ace Attorney games and loved them. It's a letdown in comparison.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Trust me when I say that these games are a It may be a spin-off from the original Ace Attorney series, but don't let your eyes be fooled. The music and sound design is very special. Different to the original trilogy, each character has a special musical theme dedicated to them. Sound effects are also very different to main line Ace Attorney. May it be a gunshot, a coughing fit, the sound of a bell ringing or a raging fire - you feel captivated by the detail put into the sound design.Another thing to add, there is voice acting inside of these games. Not everywhere but special and important moments, opening cutscenes, are fully voice acted. The animations. They're not just sprites. Each character's animation is special. Subtle changes in facial expression, subtle changes in body language... aditionally all in 3D! The scenes themselves are 3D too, camera movements feel as if you're inside of a film and the camera angles vary in amount. And the cutscenes, there are two kinds:- 3D animated with voice acting- drawn animations with voice actingAnd the storytelling. It's very obvious that the story was established first in both games, before the games were made. Of course there are plot holes, but different to following mainline games after Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney, these games have characer development. And not in a minimal sense. Each character feels human, as if they could jump out of the monitor at any moment and become real. Would that happen, they would be believably human. Check the two games out. Even if it's just the soundtrack.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game is good, however I do have some issues. _childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic game, but it could've been better. It should've been much shorter, but the music and spritework were so beautifully done that I couldn't mind the lengthiness that much. If you played Rise from the Ashes in the original trilogy, that is the vibe you get playing GAA, but with less standing in front of Detective Gumshoe and presenting every piece of evidence in your inventory three times. Too long, but interesting and heartwarming.Susato was the blandest assistant in the series, and the game could've been so much better if she was shown to be a flawed character or even just a character with quirks. Nah, she just physically harms other people and it's presented as being cute and funny. She was more a collection of plot devices than a human being, and the only unique thing about her is that she's an assistant who isn't an orphan. She was better in game 2 case 1, but any flaws she was given in that case were immediately taken away for the rest of the game. If I could wave a magic wand and change one thing about the game, it would be to make Susato a better foil character for Ryu.Oh, and Hosonaga should've been invited to the Forensic Science forum. But I only have these complaints because the game was so close to being phenomenal.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: To be clear, this is two full Ace Attorney games in one, Dai Gyakuten Saiban 1 & 2. They were released Japan-only a while ago and now finally are on PC, for some reason.This is great because, this is the best Ace Attorney experience you could ever have. If you know those games in passing or played the old ones on DS or whatever, well, here's all that gameplay perfected.So the most important part of a story-heavy VN like this is the narrative, and suffice it to say it's flawless. I've only at time of writing played the original Phoenix Wright trilogy, but going from that to this you can see Shu Takumi's writing has really evolved over time and he's just learned a lot and grown really good at making video games.Jumping in with this game is easy to do. Because this is an original story set far in the past of the original Ace Attorney series, you can freely pick up and play 'The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles' without having played any of the other games, and you'll have a great time doing so.These two games are interconnected as well and tell a complete narrative, I don't know if Shu Takumi knew he was getting exactly two games, and so wrote the scenario and the script to fit that, or if he just managed to successfully panic edit down the second and third game's script into one, forming a duology from what I assume was a cancelled trilogy because Capcom. It's perfectly satisfying though, and wraps up neatly at the end.One thing in particular that really impressed me is, most of the characters are really memorable, even side-characters, the main cast is great. Ryunosuke is instantly likeable, so's his friend Kazuma. Susato makes for a great assistant too by being useful, so she's pleasant to have around as your Maya Fey.As for the gameplay, it too is the smoothest it has ever been, all of the puzzles are logical and make sense, are easy to follow if you are paying attention, and a lot of care is taken to make sure you are able to keep up. The worst I can say about it is that you might grow a little bored. In a way, the game is almost too easy, it will sometimes accept multiple solutions to testimony, and I don't think you really get sent back at all if you 'game over' either (which is fine by me) and the gameplay overall does very little to interrupt long stretches of dialogue and plot. This is hardly a problem if you're engaged in the story, though.I think I may have game overed like, twice, over the course of two games, which is a pretty sharp contrast to the original trilogy where there are some bits where you almost just have to try every piece of evidence you have against every line of dialogue because you have literally no idea what the game wants from you, or some 'boss battle' cases like 1-4 where I think you can lose life just for pressing the witness at all during some sections? I'm okay with DGS 1 & 2 being a bit more chill than that.The graphics are spectacular, I think this was originally a 3DS game, then ported to Switch/PS4 and PC at the same time, and. It looks and feels like a PC game to my eyes, it's great. The animation is worth pointing out, all the characters are characterised by flashy mocap performed by member(s) of an all-female theatre troupe...? It's something you'll notice if you pay attention, but in a good way. Aside from that all the models are of a fine quality, the backgrounds are often hand-drawn and look great, and the 3D is good enough that it mixes nicely with the 2D elements. It's all quite modern and sleek.I really have nothing negative to say about this game, it's one of the best I've played in years.I would recommend it to pretty much anyone unless you just HATE reading, I guess.

After waiting for several years to try it I'm more than happy to say, it truly is a... no excuse me, The Great Ace Attorney!

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to preface this with the fact that i have not previously played the Phoenix wright series however i have seen an edited play-through of the first 3 games, that being said:This game/games was amazing. The story was phenomenal with each case being an interesting tale with twists at every turn, sometimes you had some cliche parts which fit in quite well and sometimes you had some stuff were you are like "eh, that could have been done better", but there was not a single part of this that i would consider bad. Obviously the cases are unrealistic with many many coincidences propelling the story forward but this is a main staple of all detective games as there isn't much to get around that and still have the case be intriguing, but i found it dosn't hinder the story at all and adds to the experience. The story follows a case by case story-line each expanding on the tale of Runo (the shortened name of the main character), showing the young lawyer's journey from nothing to greatness with a very intricate subplot that spans both games in the series and ends in an epic 2 part finale. Each of the main characters has a deep personality that has you grow attached no matter how annoying they were to start (looking at you Sholmes) and every case features a cast of wacky sub characters to help spice up the court proceedings. One thing i think people will like is the lack of magical happenings that featured in the Phoenix wright series, as much of that was used to bail-out the player in a end all scenario and its much better written in this game. The evidence and cross-examinations i found to be quite well put in without super obvious guidance but some good hints here and there, but sometimes its not clear at all what you need to choose so you just filter through the evidence list until you eventually choose the right thing. One thing that really hinders this game is if you leave a case mid-way; Cases often take 3-4 hours and everything is procedural, so if you stop playing and forget what exactly happened or how a piece of evidence relates to something past you can get stuck reloading till it just happens to be correct. One thing i really enjoyed about the evidence was the ability to view most of it in a 3d space and poke at it for clues and details, sometimes even opening things up or combining 2 pieces of evidence.The music in the game is fantastic, constantly setting the tone and allowing the player to truly put themselves in the shoes of Runo. My personal favorite theme is Iris's as it perfectly fits her character. One thing that really threw me off however was the occasional voice acting, as I played the game i built up unique voices for each character in my head and every once in a while (like every 2-3 cases) you would get a voice acted segment and while its the characters definitive voice, i feel its sparse use really clashes; The interjections in court however were fine in my opinion (Runo's did feel a little lack-luster at times) and it did add to the characters and the court experience.Overall i give this game a 10/10 but do be warned about its length, i'm fast reader and it took me ~30-35 hours to finish (though reading fast isn't a big impact because the game limits text speed  when you first read it which i understand its to properly pace and set things up but was annoying)
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: * Non spoiler bitI've played most of the Ace Attorney games throughout the years (except AAI2, PWvsPL and AA6) and I must say, out of them all these two games as a whole are the best out of the whole series. Seriously, this divergence was what the series needed. The story is phenomenal, the fact that all cases are connected and slowly build into a one giant story and that story culminating into one giant epic climax where you feel so triumphant and accomplished after this long journey. The characters are all very well written, interesting and memorable, you actually feel emotionally attached to them at the end of the game. The gameplay is such a breath of fresh air, gone are pointless gimmicks, say hello to great deductions to spice up the investigations, multiple witnesses on the witness stand to pursue and the jurist system to pit jurors arguments againts each other. The soundtrack is easily the best OST as a whole in the series, nothing comes close to it. There is only a handful of songs from the other games that can be compared ("Wanting to find the Truth" for example). For any Ace Attorney fan this is a mustplay and for any puzzle solving/thinking game enthusiast a game worth trying. The only downside is that I got a bit burned out at the begging of the second game so I had to take some breaks from it because some parts are a bit longer but otherwise it was a blast.If I overlook that one small problem I mentioned, this game is an easy 10/10.*Big Spoilers bit

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve played every English-translated game in the Ace Attorney series (including spin-offs) except Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice, so maybe my word won’t have the same bearing as another Ace Attorney fan’s would. But I will say that I think The Great Ace Attorney is one of the best games in the series, if not the best.Maybe my memory fails me since it quite literally has been more than a decade since I’ve played most of the other games, but I’ve never felt any game in the series has a story that’s so intricately and carefully woven as this one. Loose ends I thought they could never neatly tie were mostly covered by the end of the series; I was especially impressed by how flawlessly the second game flowed after the first. I had expected the second game to either have a storyline that was completely divorced from the first one, or for it to feel like an afterthought. It felt like neither of these things; it felt like it was planned from the very beginning to be a two-game series, and I mean that in the best way possible. It never felt rushed or like it was just putting filler in; it knew it’s pacing well and stuck with it for an absolutely wonderful finale.I would remark more on the wonderful balance between ridiculous comedy and tense drama that the dialogue has, but that’s honestly just a mainstay of the Ace Attorney series rather than a specifically GAA thing. The writers of this series present a masterclass of visual novel writing; they know when to pull punches, and they know when to hit hard. And boy did they use it for this game.The (relatively, for an Ace Attorney game) small cast of characters had such strong personalities and were endearing. I really cared for a lot of them, and I even felt a lot of sympathy for a lot of the ‘criminals’ in the end. Everyone felt like a fully conceived character with motives and aspirations, and I really understood where they came from, even when I didn’t agree with them or their actions.The music is phenomenal. Not only because of how it sounds because hey, it does sound great, but because of how it was used. I can’t say much on this because I don’t want to spoil anything, but there were several times a leitmotif began playing when I didn’t expect it to or there was an emotionally tense moment in the story, and it made me absolutely lose my mind. You can tell the composer paid very close attention to the script and worked with the writers, and it just… really made my experience.I was glad to see the classic mechanics were still being used. It’s always nice to have the familiar trial and investigation sequences to get back into the series. I was fascinated by the fact that the first GAA game didn’t necessarily follow the usual sequence, though. The sequence I usually expect is that the first episode is purely the trial, then the subsequent episodes are investigation-trial-investigation-trial. They revert back to that in the second GAA game, but it was refreshing that the first GAA didn’t follow the formula.It made me laugh that the jury system was brought back, it just brings wonderful flavour to the games. Sholmes’ Dance of Deductions were a nice addition to the investigation sequences, but they did drive me a little insane towards the middle of the game because you kind of have to sit there internally screaming while listening to how Sholmes is wrong at first, and THEN you have to sit through it AGAIN to correct it. I’d say eventually they were worth it to see the last Dance of Deduction, but I did wish there was a way to expedite it a little.I could go on a lot more about what I loved about this game, but I’m so scared of spoiling it for people. Most of the fun of these games is getting to the bottom of the mystery after all.  I am definitely extremely biased, but I think that the Ace Attorney games are the king of visual novel/puzzle games, and The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a must play addition to the series. Also, ultimately, while I’ll miss the cast, I hope they never make another GAA game. It’s a perfect package already.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay I like the game so far, it has some cool new features to the old games, and as usual the story is compelling and the characters likeable.I'm on the first case, but what I really don't like is that in the first case, while the other games weren't always steeped in realism, it at least remained grounded. _childDocuments_.review: Phew. This game is a bit of a drag, I won't lie. Compared to other games in the same franchise, it's pretty slow. There are some interesting things pulled from history here and there, but the game is way more dialogue than actual "game" where you get to connect the thoughts. There is like 30 minutes of core dialogue until you get to actually interact and gather actually pertinent information. I find myself putting this game on auto and doing chores before making another decision that will take a bulk of time to say nothing.The opening act was interesting, but the nonsense to entertain quickly fell off by episode 2. And yes, I also wanted to nap in the middle of these games. Good lord, sitting through the full deductions just to turn the camera 15 degrees and click something an inch away is a bit groan inducing. I only recommend this game if you're not an overthinker and like watching silly displays. Even then, I feel the older Ace Attorney games are a bit more to the point for that. I'll let this slide this time only because I think they're trying to experiment with more content in their games since departing the DS days.

_childDocuments_.review: During the six months that passed since I first completed the Chronicles, and the inclusive two months since I returned to get the rest of the achievements, I have gotten around to completing the rest of the Ace Attorney series, from the Investigations duology, to the sequel trilogy, and finally, the Professor Layton crossover.While there were games from that list that I greatly enjoyed (notably Spirit of Justice and the Layton crossover), the Great Ace Attorney Chronicles remains as what I personally consider to be the peak of the Ace Attorney games. Lovable and memorable characters, charming music, great usage of the 3D visuals, and a beautifully written overarching story. While I do admit that the first game fell a little to the mundane side (both story and pacing wise), the second game takes those problems and manages to not only polish them up, but somehow manage to bring back underdeveloped plot points and wrap them up in a natural and enjoyable way. Returning characters either keep their charm from the first game, or become even better somehow, and seemingly one-off characters are brought back in a way that makes them some of the most memorable of the cast. It's no wonder then that people comment on how the first game exists to provide the necessary bases to make the second game as good as it is.Overall, a fantastic experience, and a delightful duology. To any Ace Attorney fan contemplating on whether to give the Great Ace Attorney Chronicles a try, it'll be a definite recommendation from me. Maybe you'll like it, maybe you won't, but if you've enjoyed the original trilogy (which I do recommend you play beforehand), chances are that you'll enjoy the Chronicles just as much, or maybe even more.

_childDocuments_.review: The fact that I find it hard to come back to this game and finish it even after being 16 hours into it and only around 4-5 cases through should speak to about how long-winded this game is with relatively little payoff for your patience. I've played the original trilogy and I get what the games are supposed to be like, but I feel more draw to go play the original trilogy again rather then try to continue through this one.A new mechanic is you'll confront someone hiding something, and then "Herlock Sholmes" makes a "deduction" which is a wild assumption about what the person is hiding. There are four correct premises but he concludes them incorrectly, so you have to go back and fix them. The primary problem with these is you go through the entire deduction once, and then you go through the entire thing again to fix it, which easily takes about five minutes each time. This wouldn't be a problem if the fixing weren't extremely easy.Fixing these has been set up as "the real answer is just hidden out of view from the camera angle you are given". They look like they wanted to show off the 3D environments by letting you pan the camera around the scene, so the easiest way to find the answer is move the camera around lazily until you find something out of place (you can easily do this without even reading any of the deduction). It makes the entire thing feel like a waste of time.There is an excessive amount of filler dialogue that is not interesting to read, or just tells you about things you remember from five minutes ago. I often find myself just skipping dialogue to get to the next point that I am allowed to interact with the story.I know this game's known for having whacky characters, but Sholmes especially goes out of his way to be as completely over the top as possible and talks an excessive amount about nonsense. On this note, a lot of the animations for the models seem to be reused as much as possible just to show that they're there when they don't really fit the situation.Don't read if you don't want the first case spoiled.In the first case you defend yourself in a wrongful murder accusation with you as the suspect. The only reason you are being accused of murder is because you picked up a revolver off the ground right at the same time someone nearby was shot. Not only does this particular case have so many off the walls turn-arounds akin to "updating the autopsy report" every ten minutes, the entire premise of "you shot him because you had a gun in your hand" falls flat when you understand an undercover detective who neurotically steals evidence from the scene didn't bother to check the gun you picked up to see if it had been fired. The ENTIRE case falls apart if you point out to a single person that "it couldn't have been me because the gun was still fully loaded". Even assuming this was somehow planned for, there's plenty of other things that make zero sense as to your involvement like the position of the victim in relation to the table. This is incredibly frustrating to be unable to point out and the whole thing feels like a waste of time.It often feels like lots of things go the same way even without your input, especially in the court room. Don't read if you don't want the third case to be spoiled.During the third case an omnibus is brought in the court room as evidence, but during a scuffle and due to a smoke grenade is tampered with during the case to support a different narrative. It presents you with the moral question of if you'll use the tampering of evidence to defend your client or if you'll tell the truth. Despite me carefully examining the bus prior to being tampered in its entirety, my character still "wasn't sure" if it had been tampered with and nobody seemed to care what I picked for dialogue either way.Overall the game feels like a chore to play. Go play the original trilogy.

Unless you compared him with Layton in the crossover.And the dance of deduction is a nice gameplay. Definitely recommended in sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a much a "Grander" spin on Ace Attorney. It's presentation, it's setting, it's orchestral soundtrack, and the conspiracies that lie within, all the while introducing a new set of characters and fleshing most of them out so nicely in one self-contained story! It has everything I love about the series while also having it's own distinctive vibe.I may be in the minority when I say this, but I honestly prefer The Great Ace Attorney: Adventures (GAA1) to its sequel. It feels like a much more grounded story which you experiencing the events in real time as it happens, and it honestly makes for a really nice narrative. It's very different for Ace Attorney, and that's what I like about it!GAA2 meanwhile kind of builds everything up to one grand final conspiracy and it kinda just feels like your standard Ace Attorney affair. Nothing bad mind you, it's still a great game, but I do feel it loses a lot of its narrative charm that the first game had.It's a good collection of 2 adventure games, both very meaty and long. I'd absolutely encourage anybody who likes any of the other Ace Attorney games to give this a shot, it's a stand out entry in the franchise!

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles (TGAAC) is an amazing two-part journey of murder mysteries and courtroom encounters with some of the best characters & musical soundtrack in the Ace Attorney franchise. It was a pleasure to finally get to play this game localized, and I dare say it might be my favorite overall Ace Attorney story even though it is a spin-off from the mainline games.Visual novel, point-and-click investigations, murder mysteryTGAAC, like the mainline Ace Attorney games, largely (for most cases but not all) takes place in two halves: one half being about story exposition with sections of gathering evidence/talking to witnesses, and the other half being the courtroom battles where you take the defense attorney bench and pursue the truth in order to prove that your client is not guilty of the crime they are being charged with. Of course, in the courtroom it is your job to debunk witness statements & claims made by the prosecution by presenting evidence that contradicts their statements and in doing so, it is up to you to figure out who is actually responsible. New gameplay elements that were not present in the previous mainline Ace Attorney series come in the form of summation examinations and the Dance of Deduction. The summation examination occurs in court where you need to convince the new jury to change their stance away from guilty, and the Dance of Deduction is where you need to "fix" Herlock Sholmes's brilliant deductions by observing the environment and replacing some of his keywords with ones that make more sense. TGAAC was originally a 3DS/Mobile game so it retains much of the 3DS-era Ace Attorney games appearances, but with options like upscaled resolution and anti-aliasing available on PC. In fact, the 3D animations are very well done as many of the characters have a variety of idle poses/animations that they smoothly run through. TGAAC is set in late 19th century Japan & Great Britain and follows the story of Ryunosuke Naruhodo, an ancestor of the mainline Ace Attorney series's protagonist, Phoenix Wright. Without spoiling anything, Ryunosuke finds himself traveling from Japan to Britain on a study tour with an assigned judicial assistant, Susato Mikotaba, as a means to better immerse himself in the legal system of the most powerful nation in the world at the time. On this study tour, the pair of foreigners encounter many eccentric characters that they often befriend/defend in court. The story is told in a total of ten cases throughout the two games within, and as opposed to the story of the mainline series in the past, every case in TGAAC is largely interwoven with each other to form an overarching plot. •The localisation is excellent; I only encountered one singular (obvious) typo in the entire game (not counting the instances of choppy text to symbolize various European accents). •The game doesn't stray away from addressing issues of xenophobia felt in the game's time period by deliberately including various British negative preconceptions about the Japanese. In a time of political tension where countries were beginning to open up and form alliances, it only made sense to keep such tension intact in the dialogue of the game.•TGAAC introduces some of my new favorite Ace Attorney characters. Many characters tend to stick around for more than one case which gives them ample time to develop, and a lot of the character development is just amazing. Watching the protagonist, Ryunosuke, grow from being unsure of his ideals to being a resolute defense attorney is quite inspiring over the course of his adventure. •The overall story payoff by the end of TGAA2 beautifully ties up the ends of all the interwoven cases together into one singular narrative. A lot of anticipation is built up after every individual case as new mysteries keep popping up and becoming forcibly unexplained by the characters. In the finale, everything comes out and you finally understand why something happened previously and why that event was so significant to so many characters. •The music is phenomenal and rivals, or dare I say bests, the soundtracks of the other Ace Attorney games. The upbeat character leitmotifs are very cheerful and the downtrodden, melancholy reverberations of sad memories feel very foreboding and uncomfortable. I find myself listening to them on repeat in my free time because of how catchy they are. •There is a "story mode" option available to new players who just want to experience the story without being prompted to input "correct" responses. This option lets the game play out as a movie where every correct option is chosen for them (so it is also useful when you get stuck on one problem for a long time).•The game's voiced audio moments can be toggled between English and Japanese.•The game comes with DLC in the form of viewable key/concept art, various unreleased music tracks, supplemental unrelated story chronicles, and more. Most of the DLC comes with developer comments too and it was fun to read the designers' thoughts about scrapped ideas and concepts that didn't make it to the game's release.•Like most Ace Attorney games, there is a toss up between amazing, mind-blowing cases and mundane, slow-burn cases. The great cases make you persist towards the end to find out what happened, and the alright cases are the ones where you figured out what happened already and want the game to acknowledge your intelligence already.•Also like most Ace Attorney games, you might find yourself in the position where you think you are presenting the right evidence, but in fact you need to be presenting the other one of the same nature that the game is assigned to recognize as the actual "answer" to the question being posed. (Not particularly a weakness but more of a statement):•Sherlock Holmes was renamed Herlock Sholmes in order to avoid legal disputes in the English localisation. I see some people trash on the game just because of this, and in my opinion that is such a dumb reason to have for refusing to play a game.9.5/10TGAAC is now one of my favorite, if not my favorite, Ace Attorney games even though it is a spin-off. I thoroughly enjoyed my time playing around in a late-Victorian London setting and interacting with many memorable & charming characters. I liked the long story payoff, the music is phenomenal, and overall, this 65 hour adventure was a pleasure to behold. I would fully recommend this game to be played.

_childDocuments_.review: I will keep the spoilers minimal, as I think games like these are the best enjoyed when going in blind. If puzzle solving aspect doesn't interest you, then there is always the journalist mode that can be selected in the options menu.Adventures:The biggest weakness of Adventures is the way that the story is unnecessary stretched and presented as hopeless situations, even though any person with common sense would quickly come to a certain conclusion without having to take all the flak head-on. It becomes even more blatantly obvious on case 4 and 5, when the jurors are incompetent. As part of the jury system, the jurors are allowed to decide the fate of the defendant through their whims. As part of the mechanic, you get to convince them to overturn their verdict, but the testimony the jurors give most of the time are either blatantly racism or has nothing to do with the case on hand. There is improvement in the story writing in case 5, but the odds are unnecessarily stacked against you. The situation is always unfair and anyone who is new to the AA series will find this to be a big turnoff.Resolve:From Resolve on, the concept of science plays a much bigger role and the complexity of each case changes to reflect on the evidence being more modern. The jury is as incompetent as always in case 2, but when they pronounce guilty, at least the reason this time is somewhat more reasonable. However, case 3 shows a dramatic change in quality of the jurors, because the jurors in case 3 (among them a scientist, a magician and a police officer) are actually capable of helping our protagonist out. And most importantly, they dont have the itchy trigger finger other jurors seems to have and are willing to reason with our protagonist.Overall:I really hated how the Adventurers was narrated, but all of the shortcomings were fixed in Resolve. I have not finished Resolve yet, but I strongly recommend this game. You will have to suffer through the first five chapters of Adventurers, but once you've finally gotten over it, you will appreciate the fine story telling that is provided in Resolve.

_childDocuments_.review: If you really like the Ace Attorney series and want something more story focused and less gimmicky, this game is for you.While it lacks the gameplay "flourish" and variety of ways to investigate/interrogate of other games like Psyche Locks/Emotion Reading, it has a few hiccups in pace and conveyance on certain parts (re-inspect your items often, even if you think you know the evidence is good, the game will refuse to progress until you've done all checks and item updates!) and the two games are just one game cut in two parts, with some of the chapters are really just 2 chapters in one, so you have 8 actual chapters instead of 10...The story more than makes up for it, and has its own little quirks of its own. The story is in my opinion one of the best ones in the entire series, the characters are as varied and quirky as usual, the music is good as well.I can definitely recommend this to someone that likes Ace Attorney as a whole, though do not expect much from the "gimmicks" of this game, but instead turn yourself towards the characters and the story it offers, because it will not disappoint in that way.

_childDocuments_.review: Having finally completed  I can say this is probably my new favorite Ace Attorney game. I know it's actually two games from 3DS that only got a Japanese release in 2015 and 2017, but they were meant to be played together. The story was written as a whole by series creator Shu Takumi, who wasn't working on the mainline games anymore. It did take me about six months to complete as I took breaks between cases to not get burned out and to better absorb the story. The tone of the game is much more grounded than other Ace Attorney games. No longer set in the nebulously defined land which fans call "Japanifornia" but primarily in London *around* 1900, but don't bother looking for a definitive year that aligns with real people and events.The Japanese protagonists have to deal with quite a bit of xenophobia from the people of London who would already see them as untrustworthy, especially in a court of law. However that doesn't mean the game isn't funny or without ridiculous characters. There are many ridiculous witnesses and jury members, and of course, Herlock Sholmes. His character is already hard to describe, but he will also create inventions that mirror our current technology that put him pretty far into steampunk fantasy. Ryunosuke feels more competent than Phoenix, relying less on bluffing and more on eliminating the impossible. He's earnest but still fun with his interactions with Sholmes. I do wish his voice actor gave a stronger "Objection!" Assistant Susato is pretty calm, knowledgeable, sweet but serious, but is a total fangirl for Sholmes. Meanwhile the primary antagonistic prosecutor feels smarter when it comes to standard law practices when compared to those we've seen in the past. All of the other main characters were very enjoyable. If I didn't care for character initially, I had grown to like them by the end with their complex motivations and moral shades of gray. Most 'one-off' characters were good as well, but there were a few annoying ones too. The music is phenomenal with many songs that stick with you long after you stop playing, orchestral sounding pieces with lots of stringed instruments, accordions, and harpsichords. There isn't much else to say besides me just gushing about each song individually. The overall story is great with several shocking moments. There are are some moments that were less shocking and were more expected. I suppose that balances out but some of the unsurprising moments reminded me of events in the original trilogy. For the individual cases, most I couldn't stop once starting. The first two cases did feel a little slow, like I had figured out things out ahead of the story, and the first case took about 4 to complete. And there was one case that kinda annoyed me with its crime and characters, but the rest are some of the best cases in franchise. All of the cases are pretty long, but it's not a problem for the good ones. The game has many quality of life features that make it hard to go back to previous entries: reviewing recently mentioned text, seeing at-a-glance how many parts a witness testimony has and which part you're currently viewing, and an auto-play toggle to automatically advance dialog after short moment so you don't have to press a button to advance to the next text box. The game also has a 'story mode' setting where the game plays itself for you to watch, solving puzzles for you. I never used it to try it (it disables achievements.) I hope future games have full voice acting. Also many characters have their dialect written into their text, so I had to read some lines aloud to understand what they were saying. I can see this being more difficult for non-native English speakers, so an option for plain text would be cool to see. Graphically the game looks great. The backgrounds and character designs are fantastic, no complaints here. While the other Ace Attorney 3DS games kinda made me miss the 2D sprites, this game is how I want to see the series look going forward. Characters are able to interact and look at each and into the background. The camera pans and sweeps add a lot of flair to the scenes they're used. The game is locked at 30fps and looks fine, but if you have it on Steam, you can install a mod to increase it to 60fps and the character animations look so silky smooth. I highly recommend this game for fans of the previous game, or ones who thought the prior games were too silly, or newbies who have been interested in these silly visual novel games and want to see the best they have to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: Good games with extremely wonky pacing and a terrible PC port.First off, some housekeeping!Should you want to play this game, do yourself a favour and get the file from this guide an absolute legend has provided us: It fixes the embarassingly glaring resolution issues the game still has, heavily improves performance and ups the framerate to a buttery smooth 60 FPS, which in turn also makes the game's text flow much more smoothly - it genuinely makes a huge difference.The fact that Capcom just left the game in this state is frankly shameful, considering how easy these fixes are to implement.Also, do yourself yet another favour and avoid the community content tab for this game like the plague - that section is absolutely overflowing with spoilers, which is a bit of a problem when the game actually features a couple very good plot twists.Now, as for the games themselves - a lot of people in the Ace Attorney fandom consider this duology the pinnacle of the series. While I certainly do agree that it does a lot right - the setting is actually meaningful to the plot and develops alongside the story, the overarching plot is interwoven throughout the entirety of the games, the characters themselves develop in a far more nuanced way - the one place where the game suffers is unfortunately one that can make or break the experience. These games absolutely LOVE to reiterate points that were already well established in prior scenes over and over and over and over again, all for the sake of adding character interactions. This ends up utterly destroying any semblance of pacing in the early game and apparently remains an issue all the way through to the second case of the second game. Hell, the first game's tutorial cases (yes, there are two of them this time) can take anywhere from 3 to 4 hours each to clear, while the fourth case in that game has to be one of the most annoying, even sort of insulting things I've ever read - spousal abuse sure is funny so long as it's a man that gets hurt, huh?The third case is fine though, for what that's worth!That... does not make for an enjoyable experience if you're not already a hardened, remarkably patient VN fan. This is one of those cases where a neutral rating would honestly be welcome - hopefully the rest of the game will turn me around on the experience.Will update after finishing the collection.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: The two games are basically one single game, with complete unity of plot, and as such it must be the most ambitious entry in the Ace Attorney series. The coherence of the plot over the two games is really impressive, with some questions introduced at the start which are only solved at the end. Starting from scratch with new characters allows them to integrate character development and relationships into the plot really well. I liked all the main characters (I found Soseki a bit over the top, but not too bad). The relationship between the two main characters is more developed than in other Ace Attorney games and the way their affection for each other grows while trying to figure out a foreign country gives the game a really sweet atmosphere. Herlock Sholmes is very funny, and mostly the game avoids the risk of making him OP by making him erratic, depressive, forgetful, and overconfident (I think they do fall into the trap a bit at the end, but it doesn't do too much harm). The trials and investigations are almost all interesting (I found Chapter 4 of the first game, particularly the investigation, the weakest and unnecessarily drawn out). The investigation and trial mechanisms work pretty well (it is, somehow, possible to miss reactions from other witnesses in the cross-examinations), and there aren't many points where the inference they expect you to make turns out to be a bit groan inducing. Overall, I really liked it, and I'd love it if they were to make a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: okay, as a fan of ace attorney and one who played all of them except SoJ (sorry, i will get to eventually, Dual destinies left me kinda unsatisfied)I genuinely believe The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles IS THE BEST game (or games if you count them as two separate games) IN THE ENTIRE FRANCHISE. The atmosphere and story are interesting, the game knows how to make you see something a certain way, and then flip it upside down and surprise you. The game IS very talkative, and that means the game HAS A ♥♥♥♥ TON OF DIALOGUE TO READ, AND I MEAN A ♥♥♥♥ TON, it is still filled with humor and heartwarming moments, and i never felt as though it was just trying to fill up play time.I do admit that the first game of Chronicles is slow, like incredibly slow, and the insane amount of dialogue does not help the case (hah) . The second game does  shines through and gets you to finally experience and enjoy a bit more of every single step in your journey of becoming a defense lawyer. I had multiple times where i audibly went "WHAT" as the game surprised and intrigued me where i wouldn't believe, the over-arching plot the game has is rich, each case you get a little bit of the big puzzling mystery that is looming over the entire game and it is incredibly rewarding to get to each new point where you find out yourself, as Ryuunosuke Naruhodo, what event occurred in Great Britain in which you were thrown into out of mere coincidence as a foreigner who is  also not welcomed very nicely. Chronicles consists of 2 games, each one is around 30 hours, making it 60 hours as a whole, same amount of time as the original trilogy. I see it as one huge game with 10 chapters as both are connected with one over-arching plot, as the first game barely has a satisfying ending as a whole if i'm being honest.TIP: ENABLE TEXT-SKIP IN THE MENU TO MAKE THE GAME DIALOGUE GO FASTER, YOU CAN CLICK SPACE AND NOT WAIT FOR IT TO SLOWLY APPEAR ON SCREEN AS THE ANIMATION IS SUPER ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SLOW.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute gem, and a complete improvement over the original AA trilogy in every way. This game is, unlike that trilogy, firmly based in its historical setting in all ways. Racism, taxation, international politics, relationships and conspiracies are all key elements of every case and it feels incredibly real and immersive unlike the original series which seemed unwilling (at least in localized versions) to even acknowledge it was set in Japan. The fact that this also set in the Victorian era helps lend credibility to some of the more out there and previously non-nonsensical elements of the original trilogy. Many technologies we have today simply did not exist, and the game takes advantage of this. As a game on its own, GAAC offers an incredibly tightly wound and complex narrative that ends in a very satisfying way. Some cases definitely felt out of place in the moment, but all of the pieces eventually fall into place. The characters are also very charming, including Herlock Sholmes who brings so much to the table in both the story and gameplay. The two games together are also surprisingly long, taking me 60 hours to complete both. It did drag at times, for the most part the game has a great momentum filled with shocking twists and genuinely funny moments.I highly recommend this collection, and I desperately hope that we get a Great Ace Attorney 3 someday.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Oh wow, what a ride!I had only played the original Ace Attorney trilogy before, so I got to The Great Ace Attorney without having experienced the other installments and spin-offs. Even so, I never felt Chronicles was just more of the same, instead it really felt as a step forward with a fair share of new features that expand and refine the original formula.Since at the end of the day we are playing a series of narrative adventures, let's get straight to the most important aspect of this package: its plot and characters. It contains the usual twists and exaggerations that are commonplace in the first games, and they are masterfully handled here. The plot (the specific of each case and the overarching one that spans both games) are very well written and superbly laid out, I never felt that any scene was lacking nor had any loose end stitched like a patch. Each case is well crafted and never loses the sense of discovery or progression, and there were few times (although they do exist) when I felt it was obvious what was going to happen. Fortunately everything is properly closed and explained by the end, avoiding the inclusion of a cheap cliffhanger to squeeze new installments out of it. This is a universe with many possibilities and Great Ace Attorney still has a long way to go, but the creators do not force the ending to give rise to artificial sequels, and that is something that honors them and I am very grateful for.As for the characters, there is a great variety of them and they are all properly fleshed out. The secondary characters have a lot of charisma and their personalities are well defined, with special care put to the use of accents, dialects and other paraphernalia that contributes to make them a more colorful bunch. This is accompanied by sensational visual designs and a perfect animation work, picking up the 'minimal animation' style of the original trilogy and translating it to 3D in a quite successfully, with fantastic results.The group of main characters has a nice balance to it. On the one hand, we have the set of protagonists who are direct heirs to the Phoenix-Maya-Edgeworth trio in the original. In that sense, they are similar characters in terms of approach and personality, but they still feel different and some of them (I will not tell which one so as not to spoil the surprise to anyone) have a deep additional development in the last third of the collection. On the other hand, the remaining main characters breath new air into the formula that expands beyond themselves.I'm talking, of course, about the world-famous Herlock Sholmes, who is a more experienced and resourceful counterpoint to the lawyer-to-be protagonist, while also acting as an occasional comic relief. With Sholmes comes the first (and super fun) new feature of Great Ace Attorney: the Logic and Reasoning Spectacular events. They are a series of scenes that act as a breaking point in the exploration process' pace and consist of a kind of "dances" between the famous detective and our protagonist, where mysteries and contradictions in the crime scenes must be solved, sometimes with the presence of those involved using our observation skills to assemble together the puzzle of the event in question. These scenes are a blast and I always felt like I wanted more, the animation and sound work in them is out of this world and every time I reached one my heart started pounding with excitement. Great gameplay design here.The innovations do not end there, however, and the already classic trials have undergone an important facelift. This time, one additional "party" is included in the judicial process: the people's jury. In each trial we will have to convince not only the investigating judge but also the members of the jury of our position, sometimes using their own arguments against them and pitting them against each other to achieve our purpose. It involves an additional degree of reasoning in the trials that makes them more varied and deep. Besides, now there may be more than two witnesses testifying and being cross-examined simultaneously, so we will have to focus not only on their testimony but also on the reactions of the other people on the stand in real time. It does not have a great difficulty and it's almost impossible to fail when a reaction takes place, but again it contributes to breath additional variety and depth into the original formula.As for the remaining features, this game achieves excellence in all of them. Visually it is, for me, the most polished of all the entries I've played, with a great deal of work done in environments, effects and, especially, characters. As I have already mentioned before, I am in love with their extravagant designs and animations, full of expressivity and personality even in their simplest instances.Likewise, audio is quite amazing in this pack. The series' spirit is still there, keeping the old sound identity in menus and actions with SFX that are recognizable by any fan of the franchise, and in terms of soundtrack, this is arguably the best installment in the series. The themes have an immense quality, both the reimagined classic themes (few) and the new ones (specially all those related to Herlock Sholmes, really memorable compositions).All things considered, this was a memorable experience for me, one that I've enjoyed every second of and I'm already missing. If you are into narrative games, there are few better representatives than this one, and if you are an Ace Attorney fan then this is a must stop.

_childDocuments_.review: An Ace Attorney collection truly worthy of its name. Certainly the closest the series has come to matching the quality of the original trilogy. It has all the components for a great Ace Attorney game: It's got an interesting plot with an overarching mystery over the course of the duologyIt's got great characters who are always likeable and entertaining (making Sherlock Holmes a comedic relief character was a bold choice)It's got good puzzles, with no solutions that are absurd reaches (something the rest of the series is a tad infamous for)There are only a few things I criticise the game for. One for the amount of repetitive and unnecessary dialogue, which is never more prevalent than in the Dance of Deduction sequences. It really slows the game down, especially since the dance of deductions are so easy.Another is the fact that while the mysteries are interesting, it seems that the writers struggled to fit the discoveries in the courtroom format. This leads to witnesses and jurors sometimes saying completely irrelevant things to keep the plot progressing forward.

_childDocuments_.review: The Game is AfootThere have been very few games I have recommend at full price, this is one of them.Before you say anything, yes, £31.99 is 110% worth it.If someone were to ask, "what is an example of absolutely brilliant story telling" this is one of the first things that would pop to mind. The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is 2021's, localised bundle of the 2015, "The Great Ace Attorney: Adventures" (Dai Gyakuten Saiban: Naruhodou Ryuunosuke no Bouken) and the 2017, "The Great Ace Attorney 2: Resolve" (Dai Gyakuten Saiban 2: Naruhodou Ryuunosuke no Kakugo)After years of fans begging Capcom to bring the Japan exclusive Ace Attorney prequels to the west, we finally received them, and they are glorious, not only does TGAA improve on major problems that have plagued the Ace Attorney franchise for years, but also serve as a new story, following Ryunosuke Naruhodo, the ancestor of Phoenix Wright (Ryūichi Naruhodō in Japan), the lovable and more competent than Maya, Judicial Assistant, Susato Mikotoba, along with Sher- sorry, Herlock Sholmes, and his adopted daughter Iris. _childDocuments_.review: Wouldn't recommend unless you can grab it on discount.Both 'Adventures' and 'Resolve' felt long winded, lots of filler dialogue and fanfare during deductions made it take much longer to get to parts of the story you could interact with. There was minimal evidence collection/forensic work, and when you could interact outside of evidence, it was pretty clear what option you had to choose (deductions telling you what to change, clear notice for perusing side witnesses, and when it was peruse or drop something, you always pursue, making it feel like a pointless choice). The cases were predictable, it was pretty easy to know the ending as well as what examined parts of evidence would be used for long before it would come up. I paused the game often to do other things, because it wasn't engaging. The recurring female characters in the main cast group are young/minors, whereas the recurring males are 20s/30s/40s+. Just seemed a bit odd, would have like to see a better balance.'Adventures': I just didn't like this game. The story felt disconnected, the case plots were underwhelming, and the trails rarely had a satisfying ending. The game sacrificed a lot of character potential to prep for reveals in Resolve when it didn't need to. It could have written them better and still avoided spoiling the plot, but instead the characters seemed one-dimensional and their decisions came off as just ways to move the story along instead of purposeful character choices and motivation. If the games were offered outside of a bundle, I'd say get Resolve and just read a summary of 'Adventures'.'Resolve': Okay overall, I preferred this game to 'Adventures'. It tied up loose ends and gave a bit more depth to the characters from the previous games, but it really shouldn't take 2 games/10 cases to get to that point. Even with this game, I don't think most of the story, trails, or characters are that memorable/interesting compared to previous Ace Attorney games.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not gonna act like I didn't have fun with this game. I'm glad it got localized, the music is great, the overarching storylines are good, the graphics are good. It's more Ace Attorney for the fans who have already played all the other Ace Attorney games, and that's really the only demographic I would recommend this game to. If you want to get into the series, play the Phoenix Wright trilogy. If you played the trilogy and want more, play Apollo Justice or Miles Edgeworth Investigations.Because DEAR GOD this game is a slogfest. this game is stacks on stacks on stacks of overly explained yet entirely simple mysteries and extraneous dialogue that isn't funny enough to justify the absolute time sink of a single sentence at the slowest text scrolling speed known to man. Why bother writing two mysteries when you can write one that takes twice as long because all the characters stop at every opportunity to say "There's a mystery! "How did you not notice the mystery?" "What mystery?" "How could there be a mystery?" "Oh, we sure have to solve this mystery!"Like, the core element of Ace Attorney is the cross examination of testimony, so you'd think with such a long game you'd have lots of opportunities to press witnesses and find contradictions, right? But if you actually count the number of individual testimonies, you get maybe like... eight in a case. A trilogy case would give you twice as much, meaning more puzzles to solve, more lies to uncover, and just more exciting moments. It's not quality over quantity here, either; you're really just supposed to press every statement until some evidence or a statement gets updated, and then you know that you have to use whatever got updated, taking away half the puzzle. It's even easier when they give you a big exclamation point because a different witness wants to say something. Questioning the jury about voting guilty is similarly easy and goes just as slow, but it's a good mechanic and fits right in.The investigations... are very, very long. Investigation segments in any Ace Attorney game tend to be the less exciting half in exchange for the necessary buildup of mysteries and evidence, but the investigating in this game railroads you harder than ever. Go here, ask everything, look at something, repeat. You're not solving any puzzles besides the occasional "Dance of Deduction" (Great segment. Could go a little faster).And it's not like I hate the characters, either. They're all expressive, funny, and interesting. But the best characters in the world don't mean anything when I'm just waiting for a plot that refuses to move forward at a reasonable pace. If the writers trimmed out some lines to make the game less repetitious and gave an option to double the text speed, especially on first playthroughs where you can't skip ANY new dialogue, I'd still have some issues, but I wouldn't be giving this thumbs down. Great Ace Attorney is a 70 hour game that should be a 45 hour game at maximum, and if this review seems needlessly elaboratory on that point then I've given you a good idea of what you're in for.

_childDocuments_.review: I have long been a fan of the Ace Attorney series playing all of them as they came out on the Game Boy, This is the first time I played The Great Ace Attorney and I absolutely loved it. Taking place in the 1800's Japan and Great Britain following a different lawyer/judicial assistant combo I felt this was a very fresh take on the series. The gimmicks of this game were great, no magic/spiritual power needed, and it all fit thematically. -Simple Gameplay, basically a visual novel-Fun mysteries-Fun quirky Characters-Accessability options to turn it into a straight visual novel.-Music is great-Level select for completion once beating the game-Good voice acting for cut scenes, this is not something I often think about, but the accent work is excellent. The main characters are Japanese students in Great Britain, so they speak a British dialect, with a Japanese accent.-This is a problem persistant through the series, but there are parts where testimony can be contradicted with multiple pieces of evidence, but only one works, and then the rest are brought up to coroborate. -A few times I could piece together large chunks of the mysteries, and had to wait for my character to catch up, at one point it was obvious to me but the character had to go through multiple panic attacks.-Some evidence can only be partially investigated until something happens-Text is a bit slow, and I found myself often fast-forwarding and then reading the court history. -No fishingI took about 100 hours to beat, (I left my PC on a lot and would do other things so not sure that is true). I beat it in to segments taking a break between Game 1 and Game 2. Took less than a day to clean up achievements thanks to the chapter select. I looked up 3 solutions I could not figure out, that made sense, but I had other evidence that made more sense, or I just missed a small detail on.

_childDocuments_.review: How is anyone getting through this? Everyone takes 16 times longer to say anything than they should. Every character wastes so much time on quirks that aren't interesting or amusing, talking about plot points that go nowhere, talking about plot points that will go somewhere in what the writers probably thought was foreshadowing but was actually just needlessly drawn out filler, or they just talk about nothing. The protagonist is almost as useless as Apollo was in his first case, except this lasts for two whole games. The assistant is bland, though is at least preferable to the parts where an adult is accompanied by a 10 year old girl. I don't know the pedo laws over in Japan, judging by most anime they seem to have none at all, but over here we're not into that. This game does seem to have two unique gimmicks... one which wastes time during investigation, and one which seems like a good idea but mostly just makes every juror into an idiot who doesn't understand the stakes of a murder trial. The only good thing about this game that Trials and Tribulations badly needed was telling you where to go during Investigation. Everything else makes me wish I stopped played these games after Dual Destinies, which was much better than this and had more interesting gimmicks and characters. This is obviously just a poorly written excuse for a game made by someone who just discovered Sherlock Holmes books and wanted to include a character based on that. The inconsistent British accents of every character make it clear that they didn't care about anything besides that.In conclusion, here's an example of how most of the dialogue should have been written vs how it was written:_______________________________Prosecutor Dracula: What evidence do you have for your claim?Protagonist Useless: This - (Shows evidence)but instead we get:_______________________________Prosecutor Dracula: What evidence do you have for your claim?Judge CopyPaste: Yes, show us your evidence!Assistant Bland: Protagonist, this is the time to show the evidence!Protagonist Useless: (I need to think carefully about the evidence...)Assistant Bland: I am responding to what is supposed to be a thought because the translators didn't realize that words in parenthesis were not actually said out loud.Protagonist Useless: I am about to present the evidence that supports my claim!Prosecutor Dracula: What?!Jury Moron 1: !Jury Moron 2: It can't be...!Jury Moron 3: My preconceived notions are being challenged??Jury Moron 4: I bet I'm secretly the culprit all along, how convenient that I am a member of the jury.Jury Moron 5: I have nothing to add and will take a full 10 seconds to state that.Jury Moron 6: What?Protagonist Useless: The evidence...Prosecutor Dracula: Racist insult. I throw my glass backwards.Protagonist Useless: ...which I am about to present...Judge CopyPaste: Gasp! My hair animation will play for the 400th time!Protagonist Useless: ...is this, which would have saved a lot of people 6 hours of pointless dialogue if I had the option to present it earlier.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a case where I really wish Steam had a "mixed" review option; because this game has potential - it's just a slog to get through.As someone who bought this game immediately after finishing the original Ace Attorney Trilogy, I was honestly expecting the same thing as that game. What I got was like trying to wade through cobwebs in Minecraft with soul sand underneath and the effects of the Turtle Master potion applied - slow as hell.In the original Ace Attorney, the "tutorial" case, the "First Turnabout", was about 40 minutes long. Here, the first case, the "Adventure of the Great Departure", which was just an intro to the trial portions of the game for those unfamiliar with the Ace Attorney series, was . They could have easily condensed this down; but everyone in this game talks like I put the original lines from the Ace Attorney Trilogy, and asked ChatGPT to make them more verbose and wordy. Like, for example, something as simple as "that's a ladder" turns into "that's a climbing device known here as a 'ladder.'"Although, I will state, it nails down the Ace Attorney formula very well despite it being a mess to get through; the music is actually really good; and they definitely nailed down the 3D models in this game compared to Dual Destinies or Spirit of Justice.That being said, I would still recommend this game to Ace Attorney fans or visual novel enjoyers, just not to someone who has a fairly short attention span (like me) or expect the game to be quick and snappy like the original Ace Attorney Trilogy.

_childDocuments_.review: A Great Departure Signaling A Much-Anticipated Return to Form~!A lovingly crafted return to a much-missed series, The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is as much a treat for the eyes and ears as it is for the mind. Fully embracing its turn-of-the-20th-century Japanese setting, the game introduces its (as always) well-written and oddball characters, from our hesitant legal savant protagonist Ryunosuke to the painfully pathetic Auchi. Aside from a spoilerific segment first introduced in the second case, the game utilizes mechanics adopted across previous games and interweaves them with newer mechanics to create a smooth, enjoyable experience. Two cases in, and there's very little to complain about, so if you're a die-hard fan of Phoenix Wright, give it a try!Pros: Fresh world, fresh characters, and background conflict that's interesting and easy to understand. Music and visuals are on point, and gameplay is frustration-free and fun.Cons: Unless you own a Switch, you're not getting a physical copy of this. Oh, and one of the characters is a bit annoying, but I'm sure that'll sort itself out soon (it's a game about murder mysteries and raison d'etres. It'll fix itself one way or another, through death or character growth... or both).

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I feel like I should write something about this game. Ace Attorney is probably my favorite game series and this was an entry I was excited for. I finally finished it last night, and I have to say it is quite spectacular.There is some challenge to totally leaving the cast that your players know so well behind and constructing a brand new one, in a different time period no less, and this game succeeds on this front. The characters are marvelous and even the ones specific to one case are very strong and memorable.This game benefits in a very similar way to the way Miles Edgeworth's spin-off games Ace Attorney Investigations does, in that the first game, while good, builds toward the second game's conclusion. The final three cases in the second game of this duology, Resolve, is one of the finest sequences of the Ace Attorney franchise. The story of the two games is well laid out and the conclusion is beautiful.I think this one improves on the mechanics of the previous games in the series; the earlier games falter with me a bit with very long, boring and cryptic investigation phases where as they are a bit streamlined here will still being an interesting phase to meet new characters and learn new information about the case. The cross-examination of multiple witnesses from the Layton crossover is an excellent mainstay here and other new mechanics like the Dance of Deduction and Summation Examination are really great too.Sometimes the game feels a bit long, but that isn't necessarily a complaint for me. Some people are likely going to feel its length but I don't think its much of a problem at all.Anyway, this is a really fantastic pair of games and I can only hope that we see more access to more games in the Ace Attorney franchise on modern consoles and PC such as Apollo Justice, Investigations 1 and 2 and the 3DS-only games. I would also hope more Ace Attorney games are in the works at Capcom.If you like Ace Attorney, buy this game. If you are interested in getting into Ace Attorney, this is just as good a place to start as the original Phoenix Wright trilogy, in my opinion.And remember: pursue the truth, no matter how painful it may be.
