_childDocuments_.review: I ultimately really enjoyed this game, but I would highly recommend playing it in chunks. This is a VERY long game and the length can get tedious at times. There are also, from the very first case onwards, TONS of dangling plot threads that quite literally don't get sewn up until the very end. I will say, that every single thread does get wrapped up in a very emotionally and satisfying bow, but considering the length, just let the mysteries wash over you because it's going to take a long time for all of them to get resolved.Each Ace Attorney game seems to have a new courtroom mechanic, and this one includes two: the jury system and also the fact that more than one person takes the stand at a time very frequently. I enjoyed the jury system as it added a lot of personality and flavor the court proceedings, but it did get a bit predictable. At some point in every trial (often twice) the jury will decide that they've made up their mind on a guilty verdict and you've got to pit them against each other in order to change their mind. While I enjoyed it generally, I feel like these moments would have had greater impact if used more sparingly. The fact that more than one person can testify was an interesting idea in concept, but I sort of hated the execution. That's primarily because the game has a wonderful "auto-play" feature where you don't have to keep pressing the space bar or mouse to continue the text. This was awesome. I could sit back, sip my tea and just read along the screen until it came time to make a decision. But the way multiple testimonies work is that in the midst of a conversation with one person, another person on the witness stand will make some change of expression, and you have to catch it and pursue this other person in order to get the new bit of information or elaboration, which essentially means that when more than one person testifies (which is probably about two thirds of the time) you can't use the auto-play feature when pressing witness statements. Also, there's absolutely no deductive ability at all. It's just a way of stringing along already very long trials.I know that all that said, it might sound like I don't recommend the game, but I DEFINITELY do. The cases were typically convoluted and wonderfully complex, just how I like 'em. But by FAR the best parts of the game are the three main protagonists: Ryunosuke, Susato, and of course Herlock Sholmes.Ryunosuke and Susato are both so incredibly winsome and earnest. In a 19th century Britain teeming with jaded, cynical, and often bitter characters (though delightfully eccentric as always) Ryunosuke and Susato are constant breaths of fresh air, and the fact that they have each other's absolute decency to lean on did an amazing job of offsetting even the darkest moments. I think I prefer them to even Phoenix and Maya. I think they both have more personality, frankly, and their situation (fish out of water) and their earnest resolve made them much more easy to identify with and root for. I ended the game loving them both very much and seeing their friendship (and more....????) blossom throughout the series was my second favorite part of the game.My first being, of course, the inimitable Herlock Sholmes. We haven't had a character like Sholmes in an Ace Attorney game that I can think of and he is a DELIGHT. I actually remember being pretty put off by him during his first appearance, and I will say his mini-game during investigation sections, while interesting are VERY unchallenging. But his humor and personality grows steadily throughout the series. I found myself laughing more at this game than I have in any other than I can remember in a long time, and I'd say 85% of that was Sholmes. He is fantastic. Bumbling, often hysterically wrong, conceited, but at the same time always a source of boundless enthusiasm, joy, and unexpected wisdom. He's a singularly charismatic character, whose fun and mystery only grows with each case. I don't think I've enjoyed a video game character so much since I played Disco Elysium. A brilliantly unorthodox take on "The Great Detective" and it makes me want to retcon every iteration of Sherlock Holmes ever and make them the adventures of Herlock Sholmes instead.So all in all, highly recommend the game, but don't expect to binge it. I think I binged the first game but then after starting the second one, it got too overwhelming and I had to take a break. Just go at each case leisurely if you can. It's a lot to get through, but they really nail the conclusion and the characters grow very much throughout the course of the two games.Also: the prosecutor Von Zeiks is insane. He dresses like a Transylvanian count, is constantly crushing wine glasses and bottles, and occasionally hoists his leg up on the banister like drag queen doing a seductive stretch. He's definitely enough to give the Edgeworth shippers a run for their money.

_childDocuments_.review: Many people are praising this game, so let me put my perspective as someone who requested a refund but probably won't get it with three hours of playtime. The game is slow. The game even punishes you for thinking ahead, as you have to make obviously wrong statements, suffer through endless repetition of basic facts, and pursue useless lines of inquiry before you're allowed to make progress. The character models look nice, and some dialogue is amusing, but far more of it is not amusing enough for how slow it is.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I would like to put this on my list of recommended games... I just can't. There are several reasons for that (some of which are subjective), which have a negative effect on how entertaining this game is.-One of the reasons is the pacing. As it has been noted by several other people, GAA was meant to be one single game, but was split in two due to platform constraints. And it shows... because the game seems to drag on forever, particularly with the overarching plot. It doesn't help that parts of some cases are an obvious recycle of previous ones, like how the culprit from the first one here is a period accurate copy of Dahlia Hawthorne from PWAA Trials and Tribulations. But I could mention how painfully repetitive and predictable are the so called "twists" are, going back and forth multiple times in the same scene until you want to fast forward just to get to the point. This is just not funny.-The characters are, frankly, irritating, starting with the MC of all people. Unlike Phoenix or Apollo's introduction to the series, Naruhodo is a fumbling mess at first and while he does get better later on, his animations are pointlessly theatric even in later chapters. And he's far from the worst, as Natsume is such a jumpy mess with such inane posing that it honestly made me wish to see him cut loose. But no, there's an even worse character in GAA, the cringiest vampire ripoffs in the history of video games, van Zieks (which sounds Dutch, not even British), who, unlike any of the prosecutors from the previous games is not even remotely funny. None of the cool rebuttals Edgeworth is known for, or the mockery with which Franziska wants to whip Phoenix into shape (heh) or even Godot and his coffee addiction. No, just a 2-dimensional horrifyingly badly written antagonist vampire ripoff. Seriously, who wrote his character?Oh, and Gregson looks like Stalin without his hat.-In terms of gameplay there's plenty to criticize too. The investigations feel boring and short, with GAA ditching the best parts (like the Psy-locks) for multiple chances for... playing the straight man to another bumbling fool who goes by a name everyone would recognize. This guy's "deductions", while they do give the opportunity for the player to engage in gameplay more, only provide a feature that can't measure up to the previous games with how ridiculous they are. And they are the highlights of the investigation parts!But I could also mention the utterly pointless magnifying glass feature. The number of times it actually proves useful or needed is exactly... zero. It's only good for wasting time.Or how about the idiotic jury system? Seriously, it was only put into this game to pointlessly drag on the trials.-How about the music then? It's also a far cry from any of the soundtracks so far, though this may be a bit more subjective. It does fit the era and location decently, but nonetheless fails to achieve the same level. Exciting cross-examination theme? Nah. Character songs like Gumshoe's? Heavens no. Steel Samurai level theme song? Perish the thought. The most we get is a mixture of Eastern and Western tunes resulting in passable, but hardly noteworthy tracks.The translation also leaves something to be desired on multiple occasions, but one that really stands out is the translator's insistence on using "mass murderer" instead of "serial kiler". And that's not the only issue, really. What were they thinking?All in all, while GAA is certainly an interesting take on the classic games set in Victorian-era London and contemporary Japan, it fails to achieve the quality of the previous titles. In the absence of a neutral rating I'm settling for Not Recommended, unless bought at sale for a reduced price.

_childDocuments_.review: When first I started The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles, I was frustrated by the pacing, presentation of characters, and lack of brevity to every conversation. However, my opinion on just about everything did a complete 180 after I simply changed how I viewed the game. I approached the game from the lens of someone who has been playing Ace Attorney for years, and for better or worse, it is a series with a somewhat predictable formula. I had grown comfortable with that formula, but I only now realize, after being shown just how much that formula can be shaken up, just how stale it had become.Great Ace Attorney feels like a breath of fresh air to the Ace Attorney series. The orchestral and somber musical score is perfectly suited to the period, and every theme feels masterfully tailored to the situations they play in. By comparison, the 3DS titles we did initially got, Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice, feel almost slapdash and I am only upset we didn't get these games sooner.I genuinely feel that Great Ace Attorney should be the bar moving forward, having shaken up the storytelling formula kept so firmly in place by Ace Attorneys famous 3 day trial system, and that the mechanics introduced, the jury system and Dance of Deduction, should certainly make a return. The Dance of Deduction especially is worthy of praise, as it managed to do something I had never expected of an Ace Attorney: it made the investigation phases genuinely interesting.Overall, grand game, wonderful soundtrack, memorable characters, and a well-told, if sometimes overly verbose, story that often had me laughing and sometimes crying. I am filled with new hope for the Ace Attorney franchise and hope that Mr. Shu Takumi can continue to deliver.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney is, at the very least, on par with the original trilogy- I can guarantee that much. But when I was playing it, particularly GAA2, it occurred to me that these games, when considered as one, contiguous story, and two parts of a larger game, might actually be my favorite in the entire series.The original trilogy is incredible, no doubt about it- an enticing combination of solid characters, engaging mysteries, humor, and slowly unraveling overarching stories. Then, when I played Apollo Justice, the fourth game in the series, I thought I'd be in for more of that. Many people overlook AA4, but I really enjoyed it. AA5 and 6 didn't quite live up to my hopes. Solid games, of course, with some excellent moments, and overall quite enjoyable, but they miss the mark in a few areas, namely the writing. One particular thing that irked me was that the switch to 3D models over 2D sprites was wasted, and the classic expressiveness of Ace Attorney characters seemed to be lost.The Great Ace Attorney lives up to the promises made by the original trilogy. The writing, is, thankfully, much improved- Shu Takumi, series creator, back in the director's chair-, and unlike the second trilogy of the main series, GAA is not afraid of telling an overarching story. Crucially, it takes the same approach that AA1-3 took to its characters, where many, if not most, appear in multiple cases, allowing the world to feel vastly more connected, and creating much more affinity for the characters that appear. GAA also uses the added dimension of the 3D models to its advantage; characters look like they belong in 3D, instead of being odd, frequently uncanny translations of existing characters. The mere fact that this game allows multiple characters to appear in the same frame at once sounds minute, but brings significant improvements to the flow of dialogue and storytelling.Gameplay is mostly unchanged, with typical investigation sequences and courtroom battles, but two new mechanics make everything feel just varied enough when compared to the original. Unlike the Mood Matrix (which had its moments) and Divination Seance (which was terrible except for the literal last one in the game) of AA5 and AA6, these mechanics feel naturally integrated and match the story. The introduction of a jury addresses a common logical complaint about the Ace Attorney series- the lack of a jury in all but one case in the main series-, but having to persuade jurors in what are essentially special cross-examinations brings a new layer to the courtroom battles. In investigations, you now take part in the Dance of Deduction with Herlock Sholmes (that's not a typo), which utilize the 3D space and provide a fun break from the typical talk-investigate-move loop of investigations.The setting is one I absolutely loved; a heavily stylized Victorian London with minor steampunk elements, and an opening set in Japan. It doesn't provide any profound commentary on the period, nor would I expect it to. The game leverages its setting to create charming characters and enjoyable environments to sleuth through, frequently using the time period in its humor and often its mysteries (for example, while in the main series, fingerprints are bound to appear in almost every case, they are not yet accepted as evidence at the time of GAA).There's not a single character in either game I hated (by which I mean, a character the developers did not intend for me to hate, because there are plenty of those), and some of them have risen to be my favorites in the series. Ryunosuke also (potentially unpopular opinion) has a more defined character arc than Phoenix ever had, and Susato is one of few times where they've succeeded in giving you a companion as enjoyable as Maya Fey (Trucy Wright and Ema Skye being the others, but the series completely forgets about Trucy, and Ema is relegated to Gumshoe's replacement). Van Zieks is a strong prosecutor, perhaps not quite the series' best, but still in the upper half. The best character, of course, is Herlock Sholmes, who steals every scene he appears in, and is, at all times, entirely entertaining.I won't speak too much on the overarching narrative and the individual mysteries for spoiler reasons, but I would argue that there is no 'bad' case in GAA, and all are at the least, very good. The average quality of the cases in both game is alongside or above the original trilogy (and I'd lean towards the latter), and a very well-rounded, varied package. I didn't find too many logical inconsistencies (though I also don't spend my time nitpicking at every detail like some, so go figure) in the cases. The overarching mystery slowly unravels, but I will admit that in retrospect, the first game definitely takes a lot of its time to set up GAA2. Despite this, GAA tells its own story and still manages to exist by itself, even with the heavy connection and build-up to its sequel. To fully appreciate them, though, you must play both.I would strongly recommend The Great Ace Attorney, whether you enjoy the main series or otherwise. You can enjoy GAA without playing any of the others. Play it if you love mystery/detective stories and visual novels of this style. If you want more Ace Attorney and haven't played GAA, you really can't go wrong here, and I strongly encourage anyone with similar feelings towards AA4-6 to myself to play GAA, as it's probably what you're looking for.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: It's a return to form for the series after the questionable direction of Yamazaki during dual destinies and spirit of justice. If you want to recapture how the original three games felt in terms of how people speak and how characters are designed, look no further than this.The "racism" people harp on about is at most casual bigotry from people who are supposed to be seen as being bigoted. It's a tool the narrative uses to paint Ryu and the gang as an underdog more than anything. Don't let it dissuade you from this title.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: The story and intrigue that I always loved of Ace Attorney games. Although it drags on in some dialogues, by taking a long detour to do something as simple as a memory/flashback, it still has creative intrigue, with some I predicted, some that caught me by surprise.That being said, the second game has...Very dubious translation issues and unintentional misspelling, which become far more painful to bear in the second half of the game. The strangest of which, to me, was using the term "appreciate" instead of "understand", which comes off very strangely when a character mentions things, such as "I appreciate your pain and struggles". I wish I was kidding. Considering how early you learn the word "understand" when starting to learn english as a non-native language, it feels like the kind of mistake that could happen only by using google translate, as even AI would do a better job of translating. There are a lot of other mistakes in the translation, many that just makes it confusing, as using the wrong verb tense to link a sentence together, but this one was by far the most glaring one I could think of.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I owned the Ace Attorney trilogy, Ace Attorney Apollo Justice, Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice games on the 3DS.  I've never loved any of them enough to include them on a list of all-time favorite video games, but I've liked them well enough to buy and play them when they've been on sale.This is the first time I've played any of the games in this franchise on PC.  One thing I've always disliked about this series is that you aren't given the option to set the text display speed, nor are you allowed to click through the dialog windows at your own pace.  I was hoping that by now, having made their way to PC, that those things might finally be an option.  But no.  I still have to sit waiting for text to crawl across the frames at its own pre-set speed to read it, and wait until it's finished doing that before I can click through to the next sentence.  Nor is there any option to skip ahead (although if the game has in fact shown you some dialog before, it will remember that and allow you to move through the text faster on subsequent playback by holding down the button).  This leads me to conclude that not being given the option to do otherwise is a deliberate choice on the part of the developers in order to artificially pad/stretch out the game's length.  Which is really tedious, especially when you know what the characters are getting at but they haven't gotten to the point yet.This is a marginal thumbs down because the rest of the things about the game range from adequate to enjoyable.  As of right now I'm almost halfway through the game (I believe), but I'm close to being fed up with this aggravating UI feature.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Eh. Didn't really care for this one, even though I enjoyed every other game in the franchise. I appreciate what they were trying to do, and there are some really good cases in here. The new mechanics with the dance of deduction and summation exams are neat.  Furthermore, the overarching story is great. It's just that the journey to get there is a bit slow and tedious at times. So much to the point I can't really recommend this one or say it's worth the time I spent feeling a bit bored or feeling like the cases were going sluggish. GAA2 is better than GAA1 in that regard but.... You still have to go through GAA1 for the full story so.... Yeah. I feel maybe I'd appreciate the game more if I was a Sherlock Holmes fan as I know this game is full of references to it, but I haven't., so.... That's a lot of stuff I'm not getting. Music's not bad, but I could probably fall asleep to a number of the tracks - which doesn't really help with how poorly paced parts of this are. It made me long a bit for the music direction of other titles. So... Yeah. There's a great story in there, but the issues I have really weigh this one down for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I am still playing through this, but I am far enough along to be invested (1-4, investigation past the first save point)Firstly, I think this game does a lot well with what it is.Lets start with the background and work forward. The design of it is a lot better than the remastered trilogy, as the movement menu shows off all the locations you can currently visit and doesn't make you backtrack across various other setpieces to get to where you need to go. The mechanics are more robust than just psychelocks and occasionally pressing everything a dozen times, the examination of evidence is SO good (I so wanted to inspect the receipt in Case 1-2 early, that really could have been a save from Mia if the player didn't figure it out yet), most of the characters are better, more fleshed out versions of parallels from previous games (Giving Maya stand-in a stronger presence as the more competent one was a big plus to me, it always felt like Maya Prime was a bit underdeveloped as just a damsel in distress that is occasionally useful). The detectives (plural) are all more competent or funnier than Gumshoe, who was a catchphrase machine and local punching bag, the Edgeworth is more edgy and worthy (and actually scary. When Edgeworth Prime showed up in the original trilogy, I approached it like "Ok, so this is the REAL prosecutor who is contesting us" and when this one showed up it was "Oh ♥♥♥♥ the vampire is going to kill us all if he gets pissed off" and has more or less so far believed in justice.) The justice system is screwed not because the prosecutor took more than their fair share of the dinner but because the system is so new that nobody has a clue what is going on yet. The mechanics with the jury and the multiple witnesses adds so much to an otherwise boring process.I mean seriously, just going through the character list everyone seems better than the original:Judge: They seem like they actually care about justice, rather than some notion that the prosecutor is always right.Maya:  Competent, strong, can kick the ass of anyone who tries her.Phoenix: Has a real reason he is outwardly stumbling over every little thing. We are expected that Phoenix Prime passed the bar exam, but Naruhodo is just a student.Inspector Gumshoe: Has 3 standins, each to a varying degree of competency and fun. The first one is straightfaced, a bit eccentric, but loyal and determined. The second needs Adderall, but is generally either fun or smug and dances on either side of the line to fit what perception we need to have of him. The third is the closest to Gumshoe, but tired. Larry Butz: Not present so far, keep up the good work!Witnesses: They don't feel like one note personalities, instead they seem like 2 notes. A step in the right direction, but not bad considering the lot of them we will meet once and discard.Now onto the things I personally didn't care for in this game:The entire jury trial thing could have been handled better. At the beginning I reset because I was thinking "♥♥♥♥ I can't press willy nilly because it causes the game to make me lose without the life system." But nope that was required to continue the story. It is not a good look for the game when I can view progress as losing. That wouldn't be so bad if the game's UI glitches out if you do anything the game isn't prepared for. If you Alt Tab and do anything, or scroll using a trackpad, or walk away for a bit, the game will break itself to pieces. I have lost a bit of time just getting back to where I was in the story because I had to restart my game because the right movement key would get stuck. And then there is the fact that the entire thing is a cloud save, limiting the options of offline play on this singleplayer game. I doubt that this visual novel's file takes up *too* much storage space, we can spare a kilobyte or two on it.As for things I am neutral about, the graphics are ok, the entire theming is pretty interesting but also infuriating for entirely understandable reasons (Hate that it has to happen, do not mind that it is happening because it is accurate), 3rd case was a bit rocky, but if we consider our boss's questions as a lesson to us, we can kind of appreciate the lesson learned that we should be hunting for the truth, not a guilty verdict. I cannot feel one way or the other about the actual locations we find ourselves investigating.Overall, 7.2/10. There are a few quite annoying glitches, but the other UI is good, the characters are great and poke fun at the original trilogy and how hammy it was, the motives are more comprehensive, and the gameplay overall has improved. Well done.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney is a very special game from Capcom. This is, one of the greatest games Capcom ever made, a game that has a deep history to it, and a rough history. A title that for many years was trapped in Japan on the 3DS, unable to release anywhere else in the world, and for many, it being on this Steam page is a dream come true.Let me take you back, to 2012. Capcom is deep in development of the ambitious crossover with Level 5: Professor Layton vs Ace Attorney. Two DS mystery game icons join forces on a grand adventure filled with mystery, with the gameplay combined of both series. At the time, Ace Attorney had stagnated. Gameplay was the same, stories weren't that interesting, and there hadn't been a mainline entry in years. Development of PLvAA was a rocky road with many ideas scrapped, as not only were they on a tight deadline, but also planning to try new things Ace Attorney never tried before. This crossover was Ace Attorney's first game in the third dimension, so in light of this Capcom felt it was time to do more. More presentation, voice acting, more animations, more detail. Ace Attorney in the past relied on reusing assets a lot and using as little resources as necessary in order to create their compelling narratives. It worked wonders for the original trilogy, but it was clear that after so many games, they needed to shake things up, and my god did it pay off. Despite the rough development, the crossover was a success, and really innovated the Ace Attorney games for the better.However because of how long development took on PLvAA, Capcom needed a new mainline Ace Attorney game. Problem was, Shu Takumi, the series' main architect, was too busy with PLvAA, so the spinoff team had to make the new mainline game, Dual Destinies, themselves, given a blank slate to tell the story they wanted. Dual Destinies (as well as the following game Spirit of Justice) were amazing Ace Attorneys, however the innovations brought in PLvAA did not make the cut. Not that this is a bad thing, but what PLvAA did just felt...more, and really made the games even more fun.Enter the Great Ace Attorney in 2015. Shu Takumi has a grand idea: A new Ace Attorney storyline set years in the past the late years of the 19th Century starring fledgling Japanese lawyer Ryunosuke as he is sent to study law in the Empire of Japan's new ally Great Britain. Along the way teams up with the legendary great detective himself, Sherlock Holmes, a name I think you already know, and unravels mystery after mystery with Holmes both around London and in the courtroom defending many interesting characters.So what happened? Two things: The first, The Great Ace Attorney was not a success initially. Originally, gamers in Japan hated the new direction, and sales struggled. Not only that, but the game could not release internationally due to one character: Sherlock Holmes. The Conan Doyle Estate are ruthless copyright trolls, who despite the character being public domain, is still covered in legal red tape, and no matter what negotiations Capcom tried, the Doyle estate wouldn't budge.Given time and a sequel two years later, Japanese gamers realized just how great (pun intended) this masterpiece really is, and now both games rival even the original trilogy. But how? Because of new gameplay from PLvAA refined in this game: Multiple witnesses, extra presentation, the new Jury Examinations, and most importantly: Memorable characters, stories, and drama. The Great Ace Attorney lives up to it's name.One piece of gameplay was improved tremendously: Investigations. In the past investigating in Ace Attorney was a chore. You have to point and click everything and it was not fun, engaging, and rarely memorable as everyone just wanted to get it over with so they could get back to the more fun court sections. The Great Ace Attorney fixed this with one character: Sherlock. How? The bulk of investigating has been greatly condensed into investigating with Sherlock Holmes, and performing his "great deductions" in which you will deduct characters and crime scenes with him, and they're amazing. Converting investigation time to Sherlock Time was genius and actually make you invested in investigating.For years, this game was impossible to get internationally. Most people had to hack their 3DSs and run pirated copies of the Great Ace Attorney using fan translations, and while the translations did a good job, they were far from perfect. And honestly, this wasn't the best way to experience this masterpiece. Fortunes changed last year, as Capcom decided "screw it" and went the Arsene Lupin route of changing Sherlock Holmes' name to "Herlock Sholmes." Surprisingly this copyright dodging move actually made things even better. Sherlock now feels like he fits into the Ace Attorney universe. Combine that with the upscaling of the graphics, and both games in one massive package that will last you over 50 hours, and we have the perfect storm for a breakthrough masterpiece.So all this is to say: for the love of all that is holy, BUY IT! JUST BUY THIS ABSOLUTELY AMAZING MASTERPIECE I WAITED 7 YEARS TO FINALLY COME TO THE WEST!

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is not a bad game. It’s well made, has original characters, respects the historical setting, and pays tribute to the well-known fictional detective Sherlock Holmes. However, while you might expect it to be dialogue heavy, obviously it being a visual novel, still, it can go overboard at times, constantly repeating the same plot points as if the player had the attention span of a 5 year old. I had a really tough time going through the first chapters of the second game, which lead me to stop playing for a significant time period. But when I came back to the game and got over this hurdle, the worst part was over and the game’s story wrapped up quite nice. It was engaging enough for me to go through to the end.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan of this series since around 2015... so, basically around when DGS was released. I remember glimpsing news about it and its sequel, getting irritated that us english-speaking fans weren't receiving anything.And now, we finally get not one, but both of them!To address the complaints of others...- Yes, this game does drag on a little more than other series titles, but consider the fact they need to introduce about three new mechanics, rather than the usual singular one. Also, being that these are in an entirely new setting, they need to introduce it fully, which regrettably takes some time.- Yes, animations can be long. But personally, it adds a lot of charm to the game! I really love the expressiveness of everyone and wish they animated like this more frequently.- Some evidence choices are weird. I don't get everything 100% of the time. Using a guide is pretty much what I do for every AA title, so it isn't bad that I needed to use one for this.Basically, if you're very impatient and only want lore heavy cases, this might not be the best choice for you. If you've never played an AA game in your life, I'd suggest playing at least the first game before touching this, just to be introduced to the base mechanics.As for my rating?10/10 you can save anywhere

_childDocuments_.review: Another amazing package from the Ace Attorney series. This spin off will takes back to the past fighting the darkness in the justice system of a early 1900s london. The game as always is chuck full with colorful and memorable characters, funny as hell dialogues, heartwrenching stories and tense as hell trials. The first of the two games feels really like an introduction game, it takes its time making you feel familiar with the characters, gameplay and settings, there are some really cool and unexpected twists in the formula but the game as a whole really feels like the appetizer to the main course that is the second game. Great Ace Attorney 2 switches gear to max immediately, with the great mistery slowly unraveling, answers that raise even more questions all building up to an intense as hell final battle of a trial. Absolutely recommend this game to everyone, even if you haven played the original trilogy
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Huge props to the madmen at Capcom for localizing these two fantastic games. These games are definitely quite unique from the rest of the series, in both setting and atmosphere. You'll be spending hours and hours listening to Victorian orchestral music and staring at the depressing streets of London. This game will really give you an idea of why there's the usual depression, and then there's the BRITISH type of depression. It's a whole different beast. It also has some very interesting cases, with one of my favorites being the closed-roomed murder mystery inside a moving horse carriage. The writing quality, the mind-bending mysteries, and the "soul" of the series, which are the zany and creative characters, are still intact despite the change in setting. The second game, especially, has some of the coolest and most entertaining witnesses out of the entire franchise (Drebber and Shamspeare). Playing these games made me realize that it's been 20 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ years since the first game came out. It's been a long journey, and I'm glad that these games have been a big part of my life for so many years. Buy this collection and god save the queen.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Key success factors for a game like this: 1. the writing, pacing, dialogue 2. the clues, riddles and mysteries 3) the user interface, mechanics of interacting and taking actions.The game falls flat on all of these measures.The dialogue is incredibly drawn out, with very many irrelevant and meaningless statements. This is not "lore" or interesting background talk - characters are cardboard cutouts and almost all statements are meaningless, trite, irrelevant and boring. "Rynosuke, you need to speak up!" "Let your voice be heard" "Do not be nervous" "Tell the judge what's on your mind" "Just speak plainly" "Express yourself" "Speak without hesitation".  It feels like someone decided that the game's key success factor was rather the number of lines and how long it takes to get through it - so they ordered some poor underling to just put a LOT of effort into dragging out, reformulating, repeating, extending, even the most miniscule thought.The clues are either completely trivial or completely obscure. There's no happy medium of reasoning or deduction, like in original Ace Attorney episode 1. Some stretch credulity, like they are forced - someone thought up a logical plot point, but it's just not fully coherent, yet it's still hammered in without anyone challenging it. Mechanics are cumbersome and obtuse. It's easy to trigger a repeat of 20 lines that add nothing useful, per the above. Overall, it's a tedious disappointment. There is a small bit of value if you are a fan of this type of game. I was a fan of Ace Attorney 1, but feel my money is wasted.The first 2 hours should give you a correct impression of what the rest of the game is like. If you like them, you will like the rest, and vica versa.(Hours played is incorrect.)

However most of first game and especially the second game are really great in term of characters , story and you will find it hard to exit the game because you'll really want to know the truth of what is happening. _childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Played great on the Steam Deck. If the anime cutscenes don't play right (for example, looking like a rainbow test pattern) try switching your Proton version for the game. I was using 8.0-3. The only bug I encountered in the entire game was a single polygon on the left cheek of  that would flicker during a certain animation. It's quite long, but I liked that about it. A good relaxed game for lazing in bed or on a comfy couch.Something to keep in mind is this is basically one story segmented into two games spread over five chapters each. There are story elements that are introduced in the first game that don't have payoffs until the second game. I bring this up because one might think the game is paced very strangely or slowly if they are playing through the first game and expect the story to conclude by chapter 1-5, when that's merely the middle of the story.I liked the new mechanics, such as the "dance of deduction" mode that sometimes takes the place of trials. In trials there can now be multiple witnesses on the stand at once, and there's a jury to be persuaded. I enjoyed the game and would recommend it to any fans of the other Ace Attorney games. It might be a good stepping-on point for new players as well, since this is the beginning of a new spin-off that doesn't rely at all on previous Ace Attorney stories.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, these two games are up there with my favorites in the Ace Attorney series, (especially Resolve). The pacing is a bit slower when compared to other Ace Attorney games, but I don't think this is a bad thing. This is because by the end everything feels really well developed and fleshed out. The setting, story, and characters are all great and memorable, and overall these entries feel fresh and inspired. These games have made me very excited to see what the future holds for Ace Attorney!

_childDocuments_.review: I know this is a visual novel for the most part, but I do wish that there was a little bit more of an exploration/discovery phase for finding clues that is not just uninterrupted dialog. However, the court scenes are so fun, and digging through the evidence can actually be challenging at times. Also, I would die for Herlock Sholmes. Fully recommend

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't my usual genre of game, but man has it left an impact on me. I played this game nearly two years ago  and despite playing hundreds of games since then, this one is the one that comes back to me the most. _childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: This is without a doubt one of the best installments in the Ace Attorney Chronicles, and I say that as someone who has been playing the series since I was 13 years old. The music, character design, and localization are incredible. Love the use of steampunk London and post-Samurai Meiji Japan. The intricacies and historical nuance have been done really well and I highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the franchise. I'd argue that I like this a bit more than SoJ but again I love all of them so I am biased. The characters are so endearing, you feel strongly connected to everyone and it stands alone from the main trilogy.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: My biggest disappointment with this game is, after finally finishing it, learning that Capcom doesn't appear to have any plans for a sequel. GAAC has the same appealing story and writing found in the Ace Attorney mainline games, but with an even more appealing setting and supporting cast. The Victorian era allows for a tiny bit of steampunk "magic", but otherwise forces the investigation and logic to be reasonably grounded, with fewer plot twists dependent on deus ex machina solutions.On the other hand, GAAC is perfect to get into even if you've never played an Ace Attorney game.At around 40-50 hours total, the 10 GAAC chapters will definitely feel long at times, but all of the gameplay mechanics are at their most polished, so at least that time is spent reading the fun dialogue and interesting plotting. I'm glad I experienced the two games as a single package -- if there's one major complaint I'd make, it's that the first game is heavily tuned toward setting up the mystery and climax of the second game, so you're not wrong if you feel like it's a slog in some parts, with mysteries that feel relatively low stakes. Thankfully the setting and new characters are more than enough to keep your interest.By comparison, the second game is a real barn burner. It does feature the same Grand-Conspiracy-in-the-Justice-System seen in the other AA games, but there's enough twists and tweaks for long time series players that keep it interesting even if you can see some of the major twists a mile away.If you've liked any of the AA games then GAAC is a no-brainer to play. If you're interested in visual novel-type games in general, then GAAC is a great entry point into the Ace Attorney series
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: This is possibly the best game in the ace attorney series. a solid 10/10. the character are great as always from the series, as well as the great designs. The game is pretty long, but every second was worth it. this game had THE best last case in any of the AA games ive played so far. also the music is fabulous and also honestly the best in the games as well. really good game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: You know when you're reading a manga or watching an anime, and there are those moments when characters just keep saying what is happening and what's going on with the plot? Like during a fight scene, Goku will think "I need to use the spirit bomb I learned from King Kai, but I may not have the energy to do so, and I may not be able to hold off Android 88 while doing so." And then we'll cut to sideline characters explaining the same thing, then to King Kai on his planet saying the same thing and so on and so forth. This game has that peculiar over-explaining, where you'll see something like the judge saying "Ryunosuke, if you interrupt at the wrong time, you will be penalized." And then Ryunosuke will think "If I interrupt at the wrong time, I will be penalized." and then the person next to Ryunosuke will tell him that if he interrupts at the wrong time, he will be penalized.In the first case, I knew what evidence I should be presenting, but I kept having to wade impatiently  through endless dialogue just to get to the point where I could start interacting with the court experience. It's really poorly-paced.I never played past the first Appolo game in the main series (and I played the first Edgeworth game), but part of what made AA games appealing was the pacing. Characters' animations were snappy while the text speed seemed to speed up and slow down to match characters' excitement. GAAC is just so much more verbose and sleepy.I wanted to like this game, but I can't. I agree with most of the negative reviews that this game's script could be cut in half without any real loss. Every character just babbles on and on, explaining minor detail while the text crawls by at a snail's pace.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I played a lot of ace attorney games because i'm an fairly big mystery and detectiv game lover. Altough i think all ace attorney games are greate, i have to say that this one was the best i played. The first Game takes  a while to get going but you really start to like the character. In the second part the story gets pretty intense and embedds some complicated and connected Cases.Would recommend to Ace Attorney fans and to new joiners.

_childDocuments_.review: This is how you "modernize" Ace Attorney. All of the gameplay systems are improved, some more flair is added, but the meat and potatoes and essence of the series is intact. Buuuuut.. the actual story and writing is so much worse than Phoenix Wright. I stopped playing during the first court case of the second game and I played a lot of Phoenix Wright as a kid and I'm replaying it right now to see if it actually holds up and I'm not misremembering. _childDocuments_.review: Going to regard this duology as one game, and not as "TGAA1/TGAA2". It's only fitting, where, for all of us Ace Attorney fans, we're used to story threads usually being introduced in the first 2 chapters and all loose ends being tied up at the last chapter (the exception to this rule being Trials and Tribulations, turning AA1/AA2, 2 standalone titles into part of a trilogy, with the strong prequel storytelling.Anyway. Viewed separately, TGAA1 was honestly slightly boring and - dare I say - even slightly painful to play through at times. Mind, not because it was 'bad'. I believe this was a very deliberate storytelling direction taken by the designers. They obviously envisaged TGAA Chronicles as a duology (even more so than they viewed the first 3 AA games as a trilogy) and not as titles that would satisfy an avid AA enthusiast such as myself. As such, TGAA1 focused more on introducing mysteries/plot elements that promise a huge payoff... but not by the fifth chapter. Heck, it felt like TGAA1, as a whole, was just an "appetizer", for us to get used to Meiji Era "Phoenix Wright", and for Naruhodo Ryunosuke to get accustomed to living in London.But man oh man, when TGAA2 came along.... The kids' gloves were off. Hype and excitement just kept building for me starting from the third case, and it was an amazing ride all to the final second. Personally, I feel that if the Ace Attorney franchise were to wrap up and sent off by this prequel duology - considering that Phoenix Wright, Apollo Justice, Athena Cykes story and character arcs in the present have ostensibly been wrapped up - I'd have no complaints. None AT ALL. TGAA1: 7/10TGAA2: 9.5/10TGAA viewed as a duology: 11/10 (My favorite Ace Attorney game, even when compared to AA1 to AA6)

_childDocuments_.review: Without getting into too many details, I loved this Duology. You don't need to have played any other game in the series to understand the story in these two games, however there are many references for fans of the past Ace Attorney games and The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes. The first game has some poor pacing where some things feel like they drag on far too long, but it is still very enjoyable with it's fantastic characters and entertaining dialogue. However, you do get left on multiple cliffhangers at the end of the first game, which can feel a little awkward on its own. The second game is clearly on a budget, which is easily noticeable because of the lack of animated cutscenes and some obviously reused assets. However in spite of that, the game clearly had a lot of heart and soul put into it, because in my opinion, it still manages to surpass the first game in almost every way. The pacing is better and the cases are overall more interesting, with twists and turns that even the most veteran of Ace Attorney fans might not see coming. Also, all of the mysteries from the first game are finally solved in the second (except for Kazuma's headband, it's nonexistent wind is never explained). The second game has a near perfect conclusion for the two games and their characters, and I believe that it may have even surpassed the highest highs of the original Ace Attorney Trilogy. Oh yeah, and the soundtrack is absolutely incredible. You will find yourself jamming to multiple different tracks in both games.In short, if you're a fan of Ace Attorney, or even if you are brand new and interested in the Ace Attorney series, you will be sure to enjoy yourself throughout these two games, even with it's few downsides.

_childDocuments_.review: I must say, this is by far the best Ace Attorney games by far, it almost saddens me that every other Ace Attorney pales in comparison. The story was the best told and executed out of all the games, previous games have attempted and over-arching plot from case to case but this game not only did it the best, but also managed it over not one but two games. The way they set up things in the first game to be brought up in the second was done masterfully. The actual story contents-wise is not only my favorite out of all the Ace Attorney games, its up there with many of the greatest visual novels. The soundtrack to this game was straight fire, the best in the series, I literally have listened to both games soundtracks on Spotify from start to finish multiple times. The characters were the most like-able out of all the games, not just the main characters but I even found myself enjoying the side characters presence, even the bad guys. I won't deny that there were times I got stuck during the cases and had trouble figuring out what to do, and there was one instance during the final case that I resorted to looking up which evidence I needed to present during a cross-examination, but that's par for the course for an Ace Attorney game, and even though I didn't use it, there's a story mode option that automatically goes through the story so you can basically just watch the game without having to figure out the puzzles. Unlike typical Ace Attorney games, I felt that I enjoyed every single case in both games, even the one I considered the worse, the first case, wasn't as bad as cases in other games, I just think it was much longer than necessary and I hope it doesn't turn off newcomers from continuing because every case after that is so much better. Basically, I think this is one of the best visual novels I've ever played, I think it IS the best Ace Attorney I've ever played, I'm very glad they localized this finally so its more accessible, I hope it sells exceedingly well so Capcom will make more Ace Attorney games of this caliber. Its a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 10/10, perfect game, if this was any other game I'd be upset that I'll have to play it again to get all the off the path achievements but I'll gladly do it for this masterpiece :)

_childDocuments_.review: "Suspended disbelief, never heard of it...."Overview: A beautiful and fun story game if you're chronically bored (and possibly masochistic), and you enjoy sitting through 30 minute stints of bizarre dialogue before you're allowed to present the clue you figured out 5 minutes into the current section of the story...  "Suspended disbelief, never heard of it...."[Long form review bellow, quick checklist at the very bottom of the review]I first came across this game years ago while browsing for highly rated community games. With 94% positive reviews, I added it to my wishlist, however the high price at the time kept me from pulling the trigger. I had seen some sales come and go that almost tempted me to jump in, but it wasn't until yesterday Steam finally got me! :-DBackground---- I am not familiar with the franchise, so I came into this game a complete newbie. I have played many story based, visual novel type games, and I've enjoyed everyone I've played so far. I also am a big fan of mystery/puzzle games. I cut my teeth on classic Adventure games like Kings Quest, The Secret of Monkey Island and Discworld. Based on what little I knew about Ace Attorney, the glowing reviews, and my past history, I started the game.The Game---- You're treated to a beautiful animated cut scene introducing you to the world you'll be occupying for the next 5-6 hours as you navigate your first case. The intro is captivating, and I applaud the writers choice of introducing the game mechanics in a Japanese courtroom during the fall of Sokaku, the Japanese period of isolation from the Western world at large.As the concept of western legal proceedings was new to the Japanese people during this time, the sets the perfect pretext for character dialogue to explain game mechanics, and how trials work, without ruining the immersion of the story. In my opinion, an early indication of any truly great game is how intuitively you are introduced to the world and the mechanics. With that said, while the story flowed well initially, several mechanics were awkwardly shoehorned into conversations over the next few hours of game play. These new mechanics often felt forced and out of place.I found often I would realize I have discovered something relevant to progressing the story, but I was unable to do anything with that until 30 minutes later a new game mechanic would be introduced that would finally allow you to act on the item you figured out a lot sooner. I soon found I had been "trained" to view all new information as part of a formula, I just needed to wait until the game presented me with the question I needed to plug in my answer.The result of this is you begin to loose the story. I found myself no longer caring about the dialogue, the characters, or anything else that was happening. I knew the next thing the game was going to ask me to progress, my job now became hitting the space bar as fast as I could until the prompt finally came up for me to enter my newly discovered information. Unfortunately, that usually involves sitting through 20-30 minutes of often repetitive dialogue before you can proceed. This ultimately becomes the fatal flaw with Ace Attorney, at some point the story becomes the gatekeeper preventing you from moving to the next step. A great novel game ensures text/dialogue is always nourishing you, building tension, compelling you to root for the protagonist, misdirecting you for future surprises, and most importantly of all, a great novel game must excel at suspending your disbelief.Suspended disbelief is crucial to every story ever told. You've probably experienced how jarring it is to suddenly realize the movie you've been completely engrossed with for the past hour suddenly makes zero sense. I remember watching Star Wars: The Force Awakens when it came out in 2015, and specifically, the exact moment when Rey, who picked up a light saber for the first time about 6 minutes ago, defeated Kylo Ren in a light saber battle..... Kylo Ren, who had been trained as a Jedi his whole life... defeated by someone who just picked it up..... WTF?! I remember thinking "this makes absolutely zero sense at all...." I mean, Luke, who at least had some training with Yoda, lost his freaking hand when he battled Darth Vader, and yet here comes Rey who magically stomps all over the super villan in about 8 seconds on her first attempt.... it makes no sense at all.Not the magical mind control powers, the Faster-Than-Light spaceships, or any other of the totally ridiculous things that occurred for the first two hours of that movie.... nope..... just her sudden proficiency with a light saber..... Which goes to show how absolutely crucial the suspension of disbelief truly is to a great story. When done well, you are pulled deep into the narrative world the author has created for you to enjoy. No matter how magical or bizarre, you accept whatever is laid at your feet and become a citizen of the universe that is presented to you without questions.During the first case, the plot holes in the mystery, the formulaic dialog progression, and the forced game mechanics all combine to ruin the suspension of disbelief, and make you all to aware that you're not interacting with a great story, you're simply playing a game and mashing a space bar to get to the next step. In the end, Ace Attorney feels much more like the man behind the curtain than the Wizard of Oz, which I found very disappointing given how long I have waited to play this game and all the glowing reviews.If I was able to refund a game 5 hours in I would have with this one. With that said, since it's mine now, I'll probably try another story to see if they are able to pull me in.❤ Audience ❤ ---Casual Gamer☼ Graphics ☼ ---Beautiful♬ Music ♬ ---Good☠ Difficulty ☠ ---Easy to Average§ Bugs § ---Very Minor☯ Story ☯ ---Decent but multiple plot holes ruin the immersion ⚔ Gameplay ⚔ ---Frustratingly long$ Price / Quality $ ---Buy on sale or pass, many other great story games out there!

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, I haven’t had the chance to play too many  games, the only one (or, rather, three) I finished was the . I really enjoyed it, so I was very happy when this new collection came out on PC earlier this year.I, for one, liked the idea of moving the plot to the steampunk version of Victorian-era Britain and Japan, but at first, I wasn’t sure how to feel about the whole new set of characters. After a few hours of gameplay, I admit that I grew closer to most of them, and Ryunosuke and Susato proved to be a fun pair of protagonists, but not as much as Phoenix and Maya, at least in my opinion. Sholmes, however, was always hilarious!That said, I can’t complain about any other aspects of the game. There’s more than 70-80 hours of content here, and that’s without all the extras. The cases are sometimes surprisingly challenging, the extremely well crafted, overarching storyline puts many political thrillers to shame, the 3D graphics look gorgeous (for a visual novel, of course), and there are even a few tiny changes and improvements in the gameplay here and there.If you’re a fan of the franchise or adventure games in general, then you should definitely grab this two-game package. _childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: yep it's goodI have played through Phoenix Wright collection, and compared to that, this one fixes a bunch of things that bothered me (, lack of things that can happen in a court), adds a couple of cute mechanics to spice up the gameplay. Even though they still are pretty simple, I did enjoy them when they popped up.These games are a bit more grounded, the cast has lost some of it's craziness, which I did miss, but as a benefit - there's a much larger set of characters that can't be summed up in 1 sentence and have actual depth, so this might be seen as a plus or a minus, depending on what you prefer.It's important to note that with similar playthrough time to the Phoenix wright trilogy, this game has 10-ish cases, whereas the original trilogy had 14 (if you count tutorial ones). This means two things:1. Mysteries are more developed and not as obvious. I enjoyed discovering what really happened much more than before.2. Sometimes, the plot really drags on and stops moving. If you plan to binge all of it, lots of information dumps will be repeated again and again - this was present in previous titles also, but here I think there's more of it, because clues within the case get repeated together with overarching plot points again and again. Because of that, the game really benefits from making significant breaks in between cases, otherwise you might feel exhausted at the end, as I did.Other things that I think would really improve the experience - but I'm sure there's good reason they aren't there:1. More voice acting!2. More animated segments! I think there were none in the second game, and it was a bummerAlso huge kudos to the addition of the autoplay, I hope it's also in the Apollo Justice port.To sum up, I do think this is an improvement over Phoenix Wright trilogy, and worth playing if you liked it, or if you are a newcomer and this would be the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: Will update review later for 2nd game.I'm an Ace Attorney fan who has been parched for games since 2016. Very excited to play this, was not disappointed. I would only note that Ace Attorney originated on the small screen (the NDS) and moved on to mobile. For several reasons, I don't think the big screen of a PC fits the experience. If you can get this game elsewhere or play on a rather small screen (like a Handheld Switch), I think it will be better. The text is purposefully large for smaller devices, and it just doesn't have the same charm on big screens.This game made me laugh out loud a few times, which Ace Attorney games have rarely managed to do. I liked the characters a lot, the whole idea of setting the franchise one or two centuries back in time to 'reinvent' it. Its setting of crossing Meiji era Japan and 20th c. England is rather unique, perhaps even innovative. A point of criticism: it might feel like not a lot has happened in a case, and that might be because of the setting! One of the plot points is that science isn't all that advanced, so there's usually less evidence and more testimony. This is understandable, but it can make cases drag out. Though I've played thirty hours of the first game, it still felt 'short', and it might be because 'not much happened'. The last case of the game suffers from this greatly: probably an hour before the end, you already know what happened, but you just have to keep on proving it. This is the case in other games too, but I feel like it usually is ~20-30 minutes max?As a final note, unlike previous Ace Attorney titles, this one is obviously written as a prequel -- there's at least four unanswered major plot questions at the end, one of which is set up in the first case. Which means to say, you can't really just play the first game and be done with it! I expect at least another 30 hours from the second game.I just finished the second game (76 hrs of playtime, though sometimes I left the game running). I played the game on and off, and I enjoyed the cases. I could anticipate some of the plot twists, but I admit that (especially in the final case) the game caught me off guard! The end, unlike the first game, drags out a lot. There is a big dump of revelations at the end, and the writers want to dedicate enough time to each one; but this could have been handled better, I think. The reveals could have been fed to the player little by little, throughout the game, instead of all at once near the end. Also, in retrospect, the first case in this game really feels like a filler; even though the game otherwise is really masterful at tying in almost every single detail you've seen throughout this entry and its prequel.I prefer the first game only because this one felt like it overstayed its welcome, but maybe that's always been the case with Ace Attorney? The first game had higher highs, too (but not lower lows). In any case, you should play both of them if you want the full story. Though there are some cases I would skip if you only wanted the overarching plot (e.g. first two cases of the second game).

They throw this notion right out the window in Adventures though, and it's very easily my least favourite Ace Attorney game to date.However, then we get to Resolve. Cases 1 and 3 are fine, but case 2 is really great, surprisingly so. I'd say it's mostly due to the stupidly fun characters of Souseki Natsume and William Shamspeare. Whether it's characters like Herlock Sholmes (yes, really), or the mostly outstanding soundtrack, TGAAC definitely seems to have the highest production value of any AA game yet.Anyway, the two combined make an overall okay game. _childDocuments_.review: This game is really good, and I am really enjoying playing so far.The reviews of people saying there is "too much dialogue" is also something I have a problem with, as the game very much likes to over explain everything; which means witnesses will talk for MINUTES at a time.Another thing that also does waste time, in my opinion, is the deductions with Herlock Sholmes. Now don't get me wrong, I love this game play feature and theatrical way he dances around the room pointing out his deductions. However I find it annoying you have to hear Sholmes' wrong conclusion before you get to step in and help him. I would have very much preferred if you could press a button and butt-in with an "Objection!" when he makes an incorrect conclusion. It would mean you wouldn't have to waste 5 minutes listening to his wrong conclusion but you still get to join in and steer him in the right direction.Despite the issues I have with the game, I really believe that anyone who enjoyed the Phoenix Wright games would have a blast with this one. It improves on A LOT of the game play features from the Phoenix Wright games as well as adding some brilliant new ideas that makes the game feel fresh without losing that 'Ace Attorney feel' we all love.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is not only a return to form for the series, it is in my opinion the best game(s) in the franchise!A story so carefully planned throughout 10 cases, each being of great importance to the plot, and with a such a charming colourful cast of characters, it is truly a marvel to play though it.The investigation parts of the game has never been paced as well as here, also adding a new very fun minigame in the great Herlock Sholmes's Logic and Reasoning Spectacular absolutely stealing the show!The same goes for the court proceedings, now featuring a jury and multiple witnesses at once presenting their testimonies, making the game feel truly unique.The witnesses themselves have never been less annoying as well, in fact the whole cast of characters from more to less important ones have never been funnier and more charming. I applaud the phenomenal character and story writing that manages to beat the best entries in the Phoenix Wright's timeline, just as well as the new mechanics that reinvent the game a bit and make it feel fresh again!

_childDocuments_.review: I waited to play this game for 5 years. It was worth it.I first found out about this game in late 2016 a while after I completed the trilogy. I don't remember how, but I watched an almost full playthrough of the first game on youtube with poorly translated subtitles. I watched up until before the last trial, because I had some hope this would be localized (being only half a year after release), and I knew I would buy this game if it did.I had difficulty getting into the other two 3DS games: Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice. For some reason they didn't appeal to me in the same way The Great Ace Attorney did. It was unique, and the new gameplay concepts were legitimately interesting. The Dances of Deduction with Herlock Sholmes being one of them along with the Jury System and multiple witnesses at the stand. There was so much going for this game. It was ambitious, unique, different. It had the makings of a true masterpiece. I wanted to see this happen. I only knew of this conceptually and I really wanted to see how they were applied in the game. And you know what? Even with the terrible subtitles, the first case in the Great Ace Attorney was really good. Kazuma was cool as hell. Herlock Sholmes was also incredibly funny in his animations. I couldn't get much from this translation, but this was a really promising game for the series. A true new generation of ace attorney. For a while, I attributed my uninterested demeanor towards Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice as being because Shu Takumi wasn't involved in the projects. But Shu Takumi was the one behind the Great Ace Attorney games, just as he had been behind the Ace Attorney Trilogy, and Apollo Justice. And I loved those games dearly.Eventually news came that a sequel came out, and at this point I did not expect a localization. Regardless, I did not look up any information. Years passed, and a fan translation for the first game was in the works. Of course, when this released in 2019 I tried it immediately. However, due to the complications of getting a fan translation for a 3DS or Android game working, I dropped it.But now, here we are. In 2021 (well 2022 as I'm writing this review). An official translation of The Great Ace Attorney has been announced, and not of only the first game. BOTH games. And on steam TOO? I legitimately couldn't believe my eyes. The next ace attorney game finally being brought to the west. In all honestly, I completed expected Dual Destines and Spirit of Justice to be ported before they even bothered porting The Great Ace Attorney, let alone LOCALIZE themSo what do I think about these two games now that I've finally played and finished them? Well, to put it simply, this was everything I wanted it to be, and it was a wonderful journey. I'm so glad these two games were as good as they were. A lot of my initial conceptions were shown to be real, and even enhanced. This set of games is a journey, befitting of Ryunosuke in his personal quest of becoming a lawyer.LOCALIZATION & A CULTURAL SHIFTTo start off, the localization for this game is phenomenal. This has to be on my list of top localizations ever conceived. The writing is reminiscent of literary British, befitting of the time period, but it was written in a manner that felt like actual speech. It really gave off the vibe of Victorian England. Everything about this game feels like I'm in an era of the past, and the localization team and writing skills of Shu Takumi are completely responsible for this. Being an American, I'm not too familiar with Victorian England, and especially Meiji-era Japan, but the game expertly deals with the topics of the eras in a way modern audiences can understand. Because this is a game centered on a Japanese man travelling to a foreign land, many cultural conflicts are present in the game and discussed, even making nods on the difference in languages at parts. Most of these are humorous, but it of course does take the issue seriously. People in the game commonly remark at the fact you're Japanese, and people are prone to distrust you, including the prosecutor, Barok Van Zieks, who calls you "Nipponese".CHARACTERSI love the characters in this game. Herlock Sholmes has to be one of the best written characters in anything. He's hilarious, but also a genius. I would describe him as an "incompetent genius" in that he's clearly the Great Detective, but characters like Iris will remark about how she caught Sholmes drinking chemicals. and when asking her why, she said he said he was thirsty. It's this kind of contrast I find hilarious. I love this character, both for his faults and strengths. Susato Mikotoba is a great character as well. She's really kind in general, but I won't be forgetting the Susato Takedown anytime soon. Kazuma Asogi as Ryunosuke's best friend is a dynamic I see little of in games, and I heavily appreciate this kind of dynamic. Kazuma in general is just extremely cool. He carries his katana and wears a headband around his forehead that's just constantly waving in the wind. He also this lighthearted but cool demeanor to him. Great character. I like almost every character in this game, and I cannot possibly go through all of them, but all of their unique quirks were hilarious as they were cool.I'm going to end this section off with, I feel Barok Van Zieks has to be one of the best prosecutors in the series. I feel he truly shines in the sequel, but he's extremely well-written, and his background is surprisingly interesting. To me, Barok Van Zieks feels like he was given the best writing out of any prosecutor. Everything interesting that could be done with a prosecutor was done in this game, and it was marvelous. I did not expect to like Barok Van Zieks as much as I did. Godot still holds a place in my heart, but Barok Van Zieks is somewhere there now.MUSICThe music as always is well-written and memorable. I won't be forgetting the Pursuit theme or Barok Van Ziek's theme anytime soon. Or Kazuma's. They're all fantastic. Bravo to the composers for writing such impactful music. The composers for the first Great Ace Attorney game return for the second game, and obviously compose brand new tracks, which are similarly as great. The Pursuit theme in these games has to be a personal favorite of mine, and I loved how they delivered the music in the second game to make the actions feel truly great.WRITINGThis genuinely has to have the best writing of any Ace Attorney game. This feels like if they took Apollo Justice's final case, and stretched it into a whole game, and actually made it work. Holy, I'm surprised it worked. The pay off at the end of the Great Ace Attorney 2 genuinely cannot be matched by any trial in any other Ace Attorney game, in my personal opinion. Both games are a continuation of the same storyline, with the conclusion being at the end of the second game, and I feel the world and characters were expertly crafted over the course of both games to truly show an engaging world and story. This is the most ambitious Ace Attorney game. No doubts in my mind. It tries to tell a story that spans not only one game, but two, and it's done extremely well. Slow paced, maybe, but every point in the story has reason to exist, and I'm glad the game got the conclusion it deserved. Absolutely incredible show of writing. Thank you Shu Takumi.FINAL THOUGHTSThe second game is in my list of top games for sure. The second game is a masterpiece in every aspect. But play the first game first. I enjoyed the first game heavily, but this is a duology of games. The second Great Ace Attorney is hands down my favorite Ace Attorney game. Please play these games. I put in almost 120 hours and got all the achievements. It's well worth your time. There's not a single game like this in the world. Everything about these games is incredible. Everything is so filled with charm. I would discuss more, but I hit the word limit lol

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. It's one of the Ace Attorney/Phoenix Wright games; the latest one to be exact. Obviously it's not in the main series, but a spin-off.I'm enjoying the old-timeyness of it (since it takes places late 1800s). But it's a bit slower to start than how I remember other PW games to be. Part of it might be because it takes place 100yrs before, there's a lot more explanation about "new" tech like photography and medical knowledge and such. I often found myself mashing the next/continue key because I was like, "Yes, I know what that is commmmmeee on."The overall dialog can be that way, too. Because the main character here, Ryunosuke Naruhodo (the ancestor of Phoenix Wright, or Ryuichi Naruhodo in Japanese), isn't really a lawyer to begin with. So there's additional dialog where court and investigative concepts have to be explained more than usual.But beyond the slow dialog, I think this is one of the best installments in the whole franchise. I loved the format, with all the cases being related and intertwined, coming together at the end and wrapping everything up. Definitely has a darker-than-usual storyline, too, which I appreciated.The characters and cases are fun and interesting. Especially "Herlock Sholmes" (*obviously* no relation to another famous detective /s) Since the cases are "chapters," each is related to the other and they build off each other as you move through the story. Characters get a little more development than in past AA games. Altogether, it keeps you hooked, since you want to know "whodunit?" and the motivations for everyone. Cases can be challenging at times, but not overly so. You should never have a need to look at a guide if you take the time to look at evidence and reason through the arguments.Some new mechanics in the game include Jury Examination system and the Pursuit system. Jury Examination strains credulity a bit, but hey - there was a talking parrot as an important witness in on AA game! The system does lead to some edge-of-seat storytelling. One moment it feels like it's the end of the case, that the accused is about to be declared guilty, but then Jury Examination allows you to further argue the case and convince the jury to think again, leading to some drastic "Turnabouts."Overall, highly recommend it for anyone who's played Ace Attorney games and the like. Here's hoping for more installments on Ace Attorney!

_childDocuments_.review: By far the most polished and coherent game in the entire franchise. All of the characters are great and memorable, main cast as well as the witnesses. The soundtrack is fantastic. The 3D-models have improved massively compared to AA5 & AA6 and are used in such fun ways. The animated cutscenes were a joy to watch, and they got voice acting! + I really liked looking through the concept art and other bonus content that came with the games.The storyline is very rewarding and builds up from the start, there really is no case that feels like a "filler". The story spans across both of the games' 10 episodes so you can't really treat them as separate the same way you could with other Ace Attorney games. I honestly wished that this too was a trilogy because while the second part of the story was handled well, you could argue that it was a tiny bit rushed, but it was nothing that ruined the experience.While the game keeps the typical Ace Attorney silliness, the story has quite dark undertones throughout and keeps a sort of realism that has been absent from the trilogies. The unique gameplay mechanics feels natural to the setting and doesn't rely on some new high tech or magic system. My main criticisms of the game is that the dialogue sometimes feels a bit slow phased and there are some unclear moments during some of the second game's trials, but with that said, I wholeheartedly think that this is the greatest Ace Attorney game.
