_childDocuments_.review: Never in my life I expected these two games to ever be localized, let alone be ported to PC. But they are here and easily available to a greater audience. With that said, I’ve been trying to let them rest in my mind for a while. Despite that I can’t help but think about them every now and then and look fondly to the whole experience.Neither of them can stand too much on their own when compared to some of the best in the franchise, with the first game in this duology being an incredibly slow-paced game, even when compared to others in the same franchise, and the second one trying to come up with a resolution for most of what the first built up in just 5 cases(kinda). And I wouldn’t even be surprised if this was meant to be a trilogy and due to low sales for the original 3DS release, they decided to just wrap everything up with the second game.But despite all of that, what we got here was the duology as a whole, which ultimately works for its benefit when the games are greater than the sum of its parts. Together they stand taller than anything else in the whole franchise, and by the time you reach the cathartic finale of the second game, none of the flaws matter. These are wonderful games that stand out, not just by having the most interesting settings or presentation, but with what it comes to accomplish with its greater scope. Celebrating what makes the franchise so good while also giving a fresh cast to love for the fanbase. Like all Ace Attorney games by Takumi, there are going to be cases that you might think less than others, making some of the quality might be uneven, but that’s also part of the appeal. It is all in service for fantastic cases that come as peaks in the collection. The whole thing comes up as a package that is full of love and passion by people that care about the franchise a lot. Both knowing how to embrace what makes it special while also showing that, sometimes, it’s better to let go than dragging something to the mud. I cannot recommend these games enough; go play them.

_childDocuments_.review: For those looking to play this game or a beginner of the series, PLAY IT LAST. You learn to appreciate how far the series has gone from the typical sprite-based designs to full 3D, even if it is a prequel with very few if not any ties to the mainline series, I strongly recommend playing the games in release order.I've played through every game in this series, including the Layton spinoff and the two investigations games and I've gotta say, this is probably the best Capcom has to offer as far as far as Ace Attorney goes, if we're talking about the overall package. The music is good, the animations are fantastic and I'm really glad they didn't butcher the localization. Ultimately, without spoilers the package deal is great, you'll love the characters (arguably some more than mainline AA games), and it's mostly a joy from start to finish.If I had to complain, I'd say 1-4 and 2-2 were my personal low points, some of the other trials last way too long, and you could see the big bad coming from a mile away. It also doesn't have some of the high highs the mainline games have in terms of story (JFA 2-4, T&T 3-5, etc), but doesn't have the really bad lows (JFA 2-3, AJ 2-3, etc) which bumps my grade up just that little bit. All in all, an amazing experience that will make you want more.TL;DR: An amazing Ace Attorney game(s) from start to finish, play the older games first, you'll appreciate these two titles a lot more in the long run.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great AA Chronicles:♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ where do I begin, this was my last two games before completely finishing the series (as of June 13th 2022) and I can say this game was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ incredible.  The will be spoilers in the review but only about a sentence so read at own riskWhere do I begin I guess I should start with characters and wow what a great introduction to the new characters from Herlock to Gina, they were all written great, the music was incredible which I expect from the series. Lord Van Ziekes as a rival prosecutor was an incredible rival for the games with and incredible theme behind it and spoiler has a huge mystery behind him with him being called The Reaper Of The Bailey as everyone who has gotten an acquittal has died mysteriously which all gets solved by the final case of the second game /spoiler. Gameplay was usual AA affair however with there being multiple witnesses you can see how others react during cross examinations in order to get more information which is such a nice feature from Layton vs AA. Another mechanic the games adds is the Dance of deduction where Herlock points out several things about a witness and they look about and when he gets something wrong you must point it out, Herlock isn’t dumb in this case he is getting things wring to help you improve as a lawyer. The final big gameplay change is a jury, the jury will determine if your client is guilty or not and during points they will all go for a guilty verdict, at this point you have to perform a judicial examination against them which is like the cross examination, but this time you will need point out statements that contradict each other pitting them against each other and making them change their vote in your favour so the trial can continue. The story was great especially the second game and how it wrapped all the mysteries from the first and second and so many twists and turns in the final case was shocking and I didn’t see where the game was going in the last 3 hours, but I loved it. While not really a big issue I should complain about the dialog can be tricky to read at times due to the game being set in Britain they have over the top accents making words hard to read at times, like Naruhodo being changed to ‘Oddo but that’s simple to read but some others took a few reads to understand (saying as a Brit myself), however this is for like 2-3 characters as each has a different accents while the rest each one is easy to read so it is a very minor pick I decide to pick out. However overall, these two games were both incredible and the ending to the second game made me almost cry with the way everything wrapped up and, you know if your player gets emotional during the ending of a game cause they won’t see the characters again with fresh interactions you have truly made some fantastic characters. While I doubt, we will get a third games in the Great Ace Attorney series I would love if Capcom somehow find a way to make TGAA 3 or even a 7th instalment in the mainline series.

_childDocuments_.review: Can't recommend these games enough. I got invested in it around a year ago and I still feel completely insane about it. 7 years ago I started ace attorney as a series and fell in love with it instantly, but TGAA managed to completely take me off-guard about the sheer quality that despite it being a part of an already great series, was almost mind blowing. _childDocuments_.review: It is just not that good.Characters designs are not as memorable, and poses more forgettable.The puzzles are infuriatingly easy and/or uninspired, to the point that the steamboat mystery is literally just a Sherlock Holmes locked room mystery, with only minor details changed. I did not know about this mystery prior to playing the game, but since the game itself mentions by name the actual mystery it is just straight up ripping for its own use, I feel like that must be held against it.You can usually see the conclusion coming from a mile away and there are no big turnabout moments, which is a cardinal error for an Ace Attorney game.I personally find Herlock Sholmes to be an unsufferable character, seeing as he is portrayed here as incompetent and full of himself, essentially not deserving his reputation and relying on unnamed third parties to correct his mistakes. He does cause a lot of innocents to go through numerous ordeals and sees no consequences for his actions, which I dislike.Mechanically, you have to suffer through his entire deductions first, and then go through them again to course correct. This is not enjoyable.Another frustrating thing this game does is the "This element is the Solution of the Puzzle, but only becomes a Valid Answer after you Inspect it once", which was always terrible when the mainline games did it, and is even worse here since, I said before, the puzzles are REALLY easy. So you want to speed through it because you understand the mechanics, and the game knocks you over the head, because it presumes you are presenting at random. The way they use spatial clues (in that you have to rotate the camera to find additional information) feels extremely lazy to me. From previous titles, I am used to having to combine a relatively small or obscure detail obtained by interacting with evidence (combining pieces, etc.) with a statement, but here it is more in the spirit of "Flip the camera view 180° and what you need to pick up on is a massive visual element distinct from all the rest that takes up a tenth of the screen". There is no subtelty or attempts to lead you in the wrong direction, it is just always immediately in-your-face, glaringly obvious, uninvolving.There is a lot of stating the obvious in this game, which arguably is always a part of Ace Attorney games, but I would argue that it is all in the balance of it. In other titles, it helps because when the game throws a curveball, suddenly it is very useful to know exactly what you can take for a fact and where the rug is being pulled from. Here, you do not find that level of complexity, so it just feels padded and it removes even more of the already low stakes. It adds to the unnatural of the dialogue.Due to the game not having much of the spark of other titles, what is left is a lot of padding. While there are some moments where it threatens to pick up some steam - let us not pretend it does not have its moments or characters - it just does not feel like it has enough life into it. You experience will be: genuinely well done sequences, scenes or character moments in-between long and dull segments where not much of any interest is discussed, while uninspired character designs move about on screen, and the game occasionally whacks you for daring to try to move along too fast. Because you Inspect first, and Present second, even though Inspecting adds nothing more that could not already be seen.And I am sorry but -spoilers for the second case- a best friend that dies by cracking his head open on a bedframe as he slips on a floor stain because of a cat he couldn't see or feel in his legs is, realistic and unfortunate, yes, but also from a meta point of view a really retarded plotpoint and you cannot build a meaningful character arc for his friends out of this because his death is meaningless. It was an accident, you removed one of the most interesting characters, and you still failed at cashing in on the emotional side of things because he died a ridiculous death. You cannot fuel another person's motivation out of this kind of death since you try to find meaning and strength in the fact the poor chap split his brain matter on the wood floor because he mistep.There is also a pawnbroker who threatens to blow his brains out with a gun (this is animated) at every minor inconvenience; while I personally relate, I still find it jarring with regards to the tone of the rest of the game.But as I said, it has its moments; for example there is a joke early on about Ryunosuke's attempts at slamming the defense's desk making a wet slap sound in his greenhorn days, and committing to a firm BANG after a while. Nice touch.Finally, I think they fudged up the prosecution. The main prosecutor/antagonist does not have that Oomph to him, partly because he is just a vampire Edgeworth with less vivid clothing, and partly because his animations or facial expression feel a little too stiff and slow. He really does not mistreat equipment or appliances enough, and comes up as a static automaton. It does not help that, as stated previously, the puzzles are really simple, so when the prosecution gets flared up, it is about the Defense proving that water can be boiled, which as a reader at best evokes a faint smile if you feel generous.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to commend this game for the quality of life features that I wasn't used to from the first Ace Attorney games. While investigating, being able to tell whether you've already inspected something or not is such a relief. And having the option of letting the game play itself for you makes it accessible to a new market of people who'd be into visual novels but couldn't/wouldn't play it themselves, but more importantly it prevents players from having to look up solutions online if they ever got stuck. Brilliant!While I don't feel that Herlock Sholmes earns all the spotlight he steals, the characters are all wonderfully written and designed with tons of style and personality. And although some parts of the plot were predictable, the intensity and the stakes get raised to 11 by chapter 3 of the second part, and then it keeps rising from there! It is a thoroughly enjoyable ride with excellent music (gotta love the tapdancing as an instrument!) and Van Zieks has to be my favorite prosecutor the Ace Attorney franchise has had yet.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Finished the 2nd game. Can confirm it was an absolute masterpiece.I've currently only finished the first game in this collection, but I can say without a doubt that it's already more than worth the asking price. The Great Ace Attorney 1 is not just a good Ace Attorney game, it's the best in the series bar none.The writing, and characterisation is excellent and fits perfectly with the game's themes. Ryunosuke, the game's protagonist, goes through more character development in 3.5 cases than Phoenix has in 6 games. Susato is the best assistant, capable of both being funny and being genuinely helpful as well as having some very good development of her own. Van Zieks is the best Prosecutor in the series (sorry Edgeworth) and goes against the tired trope of being "undefeated" until they meet the protagonist. They never feel like they're being stupid for plot convenience and they manage to be sympathetic, likeable and badass in spite of being a racist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. And Herlock Sholmes, once you get past the dumb localised name, is one of the funnies and best-written characters in the series, and I feel like I've barely touched the surface of his characterisation having not played the 2nd game yet.The witnesses and perpetrators aren't just cartoonish villains who killed someone to further their own gain, they're sympathetic people whose actions are the product of their environment and way of life. And often by exposing the truth, you end up harming them in some unexpected, far-reaching way that arguably, they don't deserve.All of this is combined with the best soundtrack in the series (particularly impressive considering the Ace Attorney series is known for its banger soundtracks), some really well done character animation and some of the most fun gameplay gimmicks in the series.If you're a fan of Ace Attorney, you'll love this. If you've never played Ace Attorney and don't mind a lot of reading, you'll love this. The Great Ace Attorney 1 is so far my favourite game I've played this year, and is in serious consideration as one of my favourite games of all time.

_childDocuments_.review: A somewhat barebones but mostly competent port of an otherwise outstanding dilogy. Ironically, it is best delivered as duo-pack of the games. Both due to the interconnected story between games and the way first game handles a good chunk as more of a tutorial. Luckily, all of it makes sense once player transitions to the second game and character setups start paying off quicker, while tutorial portion of the game is much shorter.To those uninitiated in the Ace Attorney franchise - these games are rather curious take on the Visual Novel genre. Still focused on the story first and foremost, but making decent use of puzzle mechanics to keep player occupied and well stretched between dialogues. Being relatively late addition to the franchise, The Great Ace Attorney benefits from experienced and polished approach both to the transition from sprite work of early NDS games to 3D environment as well as pretty well handled gameplay mechanics that doesn't suffer from "moon logic" or overly prolonged puzzle sequences.All in all, it is a great addition (if late in terms release date) to the library of the already avid Ace Attorney fans, but also a solid point to jump into the series for new players.

_childDocuments_.review: After beating the first two cases of The Great Ace Attorney: Adventures, I sadly cannot recommend this game to anybody. The graphics and music are drastically improved to the point where I was extremely impressed with the overall presentation of the game. The music engages you more than any other game in the Ace Attorney series. I also quite enjoyed the new mechanics of this game. The first being where the player can make deductions in real time alongside Herlock Sholmes. I believe this to fit in well with the Ace Attorney franchise, it adds something new to the game that previous titles didn't have, and overall I thought it was a lot more fun than some of the gimmicks of the other games. I also enjoyed having multiple people on the stand at once. Although minor, this seems like a good way to add something more to the court sections that, again, other games don't have.However, this is about where the positives end. The cases themselves feel much more drawn out than the previous games and the logic seems lackluster at best.  The first two cases also seem to mimic the first two cases of the original games.  The humor of the game doesn't seem as funny as the game hopes it is, some characters seem extremely smart at some points and completely oblivious at others, and after the third or fourth time where a "groundbreaking discovery" was found in a case, especially when some happened mere minutes after the others, the overall impacts of these discoveries were lost. I didn't feel as though I was delving into this exciting world full of court drama where anything could happen and at any moment my world could be turned upside down. I felt as though I was in an actual court, waiting for all the information I already knew to be repeated time and time again. Plot twists aren't as fun when they come back to back to back.All in all, I believe that if you want to play an Ace Attorney game, this is definitely a decent way to scratch that itch and to delve into more cases with a similar gameplay style as previous games. However, if you want a game with a compelling story then I believe that The Great Ace Attorney series leaves much to be desired.Also, I saw some players and people online stating that the second case of this game isn't great and that The Great Ace Attorney: Adventures is more fun during/after the third case. Although that might be true, if the game doesn't start to get good until ~40% of the game is done, then it isn't that much of a good game. I also have not played any of The Great Ace Attorney 2: Resolve, so I cannot comment on that.

_childDocuments_.review: **This review is spoiler-free!** The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles are my favourite Ace Attorney games without a doubt! It was a great new direction to the series while also revisiting the series' roots. They cater to both new players and long-time Ace Attorney fans since they're standalone in the game universe- so they can be your first games or games to wind the series up and you'd still enjoy it significantly. Both games should take around 60 hours to finish. I'm currently almost done with a re-play of the third case in Game 2, but I have played this game through a fan-translation before that. PROS: * Great Storyline. These are the first Ace Attorney games since the first Phoenix Wright games to introduce a completely new cast of characters and it delivers on that front. The storyline is great and the characters are memorable- although you can see they're inspired by trilogy characters, they still manage to feel distinct and likable and not rehashed/copied. * I loved the Sherlock Holmes novels themed backdrop. * The OST is beautiful! It's a lot grander than the previous games, with a more orchestral feel to it. * Great use of 3D. Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice(imo) feel lacking in the charm the previous games had, because of the 3D sprites but these games don't feel that way. The 3D sprites in TGAAC are expressive and animated well and I enjoyed them as much as the 2D games. * Fun Mechanics. I really enjoyed the "Dance of Deduction" segments. The jurors were rather annoying, but I think it's a good take on the system. Keeping them stupid on purpose adds to the fun, in a way. CONS:* The games are VERY slow paced. The first game is a sort of preface to the second game, so it lays the foundation for the plot while the second game reaps all its benefits. However, the first game takes some rather bold choices in terms of cases which is great while the second game is a quintessential Ace Attorney game from start to finish. The enjoyment would vary from player to player.* The games are rather easy. Pressing and presenting evidence in the trilogy(for instance) makes me feel smart and accomplished, but that wasn't the case here.* There is one particular part of the story that uses the 3D features of the 3DS, but unfortunately wasn't usable here. It's not a con that ruined my enjoyment of the games in any way but still found it worth mentioning.

The second game (and this includes both games) is an amazingly good payoff for every little bit of setup.Don't treat it as two 5-case games, treat it as one 10-case game.I don't know how Ace Attorney will ever be able to top this one. The final three cases were one mind-blowing reveal after another. The characters are well written, the music is great, and the courtroom gameplay is better than ever.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the second game, and thus the whole collection. What a story... wich I won't comment further about because it's something long-time Ace Attorney fans must enjoy by their own eyes, and their own unbiased opinions.I will mention, however, that I LOVED, really LOVED, the "asymmetry" of the structure of the episodes. Obviously I won't go so much into details, but forget the classic formula of "Investigation -> Trial -> Investigation -> Trial -> Repeat as many times the plot needs it", it's gone in its majority of episodes, and it really gives some freedom to the writting of the story, and some room to give some unexpected twists in my opinion.So as far as if I recommend the duology or not. For long-time fans of the Ace Attorney series is a must, but I won't guarantee that you'll love them more or less than the rest of the games, as I said before, it's better not to be biased by somebody's else opinions.For new players, it's tricky. I strongly recommend the games (this "Chronicles" is the compilation of 2 games) as the story is simply fantastic, and the soundtrack marvelous, among other things, it really shows what Ace Attorney is all about... buuuuuuuuuut I fear that if you start the Ace Attorney series with these games, you might find the rest of the series a little lacking in comparison (The original trilogy is on Steam, and I'd say "Chronicles" is far superior than the first two games of that trilogy, but that's very subjective). This duology has its own universe and it's not connected to the rest of the series (for now at least), so you really don't need to play the rest of the series to enjoy this one.

name: White Shadows
detailed_description: White Shadows is a cinematic puzzle-platformer where you play as a little Ravengirl trying to escape a brutal dystopia founded on oppression and violence that puts her at the bottom of its hierarchical social ladder. Composed of a vast network of towers rising from the void of post-catastrophe darkness into the sky above, the city our young adventurer seeks to escape is a dangerous place to be. She will have to find ways to avoid the teeth of machinery primed to grind her into dust, leap across rickety infrastructure that bridges the cavernous darkness all around and avoid the watchful eyes of guards ready to gun her down. She will travel to the city’s brightest highs and delve to its darkest depths on her journey, discovering her destiny among the last free people alive. White Shadows ’ striking architectural forms and stunning monochrome art style combine to create a place steeped in atmosphere. It’s a world where the lies of the elite are plastered across its walls, where twisted forms of entertainment are used to keep everyone in their place, and where hope seems in short supply. A visually stunning and narratively rich dystopian setting with a distinctive art style Varied puzzle platforming with unique scenarios that keep things fresh An exciting personal story combined with social critique A simple and intuitive control scheme

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No, but it's a new Limbo clone, and I like those games. Or at least most of them. A dystopian, black and white puzzle platformer. You can run, jump and interact with hotspots, not much more. Finding your way and not getting killed along the way is all you have to do. While the game is presented in 3D, you can only run along a fixed path, so you actually play a 2D platformer with 3D graphics around it.Everything is dark, the scenario is depressing. Animals rule the world, only bulbs bring some light. Birds are the lowest class, wolfs rule the city. Unfortunately, you are a raven. So you sneak through the chapters, push crates, pull levers and climb laddders to escape from this hell, uncovering the horrible truth behind this animal society. Not bad, but not great either.Works fine on ultrawide, supports gamepads. The soundtrack is good, inspired by classics like "Danube Waltz", "Thus Spoke Zarathustra" or "The Ride of the Walkures". Dystopian puzzle platformer inspired by Limbo.

_childDocuments_.review: If you'd prefer to see a video review of the game, featuring 5 minutes of gameplay (no spoilers – all footage taken from the first two chapters of the game), check it out here: I spent a good part of my playthrough of White Shadows in a sort of trance, hypnotised by some of its awe-inspiring moments – which there are many. From the off, the game wears its influences on its sleeve. If you were to tell me Playdead, the makers of Limbo and Inside, had developed the game, I’d believe you, as it feels so much like those games, in both style and tone.Like those games, and the similarly unsettling Little Nightmares, the story is told through actions rather than words, and it’s one that slowly reveals itself over the course of five chapters. There’s no tutorial, with the player forced to discover the controls and mechanics of the game themselves. Our protagonist is a ravengirl thrust into a dystopian world called The White City, controlled by wolves. The plot takes influence from George Orwell’s 1940s Animal Farm. A novella where animals usurp the humans on their farm for a better life. In that tale, the famous slogan ‘All animals are equal’, quickly gets the contradictory addendum, ‘But some are more equal than others’, after the pigs take control, showing how ideals are quickly corrupted.Like Orwell’s story, the world of White Shadows is one where equality is but an illusion. Orwell’s maxim features, but in this game, it is the birds that are the pariahs, with our ravengirl cast as a possible saviour. To say any more would spoil the story, but be prepared for a modern fable that's relatable and filled with social criticism.Controlling Ravengirl will feel familiar to anyone who’s played Inside. With a gamepad, you move using the left analogue stick and have one button to jump and one to interact with objects in the environment. Typical platfomer mechanics feature, certainly at the start, with pulling levers, pushing crates and making death-defying jumps. Puzzles are more like little hurdles, than brain conundrums. You’ll initially think you’ve seen it all before – but, just wait! There are surprising changes to the core mechanics later in the game. Things I’ve not seen in similar 2.5D platformers.The game features some of the most breathtaking visuals of the year with its monochromatic artstyle. The film noir aesthetic reminded me of 1930s black and white movie Metropolis, with elements of Bioshock, and even, Blade Runner thrown into the mix – particularly with the verticality of White City’s towers that rise into the sky, and the ubiquitous advertisement hoardings.White Shadows is a truly cinematic experience with the way the camera zooms in and out as you move ravengirl around the city. The sheer level of detail in every frame of the game is impressive; with so much going on in the foreground and background, the city feels alive.The music is also memorable with dramatic moments set to classical pieces, such as Wagner’s Ride of the Valkryie and Strauss’ The Blue Danube. There’s something wonderfully incongruous about watching mechanical cranes move in time to an orchestral waltz.I imagine some may find the gameplay a little slow, the puzzles a little too simplistic. The black and white graphics are a little grainy, even on high resolutions, making identifying your character a bit difficult in places. The game’s length may also be a put off for some.I finished White Shadows in one 2.5hr sitting, and while that may seem short, the game never outstays its welcome. There is no filler. I was never bored, but captivated from start to finish. And don’t forget, Inside and Limbo can both be completed in a couple of hours – and they’re both hailed as indie classics. See this as an interact movie, and a beautiful one at that.

_childDocuments_.review: White Shadows is made by a company of developers who played Little Nightmares and fell short trying to create their own version of a fun side scroller.Parts of this game are fantastic, absolutely fantastic.  I just really wish there were more of them.What you'll find is a large amount of the game is simply running side to side and jumping between platforms.  The environment is great, but you're not actually doing anything.  Give me more trains.  Give me more rope ladders.  Give me even more trains.  Give me more obstacle courses, those swinging obstacle courses are great, with the crowd making funny noises when you screw up.  Give me more "bosses" -- the TV thing is absolutely brilliant presentation wise.Just... give me more actual content.  And not recycled content from previous chapters just because I'm a chicklet now.  That was irritating.Finished the game in a few hours and the replayability factor is low... so was it worth $20?  No.  Developers had a hell of a great idea and half-assed it.  Honestly wish I could recommend this game because some of it is amazing, but I just can't.

_childDocuments_.review: is a puzzle-platformer set in a Dystopian landscape of industry where light is a commodity and society are ruled by a group calling themselves “The Founders”. Ravengirl, is aware that she is at the bottom of the social hierarchy and culture depicts her as dirty and irrelevant. Her life is meaningless to many, but she has a home far away where loved ones reside and she is seen as an equal. Her only salvation is to find that promised land by travelling through the dark and dangerous landscapes to be reunited with her kin. I was mesmerized by this game. I found it emotional and thought provoking, but it was incredibly uncomfortable and chilling to play. The opening sequence warns us that there will be references to racism, suicide, violence, animal cruelty, forced labour and xenophobia. When I read this I was filled with trepidation; Although there are scenes of this nature, they are artistically presented, and although disturbing, are more provocative than frivolous.  The dystopian landscape and drudgery of everyday life is portrayed so strongly that you feel like you have been dragged down into the cesspit along with the poor souls fighting to bathe in a brief burst of light. The constant drone of machinery, and the monochrome aesthetics, make this a bleak and foreboding place, and the desperation feels tangible.The game looks absolutely gorgeous with some clever use of light and shade. Whilst the elite enjoy the comforts of light, and peddle it as a commodity, the social hierarchy dictates that others must wallow in the dark being ushered along by sentinels ready to deal punishment to any that step out of line. The game is clever at dropping hints and suggesting parallels with modern day life, and often my mind would drift away as the game subtly reminded me of events and situations that our society also practices. It got me questioning and considering my own choices and was a powerful and moving experience.The story is a little ambiguous and I must say I did not fully understand the ending. There is no narration, text or voice acting and events are there for you to interpret. I have played many games like this and most of them just feel dull and opaque but White Shadows resonated with me and stirred emotions and made me care. That is no mean feat in a game of this type.Gameplay is rather average in most departments. Platforming is not challenging and the puzzles are mainly quite easy to solve. There is nothing new or innovative in the mechanics. It’s all things I have seen before. Platforming sections are aided by generous jumping mechanics; She can leap huge gaps and not once did I struggle to make it to the other side. I was particularly impressed with the movement of Ravengirl. She looks great as she runs across the skyline and I know it sounds stupid but I really admired the way she climbed ladders. It just looked really nice.Puzzle sections involved the usual pushing and pulling of objects but there were some interesting main puzzles dotted throughout, but they won’t stump seasoned puzzle lovers. The stealth sections were quite easy to navigate too but I did enjoy certain sections involving her small bird like friends.There are some nice cinematic sequences which enrich the story and highlight social injustices, and the accompanying music feels military and regimented in style.Game length is my only real concern about recommending this game at full price. Your first playthrough will be powerful, but is quite short at two to three hours. There are achievements to pick up, which I missed on my first run, and there are generous chapter selections to aid in these, but subsequent tries don’t seem as enjoyable when you know what to expect, so replay value is low. Being a bird, Ravengirl is quite nimble; she moves fast and can jump long distances.The environment is vast, with big industry dominating the landscape. She will need to jump across chasms; navigate platforms by jumping over hazards; climb up objects and ladders; and even spread her wings and fly.Ravengirl will find herself trapped in certain situations and need to escape. She can push and pull certain things and use these items to reach platforms or trigger switches. She can pull levers to work machinery and even use her small bird allies, that she encounters on her journey, who will hide her from sentries and lift her over high walls.There are quite a few stealth sections requiring you to hide from the glare of sentinels. Sometimes, you will need to perform puzzles or platforming whilst avoiding detection. Hiding behind pillars, timing movements and using the environment and lighting conditions will help you progress.The graphics are nothing but stunning. They are imaginative and atmospheric, and the clever use of light and shade creates an unsettling eeriness and surreal impression. You get an instant sensation of vastness against the huge backdrop of towers and endless vistas. Such a tiny frame seems minute in comparison.Ravengirl is wonderfully animated with realistic and graceful movements, and one of the best ladder climbing animations I’ve witnessed in a bird like character!Sound is quite minimalistic, but the white noise, and the constant drone of machinery and industrious behaviour, creates a bleak and repetitive picture of hopelessness. There are some cinematic sequences with song tunes which switch sensations from desperation to an unnatural creepiness.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I don't know what to say. I've completed the game twice, completed all the achievements, and it seems like a normal game. But I can't shake the feeling that something is wrong. In the game, we play as a raven who learns to fly only towards the end of the game, and even that doesn't last long. The graphics and style are cool, but some places look disgusting, especially the faces and butts of the characters in the background. The game is quite small, but when I was playing it, it seemed like I had been playing for 10 hours instead of 5. But this is probably not because the game is boring, although it really is. The game lacks character sounds and normal ambient sounds. It turns out that I'm playing a game where the sounds only work once every 3 minutes. The controls are also not very responsive, and you don't feel your character. Overall, my opinion of the game is vague, and it's probably an acquired taste. But most of all, I liked the Steam cards, which paid for the game almost 5 times over.  So I don't regret it and give the game a plus.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel a bit torn about this game. I loved it - to bits. Every single Orwellian reference, every single Kubrick reference (EXCELLENT choice of music), every single cinematic moment. It's crude, brutally honest, powerful in its depiction of a dark dystopian society.BUT. My only problem with this game is that it falls short on the gameplay side. I suppose it wasn't trying to do wonders - which is why I couldn't recommend it enough. But to someone who played LIMBO/INSIDE and Little Nightmares, I can't help but feel the puzzles were lacking, and the gameplay could have been deeper.Still, I think what this game does wonderfully is tell a great dystopian story, with astounding visuals and direction, and a little touch of surrealism. There's some clear artistry in some moments of this game, and I couldn't help but sit in wonder when those bits played on screen.If this sounds like your cuppa, get this game instantly. The things this game does well will stick with you well beyond the end credits. Just don't approach it expecting the next LIMBO or INSIDE; it isn't quite there in that sense - and considering how beautiful everything else is, I think that's okay.
_childDocuments_.name: White Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Orwellian themes permeate White Shadows but nothing much is done with them, and the experience surrounding the social commentary is left wanting. Leading the way is some great world design that is appealing and consistent, and hopefully explored more in the future. Unfortunately the platforming is basic and the puzzles are too easy. It also strangely delivers its story, relying smartly on the world design until it gives an unnecessary exposition dump just prior to a sudden unsatisfying conclusion. White Shadows has some appealing visuals that could make it worth playing, but for nearly everything else, it needed more time in the incubator.
_childDocuments_.name: White Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: This game blew me away, and I loved everything about it.  I had zero technical issues and the controller support was flawless.  The puzzles and platforming were fun instead of frustrating.  The art style, the story, the game mechanics, all amazing.  I thought I was getting a Limbo rip off, but nope.  It had a bit of that feel along with Little Nightmares, but White Shadows was a unique experience.  The only thing about the game that upset me was that it was over too quickly.  It left me wanting much more.  I'll definitely be playing again for a 100% achievement run.  It's a gem and I can't recommend it highly enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Do i recommend this or not.This is a tough question as I would like to support local german devs.Sadly, I will go with no. If it was 10€ maybe. A Neutral Option would be the better choice here, but sadly i can only say yay or nay.My main gripe comes from a very in your face message, I don't mind the simple gameplay at all, I like my walking Sims, and I don't need to be hardocre challanged in every game. A well told Story with a good presentation and nice controls can work very well.Sadly the Story falls short here, the gameplay is fine, but not outstanding, walk jump using an action button is (mostly) all you do. And the End was really disappointing. If i were to get one question to the story writer, it would be "So what REALLY was your intended point in the end, what was your message?" Because I am not sure you had one, , which, sorry, is just not good enough, for me, these days.I don't regret the 3 1/2h I spend in the game, but i don't think I need to recommend this to more people, I'd say go play Limbo, go play Inside, they are just better.So if any of the Devs is reading this: You are good on the Tech Side of things (aside from this running crap on the steaqm deck for the Graphics that it presents), you are good on the controls, but you really need to up your game on the story.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most amazing games I ever played.  A side-scrolling work of art. This is obviously not for open-world gamers, and not for gamers who are seeking pure action or replayability. And in a world of roguelite, permadeath and unforgiving checkpoints, it's also very refreshing to play a game that doesn't follow this trend. This is an interactive and dark narrative with stunning visuals and a dystopian atmosphere.
_childDocuments_.name: White Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very much like Limbo and Inside, and they do everything in their power to copy both the style and feel of those games, as well as using essentially the exact same mechanics (avoiding spotlights, dragging boxes etc..)But if people want that sort of puzzle game, you should be aware that this is not a puzzle game, there's like 3 things in the entire game that might take like a minute to figure out. It also weirdly has a single 'boss fight' and then a weird section for a few minutes where it's like a timing/platformer section. It's very weird pacing.They also like set up the first 2 hours as like giving breadcrumbs of how the world works...then you hit this part they just launch into 10 minutes of exposition explaining the world and it seems really out of placeIt's still good, but just be aware it's a 'walk through an interactive story' game not a puzzle game. The just let you thumbs up/thumbs down here, so it's a thumbs up, but it's like a 3.5/5 sort of thing
_childDocuments_.name: White Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: White shadows is a nice little game.Fairly short game with a few easy puzzles.Plays like "LIMBO" or "Little Nightmares".The most important part in this game is the message.It is not just about racism, discrimination and capitalism. It goes a bit deeper if you look closely.Very reminiscent of the Youtube films "Happiness (2017)" and "MAN (2012)" by Steve Cutts.I also liked how they incorporated classical music ;)Neat little game but overpriced,Get on discount!

_childDocuments_.review: I was on the fence about recommending this game or not but for the current price ($11.99) it will be a "Not Recommended".The game is functional and I didn't run into any major bugs or glitches in general but the game is pretty short (around 2h~3h I would say) and the puzzles are very, very simple. There are a few bits in the game that I feel like they exist with the sole purpose of stretching the playtime a bit; the "soundtrack" is pretty weird/out of place and I absolutely hate the phone ringing sounds that happens a few times in the game.The biggest reason I'm not recommending this game is because I read other reviews talking about "INSIDE" and "LIMBO" and although it definitely looked like a similar game, everything in it is SO heavy handed and on the nose - I feel like if the game was a bit more subtle about its theme where the player discovers a bit more about what's going on slowly, the game/atmosphere would improve A LOT.All in all it's not really a bad game I just don't think it's worth the current price.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever asked yourself, "What if Limbo but birds? What if Inside but racism?" That's basically this game, another entry in the "cinematic platformer" genre, a mechanics-light but atmosphere heavy world where you press right a bunch and jump every now and then. "White Shadows" is a gorgeous, moody, wonderfully realized place that I recommend for vibes mostly. This is a triumph of scale and art design.Unless you were born literally 27 minutes ago, this game is a METAPHOR. And the metaphor is BAD STUFF BAD. It's so glaringly unsubtle that I felt like I was being made fun of at times, or that it's almost a parody of those types of messages? If it's sincere, there's no subtext, it's just text. It's only near the end that you get a perplexing complication on the world's conceits. What is prophecy? What is fate in a mechanical world? What is personal agency when you were born in a machine? Interesting stuff that only get brought up in the last moments, when it should have been the inciting incident.The game is 2 hours at most, a brief and punchy trek through this bizarre animal factory world. I'd pick it up if you're looking for a moody, depressing evening.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a terrible game, there's aspects of it to enjoy, but for a price tag of $20, you'll probably end up disappointed.Cons:-Lacks technical finesse. Poorly optimized graphics, and lacks an in-depth options menu.-Lacks a core tension its inspirations have. The pacing and challenges are generous, the ability to explore the world is limited to progression, and the puzzles are easy.-Short. -It's not particularly deep or shocking story-wise. This wouldn't be a problem, were it not for the price-tag and the issues above. The game starts with a trigger warning screen, despite the fact that the game is tamer than its inspirations (Inside, Little Nightmares).Pros:+Generally well-told story, complete in its balance of spectacle-to-platformer-to-puzzle challenge. The main character undergoes an interesting change.+Functional walking sim.If you enjoy Limbo/Little Nightmare-esque games where you run around as a small child in a darker world, AND enjoy reading/writing english class short story essays for fun AND find the game on sale, pick it up. Otherwise, no.

_childDocuments_.review: BEST PART: VISUALSWhite Shadows' greatest strength is the visual design which shows a world filled to largest factorial machinery, rails, flying devices, and wires all being held together by a seemingly never-ending smog. This contrasts well with the black and white colour palette as it gives clarity to what has visual importance in this world since almost all objects or creatures in this world have a radiant white glow in some place or another. This is also works well with the 1940s aesthetic since this game is pretty much a take on George Orwell's: 'Animal Farm'. If you consider yourself a "graphics tourist" then this is worth a look, but it isn't very graphically intensive, more relying on an artistic style rather than heavy graphical fidelity.OKAY PART: GAMEPLAYThe gameplay for White Shadows is almost exactly what I expect from a game like INSIDE, but that's kind of the issue since it's almost a little too similar to INSIDE. For example, there is a repeated section of this game where you need to sacrifice small birds to progress through a level which is what happens in the first couple of minutes in INSIDE once you get to the barn. That might be just one example through gameplay but even visual choices like planks conveniently being on top of boxes that fall when you pull them, or even the walking and climbing animations of the Ravengirl are all too similar to INSIDE that it feels like the developers took their favorite aspects of that game and put them in here without changing their answers enough so it won't be caught by the teacher. That's why its just considered 'okay' to me since I came to this game for that kind of gameplay but I am a little disappointed that there is nothing to differentiate White Shadows from INSIDE in that department.WORST PART: STORY !!!SPOILERS!!!The reason I put the story as the worst part of this game is because of how overwhelmingly disappointed I was with the reveal at the end of Part Four. For context, the game opens up with a warning saying that this game has depictions of "Racism, Suicide, Violence towards Women and Children, Animal Cruelty, Forced Labour, and Xenophobia". This initially excited me since I have never had a game like this come clean with the content of it's themes and social criticism before and was welcome to the idea of knowing what I was gonna get into. However, this game handles most of that subject matter without much real critical thinking or nuance as I would've expected. This may be a case of me setting higher expectations, but I expected a game that handles such subject matter better than just putting a bunch of signs everywhere that essentially say: "Bird is bad!" "We don't like bird!" "Bird deserves it!". I am not a fan of media that needs to outwardly tell me how bad something is to me when I know the implications of the subject matter. But given my gripes I pressed on hoping the game would explain to me the reason for this world hating the Ravens so much. This doesn't get revealed in full until Chapter 4 of the game where you are given a play presented to you that explains the background of this world in a theatre format. Essentially what all the racism and xenophobia boils down to is a war started that caused the sun to be "destroyed" and the animals needed to work together to bring light back to the world. However, after helping bring light back to the world and uniting all the animals together, the animals being the rats, sheep, pigs, and ravens, one of the animals gets sick out of no where and dies. After this animal dies, the wolves come around all of the sudden and say that they will make the world better and put the blame on the animal's diseased death on the Ravens by RANDOM CHOICE. And that is the reason why the birds are discriminated against in this world. I understand this game is trying to parallel Animal Farm in a way but honestly this is some very bad story telling as there is no real depth to Racism by random choice. I could look deeper into the story as to why the wolves randomly chose the birds, but the only real "theory" I have is that the wolves are afraid of the ravens, or maybe most animals to a certain extent, because the advertisements for the light showers depict birds are "The Darkness" which is something to be afraid of and requires Light Cleansing to be rid of them. But this theory gets no deeper than that since the story after that has our Ravengirl detail her backstory of how she got into the cuckoo-clock (which isn't really important to the story either btw) and she gains wings and turns off all the artificial lights for this dystopia. Story over! It's just a shame since games that White Shadows clearly take a lot from are able to depict their themes in such a nuanced way that it feels like the developers took so much of the visuals from those games into account when making this game instead of all the other parts that made those game particularly spectacular.I beat this game in about 2 hours which is short and I like to render my worth in a game as: $1 per 30 minutes for it to be worth it. So since I beat this game in 2 hours which was at a slightly brisk pace, I would be down $18 from this game if I bought it at full price. Luckily I didn't since I got this one on sale but in all honesty, you should get this game when its on sale for at least 75% off or else you aren't getting your monies worth.I would say this game is for fans of games like LIMBO, INSIDE, or Little Nightmares since it mirrors a strong visual resemblance to those games, but unfortunately it doesn't differ itself too much from those games with a terrible story in the mix and it's a game I could not recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I almost feel bad giving this game a negative review because it has so much potential, and I really believe that if the dev team gets another opportunity with more time, money, and experience they could make something really special but ultimately White Shadows just doesn't deliver. SPOILERS + HEADY THEORY AHEADThe most compelling part of White Shadows is the world it builds. A cruel, mechanized dystopia is nothing new but the 20s-esque visual design combined with the stark lighting and sometimes truly grotesque imagery is incredible. The problem is that there's nothing to do in this compelling world, and the story and message that the devs try and tell starts strong and has a lot of potential but it ultimately loses direction and just kind of peters out. When the credits started to roll my only thought was "wait, that's it?"To get into the headier stuff the game's messaging revolves around racism and xenophobia, even more specifically around the generally Marxist theory that ideology is created based on the material situation of a society instead of the other way around, applied here in the fact that the other animals seem to learn that birds are exploitable for light in a world without sun and then later justifications are made to explain why they're inferior and deserve their treatment which could be really compelling, but it just goes... nowhere. As I got closer to the end I thought that maybe it would go into the theory of recuperation, where a revolutionary symbol (our main character) is absorbed and sanitized to become something that can peacefully coexist with the establishment while placating the oppressed, but it just sort of devolves into this weird "you're the chosen one because you can fly" thing and the solid 10 minutes of effectively no gameplay that I assumed was leading to the recuperation arc seem to serve literally no purpose in the plot of the game. There's also some random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about apparently the wolves are behind everything but the villains for literally the entire game up to and after this point are the pigs, and up to this point you've seen one mechanical wolf head so that just comes outta nowhere for no reason.I could overlook all of that if the gameplay was interesting, but it's not. The mechanics are fine, standard Limbo/Little Nightmares-esque clumsy platforming, but all of the platforming is extremely basic; it's way too easy and linear to be anywhere near fun gameplay, and the "puzzles" in this "puzzle-platformer" exist almost solely of either moving boxes to climb ledges or pulling levers in the correct sequence, and the worst part of all is that most of the game isn't even the basic platforming or the boring puzzles; you just walk. A vast amount of the game is spent either walking while you watch the interesting world (that you can barely explore) exist behind you, riding a train, elevator, or helicopter while you watch the interesting world exist behind you, or floating on wings or with an umbrella while you watch the interesting world exist behind you. And while walking simulators can work if both the world and the concepts it's tackling are interesting enough, the progression of the story and the messaging in White Shadows simply aren't executed well enough to justify just how much time you spend with effectively no gameplay. And it's a damn shame. It's a damn shame because the world, if I was able to actually EXPERIENCE it instead of just watch it go by, is very interesting, and it's very clear that the team who made this game had something to say about xenophobia, racism, ideology, and exploitation, but they just really REALLY fumbled it at the end. I'll be looking for their next game with great interest because I think it could really deliver, but White Shadows, especially for the price point, simply isn't worth it.TL:DR: Gameplay is extremely slow and not very compelling, could be justified if story and messaging were good enough, and while they get close and have some really interesting ideas, they fall flat before the end,

_childDocuments_.review: White Shadows is a decent puzzle platforming game presented through the lens of a TV episode that goes through the journey of a "Plague Bird" that tries to beat the system in an oppressive industrialized black and white world where the sun is gone and racial or animal species-based oppression is the cultural norm. As you make your way up to the top of this hostile world, constant signs reminiscent of things like Jim Crow reinforce the idea of pigs being superior to birds. You jump from platform to platform avoiding trains zooming by carrying the light that powers the world and "Keeps the Darkness away". The world feels very fifties-esque due to the the colorless presentation and classical music choices including songs such as Flight of the Valkyries.  White Shadows has an intriguing concept and an eye-catching world that has decent platforming and a mildly interesting story combined with sparsely dispersed "Puzzles" which is more like moving two boxes and flipping five switches. The game is good but I just felt like you'd be better off playing a game like Inside instead. If you're genuinely interested in the plot then I'd recommend buying it on sale, but I'd leave it at that.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game, heavily inspired by Playdead's LIMBO and INSIDE games. White Shadows does a good job of presenting an intriguing, dystopian environment, which reminded me a lot of BioShock's Rapture and Columbia settings. There's a lot of environmental storytelling which will definitely make you curious enough to keep going to find out what is going on, and the game makes some nice use of classical music for it's set piece sequences.The game itself is short and not difficult, and can be completed in just a couple of hours on a first playthrough, with puzzles definitely being on the simple side of the difficulty spectrum.The gameplay, animation and movement definitely aren't as fluid and natural feeling as they are in Playdead's titles, and there are places where the sound design seems to abruptly end or not sound quite right as you enter new areas. Also, some gameplay sequences seem to be thrown into the game, with no clear reasoning behind them or proper introduction to the player. It's easy to lose track of what is going on or why things are happening the way they are. However, they do change the game up a bit and do a good job of keeping you interested.The game also abruptly limits or takes control from the player in places for some cutscenes, which play out in real-time and can cause some scenes to drag on a bit too much.Ultimately though, this is a great first game effort by Monokel, which will be thoroughly enjoyable to those who enjoyed games like LIMBO, INSIDE and Little Nightmares. I'm excited to see what they might produce next!

_childDocuments_.review: A dark and beautiful game, both in its evocative visual style and compelling narrative. My friends and I spent a long while discussing this game after I finished it on stream again. A worthwhile and compelling experience from start to finish with intuitive gameplay and intriguing worldbuilding.While the main real life parallel is anti-semitism, the creative use of allegory, multiple difficult-to-watch but morbidly fixating scenes, and moments of humanity and humour mean it will likely strike a chord with anyone who experiences oppression or sympathises with those who do. Shout out to video essayist Jacob Geller on youtube for including this game in his video "Games that won't leave the dark", without which I may never have been introduced to this game.

_childDocuments_.review: White Shadows is to games as short films are to regular films.  I cannot stress that last point enough.  White Shadows is a 2D platform/puzzler, in the same vein as games like Out of This World and Inside.  However, White Shadows is very brief, my playthrough took around two and a half hours.  White Shadows is presented in greyscale.  I appreciate the choice.  The game looks amazing.  The world that Monokel has created is visually interesting and well presented.  There are scenes with massive crowds of animals and the scale is massive and stunning.  White Shadows has a somewhat abstract narrative.  There are some relatively obvious themes, and some others that are more obscure.  I would not be surprised if some things went over my head.   The game has a surprising classical soundtrack that kicks in and unexpected but amazing times.  Additionally, the rest of the sound design is very well done.   The controls can be a little iffy at times, and there is some other technical jank as well.  The sort of issues you would expect from a small teams first outing, nothing game breaking.  The team has already issued a patch, and I am confident they will iron everything out.  White Shadows has really really high highs.  There a few transcendent moments in the game, that make playing it totally worth it.  I look forward to Monokel's next effort.  7/10

_childDocuments_.review: It would be tempting for me to say that if "White Shadows" was any more inspired by Playdead, it would possibly be named "Inside 2: Electric Boogaloo". But for all the similarities there, "White Shadows" has also many differences - some of them very big - from Playdead's games. Because if Playdead ultimately puts play above everything else, "Shadows" cares very much about its story, mood and emotions. It's a game that leaves little to our imaginations, and very much wants us to know what's going on, even if gradually. Which is not a bad idea: it may be good to see developers at Monokel - in its inaugural game - trying to do their own thing. But when this takes a toll on gameplay, that's when I have my issues.For starters, let's give credit where credit is due: "White Shadows" is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played. I know I say that a lot in my reviews, but this one delivered one of the most visually arresting and immersive experiences I've ever had in this medium. It's truly a game to marvel, a black-and-white looker that will give you plenty to look at. Not only that, but the sound mixing is also spectacular, with moments of radio cacophony, distant sounds and pitch-perfect usage of classical music, such as "Ride of the Valkyries", "The Blue Danube", "Flight of the Bumblebee" and "Dies Irae". It's a game to play either with big loudspeakers, or with headphones.But I guess this is part of the problem: it's too much about visuals and the lore they transmit, and not so much about gameplay. As I played it, I quickly realised this is not firstly a puzzle game. There is a fair share of problems to be solved along the journey, and a lot of platforming to be had, yes. But the game may feel at times like a walking simulator, with no secret paths (that I know of), and with some tedious situations that are so... well, tedious.It mostly rejects Playdead's penchant for teaching players what to do by punishing them, albeit it does have one of two situations that play out like that. That was my major issue with "Limbo" and "Inside", and it's nice to see that "White Shadows" doesn't lean much into that direction. But it can be very slow paced sometimes, with moments when control is taken from us and drag on for way too long - again, in an attempt to woo us with its visuals, with its visual storytelling. While it indeed is a truly "cinematic" game, not everyone will enjoy it, and this should have been advertised better.Characters don't talk (one sings however), but there's a ton of signs telling us what this world is, how it came to be, how it works. Even the chapters are announced in signs across the world. I hope this is not a major spoiler, but at a moment there's even this boring play meant to tell us what happened, and who our protagonist is. At two moments, the game got interrupted by an unskippable commercial break for a product within that universe. That's right: commercial breaks in my game. The same commercial, by the way. Avoiding commercials is the only reason I pay money for YouTube Premium, and now I'm stuck with two. Being upfront about lore is not much of an issue itself; it's how it's too much at front and centre.One issue I had with the game at first is that its visuals can be misleading. The game is so visually loaded that, sometimes, I confused visual elements with platforms. For instance, there's this train section that ends with this giant mechanic wolf swallowing the wagons. That felt threatening to me, so I felt it was time to abandon ship. I thought there was a platform in the environment I should jump at, and I kept on missing it. As it turned out, it was... nothing. Just a thing in the environment, and I was supposed to be indeed swallowed by the wolf thing.  The game is not what I would call original, for all its ambition. Again, it's beautifully made, and you can see a lot of time and love was poured on it. But we've already seen several things present in it, like "BioShock", "Brazil",  "Animal Farm", "Schindler's List" and "The Matrix". The game starts with this warning that we're about to see some heavy stuff, and we should be prepared, but I didn't find the game to be so disturbing. It's not like you're going to see hard rated-M stuff, but there were moments that did make me feel part of the developers were vegan.The game also introduces some gameplay variation. To break from the routine of moving, interacting and platforming, there are moments that are genuinely amazing, such as the train ride, or humiliating, like the circus. There's this moment near the end that I will not spoil, but that makes the game substantially more interesting.All in all, I do observe the issues of this output. It's a dystopian drama that is also a game, not the other way around. But all things considered, I just cannot dislike it. It's engrossing, it's fair, it doesn't overstay its welcome (it's about 3 hours long in a first playthrough) and it accomplished in bringing me emotions. Not big emotions, but enough to make me impressed. It's a game that must be played in its own terms, and while it's rough around the edges, it can also be very rewarding.I would say there's a great game in "White Shadows", and you just need to have the patience to find it. It was a huge first step for Monokel; let's hope that, for their sophomore game, they'll improve over it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a little torn on this one - White Shadows offers up a beautifully imaginative world, with emotive art direction and some incredible camera work. I hate to not recommend this game, as clearly a lot of work went into it but it unfortunately falls short in almost every other aspect:NO HDR!!! - Although the lighting has been artistically designed well, it has not been implemented (technically) very well at all. The game doesn't have HDR capabilities, which for a black and white story focused entirely on light and dark seems like a massive missed opportunity. The lack of HDR leaves the game feeling horribly washed out and I spent the whole time panicking that I was burning my screen in with all the unnecessary bright grey backgrounds. The light sources in the game disgustingly bleed into the surrounding areas, it's not pleasant at all.Story - nothing new or interesting - without spoiling it, it's all very surface level, well trodden ground, and even at that it's not fully fleshed out. The ending left me whelmed af. A lot of the environment flourishes are just lazy character and story beats literally spelled out for you. Platforming/Puzzle solving - again, nothing new or interesting. Some of the puzzles that could have had emotional heft were squandered, and if you're going to be a Limbo clone you'd think they'd want to put there own spin on some of the platforming, but they didn't.Performance - it runs respectably, but the player character and NPC's often jitter about for no reason.I feel like the developers genuinely tried to make a unique, fun experience here. But the end product is unfortunately something that ins't really close to a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: For the first game of the developer, this is a good effort.Sadly, there were a couple of issues that really hampered my enjoyment to the point where I actually quit in chapter 5, probably close towards the ending. It was actually a funny situation: I had to stop playing to do some personal life stuff, right when I was in the middle of finally figuring out how to fly (because the game does not tell you its controls, at least not in-game..), so the game was paused mid-flight. When I came back half an hour later, I clicked the button instinctively to , but the cursor was actually on . As if the universe wanted to tell me something here... After cursing my impatience, I restarted the game, only to find out that the checkpoint system put me 10 minutes before the flight scene into one of the worst chase/run away sequences in the game where you have to jump-run away (not run, that's too slow, continuously jumping is the key), but take care not to fall into some holes. Of course I fell into those holes. Twice. And then I quit for good. It just wasn't worth it.As a German, I recognized the German-ness of the game immediately. Can we have our own LIMBO? Yes, we can, just not nearly as good. Can we have a spooky dystopian story? Yes, we can, just with a silly premise and a lot of "cleverly hidden" social commentary (because in Germany everything needs to be a commentary on real-life social struggles) that we will beat you over the head with continuously with the same message. Can we have 2D platformer gameplay? Yes, we can, just with floaty jumps, some imprecise collision detection and some painful checkpoints. Oh, and your controller won't work natively, so it's just using Steam controller mapping to keyboard controls, which may or may not be part of the control issues. And the worst of all? Instead of its own sound track, let's raid the classics and use songs where the copyright has expired decades ago. It's all so German, I wouldn't be surprised to hear that this game got an official sponsorship from some German Ministry of Awful Decisions because of its thrilling social commentary.Okay, enough ranting. It's probably not half as bad as I my description makes it seem, I am just frustrated that the game for me squandered its excellent premise and a couple of really novel ideas with an overall "safe and pedestrian" execution. I may have demanded too much from it. I just lost interest less than 2 hours of actual gameplay in and probably close to the ending. And because I paid 15 € for it a year or so ago. If you try it, do so when it is on 80% or more sale, as you only get abour 2-3 hours of gameplay out of it even if you like it.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: White Shadows is the debut title of German developer Monokel. It is a cinematic platformer very much in the vein of INSIDE and especially LIMBO. It draws many elements from it's contemporaries, and is fairly short, but it's unique and striking sense of style, and thoughtful, well paced narrative make it a fascinating must play for fans of it's genre.In terms of gameplay, it's very simple and similar to most modern cinematic platformers. You run, jump, and interact with the world to solve puzzles and avoid hazards with simple controls. The physics are weighty, and help sell the physicality of the player character while still having a sense of control in the way the best cinematic platformers do. If there is one minor nitpick to the controls, it's that the ledge climbing can feel a smidge stiff. However it never gets in the way. To veterans of the genre the game may seem a tad easy, and the puzzles simple, but the sheer sense of STYLE makes up for it.The audio-visual aspect of the game is a treat. The visuals are all rendered in black and white, but it stands out by playing with light and shadow. The animation and character design are all very well done, with the player character's animation having small touches that add a bit more characterization that expected. Special mention has to go to the camera work. For a 2D platformer, it uses it's 3D environment well. The camera swings about with scene changes, zooms in and out and adds real depth to the world. However, all of that praise pales in comparison to the sound design. The world of White Shadows is a world of machines, vehicles, neon lights and electric dynamos. And it sounds gorgeous. From the patter of little feet against metal panels to the roar and squeal of trains zooming by, the soundscape is richly layered with industrial noise. There almost never seems to be a moment of silence in this world, yet the sound effects never become a painful cacophony. In fact, at several points, the sounds of industry seem to become a part of the soundtrack, like a great and terrible rhythm to an eternal machine. The soundtrack itself is mostly made up of classical pieces such as Blue Danube and Ride of the Valkyries, however the songs themselves fit the Metropolis-like silent film aesthetic of the game perfectly, and with the clatter of gears forming a percussive backing, it all feels engrossing.The narrative also deserves special mention. This section will remain spoiler free, at least to the best of my ability. Compared to most games like it, White Shadows has a much more straightforward narrative that only dips into surrealism right when it needs to. The world is a great underground city, with twisting pipes and grinding metal. The player will see the workings of this world with each new chapter, learning it's function and understanding the mega-structure they are in, but it isn't until later that a real goal beyond "survive and move forward" becomes clear. Partway through the game there is an exposition sequence that actually explains much of the world, which is somewhat unexpected, but it comes at just the right point to feel surprisingly cathartic, as it also gives the player a final concrete goal. It also hit's some occasionally heartfelt and bittersweet moments. It then ends up veering into the strange and unusual at the end, and still leaves much unexplained, but in this case leaving much up to interpretation is better than trying to answer every possible question.If there is one thing that will turn some away, it's the length. White Shadows is a short game, clocking in at around 2 to 2.5 hours. For some, this will be a deal breaker. However, I think it's short length is actually one of it's strengths. It works as a brisk, tightly paced experience that never gets mired in itself. There's no one gameplay mechanic or puzzle element that feels overused, and by the time any section get's stale, it switches gears to something new. It's short length also feels fitting for the narrative, which never feels bloated or confused. It's a great example of "All Killer, No Filler". And I am going to be watching the developer, Monokel for their next project.(This is the first steam review I've written in years, so pardon if it's long winded and full of formatting mistakes and strange wording.)

_childDocuments_.review: Peculiar little game. Immensely atmospheric, poetic even. Gameplay wise it is quite simplistic, but it didn’t bother me, for me it was more of an experience than a test of skill. _childDocuments_.review: A mixed bag, but ultimately a very lovely little game.When I first saw this advertised years ago, it felt like a hanger-on to the sub-genre of "children in danger in a dark place" sidescrollers like Limbo, Inside, and Little Nightmares, and while it does owe a lot to those games, this does have its own particular flavor to it that makes it stand out.The depth of the backgrounds and variety of what is done in the world is unique and starkly beautiful at times, with the black and white giving a suitable noir meets Kafka decor to everything. The inspirations -- from Orwell to Kubrick to Bioshock -- are all present, and would have been better toned down into something wholly original instead of directly referenced, but do not greatly detract from the experience.The gorgeously realized visuals in a world of chiaroscuro contrast marry well with the classical music, though it did become tiresome hearing the same pieces I've heard used dozens of times in other works (though the use of Blue Danube during one sequence with mechanical arms got an amused laugh out of me). The platforming was simple and the puzzles also easy to figure out, with only one or two sections frustrating me due to timing issues.A demerit is its length, at under 3 hours, $20 is a hefty price to pay, and I feel it would have gotten more love at a more manageable $12 when it was released. Maybe look for a sale, or hell, just buy it to support indie devs so they can do more projects, as this one fell through the cracks when it was released.The ending....just kind of is? I was hoping for something more grand and evocative, but it seems like it just stops and leaves you very unfulfilled. There are a lot of themes in the game about scapegoating and oppression that marinate well with the overall aesthetic of dark and light contrasting, but I feel like it never fully realizes these efforts and instead gives you a sense of incompleteness.Nonetheless, this is absolutely worth your time and a playthrough, there are some really interesting and unique ideas and executions here, but they don't quite reach the heights of the games they aspire to be.
_childDocuments_.name: White Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: As you've no doubt realized this game is thoroughly in debt to Limbo, Inside, Little Nightmares etc. It has less puizzle solving and platforming and a pretty short play time (finished in well under 3 hours).
