_childDocuments_.review: Paradise killer is a game I have been eyeing for quite sometime but only got it recently due this month's Humble choice.After playing it through and exploring every nook and cranny of Perfect 24, I would honestly like to say that Paradise Killer is one of the best detective games that I have played.Pros:Unique StyleOne of the first things that caught my attention would be the fact that this game oozes style. This is seen in the world design, unique lore, eccentric characters and art style. This is further accentuated with the amazing soundtrack making this one of the most stylish games in library.No HandholdingUnlike many other detective games such as LA Noire or Simulacra which I recently played, Paradise killer absolutely does not hold your hand. Other than letting you know the location of the suspects at the start, players are free to approach the investigation in anyway shape or form. This allows for players to make their own judgment and assumption to the evidence they find and piece them together without much of game assistance. This is something that I often felt as I found myself trying to find the necessary evidence to convict suspects that I knew were guilty. In my opinion, this encourages self exploration of the island rather than letting players autopilot.Lack of urgency or pressureAnother one of Paradise Killer's unique strengths would be the lack of urgency or pressure. This is due to the fact that the game never rushes you in your investigation or sets a deadline for you to accomplish your goal. This gives players the time needed to think and make decisions that are meaningful to them rather than pressure them in going down a certain path. Such can include the fact that the player is free to start the trials at the start of the game if they wish too even without evidence as there is no right or wrong in the game. This is no doubt a daring move by the developers but one that further increases my enjoyment playing this game.Flaws:No purposeWhile the lack of urgency and pressure is stated as one of the game's strengths, it is no doubt a turn off for those unable to find a purpose to play this game or those hoping for a linear experience.  This can result in a confusing experience or being lost as the player might not know what to do to perhaps get to a specific location or perform a specific objective.Conclusion:In conclusion. Paradise Killer is no doubt a hidden gem that deserves more attention that it is getting. It is in my opinion worth a play for those who love investigative games or looking a unique experience. Just note that this game might not be for everyone but is no doubt one of my favorite games played this year.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is a lengthy, open-world detective mystery. You explore the beautiful island as an investigator, searching for clues about a mass murder. The truth and the facts are yours to decide. Conspiracies are everywhere.The  island is beautiful and varied. Nothing is spoon-fed to you, everything is up to you to discover. There's upgrades and abilities to get and it's up to you to discover how to get them. In the current day of tutorials being overbearing and forced, I greatly enjoyed that this game trusts you to explore and learn at your own pace. The lore of how we ended up in our current situation is interesting. The characters are eccentric. The music is jazzy and upbeat. The game struck me as an indie passion project.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is a detective game in a rather open world (well, island, but there's a lot to explore) in which your goal is not to deduce the facts but to create a truth from the facts you find. Enjoy yourself as you gallivant about a surprisingly detailed island, listening to snappy 80s style funk songs, interviewing ludicrously-named characters and collecting evidence, y'know, detective stuff.It ain't perfect, but there are some really novel game design choices. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a breath of fresh air. It takes the open world exploration of old school puzzle games but instead of a series of obtuse (and often stupid) puzzles to solve, you spend your time interviewing suspects and searching for clues. It's more interested in emotional intelligence than abstract reasoning and is all the better for it. The cast are all oddballs but it's too the credit of the writers that there are no clearly evil moustache twisters, they all feel fleshed out with motivations and secrets that are logical and weirdly grounded despite the fantastical setting. Graphically the game is very basic, it could easily have come out 10 years ago BUT the design and art direction are superb. The whole game has a clean vaporwave aesthetic and a very clever use of colour to make spotting interactive objects a lot easier. It's honestly the sort of thing you could come back to many years later and still be just as impressed. And the soundtrack is a belter.

The puzzles are repetitive as all hell with only a couple of interesting ones here and there.The dialog and story are very engaging, the world created here is out of the ordinary to say the least and the characters are fun. The more you learn about the mystery the more you become engaged in it and want to solve it fully.So I guess if like me, you don't mind walking around a whole lot and picking up mostly useless knickknacks to get to a good story, this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I will admit, when I started my journey with Paradise Killer, I was frustrated and confused. Lore was being thrown at me left and right, with names and references I didn't understand. The mystery for me was not so much what the game was putting forth, but how the world worked and what they were referencing.As the game progressed, and I became more familiar with the locations on the island, I began to get more intrigued. I can now say I find the game thoroughly enjoyable and the characters and storyline engaging. Things begin to click later in the game. Although I do wish they had explained things more simply upfront, the story and lore itself is very interesting, and I liked the way the island felt and looked. If you can get past the confusion and walls of text you may not understand in the beginning, you will discover that this island utopia may not be exactly what it seems at first glance, and an intriguing storyline awaits you.So far, these are my takeaways.PROS-----> incredibly beautiful art style and world design, the aesthetic is unmatched--> cool vaporwave music--> very intriguing storyline--> interesting and complex characters and relationshipsCONS-----> i wish the storyline was easier to understand upfront. also if there was a more straightforward guide to follow on the world and intricacies within it. For example the God structure, citizens and the Syndicate itself were confusing to understand especially with no context in the beginning.--> fast travel could be more accessible, you have to pay a blood crystal (in game collectible currency) to first unlock a fast travel point and must spend one every time you fast travel. blood crystals will go fast and it's frustrating when you don't have any and need to talk to a character across the island.--> there could be more gameplay mechanics than just the nighmare computer puzzles and talking to characters. i will say i have not tried the trial yet.Overall, I totally recommend this game, especially if you're into kinda creepy concepts like cults that worship gods from space and have sacrificial rituals. Find yourself immersed in uncovering the dark secrets buried within paradise's "perfect" exterior.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first saw Paradise Killer, I instantly went “nope” and moved on. I mean, it looked like a weak attempt to mix the currently still popular 80s aesthetic with Suda51 and Danganronpa that had all of the flair, but no substance. Yet, as time went by I’ve heard more and more good things about the title and eventually decided to give it a go myself. While my original assumptions weren’t entirely disproven, Paradise Killer turned out to be a really enjoyable game.Paradise Killer is an open world investigation adventure game with elements of a visual novel and, possibly most uniquely, fully unrestricted first person traversal controls. You can walk whenever you like, crouch, jump, even unlock additional traversal options at specific points. And you can explore the island you will find yourself on any way you see fit. It’s not exactly unheard of, since the story exploration games/walking sims started similarly and the revival of first person perspective adventure games with horror themed titles of Frictional Games all played similarly, but it’s still quite unique just how completely unrestrained you are in this game. Given that the island is also full optional items (some of which can be helpful for the investigation), it’s very unusual to see the game just be totally fine with the player abusing the jumping physics or weird geometry inconsistencies and, in fact, almost expecting many people to do that.While that might not be a defining characteristic of the game, it certainly shows how open the title is. There’s a setup – a mass murder, – and a certain expectation at the start that people would at least look at the crime scene first. But you may choose to just go in a different direction and explore as you want, finding more potential leads or even new cases as you explore and talk to the weird inhabitants of this bizarre and effed up world. Suda51 comparisons are unavoidable and the developers are wearing their influences as a badge. And they do try to take this weird vaporwave meets Old Gods rule the world dystopia feel different from what you usually get from Suda51. Resulting in a universe that makes more sense, feels more consistent and doesn’t flippantly invent some crap just because it was fun. Which might be disappointing to some (not that there isn’t any “punk spirit” in the game), but I found at least interesting. And while I personally didn’t love the a e s t h e t i c or even the catchy soundtrack all that much (as it’s more “plain” and far less “quirky” than something Masafumi Takada would do), I’m sure lots of people would love this far more than I did.Now, if you want this game specifically for an investigation part, you might be slightly disappointed, as lots of it requires you to also want to explore and “hang out” with characters, and also because there are no real “bad choices” you can make up until the trials start. You can find a bunch of evidence, talk to a person and ask them about literally everything with no consequence whatsoever, you can’t say a “wrong” thing or play your cards too early here. I didn’t find that disappointing, but, as a result, it did make all of the talks work far more like just clicking through stuff to get it over with, rather than thinking about what you talk about with whom and when. Additionally, given the size of the island, you might sometimes get in the situation where you remember seeing a place you need to go to with an item you just found, but the game doesn’t keep any information on that. It actually does track pretty much everything and any, say, computer you found that you “hack” with a simple minigame, will be tracked and shown in your AR mode. And it will smartly sort all of the evidence items for you in the computer interface. Yet if it’s just a spot on the ground which you saw several hours ago and can’t remember where it was now that you can interact with it – can’t help you there.I suppose, the main strength of the game, in how nicely it flows and how open it is, is also it’s downside. Even during the final part of the game (which you can initiate whenever you feel ready) – the trials, – you usually only have to select the person you consider guilty, the rest will play itself based on the evidence you have uncovered. No need to explain yourself, no need to point out the specifics, no need to word replies carefully or not choose some options. Just select a person and go through all topics, just like with the dialogues. If you don’t have enough evidence to support the claim, it won’t fly, if you do it will, as simple as that. The game does focus on the concept that “a fact isn’t the truth”, which comes into play when you consider if you actually wish to condemn someone who is clearly involved, or let it slide and remain outside the truth of the matter. And it’s a nice concept. Yet, I can’t say that it would make you truly pause and think before acting, more likely you will have made up your mind far before it comes to making the choice.Still, I really enjoyed exploring the island, learning more about the terrible world of this game and investigating the cases. They’re nicely written and voiced and the game isn’t all style with no substance. But I can’t say that it engaged me as much as the investigative parts of, say, 999 or Danganronpa which it clearly borrows from. It’s a really nice game that’s worth checking out – it might be just the thing for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: The story’s pretty bonkers. Basically, you have this group of immortals called The Syndicate. They worship and want to resurrect some alien gods through human sacrifices on the island Paradise. The problem is, they always end up summoning demons instead of gods. That’s when the Council, the leaders of the immortals, hits the reset button and remakes the island. Things get learned along the way and they get closer to perfection with each new island. Now they are on island no. 24, island no. 25 is supposed to be perfect. But on the eve of transition someone murders several members of the Council. The crime is pinned on a citizen who doesn’t remember anything and has been the cause of trouble in the past versions of the island. As the coming of the perfect island may be in jeopardy, the remaining immortals decide to bring back Lady Love Dies, the best investigator they have. She was sent into exile after she got deceived by the false god and caused the destruction of one of the previous islands. Her punishment was watching the destruction and rebirth of several islands from a complex above. Your main job is to investigate the crime and then report back to the Judge. How you do this is entirely up to you and there is no time limit. You can explore the entire island the moment you step out of the judge’s door. Run straight to the murder scene and start investigating or simply walk the other way and enjoy the scenery. The only true boundary is water around the island, but even if you accidentally fall in, you’ll simply appear at the nearest save point. The game isn’t slow like some detective games. A sprint and jump button make exploring easy and there’s also quite a lot platforming involved. This means that if you see something interesting on a roof or hard-to-reach place, usually some sweet collectible, there’s probably a way to get to it by jumping. You might even jump off a cliff and find something that shouldn’t be found. Oh, and there’s no fall damage. But the main gameplay still consists of collecting everything interesting. The island is divided into small districts that are littered with small squares you can interact with. There’s even an occasional puzzle or two stuck in there. The things you pick up is usually directly connected and can be used in the current area so it’s always a good idea to search it thoroughly; like colored gems that need to be placed into nearby slots. Some areas are closed off and can be opened only with a simple hacking mini-game. Naturally, you’ll have to find new sets of glyphs for more important doors. Stuff you get to pick up may contain evidence, item or blood crystals, this world’s currency. You can spend them on several things: to unlock quick travel points, sacrifice at altars, visit footbaths and purchase special abilities, like double jump and meditation which shows points of interest and saves you the trouble of searching for that last collectible, on vending machines and black market where you buy information on others. Squares may also contain information or relic of this world or show you a memory from one of the island’s previous versions. Their only purpose is to build the world and don’t bring anything to the investigation. Oh, and you don’t have to worry about missing anything. Every clue or statement is stored in your personal computer Starlight. It contains information about the case, members of the council (alive, dead and those that already moved to Island 25), inventory, timeline, map, skins for your computer and music.No good mystery game goes without wacky characters and this game has around a dozen weirdos. You always know where they are as their location is displayed by simply pressing the button. They either have some connection to Lady Love Dies from the past or just hate your guts and call you’re a freak. Topics you can talk about depend on the stuff you discovered so far, including motive and alibi of others. There’s no fear of missing anything or messing up. You can respond any way you like and each response is described like “Friendly”, “Suspicious”, “Flirty”. You soon discover that choices don’t matter. You can also hang out with them and build relationship. Do it often enough and you’ll get some new piece of juicy information as reward. All this talking unfortunately does include a lot of back-tracking. You may find some unimportant clue on one side of the island and use it to interrogate someone on the other. You can use the quick travel at save points, but this costs blood crystals which are limited.You can finish your investigation at any time, whether it’s 10 minutes into the game or 10 hours. You can really sink your teeth in and find the true, definitive conclusion, or accuses the first suspicious character. And everyone’s a suspect. While investigating the main crime you might stumble upon hidden clues that connects a character to a much bigger picture. You’ll find dirt on everyone. It’s your job to piece the puzzle together and begin the trial. During the trial you’re asked questions about individual cases. You must then accuse the suspect and back it up with evidence. Depending on how thoroughly you researched a case, you either succeed in convincing the judge or fail. After the trial you can still hunt for the missing collectibles, choose the fate of surviving characters or simply end the game.Although the island isn’t that big once you get familiar with the surroundings, it still is pretty nice and has lots of detail. There’s also a day-night cycle that moves really fast and paints the island in a different light but doesn’t change the gameplay. Characters are flat 2D images placed in a 3D world so it looks weird every time they turn towards you. Similar to VN, the only voice characters make are certain words or sentences. Another major plus of this game is its soundtrack, again from the 80s. It’s that famous synthwave you’ve been hearing in almost everything lately. The type of music that makes you feel good and relaxed. You’re pretty much stuck with it throughout the game; you can collect tapes with new music you can listen at any time or make a personal playlist. The game runs fine. I encountered only one slowdown when a lot of stuff happened on the screen at the same time, but it quickly returned to normal. It’s a real shame the game doesn’t have achievements, which could lure you into playing it a few more times and make different choices or accuse other characters. Now there’s little incentive to search every nook and cranny for that last piece of collectible once you collect enough clues.It also doesn’t encourage another playthrough; you’ll probably explore everything the first time. And save often because the game doesn’t support autosave! This game feels more like an anomaly and not something that will get copied. VN mystery game mixed with open world concept can only take you so far.  Rating: 8/10Reviewed by:

_childDocuments_.review: My relationship with this game is complicated.On one hand, much of the game feels cobbled together, with parts of it seeming to be very nicely polished and yet others mysteriously held over from a time when I presume the game was much earlier in development. It's hard to pinpoint exactly which parts of the game were calculated sacrifices and which were developmental oversights. For instance there is a flashlight icon with the keybinding to toggle it on and off glued to the bottom right corner of the screen and yet I have absolutely no idea in what situation it would serve you to have a flashlight. There is a day and night cycle and yet the concept of time in the game is extraneous. The free roaming and platforming aspects of the game seem to provide no real value to the core gameplay experience (which like many games in the mystery genre is essentially a virtual novel with light evidence collecting mechanics) because the majority of the scattered puzzles in the game serve only to provide you with currency rather than to provide opportunities to freely gather evidence and examine crime scenes. The currency itself after a few hours into the game loses much of its function, changing from a means to gain upgrades to your personal computer and to buy information, to merely a means of fast travelling through stations you've already paid once for to unlock travel to and from.The game does not take itself too seriously, though. It is filled to the brim with vague, platitudinous language and stream-of-conscious-like snippets in item descriptions that reference all of the cliches of film noir, but do little to inform the player of anything except that the world you are exploring is apparently as mysterious as the murder you are trying to solve. There is a bizarre and seemingly irrelevant preoccupation with describing various liquors and beverages. The contrast between how cliche everything is and the ominous, cold and grotesque nature of the world makes the game both charming and horrifying at the same time.  And yet it is surprisingly easy for the player to accept the horrifying nature of the world and get on with their job.That said, the world is barren and empty. The game calls attention to this as often as it can with dialogue referencing the end of the world, which after awhile feels less like a well-utilized plot device and more of a convenient explanation for the lack of content. The characters feel like they did not get the patience and attention they deserved as nearly all interaction with them is either through interrogation or idle banter that focuses too much on telling and not enough on showing. Like everyone understands that it's their job to provide a history of the world to the player and that they only have a 20 hour game to do it in.I realize all of this sounds like I'm describing a very deeply flawed game. And part of the reason is because that is exactly what I am doing. To me, it is less of what an open world mystery game should be, but a demonstration on what they COULD be, and that dynamic and the understanding of how few people were involved in its development are inspiring to me.That and the music slaps.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolutely fun game. I love murder mysteries and this one did a great job. The art style and environment reminded me a lot of Danganronpa. My only complaint with the game is I wish there was a CG gallery unlocked or a way to review all your collectibles after you finish the game. They had some great artwork and world-building and it's disappointing to only be able to see the full illustration and flavor text once.I would highly recommend this if you're looking for a fun, crazy murder mystery.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: The characters are fun, the mystery is clever and pulls no cheap tricks, the exploration is engaging, even if slow at times. It's the first game in a long time that has delivered the kind of wonderfully bewildering experience I used to get from Suda51's early games. It's far from a Suda51 ripoff, but the influences from Flower, Sun, and Rain and Killer7 are obvious. The trial and epilogue sections are unfortunately under developed, with the former feeling more like a victory lap than an effort to prove my theories, and the latter feeling like it didn't have enough writing in it to justify.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: It's literally just random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nonsense and pressing E on items that talk about nothing until you trip on the item that tells you exactly what's happening. The most basic stuff gets screwed up like finding a corpse and it still listing them as MIA in your computer. Does the dumb 5% of dialog is voice acted approach too where just totally random stuff is fully voiced midway through a conversation- not important lines even just random stuff. The whole game is pretty lol random so I guess it's just being consistent.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Probably best described as a non-linear, Danganronpa-esque open world walking sim with some collectables thrown in, all played to the backdrop of some great music that truly ties it all together.There's a certain type of zen feeling as you're gradually exploring the island, finding collectables & clues, all the while peeling back the mysteries of the island/game world.I have some nitpicks - the consumable blood gems being used for fast travel can get a little annoying towards the end if you run low on them, but there are some permanent buffs you can acquire to make finding collectables & traversal much easier, so it balances itself out for the most part. The trials all taking place at the finale of the game also gives the ending an abrupt sort of feeling, especially given the trials themselves are mostly open & shut cases provided you've gathered enough evidence; there's no real opportunity for any of the defendants to throw a wrench in your prosecutorial case against them, which is a shame given how lengthy and back-and forth Danganronpa/Ace Attorney's trials tend to be, you can't help but think the conclusion here would be a bit more epic if there were more of a showdown.Overall, though; a lot better than I thought it would turn out, it's a really nice palate cleanser between other games if you fancy trying something different.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: I am a little surprised that this game does not have a "horrible" tag. The first NPC(sorry I forgot his name) really horrified me. And every time he appeared and disappeared suddenly, I got frightened. Also, the criminal scenes were so frightening. It was hard to explain. But I really got uncomfortable at many scenes. Apart from this, the game is basically acceptable.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Great fun. Some of the moment-to-moment writing falters and I wasn't convinced by the 2D character art, but the open-ended investigation is really engrossing. Loved how the game doesn't hold your hand and pretty much just sets you free on an island to figure things out, which also plays into how things are wrapped up at the end. _childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

Super unique premise and the collectathon was a fun spin on standard VN gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, never thought I would be invested in a murder mistery much less one that makes you read lore where characters have names like Lady Love Dies.But yes, I am hooked in the lore, the presentation, the mistery and traversing/collecting things is good too.Ending is a bit mid. _childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: was recommended this by a friend, picked it up on sale and gave it a try and wow i really like it, a lot more than i was expecting to! vaporwave admittedly is not my top choice of aesthetic but for some reason the vibes in this game really did a number on me, i love existing in the world, not to mention the really good music and characters. really enjoyed putting together all the evidence, and appreciated that the player is left to interpret it for themselves, leaving the explanation only for the end-game trial section. even as i was doing the trials i was still deliberating over the evidence, trying to decide who really dun it! and it was rewarding to see that my investigating and hunches led to a (mostly correct) verdict. i am rambling enough so i will leave it here for now, PLAY NOW IF YOU LIKE DETECTIVE GAMES!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer has a lot of potential but doesn't live up to it gameplay-wise.This is a crime/investigation game taking place on a big, open-world island. Scattered on the island are a few characters (suspects) to talk to, and objects to pick up. You advance through the game by interacting with them.You get a lot of freedom to do whatever you want in your investigation, you can start the final trial to end the game whenever you want, but the consequences of that is missing evidence you gather on the island and coming to the wrong conclusion.Don't expect an Ace Attorney or Danganronpa-esque way of explaining through all the facts and arriving at a satisfying truth at the end. Here, you're meant to do all the thinking on your own by reading through your evidence, and the conclusion you come to might not even be the truth of what happened. As a crime game lover, the story felt unsatisfying and a bit burdensome to get through. It would have been nice if the game helped you sort through the facts in any way.And, for the achievement hunters out there, 100%-ing this game means going around for hours and picking up every collectible on the map. The most fun way to achievement hunt. Not. It felt like I focused more on jumping around the map trying to pick up everything I found than to actually investigate the crime.I wish I had better things to say about Paradise Killer, because it at least vibes hard with the style, art and music. But it is just not fun to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Exploration-heavy detective adventure that takes place in a bizarre world. Very odd, very cool.Exiled lead investigator of a disbanded Psycho-crimes unit is called upon to solve a gruesome mystery of mass homicide in paradise. Old friends that may have turned foes, old foes that may have turned even more bitter, and demons that may have turned… no, those just stayed what they are – all making things a lot more complex and, maybe, a bit nostalgic.  There’s only one god, but he is still weak, and the rest of the pyramids stand empty waiting for powerful inhabitants. The island is dying, but the new paradise is already built and brought to life. Someone is meticulously planning kidnapping of a fresh bunch of humans from real world – residents of the island aren’t going to service themselves, of course. And there is murderer on the loose – everything falls into place for an investigator Lady Love Dies to have a grand old time. Was any of that clear? Or was it “what the hell did I just read” moment? If it’s a second option - it’s quite alright. To explain original, multi-layered and quite peculiar universe of “Paradise Killer” would be a daunting task and, in some way, a disservice to the player, as discovering all the oddities and complexities is part of the fun. This is a game with a heavy narrative element (in a Danganronpa-ish sort of manner), and Lady Love Dies would be moving investigation forward as well as exploring through loads of dialogue , much of which will contain tons of info about the brand new (to the player) world. Considering this fact, the narration is done well and flows relatively smoothly, not counting almost total confusion about surroundings and works of the society in the first quarter of the game. Occasional necessary info dump and quirky character flight of fancy included, “Paradise Killer” has a solid writing element going, maybe not to be thoroughly questioned, but enough to intrigue a player, leading straight into a rather addictive gameplay.Gameplay that is, unusually for adventure games, is built on heavy exploration of the surroundings. As a lead investigator, not only does a player get to explore extensive and colorful areas of the strange island tracking clues but also traverse this world vertically - from the sewers up to the highest towers - finding secrets, blood crystals (currency of the island), all kinds of collectibles and quick words of wisdom from one particularly vulgar demon. The exploration can be done at player’s own pace and can be as thorough or as limited as one desires. Same could be said about the mystery at the center of the game. While search for “who and how”  doesn’t provide for any kind of deductive freedom and is being logged by Lady Love Dies in a fashion that doesn’t require much input from the player, how much is being discovered, brought to trial, and used there ( and in what way exactly) is entirely up to the player. It is possible to go to trial without discovering major plot twists and end up with a wrong conclusion. It is also possible to understand what happened quite clearly and yet put everyone through a grinder just because Lady LD felt like it that morning. This combination of free exploration and carefully doled out by the game mystery makes “Paradise Killer” all about the journey rather than destination. The ending might seem slightly anticlimactic, but the process of getting there, especially if the player’s into exploring, is fun and quite addictive.The graphic element is as peculiar as the rest of the game but will seem familiar to all the Dangaronpa players as yet another, at least a little inspired by that game, element. Strange and colorful cardboard cut-out character models with no animation stand out in the surrounding 3D heavily detailed and very complex world. While said characters are drawn with a big imagination and gusto, it’s the “world” that takes the prime spot as the main visual element. Everything from eerie, opulent temple full of sacrificial blood to strange futuristic factory and agriculture set-ups to diverse neighborhoods and then some - are highly creative, intriguing and rather breathtaking examples open for exploration. All this vivid variety full of thoughtful details and colors can be viewed under the clear, sunny sky or during romantic, deep sunset that slowly descents into dusk, as it’s possible to see the passage of time while investigating murder (it has no bearing on the investigation itself and seem to simply add to the mood and atmosphere).What else adds majorly to the mood and atmosphere? Music does. What a wonderful, part romantic part relaxing techno jazz mash-up “Paradise Killer” has going on! Something to notice from the very beginning and continue to marvel at throughout this rather lengthy game. Tracks changing based on the area of the city, becoming bit more bluesy and soothing next to calmer areas, and bit more dynamic when getting closer to dangerous zones. In general though, the jazzy, smooth vibe permeates the entire game and makes the exploration absolutely wholesome. There’s also some VO here – every character has a number of lines they repeat during the dialogue (hello again, Danganronpa) and whatever is present is done well, but ultimately, it’s just a softer, less noticeable support to a great soundtrack that dominates the game.“Paradise Killer” is an oddity. It’s a detective game based on exploration and finding clues, where detection itself is curated by the game, but exploration is 100% given to a player. It’s has wholly unique universe and lore, intriguing story and fantastic soundscape. Hours put into this game tracking perpetrator and finding secrets can end up being seriously addictive and fun. Sort of a game that might not be for everybody but that most adventure players would enjoy, if that makes any sense. Most of all though, despite gruesome happenings, the game is quite relaxing and strangely light-hearted. There’s nothing like looking at blood and gore during pink sunset listening to soft jazz and planning your next sexual encounter, and “Paradise Killer” is here to give everyone this opportunity.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed the game more than I thought I would. The art style was warm and upbeat which distracted from the serious tone of solving a mass murder. Story elements were reminiscent of a cross between death loop and the myst series. It's relatively short but in this case that could be a pro because it doesn't wear out it's welcome. Even hunting down the collectibles for evidence isn't that bad once you unlock meditate. The biggest con is that the in-game puzzles can be pretty basic and repetitive. Overall I'd give it a 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: This was one of the best mystery games I've played recently.  The game's setting is fearlessly original, and by far the highlight of the game.  The writing is very good throughout, and the plot is well-constructed.  On the other hand, some of the exploration parts were a bit tedious, and I feel like I could've gotten stuck a few times if I hadn't gotten lucky.  Still, this was an enjoyable experience, and at ~20 hours it's the perfect length.  Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: The game is more of an exploration adventure game where you endlessly search the Island, turning over rocks and talking with people in an attempt to find more clues. Once you find the clues, the game basically hands you the answers, there's no need to synthesize the facts into a single truth yourself. This makes the game pretty mundane and easy, there's no risk to anything you do (aside from one conversation topic which you'll be locked out if you're not considerate, but the evidence is mostly irrelevant anyway), no need to think carefully about what to do next, no need to write up the set of events yourself, just stroll through the island at your own leisurely pace and click on every item you see. When you get to the trial, the game holds your hand all the way through it, basically making it impossible to mess up unless you was very lazy during the investigation part of the game, or very very very stupid during the trial. This is evident because literally every person I've seen discussing the ending mentions the same answer, with only a few people deliberately letting  Aside from that it's a good game, but it's best enjoyed as an interactive story rather than a detective game. I wish I could give it a neutral rating.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game alot, i recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed the finding information aspect of Outer Wilds and Return of the Obra Dinn, and also to any fans of Danganronpa because it had heavy comparisons in the story and vibe of the game. _childDocuments_.review: An absolute trip from beginning to end, Paradise Killer gives you a mystery to solve and no one way of solving it. This openness doesn't last the entirety of the game, but the journey is still worth it and the destination is satisfying. Go in as blind as possible for the ultimate experience, but also don't be afraid to look up a few things here and there as some of the more important clues are in very obscure locations. Overall, it's worth checking out and well worth the $20.

_childDocuments_.review: I fail to find much to enjoy in Paradise Killer. The world is highly abstract and seems to operate on lots of moon logic, which feels at odds with its murder mystery setting; Right from the setup I had a bunch of questions about what exactly happened, and the story didn't provide a coherent explanation. Instead, it unleashes you onto this barren open world full of meaningless collectibles, where you have to slog your way around questioning people. Questioning them involves tedious menuing through dozens of options where the characters often just insult each other and nothing gets resolved. I found the dialogue presentation poor, with character sprites being way too small and awkwardly positioned on screen, loads of punctuation errors, and obnoxious regular choices that don't add to the conversation. Also, the characters constantly interject with canned voice lines that kept pulling me out of the writing. You might say having some voice lines is better than no voice lines, but this feels like a clear showcase of the problems with a halfway implementation.And that's about all I have to say. I love detective games, and I love visual novels, and yet this just did not do it for me on any level.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is a well-written open-world mystery, set on an island dripping with lore and intrigue. The open-ended nature of the investigation and the final trial is where the game shines, as the player is given a lot of freedom. They can choose to distinguish between facts and truth to influence the final outcome. The system to organise evidence by suspect and crime is very well-organised and helpful.The weakest part of the game is unfortunately the part that the player will spend the maximum time in, traversing the island itself. While there is a fast travel option, it is limited in many aspects. The in-game map is practically useless and the absence of a compass or a minimap overlay makes it even more difficult to use. While it is understandable that the game wants players to explore the island, the impression given is that this objective was not met by encouraging players to do so but rather by discouraging them from travelling in any other way and forcing them to painstakingly tread and retread the same paths through bad navigation systems.Having said that, the mystery and its writing combined with the open-ended nature of the crimes and the trial, along with the accompanying social commentary propped up by the lore of the island and its creation make Paradise Killer a compelling package.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best-realised detective fantasies ever made, gorgeously presented with a very good cast of characters and an excellently conceived central mystery. It's not a perfect game, but these things aren't flaws! They're, uh, idiosyncrasies. It is almost aggressively quirky in a way that works for me about as often as it doesn't, and I think quite a few members of the cast are one-note, but it's a pleasant note so it works.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: I will recommend this game, but only barely. Before I go into a full review, I want to give some tips that would have made this a more positive experience had I known ahead of time. Just a heads up, this is more of a collect-a-thon, than it is a detective game. If you intend to play: here are some spoiler-free pointers to give you a more positive experience.Anyways, on to the full review. Paradise Killer was a wildly mixed bag for me. I really wanted to love this game, but there are so many flaws in the nitty gritty that I was exhausted with the game in the final hours. But just to be clear: I will be closely watching this studio to see what they come up with next, because I think their next game will be great.- Music, without a shadow of a doubt. If the music weren't so great, I honestly might not have recommended this game due to everything else.- Aesthetic. Just look at the screenshots, its a really cool looking game.- Character Designs. Very unique characters that I will very much remember.- The playable world. It seems really overwhelming and huge at first, but as you play it starts to get more and more intimate, and by the end you really feel like you know it like the back of your hand. Very unique space, that I will have fond memories of. (Smaller things that I feel a mod or patch could fix):- Clunky Platforming. Your character cannot step over the tiniest bump, so you have to jump. The problem is that you cannot change direction once you are in the air. I think the overall clunkiness could have been fixed by allowing me to move forward just a little bit while jumping. In its current state however, if you wanna get over a 2 inch bump, you have to back up, get a running start and then jump. It sounds minor, but given 80% of the gameplay is just running around, these moments really add up.- Collectible pop-ups. For every single "Blood Crystal"/(currency) pick-up, a pop-up covers the entire screen, and you have to wait about a second before you can close it. You'll probably collect near 100 of these, so the constant interruption gets really annoying after a while.- Lack of being able to call someone. You get a phone call from one of the suspects early on in the game, confirming that phones exist in this universe. I really wish that I could call suspects, but maybe limit it to only one conversation. It just pads the game out when you find a "new break in the case", and thus you now have to go visit all 10 suspects and ask them about it, only for 8/10 of them to just say "IDK". I understand that witnesses are going to not know the answer or lie sometimes, but good lord it just adds so much pointless traversal, fast travel, and wasted time on the player's behalf. This alone could have trimmed at least an hour or two off of the playtime.- Fast Travel gets annoying. I appreciated the "in-universe" explanation for fast-travel at first, but I'll admit I got tired of the little dialogue/"scene" after the first dozen times. I wouldn't mind as much if the dialogue changed at all, but given how much you have to fast travel in this game, it eventually just got old and I mashed through it. - I wish Shinji's dialogue referenced your current location more often. Out of the 30-40 times I spoke with Shinji, only twice did he ever mention where we were physically. Otherwise it just felt like he was reading through a static list of vague observations.- I feel the lore was a bit over-written. They throw far too much in your face at first. And with how exotic all of the names for things are, it was just lore overload. I think the world is cool, but there's just too much that is explained that has absolutely nothing to do with what is going on. Some of the collectibles are just wildly uninteresting, and I really didn't care about the text that came with 80% of them.- The voice acting. I get that the game might not have had the budget to do full voice acting, but it does have some. Each character has half a dozen short lines that they repeat far too often. Usually while you are trying to read something that is not even close to what they said. It just gets really annoying after a while. Special shout out to the Grand Marshal's really poor voice acting in particular though. She was insufferable.- World devoid of life. Due to an investigation going on, I can understand everyone being "locked in their homes", but some characters were just hanging out outside. I wish there was a little more life on the island, because honestly it felt like I was just running through an empty world like a level designer would or something during development. The 2D PNGs representing the suspects in the world also did not help with this. - Also, the bar cutscenes didn't really do much for me.- You also don't really need to use your intuition much in this game. If you collect 80% of the evidence, your character kinda just deduces everything for you in the end without you having to think much.All in all, a very memorable game - albeit it one littered with clunky gameplay, and some frustrations that add up. I think the team will likely take feedback for PK into account, and make a pretty great 2nd game. I will be listening to the music for the foreseeable future, and picturing this cool world in my head.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is an amazing open-world detective game. The story is gripping and the characters are (ironically) three dimensional, and the mythology the story builds is insane. It bears similarities to Mesopotamian mythology yet all the characters and stories are entirely unique which just builds this fabulous sense of wonder. The amazement is complimented by the  that makes the game visually unique too that will keep you glued to the screen and engrossed in the lore.After I beat the game, I spent weeks thinking about it and mulling over the plot in my head. Months later it still fills me with the same sense of wonder it did when I first booted it up, and I love it with a passion. It is a truly memorable experience, and is one of my new favorite games.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: This game reminds me heavily of a mix of games like Myst, and Ace Attorney, undoubtedly being an inspiration for the exploration-based gameplay and mechanics of the game respectively. It definitely focuses more on the collection and inventory aspect of it, for better and for worse, though IMO mostly for better. It's certainly a hidden gem, as overused as that term is to some extent, and it is absolutely something worth experiencing for yourself.It's not all perfect, though. The world, while absolutely immersive, was a little underwhelming, and the time I spent roaming the world was time I wish I could've spent getting more dialogue out of characters. It also felt weirdly restrictive, for lack of a better word, the entire map felt small yet huge at the same time, in that the urban sections were cramped, while the mountains were unforgiving to climb (and even punishing).Nonetheless, I enjoyed Paradise Killer, and I'm sure you will too. Close the door and stay forever, here in Paradise.
