_childDocuments_.review: Picked this up on recommendation, and I loved 90% of what this game did.  Unfortunately, the 10% I didn't was that it *completely* collapsed at the end, in a way that is difficult to articulate without spoilers.  Half of it is that there is a single piece of pre-trial evidence you can find which totally, unambiguously blows apart the game's central mystery and goes from zero to literal confession within the span of 30 seconds, so for all the game's talk about distinguishing facts from truth, the facts end up having a super clear truth which removes a huge amount of the moral dilemma it was building toward.  The other half is that, having spent all game pushing the thesis statement "Is paradise worth saving?" at you, there is no way to follow up on it whatsoever.  You never get to see the outcome of your choices (aside from everyone you convict of any crime getting the immediate death penalty); there is apparently no difference whatsoever to the structure and trajectory of the next island, whether you murder the entire main cast or find a single scapegoat.  More crucially, there is absolutely no acknowledgement when you have enough evidence to convict someone and then deliberately refuse to present it.  I replayed the final trial, and was SO looking forward to the catharsis of saving [redacted] and then talking with them later to say I knew exactly what they had done.  But there is no way to even bring the topic up in post-trial conversation, just an option to supplementarily kill (or exile) anyone you thought was guilty but couldn't prove it in court.  (And nobody even reacts to that!  It just happens and it's done.)This would have been a fantastic game if there had been any denouement whatsoever -- or, failing that, if the linchpin evidence had been treated with even a fraction of the care and thought of the rest of the game.  As it is, this is a weak recommend on the strength of its worldbuilding and atmosphere, with a warning that it will likely leave you unsatisfied, despite the good parts of it sticking in your head.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice mix of exploration puzzles and sleuthing. The plot and mystery are interesting enough. The game is designed to be forgiving, you can fall from any height and survive, you will respawn if you fall into the water, and as far as I can tell there are no dialogue options that will cause you to lose critical clues. You'll just be left to wonder whether your conclusions are all correct. It was compelling and I completed one run within 2 days.

_childDocuments_.review: A strange game, with some powerful vibes going on, and very little hand-holding.Graphics are a bit rough around the edges, but the game embraces the roughness.The character writing and storytelling is really well done, especially the environmental storytelling.There is some jankiness to the platforming, since you don't have aerial control, but it feels like the game is fully intending for you to not do any precision platforming, and so purposefully didn't give you the tools to? _childDocuments_.review: Pretty cool little game, you walk around in a big 3D world interacting with odd characters and collecting items and its a big murder mystery you have to solve. Very nice music and art and stuff, gameplay is simple but it works. Lot of things to do and collectables to get. Has a small amount of voice acting but what is in there is pretty decent. The setting and the world and all the lore is very interesting and I would like to see more of it. Runs pretty well, didn't really notice any bugs, didn't have any crashes. Ran at a good 100-144fps most of the time. If I had any critiques its probably that its a bit straightforward and as long as you go around and do everything you more or less don't have to worry too much about solving things. Would have also liked there to be achievements or at least some sort of way I could check that I've collected everything. _childDocuments_.review: I really don’t like calling things pretentious. I avoid it if at all possible, because I think claiming something doesn’t have the depth or meaning it purports to requires a level of understanding that most people (myself included) don’t reach with their media. I’d rather not say a game fails to express its intended meaning unless it’s really, truly, painfully obvious that it missed the mark. I bring this up because I’ve heard Paradise Killer criticized for being pretentious, and I don’t think that could be any further from the truth. The characters and concepts are about as far out there as you can get without becoming wholly experimental, but the gonzo themes are only setting you up for the brilliant, poignant ending. You might not be expecting it, even when the game tells you exactly what it’s going to be.Lady Love Dies is known as the “investigation freak”, or at least she was, until she was exiled from Paradise. Paradise is an island, managed by the all-powerful Council, that is unmade and remade over and over again in the hopes of forming a perfect society that will revive a host of ancient, alien gods. This reality manipulation can have nasty side effects, like demon infestations that have to be purged by remaking the island. However, the Council seems to have gotten it right with their next iteration of the island, which they’re in the process of relocating to when they are all quite suddenly murdered. This unthinkable event is enough to summon Lady Love Dies from her exile, and put her on the grisly case.If you think that’s weird, it only gets weirder once you’re in the game. You’re going to interview suspects like the cyber-enhanced Doctor Doom Jazz and the goat-headed Crimson Acid. You’re going to learn about gods that whisper dead secrets into mortal ears. You’re going to buy sodas from Dead Nebula machines, and scour cabinets and trash cans for blood crystals. And you’re going to do all this in a wide-open city that looks like some kind of insane vaporwave FPS mod, meeting up with 2D characters that transition you to pre-rendered scenes from a Windows 95 screensaver to question them about an impossible murder. It’s a lot to take in, thematically and aesthetically, and honestly this might be what makes Paradise Killer work so well.The moment you load into the game, you’re dropped into Lady Love Dies’ palace of exile, a white-marble affair accented with lush gardens and golden skulls. The plot is blasted at you by your talking computer, you’re taken down to the gates of the island on a road to nowhere, and then you’re given the full scope of your task from the Judge, a being of pure logic fused to the island through mechanical and spiritual means. Opening the game with the full gamut of the game’s weirdness honestly makes it a lot easier to accept as status quo, and helps put the player’s mind where it needs to be to comprehend the events that unfold. The plot is a complicated one, with dozens of players and elements to keep track of, and they cross in ways that would make no sense in our world, but perfect sense in the world of the Syndicate and Perfect 24.At the heart of Paradise Killer is a murder mystery, and everything you do on the island is to the end of uncovering the facts of the case. But doing that requires running around the island, exploring the deserted neighborhoods, industrial centers, shrines, cliffs, and more. This is accomplished in first-person, and is honestly some of the most fun I’ve had scrambling about a location. The wild architecture is certainly a big plus, but there’s an element of first-person platforming to it that controls exceptionally well and makes finding secrets and collectibles that much more gratifying. Perfect 24 is just a fun place to hang out, and I never got tired making laps around the island to find new things or follow up on leads.As for the mystery itself, there’s a ton to unravel and every character has something to contribute to the unraveling. You will indeed need to make several laps of the island, to ask about new evidence you uncover or refute a claim a character made earlier on. A few locations require some puzzling to get into, nothing overly complex but it does add to an overall sense of progression. There’s one revelation that came out of absolute nowhere for me, perhaps because of how I came across it, but that’s forgivable in part for the incredibly open nature of the game. Even with all the time I spent uncovering secrets and making connections, I’m still not sure I got the full picture, but fortunately that’s not necessary for the ending.I do want to mention one thing about the ending, without getting into spoilers, because it’s perhaps the most brilliant part of the game and also the most misunderstood. Early on in the game, while you’re getting your bearings and coming to grips with the bizarre setting, the Judge explains your investigation in detail. They say something about how this will all wrap up that’s meant to be taken literally, and I get the feeling some folks didn’t pick up on that. Because of this, the conclusion you get once you close your case might not be the definitive answer to the mystery you’re looking for. All I can tell you is that that’s the point, and to heed the words of the Judge both at the beginning and the end of the game.Even if the mystery angle doesn’t hit as hard for you as it did for me, Paradise Killer is absolutely a game worth experiencing. A lot of indie games go hard on unique aesthetics and themes, but this is one of the rare ones that really makes it work from start to finish. The vaporwave look, the wild architecture, the almost nonsensical characters, and the surprisingly deep lore all combine to make a world that’s utterly implausible and yet still feels real in its own way. I greatly enjoyed my time scouring the island and collecting clues, and I was incredibly impressed with how it all wrapped up. I hope it’s the same for you, because it can be one hell of a trip.Did you enjoy this review? I certainly hope so, and I certainly hope you'll check out more of them at  or on my !

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone because I can't work out who it is for.It's not a detective game. There is nothing to solve. The critical path will force you to the conclusion by just following instructions.It's not a great visual novel. It belongs to the "throwing constant nonsense with no context at the reader" school of worldbuilding and you quickly tune it all out as you got through the game.Ultimately the most enjoyment I got out of the game was hoovering up the collectibles at the end and even that is kind of a pain. The fast travel system requires a currency and the menu's are slow. "Detective vision" has to be constantly refreshed and the movement system often behaves just a little short of what you expected.Game was clearly made with a lot of effort and it has a banging soundtrack (available on Spotify) but it's a sort of hollow experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved everything about this game from the vaporwave aesthetic to the music and dialogue. It reminds me of when I explored games on the N64 as a child, finding ways to platform around to gather items. At the same time Paradise Killer has a Phoenix Wright feel to it with gathering evidence and pressing for testimony, and depending on your approach, you can form your own narrative. The game's simplicity works in its favor and has a lasting impression after completion.I really liked the world, its characters and overall story that I really hope the team decides to make a sequel. I haven't binge-played a game like this in a while.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Not everything is as it seems in paradise.This game took over my life for a couple of days. Seriously though, this was the perfect game for an achievement junky like myself. Along with all the collectibles, there are so many aspects that make Paradise Killer an extremely unique game to devour. It has a cast of memorable characters, a stylish vaporwave aesthetic, captivating lore, and a web of mysteries that just seem to spiral into more mysteries the more you delve into it. The world and map admittedly took some time getting used to, however I came to appreciate it the more time I spent on it. If there is ever a chance for a second game, little icons that show the location of key characters on the map would be helpful. I didn't really mind the parkour, as it only got tricky getting a few specific collectibles. Overall, I really enjoyed this game and hope to see more of Lady Love Dies in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: This game stands out for its unique, and stylish world and character designs. Beneath that however lies a solid detective game with interesting characters, stories and clues aplenty.  From start to finish I was gripped by the need to discover the truths for all the strange events that happened. The way the ending was done is amazing. Truly a good way to reward the player for their hard work and for taking up responsibility for EXECUTING JUSTICE!The game's level design felt very nostalgic for me. I loved navigating the geometry by jumping around aimlessly, often stumbling across clues and secrets which was something I loved to do in games when I was a kid.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is an okay game with great soundtrack and visual style, fresh setting and well-written characters. I've completed it and for the most part had a decent time.So why "Do not recommend"?Because it positions itself as a detective game and in that regard it's pretty awful. It doesn't "feel like real detective work in a way few games do" (quote GameSpot), neither does it "set a new standard for investigative gameplay" (quote PC Gamer). There is absolutely no detective work, no deductive reasoning or investigating, required from you. All you have to do to uncover the truth is: a) run around the island collecting the clues scattered throughout and b) exhaust all dialogue options with characters that just stand around and not interact with the world or story in any way. Some of the dialogue is locked behind the pointless relationship system, but ultimately, if you talk to everyone enough times, you are guaranteed to find all there is to know. And I mean, there is no reason not to - no time limit or missable content, just run around till you get everything (or get bored). All the clues you find are connected to relevant case files and suspects automatically, so no involvement needed here either. There are also a couple of "puzzles", but they are really nothing to write home about: just looking for key items and minimal trial-and-error tinkering.And then there is the final trial. Don't expect anything intense and full of dramatic twists like Phoenix Wright or Danganronpa. There are several crimes to solve, for each one you just choose who you want to accuse and dump all relevant evidence and testimonies on Judge, who, for the most part, never questions you. If you found all the clues (see above), there shouldn't be any problems with that, and even if you make a mistake, it ultimately doesn't matter, which brings me to the worst part of the game (and the reason i'm writing this review): the ending.Not to spoil to much, I'll just say that the game has an open ending, which doesn't change (as far as I've seen) whether you find all the clues or not. Moreover, for some of the crimes there are two equally possible culprits, and the game rolls with whoever you choose. I think that was the intention (it says something like "your facts have become truth"), but I really didn't like it. All in all, the ending felt really underwhelming.So, unfortunately, despite the good music and unusual setting, I can't recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is unmissable. It's preposterous, it's wild. It's innovative but also an experimental refinement of simpler things, well-worn things. It has its rough edges and its sharp corners, but lovely things do.I only have one minor gripe, and BOY is it minor. But it must be said. It must.This game is written. It uses writing. It hinges on writing. It has other things, but its core—its heart—is writing. This is great, this is what I want. But I also want the writing to make sense.You see, Paradise Killer uses wonderous mutations of terms and language. It plays with it all. Nouns mean nothing here, nouns can be anything. Characters are named Lady Love Dies and Leon Disaster and The Witness To The End and Dr. Dirge Driveloss, only one of which I made up. In a game like this—in a game where all naming conventions are defied—it is important, if not absolutely vital, that the writers understand the basics of English.Or to be less obtuse, the writers, creative and great as they are, need to learn how to use a dang hyphen correctly!In this world, it would surprise no one to find an object called, let's say, High Whiskey, and then learn that the word "High" is actually the name of an apartment complex named after an event named after an alien. High Whiskey, from High. Then maybe you have End Whiskey, named after The End. Okay, we're playing with adjectives here, that's fun. High Whiskey. End Whiskey. So then, you might get confused by "High End Whiskey." Did they mean... "High-end Whiskey"? As in, whiskey of quality?Is the whiskey high? Is the whiskey end? Or is the whiskey high-end?This would normally be a no-brainer. But in a world where anything goes in the naming of things, it's integral to the reading experience that the writers understand the nuts and bolts of the written language.One sentence started with the phrase "Criss crossing," and for a moment I had to wonder if Criss was the name of a fallen alien god who was crossing. But no, they meant "criss-crossing," and they meant to use it as an adjective, like "criss-crossing wires covered the ceiling." And in fact, later in the game, in a different piece of text, they used this correctly, hyphen and all. They don't fully know when or when not to use it.This is a massive amount of text I'm writing, but it needs to be. Sometimes small things take lots of words to explain. Sometimes things aren't easy to boil down into a few words. I'm sorry for that.But here it is. This game is rich and vibrant in lore and delivery; it's truly unlike anything I've played before. The writing is a staple. It's not a bell or whistle, it's the thing that holds it together. The unconventional nature of the world demands that the writers either dig into the real technical side of the written language, or someone (the publisher?) with a little more foresight realizes that it would benefit the reading experience of a text-based game to have an editor/proofreader who IS familiar with the aforementioned nuts and bolts of the language.This doesn't stop me in any way from giving it high praise. I love it. You love it. Let's love it. But also, let's be okay with helping the readers read it.Buy the game full price, support the devs.

_childDocuments_.review: A very cool game. If you like mysteries at all you'll love this game. I can't tell you how many times I found a clue that recontextualized everything in my mind about what went down. You can ultimately accuse anyone of anything but you better have found the evidence to back that claim up. Only downside I would say is the game uses stock art at some points and the overall art direction of the game suffers for it. But this is a very indie game I won't hold that against it. I loved it regardless.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished this gem getting all the secrets and reading through all the stories and loved every minute of it. Well worth your time and money on this one. Contrary to many google searches it is possible to get confirmation on your accusations in the end, but you have to be a thorough investigator! :D
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: What are the facts? What is the truth? Are they the same?In Paradise Killer, you take on the role of a detective solving a murder in a fantasy world, full of weird and charismatic characters and lore.This is mainly an exploration game. You'll spend most of your time walking around the island, talking to people and collecting items as you go. There are a lot of things to unlock, and the game rewards you for looking into all corners. This ties in with the movement, which while being limited presents a fun challenge, and there are a couple optional movement upgrades you can unlock that make it a lot more dynamic and fun. The game presents some tricky platforming but it's pretty easy in general, although learning to move from location to location around the island is a fun challenge on its own.The dialogue is very linear but well written. Don't expect to have to think a lot or to make tough choices. If you gather all the relevant evidence, you only need to pinpoint the culprit(s), and the game will do the reasoning for you. That didn't make it any less fun though, as you'll end up figuring it out as you go, and the final trial is more of a cutscene/climax. Or you can go ham and make false accusations ;)Oh, and the music goes really hard. It's an 80s style soundtrack that doesn't get in the way of thinking but gives you funky beats that'll get stuck in your head. Really good for setting the atmosphere.Overall, 8.5/10. A bit hard to get into, and has some rough edges; but its charm, uniqueness and writing more than makes up for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: This game is weird and wonderful.  I've never played anything like it and i wish there was more of  this clevery crafted, bizarre world, you're trying to solve a murder with the help of gods, ghosts and demons.  Find your evidence and make your case before the judge, but definitely stop and look around, a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Loved this game, got sucked right in. The world is immersive, the characters are interesting, and the story has depth. It's really a collect 'em up, that unfolds the narrative as you go about your way, I would say it's kinda a mashup between Pathologic 2 and The Other Wilds (probably with a bit of Danganronpa thrown in at the end - though I haven't played that yet). Music is top notch synthwave affair too. The only thing I would say is that I didn't find it particularly difficult, but it was very satisfying. Highly Recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: The review says I played ~5h of gameplay but I have actually played for about 15h. I didn't have internet access for a couple of days and those gameplay hours were not registered somehow.Anyway, Paradise Killer was one hell of a ride. The best thing I can say about it is that there's nothing like this game out there. It masterfully blends a lot of different gameplay elements and concepts and creates a very risky package that works surprisingly well.First off, I must say I had a lot of fun exploring the island and it never felt bloated with nonsense content just for the sake of throwing content into it; every collectible feels like a reward for your time invested in its world and I really appreciate that design decission. The character movement, albeit a bit clunky sometimes, is very comfortable and once you've unlocked every upgrade it breathes a lot of verticality into the formula like few other open-world games do.This matches surprisingly well with the main investigation topic of the game. Uncovering the island's secrets never gets old and there's always some new bit of information you can add to your court record if you take your time to properly talk to every character involved and explore every area thoroughly. This gives the progression of the game a certain degree of non-linearity (even with the plot being solid and closed) that differentiates Paradise Killer from other games such as the Phoenix Wright saga, where everything is much more linear and straight-forward. You really feel like an investigator following leads and uncovering buried secrets.Story-wise, the themes used for PK's lore are a very unique choice. Mixing religion with cosmic horror while reimagining the western concept of Paradise and afterlife and tapping into some of the biggest modern alien conspiracies was definitely a very risky move, but the creators managed to pull it off somehow. The artistic and sound design choices are also on point and help a lot in that regard, as the Vice City-esque island filled with vaporwave music gives the world this distinctive flair of fabricated reality that boosts the game's thematic choices.Paradise Killer is a game that rewards the invested player who really take their time to delve deep into it, and that's exactly how I would recommend playing: embracing it as the creators' did with their ideas. This was a very pleasant surprise and its weirdness can't be a better match for year 2020.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game over 3 or so sessions and I absolutely adored it! The setting and lore, with it's aliens as gods and demons, weird alternate realities and magic/technology balance, gripped me right away, I wanted to know more. The music is absolutely great, especially if you love synthwave bops, it helped to give the island so much more character, especially in locations where the radio didn't work. Piecing together the mystery and everything that had happened on the island while interacting with the colourful and creatively designed characters was a fun ride and I enjoyed every second of it. The art in this game was also stunning - props to the character designer!I feel myself wanting more - I want more lore, to play around more and interact with the setting more; an open world mystery rpg style game in this setting, perhaps on Perfect 25, would honestly rock my world.The only thing I feel that let the game down was the finality of the end trial. I felt a little caught in some of the options and wanted to be able to save some characters from their fate because of their level of involvement.  Would also love to see achievements added to Steam, as I think I got everything but can't be certain.If you like detective games, synth/vaporwave, a mad mix of sci-fi and fantasy and fun characters I would highly recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished it after buying it a couple days ago. If you're a fan of the Phoenix Wright or Danganronpa series, this game is for you. It's more in the same vein as the latter, but a 'lite' version. Paradise Killer definitely leans more into the exploration and story elements, as opposed to the puzzle elements in PW and Danganronpa games. Now that I think about it, the game is really an open world visual novel.The islands environment, is beautifully done. There's a significant vertical element which means there's a fair amount of exploring to do even though the area is relatively small. The game features an overall bright, detailed, kinda anime-ish Vaporwave aesthetic that permeates both visually and musically. That's something that drew me in initially. There's also a lot of what seems to be Babylonian mythological influence. I thought that was neat since that's not a mythos that we see in games very much.The story drops you "in media res." Which can be a little overwhelming initially. You're told that there's been a mass murder and you have to investigate. And that's it; very little direction, outside some leads/hints. Nearly all areas are open from the get-go. As you progress, side cases come up that obviously tie into the main murder case. Like Professor Layton games, all will be solved by the end.I thought the characters (main suspects) were interesting, if not a little shallow and cliched. Though as I made progress, constantly going around talking to the characters, bits and pieces of their background were revealed, which made me want to know more about them and this world they're in. Speaking of constantly going around, that is one of the downsides: this game is a bit of a walking simulator. Many times I found myself going from one side of the island to the other and back again by foot. However, there is a fast-travel system. You have to pay with in-game currency, but it's cheap and the currency plentiful. Still, I'd suggest getting about by foot until you've checked out all the areas.All-in-all, I enjoyed Paradise Killer. The whodunit story and exploration kept me interested, enough that I played like 12hrs straight so I could finish it during the weekend. If you're a fan of any of the games I mentioned in this review, I'd definitely recommend Paradise Killer.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: This game had an interesting story that made me want to play through the game and play until the end. You solve multiple crimes and see those responsible punished. The puzzles are super easy so there is no real skill needed. I highly recommend this game for anyone who likes a good story/mystery game.However, I suggest buying this game during a sale. This game has no replay value and is extremely linear in its nature. I completed it in less than 10 hours and that was getting every piece of information possible. I ran around for awhile to see if there was anything else I could do/collect or if I was missing anything and there was nothing. You may want to go through the story again, I won't feel inclined to for at least a few years.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent and weird free-roaming first-person mystery game set on a beautiful, eldritch vaporwave island with a very groovy citypop soundtrack. I can't go too deep for fear of spoiling anything, but you'll love it if you like mystery games - aside from the mystery you're actually brought in to solve, trying to piece together the bizarre world that you're cast into is just as much of the experience.This is an easy recommendation to fans of mystery games, odd and interesting settings, story-driven games, and even collectathons.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the story/world, just weird and crazy enough to keep me interested most of the time.  I didn't like the spiral staircase climbing and there's a fair amout of it.  The point if it appears to be to cause nausea, otherwise it feels like a totally unecessary design choice.  My main problem with the game is that things start to get a little tedious toward the end and the ending itself I found to be an unsatisfying cop-out.  Maybe it was too meta or profound for my pea sized brain.  There is a lot of good stuff in here though, it was obviously a creative bunch who put this together.  I would've easily recommended this up until the last few hours, it was fun, but the staircase nausea, last bit tedium and ending makes me lean toward no.  If there was a thumb sideways I would've chosen that.  Not a total waste of time but also not a great use of time either.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: annoying visuals (graphics are straight from 2007), absolutely dead world, tones of texts (which isn't a bad thing by itself but not in this case), blunt characters, (they are even represented as a cardboard dummies), ducking load of objects to collect, but 95% of them has 0 relations to the world or story, idk... tried to love this game, but it absolutely didn't do that to me
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the mystery behind it and loved the characters, but most importantly the soundtrack in this game is some of the most consistently great ones I've heard in a game. Of course it doesn't mean everyone will like this game and it especially might feel a bit slow at times if you're aiming to explore and uncover everything but it's still very enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: This game was impossible to put down for me, I had a lot of fun playing it. I loved the satanic-vaporwave-city pop atmosphere! I thought the lore/world-building and the story were really well done and compelling -- you have to dig up every detail about the world yourself, nothing is handed to you. Every nook and cranny seemed to be hiding something! At times it was difficult to jump around and reach some places, but using the footbaths helped a lot. If you like lovecraftian weirdness, give this game a try! I hope the developers are able to create more games in this universe they clearly worked hard on.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic investigative game. Gameplay mostly involves scanning areas for clues and interviewing the cast of unnecessarily sexy characters, but the mystery is compelling with a ton of twists and revelations. The vaporwave aesthetic is top-notch as well (The main theme being stuck in my head inspired me to write this review). The setting is also totally bonkers and I found I was playing as much to find out more about the Syndicate and their islands as I was to solve the murder.Minor complaints would be that movement is a bit clunky, as is the fast travel system. Unlockable movement upgrades help a lot, but there is still quite a bit of backtracking accross the island. Luckily exploration is rewarded with money or "relic" items that give you little backstory snippets, as well as the occasional clue in a well hidden area.The ending trial is pretty interesting in that you can choose who to accuse of each part of the crime, and what evidence to present. You might decide that some of the guilty parties don't deserve death, or you could frame someone you don't like. I highly enjoyed my time with this game and it left me wanting more. If you're at all interested in investigative games give this a shot, there's nothing else quite like it out there.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: I adored this game from start to finish. It's impossible to describe but I'll try.It's a detective game! A few things it does excellently:- It's an open world. You can explore the entire island, and nowhere is gated at first. There are a few locations that you can't get into immediately but 95% of the whole island can just be wandered into after a 10-minute intro sequence. This is AMAZING.- It also means evidence and characters can be encountered in any order. The game just... handles this. It's fine. And it adds to that feeling of flexibility and freedom. - Sometimes evidence is an object that's been dropped, or left somewhere. This means that you can't necessarily just do what you're told and assume you'll get all the evidence. A few times I had to go off the beaten track, wondering "hm, since I know this fact, I wonder if there is some key evidence hiding away over here?" Sometimes there wasn't. Often there WAS, which was a great feeling.- You can start the trial, in which you expose the conspiracy, at any time. You can accuse anyone. - Oh, and the crime is really clever too!This all means that, while you'll probably not take advantage of all of this freedom (you won't accuse someone for whom you have no evidence, for example) the fact you CAN makes the whole game feel so much more earned. YOU wandered into an area based on a hunch, found some evidence, and are now using it to accuse person D of committing a murder? You earned that.And I haven't even talked about the setting! It's a gorgeous, grotesque mix of a Miami hot pink "I left my rhinestone sunglasses in the fuchsia penthouse" aesthetic, and glitchy cosmic-horror satanism. The story and worldbuilding are absurd and SO out there. Each character fits seamlessly into this bizarre and tragic world. I find the setting completely irresistible, and I desperately want a sequel so I can see more of it.Oh and the music? IT BANGS.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: The game just starts talking about a lot of different ideas and characters without any introduction. It's already overwhelming to try and figure out what anyone is talking about from context, then you're left to investigate and find even more things you have no idea how they connect (stopped playing after talking to the judge, and finding a bunch of clues in some cabin nearby that just confused me more). It feels like the game expects all that effort before even showing what the actual puzzle gameplay is all about. It honestly felt like it was a sequel to some game where all of that was introduced, and people are talking about characters you've already met. As it is, it starts with too much text without context to feel engaged.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Though a bit hard to get into at first (a bunch of weird terms and names are thrown at you at once), once you get into the actual investigating it's one of the most original and entertaining games I've played in a long time. For fans of the Ace Attorney series gameplay and the Persona series' aesthetic, Paradise Killer asks you to travel across a weird open-world island interrogating suspects (going through the list of conversation topics you've unlocked) and finding clues until you're satisfied you can prove who's guilty and who's innocent. Navigating the island (in a first person perspective) can be quite frustrating, however. The level design is quite iffy (I would often get lost in alleys even after a dozen hours of play-time, and the island isn't that big) and the platforming is clunky, but I found the story and worldbuilding very enjoyable and was genuinely interested in revealing the truth behind the crimes. I would've enjoyed having a free fast-travel system, though, since you travel a lot when collecting all the final clues towards the end of the game and currency isn't that common unless you want to spend extra time with the clunky platforming.I would've also loved to have some puzzles along the lines of the Ace Attorney series, where you're tasked with finding inconsistencies in the suspects' arguments, but I'm fine with that not being the focus of the gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to enjoy Paradise Killer, but it had a huge problem with its scale.  It was trying to be so much more than it really is.  At its core, Paradise Killer is a visual novel that allows you to undercover all the different plots of each character, and decide the outcome at a trial.  But getting there has to be the most painful thing imaginable.First person Platformer: Scale issue: There's too many odd jumps, missed falling, and hard to see jumping in this game.  I don't like playing platform games in 3rd person.  The amount of odd jumping, falling, and using the special powerups just to get minor items in the weirdest of places was extremely tedious and painstaking.  I did a lot before the i found the powerups, because I'm insane.    This really didn't add very much to the gameplay, other than to make the game longer.  Exploration: The scale problem here is that the map is pretty wide east to west and north to south, but it's just as expansive Bottom to Top.  Why do I need to scale a 10 floor apartment building where the majority of the floors are nothing?  I had to use the motion sickness assist, because it was way too much.  To get from one side of the island to the other was crazy... it's easy to get lost and turned around.  Some sections were impossible to find the entry point (I'm looking at you Marshall Barracks) because the save point wasn't in the section you expected it to be.  There was no reason to have this huge of an exploration area, other than to just make the game longer.Blood Crystal Currency: The problem of scale with the Blood Crystals as currency, is that you're always afraid you're going to run out.  At the end of the game you're swimming in them, but early on you have no clue if you're going to have issues.  It discourages the use of Fast Travel, which should not cost any currency at all! You shouldn't be punished for moving about the island quickly at the end game, but yet I'm running from the Isolation Cell to the Yacht because I only have 10 crystals.Nightmare Puzzles:  Why even bother?  This would be something I would just have edited out of the game.  You got the Cosmos upgrade, great... now you can access these terminals.  The making of the symbols in the Nightmare puzzles was overly simple.  The interface was super clunky.  You could easily shift to the wrong spaces on the controller, so it did nothing but anger me every time I had to do one.Visual Novel: The scale of the visual novel was probably correct.  It would have been nice if this was set up more like Ace Attorney where I could go to different areas, do a little investigation, and interrogate the character there.  It would have flowed much better.  Instead, I had to keep zipping back and forth to people to do the hang outs.  The Hang Outs felt very added on, and just there to make the game longer.  Would have been nice to fast travel back and forth to people, and just burned the blood crystals, but the timer prevented you from doing that.  Another system causing conflict with the system.The sub-screen: I really wish the interface and the sub screen were better organized.  The case notes were really helpful in knowing what to do next, and the file organizations actually did organize the information well.  I thought that was well done.  But the controller would sometimes his the evidence to clear out the "!" mark and then you wouldn't be able to scroll back up to someone else's testimony forcing you to back out of the record, and then go back into it.  Which leads me to:Collectibles:  Why? This was such a tedious exercise.  I haven't gotten 1... and I mean 1... of the red crests to finish that one puzzle.  My level of caring is so low after the crazy amounts of work I did to find all the others.  When I see that "6.4% of players" have all the Island Sequence Memories, I'm left wondering if it really was worth it. It feels like a lot of the achievements just aren't worth the effort.The ending: Satisfying?  Meh.  I think the most satisfying thing is knowing that it's over.All in all, I really think Paradise Killer would have been better if it was more linear.  There's too many conflicting things to do, when the core of the game is the world building visual novel. Take away the blood crystals, excessive exploration, and collection tasks, it would have been a nice compact and tight game.  It just needs heavy editing to remove a lot of the bad pieces.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Great game for Vaporwave lovers!  Aesthetic is there, imagery, palette, retro-wave music etc.  Cast of characters is odd, and mostly compelling.  Pace is your own so it's a nice exploration game.Few gripes to be aware of:Some of the abilities to unlock that would be helpful early on, you have to find on your own and have the money to buy them when you find them.  The abilities could just be baked into the game, and it makes navigating easier.One of the abilities you have to turn on every 30 seconds for it to be meaningful if looking to find every secret.Quick travel shouldn't have a cost to use.  It makes players weary of using even though you will have plenty of currency to use it.

_childDocuments_.review: I started out just wandering around, gathering collectibles, and then I found the music tapes and became obsessed with gathering those, they music is soo nice! And every once in a while I'd run into someone I could interrogate..the game just sorta unfolded naturally, even though I had no plan. _childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, great mystery, lots of eclectic characters and a fascinating world for them to play in.Two caveats: make sure you turn off censorship in settings, or enjoy a lot of *****s. Secondly, the resolution of the mystery is a bit disappointing, since it breaks one of the Knox Rules of Mystery, but the ride trying to figure it out is still a blast, even if my theories were proven wrong.Lady Love Dies is the investigator the world needs.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: With how unique the elements of the game are, it feels strangely nostalgic playing this. With it's movement and environment design, it feels as if I'm playing half-life jumping on object on top of object and walking along sides of buildings and on top of railings just to traverse faster or to get somewhere higher. It's great fun and very satisfying. Walking around the island is relaxing with its artsy buildings, designs, and color schemes. Just traversing by itself is fun since everything on the island has collision, in theory there shouldn't be a spot on the island you can't stand on. Running, jumping, collecting, and talking can all be done in your pace since there isn't a timer or notification constantly reminding you to do something and almost everything is optional so there's no rush or push to stress you. Everything in this game is just great, if it isn't great it's fine, nothing really stood out like a sore thumb. I haven't had a game like this in a while that didn't have questionable game designs that would just piss me off randomly. It knows what it is and doesn't punch above or below. In a gaming space where every game is desperate for your attention, and when it does get it, it does every trick in the book to keep you in like making you restart constantly, grinding levels to watch stats go up, chance to win prizes with loot-boxes, tedious fetch and grab and escort missions to waste your time, this game is paradise among killers, definitely one of the best games I've played in this "modern" gaming age.Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets a big thumbs from me 👍 I really enjoyed the cast of characters, the "sound-bites" during dialog, and the blending of Visual Novel and 3D open-world exploration. Without giving anything away, some of the evidence near the end is a little too easy to miss. I also really like that the truth is what you want to make of it! Well worth playing!!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Really surprisingly great game, It's just so transfixingly weird with all the lore and interactions with other characters. It's weird in a solidly written way, though, it's not just trying to be wacky and random for the sake of it. It was also unexpectedly mechanically super satisfying unlocking your little handful of platforming abilities and door key types and just digging into every little nook and cranny of the map while you listen to the soundtrack and just soak in the aesthetic of the combination of the two
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most stylistically confident and unique adventure games of late. It is immensely fun to explore the island at your own pace and untangle not only the crime itself but the imaginative and weird world building and it's many mysteries. Add to that fleshed-out characters, nice music and a world that's at the same time comfy and deeply unsettling and you get a vivid, memorable experience. A great time.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: A slightly offputting start leads to a really fun and unusual murder mystery with an imaginative cast of characters and world, including some great worldbuilding and lore. Interesting that there was no true "canon" ending, rather the player is left to use the evidence and facts at their disposal to craft the truth narrative. Well worth playing, runs well on Steam Deck and will blast your eyes out of your head on an OLED in HDR.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is a murder mystery set in the 24th attempt by a group of demon-worshiping immortals to create paradise. You play as Lady Love Dies, one of the immortals, brought back from exile to solve the murder of the entire ruling council, and a myriad of other mysteries you discover along the way. The visuals are interesting and the whole thing has a strong vaporwave  The gameplay mainly involves wandering the island searching for clues. You have a list of leads to follow but can just as easily wander aimlessly and stumble on something worthwhile. While wandering you'll come across  which are a collectable currency that can be used to fast travel or to buy info from the info broker. There are a few other types of collectible as well.The collectibles are all 2D Doom style sprites, which actually work with the rest of the game's aesthetic.The characters are also presented as 2D sprites, and you'll spend a fair amount of time talking to them.  It may seem superfluous but raising your relationship with characters can unlock key evidence. It's clear from the beginning that the game will end with a trial. Your job is to collect all the evidence and testimony you need to reveal the truth in that trial. Or you could just present the evidence against the people you dislike and condemn them to death. That works too. My playtime represents the time it takes to solve the case (with all the evidence, as far as I can tell) and collect  so expect around 16 hours if you're a collecto like I am. I loved this game. I'm a big fan of mysteries, and exploring for hidden items, and I like vaporwave so this is pretty much right down my street. If you like those things you'll probably enjoy it too.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is an open world mystery game that borrows inspiration from Suda51's works and writing style. Because it's an open world game, the mystery, combined with visual novel elements seen in games like Ace Attorney or Dangan Ronpa, is presented in a way I have not seen in any game before. Unlike other visual novel based mysteries, the game emphasizes a freedom of choice in both movement, discovery, and pursuit of the truth by allowing players to use the facts of the case to their choosing. The facts of the mystery are the same each time, but there's room for subjectivity on the player's part.While the plot is in some ways standard mystery fare, I would say the real star of the game is the world and lore itself. The island is a gorgeous, well-designed environment with an obvious vaporwave aesthetic along with an incredible and well-considered soundtrack that's worth owning on its own. The island is enjoyable to explore and observing the different districts and how they function in this computer built society is interesting. The setting is a high concept, esoteric sci-fi involving a cult-based society that struggles to create a utopia while battling off demons and insurrection. While there are a ton of collectibles covering the island that deliver random lore tidbits, talking to other characters and finding out about the world through osmosis while playing as someone who's been away for years is plenty to understand the world you're living in.The execution of the mystery can be very subjective, but I do think if you go into this imagining something purely like Dangan Ronpa or other mystery thriller VNs, you'll do yourself a disservice. This game is not purely its mystery, but also the universe it has created for itself and if you're sold on that aspect and its aesthetic, this game is WELL worth your time. It's an absolute delight to wander around in and the amount of universe given to the player is not too little or too much to be satisfying. Definitely a game that took me by surprise and stands out to me among all the games I've played this year.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: At first the only hook I got from this game was "too weird not to keep going" with absurd character names, designs, and world building. Definitely worth it once you get over the initial style introduction - an open world detective game that mixes cute, weird, and sinister in some very compelling ways. It's dialogue heavy with minimal voice-work so be prepared to read a lot but I'm a sucker for well-written stories with developed worlds. My only complaint is the 'true' ending that moves -way- too quickly for what unfolds. The buildup makes up for it though!

_childDocuments_.review: If you love Ace Attorney/Danganronpa, you might *not* enjoy this. Despite a lot of comparisons being drawn between PK and those series, I see that as a bit of a stretch. While PK is a murder investigation game with plenty of dialogue and evidence, the similarities fall apart there. The trial does not involve punching holes through witness testimony, you don't get to know if you made errors in judgement, and there is only one grand trial for everything (albeit with multiple parts). If those are the similarities you were looking for in PK, I recommend doing a little bit of research into this game before deciding whether you want to play it.Personally, I never felt the "click" while playing this game that I did with many other mystery/detective games that I love (Ace Attorney, Danganronpa, Return of the Obra Dinn, Nancy Drew, Her Story, Shenmue, Zero Escape). However, PK was a confidently executed, fresh take on the genre and I'm excited to see what may follow after it.

It's alright, but not a spectacular game, its shortcomings come from the horrible gameplay design (yes i've 100% this game and collectables are completely useless) and it's a shame since it's not badly written.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say much that hasn't already been said. If you like Phoenix Wright and Danganronpa and you're really into the weird vibe of SUDA51 games then this game is especially made for you.95% of this game is roaming around the island and collecting clues. I assumed that there would be a great deal of thought and strategy that goes into the the trial portion similar to the contradictions logic puzzles of Phoenix Wright or even the weird minigames of Danganronpa. This makes the ending a little disappointing. Unfortunately I found that the trial is pretty on rails and takes care of itself based on the evidence collected. So it feels more like an hour long wrap up than it does an actual portion of the game. In addition to that the story kind of wraps up on a dime. One minute you're in the trail of the century and 2 minutes later its all over and justice has been served and a majority of the characters you've just spend a dozen hours with are gone and it all feels pretty anticlimactic. A few of them deserved a lot better or worse than they got, but I guess that's justice. Overall, still a great experience!

_childDocuments_.review: What a fantastic game! Let me start by saying that I am a huge fan of the Danganronpa games and the Phoenix Wright series, so I was quite interested in playing this indie detective game, and I am very glad I did! Paradise Killer is essentially a murder mystery with you as the lead detective trying to find out who killed the council of this strange 80's fusion island. The island itself, wow, I think is one of the most creatively unique game worlds I have ever seen. The story itself was also brilliant!To the comments that this game is a little pixel-huntey I would disagree, with the caveat that there are some secrets on the island that I think are perhaps a little too well hidden, but a quick google can often help you sort it out. Overall, a very warm recommendation from me. Spent about 9 hours in this fantastic unique world, and I enjoyed every minute of it. Hell I even kept hand written notes on the case as the game progressed, not because the game required me to, but because it was so fun building up notes on who did what and why.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as I know there isn't another game that has this mix of gameplay, story and style. There's something so enjoyable about having an open world to explore and trying and find secrets. Every character is strange but interesting and the mysteries they're holding onto and the wider investigation kept me interested throughout my entire experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Early on in this game I saw something behind a fence and I did some precarious parkouring to get to it. I made it and felt bad, assuming I had skipped some progression elements and cheated the game of its natural flow. Then an hour later I found a double jump powerup and realized this game was a lot more than what I thought it was. This is a great game to just experience. It's not really full of high level puzzles or all that much logical deduction. If you talk to everyone and find the collectables the case will solve itself. But this is one of those games where the journey is better than the destination. The world of Paradise Island Sequence 24 is coated in this lovecraftian vaporwave aesthetic that is as interesting as it is messed up. You're investigating the murder of a group of terrible people, with a group of suspects who are equally as terrible. The actual facts are less important than the truth you aim to prove. Don't come into this expecting Professor Layton puzzles or Danganronpa style logical leaps like the infamous "seesaw effect" moment. This game is simple, yet complicated in its delivery. If it sounds even remotely interesting to you, I say you should give breathing life back into Paradise a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: A "whodunit" game drenched in '80s style. Very limited replay once you have fully mastered the mysteries and it's not the prettiest game to look at. But I enjoyed it none the less. Interesting character designs, chill tunes and an enjoyable story make up for all of the shortcomings.Would just say that if you aren't feeling it within the first hour or so maybe use that Steam refund. Game is definitely not going to be for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: I've said it before but the hallmark of a great game, or a very good one at any rate, is whether or not you're compelled to play it until the very end. Paradise Killer is an expertly constructed murder-mystery detective story from a first person perspective that takes place on an ancient island that goes through cycles of regeneration, i.e., births & deaths. You play as Lady Love Dies, a lead investigator for the Syndicate who's been brought out of exile to solve the crime to end all crimes, lol. This game is extremely well made and runs perfectly. The island is a lot of fun to explore and the plot keeps you guessing up towards the very end. The soundtrack is very nice as well. The trial at the very end is a stellar experience that doesn't disappoint. There's not much to complain about here. But if I could point to something, it would be that perhaps the game starts to drag a bit towards the end. During the last 2 or 3 hours I must have gone back and forth between Carmelina Silence and Witness to the End at least 20 times to gather info...it just got a tad bit tedious towards the end of the game but as I mentioned, the final trial was a LOT of fun. This game could be anywhere from 15 to 20 hours long on average so there's a lot to solve here. I suppose I'd give Paradise Killer a solid 8.5 out of ten. It's a well made game that's very definitely worth playing through. Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10Pros:-Unique and interesting characters in a fantastical world that feels alive-A real banger of a soundtrack. No joke.-Vaporwave as all heck-Incredible world sound design and voice talent-Personality brimming in every nook and cranny of this game. I can tell this was a real labor of love.Cons:-Kinda drags on a little long for my taste (You can essentially go to endgame at any time, but I wanted to see as much as possible and that made for a 6-7 hour long runtime that should've really only been like 4-5 hours)-Can't pet the dog-There's a lot of text. A lot. It makes it easier on you by tracking anything of note in your case files, but towards the end I was just mainly slamming through every textwall and checking notes afterwards.-Barry "Epoch" Topping doesn't get enough credit for the OST. Give him some love, people.-Seriously, it's an amazing soundtrack and I hadn't even heard about it until now.

_childDocuments_.review: With its Vaporwave-meets-Vice-City aesthetic and Dreamcast-era art style, Paradise Killer is a tough game to categorize. It’s one part exploration and collection, one part visual novel, and one part mystery adventure, all infused with a generous layer of “weird” -- and I absolutely loved it!The game takes only a few short moments to give you the setup -- the entire ruling council has been murdered in the night, and there’s only a handful of people left on the island as suspects -- then you are given free-reign to start exploring the island paradise, talking to the suspects, finding clues, and gathering collectibles. It’s Phoenix Wright meets something like Outer Wilds or Return of the Obra Dinn, where the story organically unfolds through your exploration and the discoveries you piece together along the way.I’m not usually one to connect with games that require you to learn a lot of proper nouns, lore, and in-universe jargon, but Paradise Killer’s commitment to its style and quality writing manage to make its exposition and lore dumps intriguing and inviting. The writing is snappy and quick, never giving you more than you need at a time, while cleverly (and non-linearly) dropping the breadcrumbs of the story.A major highlight for me were the characters. They’re all incredibly distinct, from their visual appearance to their personalities, to the voice the writing gives their dialogue. The bold approach to character design that Paradise Killer takes makes every suspect immediately memorable and identifiable -- a god-send for a game that asks you to put so many pieces together -- and with names like “Crimson Acid”, “Lydia Daybreak”, and “Doctor Doom Jazz”, they’re hard to forget!But ultimately the game is about solving a crime, and in that regard I think it delivers. While every suspect has at least some evidence pointing against them, exploration and thoroughness are rewarded with surprising twists and turns, painting a detailed portrait of what actually happened while still leaving enough gaps and red herrings that you’re never really sure until you’ve presented your case at the game’s closing trial -- a wonderful culmination of your work to that point, and an event that you can technically begin at any time; starting the trial could be the first and only thing you do in Paradise Killer, if you really wanted to!The main criticism I hear about Paradise Killer is with the collectibles side of things. There are hundreds of little tokens scattered all over the place, some of which you need as currency to get certain unlocks or information. I personally got super into the collecting. I found it really peaceful to just kind of zen out and vibe with the game’s killer music while poking around in all the nooks and crannies for the telltale audio glitches that signalled a pickup. That being said, I totally understand how this part would rub people the wrong way. There are some areas that are pretty confusing to navigate, and it took me a while to form my mental map of the island (the in-game map is pretty bad). Just know that you don’t have to collect all that much to actually see everything the game has to offer!All in all, Paradise Killer was exactly my ♥♥♥♥, and despite sharing almost nothing in common with them, it still somehow sits at the weird cross-section of whatever it is that games like Outer Wilds, Return of the Obra Dinn, and Disco Elysium share, in a spiritual sense. The free-form approach of interacting with a story at your own pace, chasing the leads that interest you in the moment as you fill in the gaps and form a mental picture of events is extremely satisfying, and I’m happy to count Paradise Killer as one of my personal favourites from this past year of intensive pandemic gaming!

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer offers an intriguing blend of open-world exploration, vaporwave aesthetics, and murder mystery investigation. Set in a surreal world filled with immortal council members, gods, and bizarre characters, it hooks you with its eccentric yet deeply engaging narrative universe and the promise of uncovering the truth behind a mass murder. However, while the game boasts a unique charm, it stumbles in several key areas.Visually, Paradise Killer excels in creating a retro-futuristic world, but the actual gameplay environments feel sparse and, at times, repetitive. Despite strong world-building, the execution feels rough around the edges. The overused assets, 2D art awkwardly integrated into a 3D space, and repetitive textures create a disjointed experience. Combined with the constant collection of meaningless "relics," it’s difficult to recommend the game to players who prioritize gameplay over story.That said, the soundtrack is a standout, blending upbeat electronic tracks with soothing synthwave melodies that perfectly complement the game’s dreamlike atmosphere.Character interactions are plentiful, and each suspect offers a distinct perspective that enriches the immersive world you're thrown into. The pacing of the mystery is masterfully handled, with the investigation consistently pushing you toward new leads and revelations. I rarely found myself wondering, "What now?" as each piece of evidence led naturally to the next, driving me deeper into the mystery until the final judgment.Overall, Paradise Killer is a fascinating experiment, but one that doesn’t quite live up to its potential. It’s worth experiencing for its style, atmosphere, and incredible story, but be prepared for a rough gameplay experience. Despite the lackluster 3D visuals and the tedious collecting, the core creative aspects—story, characters, and world—manage to shine through.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: THE GREATEST DETECTIVE GAME ON STEAMParadise killer sees you, the chief investigator for a syndicate of cultists who worship dead alien gods bent on the destruction of humanity, return from your 3 million day exile to solve the murder of your leading council on a vaporwave island pocket dimension. Sounds simple right? Despite this BIZARRE premise, this game has great presentation, great investigation gameplay, and great game design that actually allows for you to feel like Sherlock rather than Watson.Uniquely for this genre, this is an open world game. The island that you are on is pretty small, but fairly dense. You wont soon run out of places to check for potential clues. This also allows you to investigate crimescenes and suspects on your own initiative, and follow up whatever leads you deem important without being told what to do, where to go, who to suspect, or what to investigate. This leads to a much more authentic "detective" experience.Another unique thing about this game is how it handles the ending. You can end the game at any time by calling for a trial once you think you have enough evidence to solve the crime. That's not all however, you can accuse anybody, and can get them convicted if you have enough evidence. This means that you can not only convict the wrong person without knowing it, you can purposely frame someone if you play things right. Why would the game let you do this? Well, it actually asks a bit of a moral question from you at the end. What is the difference between the facts and the truth? What is the difference between being guilty and deserving punishment? Does justice matter when you and your cultist friends are ultimately the bad guys?This game is well worth the money and time I put into it, and had me staying awake at night trying to wrap my head around the elaborate crime and potential suspects. I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a fun mystery game, this might not be for you. Paradise Killer is a lot of things. It has an intense style and insane world-building. But something it lacked for me was a compelling mystery.I often found exploring this game and gathering clues quite tedious. There's something to be said for the fact that you have to piece together motives for murder in a world where you're also trying to understand the basic operation of society. But, ultimately, I found those motives quite boring and so mundane for such a fantastical setting.The most interesting aspect, the characters and their relationships with the protagonist and each other, felt quite on-rails with no real room for the player to affect the story. The development of these characters and the game's mystery is stopped abruptly when it's time to go to the judge with your evidence. If you've collected all the clues, which is not hard to do - just time-consuming, it becomes a simple matter of laying down accusations and scrolling through soooo much dialogue recapping everything you've already learned. Then you shoot a bunch of people and the game is over.If you're into vaporwave and games that look intentionally kinda bad, or even just wild lore about an alternate earth history with demonic gods and cross-European wars, you might enjoy this. If you're looking for a satisfying, complex mystery game, this one might not be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is a good game, albeit one with some deep flaws and that has some difficulty establishing its own identity. It's a crime VN/platformer that's heavily inspired by Suda51's "Kill the Past" trilogy with vaporwave stuff slapped on top of it.The idea is that it's a completely open-world, non-linear detective game. The only thing set in stone is that there's going to be a trial at the end. The game more or less throws you into a world that doesn't make sense and asks you to make sense of it: the gist is that the world is an alternate reality that relies on the mass sacrifice of people kidnapped from the real world to exist. Here's my main problem with this game. Because of its open-world, non-linear format, it is entirely possible that you will stumble upon the solution to more or less all of the mysteries on the island before you actually finish even unlocking the crime scene. There's a single room that basically answers all of the questions, and I managed to find it after a few hours of wandering around - I fell off a platform with an NPC on it and as soon as I examined it I had basically sequence broken the game.The one good thing is that even finding the magic evidence room won't get you everything you need to truly finish the game, but at the same time answering all the questions involves a lot of boring stuff like spending time with every single NPC outside of just interrogating them, and none of the NPCs were really interesting enough that I felt like doing that.Another problem I have is that the game doesn't really adapt based on what order you find things in. As an example, one of the sidequests you get early on involves finding a missing person. I found that person's dead body just by wandering around before finding anything else related to them (as their house is very out of the way), but nothing in the game seemed to acknowledge that I found the body: every dialog I could initiate about it acted like I hadn't found anything. Going with that, it also suffers a bit from the same problem the Ace Attorney games have, where you know exactly what happened but the game won't let you say it.I'd say if you're going to play this game, stick strictly to doing what the game's "notes" screen tells you to do so you don't wind up sequence breaking the entire thing. That might be kind of hard, given that the game doesn't really have a map and some locations can be kind of hard to find unless you know where you're going already: I think if they added a map it would definitely help with that. It's definitely not a bad game, but it could use some work.

_childDocuments_.review: loved loved loved this game. truly insane worldbuilding I never quite understood but was still immersive, this game is not afraid to do whatever it feels like and I respect it. Characters were fun to interact with, found a lot of them very compelling. The mystery itself was interesting, and having the final scene be a trial allowed an expansion of the theme while forcing players to prove their knowledge of the case.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of detective games, I really wanted to like Paradise Killer. _childDocuments_.review: An open-world, murder-mystery, vaporwave detective game that might even be better than Return of the Obra Dinn as far as the detective/investigation genre of video games are concerned. The main character is great, the music is fantastic, the environment is vibrant, there's plenty of mystery to uncover. The only downside was that it took me a little bit to get used to the setting of this game, but once I did, everything clicked and it was really enjoyable to fully explore. Also, I really appreciate that there was an in-game mechanism to hunt down all the collectables on the island, forgoing the need for external guides.Definitely pick this up if you like being a detective, or are super into the vaporwave aesthetic.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what an absolutely stellar experience. This game is like Phoenix Wright meets Danganronpa, but open world. It is so much fun. I had a great time unraveling the mystery and discovering the lore. THE LORE. The lore is incredibly fascinating and learning about the world that Kaizen has created was so much fun. I've seen a few complaints about how the game doesn't really tell you where to go or what to do, but I loved that aspect. It allowed me to really dig into the world and discover what it had to offer.My only real complaints about the game are regarding the map and travelling around it. The map only shows you what 'zone' you're in, but you don't know which way you're facing so it can be a challenge to navigate, especially early on. Additionally, the game's Fast Travel system costs currency each time you use it, which I found frustrating and therefore I only used it when I absolutely had no other choice (As there is one area you cannot access without using Fast Travel).Despite that one gripe though, I have nothing else truly negative to say about this game. There were a few small things I think could have been executed differently, like the Trial at the end, but I'm not mad about it. This was a fantastic, fun, sometimes horrifying, but always intriguing experience. Absolutely get this game if you're on the fence. Between its brilliant sense of style, the AMAZING soundtrack, the fascinating story, and the entertaining characters, this is one of the best games I've played in a long time. I truly hope Kaizen releases a sequel because I can't wait to return to Perfect 25 and the world of Paradise Killer.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: The best detective game I've ever played.Thrilling plot, weird and captivating universe and a great cunning female protagonist. It made me really nervous going to the trials. _childDocuments_.review: The game starts off interesting, then it nosedives with the pacing and lack of a clear "mission path" so it feels overwhelming a bit, especially if you don't get the upgrades quickly.Then it becomes really good to the point I collected everything in the game. The later part of the game also feels very annoying to play since you will have to run from one character to another to progress the story, and they all stay in the same place, so that means you will know these routes by heart. _childDocuments_.review: Really great game, it's a shame it's so underrated!!! I had to go through many steam queue games to find this one.Lots of Danganronpa vibes, but it's by no means the same game. Just because you like Danganronpa doesn't necessarily mean you'll like Paradise Killer, but I think if you do then it's definitely worth a try.You only have one trial. The whole game is you gathering evidence for that trial. You don't really end up putting the pieces together yourself - the computer kind of does that for you if you find all of the evidence, logging and sorting it into where it belongs.I think Paradise Killer has a fantastic world and the thing it does best is immersing you into it. I became invested in many of the characters and couldn't put it down until I completed it. It's the type of world that I won't be able to forget and feels super nostalgic.The game looks great for what it is - it seems to have been made on a small to medium budget and kind of has a lo-fi feel where things aren't super high fidelity, but are still beautiful. (My boyfriend says that the game looks like it was made in source lol.) I loved the colors they use and their choices in aesthetic and art direction - everything fits together so well. And the music is great.There are some issues of course. Some large areas do feel kind of empty except for collectibles. And some things just feel kind of wack - I don't know, it might just be me, but there was a fair amount of platforming required for collectibles, and while the game gives you the tools to do it, the movement just doesn't feel super tight. I ended up getting stuck in some areas, but luckily there's a Respawn button in your options menu if this happens.I don't think the game is for everyone - since there's only one trial, I wish that the actions you choose at that trial have an impact on the ending - but I suppose that's kind of one of the messages the game tries to give you anyway, that in this world, things don't really matter. Regardless, I think that the game definitely makes up for these shortcomings with its environment ambiance, interesting world, great soundtrack, etc. It's a game and world worth experiencing, and I really hope this studio makes more games like this, so I fully recommend (:

_childDocuments_.review: , what an interesting title this is.At heart it’s an investigation mystery Visual Novel, the game will see you roaming the world in search for clues about both the main crime and many other side mysteries that happened on this small pocket of reality they call Island Sequence 24.The aesthetics and dialogue may seem too much at the start, lots of strange people talking in an even stranger way, until you start to unravel just what this setting is, then it all will make much more sense, if you pay attention, you’ll get used to it quite quickly.But the strangest thing it evoked was that feeling when you played a very old MMO where either boredom or curiosity will lead you to jump around the geometry of this artificial world to discover secrets that more often than not aren’t there.Yet Paradise Killer seems to double down on this premise, the game world IS both artificial and dying rewarding exploration with clues, messages and currency for every seemingly out of reach crevice you can reach, and this, I think, it’s the game biggest strength and something I never saw done in anything else.A few nitpicks I may have is that the game is not clear on what the mechanics in the climax of the story are, the game locks behind you and you have one shot at it which segways into the second problem, exploration is great at first but by the end I’ll become hours of running around to try to find everything in fear of getting a bad ending if you do not.Still, this doesn’t break the game, and that’s why I recommend it wholeheartedly, price may be steep for what is basically a single case game but it's still fresh enough to warrant a positive review.Your game deserves praise miss Love Dies, may you reach the moon.
