_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to cut to the chase - this game is a perfect example of a developer having a clear vision: aesthetic is on point, (vaporwave ftw) the characters are colorful (both literally and figuratively), the mystery is compelling... and there is a lot of subtext here, everything from social commentary to Lovecraftian horror.Overall- had a blast playing it! An extremely satisfying experience worth even more then the asking price - looking forward to a sequel!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Many investigation games (i.e. Danganronpa, Phoenix Wright) are essentially long cutscenes interrupted by the occasional crime scene and trials that follow the "use evidence A to refute statement B" formula. While I enjoy that type of game, Paradise Killer sets itself apart in a peculiar way. It has an open world in which it is up to you to find secrets and hidden evidence and to some extent, decide the truth for yourself. There is much less emphasis on trial procedure and finding the "correct" answer, and more focus on using the information you find to unravel a conspiracy. Pros:- Great story and world building- Exploration is enjoyable, there are always collectibles and/or evidence around the corner- A breath of fresh air in the investigation genre- Fantastic visual style and soundtrack- Diverse and interesting cast of characters, with many things to hide- Riveting plot twists- The player has much more freedom compared to similar games, including how justice is carried outCons:- The currency system is poorly implemented. Fast travel and some information have costs, so you feel constrained to walking everywhere for a good chunk of your playthrough. Thankfully you can get around the island somewhat quickly on foot- Certain objects around the world that seem meaningless are very important for progression, which can leave you glancing over them and becoming lost in the process. These also cost currency, which further demotivates you from interacting with them- There is a TON of backtracking. You will need to revisit characters essentially every time you obtain new information, and reuse objects once you acquire certain upgrades or key items- Hacking puzzles were a bit repetitiveOverall, I had a great experience with Paradise Killer. Unveiling the secrets the island and its inhabitants hold was thrilling, and I would highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good mystery.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: The story is garbage, characters are as flat as their sprites, map is far too large and empty w/ fast travel gated by a currency, first person controls are not good, "investigating" means "find things you can press the collect button on scattered throughout the giant world", the writing is unbelievably snarky and self-assured for being so bad (though I suppose that contributes to its badness).I should have refunded before 2 hours, but decided to give it a chance - which I now regret.[EDIT]: After talking it through with some friends (we all played through this at the same time), I think you might have a better time than I did if you're already bought into paranormal-type stories (ghosts/spirits/demons/cosmic horror/etc w/o a grounding in reality). I am not into those things myself and that in combination with the mediocrity of everything else led to the whole experience falling flat to me. If you like that kind of stuff this might have a pull for you, but for me there was nothing to pull me through w/ the 3D portion of the game lacking in the "game" department.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: So, I'm just gonna come right out and say it; I love friggin this game! One might even say I am bordering the line of obsession, and honestly, I can't say I disagree. Honestly I could write an essay about how amazing I think this game is and all the things that make it so, but you probably don't wan't to read all of that. I haven't finished the game yet, I honestly doubt I'm close to done, and I'll probably play through it a number of times and continuously realize I actually knew nothing last play through.  - For starters, it kind of reminds me Danganronpa, like if the entire game was the period between discovering a body to the class trial, but better, because it doesn't hold your hand. I haven't actually reached the trial stage yet, because there is just  much in this game, and I love that. You could start the trial at any point, regardless of whether or not you have all the facts. I love the thinking I know something, then coming back to something I found like, 10 hours ago, and realizing that it is  important to the story then I thought it would be.   - There is a lot of back and forth once you start connecting the dots, and while I like it, it might be a little to repetitive for some people.   - I kind of struggle using the little in-game computer,I just feel like it could be better with how it categorizes things.  - That map is pretty big, but there are things you can access to make traversing it quicker, although I recommend taking your time and looking around. There's lots to see   - Definitely repayable   Honestly I could write so much more but I'm scared of accidentally spoiling something. It's a great game, 13/10, do yourself a favor and play it!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: An open-world murder mystery game with a vaporwave aesthetic. You play as Lady Love Dies, an investigator brought out of her 3 million day-long exile to solve the crime to end all crimes: the murder of the island's Council. At first, the case seems pretty straightforward: a Citizen named Henry, who was possess by a demon 10 years ago and has been imprisoned ever since, broke out of his confinement and killed the entire Council. But as you explore the island, speak to its immortal inhabitants, and uncover clues, you soon realize that everything is not what it seems. Is Henry really the murderer? Or is he just a scapegoat?- Vaporwave aesthetic- Fast running speed and movement upgrades (double jump & dash) allow you to explore the entire island relatively quickly- Fast travel mechanic helps with the tedium of traveling around the island- AR and meditation mechanics help you find collectibles- Freedom to choose your own ending--you don't have to arrive at one solution to finish the game- Crimson Acid is a total MILF- First-person view can be nauseating when traversing certain regions- If you hate vaporwave you'll get tired of the background music- Conversations with characters don't have any real consequences--if you say the wrong thing and piss someone off, they'll still talk to you afterwards and give you the information you need
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Game 138 of my backlog.Spoiler freeNote: This is a Visual novel. There aren't a lot of choices to make realistically. Only looking for evidence and then watching it play out in the actual trial. I'm let down by that fact. You will not be proving or disproving anything. Only collecting, and hoping you collected enough+ Open world Phoenix Wright-esque investigation style gameplay+ Collectibles and upgrades+ Interesting Lore+ There is a decently good story to discover+ You can start the trial at any time+/- Would've loved to see a little more voice acting in there- Trial itself is a huge letdown. You get an mild option of choice simply by picking a candidate but then there is no proving or disproving anything beyond that. It just plays out. - Fast travel option is slow and tiresome. Bad implementation.- Constant backtracking, and not in a fun way, to collect all evidence, usually by talking to 2 people on opposite ends of the island, over and over again.- Dull Hang-Out mechanic.It starts fun, but ultimately I think it falls short. I feel like this is where Octopath Traveler 1 makes a nice comparison. Tons of great ideas not fully expressed very well. There is almost a golden gem of a game here that falls just short of being phenomenal if only there were some small changes in a few spots (disregarding my Voice Acting comment).
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: This game, particularly if you get it on sale, is 100% worth your time and money. In today's modern age of gaming, there are hundreds, maybe thousands of worthless and mediocre titles that demand your money in exchange for contrived, painful tropes and game-play all stolen from each other that provide nothing of substance. This is not one of those titles. While Paradise Killer does not excel in terms of its gameplay mechanics or replayability, it is absolutely stunning in terms of its visual presentation, characters and worldbuilding. It's quirky, charming, and will surprise you again and again as the plot unfolds. If you can put up with some tedious collect-a-thon stuff and bizarre exposition, you are sure to enjoy this.1) The game-play is a bit grating, comprising mostly of "find this, find that, go here, interrogate this person, solve this puzzle, etc." HOWEVER, the mystery underpinning the game is more than enough to compensate. No one mystery is spoon-fed to you or given away entirely in a single session. Out of the 14 hours I put in, I didn't determine the full shape of the mystery until about hour 12.2) The environment is just... wow. Certainly for being a smaller game, you can tell the team put a ton of love and effort into every area of the map. It feels like Vaporwave incarnate, and you will be living for every inch of it.3) The characters, my God, the characters. They're all so charming and quirky, and you get to know their ambitions, dreams, background, secrets, all of it. Some of them are more flat than others, for sure, but in general you will enjoy speaking with them at every turn.4) Without spoiling anything, the game really puts you in the driver's seat in terms of how fast or slow you go through the game. You never feel rushed, but you do always feel intrinsically motivated to learn more and comb every inch of the map. Highly appreciable, given the maddening obsession AAA studies have with map markers and "golden-path" design. The moment to moment gameplay definitely feels limited in that your dialogue choices are pre-defined, but you really get the feeling that you are determining the emotions that come into play. At no point did ANY character say ANYTHING incompatible with the conversation choices I made; it all just flowed organically, flawlessly, 100% of the time due to the way the game structures revelations.Finally, the game runs like a dream, even on max settings and ray-tracing on. No crashes, maybe 2 bugs the whole time, pitch-perfect soundtrack. I got this game for like $12 and feel like I robbed Kaizen Game Studios. Please buy this game, I beg of you. Your future self will thank you.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: If this game interests you even slightly, go play it instead of spoiling yourself! The story that unfolds as you uncover the truths of the island is spectacular with a few twists and turns in it. The world is incredible and you, the player, get to uncover that mystery as well. There's plenty of worldbuilding and almost nothing is wasted in the experience. I do wish the game had full voice acting, as the few lines there are get quite annoying. Thankfully there is a feature to turn down the frequency and even disable them entirely, which I did pretty shortly into the whole thing.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll just say it.  I am in love with .So many elements are done so well, and the whole comes together so beautifully.With all that I have gone through over these 15 hours, I wouldn't have changed a thing.  This is one of those experiences that carves out a place in your heart and makes you not want it to end - though the length is actually perfect too.  They knew the story they wanted to tell and took the right time to tell it without dragging things out and without skipping over anything.Above all,  fills me with , triggering feelings of longing for my real world past through masterful evocation of its own fictional one. _childDocuments_.review: 100% completion Paradise Killer is part visual novel murder mystery, part first person platformer, and part collectathon. The vaporwave aesthetic is well-earned by the game's critical tension with the titular paradise. That tension permeates the entire narrative, as characters both benefit and suffer in their self-imposed immortality. The mystery is enjoyable to uncover, with lots of dramatic moments if the player chooses to chase down every line of inquiry. The characters are memorable and nuanced, with complicated overlapping motives and skillsets. Unlike similar titles, there isn't a specific hard truth to uncover; rather, the player can present evidence that they feel is more incriminating in order to weave a compelling narrative of the crimes. This did make the ending slightly unsatisfying, as all the crimes have multiple plausible culprits.I also found island navigation to be a bit irritating at times. The map is useless, and the overall design is a bit mazelike. That said, it is a small enough space that this issue fades into the background as you progress. First person platforming certainly adds a retro vibe, but this implementation is not a significant improvement over its very dated predecessors. With all the upgrades unlocked I did end up enjoying jumping around the island, but there were quite a few moments of frustration mixed in there as well.Overall the imaginative world, consistent vibe, and exemplary writing made this a unique and compelling experience. I can forgive a few shortcomings when they come from a place of artistic experimentation, and the result is a game with a tremendous amount of heart and personality.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is easily one of the best detective games ever created. While most games in the ‘mystery’ genre do have you investigating a case, you are typically stuck in a very on-the-rails experience; if you do have any control it’s typically a very structured experience. Paradise killer simply drops you into the experience with a very minimal overview – and it is totally up to you what to do at your own pace. The game is set in a pocket universe/reality (referred to as islands) created by the syndicate, which is basically a religious cult of sorts. All the members of the syndicate are immortals, and sometimes they move to a new pocket universe as needed. At the time of the crime, most of the population has moved to the new island so the pool of suspects is not too large. As a result of the setting you need to learn the rules, mechanics, and norms of the society. The setting and has a very manga/anime feel to it, but overall is incredibly fun.That is not to say the game is entirely without structure, you have a computer at your disposal that keeps track of all conversations and clues, it can even analyze forensic evidence like DNA or chemical residue. And all dialogs have the typical list of generated questions to select from, based upon all the clues you have at the time. The trial at the end of the game is also highly structured, but your options will be based upon all the evidence you have collected. At the end of the game you are free to accuse anyone of the crime (except for yourself or the judge).Now just a couple of spoiler free tips, the currency, ‘blood crystals’ can be used for a variety of purposes in the game – there are plenty around in the world, so while you shouldn’t spend recklessly there will be more than enough to get you everything you need. Secondly, do not be afraid to hang out with characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Wasn't sure what to expect when I started this one.  There's a strong Japanese aesthetic running through the whole thing, and there's a weird almost 80's vibe to the color scheme and music.  You play a detective with free reign to explore an island and uncover as much evidence as you want before starting the final trial.  You could run straight to the end if you so choose, but won't have much to support your case.  In addition, there are a TON of hidden items to find, and getting them all is a challenge even with what little help the game provides. It reminded me a lot of the later Far Cry games where you collect for the sake of collecting.  All the characters are bizarre and interesting and the investigation just keeps throwing revelations at you that, thankfully, the game keeps track of for you.  The final case isn't nearly as difficult as I was anticipating given all the evidence you've collected, which I really appreciated, but I kind of wish I got some kind of final grade for my effort.  This is definitely a game if you want something more low-key that you can take your time with and enjoy the exploration.  You don't fight, kill anything, and you can't die, so all the pressure comes from being able to find what you are looking for, and they don't make it easy.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful, weird and incredibly enticing. I set a project to compile, booted the game up to try it out and stood up eleven hours later. The authors created a bizarre world, populated it with larger-than-life extravagant characters and then wrote a story to match. The tutorializing is also done wonderfully, I love the way you learn there's no fall damage - it's entirely seamless and a setpiece all on its own.If this game clicks, you won't stop until you read everything and get to know everyone (even Yuri). Two bits of advice: there's no way to waste a Blood Crystal, and get the soundtrack bundle. You'll want to buy it anyway, trust me.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice mystery game. It took a good deal of inspiration from Danganronpa, however it's its own thing : with only one, big case and little handholding, the feeling is very different. You're not reading an interactive mystery novel, you're actively investigating a crime and building your case, to the point the trial can play out in different fashions depending on your findings.Also that world building is pretty well made and understandable despise being quite alien at times.The (optional) relic hunt helps with that. Which will likely make the difference in playtime BTW : once on the island I mainly bumbled around instead of trying to meet with the inhabitants. No idea how long the game is in a more focused first run, I'm guessing around six to eight hours?Music's nice and fitting. There's no proper voice acting, but voices samples punctuate the dialogues. You can change the frequency at which they're played, always nice if you grow tired of hearing the same lines.Only little gripe I have is the graphics, they're at times quite barren and amateurishly ugly.On the other hand I guess it allowed the devs to make their big island one unique zone, complete with being able to see items from hundreds of meters sometimes, so there's that.I had a good time overall, hope we'll see more of those devs work in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Being sold as an open-world investigation game, Paradise Killer struggles with that definition. A lot of its uniqueness is derived from its off-beat design and style, but it comes at the cost of also having some polarizing features. Even as someone that's very generous to products willing to take risks, I found myself asking throughout my play through whether or not the game would have been better if it followed a more traditional design. The open-world itself is what gave me the most thought, as it really drew me into the island and every resident. The visuals and music are gorgeous, which made wandering around a blast in of itself. It's strangely fulfilling to have a physicality to what otherwise could have just been point-and-click game with conversation menus, helping my immersion with the world. Up to a certain point, that is, because while it's novel for a while, there's a wall I hit in familiarity with the island that eventually became tedious. Having to walk everywhere well over dozens of times for the full experience, even with the fast travel system as it exists, my patience started to wear thin. When several investigation threads are going on all at once, it paradoxically had less of a mental stack on me, as picking any random direction had something to follow up on. Once I was down to a single thread at a time though, having to walk back and forth between characters just to get a couple lines of dialogue became very tiring. The aforementioned fast travel system should alleviate most of this then, but it unfortunately didn't help nearly as much as it should have.The disparate density throughout the island of fast travel nodes leads to some areas having a confusing amount of options, while others still had minute-long jogs from it to its nearby point of interest. The process of using the fast travel is also weirdly inefficient, with a couple loading screens and a fairly unclear map of the area for choosing your destination. I ended up just walking most of the world in spite of the fast travel system just because of its awkwardness. The collectables scattered throughout the island are also just present, not having much use other than filling space for people into collectathons at best, and being visual clutter in front of what may actually be an important piece of evidence at worst. The actual mystery I found to be compelling enough, given how bizarre, yet seamless the world and the content of its writing is. It's nothing groundbreaking, largely consisting of exploring an area for a piece of evidence and then grilling any pertinent characters. Uncovering the juicier parts of the story as payoff for subjecting yourself to fully exploring the open-world does help the two coexist, but as mentioned before, its pace slows down as the investigative checklist whittles away. I don't think I would remove the open-world aspect if I could, as it does add something magical to the entire package. I just feel that more could have been done to mitigate its faults that come with its inclusion, especially knowing that there are friends of mine that I would recommend this to for the rest of its content. It's not like any of its eccentricity would have been lost if the game was tightened up a bit in these areas. At least you find out pretty quick whether it's for you or not. With that all said, I'd be lying if I said Paradise Killer wasn't still an overall joy to play through, it'll just require some patience.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10 Good.A solid detective game, where you play as Lady Love Dies, an exiled detective summoned back to a surreal virtual island world because all the leaders have been killed and the temporary leaders need to know whodunnit?!A colourful open-world, a ridiculous cast of characters, superb UI and design aesthetic combined with a simple investigation and chatting gameplay makes for a fairly surreal open world to explore.Genuinely an excellent idea and concept, the only let down is the finale, because although you do have a trial to conclude your investigation, where you do get to dispense justice, the actual trial itself doesn't steal the show as the highlight, the big finale of  a wonderful, weird journey.Still, in spite of this, it is a good game, and one that everyone should pick up at some point, whether on sale or for full price as it is genuinely spot on and fairly priced.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: This game should have been a playlist.There are two sides to Paradise Killer:- a inconsequential collectathon where you find yourself parkouring across a (boring) island built using Half-Life 1 technology and designed with far too much Minecraft build style inspiration- an uninspired murder mystery VN that isn't really an investigation as the player never has to connect any dots - just examine everything to find all the cluesIt's an investigation sandbox, there is no right or wrong answer to the mystery, whatever facts you choose to present end up being considered the truth. This may be a realistic image of a failed justice system, but it makes all your choices pointless, and the finale (which is a mockery of a trial, with no defense, all accusations based on hearsay and no proofs, presented linearly with just an illusion of player interaction) ends up being very unrewarding.As I played through the game I understood the "vaporware" aesthetics and themes just a cover up for cheap design and little effort put into game art. The style is incredibly inconsistent, and does not fit at all with the concepts that the story attempts to explore. Cheerful, catchy synth tunes do not resonate with the gloomy reality of the world you explore - the tracks are very faithful to '90s synth pop music, and they are brilliant on their own, but not in the context of the game. It all feels like an excuse to be inconsistent with the design and ignore any details. Perhaps it was the right bet though, seeming how other reviews seem to love the style - so it seems I'm very subjective here.I am also disappointed by the writing. Sure, there is some merit to it, but the world lore is so quirky and random, you can't possibly make any sense of it as an investigator. How can you even attempt to connect murder dots if you, the player, don't understand how all the fantasy elements in this world work? And obviously, so many plot twists are realized by disclosing a new, major fact about the world to the player, that all game characters had to know... Explaining mysteries with a "oh, so actually, this guy can telepathically sense distress, and it's a totally normal thing in this world" is cheap and insulting to the player.The main character is pretty cool though, and I enjoyed her interactions with the cast. All VA is also really good, even though only some lines are voiced.Overall, a tedious, confusing, and poorly designed game. Perhaps I would approach it with a different mindset if its base price was 3-5EUR, but at 15-20 I expected much more polish and/or more clever design.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Man I love paradise killer - the mystery isn't super in depth in and of itself, neither is this game a standard detective or puzzle game if that's what you're interested in. It's a collectathon platformer, based in truly one of the most interesting and creative sci-fi/fantasy worlds I've seen in games. Every location is just oozing style and vibes and the amount of stuff to explore and find is excellent.It's quite wordy so if that's not your thing this won't be for you, although also if you just want words it also won't be for you. The platforming is a little jank, but only imo in ways that enhance your ability to get to each nook and cranny of the game world and the story doesn't quiiiiiiiiiiiite stick the landing, but not in a way that massively impacted my enjoyment of the game.Overall highly recommend it, if it seems like it's your thing it will be.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: 'That's human nature: we need mysteries.''But a mystery can make you insane!''That's the knife edge we all walk.'Paradise Killer is a weird game to recommend. It's not without its flaws and even more importantly, its strange setting, deliberately awkward graphics and simple gameplay will be a turn off for some. In essence it's a simple whodunnit in the form of a graphic novel meets walking simulator. Interactivity is limited to exploring the environment and collecting items, which in turn will create new dialog options with the characters. Then start the ending at any time you think you have found enough 'evidence'.Where the game shines in my opinion is the lore and quite original world combined with a vibrant 90s 'Active Worlds' aesthetic and a jazzy synth soundtrack. It's as if HP Lovecraft wrote one of his stories of terrible unimaginable Elder Gods while snorting cocaine in an 80s Miami. The game drops you in the thick of it, and the earlier hours of the game it's all quite baffling. But continue playing and things become clearer, and vastly more mundane and therefore also somewhat less interesting. Basically the game is slightly too long, even though it can be finished in about 15 hours. The writing is pretty good, but the goofy design of the game gets kind of in the way if the story it tries to tell. Still, I enjoyed my time on Paradise Island 24 and hope to explore more of this world. But hopefully with slightly better graphics, since after one game of neon colors and 2D sprites I think this gimmick has now run its course.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best mystery games on Steam. It can be overwhelming to start as it dumps you in a surreal world in which you are completely unfamiliar in addition to solving a mass murder with no real starting point. The game does not hold your hand at any point and allows you to draw your own conclusions.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Solid game overall. Music was great, characters were good, and the actual murder mystery investigation was fun. Sometimes the collectible stuff was fun. Unfortunately the biggest mark against the game is the moment-to-moment platforming.Platforming in first-person is a pain and with floaty physics like these it's even worse. Blood crystals also become more work than they pay off to be, especially when you can find a blood crystal next to things that require them often enough. It's not worthwhile to collect more than 20 at a time.Otherwise would recommend for those murder mystery and trial simulation fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Not exactly what it says on the tin, but a fun, stylish piece nonetheless.Paradise Killer is an investigation-lite game. I'd call it more of a investigation-themed exploration game/collectathon. While yes, you're playing as a lovely Lady Love, an investigator, you're not really... investigating the crimes. You're just collecting evidence scattered around the island, like in Dangronpa's investigation phase (you'll hear that comparison a lot in this review) and you can honestly forget about them until it's the time for the trial. It goes something like this: talk to a suspect, they point you to a place to check out, you start walking in that direction and immediatly get sidetracked by hundreds of collectibles to be found in this world.And what a world to explore it is. Absolutely peak aesthetics, brave colours, memorable landmarks, inspired by vapourwave, brutalism, small, japanese towns, ancient, egyptian monuments and a dash of futurism and yet, it works perfectly together. Not to mention the entire lore and the worldbuilding the game has. A completly unique blend that was fascinating to learn about. What's up with these Gods? Wait, there are demons possessing people? Why's there air conditioning literally everywhere?The world is also inhabited by a colourful cast of characters (you, know like in Danganronpa), who each have their own clear goals, motivations, agendas. Who's working with who? Who's gonna gain something from the confustion and who wants to lead you astray? Also, the game has two cute dogs (you can pet them) and a possessed fish yearning for knowledge.While you're exploring the island, you'll be jamming to some killer (pun intended) soundtrack, jazzy, funky, etheral, a perfect fit to the visuals. Paradise Killer is oozing with style, especially the stylized UI elements, that really set the tone of the game. Everything's slick, flashy, bright, yet somehow tainted by some hidden force working in the shadows. You'll get it, when you realise why the hacking terminals are called "Nightmare Computers".Okay, the game seems pretty good, what's the catch?Well, while the mystery is really cool and complex, and you can find out everything about everyone, the game kinda... fizzles out at the end, when the time for the trial comes. It's just a very simple text-based scene, where you don't really do anything, except point your finger at the guilty, like you're going with the motions. I was hoping for something like, you guessed it, Dangaronpa trials, where you're more of an active participant. That would make it more memorable I think. What's more, is that the trial actually... doesn't really matter? No matter who you charge as a titular killer, the result's all the same, which is a huge shame. Why not at least put a "where are they now" kinda thing to show you how your choices affected the world, so you had an incentive to play the scheming game The Syndicate loves so much. Overall, Paradise Killer is more of a journey than a destination kind of deal. It's a beautiful, memorable journey, don't get me wrong. It's just a shame that it couldn't stick the landing. Otherwise, we would have gotten pretty close to perfection.JUSTICE HAS BEEN SERVED

_childDocuments_.review: AMAZING!In practice a collect-athon/platformer/explorer game in an incredibly creative surrealist vapor-wave pocket dimension setting.The story has you discovering secrets and clues to solve a murder mystery among a bunch of astral-super-villains who are on the run from demonic invasions and the god-hunters of the real world who seek to stop them from resurrecting and worshiping dead lovecraftian gods from beyond the stars. _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. It has a very wacky setup and setting but it is ultimately a murder mystery solving game and I really like those type of games. To be fair the setting and general wackiness of the game sort of grew on me as I played anyway.The basic premise is that you play a character called Lady Love Dies who has been exiled for 3 million days, but is then recalled to investigate the murder of the rulers of an island. And yes that is your characters actual name and yes I meant days and not years.To investigate the crime you will scour the island for clues and question a number of suspects to determine if they were or weren't involved. When you decide to finish your investigation you then move onto a trial where you will accuse the suspects you believe are guilty and present your evidence to convince the judge.As I said I did really enjoy this game and was hooked from early on. Exploring the island for clues and evidence is fun. There's also other collectibles to find, mainly crystals which are a form of currency which you'll use to fast travel, unlock fast travel points and abilities as well as buying information from one of the suspects. The other main form of collectables are relics which serve no purpose other than to serve as a bit of lore flavour.All your evidence gets collected on a laptop device and is nicely sorted by case and suspect which will aid in your investigation and guide you in determining what to look for next.So if a game that has investigating a murder as it's main focus sounds appealing then definitely give this game a try. As someone who likes investigation games, I can easily recommend it. It might not be to everyones taste but it certainly was to mine.

And I mostly enjoyed my time with it.

_childDocuments_.review: This bizarre vaporware-ish Danganronpa-inspired adventure/visual novel game turned out to be my second most favorite game of 2020.If there's one word that can describe Paradise Killer, it would be "stylish". The contrast between flat, simplified "external" elements like HUD, UI, menus, even the architectures, and the baroque fantastical visual design of characters and locations give Paradise Killer a chaotic vibration, just like how the intricate writing manifested its complex lore. Nothing comes off as gimmicky as the narrative is tightly directed. The dialogue is just as slick and distinctive as its character design. I also personally find very few of narrative pieces in this game to be filler, and even with its bizarre atmosphere, everything is constrained and developed within its internal logic. Nothing becomes too wacky, too ridiculous, too out there to believe. It's like a fever dream of a literature architect obsessed with magical realism, but the crazy part is, the realism here nails down the magical elements, unlike most of the notable works in this genre.The game's main mechanics are split into two parts - the conversations that's tied to investigation, and the exploration that actually functions like a collect-a-thon. You don't actually find too many evidences in the world, the majority of items you collect includes recording, tidbits related to lore and various artifacts that speak about the mystical history of Island 25. It is very unconventional in some senses, as the open world is on the same scale as Kamurocho found in Yakuza games, but the level of freedom is much higher with different verticality and hidden items in places you don't expect. It legit feels like a first person platformer at times due to the lack of invisible walls, which makes the open world incredibly satisfied to explore.And then there's the disco-fueled soundtrack that merged synthwave, vaporware and electronic. For a game that deals with pretty unpleasant themes, the music is uplifting and is just as colorful as the visual style. Half of the game's title is "PARADISE", after all.

_childDocuments_.review: A mash-up between a visual novel and an open-world game. It has a strong narrative and an incredible city-pop soundtrack. The exploration is very chill and peril-free, with some minor platforming puzzles. The post-game is a bit disappointing – more reactivity to the player's choices would have gone a long way. I absolutely recommend this game if you are looking for a strong narrative but want a bit more agency and mechanical depth than your average visual novels. I recommend the soundtrack to everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: "19th Island Sequence - When you sat with me and looked at the moon."I re-wrote and deleted the review 3 times by now. I can't really put it in words, but this game is an . I can't really recommend it to everyone, and I don't think it's a game that absolutely everyone should play. It took me 10 hours to 100% the game, and at its current price-per-hour point you're looking at what should feel like a nice restaurant 3-course meal, and what you end up with is a dinner at a Michelin-star restaurant where the main chef is using goat blood and demonic murmurs to spice the food, the servers look like they're on acid and they smell of whiskey, and the other patrons are loving it. So in what case would this game be a good purchase for you? Should you be able to look past minor inconveniences and don't mind an indie feel to a game, you end up with what I can only describe as a "I wish I could play this for the first time again" type of experience. Paradise Killer is very unique in a lot of ways, and I struggle to piece together a Frankenstein of similar games that can fill all of its parts - and this is is what alienates the game from the mainstream gaming audience. What you should know is that the game is an Open World Mystery, but it doesn't stop at that. The trailers also don't do justice to the game's movement, which once mastered will leave you zooming from location to location, progressing plot points and collecting bits and pieces of the world being spoon-fed through collectables and dialogue. And what a world it is! If you made it this far in the review and like what you're reading, I warmly suggest stopping and getting the game. There's more I'd love to tell you, but the experience of going in blind and reading the reviews later will do you proper justice. Is the game perfect? No. Should you play it? Maybe. Overwhelmingly positive worthy? Yup. And finally, best girl? Crimson.

_childDocuments_.review: So, this isn't really a detective game, It's an open world exploration collectathon in which you find clues, chat with npcs and present those clues to them. That might be weird to say, but the deductions made aren't explicitly required for the player to make, unlike in Obra Dinn or Outer Wilds for example. This isn't a bad thing, Paradise Killer is very good exploration game, and it has a lot of elements that would benefit a true detective game that many games I consider detective games lack, it tracks your progress really well, It lets you know what you may have overlooked and the mystery is fun to unravel on your own despite not being prompted to do so.To elaborate, let's take Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments and Danganronpa as examples of 2 elements Paradise Killer emulates but does not reach.In Crimes and Punishments and Paradise Killer you collect evidence by exploring the world, however, in Crimes and Punishments it's on the player to put that evidence together to form a connection with their deduction board mechanic. Paradise Killer makes those deductions for you.Danganronpa and Paradise Killer feature trial sections where you present evidence to find out who's guilty of a crime, in Danganronpa you have to find contradictions in various statements and prove them to be untrue using what you know; doing this wrong fails the trial, Paradise Killer simply requires you to choose who you believe committed a crime and throw all the evidence at them at once without having to parse through statements or select the correct evidence.None of this is to say Paradise Killer should have perfectly emulated the above games, I think it does a great job at being an exploration game but the detective part of it might as well be an on rails visual novel.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't expect to like this game, let alone love it. I found the graphics ugly, the character names silly and the initial plot hook bizarre. I am so, so glad I tried this out. The weird setting, the over the top characters, the insane world building all comes together in one solid neon vibe that just WORKS. I loved the free rein you are given to explore the island and discover a huge, complicated mess of characters and motives and history in a darkly funny and disturbing world. It's not really detective work, you're just finding the pieces of info and the game neatly packages it up for you. You're not performing logic leaps like in obra dinn or the golden idol, you are sifting through multiple and conflicting pieces of evidence and deciding which is true. It's this exploration that got me hooked, those moments of wonder and discovery that you can only experience once. Despite the complete difference in tone my experience playing Paradise Killer reminded me most of playing Outer Wilds. Outer Wilds was more awe and reflection though, Paradise Killer definately earned a few wtf.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most distinct games I played lately. The world and the characters are really interesting and memorable, as is the story. The player is free to progress and try to figure at the mystery at their own pace. Exploring the world is rewarding and it didn't get boring even after searching every corner of it. The length of the game is perfect too. Not too long to overstay its welcome, neither too short to feel rushed. The character designs were all really notable and probably the highlight of the game for me. The music, even though it isn't my type, felt perfect for the world. Really liked the, not so subtle, social commentary too.

_childDocuments_.review: It hurts me to write this review considering how excited I was to finally play Paradise Killer, but god was this game an absolute miss. I've had it on my wishlist forever and figured the steam sale would be a good place to pick it up! And I am so glad I waited until it was on sale because I cannot recommend buying this game at full price to anyone. There's a long list of problems I had with the story and gameplay mechanics, so I'll start with what I really enjoyed. The art for the characters and the music. Beautiful. The character sprites were so good, to the point where it made me like characters that otherwise I would think literally nothing of with how bland the writing for them is. The music was perfect for the feeling of the island/world that was being conveyed, and discovering new tracks was one of the few collectibles I actually enjoyed completing. The dialogue with the . One of the few gameplay mechanics I did like were the decryption puzzles, which there were much fewer of than I had anticipated. I wish there were more things I could compliment the game for, but unfortunately I can't.Starting off the list of cons: the story. It's bad. I don't know if I can even critique the story, because it felt like there wasn't even one there while playing. Without including spoilers, essentially your job is to figure out who murdered the elites of this island by investigating and interrogating suspects. Except it's not, because your job is in fact going up to suspects who you have just found incriminating evidence linking to them and getting a resounding "No... that wasn't me. I didn't do that." Now, you would think, 'Oh, obviously the trial is going to be more in depth with you linking these pieces of evidence. Surely there is a reason why this PROVEN piece of evidence isn't getting me any further talking with them.' And you would be so very wrong. The trial is one of the most disappointing parts of this game in my opinion. It's less deduction and more common sense Who Did This Crime, the conclusion of which is generally led to by a single piece of evidence found. Even without the way this was set up, the story is completely unfulfilling. Character hangouts felt very bland or down right intolerable, specifically Yuri's. I don't know what Shinji's interactions were meant to convey but I felt literally nothing reading them. Even the overarching story of your backstory and the islands themselves felt just... empty. The entire game feels like some cool character designs were created and they tried to shove them into an unfinished story and world. I wasn't expecting a lot from the story, but I also wasn't expecting to be left feeling absolutely nothing about the characters when I completed the game. Moving onto the actual gameplay mechanics, this is where most of the big issues lie. To preface, I love collectibles in games. Love completing side quests. This game has a lot of one of the two. A Lot. Of collectibles. And it weighs the game down an immense amount. I'd say about 80% of this game is bouncing around with the god awful physics and drowning while you slide down a mountain trying to pick up a Blood Crystal. That was my experience in a nutshell. Trying to get evidence for the murders that happened? No, it's just a crystal. And then another. And another. I understand they're the currency for fast traveling and such, but god is it annoying to try to collect evidence for the case only to find out there's nothing more and only a plethora of these crystals leftover. And to my knowledge, collecting these does literally nothing aside from purchasing items or info. Don't worry though, they aren't the only thing filled throughout this island to make it seem like there's more to do! There is so much junk to sift through, just random items with the most bland flavor text I've read in a game like this to date. The collectibles revolving around the lore just feel like weird world-building without the actual effort of doing it. Most of the stuff about the gods or the way the world works was just left up to the player to interpret, which I don't generally mind, but with a story as convoluted as this it's almost necessary. The few side quests that were available were actually good, I liked being able to go search for things residents asked for, as it gave more reason to explore the world and also gave me the most understanding of how the society worked. This would be great if there were more than like, 5 of these throughout the entire game. I feel like a lot of the issues with general storytelling about the world itself could've been solved with more of these citizen interactions, so it's just frustrating how little they were incorporated. Some issues I had that were less of an issue and more of a nuisance were the voice line loops and the map ui. I ran into multiple situations where the same voice line would play back to back, no tone change, nothing, just the same line repeated. It wasn't a huge issue but it just felt strange? Regarding the map, I didn't use it very much in my playthrough, usually only in the portions where I fast traveled, and I didn't even start using that until closer to the end of the game because I still wasn't familiar enough to remember each suspects location on this big open world map. This is where a better ui for the map would've helped immensely, at least just with the faces of people next to their closest warp point.TLDR; Do not buy this game if you're looking for a fully fleshed out story, or any sense of reasonable exploration. The game tries to bring up bigger issues of right and wrong, morality, the exploitation of the working class (i assumed), and falls completely flat. There is a murder. Is it a mystery? Not really, besides one single aspect of it. Pick up the game while it's on sale if you think you'll be able to get more enjoyment out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: A great time. After 11 hours I feel I've found all the important clues while also completing most of the side missions, but to collect everything would likely take another few hours at least. The characters were all very fun and interesting to talk to, and the open-ended nature of the mystery made each discovery and conclusion drawn feel like my own. The soundtrack and style are both intoxicating and I'd love for there to be more games in a similar style. There were a few flaws, though. Making fast travel cost a limited in game resource ensured I rarely used it and now at the end I have a bunch of blood gems I don't need stockpiled. Also, the voice lines get repetitive really fast, as each character only has a handful of voice lines that they repeat each time you speak to them.The last flaw, however, is more of a compliment; I really wanted more. I wish I could have more time interacting with all the cool characters in this really unique world. Thus, I'm really excited for whatever Kaizen Game Works puts out next, because if it's even half as good as this I'm sure I'll enjoy it.tl,dr; Buy this game if you want a cosmic horror murder mystery set in a neon-tinted nostalgia ridden vapor-wave island, and I'm sure you won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm almost four hours into the game, and ... it's tedious.I like taking things apart and putting them back together again. (I really enjoyed 'Assemble With Care', a game that's all about that.) So Shipbreaker looked like it exactly fit my interests: a zero-G environment, spaceships that are detailed inside and out, and the opportunity to take them apart!In practice, though, this game (in Early Access) has a *lot* of rough edges. I'm playing in Standard mode, where I get infinite lives but am limited by the length of each day's shift and the amount of oxygen I have. In my four hours I think I've worked on four ships so far (and also did two tutorials). It's all about using a handheld welding gun to destroy connection points, and a handheld tractor beam to pull pieces off the ship and nudge them in the direction of a furnace, a processing plant, or a barge (depending on the part). First off, the time limits really get in the way - I have to keep returning to a kiosk to purchase more oxygen several times while I'm working on a ship, and the day's usually up when I'm no more than a third of the way finished with it. There's an easier mode where time and oxygen aren't factors, but that might be too easy. I think the lengths just need some tweaking.But beyond that, so far the game seems somewhat repetitive, and maneuvering around to try to drag pieces with the tractor beam is time-consuming. Right now I would rate this game with Satisfactory, or with American Trucker: it's a neat concept, but it's a considerable amount of work and I can see it eating up as much time as I give it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you love Firefly or the Expanse, and want to have that salvager or grease-neck experience, then this is the game for you. I hope they crank up the creepiness factor of ghost ships up to 11 though. I can't wait to find out more about this game and in-game universe!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fresh new gaming perspective I find enjoyable to play.  Love the graphics and game play mechanics.  There's still a few bugs in the early access but it plays solid overall.  This does quickly turn into feeling like a real "job", it's very repetitive and it won't take long to find efficient ways to dismantle a ship; at which point it just turns into a grind for the next level.  I'm hoping we'll see some kind of variety or challenges thrown in so it breaks up some of that grinding feeling.  The tasks as you advance do get harder to achieve, but with needing 100+ completed tasks to advance to the next level; you'll be back doing the intro ships just to knock them out and there's little incentive to keep with the larger vessels.Overall, fun to play but it'll get old fairly quick I think. *Updated with full release*Not too much has changed, it's basically the same game now it was then; just with a completed story line they had been teasing us with during EA.  The same old bug/issues that were there then are still here now, though the voice actors have changed.If you enjoy single player casual games, this still makes for a good casual game and it still feels like the daily grind of a job.  There are achievements and leader boards for challenges if you want to compare yourself with others, but this is basically a simulated high-risk job in space with a slightly annoying story line that you can't skip/opt-out of in career mode.

_childDocuments_.review: Every once in a while  game comes along  that you can't walk away from. You know how it works. "just a few more minutes." "Just one more time." "I'll finish this and then I'm done." Then the next thing you know it's 3 AM and you have to work in the morning.Factorio did that to me. So did Minecraft back in the day.And so does Shipbreaker. There's something oddly therapeutic, satisfying, even zen like, about simply tearing down a space ship in 3D, zero gravity space. Well done! And what's more, it's still in Early Access. I can't wait to see what happens next.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR at the bottomEdit: With the release of the first patch, additional resolutions are now supported, so I have changed my review to a recommended review as of June 25th, 2020.So, what about the game itself? It's fun! It's sort of like Viscera Cleanup Detail meets Space Engineers. If you like either one of those games or both of them you should have fun with Hardspace. Cutting up the ships and depositing salvage is satisfying, there appear to be quite a few upgrades to the existing equipment and what I've gotten to use has been satisfying, intuitive and fun. The movement feels great and the game does utilize the zero-g environment well. The movement and equipment are easy to pickup but there's room within the mechanics to creatively problem solve, which is great! The soundtrack is great if you're a fan of any kind of Space Western soundtracks. In fact, in terms of immersion, the game is outstanding right from the moment you boot it up. Hardspace really wants you to get into your character and your role early on. Everything from the UI to the music seeks to immerse you straight away. The game is pretty, although texture quality doesn't hold up when you're smashing your face into the wall of a ship (and you will, a lot). The game also features full gamepad support which, in a game with 6 Degrees of Freedom, is a pretty big must have, personally.TL;DRPros+ Cutting up ships is fun and creatively challenging.+ Equipment is easy to pickup but complex enough to be creative + Movement is fun, satisfying and not too hard once you get used to it+The soundtrack is awesome+The game is very immersive right from the moment you boot it up+ Full Gamepad support+Additional Resolutions now supported in 21:9 aspect ratioCons:-Textures are a little muddy close up-The game is a little content light at the moment, but I suspect that will change over time.-I have had several crashes in my 14-15 hours of gameplayConsider staying away if you have a higher resolution than 1920x1080 and you don't want to play in windowed mode

_childDocuments_.review: This game is addicting and there is a great balance between complexity/danger.  I'm having loads of fun chopping these ships up.  If the game suffers from anything its odd bugs that occur with the physics and clipping, as well as having a very lame story.  The game play definitely makes up for those short comings.  The dystopian future is something quite popular in games right now, and while they seem at the beginning to be going in the right direction, the story very quickly turns bland and feel disconnected.  There's a lot of dialog that feels like its meant attach you to the other story characters in the game, but the dialog focuses on topics sometimes that don't even seem relevant to the game and that makes it feel forced, or like the game doesn't really know what it wants to do or say.  All in all the story matters little, the games about choppin up ships and choppin up these ships is fun as hell.  Wish I could bring a friend!

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of what I call "chore simulators," I will say even in Early Access, this game has strong foundations to be something genuinely brilliant... but it currently suffers from an identity crisis that leaves a lot to be desired.Like most "chore simulators," this game starts out extremely relaxing—a cathartic, at your own pace activity with a unique and visually wonderful setting. But within minutes, the game starts to punish you, adding in obstacles that continually frustrate your progress (oxygen - particularly early on), and puzzles that are only hard in that they are bewilderingly unexplained (cut guards).The game can't seem to decide whether it wants to be hardcore, forcing you to plan you every action methodically... or casual, allowing you to relax and do something rewarding.After 5 hours (and about halfway through the primary progression tree), I found myself both in love with and utterly frustrated with this game.But this game is Early Access, and with that is an extremely impressive platform with huge potential.I sincerely hope the game can find itself before launch, or at least add two clearly defined modes that are optimised for their desire behaviours.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall score: 9/10No, really. Hardspace: Shipbreaker is well thought out, with good in game progression, pretty great voice acting for the most part (there's a little bit of dialogue that's cheesy, but that's bound to happen in most games), great ship designs that overall feel pretty realistic, fluid gameplay that's satisfying and has just the right amount of challenge, fairly intuitive controls, an interesting bit of lore with fairly believable backstory, and the zero-g movement just feels right. I bought this when it was still in Early Access and missing some critical features, the catalog of ships wasn't very deep and they lacked some of the realistic, lived in feel they have now, you couldn't save progress on ships when you quit the game, you had to destroy more than I liked to salvage everything possible, and yet I still enjoyed it!Now that it's fully released and none of those problems are present, I can heartily recommend it without any caveats. Graphics: Solid 8/10. Some of the environmental textures get a little fuzzy up close, but you have to be looking for it. A few objects are very blocky when they ought to be round. Nothing that detracts from the experience.Gameplay: 9/10. There's really not much to compare this to. It's very much original and really satisfying to pull off some of the more complex maneuvers you can do. Only nitpicky thing I will mention is that there's still a handful of things that you HAVE to truly destroy in order to salvage important stuff. There used to be a lot of that, but they've done a great job of designing these ships.Soundtrack: 9/10. There's a fairly deep, original soundtrack that took a long time for me to get bored of. I did eventually get bored with it, but it has a great feel for quite some time.So, seriously, get it. Enjoy, and pay down that corporate debt to freedom!

_childDocuments_.review: This blends all the makings of a chill, relaxed-pace game but also has a fair amount of risk/challenge associated with how you work through a ship and how quickly you're able to break things down.  It's honestly a solid game and I like it a lot, but I wish there were some more granular options between the completely freeform sandbox mode and the limitations of career mode. It's by no means a hard game (honestly, it seems like it's hardest at the beginning before you get your upgrades) but I think it'd be better with the ability to mess around with the rules.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't leave many reviews, but the ending of the game brought such solid catharsis that I wanted to give the game creators support by leaving a review.This game is a gem.  It's a "small" game to be sure.  It isn't a huge budget.  But the people who made it poured a lot of love and soul into the game and it shows.  First, the MUSIC.  It is perfect for setting the tone and "flavor" of the story.  Good job to whomever lead that effort.Second, the story-telling, while not ground-breaking, is solid.  And the ending was perfect.  I didn't know it was possible to create catharsis in a game like this but son-of-a-gun they did it.  It's been a long time since I've finished a game and smiled when the credits hit.  They managed to take all of the tension of both the story and the game play and wrap a bow around it.  Too many game creators seem to rush the end with little thought.  This one conducted it like a symphony, leveraging one of the main NPCs to sum up the emotions of the story and leave us satisfied. Finally, the gameplay.  Now you may think it odd I end on this, but the truth is I'm at a stage of life that solid gameplay isn't enough for me.  I want it wrapped up in a well crafted story.  With so many game companies out there solid gameplay is a given.  It's the "spice" and "seasonings" of story that give it the flavor.  That said, the gameplay is fun.  Not ground breaking, but a neat experience that's worth the price.  There is a nice progression with new tech that develops. And some have commented that the core gameplay needed more.  But to be honest, the length of the game didn't justify expanding the core mechanics.  Thank to the devs, artists, and writers that made this little gem of a game possible.  I hope that the team behind this game makes more to come.  (Maybe even a "spiritual" sequel to this game. Where it is a different game just set in the same universe.)

_childDocuments_.review: The alarm goes off waking me from my slumber. Groggily I get up from my standard Lynx corporation rest and recuperation cot and hit the Lynx shift master 3.0 alarm clock. Some Lynx corp synthetic caffeine and space grown wheat biscuits and then I'm out the habitation shelter's airlock and off to work. The half disassembled wreck of a massive fuel hauler ship is right where I left it in the scrapyard. _childDocuments_.review: Extremely Satisfying. Time limit is a tad short per shift, but adds an urgency and much challenge. Maybe consider upgrades that increase shift time by small amounts? In the end, I believe 25-30 minutes would be optimal. Regardless, the game DOES have a free mode for pure satisfying dismantling, however, it strips the progress and sense of rushed danger. Still an awsome touch. There are not many games like this, especially none that do it so well, even with this being released in early access today. It is good, and can certainly be much greater over time. If the 15-minute time limit per shift (you can work over multiple shifts; you just pay bills along the way) scares you off, don't worry; it honestly does add urgency and challenge, which is honestly a very good thing. Maybe, just maybe, a tad longer but it honestly is a vital part of the game's challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: My last review stated that this game is amazing and a 10/10, but this game truly is flawed. The laser shoots where you point, but also collides with anything that goes into its beam leading up to the contact point. It gets very annoying considering how punishing accidentally blowing up a tank or cutting into an ECU line is. The story line could use some rework, its a bit dull. If they could add a skip dialog button that would be nice but its just not the best story in general. It has no mod support or workshop support which is pretty devastating considering that there are only a few base ships and can get boring. I feel like a game like this could REALLY get big if mods were allowed. Some of the ships are more of a pain in my ass to disassemble than it is fun due to you having to depressurize the area if you want to make a cut, and when you depressurize a room the doors to that room closes. Wish you could just go to the front of the ship and there could be a main depressurize switch or something to make it simpler. When these get fixed, rating would shoot to 9/10. With these inconveniences, 5.5/10. If you want a game to relax to, sometimes have be buggy and listen to space-themed music, I fully recommend waiting until its on sale. I don't often play anymore due to the bugs listed above but sometimes i come back and i just get annoyed.

_childDocuments_.review: Blackbird Interactive, who are the devs of this game, made Homeworld: Deserts of Kharak, which I remember reading was originally going to be called Shipbreakers. I believe many of the team came from Relic who made Homeworld. Stick with me if you can't yet see where I'm going with this.If the names Peter Elson and Chris Foss give you warm fuzzy feelings, buy this game without question. Likewise if the Terran Trade Authority books shaped your childhood dreams of a future among the stars. If you just loved the aesthetic of Homeworld and Deserts of Kharak, this is for you.If you like your science fiction blue-collar, hard-nosed with calloused hands, this is for you. If you can appreciate the irony of playing a computer game where you can and probably will die in a workplace accident doing extremely hazardous manual labour of the kind that currently happens on beaches in India, only you are in orbit with the Earth turning below you, buy this. If the powerlessness of being a tiny cog in a huge machine and the power of tearing apart huge machines with dangerous yet awesome machine tools are your jam, you need this. If you want to use your brain to figure the best way to squeeze as much value out of the ship you are salvaging, you'll pass enjoyable hours with this. If you want to play a game where the central conflict is with an uncaring system and the final boss is debt, here you go.It's great. Buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun.It feels very satisfying to chop apart spaceships with an incredibly powerful laser cutter. It has two modes: precise and slice the ship in half. The second mode is cool and fun, but unfortunately you can't control the width of the beam. Sometimes it's concentrated and just cuts a support. Other times it cuts the width of a panel. It looks like it's supposed to decide contextually, but what ends up happening is you bump into a beam, it knocks you a little to one side, and the ship gets cut in half including fuel lines that explode and kill you. I would really love the ability to choose the width, not have automatic sizing. Better yet, have a few different modes.The tethers are cool feature, but they're still a little bit buggy. Really neat idea, but they're too weak. They break constantly, get cut often, and seem to just evaporate for no reason sometimes. It also kinda sucks that you have a limited tether amount. Flying back to the refill area because you wasted all your tethers on a couple stuck pieces feels really bad.There're a few different ships, and each one has several variations, but be prepared to scrap the same ship a bunch of times. It seems like the first few times on a new ship, I blow it up or botch it in some other way, but then you start figuring it out and are able to the next one faster, and the next one. That's pretty fun.

_childDocuments_.review: The combination of puzzling through the inner workings of a ship to no blow something up, or at least to avoid damge to valuable parts, is really well made. In this game, you are a shipbreaker. A job in the near future, where you break ships appart and receycle them for three different types of valuable parts: The Furnace thakes slabs of aluminium and other raw materials that can be reforged.The Processor takes compound materials that can be reused.The Barge collects everything from chairs to computers that can be directly sold.To do you job, you have a graple gun to move stuff (upgradable with tethers for more efficient work), Laser cutter (point an line cut), demo charges (spark free! You understand it later) to break appart the harder cutting points, a scanner with three different modes (standard, object and system) and you space suit to move around and provide (limited) oxygen.The world building adds to a rich experience. You can find out a about how society has changed  (or not) in the next 500 years while expanding into the solar system. The ships are designed functional, so you have to check if the compartments are pressurized, to avoid cutting into them and cause explosive decompression, or cutting through a fuel line. It is very satisfying, if you manage to break appart a ship efficiently.I wish they will make more games in the same universe. I would like to see the jovian frontier, the asteroid mining operations, the Jupiter Gate.

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace Shipbreaker is a fantastically unique and interesting game. Its gameplay promotes a real sense of methodical flow, taking things apart piece by piece as neat as you can, trying to find the least damaging ways to break things where you have to, it's an incredible experience. There's also the experience of traversing these massive ships that you can slowly explore before taking them apart. Overall, I think it's incredibly well-realized in a mechanical and aesthetic way. I originally tried the game when it first entered into Early access, and my opinion of the gameplay then was much the same. I only spent a day or two with it, though, so that I could come back when it hit 1.0. In coming back to it I felt they'd greatly improved the variety of ships in the game (though it's still a bit limited overall, definitely better than it started though). They also added a story, and that's what got me to stay this time around. It's not some masterpiece of writing, to be fair, but it's not really trying to be. The characters feel genuine, like people I've worked retail or stocking jobs with irl, and they made me care enough about them that I wanted to continue onward. If I have a criticism I guess it's that you yourself have very little impact on the things going on around you, which is fair, it's not trying to be some massive, multiple-endings, branching-narrative-choice game here. At the end of the day though, it's a hopeful story, and a very human one, which is just what you need sometimes when your game is about being the slave of a crushing corporate machine.The game comes highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. I was searching around for a good chill game to play at the end of the day before going to sleep. I wanted something that requires focus but is not too execution or reflex heavy and that's where this game feels like a perfect fit. Unlike those Simulator series of games, this game has a lot more depth and polish to it I really appreciate. The core loop is satisfying as you move through space leveraging all your unique tools to dismantle, sort, and cut up each ship.As you progress into the game, the hazard level increases as more dangerous components are added and found throughout the ship to manage. For example, most ships will have pressurized cabins and sometimes the atmospheric control unit may be damaged or non-operational then it becomes a puzzle game to figure out what you can cut or depressurize so as not to cause a violent reaction damaging critical components.The story is decent, pretty straight forward without a lot of twists or turns but it was enough to be interested in seeing it play out. At some point you are gathering parts to repair a ship that plays into the story. While it's a functional system, it's a bit unsatisfying as it's all managed through menus. Would have enjoyed a system leveraging the salvaging mechanics to actually repair the ship in a more involved way.I've just about finished the story but feel like I'll continue playing it most nights to unwind before fully completing it.EDIT: This game does run decently on the steamdeck despite the "Unsupported" status. It runs as is just fine, maybe a little bit of a stutter on a fresh load for each effect: grappling, dismounting electronics, reactor meltdown starting, fire, electricity, coolant. After that, the rest of it runs very smooth.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a curiously soothing time-sucker of a game. Do make sure that you read through some of the community guides, and practice everything you can do in Free Play mode first: figuring out how to do things like use momentum to your advantage, mastering using your hands to grab on to surfaces, when to use precision cutting verse slicing walls willy nilly is worth the time to get a grip. The learning curve is just right, and the game never seems to throw anything at you that seems patiently unfair - it really is a matter of time and experience as you learn the best methods to "unravel" each of the major ships and their various sub-types...and also figure out which goodies are worth all the time, and when are the times where you just throw your hands and say "screw it" and toss the remaining half of the ship into the furnace. This feels like a really well fleshed out game already - the soundtrack is gorgeous, and is very reminiscent of the Firefly aesthetic - it's easy to imagine you're out in the black, trying to make you're way in the 'Verse, just another screwed over worker. I can't wait to see what develops as more and more content is added.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good. The game gives you a space ship to cut apart into bits that go into the red (metals), green (equipment) and blue (fancy metals) bins. You hack at the ship with a variety of tools for 15 minutes and then go home. The next day you can either go back to cut up more of the same ship, or take on a new ship. While you work, your oxygen supply and jet pack fuel deplete and you have some consumable tractor beams and explosives to manage. You can die, say, by accidentally blowing yourself up, setting yourself on fire, or falling into a furnace, but you generally won't and there's no significant punishment if you do. The more completely and cleanly you dismantle a ship, the more skill points you get to unlock upgrades for your tools. Each ship is given a total monetary value, e.g. $10 million, and you will get a few points for extracting $1 million from it, a higher reward for extracting the next million, and so on. extracting about 90% of the value gets you the largest reward and a little bonus. Over time, you are given bigger and more complicated ships that are harder to dismantle safely. Most ships will start having pressurised interiors that need to be vented first (most of which cannot be vented safely) and some components must be dismantled in particular ways to avoid explosions. The 15 minute time limit does enough to make you feel a little rushed - you won't want to end a session only moments away from earning the largest reward, because you then have to come back to the ship again the next day to mop up. In practice, there isn't actually any kind of punishment for taking you time though. The plot demands you make $500,000 worth of scrap each day to clear a debt, but it's almost impossible to fall short of that number and I assume there isnt even any punishment if you do fall short. So, if you want a leisurely cut-up-the-space-ship simulator to play with then this game works fine. The whole thing is generally very pretty and sounds good. I havent encountered any obvious bugs and had no crashes. Some of the mechanics arent really described very well, or at all - for example, you can slowly power down a ship and that will leave the airlocks and doors out-of-order, but this doesnt mean you can pull out electrical equipment without the danger of electrocution, but the game won't even explain what is powering the ship in the first place, let alone how that power is distributed and what it affects. So, you're going to die a few times to the game just not having a manual, but it's fine because there's no punishment for death. There is a plot, but it's pretty ropy and I mostly ignored it. It's the standard "little guy vs the big mega corporation" thing, but the big mega corporation is comically evil, while your fellow workers are super reasonable and sympathetic at all times. It can feel like those arguments you have in the shower with imaginary people, where you're so smart and reasonable and they are totally insane, and you win, and all the imaginary onlookers clap. There are some good moments, and it won't hurt you, and your character just listens silently to everything that happens anyway, so don't worry about it too much. Once the plot's over, the game just continues. I'll probably get another 10 hours or so out of it before packing it in.

_childDocuments_.review: May 2021: Keeps one on the edge of their seat. Fun game that gets confusing and complicated easily. Every new ship you try to dismantle gets you wondering how the hell are you going to do it. Many attempts later, you git gud.*EDIT* December 2021: I played in May and again now in December 2021. The game has changed quite a bit, in the sense that users are better trained on how to deal with each challenge, instead of just throwing you into the deep end. Very satisfying game and there is nothing else out there quite like this. There is also some story to it and not just slice and dice ships. The ships are amazingly designed, so well in fact you'd swear these ships will actually exist 100 years from now.Graphics are beautiful and the game play does a great job at immersing the player. The game feels very polished for an EA game. I haven't encountered any bugs.I'd highly recommend this game. It's beautiful, addictive, relaxing with intense moments.
