_childDocuments_.review: lets say, 7/10The core gameplay loop of cutting ships apart, trying to avoid damaging valuable parts, and getting every piece into the right bins as fast and efficiently as possible was a lot of fun. I think this might be the only have I've played with 6 axis of freedom that's fun to move around in. Definitely a game I could spend 100 hours on if sufficiently motivated.Unfortunately I WASN'T sufficiently motivated. About 3/4 of the way through the game, the main thing that was motivating me(getting out of debt) was removed, and I was just sitting there like "...I guess I'll stop playing then". I took the time to finish the story, but all that took was scrounging loose parts off ships, which only took me a couple hours. And I could've done THAT in 20 minutes if I didn't bother actually scrapping the ships and just focused on scavenging the parts I wanted, but I was looking for any excuse to continue playing the gameSo yeah, I liked the game, and I had fun pretty much the whole time. That being said, I did have a couple issuesThere's unskippable dialogue, which might not have been much of a problem if I'd had something to do and/or cared about the story. I did eventually get a little invested in the story, which honestly IS saying a lot for me, but it could've been done WITHOUT forcing me to literally sit listen to characters whining at me about things I don't particularly care aboutThe light political messaging was...fine, not particularly nuanced, but fine. My main issue was the world building didn't really make a whole lot of sense to me, because...well, let me explainSo, the Company is portrayed as comically evil in that corporate way: contracts that have ludicrously bad terms, massive debts being forced on you out of nowhere, the Company outright stating that it cares more about its equipment than your safety etc.The game SAYS all of that, and it seems to think it's clearly portraying a bad work environment, but - at least at the beginning - it seemed like a pretty sweet deal to me.While yes, you are $1.2 billion in debt, you're also making $5-10 million per shift. Even if you presume that these shifts are actually supposed to be 8 hour shifts, that still ain't bad. Also, presumably when you're done paying off your debt you could still keep working, making absolutely ABSURD amounts of money.But maybe there's some serious inflation in the future, and you're not actually making that much money, right? Well, for one thing that works both ways, as it would also mean you're not in nearly as much debt, but sure, lets assume that in today's dollars you were $1.2 million in debt and making $5-10,000 per day. Keep in mind that's meals and lodging included. I don't know about YOU, but I feel like that's a completely reasonable amount of debt to owe considering you could pay it off in a year and then just keep working and making money at the same rate.I get that there's issues like poor living conditions, sketchy rights abuses, and probably a significant lack of ways to amuse yourself, being out in space and all, but if you're trying to sell me on how evil this Company is, maybe don't make it abundantly clear that I could actually quite easily work my way out from all this debt and then leave. The biggest issue the Company had for me was just a lack of transparencyAnyways, good game, satisfying, kinda wish it was a bit longer, but still had fun

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker is a fantastic game about dismantling obselete and derelict spaceships. At its core, the game is about reading the architecture of a ship and how to dismantle it. It does this extremely well, even for early access alpha. There are full-priced games that release in far worse states than this. I am mainly writing this review to clarify for people afraid of having timers in this game: do not be afraid of this game. I started afraid at first, but I think this is because the game isn't great at communicating what's at stake in terms of the timer components.There are two timed components to any shift, your O2 meter, and your shift timer. O2 ticks down over the course of the shift, but can often be found inside ships you are working to top you off, and is easy and extremely cheap to refill at the Jack, which is like your base. If you are paying attention you will never run out of O2, it's just a way to get you to get out of the hull and come back with perhaps a new approach to the job.The shift timer is basically setting a 15 minute cap on your demolition, but all that actually means is you are paying an amount that can be decreased with time upgrades for a shift on the job. You can keep working on a job for multiple shifts. All you need to do is think in terms of efficiency, "how can I tear this ship apart cleanly, and quickly" is the name of the game. The only thing the timers ultimately penalize you with is debt, which is just a big red number that is more of a joke than anything. Upgrade currency is completely separate from this number, and you will always be able to finish a job even if it takes multiple shifts. The largest ships at Tier 6 take me a minimum of 3 shifts to knock out most of the work orders. Those ships are a lot of work!So if you see the timed component and turn off immediately, don't. It's not bad at all and has helped me learn how to get a job done quickly and cleanly, just like Lynx would want.

Don't get it all the first shift, you'll have to come back later or just select a new ship altogether. This makes it easier for small, quick sessions. It can get repetitive if you play long periods, but for the price its a nice little game in EA.

_childDocuments_.review: There are many games out there about building things. Whether its cities, vehicles, or structures, you can always put things together. There are even more games that have you destroying things intentionally or as a byproduct of combat. However, Hardspace: Shipbreaker is one of the first I’ve seen that has you meticulously taking things apart to save as many pieces as possible.Abbreviated Review: Shipbreaking is a real job that has workers descending upon retired ships to strip them of all useful or valuable parts before they’re fully destroyed. When a ship goes beyond its lifespan, it can cost more to repair or retrofit it than it does to build a new one from the ground up. Pulling the best parts out of these ships has been a worthwhile venture for as long as boats have been on the water.Hardspace: Shipbreaker takes this role into orbit. Yet, this time instead of a team of breakers swarming over the task, you’re a lone soul in a spacesuit with a couple of useful tools. Just like in the terrestrial version, the goal is to pull/cut/explode off as many valuable pieces of the spaceship as possible and put them in the correct area. Doing this will add to your end-of-shift payout as well as fulfill the various tasks on your work order – the goals for each ship.The breaking area, which I’m probably going to improperly refer to as a dry dock, has three types of salvaging repositories around it. Below you is a large flat barge, which is where you’re supposed to toss every fully functional part you find. Things like furniture, computers, engines, and even the valuable reactor. The second facility is the Processor where you send items that are made of the most valuable to be broken down. The final destination for everything else is the Furnace where metals are scrapped and melted down for the smallest payout.To facilitate this meticulous destructive process, you’re given two tools for the job. The tether gun allows you to grab specific items and pull them free from their mounts. It also can produce tethers that magically connect items and pull them toward each other. This is what you’ll use to get pretty most things from their location on the ship to their required processing area once cut free.Your other tool, the cutter, also has two modes. The first mode is a precision laser (Stinger) that heats and melts parts. You can use this in tight spaces without any fear of collateral damage. However, it will heat the tool and takes much longer than the “Splitsaw” mode at cutting through weak points. What you risk with the split saw is the potential for cuts that go beyond your intended range and damage other parts. Virtually every error I made in my time playing involved the Splitsaw in some way.These tools, as well as much of the rest of your gear, have several upgrades. The cutter can gain the ability to take more heat or cut further from you (which can be far more dangerous). The tether gun gets more pulling force and can hold more tethers. Even the scanning tool, with its somewhat limited use, has upgrades to allow it to have more modes and function further in your view. Upgrades to your suit give you more oxygen, movement capability, resistance to damage, and generally make the hurdles Hardspace: Shipbreaker puts in front of you a little easier to overcome.Hardspace: Shipbreaker is fun in a strange zen-like way. Methodically tearing up ships is far more fulfilling than blowing them up as you would in other games. Sure, you can accidentally blow them up, but that’s usually a bad thing (though doing it right can be effective). The seemingly insurmountable billion-dollar debt you start in and slowly chip away at a few million at a time adds another strangely rewarding feeling to the process. Trying to make as much money in every shift forces ingenuity in your efforts even when you don’t realize it.Yet the limitation of the shifts can be a bit of a problem. In early ships, you can knock out most everything in the 15-minute time limit. For larger ships, you’re revisiting three or four times just to fulfill the work orders. Finding efficient methods to cut ships apart can only go so far to resolve this, so it just feels like a chore reloading every 15 minutes. Couple that with crazy physics bugs (don’t try to pick up a fuse) and items being pulled into the wrong processing area and some big issues need to be resolved. On top of that, the UI isn’t particularly friendly and on PC currently has static keybinds that aren’t consistent across the menus.Despite those issues, the allure of zero-g space ship salvage drew me in. I’ve always loved salvaging in games so this was a must-play for me. It delivered most of what I expected and some things I didn’t even consider. Hopefully, the developers can work out the bugs and figure out a middle ground on the timer (which I do think is necessary in some form). I’d recommend this in its current form mostly for crazy sci-fi salvage-loving nerds like me.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically Debt Paying Simulator: Spaceship Edition, but the game itself is quite fun.The main HAB "UI" is rather clunky to navigate, but the rest of the game is quite responsive, and the story isn't bad, but can be mostly ignored if you don't care.Otherwise though, cutting spaceships apart and hurling the scrap into giant furnaces and processors is actually quite engaging.The 15 minute timer (per shift, and you can take as many as you want to finish salvaging a ship - but each time you do, you'll have to pay off some of that debt, so you have to ask yourself if it's worth it) is actually quite generous, especially as you get better at the game. You can just play the mode that disables it, but I find that far less fun and engaging.There's no real punishment for losing (except getting more debt) so I don't feel like the game is forcing me to finish in <15 minutes, which is quite hard to do - as most games with a timer fall into the "you'd better finish up fast or you're dead, boy!" category.Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who loves space and/or wants to toss some ship scrap around for funsies.

The mechanics are REALLY smooth for an early access game, and the visuals are gorgeous!You got yourselves a winner here!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game that continues to get better with each update. While it's not close to done yet, I'm still peeling onion layers of how to efficiently take ships apart and find new ways to do so 30 hours into the experience, and I've not seen every ship type yet!You can see that there's a lot to come - better system connections in ships, more interesting ship type puzzles, sub-systems and what they do - the developers have been great with communication and updates, so if that cadence continues, this will be a heck of a game once it's all said and done.If you don't mind relearning things as the ships get more complete / refined over updates, I'd say jump in now if you want what can either be a stress-inducing run of how fast you can get to the lucrative parts in 15 minutes, to a chill no-pressure puzzle game, this is a good one to go for, as it now offers both with the recent update.there's minor bugs, and some balancing on tools and rewards, but nothing that's detracted heavily from the experience - now that coolant and computers don't launch itself across the room at you! =)

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this on the most 'casual' of settings, infinite lives, no timer, no oxygen drain and having a blast. I can see the appeal in having some sense of urgency with managing your time and oxygen, but personally it felt like a shallow way to add complexity. Instead I play at a very relaxed pace while taking my time and really enjoying myself. Over the course of the campaign more types of hazards are introduced with different steps to handling them safely and this is what I have been really enjoying. It is incredibly satisfying to start with a large ship where I have to plan out my steps and then end with an empty bay.I highly recommend this to anybody looking for something where you take things apart. There's a lot of freedom in the settings and choices of ship(s) so in my mind this game is perfect from a more casual perspective all the way to a more competitive playstyle. The campaign is rough around the edges in presentation, but is otherwise a great way to get into the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy playing this game - when it works. Its a decent $10 game if you enjoy tedious yet simple 3d puzzles (sometimes I do!)I don't play anymore because: The story is *not good* and is tons of unskippable voice over. Whenever the game is updated, you have to restart your save file. And the story. When I first started playing this game, I really enjoyed it and looked forward to tons of content getting added - after a year, there was one (1) new ship model (three total) and they spent their entire budget on.. a really hamfisted, preachy story.Check out the steam discussions for more about that.Anyway, the actual cutting up ships is pretty fun and relaxing. I enjoy it. The physics are really, really buggy, but that can be fun to play with! Somehow there is fire and electric arcing in hard vacuum, so obviously this isn't a hard sci fi setting. In a way its like an interactive cartoon.Its always kinda cute to see how game devs in various simulation games will simplify concepts to make the game *actually fun*. Most devs seem to build on the real world, or real physics, or give some level of consideration to how the characters, world, and environment would interact with each other. These devs did not, so its.. a cartoon! Its great! But the game takes itself very seriously with a very stern story that I have yet to finish (the game crashes a lot and sometimes saves get corrupted!)

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid game here, whether you're looking for an explosively difficult speed-running challenge, or a more casual experience dismantling things. They've done a fantastic job with making sure everything feels like it's got appropriate mass, and the story that happens in audio snippets between scenes and outings is interesting. Looking forward to the story's completion and more ships being added to the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: The game is wonderful and feels extremely polished for being in early access. Even on launch day, this game seems to know exactly what it's going for.The chaos of salvaging a ship, keeping up with your oxygen and fuel, trying to beat your debt for the day, the shift lengths, all of it comes together in a very risk vs reward fashion: Do you try and clear this last piece of wreckage today with only a little oxygen and running short on time? Or do you take a loss on your quota today so you don't have to possibly pay the cloning fee if something goes wrong?All in all, 10/10 from me. I hope the devs continue to work and expand on the features and upgrades and challenges already present and hopefully add some new ones.Go buy this game if you're even only vaguely interested, it's phenomenal.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Only recommend if you can get it on saleObjective Gameplay: 8/10Controls: 6/10Physics: 5/10Story 2/10Art 7/10While I enjoyed this game and will continue to play it, there are some elements to it that were not properly communicated in the descriptions and marketing that probably would have stopped me from buying it. Overall I'm having fun, but due to steams all or nothing review style, I have to give this a not recommended at full price.Gameplay:As a simulator, gameplay mechanics should make up the majority of its value. Story is a bonus but simulation games are, at their core, about replicating a situation in detail for the player. Overall, Hardspace: Shipbreaker has solid core gameplay    Objectives: The core gameplay is pretty fun for a simulator, I’d give it an 8/10. Basically, you just tear apart a ship using a set of upgradable tools and sort the pieces into three categories (which are clearly labeled on each piece). It was very satisfying taking apart large ships methodically, coming up with plans for depressurizing compartments safely, or removing reactors before they melt down. In the career mode the progression feels good, the jobs become more complex as you go, but they retain elements of the simpler ships so every increase in difficulty felt like an upgrade to gameplay rather than leaving something fun behind for something slightly more fun. One con I would point out is that there are resources like O2 and thruster fuel that are basically pointless mechanics. To buy more costs so little it might as well be nothing and the place you buy is right next to the work area. Really all it does is interrupt your fun every couple of minutes with a blaring alarm, adding 0 difficulty to the game. My assumption is it's for realism, but it's just too low stakes to provide anything but 15 seconds of “well I guess I have to drop what I’m doing and fly over here for a second”.    Controls: The controls are ok, I’d give them a 6/10. You are in a 0G environment so you need three axis movement which can be a pain. The thrusters can be sluggish even with upgrades and reorienting yourself or navigating complex paths can be a chore. However you don’t really need rapid movements most of the time so this was not a major obstacle to enjoying the game and sometimes the stress of maneuvering added tension to the gameplay. I did really enjoy slingshotting around with the grappling tool, that was fun especially when I got the hang of it. I played with both controller and KBM, I personally would recommend controller but KBM is totally usable if that’s your preference.    Physics/Engine: The physics in this game could be pretty frustrating and probably my biggest gameplay complaint. I would give them a 4/10 or 5/10. For example to sort the pieces you need to move them into zones, there are two that are directly side by side where you put the largest pieces. The zones pull things automatically when they get close, but the pull zones overlap so with the largest pieces they can get stuck between the two zones and they are a HUGE pain to get off. This game also has a time limit on each shift so you waste a bunch of time trying to unstick bits. Another common issue is you pull off a piece from the ship and it flings back and hits you like a rubber band which sends you flying into space. If you’re still holding the piece that momentum is transferred and hits you again, rinse and repeat. Story:    I’m just going to be blunt, the story is bad, and it's a huge downer 2/10. You’re basically a space debt slave working for the most cringe heavy handed dystopian corporation. If you work a long day at a real corporation and want to come home and relax, this is not the game. Now that alone isn’t really the problem. The problem is that this is a simulator game, and when the story scenes start (and there are A LOT) it locks you into the homebase and you can’t do anything. You can’t start your shift, can’t upgrade your tools, can’t skip, just gotta sit through some heavy handed social commentary written by a teenager. The characters are all one-dimensional cliches. You’ve got the grizzled father figure, the nervous goodboy with a hard homelife, the tough-as-nails lady with a soft spot, and the most overplayed, crusty crab, greedy middle manager type.  Also the characters are just annoying oversharers. If you work in an office you know that one guy, and they are all that guy. The bad story isn't a big deal since it's a simulator, but forcing the player to sit through a bunch of unskippable dialogue made those scenes go from story to gameplay, and when all you want to do is dismantle some ships it feels incredibly out of place and just huge drag.Art:     Nothing groundbreaking, but the designs are thematically consistent and interesting. I honestly didn’t think about it too much but it has a 1979 Alien feel to it which worked well I would say. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is just... stupid fun. Have you ever wanted to tear apart old, broken down ships and salvage the valuable components, working long hours under extremely hazardous conditions with minimal benefits for an evil corporation all so you can pay off a crippling debt? Yeah, neither have I. But in a few days I logged a TON of hours doing just that.It's the far future. Everyone has a space ship. Space ships break down. What do you do with them? Well, they get sent to the salvage yard, naturally... and at that salvage yard are people like you, who are hoping to strike it rich performing one of the more dangerous jobs in the universe: tearing apart ships for salvage. You work for a fairly evil corporation that doesn't even try to hide how little it values your life ("Warning... asphyxiation can lead to missed salvage quotas" "Warning... excess CO2 can cause damage to LYNX equipment") and you're literally a billion dollars in debt. You go out, work your hardest during your shift to haul in as much valuable salvage as you possibly can... Congratulations! You pulled in two million dollars with of salvage! ...minus loan interest, minus tool rental fees, minus habitation fee, minus utilities, minus... well, you get the drift. It's a little like the real world... Great work, buddy - now we'll take our cut. (And it doesn't help that ANYTHING you need to complete your job... you've got to buy from vending machines on site.)Sound intimidating? Like something you don't want to do?Actually it's AMAZING. You learn the ships. You learn the cut points. You learn what's valuable, and what's... well, you could go for it, but is it really worth the extra thousand bucks? Eh. Chuck it into the processor and see how much you can make out of it.Along the way you have to deal with all kinds of hazards. What is the SAFEST way to extract that engine, without blowing yourself up? (After all, LYNX will remind you that if you die, your productivity levels will dip below acceptable levels.) How exactly am I going to get that unstable reactor out and into the salvage barge? First I need to clear a path... then I need to follow some safety steps to make sure it doesn't blow something else up... Ok, GO!!! EXECUTE PLAN!! GET THE REACTOR OUT!!! FOR GOD'S SAKE GET IT IN THE BARGE!!!It's absolutely beautiful (and fairly comedic in a grim way). Crawl around in the guts of ships, cutting certain points so you can loosen up outer plating or massive support beams... Pull out valuable items to chuck into the barge.. And for God's sake BE CAREFUL about opening up something that is pressurized into a space that is NOT pressurized!!I really also appreciate the way this game captures the feel of the scale of things. In a lot of games where you're dealing with "massive" things, you end up getting this feel that you're playing with little toys. For example, another favorite game of mine is Farming Simulator 2019.. Well, if you're out of one of your tractors, you can get a feel for how big the things around you are... sort of... But when you're driving them, you feel like you're playing with toy cars. Not so in this game... Not sure what exactly it is, but you always get a feel for the enormity of what you're doing - when you tether a massive side panel to get tossed into the processor, it really does feel like that side panel is absolutely enormous. When you're pulling out the huge fuel tank from a Javelin-class ship... you really do have the feel that you've got to "get out of the way," because it's an enormous item.Game also has a really quirky, grim, morbid sense of humor. I absolutely LOVE the heartless LYNX corporation. I will literally read the emails out loud to my girlfriend and we get a laugh out of how awful... and yet somehow true to life... it is. Trying not to reveal more than necessary - it's a riot.That, and it really IS pretty much "your call, cut it as you see it." I mean sure, there are a few types of metal you can't cut... But if you're short on time on your shift and you need to extract a few valuable components from a room? Cut a hole in the wall. Just do it. Get that stuff out - your work time is valuable, and all your fees are due every single day.I see some negativity about the lack of variety in ships... well, right now I guess there aren't a TON of ships... But this game is turning out to be like pizza for me: you can eat pizza, several different kinds of pizza, until you're sick of it. But at the end of the day, you're GOING to eat pizza again, because why would you NOT. Each time is so great. Same with this game... I could cut up the same exact thing a thousand times in a thousand different ways. I imagine at some point I'll take a break from it... but this is one of those games i KNOW I'll be back for. (Don't worry - there isn't such a small variety that you'd lose interest fast. There's plenty of different ship designs... and remember, these puppies are ENORMOUS... so you could find a million different ways to cut 'em up, each time getting a little more efficient.)Final verdict: mega recommend. For being "early access" I've only had a couple crashes.. and for being early access there is a LOOOOOOOT to this game. You will NOT get bored of this quickly. (I would even recommend this game full price.)Do it, you won't be sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: at the bottom this is a bit of long review. I'm an Early Access buyer and the end result was disappointing.To explain the disappointment I need to explain what I thought I was buying. When I bought the game there was a general premise. You were a ship breaker, in a salvage yard in the relatively near future. The game play loop was that you had to take apart space ships in various states of disrepair with different tools. You had to think ahead, plan how the disassembly would go for maximum profit, and, of course, not blow up and die. Essentially the game was a 3D puzzle with a equipment upgrade grind. Overall the world was fun with a simple goal, you were 1 billion dollars in debt with the mega corporation, Lynx, that run the facility. Sounds bad but after your first few ships you're making multi million dollar days. So you can pay it off after 90 or so game rounds. Lynx was tongue in cheek evil to explain game mechanics, IE making you buy extra oxygen, or pay for repairs to your equipment, or paying for clones if you die, etc. There was even a bit of an in game world building where you were finding data disks that brought up the history and recent developments of the in game world. There was even hints of an AI rebellion brewing out beyond Jupiter.When I got the game there was two ship classes and two variants of each and there was promise of a lot more.  With a lot more tools to discover and new hazards to be added to figure out. There was even talk of having a ship creator mode so you could upload to the workshop and have player made ships to take apart.That's what was suppose to happen.What really happened was that there seemed to be a change mid stream where it wasn't about the game anymore. It wasn't about the ships or the puzzles. It was about "The Message". The Dev's, for whatever reason, decided that there needed to be a more structured story, even though no one asked for it. From that point on additional content seemed to slow to a crawl. They added two additional ship classes an additional variant to each class, and an extra hazard was added but that is far from the initial goals of the game. This is over the course of two plus yearsIf you're wondering what "The Message" was it came down to a grade school rendition of unions good, corporations bad, rise up, fight the power. You are drafted into a proto union, (you literally have no choice), to fight the now cartoonishly, mustache twirling, evil Lynx. I mean, OK, Sure, Fine, Whatever, but it is so heavy handed, it's like taking a two by four to the face and then having a cinder block dropped on you just to make the point. To top it off, and why I'm so salty about this, you are completely railroaded into the story. I mean it's so bad that you are literally tied down to the train car and forced on rails to the end. You have no say, no agency. You can not influence or affect the story in any way. The story isn't even about you, you are a minor side character to the main character. I mean there are games with silent characters that follow a story script, Link, Master Chief, Doom Guy, etc. where you don't talk or barely talk but people are reacting to what you do, what you put into motion. Here? Here you're completely removed from the action, the choices. What you do doesn't matter. The hilarious thing is that the Dev's are just as authoritarian and heavy handed in forcing you to hear "The Message", completely disregarding around a year of people telling the they didn't like it, introducing such 1 and 2 dimensional characters, with grade school level understanding of business, that they actually make Lynx seem like a reasonable organization half the time despite how they act in game. There are times where you go, "Well, Lynx does have a point".Last thing. Don't take my hours played as a sign of the game I finished in about 8-10 hrs. They restarted progress multiple times during development and you have to grind to get to the new content. Plus I did try to clear my debt in one play through. On top of that, I think they made the game easier. And because you can now 'win' the game, a lot of the drive to go so long and clear the debt is now gone.So TLDR: The game has good game play, graphics, and music, but the Dev's decided to get preachy and focus on a "Message" instead of game play and content. There is between half to a third of what ship classes was originally scoped, there is no planned ship creator, no planned workshop addition, and the challenge of the game seems to have been watered down. If you can get the game for what I did $10-15 it's worth it if you can deal with the 'story' but avoid if it's not on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: To talk about Hardspace: Shipbreaker, you have to understand that there are two things going on simultaneously.The first, is the game itself. The actual gameplay of taking apart ships, sorting them into their various components, and turning them in for profit. This part is good. It's a pleasant experience, and the time in EA has made it relatively polished for how much physics is going on (there's still some wonkiness, but that's going to happen with any physics game). I don't have too much to say, but that's praise. It feels good, it's fun, it's a good experience all around. Second, we have the story. The story is basically a visual novel, and is presented as other characters expositing at you in one of four ways: Before/after the shift, in e-mails, or over comms during the shift. If you don't particularly want to listen to the exposition, sorry you have to listen to the before and after shift messages. I didn't find a way to skip them. At least the comms during a shift can be mostly tuned out while you actually play the game. The plot itself is okay. Evil megacorporation is bad, unions are good. Some of the human moments are touching and sweet, some of them are really boring because it's stopping you from playing the game.So, the story's ok, and the game's good. But there's one big problem: They don't match. They don't fit together. Most of the story revolves around corporate and managerial malfeasance. However, this malfeasance (almost) never touches the player. You're faced with "extortionate fees" of over 500,000 credits per day. Of course, you can make over 10,000,000 (ten million!) credits per day. So these extortionate fees are... maybe 5-10%? That's less than people pay in real-world taxes! But you don't get that money, it's just paying off a debt, of course. A debt of about 1.2 billion credits. So at a pace of ten million credits per day, it would take around 120 game days (or approximately 30 real-world hours) to pay your debt. If we compare this to real world student loans... um... find me someone who paid off their student loans in 120 days. I'll wait. The training (tutorial) provided to the player is more than adequate, even though we're told that other characters weren't getting sufficient training. Other characters struggle with faulty equipment, but everything provided to the player runs perfectly fine. The game gets harder at progressive points, which are laid out perfectly clearly ahead of time under "certification progress." But when you hit those points, the story acts as though you're being forced to progress. All of this creates a feeling of ludonarrative dissonance -- the unpleasant feeling when the narrative doesn't match the feelings evoked by gameplay. It's far harder to buy into the story and believe that times are tough when you're making money hand over fist.However, all this said, I still recommend the game. The core game is absolutely fun, and the feeling of progression is well-tuned. It's just a darn shame that the narrative is so divorced from the actual game.

_childDocuments_.review: Crawling around inside, outside, and through ships slated for demolition is satisfying. Pluck off the low-hanging fruit - the sensor towers, the masts, the thruster nacelles. Then go looking for the structural ties that hold the outer hull on. Peel the ship carefully, so you don't destroy the valuable components or smash your helmet with a fast moving hull plate. Cut into the soft inner hull (don't cut a pressurised fuel line!), and remove the furniture and consoles. Yank the reactor for the big payday. Then consign the metal to the furnace. Return to your hab and watch your indenture loan tick down minutely. You're not getting out of this debt quickly, but that's okay. Tomorrow is another shift. Another ship. There's always another ship.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write very many reviews but it is not often I see a game in early access that I can't wait to start playing even before 1.0 release. Every major update I dove back in to see how the polish was coming along and when they started putting in the story I grew anxious for full release day. A fantastic game to just chill and pass an hour or so in just cutting a few ships while listening to some tunes and it has a solid story that anyone who has worked or had family that has worked under the boot of their company can empathize with. Each character was well fleshed out and you had a good idea as to their personality and what kind of experiences they've had in life.  Even though  I've beaten the game.. I know I'll be back to vibe and cut again.. and possibly hear a few random lines from my fellow cutters as they go about a days work. My ONLY gripes with the game are.. Physics seems to get confused during decompression so whole sections of a ship will yeet the ♥♥♥♥ off in the direction the atmosphere is venting out (Which is not how physics works.) Doing a "1 life run" seems to be impossible in the games current state because there are some moments you will just flat out die instantly. Like cracking open a Quasar Engine after venting the fuel (When it splits down the middle.) I've died instantly after flipping that switch a few times now.. when there should be nothing at all that can crush me. So that's frustrating. Oh.. and it seems like the devs have gone out of their way to make it impossible to safely depressurize ships 100%. If you remove doors the atmosphere regulators just shut off.  So no matter what you do you are going to eventually have to "blow" out the atmosphere in a ship unsafely.. which risks the "Yeet". Feels like it takes some agency away from us to actually solve the problem with minimal risk.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 such an amazing space based story game. Ship breaker is essentially space capitalism where you are in indebted servitude to an mega corp called LYNX. Throughout the game you basically just break ships apart and sort the parts into 3 separate areas. However the level of detail in the way you are required to dismantle these ships makes it far more interesting than you might expect. The higher your level the higher class of ship you can dismantle. You also get points to upgrade your tools and you level also dictates what upgrades are available to you.The sound track in this game, the theme's of it are very similar to cowboy bebop in the sense that they are very space western. It works so well for this game seeing as you, the main character are the working class and it is a bit of a work sim.I will say, especially on the later end of the game it does get a bit grindy and repetitive. I know as well other people who got the game in early access were not as pleased as I was that it went in a more story orientated direction. But if you are looking for a cool space based fun puzzle game/job sim with a interesting and immersive story I would 100% recommend this game

_childDocuments_.review: I feel weird giving it a negative review, because I think the gameplay can be really well designed and fun. What I have an issue with is everything around the gameplay. I played through for my first time on the limited lives mode to make things more interesting for myself. I feel the rate that you unlock new ships means you get very little time to actually learn how you can better dismantle the ships you have. The other characters in the story feel they serve very little purpose, when they could be used to help show you how to more efficiently dismantle ships by seeing how they do it. The story is very anti-corporate, but it's typically when corporate steps in and micromanages that the gameplay becomes more fun or interesting. I feel the game would be a lot better if they scaled back on what they wanted to accomplish with the game, but I'm not sure if it would be the same game if they did. I walk away from the game not really having any deeper thoughts on the game other than 'man this could have been something great'. I would leave a 'mixed' review, because I don't think it's a bad game, just perhaps not worth the time you have to invest in it.

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker is a game all about salvaging as much as you can, from now defunct spacecraft.The lovely thing about the game is the freedom you have with your tools and canvas, as well as the relaxing atmosphere.You've got a cutter, which allows you to either use a focused beam to destroy connections between walls, freeing them up.Or you can switch to its alternative mode, which is a Dead Space-esque plasma cutter with either a vertical or horizontal line. You can use this to cut literally anywhere you want on soft metals. This means you can be as efficient or inefficient as possible, ranging from cutting one beautiful big square off a wall, or dicing it up into hundreds of pieces.Some metals are too strong for your cutter, which is where you'll need to get into the ship through other means, and then dislodge the bolts holding the wall in place. It's actually a lot of fun figuring out how to approach each ship. The ideal way would be to go through the airlock. If you activate it properly, this will depressurise the ship, and allow you to enter safely. If you fail to do this, and instead, say, cut a hole right into the ship, it will depressurise violently, and launch you alongside any cargo on the inside. This is bad because, first, you can die from a savage impact against a wall in your station. Or two, you damage goods that you could have salvaged, which puts a dent in your income (which I'll go further into later).Once you've gotten in successfully, and dislodged walls, you have a few options.The first would be to use your energy grabber, which allows you to manipulate objects from a distance, provided they are light enough. You throw them into the right container (furnace, processor, barge), and get a reward.If they're too heavy though, you'll find that grabbing them with your tool will pull you towards them instead.This is where tethers come in. They're super fun tools that allow you to attach objects to each other. Depending on the angles, and weight of them, you might have to put multiple tethers, which allows for some fun playing around with physics.Once 15 minutes have passed, your shift is over, and you return to your home in space. This is where you can use your earned tokens to purchase upgrades for your gear. This includes increased range, faster thrusters, increase oxygen timers, etc.Most of them are just number increases, nothing super interesting.Once you're done, you pick your next ship to work on (or continue the one you were using before), and start your next day.  That's the main loop!The game is so incredibly relaxing, despite some of the dangerous encounters you can get into. The music is some chill country guitar, and floating around feels peaceful. You can actually reach out with your hands to grab onto walls to stop yourself from floating around, and can even crawl around if you alternate your hands.The game becomes more intricate when you want to maximise your money earnings. You'll want to pick apart as many pieces as possible. For example, instead of throwing the whole back of the ship into the processor, because the majority of it requires that, you will instead go in, pull off some lamps, chairs, throw them into the barge, then get some beams and put them in the furnace, and THEN put the rest in the processor. You start to feel like you are really mastering the job.My problem with the game lies here though: The forced limitations get in the way. The 15 minute shift timer is not that fun, and just forces you to rush towards the end of your shift. On top of that, your tethers and oxygen are limited, and need refilling often. It's not a huge deal, because you can fly over to the outside of your home and refill on that stuff quickly, but it breaks the flow, and forces you to be conservative in an unfun way. I would be all for limiting how many tethers can be active at once, but the system implemented just impeded the fun for me. You can upgrade all of this stuff to allow you to carry more, but it just felt tedious until that point. It's not a dealbreaker, but it does force you to take 30 second breaks every now and again when you might not necessarily want to.There is fortunately a freeplay mode where you can pick a ship and do exactly the same thing, minus all the limitations, but the only issue there is you lack the feeling of overall progression in the career mode.Speaking of Career mode, the story is that you work for Lynx. Trying to work off your 1 Billion dollar debt! Unfortunately for you, they also charge you for renting all your tools, accomodation, and even add interest on top of that. It's actually a subtle, but silly little world that the game is based in. You can also find some lore based tapes and such, for those interested in that.Overall, I love the game. I think there are issues with it in its current state, like not properly explaining some mechanics, and being rough around the edges sometimes, but in the end its a lot of fun disassembling stuff, and I recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: Nothing like stripping a hulk for a hard days work. This game can almost be called a survival except you get to go home at the end of the shift. Nice progression through the levels, however it does appear a little fast at times. Perhaps something to be balanced. I can't wait to see what else gets released. Currently a solo game, you can race people on the web for the fastest time to process a ship. I would like to see full multiplayer implemented. This will allow the deconstruction of truely mammoth ships. A new zone might need to be created or perhaps a mobile processing ship that can be moved around a much larger ship.TLDR: a fun game worth at least 10 hours of game play and its only a beta.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the idea of being upside down, while spinning in zero-g and trying trying to grasp a slab of titanium as big as a barn door. Using an electromagnetic kinetic gun to shoot the slab into the correct processing bay then this game is for you.However this isn't a bloody fps where one man takes on an army. The only blood you'll see while ship breaking is your own as a result of you slicing through a metal bulkhead into a pressurised room. Leaving you with a whole in your body the exact shape of a computer terminal.This is when you realise that in space no one can hear you scream, gasp, gurgle, beg or pray before everything goes black.

_childDocuments_.review: Lynx Corporation (aka Weyland-Yutani Corp) exists in a dystopian future, where mankind has colonized the solar system and Earth is a scorching hot, polluted, bio-adverse hellhole. You work as an employee of Lynx, living and working on an orbital space station, bound by an enormous debt to a life of indentured servitude, spending every waking moment salvaging old vessels, like a sort of space womble with a frikkin' laser beam. Sounds great, doesn't it? Oh, and one more thing; you can't die. Well, that is to say you CAN die, over and over again, as if Bill Murray made Groundhog Day 2 with a space based protagonist. Problem is you have to pay to be reanimated, and it gets added to your tab. It's the same for absolutely everything else; you have to pay for everything and to begin with can barely make a dent in your debt!So far I have been really enjoying this game, and I felt the need to share. The physics of weightlessness is fun, as is being crushed by titanium bulkheads, or ejected by an explosive decompression. There is a learning curve and the keyboard commands can be a little clunky (seems to be no support for my Rapoo game controller anyhow), but the game does reward you when you get it right. It has the Euro Truck Simulator of "this shouldn't be enjoyable but somehow it is" vibe going on, and it's still only Early Release. DO youself a favour and buy it now! TL;DR - space wombles with laser beams and a massive overdraft attempt to unionize and take down giant megacorporation.

_childDocuments_.review: This game SUCKED... at first. When it was released it was in such poor shape and had some game-breaking and corrupting bugs that I would have given it a 1/10. However, the game has had a few updates and finally feels like it was worth the money all that time ago. There is a sufficient curve in difficulty that the game actually maintains some challenge in later ships and there are just enough features to be enjoyable without being too much. I can honestly say that this is a really chill game most of the time and it worth it to just relax and take your time tearing apart a ship in "anti-puzzle" type levels. I even went so far as to record a few teardowns for my YouTube channel. Check it out if you'd like to see me REALLY screw up this game. (Not all episodes are currently up)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game, based purely on the premise.  I think they got several things wrong, probably in the name of meeting player expectations.  First, It bugs me that the speed of an object decays over time.  In reality, an object in motion with no atmosphere present will continue to move at the same rate until it encounters some friction (an atmosphere or another object). Second, the atmosphere venting mechanics are ridiculous.  I find it very tedious that you can't vent the atmosphere of an entire ship by opening all the doors inside the vessel, and then using just one panel to suck the air out.  Instead, the game closes all the open doors, and only sucks the air out of one room.  When I cut out the doors, the atmosphere vents stop working altogether.  I know this was probably done for the sake of gameplay, but I find it ridiculous that this simple approach doesn't work.  Also, in this day in age, why in the world wouldn't you be able to save and exit the game during a salvage job?  Seriously?Gripes aside, it's a fun game.  The story is pretty lame, but the moment problem solving keeps it interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent game but don't bother playing the "No Revivals" difficulty.Random physics bugs will send the ships spinning, meaning instant death if you're inside of them.Dying results in a reset where you're forced to watch the same unskippable, flat, boring """cut-scenes""" over and over again.At least the game gives me the option to mute voice audio so I can tab out and do other things while that garbage plays on in the background.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun solo experience where you take apart old spaceships. Good graphics, immersion, and sound design.Warning that content and support for this game seems to have stopped cold after its full release. Once you finish the short story mode, all there is to do is keep taking apart the same ships.The story is interesting, but pretty cookie-cutter and entirely linear. Most of the story focuses on your role as an expendable worker in an anti-union corporation. There are sometimes corrupted/alien AI infecting the ships, but that plot goes nowhere and is just another style of hazard in the ships.Once you are familiar with the small variety of ships, it's sort of a relaxing way to zone out and feel like you're accomplishing something.

_childDocuments_.review: Great graphics, interesting gameplay, relaxed pace. I was enjoying it until it crashed, twice, within the first 2 hours. Given that this is an early access game, some bugs are expected, but game-breaking bugs like that need to be fixed before I can recommend it. I look forward to checking back at a later date to see if these issues have been ironed out.Edit: Since this review, the game has continued to get support from the devs, including numerous bug fixes. I'm not sure my specific issue has been addressed yet, but the progress indicates that this should be a relatively safe buy, so I'm changing my review to a recommend. _childDocuments_.review: It first, I wasn't impressed by the game...then I played it a second time and it made sense why it was a decent game....then by the third time I discovered that I had put hours into the game and was having lots of fun.  This game addicts you to the 'zen' mindset of comfortably organizing something, while taking things apart.  It tickles that OCD itch in several ways, and I find it extremely relaxing.  The ships increase in difficulty and complexity, so the gameplay doesn't stagnate.  The controls feel right, and the physics are good enough to feel like objects have different weights and density to them.  The game is still in development, but it feels solid enough to recommend now to anyone who can enjoy tearing something apart as much as building or organizing things.  The tutorial just gives you the basics, but there are a few other things I wish it included, such as using your hands to grab onto things/move/stop movement, using the grapple reel to pull objects to you or move towards objects, and what a Utility key or a patch kit is, and when/why you may need them.  That said, I don't see myself putting this game down any time soon, especially since new things are still being added.

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this game, it provides a challenge and does not force you into any particular order or technique for salvaging a ship as a whole. Yes, I would like the procedural generation for the ships to be more detailed and the campaign/story to have fewer "annoying" quirks, but all in all, if salvaging ships in space is something you want to do, it is a very good game. I would personally recommend waiting for the game to go on sale for $15-$20 because $35 feels a bit steep imo.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: The game designed around killing you in fun and explosive ways forces you to redo 30+ minutes of salvaging if you die. The same happens if the game crashes. Which it did at least once every 30 minutes.You will even lose progress if you end your work day, return to your habitat, cash in your salvage and then exit to the main menu and close the game. The next time you log in you will be back in the previous work day with an unsalvaged ship and no money banked.There are so many ways to lose progress in the current build.This is exacerbated by the fact that the game doesn't do a great job at explaining what you need to do. My only deaths were from putting things in the wrong place and the company shutting my life down. Great, so you didn't tell me where to put this antenna I guess I'll try to blue light bay? Dead. Ok, the furnace to melt it down? Dead .... um.... Oh, there's a green net over there, is that it? Now do that with a reactor that it takes 30 minutes to pry out of a hull where you'll have to start from scratch if it blows up or you put it in the wrong place?It's frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is relaxing and challenging at the same time. I LOVE space and the graphics and physics really help with the immersion.What REALLY makes it immersive (and both hilarious and depressing) is the fact that you're working off a massive debt and after every salvage run there's an itemized list that reminds you that you're renting equipment, paying fees and interest. Kids! This is a space-based RL simulator. It's EXACTLY like having to pay off crippling student loans, rent, utilities, and other things while working a job that barely makes ends meet.... and I love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker is one of those games you will either love or hate. It's not going to appeal to everyone, and that's OK.If the idea of breaking up spaceships is your idea of fun, then it has you covered. The story feels a bit hamfisted in and some of the dialogue is... not great, but reduce it to reducing ships and your work-related debt and there's plenty of hours of entertainment to be had here. It's decent graphically and for those of you so wondering, is a great experience on Steam Deck. (90% of my playtime is on-deck play)Campaign is a good 30+ hours, depending on your shipbreaking ability.A good chill out game for those who like to kick back and play at their own pace.Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: A rare example of a game that was incredible on release in Early Access and subsequently got worse with every update. The reason for this is a complete misunderstanding as to what made the game great.Out of the gate, you had a brief 2 minute prologue in your awful, cramped, noisy apartment, and reading a tablet with a couple text blurbs that describe how gross and awful the in-game world is. This was a fantastic opening and communicated everything that was needed to be said about the world. You were then thrust into a very satisfying and chill gameplay loop where you break apart ships, with no NPC chatter, making for a very relaxing experience.Then, with each subsequent update, rather than focusing on the incredible core gameplay loop and adding more ships, they focused on story. You have NPCs chattering in your ear constantly with poorly written dialogue. You have to watch unskippable cutscenes between missions. You have a story that really isn't good or interesting or say anything new. Corporations are bad. All they needed to do was add more ships for you to break apart, as the game is called "Shipbreaker". Instead they invested in a really mediocre story, rather than the core gameplay loop.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun and chill game, when you're not exploding that is. Go to space, put on your space suit, and strip ships down into manageable parts to salvage and get loads of money from it too. As you get to bigger ships the challenge and puzzle increases. How do i normalize the pressure here? What do i cut to split this safely? This game is a lot of fun, has great music to chill to, and good tongue in cheek humor to make a really great game.Kobold recommends

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I didn't have to put a negative review on this game but I sadly feel like I need to, especially so others can see why.This game is pretty good, and by game I mostly just mean the gameplay. The ship selection is small but there still feels like there is enough to at least hav ea couple dozen of hours of replay before it gets boring. Some people have mentioned the concept art ships for this game and yeah, they're neat, but some could have just been over ambitious to be added to this game and the system it runs on. The biggest issue with this game is the story. The story isn't one with a bad theme, but one that just doesn't add anything to the table that hasn't been said. The game takes on a whole "aren't bad corps bad?" message with nothing else to it. Comically evil suits and vigilante saints. The other issue with the story is that in the campaign, you have no means to skip dialogue or cutscenes. Some cutscenes or dialogue strings go on for a long period of time and it doesn't help that they just repeat the same thing each time with your controls taken away so you are forced to hear what they say.There's more I want to say about my issues with the story but I know i'd spend too much time ragging on it so I'll just leave it as it. It's just sad since that's really the only big issue with the game.TL;DRFine game, terrible story

But after a while of playing in the revamped version, the developers political ideology was self evident and the more it was levered in to the game, the more it became a distraction and worse, an entirely unnecessary distraction.I've had this game for ages and have given a good shot both before the major revamp (pre-ideology) and post and whilst i was able to ignore the blatant political activism, sadly this evening I actually got fed up enough to close it down and write this.  Quite sure there will be those on here finger wagging about this but i play games to escape reality and chill out. i don't play games to have certain ideology rammed down my neck.  you have my money already and there isn't a lot i can do about that hence you can have a negative response instead. _childDocuments_.review: It's a fun grind! It's not a linear game that holds the player's hand all the time. You choose the ship and the game presents you with a few items to salvage for experience and upgrades, but beyond that you can recycle whatever you want, in any order, and in any way you want for money. You can be careful and dismantle everything down to the smallest detail, or you can just go crazy and start cutting structures to salvage only the most valuable items like reactors and leave behind what isn't profitable.The microgravity movement is part of the game's challenge because there are many degrees of freedom compared to walking on the ground, but after a while it became natural for me and I was flying around at high speeds. Sometimes things go wrong, I collide at high speed and damage my helmet, get sucked into the furnace, I make mistakes when cutting and the fuel tank catches fire, or the nuclear reactor takes a hit and leak radiation. It's all part of the fun of the game.Currently, there are only 3 classes of ships in the game, but they have a lot of variety and in my 20 hours of gameplay, none of them were identical. Despite being in early access, it feels like a complete game and I didn't feel like anything was missing. I only experienced one crash and one audio bug.The negative point is the size of the shipyard, which is very cramped, and the game doesn't save the progress of the ship being dismantled when you leave. I was a bit disappointed with the short turn time (15 minutes), but it's an incentive for the player not to waste time being meticulous.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed shipbreaker and its physics based zero-g slavery gameplay. Systematically tearing a ship apart and sorting all of its bits is incredibly satisfying, as is breaking out the high explosives when I realise there is 1 minutes left in my shift and that big lump of aluminium that used to be the crew quarters isnt floating into the furnace fast enough. The tight time limit on your shifts promotes setting goals for yourself for each shift, and as you improve both as a player and unlocking tool upgrades the speed and scope of these goals organically increase. When I started I was carefully taking bits and pieces off of a small ship one by one, but by the time I was done the campaign I was tearing through freighters like tissue paper and I feel that sense of tactile improvement is one of this games greatest strengths.    Story wise it tells a small personal tale of a group of workers trying not to allow their corporate overlords grind them into paste in every sense of the word. If I had one complaint its that LYNX corp and its affiliates are so cartoonishly evil sometimes its honestly distracting. Like they may as well be drowning puppies in the space river while telling you how its actually good for them with a smile. However the final mission where  was a fantastic capstone to the story.   Overall I highly recommend it if you want a physics based puzzle/demolition game with lots of room for player improvement and a good story to back it up.

_childDocuments_.review: The core of this game is very good. Taking apart spaceships is satisfying, and they have nailed a lot of key gameplay factors like weightiness, the 'feel' of the tools, and the core setup of sizes and distances. They got so much so right at the start.They have since let themselves down in a few apparently small, but cumulatively obnoxious ways.The dialog is poorly written and - that most egregious of gameplay sins - UNSKIPPABLE. When you should be taking apart ships, you're instead stuck there twiddling your thumbs as line after bland line of poor voice acting is read out, or stuck in your Hab waiting for someone to read out the subtitles for you. And speaking of the Hab - your room between shifts, although it's actually quite a nice apartment with a beautiful view (which doesn't fit the game's narrative) - what an absolute mess. You lunge from desk to desk with lurch after sickening lurch, instead of having free movement. The menus are inexplicably spread out across the room. It's badly designed and badly implemented. It's obvious what has happened, of course. The devs spent time and money on developing the Hab, and even though it actively makes the game worse... well, they can't just remove it and go back to the far-superior simple menu system, because they spent time and money on it! So we, the players, are made to suffer pointlessly.There's also the matter of the economy/debt. What could have been an interesting, balanced drive to work the numbers and pay off your debt is instead largely meaningless. There's no nuance - they've just whacked a big number of "debt" on you at the start of the game, and that's pretty much it. And again, it doesn't quite fit with the game narrative, because if you crunch the numbers, you'll be able to pay off your debt after about six months, and then start making massive profits and be an in-game millionaire - which is completely at odds with the "worker grunt" motif in the "story",These failures add up, and it's a shame that the devs have undermined such excellent core gameplay in this way (EDiT: I just want to say this again - they really nailed the gameplay. It feels like a job, but it never feels like a chore. It can be so satisfying to swing around in zero-G and fling a section of hull directly into its receptacle. Also just want to say that I'm playing on a pad, and while one or two controls seem like odd choices at the start, it doesn't take long for everything to click. You're almost never fighting the controls, which is great to see in a game like this.). However, the last year of development suggests not an exciting future for this game, but instead a downward spiral.At this point, with the recent price rise and failure to fix simple issues over the last year or two, I'm recommending against buying the game.But I hope I'm wrong, that the devs start to work smarter, and that I can see some positive progress that allow me to recommend this game in future.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and fun game, ruined by elementary school-level writing, more concerned with flag waving than telling a story.Fantastic gameplay that kept me glued to the screen all throughout the development phase. The game is beautifully crafted and excellently balanced. Progress feels rewarding as you find yourself planning the disassembly of ever more intricate ships. The sound pulls you in and keeps you immersed in the moment, from the booming thuds of heavy metal parting to the dangerous sizzling of your tools.This was during the Beta phase, where the developers were experimenting with new systems constantly, adding features on a monthly basis but always keeping to the same core gameplay loop; - Purchase a ship. - Disassemble it as carefully as possible.- Recycle everything.- Reduce your debt.However, since the story release things have slipped from engaging to tedious. Previously what story there was took a 'show don't tell' approach.You are always aware of the greater world.  All around you is the constant bustle of activity. Massive transport ships and small hopper shuttles glide between stations.  The vast reaches of low earth orbit are turned into a veritable city of planet-sized proportions.  You are but a spec amongst it all.  A mote of dust suspended on a sunbeam.Occasionally, you stumble across audio logs and recovered data in your salvage targets. Decoding them, these hint at the events that took place onboard the ship you are now disassembling.  You could choose to ignore them, but instead, you follow the breadcrumbs, piecing together the stories of those who had once travelled in these now derelict hulk.Thousands of lives, both spectacular and mundane, lived out in the unforgiving void.  Now these vessels lay dormant after their final journey. Their stories would be forgotten by all but those who once lived them.Just as the ships are recycled, reused, and repurposed, so the stories live on through you.The story did not need some grand conspiracy. It already has a strong motivation built into its very fabric. The weight of your debt to the company is enormous, but it is surmountable (the cap had to be raised several times during development, so powerful was this as a motivator). In exchange for functional immortality, you pay off your debt to LINX, seeing that number diminish at an exponential rate as your skill improves.  You buy your tools so you no longer pay rent on them, improve them so they don’t break and earn you more credits per ton. Eventually, that enormous debt slides to zero, then climbs into positive integers as you become a master at your trade.It strikes a chord with the ceaseless desire to move forward.  This was motivation enough.Then a ‘story’ was added on top of this wonderfully simple framework.  And everything went wrong.Now the player is dropped onto the railroad tracks of the writer's puddle-deep interpretation of late-stage capitalism.  A plot in which you have no reason to move forward, surrounded by a cast of thoroughly dislikable characters while political messaging takes centre stage. I would not be surprised to find out the writing had been taken away from the core design team entirely, instead handed off to some ‘major in gender studies’ and their cronies.  At the very least this would carry some irony, mirroring the actual removal of player impetus in the game.The plot is delivered as exposition, parcelled in non-intractable dialogue.The levelling system seemed to be the trigger for each bout of exposition and I began to dread going up a rank, knowing that ‘union rep’ Lou would then interrupt the game after every job.This would be forgivable to some extent if the player could do something while the writer's novella is being read to you.  At least let me upgrade my tools while the sermon is being preached.  But that is not the case.  Instead, we were given no option but to answer the communicator when entering the habitat after finishing our work day.  Then the player character is riveted in place listening to the whiny unskippable dialogue.This occurs three times whenever you rank up, every time you finish a ship.Most importantly for the player though, you have no choice in what happens. You cannot help plot the downfall of the company or opt out of Lou’s disloyal machinations.  You cannot choose the forge closer ties with the other crew, nor speak with anyone outside pre-written and ordained set pieces. You cannot interact at all, the player is simply a spectator.This speaks to an attitude held by the writing staff; This plot is being read to you and you will listen.In the Beta, the comradery of the ever vigilant shift manager Weaver was all the interaction required.  His dulcet tones and calm demeanour could have seen this game through from start to completion.  It did not require anyone else, but that didn’t mean that the game could not be enriched by other colleagues and intractable characters.Sadly, other than Weaver and the antagonists, the other NPC workers are little more than set dressing for Lou’s soapbox.  They go underutilised and unrealised, acting more as a more of a box-ticking exercise in ‘Diversity casting’ than relatable colleagues.When the community backlash against such a farcical quality of writing was seen, the dev responded. Not by toning things down again or rolling back to a subtle background story; it was to double down.The third act sees the ‘banner-waving waste of creative writing’ Lou spontaneously vanish, replaced by a corporate entity so farcically evil, that it makes Umbrella-Corp seem relatable.  This is of course coupled with an incompetent middle manager, representative of the banality of evil ‘exclusive to white males’. Honestly, it feels as though Lou was a kind of self-insert. When the community rejected her, the conceited plot childishly robbed the players of any sense of engagement."Oh woe is me!” bemoan the remaining NPCs, “If only we had listened to the annoying one!" Meanwhile, their author remains successfully ignorant of the subtle story weaving that made this game wonderful in the first place.This writing is unworthy of the quality of this unique game.And Lou has successfully made me anti-union.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Breaking ships is fun, it's satisfying, and the progression doesn't feel grindy.  This game really is enjoyable, and it's a game for people who like to chase progression and achievement, where they can tune out the world and focus on a job, and even relax.  There's catharsis to it.Cons: The new storyline the devs introduced late into development seems to have taken away too much of the time and focus of what the game seems to have been originally envisioned to be back when I bought it in EA.Before the storyline was introduced, progression was more grindy, but not overly so.  Each of the 30 certificate ranks mattered, and you would work hard to unlock them to get access to much-needed upgrades. Now, you reach about certification level 18, and that's it. There's nothing more to look forward to. No new ships, no new variants, nothing.  Just another 10 or so certification ranks that give you nothing.But they have stickers now!  That's something!The world building was done through abandoned data drives full of mission logs, personal messages, and historical recordings, left by the people who once called home the ship you're tearing apart for salvage.There used to be a decent amount of puzzle-solving involved with more complicated ships, requiring specific buttons to be pushed and keys to be turned in specific orders to safely salvage a ship.  Much of it is still there, but it's been dumbed down and simplified.The game also has the bones and the structure to essentially add onto it endlessly, with new ship types and variants, new world-building events that introduce new challenges and hazards (e.g. like the "ghost ships"), new puzzles and challenges to overcome as we become a more and more skilled and experienced shipbreaker.But unfortunately the devs have already said that the game, for them, is done.  It's finished.  They said they have no plans for more content, and no more building on top of the foundation they've created.Which is a shame, since the game in it's current state, with the certification system now almost too easy, with the new storyline that seems to railroad you quickly to a conclusion in a game where part of the experience was that there really was no real end, and a progression system where you have everything unlocked and have seen all there is to see 2/3 of the way through - it leaves the game feeling hollow and a shell of what it could have been.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, a rare case of where the game used to be good earlier on in its development cycle, then progressively got worse.  The developers started blatantly ignoring any community feedback they got and adopted a head-in-sand approach to development.  There's still gameplay issues like higher tier ships being forced, and extremely niche use for the breach explosives.  There's also a ton of bugs still in the game that haven't been fixed.All that aside, the absolute worst offender and reason I can't suggest this game is that they entirely gave up adding any new gameplay features and actual content in order to promote what can only be described as a preachy, politically-laced story mode.  It's unskippable, constantly extols the virtues of unionization and worker rights, and is filled with one-dimensional characters defined by racial stereotyping.  The devs themselves have admitted to wanting to 'educate' people on unions, and have turned the game into a platform for their political stance, at the expense of the actual gameplay.  There are only four ship types, and they never even bothered giving us a fourth tool, leaving a slot on the HUD completely empty.If they fix all this in the future, I might change my review.  But as it stands, the game is a shallow, pitiful experience compared to what it could have been, sacrificed in the name of promoting a misplaced political agenda more suited to far different forms of media.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly challenging and rewarding space ship dismantling simulator.You play as a debt-riddled astronaut breaking apart ships during 15 minute shifts. During a shift you have a work order that consists of objectives such as collecting electronics equipment, metal parts or reclaiming the dreaded reactor core. You do this with the use of two tools: a laser cutter and a grapple lasso (think gravity gun). You float in zero gravity using a jetpack, flying around the ship in free 6 degree of motion. Fulfill work orders and do extra work for more cash. Upgrade gear and rinse repeat.What makes the process interesting is the Newtonian gravity and the sheer physics at play. To optimize you want to work quickly but taking a ship apart carefully takes time. Slowly you start learning each ship class's intricacies and optimal workflow. For example you might cut off the floor off a passenger vessel, granting direct access to the furniture within, allowing you to simply push the seats and boxes downwards towards the reclamation barge. Or you may use the tether tool to connect multiple objects together to create a linked chain of hull panels to lead them all in one go to the nanocarbon reclaimer.The career mode has excellent pacing. However if you want to just break apart ships without concerns for resources or time limits, there's a freeplay option as well. It's great for learning the ship structure on your own time.The game supports both keyboard+mouse and controller input but I felt that controller is the best way to play.

I bought this game in early access on the premise that there would be more added to the gameplay beyond more ships, but this is the same game I played a couple of years back. Grav boots, mini thrusters, remote hacking tools (for the small amount of interactibles), more heavy duty cutters, or even a thermite launcher or something that lets you hit the weak points of a structure with less tedium. _childDocuments_.review: Pull apart decomissioned space ships for salvage in order to repay your crippling debt to Earth's ruling giga-corporation!Choose a ship to be delivered to your assigned orbital salvage bay and get to work. Fly around with your jetpack in zero-g, six-degrees-of-freedom style. Open up the ship, find and cut the attachments between the various pieces, and grapple-gun the bits into the Processor, Furnace, or Barge as appropriate. You face ever more structurally and mechanically complex ships as you qualify for higher ranks. Deal with fuel/coolant pipes which can rupture, electrical equipment that arcs when damaged, and of course there's always explosive decompression! Try to keep everything intact as possible to maximize value.And of course, time is money. Each shift you work, you're being docked interest, rent for your living quarters and gear, and you gotta pay for all the thruster fuel, oxygen, and the other supplies you need to get the job done.Anyway as bleak as the backstory is, the game is very fun and addictive. Learning and improving your efficiency gives the same type of satisfaction as Viscera Cleanup Detail. If you like that sort of manual-labor-simulator like I do, then you'll like this one too.
