_childDocuments_.review: Normally I play puzzle games but I thought I'd take a break from that to try something else.  Very glad I did!What a great game Shipbreaker is....good backstory, good atmosphere (pun intended), good gameplay.  Didn't know it when I bought it but in reality it's a puzzle game...figure out the best and safest way to dismantle a ship to maximize profits while not killing yourself in the process.   There are various types of ships that come your way...they are really well designed/thought-out and each is unique in their own way so there's nothing cookie cutter about it. Game also has several variations...you can play a standard "career", or free play, or play in a relaxed mode that isn't timed and doesn't make you worry about your oxygen supply.  This is a really nice feature as sometimes it's nice to just chill out and play in relaxed mode.The only thing negative I can say about this game is that the mechanism for switching between your tools using mouse movements is a little annoying and tedious...easy to pick the wrong tool. _childDocuments_.review: This is one of these rare games where I can zen out and just have a nice podcast or video on and just enjoy the pleasure of, well, since I'm not super great, somewhat controlled deconstruction. I think I only have three gripes worth mentioning.I like the story and the characters. When I played in EA, I don't even remember if Weaver was in the game yet haha. But I'd like to hear more about what happened to Earth and more world building about the other planets. Also, the largest glaring issue is that a lot of story takes place in areas where you are kind of just forced to wait. The salvage yard is the perfect delivery system for the story and for some of the larger narratives, I wish they had been out there so I could continue to play. Although I understand the necessity of HAB based conversations.Maybe it's because I played a lot of EA, but the game is too easy. I wish there were a harder mode besides limited number of deaths. I died once in the regular playthrough, and it was because I wanted to see how much abuse a class II nuclear reactor could take. You know, tolerance tests for future extractions. A way to lessen either the durability and/or add debt would be great. As is, the current debt is easy to wipe out after a few upgrades.The upgrades themselves. I don't really understand the existence for some of the upgrades as they tend to cause more issues than they solve. Two big ones for me were grapple strength and the grapple's "shove" feature. The more strength I added to the grapple, the weirder the physics became. For example, I'd grab the top of a floating piece and then look down to pull the piece flat and the point I grappled to be closer. But often the physics reversed. Grab something and try to move it to the right and it'd move left. Eventually I had to adjust to physics being backwards. Also sometimes, even when attaching to them straight on, canisters of fuel or coolant, after being separated from their mounting, would fly off in a random direction at great speed, often causing catastrophic damage. I made sure that the beam was straight and I would be pulling the item "up" from the top of said item. This was an issue in EA as well, though it's happened twice this time, so it's 95% better.The "shove" feature causes a lot more issues than it helped. I didn't finish either the grapple strength or "shove" strength since they were causing so many issues, but upgraded, if I wanted to shove a panel towards a salvage entrance, things all around me, even behind me, would go flying and send even large structural pieces in motion. A more concentrated area would be appreciated.To be fair, those complaints are just small ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ around a very solid core. For me, the core gameplay loop is fun and as a bonus, can be a zen game I can use to destress.I definitely give it a recommendation as it can be engrossing enough to get to the point of "one more turn" of TBS games like Civ, but to me it was, "just one more shift.".

_childDocuments_.review: Do I recommend Hardspace: Shipbreaker: Yes.Will you want to play it for 487 hours like I have? Maaaaaaybe...?The thing with Hardspace is that it's still in early access and it's hard to say where exactly it will all go. Right now the biggest flaw I can say about the game is that while there are a lot of obstacles to keep in mind until recently only a few interacted meaningfully. These were cutting the fuel lines and the cooling from a Class II Reactor, getting it the hell out of the ship, and into the barge before the thing goes nuclear.The most recent update added ghost ships with hostile AI. Or at least it WILL be hostile once you piss it off as part of the required objectives of your work order. Problem is once you know what the AI can do to screw with you it's really easy to remove its fangs. So what's the point of me telling you all this?Hardspace, at this point in its development, is a game where through repetition you'll know how to conceivably deal with everything that the game can throw at you, which is both good and bad. In short: if you're coming into this expecting non-stop zany zero gravity antics where you blow your dumb ass up you'll find that is short lived. If you like games where you can achieve a zen state as you methodically disassemble a ship while thwarting a murderous AI then this is for you.That said here's an odd bit of advice for you: If you do pick this game up go to its page on tvtropes after the tutorial and look at the "Guide Dang It" section to learn some really useful stuff that, last I knew, the game does not tell you about.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay itself is GREAT. It's super relaxing to take all kinds of spaceship apart in your own way, sort them out and clean your dock. The atmosphere is fantastic: relaxing music, great view, colorful and detailed. There's a few options to make the game more laid-back (no oxygen usage, no shift timer) and through it's development the gameplay improved by fixing bugs (although some persistent ones can still ruin your experience, like decompression) and adding variations of a total of 4 ships. The future appeared bright with so many options to add: new ships, different tools, various ways of handling problems, you name it. Until...Devs threw all their promising progress out the window in favor of the narrative. Does "black lesbian fighting oppressive corporate capitalism through a socialist organization" sound like any recent cultural phenomenon to you? That's what the game is about now.Because of this change, the entire purpose of the game changed. No longer are you the "blue-collar spaceship salvager", instead you are an npc to someone else's story, literally grinding the same 4 ships over and over to progress a boring and predictable narrative. There's no opting out of it. No skipping dialogue. Break ship, get level, hear story, repeat. There's no incentive anymore. And I tried. Maybe it would get better (yes, sunken cost fallacy). But it's all so predictable. Oppression by greedy megacorp, workers rise up, revolution, good times for everyone. Doesn't matter what you do, just follow along."Just play free-play mode"... Is as weak-sauce an argument as saying "use mods" when potentially good games are bad because of dev choices. People were sold a different game, they changed it and I would not buy it in it's current form because it's lacking in content.Oh and don't get your hopes up for new content. Devs have literally posted that adding new content is "too hard" and they'd rather focus on porting to XBOX and PS5. Check out the flaming pile of dung that is the Community Discussion FAQ. No workshop, mods, new content or co-op. Just reasons why they coulda-shoulda-woulda but didn't.Do not buy. Massive disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly, highly satisfied with my getting this game. I'm usually cautious about Early Access titles, but the level of polish in previews convinced me to make the purchase and I'm happily glad that I did. That being said, I do have some criticisms that I hope will be addressed during the Early Access period, but I'm fairly confident this studio knows what it's doing. In terms of positives, the primary game play loop of salvaging parts from spaceships is great, and has that perfect work-simulator quality of being exciting and inventive. The learning curve is very fair, slowly allowing you to come to grips with specific models of spacecraft before giving you more objectives and more complexities to deal with. The sound design is top notch, from the heavy breathing in low oxygen to the cutting of metal in zero gravity. Graphics-wise, this game is a looker and I was frankly shocked to see this was a Unity-engine game. This is definitely one of the finest games to make the most of the engine and the developers should be proud.All in all, the foundation for a perfect game is here, although in its Early Access state, it remains a solid game in its own right. For the planned year or so of development, I think BBI can pull off the rare feat of releasing a truly memorable game in the final release. So now that I've done all the praising, I hope the developers will indulge a few comments/critiques I have:1. The Time Limit = while I've seen others criticize the time limit for each shift, I don't necessarily have an issue with it. Freeplay mode offers the ability to tear a ship apart with as much time as possible and leaves room for plenty of experimentation. I think however, there should be a cap as to the number of shifts you can salvage a ship with to force players to be more strategic with their cutting.2. Diversity of Ship Interiors = while I've seen the number of ships available to salvage is the most frequently cited critique I've found on Steam and elsewhere; I understand that Shipbreaker is in Early Access, and releasing only two types of ships was the smart way to go to make sure bugs are addressed in an expedient and thoughtful manner. But after several hours with the game, the Gecko and Mackerel do feel pretty same-y when their interiors are effectively identical each time I enter them. The biggest issue is that my solution for salvaging them is the same process every time. After an hour each for the Gecko and Mackerel, I developed the best strategy to get the most valuable parts of the ship in the most timely manner. Perhaps something can be done about the cosmetics of the interiors as with the coat of paint on the exterior. But my main issue is the placement of certain valuable parts. Following a few play throughs, players will be immediately attuned to where all the most valuable salvage parts will be. I know the game randomizes consumables and the placement of excess fuel and coolant (which is great by the way), but perhaps other major parts like the ECU and power station can be diverted into other rooms. When it comes to a work-simulator game like this, repetition is practically unavoidable, and is part of the charm of the game after all. But additional hazards can be highlighted to players to address BEFORE cutting a ship apart. The possibility of a fuel rupture, for instance, is an example of a great hazard to deal with in order to remove the thrusters and reactor core. Perhaps the player could also deal with malfunctioning electronics or mechanics that could cause problems in removing valuable parts like the ECU and power station as well.The reactor core is the heart of the ship, and the game makes it abundantly clear it's the most valuable part to remove. As a suggestion to the developers, perhaps higher difficulty ships require the core to be removed LAST. Or perhaps the core is already unstable, and players can perform tasks aboard the Vessel to ensure the core doesn't meltdown prematurely, like slathering it with coolant or diverting power to other parts of the ship to reduce the possibility of an explosion. Speaking of which...3. Interplay of Various Ship Systems = on paper, the idea of the radiation, coolant, and electrical systems is ingenious. It gives a sense of purpose to salvaging as well as forcing players to think critically. While the example of removing coolant supplied to the reactor can cause the reactors ticks to go down faster, I feel there needs to be more interaction between the three systems. Fuel, for instance, doesn't appear to be hooked up to either the reactor, even though the reactor is supplying power to the thrusters. Meanwhile, the electrical system seems to only be supporting the controls for the reactor console. More interplay of these three systems will probably lead to all sorts of hazards that must be addressed before cutting which will help alleviate my concerns of repetition above. Post-Launch "Pie-in-the-sky-idea" of Customizable Ships = Ok this comment is purely a fun idea that I'm not sure is feasible at the present state of the game, nor do I believe should be a priority for the developers right now. My three points above are the only things I would like to see for me to slot this game as "best in its genre" material. But as a fun idea to help expand Hardspace's appeal is an ability for players to design their own ships for other players to salvage. Effectively, these would be custom levels that players can share with each other to challenge others with dismantling in the fastest way possible.As a further idea, this mode can be introduced AFTER the player has wiped their debt and begins salvaging parts to install in their own ships to sell for a higher price. Giving this game a more business-simulator feel in the endgame would be a logical progression from the blue-collar roots the game is going for. All in all, fantastic job Blackbird Interactive. Congrats on releasing one of the best early access games in years!

_childDocuments_.review: "The best virtual job I've ever held!"This is a game about you taking a laser cutter and a gravity gun, then cutting up a spaceship in zero gravity and tossing the pieces into various receptacles to process them and make money off of them. You get to cut away hull panels, occasionally explode fuel lines by accident, risk reactor meltdowns and even explosively decompress entire ships if you're not careful!If all of that doesn't sound awesome and fun to you, you might need to see a doctor or something. For me it was one of the most entertaining things I've played in a long time.Seeing how the different ships are structured, figuring out how their hulls come apart in nice, clean chunks and how to most effectively and quickly disassemble the juiciest and most valuable parts is a great little puzzle unto itself. Atop it all the visuals are very nice, with all sorts of cool details to discover, and there's even some clever worldbuilding going on to establish a story and setting.Sadly I found the weakest part of the game to be its story. I feel the tale of downtrodden workers being forced to work and exploited rang kind of hollow to me simply due to how much I freakin' loved starting a shift and getting to work again! The individual characters, and especially the voice actors, are excellent, though. While you never get to see these distant colleagues in person, you get to know a bit about their history and life.Along with the excellent voice cast, the rest of the games audio is pristinely done as well. From the twangly country music that embodies hard but chill work to the various sounds you hear in your suit, whether it be the eerie hum of pressurized spaceship interiors or the rattle of metallic microfragments raining on your visor as you cut through a support beam.I'm definitely keeping this game as one of my relaxing games to pass the time with, and if there is ever expansions or sequels for it, I'll be happy to take the plunge!An easy recommendation from me.Playtime: 20+ hours (Single playthrough)Ratings (1-10)Visual: 9Audio: 9Story: 7Gameplay: 10Overall: 9

_childDocuments_.review: This review is written after 8 hours of playtime, and at version 0.3.0 of Early Access.I bought this game as soon as it was released because I thought it sounded a) very cool and b) very different to everything else in my library.I'm happy that the devs have implemented easy mode where you can turn off the timer and O2 depletion, now I can relax, take my time and enjoy taking a ship apart.If you want a challenge you can try to solve the puzzle under some tight time constraints, but that's not the way I like to play it - way too stressful :)Gameplay is incredibly satisfying, it takes practice and you have to learn the layout of each ship, how it comes apart, and what mistakes not to make - there are plenty of ways to electrocute and incinerate yourself.There's a progression system that comes in the form of certification, complete tasks to unlock better equipment and have a shot at more complicated ships.There must be some really smart devs on the team, I can't even begin to imagine the challenges of implementing all the realistic physics and engineering systems that underpin the whole thing.The game is still very much in active development, updates are coming all the time and a new class of ship was just released called the Javelin.Highly recommended - please buy a copy and support continued development.

_childDocuments_.review: Even right out of the gate in early access, this game has definite potential, and there's already enough content for some satisfying game time for the price.It's a lot of fun identifying cut-points and how the ship is put together, and forming a strategy to take it apart as quickly as possible. Time is money, after all.I hope the devs seriously explore the co-op potential of the game, because I can already see that being a lot of fun. There's so many little things can be cut, pulled off, salvaged, that there's plenty of work that could be divvied up between 2-3 people. In fact, I think having something like 4 player co-op for much larger ships could be fantastic.Cons? I think there's too many 'bars' to keep in check. You only have about 15 minutes per work shift, and you have to manage oxygen, jetpack fuel, tethers, AND health. I suggest either drop the fuel or the oxygen, because having to worry about both on top of everything else and the overall time limit is a bit much. Sure, you can sometimes find oxygen or fuel canisters inside ships to save you time, but it isn't guaranteed.

Refunded it after about 30 minutes.So, the big problems with this game are, the drifting physics, the focus on timed missions, and no multiplayer.The drifting physics:Floating around in Hardspace is just unfun. I came to Hardspace after playing Outer Wilds and was super sad by the feel of navigation in this game. I enjoy space sims, and at the time of launch, this has some of the slowest controls of any space sim out there. I found myself mashing my fingers into the keyboard unconsciously for how sluggish I felt. Maybe this has been resolved by now.No Co-Op:I predominantly bought this game to replace Viscera Cleanup Simulator. Without multiplayer, it can’t do that.Timed Missions:So at the time of writing this review, Hardspace added a few extra untimed modes. However, this doesn’t really address the issue at its heart. The problem wasn’t that there were no untimed modes in the game, the problem is that the game is designed around the rush of a score attack under time, when the core concept of the game doesn’t feel like it was ever meant to put time pressure on you.Taking apart ships should be like cleaning your room or deconstructing a lego set. Imagine if Marie Kondo came into your house and asked you to declutter your life in 15 minutes or you fail. Walking into this game expecting a soothing activity will leave you frustrated and disappointed.The weird thing is, if the game was meant to be a race in its core design, why do you move so slowly? This game feels like a grab bag of ideas that never had a consistent vision of what it wanted to be. Hardspace knows what it wants to do, but not why you should be doing it. This isn’t something that can be magically fixed with more game modes, this is a fault in the design vision itself.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: This game can be equal parts relaxing or stressful, depending on your settings (e.g.: you can disable oxygen drain and time limit).  It's also a slow burner that you might just get back to from time to time: the basics of gameplay are easy to pick up, and the game only became more playable since the beta days.The storyline is nice, relevant though every bit as cheesy as the western/country-themed music.Graphicswise, it ran fine on ultra at roughly ~70fps @ 3440x1440 on a 3900X + 2080Ti combo, and slightly better (80-120) on a 5800X3D. The thing that will eat your frames is the number of separate ship parts you see. So don't be like me and blow a ship into a gazillion parts because that will tank it down to half or worse. It is fun to do so though.Anyway, fun, relaxing, great game to turn off your brain (the biggest ships currently can take up to a few hours to totally salvage), did not touch the race mode that has leaderboards. Would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Great relaxing game, and devs are updating it quite frequently and interacting really well with the community. I can't wait to see what's next for this game. I'm personally hoping for bigger ships and new game modes. I'd love to see a sort of "Storage Wars" game mode where instead of a time limit, you are borrowing money to bid on ship or even "lots" of debris and hoping to extract enough from it to make up your costs.Speaking of the timer, a lot of people have had a lot to say about it. I find the timer is only an issue in the start, later on you get more comfortable with the ships, not to mention the components themselves are worth a lot more, so you almost always end up making a profit unless you mess up, which is how it should be.Highly recommend, 9/10, could turn into a 10/10 with future updates!

_childDocuments_.review: Let's be honest here, I dare anyone playing this game for the very first time not to sit there leaning your head to one side or the other as your Cutter spins about - you just can't help yourself.That aside, if you enjoy lateral thinking, tactical planning, solving problems involving the deconstruction of machinery, or you're just a welder at home twiddling their thumbs, you will love this game. It can be frustrating to begin with, due to moving about in three dimensions via your keyboard, but by level 5 you should have it nailed. Initially oxygen is your limiting factor, but on more difficult ships you will find plenty of spare oxygen cylinders inside the doomed ship. If you are like me, there will come a point when you decide to see what happens if you remove the glass shield before entering the ship, or if you purposely rupture the drive. Try it. It's impressive.Graphically this game ticks all the boxes, and the sound of your cutter is highly satisfying, but most impressive is the destruction model and the physics engine. Brilliant. As for sound, well the background music is quite soothing, but don't expect anything else along the lines of 'Hunt: Showdown' in terms of acoustics.With more being added, this game just gets better.

_childDocuments_.review: I grudgingly recommend this game, solely due to the fact that its central premise - breaking apart ships - remains fun. It's a strangely meditative, problem-solving game, that unfortunately falls far short of what it could have been. The game will throw you a story; ham-fisted, poorly told, and absolutely without any player interaction.  At the end, the impression that stuck with me, is of a game that was pushed out the door by a team that is already working on its next game. It's fine for what it is, but a shame for what it is not: A little bit more work could have produced a few more ships and variants, player records, a count of shifts working this salvage, a real tutorial, some sort of efficiency measure, something  to buy with all this money, salvaging in the earth's shade, maybe real customization for your pod/suit, some real choices when buying upgrades, and maybe some ability to interact with the story. _childDocuments_.review: TL:DR - High replayability, great story, soothing, fun, great physics.  A must have.This may just be the most polished Early Access Game you'll ever play.  The physics are incredible, and the ships are a delight to puzzle through as you work your way towards disassembling them.If I had to nitpick I would say the tutorial could use some work (and as a pro tip: do EXACTLY what the tutorial says, no more, no less, and you'll get by just fine), and there are a very few minor bugs that can be annoying at times... but they are aware of them.That being said, the game has a pretty great back story, and the  guy you "work with" seems like he'd genuinely be someone you'd want to grab a drink with.  The ships do get a bit repetitive (BUT... it's early access, and there are still a ton of ships to work through in all the different iterations).  However, the work orders are spot on, and if you accidentally destroy a component needed for one of them it simply brushes that work order item aside and keeps going flawlessly.  This game is incredibly laid back, requires some thinking, has a calming property to it, and gives a glimpse into a dystopian future that is quite possibly real.  The open-ended nature of the game makes replayability quite high, and short of CIV V, and Battle Brothers, this is my third favorite replayable game.TS:DR - Need more?  This one time, when I was 14, I was alone at home, and I was chasing my cat.  I ran through the kitchen and stepped on the edge of our industrial dustpan.  It's actually pretty amazing how quickly a toe can come off, and it's even more amazing how quickly a cat can do a 180, grab your loose toe, and run like hell.

_childDocuments_.review: A bit of good fun for the price (50% off sale), I like having to explore each ship and figuring out how to safely remove components without them exploding etc.However the core gameplay loop does get a bit boring, and the 15 minute timer is a bit odd - I know there's a game mode without it, but it doesn't really seem to matter either way.  Playing with the timer on just means I can't salvage the whole ship in one sitting, but it allows to go back to the ship multiple times if you want to salvage it all anyway so it feels a bit pointless.I'd like it if there were more meaningful upgrades to the tools instead of just "range" or "power".  And the beginning of the game gets annoying when you're moving really slowly and have hardly any oxygen.As it is, it's a bit of relaxing fun and appeals to someone with the kind of mindset where it's satisfying doing 'menial' tasks for the satisfaction of an overall goal being achieved.  Good time waster :)

The first time you accidentally used that completely new demo charge tool on the outside of a ship only to learn it can blow up the reactor clearly too far away from the proposed blast radius.But man, whenever you woke up and heard some new dialogue, that really drove the day away and made you want to grind for more story.The story is great, but honestly if you put it all on a piece of paper, that single piece of paper might not even be a full page. _childDocuments_.review: Shipbreaker is one of the most satisfying, fascinating games I've ever played. It can be incredibly zen meticulously removing all the computers or furniture or whatever your current work order says. It can also be incredibly tense and exciting. There's enough challenge to force you to be careful while cutting the ship apart, and each piece of the ship requires a slightly different procedure. It's a unique, fun idea in a sea of copycat games. Almost a new genre of game. I'm excited to see new ships get made.The simulation is just complex enough to be really Fun*. If you cut into a pressurized room you can have explosive decompression. There are cut points protected by ceramic coating, but you can break it off by throwing something at it, which allows you to cut the cut point, but don't accidentally hit a coolant line (I blew myself up that way lol). If you cut into the wrong wall, you could hit a computer terminal which sparks and the sparks carry along something metal nearby and damage a fuel line which causes a small explosion that damages a coolant line which makes the reactor start to melt down. If a reactor is melting down you better hope that you've removed enough of the superstructure that you have a big enough hole to remove the reactor and get it onto the barge before it melts down and you get a big, colorful explosion. It can be infuriating to lose 15 minutes of progress and all that money, but my god the explosions in this game are good.There is, of course, a sandbox mode for people who don't want the stress of having to worry about the budget or the 15 minute shifts in Career mode. Meticulously take apart every piece of a ship with no time pressure, or find the fuel tanks and throw them at strategic points on the ship to your heart's content. Some of us want it to be a Game, with constraints and challenges, but it can also just be a Simulator that you interact with.I give it 10 out of 10 deadly sparking computers.*Fun as in it takes a lot of time to learn, but it feels worth it

The repetitiveness is quite relaxing, even.Each ship is like a puzzle where if you fail you loose out on money and die.I really REALLY recommend this game. It is worth the price.Only issue? No multiplayer co-op. However, they are making the "best single-player experience they can," and I can respect that.Wouldn't mind it as a mod though. That would be cool.To be fair I can't find any fault for this game. You either like the gameplay or you don't.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start this review first by saying that this is a really good game, and given the Devs continue to fix it, I will be happy to change this review. However, in its current state, it is not something I can recommend to the person sifting through reviews trying to figure out if they'd like this game. Hard crashes come every two or three hours, without rhyme or reason. The same visual bug appears every time I resume a salvage operation, although it is fixed by doing a 360 rotation, oddly enough. While these are all minor inconveniences, the real issues lie in the gameplay itself. You can be in the process of stripping the outer hull off of a ship, and without even having one in sight, or nearby, you can randomly rupture a coolant pipe, resulting in a reactor meltdown before it's time to pull it out safely. Same things happen to fuel pipes, but you can mitigate this by using the utility keys in the reactor console. The same cannot be said for the coolant pipes, because coolant must be flowing to the reactor until you're ready to remove it. It's unfortunate because the random nature of this ruins the mechanic of being aware of what you're cutting and what's behind it. It feels like even though you're aware of the danger, you can still get punished randomly, with no mechanic to prevent this.Pressurization is another mess in this game. Without using an airlock, you can explosively decompress a ship if you don't depressurize it properly from inside. Just use the atmosphere regulator. Easy enough, right? Wrong. Every cabin has it's own unique pressure, and with no airlocks between interior cabins, there will always be rapid decompression when opening doors. So, even if you play the smart play, and void the largest interior, before opening the smaller ones, you still run the risk of a bag of chips whipping out of an airlock and killing you. This is of course, a much more merciful outcome than the random explosive decompression that occurs. And by explosive, I mean destroying the compartment in question, and more than likely the nearby compartments, yourself, and killing your desire to continue playing.Next up, something more personal annoyance based on design choices. If you're unaware to how the scrapping gameplay goes down, imagine the ship in the middle of the letter U. On either sides of the U, near the base, are the furnaces, and beside those, moving towards the open end, are the reprocessors. Both of these openings have a suction mechanic when nearby to help draw in the scraps. Basic metals go in the furnace, and carbon based products in the reprocessors. About 90% of a ships hull will go in the reprocessor, and about 90% of the interior structures (walls, floors) will go in the furnace. The problem arises when trying to move the outer portions of the outer hull past the furnace, and into the reprocessor. Even with 4 tethers pulling it as far away from the furnace, without running into the ship, removing the rear section of the outer hull is difficult as it can often get sucked into furnace. A smaller annoyance is the equipment durability. Repair kits can only be bought in mission, but equipment can only be repaired out of mission. So if you forget to buy repair kits, or you forget to repair your equipment, you're screwed until you can get in/out of a job to do what you need. With equipment durability offering nothing other than a broken cutter cutting slower, it's just an annoying mechanic that's not essential for gameplay.At the end of the day, these bugs aren't frequent, but they're often enough they can make enjoying the game difficult. I hope that sooner, rather than later, I have a reason to change this review, but at this time, there are design choices and bugs that need fixed.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: It does what it says on the tin. If you're a fan of those "oddly satisfying" videos this game may well be for you!Some teething issues, but that's what early access is for. The game is very basic at the moment but it's not a plot driven game. You pick a ship and get 15 minutes per shift to break it down. You can use multiple shifts to do it, but each shift incurs a rental fee; not really much of a penalty. There's also a free play mode to skip that.Your cutter can only do softer metals, so you have to plan around the stronger stuff. There is an upgrade way down the tree to cut through anything, but getting to that point will take a while in career mode. The ships are also packed full of explosive or sparky stuff that you don't react well to, so be careful when cutting around tanks or pipes!As mentioned, there's a certain satisfaction when you pause for a moment and just see a skeletal structure after you've torn the panels off a ship and hurled them into the processor bins. The bigger ships are much trickier, but I find the little ones (mackerels) perfectly sized for jumping in and quickly stripping down in a shift for a quick gameplay fix. Hopefully the devs integrate all the feedback in the discussion area, but as-is the game's a great time sink.

_childDocuments_.review: Edited Review;  I'm hard on this game because it's a brilliant idea and mostly well executed. I initially gave it a thumbs down because I wanted my review to be visible to the devs, if they care, which is obvious that they do.  This game is very fun and scratches a nice itch. I can see a shipbreaker two, or an expansion pack with more ships being viable. I would purchase more content for this game. They did a really good job.The game play is tight, controls take a bit of getting used to. It isn't immediately clear how you are supposed to handle certain situations, like pressurized ships with broken atmo controls.  Once you figure it out it's basically the same. The game gets a little repetitive, but a little repetition isn't a bad thing. With a little self motivation you can possibly get enjoyment from seeing how quickly you can dismantle ships. I mean anyone can safely dismantle a ship in five days. How many players can dismantle a ship completely in two? I had my debt paid off Whoever wrote the character of Administrator Hal Rhodes deserves an award. Whoever voiced the character deserves an award. I work in industry and Hal is so unnervingly on point that I literally felt like I was being berated by my real life operations manager. It's uncanny how accurate they got it. Right down to the stupid little catch phrases, the gaslighting, the pompous sense of self importance from "working their way up", the clear disregard for safety, and the blatant abuse of power. Seriously, Hal is flawless to a real life counterpart.This game deserves your attention and I sincerely hope the devs continue to develop content for this game.Original Review: The dialogue needs to be skippable. it's seriously trashing the pacing of this game. The 15 minute day is tight, allows for racing against the clock, inspires multi day plans of attack. But sitting in the hab listening to my drunken coworkers drunkenly stumble through their emotions really kills it for me.I do like the story, i've got theories of what's going to happen. The voice acting is good. You can tell effort went into it. It's just so disruptive to the core game loop.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: It does have both M/KB and controller support, but not changing keys yet. It is stated that they will add it for both. Controller scheme works except that they attached left/right thumbsticks to rotate your character. It would have been better RB/LB.It comes with a tutorial and explains everything very well, except maybe where to put it. It took me a while to figure it out.Performance seems decent it did start me of at 640x480p.I had one crash, I chose a ship tried to load it in and the program just ended.WishlistAll in all very happy with the game I can only imagine if co-op would be allowed and splitscreen.As well as versus mode, where you see your opponent in a small window while you square of against each other.Still loving it.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Game in is actually rather fun. It is still in EA, but so far developers appear to be actually carrying on developing the game forward.There are only couple of ships that can be dismantled, and little variation within those types that you can break up and recycle to try to grind your way out of massive debt.Game concept is actually fun, making most of the ship by tearing off, cutting and generally removing bits and pieces of ship and forwarding them to appropriate recycling facilities. The fascination of the game comes from breaking up those ships in a ways that you find most fun and/or efficient for yourself. And playing with big pieces of ships using physics engine, pulling large pieces with tethers and smaller ones with your own grapple.And amusing (or not) accidents that start to happen when you get bit too overconfident with your skills and cut or bump something you shouldn't have. Triggering reactor meltdowns for VERY fast disassembly (and loss of recycle value as they end up mainly as scrap) of vessel being just one way of things going really wrong.You will also be finding old recordings from ships that you can listen or read in the hub after getting them defragmented (voice recordings can be listened during shift if so desired).You can opt to either work on defined duration shifts or go for open shift where you can keep going until you are finished. If running open shift please notice! Make sure to end shift before tossing big pieces of Gecko into the furnace. My crashes have tended to take place when large portion of Gecko is put into furnace with resulting slowdown of the game. If you have not ended shift, everything you have done prior to that will be lost, but if you ended shift you get to keep all the progress made at end of previous shift.Biggest issue is just that, there will be massive slowdown in the game if and when furnace has large amounts of material pushed into it at same time. Entire inner hull of Mackarel is no big deal, but large portions of Gecko can lead even to crash. Beyond that game is quite stable at least for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Solid Early Access Title, Gameplay is very different from most games and is quite well implemented.  There is plenty to do, but there is not much in ship variety at the moment - and since breaking ships is the idea, it can get a little repetitive on the eyes!I found the game to be very stable on my setup with good graphics and audio.  The Devs are quite active on the forums and Discord which bodes well for the future of the game.Recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Man... This game is the epitome of "one step forward, two steps back".  The game-play is awesome.  It's atmospheric to the point where accidentally blowing an airlock makes you jump in your chair.  The dangers that loom all around you can make your hair stand up on end.  Accidentally pushing yourself towards the furnace makes your hair stand up on end...  It's such a great game.  At least it was.With the addition of the "interactive" hub or living quarters, the game kinda took a downturn.  It's super clunky and not intuitive.   The original way of doing things kept things simple and kept the focus on breaking down ships.  Now you spend too long trying to navigate the useless parts of your living quarters instead of getting back out there to work, which is what Lynx would want from their employees.  It's too cushy now.  Also the story is not needed.  I loved hearing the faceless Southern drawl of my supervisor telling me what to do.  Now I have a face to put to the voice and it ain't pretty.  Not only that, but now I have all these other people chatting away in my helmet which takes away from the solitary confinement of my work-space.  I don't care about the other people when they're trying to weasel their way into my heart with their sob stories of the corporation or trying to start a union, etc.  I had a good-enough time reading about all that in my emails a-la Subnautica.  There was no need to have these people join in and ruining my solitary existence in space.Oh well, hopefully the 1.0 release will be better.  I just want more ships and game-play mechanics.  I don't care about the story presented the way it is now.  I wish they had stuck with the vague emails and messages.I still recommend this game, though.  You'll definitely get plenty of fun out of it.  Here's hoping the release will make this game even better and not take another step back.Edit: So far the 1.0 release is a nice improvement. _childDocuments_.review: If you've ever disassembled something technical, you know there's a kind of peacefulness to it. Discovering how something is put together by taking it apart is something curious kids have been known to do forever, and with this game you aren't expected to be able to put it back together again! (which is good, because you're feeding the parts into various furnaces for money). In Hardcase: Shipbreaker, you'll be disassembling run-down spaceships by meticulously lasering apart their seams and sorting all the goodies inside. As you do, you'll learn the ins and outs of how their systems work; each class of ship becomes a puzzle, and you'll need to figure out how to get the most from each ship without causing a catastrophe due to electrocution, nuclear meltdown, explosive decompression, and so on. Along the way you'll earn upgrades and unlock new tools to more efficiently do your job of turning giant ships into relatively smaller pieces.The story sees you take on a job in a grimy, corporate-driven capitalist hell in high Earth orbit, but it's still better than life planetside at first. Being a billion dollars in debt has a way of eating at you, and the plot and lore partake in not-subtle-at-all jabs at how corporations are increasingly building stairways to the stars on the broken backs of the people who do the actual work. This is entirely in the background, as you'll be listening to audio messages while you do your own thing. If social commentary doesn't float your boat, there's a Freeplay mode and even a daily speedrun challenge. Each "shift" is roughly 15 minutes, and you can stop and come back to a partially deconstructed ship or choose a new one before each session.The gameplay itself is actually quite soothing. Meticulously peeling away a ship's layers to get at the precious tech within takes some skill and maneuvering in microgravity, and without any enemies the only opponent is the clock in the form of your oxygen levels (and even this can be lightened or removed in some difficulty levels). The rustic soundtrack works well with the zenlike state you may find yourself in, and your main contact's VO is generally pleasant to listen to, and he will shut up and let you work in peace for the most part.This review was written after 4 hours of play on the launch version (with 44 hours total in early access), and progress along the upgrade track does not feel like a chore yet. This is a low-pressure game that is usually chill with the occasional moment of personal terror when, say, you remember how little protection a spacesuit is when you accidentally whip yourself in the face with several tons of aluminum going 50 m/s.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of games will say they offer a 'unique experience' but often these are actually a take on a theme; an FPS, RPG et-al. Trying to explain Hardspace Shipbreaker is hard because it's essentially a first person puzzle game, but that doesn't even remotely do the game justice.Your aim is to dismantle out-of-service space ships and salvage useful parts; basic materials go into a furnace, ship hull and structural elements to into a processor and equipment such as computers and engines, go into the barge to be sold on. There are currently four hull designs with two to four variants of each, making for a good variety of ships, and after selecting your next job, you have as many 15 minute shifts to complete the job as you need. But you incur a daily set of charges, meaning you have a minimum bar to remain in gain or you potentially make a loss if you're too slow. The ships are logically designed, something I really like and there are several hazards; pressurised sections that need to be depressurised, reactor cores that will explode if not handled correctly, fuel and coolant tanks, electrical hazards, power systems and with each set of options varying each time,  it's very difficult to get bored. (I'm not certain if the ships are proceeduraly generated each time or not, but it feels like it)The controls feel very intuitive, even using a keyboard and mouse, and while I'm glad the development focus is fully on the campaign, if ever there was a game begging for a VR-Edition, it's this. In VR, this game could be mind-blowingly immersive. The developers have even got a work-around for perma-death not being a thing for the player when you die; the "Everwork Program" which clones a 'Spare' you each time you die. For a fee of course.The story is also intriguing. You and four other breakers form a crew and each has their own traits; you have Weaver, the ageing hand, Lou, the idealist, Kaito, the clumsy new-comer and Dee, the cynical veteran. You get to know these characters as you play, and I became genuinely attached to them, which means, when the Administrator, Hal Rhodes shows up, things get interesting... There's even very interesting social commentary about locking new workers into debt, fees and payments that result in permanent personal debt, corporate human rights abuses and even climate change nods. It's all very subtle; background and backdrop, adding to the story rather than smothering it. For example, after applying to become a shipbreaker, you are put into $1.2bn of debt for the privilege of coming to work for Lynx. Plus the daily charges for your habitat module, air, food, the kit you need to do your job, plus interest on your debt. Also, take care to read the 'contract' at the start and pay attention to the text when your 'Spare' is first being programmed... It will become important. The closest thing I can think of to this game is a scene in the animated film Titan AE, where the main character is working at a ship yard cutting up space ships. I'd always thought that would make a fun game and turns out, it does, because Hardspace Shipbreaker is a genuinely unique, engaging and fun game, but also somehow very relaxing with the music, atmosphere and gameplay and is well worth buying, even in Early Access. The encouraging part is the core concept hasn't been diluted from the Early Access version, meaning the core theme and premise to buy the game on didn't suddenly change, it showed the Dev Team had a clear vision for the game from early on and have absolutely delivered an absolutely great game.Would I recommend this game? Yes, absolutely.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very promising early access title and I've really enjoyed my time with it so far. Tearing apart ships in zero gravity, piece by piece, is immensely satisfying. There are lots of little environmental puzzles that you'll need to solve and hazards that you'll need to navigate as you figure out the best way to break apart the ship's hull, extract the reactor, and collect and process the various components. It takes a little bit of practice to get the hang of the floaty, zero-G controls, but once you're comfortable with it it's a lot of fun. Currently, the game offers both a career mode and an open play option. Career mode is where I've spent my time - your goal is to work off an enormous debt by processing ships. Each day is a 15 minute "shift"; and while this may sound stressful, the time limit is of little concern once you get the hang of things. Instead, it acts as a means of keeping you motivated towards making a profit on each shift, as the daily running costs will eat into your debt if you're not getting your work done. Fortunately, it's very easy to meet and exceed that daily quota, so you'll be able to focus more on solving the puzzle of each ship and getting your work objectives done. The fantastic soundtrack and art design also help to make the minute-to-minute gameplay relaxing and enjoyable.There's a simple upgrade system in place; I do hope to see some more elaborate and interesting upgrades with future updates to the title, as the current upgrades are primarily limited to simple stat boosts (extra O2 capacity, faster thrusters, etc.). As you unlock upgrades, earn money, and complete objectives, you'll also earn higher level certifications, which allow you to take on bigger, more complex, and more profitable ships. This is where the main limitation of the game, in its current state, becomes apparent. There's just not very many ships. You'll end up grinding through the same ship models again and again to rank up, which can become a bit tedious overtime. Of course, this is just the very beginning of early access, and the devs have already stated that they're working on adding lots of new ships to the game.Should you buy it now? If the concept of the game appeals to you, I'd say yes. For $20 you'll get plenty of hours of fun out of this one, even in its early state. It's a great game to just sit down and play in short bursts. I'll be coming back to this one frequently, especially as new updates come out.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best "job simulator" games I've tried. The concept is pretty simple - you tear apart ships in space to scrap. The hook comes in upgrading your equipment, along with a solid story told out through conversations with your fellow scrappers over space walkie-talkies.I appreciate the ability to play the game without shifts, as that makes it a much more relaxing experience, which was exactly what I wanted out of this. I love puzzling out how to take a ship apart without doing too much damage, but it's a completely viable way to play just going in and wrecking the ships fast.The controls are spot-on, the space movement just right. The tools are all easy to figure out, while the game keeps you on a treadmill with plentiful upgrades.If I have one major complaint, it's the soundtrack, and it's largely one I level at the space game genre in general. The space truckin' thing was played out a long, long time ago. We get it. Firefly was great. Let's go for something new or different when it comes to space music.Apart from that, the game just needs more variation in its ships. You get some new ships to take apart as the game progresses but I'd still like to see more, especially since the core ideas for so many of these feel so similar. Fixed lights that you could move around to different angles while working would also be a cool and much needed fix for the somewhat problematic lighting from the helmet, but that's just an idea.Overall, a fantastic game, and highly recommended if you need a podcast/audiobook game or something to just Zen out to.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept executed very professionally. I wish there were more games that allowed for interacting with large machinery in such a detailed simulated way. _childDocuments_.review: At its core, Hardspace: Shipbreaker is basically a physics puzzle game. Each ship type (and each variant of each type) is like a giant jigsaw puzzle that you have to take apart by cutting, pulling, and sometimes exploding the right pieces in a safe, but timely, order. Because of this, it's a great game for relaxing with music or a podcast in the background.But it's also a game that can go from 0 to 100 in an instant. One minute you're happily peeling away the outer hull of a ship, and the next, you're careening toward the furnace after a stray cutter shot violently decompresses the compartment you were in. Whether you like to play slow and safe or fast and reckless, Shipbreaker is fun and satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Deconstruction simulator with a store for buying upgraded gear and a series of increasingly complicated ships to deconstruct. Each ship is made of different parts that need to be thrown into different bins but individual working days are time limited and come with rent costs so there is a constant tradeoff between maximising value vs the time spent to gain that value. There is a story bringing it all together about a labour union seizing the means of production that is well done and some brief asides about what it means to be a clone. Would maybe have benefited from more ship types as every archetype is identical in structure even if the inside is randomly generated, so they all come apart the same in the end. Otherwise a solid game for relaxing to without too much to think about.

_childDocuments_.review: It's really quite good.  I was hesitant to buy this one, because the premise sounded dumb and boring.But actually, there's a very relaxing, methodical groove to it.  Starting with a huge ship and slowly but deliberately tearing it down, piece by piece, until it's just a metal skeleton that can be sliced up and put in the furnace is immensely satisfying.  Doing so without accidentally destroying big pieces especially so.I also like that, while the game does have failure states, they're not extremely punishing, and that encourages you to experiment a bit more.The story is meh, however.  It's serviceable, but fairly predictable and humdrum so far.Now for the complaints:Money is absolutely meaningless in this game.  You can buy refills for your gear for a few thousand dollars, but compared against your 1+ billion dollar debt and multi-million dollar salvage days, it's literally valueless.The pressurization mechanic needs *work*.  It seems to simulate "rooms" individually without any understanding of how the concept of rooms morphs as a ship is disassembled.  This leads to odd behaviours like not being able to merge rooms by removing walls between them (that just disables the atmo regulators and prevents them from working... a bug?) or explosive decompression events between two equally pressurized rooms.  In theory, this mechanic could be a really cool addition.  In practice, it's one of the few things that's pure luck and you can't skill or experience your way around.There's a couple of "guide-dang-it" moments in the game that need to be smoothed out too.  For example, when you're supposed to take the coolant tanks out of the coolant machine or the radiation filters out of their slots, there's an access panel that you have to remove with your grapple gun, but that's never explained, and pretty much everything else is just used with the interact button, so it's not intuitive that you need to use the grappler for smaller disabling actions.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game that can't get out of its own way and let you have fun. The main game mechanic has potential but every other feature is built around detracting from it. If you play with the survival elements you're constantly interrupted by tedious busy work, having to coast slowly back to a console to press the "don't die" button every few minutes; if you turn them off it all feels a bit easy and pointless.It's got an incongruous cowboy/frontier vibe, with the tutorial guy talking to you like you're his new rancher, and the music follows the same theme (which can thankfully be muted).The entire idea of putting you in massive debt at the start just sucks the fun out of earning anything, and the whole "lol aren't corporations evil???" brand of scifi humour was already exhausted when Outer Worlds did it and it certainly hasn't been revived here.There's a bunch of boring and unskippable dialogue - you can't even listen to it in the background while you do other stuff like look into equipment upgrades, the UI locks while the dialogue is playing. And for a game so built around physics, the physics are occasionally quite wonky.I wish I had stopped trying to find the fun before 2 hours were up so I could refund. It's a game that desperately needed some better high-level design work.

_childDocuments_.review: A first impression:It's surprisingly well-made for its development phase. Neat intro, music is incredibly fitting and relaxing and there's some good dialog. From the roadmap it seems the core gameplay is in position, with additional (comparatively minor) addons coming later on.It's already a good game in this stage. The tutorial starts you off with the basics of tools, the hazards of reactors and how to cycle airlocks. There's not much info on how to tackle certain problems, such as "I've removed the hardpoints for the ship, why is this panel not moving" or  "How do you detach the atmospherics console from the wall?"Other than that, gameplay is fairly straightforward, and your tools tell you to which salvage processor your parts should go.One of my favorite parts of this game is its soundtrack. It's a warm-sounding country soundtrack, with steelstring guitar, banjo and lots of reverb.It adds a lot to the relaxing nature of this game. It also fits the voice actor of Weaver, who teaches you the basics at the start of the game.I'm hoping this will eventually be released as a soundtrack since it's really good.That said, if your google-fu is decent enough, you can find some tools to rip the audio from the game yourself.Some notes from my first time playing this:The navigation took some time to get used to, as I'm more experienced with Space Engineers, where your jetpack suit has automatic dampeners. Instead, H:S has a manual dampener (Ctrl) which you need to press to stop moving. This also doesn't seem to work while grappling onto something, but that might be an upgrade later on.Having to press this key while also navigating around the ship is a little too much effort at certain points, an automatic version would be neat to have.Rotating your view by moving your mouse also has some drag to it, so you need to overshoot and move back to compensate for this. I'm hoping later upgrades minimize this, as precision movement isn't trivial. (I'm not saying it shouldn't be there at all, it's a realism-oriented simulator, after all!)One feature I'd also like to see is being able to control the length of the grappling beam. A mechanic like the Physics Gun in Garry's Mod would be nice, where you can move the object towards/away from you by scrolling the scroll wheel, like 'reeling in the fishing line'.If you deposit salvage in one of the processors, it tells you that salvage was accepted and credits have been added, but I haven't yet noticed how many credits you get (other than the screen at the end of your shift).Finally, the 15 minute timer adds quite some stress to an otherwise relaxing game. I'm hoping this can be changed to a user-set time limit, so you can work for longer (but you should also be reminded to take breaks to avoid an 8 hour shift :).Anyhow, for a first experience I had quite some fun. 9/10 would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is in early access and it shows. Due to that there are some physics and performance problems but the devs are working on that. Another feature I (and rest of community) am waiting for is community content so there are new types of ships to figure out. There’s a lot of space for  improvement and devs stay active on the game’s discord.Overall – even with this early version I feel I already got my money’s worth and it can only get better from here. It’s worth to give the game a try (you can easily figure out in 2 hrs if you like how it works). Also for the time being this has replaced my previous “zen” game – it’s great to start a movie and relax cutting ships and watching.There’s already a lot here to love. Various ship systems you have to figure out. Interesting tidbits of environmental storytelling via logs found in the ships, progress curve gradually introducing new subsystem in the ships you cut, work orders that give “currency” to upgrade your gear. The music that just  the feel of the game.Be aware though that it’s quite early version! There are 2 types of hulls to cut (with varying degrees of complication – the subsystems are introduced step by step so one hull results in many options) and getting to higher certifications requires noticeable amount of grinding.The timer people get so annoyed about doesn’t make the game worse at all – it just imposes some (but not too much) urgency on what you do and getting a positive end-day balance is absolutely no problem regardless if you’re cutting a bigger or a smaller ship. You can also get to know the layout of each ship in free mode (sandbox) but this doesn't count towards progress in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Very polished for Early Access.Unique and addictive gameplay loop, nice Firefly-esque setting. The 15 minute shifts break down the game into manageable chunks, though you can zone out and chill in free play if you don't want that timed / career progression experience.My only real critique so far is that the initial hour of the game is pretty rough around the edges. The game attempts to give you a tutorial, but isn't really clear that it's a tutorial, and it isn't real upfront that it's giving you unlimited time/health/oxygen that it will then severely limit later on. The tutorial bounces wildly between spoonfeeding you (press the roll for X seconds!) and expecting you to figure things out with no explanation (you're running out of oxygen with seconds to spare! go find and figure out how to interact with this kiosk that we've never mentioned to the player even once).Frustrations like these can turn a "wow this is cool" moment into a "this is stupid BS" moment for people playing the game for the first time. I almost ragequit twice in the first hour.Also, if you play with an Xbox controller, there's no way (at the moment) to remap buttons, so expect some very sore thumbs from constantly pressing down on the sticks to brake/roll. Remapping these to LB/RB would make much more sense to me.

_childDocuments_.review: -- EDIT -- so apparently in the release version developers decided to make playing open shift more annoying. Now it actually asks you whether or not you want to enable oxygen drain every time you start the game. The game is basically being condescending to the player asking whether or not to remove a "hard" mechanic even though I already made this choice. I am not playing open shift because I want the game to be easy, you idiots. I am playing open shift because your game doesn't make sense in standard mode.---I really like this game. I didn't at first, before open shift was introduced, but with open shift it is a much better experience.I am not sure why developers have decided to bundle open shift with unlimited oxygen, but whatever, fortunately I can opt into one without opting into the other.Below is my take on open vs. timed shift. There are plenty of reviews describing the game, so I am not going to.-- SPOILERS BELOW --A lot of people complained about the "standard" 15 min per shift mode, but I think most of the complaints were for a wrong reason. By itself, the timed shift mode is a perfectly valid gameplay, like timed puzzle solving. It might not be my thing, but there are plenty of people out there who enjoy this type of game.The problem with timed shifts is that it breaks the narrative. The game goes to a great length to establish that you are a desperate, low level worker, basically indentured labor, working for a decidedly evil, slave driving, AI killing, terrible secrets hiding corporation. You are in deep-deep debt with them, they nickel and dime you for everything, the work environment is dangerous and unforgiving and they don't care, if you die they will just replace you.In this narrative, open shift makes sense. You work crazy hours and you "use the whole buffalo", you pull every cent of salvage out of that ship, so you can crawl your way out of this crap as fast as possible.But timed shifts don't make sense. All the talk about "using the whole buffalo" goes right out of the window. I just watched one of the best speedrunners and at the end they still had a large part of the ship still intact. And once you yank out more valuable components it becomes economically unfeasible to return to the same ship on the next shift. So it makes more sense as a regular player to yank out the reactor and maybe the thruster and move on to the next ship. So the same company that will charge you for every bit of oxygen and complain when you burn an aluminum panel worth maybe a few hundreds is perfectly fine with you discarding millions of credits worth of salvage just because your shift is over and it is not worth your while. This breaks the suspension of disbelief.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has to go on that pile of recommended games labelled, "disappointments."  I write this not to suggest that Hardspace is not worth your time.  The core loops works, and it can be very engaging and fun to dice up ships and salvage them for parts.  The unfortunate part is that opening salvo of promise doesn't hold up for the length of the game.Early Access can be a boon, it allows developers to show off a core loop and demonstrate the idea they have for a project.  Projects like these are why I'm more wary of Early Access than outright failures: Hardspace is fine.  6 out of 10.  It does what it says, but fails to expand from there.  That's the problem.  The core loop works here, and slicing up ships is fun.  There's just ... not much else to it.  There are some light hazards in ships to deal with but they don't really change the game in an exciting way.  Upgrading your equipment feels token and minor.  Even paying off your debt is pretty vestigial.  In short, if you aren't here for that proof-of-concept, slice a ship up and dump it in the furnace, it's not going to hold your attention.This is demonstrated in my playtime.  I'd hate to say it's artificially inflated, but I waited periodically for the big, meaty updates to release new ships, new mechanics or the story and gave it another try.  Each time I found myself less engaged and more disinterested.  Hardspace isn't bad, but it is disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker is a completely unique, brilliantly crafted experience that transcends the genres of simulation and science fiction by fusing them into something that no one would ever have thought they could want to play until they sat down to chop up their first Mackerel with a splitsaw. I've been wielding my multipurpose grapple tool since the early days of early access for Shipbreaker, and I've watched it evolve from an amusing and creative sandbox experience to a deeply immersive and satisfying gameplay loop, not to mention the surprisingly compelling and relevant narrative that now accompanies it. And after all of these hours, I'm finally in the midst of my first playthrough of the full campaign since release.This game is supremely underrated, and if you're even the least bit interested, I promise it will impress you. During early access, I remember enjoying it thoroughly, but being a bit worn out by repetitive ship layouts. Now, I feel like there are so many that it really will take me until I work off my 1.2 billion credit debt to master them all, from the long and narrow Atlas Scouts to the densely packed salvage Geckos. And even then, the competitive Cutter's Race mode could potentially keep me occupied until the end of time, trying to figure out how to creatively cut apart a vessel as fast as possible.The features on display are certainly worth noting, but perhaps the best part of the experience is the painstakingly crafted world in which the game sits. The realism is bolstered by the fine details that litter the interior of the various ships you cut apart, from the occasional poster (which you can now swipe to decorate your personal HAB) to the idly drifting data drives you can delve into for nuggets of gritty space lore. And all of this detail speaks to the love with which it has all been intimately fabricated. Because of this, it is easy to become fully immersed, and to cringe when you accidentally chop an air filter in half because you forgot to switch to your stinger instead of your splitsaw, or to feel your stomach clench when you realize you pulled out the power supply before disconnecting the thrusters, meaning you now have pipes of volatile fuel that will easily detonate if you so much as jostle them. But on the flipside, it is also what makes it tremendously satisfying when you learn that you can bash the fuel pipes with a cannister of coolant to freeze them up, making them safe to cut. That kind of lesson is something the game doesn't directly teach you (it might be found in an obscure data drive, but it's definitely not in a tutorial), so discovering it on your own or through online forums lends a sense of discovery and authenticity to the game that makes you feel like you are truly becoming a professional shipbreaker as you play. If, like me, you played this during the early days, boot it back up and give it a whirl. You will absolutely not regret it. If you've been considering it for a while, but are unsure if it deserves your time when your steam library is already full of games yet to be played (a problem which I attribute almost entirely to Humble Bundle), then consider no more. This game will blow you away with the force of a Class II Reactor meltdown.

_childDocuments_.review: Why. Why in the world is this game as addicting as it is? You're just a wrecker. Ripping apart space ships right? Right. But also, wrong.As I write this the game is only on version 0.4.0 but the story is actually pretty interesting which I won't spoil anything here, youtube it I'm sure someone's done something on it. I am eagerly awaiting the next major update that expands the story, let alone updates that add more ships to tear apart. So far there's a limited number of ships to wreck, yet each has their own challenges. And even though some may be the same Mackrel class transport, their power cells, fuel cells or other hazards can be different or arranged in different patterns. Maybe it's pressurized? Maybe evil AI is causing trouble? There's so many different ways to tackle every ship breakdown. Do you go carefully? trying to get every last buck out of your salvage? Decompressing chambers, opening doors with control panels and such. Or go for some "Rapid Disassembly" AKA, blow it up with explosives. Cause that is an option. Just... watch out, flying debris can damage your suit, causing oxygen leaks, cracking your visor or kicking you onto another radio station.If you enjoy games where attention to detail is important then by all means try this game. If you don't like taking your time and would rather rush stuff? maybe this game isn't for you. It's about patience, taking your time and trying not to make your already substantial debt any worse. Admittedly progression can be a LITTLE slow, but this is also affected by what kind of ship you're breaking and whether or not you're using all your tools. I neglected using tethers for the longest time and now that I'm using them my salvaging speed has increased substantially. (though even doing this progression seems slow, and needs improvement or fine tuning. Though at least the DEV's are more concerned with adding more gameplay and FINISHING the game rather then balancing it at every update prior to the full launch.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is alright. It *is* satisfying to tear apart a ship when you do it right. I think the game balance is good - money and needing to repair tools, upgrading etc. You'll wish you can get rid of the breath timer, and might be tempted to start over on an easier difficulty to do so, but don't - there's no autosave and being forced back to bed every ten minutes means you don't lose much progress on a crash.Storyline is poor. Pacing is glacial. You can get up to level 20, and there's a new set of dialogue per level. Access to advanced tools is gated behind levels and therefore behind story beats. Sometimes this works really well. Sometimes it doesn't - there's clearly only about 12 to 15 actual story beats in the game, and a /lot/ of filler. You can't skip post-shift dialogue, either, so you just have to wait it out, and it's normally not interesting enough to spend even your next shift ruminating on.The ending of the game (spoilers, I guess) is almost embarrassing in how crudely it delivers its message - and boy does it have a message - this game is no allegory, it is propaganda (that I happen to agree with). The final cutscene feels taken straight from a corporate welcome pack, complete with soulless music designed by committee, while the game's worst character narrates the most predictable outcome. And that's following a final mission where you're very clearly given a choice, but what you choose doesn't actually matter.The minute-to-minute gameplay is good. Great, even. But I couldn't recommend this game to someone knowing how much stuff they will have to sit through, thinking that I endorse it in its entirety. It'd have to be rewritten, or even removed, even though I support the message.

_childDocuments_.review: What a phenomenal game this is, I can't believe I didn't find it when it was released considering how frequently I peruse the store. In any case, its a game totally unlike any other I've played. The career has you working - effectively - as a serf for a space-salvage company working off the debt they incurred to bring you up and train you. Its hazardous work, to be sure, but thankfully they provide cloning services to keep you going should the worst befall you. As you prove yourself, you gain access to upgrades to your equipment, more complex ships to salvage, and ever-greater fortune. Even with the game as it is now, it was easily worth the $20 I paid, and I'm really looking forward to what Blackbird Interactive can make happen in the near future.I highly recommend it!
