_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Don't buy this even when it's out of EA. The devs have no clue what they are doing. They should have launched the game as complete when it went into EA. It was a much more fun game then and the few QL changes they made are the only good updates.This game is very pretty. The graphics alone are enough to make you drool. I have changed my view on this game otherwise sadly. I don't honestly think this game is worth anyones time. Countless issues pop up with every update, and the number of bugs they fix seem to only be really small stupid things like a minor visual glitch instead of game breaking bugs. I used to have quite a bit of fun with this game when it first came out, but now with all of the changes it's hardly the same game. The HUD when ship breaking is absolute trash. The old system had timers on your oxygen so you could actually time when you needed to go back to the hub and refill but now it's just some obscure bar with no good indication of fill level. Their story aspect is boring and stupid as well. But I can deal with the HUD being hard to read, that's fine. The real issue... what in the ♥♥♥♥ is the terminal UI change? Holy hell is it ugly as hell and super painful to even look at for more than a few seconds. Then, with the most recent update (Act II), they have now split up the terminal into several "interactable" spots around the hab. So cool, we can now move around a space in order to do stuff... that's cool, right? It's a glorified point and click interaction with long and weird camera shifts to get around the room, and it's not even a point and click, it's just click. It's not easy to use, and just makes it even harder to repair you gear, upgrade gear, check messages etc. . I really feel like this dev team has just said ♥♥♥♥ it to what worked in the past, we need to be new every update to keep attention and let me tell you, it's not keeping anyones attention.The new Javelin class ships are super cool to look at, but that's about it. There are so many problems with this new ship that it is just too hard to actually make use of them. If you want to disconnect the parts of the ship, you have to destroy other parts such as the air locks because the outer hull is solid rings instead of segmented panels like ALL of the other ships. The air locks get stuck between the outer hull parts that need to go to the processor, and the inner living spaces that need to go to the furnace. So say goodbye to using the airlocks and sending them into the barge. So many things are attached in unexpected ways, that you literally wont even see the attachment, because there isn't a physical one. The big fuel tanks in the middle of these new ships are connected via KSP's magic quantum struts that you can't see. You have to cut up areas of the ship that make no sense, just to get it loose from the rest of the ship that it isn't physically in contact with. No it's not just getting stuck, it is literally anchored to parts with out a physical anchor.  My other gripe is about the new demo charges. Why in the hell, do they have the power of an atomic bomb? Just place one of these tiny, 5inx5in pads on the ship, detonate, and send the ENTIRE ship flying into the damn furnace. I understand it's space and they should have a little push, but these things can literally fling the whole ship from one side of the bay to the other and ruin your salvaging. I personally didn't have a problem with the laser cutter chopping up the hull pieces. I was smart enough to not just willy nilly cut the ♥♥♥♥ out of a ship which I feel like is part of this games angle. Being smart with your cuts, so you don't destroy the ship but can salvage it. So making the laser ONLY a lvl 1 cut, and demanding the use of the det charges is horrible. I like the charges, they are very cool and I enjoy using them. But with the force they apply, it's worthless to me. I don't know if I will put much more time into this game now. If I have to be using these charges on the internal parts of ships... I wont play it more than a few more hours, if any at all. This game was so much fun before the det charges were added and they may just have single handedly ruined the game for me. This game is still very cool, and beautiful. I love the new Javelin because it looks really cool and who doesn't like new free content? But it's kind of unplayable for me. Maybe these are super specific issues that someone else has a solution to, but I have yet to find one. I have tried putting the det charges in opposing directions to fight the force of eachother to little success. Since they are sequential, and there (as far as I know) isn't a simultaneous detonation option, you can't fight the pushing they do. The ship will still be flung around. I'm one of those people that want to salvage everything, and forcing us into a corner where we HAVE to blow up something, or break tons of stuff just to get one other item isn't a fun thing. I have mastered all of the other ships. I can get 100% scrap all of the other ships with almost no loss of valuable material. I can even get the damn reactors out of the giant Geckos with out any kind of reactor issue and that's a chore. I'll leave this as recommended because I do like this game a lot and it is very pretty. But the new changes have ruined many of the things I liked so much about this game.New Update to game as of 5/7/2021:Doesn't look like any of the weird issues have been fixed, just more added. The game now crashes rather frequently on the first cut you do on a ship so that's nice. They have added a new 20 cert levels, removed the objectives for collecting certain things in the certs and work orders are non-existent. So what has this update done?1. Dumbed down the entire game. They removed the specifics in favor of a really generic percentage of ship salvaged (which doesn't actually show you a percentage).2. Dumbed down the HUD. There are no longer numbers for health, O2, or fuel, there's just some obscure bar that drains which is totally better than seeing an actual number on how much you have of those... The timer on your shift is now obscure and hard to notice at first and is kind of hard to actually read. 3. Added, from what I can tell at cert 8, 1 new type of ship.4. Spread out the progression to extend play time, aka, more grinding to get to the same spot as before.5. Increased the max debt while making it seemingly harder to money.6. Released about 4 campaign driven events (just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialogue that doesn't change anything about how you play).7. Introduced a bug where pieces of the ship will just not move no matter how many tethers are on it. 8. Changed the barge, furnace, and the processor to be turned off when you enter the yard every time. This sounds cool since you get to see the really cool barge start up sequence and giant puffs of blue/red smoke come out of the holes, but in reality it just causes tons of lag and weird issues. You have to wait about 15 seconds before the barge can be used so if you throw something down there, make sure you watch it and see that it doesn't hop back out.9. Screwed up the way the barge handles items it doesn't want. Say you put a reactor cap in the barge and it had a shield still on it, well, that shield is now one with the barge. Since the barge is now a volume box instead of just a snapping grid, things get stuck under the top level of it if it doesn't score them.

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker is a pretty notable game in a couple of different ways, being not only the only shipbreaking simulator I know of but also an explicitly leftist and pro-labor game. You get to tear apart old spaceships as methodically as possible as they gradually increase in size and complexity, learning new ways to deal with all kinds of different components, and then you also build a union and secure your own rights alongside your coworkers as the company you work for tries to grind you down by every means available. In both of those aims, it acquits itself well; not flawless, but pretty damn solid overall.The primary draw, the gameplay, is probably the most novel aspect of it. You get to float around in zero-G, with pleasantly well-realized freeform movement, using a laser and a grapple gun (and later demolition charges) to disassemble impounded spaceships and deal with each component in the correct fashion. It's like nothing I've played before, but the game manages to make it feel familiar and welcoming regardless, and flipping the normally constructive goal of most simulator games on its head is an engaging concept. As time goes on, the ships get bigger and more structurally complex, and new hazards such as pressurized interiors and live reactors are introduced that require their own procedures to resolve. About 2/3 of the game, this progression largely levels off and settles into tedium when I'd prefer it moved into stripping down huge battleships over dozens of hours, but the game manages to justify this with the story beats happening at the same time, and at the end introduces a delightful twist on the formula that feels joyful and deserved after everything you've worked through thus far. If you are just into breaking down the same three mid-sized ships once the story is resolved, that's fine too; the game is happy to let you for as long as you like.That story is probably the aspect of the game that most appealed to me over the long term. The characters and individual beats are pretty broadly drawn, and nothing that happens at any point is surprising, but I liked what it was saying—about the value of labor and the humans that carry it out, things you don't hear games say nearly enough—and the degree to which it's intertwined with the gameplay, especially with regards to how the setting is realized, is genuinely impressive. Every scrap of flavor text, attached to every upgrade and menu, further makes you feel enmeshed in the game's future of a metastasized gig economy, and as previously mentioned, the gameplay progression ebbs and flows in response to what the plot is doing. The dialogue, while rote in terms of narrative function, is generally pleasant and believable, bolstered by some strong vocal performances, and when the gameplay novelty petered out it's what kept me coming back. It's just nice, from top to bottom.While no aspect of Hardspace: Shipbreaker is perfect—the gameplay is innovative but fails to maintain interest after a while, while the writing and presentation are just the opposite—it's a good package all around, full of cool ideas and smart things to say. When I started this review I was unsure if I'd recommend it at full price, but I just noticed that I spent over 60 hours on it, and it felt like a third of that, so I suppose it's a perfectly reasonable investment. Give it a shot, unreservedly.

_childDocuments_.review: For quite a while now, I've been looking for a game that fits the "Simulator" genre, but isn't just a glorified clicker. Hardspace: Shipbreaker seems to be exactly that game.The game supports two vastly different playstyles: You can either comb the ships for their most valuable resources, or completely dismantle them until literally nothing is left; how long you work on each individual ship is completely up to you. If you choose to salvage as much as possible from each craft, you'll be facing a lot of busywork, since you'll have to pick off dozens of little components. But if you enjoy that kind of gameplay, it can be an incredibly satisfying experience.Dying is more or less meaningless in this game, but that doesn't mean that failure doesn't exist. There are many ways to break valueable components or even entire parts of the ship, and if you cause too much damage, you'll be locked out of the most lucrative rewards for each job. Progressing through the story and unlocking upgrades is more or less automatic, but completing all of the optional objectives for each salvage operation can actually be quite challenging.Even at this stage, there's a ton of content to sink your teeth into. After more than 10 hours, I have barely dented the upgrade tree, and I'm still regularly unlocking major new gameplay features. The game does have bugs (such as objects flying off into space for no reason) which remind you that you're playing an Early Access game, but it's already in a better state than some recent AAA games have been in at launch. That being said, the developers regularly wipe players' save games and have already stated that save data from the Early Access version will not carry over into the 1.0 release, so keep that in mind when you decide whether the game is worth getting into at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is decent for a bit. The first half of my playtime made me think of cleaning/sorting games (Shipyard Simulator, House Flipper, Viscera Cleanup Detail, etc.), and I quite like sci-fi settings in games. However, breaking apart the ships eventually felt like a chore. The thing about these types of games is that they are literally video game implementations of chores, except they're typically pretty darn fun. With Hardspace: Shipbreaker, however, I got bored by the halfway mark.The music is kinda nice, with a sort of "melodic country" vibe to it, but that's probably my only compliment about the game which doesn't ever "get old" or frustrate me. The storyline, however, features an impossibly evil corporation presented in a world which could only allow its contract to exist by way of society becoming so corrupt that it would not care about indentured servitude and being effectively "owned" by companies in every sense of the word...while also wanting to pretend that the same world would recoil and reject the evil corporation. The story lacked logic very often and the only good, high-stakes moment of the entire storyline was flubbed in its conclusion, just making me all the more dissatisfied with it.Hardspace: Shipbreaker feels like a strong 7 or 8 in the first couple of hours, but by the time I was at the end, I think it was at a 4 or a 5 at best. If you turn off the NPC voices so that you can't hear the atrocious storyline and ignore the plot every chance you get, you might be able to enjoy the game for a fair few hours.

_childDocuments_.review: When you strip away all the eye candy this is basically a life simulator.You start out with a huge debt, every time you end your work shift you get presented by many many bills to pay and the scraps that are left is what you hand in to pay off your HUGE debt. (So if your rich and ever wondered what 99% of the people of this planet do, well play this game and laugh at us poor peasants.)Seriously though, this game is a gem in the pile of early access games that are [self censored].The game is for an early access game very playable although not to many different ships yet for breaking up.  I did not notice any game breaking bugs (3 hours gameplay) just a lot of placeholder menu's which will be updates in the future.The main gameplay loop is basically:- Pick a ship to recycle- Rip everything off that's in your work order for the most value- Bump your helmet a few times while doing this- Ruin your tools with your own bad maintenance schedule- Die while getting crushed between huge panels- Die in explosions- Die from electrocution- Die from flying into the waste burner- Die from explosive decompressions- Die from forgetting to refill your oxygen- Learn from the mistakes of your previous clone- Make the same mistakes again- Have fun while dying- Refill your oxygen about 2 to 3 times every 15 minute shift or again... DIE- Get paid so you can pay the bills for working- See the rest disappear into your debt- Upgrade your tools and suit/helmet from skill points you get through work order completion- Repeat in the next shiftFYI about the timer, you do only get 15 minutes realtime in a shift. Every shift in the beginning will cost you about 500000 credits and usually you'll make about 700000 (again, in the beginning!). BUT!!! You can work on a ship and work order in several shifts so time isn't really an issue unless you forget to refill your oxygen in time...It's been a long time since I could give a thumbs up to an early access project, but this seems to be another good one like Space Engineers and Subnautica was when they were in early access.p.s. This game has a lot more to offer then my short description, always check multiple sources before you decide to invest your money into it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is wonderful. It has an incredible amount of potential and it just released. They wanted to capture a "space cowboy" aesthetic and I think they nailed it. The themes of overbearing corporatism are present without feeling like it's beating you over the head, you really feel like you're just working day in day out.   In its current state there are two variations of ships and variables within those that alter the way you deconstruct them. The level of freedom in how you go about doing things, and how the gameplay loop flows is very unique even among a genre where you can point to several similar games. The amount of world building and lore is shocking, delivered through text documents and audio logs found in the midst of gameplay.  Also in its current state: a large number of bugs, and several crashes. The bugs generally don't get in the way of gameplay, but the crashes sometimes seem to just *happen*. They've already made bug and crash fixes a priority, so expect that to get better.I can already tell this game is going to be sorely under rated, and urge that if you think you like what you see in gameplay footage, to give it a fair shake. There's easily 15~ hours of unique content at this early stage, and more than that if you want to finish the progression.

Zero g doesn't feel like zero-g. Look at Elite Dangerous, a true proper space game. If you turn off flight assist you will spin forever unless you apply an equal and opposite force or hit something. If you cut your thrust you will maintain your velocity until you apply an equal amount of thrust in the opposite direction. Elite Dangerous did it right, and this game feels like ass coming from something like that.   Yes I really am going to not recommend the game just because the Dev's can't implement proper physics. _childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker. It’s disappointing to give this game a thumbs down, considering its enormous potential, but here’s why.First, let’s talk about what’s great. I pre-purchased this game as soon as I could and was thrilled with the early access in 2020. Back then, it offered truly innovative first-person zero-g gameplay, amazing physics and destruction simulations, over 15 hours of content, and three starting ships with multiple variations. However, not much has changed since then, and that’s where the issues start.This game lacks content—it feels like 70% of a game with no hope of completion. The last content update was in June 2022, just a month after release. Since then, no new content has been added. Since the initial version in 2020, they’ve added only one ship and some variations, bringing the total to four ships. The ship size also falls short in the endgame. In career mode, you unlock new ships, variations, and upgrades from levels 1-30, but the last 10 levels are devoid of content, just existing for the sake of it. Initially, players felt a sense of unease with atmospheric storytelling when exploring abandoned ships, occasionally making the game feel creepy. I was excited when AI ships, which have a will of their own, were introduced. The game presents them as spooky and dangerous, but this falls flat. Instead of haunted ships with traps and scares, it’s a disappointing scavenger hunt for little red orbs to destroy. The AI’s worst gameplay feature is closing a door on you, forcing you to hunt for small items to destroy by hand.Now, onto the story. It could have been much more enjoyable with classic freelance spacer tropes, interplanetary conspiracies, and maybe some aliens. Instead, we get boring sob stories while trying to detach a fusion reactor without getting blown up. I’d happily join their union if they gave me a "mute" button! I’d even side with the corporation if it meant no more unskippable dialogue and cutscenes. The other characters are dull and distract from the gameplay with inane chatter. Nothing is more annoying than listening to boring conversations when you just want to scrap spaceships.Before its release, the game had no overbearing dialogue or terrible voice acting. There was a tutorial character who occasionally popped in with background dialogue while you salvaged, but it didn’t take control away from the player. Now, the dialogue is poor quality and excessively grating. All the characters are insufferable. The writing is so bland, annoying, and uninteresting that it’s maddening. The game is brilliant, so I put up with it, but the lack of a skip button is baffling. I’d skip Lou, but I want to hear training explanations, so muting the game isn’t ideal. It’s not people talking to you; it’s people talking at you with monologues and one-sided conversations. In the hab, these forced conversations are the worst. In space, I can work while they talk, but in the hab, I’m forced to sit and listen. I usually end up watching YouTube or walking away while the unskippable nonsense continues.And then there’s the lack of control over "decisions." I support unions if they work as intended and am all for taking down the company in the game. But being signed up to a union without consent is just as grating as the sudden $1,000,000,000 debt that appears out of nowhere. At least the debt has some justification as the premise for why you work there.In conclusion, Hardspace: Shipbreaker had so much potential but ultimately falls short due to its lack of content and frustrating dialogue. The innovative gameplay and impressive physics can only carry it so far when there’s so little to do and the story elements are more irritating than engaging. While the initial experience was promising, the game hasn't evolved enough since its early access days to keep it compelling. It’s a brilliant concept bogged down by poor execution, and that’s why I can't recommend it in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Hardspace: Shipbreaker since early access, around Nov 2020. I've spent a *lot* of time in this game (almost Skyrim numbers... :P ), and it's pretty great.I describe this game to friends as a reverse jigsaw puzzle: you're taking ships apart, but you need to select the correct piece at the correct time. People like to discuss decompression, but I don't see much talk about the power systems: in order to have a controlled reactor shutdown, you need to switch off the fuel from the reactor to the thrusters. But if you pulled the main power grid, those switch aren't powered any more. Dig yourself out of that one. :PThe game is gorgeous. There are 4 main ship hulls, there's a wide variety of internal layouts. For example, a Gecko Heavy Transport and a Gecko Station Hopper are both Geckos (so look almost identical from the outside), but the internals are radically different. The former has minimised its internal compartments in order to maximise cargo capacity, whereas the other has maximised its internal compartments in order to maximise seating. As such, there's a huge amount of replayability here.I see a large number of complaints about the story, about it both being "over the top" and "rammed down my throat". It's a story about unionisation at an anti-union workplace. The conversations (that no, you can't skip) last at most 20-30 seconds. There *might* be one that goes on for about 1min.  Usually these are happening during your shift, so you can just work away while they discuss their ♥♥♥♥♥♥ working conditions. And it's true that (rarely) there's a voicemail waiting for you inside the Hab that you can't skip. What a hard life one must have for a couple of 30sec voicemails to ruin a game for you.(Really though, it's about twerps so immersed in anti-union propaganda that any kind of pro-union discussion gives them a sadface)Personally, I found the story refreshing: especially here in North America, there's a distinct lack of positive portrayals of union-formation. Unions are almost always portrayed as connected with the mafia, or otherwise just negatively represented. While there are certainly issues with unions (and all other kinds of 'organised people'), it's nice to see a pro-union narrative for once. Especially at this time when North Americans are (slowly) starting to realise that unions are needed to negotiate on an even footing with large corporations.Anywho.Hardspace: Shipbreaker.It's gorgeous.It's fun.It's relaxing.It goes wrong hilariously from time to time.Worth paying full-price, and then some.

The movement in zero G becomes second nature, as you whip around the bay with your tether, like some kind of space spider man.The game also tells an important story, it at first seems that it represents some dystopian future, but upon closer inspection, you realise that debt, unsafe work conditions and union-busting are real now, it's just the space ships that are missing (and the clones for infinite retries).The end of the game feels absolutely earned, it's truly worth it. "Bunny Character D" FTW!And the best part is, even after finishing the campaign I'm not done! There are still loads of audio and text logs to be found, more to be discovered about the creepy ghost ships, more hazardous ships. Who knows, maybe I'll try the race mode once, although from what I've seen, the highscores are absolutely crazy. :D

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: Since I wrote this review the devs have pushed updates adding more variety and challenge and addressing some of the drawbacks I mention, so don't take those aspects too seriously now. I really like the direction they're taking and most of my doubts on replayability have vanished.tl;dr: really cool concept, fun core loop, but limited content/game time currently and more of a chilled-out experience than an actual challenge. Looking forward to future updates to see what the devs have planned to add more variation.I'm really intrigued about this game. It's a pretty unique idea which has a lot of potential, but at this stage is a very bare-bones experience. The gameplay is fun and really kind of relaxing, but there are only a few ship classes to choose from just now (although the interior layout varies for them).In general I've found performance to be decent for a game this new. There are a few bits of physics weirdness when grabbing stuff like fuel tanks or powered components sometimes but nothing you can't work around, and I imagine those things will be ironed out over time. On that subject, the devs so far have been really good. Regular patches and some content put out since release into EA, and they listened to community feedback and added a no-timer mode (although personally, I don't know why they also removed oxygen use too).The cutting 'physics' are pretty impressive - cuts will actually appear exactly where you aimed at whatever angle you aimed it at, not along some predefined break point just-near-enough. You can be as precise or rough as you want. Destruction simulation is also pretty cool. Explosions or decompression events will genuinely shred the nearby metal. I can't say I'm any kind of expert on what space ships look like after exploding but I can definitely believe it would look something like the expanding ball of twisted metal shards and buckled plating that you have to deal with in this.My concern with the game long-term is replayability. At the moment the hazards are kind of easy (I only actually killed myself once, before I realised properly how power works) and once you've handled a couple of them there's no real danger. Even with the timer on, the layout of the key components is always pretty similar so after your first attempt it's pretty easy to complete the work orders in the time window. Greater variation in ships etc. will help but I hope there is a greater puzzle element added as more complex ships come along, rather than just scaling up the current challenge. Something like daily challenges might be good too, to give some competitive element, or high-hazard jobs with ships that are already partially wrecked when you start and are more unstable than usual.I'm kind of waiting to see what the devs add in future before I decide whether I really love this game or not, but if you like the space-y engineering concepts, or like me will happily spend an hour on one ship trying to correctly salvage every single component, then I'd highly recommend giving it a go. Even in it's current state, I'll definitely drop back in now and then to chill and tear a ship apart, and I don't regret spending the money at all.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm nearing 60 hours of playtime at this point, so I feel like it's time to update my review.No other game (and believe me, I've looked) captures quite the same feel this one does, its truly unique. In case you couldn't gather from the trailer and store page, the general vibe is sort of dystopian sci-fi Americana, as weird as that sounds.Overview:You are LYNX cutter 9346-52. Your job, as you could probably tell, is to cut apart ships for salvage, bringing each part into the processor, furnace, or salvage barge. These derelict ships are incredibly dangerous, with fuel, electrical, cryo, and nuclear systems that all threaten to tear you to pieces, not to mention the risk of becoming a casualty of physics should you mishandle your equipment or forget to safely decompress the ship's atmosphere (yes this game has an atmosphere simulation for ships, and it's pretty advanced!).LYNX Equipment:As a LYNX Salvage shipbreaker you're equipped with a pretty sturdy suit, a not-so sturdy helmet, and a scanner to help figure out what's inside a ship as well as know what parts of the ship are pressurized. You have some thrusters for full attitude control, a grappler for hauling all sorts of heavy objects, a laser cutter for precision disassembly (with single-point "stinger" and wide-angle "slicer" modes), and finally, remote demo charges for when your precise disassembly needs to be a little more...  All of this equipment can be upgraded with LYNX tokens you earn for carrying out your duties.Controls:The controls are very intuitive, WASD for forward, back, and strafe, Q and E for roll, space for up, C for down, and CTRL (or Q and E at the same time) for retro-thrusters (brakes). The controls feel, for lack of a better word, floaty, which makes sense.  I think this works well for the game as it is very momentum based, this makes dealing with huge chunks of ships difficult (as it should be) and makes it more stressful when you need to do something quickly but precisely (as it should be).Graphics:I'm not gonna stand here and say it's the best looking game of all time, but this game looks really good during just regular play, and looks incredible when something goes awry. seeing interior walls give way during explosive decompression as debris flies through the gaping hole you cut in the ship, or seeing a nuclear reactor go critical and explode, because you accidentally cut a nuclear fuel line, or rushing towards a fuel cut-off valve as fuel lines burn and threaten to explode the fuel injectors, no matter what's going wrong during your salvage, you better believe it gonna look cool doing it.Music:This was my main reason for saying "Americana" as the vibe. The Americana style music in this game feels spot on, despite being, theoretically, out of place for a sci-fi game set in the early 24th century. The music is very chill and nice to listen to. The soundtrack is adaptive as well, when you go into a pressurized ship, the music has an eerie feel to it, when things are catching on fire, electronics are arcing, or you're extracting a nuclear reactor, the music becomes tense and your character starts breathing heavy, the sound work in this game, overall, is very well done.Conclusion:Even though I finished this game at 30-something hours of play-time, I keep coming back to play more since it's just that fun to take apart a couple of ships every once in a while. You can tell in every facet of this game that love and care was put into it, and this game is one of my favorites because of that. The game's price is a little steep, but even at $35 I'd recommend buying it, even at full price. If you're seeing this Blackbird Interactive, I love y'all's game and would love to see a DLC (or sequel) for it. It does have an unused hazard type and hazard level, after all, maybe that and a couple extra ships and I'd happily buy that DLC for another $10 or so.

_childDocuments_.review: An aesthetically pleasing game with extremely enjoyable physics-based gameplay that induces a flow state in you like no other, with impeccable sound design. Like seriously, these people know their sound design. This game has gotten flak from some Steam users for two reasons: 1) having a story, and 2) not having enough different ship hulls. I think the narrative is actually critical, because without any emotional stakes the game would be just a toy to play around with. There is a free mode for people who want to just break ships and not think about a narrative. The second criticism about the content is reasonable, though I think it's mostly people who played this game in early access and exhausted the content. This is unfortunate and shows the failings of an early access model for a game which is supposed to be narrow and deep rather than broad and shallow. To me an essential element of this game is the three phase process where you 1) get familiar with the game, 2) get extremely good at the game, and 3) start finding the game repetitive. I think 3) exists for a ludonarrative reason - the job is a JOB and it's supposed to become rote - but I realize for a game that might be a bit of an excuse. But I think the main draw here is phase 2): getting really good at the game by repeatedly breaking down similar hulls with some variation in between (like hazards and pressurization). This is what induces the flow state. This is where you start feeling the mastery and skill you have accumulated over the game. But you can't have 2) without 3). The game needs to have a limited amount of hulls for you to get good at it, unless you're someone who can pour 1000 hours into a game (and there aren't very people like that, and they are already pouring their time into something else). So for a game aiming at a length in the dozens of hours, having fewer hulls is a perfectly justifiable design decision.There is also the same old "this game is political!" argument. This game doesn't exactly hide its politics. You should realize within the two hour refund window that this game is about how capitalism sucks people dry. The corporation literally kills you and gives you a billion dollar bill for the trouble. In fact making a game about a job like this and not highlighting the issues of exploitation would, itself, be political.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If you enjoyed Viscera Cleanup Detail or Powerwashing Simulator, but want something that requires just a little bit more thought and consideration before you "clean" something, this game is perfect... in free-play mode (the story in career mode is garbage). Also, choose the "easy" difficulty with no timer. You can choose to still have oxygen drain. Trust me, the timer is dumb.___I do recommend this game... but only just. And I've flip-flopped on that decision a few times even as I wrote this.The game itself, the core gameplay loop, is great. It's interesting without being exhausting, fun without being stressful, and satisfying without being monotonous. This is why I ultimately decided to mark it recommended, because despite its problems, I still keep coming back to this game. Also it makes respawning a canon event in-world, which is pretty neat. (I do think the fee is too low--it's completely inconsequential compared to the magnitude of your debt and how expensive the process must be, so there's effectively zero penalty to dying as many times as you want. It would take multiple deaths per day multiple days in a row with extremely slow and inefficient salvaging to actually have an impact). However, like most people here, my primary complaints lie with the story. Frankly, it's just awful. The characters are two dimensional and the plot is about as subtle as a teenager's first fanfiction novel with no sign of getting better anytime soon.You know that scene in Home Alone where Kevin throws a brick at the guy's head from the roof of the building? Then he does it again? Then he does it AGAIN? Yeah, that's what this story feels like. Just repeatedly bludgeoning you over the head with incredibly shallow, obvious, and predictable plot points. It is painfully obvious the "writer" for this game is very inexperienced.And to make things worse, the cutscenes are UNSKIPPABLE. The real penalty to making a serious mistake and wanting to restart the day is needing to listen to the same dialogue a second time, especially if there's a transmission call for you--at least the dialogue when you load into the bay can be tuned out while you proceed with your salvaging.And the timer. God, the timer. I made the mistake of starting my game under the "normal" difficulty, which means that I get a whopping 15 minutes to do all my salvaging for the day. That's fifteen minutes before the salvage yard forcibly shuts off and kicks me back into the hab where I seem to do absolutely nothing except eat and sleep. That's fifteen minutes PER DAY. It's utterly ridiculous and breaks my immersion big time. What on earth were the devs thinking? Unfortunately now I'm a few dozen "days" into the story and like hell I'm listening to all that tripe again, nevermind all the upgrades to my gear and rank.Edit: Oh, I almost forgot: the AI "ghost ships" are just dumb. They got hyped up to be so scary and dramatic, with multiple mentions by characters, eerie music and warping your systems... and then all the AI nodes ever did was open and close some doors. And the ship wasn't even all that valuable! Very underwhelming, felt like a total waste of time.Anyway. Choose no-timer, with oxygen drain, and stick to free-play mode instead of career, and this game is fantastic.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid blue-collar labor simulator in space, with an emphasis on figuring out how best to take apart the spaceships entrusted to you for salvage, both in terms of speed and safety -and minimizing damage to the ship and any valuable equipment, of course.Original and fun gameplay wrapped around a central cautionary tale of what happens when people just keep accepting corporate abuse, day after day. It's entirely possible to do serious bodily harm to your in-game self and be charged for a replacement body, and you as a player should be mindful of bright flashing lights; epileptics would probably do best to steer clear of this particular game, unless an option is added to dim the flashes or something.Your job is to throw stuff in the correct receptacles; the furnace, processor, and barge, depending on type; this gets you points to upgrade your rank and your gear, along with money to gradually pay off your debt to the company for various absurd hiring costs. To do this, you have a set of tools; a space suit, of course, with thrusters to help move you around. A grabby beam that can also fire a kinetic push blast; careful you don't launch yourself instead of whatever you're pointed at. Then there's your laser cutter, with your choice of pinpoint single-part melting mode and sweeping, vertical/horizontal line cutting mode. Your scanner, for identifying valuables or confirming material types of hull and inner structure through handy blueprint-style visual filters. And, eventually, the demolition charges - good for blowing holes in stuff that's beyond the power of your cutting tool. Also great for blowing up poorly placed fuel tanks and yourself, so watch out.Ships come in a handful of basic models, split into sub-variants and with each variant coming in different varieties, randomly and also based on your current hazard level clearance (difficulty of ships, essentially). This averages out to quite a bit of variety and with the element of challenging yourself to find new and better ways to do stuff (potentially getting creative with demo charges, for one), the game feels fresh and engaging for a remarkable length of time.All in all, highly recommended for anyone looking for a fairly chill experience that's not without its tense moments and a certain amount of drama over the communication channels. Weaver's a delight!

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace Shipbreaker stands out in its own way from many other casual simulation games in the genre. The premise is simple, you cut ships and break them apart to salvage the valuables.The job is never easy though. Nuclear, radiation, fire, explosive decompression, electric discharges and crush hazards impact your workflow and can very much kill you. But then your employers just rebuild you so you can carry on, of course.Hardspace Shipbreaker comes with a well thought-out campaign mode, where although the salvaging is routine, the introduction of new hazards, new faces on the comms and randomised ship layouts mean you never really get bored of it. If you like space games and cutting things open repeatedly, Hardspace Shipbreaker is worth every penny of the debt you incur as a LYNX employee.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost this is an Early Access game.There are bugs.It does crash sometimes.The game is not complete.That being said... it's just simple fun. I am not sure why I am mindlessly enjoying this as much as I am. Each new rank of ship gets progressively harder and once you understand the ship your time to tear it down just keeps getting faster and faster and the end goal being to eventually get out of debt and make money.At my current rate, that will be quite some time. But it does look achievable. Which when I saw my debt, I laughed quite hard and was like.. ok this won't ever happen.The only complaint that some may feel is there is the game doesn't hold your hand. It lets you know the basics and it's totally up to you on how to tear the ships apart. The starter ships have a set pattern but once you get to rank 6+ it jumps. Yeah there are still patterns but there is a lot more you have to consider as you move forward. Such as.. oh I should have looked to see if this one room was pressurized before I popped it.. whelp.. that just blew up 1/3 of the rig. Oh and hey.. I got my face mask punctured and I was already low on Oxygen.. oh god can I make it back to the hab to repair in time?!It definitely starts slow but starts to pick up by rank 6 out of 10. Which does not take long to get it. And each jump feels like a decent jump in difficulty. I cannot wait to see how crazy rank 10 is.For an Early Access game, I'm having way to much fun already.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I have played since very early access. It's an example of EA done right. The game was fun in an unfinished state. It's been interesting to see how the game has evolved and refined in this time, and the final product is absolutely a unique gem of PC gameplay. You're breaking apart and recycling ships in space, I can't think of anything like this.The controls take a little bit of getting used to. Experience with zero G and flight sim games can help. I use an xbox controller, and I found them rather easy to master once I got em down, but I have a knack for the aforementioned game genres. Learning the order to break apart a ship lest it break you apart, and destroy valuable salvage in the process... well that's the real gameplay. The story they've added has been interesting so far, all revealed by voice overs between days on the job, and at the start of new ones. While it won't win awards for best story, the voice acting is well done, and the story is enough to keep me curious about where it's going. The back-lore that's revealed in messages, and tool tips has me very intrigued.My old complaint about the game was the shift timers. You had a short period of time to be out scrapping, before having to call it a day (which would incur your daily fees). My big problem is I always needed just 1 minute more, or 30 seconds in some cases. Having the option to turn this shift timer off was just what I wanted. Now I can go strip an entire ship in one sitting, not having to constantly be freaking out over how much time I have left, wasted time, etc. I can take 45 minutes to 90 minutes depending on the ship, and dismantle it on my own time, and make sure I get everything. It's made the game the right kind of relaxing for me. Just don't play while you're dozey, you're liable to heat a fuel line and vaporize a million bucks worth of salvage!

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get the cons out of the way, first...CON: The story-line is a bit dumb. It's like a walking advertisement for unions and a protest against capitalism. If that influenced an already compelling story, that would be fine, but it's so ingrained that I wouldn't be surprised to learn that this game was actually funded by a union ad campaign. It doesn't influence the plot, it IS the plot.What makes it worse is that the game actively forces you to listen to every voice line after just about every ship you break down. If I could just ignore the plot and play the game, I'd be fine, but they are REALLY on a mission to sell unions with this game. It's super annoying.CON: The progression mechanics are also pretty mediocre. The plot centers around your "debt", but it really doesn't affect progression at all. You have to click through UIs related to how much you earned and all of that and you buy upgrades on your equipment to reduce your debt, etc... but ultimately, it doesn't mean anything!With all of that said, the game-play is super fun. It's so calming and casual. When I am bored, I just fire up this game and take apart a ship or two. Each ship is a fun puzzle that is just challenging enough that you don't have to do any math, but can still feel engaged with the objectives.I actually came here to see if there was any news on DLC to add more ships or any plans for a 2nd title, so, obviously I recommend that people buy this game and I, myself, will probably be buying whatever DLC they come up with and will, almost certainly, be purchasing ShipBreaker 2, if there ever is such a thing.Hopefully this time they will find a way to make a plot that isn't horrible and will give us something that increases replayability (like, user submitted ships in the workshop?)Anyway... that's my take... go ahead and buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I have a love-hate relationship with this game. I've watched it grow from day one, bought a copy the second it was in open-beta. I had really high hopes for this game, the potential, and the developers. But, I feel like we (all those who backed this project from the start) were a little let down. The variety (or lack there of) had me disappointed. 4 ships in total, the variants feel pretty repetitive. I'm sure there's a lot of other people like me who would've rather have a wider variety of unique ships rather than minor variations of the same ship over and over again.Then, there's the "story". it's really underwhelming. The amount that was added in "Act III" is laughable at best. The "Ghost Ships" are touched on breifly but it's never really expanded upon. The progression is slow and doesn't really feel rewarding at all. I feel that there's a lot more that could've been done had the devs actually cared to put more effort. This isn't to say they haven't already, but it overall just feels they were really lazy and didn't care enough to put in the effort to create a proper well developed story that sees proper character development/agency. The characters all feel very bare-bones with underdeveloped story-lines/arcs which is hard to believe considering the story has been in "development" from day 1, only for them to get lazy after a few months and just do the bare minimum just to say that they did do something.I want to love this game, I really do. I love the concept, the graphics, the in-game art style, the sound design, the physics, I want to love it all. But there's just a bunch of stuff that fell short and to the point where I wouldn't recommend the game. Not because it's not fun, but, because I don't want others to be let down like me and many others were.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is immensely fun to play. The world you are in is dangerous, and your employers see you as expendable. But if you want to dive into the meat of the game be aware that the trailers do represent that well -- you are alone in the vastness of space, and you can make mistakes, and they do cost you.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to give full-throated support for this game because it feels like two games. On the one hand, Hardspace Shipbreaker is a wonderful meditative experience and enjoyable puzzle game with enough of a dusting of danger and consequence that you'll get a pleasant jerk out of the zone once you (almost inevitably) mess up. On the other hand, Hardspace Shipbreaker is a too-fast, too-simple morality tale about exploitative corporations and the wonders of worker unity that gives the player no choice or agency in the course of its story.Let's start with the good. The gameplay is extremely enjoyable. The methodical process of breaking down ships and maneuvering large components in cramped spaces, juggling awkward piping and sensitive components, all the while keeping an eye on your oxygen and fuel meters and the shift clock, is a wonderfully engaging experience. The shock of an errant cut leading to sudden explosive decompression affected me more viscerally due to the otherwise placid and deliberate pace of the game than any death in any other game I've played recently. The moment-to-moment experience of playing the game is great; I can well imagine loading this up for a couple of shifts to relax and listen to a podcast. While there aren't a ton of ships (four different chassis, each with three variants) they each are different enough from one another that the player feels engaged with learning their intricacies and the most efficient way of breaking them down. Content-wise, the game lasted me 20 hours, and I don't feel like it was padded to any real extent.On the contrary, in fact, I felt that progression was entirely too quickly. Apparently shortly before release, the developers increased the rate at which Mastery Points, the progression tokens indicating what equipment and ships the player has access to, are earned. The progression is entirely too fast, unlocking too many hazards and ship types and front-loading a great deal of content that the game would be better served doling out slowly. I have heard that this change was due to player feedback, which is unfortunate; players don't necessarily recommend changes that improve the game overall. This is especially true of those who have already played the game in early access, and who might desire a quicker return to their normal level of content after a progress reset, which is what I think happened here.The problem of the rapidity of progression is most keenly felt in the story, which the player is hurtled through at breakneck speeds. There was barely any time for me to learn who the characters were before the first act was over and the "conflict" of the story kicked off. A slower progression would have allowed more time with the characters and allowed the player to actually build a connection with them, I feel. Unfortunately, I don't think there was much salvaging that could be done on the story proper, which is about as cut and dry as they come. You can probably predict the plot beat for beat by the second hour of playing. It rarely gets in the way of the gameplay, thankfully, but I wish that more had been done to tell a nuanced and, frankly, mature story than what ended up in the finished product. "Corporation bad, union good" isn't a particularly ground-breaking narrative. Why not make the issue even an iota more complex?And the complete lack of player agency in that plot gives it a tacked-on feel. Not every game has to be an RPG, of course, but the strength of story-telling in games is the agency that the player has in the events. The gameplay in Hardspace Shipbreaker is so disconnected from the actual story being told, besides the last part of the game, that it's hard to feel like you're an active participant in it.Here are some suggestions for how it could have been more tightly integrated. Each of these could have been expanded to reveal more of the world or the characters within it, if the developers actually wanted the story to have a greater focus in the game.I didn't encounter many bugs while playing; the only one of real note was that for some reason the game skipped the entire tutorial for me, giving me no instruction on several key aspects of the game. I was able to figure things out by reading the control mappings and watching a few YouTube videos, but starting a new game and just being Rank 3 and told to just go at it was a little disorientating.I still recommend the game, despite my comments about the story. Ignoring that part, it's a fun and engaging game. Just don't expect much from a story front. I would recommend playing on the limited lives mode, as well. Thirty is more than enough to beat the game, but risk of true failure heightens the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker stands as a masterpiece, seamlessly blending finely tuned gameplay with a compelling narrative. It's a rare gem that effectively communicates its message solely through mechanics; even without dialogue, players would grasp the game's commentary on the oppressive cycle of worker exploitation within capitalism. The developers' dedication to crafting a believable world and compelling characters demonstrates their commitment to delivering the utmost quality in their creation, allowing players to empathize with those ensnared in the corrupt system.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a few games that have mechanics somewhat similar to Shipbreaker, but this is the first I've seen put it together in such a package.  At present, there is a fair bit to do in the game, but it is still lacking several implementations that would be rather nice, such as multiplayer and additional ships/scenarios.  The future of these things ranges from bleak to dead.  More ships MIGHT come eventually, but coop and multiplayer has been stated as being something that will not come to the game.What is presently available is a fantastic mix of relaxation and stress, serious circumstances and humor, complexity and simplicity.  The scope of the game would certainly be challenging to increase further without making ships that would take potentially multiple hours to dismantle, but for what is there it's a very nice package.  Especially with the price, I would be hard pressed to think that many who like to tinker and see how things work would not find this game enjoyable after getting over the several learning curves.**UPDATE**Given the developers are constantly pushing a story without the option to 'skip' it and it being intrusive to the actual game play, along with a changing of how the game starts and your character not being your own, my opinion on this has changed to not recommend it.  What was great about this game has been minimized and what was minor and elusive has gotten a spot light while being shown to be hideous.  The review opinion will change if the developers change their mistakes of pushing story over game play, but that is for them to do.  For the time being though, I've just been getting through the laughable, disrupted and one-sided story line so it can just be done.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though I enjoy the really unique, meditative game play that Hardspace has to offer, I can't recommend it on the grounds that there are some pretty sinister glitches in the full release and that the clunky narrative often hijacks game play. For people who are relatively patient with those things, there's still a lot to love here.Taking apart ships is fun for me, and I assume you'll know right off the bat if you find that fun too, so I won't speak much on it. If you've ever worked a job you enjoyed, this game really simulates that positive feeling of doing things well. It can be repetitive, but even after clearing the game I still went back for more because I wanted to improve on disassembling certain ships better.To start with the negative aspects, there are modes in the game that would have you go through the entire game with either a limited number of lives, or just one life. The big problem is that As of October 2022, some ships will spontaneously kill you upon flicking a switch because of a glitch. There are also problems with the game's laser cutter that will cause massive explosions that will kill you if you fire it while something explosive is too close to your right side. Even though your laser will never make contact with the explosive, it will still go off. In fact,  as long as you move in between whatever it is you're trying to cut, and an explosive container while you're cutting the thing behind it.To summarize, things explode when your laser doesn't touch them, and they sometimes don't explode when you laser them right down the center. It will likely be very hard for anyone to figure out what's going on with this, because your deaths will be spontaneous and far apart from each other.Virtually all of my 18 deaths in my first play through were because of these two glitches. It is completely unacceptable to me that the game supports these game modes despite the way it currently functions.For me, the narrative falls really flat because it's so over the top it comes across as a lecture instead of a meaningful commentary or an argument for something. Everyone should be able to agree that worker's unions are sometimes good to protect workers (the central thesis of the game). It would have been nice to have had a more subtle approach with a broader critique, like I thought would happen with  Addressing basic stuff from a kinda anti-union perspective would have been great, but as far as I remember there was like one throw away line at the end of the game. Seeing unionization, and then a few workers be decentivized from working and maybe some healthy negotiation to refine the rules would have been great, for example.In my opinion, the entire narrative is infected with an insidious poison.  You're told you are doing hard work and you deserve more rights, but the rights you acquire are totally irrelevant for the purposes of game play. Even worse, getting those rights is actually super annoying except for one section later on that flips part of the game on it's head. Lou and the crew actually bugged me so much with un-skippable blank cut-scenes that I almost wanted the evil corporation to win at times.Lou feels like a pretty great character to me, and I can't help but feel that some of the over the top reactions to her are because of the unfortunate role she fills.   I would have liked to see a more successful integration of game and story than what this game offered.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't get this if you're expecting a lot of action, it's not an action game. I enjoy the game a lot though! It's almost a 3D puzzle to me with some of the later levels, figuring out how to detach certain parts without blowing something up. I'd like it if it was an even more complex puzzle, with bigger ships later on too! That said, one setting I would love to have but can't seem to find yet is to disable the timer. While the timer adds some challenge to the game, I would love to just relax and treat it as a more casual game where I'm not racing against the clock, just taking apart the ship and trying to salvage as much as possible. A career mode with the timer disabled could also open up the possibility of leaning into the almost puzzle like part of the game. Right now those puzzles are really simple; find the switch to turn off the fuel lines,before trying to remove the engine. Forget to do that, get blown up, for example. Why not make it more complex, with ships that also have shielded sections that the scanner can't see into?All in all, a game that is already appealing to play, with a lot of untapped potential. As it's early access, I look forward to seeing how much of that potential they tap into by the time it's done. I'll already recommend this game if you like casual game-play.

name: Windbound
detailed_description: The Forbidden Islands are Calling, Unlock their Secrets Shipwrecked alone on an uncharted island, explore, adapt and navigate the land and perilous seas to stay alive. As Kara, you are a warrior, caught at sea in a fierce storm, adrift from your tribe. Thrown from your boat, at the mercy of the turbulent waters, you are tossed on to the shores of the Forbidden Islands, a mysterious paradise. With no boat, no food or tools, just the will and skill to survive, uncover this beautiful island’s rich resources. Craft tools and weapons to hunt and defend yourself against nature itself with its wild and fantastical creatures. Whilst exploring further islands and the scattered ruins across their lands, secrets of the past and glimpses of the future are revealed. Unravel the mystery behind them all and you may find more than just your way home. Uncover the Secrets Within Embark on a personal journey and discover the history of the idyllic Forbidden Islands; each holding the key to a mystery and unexpected revelations. Explore As Far As The Eye Can See Head towards the horizon, advancing across the islands, each with their own diverse wildlife, landscapes and challenges to face. Live Off The Land Scavenge the islands’ untamed terrain for resources that you can use to craft a full range of tools and weapons to hunt wildlife and upgrade your boat. You must set sail when resources become scarce. Build Your Perfect Seacraft Your boat is your key companion on this journey, carefully craft your own custom sailing vessel to take on the treacherous waters, traversing from one island to the next. Design your boat to battle tempestuous winds, monstrous waves, and deadly sea creatures.'

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased Windbound despite a lot of negative reviews simply because I loved Satellite Reign, the studio's previous project, and wanted to thank them for some great fun I had with it.With this perspective my expectations for Windbound were extremely low, and it has failed to meet them.Within the first fifteen minutes of control glitches and minor interface errors, I hopped down from a basalt column, ragdolled permanently, trapped hanging off the edge of a stone, and sat there with the camera wildly jerking and twitching for two minutes of poking buttons before simply turning the game off.On my second attempt, I lasted another 30 minutes of the punishing survival mode, eating fish that take so long to cook you seem to lose more stamina finding them, spearing them and cooking them than you gain from eating the results, before my boat's tail-end lightly touched a coral reef.The boat didn't crumble, or explode.. It simply deleted. Vanished neatly, instantly, without a trace, dropping me neatly onto the reef.I didn't have enough grass stuffed into my pockets to build another hull, or access to more, as the only nearby island was completely lifeless, a plot/progression island existing only for a scripted sequence.Game over. Hard-locked, trapped on a lifeless island without any means of progression/escape/alternative, because of the second game-breaking glitch in less than an hour.Windbound doesn't seem finished even after all this time and three DLC releases, and doesn't seem to know what it is, or is trying to be.For comparison with their previous game, Satellite Reign was not what it claimed to be, but once you wrap your head around the reality as compared to the confused marketing, it's still a really damn good, and rather unique game. Satellite Reign was confused, but it had a solid identity beneath the conflicted pre-release interviews and advertising, and a compelling gameplay loop. It had a rough learning curve but it worked, and you always had a way to recover and continue if you made a mistake.This game seems to want to be a cute minimalistic Zelda-inspired take on survival games, and also a remarkably hardcore/KEEP EATING CONSTANTLY OR DIE type survival grind. It is trying to come at the genre from both ends of the spectrum and the result is a curious mash of 'everything is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ adorable' and 'you must kill everything and turn their skulls into your basic tools, and eat every scrap of meat, leaving nothing alive in your wake'. Seriously, it's morbid, the incentive to kill absolutely everything because the player-character's metabolism is supercharged.I'm not sure I've ever seen such a clash between the artists on a project and the gameplay designers - between pretty, cute, musical adventure and KILL KILL DIE KILL, and while either of those things I can enjoy, here they just feel tonally dissonant in the extreme.As much as I want to see 5 Lives free to continue developing games, I can't recommend purchasing Windbound. Do go back and pick up Satellite Reign if you haven't played it yet, though.TL;DR - Windbound. Still genuinely broken, and very poorly designed.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that's very difficult to decide if it deserves a thumbs up or not. I lean towards being charitable towards this game because it's not very expensive, and I blew past the refund window in one sitting, so clearly it does something right. It's a game with some real strengths and glaring weaknesses. Aesthetically it's a very pleasant game. The graphics are charming, with a slightly cartoonish flair and bright colors. Cutting across the waves towards a furtive grey spire in the hazy distance while light piano and chime music plays has a very calming effect. There's a nice variety of different island types, from tropical, to savanna, to canopied jungle. Sure, it doesn't make sense that islands mere kilometers apart would have completely distinct climates, but the variety makes exploring them more enjoyable.The sailing mechanics are the shining core of this game. They're quite deep including wind and sail directions, dynamic weather such as storms and fog, dangerous terrain such as reefs and rocks that poke out of the water, and some degree of vessel customization. Getting from island to island is consistently engaging, and as you progress through chapters it becomes very treacherous. The survival mechanics are also well balanced. You'll rarely have a surplus of food, but you don't get hungry fast enough for it to become a constant annoyance. Hunting animals for crafting materials and food is simplistic, but serviceable mechanically. The negatives are a bit heartbreaking when the rest of the game is really great. Sadly, the combat in this game is just plain bad, and later chapters make combat unavoidable. To not sugar coat it, the combat mechanics are just plain bad. It's your fairly standard suite of Zelda-like moves (minus any form of blocking/ shield), but all of them are clunky, floaty, or clunky and floaty. You walk fast enough that you would probably sidestep 90% of attacks without dodging if enemies didn't slide full meters towards you during their windup to prevent that. The feedback on hitting or being hit isn't great. You have a single attack animation that cannot be chained nor acted out of until Kara completes the *entire* animation, and mobs seem to have a guaranteed dodge if they aren't in their own postswing. Combat devolves into circling around your target until they attack, dodge it, and then hopefully getting into range to poke them a single time with your spear because doing a second takes so long that you'll get smacked during your post-swing. Most non-passive mobs require 3-5 jabs with an upgraded spear to kill, so you're looking at 30-60 seconds of combat per enemy. There are also some upgrades for parrying, charged attacking, and dodge attacking, but for some reason they're expensive craftables that you lose on death if you play the original roguelike mode. It's such a shame that possibly the last major update this game will get was spent on making the awkward combat system more plevalent instead of fixing its deep-rooted issues or expanding on what the game does right.TL;DR: If you like the idea of a peaceful survival/ sailing game and are able to put up with a glaring lack of polish in certain areas, then I heartily recommend. Just know that you're buying a diamond in the rough rather than a shining hidden gem.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited until a bit to write this to have clearer thoughts. Frankly, this game made me some of the saltiest I have ever been due to sheer game mechanics. I was SUPER excited about this game, I could hardly wait until download day and announced it all over how I was looking forward to playing!! It was gorgeous, gave windwaker vibes, and seemed like something that would give me hours of enjoyment...Please note, I played using a controller.What it does right:-Graphics: They are gorgeous. The art style is absolutely winderwaker-ish and it was what drew me to the game in the first place. In this regard, it does NOT disappoint.-Music: I love the concept of the animals having unique sounds, especially when a few types run around together and make a sort of song. It's also cool to hear them and start recognizing what they are by the sounds. The sailing music is gorgeous (though it is a bit repetitive after a bit)-Story: I did NOT finish this game (will get into that later) but the story up until this point (i was past chpt 3) was for the most part very emotional. It was definitely an interesting concept.. but they just sort of throw you into the fray without much explanation.-Sailing: It is like a lot of sailing in games. It does feel like you are against the wind a LOT but that is nothing tacking doesn't solve (allowing rowing w/ sail would fix). The water and just sailing around freely was as advertised. I spent a lot of time just excited to be running around with pretty music in the gorgeous waves. It gets even better as you upgrade ships.The disappointments:-Combat: It's a bit awkward. I played through and just found so many awkward weird things happening. It didn't feel polished. It got very monotonous after a while just kill, harvest, kill, harvest. Things rag doll or freeze in animations periodically. I either used my bow or just stab/doged-The bugs: This game is not being released as alpha or beta. That being said, there were a lot of bugs in this game for the price. It felt like they didn't bother letting people playtest it. Example: one of the tigers on the island was stuck in the jump down animation and glided around not animated. Periodic ragdolls, stuff disappearing, etc. They have been fixing things per the updates apparently. It takes time, but I am talking a bit too many for it being advertised as a finished game. They JUST fixed some of these things end of September.-"Survival": The survival mechanics in this are ridiculous. Definitely a huge make or break. I feel like 80% of this game is me struggling to keep her fed. One moment I have tons of food, the next it is all rotten and I am starving. There is no in between with this. It added nothing to my experience having to struggle with this. Did I mention I was in STORY MODE?! It doesn't keep you fed long and it rots super quick even in storage. What is the point here? (they have allegedly adjusted this though I have not experienced it)-You snooze you lose: If you do the 'real' game mode, death means you lose EVERYTHING and start completely over. Die in story mode, lose everything except your inventory.... so you still lose. Have your boat hardcore upgraded and lots of high tier stuff you were saving to upgrade something?... too bad. It again adds nothing to the game but frustration and forcing people to replay and regather things adding unnecessary grind. It felt lazy...  instead of giving us actual content, the gameplay puts all bets into you dying and having to grind back to where you were more than a few times. If you do respawn in story mode, it doesn't mean you can get all the stuff back you had, resources are so limited you probably can't rebuild your boat to even a fraction of where it was. (They apparently updated this end of September but I'm so burnt out on this game I probably wont try again until a while from now)-Music: I had to keep clicking in and out of the game to a music player for stream so that they weren't listening to just nothingness for large extents of time. If you are on an island, you will have a LOT of time in a musical black hole. It really is a pity because what music there is, is extremely high quality and wonderful to listen to.-Scarcity: I thought the scarcity stuff was interesting but you can't have crazy material requirements for recipes AND make everything hard to find/limited. Pick one or the other because this aspect was NOT balanced. There was a point I had to sail around EVERYWHERE just to try to find grass... spending more than 30 minutes doing so. Same with things breaking... if weapons are going to break that fast, then don't make materials that scarce or give a way to repair them.-As far as the eye can see...?: It talks about procedurally generated islands and such but really it doesn't add much at all. The islands may 'generate different' but that difference only means shapes of them and location for the most part. It's the same stuff. Sure, each new chapter gives you some new animals/biomes/items but that is very short lived excitement.-Storage: The storage situation was a constant issue. Many types of items and the talked about 'scarcity'; yet there is a constant need for lots of mats for recipes including things like campfires you have to constantly refuel... the storage is NOT good. It gets better later on in the game once you upgrade containers but there is a lot of inventory management that again does not fit well with the scarcity of resource concept. (They allegedly fixed this but again I am reviewing what I played and cannot comment on that fix)-So much wasted: No autosave... forget to save and lose potentially hours of progress.My Final Thoughts: This game had so much potential. It promised a lot of things but it seems to not be sure of it's own identity as a game. There needs to be more beyond adding a few more material and animal types each level. They talked about how things generate but it felt so cookie cutter each time I finished the 'level'. After the 3rd, I was sort of bored... I knew I would resource grind some more, try to upgrade some stuff,  kill things, try not to starve, activate alters....that's about it. Why should I feel for this protagonist? What is my emotional connection to her and her quest?...  I don't know many people who want to have a feed/respawn simulator. It just needs... more, even side quests on each level that help us understand our character and what is going on better or SOMETHING. I see her fall into water at the beginning and then?.... It really lacks in giving us a compelling reason to have any sort of connection or care of what is going on.... the story reveal at each chapter is just not cutting it, you can't bank everything on it which is exactly what they did. About my saltiness and stating I had not experienced the update? Frankly, I rage quit mid stream. I died a second time from hunger, lost my boat and all my stuff and I was done. D.O.N.E. I had pushed through the insane hunger/spoil rates, I sailed through the repetitiveness, I fought my way through the landscape of bugs and uncertainty... until I couldn't do it anymore. Having nothing and knowing even decimating the entire map strip mining it of everything would not get me close to what I had back and that I would not be able to get my ship back to even half of what it was due to the material requirements... It was a hard NO for me and I quit and never opened it again.  (this was back at the end of August)If you have no issue with dark souls; maybe, just maybe you will be alright with this level of grind/repeat. Beyond that, I expect a LOT more for $30 in terms of story/quest and content. Wait for it to be on sale if you truly want to try it. I streamed every second of my elation and frustration and it is painful to rewatch but when I feel maybe I should give this a try again, I do it to remind myself... save yourself the agony until they change A LOT of things.

_childDocuments_.review: A genuine slog to get through, Windbound is trying to be too many things at once, and isn’t good at any of them.Let me just say firstly, the music is lovely, and the art style is also great. The story is your typical indie, ambiguous nonsense but its fine overall, everything on the surface, conveys a rather tranquil experience (this is ruined by the gameplay, but we’ll get to that) And performance was mostly fine for me, with everything maxed, it isn’t an intensive game though.Survival mechanics that add nothing to the game, and just serve to annoy. Kara is hungry  the time, and it really gets repetitive having to constantly keep her hunger bar in check. Crafting is fine mostly, but it is nothing special or new, its just  in that regard.Frustrating sailing mechanics that never feel tight enough to be enjoyable. Constantly sailing against the wind to get to the next island is just not fun, at all.Combat is meh, very basic and enemies are annoying to fight, this is compounded by a roguelike death system of all things  that is just unfair and doesn’t give any incentive to play again, have fun going right back to the beginning of the game and losing hours of progress because of a loose combat system.The game is also rather short. I saw a comment left by the publisher that stated that the game has over 40 hours of content,, I’m sorry. The main story takes 7-8 hours, at a push, and that was with me really taking my time. I’m sure you can stretch the game out for a few more hours if you really wanted to get stuck in with the crafting (not sure why you would want to though) but 40 hours?
