_childDocuments_.review: I would say that the main characteristic of this game for me is flashes of brilliance and equally frequent bouts of deep frustration. Interesting enough concept, the graphical style is charming, the game-play loop is promising; it has all the moving parts of a game that I really want to enjoy, but they all fall slightly flat for largely mechanical or technical reasons. As its core inspiration, it clearly draws heavily from Legend of Zelda: Windwaker and Breath of the Wild, both highly polished and beloved games. The stylistic inspiration for the murals through which Windbound tells its story are very reminiscent of Abzu. The biomes and the various creatures you progress through are all distinct and interesting. It's a beautiful game, without being too flashy or relying on impressive graphics. Visually and aesthetically, I have no real complaints. It's when interacting with this environment that things start to unravel. On the tin, the core gameplay loop of gathering and managing resources, crafting supplies, and retrieving key items to progress through the procedurally generated archipelago is a slight variation on the tried and true open-world-survival-craft game genre. But the devil is in the details. The inventory system is stiflingly restrictive with a hard maximum of 26 carry slots, and storage solutions are heavily limited by the arbitrary limit of one placement slot per boat section. The maximum stack size for many critical items feels small compared to how many of them you’ll use throughout your journey. I spent all my time in adventure mode, where inventory is preserved on death and through level transitions; I can’t even imagine the frustration of losing all but your 7 (8 if upgraded) held item slots as not all archipelagos seem to provide access to the full suite of resources available. The primary goals when exploring the islands is the recovery of shell amulets from stone towers, which are used to unlock the next series of islands in the progression. There are some limited attempts at puzzles in some iterations of these towers, but they all fall flat and leave me wanting something with more meat. Hitting a gong with a ranged weapon, or sailing to another island to retrieve a key, hardly qualify. A handful of towers are guarded by enemies or gated behind a fight with a more powerful version of a creature, but by and large, these central pillars of the gameplay loop are resolved by just climbing a pile of rock, and the edge detection to facilitate this process is frustratingly faulty. As for the combat, it technically has all the moving parts you’d want in a moderately shallow combat system: melee and ranged options, target locking, dodging, and a handful of special scenario-dependent attacks. Added together, it just manages to feel clunky and frustrating. The dodge seems to lag about half a second behind the player actually issuing the prompt, and there are no i-frames during the extensive ragdoll animation after getting hit by an enemy, resulting in the frustrating and common experience of getting hit once by a relatively low-level enemy and having no opportunity to retaliate until your health is entirely exhausted. On the opposite end of the spectrum, the enemy AI is deeply flawed and exploitable. There seems to be a complete lack of pathfinding, such that standing on a rock one or two feet off the ground completely confounds all but one or two of the enemy and creature types. And bizarrely, one hit from a ranged weapon of any type instantly disengages combatants and causes them to absently wander around whatever island they’re inhabiting. I came to rely so heavily on these flaws in the AI that the four boss battles, where you are trapped in a level arena, were frustrating and exaggeratedly difficult in comparison. When it comes to the boat and its maximum of three multipurpose placement slots (despite a surplus of visible space on deck), the game plays you absolutely dirty and breaks its own rules regarding the preservation of materials when constructing and deconstructing components. Late in the game, you find yourself with metal as a new resource, which allows you to smith metal weapons and armor and craft a cauldron for potion-making. The cauldron must be placed on a fire, and the potion making process requires clay pots that are crafted in a kiln which also requires a fire. Both the cauldron and the kiln are resource-intensive to craft, both have repeat functionality as the kiln is also used in smithing. However, both mean that the fire below them can no longer be used for the absolutely critical function of cooking food. The crux of my issue is that, unlike anything else on your boat, you do not recover their resources when deconstructing them, because you are technically not deconstructing them but instead the fire on which they sit. And because of the aforementioned arbitrary limit of only three build slots on your fully-upgraded boat and the fact that the fires in question are not usable for cooking, you have to choose between storage, expensive resources, and a full stamina bar. If this were intended to be a core conflict in the gameplay, I might understand, but the contrast with the full retrieval of resources used to build other parts of your boat, this can’t help but feel like a frustrating oversight.Repeatedly, in almost every aspect, this is a game doesn’t manage to make a whole that is greater than the sum of its parts, through specific and identifiable technical or mechanical issues that I can hardly believe made it past the first round of play-testers. I enjoyed moments, enjoyed the story the developers were trying to tell, but found myself repeatedly frustrated enough that I had to set the whole thing aside. This is a game that I really wanted to enjoy, and was in fact looking forward to prior to release. Disappointingly, it just didn’t live up to my expectations. If you can snag this on a steep sale like I did, give it a shot. Otherwise, I can’t recommend the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Beautiful art style and detailed assets- Interesting progression- Satisfying sailingCons:- Buggy enemy AI- Buggy combat system- Limited inventory space- Extremely limited build space- Clunky/dodgy climbing system- Very limited difficulty settings (two)The game could be really relaxing and joyful to play, but the gather-craft-combat loop is severely stopped at every corner.1. GatheringGathering is has slow animations and is extremely gimped by your inventory space. It is possible to build storage on your ship - but that is also gimped by providing very few building spots.Later on you are able to build massive ships as far as I've read - but by that time you're basically done with the game.It's also very disheartening that the only viable food source is meat in the form of jerky, reducing mushrooms and berries to something you eat directly rather than cooking with it.That ties into the drastic stamina loss - you're forced to engage in combat regularly to obtain meat for jerky. This prevents from being able to enjoy the scenery, planning and sailing in peace. Even in the crossing between the first and second set of islands I've lost half my stamina due to hunger.2. CraftCrafting is fine, except that often you have to stop crafting and dump items on the ground to be able to continue crafting because your inventory is so small.Also it doesn't auto craft any necessary items, so on more complex recipes you have to scroll back and forth to check what you need.3. CombatOh boy, the combat. It is strongly inspired by Breath of the Wild and FromSoftware games.The problem is - the enemy attacks reach far wider than they should. For example the big hogs hit you even though neither the model of the hog nor the effect animation hits you.The dodging is extremely floaty and due to the attacks reaching far wider that they should you're getting hit even though you dodged and didn't connect with the mob.Similarly - the ragdoll after being hit is so long that the enemies can attack you again before you can get up.On the other hand you own attacks don't connect even when your spear is connecting with the enemies model.In three out of five fights I've also had an issue where the camera lock on would turn my camera and character away from the mob, instead of focusing on it. The only way to reset this was to abort the fight by running away and reengaging.It'd also be great if the game mentioned that your weapons can _break_ before entering a mini boss fight with the first hog.On my second island I've killed three of the little hogs before the big hog spawned and on the second attack the game was like 'oh no, your spear is about to break!'.I can see what type of game they were going for - but the bugs just make it not enjoyable to play. In addition to that the enemies that must be killed are severely stronger than you, double-dip on attacks and don't have interesting mechanics.In sum this makes the game not fun, engaging, rewarding or enjoyable.I also have a gripe with the difficulty settings. These are either:1. Babys first adventure game2. Get rektAlso the endless mode can only be played on the "get rekt" difficulty.I don't know why the devs are only offering these two, but neither are appealing to me as a more casual player.I think the game has great potential as a relaxing and beautiful game. But the developer desperately wanted to make a hard rogue-lite. Which would be fine if the combat systems was up to par and the enemies were interesting.Offering more difficulty options (or even entirely customizable difficulties) - especially for people who don't want to deal with the buggy combat system - would make the game much, much better.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really wanted to be able to recommend this game, because there's a lot to love about it. It's very beautiful and atmospheric, and it's got some good crafting mechanics. However, the resource management mechanic is really, really broken in the first chapter. From reading on this issue, whether or not you get food or other higher-level resources like wood or sticks seems to be a matter of complete procedurally-generated chance, and there doesn't seem to be any sort of corrective mechanic that makes sure you get drops if you've come up empty for long enough. So you can tour half a dozen islands and find edible animals but no sticks to spear them, and other than that just one or two bushes of berries and a mushroom. Then you starve to death. That doesn't wipe your story and resource progress (in Adventurer mode - it does in Hunter), but it does wipe your map. So you lose your record of where you've been, and you start again at the bottom of the map, some minutes of rowing from anywhere, which gets pretty old, especially after you've starved a few times as well. There is a sinking feeling that comes as you round the side of your fourth or fifth island and you can see already that it only has grass and rocks, but you still have to check it out, just in case there's one animal here you can kill with only your starting-out knife. But your hunger bar is running low and you know if this one doesn't work out, you're in for another slow death followed by another long, long row from the bottom of the world. I gather from discussions of this topic that it does resolve once you get past the first chapter and have more tools at your disposal, and I really, really tried to get far enough for that, but in the end it crossed the line of too much work for not enough progress-reward.

_childDocuments_.review: Windbound is a fun game, that clearly has elements from other games, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing. When I play, I have fun seeing how other ideas have been improved, and how they've been reimagined in general. It can be a bit frustrating at times, but in some aspects, it adds to its charms.Here's a list of Pros and Cons I've compiled. Please keep in mind I have yet to finish the game at time of writing this:Pros:- The graphics are AMAZING. I play on a gaming laptop with the graphics on the highest settings, and this game is a beauty.- It is a mix of both relaxing, and adrenaline-inducing. You may find an island with no enemies and it may only be a resource spot at one place, and then go to the next island and find 3-4 different bosses you didn't see. Or get the piss scared out of you by Silkmaws.- It is interesting. The way to collect things and the degrading of certain items is an interesting twist. Most likely, the weapon/item degrading system is from Breath of the Wild, which again, isn't a bad thing. I believe Windbound has found a good balance to this system and pulled it off better than BOTW did. I also like how the food can decay, and this can be prolonged, but not gotten rid of entirely. Though I don't think the food should degrade so fast, it is a thing that would happen if this game were to occur in real life.- Each Island is unique. As I said before, you never know what might be on one island from the next. That being said, there are general groups of islands, such as Bamboo forests, which have distinctive red trees you can see from a distance, Forests, which have "regular" deciduous trees, Fields, which typically have little to no trees, and what appears to be Swamps, which have weeping willows. Please keep in mind this may not be an extensive list, as I am still on my first play-through, and have obviously not found everything there is to discover yet. However, each island type have their own ecosystem, and their own bosses that they provide. They offer their own unique things, and offer great ways to find ingredients needed to craft items.- Wildlife. The wildlife in this game are beautiful, and well-thought-out. Each breed has their own attack style, and you must adapt to them quickly, or else you may be killed! It can be exhilarating! Each offer something you will need later on in the game.- Environment. The environment plays a huge roll in the game. You can use it to your advantage if you're smart enough, as well! But you must be able to adapt easily. What works for the Gorehorn definitely won't work against a Plainstalker! In the game, I managed using large rocks to climb up on and help me take down the Gorehorn without taking damage. When I tried doing something similar with the Plainstalker, it didn't work out well and I quickly had to adapt to a new fighting style.- Easy to learn. The mechanics are simple for even the most beginners. And it's easily to figure out what you need to do, because there is no real path to travel.- Sailing. I know people have been complaining about the sailing mechanic, and I personally disagree. What do you expect when you have a sail on your boat? If you aim it correctly, you can sail against the wind, it's just a matter of finding the correct position. My only problem with sailing is that you cannot row after putting a sail on your boat. Realistically, this should fix the "problem" many people are having with it. Even on sail boats, you can row in real life. :)Cons:- The game can be extremely unforgiving. I had almost finished chapter 3, and had all the Nautilus beacons lit. I was about to head to the passage after collecting more resources. Obviously, I saved, but unfortunately, this was when I met the Plainstalker for the first time, and it managed to kill me. I had to start back at the beginning of chapter 3 with only the stuff I had on my person. It was like the bosses I had killed previously didn't even happen, and that was a bit disheartening.- Story. While the story itself seems to be interesting, and is told in a unique way, it is also... Lacking. Yes, it seems interesting, but I would like a little more context. Not everyone will interpret the murals the same way as another. It would be best to give maybe a sentence or two with each painting piece, so we know officially what is going on.- Beacons. Beacons, beacons, beacons... Every chapter is essentially the same as the last, go find these beacons and make your way to the passage. That's really it. This does allow a lot of freedom, and lets you play at your own pace, but I think it would be interesting to add something else so you can get more story. For instance, maybe you have to find ruins and free the souls of some of the ancient people, for example. I think a lot could be done with this!- Boat killers! Okay, I HATE the Crobsters. They're a good idea in theory, but they can be annoying as hell. In a good way, though. Your boat takes damage as they attack it. That's great! What's not great is that I have to stop my boat, or let it possibly hit something as I go to defend it. I risk doing more damage or even losing it entirely. That being said, I dislike one aspect. When I don't get there in time, and I have to lose part of my boat, the chest gets completely destroyed, and I lose everything in it. This could be fixed by just making the items float. When I first started, I had to have a grass hull on one side, and I put my enemy stuff in the basket on that hull. I lost a lot of good materials to a Crobster, and I was extremely angry. At least let me collect my stuff again!- Placements. Why can I only put one thing on my decks and pontoons? That makes no real sense to me. Instead, I could put at least 3 things on a deck or pontoon. Instead, I have to make 4 different decks just to have a decent amount of storage. Everything only goes to one corner, and it bothers me I can't have more than one item on a boat piece, excluding the sail.- Wonky physics. This can be both good and bad. You can toss your boat like it's weightless, but also, sometimes animals get stuck in the ground, (poor collision) or you get launched or stopped completely by rough seas, even if your boat is well made, logically. It can be a bit annoying.I think that is it, at least for now. I think this is a good game, and that people should get it, but maybe wait for a little bit, so they can work out the bugs! I can't wait to see it improved later on!

_childDocuments_.review: No time for a detailed review so I give this game a rank C.Okay game - not bad but you can skip it or try on sale.See my profile for more details about my reviews.Additional notes: this game was a bit of a rollercoaster in terms of experience. The first hour I played it was really mediocre, I was about to uninstall it, I would have given it about a 40%-50%. It basically felt like a student project completely inspired (too inspired...) by Zelda, mostly Wind Waker and Breath of the Wild. Then I read a bit more about it, about the experience it tried to convey... and I got sucked into it, spent 20 hours! If you are forgiving towards its flaws, its bugs, its very limited content and design... there is some good into it, and quite some heart poured into this little game! Imagine a roguelike, based on Wind Waker/Sea of Thieves (island hopping and exploring), with Breath of the Wild features: survival (foraging, cooking, crafting), graphics (soft cell shading, illustrations for the "story"), combats (lock, mini boss fights, etc) and finally a bit of a very casual Souls-lite combat feature (learn enemy patterns). Finally, one of the most interesting point of the game is to gather various materials to upgrade your little raft into a ship, and more and more into a better boat, without any explanation or tutorial - that is cool, you really want to know to what point you can upgrade your ship up. The game is very relaxing (repetitive exploration) and very stressful at the same time (quite unforgiving, clunky and buggy at times, you have to restart the entire current world if you die). I reached , and it was mostly pleasant and nice. But towards the end of my playthrough I felt more and more the efforts and perseverance I was putting into it felt unrewarded, or at least not enough to justify pushing in. I gave up a game like Tears of the Kingdom because of how boring and repetitive I thought it felt, so I could not justify putting more into this little sketch of Zelda. The story is abstract and insipid, and the music very underwhelming/amateurish. Still, if you have time, and on sale, it can be very refreshing!

_childDocuments_.review: Fair warning this portion of my review will obviously cover the entire story line so any desire by yourself to look under the curtain at what I've written is entirely on you.  I've seen a lot of comments on the Community page talking about combat, and most seem pretty negative. I believe I understand why the general dislike of the combat, but overall I have to disagree with the masses. The developers' narrative is that Kara isn't clueless about how to survive, which is obvious when you see her in the opening cinematic soloing a vessel. Any seafaring people with that level of nautical expertise and a lot of group and personal knowledge of the practical. However I have to ask, if Kara is used to the swing of her knife or the thrust of a spear, why is she unable to manage a combination of more that one strike at a time? To be honest ranged combat shines far brighter than the former; bordering on refreshing with it's unique boons, and approaches.  I'd venture to say that the Developers wanted players to focus more on ranged combat as the bows are the only weapons to gain enchantments (That I'm aware of). While I'm not the sea salt encrusted sailor that some here may claim to be I have set foot on a vessel a time or two, but this is a video game...not a review on a yacht I don't have. The sailing mechanics are intuitive to myself (and I hope others) and I rarely found myself dead in the water. Occasionally when I did, it was like kicking a coffee table or cracking my shin into a trailer hitch. Getting the "Speed Racer" achievement one second and my ship is a submarine the other, or when a tailwind completely refuses to carry my vessel and I'm forced to frantically turn away before the drumbeats of impending doom strike my vessel. While I admit some of this is likely the fault of my boat building (lack of additional masts/sails and general layout of the ship) I still think it's worth mentioning.  I found the crafting very interesting and refreshing. The developers gave Kara multiple ways to discover crafting recipes, through necessity and through expanding ideas. Want a tree down? Maybe some chopping implement. Got the tree down? Bet I can make some boat parts with this! The boat itself is very limited for usable space or customizing features, it's a very spartan and functional companion. Overall the crafting development felt very natural. What DIDN'T feel natural was how long it took for me to acquire tools to work materials which forced me to look back at prior stages and acknowledge how much I had been forced to leave behind. Which brings me to my next point... Firstly, Achievements. While some and obvious and well obtainable by the common man, others are so obtuse...no one but a maniac would attempt them (carry 5000 stones!?!) The Boon system was clever and I enjoyed it, however the whole Rogue-like dimension mixed with a linear survival format didn't sit too well with me, ultimately pushing me to share my thoughts in text like this rather than starve in a few more moments of AFK time like Kara did so often ( I swear I was paused..or was I?). My face at the end of the game went from one of mild confusion to mild disappointment. Where was I to go now? A new game? Usually this isn't the worst thing to me, but the VERY linear style of the story mixed with the survival element left me asking "Where is the rest? Isn't there something more.? It feels like something else should be here." The game also seemed to have a hiccup in the first week or so where people who had made sure to order before launch hour weren't able to access or didn't even receive notification of their pre-order bonus. A small issue, but also a very small issue to fix I feel and I have yet to see any announcement from the Developers outside of a Community Page forum. If you have your product for sale on a platform you owe it to yourself and your clients to keep your personal site updates and the outlying platform updates on the same page. This is something i have an issue with in general and not these Developers specifically. Lastly I spent a good portion of the game waiting for something evil and menacing to test my ability at the rudder, but besides the infrequent shark that was easily avoided and some jellyfish landmines during one of the Crossings I was left longing for that evil monster from the deep.  As I mentioned before when I finished the game I was left wanting. While I'm not one to ask or demand Developers to take something they've worked hard on and make it into something else I would not be upset if they decided to expand the game some more.  Either a mode to continue trapped in limbo with your current progress or an overall open world to build and develop in would be a plus I think. I will absolutely be returning to this story again and following any further development that they choose to pursue. In conclusion I enjoyed this game, but the issues I did have with it were enough to nag me into writing this review. We're in a very curious place right now with game development and I'm intrigued every time I pick up a new game to see what Developers bring to the table, what their customer service is like and what they have planned for dessert.

_childDocuments_.review: Beat the game in about 18 hours. It was a cozy, epic story, and quite challenging.I don't expect a lot of players to enjoy it though, as there are many things the game can't quite figure out for itself, and that will frustrate the hell out of most. I am very patient. An example is the climbing system. It will jump up for you if a cliff is at waist level, or even higher than you, but it wont jump for you. This is what I mean by "it needs to make up its mind". Either jump for the player all the time, or don't at all.Another thing it does awkwardly is the targeting system. Middle mouse click locks on, but no option exists to switch target, so you must middle mouse click to untarget, and then do it again to switch targets. That needs to get better. Lots of fun weapons and abilities to find and use, so its got that going for it. The format is like so: You sail around in a fairly large circle map (think valheim but way smaller) and island hop gathering materials and fighting very interesting and well done enemies that challenge you quite a bit, all while lighting three beacons. Then you go fight a boss on another island that you can now open all three bridges to. Once you beat it, you run your ship through a gauntlet, so to speak, and its quite exhilarating. Especially if you really work to upgrade the ship. Then you have completed a chapter. There are six if i remember correctly.The survival aspect isn't anything novel, but it does cut water out of the equation. So, food is your stamina. Attacking and running, as well as dodging uses stamina. Some items use stamina too. So keep eating to keep your stamina pool up. The ocean is lovely and dynamic enough to present a nice mechanic on its own. This is what drew me to the game. I've played other games with most of the rest of the mentioned mechanics, but the sailing here is really challenging, and it was fun to master.All in all, if you can grab it on sale i'd say go for it. Even full price would be fine, because it's about 18 hours of solid gameplay. The story is complete. It's a nicely put together game. Needs some polish on a few things to make gameplay less annoying and more fluid, but other than that, good game.

_childDocuments_.review: At $30 this game might be a little overpriced, but I'm giving it a thumbs up because I don't think it deserve only 54% positive reviews. The sailing mechanics and physics are great. At one point, I started building a deck before I had enough supplies for a hull and was forced to sail on a square raft that flipped over constantly. Good times. The stamina mechanics are simple and elegant, probably among the best I've seen. I especially love how they made your max stamina decrees the hungrier you get. It's not a story heavy game because you are meant to create your own story in the way you play and decisions you make. The games aesthetics are amazing and go a long way to create a strong sense of immersion.As far as gripes go, the boat design mechanics cap out too quickly. You can build your boat longer and wider, but you sacrifice speed and maneuverability as you do. Which, by the way, why are we limited to longer or wider? Shouldn't there be a way to build up, add taller masts and higher decks? Also, almost invariably, the bigger the boat gets the more ridiculous it looks.The ending is not especially satisfying. Without spoiling it, there are several references to something very intriguing, which doesn't seem to pay off in any significant way. This game really needs some sort of climax, a big boss battle or something like that. Unlocking beacons and preceding to the next stage where you do the same thing as a central premise is pretty weak.For $20, I'd say this game is a reasonable purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite nice!The flame in the flood, more complex.Just finished the first chapter. It took me close to 4h. Died twice and crafted stuffs not even required to pass the chapter. Learning how to play. And I did not see the time going.It is quite pleasant.The story mode is not much punitive. You die, you reappear at the beginning with all you had before dying and even a gift to ease your next game. You will have to re-explore. The environment have slightly changed. This is a one slot but permit to not restart when you need to abandon the screen.Fights are just a matter of getting into them. Once you get the trick, then it is all fine. _childDocuments_.review: A frustrating experience. Constantly having to juggle items due to limited inventory space; this leaves you the feeling you're doing something wrong by being penalised via dropped items. Raft and sail upgrade should give you something more efficient, instead it is bothersome to operate and (seemingly) less useful than the canoe. Combat is a test of patience rather than skill. On the other hand, the game has beautiful visuals that would do justice to an animated film. However, somehow it feels a bit 'strung out': the player would feel more rewarded if the game mechanics provided a surer sense of progress, and more of an idea what is actually going on.... All the fine work feels a little wasted. Locations are well drawn and the animals and player-character are really nicely done. Smoothing out the game mechanics should make it a much more satisfying experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has nice graphics and good music. Combat is basic but feels good. Sailing takes a little getting used to but feels right. Heard complaints about sailing against the wind but of course that's gonna be tough, you just need to sail around and come from another direction. Navigating the Crafting and Inventory using a controller is a bit fiddly at first, kept wanting to hit LB to select Crafting but only RB switches between them.The game has 2 modes, Survival and Story, so those that don't like having to restart when they die can still enjoy the game. I don't really understand people complaining about having to restart, they tell you whats gonna happen at the start and let you choose how to play. My first death was when I was still learning the combat system, 2nd from a Gorehorn, didn't expect them to kick me. After my first death I learned to keep some Palm Fronds on me so I could craft a bag right at the start and to keep my weapons on me. Proper item management is important so that even if you die you can start better off than last time. They have trees you could cut down if you had an axe but can't craft one until later in the game, so if you started over with one you'd get certain resources much earlier. Finding Food isn't hard once you get used to the combat system, I've even had some go rotten before I needed it.I nearly lost my ship right after upgrading it due to Crobsters that jumped aboard, surprised me so much I ran over a rock and lost part of my ship. Didn't have enough resources to repair it and lost one of the supports, had to dismantle my mast in order to row to the next island as sailing in that condition was next to impossible at the time. I also found a Stamina Shrine in Chapter 1 from exploring that increased my max stamina so it pays off to explore.

_childDocuments_.review: A challenging roguelike survival game that reminds me of both Windwaker and Breath of the Wild. If that sentence ticks boxes for you, I expect you'll love Windbound.Beautiful, challenging, dangerous and unforgiving! What a terrific survival game. The first couple of levels lulled me into a false sense of security about how challenging the game is, but it really steps up and gets positively dangerous. The sailing is terrific, especially as you craft larger boats. Boat design seems to have a significant impact on handling, and just getting from one island to the next can be a rollercoaster in the bigger/faster boats!The graphics are stunning, and the world is very atmospheric. Some islands are shrouded in mists, others hidden behind dangerous rock outcrops and coral reefs. The later levels feel huge, and with no maps, you're very much left feeling insignificant on the sea sometimes.The monsters are varied and challenging to kill. There are a couple of new ones on level 5 that I haven't dared fight yet. Maybe on subsequent runs :-D. I'm playing in the rogue-like mode, in which death puts you back to level 1, but still carrying held (not bagged!) items, so getting going after a death is not a full reset for me, but the risk means the game's danger is enhanced. As with all games, there are some bugs and things that could be improved. I've had one crash during my 10 hours (but I'd saved shortly before it, so lost nothing), and I've once killed something that got bounced unnaturally far upon death, but I still got the corpse (some people have had them flick into the sea). That said, the game is very polished, it's terrific.I've played a few survival games this year, Outward, The Long Dark, Population Zero, Grounded and this one. They all have their merits (Pop Zero is probably the weakest of them all), but Windbound has the most replayability for me. The procedurally generated world is the biggest win for me, as every playthrough is different, and you can discover special items that allow you to craft quite tasty gear quite early on sometimes.Absolutely beautiful, terrifying at times, and so rewarding to play. -----------------------------------------These were my thoughts earlier on:I've played about 6 hours so far, and managed to complete two "crossings".The game is beautiful. I love the graphics and the atmosphere generated in the changing weather conditions. The animals and plants are beautifully designed and there is more than enough danger to make it a challenge to survive (for me!). The game frequently requires you to get in your boat and sail to another island. I really enjoy the sailing, the mechanics of the sea and the handling of the boats feels brilliant to me. It's a real challenge sometimes to tack effectively in the desired direction while avoiding coral and rocks. Some of the sailing during the crossings (large swell and dodging plenty of rocks) is very challenging. I imagine that a number of players will get frustrated with the sailing element, but I really enjoy it, it's a peaceful interlude between the true 'survival' portions of the game. The combat is complex enough, but clunky in places and will likely be improved. Maybe I'm just not reading the cues right, but sometimes it's difficult to get a hit in on a mob without getting smacked (hard!). The weapon upgrades seem good, and aren't too hard to craft. I managed to find the ingredients for what feels like quite a powerful bow, which seems to have trivialised some of the combat for me, so maybe without the bow folks will be complaining about fighting the harder beasts, but I took down a few of the blue buffalo-like mobs with just a basic spear, so it isn't too far off imo.I'm 5 hours in and on level 2 of what looks like 5 levels. If the levels keep getting harder, and there are at least another 3, there should be many hours still for me to finish a play through. I'm doing the Roguelite version at the moment, and much enjoying that. Died twice so far. The content will be shorter if you don't reset.As with all games, there is room for improvement in some areas. Some of the mob AI (especially pathing on and around rocks) is weak, some of the tutorial text could be clearer, some crafting hierarchies aren't obvious, the crab things that nuke boats seem OP, but nothing game breaking.I love it. It's a more peaceful survival game than any I've played before, and I like that, it's relaxing to play and a beautiful world to be in. It offers real danger at times, as some of the mobs hit really hard, and the sea can be unforgiving. I'm really looking forward to playing more of it! I'll update this review as I get further.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really doesn’t deserve the ‘mixed’ rating it’s currently laboring under at the start of September 2020. From the excellent sailing mechanics, through the uplifting score by Zander Hulme to the near perfect crafting tree… It’s obvious a lot of love has gone into this game. It’s a love that’s short-lived, graphically quirky at times and not without its frustrations, but love all the same.While comparisons have been drawn to Zelda:  Breath of the Wild, this game isn’t as expansive or as deep. It also has more than its fair share of derivative elements – seen one Journey mural exposition, seen five! Which is where the struggle regarding the ‘mixed’ rating comes in. Consider Rime by Tequila Works and you’ll find an Ico-lite with illustrative graphics, and yet this sits at a ‘very positive’ rating on Steam. Windbound is easily – almost weirdly - comparable, and yet for some reason it’s not landing as well.Regardless of all the foibles of Steam’s feedback loop (played 200hrs “hate this game”, oh boy) 5 Lives Studios’ take on island hopping survival really is worth your time. Alongside its charming graphics and compelling gameplay loops, it also offers plenty of standout moments. Clear your first ‘crossing’, and the rocky flume ride to the game’s level-up backwater is replete with jeopardy and a driving piano track that’ll have you smiling as you frantically dodge obstacles. It really is a torrent of well-executed ideas, just a shame it’s getting a damp reception from the ‘salty’ old sea dogs on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: My review of the game.Pros.Visuals are nice.Exploration is great.Crafting is good.Cons.Combat... Is this a Survival Crafting Game or a Souls Like game? Yes you get hungry very fast, so it puts you into Panic Mode when you just start the game. What's the idea with that? Is this a Rogue Like game while having Souls Like combat? Make up your mind.Fun Factor is between Catastrophically Bad to Meh, Hunger and Combat is just Atrociously Horrendous. How can you have fun when you get Hungry too fast, and when you depend on Stamina on everything to even enjoy any mechanics?Game has potential, but it just isn't fun in Survival and Combat sense.Will revise once things gets fixed, so my total score for the game is.3/10

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game deserved better in reputation.It is incredibly rough and I was turned away as well but came back a year after with a new mindset and a sincere attempt to discover what was quite fun.The games exploration, sense of journey and story can all be really interesting and fun.It's glaring and most obvious short-comings are definitely in the inventory, slightly in the boat building, the sailing sometimes falls short, rng can be intensely cruel and combat can be simplistic and tedious but overly punishing off the top of my head.Yet I still consider it a fun game worth playing, I don't think it's for those who require a lot of guidance sadly.I always thought boat customisation could have been a little more open and less restrictive with how you could only put a single item on any piece, even platforms and some combinations of boat parts didn't seem to work.The rng element is definitely the roughest part of the game, sometimes giving you barely anything you'll need to step up your gear and craft; or perhaps even to survive.Though I also believe that this inherent randomness could be navigated and even fun with the right mindset and adjusting your playstyle when things get rough.The inventory management is tough to comment, being a game in which crafting and resources are hugely important and you'll need to hoard quite a few different ones as much as possible.Even with all of these, I think it's a fun twist on survival and rogue-likes combined that lends a mix of pleasant journey and discovery, harsh survival, terrifying moments, danger and overcoming it; all into one game which while short, is hard to stop persisting through and difficult to reach the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Windbound, its seems like a lovely game to play from the store page. It is, until you consider the new DLC that was added. It has absolutely beautiful scenery and a cute art style.I've been a follower of this game since it first came out. I've only recently came back on another platform to see what its like again. Like all Survival Games this one isn't the typical easy survival game many people would believe. Even on the Easiest mode, its a challenge, considering the Loathing and the corruption that saps most of your health bar away if you aren't careful.You will have to face many challenges and dealing with its clunky combat system that's not changed since the start. Items break too easily, there's not enough materials to keep you going if you don't know where to put your resources in. I've wasted so many materials crafting weapons that break in no time.The DLC further makes the combat more difficult and rather frustrating with the fact you can get pummelled by the new spectral monsters. Worst thing is. You can't turn it off. It sucks. It doesn't even tell you much about how to get rid of the corruption, Except the fact reloading the save area gets rid of it. Nothing else.While there is so much potential that this game has, there has not been much in the way of fixing many of the problems. The AI combat, the constant pointless tutorials that tells you to lock onto an enemy if you get hit once, Wind that constantly works against you that can throw you off your boat if you aren't careful (I'm aware that the sailing mechanic can be difficult for some), The Loathing/corruption that is almost on every island that you require the better resources is placed and then the inventory storage, again, some of the ingredients are random or difficult to come by.I don't recommend this game for those who fall under the guise that it's like a Zelda-esk type game like Wind Waker. It's not even remotely close. For those, who enjoy a good challenge and a problematic combat style its a good choice.

_childDocuments_.review: Windbound is a survival games that asks the player to build his own boat at set sail around the sea. If the game is beautiful and offers a rather unique take on the survival genre it can also be repetitive and frustrating at times. Overall, the game offers an amazing experience with a really nice and relaxing atmosphere. If you can look pass the occasional glitches, this game is an experience worth taking. Windbound has those really nice cel-shaded graphics similar to TLOZ: The Wind Waker. I would say that even though most of the game is just plain sea, it is still gorgeous. The vivid colours bring the islands to life, the blue of the sea contrasts nicely with your boat and many times you feel like what is on your screen would make a nice postcard picture. Music is both nice and absent, usually it really adapts to the speed of your boat or what is happening, but often, you feel like the game is a bit too quiet. I really liked the sequences in-between the levels where the music got really intense. It’s hard to say if Windbound’s gameplay is good or bad. On one hand, the fact that you can build your own boat, the way you want is quite unique and is probably the most compelling aspect of the game. On the other hand the game is very repetitive, you need to find three keys to open the gate to the next level, rinse and repeat with different types of islands. This repetitiveness is made worse by the survival aspects of the game. You need to hunt, eat, repair your boat, craft weapons that keep breaking and because of that more often than not you feel like a simple level takes ages to complete.Add to this some glitches and elements that ruin your experience. In my case, my character fell in between two rocks and I had to restart that game. When I came back my boat was still on the map but on the other side of the world. I found it stuck on top of rocks where it couldn’t move and had to glitch it out of it with the building function. Frustrating. I will also add that combat is a bit clunky, the character feels quite heavy and it is easy to get hit for random reasons such as an uneven floor. It is especially infuriating against the few bosses the game throws at you. The story is very simple and revolves around a woman lost at see discovering mysterious ruins of a lost civilisations that betrayed their gods. She is obviously linked to that civilisation and has to keep going through the levels to discover all their secrets. After the story, Windbounds offers an infinite mode where you can try to survive as long as possible. Sadly it doesn’t help the repetitiveness of the game.  Windbounds has 29 achievements for you to get. However, I’d say most of them are quite annoying to get and sometimes a bit technical.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with the Pros:- Wonderful art and sound designMusic kicks in right as you're sailing away from the island, and at important story points- Awesome sailing mechanicsNice and easy to use- A good basic story to the gameI would love to continue and see what the story behind the giant shell creature is and the ancient artifacts- The player upgrade system when progressing the storyGetting upgrades for the player like better sprinting really feels like your character is growing somehowAnd now the negatives:- The hunger mechanics feel tacked onthe player gets hungry way too fast for the very little amount of food you get. and you can't make use of good food until you're starving. this could easily be fixed by increasing berry bushes on the first island.- Combat isn't easyyou have to craft certain abilities in order to use them, like a mask for example. rather than just giving the basic abilities.- Difficulty isn't scaled rightthe hogs are really easy. However those buffalo looking things are way too difficult for an early enemy, especially considering that their drops are needed for so many basic tools.- Control scheme different from most gamesA minor point, but the defaults are quite strange, like crafting with the right bumper- Sprinting is annoyingThe sprint mechanic is tied to the amount of hunger you've lost, so if you're starving you can barely run. Which is unique and realistic, but realistic isn't always beneficial to the player, especially in this caseSo given all that I can't recommend the game and i'll be requesting a refund. If some of the mechanics were ever fixed or changed in the future I would come back to the game, but in its current state, it's just not fun to play

_childDocuments_.review: It's one of those games that could be great if not for certain things. In this case the game just struggles to juggle too many mechanics at once, two in specific are hardly compatible with each other and those are Rogue-Like mechanics and Survival/Crafting. I don't think those mix good.The Rogue-Like mechanic is that when you die, you start the complete chapter over again, no matter how far you get. That alone could be not too terrible, but then you also constantly lose stamina and struggle with gaining enough food and also you have to constantly search for crap to improve/repair your ship and repair + build new weapons (wich break really fast).After each chapter you can chose some gifts from the gods wich are slowly nullifying some of the survival aspects, wich makes you even question why they are there in the first place.The combat itself is terrible at first, but slowly gets improved with better weapons and adding new mechanics over time. I think they also should all be standard from the beginning, because it really takes away the fun when you don't have them.Then it's also tagged as an RPG and it's not, it has the adventure aspects of a Zelda game, but you don't level up. All the character improvements come from equipment or things you collect.The story is nothing new either, it's something I've seen in a lot of those walking sims and it bores me to death.Time to finish: I only finished 3-4/5 of the game and just can't get myself to keep going.

_childDocuments_.review: So for anyone wondering if you want to get this game all I can say is to read this review as their main thing to do.This game is awesome, yes, I have read other negative reviews as well, but this game is awesome. Main reason why so many people liked this game is because they do not like rogue-like games. You heard me, this game is survival ROGUE-LIKE. If you play in story mode you will definetly not feel this. But as someone that is on my 4th "run" with bow and an actual mage staff instead of a spear I can say that this game has content, but if you speed through it like mad man it will all feel horrible. Havent switched to story mode, neither planning on doing so. You will be thrown into game with little tutorial on what to do, because you are supposted to find it out yourself. Each "run" is generated so that it feels new while being familiar. Each run you know more and are better at the game. Each cutscene CAN be skipped so it is not repetitive. Fighting mechanics are made to be easy when you do them numerous times with constant fear of starting over. While you have limited resources every chapter, food is not limited, you just have to farm it constantly in small amounts. Sailing is bit weird, hard to understand for those that have never sailed before but you will get used to it. So basically, if you want to play it "properly" you need to understand how the game wants to be played, if you have any questions, you can ask them under this review.In conclusion, I love this game, probably will play it long after buying and I recomend it to anyone that likes rogue games

_childDocuments_.review: I came into this game with skepticism and it was justified.      The game is presented as a open world but it is linear with small islands in between each chapter. That would be fine if the islands had variety but they are pretty cookie cutter until you move to the next chapter.      The sailing is slow and windy. There isnt any indicator if your sail is "catching the wind." So i have no idea if im going the optimal path and then I end up not moving in the middle of the ocean. I would recommend your sails making sound or puffing out when it is in the optimal path.       The combat is janky and difficult to tell if youre too far to make contact. By the time I get close enough and hit, the slow attack animation leaves me exposed for a solid second before I can dodge so it seems to stutter on trivial enemies.       The story is actually interesting but it is heavily overshadowed by the lackluster gameplay.

(Also the in game photo mode is damn brilliant, i wish other games had a photo mode as good as this one does)Only bad thing i can say about the game is that some animations feel a bit rough at times (specifically when standing up after taking damage) and can feel a bit clunky too control, although nothing major honestly, and collision detection could be improved by a tiny bit.Other than that the game is on a good way and i feel like, if they make the world even more lively and dynamic this could even turn out to be a hidden masterpiece.I post this review mainly because im quite shocked about the relatively mediocre reception the game has gotten so far and i may hope that there will be additional interest for this game since i sincerely believe it deserves it.Anyways i hope the devs read this and i hope this was in some way helpful to others :) If anyone has questions about the game ill gladly answer them (as long as i can of course)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the nicer survival games out there, and feels more like an animated film. The survival aspects are real - food, water and resources are a challenge, and hoarding is difficult because things decay. Eventually you can make jerky etc. and that helps.The sailing aspect is fantastic, and feels more real than most (depending on settings.), and an important part of the game.Base building - or canoe building - is interesting. You get more bits as you experiment and find new materials. You need to progress to new areas to find new materials; balancing how fast you progress with consolidating what you have is important. Exploration is rewarding, and you can find islands, reefs and other things with varied stuff on them - with the later DLC's, that includes more 'special' things.Combat - you are a hunter and it tries to be realistic with sneakiness and fairly reasonable tradeoffs. Try the wrong fight the wrong way and you will die. Adaptability is key. DLC's - they are free, and on the whole they are good, but they feel a little jarring - they add things that do not feel entirely part of the setting, and I'm not too fond of that. As detractions go, though, that is quite minor. There are a few things that feel a little stiff. The pacing doesn't feel entirely right. Overall, though, this is a very nice little game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the concept of this game and wanted to continue exploring the isolated archipelagos but found myself constantly getting frustrated with various mechanics. If you can overlook these frustrations it may be a great game for you. Giving a pro-con for easier viewing with a little more detail afterwards.Pros:- The sailing feels good and is mostly a fun experience once you get the sail- The item progression starts simple and gets complex slowly in that feels good- The isolated chapters are stylized in a way that make them fun to explore and are enjoyable to look at.- Pelting enemies at range feels accurate and fun with the bow.Cons:- Combat is super frustrating. Enemies can get multiple hit combos in that will lock you out.- The player cannot dodge outside of being locked onto a target.- Range does not have a lock on mechanic when enemies are close to the player and dodge seems inconsistent and only backwards in range- Sailing into the wind can be frustrating when in kills all momentum if you get a angle slightly wrong.Combat was the real killer for me. By the third archipelago, with no meaningful buffs to health or ways to have additional protection, it was a mood killer. I personally never could get a parry to work so that might highly alter the experience for someone else. I didn't list this as a con as I don't think its a negative more a design over site. Each archipelago also provides a new resource to build a boat with but never enough to fully upgrade it unless you just lingered there. The second archipelago provides the bamboo material and a way to build a two pontoon boat but just not enough if you only spend a few in game cycles. Which I didn't and went to the third archipelago it moves onto wood planks for the next style. If I played longer it may have leveled out but that didn't feel good to me as a player.

_childDocuments_.review: Adding a 'Hardcore Survival' tag to the game because of food management.  While possibly realistic, the food management system is just too much and takes the fun out of the game.  Islands with only scraps and somehow you are meant to spend time there and collect resources.  Even in Story mode this aspect of the game made it significantly less fun than it could have been.  Things the developers could do:- Hunger optional (make it a checkbox in either mode)- Eating should represent more healing, even if as a heal over time (longer period)- Plants and sticks should regrow, even over longer periods of time, like the berries- Add a fast travel option to the towers so you can get back to previous islands for resources- ^ build a dock and your boat comes with you, otherwise it stays where it was- ^ Fast travel lets you put down one set of kilns in one place and get back to them- 'W' should not raise the sail, should be able to paddle against the wind- ^ Chastise whoever thought it was a good idea to need to disassemble your boat/sail to fight the windI could go on, but other people have called out good ideas, please read them and fix the game.  Overall, I feel like the game is rushing me along.  (but it has to because of the food problem)  I want to take my time exploring islands and building up resources.  Give me more islands to explore, let me spend more time in each act.  - If the boat is destroyed, all items in containers should float around waiting to be picked up.  (and be accessible swimming)- Some of the boat materials should remain behind and float, letting the player build on that for a new boat. (heck, enough for an emergency raft)- ^ emergency raft please...

_childDocuments_.review: You may have heard of "Metroid-Vania"s or "Souls-Like" games. In this case I'd say this game is a damn good approximation of a game in the "Legend of Zelda" series (please note this isn't in the same way a game like "The Binding of Isaac" is like the old Zelda games). The game as a whole is Linear, but each chapter is a procedural-ly generated "world" for you to explore, and you get to leave when you want (provided you can beat that chapter's boss).You can make a catamaran/pontoon boat in almost any shape you want, as long as you have the materials.RPG/Roguelike elements exist, too, where you pick upgrades as you go, and lose access to ones you don't select unless chance has you come across them again.I absolutely adore the soundtrack, and you can tell the composer loves his craft.There are also a few oddities: You can't opt out of past updates, which include some crazy enemies who almost seem out-of-place in the world. Tutorials seem nigh-impossible to get rid of Combat is quite clunky Performance isn't that greatThere are a few stylized decisions Player Inventory is quite small, but if you have the materials, you can make bags, and store them on parts of your  catamaran. Sailing doesn't let you paddle, so you have to use the wind or you can just sit there, unmoving.Overall, it is quite a good game, and I would recommend playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game because I absolutely loved the sailing element of Windwaker and watching the trailers for this game really brought back that itch. I've been playing for 8 hours and it really is scratching it. However, if you are expecting a game with an epic story and fluid combat like the Zelda titles, then this is not the game for you. If you enjoyed the sense of exploration and the sailing element of Windwaker, then this is definitely a game worth considering. I've been playing survival mode for 8 hours, and have been taking it slowly. Combing over islands and gradually upgrading my boat and learning what items are the most useful to keep on my person in the event that I die and need a restart and it has been very relaxing. The cell shaded graphics are wonderful to look at and the music really harmonises with the environment and the overall vibe of the game which makes just simply being in the game world an absolute pleasure. It's because of this that it has been really easy for me to overlook the bugs I have encountered.Some of the issues that I have encountered have been:- Animals being launched into the air when I killed them (3 or 4 times) which is annoying as you do lose any arrows you shot into them and the resources you were after.- Animals getting stuck on terrain making for easy kills which does detract a little from the immersion- Odd jerky boat movements when boarding and alighting from your boat on the beach which can be a pain if you have been crafting on your boat and have left items on the deck as these can be pushed into the sea where they are too deep to retrieve.The movement is not as polished as some titles released by bigger studios and the combat is not as fluid as a lot of people had hoped for (restricted to straight lunges with the spears and slings are very slow) but as with any game, once you get used to using the lock on and dodging it really isn't as bad as people are making it out to be and, as I said before, since I like the setting it is certainly not a deal breaker, far from it.TL:DRIf you want a fast paced action-adventure, do not buy this game, you will probably hate it.If you loved the sailing in Windwaker (even without control over the wind direction) and you like a slower paced exploration style game with some crafting thrown in, then at least give it a go, especially if it is on sale.It's a beautiful game. If you take your time with it, you will enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to talk a bit about the negatives of this game before anything else. What I didn't like is honestly all things I can live with when it comes to this game but I must talk about regardless. The combat feels too stiff in comparison to what it's trying to mimic with action oriented RPG games. The transitional levels between the main over-worlds are a bit dull and felt too cumbersome to traverse in comparison to the majority of the game, but again, these are things I can live with. I adore this game to no end, even with its faults.This game is absolutely breathe taking, and surprisingly fluid. Windbound tries to be a lot of things, and while it may not succeed in some of them, it thrives in its atmosphere and sailing mechanics. As a kid, I loved playing Windwaker, and Windbound brings out a age old nostalgia that I had completely forgotten about until I had built my first boat, and set sail to the hauntingly beautiful music of Zander Hulme. If you have the time, please play this game, you won't regret it at all.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is weird, the combat is repetitive, the sailing can can be a chore, and the scope of items you can craft doesn't feel necessary given the small scope of enemies, with only one optional one that could be considered a boss. Yet, I still find it all engaging. A lot of it has to do with the visuals; they're gorgeous with stunningly fluid animations for an indie title. The deliberate pacing feels oddly refreshing, with its emphasis on wonder and discovery. Like with Ocarina of Time, my all-time favorite, a lot of it is sold more by atmosphere than by challenge, but that atmosphere draws me in despite the overall delivery being less than what's promised.

_childDocuments_.review: So far I am loving this game, as a fan of the survival genre its a big hit for me, i love the blend of how your boat is also your base, you craft from it, you store things on it, and so on. The combat is pretty straight forward so far, I really enjoy the use of the sling, i though it would be rendered useless after I got a bow, but you can craft grenades and stuff later on. I'm playing on the survival difficulty because that's what was recommended, I appreciate how when you die you have to start over from the first chapter of the game, you get to keep all the items on your held bar which is super helpful but not too much of an early start, as you progress you find these blue shards that are basically a currency to trade with the gods to get perks, and these perks carry over, so it makes for a fun loop even if you die and have to start over because it isn't too unforgiving.If you have the 30$ and enjoy Survival exploration games, with dynamic storytelling (no voice acting afaik) the musical score is a treat, the gameplay loop is solid, and taking down those big enemies feels so rewarding in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a game in here for someone, but not for me[I'm a big fan of gameplay of the nomadic survival type, itches that can be scratched by ATLAS, World's Adrift, No Man's Sky and the like. And, by all accounts, Windbound should scratch that itch, and combine it with another of my favourite genres, action combat.Unfortunately, there is a genre I also can't stand. Roguelikes.Despite it's presentation of breath of the Wild like graphics and cute fluffy animals, Windbound's gameplay is strongly bound up in the rogue-like formula. Dying even in casual mode sets you back to the start of the chapter and takes away almost everything you've earned. Dying in Survival difficulty is outright permadeath and the whole game starts over.This'd be less of a concern if it wasn't for the fact hostile wildlife can respawn practically on top of you without warning, and often dead animals will fly into the stratosphere, denying you their precious food and resources, without which your survival chances are greatly diminished and the odds of you ending up back at square one rise sharply.Meanwhile the gathering lacks a certain something that is difficult to pin down, and the combat can only really be described as 'there', while infinitely better than the mess that is the majority of survival titles like ARK, the 'action combat' elements feel ponderously slow and basic, with the dodge button having a noticeable delay to trigger. Outside of combat your character gets winded after a short doggy paddle or stiff jog up a flight of stairs, and has to eat like she has a wasting disease to avoid starving.I want to like this game, and maybe the devs will make adjustments to appeal to players like me. But as it stands, this game just isn't for me. It's a Don't starve style survival roguelike dressed up as Breath of the Wild

_childDocuments_.review: Upon starting a new game you’ll have the choice of two game difficulties, Survivalist and Storyteller. Survivalist are for those players who want the full Windbound experience. The game difficulty options include, only items in “Held” inventory slots are retained upon death, Return to Chapter One upon death and Standard combat difficulty. Storyteller difficulty is for those players who want to focus on the Windbound story. The settings for this difficulty include, Full inventory is retained upon death. Chapter Progress is retained upon death and combat difficulty is reduced. You can change the difficulty setting at any time from within the Gameplay options menu. There’s a storm raging on the open sea, the waves crashing against your raft as you try to stay afloat. You can see the dim lights fastened to the masts of other rafts as they ride the waves up and down. Suddenly a giant Nautilus appears, tentacles flaying about when it comes crashing down upon your raft casting you in to the rough sea. You slowly sink beneath the waves, when suddenly you appear on the surface. The storm and waves have gone, everything is calm as you stand upon the water. Before you is a bright swirling light in the centre of some stone ruins, arches which rise from out of the calm sea.  You make your way towards the light, walking through you find yourself washed up on a beach … The Lost Islands (Chapter One). You begin with a knife and there are some resources across the island to help you survive. However, you’re not going to be able to survive on the island for long. At the far side of the island there’s some ancient ruins, on what looks like an altar is an object with a blue crystal at one end. After picking the object up it transforms into the Oar of the Ancestors. A mysterious, ornate and ancient oar which occasionally trembles in your hands as though something resides in it.  Now that you have this mysterious oar, you’ll have to put it to use. This means you’ll have to build a boat so that you can move between the islands. With limited resources you’re not going to be building any speedboats or luxury cruise liners for now though you’re going have to with a canoe made of Thick Grass. You can find Thick Grass growing most places and can be cut down using your knife. Once you have enough grass head over to the shore and select canoe in the crafting options and you’ll craft your first means of transport in this mysterious place.  When you collect resources, they may unlock new items for you to craft. There are also some animals on the islands, some big and some cute n cuddly ones. However, all will provide some resources when you ring their bloody necks. Resources such as bone, silk thread, raw meat, skins, jaws and other wonderous creature parts. Sticks, wood, rocks, palm fronds, flowers, berries, fish, bamboo are just a few of the resources available for you to find and craft into new items.  On some of these islands stand these mysterious structures with blue crystals at the top. Climbing these structures to the top will reveal a Nautilus Key, three of these keys are required to unlock the exit to the current chapter. Once you collect a Nautilus key a blue beam of light heads upwards to the heavens. There is also another light which can be seen somewhere in the distance, this is the exit point once you have collected all three keys. After going through the exit, you find yourself in a large courtyard with five sides and a pathway leading out of the courtyard, The First Crossing. A mural starts to appear on one of the sides which depicts a story of worship to the Nautilus.  At the end of the pathway there’s your canoe, which you’ll use to paddle your way under the stars over rolling waves. Eventually you spot a small plot of land with the same bright swirling light you first seen in the storm. On the bit of land though are a couple of statues, here you can make an offering and have a blessing bestowed upon you. To make an offering you need Sea Shards, these can be found in blue jars once they’ve been smashed. You can also collect shards at any shrines you may come across on your journey. Once you’ve finished with your offering and blessing then head towards the light and you’ll then find yourself on Chapter Two. As you progress, you’ll encounter different creatures which will pose far more deadly than the cute n cuddly Bleenk. Luckily for you, you will be able to upgrade your grass canoe to a sturdier boat using bamboo and later wood. Adding sails will help you travel faster than paddling. However, it can be quite frustrating trying to keep the speed up if you don’t keep the wind in your sails. Also watch out for those reefs especially in a grass canoe, hiding in those reefs are Crobsters which will jump onboard and if left will destroy your boat. I did lose some items had stored on my boat from one of those little blighters the first time I came across them. In the options you’ll find settings for Display (Full Screen, Resolution, Refresh Rate, V-Sync, Field of View and Brightness). Quality (Shader Quality, Shadow Resolution, Soft Shadows, Antialiasing, Anisotropic Filtering, Textures, LOD Quality, SSAO, Bloom and Volumetrics). Sound (Master, Sound Effects, Background Music and Creature Music Volume Sliders). Gameplay (Mouse Sensitivity, Aim Sensitivity, Invert Aim Y-Axis, Show Contextual Controls, Tutorials, Difficulty, Outfit and Vibration). Language (English, French, Italian, German, Spanish, Russian, Polish and Chinese).  Positives + Great looking graphics + Enjoyable and relaxing game to play + Two game difficulties + Good music + Has achievements  Negatives - Sailing can be a bit frustrating - No cards currently Craft yourself a seaworthy boat, let the winds guide you as you explore and unlock the secrets of the Forbidden Islands in Windbound.  8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game gets more dislikes than it deserves:Lore wise it's very rich, and Gameplay wise I think this is honestly pretty good; much of its mechanics/gameplay caters to a good deal of people. The sailing and camping qualities are really quite relaxing, while the ship building options and crafting interface are fun to play around with. The combat- while not the greatest- is still enjoyable, and every chapter unlocks new beasts to fight and gear for your character. Players can select between several different difficulties/modes when starting their game, which includes an endless mode and a peaceful mode. The entire game has a good deal of replayability, as the levels are procedurally generated and hold different challenges and treasures each time you play. This game seems to get a bad rep, and I enjoyed this game more than I expected I would, from sailing to gathering to hunting: the game itself is solid and made with passion, and I'm glad I got it- If any of this piques your interest, I think it is worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: Neat little game which could be a lot neater with some fairly simple improvements. This is a case where a bit of judicial modding would definitely come in handy.Pros: Gorgeous art design, nice soundtrack. The water effects are really stunning, and lend a lot to this game's atmosphere and mechanics. Exploration's fun, and there's a decent amount of variety in the exploration. Cons: Can't rebind the keys, and especially in water navigation, the WASD binding becomes really tedious. There's also moments where the camera becomes locked, and cannot be mouse-turned, which makes WASD even more egregious.  The combat's clunky, again, because of the forced bindings.  Once you've built your first sail, you may find as I did that while paddling is slower, it's also much more reliable and less complicated. Beyond that, simple quality of life adjustments would be nice: length of days, stamina degradation (which is entirely too fast, and leaves you spending far too much time just hunting for food.) At times, basic and essential resources become entirely too scarce. (Can't build a fire without long grass... which is slow to respawn, for example.)  Overall, if you're patient with it's flaws, I feel it's worth a few bucks, and a few hours of your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Fair warning the sail mechanics are really tough but more importantly even in the easy mode the combat can be frustrating with possible deaths.  After 6 hours I barely grasped sailing, with constant crashing into islands and reefs even destroying my ship mid sea with no recourses to rebuild it. As for combat a lot of rage quits over dying since I still haven't been able to dodge properly once (as the game I think forces you to target something to dodge it I still havent been able to successfully dodge once hence my rage towards combat). And let me make this clear, dying sucks. When you die in this game you lose a ton of progress. On harder difficulty all but a handful of items are kept with story progress being lost. But even if you choose the easy mode all bags on your ship are lost and you reset your progress to the start of the act. Nothing hurts more than having farmed up a lot of stuff for hours trying to find that one item you need to make a better ship only to die to an enemy you've just seen for the first time and losing 30 slots of items. If there was creative mode I'm sure the game would lose its charm very quickly since there is very little you can do, all the gameplay comes from low resources and hard mechanics. There is a charm to the ship making but you are given so little resources that building a large ship would take a lot of effort. But even then the limitations are obvious, once you see a few parts you've seen them all and the combinations are not endless.I was curious about the barely minimum story however the frustration over the controls and the amount of progress lost really outshines everything. The main mission is boring and repetative; as every single time you find 3 islands with towers, climb them to unlock another island, then rinse and repeat 5 times I presume (I was on act 4 when I had  enough) The game is gorgeous to look at with beautiful sounds I'll give it that. Though perfect for casual gamers, or else it would have been if not for the difficult combat and lack of progress save, so who is this game for exactly? Hardcore survival gamers I suppose. So if you like dark souls but wished when you died going back to your corpse to regain lost items was for losers and you wanted everything you worked for to be lost everytime you encountred an enemy you couldn't figure before they killed you, then go right ahead, you have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game despite the negative reviews while it was on sale, and I can honestly say its quite good so far. First off, what I like about the game:- fantastic art style- good combat mechanics- lots of exploration possible- challenging, but also playable on lesser difficulties so its playable for everyoneHere I'll adress some common downsides:1. Glitches. I haven't experienced any game breaking glitches yet. Sure some things are a bit frustrating like the climbing but its not nearly as bad as its made out to be (imho)2. Camera. It is a bit tricky as the camera is a bit wild sometimes, but again not too bad imo.3. Controls. controls are good overall, unfortunately not customisable. _childDocuments_.review: As an old school player, I enjoy difficulty. Survival games really entertain me and Windbound is one of my favorites right now. I don't mind losing the items everytime I die and restart the chapters because it's part of the adventure.The world is random generated, so you will never sail the same ocean twice, even when you back to chapter 1.Your sailboat is the focus of everything, since you are a castaway trying to get back to your family/tribe.I deeply enjoyed sail through the isles, face storms and fogs, fight the wind and explore. The sail system is "realistic", so if you enjoy this activity the fun in guaranteed.Kara is beautiful and her animations was clearly made with care. She carries everything with her and even the arrows have their spot and number acknowledged.The energy management was cleverly implemented and together with the inventory, offer a good challenge, since you can't carry everything until pass this barrier. For any survival game player, I believe this will be a fun "puzzle" to solve.There is a good amount of practical items to craft, from food, inventory and weapons, as parts for your sailboat, and not enough resources for everything. The animals respawn tho. Ah, the boat can be destroyed, so you need to repair it sometimes.I didn't encountered any bug, but sometimes the camera focus the wrong enemy and you need to release and click the button until the right one is selected (like in For Honor).The pace can be slow if you want, exploring, looking for food and resources, crafting everything possible in the chapter and then moving to the next, which will offer new challenges and more difficulty.I recommend Windbound for any survival player who enjoy a lonely adventure full of discoveries.
