_childDocuments_.review: 🎵🎵If you’re on this store page, chances are you are familiar with the Angry Video Game Nerd (AVGN). For those of you who aren’t, I can provide a quick summary but it’s probably best if you check out his  In short, AVGN is a persona who dedicates his life to playing and describing how bad some video games are (typically older ones). As the name suggests, he is best known for his anger and very liberal use of profanity.  (AVGND) is the embodiment of the AVGN series. Everything you’ve come to expect, such as his infamous potty mouth and extreme depictions of violence, alongside bucketloads of AVGN references, is incorporated in this pixelated adventure. Despite constantly being referred to as a “sh***y game” (by the Nerd himself), I quite enjoyed my playthrough.AVGND is essentially a parody of terrible games that continuously criticises itself for also being a terrible game. Despite this, AVGND is actually a good blend of challenging and fun (at least on normal difficulty). Since this is a play on terrible games, it only makes sense that the developers intentionally designed many segments to be unfair and/or trap the player. Funnily enough, this never pushed me to the point of frustration since the game is quite fair (I know this is contradictory but bear with me). Movement is reliable and familiar (feels like playing MegaMan), checkpoints are evenly spaced out, there is minimal RNG (except for boss fights), and respawns are infinite and quick. With a little patience you will know what to expect, allowing you to progress through the levels. Additionally, both games control in the same way, which makes for a smooth transition between AVGN I and II. Level design is surprisingly diverse. Each level (AVGN I) or zone (AVGN II) has a specific visual style, background music, gimmicks, and enemy types. For example, in AVGN I there is a level based on old erotic games - I don’t imagine I need to specify what the enemies are here. There is also a zone based on the TMNT NES game, complete with the awful electric seaweed and the  mini gap. Better graphics, map design, difficulty settings, etc - rest assured that everything stated on the store page is delivered. Since I have played AVGN I before, I could tell there were significant improvements in graphics and playability, which made the experience as a whole more enjoyable (AKA less rage-inducing). This deluxe version also comes with four additional levels (of which one is a boss fight) that can be accessed once you beat both I and II. Additionally, since all games (I, II and bonus) are built on the same game engine, the experience is quite streamlined. You can really feel that this is the definitive version of the AVGN games.Nevertheless, the core game is still practically the same. Although I can only speak for AVGN I, I don’t imagine AVGN II has changed much either in this version. If you haven’t played either AVGN game, I would recommend picking up the deluxe version. If you’ve already played both, it doesn’t make much sense to buy this version since it is hardly different from the originals (unless you feel like financially supporting the Nerd). Assuming you don’t get stuck and die a lot, most levels/zones should not take more than 15 minutes to complete. Altogether, my casual playthrough of AVGN I, II & bonus levels (on normal difficulty) only took about 4 hours. More content is included in the form of hidden characters/secrets and four collectable video game cassettes per level but once you’ve collected them all, there isn’t much left to do. If you’re really hungry for more AVGN, you can always attempt to complete every level without dying or increase the base difficulty.Dialogue is caked with insults and profanity, turd references are plentiful and enemies explode into gory messes when they die. This is exactly what we have come to expect from the AVGN series and the developers definitely managed to capture it here.  Honestly, I had completely forgotten how vulgar AVGN is. My teen self would have had the time of his life with this game but at this point in my life I don’t care for it much. Regardless, a very faithful representation of AVGN.Yep, that’s right, you can fire as quickly as you can button mash. This is especially broken if you have a controller with a turbo function - I imagine it would just look like a stream of white squares extending across the screen. Evading is still necessary but it feels cheap to cheese through boss fights mostly by mashing; generally speaking, they did not take more than 3 attempts to beat. Perhaps this was designed this way to make boss fights more viable at harder difficulties. There is limited time to read the dialogue as it proceeds automatically. This usually isn’t a problem but I find that the time allocated here is very short, forcing me to quickly gobble down the words on the screen. The writing isn’t Shakespearian but I would have liked to read it properly regardless. I’m not sure why the dialogue progression isn’t gated by the player’s input. Although it may seem that I have outgrown my appreciation for the vulgar, I actually quite enjoyed playing AVGND. Besides being a nice shot of nostalgia, this game is more fun than it is frustrating (at least on normal difficulty), especially when compared to AVGN I. Just bear in mind this deluxe version is essentially a remaster of the two previous games.To simplify things, I made this flowchart to help you decide whether you should get this game or not:

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of AVGN, I found these games to be a great supplement to the series. There are plenty of references and the same charm of the AVGN. Though this may turn off many who do not watch it, I do think that on its own this game holds up very well.	The part that stuck out to me the most was the gameplay. It is very satisfying. I found that movement was tight as a platformer, the game was generally fair, the level design was well done, and the gameplay was fun the entire time to the point where I 100%ed the game pretty much all in the same week. I do feel though that many people will find that this game is unbelievably punishing. When my brother played the original version he ended up throwing in the towel just because of how damn hard it was. This game on the other hand has far more difficulty options and that was perhaps this versions greatest advantage, it allows this game to be played by far more people, and on the easy difficulty will be far easier to beat while still maintaining a large portion of the challenge that the game has in its level design.	Graphically the game has a style that I appreciate, I am a sucker for pixel graphics and this game does it well. It is very colorful, backgrounds are very detailed, enemies have a great variety, and the UI and menu design is fitting. I have always disliked the gross-out stuff that the AVGN does and some of that is reflected in the game and its visuals, but honestly, that is my only gripe and I do not think that that is a real criticism since that is very much just a personal thing.	The controls are great, I had zero issues. Everything felt tight and I liked how the menus and games control.	I did not think I would say this, but I thought the soundtrack was fire. I really enjoyed it to the point I have gone out of my way to listen to some of it. The other sounds in the game are really good as well.	Lastly, this game vaguely has a story, and it is serviceable. It sucks that it is pretty minimal, but not surprising given that it is emulating older games. I don’t really have any praise for it beyond that it has the standard Nerd humor.I think this is a fantastic game. It is exactly what it should be; an old-style platformer, with AVGN humor, good graphics and music, and overall plays well. I am not a huge fan of platformers but this is definitely a good one and I found that I ate this game up and had a great time playing it. I do think that some may find this game a little lackluster for the price. I got under 12 hours out of it and it goes for 15, so I think it would be wiser to wait for a sale to get your best bang for your buck.

_childDocuments_.review: Given that this is a compilation the two official AVGN games, it has to have some quality-of-life improvements which I embraced. For one, the flood of death blocks, especially in AVGN I, was a source of frustration for many. Thankfully, they have been cut down in the DX edition, especially on lower difficulties. And despite playing this compilation on Easy, some levels forced me to be really good at platforming. Good thing I learned from my mistakes and strove to get better. This is one of those "tough, but fair" action platformers that should be given more recognition.On the other departments, the sprite work is awesome, and the music is as good as it is. The in-game story is basic, but at least it carries the spirit of the Nerd.This improved edition is the one you should get.

_childDocuments_.review: CHECK OUT MY VIDEO REVIEW AT THE BOTTOM AS WELL!I give details on the difference between the versions and go over each level.I received a review copy of this game a while ago and cannot get enough of it. This is more than just a compilation of the first two games. It's a complete overhaul of the first, a tweaking of the second, and a brand new third for the grand finale!Refitting the first game into the engine the second used, we get a lot of improved graphics. The colors really pop! Also no more "Continue/Quit" screens! When you die, you immediately reform at the checkpoint! So you don't loose any momentum! At least one boss has been replaced but I'll leave that for you to find out (Or you can watch my video). Also the Cameos/Collectibles are intact (Although the Cameos are now Future Nerd appearances) PLUS you can now find the NERD letters like you would in II. And best of all, the difficulty has been curved for the better! 3/4 of the death blocks have been replaced with spikey balls! It can still be a pain but not as infuriating.Most of the changes in the second game are cosmetic. A few characters/bosses were reworked to make it more self contained (meaning it's no longer a movie tie in) any Cameos are nixed, and at least one level has been overhauled for the better! This was a great fine tuning of a great game.Lastly there's the new chapter! A four level (three plus one boss battle) gauntlet that's equal to the Wiley Tower levels of Mega Man the Wiley Wars! It is a gauntlet of some pretty challenge levels! And a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane final boss as well to wrap things up!Now for the more technical details.Graphics: Like I said they're gorgeous! For a retro game this is one of the bests!Controls: Perfect! Never had much of a problem either with M&KB or a controller! No delays or anything.Difficulty: You can select your difficulty now and they really show! You can also receive all the achievements on Easy mode alone. Pick the difficulty you wish for whatever challenge you want! It's rather balanced.So yeah I'd give this game a 9 out of 10! It is a great game, a terrific remaster! If you love the first two, this one improves on them and then some! Get it now!
_childDocuments_.name: Angry Video Game Nerd I & II Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game, it can be a little frustrating at times, but no level will make you want to throw your controller through your monitor, or at least not in my experience.The game may be difficult but it is always fair, nothing was made to be impossible without hundreds of deaths, but rather just to test how good at the game you really are. If you like games like Cuphead or Celeste, and how you have to learn to master the mechanics to complete levels, you will likely enjoy this game.A truly great experience that I had a blast playing through. _childDocuments_.review: Fairly challenging ( in very unfair ways ) enemies knock you back into pits, tons of death blocks ( instant death )enemies take a bunch of hits to kill, plenty of intentionally placed hazards designed to make you pull your hair out.UNike the original release, this one removes the randomly generated Nerd swears when you die, and it saves you a lot of time getting back into the action. I have nearly completed AVGN1 ( just gotta beat Fred ♥♥♥♥♥ ) But I did check out the sequel a little bit to see what to look forward too.the sequel is WAY huger than this game, you get some smaller levels, but there;s tons and tons of em. You also get new powerups, like a wall jumping move similar to Megaman XThere's also some more gimmick stages, like riding on a crossfire piece through parts of a level, it's pretty neat.I'd say this is worth the dosh, it's fairly priced, there's some new bits and bobs ( and a couple boss replacements ) Also some newer content after you beat first and second game ( you may also hav to collect all the NERD carts in each level ( which appears ot be new ) The Ghost Mansion level on the first game is pretty ruthless, I lost more live there than anywhere else, mostly due to how dark it is. And the boss was a pain as well.Ben having a blast dying over and over as I learn the stages - each time, getting slightly farther than before.there's 5 difiiculty settings ( I stuck with old school, feels appropriate ) and they basically change how many lives you have, and continues as well.Iirc, the hardest difficulty gives you 1 life, andno continues - truly old school.HIghly recommend this, and if anything else comes up while playing the sequel, and the newer content - I'll add it to the bottom.Quick break down for AVGN 2 and TowerMore levels, but smaller and more focused - 3 per area, plus a final boss level ( with NERD carts in each but boss ) The upgrade system should be explained better, as it makes most of the game a lot easier.  ( for example, in monster madness, there's an entire section where the pit is covered in hidden blocks you only get with the head scanner ) Bosses weren't too difficult ( aside of Tower ) Fred F's final boss was WAY easier to beat this time around, due to rng giving me to mecha jesus powerup attacks in a rowI think overall, AVGN1 is the better game, it encapsulates the old school feeling well, while AVGN 2 brings more modern implementaitons to the series ( and shorter levels means much easier to tread ) The tower bonus content is pretty much just an additional level for AVGN 2, so 3 more hard as balls levels + a final final boss ( which was very fun )The levels there iomplemented everything in the entire 1 + 2 , and I enjoyed that.I think AVGN 2 is a bit tougher to 100%,  but I think overall level design shines in favor of AVGN 1.AVGN 2 had me getting frustrated with each death ( especially in virtual insanity ) while AVGN 1 had me chompin at the bit to retry when I died. overall, I still recommend this remASStered pack.Two slight complaints the audio mixing seems to be done poorly here, and if you play over 144 FPS, you just invented a new difficulty mode - bc the game doesn't work as it should when you play above 60 fps. This includes ( but not limited to ) being thrown back further on hit, powerups dealing incorrect damage, and wall jump in AVGN2 not working properly. A slight mar on an otherwise fantastic game collection.Here's hoping we get to bring the NERD out of hell in AVGN in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the most mixed I have felt in awhile.This game is definitely based on those old NES games... even to their faults of poor design at times. The first game was infamous for this so much that for the version of AVGN1 in this bundle, they made several changes to the levels to get rid of some of that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I played both games in [Old School] mode to get a feel for the original difficulty of the games, especially with AVGN1.I also 100% all three chapters for context. (All perfects on all levels still pending)Out of the two, I recommend AVGN2 on Old School while I only suggest AVGN1 Old School if you're into those types of harder retro styled games. In general, AVGN2 is the better game here, and the new chapter they added has good levels as well (the addition of Bugs B- I mean 'The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Rabbit' adds an additional AVGN element that was missing before).Try this game with caution.Good things:- Music is really good, whoever they got knew what they were doing for the OST of both games (Tower of Torment has some of the best tracks).- The main movement controls are pretty good, the lock-on button for aiming makes shooting easier to perform.- The level tilesets and backgrounds have some really nice pixel art to them, all of the new art in AVGN1 is such an upgrade.- Most of the boss fights are fairly fun once you learn how they work (Not a fan of the boss in Boo! Haunted House.)- Stages can be really fun to play due to their stage gimmicks and theming, AVGN2 has much more variety in stages.- Difficulty options as well as an Auto-Fire option help tame the difficulty or add to it depending what you're looking forIssues:Some of the mechanics are inconsistent which can cause frustration with the type of game this is.-Walljumping doesn't always grab onto a wall when trying to reach for one.- Walking on stairs while aiming messes with how you move on them.- Cape gliding sometimes doesn't work which can get you killed.- Some stage hazards have different timing depending on how you load them in.- Shooting next to the beams in the final level of AVGN1 causes you to get killed by it.- I also found a bug where I broke B.S Man's animation statesThe biggest issue is what they were going for and fully intentional with how they did it, however intention doesn't fully justify bad game design choices.The game has very poor enemy and hazard placement in a good amount of screens in the levels (Just because it's intentional doesn't justify it.) Death Blocks EVERYWHERE as well as enemy spamming, and offscreen hazards/enemies that WILL hit/kill you until you remember where they are

_childDocuments_.review: I've been watching some AVGN videos recently, including the 20 minute video released late November in 2020, that discussed the work that went into creating The Angry Video Game Nerd I & II Deluxe (AD). The video made it seem like this was a passion project, where more creativity was instilled into the process of blending both games into a definitive version. As another benefit, the developer learned from making other games, which would further tighten up the gameplay and level design. Surely this must have made a big impact on the final product. At least, that was the impression I got from the video, but how much of that was just hype or self-aggrandizing for the new release?Appropriately enough, AD plays similarly to NES era run and gun platformers, with the benefit of being able to play the stages in whatever order you wish. The first game has nine stages that end with boss fights, all built around a retro game theme, such as spooky monsters, and even more terrifying, Hell itself. In the second game, there are five small worlds, made up of three stages, followed by a separate boss fight. I believe what led to this change is that more stages allow for more versatility, as it's easier to build game mechanics that will be maintained throughout the level when it's smaller. For instance, with the second game, some stages are particularly short because it's an auto-scroll or chase level, whereas the first game's longer stages occasionally switched to a SHMUP section, before returning to normal again. When I played with my controller, AD seemed responsive and was reading my inputs correctly. One aspect I didn't like is that I have to rapidly mash 'X' to fire weapons instead of being able to hold the button down. There's a reason for that in the second game, but that could have been included with the first one. Otherwise, I find the controls work pretty well, as I didn't find the controls slippery or laggy.Some changes were made to the story, with most of them pertaining to the second game. All references to the AVGN movie were replaced with the antagonist from the first game, as Fred is trying to thwart a machine he made that's turning the real world into lousy games. Otherwise, both games follow the AVGN getting into antics with games going awry at the hands of his nemesis, Fred, before concluding with a fight against that rascally rabbit in the additional area made for the deluxe version. It's not Shakespeare or anything, but redirecting the 2nd game's story to fit a larger, more consistent narrative, was the right choice. Overall, I'd say that the game looks pretty good. The pixelated visuals provide plenty of detail due to good shading, with backgrounds supporting the atmosphere of each themed world. However, I found that this was undermined in certain parts of the 2nd game, as they'd be ruined by effects. For instance, the Cinemassacre inspired levels utilize a grainy effect on top of removing the color, which simply doesn't look good. The Nerd Gaiden levels and the autoscrolling Board James level put in so many visual elements, such as lightning bolts, enemy spam, and neon signs that it oversaturates the screen. Even for someone who likes bold colors, I find the color scheme of Alien 52 incredibly harsh. It's such a waste of otherwise quality visuals.The sound track for AD is solid, and I think many of them would qualify as chip tunes. Instead of using conventional instruments, the beats and music is built with sound effects. I notice a different emphasis between the 1st and 2nd games, as the 1st seemed a bit more constrained in its use of noises, so though they both sound pretty good, the 2nd one has more range. There were only a few songs amongst them all I didn't care for, which isn't uncommon for any musical composition. Similarly with the sound effects, a few could have been improved upon, but they otherwise do the job, and I wouldn't have much reason to complain.🌟 Theoretically, patches will be released so you can see more information on the overworld. For instance, which stages you missed secrets on.🌟 If you really liked the original games, at the very least, this is slightly better than they were.❌ The boss fights were really unbalanced, particularly in the 1st game. Some of them don't seem to behave consistently or have a defined pattern. For instance, Hyde would jump at random intervals and heights, and even tire out at different times instead of after a set number of moves. The green head initially follows an infinity symbol loop, but as you blast away the heads, its pattern disintegrates completely, and I couldn't find a way to dodge it consistently. ❌ Since the AVGN focuses on playing lousy games, I think some traps are made because it's supposed to be the jerk developer purposely screwing over the nerd. Including a few of these tongue-in-cheek cheap tricks fits the motif. However, I also think the crappy game mindset is used to justify lackluster design choices or oversights, “That was done on purpose. Probably?” 🔍 Many threats, including enemies, are made inert or much easier if you move forward incrementally. Instead of jumping all the way forward to kill an enemy, shoot it from a distance. I'd say this was intentional if it didn't completely neuter some encounters, and simply make them a waste of time. 🔍 Unless you have previous experience with these games, I'd suggest going for Normal difficulty on the first playthrough. That way you don't have to worry about restarting a level from the very beginning if you die too many times. 🔍 Due to the way the secrets are hidden in the game, it's probably easier if you just look up a guide in advance. It'd save a significant chunk of time.Frankly, I found myself disappointed by AD. It's clear that improvements were made to how the first game looks, and the rebalanced difficulty options helps make the game more accessible and less frustrating. Also, the ascent up the Tower of Torment is a nice inclusion to give the package deal more value, but with it ending on a cliffhanger, it seems more like a way to shoehorn in a connection to a concluding sequel. Since this was supposed to be an improvement on the original games for a definitive, all in one package, I can't help but think that other changes could have been made. Looking at AD, the price is the same as if you were to buy both original games at full price. Even if it were cheaper, I'd still find $10 steep for a game that can easily be finished in an afternoon. Like games of old, the playtime relies on difficulty and players intentionally challenging themselves with repeated attempts on harder difficulty settings, as there's not much content. Seeing as how level design and boss fights could have used more work and refinement, I don't see how this is a deluxe version of the AVGN games. There's enough quality here to say that they didn't just polish a turd, but I wouldn't recommend getting it either.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a fan of the Angry Video Game Nerd (or, "AVGN", for short) since I first saw his angry game reviews on YouTube during the summer of 2006. At the time, I was going through an extremely bad breakup and was feeling incredibly depressed and hopeless. However, upon watching AVGN's review of the original TMNT on NES (his first video I ever saw), I found myself laughing at the crude, vulgar humor. While it did not make me feel completely better, it at least cheered me up a little bit. In fact, it inspired me to check out his other game reviews and, to this day, I never get tired of watching them. Without a doubt, AVGN/James Rolfe is one of my favorite YouTubers of all time and his warped sense of humor never ceases to amuse me. For the longest time, I had seen footage of "Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures" and "Angry Video Game Nerd II: ASSimilation", but put myself off from playing them, myself. I am glad I finally decided to try them out! Admittedly, I never played the original versions of these games, so I decided to simply buy this Deluxe Edition. I was NOT disappointed!For only $10, you are getting TWO games for the price of ONE, and it is well worth it! Both titles consist of classic old-school 8-bit/16-bit sprite designs, catchy music, clever level designs, and challenging (but fair) game play. In addition, some of the levels also made me feel nostalgic for the days of when I would play Super Nintendo with my siblings or regular Nintendo over at a friend's house (The Castlevania-esque stage, humorously titled, "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥", comes to mind). Although I DID die multiple times, most of the time, it did not feel cheap or unfair. In fact, there were more than enough checkpoints to help me get by. Furthermore, I loved collecting all of the secrets in each stage (including the letters to spell 'NERD' and hidden playable characters that can be unlocked) and the bosses were very fun to fight. Of course, the humorous elements worked perfectly!While playing through the first installment, I could not help but laugh several times at the crude jokes, which truly captured the spirit of the AVGN show (the "Blizzard of Balls" stage especially had me cracking up). The dialogue (spoken by AVGN/James Rolfe and the enemies/bosses) was also utterly hilarious from start to finish! Truth be told, I needed a good laugh today and after completing the 'AVGN Adventures', I can now easily say that it most definitely did the trick! Now I need to go and play the sequel, 'ASSimilation'.Containing classic sprite designs, an addicting soundtrack, nicely constructed levels, and challenging (but fair) gameplay, this is, undoubtedly, one of the best platformers I have EVER played! If you are a longtime fan of AVGN (like me), do NOT hesitate. Get this collection NOW!EDIT: Played through all of AVGN II. I thought it was just as fun as the original! I truly do hope that there will someday be a third installment.

(scene switches to an animated scene of HappySoft, rising from a fiery pit, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out Hong Kong 97) On this one occasion, they rose from the depths of Hell, EXCRETED this unholy turd onto the Earth and then descended back to where they came! It's SO rare that to this day, not a single cartridge or physical copy has shown up at all! I can't even find a PICTURE of one! So the only way I can experience this game... is the same way as the rest of the Internet.(The game's language selection shows up with a 5-second loop of "I Love Beijing Tiananmen" playing. The Nerd is surprised.)​The Nerd: Nooooooooo! No way! (chuckles) How do you like THAT soundtrack? THAT won't get annoying at all! I've heard games with 5-second music loops before, but... not with LYRICS! There's options for three different languages. Strange, considering how the game didn't travel very far, at least not until the Internet got ahold of it. Alright, I'm picking English. (reading) "We will sell your original S-NES [sic] games, 1/3 of the gross profit will be yours. We welcome games of any kind." Oh, I bet. "So please send us your floppy." (chuckles) Hee-hee, send us your floppy. "Would you like to sell our products at your store? We are looking for dealers worldwide." Enough already! How desperate could they be to sell this game? And I guess still nobody bought it because nobody can find a physical copy! Then finally the title screen appears. (laughs) Jackie Chan?! Apparently, Jackie Chan is in the game! Who I doubt gave any consent to HappySoft, or was even AWARE of it. The image is stolen from the film Wheels on Meals. The game was released, uh, made, or at least copyrighted in 1995, but set in the future... of 1997.​The Nerd: "The year 1997 has arrived. A herd of..." (stops, sees the text saying "a herd of ♥♥♥♥♥♥' ugly reds") This can't be real. No. NO! Somebody's pullin' my leg! A herd of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ugly reds?! Was "A herd of ugly reds" too weak? Did they really need the F-word to ♥♥♥♥♥♥' drive home the ♥♥♥♥♥♥' point?! This was before cursing in games was common. I remember how shocked I was when I first played Rambo on NES and saw the word "Hell." But here, they dropped the F-Bomb! THEY DID IT! A game made for the Super Famicom! (scene cuts to Mario flying past the Super Nintendo logo, with the word "♥♥♥♥" appearing on screen) It's the closest you'd ever get to a Super Nintendo game that says "♥♥♥♥"!(The 5-second loop of "I love Beijing Tiananmen" continues.)​The Nerd: And the music is still goin'. (blankly bobs his head side to side to the music before he continues reading) "A herd of ♥♥♥♥♥♥' ugly reds. Period. Are rushing from the mainland. Crimes rates skyrocketed! Hong Kong is ruined! Therefore, the Hong Kong government called Bruce Lee's relative, Chin." Bruce Lee's relative. Just HAPPENS to be as skilled as Bruce Lee. Not a brother, a son, or even a cousin. Just some unspecified relative. Doesn't make any sense. Like, if you were related to... I don't know, Michael Jordan, would that mean that you're automatically good at basketball? OK, so Bruce Lee is in the background, the guy at the podium is Chris Patten, former governor of Hong Kong, and over there is Jackie Chan. Which one is "Chin"? (he keeps reading more) "For the massacre of the reds. Chin is a killer machine." That's Chin?! (laughs at the irony) Is Jackie Chan playing Bruce Lee's relative, Chin?! Ohhhh, Chin! What a name! Could it be any more common?! (groans and resumes reading) Ohhhh, "Wipe out all 1.2 billion of the red communists!" (laughing) Stop! I can't- I can't take anymore! I haven't even seen the game yet! Ohhhh-ho-ho-ho! Ohh! (laughing) Wipe out 1.2 billion people! (becomes serious again) And if I'm not mistaken, in 1995, that would have been the ENTIRE POPULATION OF CHINA! Bruce Lee's relative is SO powerful, he's the equivalent of a thousand nukes! He's gonna murder the entire population of China by breakin' their necks! Even when Bruce Lee would take down 20 people, it took him a little bit of time. But now comes Chin! You don't ♥♥♥♥ with Chin!​The Nerd: (reading) "However, in mainland China there was a secret project in progress! A project to de- tran- tran- (laughing) to transform the DECEASED Tong Shau Ping into an ultimate-" (laughs before finishing) It's killin' me! (sighs, and becomes serious again) So apparently, for the character of Tong Shau Ping, they used an ACTUAL IMAGE of a real Chinese leader, Deng Xiaoping! Spelled differently, but pronounced very similar. When the game was made, this guy was still alive! Couldn't they have at least had the courtesy to wait for him to die before transforming him into an ultimate weapon?! This is the most EPIC, ABSURD opening to any video game I've ever seen! Nothing compares! That'd be like if I made a game called New York 2017. (Reading as images from the proposed "New York 2017" appear) "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥' demons from the planet Jupiter have arrived through the Manhattan portal. The leader of... United States calls upon Master Joe, John Wayne's half-cousin's step-son to annihilate the 2.5 octodecillion alien scum of the universe. However, on Jupiter's secret moon, a master plan is conceived to resurrect the astro-demonoid Dill Clyntin into a mecha-doomsday machine."​The Nerd: Now that I've digested all that, let's play the game. (The game begins, playing the 5-second loop of "I Love Beijing Tiananmen". Chin runs at the bottom of the screen shooting at enemies coming from the top. He gets hit and dies.) One hit, and the game's over. Why would I expect anything more? (A real surveillance image of a man lying motionless appears) NO... Oh, please. I hope that's not a real dead body. NO. There-there's no way they'd have such bad taste. That's gotta be an actor. Or... we're lookin' at some guy who died... on that date and time in 1992. Oh, this couldn't get the Nintendo endorsement? I'm so shocked that this didn't come out on Super Nintendo! Every time you die, it resets the whole game. You have to go through the whole introduction again. This is almost as tedious as Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. Great game, but ya have to wait through a long, drawn-out Game Over screen, just to get back to the title screen, select your file, and load the game all over again. THAT is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! But THIS is a game that isn't even good! Not even close! And no, the song never stops. No sound effects, either. Just that same loop. Even when the game restarts, it doesn't interrupt it. The song never needs to reboot! It's quite impressive, actually! NOTHING can stop that loop! You'll be hearing that in your dreams!​The Nerd: So let's talk about what's happening here. Obviously, it's a 2D shooter. Nothing more to say. What ya see is what you get. Chin's only method of attack is throwing projectiles, because if you're related to Bruce Lee, that means you can shoot white balls. This guy's so good, he does it all with his back turned. _childDocuments_.review: Improved level design????? More like IMPROVED BIG ♥♥♥♥♥♥' PILE OF ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!!!!!!This is the worst lie you'll hear about this game and the main reason I wanted to play these games again. YOU LIED TO ME, YOU PIECES OF ♥♥♥♥!!!Let's start from the original games: they failed at being a parody of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games' game design by doing the exact same things, like being unfair and presenting artificial challenges most of the time. _childDocuments_.review: While I'm a huge fan of AVGN, I'm not generally the type of person that gets a lot of joy out of a coat of paint that simply references something I like. For some reason there was a disconnect while playing this game, in that there were a ton of references to stuff I was familiar with, but none of it felt deep enough to actually connect with... more like pandering.To a certain degree this is probably inescapable when you're designing something based on an external IP, but it's a difficult feeling to shake that this game might not function on its own without the AVGN branding.For that reason I attempted to play these games mostly as pure platforming experiences, and to judge them based on their merits purely in that category.As a result, I feel like my ultimate verdict is to not recommend this package. The first game still holds up in a weird way, probably heavily benefiting from a secondary difficulty pass and extra modes. The second game, however, feels much more grating, and almost like it was designed to be difficult by someone or someones without a perfect understanding of what makes difficulty 'good'.An example of this is how cycle-based platforming works almost always in this game: you start at a save point and there is a set of obstacles in front of you that requires timing to navigate. The obstacles almost always start in the ON position, however, meaning that if there's one adjacent to your save point, and there almost always is, you will have to add an obligatory 3 second wait at the start of every single attempt you make from that savepoint.Because of the relative simplicity of the controls and mechanics, as well as the sometimes blatantly malicious level design, it was easy for me to compare this game to fangames of IWBTG and determine immediately there were things missing. An instant level or checkpoint button, for example, isn't in the default control mapping, so if you want to retry a checkpoint you'll have to kill yourself manually. You have the obligatory waiting periods, and the respawning is fast, but not instant, which adds up over time as well.When the platforming *isn't* cycle based it can be genuinely enjoyable in terms of the layout of the stages and enemy placement, but it also far more often devolves to mindless corridors of garbage mobs you're meant to blast or instant death auto-scrollers that suck time out with every failed attempt. The bosses are potentially interesting, but almost all of them have an incredibly small set of attacks, and there are random difficulty spikes in both games with one or two bosses having required waiting phases that make them take 4x as long as any other boss and also make them feel that much more frustrating.The third game added as a reward for beating the main two games is so short I feel it barely counts as content, and the extra boss that waits at the end is the worst in the entire game, involving long obligatory waiting periods and a vulnerability period that functions almost purely on how much beer you get via rng. It felt like there was legit nothing I could do to mitigate how random this boss's projectiles are, and when I finished the game I was much more relieved than happy or triumphant.My take is that as pure platformers, this game/pack of games has too many serious problems to be worth playing over something like Shovel Knight or Cyber Shadow or Gravity Circuit. All of those games are amazing examples of retro game design in action platformers, and the AVGN games are examples of purely regressive and clumsy design under the guise of retro. There is a difference between 'old' and 'retro', and also a difference between 'frustrating' and 'challenging', both distinctions which these games seem to struggle with.tl;dr: nyehhh, this game ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sucks! what a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of ♥♥♥♥! nyehhhhh, what were they thinking? AAAASSSSSS♥♥♥♥ this game, watch it go

The graphics are slightly upgraded with better effects in the 2nd game. The music is pretty good, especially in the 2nd game. Worth the price if your a fan of the nerd.
_childDocuments_.name: Angry Video Game Nerd I & II Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10For what you get in this compilation, it is a very solid purchase. This game combines AVGN Adventures 1 and 2 and adds on a 15 minute long final area with more levels and challenges. I would strongly recommend buying this if you question which purchase to make.AVGN Adventures 1 & 2 are 2D action plattformers with a lot of focus on tight platforming and shooting. Lots of shooting. You play as The Angry Video Game Nerd, the famous character on YouTube. These games are naturally made for fans of the character and the media he appears in and a lot of references and gags lean in towards the fanbase. If you know nothing of the character or the media, I would recommend watching the show on YouTube first and see if the humor is your thing, otherwise the game might fly over your head. The gameplay is tight, with precise controls, adjustable difficulty and stages that are between 3-5 minutes long. If you only play to complete it, this entire bundle with last you about 3 hours maximum, but there are secrets to find and achievements to get. The soundtrack is nice and the presentation really nails the AVGN-universe. I had a good time playing this and I think it was well worth the price. Note that the gameplay is nothing fenomenal or groundbreaking, it is just a solid experience that lasts a few hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Angry Video Game Nerd I & II Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Even though i didn't 100 % it, it's still a great game specially the sequel, with slight improvements and probably more references that i think people will recognize more. Levels thoughout the games can be challenging but never impossible do achieve, but i suppose that for a completionist it will be extremely frustrating.Otherwise still a collection of small pixelated platforming games that are just great for the AVGN fan and more.
_childDocuments_.name: Angry Video Game Nerd I & II Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent remaster of the first two games. The first game has been remade in the second game's engine (Unity) rather than the original (Clickteam Fusion), and it shows.The cameos from the original game have been replaced by "Future Nerds" who travel back in time to bring you weapons and upgrades from AVGN II. I feel like this change works well, and is a welcome addition. There was also a boss fight that got updated to reference a gag from another AVGN episode, though I won't spoil which one. The character sprites for the final boss have also been updated to reflect his depiction on the show.AVGN II seems to have had more changes than AVGN Adventures did. The aliens in the Area 51 stage now look different for some reason, as if it's trying to distance itself from the movie. I believe the boss sprites in that level were changed as well, but can't quite remember at the moment. The fight handled the same though. Some level names were also changed from the original AVGN II, and the story has been changed to remove the Nostalgia Critic and replace him with Fred.After you've finished both games, you unlock the Tower of Torment, a small set of new levels with a new final boss fight that's fairly amusing. This reminds me a lot of the Wily Tower from Mega Man: The Wily Wars.All in all, I feel this is a worthwhile update to the original games, with a few new surprises for those of us who have played through the original games.
_childDocuments_.name: Angry Video Game Nerd I & II Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Definitive version of the first two games in one bundle, + a third chapter that serves as a final sendoff to this game's series Certainly recommend getting so that you don't have to get the first two games, adding to the fact that the difficulty has been properly tweaked in many areas and there are LOTS of extra content goodies and QoL features that they added here.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever considered yourself a fan of the AVGN show, I confidently recommend this bundle set of both games.The pros of both games include the enjoyable music, vibrant pixel art, and their faithfulness to the show.As for the cons, I found the difficulty to be sporadic at times, and the gameplay can feel a bit repetitive when moving from level to level, especially in AVGN 1. However, overall, I believe it's a good value for a solid game, particularly when purchased during a sale (I got it for $7.49). If you appreciate the AVGN style of comedy, it's something you'll undoubtedly enjoy.Review Score: 7.5/10

Grab your Zapper, don your Power Glove, and blast your way through an absolutely fantastic gaming experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Contrary to what some say, you don't need to be a follower of the Angry Video Game Nerd on youtube. While, some of the jokes work better if you are a fan, this game is a homage to the 2D platformers that were criminally popular during the NES years. As a matter of fact, these games were so huge, that even the 16 bit era continued the development of more games in the genre. In addition, with all the nostalgia around, a lot of game developers have created "new old" games that follow the trend. This one being quite a decent one. This games work better for those who were around in those days, as you will recognize hundreds of nods to classic videogames. This "Deluxe" edition updates the graphics, soundtrack and some levels (plus a brand new unlockable game once you complete the first two) However, the most important update is playability. Some levels were nearly impossible in the older versions. Here, you have more balanced chances and even a difficulty setting. It's an excellent compilation. Make sure it's on your collection no matter how many ♥♥♥♥♥ you give about this heavily criticized youtuber.

I got through both remakes and the new tower added to the end. It's all just the perfect amount of hard to frustrate you sometimes, but never enough to want to give up. I honestly expected to give this game no more than an hour, but so much care was put into pulling pretty much ONLY from the AVGN "universe". Every other screen, if there wasnt some new gross enemy, there was a quick hilarious reference to something the nerd has yelled about before. Solid game, great comical pacing, awesome challenges.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an adrenaline-pumping romp through not just the world of the AVGN, but of Cinemassacre as a whole. For those who'd like a pleasant trip down nostalgia lane, this game offers easier difficulties where you can experience everything it has to offer without needing to be a hardcore gamer. _childDocuments_.review: When I was a kid playing SNES I used to get so pissed with games that I threw my controllers at the wall.  I've never done it since but this game got me REALLY close to doing it again...That's not because it's a bad game but because it's a retro platformer made by people who clearly know what makes platformers great (and ♥♥♥♥♥♥).  It's everything that an old school platformer should be - you need quick thinking and quick reactions to beat the levels and you get a sense of achievement every time you nail a particularly tricky section.If you're a AVGN Nerd then the whole game is full of references to the show.  Some are subtle and some are blatant but you'll definitely get a kick out of them.  I can't remember the last time I laughed at a plaformer but when I saw Fred ♥♥♥♥♥ say "you were expecting maybe the Addams Family?" I LOLed at the screen.That's not to say the game is perfect.  There are some sections where I genuinly beleive that the game is more to do with luck than skill from the player. You just have to take a few hits and hope you have enough life left to get through. But then again sometimes you think the devs made a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ decision and it turns out it was quite intentional.  An annoying autoscrolling level that is reference by the boss at the end of the stage about how annoying it is springs to mind.  Part of me thinks that this is maybe AVGN gettting revenge for being forced to play ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games for the last 10 years.But for anyone who grew up playing platformers like this it's an amazing throwback.  Big ass sprites, obnoxious music, garish colours, seizure inducing background animation, insane bosses... and the urge to throw your controller at the wall!9/10 Rotten Skunk ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

name: The Making of Karateka
detailed_description: Prince of Persia creator Jordan Mechner was a college student when he created one of the biggest-selling games of 1984: Karateka. Now, in a new interactive documentary from Digital Eclipse, the story of how a teenager with an Apple II created one of the most groundbreaking, influential games of all time. THE ORIGIN STORY OF A LEGENDARY GAME CREATOR Discover how Karateka was made through an exhaustive archive of design documents, playable prototypes, and all-new video features. Like walking through a museum, you can explore the interactive timelines at your own pace. PLAY THE ACCLAIMED ORIGINALS Enjoy pixel-perfect versions of the original Karateka games and a variety of never-before-seen early prototypes, with rich quality-of-life features like save anywhere, rewind, chapter select, and director's commentary. TWO REMASTERED GAMES Karateka Remastered is an all-new version of the original game featuring cutting-room-floor content, commentary, achievements, and more. Deathbounce: Rebounded is a fast and frantic twin-stick shooter based on Jordan's unpublished prototype. A GROUNDBREAKING MASTERPIECE Discover how Karateka became one of the first games to include cinematic scenes, a moving original soundtrack, rotoscoped animation, and a Hollywood-style love story, influencing the decades of games that followed. THE GOLD MASTER SERIES New from Digital Eclipse (Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection, Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration), the Gold Master Series presents iconic games in an innovative 'interactive documentary' format, putting the shared history of games and their creators into one comprehensive package.

_childDocuments_.review: I've always thought more can be done with games as a medium, and this documentary game really highlights how much more can be done with some outside the box thinking. The execution of preserving the original game, telling its story, and making it comfortably playable on modern devices, with every single version they could find, is amazing. A game from almost 40 years ago, comfortable, and fun to this day, with the love and care that it (any many other games) deserve.This is a shining light of what game preservation needs to be going forward.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up: A really amazing documentary in interactive and playable format, containing multiple (prototype and final, with ports of Karateka as well) versions of Asteroids, Deathbounce, Karateka. The last two games also have reimagined versions, with Deathbounce being a real glowup. Thumbs sideways: One issue is that Karateka really is not a very fun game: a series of mirror matches with AI opponents and confusing hitboxes and hurtboxes, and you do have to learn how to cope with this in order to get anywhere.First conclusion: Thumbs up for the package, moreso than for the outdated game design... but this is museum piece, after all.Karateka Remastered thoughts: it's a much better version, EXCEPT for the panther fight. This gameplay is horribly unforgiving in terms of timing, taking the gate timing puzzle and just making it feel far worse to engage with successfully. HOW TO WIN - look up "The Making of Karateka Remastered Playthrough" on YT for the answer, and skip to 11:50.However, it's then redeemed somewhat by the improved bird fight in Level 3. The animation means that you can react with a kick correctly every time.The solution would simply be some kind of clue as to how to beat the panther, and fairer timing on getting through the gate without dying. I swear it doesn't work the same as the level 2 gate puzzle.Final conclusion: As a celebration of gaming, as a museum piece, as interactive history - amazing. As a series of fun games to play, not without issues. This is shown by how few people have the achievements for finishing the Karateka prototype / Apple II game / ports.Other thoughts: The initial Asteroids ripoff is considerably more fun to play than Deathbounce, and I can see why Deathbounce didn't lead to a published game. Just goes to show how it's not easy to design a 'simple' game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting and well-made interactive documentary about one of the most important titles of videogames' history, and the people who contributed to its creation and success, with also interviews with a few developers who were inspired and influenced by Mechner's masterpiece. There are also several games to play, including a few prototypes and complete versions, and two modern revisions of Karateka and Deathbounce, one of the very first games Mechner worked on before Karateka, but that was never published.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played Karateka as I was about 4 years too young for that at the time. But Prince of Persia sprung into my life on both my Amiga and on the PC's at my school. And I recall making animations in Deluxe Paint that mimicked what Mechner did in PoP. I loved that game.The distinct "flat" style was a particular thing I loved about it. And I also recall being incredibly disappointed with PoP2 which had a very odd and much more cartoonish style. I didn't like that game at all.But I've since learned of Karateka and appreciate what it did for computer games. And this interactive telling of the story is a perfect way to learn about the story behind it.I've seen the rotoscoping material many times online. But this pulls it all together.The menu system in the experience takes some getting used to. There's some odd horizontal vs vertical vs "click enter" stuff going on with the different selections. So I had to backtrack after a while as only then did I realize I could press enter to view more images under the same selection. But it's no biggie.Enjoyed it!

_childDocuments_.review: Getting this out of the way first: the experience was not "structured" the way I thought it would be. I'll get more into this later but be aware that there is a fair amount of work on the player to "assemble" the experience here.I'm really enjoying what this groundbreaking release is: a combination of  a gaming documentary with actual gameplay to help create a whole new experience. This is a must-try for any retro game enthusiast whether you've heard of Karateka or not. I really, really hope to see more of these and a Nintendo or Sega one would be incredible.My only criticism is this felt a little half-baked/unpolished and could have benefited from a more "guided" experience - less input from the player in order to advance the content. They did a wonderful job with the documentary footage and the structure of the documentary in general (having you play the prototypes first and then watching the story behind them) but I hated getting booted back to the UI where I needed to navigate to the next section. It totally took me out of the experience and it made it diffcult to enjoy the experience with other people who wanted to watch too.I was going into this figuring the experience went like this:Video footage > player taken directly into a game while commentary continued > once player was ready to move on they'd press a button > right back into video footage > repeat till endInstead it was like:Navigate slightly confusing UI to start the experience > first video ends....booted back to UI > manually cycle through things but I wanted to get back to the movie > finally found the selection for back to the movie > back to the UI > now I'm playing a prototype thats awesome > ok where is the next part of the movie I dont want to look at photos just put them in the movie! > back to the movie finally > another game to play, cool > ugh more non-movie/non-game stuffI really just wanted them to take me through the movie and games without needing to return me to the navigation UI. This would've worked so much better as a Netflix "experience" like Bandersnatch.

_childDocuments_.review: I got to interview Karateka creator Jordan Mechner about this project for , and I'll slap a telling quote here:---"Karateka was really the culmination of a six-year timeframe," Mechner says. "From getting my first Apple II in 1978 as a freshman in high school, I made games, and each time I kind of hoped that it would get published. All of those 'almosts,' each raised the bar a little bit. All that time, the industry was evolving very fast as I was trying to evolve as a game developer. So Karateka really brought together everything I’d learned on the previous attempts—and it makes the most sense in the context of those earlier games."When pressed on this point, Mechner offers a rare tinge of regret: “Especially when I was a young developer, I would have loved to have an exhibit like [Making of Karateka] about any game I had played and liked! At age 16, 17, I was in the dark. Not just about the technical aspects, but also the human side of programming. How does it work? What’s your relationship like as an author with the publisher, with players, with other people? To see somebody else go through that, all the emotional ups and downs. The excitement, the disappointment, the blind alleys: I love that.”---As far as a "review," Making of Karateka is a fantastic opening salvo from the Gold Master Series, and I hope it's indicative of much more to come. If you've seen Atari 50, the setup is similar, only instead of telling the story of an entire company, this collection uses old documentation, recent interviews, *and* freshly unearthed prototypes of prior games to focus its lens on a single masterwork game, Karateka. The approach does a great job showing how Jordan Mechner started as a teenager making Asteroids clones, only to mature rapidly to make a game unlike anything else of its time. Context matters when approaching older games, and that's why I love Digital Eclipse's approach here.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: Here you will find a list of problems about Digital Eclipse: Interactive documentary (same interface as the Atari 50) that brings a lot of information about the development of Karateka and other games by Jordan Mechner (creator of Karateka and Prince of Persia).List of "14" games:Karateka - Apple IIKarateka C64Karateka - Atari 8-bitKarateka RemasteredDeathbounce: ReboundedDeathbounce First PrototypeDeathbounce "Colored Balls" PrototypeDeathbounce "Little Man" PrototypeDeathbounce "Space Train" PrototypeKarateka Jordan's PrototypeKarateka Brøderbund Prototype 1Karateka Brøderbund Prototype 2Asteroid BlasterStar BlasterPositive points:Good emulation;Extras that are interesting to watch.Negative points: Karateka had several versions, both for computers from the 80s and video games, but it only includes the c64, Apple 2 and Atari 800 versions, because the devs say that these are the best versions. As someone who thinks the preservation of games is important, they could have included all versions of the game, and I still think there are several versions of Karateka that are not present in the collection, but it is better than the c64 version. Missing versions: Atari 7800, NES, MSX, NEC PC 9801, ZX Spectrum, Atari ST, IBM PC/DOS, Amstrad CPC, Game Boy. Ask anyone who bought the game if they wanted more versions (even if they weren't as good as the originals).BUGS: It happened a few times that I played Karateka c64 or Karateka Remastered, and the space image appeared when I ctrl-clicked.Once it happened that I couldn't play the c64 version, and I was forced to leave and enter the game.I played on the keyboard and could identify these bugs, but there are also controller bugs that some users are reporting in the community tab.Conclusion: I particularly enjoyed the collection, both the interactive documentary and the included games. It's worth the price, but I was very disappointed that not every game was included (and Digital Eclipse could have done that).6,5 (I wish there was a neutral review option.)The low score was because Digital Eclipse has a history of leaving several bugs and not correcting them, as is the case with SNK 40th ANNIVERSARY COLLECTION and Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: The Making of Karateka is a master class in game preservation and is essentially a digital museum. It's amazing that Jordan Mechner held on to all of this material for 40 years and that we get to glimpse into how the games industry operated in it's infancy thanks to his efforts to preserve all of this material. Digital Eclipse did an amazing job with presentation from the interface down to the sound design. It feels great being able to flip through concept art, listen to Kirk Hamilton talk about the importance of Francis Mechner's influence on game composition, examine 3D mockups of game disks and box art, and play various iterations of both Deathbounce and Karateka. A wonderful and masterful work of video game preservation by Digital Eclipse and Jordan Mechner.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: This is amazing. It manages to squeeze a gripping narrative from the act of parsing old docs, it’s really good in telling its story, it lets you play with prototypes and put your hands on stuff that is usually not accessible, it contains well emulated classics and also adds two very good modern remakes, that let you play in a more welcoming way games from forty years ago. It’s full of great ideas and unexpected ways of deconstructing an old game. I hope they will make dozens of these, if only because it seems like it could be a very versatile approach, with very different ways of doing a similar thing.

_childDocuments_.review: A fascinating in-depth look at the making of a video game classic.I’ve known about Karateka for decades but never had the chance to play it.  As a young teen in the 1980s, I would watch with fascination as the demo ran at my local computer shop until I saved up enough money to buy my own copy for the Commodore 64, but, unfortunately, the third party disk drive my dad had bought was apparently only 99.99% compatible with Commodore’s own 1541 disk drive, and it seems Karateka was the only disc it wasn’t compatible with, and so, sadly, I had to return it for a refund.And now, four decades later with “The Making of Karateka”, I finally have the opportunity to not only play this piece of video game history, but to also learn about the history behind the history.  Developer Digital Eclipse has created one of the best documentary packages I’ve ever seen, with video interviews and archival footage, photographs, original concept art, design documents, correspondence, and, of course, the multiple versions of the games themselves, all combined into an interactive timeline that takes you on a journey from designer Jordan Mechner’s childhood and early fascination with computers, through several failed video game projects, to the making of the titular game, and, finally, a look at the genesis of the never developed sequel which eventually morphed into Prince of Persia (“But that's a story for another time…”).Along the way, you'll find a number of playable games that include Mechner’s earliest effort for the Apple II called Asteroid Blaster, a pixel perfect clone of Atari’s Asteroids, which turned out to be a little  perfect since the publisher who bought it was immediately slapped with a cease and desist from Atari!  Next is Mechner’s followup project, the absurdly titled Death Bounce which went through a number of iterations but was never finished to publisher Broderbund’s satisfaction, and as you play the various prototypes and multiple attempts at a finished game, you can’t help but agree with their decision.  Finally, there’s Karateka which is presented through several prototypes showcasing its evolving development, and three versions of the finished game for the Apple II, Commodore 64, and Atari 800 computers.  While Karateka was ported to many other systems, Digital Eclipse decided to focus on only the versions that Mechner was directly involved with.  The emulation here is perfect, and the games all look and play exactly like they did on original hardware.  To enhance the authenticity, the screen is bordered by the outlines of a bulky monitor and rendered with simulated scanlines and a slight barrel distortion to mimic the CRT displays of old, but this can be disabled in the settings if you find it objectionable.  There are also options to switch from the original one- and two-button control schemes to a six-button variation that is a bit easier to play, and you can lock the framerate for consistent performance, but I personally prefer to leave those settings off to enjoy these games as they originally were.As if that wasn’t enough, developer Digital Eclipse went above and beyond, creating two new games, a remaster of both Death Bounce and Karateka, to round out this collection.  Each remaster retains the old school charm of the originals with high fidelity pixel art, but they play with the speed and fluidity of a modern game.  Now Death Bounce might sound like an odd inclusion given Broderbund’s dissatisfaction with Mechner’s attempts to bring it to completion, but with this remaster, you can see that there was actually a really good idea there for a fun game even if Mechner was unable to realize it at the time, due, perhaps, to his inexperience and the limited hardware of the Apple II.  As for the Karateka remaster, it simply plays like a better looking, more fluid version of the original, and while it’s still great fun and has added value with developer commentary, a time trial mode, and achievements, I prefer the look and feel of the originals.  There's just something about those chunky sprites that I find endearing.It took me about five hours to get through this interactive documentary, and I enjoyed every moment of it learning a lot of things I didn't know before, such as a letter from Broderbund to Mechner that mentioned a special fast loader on the Commodore 64 disc that was likely the culprit that stopped me from playing the game all those decades ago!  And the games themselves naturally have tremendous replay value which makes “The Making of Karateka” well worth the asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: A really well-crafted piece of interactive media, that sets a very high bar for future video game "making of" projects. _childDocuments_.review: As a huge Jordan Mechnerd, this game/documentary is incredible.
