_childDocuments_.review: My review video: This is the first entry in Digital Eclipse's new Gold Master Series, where they take a single game or series and do a deep dive on it, working in partnership with its creator. It's less a game and more an interactive documentary, with a timeline including video interviews, historical clips, high-res scans of art and development assets, among other things that detail not only how the game was made, but how it influenced the industry today. It's presented in a slick interface that's easy to navigate. You also have access to various different versions of Karateka, including prototypes of both this and some of Jordan Mechner's other earlier games, plus modern remakes of Karateka and Deathbounce made by Digital Eclipse that look and play great, complete with in-game goals and developer commentary.To most younger players, Karateka isn't a name that necessarily means anything, but it is formative and critical to many of the mechanics and trends that came in gaming after it, even to this day. Packages like this aren't for everyone and Digital Eclipse knows this, but if you have an interest in gaming and industry history, this is a great and importantly, interactive way to learn some cool things about a game that's heavily contributed to games that we know today. Even as someone who knew a lot of the history of this beforehand, I still very much enjoyed myself and highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: A remarkable achievement, and a must-play for anyone interested in game history or in the possibilities of interactive documentaries, for which this (hopefully) represents the new standard. To be fair, I don't imagine many other subjects would offer such a depth of primary sources to work from (multiple playable prototypes of a 40 year-old unpublished game? Really?). But here's hoping!Random stuff I learned:
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: If you are at all interested in early video game history or have enjoyed Karateka at some point, I highly recommend picking this up. It's a very rich multimedia documentary of sorts with most playable versions of Karateka as well as a variety of other early games Jordan Mechner developed during that time. It also contains a brand new Karateka and Deathbounce remaster by Digital Eclipse that is worth the price alone. Just a fantastic experience all around.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: The Making of Karateka is a must-have for any fan of classic video games and anyone interested in the medium as an art form. This interactive documentary tells the story of the creation of one of the most influential games of all time, from its humble beginnings as a college project to its current cult status (and I was there when it was originally released).The documentary is packed with fascinating details, including never-before-seen concept art, interviews with the original developers, super-interesting official documents between Jordan and the publisher, and even playable prototypes of various games. It's a fascinating look at the creative process as a whole.They also added Deathbounce: Rebounded, a new game inspired by the original Deathbounce prototype. It's amazing what they've done to honor the original concept.Digital Eclipse's work exceeds all expectations that a retro game fan could have. The documentary is well done and informative, the interviews with the original developers are fascinating, and the playable prototypes are a great bonus. I did not expect it to be this good, this is something that should be preserved in a museum, this is the well documented history of the pioneers who contributed to create this multi-billion dollar industry. Thank you, Digital Eclipse.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: After this game and the equally excellent Atari50, Digital Ellipse has become the gold standard for presenting older games in their proper historical context, with the necessary background information that helps people understand why these games were so important to video game history.The information is provided via an interactive timeline that's intuitive to use and easy to follow and understand. Digital Eclipse has organized everything here in a way that naturally tells a story and properly puts the context needed around Karateka to understand its impact. I wasn't familiar with the game before playing this, and now I *get* it. The older, mostly unmodified games play ... pretty similarly to how you'd expect. Your mileage will vary on those, but it's at least nice to play through the stuff you've been reading/watching about. Having modern touches such as rewind is also nice. The new remastered games are excellent, and play as well as anything you'd buy on the market today. If you're at all interested in video game history and how this medium came to be what it is today, feel you owe it to yourself to play this game. Karateka may not ultimately be the most important game in the world, but packages like The Making of Karateka are a crucial way to bring back the context and background needed to understand how we got from Karateka to the games of today. Really hope this is the start of a long-running series by Digital Eclipse, but even if it's not, this is well worth a look.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: For anyone who played this game back in the day then I HIGHLY recommend this, also for those interested in game history. For anyone younger or haven't experienced older games such as Karateka then I would say pass on it. It will just feel archaic to you. Broght back so many memories for me and finally explained to me why that damn bird always killed me. (Apparently it's insta-kill if you had a pirated copy, which my parents had gotten this copy from a neighbor on our Commodore 64. Hope no-one comes and arrests them now 40 years later.)
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: The Making of Karateka is the flagship entry of Digital Eclipse's new Gold Masters Series, a line of interactive documentaries using the format of their previous release Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration and paring it down for smaller, more specific stories. As the title indicates, this one covers the development of Karateka, a mid-1980s action game that incorporated cinematic elements. It dives into the background of developer Jordan Mechner, including his previous releases and a canceled prototype for a commercial game, the process of porting the game to other platforms, and even how it led into his next game, Prince of Persia. It does so with large library of documentary featurettes, design documents, business letters, and marketing materials, and it even has a interactive demonstration of the game's animation process. Of course, it also includes multiple versions of Karateka itself, including a number of prototypes, multiple ports, and even a new remaster that tightens up the experience, as well as prototypes for the aforementioned canceled title Deathbounce. And all of this is arranged in a compelling chronology that's easy to follow and navigate.Karateka gets little in the way of fanfare nowadays, but The Making of Karateka makes a strong case for the game's place in the canon of video game history, as well as a strong case for future Gold Masters Series releases.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorites as a young teen and now I know the story behind it! Hot from the heels of Atari 50, Digital Eclipse has done it again with The Making of Karateka. Until now, I only played the Atari 8-Bit version - it was wonderful expierencing the Apple II & Commodore 64 versions as well as the prototypes. Remastered versions of pre-Karateka game, Deathbounce and of course, the remasterd Karateka our my faves and I can't stop playing them. The interviews and archival footage and photos make this package a must for retro fans.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent interactive documentary and a thorough preservation of a landmark title. Tons of fascinating photos, concept art, interviews and archive footage, what I like most are the old prototypes Jordan Mechner coded, now made available to play, plus a really cool remaster of Deathbounce, with modern twin stick shooter controls. And of course the crown jewel of the whole set, a terrific remaster of Karateka, with a lovely look, great attention and love spent on it, and it plays better than ever. I am excited to see what Digital Eclipse can do next with this Gold Master series, I would absolutely love a similarly comprehensive package for Prince of Persia 1&2.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: This is a medium-pushing work, and I'd call it a new standard were it not for the fact that Karateka is one of the most well-documented classic games, so it'd be unreasonable to expect this much of all video game documentaries. That said, this new documentary format is one I can get behind fully. The ability to explore all the scans and games at my own pace rather than be told about it in a linear movie format is something I've never experienced with a documentary before, and I want more of it. I highly anticipate the next game this studio covers, whatever that may be.My only real criticism would be that it relies heavily on screenshots for representing the ports of Karateka that are not included, which made me want to play them and mildly disappointed that I couldn't do so within this collection. The versions that are included are very solid though with great emulation and unexpectedly good screen options.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: Digital Eclipse’s Making of Karateka is a fantastic interactive documentary giving a Criterion Collection quality exploration of a game as well as persevering it to allow people to play it. The collection focuses on Jordan Mechner’s early years in game dev up until the release of Karateka and its ports. The collection is structured in chapters chronologically with each chapter being comprised of timelines that showcase a smorgasbord of information dealing with Mechner’s early works and Karateka. This information includes content such as concept art, magazine articles, interactive viewers that allow you to see how the animation process of Karateka was designed, and present day interviews with people like Mechner, some of the old Broderbund crew who worked on Karateka, and game devs inspired by the game such as Tom Hall and John Tobias. The way this all is structured is really engaging. The interviews dealing with Mechner’s early years are especially charming as he and his dad reminisce how the whole family inspired and worked to help Jordan make Karateka like how his dad dressed up in a karate gi and essentially did the motion capture for the Karateka MC and how he composed the whole soundtrack. Making of Karateka also does a splendid job preserving not only Karateka and two of its most popular ports, but it also has playable prototype builds. It also has previously unreleased games Mechner made before Karateka complete with earlier design builds as well, one of them being Death Bounce, an Asteroids inspired space shooter. There’s just so much clear love and care put in this collection’s creation and it’s truly splendid to see, especially because video game history and preservation isn’t considered as a serious undertaking compared to older artistic mediums such as literature and film. Video games, being the youngest of the mediums, was born in the age of mass corporatization where being a product that sells is considered to be far more important than being of piece of artistic media that should be celebrated. Films managed to emerge right before rampant commercialization happened so they were still able to be considered art that needed to be preserved, but games haven’t been as lucky and tend to just be considered expendable products, especially by major publishers. It’s just so heartening to see something like this exist. I do have one problem when it comes to this whole package though, I think Karateka is just a straight up bad game. Karateka may have been a technical marvel at the time, as the documentary materials extensively shows, but it has completely aged like milk and is just not a good game to actually play anymore, especially in the present when a vast plethora of games have surpassed it in all regards. It’s slow, clunky, and repetitive, combat is just mainly spamming kick and moving and back forth, the hitbox on the eagle is an absolute pain in the ass, and running is super awkward and can lead to enemies’ one-shotting you if you don’t get into combat stance fast enough. There’s no lives or continues so you just gotta slog through all those boring fights and unskippable cutscenes all over again. I’m admittedly not a big fan of 80’s games, but I can pick up games like Super Mario Bros., Tetris, or Galaga and have fun with them and respect their quality, plus they’re still quite accessible. Karateka is just miserable, to the point I’m surprised people even liked it at the time. Like it’s kinda sad to me the most fun I had with Jordan Mechner’s older games in this collection was his blatant ripoff of Asteroids he made in high school. Similar to my thoughts on Night Dive’s remaster of Rise of the Triad this year, I feel Digital Eclipse gave a gold star treatment polishing to a turd, an influential one, but a turd nonetheless. Digital Eclipse also did their own remasters of Karateka and Death Bounce, they’re more playable but they still don’t really salvage the games at all to me. The Karateka remaster does add the option of giving yourselves extra lives and it does play a little better but it adds the leopard that got the cut from the original game and that section is just awful. The Death Bounce remaster is okay, though I feel the Rover is just kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, though arcade space shooters ain’t really my forte.Overall Making of Karateka is a wonderful documentary and preservation package for a game that has unfortunately not stood the test of time at all. Regardless if you have any interest in video game history I whole-heartedly recommend it. Definitely looking forward to Digital Eclipse possibly making this an entire series and cover games that were influential and actually good, like Doom or Monkey Island. Man, I want a Doom one so bad…
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent, excellent implementation of this classic game -- get every variation, every prototype, every scrap of every piece of documentation they could find along with great interviews. And heck, even the modernized Deathbounce is kind of worth the price of admission alone!It feels like the next step would be to do Prince of Persia, but with Digital Eclipse being purchased outright by Atari and PoP being a UbiSoft rights hell thing, I have my doubts.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: This is magnificent from start to finish.The ethos of the Gold Master Series complements the interdisciplinary design innovations that defined Karateka, which is likely the primary reason the making of this game is the showcase debut for this series.  Just as the game uses tropes from action/adventure stories, cinema generally, and martial arts movies in particular, the series uses existing formats and techniques--video interviews, design specs, process docs--with elements that are singular to gaming--interactivity, playable prototypes and remasters, analyses of game bugs and how bugs can turn into features and vice versa--to elevate what could have been a stale hagiographic making-of yarn into something genuinely intriguing and engaging that forefronts gaming's best, most definitive attributes.There are some things I didn't like, and would appreciate seeing improved as this series progresses.  First, there were a lot of personal, hand-written documents, which is great!  I think that you can't get a fuller, better source of the who, how, and why of a game than from the pen of the creator, but only if the hand-written material is clearly legible.  I understand the importance and the authenticity driving the use of these sources, and I don't suggest eliminating them; I recommend complementing them with a type-written transcription, so that you get the original documents in concert with text that is clearly legible.  The game does something similar to this already; multiple pages are quoted directly from Mechner's journals during the time he spent conceptualizing and realizing Karateka, and these are all typed transcriptions, not hand-written.  In cases where the handwriting quality of the author interferes with audience understanding--as here, for me--I'd like to see typed transcription complementing all of the handwritten sources, not just some isolated cases.The biggest criticism I have of this game specifically (and what I'd like most to see addressed as the series progresses), is that the making of Karateka wasn't acculturated enough, meaning that, beyond three game makers who were clearly enamored with and influenced by Karateka, attesting as they did in their interviews, what was the game's larger influence on gaming culture and pop culture, and how did contemporaneous culture influence the game as it was being made?  This is especially pertinent in Karateka's case, where explicit racism was used as a marketing tactic--the hero looks like Don Johnson just walked off the set of Miami Vice and into Medieval Japan, and the villain's primarily villainous quality is that he's Japanese, according to some character concept documents--to promote the game, echoing the methods and strategies of sibling media from that era like the Karate Kid.  The Digital Eclipse-developed remaster included in this game addresses this by making the player character and Mariko Japanese, although they saddle the PC with a truly embarrassing haircut as an apparent homage to the white savior of the original game.  A distillation of what I'd like to see in future titles in this series is this:  How did this game fit within the culture of the time it was made, and how did pop culture respond to the existence of this game?Overall, this is an excellent game, and an awesome exemplification of the techniques and artistry that make games great, as well as spotlighting the interesting and influential people who make those games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: I was a lucky little kid. I got to play all kinds of great computer games on my granddad's IBM compatible 286 and my mom's Commodore VIC-20, Commodore 64 and Atari 2600. Unfortunately for me, the only place I got to play Karateka was on DOS in EGA mode (not one of the 3 best versions). It still struck me as something amazing and has been in my brain ever since.The Making of Karateka is a fantastic product, and I loved hearing the story of Jordan and his father Francis. Everyone associated Jordan Mechner with Prince of Persia, but this truly is where it his career picked up steam. If you're at all interested in the history of video games, do yourself a favor and pick up a copy of this and savor every minute... and go get Atari 50 while you're at it haha
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic museum piece about a foundational game and what went into its creation  - including design documents, prototypes, and interviews with the creator and publisher.  A unique package that helped me understand why a game that is almost as old as I am captured the hearts and imagination of so many game developers, and why it deserves a place in history.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: As someone curious about game design and history, I feasted with this, even though I'd never played Karateka before and was only faintly aware of its existence. The whole "interactive documentary" format is a slam-dunk of an idea, and I'm already looking forward to checking out Atari 50 and digging into the next entries in the Gold Master Series entries as they come out!

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★★Karateka, a classic that captivated a generation, has been masterfully reborn in its Steam version, 'Making of Karateka.' This game not only pays homage to the original but elevates it to new heights with its intricate storytelling and innovative gameplay mechanics.From the opening scene, you're drawn into a beautifully crafted world that blends nostalgia with cutting-edge graphics. The developers have done a phenomenal job of preserving the essence of the original while infusing it with modern elements that resonate with today’s gaming community.The combat system is a standout feature, striking a perfect balance between challenging and rewarding. It maintains the original's rhythm-based mechanics but enhances them with a variety of new moves and strategies, keeping the gameplay fresh and engaging.The narrative aspect of 'Making of Karateka' is another area where the game truly shines. The story is rich and immersive, with well-developed characters and a compelling plot that keeps you hooked from start to finish.The attention to detail in this game is remarkable. From the authentic sound effects to the culturally rich landscapes, every aspect has been crafted with care and respect for the source material. It’s evident that the developers are not only skilled but also passionate about this project.In conclusion, 'Making of Karateka' on Steam is a triumphant revival of a beloved classic. It offers a seamless blend of old and new, making it a must-play for both fans of the original and newcomers to the franchise. It’s a testament to how classic games can be reinvented for the modern era while respecting their roots. An absolute masterpiece and a jewel in the crown of Steam's game library
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed learning the history of a game I never even played before. I didn´t know how many things Karateka did first and how important it really was for Video Games as a whole. I also love that there are builds for games Jordan did before Karateka included in here. The Beta builds of Karateka itself a re a really nice touch too of course. I had a lot of fun with the several builds of Deathbounce and I think that Deathbounce: Rebounded really could, and should be, a available as a  stand-alone release for a few bucks.What I do find puzzling, and a bit disappointing really, is the fact that there are "only" 3 historical retail versions here. You get the Apple II, Commodore 64 and Atari 8-Bit versions in here. All other versions are either just mentioned, or at best showcased with a few screenshots. It kinda feels a bit incomplete by not having those other historical ports in here.Still very recommended to anyone interested in Video Game History.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first interactive documentary I've experienced, and it is amazing!The amount of effort Digital Eclipse put into documenting the making of the game, allowing us to play the classic games made by Jordan Mechner, and even allowing us to play the remakes of the original games was worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: (for whatever reason, my steam deck didn't sync up all of my playtime, which is higher than listed)As someone who loved Atari 50, I had to pick this up, despite not knowing anything about this game other than it being a precursor to the massive hit Prince of Persia, a franchise that continues on and off to this day. A great thing about Atari 50, which this continues, is that largely if I played Karateka in a vacuum I'd shrug and say "ok well that's kind of interesting for the time, so what?" This thoroughly makes you care about the game, explain why its so important, how it developed (including prototypes and a ditched previous game he was working on), and beyond that its just a nice sweet documentary about a very supportive dad allowing his son to follow his muse even though it was just murdering him academically. If you have any interest in the history of influential videogames I can highly recommend this and I'm excited to see what else will get this treatment in the future. _childDocuments_.review: The faithful recreation of Karateka provided nostalgia as I replayed it just as it was originally on the Apple II. The collection includes several other versions, and prototypes as well. The presentation of the game, and the history around its creation was an excellent museumesque experience, and an wonderful example of video game preservation.Not only is Karateka included but also a few other games and protypes that Mechner created while a student at Yale. The developers of this title remade both Karakeka, and Deathbounce as with improved graphics, and some changes in design while preserving the identity of the originals.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: Even leading up to its release, I wasn’t sure what exactly The Making of Karateka would turn out to be. A collection of games? A documentary with interviews? Some remasters or reinterpretations of the original titles? All of it, turns out. And it’s a fascinating compilation that, in a way, was possible due to how impactful and important Karateka was and because Jordan Mechner, its creator, detailed his experiences in a diary that was published as a book years ago.While I can’t say that Karateka had a huge impact on me directly, after all it was released before I was born, I still vividly remember encountering it in my childhood and being fascinated by it. I’m not sure if I had already experienced Prince of Persia by that point or not, a game that had a far greater influence on how I saw games, I still liked elegant simplicity of its design in both gameplay and storytelling. I also remembered how incredibly rude several traps and enemies were, which was unfortunately reflective of the game design school of the time. Though, I’ll still give Karateka that it, at least, had not too many cheap ways of killing you that you could not predict. Those that were there were very cruel, however.So it was very curious to see how exactly this game came to be and the experience of doing it through The Making of Karateka felt very novel. You get your interviews and videos, as one would expect from a documentary, and those are full of interesting facts and details. But also you get scans of documents, photographs and physical objects that you can rotate and read. And on top of that, and most interestingly, you get faithful recreations of different versions of two games. An unreleased title Deathbounce, that was developed right before switching to Karateka, and the main game itself. And by different versions I mean several prototype versions and games that were never released before, the retail versions of Karateka on Apple II, Commodore 64 and Atari 8-bit and new remastered versions created specifically for this collections. You can just play the games from the game library, but the intended experience is going through the timeline of events that mix all of these mediums together into one coherent journey.Of course, the question is – how fun is it to play Karateka today in any of the available versions? Well… That’s a bit of a tough one. I would say – yes. Even if only for historic value. While the game might feel slow and even sluggish, even in the Remastered version, and some occasional traps are genuinely unfun, there’s still a lot of wonderful craft behind the title. And some of the ideas feel ingenious. The two stances, that would become even more important in Prince of Persia, have since defined entire genres, where you have different sets of controls depending on you’re attacking or exploring. The way your and enemy health regenerates during battle and between battles strikes a really curious balance between being patient but also being aggressive. Some of the cinematic techniques and general framing of the shots in the game still look fantastic. And while I question the desire to keep some of the jank of the original games and even add new one by restoring originally not implemented ideas, I also appreciate how original versions of the game allow some quality of life features and a rewind feature while the Remastered version allows you to have more than one life.It looks like Digital Eclipse is marketing this as a start of a collection of interactive documentaries and I can’t wait to see what other games will get a similar treatment. But starting with Karateka seemed like a very smart choice and I recommend checking The Making of Karateka to people who grew up playing this game at some point in their life and those, who love videogames but have never heard about this classic gem before.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: I played Karateka on Apple II and C64 in the mid 80's and this is some welcome nostalgia 40 years later!  Really well produced collection and brings back a lot of fond memories.  Enjoying the remaster which is very true to the original.  The documentary on Mechner's history and the making of Karateka is top notch and really shows how groundbreaking it was.  I hope Digital Eclipse produces more of these collections.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: The new standard in game preservation. Similar to Digital Eclipses's other interactive documentary Atari 50 this allows you to explore videos, documents and historical information relevant to development on a Timeline.By focusing on one breakthrough game they can dig really deep into every aspect of production. The playable versions of Jordan Mechner's pre-Karateka prototypes, and many versions of Karateka are presented in the appropriate context to appreciate them. Top-notch emulation and modernized remakes.Absolutely worth it if you have any interest in game development. Doesn't really matter if you have even heard of Karateka before. Would be a real shame if we don't get more of this Gold Master Series.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review:
Prince of Persia creator Jordan Mechner was a college student when he created one of the biggest-selling games of 1984: Karateka. Now, in a new interactive documentary from Digital Eclipse, the story of how a teenager with an Apple II created one of the most groundbreaking, influential games of all time.

THE ORIGIN STORY OF A LEGENDARY GAME CREATOR

Discover how Karateka was made through an exhaustive archive of design documents, playable prototypes, and all-new video features. Like walking through a museum, you can explore the interactive timelines at your own pace.

PLAY THE ACCLAIMED ORIGINALS

Enjoy pixel-perfect versions of the original Karateka games and a variety of never-before-seen early prototypes, with rich quality-of-life features like save anywhere, rewind, chapter select, and director's commentary.

TWO REMASTERED GAMES

Karateka Remastered is an all-new version of the original game featuring cutting-room-floor content, commentary, achievements, and more. Deathbounce: Rebounded is a fast and frantic twin-stick shooter based on Jordan's unpublished prototype.

A GROUNDBREAKING MASTERPIECE

Discover how Karateka became one of the first games to include cinematic scenes, a moving original soundtrack, rotoscoped animation, and a Hollywood-style love story, influencing the decades of games that followed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka
